documents.t: Starting from the two-sample (Allan) variance σy²(τ)=⟨½(ȳ_{k+1}−ȳ_k)²⟩, we derive step by step the frequency-domain integral σy²=2∫S_y sin⁴(πfτ)/(πfτ)² df with S_y=(f²/f0²)S_φ, and build the ADEV slope table for the five power-law noise types (white/flicker PM τ⁻¹, white FM τ⁻¹ᐟ², flicker FM τ⁰ floor, RW FM τ^{+1/2}), explaining why the clock community uses ADEV rather than the ordinary frequency variance. We then derive the complete prefactor table in-house: proving ∫sin⁴u/u³du=ln2 gives the flicker-FM floor constant σy²=2·ln2·h₋₁; from the canonical 1/f³ corner we compute floor=1.06e-9 and τ_knee=113 μs, and lab_19 verifies the absolute level (measured/theory=1.004). Embeds the allan_deviation and allan_flicker_floor figures, with 3 worked examples.

The verbatim transcription and factor-by-factor reconciliation of [P2] Appendix A (Eq.(40)–(51), pp.802–803) now lives on its own page (p2_appendix_a_reconciliation), with only a pointer left here; a new figure of the three kernel shapes (TIE=1, 4sin², 16sin⁴, with peaks and f²/f⁴ asymptotes marked) follows Step 3.

documents.t: Step-by-step derivation of Δt=Δφ/(2πf₀), σ_φ²=∫S_φ df, σ_t=σ_φ/(2πf₀), L≈½S_φ; dBc/Hz to linear; the four kinds of jitter; canonical Example C (5GHz, -100dBc/Hz → 447.9 fs).

documents.t: Derive the quality factor Q cleanly from the parallel RLC tank — three equivalent forms (R_p√(C/L), ω0 R_p C, R_p/(ω0 L)) and the energy definition Q = ω0 · stored energy / dissipated power; show that the active core must supply −R to cancel the tank loss R_p, and that this same R_p is the physical origin of the 4kT/R_p thermal-noise current; connect to phase noise (high Q → narrow band → steep phase slope) and to the Q↔Γrms/qmax correspondence, plus the practical ceiling on on-chip inductor Q. documents.t: The white-noise assumption Var[Δφ]=2D|t| gives a Lorentzian; flicker FM makes Var[Δφ] grow as t²×log (including the role of the low-frequency cutoff f_l), and the characteristic function then yields a near-Gaussian line core, not a Lorentzian. Rigorously, the free-running oscillator phase is a random walk, S_φ strictly does not exist as a stationary PSD, and what the instrument measures is the spectrum of the stationary V(t) (the Demir view); this site's S_φ formulas are conditional spectra under finite observation time and offset ≫ linewidth. Full numerical verification in lab_29.

documents.t: Supply/substrate noise hits all N ring nodes at once (strongly correlated), so the effective ISF becomes the SUM of N per-stage ISFs shifted by 2π/N — a finite geometric sum cancels every Fourier component except n≡0 (mod N). N=5 toy-ring verification: the |c_n| comb keeps only n=0,5,10,15 (165.8 dB selection); a common time-domain injection at n·f0+Δf responds only at n=0,5,10 (66 dB, coherent gain 4.998≈N). Design rule: correlated noise up/down-converts only from DC and k·N·f0.

documents.t: Two transient faces of the same Adler equation: (i) lock acquisition — separation of variables + tan half-angle gives an exact closed-form solution whose settle rate is exactly the pull-in frequency ω_c=√(ω_L²−Δω²) of [P3] Eq.(40), with critical slowing at the lock edge; (ii) with white FM noise, the tilted-washboard potential U(θ)=−Δω·θ−ω_L cosθ yields the barrier ΔU=2ω_L[√(1−r²)−r·acos r] step by step, and a Kramers escape estimate (external reference) predicts the cycle-slip rate, verified by a 512-walker SDE with fitted slope 0.993.

documents.t: Verifies every closed form on the subharmonic_injection page with two independent engines — (1) a linearized impulse-train map, (2) the unaveraged time-synchronous ODE (RK4 through the finite pulse width). Six experiments: (a) lock range vs. N follows a −1.000 power law; (b) lock range vs. pulse width follows a sinc (LC) vs. a box-averaged ISF (ring, whose energy spreads across many harmonics); (c) at equal rms current, the pulse train locks at 15/15 grid points while a pure sine locks at 0/15; (d) the realignment factor β's ODE step response against the first-order prediction, off by O(q_inj/q_max); (e) the locked phase noise is first-order discrete high-pass shaped, with the corner measured at 1.934 MHz; (f) output jitter ∝ √N (2.226 fs at N=20) and a reference spur (−67.96 dBc at 100 kHz detuning). Canonical f₀=5 GHz, N=20, q_inj=50 fC, τ_p=10 ps.

documents.t: First-principles derivation of SNR_jitter = -20log10(2π f_in σ_t) and ENOB=(SNR-1.76)/6.02; an honest design table of SNR/ENOB at 1/2.5/5/10 GHz inputs using this site's canonical σ_t=447.9 fs; back-solving 10 ENOB @ 5 GHz to σ_t ≤ 25.4 fs; wiring up the full chain L(Δf)→σ_t→SNR (verified by the lab_30 simulation).
documents.s: ADC aperture jitter: how clock jitter eats SNR and ENOB

documents.t: An ADPLL (all-digital PLL) replaces the PFD/charge-pump with a TDC and the VCO with a DCO, so the budget gains two quantization-noise sources: the TDC in-band floor L_TDC=(2π)²/12·(Δt_res/T_V)²/f_R (Δt_res=10 ps → −97.8 dBc/Hz, 23.4 dB above the analog PLL's in-band floor of −121.2 (ref×N² + CP); 0.675 ps to break even) and DCO frequency quantization L_DCO=(1/12)(Δf_res/Δf)²(1/f_R)sinc²(Δf/f_R) (Δf_res=10 kHz@1 MHz → −127.8 dBc/Hz, −20 dB per decade); ΔΣ dithering shapes the DCO LSB down to −178.7; budget S_out=(S_ref N²+S_TDC)|H_lp|²+(S_DCO+S_vco)|H_hp|², with the same 'no ×N²' and the same SSB-vs-S_φ ×2 flag.
documents.s: All-digital PLL: TDC and DCO quantization noise are the same ISF bookkeeping

documents.t: What a real SerDes clock-and-data-recovery (CDR) loop looks like: the Alexander bang-bang phase detector's sign(Δt) output, the linearized gain under Gaussian jitter K_bb=√(2/π)/σ_j (this site's σ_t=447.9 fs → 1.78e12 s⁻¹ = 71.3/UI), phase-interpolator (PI) UI/2^b quantization and the (2D+1)K_p hunting limit cycle, JTOL(f)=(UI−TJ_eye)/|1−H(f)| with its −40/−20 dB/dec mask segments, and why PCIe-style spread-spectrum clocking (SSC: −0.5 %, 30 kHz triangular FM → 521 UI peak-to-peak phase) demands a type-II loop. Every number is runnable.
documents.s: Bang-bang CDR: turning the ISF's σ_t into K_bb, JTOL and SSC tracking

documents.t: Rigorous derivations of the five clock-chain accounting rules — ×N multiplication +20logN (φ_out=Nφ_in), ÷N division −20logN (edge-picking), through a PLL (reference ×N² and lowpassed, VCO highpassed), the additive noise floor of buffers/dividers (power addition), and a DLL delay line that does not accumulate random walk because it has no oscillator (σ²_out=σ²_ref+Nσ²_stage) plus phase-interpolator UI/2^b quantization — plus a complete worked chain 100 MHz → ×50 PLL → 5 GHz → ÷2 → 2.5 GHz → buffer: per-stage L at 100 kHz and 10 MHz, the final 27.6 fs integrated jitter, and an honest brick-wall-accounting vs full type-II-shaping comparison.
documents.s: Clock-chain noise accounting: ×N, ÷N, PLL, buffer — a one-page lookup table

documents.t: 13 real, verifiable common mistakes in phase-noise / jitter work — κ² mistaken for D, SSB /4 vs /2 mixed up, single-sideband PSD plugged into the wrong jitter kernel, ΔV/slope intuition inverting the ISF, corner confusion, 8/(3γ) misremembered, forgetting the ×2 in an integral, treating the 1/f² divergence as physical, DJ_pp plugged into the TJ formula, RBW smearing out close-in noise, ÷2 mistaken for halving the jitter in seconds, applying √N to flicker, assuming a pure-sine subharmonic injection would lock — each with a physical explanation, the correct version, and an on-site reference.
documents.s: Common Mistakes Showroom: 13 Real-World Landmines

documents.t: A reverse design flow: spec L(1 MHz)≤−120 dBc/Hz @ 5 GHz, P≤5 mW, TR 10% → required FOM 187.0 dB → against the fom_limit ceilings, ring (168.3) is infeasible and LC Q=10 (197.6) is feasible → tank C=1 pF, L=1.013 nH, Rp=318 Ω → V_max=1 V, q_max=1 pC, I_bias=2.47 mA → S_i=4kT(1+γ)/Rp=1.04e-22 A²/Hz → [P1] Eq.(21) gives −124.8 dBc/Hz (4.8 dB margin, FOM 194.9 dB) → 1–100 MHz integrated jitter 25.7 fs; plus iteration rules (how many dB each knob buys and at what power) and the FOM_T definition.
documents.s: Spec-Driven Design Recipe: 7 Steps from Spec to Jitter

documents.t: Map transistor white/flicker noise onto ISF harmonics and c0/Gamma_rms; cyclostationary (effective ISF); which knobs move Gamma_rms and which move q_max.
documents.s: Device noise → ISF harmonics mapping

documents.t: Decomposition into RJ (unbounded Gaussian, from phase noise) and DJ (bounded: ISI, duty-cycle distortion, supply spurs); step-by-step derivation of the dual-Dirac model: Q-function tail integral, bathtub derived from the jitter CDF, TJ(BER)=DJ_δδ+2Q·σ with Q(1e-12)=7.03; plus an honest account of why DJ_δδ ≤ DJ_pp — the deliberate under-report is exactly what makes the extrapolation accurate. With lab_31 numerical verification.
documents.s: DJ and the Dual-Dirac Model: The Industry-Standard Tool for TJ@BER

documents.t: Complete exercise set for the design chapter — q_max/Γrms design back-calculation, symmetry design back-calculation, ring vs LC comparison, PLL optimal loop BW, σt→BER, tail-noise countermeasures. Every problem comes with a step-by-step solution, units and a dimension check, a numerical answer, and a one-line Python verification.
documents.s: Design Chapter Exercises (with Full Solutions)

documents.t: From [P1] Eq.(21) and [P2] Eq.(23), derive "the FOM of any topology can be written as 173.8 − 10log10(F_eff) dB (300 K)"; verify that the reference constant 173.8 corresponds to 1·kT (not 2kT), the ring ceiling is 168.3 dB, the LC ceiling rises with Q, and quantify how many dB good published LC designs and ring designs each sit below their ceiling.
documents.s: The Theoretical Ceiling of FOM

documents.t: Promotes the M:N sub-/super-harmonic locking math of [P4] Eq.(28)-(30), p.2129 into a standalone teaching page: why use an injection-locked frequency divider (ILFD) instead of a static divider, how the lock range omega_L = (1/2) I_inj |Gamma_tilde_N| is carried by the ISF's N-th harmonic, why a half-wave-symmetric ISF cannot divide by 2 (the payoff), lab_37's numerical verification, how to create c2 with asymmetric/single-ended topologies and tail injection, the duality between dividers (which spend ISF harmonics) and multipliers (which need injection harmonics), and how the divider's -20log10(N) accounting connects to the locked oscillator's own noise shaping.
documents.s: Injection-Locked Frequency Division (ILFD): M:N Sub-/Super-Harmonic Locking and Design

documents.t: From [P3]'s generalized Adler (Eq.30, plus-sign convention), degenerate to classical Adler, linearize to get a first-order PLL — self-noise high-pass (corner ω_c=√(ω_L²−Δω²)=[P3] Eq.40's pull-in frequency), reference-noise low-pass, suppression vanishing at the lock edge; then solve the unlocked quasi-lock case, deriving step by step the beat frequency ω_b=√(Δω²−ω_L²) ([P4] Eq.34) and the one-sided asymmetric sideband comb. The final section follows [P3] Sec. VI and uses Cauchy–Schwarz to derive the optimal injection waveform and the lock-range ceiling ω*_L=I_rms·Γ̃_rms at fixed I_rms (Eq.43–45). Three simulations cross-checked term by term. Advanced page.
documents.s: Noise shaping under injection locking and the injection-pulling spectrum

documents.t: Use the ISF framework to compare LC and ring oscillators item by item — waveform, amplitude restoration, transition slope, tank energy, number of noisy devices, phase-sensitivity distribution, jitter accumulation, design knobs.
documents.s: LC vs ring oscillator through the ISF lens

documents.t: Three methods for measuring L(f) (direct spectrum-analyzer method, PLL/delay-line frequency discriminator, cross-correlation and its three practical pitfalls), how to distinguish deterministic spurs from random phase noise and their causes/countermeasures, how to read a real PN plot — back-solving design information from the 1/f³/1/f²/floor three-segment structure — and a closed-form method for integrating jitter from a datasheet segment table.
documents.s: Phase-noise measurement and spurs

documents.t: The transfer of each of five noise sources (reference, PFD/charge-pump, divider, loop filter, VCO) and their sum S_out=(S_ref N²+S_cp)|H_lp|²+S_vco|H_hp|², the in-band vs out-of-band handoff, reference spur, and minimizing the integrated jitter to find the optimal loop BW (fn≈6.9 MHz, σt≈259 fs); plus the closed-form type-II peaking (ζ=0.707→2.09 dB @0.786fn, the cascaded 0.1-dB rule) and the fractional-N ΔΣ quantization-noise third term (MASH-m, +40 dB/dec ramp), the closed-form loop-filter resistor noise, and the PLL jitter–power FOM (σt=259 fs, 10 mW → −241.7 dB).
documents.s: Complete PLL phase-noise budget and optimal loop BW

documents.t: Phase-noise cost of the three quadrature (I/Q) generation methods (parallel/series coupled QVCO, divide-by-2 ILFD, RC-CR polyphase); the coupling-strength vs I/Q phase-error vs phase-noise triangular trade-off in the coupled QVCO; common-mode / differential-mode noise correlation of the coupled pair and the ~3 dB; finally wiring the coupling injection back into the ISF / generalized-Adler machinery of [P3]. Advanced page.
documents.s: Quadrature generation and coupled-oscillator phase noise

documents.t: At the hand-calculation level, walks the full chain device noise → ISF harmonics → close-in phase noise for three mainstream oscillator topologies — the cross-coupled LC VCO's differential tank (pure c1) versus its tail current source's effective ISF (c0 upconversion, c2 fold-back, tail filter tuned to 2f0), why Colpitts ISF concentrates in a narrow phase window, and the CMOS inverter ring stage's ISF derived from switching slope. Includes multiple worked examples, marked illustrative; §(d) tells class-C / class-D / class-F waveform engineering with the ISF (lab_43).
documents.s: ISF in real topologies: cross-coupled LC VCO, Colpitts, CMOS ring stage

documents.t: Why crystal/MEMS references are the low-offset anchor of every clock chain — a crystal is just an extreme LC tank with Q up to 10⁴–10⁶; using the site's tank_Q page Q↔Γrms/qmax bridge, we derive step by step that close-in L and the Lorentzian linewidth both scale as ∝1/Q²; a checkable worked block (Q=50,000@100 MHz vs Q=10@5 GHz, same-offset Leeson term differs by ~105 dB, ~71 dB after normalizing to the same carrier); a typical-magnitude table for XO/TCXO/OCXO/MEMS (industry convention, external); and why aging/temperature (the ppm slow axis) and phase noise (the dBc/Hz fast axis) are two distinct spec axes.
documents.s: Reference oscillators (crystal / MEMS): the low-offset anchor of the clock chain

documents.t: Why the classic charge-pump PLL's in-band floor is stuck at CP+divider ×N²; the sub-sampling PLL samples the VCO sinusoid directly with the reference (K_PD=g_m·A, slope A·ω₀) — the divider term disappears entirely, CP noise is no longer ×N² (illustrative suppression of 57.9 dB), in-band floor −118.9→−126.0 dBc/Hz (7.1 dB), now reference-limited; the price is kT/C folding (aliasing), reference spurs, and harmonic lock; sampling at the zero crossing is the elegant dual of sampling where the ISF is most sensitive.
documents.s: Sampling / sub-sampling PLL — kicking the divider out of the loop

documents.t: How oscillator phase noise becomes clock jitter, how it affects sampling and the eye; how to choose the integration bandwidth; RJ/DJ/accumulated jitter; CDR/PLL high-pass filtering of VCO noise; practical intuition for TX/RX PLL, LC-VCO/ring-VCO, with phase→time and jitter-integration derivations.
documents.s: From ISF to SerDes Clocking

documents.t: Injecting f_ref pulses into an oscillator running at N·f_ref (injection-locked clock multiplier): from the M:N average of [P4] Eq.(29) we derive that subharmonic locking is carried by the N-th harmonic of the INJECTION waveform times the ISF fundamental (ω_L=½|I_N||Γ̃₁|; a pure sinusoid cannot lock), and reconcile it term by term with the [P3] Sec. IV impulse-train arithmetic with one pulse every N periods (Δω_L=q_inj|Γ̃|max/(N·T₀) ∝ 1/N); linearizing the per-pulse map gives the realignment factor β=−q_inj·Γ̃′(θ_ss), stability 0<β<2, settling ≈1/β injections; the first-order discrete-time noise shaping H_ref=β/(1−(1−β)z⁻¹), H_osc=(1−z⁻¹)/(1−(1−β)z⁻¹), in-band ×N², corner ≈βf_ref/2π, closed-form output jitter σ²=κ²NT₀(1−β+β²/2)/(β(2−β)) (Monte-Carlo ratio 0.999), detuning-sawtooth reference spur 20log₁₀(Δf₀/f_ref); pulse-width sinc, ring vs LC, the N and β trade-offs, an ILCM vs PLL vs sub-sampling PLL table; canonical numbers f₀=5 GHz, N=20, q_inj=50 fC.
documents.s: Subharmonic Injection: From the Impulse Train to ×N Multiplication (ILCM / ILFM)

documents.t: Why a waveform with symmetric rise/fall "blocks" 1/f device noise from close-in — how the ISF's c0 sets the 1/f³ corner, and the design knobs for lowering c0.
documents.s: Waveform Symmetry and Flicker Upconversion

documents.t: Why larger signal swing lowers phase sensitivity — phase noise is proportional to 1/q_max² ([P1] Eq.(21)), and the power / voltage-headroom trade-off.
documents.s: Tank swing, qmaxq_{max}qmax​, and phase noise

documents.t: Define K_VCO=∂f0/∂V_tune and supply pushing K_push=∂f0/∂V_DD; derive how low-frequency noise voltage on the tune/supply node FM-modulates the carrier to give S_φ=K_VCO²·S_v/Δf² (white→1/f², 1/f→1/f³, paralleling the device flicker c0 mechanism); AM-PM from varactor C(V) nonlinearity; design knobs — split tuning, flat bias point, LDO/common-mode rejection; worked example K_VCO=50 MHz/V, 100 nV/√Hz @ 1 MHz, f0=5 GHz → L=-109 dBc/Hz; lab_38 measures K_push=2.936 GHz/V from first principles on the Level-1 ring and verifies it via FM sidebands (β ratio 1.002).
documents.s: Tuning-line and supply-pushing phase noise

documents.t: Why injecting noise at low waveform slope (near the peak) is more dangerous, and why fast transitions (steep zero-crossings) help — starting from the inverse relation between ISF and slope.
documents.s: Waveform slope and phase sensitivity

documents.t: Using three steps — the two-time autocorrelation of the LTV phase derivative, period-averaging over absolute time, and Wiener-Khinchin — this page rigorously redoes the heuristic Eq.(19)→(20)→(21) derivation route from white_noise_to_phase_noise, letting Σcₙ²=2Γrms² fall out naturally from the period-averaged autocorrelation, and compares it item by item with the heuristic version.
documents.s: Autocorrelation to Wiener-Khinchin Rigorous Derivation

documents.t: From Floquet theory of linear systems with periodic coefficients, to the monodromy matrix and Floquet exponents, the first principal vector v1(t), the adjoint system, and the PPV — a step-by-step proof of ϕ̇=v1ᵀ(t)B(t)ξ(t), mapped onto ISF Γ/q_max. Explicitly marked as external literature, not among the five downloaded PDFs.
documents.s: Floquet / adjoint / PPV: the rigorous foundation of the ISF

documents.t: Starting from tank thermal noise, feedback, and quality factor Q, build up the Leeson empirical phase-noise model step by step, then compare it term-by-term against the ISF results of [P1] Eq.(21),(23),(24) (Q↔Γrms/qmax, empirical F vs ISF physical, 1/f³ corner), then uses [P1] Sec.III-F Eq.(28)–(29) to show how the general ISF expression reduces to the LTI special case (including the Craninckx–Steyaert 2× difference), with an embedded Leeson-vs-ISF overlay plot. Explicitly flags that Leeson 1966 is not among the five downloaded source PDFs.
documents.s: Leeson Model Derivation and ISF Comparison

documents.t: Chinese–English pairing of ISF-related terminology, each with a one-line Chinese intuition and a link to the source page on the site.
documents.s: Chinese–English Glossary

documents.t: Starting from signals-and-systems convolution/LTI, we derive the LTV relation y(t)=∫h(t,τ)x dτ and Zadeh's time-varying transfer function H(f,t); we prove that a periodic LTV system maps input frequency f to f+k f0 with gain equal to the k-th Fourier coefficient cₖ of the ISF — i.e., the harmonic transfer matrix; finally we prove "the ISF is exactly the phase-output conversion vector for each harmonic," tying back to [P1] Eq.(13) and the fourier page. External mathematical framework (Zadeh 1950), not among the five source PDFs.
documents.s: Rigorous LTV framework: Zadeh's time-varying transfer function and the harmonic transfer matrix

documents.t: The math tools this site's derivations use repeatedly — Fourier series/Parseval, LTV convolution, Wiener–Khinchin, dB conversion, integrator response, small-angle PM, trigonometric identities, random-walk variance — each with a short proof and the pages that use it.
documents.s: Math Toolbox — Math Identities

documents.t: Verbatim transcription and factor-by-factor reconciliation of [P2] Appendix A, "Relationship Between Jitter and Phase Noise" (p.802-803): the white-noise time-domain autocorrelation route Eq.(40)-(44) and the autocorrelation + Khinchin route Eq.(45)-(51), mapped step by step against Steps 3 and 4 of the jitter_kernels page, with an honest account of what each route skips and what it spells out in full, plus a Python replay of both routes landing on the same kappa^2*DeltaT.
documents.s: [P2] Appendix A Verbatim Reconciliation: The Time-Domain Autocorrelation Route and the Khinchin Route

documents.t: How to set up the environment (Python 3.12, numpy/scipy/matplotlib, auto-detected CJK font), directory layout, running run_all_sims.py, an overview of the common module's seven modules and their functions, and reproducibility via fixed rng seed.
documents.s: Python Environment

documents.t: Full citations for the 5 source PDFs [P1]-[P5], plus external supplementary literature (Leeson 1966, Demir PPV 2000, Kaertner — explicitly flagged as not in the download folder), with citation conventions and a TODO list for manual verification.

documents.t: From paper to design intuition. This site takes the Hajimiri–Lee Impulse Sensitivity Function (ISF) theory from first principles all the way to hands-on design feel for SerDes clock jitter. Every formula is derived step by step, with units, numerical examples, Python code and figures, and explicit paper citations.
documents.s: ISF and Oscillator Phase Noise: From Paper to Design Intuition

documents.t: We assume you are an EE graduate: you know circuit theory, electronics, signals and systems, random processes, the Fourier transform, and basic DSP, but you have not yet truly mastered oscillator phase noise, timing jitter (the deviation of a clock edge from its ideal instant), the ISF, cyclostationary noise, or the LTV (linear time-variant) oscillator model. After finishing this site, you should be able to: read and re-derive on your own the core equations of [P1] Hajimiri–Lee 1998; explain "why an oscillator is LTV — not LTI — with respect to noise"; compute phase noise from the ISF and convert phase noise into rms jitter; name the design knobs that lower 1/f² and 1/f³ phase noise; connect all of this to practical SerDes clocking intuition (LC-VCO / ring-VCO / PLL / CDR).
documents.s: Who this site is for

documents.t: The full 12-step sequential path (a nine-step backbone plus three advanced steps) is in the Learning Path; but if you already have a concrete goal in mind, it is faster to jump in through one of the three "entry cards" below.
documents.s: Start from your goal

documents.t: You are not in a hurry and want to understand oscillator phase noise (the random fluctuation of an oscillation signal's phase) from the ground up. First build the physical intuition of "what an oscillator's phase actually is", then follow the planned path. What is oscillator phase? — phase vs. amplitude seen from the limit cycle Learning Path — the complete 12-step route, from basics to advanced (a nine-step backbone plus three advanced steps)

documents.t: The five source papers and external supplements are in references; per-paper close readings are in the paper deep dives; the paper map is in paper_summary_table. Honest disclosure: the source folder contains 5 PDFs. 4 of them are Hajimiri-series oscillator phase noise / injection papers, but 1 (Hajimiri_ISCS_98.pdf) is actually a cross-coupled sense amplifier paper, unrelated to the ISF. This site labels it honestly and uses it only as a side note. See the build_report for details.

documents.t: This site has had 3 incidents where an audit mistakenly "corrected" already-verified content into an error and mislabeled it "verified" — each was only caught by going back and cross-checking the original PDF at high zoom, a numerical anchor, and independent algebra: Ring FOM prefactor: v2 mistakenly changed it to 8/(3γ)8/(3\gamma)8/(3γ) (mislabeled "verified verbatim") → v4 restored 8/(3η)8/(3\eta)8/(3η) against PDF p.796. The D mapping in the Lorentzian linewidth: v3 took the variance growth rate κ² as the diffusion constant D → v5 adjudicated with MC + analytic fit and restored D=κ2/2D=\kappa^2/2D=κ2/2. [P2] Eq.(16) Γrms's N-scaling: v3 misread the radical's scope and "corrected" v1's originally-correct N−3/2N^{-3/2}N−3/2 to N−3/4N^{-3/4}N−3/4 → v7 restored N−3/2N^{-3/2}N−3/2 after triple-checking the paper's body text ("1/N1.51/N^{1.5}1/N1.5" wording), the η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75 numerical anchor, and App.B's algebra. Full incident details (exactly what was wrong, how it was caught, and which pages were updated site-wide after the fix) are in the v2/v3, v4, v5, and v7 entries of the changelog.

documents.t: Toy models are always flagged as "a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level." Content from external literature (PPV / adjoint / Floquet / Leeson / Demir) is always flagged as "not among the 5 downloaded PDFs, supplemented from standard literature." Uncertain constants/figures/citations are always written as TODO: manual verification needed ... — never guessed to fill a gap. [P5] is always honestly explained as a sense-amplifier paper unrelated to ISF, used only as a conceptual side note. Any "correction claimed by an audit" must be triple-verified in person — original PDF at high zoom, numerical anchor, and independent algebra — before being applied site-wide. This site has 3 real counterexamples where that discipline mattered (see item 5 above); the principle is not just theoretical. Printing errata in the papers themselves (e.g. [P2] Fig.16's ζ=2.5e5 which should read 2.5e-5, and [P1] p.191's "58.8 fF" which should read fC) are also honestly flagged, not silently "corrected" without a note.

WF-4 + round-2/3 re-review: page-by-page deep reading caught round-1 leftovers and new bugs, then fixed them. Key outcomes (all verified against the original PDFs): Ring FOM prefactor re-corrected 8/(3γ)→8/(3η) (v2 had mis-edited it and mislabeled it "verified verbatim"; γ enters only through V_char=ΔV/γ); the worked example moved −89.2→−91.0 dBc/Hz, 57 dB from ideal LC. [P4] ISF/APF figure Fig.3→Fig.5, p.2126; APF definition Eq.(18)–(22), ideal-LC quadrature Eq.(26) p.2128 (not the old "Eq.25/26/27" labels). Citation page/equation corrections: Fig.17 p.800→p.802, Sec.VIII p.1163→p.2135, Fig.4 p.182→p.181, f₀=1/(2Nτ_D) citation Eq.(14)→Eq.(15) (Eq.14 is actually the normalized stage delay t̂_D). Closed the closable TODOs: cyclostationary [P1] Eq.(25)–(27) p.186, generalized Adler [P3] Eq.(30)/(35), Γrms Eq.(16) p.794; unified the Chinese term for "cyclostationary" site-wide. Code bugs: lab_05 Parseval DC double-counted (c₀²→c₀²/2, giving 2Γ²rms after the fix), accumulated_jitter_curve broken call signature; lab_06/07/15 gained numerical-consistency metrics; lab_10/20 figure fixes; verify_examples regex tightened. Honestly blocked one false fix: the audit claimed "κ Eq.(12) is missing ω₀"; zooming into the original PDF p.793 confirmed Eq.(12) never had ω₀ — κ√Δt is the phase jitter σ_Δφ (Eq.11), and only the time jitter is ÷ω₀ (Eq.10). No blind edit was made. External literature now carries CrossRef-verified DOIs: Leeson 1966 (10.1109/PROC.1966.4682), Demir PPV 2000 (10.1109/81.847872), Kärtner 1990 (10.1002/cta.4490180505), Adler 1946 (10.1109/JRPROC.1946.229930). Convergence (loop is dry): all substantive findings from 3 audit rounds are handled; verify_examples shows, of 88 verifiable blocks, 73 pass with 0 errors; the remaining 13 are verifier false positives on "formula constants / contextual numbers / deliberately blank exercises" (manually confirmed correct). Final site size: 74 pages, 30 figures, 25 simulation scripts, 6 interactive widgets; final gate: build green, 0 broken links, 0 KaTeX errors, 0 content issues, 0 soft warnings. Process limitation (honest disclosure): WF-4's parallel fix agents repeatedly hit Anthropic-side server throttling ("not your usage limit", i.e. not an account usage cap), so citation-type and mechanical fixes were completed inline instead and verified item by item.

documents.t: The v4 deep audit (see the v4 entry above) closed most of them: [P2] ring constants (FOM 8/(3η), Γrms Eq.16), [P3]/[P4] citations and page numbers (generalized Adler Eq.(30)/(35), APF Fig.5/Eq.(18)–(22)), cyclostationary [P1] Eq.(25)–(27), external-literature DOIs — all verified verbatim against the original PDFs. documents.t: Publicly deployed as a GitHub Pages (project page): Site: https://gmcycle7.github.io/isf-teaching-site/ Source (public): https://github.com/gmcycle7/isf-teaching-site baseUrl set to /isf-teaching-site/; KaTeX CSS/fonts bundled via webpack (baseUrl-safe, fully offline). Deployment mechanism: local npm run build, then push build/ to the gh-pages branch (with .nojekyll); Pages serves from that branch. Each update is just re-build + force-push gh-pages — packaged as the one-click script ./scripts/deploy.sh (needs only repo scope, no workflow scope). Copyright handling: the full text and PDFs of the 5 papers are not committed (.gitignore excludes extracted/raw_text/ and *.pdf); the footer and each page state that copyright belongs to the original authors and the content is for teaching purposes. CI (optional): .github/workflows/deploy.yml is ready; pushing the workflow file requires a token with workflow scope (gh auth refresh -s workflow) to enable push-to-deploy. The bilingual build is ~200MB; Pages once hung at "building" for 35 minutes, and a rebuild via POST /pages/builds finished in 30 seconds — use this trick when a large deployment gets stuck (recorded in v6).

documents.t: [P1] Hajimiri–Lee 1998: the ISF theory itself (the oscillator is LTV). [P2] 1999: ISF applied to rings — closed-form jitter/PN, NNN-independence. [P3] Hong 2019 I: ISF generalizes Adler → generalized injection locking. [P4] Hong 2019 II: the APF (amplitude counterpart of the ISF), τ0=2Q/ω0\tau_0=2Q/\omega_0τ0​=2Q/ω0​, frequency division. [P5] a sense amplifier paper, unrelated to the ISF (honestly labeled). Full cross-reference: paper_summary_table, equation_index.
documents.s: The five papers in one line each

documents.t: This page expands the nine steps from the home page into a learning path you can actually follow, and extends the backbone with three advanced steps (Steps 10–12), for 12 steps in total. Each step tells you: What to achieve (the learning goal of this step); Which pages to read (in order); Prerequisites (you will get stuck without these); Expected outcome (what you should be able to do afterwards). At the end there are two tracks: a fast track (roughly the nine-step backbone — grasp the ISF backbone in one afternoon) and a full track (all twelve steps: re-derive every formula yourself and run every lab yourself). How to use this page: on a first pass, take the "full track" and come back to tick the checkbox after each step. For later review, the "fast track" is enough. A TODO: marker means that spot still needs manual verification against the original PDF; a "toy model" label means it is a pedagogical simplification, not transistor-level. Course Progress 0/12 doneClear all Step 1: What an oscillator's "phase" actually is Step 2: Noise is a small perturbation; the oscillator responds as LTV, not LTI Step 3: The operational definition of the ISF (impulse → phase) Step 4: From a single impulse to arbitrary noise (convolution) Step 5: White noise → 1/f², flicker → 1/f³ Step 6: The Fourier view of the ISF (c₀, cₙ, upconversion) Step 7: Simulation labs — build numerical feel Step 8: Design takeaways (swing, slope, symmetry) Step 9: Connect to SerDes clocking (jitter, eye, PLL/CDR) Step 10: Advanced theory — from κ to lineshape Step 11: Injection locking and frequency conversion Step 12: System integration and measurement Progress is stored in the browser's localStorage (key isf-progress-v1), and only applies on this device and this browser.

documents.t: Before you start, keep these three pages nearby; whenever you meet an unfamiliar symbol or paper reference, look it up there: notation — the unified symbol table (site-wide symbols, units, per-paper cross-reference). paper_summary_table — the five papers at a glance (who is responsible for what). equation_index — every formula → derivation page → source. Quick lookup (when unsure about a symbol / formula / English term, jump via the table below; when stuck, return to these four pages first): What you want to look up Where to go All formulas on one page, canonical numerical examples A/B/C Cheat Sheet The meaning and units of a symbol (e.g. Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, qmaxq_{max}qmax​, c0c_0c0​) Notation An intuitive explanation of an English term (e.g. ISF, cyclostationary, limit cycle) Glossary Which paper and Eq. a formula comes from, and where it is derived Equation Index
documents.s: Keep these three pages at hand as "dictionaries"

documents.t: What to achieve: build the geometric picture of the limit cycle (the closed steady-state trajectory of an oscillator), and clearly separate phase (tangential along the cycle, no restoring force) from amplitude (radial away from the cycle, with a restoring force). Pages to read: oscillator_phase → phase_vs_amplitude_noise → tank_Q_and_energy_restoration (the three equivalent forms of the parallel-RLC-tank quality factor QQQ and its energy definition — every later page that says "high QQQ" is using the result derived here). Prerequisites: 2-D state space, the phase plane, the basic picture of RLC oscillation. Expected outcome: you can explain "why a tangential perturbation persists forever while a radial one is pulled back" — this is exactly claim C2 (see claims_cross_reference).
documents.s: Step 1: What an oscillator's "phase" actually is

documents.t: What to achieve: understand that with respect to noise an oscillator is LTV (linear time-variant) — the same impulse injected at different phases produces a different phase shift, unlike an LTI system which only depends on t−τt-\taut−τ. Pages to read: lti_vs_ltv. Prerequisites: Step 1; linear systems, impulse response, convolution. Expected outcome: you can sketch the difference between the LTI h(t−τ)h(t-\tau)h(t−τ) and the LTV hϕ(t,τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)hϕ​(t,τ), corresponding to the figure lti_vs_ltv_impulse_response.png. This is claim C1.

Expected outcome: you can do canonical example B — the same set of numbers plugged into Eq.(21) gives L=−148.0\mathcal{L}=-148.0L=−148.0 dBc/Hz; and you understand the famous factor-of-2 SSB bookkeeping controversy mentioned in Section 3 of the spec.
documents.s: Step 5: White noise → 1/f21/f^21/f2, flicker → 1/f31/f^31/f3

documents.t: What to achieve: expand the ISF into the Fourier series Γ=c02+∑cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\Gamma=\frac{c_0}{2}+\sum c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)Γ=2c0​​+∑cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​) ([P1] Eq.(12), p.183), understand that each cnc_ncn​ "downconverts" the noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ to the carrier, and that ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ (Parseval, [P1] Eq.(20)). Pages to read: fourier_series_of_isf → rms_isf. Prerequisites: Step 5; Fourier series. Expected outcome: you can state the mathematical basis of the design rule "symmetric waveform → c0≈0c_0\approx0c0​≈0 → suppressed 1/f31/f^31/f3" (for the closed form that computes c0c_0c0​ and the corner directly from topology parameters, see Step 10's asymmetric_isf_closed_form).
documents.s: Step 6: The Fourier view of the ISF (c0c_0c0​, cnc_ncn​, upconversion)

documents.t: What to achieve: run the preceding formulas with your own hands, look at the figures, check the numbers, and turn the conversions between rad, fs, dBc/Hz and jitter into reflexes. Pages to read: first numerical_feeling (three must-do mental calculations), then open the Interactive Calculator (drag the sliders to verify examples A/B/C live — change qmaxq_{max}qmax​, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, SiS_iSi​, f0f_0f0​ and watch L\mathcal{L}L and σt\sigma_tσt​ move; this builds more feel than numbers alone), then in order lab_01, lab_02, lab_04, lab_05, lab_06, lab_07, lab_08. Prerequisites: Steps 3–6; a little Python/NumPy. Expected outcome: you can verify canonical examples A/B/C in one line with the functions in simulations/common/; every figure is traceable to its script and formula in the figure_index.
documents.s: Step 7: Simulation labs — build numerical feel

documents.t: What to achieve: translate the formulas into design knobs — increase qmaxq_{max}qmax​, lower Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, enforce waveform symmetry to suppress c0c_0c0​; and understand the ring result Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 and "at fixed power and frequency, ring phase noise is almost independent of the number of stages NNN" (claims C7/C8). Pages to read: tank_swing (the most direct knob — enlarging qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=CV_{max}qmax​=CVmax​, with L∝1/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto1/q_{max}^2L∝1/qmax2​) → waveform_slope (how the switching-edge slope directly sets how large the ISF is over that stretch) → device_noise_mapping (which phase window each device's noise current maps onto, and how the effective Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ sums up) → symmetry → lc_vs_ring. Prerequisites: Steps 1, 5 and 6 (tank_Q_and_energy_restoration, white/flicker upconversion, the ISF Fourier coefficients). Expected outcome: given an oscillator spec, you can say, in order, "which knob to turn first" — first swing (qmaxq_{max}qmax​), then how edge slope and device-noise mapping feed Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and c0c_0c0​, and only then the topology-level symmetry/LC-vs-ring trade-off (for the quantitative version of "how many dB from the theoretical ceiling", see Step 12's fom_limit); to run these knobs in reverse — from a spec sheet all the way to component values and jitter in one complete 7-step recipe — see design_recipe.
documents.s: Step 8: Design takeaways (swing, slope, symmetry)

documents.t: What to achieve: integrate phase noise into rms jitter and connect it to eye closure and BER in a SerDes link, and reach the first stop on the way to book-keeping a single oscillator's L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) into a whole PLL loop. Pages to read: (optional) dsp_view_of_phase_noise (the DSP/sampling view of Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) — a warm-up for psd_phase_noise_jitter) → psd_phase_noise_jitter → serdes_clocking_connection → pll_noise_budget (the five noise sources plus the ∣Hlp∣2/∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2/\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2/∣Hhp​∣2 transfers and the optimum loop BW — final-exam Q8 and 06-chapter exercises Q4/Q8 both live on this page). Prerequisites: Steps 5 and 7 (especially lab_08). Expected outcome: you can do canonical example C — f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, L(1MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz, 1/f21/f^21/f2 slope, integrating 1→100 MHz ⇒σϕ=14.07\Rightarrow\sigma_\phi=14.07⇒σϕ​=14.07 mrad, σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs — and you know the integral is dominated by its lower limit (for the rigorous period/cycle-to-cycle kernels see Step 10's jitter_kernels; for the RJ/DJ decomposition and TJ@BER see Step 12's dj_dual_dirac); and you know how a PLL's output noise sums from five sources and how the loop BW is chosen to minimize total jitter (Step 12's clock_chain_budget reuses this page's result directly, without re-deriving it).
documents.s: Step 9: Connect to SerDes clocking (jitter, eye, PLL/CDR)

documents.t: The backbone (Steps 1–9) builds the ISF machinery for a single free-running oscillator. The next three steps push the same machinery in three directions: deeper theory (Step 10), the injected oscillator (Step 11), and the whole clock system (Step 12). The former "Advanced (optional)" section has been expanded and absorbed: paper_003 and paper_004 now live in Step 11; effective_isf (the cyclostationary correction Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α, claim C9, plus the external mathematical foundations PPV/adjoint/Floquet, claim C13, not in these 5 PDFs, supplemented from standard literature) remains optional — read it before starting Step 10 if you can.
documents.s: Steps 10–12 (advanced): from deep theory to system integration

documents.t: What to achieve: take "white-noise phase diffusion has only one free parameter" all the way — the same phase-variance growth rate κ2\kappa^2κ2 wearing five outfits (κ\kappaκ, DDD, linewidth, ADEV, the 1/f21/f^21/f2 coefficient); the rigorous frequency-domain kernels of the three jitters (TIE / N-period / cycle-to-cycle); when the lineshape stops being Lorentzian under flicker FM; the closed form for c0c_0c0​ and the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner; and the three ways to compute Γ\GammaΓ directly from the waveform. Pages to read (one line of "why" each): diffusion_dictionary — κ\kappaκ, DDD, linewidth, ADEV, and the 1/f21/f^21/f2 coefficient are five outfits of the same number; get the conversion dictionary first (canonical κ2=0.125\kappa^2=0.125κ2=0.125 rad²/s). jitter_kernels — the three jitters are the 0th/1st/2nd-order differences of ϕ\phiϕ; the prefactors and every single 2 are derived from first principles. stochastic_noise_basics — stationarity, autocorrelation, Wiener–Khinchin: the beyond_lorentzian lineshape derivation is built directly on this page, and skipping it leaves you stuck on "what exactly is a PSD the Fourier transform of". beyond_lorentzian — flicker FM turns the lineshape from Lorentzian into near-Gaussian, and rigorously answers "what does the instrument actually measure". asymmetric_isf_closed_form — the [P2] App. B closed form: compute Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, c0c_0c0​ and the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner directly from the stage count NNN and the asymmetry AAA. isf_from_waveform — the three methods of the [P1] appendix (impulse injection / closed form / first derivative), and where each extra approximation starts to fail. Prerequisites: Steps 5, 6 and 9; plus lorentzian_linewidth and allan_variance (direct prerequisites of diffusion_dictionary — catch up on them first if needed). Expected outcome: you can convert any jitter spec into any other representation, and you know the failure point of every approximation. Self-check checkpoints: With the canonical numbers (Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz), κ2=0.125\kappa^2=0.125κ2=0.125 rad²/s; switching to the true ideal LC (Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​), why is it exactly 2× (0.250.250.25 rad²/s)? Under the "single-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​, ∫0∞\int_0^\infty∫0∞​" convention, the period-jitter kernel's prefactor is 1/ω021/\omega_0^21/ω02​; stuffing a single-sided spectrum into the 2/ω022/\omega_0^22/ω02​ version common in the literature overcounts the variance by 2× (jitter by 2\sqrt22​) — which bookkeeping convention does that 2 belong to? Same L(10 kHz)\mathcal{L}(10\,\text{kHz})L(10kHz) spec: white-FM linewidth 50 Hz, flicker-FM about 3.1 kHz — why does a dBc/Hz number at a single offset not determine the linewidth at all?
documents.s: Step 10: Advanced theory — from κ to lineshape

documents.t: What to achieve: extend the same Γ\GammaΓ from phase noise into the "injected" world — the generalized Adler equation, in-lock noise shaping and out-of-lock pulling, acquisition transients and cycle slips, M:N subharmonic locking and the ILFD, mutual injection (QVCO), and finally the sub-sampling PLL that kicks the divider out of the loop. Pages to read (one line of "why" each): paper_003 — the generalized Adler equation: a single first-order equation written with the ISF, giving the lock range for any topology and any injection waveform (claim C10). injection_locking_noise — a locked oscillator is a first-order PLL: its own noise is high-passed (corner ωc\omega_cωc​), the reference low-passed; when lock fails, the one-sided pulling comb. lab_36 — the missing transient pieces: the exact closed-form acquisition trajectory, critical slowing at the lock-range edge, noise-induced cycle slips. paper_004 — the APF (the amplitude counterpart of the ISF, claim C11) and M:N subharmonic locking / ILFD. injection_locked_division — the ÷N direction of M:N locking gets its own page: the lock range rides the ISF's NNN-th harmonic, and half-wave symmetry can't divide by 2. subharmonic_injection — the other half of the duality: multiplication rides the injection waveform's own NNN-th harmonic, with a realignment factor β\betaβ and discrete-time noise shaping. lab_40 — an independent numerical check of subharmonic injection: lock range ∝1/N\propto1/N∝1/N, β\betaβ's ODE step response, and the closed-form output jitter. quadrature_and_coupled_oscillators — mutual injection = two Adler equations: the QVCO's coupling-strength ↔ phase-error ↔ phase-noise triangular trade-off and that famous ∼3\sim3∼3 dB. sampling_pll — sampling the zero crossing = sampling the ISF's most sensitive point: sub-sampling makes the divider noise vanish and the CP noise no longer ×N2\times N^2×N2. Prerequisites: Steps 6 and 8; catching up on effective_isf first is recommended (cyclostationary correction, see the top of this section). Expected outcome: from the generalized Adler equation all the way to the noise shaping of ILFD / QVCO / sub-sampling — you can explain injection-related locking, pulling and frequency conversion along the same single Γ\GammaΓ. Self-check checkpoints: With sinusoidal injection and the ideal-LC ISF, the generalized Adler equation reduces to θ˙=Δω−ωLsin⁡θ\dot\theta=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\thetaθ˙=Δω−ωL​sinθ with ωL=Iinj/(2qmax)\omega_L=I_{inj}/(2q_{max})ωL​=Iinj​/(2qmax​); in lock, the oscillator's own noise is high-pass shaped with corner ωc=ωL2−Δω2\omega_c=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωc​=ωL2​−Δω2​ (the pull-in frequency of [P3] Eq.(40)) — why does the noise suppression vanish at the edge of the lock range? Out of lock, the beat frequency is ωb=Δω2−ωL2\omega_b=\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}ωb​=Δω2−ωL2​​ ([P4] Eq.(34)) and the sideband comb grows on one side only; with the canonical numbers (fL=5f_L=5fL​=5 MHz, true-LC noise) at r=0.8r=0.8r=0.8 the cycle-slip rate is ∼10−1.86×107\sim10^{-1.86\times10^7}∼10−1.86×107 — why do we say thermal slips are a "cliff", not a "slope"? M:N subharmonic locking gives ωL=Iinj∣Γ~N∣/2\omega_L=I_{inj}\lvert\tilde\Gamma_N\rvert/2ωL​=Iinj​∣Γ~N​∣/2 ([P4] Eq.(28)–(30)): which harmonic does the ÷2 ILFD ride on? The sub-sampling PLL's in-band floor drops from −118.9-118.9−118.9 to −126.0-126.0−126.0 dBc/Hz (illustrative example) — where did the divider term go?
documents.s: Step 11: Injection locking and frequency conversion

documents.t: What to achieve: finish at the system level — book-keep a single oscillator's L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) down the clock chain to every node, compare against the FOM theoretical ceiling, understand what a reference oscillator actually buys, compute an ADC's SNR/ENOB, book-keep RJ/DJ separately into TJ@BER, read measurement plots and spurs, dodge the 12 mines, and finally use the capstone to validate the whole site end to end. Pages to read (one line of "why" each): pll_noise_budget — the transfer and sum of five noise sources (reference / PFD-CP / divider / loop filter / VCO) and the optimum loop BW; clock_chain_budget's Rule 3 (PLL) reuses this page's ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 / ∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hhp​∣2 results directly, without re-deriving them, so read it first. clock_chain_budget — the four bookkeeping rules (×N / ÷N / PLL / buffer) plus a complete worked chain 100 MHz→5 GHz→2.5 GHz. adpll_tdc_dco — swap pll_noise_budget's five analog sources for the all-digital picture: TDC quantization floor, DCO frequency quantization, ΔΣ dithering — the same ∣Hlp∣2/∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2/\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2/∣Hhp​∣2 bookkeeping still applies. fom_limit — the FOM ceiling =173.8−10log⁡10(Feff)=173.8-10\log_{10}(F_{eff})=173.8−10log10​(Feff​) dB (300 K): know how many dB your design is from the physical limit. reference_oscillators — a crystal is just an LC tank with an outrageously high QQQ: why nothing downstream can fix the reference's close-in noise. adc_aperture_jitter — sampling error = slope × timing error: clock quality directly sets the data converter's effective number of bits. dj_dual_dirac — RJ unbounded, DJ bounded: the dual-Dirac model and the industry-standard TJ@BER bookkeeping. cdr_bang_bang_jtol — a real SerDes CDR is bang-bang, not a linear PLL: the KbbK_{bb}Kbb​ linearized gain, the JTOL mask, and SSC spread-spectrum tracking. measurement_and_spurs — the three ways to measure L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f), telling spurs from random noise, and how to read a real PN plot. common_mistakes — 12 real mines: a full review of the site's factor-of-2 discipline. capstone_lc_end_to_end — the site's main spine end to end: state equations → ISF → spectrum → linewidth → jitter → BER. The finale. Suggested optional reading (topology-level, off the main line of this step but frequently asked about): real_oscillator_topologies (hand-calculated ISF for cross-coupled LC / Colpitts / CMOS ring stage and class-C/D/F waveform engineering), varactor_tuning_supply_pushing (how low-frequency noise voltage on the tuning line / supply FMs the carrier into close-in phase noise). Prerequisites: Steps 7–9 (pll_noise_budget already appeared once, in Step 9); Step 10 (the jitter kernels and the diffusion dictionary are used repeatedly); Step 11 helps too (sampling_pll already appeared in Step 11). Expected outcome: you can draw up — and defend — a clock noise budget: from the reference to the sampler, every stage's L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) and the final jitter have a traceable source. Self-check checkpoints: The worked chain (100 MHz → ×50 PLL → 5 GHz → ÷2 → 2.5 GHz → buffer) ends at an integrated jitter of 27.6 fs; under ideal ×N / ÷N, why does σt\sigma_tσt​ in seconds not change by a single fs? Feeding a 5 GHz input with the canonical σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs clock: SNRjitter=37.0\text{SNR}_{jitter}=37.0SNRjitter​=37.0 dB, ENOB =5.86=5.86=5.86 bit; 10 ENOB @ 5 GHz requires pushing σt\sigma_tσt​ down to ≤25.4\le25.4≤25.4 fs — which formula is doing the conversion? (SNR=−20log⁡10(2πfinσt)\text{SNR}=-20\log_{10}(2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t)SNR=−20log10​(2πfin​σt​)) TJ(BER)=DJδδ+2Q⋅σ\text{TJ}(\text{BER})=\text{DJ}_{\delta\delta}+2Q\cdot\sigmaTJ(BER)=DJδδ​+2Q⋅σ with Q(10−12)=7.03Q(10^{-12})=7.03Q(10−12)=7.03: why is DJδδ≤DJpp\text{DJ}_{\delta\delta}\le\text{DJ}_{pp}DJδδ​≤DJpp​ a deliberate under-report? And why is a spur specified in dBc and not dBc/Hz?
documents.s: Step 12: System integration and measurement

documents.t: This corresponds to the Steps 1–9 backbone (Steps 10–12 are not part of the fast track). The goal is "understand what the ISF is and how it determines phase noise". You do not re-derive anything and do not run the simulations yourself: oscillator_phase (only the limit cycle and the phase/amplitude picture) lti_vs_ltv (the core LTV conclusion and figure) impulse_to_phase_shift (memorize the operational definition + example A) white_noise_to_phase_noise (memorize Eq.(21) and example B) fourier_series_of_isf (the intuition of c0c_0c0​ suppressing 1/f31/f^31/f3) numerical_feeling (the three mental calculations) serdes_clocking_connection (the jitter and eye conclusions) After this you should be able to answer: what the ISF is, why LTV, L∝Γrms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​/qmax2​, why symmetry matters, and how phase noise becomes jitter.
documents.s: Fast track (about one afternoon, backbone only)

documents.t: Follow Steps 1 through 12 above in order, cover the answer and re-derive every formula yourself, run every lab yourself with python scripts/run_all_sims.py and check figures against numbers (the advanced labs referenced in Steps 10–12 included). Suggested pace: Stage Steps Key deliverable (self-check) Geometric intuition 1–2 Can draw the limit cycle; can state LTV vs. LTI ISF core 3–6 Can re-derive Eq.(9)→(11)→(12)→(20)→(21)→(24) Hands-on 7 Can reproduce examples A/B/C; orders of magnitude match Design 8–9 Can list the design knobs; can integrate L\mathcal{L}L into σt\sigma_tσt​ Advanced theory 10 Can convert freely among κ\kappaκ, DDD, linewidth, ADEV and the 1/f21/f^21/f2 coefficient; can name where every 2 comes from Injection & conversion 11 Can derive ωc\omega_cωc​, ωb\omega_bωb​ and the M:N lock condition from the generalized Adler equation; can say where sub-sampling wins System integration 12 Can book-keep L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) down a full clock chain; can draw up and defend a jitter budget
documents.s: Full track (re-derive every step + run every lab)

documents.t: Twelve steps = the nine-step backbone (phase geometry → LTV → ISF definition → convolution → white/flicker noise → Fourier → labs → design → SerDes) plus three advanced steps (Step 10 κ and lineshape → Step 11 injection locking and frequency conversion → Step 12 system integration and measurement). The four quick-lookup pages (return there first when stuck): cheat_sheet, notation, glossary, equation_index (see the "Quick lookup" table at the top of this page). The fast track covers the nine-step backbone; the full track walks all twelve steps: re-derive every formula, run every lab. Steps 10–12 are advanced: injection/APF now live in Step 11; PPV/adjoint and much of the instrument/architecture knowledge in the system-integration pages come from external literature (not in the 5 PDFs) — every such page carries an honest disclaimer.

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Different papers write the same thing with different symbols. This page unifies them; every later chapter follows this table. If you encounter a different convention in one of the papers, come back here to cross-reference. How to use this page: skim it once to get acquainted; when actually reading the derivations, come back and look up any symbol you do not recognize. Every quantity is labeled with its unit — doing a dimension check is the fastest way to catch mistakes.

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: learning_path (the page order of the twelve-step spine; this page highlights the corresponding nodes in gold), notation (the symbol table — this page introduces no new symbols, but every page name in the graph can be looked up there) | Next: cheat_sheet, paper_summary_table This page does exactly one thing: it draws the "who must be read before whom" relationship among the site's 101 pages (Chinese originals; every page also has an English mirror under i18n/en/) as a single graph. The graph was not hand-drawn — its edges were extracted programmatically by scanning the "> Prerequisites: … | Next: …" breadcrumb line (or the lab-page variant, "> Breadcrumb: … upstream/downstream: …" — see "How to read this map" below) at the top of every page and pulling out the markdown links, so it reflects the site's actual link structure, not an idealized sketch drawn from memory. v11 (2026-09-14) folds in the 9 pages added in waves 2-3 (subharmonic_injection, injection_locked_division, adpll_tdc_dco, cdr_bang_bang_jtol, design_recipe, lab_40_subharmonic_injection, paper_004_large_injection_transient, derivation_autocorrelation_wiener_khinchin, p2_appendix_a_reconciliation) — the v10 version had stalled at 92 pages / 56 nodes, with this whole injection-locking cluster and the two appendix pages entirely missing from the map. That gap is the direct reason this page was regenerated.

documents.t: Arrow direction = prerequisite relation: A --> B reads "A is a prerequisite of B / what A teaches is used directly by B." Following the arrows gives a valid reading order; conversely, a node's incoming edges are the prerequisite pages it lists, and its outgoing edges are the downstream pages that list it as a prerequisite. Rectangular nodes = a single page (chapters 02 Foundations and 03 Core Theory are the main spine, so every page there gets its own node, per the map's editorial rule; the three small chapters 00/01/05 are also drawn page-by-page). Rounded (stadium) nodes = several pages clustered into one node (all of chapter 04 Simulation Labs is clustered; chapter 06 Design Insights and chapter 99 Appendix cluster their lower-degree pages), because drawing all 101 pages as separate nodes would be unreadable — after clustering, the whole graph has only 57 nodes (see the "How 101 pages compress to 57 nodes" table below). Exactly which pages sit inside each clustered node is listed in the "Grouped-Node Legend" section below. Gold highlight = nodes touched by the 12 steps of the learning path. This is the site's recommended main spine; every other node is an extension, a deeper dive, or reference material beyond the spine. A clustered node is marked gold as soon as any one of its member pages falls inside the 12 steps (e.g. "Systems & Advanced Labs" is entirely gold because it contains lab_36 — that does not mean every page in the cluster is on the spine). Click a node to open its page: every node carries a mermaid click directive that opens the page in a new tab (clustered nodes have no single destination, so they carry no click — use the legend table below instead). If your browser or viewer blocks the navigation, every link in the legend table and the rest of this page still works normally. This is not a strict DAG: a handful of pages list each other as prerequisites in both directions (page A explains half a concept and links to B for the rest; B in turn lists A under further reading) — the graph shows this as a back-and-forth pair of arrows. That is a faithful reflection of the site's actual cross-referencing, not an extraction error. Edge source and exceptions (v11 update): of the site's 101 pages, 77 carry a standard "Prerequisites / Next" breadcrumb line (or, on lab pages, the "breadcrumb … upstream/downstream" variant) at the top of the page, and every edge on this map is extracted verbatim from those 77 pages' breadcrumb links — nothing is added by hand. (In an earlier version, tank_Q_and_energy_restoration and capstone_lc_end_to_end lacked a standard breadcrumb and used "Further Reading" links instead; re-scanning for v11 found that both pages now carry a standard breadcrumb, so that exception no longer applies and is not special-cased here.) The other 24 pages (most of chapter 00's navigation pages, the three chapter-01 index pages, chapter 04's lab_01-lab_08 plus numerical_feeling / worked_examples / interactive_calculator, and the 4 chapter-99 reference pages) are reference-type pages by design and do not carry a prerequisite breadcrumb at the top, so they contribute no outgoing edges — but they still appear as nodes on the map, and may still gain incoming edges from other pages that list them as a prerequisite or next step (for example, 01_paper_map/claims_cross_reference has only a "Next" clause and no "Prerequisites" clause). Extracted at the page level (before clustering) this yields 270 directed edges; after clustering into 57 nodes and removing intra-cluster and duplicate edges, the graph actually draws 204 edges.

documents.t: "Degree" = a page's in-degree + out-degree in the page-level directed graph (before clustering) extracted from the breadcrumbs. A high in-degree means "this page itself lists many prerequisites"; a high out-degree means "many downstream pages list this page as their prerequisite" — pages with a high out-degree are usually the site's real conceptual hubs. Ties are broken by: higher degree first, then higher in-degree, then alphabetically by page id (see the note below). documents.t: Every edge on this map comes from a page's own declared "Prerequisites / Next" breadcrumb (the pre-v11 "Further Reading" exception for two pages no longer applies, see above) — it is a mirror of the site's actual dependency structure, not a redesigned "ideal" teaching order (the ideal order is still the learning path's twelve steps, highlighted in gold here). 101 pages -> 57 nodes: the two core chapters (02/03) keep one node per page as the authoring spec requires; chapter 04 is fully clustered, and 06/99 are partially clustered by connectivity, so the map stays a size you can scan at a glance. All 9 pages added in v11 (the 5-page injection cluster, lab_40, paper_004_large_injection_transient, and the 2 appendix pages) are folded in under the same rules. The highest-degree hubs are not in 00/01 (reference/dictionary pages are rarely listed as anyone's prerequisite, so their breadcrumb-degree is naturally low) — they are white-noise-to-1/f², the chapter-06 exercise page, SerDes clocking, the PLL noise budget, Phase-Noise-to-Jitter, the ISF Fourier series, clock-chain accounting, and waveform symmetry. These are where the site's teaching logic genuinely converges. The graph is not a strict DAG: a few pages list each other as mutual prerequisites — that is a faithful reflection of the site, not an extraction bug.

documents.t: These claims are supported by more than one paper, or reappear in different papers in different forms, corroborating each other: C2 (phase persists / amplitude decays): [P1] argues from the limit cycle that "phase has no restoring force"; [P4] corroborates from the amplitude side with the APF and the amplitude decay function that "amplitude perturbations are pulled back". Same physics, two angles. C3 ↔ C6 (Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​): the phase noise in [P1] Eq.(21) and the jitter proportionality constant κ2\kappa^2κ2 in [P2] share the same Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ ratio — phase noise and accumulated jitter are the same physics in the frequency and time domains. C4/C5 (symmetry suppresses 1/f31/f^31/f3): [P1] derives it theoretically from Eq.(23)(24); [P2]'s Fig. 17 corroborates it by measurement (phase noise minimum at the symmetric control voltage). Theory + experiment. C1 (LTV) and C10 (injection): the same Γ\GammaΓ determines both noise→phase ([P1]) and injection→phase ([P3]); the LTV viewpoint runs through both papers.

documents.t: This site has two kinds of figures: (a) figures we generate with Python (all teaching toy/conceptual models, not transistor-level), and (b) figures inside the cited paper PDFs. This page files every one of them, so you can trace any figure back to "which script, which function, what parameters, which formula behind it, which paper it comes from". How to read this table: Toy? = whether it is a simplified teaching model (not transistor-level). Redrawn? = whether it was redrawn directly from a paper figure (our generated figures are always re-simulated, never traced, so mostly No). Verify? = manual_verification_needed; entries flagged ⚠️ still need manual confirmation of constants/correspondence. Re-run everything in one shot: python scripts/run_all_sims.py (outputs to static/figures/). Data comes from extracted/extracted_figures.json.

documents.t: All 60 generated figures are fully traceable to script/function/parameters/formula/source, and none are orphaned (every one is embedded on at least 1 page; comm -23 between static/figures/*.png and this page's logged names, and between the logged names and the ![...](/figures/...) references actually found in docs/, both return the empty set). Except for phase_noise_to_jitter_integration.png, most are teaching toy/conceptual models; mos_level1_ring_isf.png and supply_pushing_ring.png are device-equation-level (MOS Level-1, not SPICE — closer to a real circuit than a toy). The 10 PDF figures are only cited and described, never redrawn; among them [P2] Fig. 17 (p.802) and [P4] Fig. 5 (p.2126) have been verified against the original PDFs. Embed syntax: ![description](/figures/<name>.png). Re-run: python scripts/run_all_sims.py.

documents.t: The source folder contains 5 PDFs. This page lays them out in a single table, then organizes their division of labor from a teaching viewpoint: which paper is the ISF core, which extends to rings, which covers injection, which is actually off-topic, and which equations are the same thing written differently, plus which notation differs and needs to be unified. Honesty note (up front): of these 5, 4 are Hajimiri-series oscillator phase-noise/ injection papers, and 1 (Hajimiri_ISCS_98.pdf = [P5]) is actually a cross-coupled sense-amplifier paper, unrelated to ISF — this site treats it only as a footnote. Also, the frequently co-mentioned PPV / adjoint / PSS / PNoise / Floquet topics have no dedicated paper among these 5 PDFs — they belong to external literature and are honestly flagged below.

documents.t: [P1] is the foundation of the whole site. Every LTV/ISF concept — Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ), the qmaxq_{max}qmax​ normalization, the convolutional phase response, Fourier downconversion, the 1/f21/f^21/f2/1/f31/f^31/f3 closed forms — all comes from here. Chapters 02 (foundations) and 03 (isf core theory) map almost section-by-section to [P1] Secs. III–IV, and lab_01/02/04/05/06/07 all reproduce figures and equations from [P1].
documents.s: Which paper is the ISF core foundation

documents.t: [P2] grounds [P1]'s general theory in the ring oscillator: the same Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ logic yields accumulated jitter (claim C6), Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 (claim C8), and "ring phase noise nearly independent of NNN at fixed power/frequency" (claim C7). Chapter 06's lc_vs_ring, symmetry and lab_03 use it.
documents.s: Which paper extends to rings

documents.t: Honestly: none of these 5 papers is dedicated to PPV/adjoint/PSS/PNoise. PPV (perturbation projection vector) / adjoint method / Floquet theory is the rigorous mathematical foundation behind the ISF, but it comes from the broader literature (e.g. Demir–Mehrotra–Roychowdhury 2000, Kaertner), not among the 5 downloaded PDFs. This site treats them as standard external literature, explicitly flagged in effective_isf (claim C13). PSS (periodic steady-state) / PNoise are numerical methods in commercial simulators (e.g. SpectreRF) for extracting ISF/ phase noise, and likewise are not the subject of any of these 5 papers; this site cites them only conceptually and does not claim they come from the downloaded PDFs. The closest thing to "simulation" is actually [P1]'s own limitation that "real circuits require transient impulse response or adjoint/PSS methods to extract the ISF" — i.e., simulation extraction is mentioned, but has no dedicated paper. All labs on this site are teaching toy models (not transistor-level), reproducing the concepts in Python, not a real PSS/PNoise flow.
documents.s: Which paper covers adjoint / PPV / PSS / PNoise / simulation

documents.t: [P1] supersedes Leeson's empirical formula. Leeson 1966's L\mathcal{L}L expression (with 2FkT/Ps2FkT/P_s2FkT/Ps​, (ω0/2QΔω)2(\omega_0/2Q\Delta\omega)^2(ω0​/2QΔω)2, 1+ω1/f3/∣Δω∣1+\omega_{1/f^3}/|\Delta\omega|1+ω1/f3​/∣Δω∣) is an empirical fit: it can draw the 1/f31/f^31/f3, 1/f21/f^21/f2, floor regions, but FFF (noise factor) and the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner are after-the-fact fitting parameters, not computed from first principles. [P1]'s contribution is precisely to compute these three regions from first principles with the ISF, and to point out that the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner is not the device's 1/f1/f1/f corner, but ω1/f(c0/c1)2\omega_{1/f}(c_0/c_1)^2ω1/f​(c0​/c1​)2 ([P1] Eq.(24), claim C5) — a key correction to the Leeson empirical model. The Leeson formula itself is not one of the 5 downloaded PDFs; this site uses it only for comparison (see equation_index row 19, flagged reference ⚠️). In addition, [P3] extends/generalizes Adler 1946's injection-locking equation, and [P4] supplies the amplitude dimension (APF) missing from [P1]/[P3]. Neither Adler's nor Leeson's original paper is among these 5 PDFs.

documents.t: Different papers use different symbols for the same quantity; this site always follows notation: Offset frequency: [P1] mostly uses Δω\Delta\omegaΔω (rad/s), datasheets/SerDes use Δf\Delta fΔf (Hz); this site uses both, Δω=2πΔf\Delta\omega=2\pi\Delta fΔω=2πΔf. The ISF's DC: note that c0c_0c0​ is a Fourier coefficient, while the ISF's DC value is c0/2c_0/2c0​/2 (Eq.(12)) — very easy to get wrong when computing the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner (Eq.(24)); this site repeats the reminder. Amplitude sensitivity: [P4]'s APF is written Δ(ϕ)\Delta(\phi)Δ(ϕ) with units A−1\mathrm{A^{-1}}A−1; it has different dimensions from the dimensionless ISF Γ\GammaΓ and must not be mixed up. PPV/adjoint/Floquet: this site does not use their dedicated notation (e.g. Demir's v1T(t)v_1^T(t)v1T​(t)) in the main track, mentioning them only as external literature in effective_isf. For the full symbol comparison (including a "per-paper notation / remarks" column) see the "per-paper notation comparison" section of notation.

documents.t: [P1] = ISF core; [P2] = ring extension; [P3]/[P4] = injection locking / APF advanced; [P5] = sense amplifier, unrelated to ISF (honestly flagged). None of the papers is a dedicated PPV/adjoint/PSS/PNoise paper; those belong to external literature (e.g. Demir 2000). [P1] supersedes the Leeson empirical formula from first principles, and corrects "1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ≠ device 1/f1/f1/f corner". Across papers, Γ\GammaΓ, the phase equation, and Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ are often the same thing seen from different angles; notation is always unified per notation.

documents.t: Prerequisites: psd_phase_noise_jitter · white_noise_to_phase_noise ｜ Next: serdes_clocking_connection The previous pages all viewed oscillator imperfection from the frequency domain: jitter was written as SSB phase noise L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) (in dBc/Hz) or as the phase PSD Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) (in rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz), then integrated into an rms jitter σt\sigma_tσt​ (see psd_phase_noise_jitter). That language is the natural one for RF/communication circuits. But the people who work on clocks, frequency standards, GPS, and atomic clocks speak another language: the Allan variance and its square root, the Allan deviation / ADEV σy(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)σy​(τ). This page answers: What does σy(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)σy​(τ) actually measure? Why is it defined as the mean square of the "difference between two adjacent gated frequency averages"? How does it convert to the familiar Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) and L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf)? Why does each of the five power-law noise types trace a characteristic slope on the ADEV log–log plot, so that the slopes "read out the noise type at a glance"? Why does the clock community prefer ADEV over the ordinary sample variance of frequency? Physical intuition (conclusion first): take a stopwatch (the oscillator under test) and compare it against a perfect clock; every τ\tauτ seconds record "over this τ\tauτ-second gate, how much faster/slower was my average frequency than nominal", producing a string of fractional frequency deviations yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​. The ordinary variance asks "how far are these yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​ from their grand mean" — but for flicker (1/f1/f1/f) and random-walk noise, the grand mean simply does not exist (it keeps drifting the longer you collect data), so the ordinary variance grows and grows without converging. Allan's trick: do not compare against the grand mean — compare only against the neighboring gate — 12⟨(yˉk+1−yˉk)2⟩\tfrac12\langle(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k)^2\rangle21​⟨(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​)2⟩. The adjacent subtraction cancels out the "slow drift", so even for flicker/RW noise the result converges and can be measured repeatably as a stable number. The price: it becomes a function of τ\tauτ — the gate length τ\tauτ you choose sets the time scale at which you probe stability. ADEV is "phase noise in the time domain": the same physics (the same Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f)), just viewed in a different coordinate. Below we connect the two sides step by step.
documents.s: Allan Variance: The Time-Domain Counterpart of Phase Noise

documents.t: First, define the protagonist. Let the instantaneous phase of the signal under test be ω0t+ϕ(t)\omega_0 t+\phi(t)ω0​t+ϕ(t), where ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) is the excess phase (the random offset relative to the ideal linear phase, in rad). The instantaneous fractional frequency deviation (dimensionless) is defined as the time derivative of the phase deviation divided by the nominal angular frequency: y(t)=1ω0dϕ(t)dt=12πf0 ϕ˙(t).y(t)=\frac{1}{\omega_0}\frac{d\phi(t)}{dt}=\frac{1}{2\pi f_0}\,\dot\phi(t).y(t)=ω0​1​dtdϕ(t)​=2πf0​1​ϕ˙​(t). Physical meaning: yyy is "by what fraction the frequency right now exceeds the nominal frequency". y=10−9y=10^{-9}y=10−9 means the frequency is off by 1 ppb (one part per billion). Unit check: ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ is rad/s\text{rad/s}rad/s, ω0\omega_0ω0​ is rad/s\text{rad/s}rad/s; the ratio is dimensionless ✓. yyy being dimensionless is exactly what "fractional" means. Relation between the PSD of yyy and the PSD of ϕ\phiϕ. Differentiation multiplies by j2πfj2\pi fj2πf in the frequency domain, so the power spectrum is multiplied by the squared magnitude (2πf)2(2\pi f)^2(2πf)2. Hence (spec §11.2): Sy(f)=(2πf)2(2πf0)2 Sϕ(f)=f2f02 Sϕ(f).S_y(f)=\frac{(2\pi f)^2}{(2\pi f_0)^2}\,S_\phi(f)=\frac{f^2}{f_0^2}\,S_\phi(f).Sy​(f)=(2πf0​)2(2πf)2​Sϕ​(f)=f02​f2​Sϕ​(f). Math used: for a stationary process a(t)→a˙(t)a(t)\to\dot a(t)a(t)→a˙(t), the PSD is multiplied by ∣j2πf∣2=(2πf)2|j2\pi f|^2=(2\pi f)^2∣j2πf∣2=(2πf)2 (the LTI filter H(f)=j2πfH(f)=j2\pi fH(f)=j2πf). Unit check: SϕS_\phiSϕ​ is rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz; multiplied by the dimensionless f2/f02f^2/f_0^2f2/f02​, SyS_ySy​ has units 1/Hz1/\text{Hz}1/Hz (the PSD of a dimensionless quantity) ✓. Key marker: this Sy=(f2/f02)SϕS_y=(f^2/f_0^2)S_\phiSy​=(f2/f02​)Sϕ​ is the adapter between "phase noise ↔ frequency noise" — the entire slope table below hinges on it. Differentiation adds 2 to the power of fff: Sϕ∼f−2S_\phi\sim f^{-2}Sϕ​∼f−2 (our signature 1/f21/f^21/f2) corresponds to Sy∼f0S_y\sim f^{0}Sy​∼f0 (white FM).

documents.t: Slice the continuous y(t)y(t)y(t) into gates of length τ\tauτ; the average fractional frequency of the kkk-th gate is yˉk=1τ∫tktk+τy(t) dt=x(tk+τ)−x(tk)τ,x(t)≡∫ty(t′) dt′=ϕ(t)2πf0.\bar y_k=\frac{1}{\tau}\int_{t_k}^{t_k+\tau}y(t)\,dt=\frac{x(t_k+\tau)-x(t_k)}{\tau}, \qquad x(t)\equiv\int^{t}y(t')\,dt'=\frac{\phi(t)}{2\pi f_0}.yˉ​k​=τ1​∫tk​tk​+τ​y(t)dt=τx(tk​+τ)−x(tk​)​,x(t)≡∫ty(t′)dt′=2πf0​ϕ(t)​. Here x(t)x(t)x(t) is the time error (the accumulated time offset of the clock under test relative to an ideal clock, in s) — note that it is exactly the phase divided by 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​, i.e. the Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0)\Delta t=\Delta\phi/(2\pi f_0)Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0​) of psd_phase_noise_jitter. So yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​ is nothing but "the difference of the time error at two adjacent instants, divided by the gate length". The two-sample (Allan) variance is defined as the mean square of the difference between adjacent gated frequency averages, times 12\tfrac1221​ (spec §11.2): σy2(τ)=⟨12(yˉk+1−yˉk)2⟩.\sigma_y^2(\tau)=\Big\langle\tfrac12\big(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k\big)^2\Big\rangle.σy2​(τ)=⟨21​(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​)2⟩. ADEV is its square root, σy(τ)=σy2(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)=\sqrt{\sigma_y^2(\tau)}σy​(τ)=σy2​(τ)​. What the 12\tfrac1221​ is for: if yˉk+1\bar y_{k+1}yˉ​k+1​ and yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​ are mutually independent, each with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, then ⟨(yˉk+1−yˉk)2⟩=2σ2\langle(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k)^2\rangle=2\sigma^2⟨(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​)2⟩=2σ2, and the factor 12\tfrac1221​ restores exactly σ2\sigma^2σ2. In other words, for white FM (independent adjacent gates) this normalization makes ADEV equal to the classical standard deviation — Allan chose it deliberately so that in the most common case the two languages agree numerically. Why "adjacent differences": differencing is a high-pass operation that blocks DC and very low frequencies (slow drift, aging, the unknown grand mean). This is the secret of its convergence even for flicker/RW noise (detailed in Step 5). Unit check: yˉ\bar yyˉ​ dimensionless → σy2\sigma_y^2σy2​ dimensionless, σy\sigma_yσy​ dimensionless ✓. Written as a "second difference" of the time error xxx. Substituting yˉk=[x(tk+τ)−x(tk)]/τ\bar y_k=[x(t_{k}+\tau)-x(t_k)]/\tauyˉ​k​=[x(tk​+τ)−x(tk​)]/τ, for adjacent gates (tk+1=tk+τt_{k+1}=t_k+\tautk+1​=tk​+τ): yˉk+1−yˉk=xk+2−2xk+1+xkτ,\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k=\frac{x_{k+2}-2x_{k+1}+x_k}{\tau},yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​=τxk+2​−2xk+1​+xk​​, where xk≡x(tk)x_k\equiv x(t_k)xk​≡x(tk​) and the sampling interval is τ\tauτ. The numerator xk+2−2xk+1+xkx_{k+2}-2x_{k+1}+x_kxk+2​−2xk+1​+xk​ is exactly the second difference of the time error (a discrete second derivative). This is precisely what the line d = x[2m:] - 2*x[m:-m] + x[:-2m] does in the simulation script lab_19_allan.py.

documents.t: The target we want to prove is (spec §11.2): σy2(τ)=2∫0∞Sy(f) sin⁡4(πfτ)(πfτ)2 df.\sigma_y^2(\tau)=2\int_0^{\infty}S_y(f)\,\frac{\sin^4(\pi f\tau)}{(\pi f\tau)^2}\,df.σy2​(τ)=2∫0∞​Sy​(f)(πfτ)2sin4(πfτ)​df. We only need to find the transfer function H(f)H(f)H(f) of the operation "from y(t)y(t)y(t) to 12(yˉk+1−yˉk)\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k)2​1​(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​)" and compute its ∣H(f)∣2|H(f)|^2∣H(f)∣2. Step (i): gate averaging = convolution with a rectangular window. yˉk=1τ∫tktk+τy dt\bar y_k=\frac1\tau\int_{t_k}^{t_k+\tau}y\,dtyˉ​k​=τ1​∫tk​tk​+τ​ydt is yyy convolved with a rectangular window of width τ\tauτ and height 1/τ1/\tau1/τ, sampled at tkt_ktk​. The frequency response of the rectangular window is a sinc: Havg(f)=1τ∫0τe−j2πft dt=e−jπfτ sin⁡(πfτ)πfτ.H_{\text{avg}}(f)=\frac{1}{\tau}\int_0^{\tau}e^{-j2\pi f t}\,dt=e^{-j\pi f\tau}\,\frac{\sin(\pi f\tau)}{\pi f\tau}.Havg​(f)=τ1​∫0τ​e−j2πftdt=e−jπfτπfτsin(πfτ)​.
