Step (ii): adjacent subtraction = multiplication by a first-difference kernel. yˉk+1−yˉk\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_kyˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​ shifts the same gate average by τ\tauτ and subtracts, which in the frequency domain multiplies by (e−j2πfτ−1)\big(e^{-j2\pi f\tau}-1\big)(e−j2πfτ−1), whose squared magnitude is ∣e−j2πfτ−1∣2=2−2cos⁡(2πfτ)=4sin⁡2(πfτ).\big|e^{-j2\pi f\tau}-1\big|^2=2-2\cos(2\pi f\tau)=4\sin^2(\pi f\tau).​e−j2πfτ−1​2=2−2cos(2πfτ)=4sin2(πfτ). (Using the half-angle identity 1−cos⁡2θ=2sin⁡2θ1-\cos2\theta=2\sin^2\theta1−cos2θ=2sin2θ with θ=πfτ\theta=\pi f\tauθ=πfτ.) Step (iii): multiply the three pieces together. The overall operation g(t)=12(yˉk+1−yˉk)g(t)=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k)g(t)=2​1​(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​) (the 12\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}2​1​ is the square root of the 12\tfrac1221​ in the definition) has the transfer-function magnitude squared: ∣H(f)∣2=12⏟def. 12⋅(sin⁡(πfτ)πfτ)2⏟gate average⋅4sin⁡2(πfτ)⏟adjacent difference=2sin⁡4(πfτ)(πfτ)2.|H(f)|^2=\underbrace{\tfrac12}_{\text{def.}\,\frac12}\cdot\underbrace{\Big(\frac{\sin(\pi f\tau)}{\pi f\tau}\Big)^2}_{\text{gate average}}\cdot\underbrace{4\sin^2(\pi f\tau)}_{\text{adjacent difference}}=\frac{2\sin^4(\pi f\tau)}{(\pi f\tau)^2}.∣H(f)∣2=def.21​21​​​⋅gate average(πfτsin(πfτ)​)2​​⋅adjacent difference4sin2(πfτ)​​=(πfτ)22sin4(πfτ)​. Step (iv): apply Wiener–Khinchin (power = ∫ PSD × |H|²). Using the single-sided PSD (∫0∞\int_0^\infty∫0∞​): σy2(τ)=∫0∞Sy(f) ∣H(f)∣2 df=2∫0∞Sy(f) sin⁡4(πfτ)(πfτ)2 df.✓\sigma_y^2(\tau)=\int_0^{\infty}S_y(f)\,|H(f)|^2\,df=2\int_0^{\infty}S_y(f)\,\frac{\sin^4(\pi f\tau)}{(\pi f\tau)^2}\,df.\qquad\checkmarkσy2​(τ)=∫0∞​Sy​(f)∣H(f)∣2df=2∫0∞​Sy​(f)(πfτ)2sin4(πfτ)​df.✓ This is the frequency-domain integral of spec §11.2. Physical meaning: sin⁡4/(⋅)2\sin^4/(\cdot)^2sin4/(⋅)2 is a band-pass kernel: near f→0f\to0f→0 it behaves like f2f^2f2 (high-pass, blocking slow drift), at high frequency like 1/f21/f^21/f2 (low-pass, suppressing ultra-fast noise), with its peak near fτ∼0.5f\tau\sim 0.5fτ∼0.5. Choosing τ\tauτ means choosing which frequency band this band-pass looks at — large τ\tauτ probes low frequencies, small τ\tauτ high frequencies. Unit check: SyS_ySy​ is 1/Hz1/\text{Hz}1/Hz, the kernel is dimensionless, dfdfdf is Hz; the integral is dimensionless → σy2\sigma_y^2σy2​ dimensionless ✓. This is the bridge showing "time domain ↔ frequency domain are the same thing": given any Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f), first convert it to SyS_ySy​ via Step 1, then substitute into this integral to get ADEV; conversely, a measured ADEV can be inverted back to SyS_ySy​ and SϕS_\phiSϕ​. The entire slope table below is nothing but this integral evaluated for power laws Sy∼fαS_y\sim f^\alphaSy​∼fα.

documents.t: The frequency-standards community writes noise as a superposition of power laws (the power-law model). Each type is described by Sy(f)=hαfαS_y(f)=h_\alpha f^\alphaSy​(f)=hα​fα, with α\alphaα running from −2-2−2 to +2+2+2. Substituting each into the Step-3 integral gives the characteristic slope σy(τ)∝τμ\sigma_y(\tau)\propto\tau^\muσy​(τ)∝τμ. The table below is the core reference table of frequency metrology (PM = phase modulation, FM = frequency modulation): Noise type Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) slope Sy(f)=f2f02SϕS_y(f)=\frac{f^2}{f_0^2}S_\phiSy​(f)=f02​f2​Sϕ​ slope σy2(τ)∝\sigma_y^2(\tau)\proptoσy2​(τ)∝ ADEV σy(τ)∝\sigma_y(\tau)\proptoσy​(τ)∝ white PM f0f^{0}f0 f+2f^{+2}f+2 τ−2\tau^{-2}τ−2 τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1 flicker PM f−1f^{-1}f−1 f+1f^{+1}f+1 τ−2\tau^{-2}τ−2 (with ln⁡\lnln correction) τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1 white FM f−2f^{-2}f−2 f0f^{0}f0 τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1 τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2 flicker FM f−3f^{-3}f−3 f−1f^{-1}f−1 τ0\tau^{0}τ0 τ0\tau^{0}τ0 (floor) random-walk FM f−4f^{-4}f−4 f−2f^{-2}f−2 τ+1\tau^{+1}τ+1 τ+1/2\tau^{+1/2}τ+1/2 Note the single most important row: our signature white FM (Sϕ∼1/f2S_\phi\sim1/f^2Sϕ​∼1/f2, produced from white noise by phase integration; see white_noise_to_phase_noise) corresponds to an ADEV slope of τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2. In other words, the −20-20−20 dB/decade phase-noise skirt appears on the time-domain ADEV plot as a line of slope −1/2-1/2−1/2.

documents.t: (a) white FM → τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2 (the one to remember). Sy∼f0S_y\sim f^0Sy​∼f0 is white; y(t)y(t)y(t) is white noise. yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​ averages white noise over a gate τ\tauτ — averaging NNN independent samples of white noise reduces the variance by 1/N∝1/τ1/N\propto1/\tau1/N∝1/τ, hence σy2∝1/τ\sigma_y^2\propto1/\tauσy2​∝1/τ and σy∝τ−1/2\sigma_y\propto\tau^{-1/2}σy​∝τ−1/2. Intuition: the longer you measure, the steadier the average — the standard error falls like 1/τ1/\sqrt{\tau}1/τ​; this is the familiar N\sqrt NN​ law of "under white frequency noise, longer averaging is more accurate". Equivalently, yyy white ⇒ the time error x=∫yx=\int yx=∫y is a random walk; the variance of adjacent-gate differences ∝τ\propto\tau∝τ, and dividing by τ2\tau^2τ2 gives ∝1/τ\propto1/\tau∝1/τ. (b) flicker FM → τ0\tau^{0}τ0 (the floor). Sy∼1/fS_y\sim1/fSy​∼1/f (1/f1/f1/f frequency noise). The remarkable property of a 1/f1/f1/f process is scale invariance: it looks statistically the same at every time scale. Feed it into the band-pass kernel and the integral comes out independent of τ\tauτ — ADEV becomes a horizontal line. Intuition: the device's 1/f1/f1/f (flicker) noise upconverts into 1/f31/f^31/f3 phase noise (see flicker_noise_upconversion); in the time domain it becomes the floor where "no amount of extra averaging time makes you any more stable". This floor is the fundamental limit of long-term stability in quartz/atomic oscillators, known in engineering as the flicker floor. (c) random-walk FM → τ+1/2\tau^{+1/2}τ+1/2 (heading upward). Sy∼1/f2S_y\sim1/f^2Sy​∼1/f2; y(t)y(t)y(t) itself is a random walk (integrated white noise). The longer the averaging time, the further yyy itself has already wandered, so the adjacent-gate differences actually grow: σy2∝τ\sigma_y^2\propto\tauσy2​∝τ, σy∝τ+1/2\sigma_y\propto\tau^{+1/2}σy​∝τ+1/2. Intuition: temperature drift, precursors of aging — low-frequency processes that "wander ever farther" — get worse the longer you measure. The right half of an ADEV plot bending upward is usually this. (d) white PM and flicker PM → both τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1 (steepest, left side). PM-type noise is concentrated at high frequency (Sy∼f+2S_y\sim f^{+2}Sy​∼f+2, f+1f^{+1}f+1) and is strongly suppressed by the sinc2\text{sinc}^2sinc2 of the gate average, so it drops off quickly as τ\tauτ is stretched: ADEV ∝τ−1\propto\tau^{-1}∝τ−1 (steeper than white FM's τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2). Intuition: pure phase noise (e.g., additive white noise of the measurement system, buffer thermal noise) is prominent at small τ\tauτ and gets averaged away at large τ\tauτ. Note: white PM and flicker PM have the same ADEV slope (both τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1) and cannot be distinguished — this is a real weakness of ADEV, which motivated the improved MDEV (modified Allan deviation): under MDEV, white PM follows τ−3/2\tau^{-3/2}τ−3/2 and flicker PM follows τ−1\tau^{-1}τ−1, making them separable (MDEV is an extension topic not developed here). Mnemonic: from left to right, as τ\tauτ grows from small to large, the ADEV slope walks −1→−1/2→0→+1/2-1\to-1/2\to0\to+1/2−1→−1/2→0→+1/2 — a bathtub curve that "drops, bottoms out, then climbs". The minimum at the bottom corresponds to the optimal averaging time τopt\tau_{\text{opt}}τopt​ — the τ\tauτ to pick for the most stable measurement or timekeeping.
documents.s: Why each slope is what it is

documents.t: This is the "why" at the heart of this page. Suppose you want the most intuitive description of frequency stability: take MMM frequency samples yˉk\bar y_kyˉ​k​ and compute the ordinary sample variance (also called the N-sample / standard variance) σstd2(M,τ)=1M−1∑k=1M(yˉk−yˉ‾)2,yˉ‾=1M∑kyˉk.\sigma^2_{\text{std}}(M,\tau)=\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{k=1}^{M}\big(\bar y_k-\overline{\bar y}\big)^2,\qquad\overline{\bar y}=\frac1M\sum_k\bar y_k.σstd2​(M,τ)=M−11​k=1∑M​(yˉ​k​−yˉ​​)2,yˉ​​=M1​k∑​yˉ​k​. The problem is that it subtracts the "grand mean" yˉ‾\overline{\bar y}yˉ​​. For white FM, no problem. White FM is stationary, yˉ‾\overline{\bar y}yˉ​​ converges to the true value, and σstd2\sigma^2_{\text{std}}σstd2​ converges too, consistent with ADEV. For flicker FM and random-walk FM it blows up. These two have strong (even divergent) low-frequency energy: They are non-ergodic in the mean: yˉ‾\overline{\bar y}yˉ​​ does not converge; the longer you measure and the larger MMM gets, the more yˉ‾\overline{\bar y}yˉ​​ itself keeps drifting. Consequently σstd2(M,τ)\sigma^2_{\text{std}}(M,\tau)σstd2​(M,τ) grows monotonically with the sample count MMM and never converges — the "frequency instability" you report depends on "how long you measured", which is a metrological disaster (not repeatable, not comparable). Mathematically: the equivalent kernel of the standard variance against Sy(f)S_y(f)Sy​(f) behaves only like f0f^0f0 as f→0f\to0f→0 (DC is not blocked); against Sy∼1/fS_y\sim1/fSy​∼1/f or 1/f21/f^21/f2, the integrals ∫0dff\int_0\frac{df}{f}∫0​fdf​ and ∫0dff2\int_0\frac{df}{f^2}∫0​f2df​ diverge at low frequency. ADEV's fix: replace "subtract the grand mean" with "adjacent differences". Step 3 showed that ADEV's equivalent kernel behaves like f2f^2f2 as f→0f\to0f→0 (sin⁡4(πfτ)∼(πfτ)4\sin^4(\pi f\tau)\sim(\pi f\tau)^4sin4(πfτ)∼(πfτ)4, divided by (πfτ)2(\pi f\tau)^2(πfτ)2, gives ∼f2\sim f^2∼f2). This f2f^2f2 high-pass tames the low-frequency divergence: flicker FM (Sy∼1/fS_y\sim1/fSy​∼1/f): the integrand ∼f2⋅f−1=f\sim f^2\cdot f^{-1}=f∼f2⋅f−1=f, convergent as f→0f\to0f→0 ✓. random-walk FM (Sy∼1/f2S_y\sim1/f^2Sy​∼1/f2): the integrand ∼f2⋅f−2=f0\sim f^2\cdot f^{-2}=f^0∼f2⋅f−2=f0, still convergent as f→0f\to0f→0 (a borderline case, but finite) ✓. So ADEV is a convergent, repeatable, measurement-duration-independent well-defined quantity all the way up to random-walk FM. That is the fundamental reason David Allan proposed it in 1966 and the frequency-standards community (NIST, IEEE) adopted it as the standard: In one sentence: the ordinary frequency variance does not converge for flicker/RW noise (it diverges the longer you collect data); ADEV uses the first difference "subtract the adjacent gate" to block the low-frequency drift, buying a stability metric that is convergent in τ\tauτ and repeatably measurable. Extensions: if you also need to distinguish white PM from flicker PM, use MDEV; to ask "is a given time error bounded", use TDEV / time variance. This page focuses on the most commonly used overlapping ADEV.

documents.t: lab_19 (simulations/lab_19_allan.py) generates the fractional frequency y(t)y(t)y(t) for the three FM noise types by FFT shaping, integrates it into the time error x(t)=∫y dtx(t)=\int y\,dtx(t)=∫ydt, and then estimates the overlapping Allan deviation: for each τ=mτ0\tau=m\tau_0τ=mτ0​, take the mean square of the second difference xk+2m−2xk+m+xkx_{k+2m}-2x_{k+m}+x_kxk+2m​−2xk+m​+xk​ and the square root. In the figure, solid lines are the simulated ADEV, dashed lines the theoretical slopes; the three slopes land precisely on −1/2-1/2−1/2, 000, and +1/2+1/2+1/2: Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Title reads: "Allan deviation：每種 FM 雜訊有特徵斜率（虛線 = 理論斜率）" = Allan deviation: each FM noise type has a characteristic slope (dashed = theoretical slope). Item Value Notes Model toy / illustrative (not transistor-level) synthesizes Sy∼fαS_y\sim f^\alphaSy​∼fα by FFT power-law shaping white FM Sy∼f0S_y\sim f^{0}Sy​∼f0 ADEV slope τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2 (blue) flicker FM Sy∼f−1S_y\sim f^{-1}Sy​∼f−1 ADEV slope τ0\tau^{0}τ0, flicker floor (green) random-walk FM Sy∼f−2S_y\sim f^{-2}Sy​∼f−2 ADEV slope τ+1/2\tau^{+1/2}τ+1/2 (red) Estimator overlapping ADEV second-difference kernel xk+2m−2xk+m+xkx_{k+2m}-2x_{k+m}+x_kxk+2m​−2xk+m​+xk​ Vertical axis normalized σy/σy(τ0)\sigma_y/\sigma_y(\tau_0)σy​/σy​(τ0​) compares slopes only; absolute scale arbitrary Core Python (full script: simulations/lab_19_allan.py, function overlapping_adev): import numpy as np def overlapping_adev(x, tau0, ms): """Compute the overlapping Allan deviation from time-error samples x (spacing tau0).""" x = np.asarray(x); N = len(x); out = [] for m in ms: if N - 2 * m < 1: out.append(np.nan); continue d = x[2 * m:] - 2 * x[m:-m] + x[:-2 * m] # second difference of the time error avar = np.sum(d ** 2) / (2 * (N - 2 * m) * (m * tau0) ** 2) out.append(np.sqrt(avar)) return np.array(out) The d line is the second difference xk+2m−2xk+m+xkx_{k+2m}-2x_{k+m}+x_kxk+2m​−2xk+m​+xk​ of Step 2; dividing by 2(N−2m)(mτ0)22(N-2m)(m\tau_0)^22(N−2m)(mτ0​)2 corresponds to the discrete estimate of σy2=⟨12(yˉk+1−yˉk)2⟩\sigma_y^2=\langle\tfrac12(\bar y_{k+1}-\bar y_k)^2\rangleσy2​=⟨21​(yˉ​k+1​−yˉ​k​)2⟩ (with τ=mτ0\tau=m\tau_0τ=mτ0​).

documents.t: The lab_19 figure above tells you the three slopes a priori. In practice, though, you only ever have one finite-length measured time series, and ADEV is a statistic estimated from that series — not an analytic curve handed down from above. The widget below moves the full "generate → estimate" pipeline into the browser, complementing the AllanDeviationExplorer on the interactive_calculator page (which plots the pure analytic slope with no randomness at all): A seeded pseudo-random number generator (PRNG — meaning the same seed always reproduces the same series) generates a fractional-frequency series y[k]y[k]y[k] of length N=4096N=4096N=4096, made of slider-controlled white FM + random-walk FM, plus an optional flicker FM approximated with a simple −10-10−10dB/decade filter cascade (an honest approximation — see the note below). The series is integrated into a time error x[k]=∑y[k]τ0x[k]=\sum y[k]\tau_0x[k]=∑y[k]τ0​, and the same overlapping second-difference formula from Steps 2–3 is applied to estimate ADEV directly at τ=τ0,2τ0,4τ0,…\tau=\tau_0,2\tau_0,4\tau_0,\dotsτ=τ0​,2τ0​,4τ0​,… (octaves, up to N/4N/4N/4), with ±σ/pairs\pm\sigma/\sqrt{\text{pairs}}±σ/pairs​ error bars overlaid. The dashed line is the analytic closed form for the same mixture of hhh coefficients (Step 4 / the prefactor table, variances of independent processes add) — the blue points should scatter around it. Click "re-seed" to draw a new seed: the small-τ\tauτ points barely move (thousands of independent pairs, statistically stable), while the large-τ\tauτ points visibly jump around (only about 4 independent pairs remain at τ=N/4\tau=N/4τ=N/4). This is exactly the lesson of this section: the "floor" or "upturn" you see at the far right of an ADEV curve can look like a definite physical feature, but if it is only supported by a handful of independent samples, those last few points carry large statistical uncertainty of their own — the fix is a longer total record, not taking the shape of the rightmost points at face value. Live ADEV from a synthetic time series (N=4096) — statistics vs. analytic Generates one fractional-frequency series y[k] with a seeded PRNG, integrates it to a time error x[k], then estimates overlapping ADEV directly (second-difference of x) at each octave τ = m·τ₀. The dashed line is the analytic closed form for the same mixture (variances add). white FM level h₀ = 10^x-19.0 random-walk FM: ONflicker FM (approx.): off random-walk FM level h₋₂ = 10^x-24.0 ↻ Re-seed (new random draw)seed = 1234 10⁰10¹10²10³10⁻¹¹10⁻¹⁰10⁻⁹τ = m·τ₀ (arbitrary units)σ_y(τ)overlapping ADEV (±σ/√pairs)analytic (same h) largest τ pairs 2048 τ = 1024 smallest τ measured/theory 0.993 (white-FM-only closed form) Estimator: overlapping ADEV σ_y²(mτ₀) = Σᵢ(x[i+2m]−2x[i+m]+x[i])² / (2·pairs·(mτ₀)²), the discrete second difference of the time error x = ∫y dt (identical formula to lab_19 / the analytic page above). Error bars use the rule-of-thumb ±σ/√pairs — a simplification (overlapping windows are correlated, so this understates the true uncertainty somewhat), but it correctly shows the qualitative point: the largest τ has few independent windows (N/τ ~ 4 at τ=N/4), so its ADEV point is noisy and jumps a lot between re-seeds, while small-τ points (thousands of pairs) are stable run to run. Flicker FM here is only an honest approximation: a cascade of 8 log-spaced one-pole (leaky-integrator) filters gives an effective PSD slope around −0.8 to −0.9 decade⁻¹ (not the exact −1 of true 1/f) over the covered band — good enough to see the τ⁰ floor bend into view, not a rigorous flicker generator. Verified in Node against a pure white-FM case (h₀=10⁻¹⁹, random-walk and flicker off): averaged over 200 reseeds the measured/theory ratio is 0.94–1.00 across all 11 octaves (worst at the largest τ, where pairs are scarcest — see below), and the fitted log–log slope of the seed-averaged curve is −0.508 (expected −1/2); a single seed (default seed 1234) already gives ratio 0.993 at the smallest τ. Independent check of the estimator: switching the generator to pure white FM (random-walk and flicker off) with h0=10−19h_0=10^{-19}h0​=10−19 and running the same algorithm in Node over 200 re-seeds, the measured/theory ratio (against the closed form h0/2τh_0/2\tauh0​/2τ) at every octave of τ\tauτ falls in the range 0.940.940.94–1.001.001.00 (worst at the largest τ\tauτ, where pairs are scarcest — exactly the effect described above); the log–log slope fitted to the 200-seed-averaged curve is −0.508-0.508−0.508 (theory: τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2), and a single run with the default seed (1234) already gives a ratio of 0.9930.9930.993 at the smallest τ\tauτ. The widget's "smallest τ measured/theory" readout is a live version of this same self-check. Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Keeping the explorer at its default settings (white FM h₀=10⁻¹⁹, random-walk FM h₋₂=10⁻²⁴ enabled, seed=1234), what does the gray dashed line (the analytic overlay, independent of the noisy blue measured points) give for σ_y(τ) at τ = 64 s? (Hint: add the white-FM and random-walk-FM closed forms from Step 4.) CheckShow answer Graded correct within ±3% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Verification: reproducing the dashed-line value at τ=64 s (mirrors AdevLiveExplorer.js's analyticSigma) import math TWO_PI = 2 * math.pi LN2 = math.log(2) def analytic_sigma(tau, h_white, h_rw, h_flicker): # AdevLiveExplorer.js analyticSigma() var_white = h_white / (2 * tau) if h_white > 0 else 0.0 var_flicker = 2 * LN2 * h_flicker if h_flicker > 0 else 0.0 var_rw = (TWO_PI ** 2) / 6 * h_rw * tau if h_rw > 0 else 0.0 return math.sqrt(var_white + var_flicker + var_rw) # widget defaults: logHWhite=-19, logHRW=-24, rwOn=true, flickerOn=false, seed=1234 # (AdevLiveExplorer.js:196-201) h_white = 10 ** -19 h_rw = 10 ** -24 h_flicker = 0.0 tau0 = 1 # TAU0, arbitrary "s" unit tau = 64 * tau0 # one of the octave-spaced m values (m=64) sigma_y = analytic_sigma(tau, h_white, h_rw, h_flicker) print("sigma_y(tau=64 s) =", sigma_y) # -> 3.467e-11

documents.t: Problem: an OCXO (oven-controlled crystal oscillator) measures σy(1 s)=2×10−12\sigma_y(1\,\text{s})=2\times10^{-12}σy​(1s)=2×10−12 and σy(10 s)=6.3×10−13\sigma_y(10\,\text{s})=6.3\times10^{-13}σy​(10s)=6.3×10−13. Which noise type dominates in this range? Extrapolate σy(100 s)\sigma_y(100\,\text{s})σy​(100s). Steps: Compute the slope μ\muμ (σy∝τμ\sigma_y\propto\tau^\muσy​∝τμ): μ=log⁡10 ⁣(σy(10)/σy(1))log⁡10(10/1)=log⁡10(6.3×10−13/2×10−12)log⁡1010=log⁡10(0.315)1≈−0.5.\mu=\frac{\log_{10}\!\big(\sigma_y(10)/\sigma_y(1)\big)}{\log_{10}(10/1)}=\frac{\log_{10}(6.3\times10^{-13}/2\times10^{-12})}{\log_{10}10}=\frac{\log_{10}(0.315)}{1}\approx-0.5.μ=log10​(10/1)log10​(σy​(10)/σy​(1))​=log10​10log10​(6.3×10−13/2×10−12)​=1log10​(0.315)​≈−0.5. Consulting the Step-4 table: μ=−1/2\mu=-1/2μ=−1/2 ⇒ white FM dominates (Sy∼f0S_y\sim f^0Sy​∼f0, equivalently Sϕ∼1/f2S_\phi\sim1/f^2Sϕ​∼1/f2). Extrapolate to τ=100 s\tau=100\,\text{s}τ=100s (still white FM, τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2): σy(100)=σy(1)×(100)−1/2=2×10−12×110=2×10−13.\sigma_y(100)=\sigma_y(1)\times(100)^{-1/2}=2\times10^{-12}\times\frac{1}{10}=2\times10^{-13}.σy​(100)=σy​(1)×(100)−1/2=2×10−12×101​=2×10−13. Result: white FM dominates; σy(100 s)≈2×10−13\sigma_y(100\,\text{s})\approx2\times10^{-13}σy​(100s)≈2×10−13. Dimension check: σy\sigma_yσy​ is dimensionless throughout (fractional frequency); the slope μ\muμ is a ratio of logs of two dimensionless quantities, hence dimensionless ✓. import numpy as np mu = np.log10(6.3e-13/2e-12)/np.log10(10) # -> -0.50 => white FM adev_100 = 2e-12*(100/1)**mu print(round(mu,2), f"{adev_100:.2e}") # -> -0.5 2.00e-13

Steps: dBc/Hz → linear L\mathcal{L}L: L(1 MHz)=10−100/10=10−10 rad2/Hz\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})=10^{-100/10}=10^{-10}\,\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}L(1MHz)=10−100/10=10−10rad2/Hz (single-sided). Write the explicit 1/f21/f^21/f2 form: in the white-FM segment Sϕ(f)=h−2f2S_\phi(f)=\dfrac{h_{-2}}{f^2}Sϕ​(f)=f2h−2​​. Substituting f=106f=10^6f=106: h−2=Sϕ(106)⋅(106)2=2×10−10×1012=2×102=200 rad2 Hzh_{-2}=S_\phi(10^6)\cdot(10^6)^2=2\times10^{-10}\times10^{12}=2\times10^{2}=200\,\text{rad}^2\,\text{Hz}h−2​=Sϕ​(106)⋅(106)2=2×10−10×1012=2×102=200rad2Hz. documents.t: The Step-4 slope table only answers "σy∝τμ\sigma_y\propto\tau^\muσy​∝τμ" — it says nothing about the absolute level. What engineering actually needs is: given the power-law coefficients of SyS_ySy​, the exact numerical value of each segment of the ADEV curve — above all, how high the flicker-FM floor sits, the level that "no amount of averaging gets you below". This section evaluates the Step-3 integral for each of the five power laws one by one: the centerpiece is the flicker-FM floor constant, which turns out to be a beautiful ln⁡2\ln 2ln2; white FM and RW FM fall to the same trick along the way; and the two PM types will show us "why a high-frequency cutoff fhf_hfh​ is unavoidable".

Notation warning: the hαh_\alphahα​ always attach to SyS_ySy​ (the standard IEEE 1139 usage). In Example 2 above we casually wrote the 1/f21/f^21/f2 coefficient of SϕS_\phiSϕ​ as h−2h_{-2}h−2​ — that is the SϕS_\phiSϕ​-side coefficient, not the same object as the RW-FM h−2h_{-2}h−2​ here (which lives on the SyS_ySy​ side, with units Hz). From this section on, SϕS_\phiSϕ​-side coefficients carry a superscript ϕ\phiϕ: the white-FM segment is written Sϕ=h−2ϕ/f2S_\phi=h^{\phi}_{-2}/f^2Sϕ​=h−2ϕ​/f2 (with h−2ϕh^{\phi}_{-2}h−2ϕ​ in rad2⋅Hz\text{rad}^2\cdot\text{Hz}rad2⋅Hz).

Each term alone diverges as u→0u\to0u→0 (∫du/u\int du/u∫du/u), but the combination is integrable (cos⁡2u−cos⁡4u=6u2+O(u4)\cos2u-\cos4u=6u^2+O(u^4)cos2u−cos4u=6u2+O(u4), integrand ∼6u→0\sim6u\to0∼6u→0). Therefore: I3=∫0∞sin⁡4uu3 du=ln⁡2⟹σy2(τ)=2ln⁡2⋅h−1 (independent of τ),σy,floor=2ln⁡2⋅h−1≈1.1774 h−1 \boxed{\ I_3=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\sin^4u}{u^3}\,du=\ln2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sigma_y^2(\tau)=2\ln2\cdot h_{-1}\ (\text{independent of }\tau),\quad \sigma_{y,\text{floor}}=\sqrt{2\ln2\cdot h_{-1}}\approx1.1774\,\sqrt{h_{-1}}\ } I3​=∫0∞​u3sin4u​du=ln2⟹σy2​(τ)=2ln2⋅h−1​ (independent of τ),σy,floor​=2ln2⋅h−1​​≈1.1774h−1​​ ​ Physical intuition: ln⁡2=ln⁡42\ln2=\ln\frac{4}{2}ln2=ln24​ is the log of the frequency ratio of the two harmonics 2u2u2u and 4u4u4u produced by the power reduction. A 1/f1/f1/f process contributes equal power per octave; the ADEV band-pass kernel, on a log-frequency axis, is a window of fixed shape that merely slides with τ\tauτ (weighted by Sy∼1/fS_y\sim1/fSy​∼1/f, the contribution density per decade is ∝sin⁡4u/u2\propto\sin^4u/u^2∝sin4u/u2, peaking at tan⁡u=2u\tan u=2utanu=2u, i.e. u≈1.17u\approx1.17u≈1.17, f≈0.37/τf\approx0.37/\tauf≈0.37/τ) — the window slides without changing shape, so the "number of octaves" it sees does not depend on τ\tauτ, and the integral is a constant. That is the frequency-domain picture of why the flicker floor is "τ\tauτ-independent". Numerical verification (scipy.integrate.quad up to 200π200\pi200π plus the analytic ⟨sin⁡4⟩=3/8\langle\sin^4\rangle=3/8⟨sin4⟩=3/8 tail correction; printed by lab_19): import numpy as np from scipy.integrate import quad U = 200*np.pi I3, _ = quad(lambda u: np.sin(u)**4/u**3, 0, U, limit=4000) I3 += (3/8)/(2*U**2) # tail ∫_U^∞ (3/8)/u^3 du print(f"{I3:.4f} {np.log(2):.4f}") # -> 0.6931 0.6931 Factor-2/4 bookkeeping (the origin of every 2 and 4 in this section, settled once and for all): The leading 2 in σy2=2ln⁡2⋅h−1\sigma_y^2=2\ln2\cdot h_{-1}σy2​=2ln2⋅h−1​: from the Step-3 kernel ∣H∣2=2sin⁡4u/u2\lvert H\rvert^2=2\sin^4u/u^2∣H∣2=2sin4u/u2 (the definition's 12\tfrac1221​ × the adjacent-difference 4sin⁡24\sin^24sin2) — this is ADEV mathematics, and has nothing to do with the phase-noise SSB /2/2/2-vs-/4/4/4 bookkeeping. The 2 and 4 in cos⁡2u\cos2ucos2u and cos⁡4u\cos4ucos4u: the second and fourth harmonics from power-reducing sin⁡4\sin^4sin4; ln⁡2=ln⁡(4/2)\ln2=\ln(4/2)ln2=ln(4/2) is precisely their frequency ratio. The 2 in the white-FM denominator h0/(2τ)h_0/(2\tau)h0​/(2τ): 2⋅I2π=2⋅π/4π=122\cdot\frac{I_2}{\pi}=2\cdot\frac{\pi/4}{\pi}=\frac122⋅πI2​​=2⋅ππ/4​=21​ — again ADEV mathematics, not SSB bookkeeping. The 4 in the denominator of τknee\tau_{knee}τknee​ in Example 3: =2×2=2\times2=2×2 (the 2 of h0/2τh_0/\mathbf{2}\tauh0​/2τ × the 2 of 2ln⁡2\mathbf{2}\ln22ln2). documents.t: Prerequisites: stochastic_noise_basics · white_noise_to_phase_noise ｜ Next: psd_phase_noise_jitter The previous two pages computed phase noise from the circuit and from the frequency domain; this page puts on a different pair of glasses — re-examining the same thing from a signal-processing (DSP) viewpoint: treat the excess phase ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) as the output of a linear system whose input is the noise current, passing through two blocks: (1) a time-varying gain Γ(ω0t)/qmax\Gamma(\omega_0 t)/q_{max}Γ(ω0​t)/qmax​ (ISF weighting), and (2) an ideal integrator ∫dt\int dt∫dt. The payoff of this viewpoint is large: once you draw it as a block diagram, you immediately see that the −20-20−20 dB/dec (1/f²) slope of phase noise is no coincidence at all — it is simply the frequency response of the integrator. At the same time, this is the bridge that translates the continuous-time integral of [P1] Eq.(11) into the "discrete-time simulation code" (lab_06). Physical intuition (big picture first): an integrator turns "something white" into "something that grows toward low frequency". Feed white noise through an integrator and the output PSD carries a 1/ω21/\omega^21/ω2 — that is 1/f² phase noise. The ISF merely "phase-weights and downconverts" the input before the integration. Phase noise = ISF-weighted white noise, shaped by the integrator.
documents.s: The DSP View of Phase Noise

documents.t: The central equation of [P1] (spec §3, formula 4): ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ.\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau .ϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ. The DSP decomposition: first define the "ISF-weighted equivalent noise current" y(τ)≡Γ(ω0τ)qmax in(τ),y(\tau)\equiv\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,i_n(\tau),y(τ)≡qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​in​(τ), so that ϕ(t)=∫−∞ty(τ) dτ\phi(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}y(\tau)\,d\tauϕ(t)=∫−∞t​y(τ)dτ — ϕ\phiϕ is the running integral of yyy. As a block diagram: Block B (ISF weighting) is LTV (linear time-varying): the gain varies periodically in time (period TTT) — this is the mathematical embodiment of [P1]'s emphasis that "an oscillator is time-variant, not time-invariant, toward noise" (claim C1). Its role is frequency translation: it "downconverts" noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ to baseband ([P1] Eq.(13), Fig. 8). Block C (the integrator) is LTI (linear time-invariant): its frequency response is exactly 1/(jω)1/(j\omega)1/(jω).

documents.t: An ideal integrator ϕ(t)=∫y dt\phi(t)=\int y\,dtϕ(t)=∫ydt divides by jωj\omegajω in the frequency domain: Φ(jω)=1jω Y(jω)⟹∣Hint(jω)∣2=1ω2.\Phi(j\omega)=\frac{1}{j\omega}\,Y(j\omega)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |H_{\text{int}}(j\omega)|^2=\frac{1}{\omega^2}.Φ(jω)=jω1​Y(jω)⟹∣Hint​(jω)∣2=ω21​. The rule for PSDs through a linear system is Sout=∣H∣2 SinS_{\text{out}}=|H|^2\,S_{\text{in}}Sout​=∣H∣2Sin​. If the ISF-weighted equivalent input yyy is approximately white in the offset band we care about (power ∝Γrms2Si/qmax2\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/q_{max}^2∝Γrms2​Si​/qmax2​), then: Sϕ(Δω)=∣Hint∣2 Sy=1Δω2⋅Γrms2qmax2 Si \boxed{\ S_\phi(\Delta\omega)=|H_{\text{int}}|^2\,S_y=\frac{1}{\Delta\omega^2}\cdot\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\,S_i\ } Sϕ​(Δω)=∣Hint​∣2Sy​=Δω21​⋅qmax2​Γrms2​​Si​ ​ dimension check: [1/(rad/s)2]×[(rad2)⋅A2/Hz/C2][1/(\text{rad/s})^2]\times[(\text{rad}^2)\cdot\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}/\text{C}^2][1/(rad/s)2]×[(rad2)⋅A2/Hz/C2]. Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless, qmaxq_{max}qmax​ is C, SiS_iSi​ is A2/Hz=C2/(s2⋅Hz)\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}=\text{C}^2/(\text{s}^2\cdot\text{Hz})A2/Hz=C2/(s2⋅Hz); collecting terms gives rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz (treating the rad² in 1/(rad/s)21/(\text{rad/s})^21/(rad/s)2 as phase rad²), consistent with the units of SϕS_\phiSϕ​ ✓. This is the 1/f²: Sϕ∝1/Δω2S_\phi\propto1/\Delta\omega^2Sϕ​∝1/Δω2, i.e. −20-20−20 dB/dec on a log-log plot. Expressed in dBc/Hz (L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\frac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​), the skirt is still −20-20−20 dB/dec. Comparison with [P1] Eq.(21) (including the famous factor-of-2): the clean time-domain derivation "white noise × ISF → integrate" gives L=Γrms2Si/(2qmax2Δω2)\mathcal{L}=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(2q_{max}^2\Delta\omega^2)L=Γrms2​Si​/(2qmax2​Δω2), whereas [P1] Eq.(21) is written with /(4Δω2)/(4\Delta\omega^2)/(4Δω2). The factor of 2 comes purely from the SSB bookkeeping convention (L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\frac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​), and does not affect the Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ scaling or the −20-20−20 dB/dec slope. Full discussion in white_noise_to_phase_noise. Extension to flicker: if the input is not white but 1/f ([P1] Eq.(22)), the same 1/ω21/\omega^21/ω2 integrator produces 1/ω31/\omega^31/ω3 at the output — the close-in 1/f³ phase noise ([P1] Eq.(23)). The DSP view unifies "1/f² and 1/f³" as "the same integrator acting on inputs of different colors". This also explains "why phase accumulates but amplitude does not": the integrator has infinite DC gain (1/ω→∞1/\omega\to\infty1/ω→∞ when ω→0\omega\to0ω→0), so phase is infinitely sensitive to very-low-frequency perturbations and random-walks away (no restoring force); the amplitude path instead has a decaying (restoring) pole — high-pass / finite gain — so perturbations get pulled back. Compare phase_vs_amplitude_noise (claim C2).

documents.t: To verify the theory on a computer, the continuous integral must be replaced by a discrete accumulation. With sampling frequency fsf_sfs​ and interval Δts=1/fs\Delta t_s=1/f_sΔts​=1/fs​, the discrete version of [P1] Eq.(11) is a cumulative sum: ϕ[k]=Δtsqmax∑m=0kΓ(ω0 m Δts) in[m].\phi[k]=\frac{\Delta t_s}{q_{max}}\sum_{m=0}^{k}\Gamma(\omega_0\,m\,\Delta t_s)\,i_n[m].ϕ[k]=qmax​Δts​​m=0∑k​Γ(ω0​mΔts​)in​[m]. The role of Δts\Delta t_sΔts​: it calibrates the "discrete sum" back to the physical dimensions of an "integral". Dropping Δts\Delta t_sΔts​ is the most common discretization mistake (the units end up off by a factor of fsf_sfs​). PSD of discrete white noise: to generate a white sequence with single-sided PSD SiS_iSi​, the variance of each sample must be set to σ2=Si⋅fs/2\sigma^2=S_i\cdot f_s/2σ2=Si​⋅fs​/2 (the single-to-double-sided factor of 2 and the sampling bandwidth fs/2f_s/2fs​/2). This constant must match the analytic expression, or the numerics will not lie on the theory line. cumsum = the integrator: numpy.cumsum is the discrete integrator; its frequency response approaches 1/ω1/\omega1/ω at low frequency — exactly the source of our 1/f². The corresponding core code (using the real functions of spec §5): import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import white_noise, estimate_psd from simulations.common.isf_utils import apply_isf_weighting, gamma_lc_ideal # 0) time axis t = np.arange(N) / fs # 1) generate the white noise-current sequence i_n[m], single-sided PSD = S_i i_n = white_noise(n=N, psd=1e-24, fs=fs, rng=rng) # A, white # 2a) ISF weighting (time-varying multiply only, with NO integration): y[m] = Gamma(w0 t)/qmax * i_n y = apply_isf_weighting(t, i_n, gamma_func=gamma_lc_ideal, qmax=1e-12, omega0=2*np.pi*5e9) # 2b) integrator: phi[k] = dt * cumsum(y) — cumsum×dt is the true discrete integral dt = 1.0 / fs phi = np.cumsum(y) * dt # 3) Welch PSD estimate, verify S_phi ∝ 1/f^2 f, S_phi = estimate_psd(phi, fs=fs, nperseg=4096) Full script: simulations/lab_06_white_noise_phase_noise.py (see lab_06). This is a pedagogical toy model (ideal-LC Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ, a single white-noise source), not transistor-level.

documents.t: You have simulated a time series ϕ[k]\phi[k]ϕ[k]; how do you recover its PSD Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) to compare against the theoretical 1/f²? A single FFT with the squared magnitude (the periodogram) has an estimator variance that does not decrease as the record gets longer — the estimate stays wildly noisy. Welch's method solves this: Split the long sequence into segments (each nperseg points long), optionally overlapping (typically 50%). Multiply each segment by a window (a window function, e.g. Hann, to suppress spectral leakage). Take the periodogram of each segment, then average. Averaging KKK segments lowers the estimator variance by about 1/K1/K1/K. trade-off: shorter segments → more segments to average, smoother, but worse frequency resolution (Δf≈fs/nperseg\Delta f\approx f_s/\text{nperseg}Δf≈fs​/nperseg) — the close-in 1/f² details get smeared out. Longer segments → better resolution but noisier. Seeing the close-in 1/f² requires long segments + long records. This site uses estimate_psd(x, fs, nperseg) (spec §5, noise_utils) for this; the lab_06 figure overlays the Welch estimate (dots) on the analytic 1/f² line (solid), and the two agree. The figure above (simulations/lab_06_white_noise_phase_noise.py, corresponding to spec §4 white_noise_phase_noise_psd.png) is the "seeing is believing" of this DSP chain: white-noise input → ISF weighting → cumsum integrator → Welch estimate, giving an SϕS_\phiSϕ​ that is a clean −20-20−20 dB/dec on log-log, coinciding with the analytic 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 of Section 2.

documents.t: When moving a continuous system into a discrete simulation, aliasing (frequencies above Nyquist folding back to low frequency and masquerading as others) is the number-one pitfall, and ISF simulations require particular care: The Nyquist iron law: fsf_sfs​ must be ≥2×\ge2\times≥2× the highest signal frequency. The ISF weighting contains Γ(ω0t)\Gamma(\omega_0 t)Γ(ω0​t) and its harmonics nω0n\omega_0nω0​, so your fsf_sfs​ must be not merely >2f0>2f_0>2f0​ but ideally ≫f0\gg f_0≫f0​ (covering the few ISF harmonics nω0n\omega_0nω0​ you care about); otherwise the downconversion of higher harmonics gets contaminated by aliasing, and the 1/f² line kicks up at high offsets. White noise is inherently aliased: ideal white noise has infinite bandwidth, and discrete sampling inevitably folds all frequencies into [0,fs/2][0,f_s/2][0,fs​/2]. That is fine — as long as fsf_sfs​ is high enough and we only interpret the offset band ≪fs/2\ll f_s/2≪fs​/2. When reporting a PSD, trust only the band far below Nyquist. The integrator's DC singularity: 1/ω1/\omega1/ω diverges as ω→0\omega\to0ω→0; a discrete cumsum manifests as a random walk (unbounded drift). In simulation, either look only at a finite offset band or detrend ϕ\phiϕ; otherwise the lowest few PSD bins are dominated by drift — this is exactly the numerical version of "ϕ\phiϕ is not stationary; do statistics on phase differences/frequency" mentioned in Section 5 of stochastic_noise_basics.

documents.t: The DSP model of phase noise: white noise →\to→ ISF time-varying weighting (LTV, frequency translation) →\to→ integrator 1/(jω)1/(j\omega)1/(jω) (LTI) →ϕ\to\phi→ϕ. The integrator's ∣H∣2=1/ω2|H|^2=1/\omega^2∣H∣2=1/ω2 is the source of the 1/f² (−20-20−20 dB/dec) slope; a 1/f input → 1/f³. Discretization: integral = cumsum × dt; white-noise variance =Sifs/2=S_i f_s/2=Si​fs​/2; do not drop Δts\Delta t_sΔts​. Welch PSD: segment + window + average to lower the estimator variance; trade segment length against resolution. Aliasing: fs≫f0f_s\gg f_0fs​≫f0​ and cover the harmonics of interest; trust only offsets ≪fs/2\ll f_s/2≪fs​/2; detrend ϕ\phiϕ to avoid drift domination. Matches the analytic result (lab_06 figure); the factor of 2 is just SSB bookkeeping and changes neither the scaling nor the slope.

Exercise 3 solution (Parseval: Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ from the ISF) (a) Compute Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ by direct integration. Using the fact that sin⁡2θ\sin^2\thetasin2θ averages to 12\tfrac1221​ over one period: Γrms2=12π∫02π(−sin⁡θ)2 dθ=12π∫02πsin⁡2θ dθ=12π⋅π=12.\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}(-\sin\theta)^2\,d\theta=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\pi=\frac12.Γrms2​=2π1​∫02π​(−sinθ)2dθ=2π1​∫02π​sin2θdθ=2π1​⋅π=21​.Γrms=12≈0.707.\Gamma_{rms}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx0.707.Γrms​=2​1​≈0.707. (b) Find ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ with Parseval. Spec Eq. 11 ([P1] Eq.(20), p.185): ∑n=0∞cn2=2 Γrms2=2×12=1.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2=2\times\frac12=1.n=0∑∞​cn2​=2Γrms2​=2×21​=1. Which cnc_ncn​ is nonzero: Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ=cos⁡(θ+π2)\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\theta=\cos(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{2})Γ(θ)=−sinθ=cos(θ+2π​) is a pure first harmonic, so only c1=1c_1=1c1​=1 (with θ1=π/2\theta_1=\pi/2θ1​=π/2); all others c0=c2=⋯=0c_0=c_2=\dots=0c0​=c2​=⋯=0. Check: ∑cn2=c12=1\sum c_n^2=c_1^2=1∑cn2​=c12​=1 ✓. Result: Γrms=1/2≈0.707\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2\approx0.707Γrms​=1/2​≈0.707, ∑cn2=1\sum c_n^2=1∑cn2​=1, the only nonzero coefficient is c1=1c_1=1c1​=1. Dimension check: Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless (spec notation table), so Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ and ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ are both dimensionless ✓. import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, gamma_rms, compute_fourier_coefficients theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 4096, endpoint=False) g = gamma_lc_ideal(theta) # = -sin(theta) print(gamma_rms(theta, g)) # -> 0.7071 a0, a, b, c, ph = compute_fourier_coefficients(theta, g, n_harmonics=5) print(np.sum(c**2)) # -> ~1.0 (== 2*Gamma_rms^2) Exercise 4 solution (phase variance from PSD integration) Step-by-step substitution (with units). Phase variance (spec Eq. 18), substituting Sϕ(f)=K/f2S_\phi(f)=K/f^2Sϕ​(f)=K/f2: σϕ2=∫f1f2Kf2 df=K[−1f]f1f2=K(1f1−1f2).\sigma_\phi^2=\int_{f_1}^{f_2}\frac{K}{f^2}\,df=K\left[-\frac1f\right]_{f_1}^{f_2}=K\left(\frac{1}{f_1}-\frac{1}{f_2}\right).σϕ2​=∫f1​f2​​f2K​df=K[−f1​]f1​f2​​=K(f1​1​−f2​1​). Substituting K=10−4 rad2⋅HzK=10^{-4}\ \text{rad}^2\cdot\text{Hz}K=10−4 rad2⋅Hz, f1=103f_1=10^3f1​=103 Hz, f2=106f_2=10^6f2​=106 Hz: σϕ2=10−4(1103−1106)=10−4×(10−3−10−6)=10−4×9.99×10−4=9.99×10−8 rad2.\sigma_\phi^2=10^{-4}\left(\frac{1}{10^3}-\frac{1}{10^6}\right)=10^{-4}\times(10^{-3}-10^{-6})=10^{-4}\times9.99\times10^{-4}=9.99\times10^{-8}\ \text{rad}^2.σϕ2​=10−4(1031​−1061​)=10−4×(10−3−10−6)=10−4×9.99×10−4=9.99×10−8 rad2.σϕ=9.99×10−8≈3.16×10−4 rad=0.316 mrad.\sigma_\phi=\sqrt{9.99\times10^{-8}}\approx3.16\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}=0.316\ \text{mrad}.σϕ​=9.99×10−8​≈3.16×10−4 rad=0.316 mrad. Result: σϕ2≈9.99×10−8 rad2\sigma_\phi^2\approx9.99\times10^{-8}\ \text{rad}^2σϕ2​≈9.99×10−8 rad2, σϕ≈0.316\sigma_\phi\approx0.316σϕ​≈0.316 mrad. Intuition: the 1/f21/f^21/f2 integral is dominated by the low-frequency end f1f_1f1​ (1/f1≫1/f21/f_1\gg1/f_21/f1​≫1/f2​) — which is exactly why close-in phase noise contributes most of the total jitter. Dimension check: [K]⋅[1/f]=(rad2⋅Hz)⋅(1/Hz)=rad2[K]\cdot[1/f]=(\text{rad}^2\cdot\text{Hz})\cdot(1/\text{Hz})=\text{rad}^2[K]⋅[1/f]=(rad2⋅Hz)⋅(1/Hz)=rad2 ✓ (σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​ is in rad²). import numpy as np K, f1, f2 = 1e-4, 1e3, 1e6 var = K*(1/f1 - 1/f2) print(var, "rad^2 ->", np.sqrt(var)*1e3, "mrad") # -> 9.99e-8 rad^2 -> 0.316 mrad Exercise 5 solution (LTI vs LTV: same impulse, different phase) Step-by-step substitution (with units). Using the operational ISF (spec Eq. 5) Δϕ=Γ(θ) Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma(\theta)\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=Γ(θ)Δq/qmax​. Δq/qmax=10−15/10−12=10−3\Delta q/q_{max}=10^{-15}/10^{-12}=10^{-3}Δq/qmax​=10−15/10−12=10−3. (a) Zero-crossing θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2 (Γ=−sin⁡(π/2)=−1\Gamma=-\sin(\pi/2)=-1Γ=−sin(π/2)=−1, maximum sensitivity): Δϕa=(−1)×10−3=−1×10−3 rad=−1 mrad.\Delta\phi_a=(-1)\times10^{-3}=-1\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad}=-1\ \text{mrad}.Δϕa​=(−1)×10−3=−1×10−3 rad=−1 mrad. (b) Peak θ=0\theta=0θ=0 (Γ=−sin⁡0=0\Gamma=-\sin 0=0Γ=−sin0=0, zero sensitivity): Δϕb=0×10−3=0 rad.\Delta\phi_b=0\times10^{-3}=0\ \text{rad}.Δϕb​=0×10−3=0 rad. Result: injection at the zero-crossing produces a phase step of ∣Δϕ∣=1\lvert\Delta\phi\rvert=1∣Δϕ∣=1 mrad; injection at the peak produces 0 phase step (there the charge only changes the amplitude, which is subsequently pulled back by amplitude restoring). Why this is LTV, not LTI: the impulse response of an LTI (linear time-invariant) system depends only on the elapsed time t−τt-\taut−τ, not on the injection instant τ\tauτ. Here, however, the same Δq\Delta qΔq at θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2 versus θ=0\theta=0θ=0 produces completely different Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ — the response explicitly depends on the absolute injection phase Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ), which is precisely the defining signature of an LTV (linear time-varying) system (see lti_vs_ltv). Dimension check: Γ\GammaΓ dimensionless × Δq/qmax\times\ \Delta q/q_{max}× Δq/qmax​ (C/C, dimensionless) === rad ✓. from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, impulse_to_phase_step import numpy as np dq, qmax = 1e-15, 1e-12 for name, theta in [("zero-crossing", np.pi/2), ("peak", 0.0)]: g = gamma_lc_ideal(theta) # -sin(theta) dphi = impulse_to_phase_step(dq, g, qmax) print(name, dphi*1e3, "mrad") # -> -1.0 mrad ; 0.0 mrad Exercise 6 solution (phase diffusion from the Lorentzian linewidth) Note: Lorentzian linewidth and phase diffusion are external literature ([E2] Demir 2000), not among the 5 source PDFs; the formulas are taken verbatim from spec §11.2. (a) Back-solve DDD. FWHM linewidth (spec §11.2): Δf3dB=Dπ⟹D=π Δf3dB=π×103 Hz=3.142×103 rad2/s.\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\frac{D}{\pi}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D=\pi\,\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\pi\times10^{3}\ \text{Hz}=3.142\times10^{3}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}.Δf3dB​=πD​⟹D=πΔf3dB​=π×103 Hz=3.142×103 rad2/s. (b) Estimate the time to accumulate 1 rad². Phase diffusion (spec §11.2) Var⁡[Δϕ(t)]=2D∣t∣\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(t)]=2D\lvert t\rvertVar[Δϕ(t)]=2D∣t∣; setting it =1 rad2=1\ \text{rad}^2=1 rad2: t=12D=12×3.142×103≈1.59×10−4 s=159 μs.t=\frac{1}{2D}=\frac{1}{2\times3.142\times10^{3}}\approx1.59\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}=159\ \mu\text{s}.t=2D1​=2×3.142×1031​≈1.59×10−4 s=159 μs. Result: D≈3.14×103 rad2/sD\approx3.14\times10^{3}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}D≈3.14×103 rad2/s; accumulating ≈1 rad2\approx1\ \text{rad}^2≈1 rad2 of phase variance takes about 159 µs (i.e., a coherence time of order τc∼1/(2D)\tau_c\sim1/(2D)τc​∼1/(2D)). Note that 1/Δf3dB=11/\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=11/Δf3dB​=1 ms is of the same order — the narrower the linewidth, the longer the coherence time; the two are reciprocals. Dimension check: (a) [ Δf ]=Hz=1/s[\,\Delta f\,]=\text{Hz}=1/\text{s}[Δf]=Hz=1/s, multiplied by π\piπ (dimensionless), gives DDD in rad²/s (rad² being the square of the dimensionless "rad" of phase variance, per second) ✓. (b) rad2rad2/s=s\dfrac{\text{rad}^2}{\text{rad}^2/\text{s}}=\text{s}rad2/srad2​=s ✓. import numpy as np df_3db = 1e3 # Hz (FWHM) D = np.pi*df_3db # rad^2/s t = 1/(2*D) # Var = 2 D t = 1 rad^2 print(D, "rad^2/s ;", t*1e6, "us") # -> 3141.6 rad^2/s ; 159.2 us (Background and full derivation: lorentzian_linewidth.) Exercise 7 solution (reading Allan-deviation slopes) Note: The Allan variance is external literature (Allan 1966), not among the 5 source PDFs; the slope table is taken verbatim from spec §11.2. Slope reference (spec §11.2). On a log–log σy(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)σy​(τ) plot: Measured slope σy(τ)∝τ?\sigma_y(\tau)\propto\tau^{?}σy​(τ)∝τ? Noise type Physics τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2 white FM (white frequency modulation) frequency is white noise → phase is a random walk; the longer you average, the more stable τ0\tau^{0}τ0 (plateau/floor) flicker FM (1/f frequency) σy\sigma_yσy​ is independent of the gate time τ\tauτ → ADEV forms a flat floor τ+1/2\tau^{+1/2}τ+1/2 random-walk FM (random walk of frequency) the frequency itself drifts → the longer you average, the worse it gets; slope turns upward Why flicker FM forms a plateau: substitute Sy(f)∝1/fS_y(f)\propto1/fSy​(f)∝1/f (flicker FM) into the spec §11.2 expression σy2(τ)=2∫0∞Sy(f)sin⁡4(πfτ)(πfτ)2 df\sigma_y^2(\tau)=2\displaystyle\int_0^\infty S_y(f)\dfrac{\sin^4(\pi f\tau)}{(\pi f\tau)^2}\,dfσy2​(τ)=2∫0∞​Sy​(f)(πfτ)2sin4(πfτ)​df and change variables to u=πfτu=\pi f\tauu=πfτ: τ\tauτ cancels completely out of the integrand — the integral becomes a pure numerical constant independent of τ\tauτ, so σy2(τ)=\sigma_y^2(\tau)=σy2​(τ)= constant ⇒σy(τ)∝τ0\Rightarrow\sigma_y(\tau)\propto\tau^0⇒σy​(τ)∝τ0, a horizontal line (floor) on the log–log plot. This floor is the signature long-term-stability feature of quartz/atomic clocks, marking the limit that no amount of extra averaging time can push down. Result: τ−1/2→\tau^{-1/2}\toτ−1/2→ white FM, τ0→\tau^{0}\toτ0→ flicker FM (floor), τ+1/2→\tau^{+1/2}\toτ+1/2→ random-walk FM. Dimension check: σy(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)σy​(τ) is the dimensionless fractional-frequency stability (y=Δf/f0y=\Delta f/f_0y=Δf/f0​); its power-law relationship with τ\tauτ only compares slopes and carries no dimension ✓. import numpy as np # Read off by the slope definition: fit the log-log slope of a sigma_y(tau) segment tau = np.logspace(-3, 1, 200) for label, slope in [("white FM", -0.5), ("flicker FM", 0.0), ("random-walk FM", 0.5)]: sy = tau**slope fit = np.polyfit(np.log10(tau), np.log10(sy), 1)[0] print(label, "slope =", round(fit, 2)) # -> -0.5 ; 0.0 ; 0.5 (Full derivation and plots: allan_variance.) Exercise 8 solution (from a single L\mathcal{L}L point to SϕS_\phiSϕ​ to jitter) (a) L→Sϕ\mathcal{L}\to S_\phiL→Sϕ​. First convert dBc/Hz back to linear: Llin(1 MHz)=10−120/10=10−12 (per Hz).\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}(1\,\text{MHz})=10^{-120/10}=10^{-12}\ \text{(per Hz)}.Llin​(1MHz)=10−120/10=10−12 (per Hz). The small-angle relation (spec Eq. 16) L≈12Sϕ⇒Sϕ=2Llin\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12 S_\phi\Rightarrow S_\phi=2\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}L≈21​Sϕ​⇒Sϕ​=2Llin​: Sϕ(1 MHz)=2×10−12=2×10−12 rad2/Hz.S_\phi(1\,\text{MHz})=2\times10^{-12}=2\times10^{-12}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}.Sϕ​(1MHz)=2×10−12=2×10−12 rad2/Hz. Phase variance (spec Eq. 18), integrated f1=106→f2=107f_1=10^6\to f_2=10^7f1​=106→f2​=107 Hz: σϕ2=∫f1f2Kf2df=K ⁣(1f1−1f2)=2(1106−1107)=2×9×10−7=1.8×10−6 rad2.\sigma_\phi^2=\int_{f_1}^{f_2}\frac{K}{f^2}df=K\!\left(\frac{1}{f_1}-\frac{1}{f_2}\right)=2\left(\frac{1}{10^6}-\frac{1}{10^7}\right)=2\times9\times10^{-7}=1.8\times10^{-6}\ \text{rad}^2.σϕ2​=∫f1​f2​​f2K​df=K(f1​1​−f2​1​)=2(1061​−1071​)=2×9×10−7=1.8×10−6 rad2.σϕ=1.8×10−6≈1.342×10−3 rad=1.342 mrad.\sigma_\phi=\sqrt{1.8\times10^{-6}}\approx1.342\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad}=1.342\ \text{mrad}.σϕ​=1.8×10−6​≈1.342×10−3 rad=1.342 mrad. rms jitter (spec Eq. 19), with f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz: σt=σϕ2πf0=1.342×10−32π×5×109≈4.27×10−14 s=42.7 fs.\sigma_t=\frac{\sigma_\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{1.342\times10^{-3}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{9}}\approx4.27\times10^{-14}\ \text{s}=42.7\ \text{fs}.σt​=2πf0​σϕ​​=2π×5×1091.342×10−3​≈4.27×10−14 s=42.7 fs. Result: Sϕ(1MHz)=2×10−12 rad2/HzS_\phi(1\text{MHz})=2\times10^{-12}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}Sϕ​(1MHz)=2×10−12 rad2/Hz, σϕ≈1.34\sigma_\phi\approx1.34σϕ​≈1.34 mrad, σt≈42.7\sigma_t\approx42.7σt​≈42.7 fs (1→10 MHz band). documents.t: Prerequisites: psd_phase_noise_jitter · stochastic_noise_basics · dsp_view_of_phase_noise ｜ Next: allan_variance · serdes_clocking_connection psd_phase_noise_jitter already gave the "operational versions" of the three jitter weighting kernels; this page derives them rigorously from first principles, and answers the question that has been left hanging: what exactly is the prefactor? Which 2 belongs to which convention? The answer is calibrated with three independent rulers: (1) the step-by-step derivation, (2) exact agreement with the verified σΔϕ=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta\phi}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔϕ​=κΔt​ of [P2], (3) Monte-Carlo time-domain measurement (simulations/lab_24_jitter_kernels.py) — all three agree to ~0.1%. This page supersedes the earlier external-convention TODO: this site previously marked the prefactor of the period-jitter kernel in worked_examples Example C3 as "external literature, to be confirmed". This page has now derived it from first principles and verified it by Monte Carlo: under the "one-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​, ∫0∞\int_0^\infty∫0∞​" convention the prefactor is exactly 1/ω021/\omega_0^21/ω02​ (not 2/ω022/\omega_0^22/ω02​ — that 2 belongs to the two-sided-spectrum or L=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12 S_\phiL=21​Sϕ​ bookkeeping; see the conversion table in Step 0). The kernel and constant used in Example C3 are correct; its value 27.6 fs is the closed-form 28.28 fs after truncating the band to 10310^3103–101010^{10}1010 Hz (Section 7 of this page has markers reconciling each number). Physical intuition (conclusion first): the three jitters are three ways of reading the same phase process ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) — read it directly (TIE), read the difference NNN beats apart (N-period), or read the difference of adjacent differences (cycle-to-cycle). In the frequency domain, "taking a difference" is multiplication by a deterministic filter; multiply Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) by that filter's ∣H∣2\lvert H\rvert^2∣H∣2 and integrate, and you get that jitter's variance. The kernel's shape decides "which part of the frequency axis of the phase noise gets counted": TIE eats the low end, period is a first-order high-pass, c2c is a second-order high-pass. Every 2 and 4 can be traced to its origin.

documents.t: This page uses exactly one convention: Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) is the one-sided power spectral density of the excess phase, in rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz, defined for f≥0f\ge0f≥0; all integrals are ∫0∞df\int_0^\infty df∫0∞​df. Its relation to the variance is σϕ2=∫0∞Sϕ(f) df[rad2].\sigma_\phi^2=\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\,df\qquad[\text{rad}^2].σϕ2​=∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)df[rad2]. No extra factor of 2 anywhere. documents.t: The total phase of the oscillator output is Φ(t)=ω0t+ϕ(t)\Phi(t)=\omega_0 t+\phi(t)Φ(t)=ω0​t+ϕ(t) (the phase term of [P1] Eq.(1), p.180; ϕ\phiϕ is the excess phase, rad). The kkk-th rising zero crossing tkt_ktk​ is defined by "the total phase has completed kkk full turns": ω0tk+ϕ(tk)=2πk.\omega_0 t_k+\phi(t_k)=2\pi k.ω0​tk​+ϕ(tk​)=2πk. Solve for tkt_ktk​ (treat ϕ\phiϕ as a small perturbation and expand to first order about tk=kTt_k=kTtk​=kT): tk=kT−ϕ(tk)ω0≈kT−ϕ(kT)ω0.t_k=kT-\frac{\phi(t_k)}{\omega_0}\approx kT-\frac{\phi(kT)}{\omega_0}.tk​=kT−ω0​ϕ(tk​)​≈kT−ω0​ϕ(kT)​. Approximation used: first-order expansion; requires the effect of ∣ϕ(tk)−ϕ(kT)∣≪∣ϕ(kT)∣\lvert\phi(t_k)-\phi(kT)\rvert\ll\lvert\phi(kT)\rvert∣ϕ(tk​)−ϕ(kT)∣≪∣ϕ(kT)∣ to be negligible, equivalent to ∣ϕ˙∣≪ω0\lvert\dot\phi\rvert\ll\omega_0∣ϕ˙​∣≪ω0​ (instantaneous frequency offset far below the carrier) and σt≪T\sigma_t\ll Tσt​≪T (jitter far smaller than the period). Practical oscillators have fs-level jitter with periods of hundreds of ps, so this holds easily. Failure conditions: cycle slips (Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ accumulating to ∼\sim∼rad within one correlation time), strong injection pulling, or non-negligible AM-PM conversion — then edges and phase are no longer one-to-one. Units: [ϕ/ω0]=rad/(rad/s)=s[\phi/\omega_0]=\text{rad}/(\text{rad/s})=\text{s}[ϕ/ω0​]=rad/(rad/s)=s ✓. So the timing error of the kkk-th edge (TIE, time interval error, deviation from the ideal clock) is TIEk=tk−kT=−ϕ(kT)ω0.\text{TIE}_k=t_k-kT=-\frac{\phi(kT)}{\omega_0}.TIEk​=tk​−kT=−ω0​ϕ(kT)​. The minus sign just says "phase leads = edge arrives early"; after taking the variance it affects nothing.
documents.s: Step 1: edge timing error = a sample of the phase (time-domain starting point)

documents.t: Following the definitions of notation (conventions Section 2), rewritten entirely in the language of ϕ\phiϕ: TIE (absolute):TIEk=−ϕ(kT)ω0(0th order: direct sampling)N-period jitter:Pk(N)=(tk+N−tk)−NT=−ϕ((k+N)T)−ϕ(kT)ω0(1st-order difference, spacing NT)cycle-to-cycle:Ck=Tk+1−Tk=−ϕ((k+2)T)−2ϕ((k+1)T)+ϕ(kT)ω0(2nd-order difference).\begin{aligned} \text{TIE (absolute):}\quad &\text{TIE}_k=-\frac{\phi(kT)}{\omega_0} &&(\text{0th order: direct sampling})\\ \text{N-period jitter:}\quad &P_k(N)=\big(t_{k+N}-t_k\big)-NT=-\frac{\phi\big((k{+}N)T\big)-\phi(kT)}{\omega_0} &&(\text{1st-order difference, spacing }NT)\\ \text{cycle-to-cycle:}\quad &C_k=T_{k+1}-T_k=-\frac{\phi\big((k{+}2)T\big)-2\phi\big((k{+}1)T\big)+\phi(kT)}{\omega_0} &&(\text{2nd-order difference}). \end{aligned}TIE (absolute):N-period jitter:cycle-to-cycle:​TIEk​=−ω0​ϕ(kT)​Pk​(N)=(tk+N​−tk​)−NT=−ω0​ϕ((k+N)T)−ϕ(kT)​Ck​=Tk+1​−Tk​=−ω0​ϕ((k+2)T)−2ϕ((k+1)T)+ϕ(kT)​​​(0th order: direct sampling)(1st-order difference, spacing NT)(2nd-order difference).​ Pk(1)=Tk−TP_k(1)=T_k-TPk​(1)=Tk​−T at N=1N=1N=1 is what is commonly called the period jitter; CkC_kCk​ is the difference between two adjacent period lengths (the difference of the difference). All three are linear operations on ϕ\phiϕ, so the next step can process them all at once in the frequency domain.
documents.s: Step 2: three jitters = 0th/1st/2nd-order differences of the phase

documents.t: What we need is Var⁡[ϕ(t+τ0)−ϕ(t)]\operatorname{Var}\big[\phi(t+\tau_0)-\phi(t)\big]Var[ϕ(t+τ0​)−ϕ(t)] (τ0=NT\tau_0=NTτ0​=NT). Two mutually independent derivation routes follow; the second is mathematically stronger — it holds even when ϕ\phiϕ itself is a random walk (non-stationary).
documents.s: Step 3: variance of a difference ← frequency-domain kernel (the core lemma, derived two ways)

documents.t: Step 1: expand the square. Let ϕ\phiϕ be WSS and zero-mean, with autocorrelation Rϕ(τ)=⟨ϕ(t)ϕ(t+τ)⟩R_\phi(\tau)=\langle\phi(t)\phi(t+\tau)\rangleRϕ​(τ)=⟨ϕ(t)ϕ(t+τ)⟩: Var⁡[ϕ(t+τ0)−ϕ(t)]=⟨ϕ2(t+τ0)⟩+⟨ϕ2(t)⟩−2⟨ϕ(t)ϕ(t+τ0)⟩=2[Rϕ(0)−Rϕ(τ0)].\operatorname{Var}\big[\phi(t+\tau_0)-\phi(t)\big] =\big\langle\phi^2(t+\tau_0)\big\rangle+\big\langle\phi^2(t)\big\rangle-2\big\langle\phi(t)\phi(t+\tau_0)\big\rangle =2\big[R_\phi(0)-R_\phi(\tau_0)\big].Var[ϕ(t+τ0​)−ϕ(t)]=⟨ϕ2(t+τ0​)⟩+⟨ϕ2(t)⟩−2⟨ϕ(t)ϕ(t+τ0​)⟩=2[Rϕ​(0)−Rϕ​(τ0​)]. Step 2: Wiener–Khinchin. The autocorrelation representation with the one-sided spectrum (as in stochastic_noise_basics; [P2] takes this same Khinchin route on p.803, its Eq.(46)–(48)): Rϕ(τ)=∫0∞Sϕ(f)cos⁡(2πfτ) df.R_\phi(\tau)=\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\cos(2\pi f\tau)\,df.Rϕ​(τ)=∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)cos(2πfτ)df. Step 3: substitute back and use the half-angle identity. 1−cos⁡θ=2sin⁡2(θ/2)1-\cos\theta=2\sin^2(\theta/2)1−cosθ=2sin2(θ/2) with θ=2πfτ0\theta=2\pi f\tau_0θ=2πfτ0​: Var⁡[Δϕ(τ0)]=2∫0∞Sϕ(f)[1−cos⁡(2πfτ0)]df=∫0∞Sϕ(f) 4sin⁡2(πfτ0)⏟kernel df.\operatorname{Var}\big[\Delta\phi(\tau_0)\big] =2\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\big[1-\cos(2\pi f\tau_0)\big]df =\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\,\underbrace{4\sin^2(\pi f\tau_0)}_{\text{kernel}}\,df.Var[Δϕ(τ0​)]=2∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)[1−cos(2πfτ0​)]df=∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)kernel4sin2(πfτ0​)​​df. That is the entire origin of the 4sin⁡24\sin^24sin2 kernel: one factor of 2 comes from "variance of a difference =2[R(0)−R(τ0)]=2[R(0)-R(\tau_0)]=2[R(0)−R(τ0​)]", the other 2 from the half-angle identity; the two 2's multiply to 4, with not a single factor to spare. Equivalently, in filter language: y(t)=ϕ(t+τ0)−ϕ(t)y(t)=\phi(t+\tau_0)-\phi(t)y(t)=ϕ(t+τ0​)−ϕ(t) is LTI filtering with H(f)=ej2πfτ0−1H(f)=e^{j2\pi f\tau_0}-1H(f)=ej2πfτ0​−1, ∣H(f)∣2=(cos⁡(2πfτ0)−1)2+sin⁡2(2πfτ0)=2−2cos⁡(2πfτ0)=4sin⁡2(πfτ0),\lvert H(f)\rvert^2=\big(\cos(2\pi f\tau_0)-1\big)^2+\sin^2(2\pi f\tau_0)=2-2\cos(2\pi f\tau_0)=4\sin^2(\pi f\tau_0),∣H(f)∣2=(cos(2πfτ0​)−1)2+sin2(2πfτ0​)=2−2cos(2πfτ0​)=4sin2(πfτ0​), and a WSS process through an LTI filter obeys Sy=∣H∣2SϕS_y=\lvert H\rvert^2S_\phiSy​=∣H∣2Sϕ​ (one-sided in, one-sided out); integrating gives the same formula.

documents.t: Step 2's CkC_kCk​ is "a first-order difference differenced once more"; the filter is two first-order differences in cascade: Hc2c(f)=(e−j2πfT−1)2⟹∣Hc2c(f)∣2=∣e−j2πfT−1∣4=[4sin⁡2(πfT)]2=16sin⁡4(πfT),H_{c2c}(f)=\big(e^{-j2\pi fT}-1\big)^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lvert H_{c2c}(f)\rvert^2=\big\lvert e^{-j2\pi fT}-1\big\rvert^4=\big[4\sin^2(\pi fT)\big]^2=16\sin^4(\pi fT),Hc2c​(f)=(e−j2πfT−1)2⟹∣Hc2c​(f)∣2=​e−j2πfT−1​4=[4sin2(πfT)]2=16sin4(πfT), σc2c2=1ω02∫0∞Sϕ(f) 16sin⁡4(πfT) df \boxed{\ \sigma_{c2c}^2=\frac{1}{\omega_0^2}\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\,16\sin^4(\pi fT)\,df\ } σc2c2​=ω02​1​∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)16sin4(πfT)df ​ Kernel shape: as f→0f\to0f→0 it behaves like (2πfT)4∝f4(2\pi fT)^4\propto f^4(2πfT)4∝f4 (a second-order high-pass — the least sensitive to close-in noise); the peak of 16 sits at f=1/(2T)=f0/2f=1/(2T)=f_0/2f=1/(2T)=f0​/2, and the oscillation average is 6. Where 16 comes from: 424^242. Each differencing contributes one factor 4 (each containing one 2 from the "variance of a difference" and one 2 from the half-angle identity); squaring gives 16. Every 2 is accounted for by name. Plotting the shapes of the three boxed kernels together makes the peaks and low-frequency roll-off easy to read at a glance: Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Axis labels/title read: "fT（正規化頻率，無因次；N-period 核以 N=1 繪示，一般為 fNT）" = fT (normalized frequency, dimensionless; the N-period kernel is drawn with N=1, in general fNT); "|H(f)|²（無因次）" = |H(f)|² (dimensionless); "三種 jitter 核的正規化 |H(f)|²：TIE、N-period、cycle-to-cycle" = normalized |H(f)|² of the three jitter kernels: TIE, N-period, cycle-to-cycle. Formulas: kernel (a) =1=1=1, kernel (b) =4sin⁡2(πfT)=4\sin^2(\pi fT)=4sin2(πfT) (with N=1N=1N=1), kernel (c) =16sin⁡4(πfT)=16\sin^4(\pi fT)=16sin4(πfT) — exactly the integrands of the three boxed formulas above, plotted against the normalized frequency fTfTfT (dimensionless) on the horizontal axis. script / function: simulations/lab_24_jitter_kernels.py (make_figure_kernels), writing static/figures/jitter_kernel_shapes.png. How to read it: on the log-log plot the three curves peak at 111 (TIE — unfiltered, constant), 444 (period — peaking at fT=0.5fT=0.5fT=0.5), and 161616 (c2c — also peaking at fT=0.5fT=0.5fT=0.5, marked on the plot with horizontal dashed lines and numbers); the low-frequency dashed lines are the f→0f\to0f→0 asymptotes (2πfT)2(2\pi fT)^2(2πfT)2 (period) and (2πfT)4(2\pi fT)^4(2πfT)4 (c2c) — a first-order and a second-order high-pass, respectively: the higher the differencing order, the less close-in phase noise gets counted. This single figure condenses the full shape information of this section's three boxed formulas for later reference whenever a kernel's shape matters.

Example: b3=1 rad2Hz2b_3=1\ \text{rad}^2\text{Hz}^2b3​=1 rad2Hz2, fl=100f_l=100fl​=100 Hz, N=1N=1N=1, T=200T=200T=200 ps: 2πNTfl=1.26×10−72\pi NTf_l=1.26\times10^{-7}2πNTfl​=1.26×10−7, bracket =0.9228+15.89=16.81=0.9228+15.89=16.81=0.9228+15.89=16.81, σΔϕ2=1.579×10−18×16.81=2.65×10−17 rad2\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=1.579\times10^{-18}\times16.81=2.65\times10^{-17}\ \text{rad}^2σΔϕ2​=1.579×10−18×16.81=2.65×10−17 rad2. Changing flf_lfl​ by 10× only shifts the bracket to 16.81∓2.3016.81\mp2.3016.81∓2.30 (∓14%\mp14\%∓14% in variance) — the log's sluggishness is good news, but it is not zero. Growth law in NNN: σΔϕ(N)∝Nln⁡(⋅)\sigma_{\Delta\phi}(N)\propto N\sqrt{\ln(\cdot)}σΔϕ​(N)∝Nln(⋅)​ — almost linear (lab_24 prints σ(N=10)/σ(N=1)=9.29\sigma(N{=}10)/\sigma(N{=}1)=9.29σ(N=10)/σ(N=1)=9.29; white FM would give 10=3.16\sqrt{10}=3.1610​=3.16). This is exactly what [P2] Eq.(9), p.792 says: correlated (low-frequency/flicker) noise makes jitter ∝Δt\propto\Delta t∝Δt while white noise makes jitter ∝Δt\propto\sqrt{\Delta t}∝Δt​ — the two segments of slope 1 and 1/2 on a log-log plot ([P2] Fig. 4). Solid-State Circuits, vol. 32, no. 6, pp. 870–879, Jun. 1997 (external literature, not among the 5 source PDFs).

documents.t: Fig. 16 caption (p.802): "RMS jitter versus measurement interval for the four-stage, 2.8-GHz differential ring oscillator (oscillator number 12)." The vertical axis reads "Rms jitter (second)", the horizontal axis "ΔT\Delta TΔT (second)"; the two asymptote fits on the plot are annotated κ=6.18e-9 sec0.5\kappa=6.18\text{e-}9\ \text{sec}^{0.5}κ=6.18e-9 sec0.5 and ζ=2.5e5\zeta=2.5\text{e}5ζ=2.5e5. Definitions of the two proportionality constants (p.792): Eq.(8) σΔT=κΔT\sigma_{\Delta T}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta T}σΔT​=κΔT​, "where κ\kappaκ is a proportionality constant determined by circuit parameters"; Eq.(9) σΔT=ζ ΔT\sigma_{\Delta T}=\zeta\,\Delta TσΔT​=ζΔT, "where ζ\zetaζ is another proportionality constant". The premise of Eq.(9) is fully correlated noise sources — in the paper's words: "when the noise sources are totally correlated with one another … the standard deviations rather than the variances add"; substrate/supply noise and low-frequency 1/f noise belong to this class. Same page, the conclusion: "a log–log plot of the timing jitter σΔT\sigma_{\Delta T}σΔT​ versus the measurement delay ΔT\Delta TΔT for an open-loop oscillator will demonstrate regions with slopes of 1/2 and 1, as shown in Fig. 4." Measurement cross-check (p.801): "The best fit κ\kappaκ for the data shown in Fig. 16 is κ=6.18×10−9s\kappa=6.18\times10^{-9}\sqrt{s}κ=6.18×10−9s​. Equations (12) and (35) result in κ=5.95×10−9s\kappa=5.95\times10^{-9}\sqrt{s}κ=5.95×10−9s​ and κ=6.07×10−9s\kappa=6.07\times10^{-9}\sqrt{s}κ=6.07×10−9s​, respectively." — ISF theory lands within 2–4% of measurement, one of the most beautiful closed loops in all of [P2]. The slope-1 attribution is on the same page: "The region of the jitter plot with the slope of one can be attributed to the 1/f1/f1/f noise of the devices, as discussed at the end of Section VI." (End of Section VI, pp.797–798: "Low-frequency noise can also result in correlation between uncertainties introduced during different cycles … the uncertainties add up in amplitude rather than power, resulting in a region with a slope of one … even in the absence of external noise sources".) Printing erratum (honesty note): the figure prints ζ\zetaζ as "2.5e5". But Eq.(9) σ=ζΔT\sigma=\zeta\Delta Tσ=ζΔT (seconds =ζ×=\zeta\times=ζ× seconds) makes ζ\zetaζ dimensionless, and the slope-1 fit line passes through (10−610^{-6}10−6 s, ≈2×10−11\approx2\times10^{-11}≈2×10−11 s), so ζ=σ/ΔT≈2.5×10−5\zeta=\sigma/\Delta T\approx2.5\times10^{-5}ζ=σ/ΔT≈2.5×10−5 — the printed exponent is missing its minus sign. This page uses ζ=2.5×10−5\zeta=2.5\times10^{-5}ζ=2.5×10−5 throughout. (Incidental dimension check: κ\kappaκ is annotated sec0.5\text{sec}^{0.5}sec0.5 ✓, s/s=s\text{s}/\sqrt{\text{s}}=\sqrt{\text{s}}s/s​=s​.)

documents.t: White FM (device thermal noise) and flicker FM (device 1/f) come from distinct physical mechanisms and are statistically independent; the variance of a sum of independent random variables is the sum of the variances (the cross term has zero expectation): σΔt2(Δt)=κ2 Δt⏟Step 4 (white)+ζ2 Δt2⏟Step 5 (flicker)\sigma_{\Delta t}^2(\Delta t)=\underbrace{\kappa^2\,\Delta t}_{\text{Step 4 (white)}}+\underbrace{\zeta^2\,\Delta t^2}_{\text{Step 5 (flicker)}}σΔt2​(Δt)=Step 4 (white)κ2Δt​​+Step 5 (flicker)ζ2Δt2​​ σΔt(Δt)=κ2 Δt+ζ2 Δt2 \boxed{\ \sigma_{\Delta t}(\Delta t)=\sqrt{\kappa^2\,\Delta t+\zeta^2\,\Delta t^2}\ } σΔt​(Δt)=κ2Δt+ζ2Δt2​ ​ Honesty note on provenance: this composed formula does not appear verbatim in [P2] — the paper gives the two limiting behaviors Eq.(8)/(9) and the two-segment plots of Fig.4/Fig.16; adding in quadrature is the direct corollary of "independent ⇒ variances add" ([P2] p.792 says "standard deviations add" for correlated sources and variances add for independent ones; between the two noise classes, white and 1/f, it is the latter). Units (time version): the κ,ζ\kappa,\zetaκ,ζ of this section are the time versions — [κ]=s[\kappa]=\sqrt{\text{s}}[κ]=s​ (κ2Δt: s⋅s=s2\kappa^2\Delta t:\ \text{s}\cdot\text{s}=\text{s}^2κ2Δt: s⋅s=s2 ✓), ζ\zetaζ dimensionless (ζ2Δt2=s2\zeta^2\Delta t^2=\text{s}^2ζ2Δt2=s2 ✓). The phase versions (rad bookkeeping) carry an extra ω0\omega_0ω0​ each: κϕ=ω0κ\kappa_\phi=\omega_0\kappaκϕ​=ω0​κ (Section 4.2), ζϕ=ω0ζ\zeta_\phi=\omega_0\zetaζϕ​=ω0​ζ ([ζϕ]=rad/s[\zeta_\phi]=\text{rad/s}[ζϕ​]=rad/s). The corner: set the two terms equal, κ2Δtc=ζ2Δtc2\kappa^2\Delta t_c=\zeta^2\Delta t_c^2κ2Δtc​=ζ2Δtc2​, and solve: Δtc=κ2ζ2 [s1]=s ✓\boxed{\ \Delta t_c=\frac{\kappa^2}{\zeta^2}\ }\qquad \Big[\frac{\text{s}}{1}\Big]=\text{s}\ \checkmark Δtc​=ζ2κ2​ ​[1s​]=s ✓ For Δt≪Δtc\Delta t\ll\Delta t_cΔt≪Δtc​ white noise dominates (slope 1/2); for Δt≫Δtc\Delta t\gg\Delta t_cΔt≫Δtc​ flicker dominates (slope 1); at Δtc\Delta t_cΔtc​ the composed curve sits 2\sqrt22​ (3 dB) above either asymptote — each term contributes half.

documents.t: Step 5's rigorous result (converted to time units, dividing by ω02\omega_0^2ω02​) is σΔt,flicker2(Δt)=4π2b3ω02 Δt2[32−γ−ln⁡(2πΔt fl)]⟹ζeff2(Δt)=4π2b3ω02[32−γ−ln⁡(2πΔt fl)],\sigma_{\Delta t,\text{flicker}}^2(\Delta t)=\frac{4\pi^2 b_3}{\omega_0^2}\,\Delta t^2\Big[\tfrac32-\gamma-\ln(2\pi\Delta t\,f_l)\Big] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \zeta_{\rm eff}^2(\Delta t)=\frac{4\pi^2 b_3}{\omega_0^2}\Big[\tfrac32-\gamma-\ln(2\pi\Delta t\,f_l)\Big],σΔt,flicker2​(Δt)=ω02​4π2b3​​Δt2[23​−γ−ln(2πΔtfl​)]⟹ζeff2​(Δt)=ω02​4π2b3​​[23​−γ−ln(2πΔtfl​)], i.e., ζ\zetaζ is not a constant — it shrinks slowly with Δt\Delta tΔt as log⁡\sqrt{\log}log​ (unit check: b3/ω02=[rad2Hz2]/[rad/s]2=b_3/\omega_0^2=[\text{rad}^2\text{Hz}^2]/[\text{rad/s}]^2=b3​/ω02​=[rad2Hz2]/[rad/s]2= dimensionless ✓). The local log-log slope deviates from 1 accordingly: dln⁡σdln⁡Δt=1−12[32−γ−ln⁡(2πΔtfl)].\frac{d\ln\sigma}{d\ln\Delta t}=1-\frac{1}{2\big[\tfrac32-\gamma-\ln(2\pi\Delta t f_l)\big]} .dlnΔtdlnσ​=1−2[23​−γ−ln(2πΔtfl​)]1​. The lab_24 Part 5 MC (fl=298f_l=298fl​=298 Hz, set by the simulation length) fits a slope of 0.909 in the flicker region, while the exact curve over the same window gives 0.911 — the MC's deviation from 1.0 is physics (the log correction), not noise. In real measurements flf_lfl​ is set by the measurement duration (seconds ⇒ fl∼1f_l\sim1fl​∼1 Hz), the bracket is ≈13\approx13≈13–161616, and the local slope is 0.9670.9670.967 (Δt=10−7\Delta t=10^{-7}Δt=10−7 s, fl=1f_l=1fl​=1 Hz, printed by lab_24) — which is why [P2] Fig.16 can be fitted with a clean slope-1 straight line: the log correction is invisible over hardware decade spans. The paper's constant ζ\zetaζ is the tangent approximation "bracket frozen at its corner value"; our figure (below) draws both, and they nearly coincide.

documents.t: Define the spectral corner f1/f3≡b3/b2f_{1/f^3}\equiv b_3/b_2f1/f3​≡b3​/b2​ (the offset frequency at which the 1/f31/f^31/f3 and 1/f21/f^21/f2 segments of SϕS_\phiSϕ​ are equal). Because it is a ratio within one and the same spectrum, the SSB /2/2/2 vs /4/4/4 bookkeepings cancel between numerator and denominator — a rare corner of this page where no convention needs minding. Insert Step 4's κϕ2=2π2b2\kappa_\phi^2=2\pi^2b_2κϕ2​=2π2b2​ and the ζeff\zeta_{\rm eff}ζeff​ above into Δtc=κ2/ζ2\Delta t_c=\kappa^2/\zeta^2Δtc​=κ2/ζ2 (the time and phase versions give the same ratio; ω02\omega_0^2ω02​ cancels): Δtc=2π2b24π2b3[⋅]= 12[⋅] f1/f3 ,[⋅]=32−γ−ln⁡(2πΔtcfl) (self-consistent).\Delta t_c=\frac{2\pi^2 b_2}{4\pi^2 b_3\big[\cdot\big]} =\boxed{\ \frac{1}{2\big[\cdot\big]\,f_{1/f^3}}\ },\qquad \big[\cdot\big]=\tfrac32-\gamma-\ln(2\pi\Delta t_c f_l)\ (\text{self-consistent}).Δtc​=4π2b3​[⋅]2π2b2​​= 2[⋅]f1/f3​1​ ​,[⋅]=23​−γ−ln(2πΔtc​fl​) (self-consistent). This 2 is not an SSB bookkeeping 2: the 2 in the denominator is the ratio of the two kernel-integral constants — the white-noise integral ∫sin⁡2(ax)/x2 dx=πa/2\int\sin^2(ax)/x^2\,dx=\pi a/2∫sin2(ax)/x2dx=πa/2 (Section 4.1) against the flicker log form (Step 5) — a convention-free physical constant. Order-of-magnitude intuition: [⋅]≈10[\cdot]\approx10[⋅]≈10–161616, so Δtc\Delta t_cΔtc​ is 20–30× shorter than the naive guess 1/f1/f31/f_{1/f^3}1/f1/f3​. "The spectral corner is at 1 MHz, so the time-domain knee is at 1 µs" is wrong by a decade and a half — the log bracket is the culprit. Not the same thing as [P2] Eq.(57): App. B's f1/f3=f1/f⋅32ηN(1−A)21−A+A2f_{1/f^3}=f_{1/f}\cdot\frac{3}{2\eta N}\frac{(1-A)^2}{1-A+A^2}f1/f3​=f1/f​⋅2ηN3​1−A+A2(1−A)2​ is the circuit-level mapping "device 1/f corner → spectral corner"; this section's f1/f3=b3/b2f_{1/f^3}=b_3/b_2f1/f3​=b3​/b2​ is the observational definition of the spectral corner itself. Same corner, different routes to it.

Against Fig.16, the two fit lines indeed cross near ΔT≈6×10−8\Delta T\approx6\times10^{-8}ΔT≈6×10−8 s ✓. documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: oscillator_phase · phase_vs_amplitude_noise | Next: From impulse to phase shift — the derivation What this page answers: LTI's h(t−τ)h(t-\tau)h(t−τ) versus LTV's hϕ(t,τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)hϕ​(t,τ) — which extra independent variable makes the difference? Why does the same impulse produce completely different phase effects at the waveform peak versus at a zero crossing — 000 vs −1-1−1 mrad for Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC? Why is this time-variance exactly the reason the ISF exists? Signals-and-systems courses teach us to describe linear systems with an impulse response h(t)h(t)h(t) and convolution. But that is the LTI (Linear Time-Invariant) story. The single most important insight of Hajimiri–Lee in [P1] is: An oscillator's phase response to noise is not LTI — it is LTV (Linear Time-Variant). This page spells out how LTI and LTV differ, why an oscillator is necessarily LTV, and why this difference is exactly the reason the ISF (Impulse Sensitivity Function) exists. Physical intuition (conclusion first): an LTI system "does not care what time it is" — the same impulse applied today or tomorrow produces exactly the same response shape, merely shifted in time. An oscillator is not like that: because its state keeps rotating around the limit cycle, the same noise current injected at the peak versus at a zero crossing produces completely different phase shifts. The system's sensitivity to the input itself varies periodically with time (with the injection phase) — this is "periodically time-varying sensitivity", and packaging it into a 2π2\pi2π-periodic, dimensionless function gives the ISF Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ).
documents.s: LTI vs LTV — an Oscillator's Noise Sensitivity Is Periodically Time-Varying

documents.t: A linear time-invariant system has two properties: linearity (superposition holds) and time invariance (delay the input by Δ\DeltaΔ and the output is simply delayed by Δ\DeltaΔ, shape unchanged). The consequence of time invariance is that the impulse response depends only on the time difference t−τt-\taut−τ: y(t)=∫−∞∞h(t−τ) x(τ) dτ(LTI convolution).y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h(t-\tau)\,x(\tau)\,d\tau\qquad\text{(LTI convolution)}.y(t)=∫−∞∞​h(t−τ)x(τ)dτ(LTI convolution). Why only t−τt-\taut−τ: inject a unit impulse at τ1\tau_1τ1​ and you get h(t−τ1)h(t-\tau_1)h(t−τ1​); inject at τ2\tau_2τ2​ and you get h(t−τ2)h(t-\tau_2)h(t−τ2​) — the same shape, merely shifted. The system does not care about "the absolute time τ\tauτ", only about "how long ago". Unit check: the dimension of the convolution kernel hhh is set by output/input; the point here is "shape invariance", not the numerical value. This is the undergraduate story: RLC filters, small-signal amplifier equivalents — as long as the operating point is fixed, they are LTI.
documents.s: 1. Review: the LTI h(t−τ)h(t-\tau)h(t−τ)

documents.t: An oscillator has no fixed operating point — its state keeps moving along the limit cycle (see oscillator_phase). So "how sensitive the system is to a perturbation right now" changes with the state (that is, with the injection phase ω0τ\omega_0\tauω0​τ). The impulse response therefore depends on two times at once: hϕ(t,τ)≠hϕ(t−τ) (LTV: depends on the absolute injection time τ, not only t−τ).\boxed{\;h_\phi(t,\tau)\neq h_\phi(t-\tau)\;}\qquad\text{(LTV: depends on the absolute injection time }\tau\text{, not only }t-\tau\text{)}.hϕ​(t,τ)=hϕ​(t−τ)​(LTV: depends on the absolute injection time τ, not only t−τ). The excess-phase impulse response [P1] writes down is exactly of this form ([P1] Eq.(10), p.182): hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ).h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau).hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ). Unpacking it, the two independent variables of the LTV response map neatly onto the two factors, each with a clear meaning: Step height Γ(ω0τ)qmax\dfrac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​: depends only on the injection phase ω0τ\omega_0\tauω0​τ. This is the "time-varying" part — the same-size impulse jumps by a different height at a different injection phase. Time shape u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ): a unit step, depending only on t−τt-\taut−τ. It encodes "once a phase shift occurs it is retained permanently" (phase has no restoring force; see phase_vs_amplitude_noise). Unit check / dimension: Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless, qmaxq_{max}qmax​ has units of C, uuu is dimensionless, so hϕh_\phihϕ​ has units of C−1\mathrm{C^{-1}}C−1; convolving with a current (A), ∫hϕ i dτ\int h_\phi\,i\,d\tau∫hϕ​idτ gives C−1⋅A⋅s=C−1⋅C=\mathrm{C^{-1}\cdot A\cdot s}=\mathrm{C^{-1}\cdot C}=C−1⋅A⋅s=C−1⋅C= dimensionless = rad ✓. Why Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) and not Γ(τ)\Gamma(\tau)Γ(τ): the sensitivity varies periodically with the "waveform phase", with period 2π2\pi2π (every lap around the limit cycle returns to the same sensitivity). So the argument of Γ\GammaΓ is the phase ω0τ\omega_0\tauω0​τ, and Γ\GammaΓ is a 2π2\pi2π-periodic function — this is "periodically time-varying sensitivity".

documents.t: Plug the step height of Step 2 into the operational ISF definition (the impulse limit of [P1] Eq.(11)): Δϕ(τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax Δq.\Delta\phi(\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q.Δϕ(τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​Δq. Fix Δq\Delta qΔq and sweep the injection phase θ=ω0τ\theta=\omega_0\tauθ=ω0​τ: Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ rises and falls following the shape of Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ). For an ideal LC, Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ: Injection phase θ\thetaθ Waveform position Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ Result 000 Peak (0 slope) 000 Δϕ=0\Delta\phi=0Δϕ=0, pure amplitude change π/2\pi/2π/2 Falling zero crossing (most negative slope) −1-1−1 ∣Δϕ∣\vert \Delta\phi\vert ∣Δϕ∣ maximum π\piπ Trough (0 slope) 000 Δϕ=0\Delta\phi=0Δϕ=0, pure amplitude change 3π/23\pi/23π/2 Rising zero crossing (most positive slope) +1+1+1 ∣Δϕ∣\vert \Delta\phi\vert ∣Δϕ∣ maximum, opposite sign Physical reason (continuing Step 4 of oscillator_phase): the size of the phase shift is set by the component of the voltage jump projected onto the tangential direction of the limit cycle. At a zero crossing the state velocity (tangent) lies exactly along the voltage axis, so a fixed ΔV\Delta VΔV turns almost entirely into tangential displacement → maximum Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ; at the peak the tangent is perpendicular to the voltage axis, so ΔV\Delta VΔV is almost entirely radial (pure amplitude) → Δϕ≈0\Delta\phi\approx 0Δϕ≈0. The tangential component is ∝sin⁡θ\propto\sin\theta∝sinθ, hence Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ for a sinusoid. This is the fingerprint of LTV: if the oscillator were LTI, Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ would be independent of τ\tauτ (only t−τt-\taut−τ would matter) — but in reality Δϕ(τ)\Delta\phi(\tau)Δϕ(τ) rises and falls periodically. The sensitivity itself varies with time = time-variant. Putting LTI and LTV side by side makes it clearest: LTI LTV (oscillator phase) Impulse response h(t−τ)h(t-\tau)h(t−τ) (time difference only) hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmaxu(t−τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)=\dfrac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}u(t-\tau)hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ) Changing the injection time τ\tauτ Shape unchanged, only shifted Step height changes with ω0τ\omega_0\tauω0​τ Sensitivity Independent of absolute time 2π2\pi2π-periodically time-varying (= ISF) Convolution ∫h(t−τ)x dτ\int h(t-\tau)x\,d\tau∫h(t−τ)xdτ 1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ)in(τ) dτ\dfrac{1}{q_{max}}\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)i_n(\tau)\,d\tauqmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ The LTV convolution in the bottom-right cell is [P1] Eq.(11), p.182 — the next chapter's convolution_derivation uses it to superpose an arbitrary noise current into ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t).

documents.t: Historically, treating oscillator noise as LTI (e.g., simply multiplying the noise by the tank transfer function) misses two things that only LTV/ISF can capture: Frequency translation: because the sensitivity Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) is itself periodic (containing harmonics of ω0\omega_0ω0​), it mixes noise near 0, ω0, 2ω0,…0,\,\omega_0,\,2\omega_0,\dots0,ω0​,2ω0​,… down next to the carrier. LTI does not mix, and therefore cannot explain why device noise both at DC and at nω0n\omega_0nω0​ shows up in close-in phase noise. This is described by the Fourier coefficients cnc_ncn​ of the ISF ([P1] Eq.(12)–(13), p.183). 1/f1/f1/f upconversion into 1/f31/f^31/f3: the device's low-frequency 1/f1/f1/f noise reaches the vicinity of the carrier through the ISF's DC coefficient c0c_0c0​ ([P1] Eq.(23)); a purely LTI view cannot explain it. Waveform symmetry → small c0c_0c0​ → suppressed 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ([P1] Eq.(24)). In other words, LTV is not a gratuitous complication — the oscillator is physically time-varying; forcing an LTI model misses mixing and 1/f1/f1/f upconversion, two real phenomena, already at the qualitative level.
