documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: Notation · Learning path | Next: phase_vs_amplitude_noise What this page answers: Why is "phase" a tangential coordinate on the limit cycle, rather than corresponding to some absolute time reference? Why is a radial (amplitude) deviation pulled back while a tangential (phase) deviation is left permanently? How does this geometric picture turn directly into phase noise and timing jitter? Before talking about the ISF (Impulse Sensitivity Function), one thing must be made absolutely clear: what physical quantity an oscillator's "phase" actually is, how it differs from "amplitude", and why one persists forever while the other is automatically corrected. This page answers that question. It is the foundation of the entire ISF theory — the later derivation from impulse to phase shift stands entirely on the geometric intuition built here. Physical intuition (conclusion first): draw the oscillator's state in a 2-D plane; in steady state it circles endlessly along a closed loop (the limit cycle). A noise impulse pushes the state point off this loop. The displacement can be split into two directions: along the tangent of the loop = a phase perturbation, perpendicular to the loop, pointing toward the center (radial) = an amplitude perturbation. The oscillator has an "amplitude restoring force" that slowly pulls radial deviations back onto the loop; but no force whatsoever corrects a deviation along the tangent, because the oscillator simply has no absolute reference for "what time it is". So phase errors accumulate, kick after kick — this is the root of phase noise and timing jitter.
documents.s: What Is Oscillator Phase?

documents.t: Any oscillator can be described completely by a few "state variables". The archetypal LC oscillator has two energy-storage elements: a capacitor (stores voltage) and an inductor (stores current), so its state is a 2-D vector z(t)=(x(t), y(t)),\mathbf{z}(t)=\big(x(t),\,y(t)\big),z(t)=(x(t),y(t)), where we may take xxx = the capacitor voltage (normalized) and yyy = a quantity proportional to the inductor current (normalized). As time evolves, z(t)\mathbf{z}(t)z(t) traces a curve in this "state plane", called the state trajectory. Physics used: energy sloshes back and forth between the capacitor and the inductor — when the voltage is maximal the current is zero (all energy in the capacitor); when the voltage is zero the current is maximal (all energy in the inductor). This is precisely the picture of a point going around a circle in the xxx–yyy plane. Unit check: both axes are first normalized to be dimensionless (each divided by its maximum swing); the radius r=x2+y2r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}r=x2+y2​ represents "the total oscillation energy", and the phase angle θ=arctan⁡(y/x)\theta=\arctan(y/x)θ=arctan(y/x) represents "where in the rotation we are right now". Why 2-D: as taught in signals-and-systems, the free response of a second-order system is a trajectory in the plane. The ideal lossless LC is marginally stable, and its trajectory is a circle of fixed radius. This site's toy model (oscillator_models.py, used by lab_01) generates this trajectory from a normalized 2-D equation (a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level): dxdt=−ω0 y+μ (1−r2) x,dydt= ω0 x+μ (1−r2) y,r2=x2+y2.\begin{aligned} \frac{dx}{dt}&=-\omega_0\,y+\mu\,(1-r^2)\,x,\\ \frac{dy}{dt}&=\ \ \omega_0\,x+\mu\,(1-r^2)\,y,\qquad r^2=x^2+y^2. \end{aligned}dtdx​dtdy​​=−ω0​y+μ(1−r2)x,= ω0​x+μ(1−r2)y,r2=x2+y2.​ The first term ±ω0\pm\omega_0±ω0​ is pure rotation (ideal LC); the second term μ(1−r2)\mu(1-r^2)μ(1−r2) is a Van der Pol-style amplitude restoring term: when r>1r>1r>1 it removes energy, when r<1r<1r<1 it supplies energy, pushing the trajectory back to the unit circle. μ=0\mu=0μ=0 degenerates to the lossless LC (pure rotation); μ>0\mu>0μ>0 models the AGC/device nonlinearity that every real oscillator must have.
documents.s: Step 1: describing an oscillator with a state trajectory

documents.t: When μ>0\mu>0μ>0, no matter where the trajectory starts (say from radius 1.71.71.7), it eventually converges to the same closed curve — this attractor is the limit cycle: Definition: a limit cycle is an isolated, periodic, closed trajectory in the phase plane; neighboring trajectories are attracted to it (a stable limit cycle) or repelled by it. Steady-state oscillation = circling the limit cycle at constant speed, with period T=1/f0T=1/f_0T=1/f0​. Why every oscillator must have a limit cycle: stable, fixed-amplitude oscillation requires a mechanism that locks the amplitude at some value. A linear system cannot do that (it either decays or diverges), so every real oscillator is nonlinear — and that very nonlinearity is what creates the limit cycle. This point comes back in LTI vs LTV. Unit check: one lap advances the phase by 2π2\pi2π rad and takes time TTT, so the angular velocity is ω0=2π/T=2πf0\omega_0=2\pi/T=2\pi f_0ω0​=2π/T=2πf0​ rad/s ✓. The figure below is the limit cycle simulated with the toy model: the black dashed line is the steady-state unit circle, and the blue curve starts outside the loop (radius 1.71.71.7) and is pulled back onto it, lap by lap, by the amplitude restoring term. The two perturbation directions at the operating point are marked on the figure. Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Labels/legend/title read: 穩態軌跡 = steady-state trajectory, "amplitude 擾動後鬆弛回 limit cycle" = relaxes back to the limit cycle after an amplitude perturbation, "phase 擾動 Δφ（切線方向，持續累積）" = phase perturbation Δφ (tangential direction, accumulates persistently), "amplitude 擾動 ΔA（徑向，會被拉回）" = amplitude perturbation ΔA (radial, pulled back), 電容電壓 = capacitor voltage, 電感電流 = inductor current, "擾動" in the title = perturbation. How to read this figure: Black dashed circle = the limit cycle (steady-state trajectory). The state point rotates counterclockwise along it at constant angular velocity ω0\omega_0ω0​. Green arrow (tangential direction) = phase perturbation Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ: motion along the loop, equivalent to "arriving earlier or later at a given phase". No restoring force — it keeps accumulating. Red arrow (radial direction) = amplitude perturbation ΔA\Delta AΔA: pushes the state point off (or into) the loop; the amplitude restoring term slowly pulls it back. The blue curve demonstrates the fate of a radial perturbation: starting from radius 1.7, it relaxes back to the unit circle within a few laps — the radial information is "forgotten". Corresponding formula: project the perturbation vector δz\delta\mathbf{z}δz onto the limit cycle's tangential unit vector t^\hat{\mathbf{t}}t^ (the phase direction) and radial unit vector r^\hat{\mathbf{r}}r^ (the amplitude direction) at that point: δz=(δz⋅t^)⏟→ Δϕt^+(δz⋅r^)⏟→ ΔAr^.\delta\mathbf{z}=\underbrace{(\delta\mathbf{z}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{t}})}_{\to\ \Delta\phi}\hat{\mathbf{t}}+\underbrace{(\delta\mathbf{z}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{r}})}_{\to\ \Delta A}\hat{\mathbf{r}}.δz=→ Δϕ(δz⋅t^)​​t^+→ ΔA(δz⋅r^)​​r^. The tangential component determines the phase shift; the radial component determines the amplitude shift. The ISF is precisely the ratio function "how much of a unit injected charge ends up in the tangential component at a given injection phase" (formal definition in the impulse-to-phase-shift derivation).
documents.s: Step 2: what a limit cycle is

documents.t: This is the most crucial — and most often overlooked — sentence in the whole theory: The differential equations of an autonomous oscillator contain no explicit time ttt. That is, the equations only know "the state z\mathbf{z}z", not "what time it is". The mathematical consequence: if z(t)\mathbf{z}(t)z(t) is a solution, then z(t−Δτ)\mathbf{z}(t-\Delta\tau)z(t−Δτ), time-shifted by any constant Δτ\Delta\tauΔτ, is also a perfectly valid solution with the same energy and the same waveform. Math used: an autonomous system z˙=F(z)\dot{\mathbf{z}}=F(\mathbf{z})z˙=F(z) is invariant under time translation (time-translation invariance). Displacement along the limit cycle corresponds exactly to this degree of freedom. Physical meaning: no external clock tells the oscillator "which phase it should be at". Sliding along the loop (= changing phase) costs no energy and is opposed by no restoring force. This is why phase is a marginally stable (neutrally stable) degree of freedom — corresponding to the system having one zero eigenvalue (Floquet exponent = 0). Contrast with amplitude: the direction perpendicular to the loop (amplitude) corresponds to a negative eigenvalue, so perturbations decay exponentially back onto the loop. (Rigorous Floquet/PPV theory is not among the 5 downloaded PDFs — it is external literature, e.g. Demir et al.; this site uses only the geometric intuition. See the supplementary note in effective_isf.) One-sentence summary: phase is the only state direction of an oscillator with no restoring force, so noise affects phase permanently and cumulatively, whereas its effect on amplitude is temporary and gets absorbed.
documents.s: Step 3: why an oscillator has no absolute time reference

documents.t: Since a perturbation decomposes into tangential and radial parts, where in the waveform you kick it determines the tangential/radial split. Take the pure sinusoid V(t)=cos⁡(ω0t)V(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t)V(t)=cos(ω0​t): At the peak, θ=0\theta=0θ=0: the state point sits at the far right of the xxx axis, and the state velocity (tangent) is purely along yyy. A voltage jump along xxx is almost entirely radial — it changes only the amplitude, barely the phase. Corresponds to Γ≈0\Gamma\approx 0Γ≈0. At the zero crossing, θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2: the state point sits at the top of the yyy axis, and the tangent is purely along xxx. The same voltage jump along xxx is almost entirely tangential — it changes only the phase, barely the amplitude. Corresponds to maximum ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣. The figure below draws this on the time-domain waveform: Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Annotations/title read: "impulse @ peak → 只有 ΔA, 無 Δφ (Γ≈0)" = only ΔA, no Δφ (Γ≈0), "impulse @ zero crossing → 最大 Δφ, 無 ΔA (|Γ| 最大)" = maximum Δφ, no ΔA (|Γ| is maximum), title "同樣大小的 impulse，注入相位不同 → 效果完全不同 (LTV 本質)" = same-size impulses injected at different phases → completely different effects (the essence of LTV). How to read this figure: The blue curve V(t)=cos⁡(2πf0t)V(t)=\cos(2\pi f_0 t)V(t)=cos(2πf0​t) is the steady-state waveform. Red marker (peak): inject the impulse here → only ΔA\Delta AΔA, almost no Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ (Γ≈0\Gamma\approx 0Γ≈0). Green marker (zero crossing, where the slope is largest): inject the impulse here → maximum Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ, almost no ΔA\Delta AΔA (maximum ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣). Conclusion: phase sensitivity correlates strongly with "the waveform's instantaneous slope" — where the slope is large, the same voltage jump is equivalent to a larger time (phase) displacement. This is the geometric reason the ISF of an ideal LC comes out as Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ (a sinusoid has maximum slope at the zero crossings and zero slope at the peaks). Corresponding formula (the operational ISF definition, [P1] Eq.(10)–(11), p.182; full derivation in the next chapter): Δϕ=Γ(ω0τ)qmax Δq,ΓLC(θ)=−sin⁡θ.\Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q,\qquad \Gamma_{LC}(\theta)=-\sin\theta.Δϕ=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​Δq,ΓLC​(θ)=−sinθ. The fact "same impulse, different phase → different effect" goes by the formal name periodically time-varying sensitivity, and it is the core reason [P1] treats the oscillator as an LTV (linear time-variant) system (see LTI vs LTV).

documents.t: Chaining the four steps together, look at the long-term consequence of noise kicking continuously: Amplitude error: each time noise pushes the state slightly off the loop (radially), the amplitude restoring term pulls it back within a few time constants. Its effect on the output is bounded and decaying — which is why amplitude noise is usually suppressed naturally (see phase_vs_amplitude_noise). Phase error: each time noise pushes the state slightly along the loop (tangentially), there is no restoring force, and that Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ stays forever. The next noise kick adds another Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ… the phase performs a random walk. Written in continuous form, this random walk is the next chapter's LTV convolution ([P1] Eq.(11), p.182): ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ.\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau.ϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ. The upper integration limit is ttt (the system has memory), so the phase contributions of all past noise add up — this is the mathematical reason phase error accumulates, and the essence of phase noise/jitter.
documents.s: Step 5: amplitude error is pulled back, phase error accumulates → phase noise / jitter

documents.t: The same thing (the random wobble of phase) has two views, differing only by the conversion constant 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​: Phase noise: the frequency-domain view. Plot the power spectrum of the phase fluctuation: Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) (rad²/Hz), or the engineering-standard single-sideband (SSB) L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) (dBc/Hz). The random walk of accumulated phase appears in the frequency domain as a 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt close to the carrier. Timing jitter: the time-domain view. Convert the phase error into "the timing error of an edge crossing zero", using Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0)\Delta t=\Delta\phi/(2\pi f_0)Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0​). Conversion formulas (Eq.17 and Eq.19, Section 3 of the spec): Δt=Δϕ2πf0,σt=σϕ2πf0=12πf0∫f1f2Sϕ(f) df.\Delta t=\frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi f_0},\qquad \sigma_t=\frac{\sigma_\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{1}{2\pi f_0}\sqrt{\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_\phi(f)\,df}.Δt=2πf0​Δϕ​,σt​=2πf0​σϕ​​=2πf0​1​∫f1​f2​​Sϕ​(f)df​. Dimension check: [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] ✓ (note that 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ is in rad/s, not Hz). Random-walk signature: a phase random walk corresponds in the time domain to accumulated jitter σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ ([P2] Eq.(8), p.792; κ from Eq.(12), p.793) — the longer the measurement interval, the larger the rms of the accumulated error, exactly the fingerprint of "no absolute time reference". See psd_phase_noise_jitter.

documents.t: Using the canonical numbers of Section 8 of the spec, let us turn the geometry above into concrete figures. Example A: qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC, Γ=0.5\Gamma=0.5Γ=0.5, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz. A charge impulse of Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC injected at a phase where Γ=0.5\Gamma=0.5Γ=0.5 (between the peak and the zero crossing): Δϕ=Γ Δqqmax=0.5×(1×10−15 C)1×10−12 C=5×10−4 rad (≈0.0286∘),\Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma\,\Delta q}{q_{max}}=\frac{0.5\times(1\times10^{-15}\,\text{C})}{1\times10^{-12}\,\text{C}}=5\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}\;(\approx0.0286^\circ),Δϕ=qmax​ΓΔq​=1×10−12C0.5×(1×10−15C)​=5×10−4 rad(≈0.0286∘), converted into a timing error: Δt=Δϕ2πf0=5×10−4 rad2π×5×109 Hz≈1.59×10−14 s=15.9 fs.\Delta t=\frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{5\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{9}\ \text{Hz}}\approx1.59\times10^{-14}\ \text{s}=15.9\ \text{fs}.Δt=2πf0​Δϕ​=2π×5×109 Hz5×10−4 rad​≈1.59×10−14 s=15.9 fs. Feel for the numbers: at 5 GHz (period 200 ps), a 1 fC charge (about 6240 electrons) at a moderately sensitive phase causes only ~16 fs of timing error. Each kick is tiny, but phase has no restoring force, so as noise keeps kicking, the error integrates and accumulates — exactly the random walk of Step 5. If the same 1 fC lands on the peak (Γ≈0\Gamma\approx 0Γ≈0): Δϕ≈0\Delta\phi\approx 0Δϕ≈0, Δt≈0\Delta t\approx 0Δt≈0 — the energy goes almost entirely into amplitude and is absorbed by the restoring term within a few time constants, with no permanent effect on phase.

documents.t: The oscillator state, drawn in a 2-D plane, circles the limit cycle at constant speed; phase = the angular position along the loop. An autonomous oscillator has no absolute time reference (no explicit ttt in the equations) → sliding along the loop costs no energy and is opposed by no restoring force. Perturbation decomposition: tangential = phase perturbation (accumulates permanently), radial = amplitude perturbation (pulled back by the restoring force). The same impulse at the peak (Γ≈0\Gamma\approx 0Γ≈0) vs at the zero crossing (maximum ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣) has drastically different effects → periodically time-varying sensitivity → the ISF. The accumulated phase random walk is, in the frequency domain, phase noise L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf); in the time domain, timing jitter σt=σϕ/(2πf0)\sigma_t=\sigma_\phi/(2\pi f_0)σt​=σϕ​/(2πf0​). Example A: 1 fC @ Γ=0.5\Gamma=0.5Γ=0.5, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, 5 GHz → Δϕ=5×10−4\Delta\phi=5\times10^{-4}Δϕ=5×10−4 rad → 15.9 fs. Sources: [P1] Fig. 4, Sec. III-A; toy model from lab_01.

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: oscillator_phase · Unified notation table | Next: lti_vs_ltv The previous page, oscillator_phase, showed geometrically that a noise perturbation to an oscillator decomposes into a tangential (phase) component and a radial (amplitude) component. This page answers the two most practical engineering questions: Why do we worry almost exclusively about phase noise, and hardly at all about amplitude noise? Can the fact that "amplitude perturbations get pulled back" be written as a sensitivity function, just like the ISF? The key term in the answer is the APF (Amplitude Perturbation Function) — introduced by [P4] as the amplitude-domain counterpart of the ISF. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the limit cycle's "stability" is completely different in the two directions. The radial (amplitude) direction has a restoring force (negative Floquet exponent): perturbations decay exponentially back onto the cycle, so the oscillator suppresses amplitude noise by itself. The tangential (phase) direction has no restoring force (zero Floquet exponent): perturbations accumulate permanently, so phase noise random-walks without bound. For one and the same noise current, the share injected into phase stays, and the share injected into amplitude gets eaten — the ISF Γ\GammaΓ describes "how much goes into phase", the APF Δ\DeltaΔ describes "how much goes into amplitude".
documents.s: Why phase noise matters and why amplitude noise is suppressed

documents.t: Write the oscillator output in the standard decomposition ([P1] Eq.(1), p.180): Vout(t)=A(t) f ⁣(ω0t+ϕ(t)).V_{out}(t)=A(t)\,f\!\big(\omega_0 t+\phi(t)\big).Vout​(t)=A(t)f(ω0​t+ϕ(t)). Here A(t)A(t)A(t) is the instantaneous amplitude, ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) is the excess phase (the deviation beyond the ideal phase), and fff is the periodic steady-state waveform. The noise hides inside the two modulations A(t)A(t)A(t) and ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t). Their impact on "clock quality" is asymmetric: Phase noise turns directly into timing jitter: clocked circuits care about "when the edge crosses the threshold". That instant is set by phase: Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0)\Delta t=\Delta\phi/(2\pi f_0)Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0​). Phase jitter = edge timing jitter = SerDes eye closure and mis-timed sampling. Phase errors accumulate, with no upper bound: since phase has no restoring force (Step 3 of the previous page), ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) performs a random walk and its variance grows with time. In the frequency domain this shows up as the tall 1/f21/f^21/f2 (and, closer in, 1/f31/f^31/f3) skirts beside the carrier. This is the fundamental reason the oscillator spectrum is not an ideal delta but has finite width. Amplitude errors are bounded, and mostly never reach the threshold decision: near the threshold, amplitude effects mostly convert back into timing error (see AM–PM below), but pure amplitude fluctuations themselves are squeezed out by the restoring force, and receivers commonly use limiters/comparators that are insensitive to amplitude. Phase noise has two more customers on the receiver side: the local oscillator's (LO's) L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) skirt "sweeps" a strong nearby interferer (a blocker) down into the IF noise floor (reciprocal mixing); and in a digital modulation system, σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ integrated over the relevant frequency span is directly the EVM (error vector magnitude) read off the constellation diagram. These two effects pull RF-receiver design — beyond SerDes/clocking — into the same L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) and σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ language — see the short subsection at the end of this section. In one sentence: for communication and clocking systems, timing jitter = a phase matter. That is why the entire Hajimiri–Lee theory bets everything on ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) and first "legitimately throws away" the amplitude degree of freedom — the next section explains why that is allowed.
documents.s: 1. Why phase noise matters

documents.t: External-literature disclosure: the reciprocal-mixing bookkeeping and the EVM relation in this subsection are standard textbook results for RF receivers and digital modulation (external literature, not one of the site's 5 PDFs) — they do not come from [P1]–[P4]. Cite B. Razavi, RF Microelectronics, 2nd ed., Prentice Hall, 2012 (the reciprocal-mixing section; exact section number TBD). EVM ≈σϕ\approx\sigma_\phi≈σϕ​ (small-angle, outside the carrier-recovery loop bandwidth) is a standard OFDM/QAM result (exact textbook passage TBD). The L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) and σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ machinery derived earlier on this site (see white_noise_to_phase_noise, psd_phase_noise_jitter) is reused here unchanged — only the "customer" changes. The first bullet above — "phase jitter = edge timing jitter" — is the time-domain customer (SerDes, ADC). But the same L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf), σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ numbers have two equally important customers on the receiver / frequency-domain side: (a) Reciprocal mixing — the LO's skirt sweeps a nearby interferer into the band. A mixer multiplies the RF signal by the LO: vRF(t)cos⁡(ωLOt+ϕn(t))v_{RF}(t)\cos(\omega_{LO}t+\phi_n(t))vRF​(t)cos(ωLO​t+ϕn​(t)). If an adjacent channel carries a strong interferer (a blocker), it too gets down-converted by the same LO; but the LO is not an ideal delta function — it carries a finite-width L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) skirt — so the small slice of that skirt sitting an offset Δf\Delta fΔf away from the blocker mixes the blocker straight into the IF noise floor, even though the blocker itself was never on the wanted channel. If L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) is roughly flat over the bandwidth BBB, the noise power referred to the input is Pn,in(Δf)=Pblocker+L(Δf)+10log⁡10(B)[dBm],P_{n,in}(\Delta f)=P_{blocker}+\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)+10\log_{10}(B)\qquad[\mathrm{dBm}],Pn,in​(Δf)=Pblocker​+L(Δf)+10log10​(B)[dBm], (where PblockerP_{blocker}Pblocker​, Pn,inP_{n,in}Pn,in​ are in dBm, L\mathcal{L}L is in dBc/Hz, and BBB is in Hz; 10log⁡10B10\log_{10}B10log10​B turns the "per-Hz density" into "total power within that bandwidth" — dBc/Hz +++ dB(Hz) === dBc, then stacked on the blocker's dBm reference). To keep this floor from eating the receiver's SNR budget requires L(Δf) ≤ Psig−Pblocker−SNRmin−10log⁡10(B)[dBc/Hz],\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\ \le\ P_{sig}-P_{blocker}-\mathrm{SNR}_{min}-10\log_{10}(B)\qquad[\mathrm{dBc/Hz}],L(Δf) ≤ Psig​−Pblocker​−SNRmin​−10log10​(B)[dBc/Hz], which turns a blocker spec (from the system or a regulatory mask) directly into a hard requirement on LO phase noise — one of the real design drivers for pushing down far-out L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) in an RF synthesizer (the other being this site's main-line 1/f² skirt that sets close-in phase noise). (b) EVM — reading integrated σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ straight off the constellation as an error vector. In QAM/OFDM-style digital modulation, each symbol is a point on the constellation; LO phase noise makes the actual down-conversion phase deviate from the ideal by ϕn(t)\phi_n(t)ϕn​(t), rotating the whole constellation by a small angle. Under the small-angle approximation, the resulting error vector length equals the rotation angle itself (arc length ≈\approx≈ angle for small angles), and only the portion outside the carrier-recovery loop's bandwidth counts — the carrier-recovery loop locks out the low-frequency phase drift it can track, and what is left over becomes random residual error: EVMrms ≈ σϕ = 2∫f1f2L(f) df[rad],EVM[dB]=20log⁡10σϕ.\mathrm{EVM}_{rms}\ \approx\ \sigma_\phi\ =\ \sqrt{2\int_{f_1}^{f_2}\mathcal{L}(f)\,df}\qquad[\mathrm{rad}],\qquad \mathrm{EVM}[\mathrm{dB}]=20\log_{10}\sigma_\phi.EVMrms​ ≈ σϕ​ = 2∫f1​f2​​L(f)df​[rad],EVM[dB]=20log10​σϕ​. The σϕ2=2∫L df\sigma_\phi^2=2\int\mathcal{L}\,dfσϕ2​=2∫Ldf here is the exact same integral as this site's rms jitter integration (Example C: Sϕ=2LS_\phi=2\mathcal{L}Sϕ​=2L, σϕ2=∫Sϕ df\sigma_\phi^2=\int S_\phi\,dfσϕ2​=∫Sϕ​df) — the only difference is that the last step does not divide by 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ to get a time; it stays in radians and is read as EVM directly. Convention flag (SSB/4 vs. time-domain/2, ±3\pm3±3 dB): exactly as in white_noise_to_phase_noise — if L\mathcal{L}L is taken as the canonical −148-148−148 dBc/Hz (SSB /4 convention) instead of −145-145−145 dBc/Hz (time-domain /2 convention), the integrated σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​ differs by 2×\times×, σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ by 2\sqrt22​, and EVM[dB] by 20log⁡102≈3.020\log_{10}\sqrt2\approx3.020log10​2​≈3.0 dB — pick one convention and stay consistent through the whole chain. This page and the worked examples below use the SSB /4 anchor throughout: −148-148−148 dBc/Hz for the canonical case, −100-100−100 dBc/Hz for Example C. Applicability: small angle (σϕ≪1\sigma_\phi\ll1σϕ​≪1 rad), counting only the part outside the carrier-recovery loop bandwidth, and treating phase noise as the sole contributor to EVM (real systems also have I/Q imbalance, nonlinearity, quantization, etc., which combine by RSS — not expanded here). Worked (reciprocal mixing, continuing Example C's L(1 MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\,\mathrm{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz): a −40-40−40 dBm blocker at 1 MHz offset, IF bandwidth B=1B=1B=1 MHz: Pn,in=−40+(−100)+10log⁡10(106)=−40−100+60=−80 dBm.P_{n,in}=-40+(-100)+10\log_{10}(10^6)=-40-100+60=-80\ \mathrm{dBm}.Pn,in​=−40+(−100)+10log10​(106)=−40−100+60=−80 dBm. If the wanted signal itself is only −90-90−90 dBm, it sits 10 dB below this floor — reciprocal mixing buries the signal under the noise floor and the receiver cannot recover it. Turning the inequality around: for SNRmin=10\mathrm{SNR}_{min}=10SNRmin​=10 dB, the required LO cleanliness is L(Δf)≤−90−(−40)−10−60=−120\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\le-90-(-40)-10-60=-120L(Δf)≤−90−(−40)−10−60=−120 dBc/Hz — 20 dB below the −100-100−100 dBc/Hz used in Example C. The canonical Example B LO (L(1 MHz)=−148\mathcal{L}(1\,\mathrm{MHz})=-148L(1MHz)=−148 dBc/Hz, SSB /4 anchor) against a 0 dBm blocker instead gives Pn,in=0−148+60=−88P_{n,in}=0-148+60=-88Pn,in​=0−148+60=−88 dBm — same LO, a stronger blocker raises the floor, but the coefficients and sign are unchanged. Worked (EVM, continuing Example C's σϕ=14.07\sigma_\phi=14.07σϕ​=14.07 mrad from the 1–100 MHz integral): EVMrms≈σϕ=1.407×10−2 rad=1.41%,EVM[dB]=20log⁡10(1.407×10−2)=−37.0 dB.\mathrm{EVM}_{rms}\approx\sigma_\phi=1.407\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}=1.41\%,\qquad \mathrm{EVM}[\mathrm{dB}]=20\log_{10}(1.407\times10^{-2})=-37.0\ \mathrm{dB}.EVMrms​≈σϕ​=1.407×10−2 rad=1.41%,EVM[dB]=20log10​(1.407×10−2)=−37.0 dB. This −37.0-37.0−37.0 dB and the SNRjitter=37.0\mathrm{SNR}_{jitter}=37.0SNRjitter​=37.0 dB on the adc_aperture_jitter page are two readings of the same number — the same σϕ=14.07\sigma_\phi=14.07σϕ​=14.07 mrad, just applied to sampling an fin=f0f_{in}=f_0fin​=f0​ sinusoid rather than a modulated constellation. The difference is only sign convention: EVM is conventionally negative (an error fraction relative to the signal — cleaner signal, more negative EVM), SNR is positive; the cross-link on that page is added by R11-30. A line-by-line check (self-contained, # -> marks actual script output; uses leeson_one_over_f2 and integrate_rms_jitter from simulations/common/noise_utils.py, the same functions behind Example C / lab_08): import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import leeson_one_over_f2, integrate_rms_jitter f0 = 5e9 # [Hz] canonical # Example C: 1/f^2 skirt anchored at L(1 MHz) = -100 dBc/Hz, integrated 1-100 MHz f = np.logspace(np.log10(1e6), np.log10(100e6), 200_000) L = leeson_one_over_f2(f, -100.0, 1e6) sigma_t, sigma_phi = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L, f0, 1e6, 100e6) print(round(sigma_phi * 1e3, 2)) # -> 14.07 (mrad, matches Example C) print(round(sigma_t * 1e15, 1)) # -> 447.9 (fs, matches Example C) # EVM evm_rms = sigma_phi # small angle: EVM_rms ~= sigma_phi [rad] evm_pct = evm_rms * 100 evm_db = 20 * np.log10(evm_rms) print(round(evm_pct, 2)) # -> 1.41 print(round(evm_db, 1)) # -> -37.0 # reciprocal mixing floor: worked example (blocker -40 dBm, L(1MHz)=-100 dBc/Hz, B=1MHz) P_blocker, L_1MHz, B = -40.0, -100.0, 1e6 floor_example = P_blocker + L_1MHz + 10 * np.log10(B) print(round(floor_example, 1)) # -> -80.0 (dBm) # canonical example B: blocker 0 dBm, L(1MHz) = -148 dBc/Hz (SSB /4 anchor) floor_canonical = 0.0 + (-148.0) + 10 * np.log10(B) print(round(floor_canonical, 1)) # -> -88.0 (dBm) # signal -90 dBm vs floor_example: how far below the floor P_sig = -90.0 print(round(P_sig - floor_example, 1)) # -> -10.0 (dB, signal is 10 dB below the floor) # required L for SNR_min = 10 dB given the same blocker/signal/B SNR_min = 10.0 required_L = P_sig - P_blocker - SNR_min - 10 * np.log10(B) print(round(required_L, 1)) # -> -120.0 (dBc/Hz) print(round(L_1MHz - required_L, 1)) # -> 20.0 (dB short of the requirement)

documents.t: The ISF writes "injected charge → phase shift" as ([P1] Eq.(10), p.182) Δϕ=Γ(ω0τ)qmax Δq.\Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q.Δϕ=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​Δq. [P4] does the exact parallel for amplitude, defining the APF Δ(ϕ)\Delta(\phi)Δ(ϕ) (amplitude perturbation function): the same injected current impulse, projected onto the radial direction of the limit cycle, produces how much instantaneous amplitude deviation. Conceptually ([P4] Sec. III-D; the APF is defined near p.2127): ΔA0 ∝ Δ(ω0τ) Δq⟺the APF is the amplitude-domain counterpart of the ISF.\Delta A_0\;\propto\;\Delta(\omega_0\tau)\,\Delta q \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{the APF is the amplitude-domain counterpart of the ISF}.ΔA0​∝Δ(ω0​τ)Δq⟺the APF is the amplitude-domain counterpart of the ISF. Units: [P4] gives the APF units of A−1\mathrm{A^{-1}}A−1 (1/ampere) — it maps "injected current" to "relative amplitude deviation". Contrast the dimensionless ISF Γ\GammaΓ: the two are structurally parallel but normalized differently. Notation note: the argument-carrying Δ(⋅)\Delta(\cdot)Δ(⋅) here is the APF function (site convention, see the unified notation table), distinct from the difference prefix Δq\Delta qΔq, ΔA0\Delta A_0ΔA0​, Δω\Delta\omegaΔω — tell them apart by whether there is a function argument (parentheses); in Δ(ω0τ) Δq\Delta(\omega_0\tau)\,\Delta qΔ(ω0​τ)Δq above, one Δ\DeltaΔ is a function and the other a difference quantity, not the same Δ\DeltaΔ multiplied by itself. The key difference — different fates: the phase deviation carries a unit step u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) (kept forever, [P1] Eq.(10)); the amplitude deviation is instead multiplied by an amplitude decay function that relaxes exponentially back to zero. Conceptually: hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ)⏟phase: step, permanentvshA(t,τ) ∝ Δ(ω0τ) d(t−τ)⏟amplitude: impulse×decay, d→0.\underbrace{h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau)}_{\text{phase: step, permanent}}\qquad\text{vs}\qquad \underbrace{h_A(t,\tau)\;\propto\;\Delta(\omega_0\tau)\,d(t-\tau)}_{\text{amplitude: impulse}\times\text{decay,}\;d\to 0}.phase: step, permanenthϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ)​​vsamplitude: impulse×decay,d→0hA​(t,τ)∝Δ(ω0​τ)d(t−τ)​​. Here d(t−τ)d(t-\tau)d(t−τ) is the amplitude decay function. [P4] Sec. III-F, p.2128 (the body text immediately before Eq.(25)) gives the exact closed form (verified verbatim against the original PDF rendering; note that Eq.(25) itself is Δ(ϕ)=τ0 Λ~(ϕ)\Delta(\phi)=\tau_0\,\tilde\Lambda(\phi)Δ(ϕ)=τ0​Λ~(ϕ), APF = τ0\tau_0τ0​ × amplitude ISF Λ~\tilde\LambdaΛ~, while the decay closed form below is the body text preceding it): d(t,ϕ)=e−t/τ0,τ0=2Qωoscd(t,\phi)=e^{-t/\tau_0},\qquad \tau_0=\frac{2Q}{\omega_{osc}}d(t,ϕ)=e−t/τ0​,τ0​=ωosc​2Q​ That is, τA=τ0=2Q/ωosc\tau_A=\tau_0=2Q/\omega_{osc}τA​=τ0​=2Q/ωosc​ — the amplitude recovery time constant is proportional to QQQ. Intuition: a high-QQQ LC recovers its amplitude slowly (τ0\tau_0τ0​ large), but it does eventually recover (exponential decay); phase has no such restoring force (unit step, infinitely long memory). This is the most quantitative one-liner for "why amplitude noise is bounded while phase noise diverges". Verified: d(t,ϕ)=e−t/τ0d(t,\phi)=e^{-t/\tau_0}d(t,ϕ)=e−t/τ0​ and τ0=2Q/ωosc\tau_0=2Q/\omega_{osc}τ0​=2Q/ωosc​ come from the body text of [P4] Sec. III-F, p.2128 (the unnumbered expression immediately before Eq.(25); Eq.(25) itself is the APF relation Δ(ϕ)=τ0 Λ~(ϕ)\Delta(\phi)=\tau_0\,\tilde\Lambda(\phi)Δ(ϕ)=τ0​Λ~(ϕ)). (Decay rates for more general oscillators belong to the Floquet/PPV framework, not among the 5 downloaded PDFs; see derivation_floquet_ppv.) Why "decays" equals "suppressed": think of amplitude noise as a convolution with hAh_AhA​. Because d(t−τ)d(t-\tau)d(t−τ) is integrable and returns to zero, past amplitude perturbations do not accumulate, and the output amplitude variance converges to a finite value (the steady-state variance of a first-order low-pass system with a restoring force). Phase convolution instead uses u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) (non-integrable, never returns to zero), so the variance diverges — this is the mathematical watershed between phase noise accumulating and amplitude noise not accumulating. documents.t: [P4] Fig. 5, p.2126 plots, for the ideal LC oscillator, the ISF, APF, amplitude decay function, and how the three relate; the most elegant conclusion is: In the ideal LC oscillator, the ISF and the APF are in quadrature (90° apart). This matches the geometry of the previous page exactly: tangential and radial are everywhere mutually perpendicular on the circle. The ideal LC's ISF is Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ (maximal at the zero crossings, zero at the peaks); the radial sensitivity (APF) should then be maximal at the peaks and zero at the zero crossings, i.e. shaped like cos⁡\coscos: ΓLC(θ)=−sin⁡θ(tangential),ΔLC(θ) ∝ cos⁡θ(radial, orthogonal to Γ).\Gamma_{LC}(\theta)=-\sin\theta\quad\text{(tangential)},\qquad \Delta_{LC}(\theta)\;\propto\;\cos\theta\quad\text{(radial, orthogonal to }\Gamma\text{)}.ΓLC​(θ)=−sinθ(tangential),ΔLC​(θ)∝cosθ(radial, orthogonal to Γ). Physical meaning: kick at the peak (θ=0\theta=0θ=0) → Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0, Δ\DeltaΔ maximal → pure amplitude change (gets eaten). Kick at the zero crossing (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2) → ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ maximal, Δ=0\Delta=0Δ=0 → pure phase change (kept forever). This is exactly the red/green markers in the previous page's waveform_with_impulse_markers. Unit check / dimension: Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless, Δ\DeltaΔ has units A−1\mathrm{A^{-1}}A−1; quadrature refers to the phase (angle) relation, not equal dimensions. "90° apart" means that, as periodic functions of θ\thetaθ, one is a sin⁡\sinsin and the other a cos⁡\coscos in Fourier terms. Verified ([P4] Eq.(26), p.2128): the proportionality constant in ΔLC∝cos⁡θ\Delta_{LC}\propto\cos\thetaΔLC​∝cosθ above and the exact normalization of the APF must be checked against PDF Fig. 5, p.2126. This page only claims the qualitative quadrature relation (stated explicitly by [P4]) and does not pin down the amplitude constant.

documents.t: If amplitude perturbations get eaten, why should design still care about them? Because there is a back door called AM–PM conversion (amplitude-to-phase conversion): Mechanism: a real oscillator's effective oscillation frequency varies with amplitude (e.g. a nonlinear capacitance C(V)C(V)C(V) that changes with swing, or a tank whose effective phase shifts with amplitude). So "amplitude fluctuation ΔA\Delta AΔA" leaks through ∂ω∂A\dfrac{\partial\omega}{\partial A}∂A∂ω​ into "phase/frequency fluctuation", which the phase's lack of restoring force then accumulates permanently. Consequence: amplitude noise that should have been squeezed out becomes long-lived phase noise via AM–PM — in particular, it upconverts the device's 1/f1/f1/f amplitude fluctuations into close-in phase noise, degrading the 1/f31/f^31/f3 region. Design implications: (i) drive ∂ω/∂A→0\partial\omega/\partial A\to 0∂ω/∂A→0 (e.g. bias at a flat spot of the capacitance curve, add AM suppression/limiting); (ii) under the quadrature picture, arranging the dominant noise injection at the phases where the radial direction is least sensitive also helps. The detailed AM–PM and amplitude-modulation analysis is the core of [P4] (advanced — this site gives only the intuition). Connections to other pages on this site: AM–PM is one of the common reasons "why the real 1/f31/f^31/f3 sits higher than the pure c0c_0c0​ mechanism predicts"; for the purely ISF-c0c_0c0​ upconversion of 1/f1/f1/f, see flicker_upconversion and [P1] Eq.(23)–(24).

documents.t: Section 2 described the fate of a single kick: the amplitude deviation decays as d(t)=e−t/τ0d(t)=e^{-t/\tau_0}d(t)=e−t/τ0​ with τ0=2Q/ωosc\tau_0=2Q/\omega_{osc}τ0​=2Q/ωosc​ ([P4] Sec. III-F, p.2128, verified on this site). But real noise is not a single kick — it is a continuous stream of white-noise current. This section upgrades "single-kick decay" to "the steady-state spectrum under continuous drive", answering two questions: What does the full amplitude-noise spectrum Sa(ω)S_a(\omega)Sa​(ω) look like? (Answer: a "flat-top Lorentzian" with the corner at ω0/2Q\omega_0/2Qω0​/2Q.) Why does the measured oscillator spectrum "flatten" far from the carrier? Besides the instrument floor there is a second physical reason — the AM plateau. Physical intuition (conclusion first): white noise = a dense stream of small random kicks. On the phase side every kick is kept forever (unit step) → they pile up into a random walk → spectrum ∝1/ω2\propto 1/\omega^2∝1/ω2 all the way down. On the amplitude side every kick carries an e−t/τ0e^{-t/\tau_0}e−t/τ0​ "shelf life" → after superposition only the kicks within the last τ0\tau_0τ0​ are still alive → finite variance, spectrum flattens for ω<1/τ0\omega \lt 1/\tau_0ω<1/τ0​. At observation frequencies above 1/τ01/\tau_01/τ0​ (time scales shorter than τ0\tau_0τ0​) the restoring force has no time to act and the amplitude also looks like a free integrator — so at the high-frequency end the AM and PM spectra have the same shape.

documents.t: Linearize the amplitude dynamics of Section 2 (small perturbation): the restoring force pulls the amplitude deviation back at rate 1/τ01/\tau_01/τ0​ while white noise keeps pushing it. Define a(t)≡ΔA/A0a(t)\equiv \Delta A/A_0a(t)≡ΔA/A0​ as the relative amplitude deviation (dimensionless, so it can be compared fairly with ϕ\phiϕ [rad]); its stochastic differential equation (Langevin equation) is: da=−aτ0 dt+c dW(t).da=-\frac{a}{\tau_0}\,dt+\sqrt{c}\,dW(t).da=−τ0​a​dt+c​dW(t). Term by term, physical meaning and units: −aτ0dt-\dfrac{a}{\tau_0}dt−τ0​a​dt: the restoring term — the linearization of amplitude control (limiting, nonlinear saturation), precisely the differential form of [P4]'s single-kick decay d(t)=e−t/τ0d(t)=e^{-t/\tau_0}d(t)=e−t/τ0​. [a/τ0]⋅[dt]=(1/s)⋅s[a/\tau_0]\cdot[dt]=(1/\text{s})\cdot\text{s}[a/τ0​]⋅[dt]=(1/s)⋅s × dimensionless = dimensionless ✓. τ0=2Q/ω0\tau_0=2Q/\omega_0τ0​=2Q/ω0​ [s] ([P4] Sec. III-F, p.2128, verified). c dW\sqrt{c}\,dWc​dW: the white-noise drive. W(t)W(t)W(t) is a standard Wiener process, Var[dW]=dt\mathrm{Var}[dW]=dtVar[dW]=dt, [dW]=s[dW]=\sqrt{\text{s}}[dW]=s​; ccc is the drive strength, [c]=1/s[c]=1/\text{s}[c]=1/s (with aaa dimensionless), so [c dW]=1/s⋅s=[\sqrt{c}\,dW]=\sqrt{1/\text{s}}\cdot\sqrt{\text{s}}=[c​dW]=1/s​⋅s​= dimensionless ✓. The phase equation = the same equation with the restoring term removed: dϕ=c dWd\phi=\sqrt{c}\,dWdϕ=c​dW ([c]=rad2/s[c]=\text{rad}^2/\text{s}[c]=rad2/s). This is the minimal mathematical model of "one white-noise source, two fates". A process of this kind — "exponential restoration + white-noise drive" — is called an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process. Honesty note: the OU process and the solution below are standard stochastic-process mathematics (external literature, not among the 5 source PDFs): G. E. Uhlenbeck and L. S. Ornstein, "On the Theory of the Brownian Motion," Physical Review, vol. 36, pp. 823–841, 1930. The only ingredient taken from the papers on this site is the decay time constant τ0=2Q/ω0\tau_0=2Q/\omega_0τ0​=2Q/ω0​ ([P4] Sec. III-F, p.2128, verified verbatim); plugging it into the OU machinery is a standard pedagogical assembly.

documents.t: The sidebands a spectrum analyzer (SA) sees beside the carrier are the sum of PM and AM. The AM sideband bookkeeping is exactly parallel to the small-angle PM derivation of white_noise_to_phase_noise: take x(t)=[1+a(t)]cos⁡ω0tx(t)=[1+a(t)]\cos\omega_0 tx(t)=[1+a(t)]cosω0​t, a(t)=apcos⁡ωmta(t)=a_p\cos\omega_m ta(t)=ap​cosωm​t (ap≪1a_p\ll1ap​≪1): x(t)=cos⁡ω0t+ap2cos⁡((ω0+ωm)t)+ap2cos⁡((ω0−ωm)t),x(t)=\cos\omega_0 t+\frac{a_p}{2}\cos\big((\omega_0+\omega_m)t\big)+\frac{a_p}{2}\cos\big((\omega_0-\omega_m)t\big),x(t)=cosω0​t+2ap​​cos((ω0​+ωm​)t)+2ap​​cos((ω0​−ωm​)t), each sideband's power relative to the carrier =(ap/2)2=(a_p/2)^2=(ap​/2)2; and the power density of aaa gives Sa=ap2/2S_a=a_p^2/2Sa​=ap2​/2, so each sideband density =Sa/2=S_a/2=Sa​/2 — exactly the same coefficient as PM's L≈Sϕ/2\mathcal{L}\approx S_\phi/2L≈Sϕ​/2 (under the same convention). The only difference is the sign: the AM upper and lower sidebands have the same sign, PM's have opposite signs (−ϕp2cos⁡(ω0−ωm)t+ϕp2cos⁡(ω0+ωm)t-\tfrac{\phi_p}{2}\cos(\omega_0-\omega_m)t+\tfrac{\phi_p}{2}\cos(\omega_0+\omega_m)t−2ϕp​​cos(ω0​−ωm​)t+2ϕp​​cos(ω0​+ωm​)t). In power an SA cannot tell them apart; a quadrature-mixer phase-detector measurement naturally rejects AM (see measurement_and_spurs). Hence: Ltot(Δf)≈Sϕ(Δf)+Sa(Δf)2(same /2 convention; comparing PM/AM only requires comparing Sϕ vs Sa).\mathcal{L}_{tot}(\Delta f)\approx\frac{S_\phi(\Delta f)+S_a(\Delta f)}{2}\qquad(\text{same }/2\text{ convention; comparing PM/AM only requires comparing }S_\phi\text{ vs }S_a).Ltot​(Δf)≈2Sϕ​(Δf)+Sa​(Δf)​(same /2 convention; comparing PM/AM only requires comparing Sϕ​ vs Sa​). Case 1: equal drive (ca=cϕ=cc_a=c_\phi=cca​=cϕ​=c). For the ideal LC this is the natural baseline: the tangential/radial projections are −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ and cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ respectively (the quadrature of [P4] Eq.(26), p.2128, verified; per Section 3 this page does not pin down the normalization constant), so the two have the same rms. Then: The PM-skirt asymptote c/ω2c/\omega^2c/ω2 and the AM flat top cτ02c\tau_0^2cτ02​ intersect at c/ω2=cτ02⇒ω=1/τ0=ωcc/\omega^2=c\tau_0^2\Rightarrow\omega=1/\tau_0=\omega_cc/ω2=cτ02​⇒ω=1/τ0​=ωc​ — the asymptote intersection is exactly the corner. The actual curves never cross (the ratio above is ≤1\le1≤1); far out, the AM contribution raises the total sideband by at most 10log⁡102≈310\log_{10}2\approx310log10​2≈3 dB. Case 2: stronger AM drive (R≡ca/cϕ>1R\equiv c_a/c_\phi \gt 1R≡ca​/cϕ​>1). Common in real circuits: bias/tail noise and weak limiting all push the AM drive up. The crossover condition in three lines: cϕω2=R cϕ τ021+ω2τ02 ⟹ 1+ω2τ02=R ω2τ02 ⟹ ωx=ωcR−1 ⟺ fx=fcR−1 \frac{c_\phi}{\omega^2}=\frac{R\,c_\phi\,\tau_0^2}{1+\omega^2\tau_0^2} \;\Longrightarrow\;1+\omega^2\tau_0^2=R\,\omega^2\tau_0^2 \;\Longrightarrow\;\boxed{\ \omega_x=\frac{\omega_c}{\sqrt{R-1}}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ f_x=\frac{f_c}{\sqrt{R-1}}\ }ω2cϕ​​=1+ω2τ02​Rcϕ​τ02​​⟹1+ω2τ02​=Rω2τ02​⟹ ωx​=R−1​ωc​​ ⟺ fx​=R−1​fc​​ ​ (As R→1+R\to1^+R→1+, fx→∞f_x\to\inftyfx​→∞, consistent with "equal drive never crosses" ✓; no solution for R≤1R\le1R≤1.) For fx<Δf<fcf_x \lt \Delta f \lt f_cfx​<Δf<fc​ the AM flat top sits above the PM skirt: the measured spectrum first falls at −20-20−20 dB/dec, bends flat at fxf_xfx​, stays flat out to fcf_cfc​, and only then resumes −20-20−20 dB/dec (by now AM-dominated). This "pedestal" occurs above and before the instrument floor — this is the second reason a measured spectrum flattens far out (the first being the additive/instrument floor; the close-in flattening is a different story — the Lorentzian lineshape, see lorentzian_linewidth).

documents.t: The jitter that communication and clocking systems care about = a phase matter; phase has no restoring force → accumulates → 1/f21/f^21/f2, 1/f31/f^31/f3 skirts. Amplitude has a restoring force → perturbations decay exponentially (amplitude decay function d(t−τ)→0d(t-\tau)\to 0d(t−τ)→0) → bounded variance, suppressed. The APF Δ(ω0τ)\Delta(\omega_0\tau)Δ(ω0​τ) (units A−1\mathrm{A^{-1}}A−1) is the amplitude-domain counterpart of the ISF; the phase kernel is a step uuu, the amplitude kernel is impulse × decay. Ideal LC: Γ∝−sin⁡θ\Gamma\propto-\sin\thetaΓ∝−sinθ (tangential) and Δ∝cos⁡θ\Delta\propto\cos\thetaΔ∝cosθ (radial) are in quadrature (90° apart) — [P4] Fig. 5, p.2126. AM–PM is the back door through which amplitude noise leaks back into phase: beware when ∂ω/∂A≠0\partial\omega/\partial A\neq 0∂ω/∂A=0. Example A: 1 fC injected at the zero crossing → 31.8 fs of permanent jitter; at the peak → ~0 permanent effect. Continuous white-noise drive + exponential restoration ([P4] τ0=2Q/ω0\tau_0=2Q/\omega_0τ0​=2Q/ω0​) = an OU process: Sa=cτ02/(1+ω2τ02)S_a=c\tau_0^2/(1+\omega^2\tau_0^2)Sa​=cτ02​/(1+ω2τ02​) — a flat-top Lorentzian with corner fc=f0/2Qf_c=f_0/2Qfc​=f0​/2Q (Q=10Q=10Q=10, 5 GHz → τ0=0.64\tau_0=0.64τ0​=0.64 ns, fc=250f_c=250fc​=250 MHz); phase, with no restoring force → c/ω2c/\omega^2c/ω2 all the way down. The second reason a measured spectrum flattens far out is the AM flat top (the first is the instrument/additive floor): under equal drive the asymptotes intersect exactly at fcf_cfc​ and AM adds at most +3 dB; with stronger AM drive (R>1R\gt1R>1) the crossover is fx=fc/R−1f_x=f_c/\sqrt{R-1}fx​=fc​/R−1​, e.g. R=10→83.3R=10\to83.3R=10→83.3 MHz. An SA measures AM+PM; phase-detector methods reject AM. Sources: [P4] (APF / amplitude decay / quadrature, Sec. III-D–E, Fig. 5, p.2126, verified); the phase side from [P1] Eqs.(1),(10); the OU process is standard stochastic-process mathematics (external literature, Uhlenbeck–Ornstein 1930).

documents.t: Prerequisites: white_noise_to_phase_noise · stochastic_noise_basics | Next: serdes_clocking_connection This page answers the question engineers ask most often: you are handed a phase-noise plot (L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f), dBc/Hz) — how do you turn it into a single time-domain number, the rms jitter σt\sigma_tσt​ (fs)? This is the bridge between the frequency domain (the language of communications/RF) and the time domain (the language of digital/SerDes). The full chain is four steps: L(f) → ×2, de-dB Sϕ(f) → ∫f1f2 σϕ2 → σϕ → ÷(2πf0) σt.\mathcal{L}(f)\ \xrightarrow{\ \times2,\ \text{de-dB}\ }\ S_\phi(f)\ \xrightarrow{\ \int_{f_1}^{f_2}\ }\ \sigma_\phi^2\ \xrightarrow{\ \sqrt{\ }\ }\ \sigma_\phi\ \xrightarrow{\ \div(2\pi f_0)\ }\ \sigma_t.L(f) ×2, de-dB ​ Sϕ​(f) ∫f1​f2​​ ​ σϕ2​ ​ ​ σϕ​ ÷(2πf0​) ​ σt​. We take each step apart, carrying units and a dimension check throughout, and finish with canonical Example C (5 GHz, −100-100−100 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, 1/f² slope, 1→100 MHz) to obtain σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the phase error Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is "how far the clock hand has strayed in angle"; divide that angle by the angular velocity 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ and you get "how far the hand has strayed in time," Δt\Delta tΔt. The phase-noise plot tells you how much phase power density sits at each offset frequency; adding it all up (integrating) gives the total phase variance; the square root is the rms phase; dividing by 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ gives the rms timing jitter. The whole plot is compressed into one fs number.

documents.t: An ideal oscillation cos⁡(2πf0t)\cos(2\pi f_0 t)cos(2πf0​t) becomes cos⁡(2πf0t+Δϕ)\cos(2\pi f_0 t+\Delta\phi)cos(2πf0​t+Δϕ) once excess phase is added. Factor the phase term out and look at where the zero crossing lands: 2πf0t+Δϕ=2πf0(t+Δϕ2πf0⏟= Δt).2\pi f_0 t+\Delta\phi=2\pi f_0\Big(t+\underbrace{\frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi f_0}}_{=\ \Delta t}\Big).2πf0​t+Δϕ=2πf0​(t+= Δt2πf0​Δϕ​​​). In other words, an extra phase Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is equivalent to shifting the entire waveform along the time axis by Δt\Delta tΔt (spec §3, Eq. 17): Δt=Δϕ2πf0 \boxed{\ \Delta t=\frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi f_0}\ } Δt=2πf0​Δϕ​ ​ Physics used: the conversion rate between phase and time is the angular frequency ω0=2πf0\omega_0=2\pi f_0ω0​=2πf0​ (rad/s). Dimension check: [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] ✓. Note the denominator is 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ (rad/s), not f0f_0f0​ (Hz) — dropping this 2π2\pi2π is the most common mistake. Why it is reasonable: at small phase (Δϕ≪1\Delta\phi\ll1Δϕ≪1 rad), phase offset and edge-time offset are linear and one-to-one. Timing jitter is the time error of the zero crossing, so it equals Δϕ/(2πf0)\Delta\phi/(2\pi f_0)Δϕ/(2πf0​). Feel: at 5 GHz, Δϕ=1\Delta\phi=1Δϕ=1 mrad ⇒Δt=31.8\Rightarrow\Delta t=31.8⇒Δt=31.8 fs (see numerical_feeling Example 1).
documents.s: Step 1: why a phase error becomes a timing error

documents.t: The vertical axis of a phase-noise plot is L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f), the SSB phase noise (single-sideband phase noise), in dBc/Hz — meaning "at offset fff, within a 1 Hz bandwidth, how many dB below the carrier the single-sideband noise power sits" (dBc = dB relative to carrier). de-dB (from dB back to linear): dBc/Hz is 10log⁡10(⋅)10\log_{10}(\cdot)10log10​(⋅), so Llin(f)=10L(f)/10[1/Hz].\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}(f)=10^{\mathcal{L}(f)/10}\quad[\text{1/Hz}].Llin​(f)=10L(f)/10[1/Hz]. Then connect to the phase PSD: under the small-angle approximation, the SSB phase noise relates to the single-sided phase PSD as (spec §3, Eq. 16): L(f)≈12 Sϕ(f) ⟹Sϕ(f)=2⋅10L(f)/10 [rad2/Hz].\boxed{\ \mathcal{L}(f)\approx\tfrac12\,S_\phi(f)\ }\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S_\phi(f)=2\cdot10^{\mathcal{L}(f)/10}\ [\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]. L(f)≈21​Sϕ​(f) ​⟹Sϕ​(f)=2⋅10L(f)/10 [rad2/Hz]. Units: SϕS_\phiSϕ​ is rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz (the density of phase variance). Llin\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}Llin​ itself is dimensionless per Hz; after multiplying by 2 it is read as rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz. Where this 12\frac1221​ comes from: phase-modulation power splits evenly between the upper and lower sidebands, and L\mathcal{L}L counts only one side, so it is half of SϕS_\phiSϕ​. This is exactly the bookkeeping convention discussed in the spec §3 "factor-of-2 teaching note"; for jitter integrals this site always uses Sϕ=2LlinS_\phi=2\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}Sϕ​=2Llin​. For a deeper discussion see white_noise_to_phase_noise.

documents.t: That 12\frac1221​ above is not pulled out of thin air; it is a direct consequence of narrowband phase modulation (PM with a very small phase swing). We derive it step by step and make "one sideband's power =(ϕp/2)2=(\phi_p/2)^2=(ϕp​/2)2" explicit. Step 1: write a carrier phase-modulated by a single tone. Let the phase be modulated at a single frequency ωm\omega_mωm​ (offset angular frequency) with a small amplitude ϕp\phi_pϕp​ (peak phase, the peak of the phase swing, rad): v(t)=cos⁡(ω0t+ϕ(t)),ϕ(t)=ϕpsin⁡ωmt,ϕp≪1 rad.v(t)=\cos\big(\omega_0 t+\phi(t)\big),\qquad \phi(t)=\phi_p\sin\omega_m t,\quad \phi_p\ll 1\ \text{rad}.v(t)=cos(ω0​t+ϕ(t)),ϕ(t)=ϕp​sinωm​t,ϕp​≪1 rad. Physics used: this is Step 1's excess phase Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ replaced by a phase that swings sinusoidally in time; ϕp\phi_pϕp​ is its amplitude. Units: ϕp\phi_pϕp​ and ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) are both rad; ω0,ωm\omega_0,\omega_mω0​,ωm​ are both rad/s. Step 2: expand the phase modulation with a trig identity. Use the angle-sum formula cos⁡(A+B)=cos⁡Acos⁡B−sin⁡Asin⁡B\cos(A+B)=\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin Bcos(A+B)=cosAcosB−sinAsinB with A=ω0tA=\omega_0 tA=ω0​t, B=ϕ(t)B=\phi(t)B=ϕ(t): v(t)=cos⁡ω0t cos⁡ ⁣(ϕpsin⁡ωmt)−sin⁡ω0t sin⁡ ⁣(ϕpsin⁡ωmt).v(t)=\cos\omega_0 t\,\cos\!\big(\phi_p\sin\omega_m t\big)-\sin\omega_0 t\,\sin\!\big(\phi_p\sin\omega_m t\big).v(t)=cosω0​tcos(ϕp​sinωm​t)−sinω0​tsin(ϕp​sinωm​t). Step 3: the small-angle approximation (this is all "small-angle" means). Because ϕp≪1\phi_p\ll1ϕp​≪1: cos⁡ ⁣(ϕpsin⁡ωmt)≈1,sin⁡ ⁣(ϕpsin⁡ωmt)≈ϕpsin⁡ωmt.\cos\!\big(\phi_p\sin\omega_m t\big)\approx 1,\qquad \sin\!\big(\phi_p\sin\omega_m t\big)\approx \phi_p\sin\omega_m t.cos(ϕp​sinωm​t)≈1,sin(ϕp​sinωm​t)≈ϕp​sinωm​t. Math used: Taylor expansions cos⁡x≈1−x2/2\cos x\approx1-x^2/2cosx≈1−x2/2, sin⁡x≈x\sin x\approx xsinx≈x, keeping first order only (x=ϕpsin⁡ωmtx=\phi_p\sin\omega_m tx=ϕp​sinωm​t, whose x2x^2x2 is O(ϕp2)O(\phi_p^2)O(ϕp2​) and can be dropped). This is exactly the small-amplitude limit of the Bessel expansion J0≈1, J1≈ϕp/2J_0\approx1,\ J_1\approx\phi_p/2J0​≈1, J1​≈ϕp​/2. Substituting back: v(t)≈cos⁡ω0t−ϕpsin⁡ω0t sin⁡ωmt.v(t)\approx\cos\omega_0 t-\phi_p\sin\omega_0 t\,\sin\omega_m t.v(t)≈cosω0​t−ϕp​sinω0​tsinωm​t. Step 4: split sin⁡×sin⁡\sin\times\sinsin×sin into the two sidebands. Use the product-to-sum identity sin⁡αsin⁡β=12[cos⁡(α−β)−cos⁡(α+β)]\sin\alpha\sin\beta=\tfrac12[\cos(\alpha-\beta)-\cos(\alpha+\beta)]sinαsinβ=21​[cos(α−β)−cos(α+β)] with α=ω0t\alpha=\omega_0 tα=ω0​t, β=ωmt\beta=\omega_m tβ=ωm​t: v(t)≈cos⁡ω0t−ϕp2[cos⁡(ω0−ωm)t−cos⁡(ω0+ωm)t]=cos⁡ω0t⏟carrier−ϕp2cos⁡(ω0−ωm)t⏟lower sideband+ϕp2cos⁡(ω0+ωm)t⏟upper sideband.\begin{aligned} v(t)&\approx\cos\omega_0 t-\frac{\phi_p}{2}\Big[\cos(\omega_0-\omega_m)t-\cos(\omega_0+\omega_m)t\Big]\\ &=\underbrace{\cos\omega_0 t}_{\text{carrier}}-\underbrace{\frac{\phi_p}{2}\cos(\omega_0-\omega_m)t}_{\text{lower sideband}}+\underbrace{\frac{\phi_p}{2}\cos(\omega_0+\omega_m)t}_{\text{upper sideband}}. \end{aligned}v(t)​≈cosω0​t−2ϕp​​[cos(ω0​−ωm​)t−cos(ω0​+ωm​)t]=carriercosω0​t​​−lower sideband2ϕp​​cos(ω0​−ωm​)t​​+upper sideband2ϕp​​cos(ω0​+ωm​)t​​.​ Physical meaning: phase modulation grows a symmetric pair of sidebands next to the carrier, at ω0±ωm\omega_0\pm\omega_mω0​±ωm​, each with amplitude ϕp/2\phi_p/2ϕp​/2. This is the time-domain origin of the "carrier smeared into a skirt" picture of [P1] Fig. 8. Step 5: each sideband's relative power. The carrier has amplitude 111, power ∝1\propto 1∝1 (taking 12⋅12\tfrac12\cdot1^221​⋅12); a single sideband has amplitude ϕp/2\phi_p/2ϕp​/2, power ∝(ϕp/2)2\propto(\phi_p/2)^2∝(ϕp​/2)2. So the single-sideband-to-carrier power ratio is P1 sidebandPcarrier=12(ϕp/2)212(1)2=(ϕp2)2=ϕp24.\frac{P_{\text{1 sideband}}}{P_{\text{carrier}}}=\frac{\tfrac12(\phi_p/2)^2}{\tfrac12(1)^2}=\Big(\frac{\phi_p}{2}\Big)^2=\frac{\phi_p^2}{4}.Pcarrier​P1 sideband​​=21​(1)221​(ϕp​/2)2​=(2ϕp​​)2=4ϕp2​​. Dimension check: a power ratio is dimensionless ✓; ϕp\phi_pϕp​ (rad) squared is read as rad2\text{rad}^2rad2 in the "phase power" context. Step 6: connect it to SϕS_\phiSϕ​. For ϕ(t)=ϕpsin⁡ωmt\phi(t)=\phi_p\sin\omega_m tϕ(t)=ϕp​sinωm​t, the mean square (variance) of the phase is ⟨ϕ2(t)⟩=ϕp2⟨sin⁡2ωmt⟩=ϕp22.\langle\phi^2(t)\rangle=\phi_p^2\langle\sin^2\omega_m t\rangle=\frac{\phi_p^2}{2}.⟨ϕ2(t)⟩=ϕp2​⟨sin2ωm​t⟩=2ϕp2​​. All of this single tone's phase power ϕp2/2\phi_p^2/2ϕp2​/2 is concentrated in the one spectral line at ωm\omega_mωm​; reading it as "the single-sided phase-PSD strength at ωm\omega_mωm​" gives Sϕ(ωm)=ϕp2/2S_\phi(\omega_m)=\phi_p^2/2Sϕ​(ωm​)=ϕp2​/2 (per-Hz, taken as the weight of one line). Step 7: divide the two, and the 12\frac1221​ appears. L\mathcal{L}L (SSB) = single-sideband power ratio =ϕp2/4=\phi_p^2/4=ϕp2​/4; Sϕ=ϕp2/2S_\phi=\phi_p^2/2Sϕ​=ϕp2​/2. So L=ϕp2/41=12⋅ϕp22=12Sϕ \boxed{\ \mathcal{L}=\frac{\phi_p^2/4}{1}=\frac12\cdot\frac{\phi_p^2}{2}=\frac12 S_\phi\ } L=1ϕp2​/4​=21​⋅2ϕp2​​=21​Sϕ​ ​ One-sentence summary: L\mathcal{L}L counts one sideband (power (ϕp/2)2=ϕp2/4(\phi_p/2)^2=\phi_p^2/4(ϕp​/2)2=ϕp2​/4), while SϕS_\phiSϕ​ is the total phase power density (ϕp2/2\phi_p^2/2ϕp2​/2, i.e. the two sidebands combined). One side ÷ total =12=\tfrac12=21​ — that is the entire origin of the factor-of-12\tfrac1221​. Failure condition: once ϕp\phi_pϕp​ is no longer ≪1\ll1≪1, the higher-order Bessel terms of Step 3 (J2,J3,…J_2,J_3,\dotsJ2​,J3​,…) grow additional sidebands and L=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12 S_\phiL=21​Sϕ​ no longer holds — at large phase the carrier also "loses power" to the higher-order sidebands. Small-angle condition: L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\frac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​ holds only for σϕ≪1\sigma_\phi\ll1σϕ​≪1 rad (Bessel expansion kept to first order). Here σϕ=14\sigma_\phi=14σϕ​=14 mrad ≪1\ll1≪1, OK. Canonical numbers: at 1 MHz, L=−100\mathcal{L}=-100L=−100 dBc/Hz: Llin=10−100/10=10−10\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}=10^{-100/10}=10^{-10}Llin​=10−100/10=10−10; Sϕ(1MHz)=2×10−10 rad2/HzS_\phi(1\text{MHz})=2\times10^{-10}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}Sϕ​(1MHz)=2×10−10 rad2/Hz.

documents.t: This step is pure Parseval / Wiener–Khinchin: integrate the PSD over frequency to obtain the time-domain variance (spec §3, Eq. 18): σϕ2=∫f1f2Sϕ(f) df \boxed{\ \sigma_\phi^2=\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_\phi(f)\,df\ } σϕ2​=∫f1​f2​​Sϕ​(f)df ​ Math used: Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) is "phase power per unit bandwidth"; summing (integrating) it over the offset band of interest [f1,f2][f_1,f_2][f1​,f2​] gives the total phase power = the variance σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​. This is the same move as integrating the current PSD into in2‾\overline{i_n^2}in2​​ in Section 3 of stochastic_noise_basics. Dimension check: (rad2/Hz)×Hz=rad2(\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz})\times\text{Hz}=\text{rad}^2(rad2/Hz)×Hz=rad2 ✓. Why the integration band [f1,f2][f_1,f_2][f1​,f2​] matters: the phase PSD at low offset is typically 1/f² (or even 1/f³), so the integral is dominated by the lower limit f1f_1f1​. Moving f1f_1f1​ by one decade can change the jitter by several times. So a reported jitter number must state its integration bandwidth, otherwise it is meaningless. Upper limit f2f_2f2​: physically set by the system bandwidth (for SerDes, the PLL loop bandwidth or Nyquist). Lower limit f1f_1f1​: for an open-loop oscillator the integral diverges toward DC (random walk); in practice it is set by the measurement time or by the frequency at which a PLL "holds" the phase. Small-angle approximation (sin⁡Δϕ≈Δϕ\sin\Delta\phi\approx\Delta\phisinΔϕ≈Δϕ): approximating the phase-modulation power as σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​ likewise requires σϕ≪1\sigma_\phi\ll1σϕ​≪1 rad.

documents.t: Anchor the 1/f² shape from Step 2 at fref=1f_{ref}=1fref​=1 MHz: Sϕ(f)=Sϕ(fref)(freff)2=2×10−10(106f)2.S_\phi(f)=S_\phi(f_{ref})\Big(\frac{f_{ref}}{f}\Big)^2=2\times10^{-10}\Big(\frac{10^6}{f}\Big)^2.Sϕ​(f)=Sϕ​(fref​)(ffref​​)2=2×10−10(f106​)2. Substitute into the integral (note ∫f−2df=−1/f\int f^{-2}df=-1/f∫f−2df=−1/f): σϕ2=2×10−10 (106)2∫106108dff2=2×102(1106−1108)=200×(10−6−10−8)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2.\begin{aligned} \sigma_\phi^2&=2\times10^{-10}\,(10^6)^2\int_{10^6}^{10^8}\frac{df}{f^2} =2\times10^{2}\Big(\frac{1}{10^6}-\frac{1}{10^8}\Big)\\ &=200\times(10^{-6}-10^{-8})=200\times9.9\times10^{-7}=1.98\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}^2. \end{aligned}σϕ2​​=2×10−10(106)2∫106108​f2df​=2×102(1061​−1081​)=200×(10−6−10−8)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2.​ Take the square root: σϕ=1.98×10−4=1.407×10−2 rad=14.07 mrad.\sigma_\phi=\sqrt{1.98\times10^{-4}}=1.407\times10^{-2}\ \text{rad}=14.07\ \text{mrad}.σϕ​=1.98×10−4​=1.407×10−2 rad=14.07 mrad. Feel check: inside the parentheses 10−6≫10−810^{-6}\gg10^{-8}10−6≫10−8, so the "1/f11/f_11/f1​" term dominates — confirming again that the lower limit dominates. Raising f2f_2f2​ from 100 MHz to 1 GHz barely changes the answer; lowering f1f_1f1​ from 1 MHz to 100 kHz blows the jitter up by 10≈3.2×\sqrt{10}\approx3.2\times10​≈3.2×.

documents.t: Apply Step 1's Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0)\Delta t=\Delta\phi/(2\pi f_0)Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0​) to the rms quantities (spec §3, Eq. 19): σt=σϕ2πf0=12πf0∫f1f2Sϕ(f) df \boxed{\ \sigma_t=\frac{\sigma_\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{1}{2\pi f_0}\sqrt{\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_\phi(f)\,df}\ } σt​=2πf0​σϕ​​=2πf0​1​∫f1​f2​​Sϕ​(f)df​ ​ Substituting this example (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, σϕ=1.407×10−2\sigma_\phi=1.407\times10^{-2}σϕ​=1.407×10−2 rad): σt=1.407×10−2 rad2π×5×109 Hz=1.407×10−23.1416×1010 s=4.479×10−13 s=447.9 fs.\sigma_t=\frac{1.407\times10^{-2}\ \text{rad}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{9}\ \text{Hz}} =\frac{1.407\times10^{-2}}{3.1416\times10^{10}}\ \text{s} =4.479\times10^{-13}\ \text{s}=447.9\ \text{fs}.σt​=2π×5×109 Hz1.407×10−2 rad​=3.1416×10101.407×10−2​ s=4.479×10−13 s=447.9 fs. Dimension check: [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] ✓. This is canonical Example C (spec §8): 5 GHz, −100-100−100 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, 1/f², integrated 1→100 MHz ⇒σϕ=14.07\Rightarrow\sigma_\phi=14.07⇒σϕ​=14.07 mrad, σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs. Scaling feel: 10 dB better phase noise (L=−110\mathcal{L}=-110L=−110) ⇒Sϕ\Rightarrow S_\phi⇒Sϕ​ 10× smaller ⇒σt\Rightarrow\sigma_t⇒σt​ smaller by 10≈3.2×\sqrt{10}\approx3.2\times10​≈3.2× →∼142\to\sim142→∼142 fs. 20 dB better (−120-120−120) ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ 10× smaller →∼45\to\sim45→∼45 fs (see the reference points in numerical_feeling). The figure above (simulations/lab_08_jitter_integration.py) plots the 1/f² skirt at −100-100−100 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz and how the cumulative integral converges to 447.9 fs with bandwidth; the numerical integration matches the hand-computed analytic result above exactly. This is a toy / analytic demo (single 1/f² source, small-angle approximation), not transistor-level.

documents.t: import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import leeson_one_over_f2, integrate_rms_jitter f = np.logspace(6, 8, 4000) # 1 MHz -> 100 MHz L = leeson_one_over_f2(f, L_ref_dbc=-100, f_ref=1e6) # 1/f^2 skirt sigma_t, sigma_phi = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L, f0=5e9, fmin=1e6, fmax=100e6) print(sigma_phi*1e3, "mrad ;", sigma_t*1e15, "fs") # -> 14.07 mrad ; 447.9 fs

documents.t: The same word "jitter" can refer to entirely different measured quantities. The table below follows the definitions of notation (spec §2): Name Definition Intuition Relation to phase noise random jitter (RJ) Gaussian, unbounded, described by σ\sigmaσ wander from random kicks exactly the σt\sigma_tσt​ integrated above; SerDes BER uses it to estimate eye closure period jitter Tk−TT_k-TTk​−T (a single period relative to nominal) how long/short this one beat is integrate SϕS_\phiSϕ​ after applying a sin⁡2(πf/f0)\sin^2(\pi f/f_0)sin2(πf/f0​)-type high-pass weight cycle-to-cycle jitter Tk+1−TkT_{k+1}-T_kTk+1​−Tk​ (difference of adjacent periods) how fast the beat changes beat to beat differences adjacent periods; even stronger high-pass weighting, least affected by close-in accumulated / long-term jitter edge error over separation Δt\Delta tΔt, σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ an open-loop oscillator drifts further the longer it runs random walk; corresponds to integrating 1/f² down to very low offset ([P2] Eq.(8)) Why the distinction matters: period / cycle-to-cycle jitter apply a high-pass weight to SϕS_\phiSϕ​ (differencing suppresses low frequencies and amplifies high ones), so they are not dominated by close-in 1/f²; whereas the random / integrated jitter computed above (the absolute zero-crossing time error) is dominated by the lower limit. When reporting a number, say which kind it is, or the figures can differ by orders of magnitude. accumulated jitter: a free-running oscillator has no absolute time reference; its phase is a random walk, σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ ([P2] Eq.(8), p.792, claim C6). For ring details see [P2] and serdes_clocking_connection.

documents.t: The "high-pass weighting" in the table above is not hand-waving; it has exact kernels. Key idea: the different kinds of jitter are different "differences" of the same phase process ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t), and a time-domain difference is, in the frequency domain, multiplication by a transfer function. We derive the kernels step by step. Step 1: write each edge's time error as a sample of the phase. The kkk-th edge nominally lands at tk=kTt_k=kTtk​=kT; its time error is the phase at that instant divided by the angular velocity (reusing Step 1's Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0)\Delta t=\Delta\phi/(2\pi f_0)Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0​)): Δtk=ϕ(kT)2πf0.\Delta t_k=\frac{\phi(kT)}{2\pi f_0}.Δtk​=2πf0​ϕ(kT)​. Step 2: three jitters = three differences. By definition (spec §2): period jitter:Jkper=Δtk+1−Δtk=ϕ((k+1)T)−ϕ(kT)2πf0(first difference of the phase),cycle-to-cycle:Jkc2c=Jk+1per−Jkper(second difference of the phase),accumulated:Δtk=ϕ(kT)2πf0(no differencing; the phase itself).\begin{aligned} \text{period jitter:}\quad &J^{\text{per}}_k=\Delta t_{k+1}-\Delta t_k=\frac{\phi((k{+}1)T)-\phi(kT)}{2\pi f_0}\quad(\text{first difference of the phase}),\\ \text{cycle-to-cycle:}\quad &J^{\text{c2c}}_k=J^{\text{per}}_{k+1}-J^{\text{per}}_k\quad(\text{second difference of the phase}),\\ \text{accumulated:}\quad &\Delta t_k=\frac{\phi(kT)}{2\pi f_0}\quad(\text{no differencing; the phase itself}). \end{aligned}period jitter:cycle-to-cycle:accumulated:​Jkper​=Δtk+1​−Δtk​=2πf0​ϕ((k+1)T)−ϕ(kT)​(first difference of the phase),Jkc2c​=Jk+1per​−Jkper​(second difference of the phase),Δtk​=2πf0​ϕ(kT)​(no differencing; the phase itself).​ Step 3: differencing in the frequency domain = multiplying by (1−e−j2πfT)(1-e^{-j2\pi fT})(1−e−j2πfT). For a frequency component ϕ(t)∝ej2πft\phi(t)\propto e^{j2\pi ft}ϕ(t)∝ej2πft, a delay of one period TTT is multiplication by e−j2πfTe^{-j2\pi fT}e−j2πfT. So the frequency response of the first-difference operator "now minus one period ago" is Hper(f)=1−e−j2πfT,∣Hper(f)∣2=∣1−e−j2πfT∣2=4sin⁡2(πfT).H_{\text{per}}(f)=1-e^{-j2\pi fT},\qquad \lvert H_{\text{per}}(f)\rvert^2=\big\lvert 1-e^{-j2\pi fT}\big\rvert^2=4\sin^2(\pi fT).Hper​(f)=1−e−j2πfT,∣Hper​(f)∣2=​1−e−j2πfT​2=4sin2(πfT). Algebraic expansion: ∣1−e−jθ∣2=(1−cos⁡θ)2+sin⁡2θ=2−2cos⁡θ=4sin⁡2(θ/2)\lvert 1-e^{-j\theta}\rvert^2=(1-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta=2-2\cos\theta=4\sin^2(\theta/2)∣1−e−jθ∣2=(1−cosθ)2+sin2θ=2−2cosθ=4sin2(θ/2); substituting θ=2πfT\theta=2\pi fTθ=2πfT gives 4sin⁡2(πfT)4\sin^2(\pi fT)4sin2(πfT). Why it is high-pass: as f→0f\to0f→0, sin⁡2(πfT)≈(πfT)2→0\sin^2(\pi fT)\approx(\pi fT)^2\to0sin2(πfT)≈(πfT)2→0 — low frequencies get crushed; the maximum of 444 occurs at f=f0/2=1/(2T)f=f_0/2=1/(2T)f=f0​/2=1/(2T). This is the mathematical reason period jitter is "not dominated by close-in 1/f²". Step 4: put the kernel into the phase-variance integral. Multiply the phase-variance density by ∣H∣2\lvert H\rvert^2∣H∣2, integrate, then divide by (2πf0)2(2\pi f_0)^2(2πf0​)2 to convert to time (spec §10.2, period/cycle-to-cycle jitter kernels): σT2=1(2πf0)2∫0∞Sϕ(f) ∣1−e−j2πfT∣2 df=1(2πf0)2∫0∞Sϕ(f) 4sin⁡2(πfT) df.\sigma_{T}^2=\frac{1}{(2\pi f_0)^2}\int_0^{\infty}S_\phi(f)\,\big\lvert 1-e^{-j2\pi fT}\big\rvert^2\,df =\frac{1}{(2\pi f_0)^2}\int_0^{\infty}S_\phi(f)\,4\sin^2(\pi fT)\,df.σT2​=(2πf0​)21​∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)​1−e−j2πfT​2df=(2πf0​)21​∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)4sin2(πfT)df. Cycle-to-cycle takes one more difference, so the kernel is squared once more (a second difference = the first-difference operator applied twice): σcc2=1(2πf0)2∫0∞Sϕ(f) ∣1−e−j2πfT∣4 df=1(2πf0)2∫0∞Sϕ(f) 16sin⁡4(πfT) df.\sigma_{cc}^2=\frac{1}{(2\pi f_0)^2}\int_0^{\infty}S_\phi(f)\,\big\lvert 1-e^{-j2\pi fT}\big\rvert^4\,df =\frac{1}{(2\pi f_0)^2}\int_0^{\infty}S_\phi(f)\,16\sin^4(\pi fT)\,df.σcc2​=(2πf0​)21​∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)​1−e−j2πfT​4df=(2πf0​)21​∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)16sin4(πfT)df. Accumulated jitter has no differencing kernel (kernel =1=1=1), so it is dominated by low frequencies (the 1/f² integral diverges once carried to very low offset), which is precisely the frequency-domain counterpart of its Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ random-walk growth ([P2] Eq.(8), p.792; κ from Eq.(12), p.793). Dimension check: SϕS_\phiSϕ​ (rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz) × dimensionless kernel × Hz\text{Hz}Hz = rad2\text{rad}^2rad2; dividing by (2πf0)2(2\pi f_0)^2(2πf0​)2 (rad2/s2\text{rad}^2/\text{s}^2rad2/s2) gives s2\text{s}^2s2 ✓, and the square root yields seconds. Three-line comparison: accumulated kernel =1=1=1 (low-frequency dominated); period kernel ∣1−e−j2πfT∣2\lvert1-e^{-j2\pi fT}\rvert^2∣1−e−j2πfT∣2 (first-order high-pass); cycle-to-cycle kernel ∣1−e−j2πfT∣4\lvert1-e^{-j2\pi fT}\rvert^4∣1−e−j2πfT∣4 (second-order high-pass, least sensitive to close-in). Note (constant conventions): the expressions above use the "single-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​, ∫0∞\int_0^\infty∫0∞​" convention; with a double-sided PSD or a different SSB bookkeeping, the prefactor can differ by a factor of 2 — same root cause as the spec §3 factor-of-2 teaching note. For jitter this site always uses Sϕ=2LlinS_\phi=2\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}Sϕ​=2Llin​ with single-sided integration. For exact constants consult each reference's definitions.

documents.t: Continuing Example C: f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz (T=200T=200T=200 ps), L(1MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz, 1/f² slope. Find the period jitter σT\sigma_TσT​ (integrate 1 MHz→100 MHz, the same band as Example C for comparison). Insert the 1/f² shape from Step 3, Sϕ(f)=2×10−10(106/f)2S_\phi(f)=2\times10^{-10}(10^6/f)^2Sϕ​(f)=2×10−10(106/f)2, into the period kernel. First check the kernel's size over this band: T=2×10−10T=2\times10^{-10}T=2×10−10 s; πfT\pi fTπfT at f=106f=10^6f=106 is π×106×2×10−10=6.28×10−4≪1\pi\times10^6\times2\times10^{-10}=6.28\times10^{-4}\ll1π×106×2×10−10=6.28×10−4≪1, and at f=108f=10^8f=108 it is 6.28×10−2≪16.28\times10^{-2}\ll16.28×10−2≪1. So the small-angle form sin⁡2(πfT)≈(πfT)2\sin^2(\pi fT)\approx(\pi fT)^2sin2(πfT)≈(πfT)2 applies over the whole band: ∣1−e−j2πfT∣2≈4(πfT)2=(2πfT)2.\big\lvert 1-e^{-j2\pi fT}\big\rvert^2\approx 4(\pi fT)^2=(2\pi fT)^2.​1−e−j2πfT​2≈4(πfT)2=(2πfT)2. Substitute into the period integral: σT2=1(2πf0)2∫106108 ⁣2×10−10(106f)2(2πfT)2 df=(2πT)2(2πf0)2 2×10−10(106)2∫106108 ⁣df=T4⋅2×10−10(106)2∫106108 ⁣df.\begin{aligned} \sigma_T^2&=\frac{1}{(2\pi f_0)^2}\int_{10^6}^{10^8}\!2\times10^{-10}\Big(\frac{10^6}{f}\Big)^2(2\pi fT)^2\,df\\ &=\frac{(2\pi T)^2}{(2\pi f_0)^2}\,2\times10^{-10}(10^6)^2\int_{10^6}^{10^8}\!df =T^4\cdot 2\times10^{-10}(10^6)^2\int_{10^6}^{10^8}\!df. \end{aligned}σT2​​=(2πf0​)21​∫106108​2×10−10(f106​)2(2πfT)2df=(2πf0​)2(2πT)2​2×10−10(106)2∫106108​df=T4⋅2×10−10(106)2∫106108​df.​ Collect the constants: (2πT)2/(2πf0)2=T2/f02=T2⋅T2=T4(2\pi T)^2/(2\pi f_0)^2=T^2/f_0^2=T^2\cdot T^2=T^4(2πT)2/(2πf0​)2=T2/f02​=T2⋅T2=T4 (since f0=1/Tf_0=1/Tf0​=1/T), and the two powers of fff cancel (f−2⋅f2=1f^{-2}\cdot f^{2}=1f−2⋅f2=1), so the integral becomes ∫106108df=9.9×107\int_{10^6}^{10^8}df=9.9\times10^7∫106108​df=9.9×107 Hz: σT2=T4⋅2×10−10⋅(106)2⋅(9.9×107)=(2×10−10)4⋅2×10−10⋅1012⋅9.9×107.\begin{aligned} \sigma_T^2&=T^4\cdot 2\times10^{-10}\cdot(10^6)^2\cdot(9.9\times10^7)\\ &=(2\times10^{-10})^4\cdot 2\times10^{-10}\cdot10^{12}\cdot9.9\times10^7. \end{aligned}σT2​​=T4⋅2×10−10⋅(106)2⋅(9.9×107)=(2×10−10)4⋅2×10−10⋅1012⋅9.9×107.​ Term by term: T4=(2×10−10)4=16×10−40=1.6×10−39T^4=(2\times10^{-10})^4=16\times10^{-40}=1.6\times10^{-39}T4=(2×10−10)4=16×10−40=1.6×10−39; 2×10−10⋅1012=2×1022\times10^{-10}\cdot10^{12}=2\times10^{2}2×10−10⋅1012=2×102; multiplying by 9.9×1079.9\times10^79.9×107 gives 1.98×10101.98\times10^{10}1.98×1010. So σT2=1.6×10−39×1.98×1010=3.17×10−29 s2 ⇒ σT=5.6×10−15 s=5.6 fs.\sigma_T^2=1.6\times10^{-39}\times1.98\times10^{10}=3.17\times10^{-29}\ \text{s}^2 \;\Rightarrow\;\sigma_T=5.6\times10^{-15}\ \text{s}=5.6\ \text{fs}.σT2​=1.6×10−39×1.98×1010=3.17×10−29 s2⇒σT​=5.6×10−15 s=5.6 fs. Feel, side by side: same phase-noise plot, same integration band — the accumulated/RJ σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs (Example C, lower-limit dominated), yet the period jitter is only ∼5.6\sim5.6∼5.6 fs — almost two orders of magnitude smaller! The reason is exactly the high-pass kernel (2πfT)2(2\pi fT)^2(2πfT)2 crushing the close-in end (the 1 MHz end, the main contributor to RJ); period jitter instead accumulates from the high-frequency end. This is the best possible teaching example of "always say which kind of jitter you are reporting." Dimension check: T4T^4T4 (s4\text{s}^4s4) × (rad2/Hz)×Hz×f0\times\,\text{(rad}^2/\text{Hz)}\times\text{Hz}\times f^{0}×(rad2/Hz)×Hz×f0 collapses to s2\text{s}^2s2 ✓. import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import phase_psd_to_l_dbc_per_hz # noqa: F401 # period jitter: multiply S_phi by |1-e^{-j2πfT}|^2 = 4 sin^2(πfT), integrate, divide by (2πf0)^2 f = np.logspace(6, 8, 200000) f0 = 5e9; T = 1.0/f0 S_phi = 2e-10 * (1e6/f)**2 # 1/f^2, reconstructed from -100 dBc/Hz @1MHz kernel = np.abs(1 - np.exp(-1j*2*np.pi*f*T))**2 # = 4 sin^2(πfT) high-pass kernel sigma_T = np.sqrt(np.trapezoid(S_phi*kernel, f)) / (2*np.pi*f0) print(sigma_T*1e15, "fs period jitter") # -> ~5.6 fs (far below the 447.9 fs RJ)
