documents.t: Problem: a real oscillator is never driven by just one noise source. This example demonstrates multi-source superposition — two independent white-noise sources hitting the same ideal-LC node at once. How do we combine them into a total phase noise? Reuse the oscillator parameters from white_noise_to_phase_noise Example 1 (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC). Superpose two statistically independent white-noise current sources on the node: Device A (e.g. the main transconductor, which sees the full ISF): ΓA,rms=0.5\Gamma_{A,rms}=0.5ΓA,rms​=0.5, Si,A=in,A2‾/Δf=1×10−24 A2/HzS_{i,A}=\overline{i_{n,A}^2}/\Delta f=1\times10^{-24}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si,A​=in,A2​​/Δf=1×10−24 A2/Hz. Device B (a tail-current-source-type device, which only contributes noise during part of the cycle because of cyclostationary gating — see effective_isf and Γeff=Γα\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\alphaΓeff​=Γα): effective Γeff,B,rms=0.25\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}=0.25Γeff,B,rms​=0.25 (half of A's — an illustrative value), but with larger current-noise power Si,B=4×10−24 A2/HzS_{i,B}=4\times10^{-24}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si,B​=4×10−24 A2/Hz (e.g. a device biased with a larger current). The two are distinct physical noise sources and are independent (uncorrelated), so the question is: what is the combined Ltotal(1MHz)\mathcal{L}_{total}(1\text{MHz})Ltotal​(1MHz)? The formula is the same [P1] Eq.(21) shared with white_noise_to_phase_noise. Step 0: why independent sources add in SϕS_\phiSϕ​ (power), not in dB. Each noise source is separately weighted by its (possibly different) ISF and independently integrated into a phase perturbation ϕA(t)\phi_A(t)ϕA​(t), ϕB(t)\phi_B(t)ϕB​(t) (see [P1] Eq.(11)); the total excess phase at the node is the linear superposition ϕ(t)=ϕA(t)+ϕB(t)\phi(t)=\phi_A(t)+\phi_B(t)ϕ(t)=ϕA​(t)+ϕB​(t). For independent (uncorrelated) random processes, the variance/power spectral density adds and the cross term has zero expectation: Sϕ,total(Δω)=⟨(ϕA+ϕB)(ϕA+ϕB)⟩spectrum=Sϕ,A(Δω)+Sϕ,B(Δω)+2 Re⟨ϕAϕB∗⟩⏟=0 (independent).S_{\phi,total}(\Delta\omega)=\big\langle(\phi_A+\phi_B)(\phi_A+\phi_B)\big\rangle_{\text{spectrum}}=S_{\phi,A}(\Delta\omega)+S_{\phi,B}(\Delta\omega)+\underbrace{2\,\text{Re}\langle\phi_A\phi_B^*\rangle}_{=0\ (\text{independent})}.Sϕ,total​(Δω)=⟨(ϕA​+ϕB​)(ϕA​+ϕB​)⟩spectrum​=Sϕ,A​(Δω)+Sϕ,B​(Δω)+=0 (independent)2Re⟨ϕA​ϕB∗​⟩​​. This is the "one-line rule" for this problem: independent sources add in SϕS_\phiSϕ​ (linear power) — you must never add or average two dBc/Hz numbers directly. You have to convert each back to linear, add, and only then take a single 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​. Step 1: compute Device A alone (same recipe as white_noise_to_phase_noise Example 1, using [P1] Eq.(21)). LA=10log⁡10 ⁣(ΓA,rms2qmax2⋅Si,A4 Δω2),Δω=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s, Δω2=3.948×1013.\mathcal{L}_A=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{A,rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_{i,A}}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right),\qquad \Delta\omega=2\pi\times10^6=6.283\times10^6\ \text{rad/s},\ \Delta\omega^2=3.948\times10^{13}.LA​=10log10​(qmax2​ΓA,rms2​​⋅4Δω2Si,A​​),Δω=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s, Δω2=3.948×1013.ΓA,rms2qmax2=0.2510−24=2.5×1023 C−2,Si,A4Δω2=10−241.579×1014=6.332×10−39.\frac{\Gamma_{A,rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}=\frac{0.25}{10^{-24}}=2.5\times10^{23}\ \text{C}^{-2},\qquad \frac{S_{i,A}}{4\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{10^{-24}}{1.579\times10^{14}}=6.332\times10^{-39}.qmax2​ΓA,rms2​​=10−240.25​=2.5×1023 C−2,4Δω2Si,A​​=1.579×101410−24​=6.332×10−39. Linear value inside the parentheses: ℓA=2.5×1023×6.332×10−39=1.583×10−15\ell_A=2.5\times10^{23}\times6.332\times10^{-39}=1.583\times10^{-15}ℓA​=2.5×1023×6.332×10−39=1.583×10−15, so LA=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15)≈−148.0 dBc/Hz\mathcal{L}_A=10\log_{10}(1.583\times10^{-15})\approx-148.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}LA​=10log10​(1.583×10−15)≈−148.0 dBc/Hz (matches white_noise_to_phase_noise Example 1 — same parameters). Step 2: compute Device B alone (same formula, with Γ→Γeff,B,rms\Gamma\to\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}Γ→Γeff,B,rms​, Si→Si,BS_i\to S_{i,B}Si​→Si,B​). Γeff,B,rms2qmax2=0.25210−24=0.062510−24=6.25×1022 C−2,Si,B4Δω2=4×10−241.579×1014=2.533×10−38.\frac{\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}=\frac{0.25^2}{10^{-24}}=\frac{0.0625}{10^{-24}}=6.25\times10^{22}\ \text{C}^{-2},\qquad \frac{S_{i,B}}{4\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{4\times10^{-24}}{1.579\times10^{14}}=2.533\times10^{-38}.qmax2​Γeff,B,rms2​​=10−240.252​=10−240.0625​=6.25×1022 C−2,4Δω2Si,B​​=1.579×10144×10−24​=2.533×10−38. Linear value: ℓB=6.25×1022×2.533×10−38=1.583×10−15\ell_B=6.25\times10^{22}\times2.533\times10^{-38}=1.583\times10^{-15}ℓB​=6.25×1022×2.533×10−38=1.583×10−15, so LB=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15)≈−148.0 dBc/Hz\mathcal{L}_B=10\log_{10}(1.583\times10^{-15})\approx-148.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}LB​=10log10​(1.583×10−15)≈−148.0 dBc/Hz. "You'd think A dominates — it doesn't": at first glance Γeff,B,rms=0.25\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}=0.25Γeff,B,rms​=0.25 is only half of ΓA,rms=0.5\Gamma_{A,rms}=0.5ΓA,rms​=0.5, so intuition suggests Device B's ISF-weight term Γeff,B,rms2/qmax2\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γeff,B,rms2​/qmax2​ is 4×4\times4× smaller (−6-6−6 dB) and B should be completely swamped by A and safely ignored. But Device B's current noise Si,BS_{i,B}Si,B​ happens to be exactly 4×4\times4× larger (+6+6+6 dB) — the two ±6\pm6±6 dB effects exactly cancel, giving LA=LB≈−148.0\mathcal{L}_A=\mathcal{L}_B\approx-148.0LA​=LB​≈−148.0 dBc/Hz: B is just as strong as A and contributes equally — it cannot be neglected. This is exactly the trap you fall into by judging a noise source's contribution from Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ alone: what actually sets the contribution is the product Γrms2⋅Si\Gamma_{rms}^2\cdot S_iΓrms2​⋅Si​, and both factors must be considered together. Step 3: power-sum (add in the linear domain, not in dB). Ltotal=10log⁡10(ℓA+ℓB)=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15+1.583×10−15)=10log⁡10(3.166×10−15).\mathcal{L}_{total}=10\log_{10}\big(\ell_A+\ell_B\big)=10\log_{10}\big(1.583\times10^{-15}+1.583\times10^{-15}\big)=10\log_{10}(3.166\times10^{-15}).Ltotal​=10log10​(ℓA​+ℓB​)=10log10​(1.583×10−15+1.583×10−15)=10log10​(3.166×10−15). Cross-check with the equivalent "dB-domain power-combining formula" (convert each back to linear via 10L/1010^{L/10}10L/10, add, then take a single 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​): Ltotal=10log⁡10 ⁣(10LA/10+10LB/10)=10log⁡10 ⁣(10−148.0/10+10−148.0/10).\mathcal{L}_{total}=10\log_{10}\!\Big(10^{\mathcal{L}_A/10}+10^{\mathcal{L}_B/10}\Big)=10\log_{10}\!\Big(10^{-148.0/10}+10^{-148.0/10}\Big).Ltotal​=10log10​(10LA​/10+10LB​/10)=10log10​(10−148.0/10+10−148.0/10). Result: Ltotal(1 MHz)≈−145.0 dBc/Hz\mathcal{L}_{total}(1\,\text{MHz})\approx-145.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}Ltotal​(1MHz)≈−145.0 dBc/Hz. What just happened arithmetically: AAA and BBB have equal power, so together they give exactly twice the power ⇒10log⁡102≈3.01\Rightarrow 10\log_{10}2\approx3.01⇒10log10​2≈3.01 dB, so Ltotal≈LA+3.0 dB=−148.0+3.0=−145.0\mathcal{L}_{total}\approx\mathcal{L}_A+3.0\ \text{dB}=-148.0+3.0=-145.0Ltotal​≈LA​+3.0 dB=−148.0+3.0=−145.0 dBc/Hz. Device B's contribution to the total noise, expressed as "how much worse than A alone," is X = 3.0 dB — not the 0 dB you'd wrongly conclude by reasoning that "Γeff,B,rms\Gamma_{eff,B,rms}Γeff,B,rms​ is only half" and therefore negligible. One-line rule (memorize this): uncorrelated (independent) noise sources add in SϕS_\phiSϕ​/power — never add dBc/Hz numbers directly, and never average them. Two equal-power sources combine to ×2=+3.0\times2=+3.0×2=+3.0 dB, not +6+6+6 dB (that would only happen for coherent/voltage-amplitude addition; white-noise sources here are uncorrelated). Dimension check: ℓA\ell_AℓA​ and ℓB\ell_BℓB​ each have the form Γrms2/qmax2⋅Si/(4Δω2)\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2\cdot S_i/(4\Delta\omega^2)Γrms2​/qmax2​⋅Si​/(4Δω2), just as in white_noise_to_phase_noise Examples 1 and 2, and both reduce to s\text{s}s (per-Hz, see that page's Example 1 dimension check) — only quantities with the same dimension may be added; the sum is still s\text{s}s, and after 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ it reads as dBc/Hz ✓. import numpy as np qmax = 1e-12 # C dw = 2*np.pi*1e6 # rad/s (offset Δf = 1 MHz) # Device A: main transconductor, sees the full ISF gamma_A, Si_A = 0.5, 1e-24 # (–, A^2/Hz) # Device B: tail device; smaller effective Gamma_eff,rms after cyclostationary gating, but larger current noise gamma_effB, Si_B = 0.25, 4e-24 # (–, A^2/Hz) def bracket(gamma_rms, Si, qmax, dw): return (gamma_rms**2 / qmax**2) * (Si / (4 * dw**2)) # linear value inside [P1] Eq.(21) ell_A = bracket(gamma_A, Si_A, qmax, dw) ell_B = bracket(gamma_effB, Si_B, qmax, dw) L_A = 10*np.log10(ell_A) L_B = 10*np.log10(ell_B) print(round(L_A, 1), "dBc/Hz (A alone)") # -> -148.0 dBc/Hz print(round(L_B, 1), "dBc/Hz (B alone)") # -> -148.0 dBc/Hz # Correct approach: sum the power (linear S_phi), then take one log; never add two dB numbers L_total_via_linear = 10*np.log10(ell_A + ell_B) L_total_via_powersum = 10*np.log10(10**(L_A/10) + 10**(L_B/10)) # equivalent form, for cross-check print(round(L_total_via_linear, 1), "dBc/Hz (A+B power-summed)") # -> -145.0 dBc/Hz print(round(L_total_via_powersum, 1), "dBc/Hz (cross-check)") # -> -145.0 dBc/Hz X_dB = L_total_via_linear - L_A # degradation contributed by B: here A and B contribute equally print(round(X_dB, 1), "dB (B's contribution, even though Gamma_eff,B,rms is only half of Gamma_A,rms)") # -> 3.0 dB (This example continues the [P1] Eq.(21) SSB /4/4/4 convention; both sources use the same formula, each with its own Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (or Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​) and SiS_iSi​, and are summed in power. Using the lab_06 clean time-domain /2/2/2 version instead would shift LA\mathcal{L}_ALA​, LB\mathcal{L}_BLB​, and Ltotal\mathcal{L}_{total}Ltotal​ all up by 333 dB together — leaving the 3.0 dB gap between them unchanged. This echoes the factor-of-2 note in white_noise_to_phase_noise: the constant convention does not affect scaling/relative relationships. The full rule for multi-source superposition and the derivation of the cyclostationary Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ are in effective_isf; full libraries: simulations/common/noise_utils.py, simulations/common/isf_utils.py.)

documents.t: Prerequisites: lti_vs_ltv · Notation | Next: white_noise_to_phase_noise This page answers a prerequisite question: before we can talk about the ISF, we have to pin down "noise" as a stochastic process. Phase jitter in an oscillator originates from the random currents in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) of transistors and resistors. Before feeding it into the phase integral of [P1] Eq.(11), we need to know: how to quantify the "strength" of this random current (PSD), how to recover time-domain power from the PSD (Parseval), whether it is correlated across time instants (autocorrelation), whether a single measurement can represent the whole ensemble (ergodicity), and — most critical for oscillators — whether the noise intensity itself varies periodically with the oscillation phase (cyclostationary). That last point is the core of effective_isf later on: the transistor leaks noise only during the short window when it conducts, and where that window falls in the waveform's phase determines which segment of the ISF weights it. Physical intuition (big picture first): think of noise as "an invisible hand randomly kicking the oscillator at every instant." We need two independent pieces of information: (1) how hard the hand kicks on average (intensity, measured by the PSD); (2) when the hand kicks hardest (time modulation, described by cyclostationarity / the NMF). The ISF is the third item: "at which phase of the waveform a kick changes the phase the most." Multiply the three together and integrate — that is phase noise.
documents.s: Stochastic Noise Basics

documents.t: White noise (a stochastic process whose power spectrum is flat at all frequencies). The name comes from white light — all frequency components with equal strength. Its single-sided PSD (power spectral density) is constant: Si(f)=in2‾Δf=const.S_i(f)=\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=\text{const}.Si​(f)=Δfin2​​​=const. Units: current-noise PSD is in A2/Hz\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}A2/Hz (mean-square current per Hz of bandwidth). Typical thermal-noise expressions: in2‾/Δf=4kT/R\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=4kT/Rin2​​/Δf=4kT/R (resistor) or 4kTγgm4kT\gamma g_m4kTγgm​ (MOS channel). Dimension check: in2‾\overline{i_n^2}in2​​ is A2\text{A}^2A2; dividing by the bandwidth Δf\Delta fΔf (Hz) gives A2/Hz\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}A2/Hz ✓. Physical origin: thermal noise (random thermal motion of carriers) and shot noise (discreteness of carriers crossing a barrier) can both be treated as white over the frequency range we care about. Canonical value: this site's white-noise source uses Si=10−24 A2/HzS_i=10^{-24}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si​=10−24 A2/Hz (see canonical example B). This corresponds to a current-noise density of Si=10−12 A/Hz=1 pA/Hz\sqrt{S_i}=10^{-12}\ \text{A}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}=1\ \text{pA}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}Si​​=10−12 A/Hz​=1 pA/Hz​. Why oscillators care about white noise: white noise has equal-strength components near every nω0n\omega_0nω0​; each ISF harmonic cnc_ncn​ "downconverts" the white noise of the corresponding band to near the carrier, forming the 1/f² (−20-20−20 dB/dec) phase-noise skirt. This is exactly the content of [P1] Eq.(21) — see white_noise_to_phase_noise.

documents.t: Flicker noise (also called 1/f noise: low-frequency noise whose power rises inversely with frequency). In MOS devices it mainly comes from carriers being randomly captured/released by interface traps. Its PSD is not flat: Si,1/f(f)=in2‾⋅ω1/fΔω(Δω<ω1/f),S_{i,1/f}(f)=\overline{i_n^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}\qquad(\Delta\omega < \omega_{1/f}),Si,1/f​(f)=in2​​⋅Δωω1/f​​(Δω<ω1/f​), which is exactly the device flicker model of [P1] Eq.(22), p.185 (site spec Section 3, formula 13). Units: still A2/Hz\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}A2/Hz. ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ is the device's 1/f corner (angular frequency, rad/s) — the frequency at which the 1/f component's strength equals the white-noise floor. Dimension check: in2‾\overline{i_n^2}in2​​ (A2/Hz\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}A2/Hz) × ω1/f/Δω\times\ \omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omega× ω1/f​/Δω (dimensionless ratio) =A2/Hz=\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}=A2/Hz ✓. Key pitfall: the device 1/f corner ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ is not equal to the phase-noise 1/f³ corner. The latter is Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c02/(2Γrms2)\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅c02​/(2Γrms2​) ([P1] Eq.(24)), upconverted only through the ISF's DC coefficient c0c_0c0​. A symmetric waveform (small c0c_0c0​) can push the 1/f³ corner far below the device corner — see symmetry (claim C5). Noise type PSD shape Physical origin Becomes, in phase noise white flat (const A2/Hz\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}A2/Hz) thermal / shot 1/f² (−20-20−20 dB/dec) flicker (1/f) ∝1/f\propto 1/f∝1/f trap capture/release 1/f³ (−30-30−30 dB/dec), via c0c_0c0​ only
documents.s: 2. Flicker (1/f) noise

documents.t: The PSD (power spectral density) tells you "how much power per unit bandwidth." Integrating it over frequency gives the total time-domain power (variance). This is Parseval's theorem (time-domain energy = frequency-domain energy) in its stochastic-process form: in2‾=∫0∞Si(f) df(單邊 PSD).\overline{i_n^2}=\int_0^{\infty}S_i(f)\,df\qquad(\text{單邊 PSD}).in2​​=∫0∞​Si​(f)df(單邊 PSD). Units: left side A2\text{A}^2A2; right side (A2/Hz)×Hz=A2(\text{A}^2/\text{Hz})\times\text{Hz}=\text{A}^2(A2/Hz)×Hz=A2 ✓. Intuition: the PSD is a "density of power," and integrating means "multiply density by bandwidth and add it up." For white noise this integral diverges — so any real system has a finite bandwidth, and white noise is only an in-band approximation. Why it matters: phase noise plays the same trick — integrate the phase PSD Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) over offset frequency to get the phase variance σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​, then convert to rms jitter. Full derivation in psd_phase_noise_jitter. Convention: this site uses the single-sided PSD (positive frequencies only, 0≤f<∞0\le f<\infty0≤f<∞). If you switch to the double-sided (−∞<f<∞-\infty<f<\infty−∞<f<∞) PSD, the value at each frequency is divided by 2. This factor-of-2 convention is the same class of bookkeeping issue as the SSB phase-noise relation L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\frac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​, discussed in detail in white_noise_to_phase_noise.
documents.s: 3. PSD and Parseval: frequency-domain intensity ↔ time-domain power

documents.t: Autocorrelation (how correlated one stochastic process is between two time instants): Ri(τ)=in(t) in(t+τ)‾.R_i(\tau)=\overline{i_n(t)\,i_n(t+\tau)}.Ri​(τ)=in​(t)in​(t+τ)​. Units: A2\text{A}^2A2 (the expectation of a product of two currents). Wiener–Khinchin theorem: autocorrelation and PSD are a Fourier pair. White noise has a flat PSD, corresponding to a delta-function autocorrelation: Ri(τ)=in2‾Δf δ(τ)R_i(\tau)=\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}\,\delta(\tau)Ri​(τ)=Δfin2​​​δ(τ). Intuition: white noise's "value now" is completely uncorrelated with its "value the next instant" (zero memory). This is exactly why, in the phase integral of [P1] Eq.(11), noise contributions at different instants can be superposed independently — it turns the phase-variance calculation into "square and add term by term" with no cross-correlation terms to handle. Flicker counterexample: 1/f noise has a long autocorrelation tail (long memory, strong correlation), which is also why it is hard to integrate and hard to simulate (see the aliasing caveats on the DSP page).
documents.s: 4. Autocorrelation and the real definition of "white"

documents.t: Ergodicity (the property that "time average = ensemble average"). Plain language: you have only one oscillator and measure one long waveform (time average); the theory speaks of the statistics of infinitely many identical oscillators at the same instant (ensemble average). Ergodicity guarantees the two are equal — otherwise "measuring one device" could never validate "the ensemble statistics predicted by theory." Applicability: the process must be stationary (statistics do not drift with time) before ergodicity is even on the table. Thermal noise qualifies. Failure warning: the oscillator's excess phase ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) itself is not stationary — it is a random walk (variance grows linearly with time; see accumulated jitter σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​, [P2] Eq.(8)). So we do statistics on "the time derivative of phase (frequency)" or on "phase differences," not on the absolute value of ϕ\phiϕ. This subtlety is retold in dsp_view_of_phase_noise from the "1/(jω) integrator turns white noise into 1/f²" viewpoint.
documents.s: 5. Ergodicity

documents.t: Cyclostationary noise (a stochastic process whose statistics vary "periodically" with time). [P1] Sec. III-D, p.186 says it plainly: "the channel noise of a MOS device in an oscillator is cyclostationary because the noise power is modulated by the gate-source overdrive which varies with time periodically." ([P1], p.186, cyclostationary paragraph) In other words: the transistor does not leak the same amount of noise at every instant. It is noisy only during the short window when it conducts (large current, large overdrive); the rest of the time it is nearly silent. And "conducting" is locked to the oscillation waveform — repeating once per period TTT. That is "cyclostationarity." [P1] decomposes a white cyclostationary current as ([P1] Eq.(25), p.186): in(t)=in0(t)⋅α(ω0t),i_n(t)=i_{n0}(t)\cdot\alpha(\omega_0 t),in​(t)=in0​(t)⋅α(ω0​t), where in0(t)i_{n0}(t)in0​(t) is a white stationary process (fixed intensity) and α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0 t)α(ω0​t) is a deterministic, periodic, normalized (max = 1) function describing "when the noise amplitude gets turned up or down." This site calls it the NMF — noise-modulating function, symbol α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0 t)α(ω0​t), 0≤α≤10\le\alpha\le10≤α≤1, dimensionless (see the notation page). Units: α\alphaα is dimensionless (it is a normalized envelope); in0i_{n0}in0​ and ini_nin​ are both in A. Dimension check: A=A×(無因次)\text{A}=\text{A}\times(\text{無因次})A=A×(無因次) ✓. Meaning of α2\alpha^2α2: because the PSD deals in power (i2i^2i2), the noise's instantaneous mean-square power is proportional to α2(ω0t)\alpha^2(\omega_0 t)α2(ω0​t). The maximum instantaneous PSD =in2‾/Δf=\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=in2​​/Δf; at all other times it is suppressed by α2≤1\alpha^2\le1α2≤1.
documents.s: 6. Cyclostationary noise — this page's focus, straight into the effective ISF

documents.t: Substitute the cyclostationary decomposition into the phase integral [P1] Eq.(11): the noise contribution at instant τ\tauτ is weighted by Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ), while its own intensity is modulated by α(ω0τ)\alpha(\omega_0\tau)α(ω0​τ). The product of the two periodic functions can be packaged into a single effective ISF ([P1] Eq.(27), p.186): Γeff(ω0τ)=Γ(ω0τ)⋅α(ω0τ) \boxed{\ \Gamma_{eff}(\omega_0\tau)=\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\cdot\alpha(\omega_0\tau)\ } Γeff​(ω0​τ)=Γ(ω0​τ)⋅α(ω0​τ) ​ In [P1]'s own words: "the cyclostationary noise can be treated as a stationary noise applied to a system with an effective ISF." ([P1], p.186) Meaning: just replace Γ\GammaΓ with Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α, and every downstream formula (cnc_ncn​, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, Eq.(21), Eq.(23)) carries over unchanged. Cyclostationarity does not need a new theory; it only changes which curve you take the Fourier coefficients of. Units: Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ is still dimensionless (dimensionless Γ\GammaΓ × dimensionless α\alphaα) ✓. Teaching point: when computing cnc_ncn​ and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, use Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ (i.e., as [P1] puts it, "the effective ISF should be used in all subsequent calculations"), not the bare Γ\GammaΓ.
documents.s: Why this leads straight to the ISF: the effective ISF

documents.t: [P1], p.186 gives two contrasting examples of great pedagogical value: Oscillator Large current (large α\alphaα) occurs at Γ\GammaΓ there Cyclostationary impact Colpitts LC tank-voltage minimum (trough) small (ISF is small at peaks/troughs) Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ differs a lot from Γ\GammaΓ; cannot be ignored ring (single-ended) transitions (zero crossings, max slope) large (ISF is large at transitions) Γeff≈Γ\Gamma_{eff}\approx\GammaΓeff​≈Γ; small impact [P1]'s reading: the Colpitts transistor "turns on only where the ISF is small" — nature effectively injects its noise at insensitive phases, so cyclostationarity helps the LC. The ring is unlucky: the maximum current occurs exactly at the most sensitive transitions, so noise and sensitivity peak simultaneously. [P1] calls it out directly: "This unfortunate coincidence is one of the reasons why ring oscillators in general have inferior phase noise performance compared to a Colpitts LC oscillator." ([P1], p.186) This is one of the two big reasons "LC is cleaner than ring" (the other: a ring burns all of its stored energy every period). Quantitative discussion in [P2] and lc_vs_ring. Toy-model reminder: later pages use toy shapes for α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0 t)α(ω0​t) (e.g., setting the NMF to a conduction window) to demonstrate how Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α changes c0c_0c0​ and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​; these are pedagogical toy models, not transistor-level. The real α\alphaα must be extracted from the device noise model and operating point ([P1] states "α\alphaα can be derived easily from device noise characteristics and operating point").
documents.s: LC vs ring: the cyclostationary impact differs enormously ([P1]'s beautiful conclusion)

documents.t: The full phase-noise recipe is the product of three periodic/stochastic quantities, then integrated: The two "×" signs in the middle are the origin of the effective ISF Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α; the final integrator is what turns white noise into 1/f² (see the DSP viewpoint linked in the next section).

documents.s: Applicability and failure conditions

documents.t: White noise: flat PSD (A2/Hz\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}A2/Hz), delta autocorrelation, memoryless; becomes 1/f² under the ISF. Flicker (1/f) noise: S∝1/fS\propto1/fS∝1/f ([P1] Eq.(22)); upconverts to 1/f³ only via c0c_0c0​; device corner ≠\neq= 1/f³ corner. PSD ↔ Parseval: integrating the PSD gives time-domain power (variance); units self-consistent A2/Hz×Hz=A2\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}\times\text{Hz}=\text{A}^2A2/Hz×Hz=A2. Autocorrelation: white = delta (memoryless); 1/f = long tail (strongly correlated). Ergodicity: time average = ensemble average; but ϕ\phiϕ is a random walk, non-stationary — do statistics on phase differences/frequency. Cyclostationary (this page's protagonist): noise intensity varies periodically with the oscillation phase (the transistor leaks noise only while conducting); described by the NMF α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0 t)α(ω0​t) and packaged as Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α ([P1] Eq.(25)–(27)); LC benefits, ring suffers. Sources: [P1] Sec. III-D (cyclostationary) Eqs.(25)–(27), p.186; device flicker Eq.(22), p.185; claims C9.

documents.t: Prerequisites: oscillator_phase | Next: tank_swing The "quality factor QQQ (the measure of how 'sharp' a resonance is and how much energy is lost per cycle)" appears on almost every page of this site: the Leeson model writes it as 12Q\dfrac{1}{2Q}2Q1​ (derivation_leeson), the LC-vs-ring comparison hinges on it (lc_vs_ring), and the tank-swing trade-off needs it too (tank_swing). Yet on all of those pages it is used as a given — it has never been cleanly derived from the circuit. This page fills that hole: starting from the most basic parallel RLC tank, we derive the three equivalent forms of QQQ and its energy definition step by step, then show how it connects to the active core's −R-R−R, to the tank thermal noise 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​, and finally to how it determines phase noise. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the tank (resonant tank — the energy-storage element in which LLL and CCC exchange energy back and forth) is like a pendulum. QQQ measures "how reluctant this pendulum is to stop" — per radian of oscillation it leaks only a tiny fraction of its stored energy into the loss resistance RpR_pRp​. The higher the QQQ, the sharper the resonance peak, the narrower the bandwidth, and the steeper the phase-vs-frequency slope. Think of noise as a force trying to push the oscillation frequency off: the higher the QQQ, the harder the tank "bites down" on ω0\omega_0ω0​ and refuses to be pushed, so the same lump of noise buys less phase noise. That is why the first slogan of low-phase-noise design is always "make QQQ high." This page answers three questions: What exactly is QQQ? Why are the three forms Q=RpC/L=ω0RpC=Rp/(ω0L)Q=R_p\sqrt{C/L}=\omega_0 R_p C=R_p/(\omega_0 L)Q=Rp​C/L​=ω0​Rp​C=Rp​/(ω0​L) equivalent, and why does it equal ω0×\omega_0\timesω0​× (stored energy / dissipated power)? A real tank always has loss RpR_pRp​, so the oscillation decays — how does the active core restore it with −R-R−R? And why is that cancelled RpR_pRp​ precisely the source of the tank thermal noise 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​? How does QQQ connect to phase noise? Why "high QQQ → narrow band → steep phase slope → less noise per unit offset," and why is this the same thing as the ISF's Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​? Honesty note (read first): this page's RLC tank, definition of QQQ with its three equivalent forms, and 4kTR4kTR4kTR thermal noise are all standard circuit-theory / microwave-engineering textbook material (external literature, not among the 5 source PDFs) — e.g., Razavi, RF Microelectronics; Pozar, Microwave Engineering; Lee, The Design of CMOS RFICs. This site does not reinvent these constants; it only derives them cleanly and connects them to the verified ISF results within the 5 PDFs ([P1] Eq.(21), etc.). Every connection to [P1]/[P2] is tagged with paper id + equation.
documents.s: Tank Q and Energy Restoration

documents.t: The most basic LC-oscillator tank is a parallel RLC: an inductor LLL, a capacitor CCC, and one parallel loss resistor RpR_pRp​ (all tank losses — inductor series resistance, capacitor dielectric loss, radiation — lumped into this single equivalent parallel resistance). First define the resonant angular frequency. At one particular frequency, the parallel LC's inductive and capacitive susceptances cancel, the impedance is purely resistive, and the energy swaps entirely back and forth between LLL and CCC: ω0=1LC.\omega_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}.ω0​=LC​1​. Physics used: inductor impedance jωLj\omega LjωL, capacitor impedance 1/(jωC)1/(j\omega C)1/(jωC). In parallel, susceptances add: 1jωL+jωC=j(ωC−1ωL)\dfrac{1}{j\omega L}+j\omega C=j\big(\omega C-\dfrac{1}{\omega L}\big)jωL1​+jωC=j(ωC−ωL1​); setting the bracket to zero gives ω02=1/(LC)\omega_0^2=1/(LC)ω02​=1/(LC). Unit check: [LC]=H⋅F=(V⋅s/A)(A⋅s/V)=s2=s[\sqrt{LC}]=\sqrt{\text{H}\cdot\text{F}}=\sqrt{(\text{V·s/A})(\text{A·s/V})}=\sqrt{\text{s}^2}=\text{s}[LC​]=H⋅F​=(V⋅s/A)(A⋅s/V)​=s2​=s, so 1/LC1/\sqrt{LC}1/LC​ is in rad/s ✓. Unloaded vs loaded QQQ — settle the distinction up front: Unloaded QQQ (Q0Q_0Q0​, unloaded quality factor): the QQQ counting only the tank's own losses (RpR_pRp​ purely from the tank elements). It is the intrinsic "quality" of the tank components themselves. Loaded QQQ (QLQ_LQL​, loaded quality factor): the QQQ after external loading (downstream circuitry, measurement instruments, buffer input impedance) is folded in. The external load is effectively another parallel resistor RextR_{ext}Rext​; the total parallel resistance Rp∥RextR_p\parallel R_{ext}Rp​∥Rext​ is smaller than RpR_pRp​, so QL<Q0Q_L<Q_0QL​<Q0​. Relation between the two: 1QL=1Q0+1Qext\dfrac{1}{Q_L}=\dfrac{1}{Q_0}+\dfrac{1}{Q_{ext}}QL​1​=Q0​1​+Qext​1​ (conductances add → reciprocal QQQ's add, since Q∝Rp∝1/GQ\propto R_p\propto 1/GQ∝Rp​∝1/G). What this page derives, and what determines phase noise, is primarily the loaded QQQ (what the oscillator actually sees); inductor design, however, cares about the unloaded QQQ. Below, unless stated otherwise, QQQ means the oscillation loop's actual effective (loaded) QQQ. Now derive QQQ. The circuit definition of the parallel-RLC QQQ is "at resonance, the energy flow stored in a reactive element (LLL or CCC) relative to the dissipation rate in the resistor RpR_pRp​." The most convenient equivalent algebraic definition is the ratio of the capacitor's (or inductor's) susceptance magnitude to the conductance at resonance: Q=∣BC(ω0)∣G=ω0C1/Rp=ω0RpC.Q=\frac{|B_C(\omega_0)|}{G}=\frac{\omega_0 C}{1/R_p}=\omega_0 R_p C.Q=G∣BC​(ω0​)∣​=1/Rp​ω0​C​=ω0​Rp​C. Physics used: in a parallel RLC, the conductance G=1/RpG=1/R_pG=1/Rp​ is the only dissipative element; the capacitive susceptance BC=ω0CB_C=\omega_0 CBC​=ω0​C measures how large the "reactive current" is. QQQ is the ratio of reactive current to real (dissipative) current. Unit check: [ω0RpC]=(rad/s)(Ω)(F)=(1/s)(V/A)(A⋅s/V)=[\omega_0 R_p C]=(\text{rad/s})(\Omega)(\text{F})=(\text{1/s})(\text{V/A})(\text{A·s/V})=[ω0​Rp​C]=(rad/s)(Ω)(F)=(1/s)(V/A)(A⋅s/V)= dimensionless ✓. Substituting ω0=1/LC\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}ω0​=1/LC​ gives the second form: Q=ω0RpC=RpCLC=RpC2LC=RpCL.Q=\omega_0 R_p C=\frac{R_p C}{\sqrt{LC}}=R_p\sqrt{\frac{C^2}{LC}}=R_p\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}.Q=ω0​Rp​C=LC​Rp​C​=Rp​LCC2​​=Rp​LC​​. Every algebra step: ω0C=C/LC=C2/(LC)=C/L\omega_0 C=C/\sqrt{LC}=\sqrt{C^2/(LC)}=\sqrt{C/L}ω0​C=C/LC​=C2/(LC)​=C/L​; multiply by RpR_pRp​ and you are done. Unit check: C/L=F/H=(A⋅s/V)/(V⋅s/A)=A2/V2=A/V=1/Ω\sqrt{C/L}=\sqrt{\text{F/H}}=\sqrt{(\text{A·s/V})/(\text{V·s/A})}=\sqrt{\text{A}^2/\text{V}^2}=\text{A/V}=1/\OmegaC/L​=F/H​=(A⋅s/V)/(V⋅s/A)​=A2/V2​=A/V=1/Ω, times RpR_pRp​ (Ω\OmegaΩ) → dimensionless ✓. The quantity L/C\sqrt{L/C}L/C​ has units of resistance and is called the tank's characteristic impedance R0=L/CR_0=\sqrt{L/C}R0​=L/C​, so we may also write Q=Rp/R0Q=R_p/R_0Q=Rp​/R0​ — "how large the parallel loss resistance is relative to the characteristic impedance." The third form uses ω0=1/LC\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}ω0​=1/LC​ to swap CCC for LLL. Because at resonance the inductive susceptance magnitude equals the capacitive susceptance magnitude (ω0L\omega_0 Lω0​L and 1/(ω0C)1/(\omega_0 C)1/(ω0​C) are reciprocals of each other), the same ratio can also be written as the reciprocal of conductance ×\times× inductive reactance: Q=ω0RpC=Rpω0L.Q=\omega_0 R_p C=\frac{R_p}{\omega_0 L}.Q=ω0​Rp​C=ω0​LRp​​. Algebraic verification: ω0RpC⋅ω0L=ω02LC Rp=Rp\omega_0 R_p C\cdot\omega_0 L=\omega_0^2 LC\,R_p=R_pω0​Rp​C⋅ω0​L=ω02​LCRp​=Rp​ (since ω02LC=1\omega_0^2 LC=1ω02​LC=1); divide both sides by ω0L\omega_0 Lω0​L to get ω0RpC=Rp/(ω0L)\omega_0 R_p C=R_p/(\omega_0 L)ω0​Rp​C=Rp​/(ω0​L) ✓. Unit check: Rp/(ω0L)=Ω/[(rad/s)(H)]=Ω/Ω=R_p/(\omega_0 L)=\Omega/[(\text{rad/s})(\text{H})]=\Omega/\Omega=Rp​/(ω0​L)=Ω/[(rad/s)(H)]=Ω/Ω= dimensionless ✓. The three forms are equivalent — collected here (cited directly across the site): Q=ω0RpC=RpCL=Rpω0L=RpR0,R0≡LC.Q=\omega_0 R_p C=R_p\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}=\frac{R_p}{\omega_0 L}=\frac{R_p}{R_0},\qquad R_0\equiv\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}.Q=ω0​Rp​C=Rp​LC​​=ω0​LRp​​=R0​Rp​​,R0​≡CL​​. Physical reading (extremely important): note that RpR_pRp​ is in the numerator. In a parallel tank, larger RpR_pRp​ means higher QQQ (in parallel, a large resistance = a small loss conductance = less leakage). This is the opposite of the series-RLC intuition (series Q=ω0L/RsQ=\omega_0 L/R_sQ=ω0​L/Rs​ with RsR_sRs​ in the denominator) — the classic beginner mix-up. This site models oscillators exclusively with the parallel form; remember "parallel: large RpR_pRp​ → high QQQ." Form When to use it One-line reading Q=ω0RpCQ=\omega_0 R_p CQ=ω0​Rp​C CCC, RpR_pRp​, ω0\omega_0ω0​ known (most common) loss resistance ×\times× capacitive susceptance Q=RpC/L=Rp/R0Q=R_p\sqrt{C/L}=R_p/R_0Q=Rp​C/L​=Rp​/R0​ when comparing "RpR_pRp​ against the characteristic impedance" how large the loss resistance is relative to R0=L/CR_0=\sqrt{L/C}R0​=L/C​ Q=Rp/(ω0L)Q=R_p/(\omega_0 L)Q=Rp​/(ω0​L) LLL, RpR_pRp​ known loss resistance relative to inductive reactance

documents.t: The most physical, most field-agnostic definition of QQQ is the energy definition: Q=ω0 EstoredPdiss=2π 每週期儲存的能量每週期耗散的能量.Q=\omega_0\,\frac{E_{stored}}{P_{diss}}=2\pi\,\frac{\text{每週期儲存的能量}}{\text{每週期耗散的能量}}.Q=ω0​Pdiss​Estored​​=2π每週期耗散的能量每週期儲存的能量​. Meaning: Q/(2π)Q/(2\pi)Q/(2π) = stored energy / energy dissipated per cycle. The higher the QQQ, the smaller the fraction 2π/Q2\pi/Q2π/Q of the stored energy leaked per oscillation cycle. Hence "QQQ is roughly the number of radians for a free oscillation to decay to 1/e1/e1/e" (more precisely: the energy envelope is e−ω0t/Qe^{-\omega_0 t/Q}e−ω0​t/Q; see below). Unit check: ω0E/P=(rad/s)(J)/(W)=(rad/s)(J)/(J/s)=\omega_0 E/P=(\text{rad/s})(\text{J})/(\text{W})=(\text{rad/s})(\text{J})/(\text{J/s})=ω0​E/P=(rad/s)(J)/(W)=(rad/s)(J)/(J/s)= dimensionless (rad) ✓. Proof that it equals Step 1's ω0RpC\omega_0 R_p Cω0​Rp​C. At resonance, let the voltage across the tank be v(t)=Vpcos⁡ω0tv(t)=V_p\cos\omega_0 tv(t)=Vp​cosω0​t. (1) Stored energy: at resonance the energy swaps entirely between LLL and CCC; the total stored energy is conserved and equals the peak capacitor energy (at the voltage peak, all the energy is in CCC): Estored=12CVp2.E_{stored}=\frac{1}{2}C V_p^2.Estored​=21​CVp2​. Conservation check: capacitor energy 12Cv2=12CVp2cos⁡2ω0t\tfrac12 C v^2=\tfrac12 C V_p^2\cos^2\omega_0 t21​Cv2=21​CVp2​cos2ω0​t; inductor energy 12LiL2\tfrac12 L i_L^221​LiL2​, where iL=1L∫v dt=Vpω0Lsin⁡ω0ti_L=\tfrac1L\int v\,dt=\tfrac{V_p}{\omega_0 L}\sin\omega_0 tiL​=L1​∫vdt=ω0​LVp​​sinω0​t, so the inductor energy =12LVp2ω02L2sin⁡2ω0t=12Vp2ω02Lsin⁡2ω0t=\tfrac12 L\tfrac{V_p^2}{\omega_0^2 L^2}\sin^2\omega_0 t=\tfrac12\tfrac{V_p^2}{\omega_0^2 L}\sin^2\omega_0 t=21​Lω02​L2Vp2​​sin2ω0​t=21​ω02​LVp2​​sin2ω0​t. Using ω02L=1/C\omega_0^2 L=1/Cω02​L=1/C, this becomes 12CVp2sin⁡2ω0t\tfrac12 C V_p^2\sin^2\omega_0 t21​CVp2​sin2ω0​t. The sum =12CVp2(cos⁡2+sin⁡2)=12CVp2=\tfrac12 C V_p^2(\cos^2+\sin^2)=\tfrac12 C V_p^2=21​CVp2​(cos2+sin2)=21​CVp2​ — indeed conserved ✓. (2) Dissipated power: only RpR_pRp​ dissipates; the average power (mean square of a sinusoid = half the peak squared): Pdiss=v2‾Rp=Vp2/2Rp=Vp22Rp.P_{diss}=\frac{\overline{v^2}}{R_p}=\frac{V_p^2/2}{R_p}=\frac{V_p^2}{2R_p}.Pdiss​=Rp​v2​=Rp​Vp2​/2​=2Rp​Vp2​​. (3) Substitute into the energy definition: Q=ω0EstoredPdiss=ω0⋅12CVp2 Vp2/(2Rp) =ω0⋅12CVp2⋅2RpVp2=ω0RpC.Q=\omega_0\frac{E_{stored}}{P_{diss}}=\omega_0\cdot\frac{\tfrac12 C V_p^2}{\,V_p^2/(2R_p)\,}=\omega_0\cdot\frac{\tfrac12 C V_p^2\cdot 2R_p}{V_p^2}=\omega_0 R_p C.Q=ω0​Pdiss​Estored​​=ω0​⋅Vp2​/(2Rp​)21​CVp2​​=ω0​⋅Vp2​21​CVp2​⋅2Rp​​=ω0​Rp​C. Vp2V_p^2Vp2​ and the factors 12,2\tfrac12,221​,2 all cancel, landing exactly back on Step 1's ω0RpC\omega_0 R_p Cω0​Rp​C ✓. The energy definition and the circuit definition are the same QQQ — no coincidence: both measure the same thing, the fraction of stored energy leaked per radian. Unit check: ω0⋅[F][V2][V2]/[Ω]=(rad/s)[F][Ω]=(rad/s)[s]=\omega_0\cdot\dfrac{[\text{F}][\text{V}^2]}{[\text{V}^2]/[\Omega]}=(\text{rad/s})[\text{F}][\Omega]=(\text{rad/s})[\text{s}]=ω0​⋅[V2]/[Ω][F][V2]​=(rad/s)[F][Ω]=(rad/s)[s]= dimensionless ✓. The free-decay rate falls out as a bonus (for the "QQQ = so many radians" intuition): with no active core replenishing energy, the tank dissipates Pdiss=ω0E/QP_{diss}=\omega_0 E/QPdiss​=ω0​E/Q per second, i.e. dEdt=−ω0QE\dfrac{dE}{dt}=-\dfrac{\omega_0}{Q}EdtdE​=−Qω0​​E, whose solution is E(t)=E0 e−ω0t/Q⇒v(t) 包絡 ∝e−ω0t/(2Q).E(t)=E_0\,e^{-\omega_0 t/Q}\quad\Rightarrow\quad v(t)\ \text{包絡}\ \propto e^{-\omega_0 t/(2Q)}.E(t)=E0​e−ω0​t/Q⇒v(t) 包絡 ∝e−ω0​t/(2Q). Reading: energy decay time constant τE=Q/ω0\tau_E=Q/\omega_0τE​=Q/ω0​; oscillation-amplitude decay time constant 2Q/ω02Q/\omega_02Q/ω0​. For a Q=100Q=100Q=100, 5 GHz tank (ω0=2π×5×109\omega_0=2\pi\times5\times10^9ω0​=2π×5×109), the free amplitude-decay constant is about 2×100/(2π×5×109)≈6.42\times100/(2\pi\times5\times10^9)\approx6.42×100/(2π×5×109)≈6.4 ns, roughly 32 cycles — this is why a real oscillator must have an active core continuously restoring energy, or it stops within a few tens of cycles. Which brings us to Step 3.

documents.t: Step 2 showed: as long as RpR_pRp​ is there, the oscillation decays as e−ω0t/(2Q)e^{-\omega_0 t/(2Q)}e−ω0​t/(2Q). To sustain steady oscillation, the oscillator's active core (e.g., the negative conductance provided by a cross-coupled differential pair) must replenish, cycle by cycle, the energy that RpR_pRp​ leaks. The cleanest view: the active core presents a negative resistance −R-R−R (negative conductance −Gm-G_m−Gm​) across the tank, in parallel with RpR_pRp​. 1Rtank=1Rp−Gm,起振條件: Gm≥1Rp (即 −R≤−Rp).\frac{1}{R_{tank}}=\frac{1}{R_p}-G_m,\qquad \text{起振條件}:\ G_m\ge\frac{1}{R_p}\ \big(\text{即 } -R\le -R_p\big).Rtank​1​=Rp​1​−Gm​,起振條件: Gm​≥Rp​1​ (即 −R≤−Rp​). Physical meaning: positive resistance absorbs energy; negative resistance supplies it. When the active core's negative conductance GmG_mGm​ exactly equals RpR_pRp​'s conductance 1/Rp1/R_p1/Rp​, the total loss is zero and the oscillation holds constant amplitude (the Barkhausen start-up boundary). In practice, GmG_mGm​ is designed slightly larger than 1/Rp1/R_p1/Rp​ (loop gain >1>1>1) to guarantee start-up, and nonlinear saturation then pulls the effective GmG_mGm​ back to exact cancellation — the circuit-level incarnation of the limit-cycle amplitude-restoring mechanism described in oscillator_phase. Unit check: GmG_mGm​ and 1/Rp1/R_p1/Rp​ are both in siemens (S) ✓. Key clarification: what the active core cancels is RpR_pRp​'s deterministic energy loss (keeping the oscillation from decaying). It does not — and cannot — cancel the random thermal noise that RpR_pRp​ brings. That is the point of the next paragraph, and the bridge from this whole page to phase noise. RpR_pRp​ is the physical source of the tank thermal-noise current 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​. Any dissipative resistance (including the equivalent loss RpR_pRp​) is necessarily accompanied by thermal noise, per the Johnson–Nyquist theorem. A parallel resistance is most conveniently represented by its Norton-equivalent noise current source, with single-sided PSD: in,R2‾Δf=4kTRp.\frac{\overline{i_{n,R}^2}}{\Delta f}=\frac{4kT}{R_p}.Δfin,R2​​​=Rp​4kT​. Physics used: the fluctuation–dissipation theorem — where there is dissipation, there is fluctuation. The resistor thermal-noise voltage PSD is 4kTRp4kTR_p4kTRp​ (covered in psd_phase_noise_jitter); converting to a parallel Norton current source means dividing by Rp2R_p^2Rp2​: in2‾/Δf=(4kTRp)/Rp2=4kT/Rp\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=(4kTR_p)/R_p^2=4kT/R_pin2​​/Δf=(4kTRp​)/Rp2​=4kT/Rp​. Unit check: [4kT/Rp]=J/Ω=(V⋅A⋅s)/(V/A)=A2s=A2/Hz[4kT/R_p]=\text{J}/\Omega=(\text{V·A·s})/(\text{V/A})=\text{A}^2\text{s}=\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}[4kT/Rp​]=J/Ω=(V⋅A⋅s)/(V/A)=A2s=A2/Hz ✓ (single-sided current PSD, consistent with the spec's notation of in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf in A²/Hz). The deep point: you cannot cancel this noise with −R-R−R as well. The active core's −R-R−R cancels RpR_pRp​'s loss term on the "energy balance" ledger; but the random 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​ current that RpR_pRp​ injects on the "fluctuation" ledger is sustained — equally amplified — by the very energy the active core pumps back in. So the tank loss RpR_pRp​ is simultaneously the source of two things: it forces you to add an active core to restore energy, and it hands you an unavoidable baseline thermal-noise floor. This is the physical root tying QQQ to phase noise. (The active core's own devices add still more noise — that is the topic of device_noise_mapping; this page covers only the tank's own 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​.) Expressing RpR_pRp​ in terms of QQQ (to hook into phase noise next): from Step 1, Rp=Q/(ω0C)=Q ω0L=Q R0R_p=Q/(\omega_0 C)=Q\,\omega_0 L=Q\,R_0Rp​=Q/(ω0​C)=Qω0​L=QR0​, so at the same capacitance/frequency, 4kTRp=4kT ω0CQ⇒in,R2‾/Δf ∝ 1Q.\frac{4kT}{R_p}=\frac{4kT\,\omega_0 C}{Q}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \overline{i_{n,R}^2}/\Delta f\ \propto\ \frac{1}{Q}.Rp​4kT​=Q4kTω0​C​⇒in,R2​​/Δf ∝ Q1​. Reading: higher QQQ → larger RpR_pRp​ → smaller tank-injected thermal-noise current PSD (∝1/Q\propto 1/Q∝1/Q). This is the first layer of "high QQQ → low phase noise" (the noise source shrinks); the "narrow-band / steep-slope" effect of Step 2 is the second layer. Stack the two and you get the next step.

documents.t: (a) High QQQ = narrow bandwidth = steep phase slope. The standard relation between QQQ and the 3-dB bandwidth: Q=ω0Δω3dB⇔Δω3dB=ω0Q.Q=\frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega_{3\mathrm{dB}}}\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad \Delta\omega_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\frac{\omega_0}{Q}.Q=Δω3dB​ω0​​⇔Δω3dB​=Qω0​​. Derivation sketch: the parallel-RLC impedance is Z(ω)=(1Rp+jωC+1jωL)−1Z(\omega)=\big(\tfrac{1}{R_p}+j\omega C+\tfrac{1}{j\omega L}\big)^{-1}Z(ω)=(Rp​1​+jωC+jωL1​)−1; expanding to first order near ω0\omega_0ω0​ with ω=ω0+Δω\omega=\omega_0+\Delta\omegaω=ω0​+Δω, the susceptance part is ≈j 2CΔω\approx j\,2C\Delta\omega≈j2CΔω, giving Z≈Rp/(1+j 2QΔω/ω0)Z\approx R_p/(1+j\,2Q\Delta\omega/\omega_0)Z≈Rp​/(1+j2QΔω/ω0​). ∣Z∣|Z|∣Z∣ drops to 1/21/\sqrt21/2​ of the peak (−3 dB) when 2QΔω/ω0=12Q\Delta\omega/\omega_0=12QΔω/ω0​=1, i.e. half-bandwidth Δω=ω0/(2Q)\Delta\omega=\omega_0/(2Q)Δω=ω0​/(2Q), full bandwidth ω0/Q\omega_0/Qω0​/Q ✓. Phase slope: the phase of the above is ∠Z=−arctan⁡(2QΔω/ω0)\angle Z=-\arctan(2Q\Delta\omega/\omega_0)∠Z=−arctan(2QΔω/ω0​), whose slope with respect to ω\omegaω at ω0\omega_0ω0​ is d∠Zdω∣ω0=−2Qω0\dfrac{d\angle Z}{d\omega}\big|_{\omega_0}=-\dfrac{2Q}{\omega_0}dωd∠Z​​ω0​​=−ω0​2Q​. The higher the QQQ, the steeper the phase-vs-frequency slope. Physical meaning (why a steep phase slope = low phase noise): the oscillation locks to the frequency where "the total loop phase shift = 0." If noise tries to push the phase away from 0, the tank's steep phase slope applies a large "frequency restoring force" pulling it back to ω0\omega_0ω0​ — the steeper the phase slope dϕ/dωd\phi/d\omegadϕ/dω, the smaller the frequency (and hence long-term phase) offset that a given phase perturbation corresponds to. The tank acts like a very stiff spring clamping the oscillation frequency at ω0\omega_0ω0​. This is precisely the physical origin of the Leeson shaping term (ω02QΔω)2\big(\tfrac{\omega_0}{2Q\Delta\omega}\big)^2(2QΔωω0​​)2 (derivation_leeson, Step 2). (b) 1/Q21/Q^21/Q2 scaling (Leeson). Stack (a)'s narrow-band shaping on top of Step 3's 1/Q1/Q1/Q noise source, then run it through the autonomous oscillator's phase integration (1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2): the QQQ dependence of phase noise lands at 1/Q21/Q^21/Q2: L(Δω) ∝ (ω02Q Δω)2 ∝ 1Q2.\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega)\ \propto\ \Big(\frac{\omega_0}{2Q\,\Delta\omega}\Big)^2\ \propto\ \frac{1}{Q^2}.L(Δω) ∝ (2QΔωω0​​)2 ∝ Q21​. Reading: doubling QQQ → phase noise improves by 10log⁡10(22)=6.0210\log_{10}(2^2)=6.0210log10​(22)=6.02 dB. This is the same inverse-square law as tank_swing's "double qmaxq_{max}qmax​ → −6 dB" — QQQ and qmaxq_{max}qmax​ are two independent levers that each "pay off quadratically" toward low phase noise. Note: the shaping expression (ω02QΔω)2\big(\tfrac{\omega_0}{2Q\Delta\omega}\big)^2(2QΔωω0​​)2 belongs to the Leeson model (external literature, not among the 5 source PDFs; see derivation_leeson). (c) Q ↔ Γrms/qmax equivalence (this site's core correspondence). derivation_leeson (Step 5, comparison table) asserts: Leeson's 12Q\dfrac{1}{2Q}2Q1​ and the ISF's Γrmsqmax\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}}{q_{max}}qmax​Γrms​​ describe the same thing — "the efficiency of converting tank/device noise into phase skirts." Putting the two 1/f21/f^21/f2 results side by side makes it clear: Model 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase skirt "noise → phase" efficiency factor Source Leeson (external, not among the 5 PDFs) ∝(ω02Q Δω)2\propto\big(\dfrac{\omega_0}{2Q\,\Delta\omega}\big)^2∝(2QΔωω0​​)2 12Q\dfrac{1}{2Q}2Q1​ (high QQQ → low efficiency → less noise) [E1] Leeson 1966 ISF ([P1], within the 5 PDFs) Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4Δω2\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\Delta\omega^2}qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​ Γrmsqmax\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}}{q_{max}}qmax​Γrms​​ (small → less noise) [P1] Eq.(21), p.185 The correspondence: 12Q ⟷ Γrmsqmax×(載波/雜訊功率正規化).\frac{1}{2Q}\ \longleftrightarrow\ \frac{\Gamma_{rms}}{q_{max}}\times(\text{載波/雜訊功率正規化}).2Q1​ ⟷ qmax​Γrms​​×(載波/雜訊功率正規化). How to read it: high QQQ ⟺ low Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ ⟺ low phase noise. Both are the ratio of "how much phase the same lump of noise buys." Why the ISF is more general: QQQ is an LC-tank concept (you need a resonant energy-storage element to even have a QQQ); a ring oscillator has no high-QQQ tank — no QQQ at all — yet it still has Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and qmaxq_{max}qmax​, so [P1]'s Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ holds for rings just as well, while Leeson's 1/(2Q)1/(2Q)1/(2Q) fails for rings (see lc_vs_ring). QQQ is the incarnation of Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ in the special case "a resonant tank exists." That is the full meaning of the Q↔Γrms/qmaxQ\leftrightarrow\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Q↔Γrms​/qmax​ equivalence claimed in derivation_leeson.

documents.t: In theory you could keep raising QQQ by making RpR_pRp​ large, but in a silicon process QQQ hits a hard ceiling, and the causes almost all trace back to the inductor and parasitics: Limiting source Why it suppresses QQQ Typical magnitude / consequence spiral-inductor metal series resistance RsR_sRs​ finite metal conductivity + skin effect / proximity effect raise RsR_sRs​ at high frequency; the series RsR_sRs​ converted to parallel, Rp≈QL2RsR_p\approx Q_L^2 R_sRp​≈QL2​Rs​, is capped on-chip inductor unloaded QQQ is often only 5–15 (~20 in advanced nodes); only discrete/MEMS reach the hundreds substrate loss the silicon substrate conducts: magnetically induced eddy currents + capacitive coupling leak energy into the substrate worst at high frequency; drags QQQ down further capacitor / varactor loss the varactor (voltage-controlled capacitor used to tune f0f_0f0​) has series resistance and finite QCQ_CQC​ the wider the tuning range, the larger the varactor's share and the more it drags down the tank QQQ external loading (loaded QQQ) the buffer / next stage effectively parallels in an RextR_{ext}Rext​, so QL<Q0Q_L<Q_0QL​<Q0​ (Step 1) the heavier the measurement or drive loading, the lower the effective QQQ → worse phase noise parasitic capacitance wiring/device parasitics CparC_{par}Cpar​ parallel into the tank, eating the usable CCC tuning range and possibly adding extra loss limits the maximum f0f_0f0​ and the swing Design implication: because on-chip QQQ is stuck at ~10–20, LC-oscillator phase-noise improvements often come not from raising QQQ (there is little headroom) but from enlarging the swing to raise qmaxq_{max}qmax​ — exactly the theme of tank_swing. The design knob "raising tank QQQ is nearly-free swing" (at the same IbiasI_{bias}Ibias​, larger RpR_pRp​ → larger swing ≈4πIbiasRp\approx\tfrac{4}{\pi}I_{bias}R_p≈π4​Ibias​Rp​) has its upper limit locked by this inductor-QQQ ceiling. Why rings do not rely on QQQ: a ring oscillator has no resonant tank at all (no QQQ); it uses the number of stages NNN and per-stage current/swing as levers instead — another reason the ISF's Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ framework (which needs no QQQ) is more general than Leeson (see lc_vs_ring). Honesty note: this section's typical inductor-QQQ values (5–20), skin/proximity effects, substrate loss, and varactor QQQ are all standard RFIC design knowledge (external, not among the 5 source PDFs; e.g., Lee, CMOS RFICs; Razavi, RF Microelectronics; Niknejad's inductor work). Exact numbers vary widely across process generations; only order-of-magnitude feel is given here. TODO: to cite a specific process's inductor-QQQ curves, consult that process's documentation.

documents.t: The parallel-RLC QQQ has four equivalent forms: Q=ω0RpC=RpC/L=Rp/(ω0L)=Rp/R0Q=\omega_0 R_p C=R_p\sqrt{C/L}=R_p/(\omega_0 L)=R_p/R_0Q=ω0​Rp​C=Rp​C/L​=Rp​/(ω0​L)=Rp​/R0​ (R0=L/CR_0=\sqrt{L/C}R0​=L/C​); in parallel, RpR_pRp​ sits in the numerator — large RpR_pRp​ → high QQQ. The energy definition Q=ω0 Estored/PdissQ=\omega_0\,E_{stored}/P_{diss}Q=ω0​Estored​/Pdiss​ agrees exactly with the above (substituting v=Vpcos⁡ω0tv=V_p\cos\omega_0 tv=Vp​cosω0​t yields ω0RpC\omega_0 R_p Cω0​Rp​C; Vp2V_p^2Vp2​ cancels entirely). Without an active core the energy decays as ∝e−ω0t/Q\propto e^{-\omega_0 t/Q}∝e−ω0​t/Q; the active core uses −R-R−R (negative conductance Gm≥1/RpG_m\ge1/R_pGm​≥1/Rp​) to cancel RpR_pRp​'s energy loss, but cannot cancel RpR_pRp​'s thermal noise. RpR_pRp​ is the physical source of the tank thermal-noise current 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​ (single-sided PSD, A²/Hz); Rp=Q R0R_p=Q\,R_0Rp​=QR0​, hence 4kT/Rp∝1/Q4kT/R_p\propto 1/Q4kT/Rp​∝1/Q. Q=ω0/Δω3dBQ=\omega_0/\Delta\omega_{3\mathrm{dB}}Q=ω0​/Δω3dB​: high QQQ → narrow band → steep phase slope −2Q/ω0-2Q/\omega_0−2Q/ω0​ → frequency clamped → phase noise ∝1/Q2\propto1/Q^2∝1/Q2 (−6 dB per doubling of QQQ; Leeson, external, not among the 5 source PDFs). Q↔Γrms/qmaxQ\leftrightarrow\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Q↔Γrms​/qmax​: Leeson's 1/(2Q)1/(2Q)1/(2Q) and [P1] Eq.(21)'s Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ are the same "noise → phase" efficiency; high QQQ = low Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ = low phase noise. The ISF version also holds for rings, which have no QQQ. Example: L=1L=1L=1 nH, C=1.013C=1.013C=1.013 pF, Rp=314 ΩR_p=314\ \OmegaRp​=314 Ω → f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Q=10Q=10Q=10, Δf3dB=500\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=500Δf3dB​=500 MHz, 4kT/Rp≈5.3×10−234kT/R_p\approx5.3\times10^{-23}4kT/Rp​≈5.3×10−23 A²/Hz. Practical ceiling: on-chip spiral-inductor QQQ is only ~5–20 (metal RsR_sRs​, skin/proximity, substrate loss, varactor), so LC phase-noise reduction usually shifts to enlarging the swing instead (tank_swing). documents.t: Prerequisites: fourier_series_of_isf (c0c_0c0​ and Parseval), rms_isf (definition and role of Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​), flicker_noise_upconversion (why c0c_0c0​ is the only gate for flicker upconversion) | Next: symmetry (turning these closed forms into design knobs), lab_32 (equation-level ring ISF extraction — where the triangular approximation breaks) The symmetry page gives the qualitative rule "symmetric rise/fall → c0→0c_0\to0c0​→0 → 1/f³ suppressed," but its numerical example plugs in an assumed c0c_0c0​. This page fills the missing piece: given a ring oscillator's stage count NNN and how asymmetric its waveform is, what exactly are Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, c0c_0c0​, and the 1/f³ corner? [P2] Appendix B (p.803) answers with a full set of closed forms, Eq.(52)–(57), built on an asymmetric triangular ISF model — one of the very few places on this site where c0c_0c0​ is computed directly from topology parameters, so it is worth walking through step by step. Physical intuition (conclusion first): a ring's ISF concentrates at the two transitions: a positive lobe at the rising edge and a negative lobe at the falling edge, with lobe height inversely proportional to that edge's slope (steeper edge → less sensitive). If the rise is steeper than the fall (A=frise′/ffall′>1A=f'_{rise}/f'_{fall}>1A=frise′​/ffall′​>1), the positive lobe is short and narrow while the negative lobe is tall and wide — the two lobe areas no longer cancel, and the leftover net area is exactly Γdc\Gamma_{dc}Γdc​ (i.e. c0/2c_0/2c0​/2), which upconverts device 1/f noise into close-in 1/f³. The closed forms turn this geometric picture into three formulas — Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ (Eq.55), Γdc\Gamma_{dc}Γdc​ (Eq.56), corner (Eq.57) — and the corner depends on only two dimensionless numbers, AAA and NNN.
documents.s: Closed Forms for the Asymmetric Triangular ISF ([P2] Appendix B)

documents.t: [P2] Fig. 18, p.803 (verified against the rendered PDF page for this unit): "Approximate waveform and the ISF for asymmetric rising and falling edges." The figure plots Γ(x)\Gamma(x)Γ(x) over one period (xxx from 000 to 2π2\pi2π) as two triangular lobes: Lobe Height (peak) Base width Corresponds to positive 1/frise′1/f'_{rise}1/frise′​ 2/frise′2/f'_{rise}2/frise′​ rising edge negative 1/ffall′1/f'_{fall}1/ffall′​ (depth) 2/ffall′2/f'_{fall}2/ffall′​ falling edge Here frise′f'_{rise}frise′​, ffall′f'_{fall}ffall′​ are the maximum slopes of the normalized waveform (f(x)f(x)f(x) normalized to amplitude 1, x=ω0τx=\omega_0\taux=ω0​τ) during the rising/falling edges (verbatim: "where frise′f'_{rise}frise′​ and ffall′f'_{fall}ffall′​ are the maximum slope during the rising and falling edge, respectively", p.803). Unit check: x=ω0τx=\omega_0\taux=ω0​τ is [rad/s]⋅[s]=[rad][\text{rad/s}]\cdot[\text{s}]=[\text{rad}][rad/s]⋅[s]=[rad], and this site treats rad as a dimensionless pure number; f(x)f(x)f(x) is dimensionless, so f′=df/dxf'=df/dxf′=df/dx and 1/f′1/f'1/f′ are also dimensionless — consistent with Γ\GammaΓ being dimensionless ✓. Why the height is 1/f′1/f'1/f′: the ISF peak is inversely proportional to the waveform slope — the steeper the edge, the smaller the phase shift caused by the same charge perturbation (see waveform_slope; this is the starting point of the triangular approximation in the main text of [P2]). Key geometric observation (slope = 1): each lobe has "height =1/f′=1/f'=1/f′, base width =2/f′=2/f'=2/f′", so the half-width equals the height and the two sides of the triangle have slope ±1\pm1±1 in the xxx coordinate. This is no accident: the sensitivity peak is ∝1/f′\propto 1/f'∝1/f′ and the sensitive window (the phase width the transition occupies) is also ∝1/f′\propto 1/f'∝1/f′; they share the same origin, so their ratio is fixed at 1. This "unit slope" makes the integrals below extremely clean. The positions of the lobes along xxx (where the positive and negative lobes sit) do not affect Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ or Γdc\Gamma_{dc}Γdc​ (they only affect the harmonic phases θn\theta_nθn​), so the derivation may place the lobes at any non-overlapping positions.

documents.t: Start from the definition of Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (the [P1] Eq.(20) form, see rms_isf) and integrate the two triangular lobes piecewise. Because the sides have slope =±1=\pm1=±1, on each half-side we can use the "value of the ISF" itself as the integration variable (Γ\GammaΓ walks linearly from 0 to the peak 1/f′1/f'1/f′, with dΓ=± dxd\Gamma = \pm\,dxdΓ=±dx); one lobe = two half-sides = 2∫01/f′x2 dx2\int_0^{1/f'}x^2\,dx2∫01/f′​x2dx. Verbatim ([P2] Eq.(52), p.803, verified against the render): Γrms2=12π∫02πΓ2(x) dx=1π ⁣[∫01/frise′x2 dx+∫01/ffall′x2 dx]=13π(1frise′) ⁣3(1+A3)\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)\,dx =\frac{1}{\pi}\!\left[\int_0^{1/f'_{rise}}x^2\,dx+\int_0^{1/f'_{fall}}x^2\,dx\right] =\frac{1}{3\pi}\left(\frac{1}{f'_{rise}}\right)^{\!3}(1+A^3)Γrms2​=2π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx=π1​[∫01/frise′​​x2dx+∫01/ffall′​​x2dx]=3π1​(frise′​1​)3(1+A3) Expanding the middle step into the last step, one line at a time: 12π ⁣[2 ⁣∫01/frise′ ⁣x2dx+2 ⁣∫01/ffall′ ⁣x2dx]=1π ⁣[x33∣01/frise′+x33∣01/ffall′]=13π ⁣[(1frise′) ⁣3+(1ffall′) ⁣3]=13π(1frise′) ⁣3(1+A3).\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2\pi}\!\left[2\!\int_0^{1/f'_{rise}}\!x^2dx+2\!\int_0^{1/f'_{fall}}\!x^2dx\right] &=\frac{1}{\pi}\!\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\Big\vert_0^{1/f'_{rise}}+\frac{x^3}{3}\Big\vert_0^{1/f'_{fall}}\right] \\[4pt] &=\frac{1}{3\pi}\!\left[\left(\frac{1}{f'_{rise}}\right)^{\!3}+\left(\frac{1}{f'_{fall}}\right)^{\!3}\right] \\[4pt] &=\frac{1}{3\pi}\left(\frac{1}{f'_{rise}}\right)^{\!3}\left(1+A^3\right). \end{aligned}2π1​[2∫01/frise′​​x2dx+2∫01/ffall′​​x2dx]​=π1​[3x3​​01/frise′​​+3x3​​01/ffall′​​]=3π1​​(frise′​1​)3+(ffall′​1​)3​=3π1​(frise′​1​)3(1+A3).​ Line 1: each lobe has two half-sides; the sign disappears after squaring, so the positive and negative lobes each contribute 2∫0hx2dx2\int_0^{h}x^2dx2∫0h​x2dx (hhh = peak height). Line 3: factor out (1/frise′)3(1/f'_{rise})^3(1/frise′​)3 using 1ffall′=Afrise′\dfrac{1}{f'_{fall}}=\dfrac{A}{f'_{rise}}ffall′​1​=frise′​A​, where AAA is the asymmetry ratio ([P2] Eq.(53), p.803, verbatim): A≡frise′ffall′A\equiv\frac{f'_{rise}}{f'_{fall}}A≡ffall′​frise′​​ Dimension check: [x2 dx]=rad3[x^2\,dx]=\text{rad}^3[x2dx]=rad3 (dimensionless), divided by π\piπ (rad) → dimensionless; Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ is dimensionless ✓. Sanity check: at A=1A=1A=1 (symmetric), 1+A3=21+A^3=21+A3=2 and the two lobes contribute equally; for A>1A>1A>1 (steep rise), 1/ffall′1/f'_{fall}1/ffall′​ is large and the negative lobe dominates Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ — the slower edge sets the rms sensitivity.

documents.t: Eq.(52) still contains the waveform slope. To express it in "parameters a designer holds" (the stage count NNN), use the ring's period constraint. [P2] Eq.(14), p.794 defines the normalized stage delay t^D=η/fmax′\hat t_D=\eta/f'_{max}t^D​=η/fmax′​ (η≈1\eta\approx1η≈1 is a proportionality constant: one stage's delay is roughly the inverse of the transition slope, times η\etaη). In a single-ended inverting ring, the signal travels around the loop twice per full period (every node rises once and falls once), i.e. 2N2N2N stage delays — NNN of them rising-edge delays η/frise′\eta/f'_{rise}η/frise′​ and NNN falling-edge delays η/ffall′\eta/f'_{fall}η/ffall′​. Writing the period's phase length 2π2\pi2π as the sum of these delays ([P2] Eq.(54), p.803, verbatim): 2π=ηN ⁣(1frise′+1ffall′)=ηNfrise′(1+A)2\pi=\eta N\!\left(\frac{1}{f'_{rise}}+\frac{1}{f'_{fall}}\right)=\frac{\eta N}{f'_{rise}}(1+A)2π=ηN(frise′​1​+ffall′​1​)=frise′​ηN​(1+A) Solving for the positive-lobe peak height: 1frise′=2πηN(1+A),1ffall′=2πAηN(1+A).\frac{1}{f'_{rise}}=\frac{2\pi}{\eta N(1+A)},\qquad \frac{1}{f'_{fall}}=\frac{2\pi A}{\eta N(1+A)}.frise′​1​=ηN(1+A)2π​,ffall′​1​=ηN(1+A)2πA​. Dimension check: both sides are rad (dimensionless) ✓; η,N,A\eta,N,Aη,N,A are all dimensionless. Sanity check: at A=1A=1A=1 this reduces to the symmetric case 2π=2Nt^D2\pi=2N\hat t_D2π=2Nt^D​ (exactly the phase-domain form of [P2] Eq.(15), f0=1/(2NτD)f_0=1/(2N\tau_D)f0​=1/(2NτD​)); larger NNN or larger A+1A+1A+1 shrinks the positive lobe — every piece of the geometry is "diluted" by the fixed 2π2\pi2π budget.

documents.t: Γdc\Gamma_{dc}Γdc​ is the average of the ISF over one period. Triangle area =12⋅=\tfrac12\cdot=21​⋅base⋅\cdot⋅height: positive-lobe area 12⋅2frise′⋅1frise′=1frise′2\tfrac12\cdot\dfrac{2}{f'_{rise}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{f'_{rise}}=\dfrac{1}{f'^2_{rise}}21​⋅frise′​2​⋅frise′​1​=frise′2​1​, and likewise 1ffall′2\dfrac{1}{f'^2_{fall}}ffall′2​1​ for the negative lobe (with a minus sign): Γdc=12π ⁣[1frise′2−1ffall′2]=12π 1−A2frise′2=12π⋅4π2η2N2(1+A)2 (1−A2)\Gamma_{dc}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\!\left[\frac{1}{f'^2_{rise}}-\frac{1}{f'^2_{fall}}\right] =\frac{1}{2\pi}\,\frac{1-A^2}{f'^2_{rise}} =\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{4\pi^2}{\eta^2N^2(1+A)^2}\,(1-A^2)Γdc​=2π1​[frise′2​1​−ffall′2​1​]=2π1​frise′2​1−A2​=2π1​⋅η2N2(1+A)24π2​(1−A2) Using 1−A2=(1−A)(1+A)1-A^2=(1-A)(1+A)1−A2=(1−A)(1+A) to cancel one (1+A)(1+A)(1+A) gives the paper's form ([P2] Eq.(56), p.803, verbatim): Γdc=2πη2 1N2(1−A1+A)\Gamma_{dc}=\frac{2\pi}{\eta^2}\,\frac{1}{N^2}\left(\frac{1-A}{1+A}\right)Γdc​=η22π​N21​(1+A1−A​) Connecting to the Fourier coefficient: the DC value of the ISF series ([P1] Eq.(12)) is c0/2c_0/2c0​/2, so c0=2 Γdcc_0=2\,\Gamma_{dc}c0​=2Γdc​ — this is the c0c_0c0​ that feeds the [P1] Eq.(24) corner formula (same sign trap as on the symmetry page: c0c_0c0​ is the coefficient, c0/2c_0/2c0​/2 is the DC value). Sign: A>1A>1A>1 (steep rise) → Γdc<0\Gamma_{dc}<0Γdc​<0 (larger negative-lobe area); A<1A<1A<1 flips the sign. Upconversion only sees c02c_0^2c02​; the sign does not enter the corner. Scaling highlight: Γdc∝N−2\Gamma_{dc}\propto N^{-2}Γdc​∝N−2 falls faster than Γrms∝N−1.5\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-1.5}Γrms​∝N−1.5 (lobe area ∝\propto∝ peak height squared ∝N−2\propto N^{-2}∝N−2; rms squared ∝\propto∝ peak height cubed ∝N−3\propto N^{-3}∝N−3). documents.t: The corner relation in the main text of [P2] ([P2] Eq.(7), p.792, verified against the render, verbatim): f1/f3=f1/f⋅Γdc2Γrms2f_{1/f^3}=f_{1/f}\cdot\frac{\Gamma_{dc}^2}{\Gamma_{rms}^2}f1/f3​=f1/f​⋅Γrms2​Γdc2​​ Substituting Eq.(55) and (56), and factoring 1+A3=(1+A)(1−A+A2)1+A^3=(1+A)(1-A+A^2)1+A3=(1+A)(1−A+A2): Γdc2Γrms2=4π2η4N4(1−A)2(1+A)22π23η3N3⋅4(1+A3)(1+A)3=32ηN⋅(1−A)2(1+A)1+A3=32ηN⋅(1−A)21−A+A2\frac{\Gamma_{dc}^2}{\Gamma_{rms}^2} =\frac{\dfrac{4\pi^2}{\eta^4N^4}\dfrac{(1-A)^2}{(1+A)^2}} {\dfrac{2\pi^2}{3\eta^3N^3}\cdot\dfrac{4(1+A^3)}{(1+A)^3}} =\frac{3}{2\eta N}\cdot\frac{(1-A)^2(1+A)}{1+A^3} =\frac{3}{2\eta N}\cdot\frac{(1-A)^2}{1-A+A^2}Γrms2​Γdc2​​=3η3N32π2​⋅(1+A)34(1+A3)​η4N44π2​(1+A)2(1−A)2​​=2ηN3​⋅1+A3(1−A)2(1+A)​=2ηN3​⋅1−A+A2(1−A)2​ which gives the paper's result ([P2] Eq.(57), p.803, verbatim): f1/f3=f1/f⋅32ηN⋅(1−A)2(1−A+A2)f_{1/f^3}=f_{1/f}\cdot\frac{3}{2\eta N}\cdot\frac{(1-A)^2}{(1-A+A^2)}f1/f3​=f1/f​⋅2ηN3​⋅(1−A+A2)(1−A)2​ Factor-2 convention flag (flagged every time a 2 or 4 appears): substituting c0=2Γdcc_0=2\Gamma_{dc}c0​=2Γdc​ into [P1] Eq.(24), Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c02/(2Γrms2)\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅c02​/(2Γrms2​), yields 2 ω1/fΓdc2/Γrms22\,\omega_{1/f}\Gamma_{dc}^2/\Gamma_{rms}^22ω1/f​Γdc2​/Γrms2​ — exactly 2× [P2] Eq.(7)/(57). This belongs to the same family of bookkeeping issues as the SSB /4/4/4 vs time-domain /2/2/2 discussed on the white_noise page (how the DC channel is weighted in the ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ sum; [P2] Eq.(6), p.792 itself uses /(8π2f2)/(8\pi^2f^2)/(8π2f2) = the time-domain /2/2/2 convention). Each paper is internally self-consistent; the scalings (∝(1−A)2/(1−A+A2)\propto(1-A)^2/(1-A+A^2)∝(1−A)2/(1−A+A2), ∝1/N\propto1/N∝1/N) and all ratios are unaffected. This site reports the [P2] Eq.(57) value as primary and quotes the [P1] Eq.(24)-convention value (=2×) alongside. Interactive exploration: the widget below lets you drag NNN, AAA, η\etaη, and f1/ff_{1/f}f1/f​ directly and watch Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, c0c_0c0​, and the corner (from Eq.(55)–(57)) update live, alongside the Fig.18 triangular-lobe shape on the left and the corner-vs-AAA V-shaped valley on the right (the analytic version of the [P2] Fig.17 measured bowl) with the current point marked: Asymmetric triangular ISF explorer ([P2] Appendix B, Eqs. 52–57) N (級數 stages)5 A = f'rise/f'fall3.00 f_{1/f} (device corner)1.0 MHz η (stage-delay const.)1.00 Γ(x) — Fig. 18 triangular lobes x = 2πΓ(x)Γ_dc = -0.126 corner / f_{1/f} vs A (log-A, Fig.17-style V) A=0.2A=5A=1 Γ_rms — Eq.(55) 0.3035 dimensionless c₀ = 2Γ_dc — Eq.(56) -0.2513 dimensionless f_{1/f³} — Eq.(57) 171.43 kHz [P1] Eq.(24) convention (=2×) 342.86 kHz Closed forms ([P2] App. B, verbatim): Γ_rms² = (2π²/3η³)(1/N³)[4(1+A³)/(1+A)³] (Eq.55); Γ_dc = (2π/η²N²)(1−A)/(1+A), c₀ = 2Γ_dc (Eq.56); f_{1/f³} = f_{1/f}· (3/2ηN)·(1−A)²/(1−A+A²) (Eq.57). Sanity anchors: A=1 → c₀=0, corner=0 (exact symmetric-lobe cancellation); N=5, A=3, η=1, f_{1/f}=1 MHz → Γ_rms=0.3035, c₀=−0.2513, corner=171.43 kHz ([P2] Eq.57) / 342.86 kHz ([P1] Eq.24 convention). Pedagogical triangular toy model (linear-ramp edges, unit slope), valid only for N ≥ 2/η (non-overlapping lobes); see asymmetric_isf_closed_form. Eq.(57) has three structural properties, each carrying a design message: The corner vanishes quadratically as A→1A\to1A→1: the numerator (1−A)2(1-A)^2(1−A)2 — near the symmetry point the corner is second-order insensitive to asymmetry, but once you drift away the degradation also accelerates quadratically (lab_33: at A=1.01A=1.01A=1.01 corner/f1/f/f_{1/f}/f1/f​ is only 2.97×10−52.97\times10^{-5}2.97×10−5, while at A=1.10A=1.10A=1.10 it is already 2.70×10−32.70\times10^{-3}2.70×10−3 — nearly 100× apart). This is the analytic version of the bowl-shaped minimum of [P2] Fig. 17, p.802 ("phase noise vs symmetry control voltage"). Invariant under A→1/AA\to1/AA→1/A: (1−A)2/(1−A+A2)(1-A)^2/(1-A+A^2)(1−A)2/(1−A+A2) is unchanged when AAA is replaced by 1/A1/A1/A (multiply top and bottom by A2A^2A2; lab_33 verifies corner(A=2)=(A{=}2)=(A=2)= corner(A=0.5)=1.000000×10−1 f1/f(A{=}0.5) =1.000000\times10^{-1}\,f_{1/f}(A=0.5)=1.000000×10−1f1/f​). The V-shaped valley is left-right symmetric on a log-AAA axis — "which edge is steeper" does not matter. Corner ∝1/N\propto 1/N∝1/N: at fixed AAA, more stages means a lower corner. Verbatim (p.803, end of App. B): "As can be seen for a constant rise-to-fall ratio, the 1/f³ corner decreases inversely with the number of stages; therefore, ring oscillators with a smaller number of stages will have a larger 1/f³ noise corner. As a special case, if the rise and fall time are symmetric, A = 1, and the 1/f³ corner approaches zero." Reconciling with the "NNN-independence" conclusion: [P2]'s main-text Eq.(23) says that at fixed f0f_0f0​ and power, phase noise in the white-noise (1/f²) region is approximately NNN-independent (see the paper_002 deep dive and lc_vs_ring). There is no contradiction: NNN does not move the height of the 1/f² region, but it pushes the 1/f³ knee toward lower frequency (∝1/N\propto1/N∝1/N). Design message: if your pain point is close-in flicker (e.g. the PLL loop bandwidth is too narrow to clean up the VCO's 1/f³), more stages is an effective lever; if the pain point is white-region jitter, adding stages does not help. This is the new design takeaway of this page — called out by [P2] itself.

documents.t: Prerequisites: lorentzian_linewidth (the full white-noise → Lorentzian chain and the "spurious divergence"), flicker_noise_upconversion (where the 1/f31/f^31/f3 skirt comes from), stochastic_noise_basics (stationarity, Wiener–Khinchin) | Next: allan_variance (the canonical time-domain tool for characterizing flicker FM), measurement_and_spurs (instrumentation practicalities) lorentzian_linewidth resolved the spurious divergence of 1/f21/f^21/f2 as Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0 with one clean logical chain: phase random walk (Var⁡[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi]=2D|t|Var[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣) → Gaussian characteristic function → exponential autocorrelation → Lorentzian lineshape. But the first link of that chain hides an assumption: the noise driving the phase is white. In a real oscillator, the skirt closest to the carrier is usually 1/f31/f^31/f3 (flicker FM, see flicker_noise_upconversion) — so is the close-in lineshape still Lorentzian? This page answers two questions: Part A (lineshape): under flicker FM, Var⁡[Δϕ(t)]\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(t)]Var[Δϕ(t)] no longer grows linearly but as t2×log⁡t^2\times\logt2×log (with an explicit role for a low-frequency cutoff flf_lfl​); the characteristic-function step therefore yields a near-Gaussian line core, not a Lorentzian. Part B (nonstationarity): the free-running ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) is a random walk, so strictly speaking Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) does not exist (it is not a stationary process and has no stationary PSD); what the instrument really measures is the spectrum of V(t)=cos⁡(ω0t+ϕ)V(t)=\cos(\omega_0t+\phi)V(t)=cos(ω0​t+ϕ) — which is stationary (the [E2] Demir view). Every SϕS_\phiSϕ​ formula on this site is a conditional spectrum under "finite observation time, offset ≫\gg≫ linewidth"; the two descriptions agree exactly within that range. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the lineshape is set by the "speed profile of phase memory loss". Under white noise the phase variance accumulates linearly (∝t\propto t∝t), the memory-loss envelope is the exponential e−D∣t∣e^{-D|t|}e−D∣t∣, and its Fourier transform is a Lorentzian. Under flicker FM, low-frequency noise parks the frequency itself on one side for long stretches, and the phase variance accumulates almost as t2t^2t2 (up to a log) — like a "walk with drift" — so the memory-loss envelope becomes the near-Gaussian e−(const)t2log⁡e^{-(\text{const})t^2\log}e−(const)t2log, and the Fourier transform of a Gaussian is again a Gaussian: the line core becomes a bell-shaped Gaussian with shoulders far steeper than a Lorentzian's. For the very same L(10 kHz)\mathcal{L}(10\,\text{kHz})L(10kHz) spec, the white-noise version has a 50 Hz linewidth and the flicker version 3.1 kHz — a dBc/Hz number at one offset does not determine the linewidth at all; the noise "color" does. This is the main event of the lab_29 numerical demo. Try it: the lorentzian_linewidth page embeds an interactive explorer — a slider for the same L(10 kHz)\mathcal{L}(10\,\text{kHz})L(10kHz) spec, a white FM / flicker FM toggle, and a spectrum-analyzer RBW slider — so you can see this page's "same spec, 100× difference in linewidth" conclusion first-hand, plus how too-wide an RBW smears away the flattening / near-Gaussian shoulder.

documents.t: The derivation chain of lorentzian_linewidth is: Var⁡[Δϕ(t)]=2D∣t∣ ⇒ ⟨cos⁡Δϕ⟩=e−Var⁡/2=e−D∣τ∣ ⇒ Sx(Δω)∝DD2+Δω2,Δf3dB=Dπ.\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(t)]=2D|t| \;\Rightarrow\; \langle\cos\Delta\phi\rangle=e^{-\operatorname{Var}/2}=e^{-D|\tau|} \;\Rightarrow\; S_x(\Delta\omega)\propto\frac{D}{D^2+\Delta\omega^2},\quad \Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\frac{D}{\pi}.Var[Δϕ(t)]=2D∣t∣⇒⟨cosΔϕ⟩=e−Var/2=e−D∣τ∣⇒Sx​(Δω)∝D2+Δω2D​,Δf3dB​=πD​. The first link — variance grows linearly — holds only for white frequency noise (white FM: the PSD of ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ is flat). This page swaps that link for flicker FM and watches how the whole chain changes. First, nail down the bookkeeping (this site's factor-of-2 discipline). Let the single-sided PSD of ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ for white FM be W0W_0W0​ (units rad2/s2/Hz=rad2/s\text{rad}^2/\text{s}^2/\text{Hz}=\text{rad}^2/\text{s}rad2/s2/Hz=rad2/s). Step 1 will prove rigorously that Var⁡[Δϕ(t)]=W02∣t∣\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(t)]=\tfrac{W_0}{2}|t|Var[Δϕ(t)]=2W0​​∣t∣, so Var⁡=2D∣t∣\operatorname{Var}=2D|t|Var=2D∣t∣ corresponds to W0=4DW_0=4DW0​=4D, and the phase spectrum (integrator 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2) is: Sϕ單邊(f)=4D(2πf)2,Sϕ雙邊(f)=2D(2πf)2,L(Δf)=時域/2Sϕ單邊2=2DΔω2.S_\phi^{\text{單邊}}(f)=\frac{4D}{(2\pi f)^2},\qquad S_\phi^{\text{�雙邊}}(f)=\frac{2D}{(2\pi f)^2},\qquad \mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\stackrel{\text{時域}/2}{=}\frac{S_\phi^{\text{單邊}}}{2}=\frac{2D}{\Delta\omega^2}.Sϕ單邊​(f)=(2πf)24D​,Sϕ雙邊​(f)=(2πf)22D​,L(Δf)=時域/22Sϕ單邊​​=Δω22D​. Which convention: when the literature writes "Sϕ=2D/Δω2S_\phi=2D/\Delta\omega^2Sϕ​=2D/Δω2 for a Wiener phase", it is usually double-sided bookkeeping (or, equivalently, the factor of 2 has been absorbed into the definition of DDD — i.e. convention 甲 of diffusion_dictionary, D甲=2DD_{\text{甲}}=2DD甲​=2D). Site convention 11.2 (v5) agrees with this page: single-sided Sϕ=4D/Δω2S_\phi=4D/\Delta\omega^2Sϕ​=4D/Δω2, Var⁡=2D∣t∣\operatorname{Var}=2D|t|Var=2D∣t∣. lab_29 nails this numerically: for phase synthesized with Var⁡=2D∣t∣\operatorname{Var}=2D|t|Var=2D∣t∣, single-sided Welch measures Sϕ(10 kHz)÷(4D/Δω2)=1.001S_\phi(10\,\text{kHz})\div\big(4D/\Delta\omega^2\big)=1.001Sϕ​(10kHz)÷(4D/Δω2)=1.001 — it is 4, not 2. This factor of 2 between single- and double-sided does not affect the lineshape or Δf3dB=D/π\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=D/\piΔf3dB​=D/π (the linewidth is set by the envelope decay rate, independent of how the spectrum is bookkept). Relation to the SSB /4/4/4 convention: lab_29 measures the single-sided skirt of the V(t)V(t)V(t) spectrum directly and divides by carrier power, which is exactly the time-domain /2/2/2 convention's L=Sϕ/2\mathcal{L}=S_\phi/2L=Sϕ​/2 (measured vs. theory at 10 kHz: +0.12+0.12+0.12 dB); the SSB /4/4/4 bookkeeping of [P1] Eq.(21), p.185 would quote the same physics 3 dB lower — the famous factor-of-2 bookkeeping affair already covered in white_noise_to_phase_noise; this page does not reopen that debate, it only labels which convention each number uses.

documents.t: To handle FM noise of arbitrary color we need a general formula that computes Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]Var[Δϕ(τ)] directly from Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f). Derive it step by step: (i) The increment is a windowed integral of ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​. Define the phase increment Δϕ(τ)≡ϕ(t0+τ)−ϕ(t0)=∫t0t0+τϕ˙(σ) dσ\Delta\phi(\tau)\equiv\phi(t_0+\tau)-\phi(t_0)=\displaystyle\int_{t_0}^{t_0+\tau}\dot\phi(\sigma)\,d\sigmaΔϕ(τ)≡ϕ(t0​+τ)−ϕ(t0​)=∫t0​t0​+τ​ϕ˙​(σ)dσ. As long as ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ is a stationary zero-mean process (white noise, or flicker with a low-frequency cutoff, both qualify), the statistics of Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ do not depend on t0t_0t0​ — this is "increment stationarity", and Part B will come back to it. (ii) The windowed integral is an LTI filter. For a component at frequency fff, the response of a rectangular integration window of length τ\tauτ is Hτ(f)=∫0τe−j2πfσ dσ=1−e−j2πfτj2πf⟹∣Hτ(f)∣2=2−2cos⁡(2πfτ)(2πf)2=sin⁡2(πfτ)(πf)2.H_\tau(f)=\int_0^\tau e^{-j2\pi f\sigma}\,d\sigma=\frac{1-e^{-j2\pi f\tau}}{j2\pi f} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lvert H_\tau(f)\rvert^2=\frac{2-2\cos(2\pi f\tau)}{(2\pi f)^2}=\frac{\sin^2(\pi f\tau)}{(\pi f)^2}.Hτ​(f)=∫0τ​e−j2πfσdσ=j2πf1−e−j2πfτ​⟹∣Hτ​(f)∣2=(2πf)22−2cos(2πfτ)​=(πf)2sin2(πfτ)​. Unit check: [Hτ]=s[H_\tau]=\text{s}[Hτ​]=s (integration over time), [∣H∣2]=s2[\lvert H\rvert^2]=\text{s}^2[∣H∣2]=s2 ✓. (iii) Stationary process through an LTI filter → output variance = integral of PSD × ∣H∣2\lvert H\rvert^2∣H∣2. Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]=∫0∞Sϕ˙單邊(f) ∣Hτ(f)∣2 df.\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]=\int_0^\infty S_{\dot\phi}^{\text{單邊}}(f)\,\lvert H_\tau(f)\rvert^2\,df .Var[Δϕ(τ)]=∫0∞​Sϕ˙​單邊​(f)∣Hτ​(f)∣2df. Unit check: (rad2/s)⋅s2⋅Hz=rad2(\text{rad}^2/\text{s})\cdot\text{s}^2\cdot\text{Hz}=\text{rad}^2(rad2/s)⋅s2⋅Hz=rad2 ✓. (iv) Rewrite in terms of SϕS_\phiSϕ​. Substitute Sϕ˙(f)=(2πf)2Sϕ(f)S_{\dot\phi}(f)=(2\pi f)^2S_\phi(f)Sϕ˙​​(f)=(2πf)2Sϕ​(f) (differentiator), and (2πf)2⋅sin⁡2(πfτ)(πf)2=4sin⁡2(πfτ)=2(1−cos⁡2πfτ)(2\pi f)^2\cdot\frac{\sin^2(\pi f\tau)}{(\pi f)^2}=4\sin^2(\pi f\tau)=2\big(1-\cos 2\pi f\tau\big)(2πf)2⋅(πf)2sin2(πfτ)​=4sin2(πfτ)=2(1−cos2πfτ): Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]=2∫0∞Sϕ單邊(f) (1−cos⁡2πfτ) df \boxed{\ \operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]=2\int_0^\infty S_\phi^{\text{單邊}}(f)\,\big(1-\cos 2\pi f\tau\big)\,df\ } Var[Δϕ(τ)]=2∫0∞​Sϕ單邊​(f)(1−cos2πfτ)df ​ Physical meaning: the kernel (1−cos⁡2πfτ)\big(1-\cos2\pi f\tau\big)(1−cos2πfτ) is an "increment high-pass" — components slower than 1/τ1/\tau1/τ (fτ≪1f\tau\ll1fτ≪1) get suppressed to 2π2f2τ22\pi^2f^2\tau^22π2f2τ2 (slow drift is invisible within a short window), while components faster than 1/τ1/\tau1/τ contribute 2Sϕ2S_\phi2Sϕ​ on average. Precisely because of this high-pass, the increment variance can remain finite even when ϕ\phiϕ itself diverges (foreshadowing Part B). White-noise self-check (recovering 2D∣t∣2D|t|2D∣t∣): substitute Sϕ=4D/(2πf)2S_\phi=4D/(2\pi f)^2Sϕ​=4D/(2πf)2 and use the standard integral ∫0∞1−cos⁡uu2 du=π2\int_0^\infty\frac{1-\cos u}{u^2}\,du=\frac{\pi}{2}∫0∞​u21−cosu​du=2π​ (substitution u=2πfτu=2\pi f\tauu=2πfτ, see math_identities): Var⁡=2∫0∞4D(2πf)2(1−cos⁡2πfτ) df=8D(2π)2⋅2πτ∫0∞1−cos⁡uu2 du=8D4π2⋅2πτ⋅π2=2Dτ ✓\operatorname{Var}=2\int_0^\infty\frac{4D}{(2\pi f)^2}\big(1-\cos2\pi f\tau\big)\,df =\frac{8D}{(2\pi)^2}\cdot 2\pi\tau\int_0^\infty\frac{1-\cos u}{u^2}\,du =\frac{8D}{4\pi^2}\cdot2\pi\tau\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=2D\tau\ \checkmarkVar=2∫0∞​(2πf)24D​(1−cos2πfτ)df=(2π)28D​⋅2πτ∫0∞​u21−cosu​du=4π28D​⋅2πτ⋅2π​=2Dτ ✓ This also re-verifies the Step-0 bookkeeping: only the single-sided 4D/Δω24D/\Delta\omega^24D/Δω2 recovers 2D∣t∣2D|t|2D∣t∣. Link to [P2]: this general formula is the engine behind the ring paper's accumulated-jitter law — [P2] Eq.(8), p.792's σΔϕ=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta\phi}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔϕ​=κΔt​ is exactly the special case "white FM → linear variance" (the phase version κ=ω0κt\kappa=\omega_0\kappa_tκ=ω0​κt​ = the square root of [P2] Eq.(11), p.793; the printed Eq.(12), p.793 gives the time version κt\kappa_tκt​, with ω0\omega_0ω0​ in the denominator).
