documents.t: Definition (frequency domain): flicker FM means the frequency fluctuation ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ carries a 1/f1/f1/f spectrum: Sϕ˙單邊(f)=kff⟺Sϕ單邊(f)=Sϕ˙(2πf)2=b−3f3,b−3≡kf4π2.S_{\dot\phi}^{\text{單邊}}(f)=\frac{k_f}{f} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S_\phi^{\text{單邊}}(f)=\frac{S_{\dot\phi}}{(2\pi f)^2}=\frac{b_{-3}}{f^3}, \qquad b_{-3}\equiv\frac{k_f}{4\pi^2}.Sϕ˙​單邊​(f)=fkf​​⟺Sϕ單邊​(f)=(2πf)2Sϕ˙​​​=f3b−3​​,b−3​≡4π2kf​​. Units: [kf]=rad2/s2[k_f]=\text{rad}^2/\text{s}^2[kf​]=rad2/s2 (Sϕ˙S_{\dot\phi}Sϕ˙​​ is rad2/s\text{rad}^2/\text{s}rad2/s, multiplied back by fff); [b−3]=rad2⋅Hz2[b_{-3}]=\text{rad}^2\cdot\text{Hz}^2[b−3​]=rad2⋅Hz2 (SϕS_\phiSϕ​ is rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz, times f3f^3f3) ✓. In terms of fractional frequency y=ϕ˙/ω0y=\dot\phi/\omega_0y=ϕ˙​/ω0​, Sy=h−1/fS_y=h_{-1}/fSy​=h−1​/f and b−3=h−1f02b_{-3}=h_{-1}f_0^2b−3​=h−1​f02​ (this h−1h_{-1}h−1​ notation is the one used by allan_variance). Origin in ISF theory: the 1/f31/f^31/f3 skirt comes from device flicker upconverted through the ISF DC term c0c_0c0​ — [P1] Eq.(22)→(23), p.185 (derivation in flicker_noise_upconversion). Inverting the L\mathcal{L}L of [P1] Eq.(23) into SϕS_\phiSϕ​ via the small-angle relation L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​ yields the corresponding coefficient: b−3=c02qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf ⋅ ω1/f32 π3.b_{-3}=\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f\ \cdot\ \omega_{1/f}}{32\,\pi^3}.b−3​=qmax2​c02​​⋅32π3in2​​/Δf ⋅ ω1/f​​. Unit check: 1C2⋅A2Hz⋅1s=1A2s2⋅A2s⋅1s=1s2=Hz2\dfrac{1}{\text{C}^2}\cdot\dfrac{\text{A}^2}{\text{Hz}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\text{s}} =\dfrac{1}{\text{A}^2\text{s}^2}\cdot\text{A}^2\text{s}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\text{s}}=\dfrac{1}{\text{s}^2}=\text{Hz}^2C21​⋅HzA2​⋅s1​=A2s21​⋅A2s⋅s1​=s21​=Hz2 ✓ (rad is dimensionless). Convention note: Eq.(23) inherits [P1]'s SSB bookkeeping (same family as Eq.(21)); the expression above additionally stacks L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​ on top. These combinations of 2s are "packaging" and do not affect the 1/f31/f^31/f3 slope or the c02/qmax2c_0^2/q_{max}^2c02​/qmax2​ scaling — the rest of this page uses b−3b_{-3}b−3​ (directly readable from measurement: b−3=Sϕf3b_{-3}=S_\phi f^3b−3​=Sϕ​f3) as the single parameter, keeping the packaging debate out of the lineshape derivation.
documents.s: Step 2: what flicker FM is — Sϕ=b−3/f3S_\phi=b_{-3}/f^3Sϕ​=b−3​/f3, and its origin in ISF theory

documents.t: Substitute Sϕ=b−3/f3S_\phi=b_{-3}/f^3Sϕ​=b−3​/f3 into the Step-1 formula. First, why a low-frequency cutoff flf_lfl​ is mandatory: as f→0f\to0f→0 the integrand behaves as b−3f3(1−cos⁡2πfτ)≈b−3f3⋅2π2f2τ2=2π2b−3τ2f,\frac{b_{-3}}{f^3}\big(1-\cos2\pi f\tau\big)\approx\frac{b_{-3}}{f^3}\cdot2\pi^2f^2\tau^2=\frac{2\pi^2 b_{-3}\tau^2}{f},f3b−3​​(1−cos2πfτ)≈f3b−3​​⋅2π2f2τ2=f2π2b−3​τ2​, i.e. 1/f1/f1/f — a logarithmic divergence. For white noise, the f2f^2f2 suppression of the (1−cos⁡)(1-\cos)(1−cos) kernel was just enough (1/f2⋅f2=1/f^2\cdot f^2=1/f2⋅f2= constant, integrable); flicker brings one extra factor of 1/f1/f1/f that the kernel cannot hold down. So the lower limit of the integral must carry a physical low-frequency cutoff flf_lfl​: Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]=2∫fl∞b−3f3(1−cos⁡2πfτ) df.\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]=2\int_{f_l}^{\infty}\frac{b_{-3}}{f^3}\big(1-\cos2\pi f\tau\big)\,df .Var[Δϕ(τ)]=2∫fl​∞​f3b−3​​(1−cos2πfτ)df. Where does flf_lfl​ come from? Three common sources, with the same effect: (a) observation time — measuring for TobsT_{obs}Tobs​ seconds means you cannot see fluctuations slower than 1/Tobs1/T_{obs}1/Tobs​ (spectrum analyzers, and our simulations, are of this kind); (b) physical mechanism — flicker trap time constants are long but finite; (c) the system — a PLL locks the carrier, and drift below the loop bandwidth gets eaten. The cutoff's role is "logarithmically weak": below we will see that flf_lfl​ enters only inside the ln⁡\lnln. Do the integral step by step. Substitution u=2πfτu=2\pi f\tauu=2πfτ (f=u/2πτf=u/2\pi\tauf=u/2πτ, df=du/2πτdf=du/2\pi\taudf=du/2πτ, 1/f3=(2πτ)3/u31/f^3=(2\pi\tau)^3/u^31/f3=(2πτ)3/u3): Var⁡=2b−3 (2πτ)2∫u0∞1−cos⁡uu3 du≡8π2b−3τ2 K(u0),u0=2πflτ.\operatorname{Var}=2b_{-3}\,(2\pi\tau)^2\int_{u_0}^{\infty}\frac{1-\cos u}{u^3}\,du \equiv 8\pi^2b_{-3}\tau^2\,K(u_0),\qquad u_0=2\pi f_l\tau .Var=2b−3​(2πτ)2∫u0​∞​u31−cosu​du≡8π2b−3​τ2K(u0​),u0​=2πfl​τ. What remains is evaluating K(x)=∫x∞1−cos⁡uu3 duK(x)=\displaystyle\int_x^\infty\frac{1-\cos u}{u^3}\,duK(x)=∫x∞​u31−cosu​du for x≪1x\ll1x≪1. Integrate by parts twice: (i) First integration by parts (dw=u−3du⇒w=−12u2dw=u^{-3}du\Rightarrow w=-\tfrac{1}{2u^2}dw=u−3du⇒w=−2u21​): K(x)=[−1−cos⁡u2u2]x∞+12∫x∞sin⁡uu2 du=1−cos⁡x2x2+12∫x∞sin⁡uu2 du.K(x)=\Big[-\frac{1-\cos u}{2u^2}\Big]_x^\infty+\frac12\int_x^\infty\frac{\sin u}{u^2}\,du =\frac{1-\cos x}{2x^2}+\frac12\int_x^\infty\frac{\sin u}{u^2}\,du .K(x)=[−2u21−cosu​]x∞​+21​∫x∞​u2sinu​du=2x21−cosx​+21​∫x∞​u2sinu​du. (ii) Second integration by parts (dw=u−2du⇒w=−1udw=u^{-2}du\Rightarrow w=-\tfrac1udw=u−2du⇒w=−u1​): ∫x∞sin⁡uu2 du=[−sin⁡uu]x∞+∫x∞cos⁡uu du=sin⁡xx−Ci⁡(x),\int_x^\infty\frac{\sin u}{u^2}\,du=\Big[-\frac{\sin u}{u}\Big]_x^\infty+\int_x^\infty\frac{\cos u}{u}\,du =\frac{\sin x}{x}-\operatorname{Ci}(x),∫x∞​u2sinu​du=[−usinu​]x∞​+∫x∞​ucosu​du=xsinx​−Ci(x), where Ci⁡(x)≡−∫x∞cos⁡tt dt\operatorname{Ci}(x)\equiv-\int_x^\infty\frac{\cos t}{t}\,dtCi(x)≡−∫x∞​tcost​dt is the standard cosine integral, with small-xxx expansion Ci⁡(x)=γE+ln⁡x+O(x2)\operatorname{Ci}(x)=\gamma_E+\ln x+O(x^2)Ci(x)=γE​+lnx+O(x2). Here γE≈0.5772\gamma_E\approx0.5772γE​≈0.5772 is the Euler–Mascheroni constant — note it is not the ISF's Γ\GammaΓ, nor the MOS noise coefficient γ\gammaγ; to avoid the name clash we always write γE\gamma_EγE​. (iii) Combine and take the small-xxx limit (1−cos⁡x2x2→14\frac{1-\cos x}{2x^2}\to\frac142x21−cosx​→41​, sin⁡xx→1\frac{\sin x}{x}\to1xsinx​→1): K(x)=14+12[1−γE−ln⁡x]+O(x2)=34−γE2+12ln⁡1x+O(x2).K(x)=\frac14+\frac12\big[1-\gamma_E-\ln x\big]+O(x^2)=\frac34-\frac{\gamma_E}{2}+\frac12\ln\frac1x+O(x^2).K(x)=41​+21​[1−γE​−lnx]+O(x2)=43​−2γE​​+21​lnx1​+O(x2). (iv) Substitute back to obtain the main result of Part A: Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]=4π2b−3 τ2[ln⁡12πflτ+32−γE] (2πflτ≪1).\boxed{\ \operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]=4\pi^2 b_{-3}\,\tau^2\left[\ln\frac{1}{2\pi f_l\tau}+\frac32-\gamma_E\right]\ } \qquad(2\pi f_l\tau\ll1). Var[Δϕ(τ)]=4π2b−3​τ2[ln2πfl​τ1​+23​−γE​] ​(2πfl​τ≪1). Physical meaning: the dominant behavior is τ2\tau^2τ2 — not the white-noise τ1\tau^1τ1. τ2\tau^2τ2 means a "quasi-coherent frequency offset": on the timescale τ\tauτ, flicker components slower than 1/τ1/\tau1/τ act like a temporarily fixed frequency error δω\delta\omegaδω, giving phase error =δω⋅τ=\delta\omega\cdot\tau=δω⋅τ and variance ∝τ2\propto\tau^2∝τ2. The log⁡\loglog factor counts "how many decades of slow components are playing that role" (each decade from flf_lfl​ up to ∼1/τ\sim1/\tau∼1/τ contributes equally). Unit check: [4π2b−3τ2]=rad2Hz2⋅s2=rad2[4\pi^2b_{-3}\tau^2]=\text{rad}^2\text{Hz}^2\cdot\text{s}^2=\text{rad}^2[4π2b−3​τ2]=rad2Hz2⋅s2=rad2 ✓; inside the ln⁡\lnln, flτf_l\taufl​τ is dimensionless ✓. The cutoff's role (stated explicitly): flf_lfl​ appears only inside the ln⁡\lnln — changing flf_lfl​ by a factor of 10 shifts the bracket by only ln⁡10≈2.30\ln10\approx2.30ln10≈2.30 (roughly ±20%\pm20\%±20% against a typical value of ∼10\sim10∼10); the variance is finite but never forgets the cutoff. Contrast white noise: fl→0f_l\to0fl​→0 is completely invisible. This is the mathematical fingerprint of flicker's "infinite memory", and the root of Part B's "measured values depend weakly on observation time". Applicability/failure: (a) requires 2πflτ≪12\pi f_l\tau\ll12πfl​τ≪1, otherwise the O(x2)O(x^2)O(x2) corrections enter (once τ\tauτ is long enough to see the cutoff, variance growth slows); (b) requires ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ stationary for f≥flf\ge f_lf≥fl​; (c) convergence at the upper limit f→∞f\to\inftyf→∞ is unproblematic (kernel saturates, 1/f31/f^31/f3 integrable); in practice the high-frequency end is taken over first by white FM (the 1/f21/f^21/f2 segment) — this derivation only covers the close-in region where 1/f31/f^31/f3 dominates. Numerical verification (lab_29): measured increment variance ÷ closed form gives 0.9570.9570.957 at τ=1\tau=1τ=1 ms and 0.9440.9440.944 at τ=10\tau=10τ=10 ms (ensemble of 6 records of 32 s; the residual is record-to-record fluctuation of flicker's slowest components, see Part B); closed form ÷ "exact discrete-bin sum" gives 1.0001.0001.000 at 10 ms — the closed form itself is accurate.

documents.t: The characteristic-function step is identical to lorentzian_linewidth: Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is zero-mean Gaussian (our synthesis is "Gaussian white noise through a linear filter", hence exactly Gaussian; in real circuits this holds approximately), so Rx(τ)=12cos⁡(ω0τ) E(τ),E(τ)=⟨cos⁡Δϕ⟩=e−Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]/2.R_x(\tau)=\frac12\cos(\omega_0\tau)\,E(\tau),\qquad E(\tau)=\big\langle\cos\Delta\phi\big\rangle=e^{-\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]/2}.Rx​(τ)=21​cos(ω0​τ)E(τ),E(τ)=⟨cosΔϕ⟩=e−Var[Δϕ(τ)]/2. Substituting the Step-3 variance: E(τ)=exp⁡ ⁣(−2π2b−3 τ2[ln⁡12πflτ+32−γE]) \boxed{\ E(\tau)=\exp\!\left(-2\pi^2b_{-3}\,\tau^2\left[\ln\frac{1}{2\pi f_l\tau}+\frac32-\gamma_E\right]\right)\ } E(τ)=exp(−2π2b−3​τ2[ln2πfl​τ1​+23​−γE​]) ​ This is a Gaussian envelope (up to a slowly varying log): of the e−(const)τ2e^{-(\text{const})\tau^2}e−(const)τ2 type. Contrast the white-noise exponential envelope e−D∣τ∣e^{-D|\tau|}e−D∣τ∣. The Fourier transform of a Gaussian is again a Gaussian: so the line core (SxS_xSx​ near the carrier) is a near-Gaussian bell, not a Lorentzian. Freezing the log⁡\loglog at the memory-loss time τ\*\tau^\*τ\* (E(τ\*)=e−1E(\tau^\*)=e^{-1}E(τ\*)=e−1) gives the engineering approximation: Sx(Δf) ∝ exp⁡ ⁣(−2π2στ2 Δf2),στ=12πb−3L\*,Δf3dB≈22ln⁡2 b−3L\*,S_x(\Delta f)\ \propto\ \exp\!\big(-2\pi^2\sigma_\tau^2\,\Delta f^2\big),\quad \sigma_\tau=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{b_{-3}L^\*}},\qquad \Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}\approx2\sqrt{2\ln2}\,\sqrt{b_{-3}L^\*},Sx​(Δf) ∝ exp(−2π2στ2​Δf2),στ​=2πb−3​L\*​1​,Δf3dB​≈22ln2​b−3​L\*​, where L\*=ln⁡12πflτ\*+32−γEL^\*=\ln\frac{1}{2\pi f_l\tau^\*}+\frac32-\gamma_EL\*=ln2πfl​τ\*1​+23​−γE​. With lab_29's parameters, τ\*=1.64×10−4\tau^\*=1.64\times10^{-4}τ\*=1.64×10−4 s and L\*≈12.1L^\*\approx12.1L\*≈12.1, giving an approximate linewidth of 323332333233 Hz, versus the exact linewidth 317631763176 Hz obtained by "no freezing, direct numerical Fourier transform" — the freezing approximation errs by ≈2%\approx2\%≈2%. Linewidth-scaling contrast (engineering mnemonic): white noise Δf3dB=πb−2\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\pi b_{-2}Δf3dB​=πb−2​ (Sϕ=b−2/f2S_\phi=b_{-2}/f^2Sϕ​=b−2​/f2, another way of writing D/πD/\piD/π), proportional to the noise strength; flicker Δf3dB≈2.355b−3L\*\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}\approx2.355\sqrt{b_{-3}L^\*}Δf3dB​≈2.355b−3​L\*​, proportional to the square root of the noise strength (up to a log). Drop the noise by 6 dB: the white-noise linewidth shrinks to 1/4, the flicker linewidth only to about 1/2. Shape fingerprint (the −3-3−3 dB / −10-10−10 dB half-width ratio) — a directly measurable lineshape discriminant. Let x=Δf/HWHMx=\Delta f/\text{HWHM}x=Δf/HWHM: Lorentzian: S∝11+x2S\propto\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}S∝1+x21​. −3-3−3 dB (S=12S=\tfrac12S=21​) at x=1x=1x=1; −10-10−10 dB (S=110S=\tfrac1{10}S=101​) at 1+x2=10⇒x=31+x^2=10\Rightarrow x=31+x2=10⇒x=3. Ratio exactly 3.003.003.00. Gaussian: S∝e−ln⁡2 x2S\propto e^{-\ln2\,x^2}S∝e−ln2x2 (written so that x=1x=1x=1 is exactly −3-3−3 dB). −10-10−10 dB at ln⁡2 x2=ln⁡10⇒x=ln⁡10/ln⁡2=1.8226\ln2\,x^2=\ln10\Rightarrow x=\sqrt{\ln10/\ln2}=1.8226ln2x2=ln10⇒x=ln10/ln2​=1.8226. Ratio 1.821.821.82. Flicker line (exact numerical theory including the log correction): 1.861.861.86 — slightly "heavier-tailed" than a pure Gaussian, because the log makes the envelope decay a bit more slowly than the frozen Gaussian; measured 1.891.891.89. The Lorentzian's 3.003.003.00 and the Gaussian family's values around 1.81.81.8 are far apart — one measurement settles it. Honest attribution (external theory vs. computed on this site): the rigorous theory of "oscillator lineshape under f−αf^{-\alpha}f−α noise (including the near-Gaussian conclusion)" is external literature, not among the five source PDFs: [E3] F. X. Kärtner, "Analysis of White and f−αf^{-\alpha}f−α Noise in Oscillators," Int. J. Circuit Theory Appl., vol. 18, no. 5, pp. 485–519, 1990 (already listed in this site's references); the rigorous stochastic model for colored noise is A. Demir, "Phase Noise and Timing Jitter in Oscillators with Colored-Noise Sources," IEEE Trans. Circuits Syst. I, vol. 49, no. 12, pp. 1782–1791, Dec. 2002 (external literature, not among the five source PDFs); the textbook-level treatment is E. Rubiola, "Phase Noise and Frequency Stability in Oscillators," Cambridge Univ. Press, Cambridge, U.K., 2009 (external literature, not among the five source PDFs). What this page does itself: the elementary derivations of Steps 1–4 (increment filter + integration by parts + characteristic function, with no skipped steps), and all of lab_29's numerical verification (the t2log⁡t^2\logt2log variance law, the lineshape, the width ratio, the linewidth, the L\mathcal{L}L matching).

documents.t: Wide-sense stationarity requires two things: a mean that does not change with time, and an autocorrelation Rϕ(t1,t2)R_\phi(t_1,t_2)Rϕ​(t1​,t2​) that depends only on τ=t2−t1\tau=t_2-t_1τ=t2​−t1​. For a white-noise-driven Wiener phase started at t=0t=0t=0 (ϕ(0)=0\phi(0)=0ϕ(0)=0), compute RϕR_\phiRϕ​ step by step: (i) Take t2≥t1t_2\ge t_1t2​≥t1​ and split ϕ(t2)=ϕ(t1)+Δ\phi(t_2)=\phi(t_1)+\Deltaϕ(t2​)=ϕ(t1​)+Δ, where Δ=ϕ(t2)−ϕ(t1)\Delta=\phi(t_2)-\phi(t_1)Δ=ϕ(t2​)−ϕ(t1​) is the noise integral over the interval (t1,t2](t_1,t_2](t1​,t2​], independent of ϕ(t1)\phi(t_1)ϕ(t1​) (white noise is uncorrelated across disjoint intervals; for Gaussians, uncorrelated = independent). (ii) Rϕ(t1,t2)=⟨ϕ(t1) [ϕ(t1)+Δ]⟩=⟨ϕ(t1)2⟩+⟨ϕ(t1)⟩⟨Δ⟩⏟=0=2D t1.R_\phi(t_1,t_2)=\big\langle\phi(t_1)\,[\phi(t_1)+\Delta]\big\rangle =\big\langle\phi(t_1)^2\big\rangle+\underbrace{\langle\phi(t_1)\rangle\langle\Delta\rangle}_{=0} =2D\,t_1 .Rϕ​(t1​,t2​)=⟨ϕ(t1​)[ϕ(t1​)+Δ]⟩=⟨ϕ(t1​)2⟩+=0⟨ϕ(t1​)⟩⟨Δ⟩​​=2Dt1​. General form (no ordering assumed): Rϕ(t1,t2)=2Dmin⁡(t1,t2) \boxed{\ R_\phi(t_1,t_2)=2D\min(t_1,t_2)\ } Rϕ​(t1​,t2​)=2Dmin(t1​,t2​) ​ This is not a function of τ\tauτ — it depends on absolute time (how long since power-up). Moreover Var⁡[ϕ(t)]=2Dt→∞\operatorname{Var}[\phi(t)]=2Dt\to\inftyVar[ϕ(t)]=2Dt→∞: unbounded variance. Both violate stationarity. Consequence: the Wiener–Khinchin theorem (stochastic_noise_basics) presupposes stationarity. So "Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f)" as a stationary PSD strictly does not exist — expressions like Sϕ=2D/Δω2S_\phi=2D/\Delta\omega^2Sϕ​=2D/Δω2 cannot be read literally by definition. Flicker FM is worse: even the increment variance needs flf_lfl​ to be finite (Step 3). But the increments are stationary: Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]=2D∣τ∣\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]=2D|\tau|Var[Δϕ(τ)]=2D∣τ∣ is independent of t0t_0t0​ (Step 1 (i)). This is why [P2] describes ring jitter in increment language, σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ ([P2] Eq.(8), p.792) — increment statistics are well defined, the PSD is not. Time-domain jitter language is, mathematically, more fundamental than "SϕS_\phiSϕ​".

documents.t: Although ϕ\phiϕ diverges, V(t)=cos⁡(ω0t+ϕ(t))V(t)=\cos(\omega_0t+\phi(t))V(t)=cos(ω0​t+ϕ(t)) is bounded, and its statistics converge to stationary: The divergence of the "absolute" phase does not matter — VVV only sees ϕ mod 2π\phi\bmod 2\piϕmod2π, and the mod 2π\bmod 2\pimod2π distribution of a random walk tends to uniform over time (the initial phase is forgotten). The autocorrelation retains only the phase difference: ⟨V(t)V(t+τ)⟩→12cos⁡(ω0τ)E(τ)\langle V(t)V(t+\tau)\rangle\to\tfrac12\cos(\omega_0\tau)E(\tau)⟨V(t)V(t+τ)⟩→21​cos(ω0​τ)E(τ) (the Step-1 computation of lorentzian_linewidth, which uses precisely the stationary increment Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ) — depends only on τ\tauτ ✓. This is one of the core points of [E2] A. Demir, A. Mehrotra, and J. Roychowdhury, IEEE TCAS-I 47(5):655–674, 2000 (not among the five source PDFs, DOI 10.1109/81.847872): the output of a noisy oscillator converges to a stationary process, whose spectrum (a Lorentzian under white noise) is a rigorously well-defined object — and it is exactly what the spectrum analyzer measures. Part A of this page merely runs the same machinery with flicker's Var⁡(τ)\operatorname{Var}(\tau)Var(τ); the lineshape changes from Lorentzian to near-Gaussian, but "VVV is stationary and its spectrum is well defined" is unchanged (flicker needs the flf_lfl​ cutoff to make ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ stationary). One table for "what exists, and who measures it": Object Strictly exists? Who measures it the sample path ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) ✓ (but nonstationary, unbounded walk) nobody measures it directly (an infinite-range phase meter does not exist) Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) as a stationary PSD ✗ (the Wiener–Khinchin premise fails) — (a convenient notation; see Step 7) increment statistics Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]Var[Δϕ(τ)] ✓ (white: inherently; flicker: needs flf_lfl​) time-interval analyzers / jitter measurement ([P2]'s κΔt\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}κΔt​), allan_variance finite-observation spectrum Sϕ(T)(f)S_\phi^{(T)}(f)Sϕ(T)​(f), f≫1/Tf\gg1/Tf≫1/T ✓ (expectation well defined, converges) phase-noise analyzer (phase discriminator + FFT; the PLL eats the walk below the loop bandwidth) — the Welch of lab_29 panel (d) is exactly this SV(f)S_V(f)SV​(f) (the PSD of V(t)V(t)V(t)) ✓ (VVV stationary, [E2]) spectrum analyzer, directly (linewidth, lineshape, and L\mathcal{L}L are all read from it) L(Δf)=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)=\tfrac12S_\phiL(Δf)=21​Sϕ​ ✓ when Δf≫\Delta f\ggΔf≫ linewidth (and ≫1/T\gg1/T≫1/T) the number on the datasheet

documents.t: So what do the pagefuls of SϕS_\phiSϕ​ and L\mathcal{L}L formulas on this site (and in [P1]) mean? They are conditional spectra at finite observation time: take a record of length TTT (or let the PLL/instrument subtract the slow drift), and do spectral estimation on "the increments that look stationary within this record". One can show (and lab_29 panel (d) demonstrates numerically) that for f≫1/Tf\gg1/Tf≫1/T the expectation converges to Sϕ(T)(f) →f≫1/T 4D(2πf)2 （單邊，white FM）,b−3f3 （flicker FM）,S_\phi^{(T)}(f)\ \xrightarrow[f\gg1/T]{}\ \frac{4D}{(2\pi f)^2}\ \text{（單邊，white FM）},\qquad \frac{b_{-3}}{f^3}\ \text{（flicker FM）},Sϕ(T)​(f) f≫1/T​ (2πf)24D​ （單邊，white FM）,f3b−3​​ （flicker FM）, with measured ÷ theory =1.001=1.001=1.001 (10 kHz; see the marker above). So every SϕS_\phiSϕ​ formula on this site is rigorously usable in the range Δf≫max⁡(1/T, 線寬)\Delta f\gg\max(1/T,\ \text{線寬})Δf≫max(1/T, 線寬); where they fail is precisely the "spurious divergence" region of lorentzian_linewidth — for Δf≲\Delta f\lesssimΔf≲ linewidth you must switch to reading SVS_VSV​ (the Lorentzian / near-Gaussian lineshape). The two descriptions splice seamlessly over their common range of validity (Part A's 0.6 dB exercise quantifies the splice point). Flicker adds one more twist (this page's own lesson): because flf_lfl​ enters the variance through ln⁡\lnln, "finite observation" leaves a logarithmic afterimage on flicker forever — lab_29's cutoff experiment (flf_lfl​ moved from 1/321/321/32 Hz to 1 Hz halves Var⁡(10 ms)\operatorname{Var}(10\,\text{ms})Var(10ms)) and the single-record linewidth spread (2944±1422944\pm1422944±142 Hz, 6 records of only 32 s each) are direct displays of it. In practical language: for a flicker-dominated oscillator, the "linewidth" and the close-in integrated jitter are (weak) functions of "how long you measure"; quote the observation time / measurement bandwidth alongside the number — which is also why allan_variance exists (flicker FM shows up as a clean plateau on ADEV, well defined without any flf_lfl​). For the textbook treatment of this viewpoint see Rubiola 2009 (cited above, external literature).

documents.t: The Lorentzian is exclusive to white FM: it is inherited from the linear growth Var⁡[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi]=2D|t|Var[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣. The universal engine: Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]=2∫0∞Sϕ單邊(f)(1−cos⁡2πfτ) df\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]=2\int_0^\infty S_\phi^{\text{單邊}}(f)(1-\cos2\pi f\tau)\,dfVar[Δϕ(τ)]=2∫0∞​Sϕ單邊​(f)(1−cos2πfτ)df (increment high-pass kernel; single-sided bookkeeping — substituting the white 4D/Δω24D/\Delta\omega^24D/Δω2 recovers 2D∣t∣2D|t|2D∣t∣; lab_29 measures a ratio of 1.001). Flicker FM (Sϕ=b−3/f3S_\phi=b_{-3}/f^3Sϕ​=b−3​/f3, needs a low-frequency cutoff flf_lfl​): Var⁡=4π2b−3τ2[ln⁡12πflτ+32−γE]\operatorname{Var}=4\pi^2b_{-3}\tau^2[\ln\frac{1}{2\pi f_l\tau}+\frac32-\gamma_E]Var=4π2b−3​τ2[ln2πfl​τ1​+23​−γE​] — t2×log⁡t^2\times\logt2×log growth; flf_lfl​ enters only through ln⁡\lnln (a 10× change shifts it by only ln⁡10\ln10ln10). Characteristic function E=e−Var⁡/2E=e^{-\operatorname{Var}/2}E=e−Var/2 ⇒ near-Gaussian envelope ⇒ near-Gaussian line core; linewidth ≈2.355b−3L\*\approx2.355\sqrt{b_{-3}L^\*}≈2.355b−3​L\*​ (∝噪\propto\sqrt{\text{噪}}∝噪​, i.e. the square root of the noise strength; for white noise it is ∝\propto∝ noise strength). Shape fingerprint, the −10-10−10 dB / −3-3−3 dB half-width ratio: Lorentzian 3.003.003.00, Gaussian 1.821.821.82, flicker with log correction 1.861.861.86 (lab_29 measures white 2.872.872.87, flicker 1.891.891.89; Lorentzian-fit rms error 0.24 vs 4.37 dB). The same L(10 kHz)=−71\mathcal{L}(10\,\text{kHz})=-71L(10kHz)=−71 dBc/Hz: white-noise linewidth 50 Hz, flicker linewidth 3.1 kHz (61×) — single-point PN does not determine the linewidth; the noise color does. Free-running ϕ\phiϕ: Rϕ=2Dmin⁡(t1,t2)R_\phi=2D\min(t_1,t_2)Rϕ​=2Dmin(t1​,t2​), unbounded variance ⇒ nonstationary ⇒ SϕS_\phiSϕ​ as a stationary PSD strictly does not exist; what exists: increment statistics ([P2]'s κΔt\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}κΔt​), the finite-observation conditional spectrum (converging to this site's formulas for f≫1/Tf\gg1/Tf≫1/T), and the stationary SVS_VSV​ ([E2] Demir; what the spectrum analyzer measures). Flicker's measured quantities (linewidth, close-in jitter) depend as ln⁡\lnln on observation time / cutoff — quote the conditions with the number.

documents.t: Prerequisites: diffusion_dictionary | Next: final_exam What this page answers: Starting from the state equations of an ideal parallel LC, why must Floquet linearization always produce a phase direction with eigenvalue λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0? How does the geometric projection give Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ and Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​ (Parseval)? Plugged into [P1] Eq.(21), why does that come out to −145-145−145 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz (canonical example B's Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5 gives −148-148−148, a 3 dB difference)? How does the Lorentzian tame the 1/f21/f^21/f2 divergence as Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0 — where does the true-LC (D=0.125D=0.125D=0.125 rad²/s) 3-dB linewidth Δf3dB=D/π=39.8\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=D/\pi=39.8Δf3dB​=D/π=39.8 mHz come from? Integrating a measured −100-100−100 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz from 1 to 100 MHz gives σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs — why? And how does that turn into the 6.3% UI eaten out of a 10 Gb/s eye at BER 10−1210^{-12}10−12? This page is the site's main spine: take one ideal lossless parallel LC oscillator, start from the lowest-level state equations, skip nothing, keep every step rigorous and numerical, and push all the way to the BER (bit error rate) bathtub curve that a communications engineer ultimately reads. Finish this page and you hold the entire ISF phase-noise theory as one unbroken chain — every other page on the site is a zoomed-in view of some segment of this spine. Physical intuition (the whole chain up front): the LC's energy sloshes losslessly back and forth between the inductor and the capacitor → it traces a limit cycle in the 2-D state plane. A noise current pokes it; the resulting displacement decomposes into "tangential along the cycle = phase" and "radial perpendicular to the cycle = amplitude"; amplitude has a restoring force and gets pulled back, phase has no restoring force and accumulates permanently — the weight "how much permanent phase per unit injected charge" is the ISF Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ), and for the ideal LC it comes out exactly −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ. Weight the white noise by Γ\GammaΓ and integrate (the integrator gives 1/ω21/\omega^21/ω2) and you get the 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise L(Δω)\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega)L(Δω). This 1/f21/f^21/f2 appears to diverge as Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0, but near the carrier it actually flattens into a Lorentzian with a finite linewidth Δf3dB\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}Δf3dB​. Integrate L\mathcal{L}L over offset frequency, take the square root, divide by 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ to get the rms jitter σt\sigma_tσt​; finally σt\sigma_tσt​ eats the eye from both sides and sets the BER. One sentence: state geometry → ISF → integration → spectrum → linewidth → jitter → BER. The spine has 8 stations, each of which corresponds to the in-depth version on some page of the site; this page welds them into an unbroken chain and walks the same set of canonical numbers (qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz) all the way through.
documents.s: Capstone — One Ideal LC from State Equations to BER (Fully Rigorous, End to End)

documents.t: Take an ideal lossless parallel LC: inductor LLL and capacitor CCC in parallel, no resistive loss of any kind. Describe it with two state variables — the capacitor voltage vvv (V) and the inductor current iLi_LiL​ (A). KCL at the parallel node: current into the capacitor === current out of the inductor; the inductor's vvv–iii relation is v=L diL/dtv=L\,di_L/dtv=LdiL​/dt. Rearranged into a first-order state-equation system: v˙(t)=dvdt=−1C iL(t),i˙L(t)=diLdt=+1L v(t).\begin{aligned} \dot v(t)&=\frac{dv}{dt}=-\frac{1}{C}\,i_L(t),\\ \dot i_L(t)&=\frac{di_L}{dt}=+\frac{1}{L}\,v(t). \end{aligned}v˙(t)i˙L​(t)​=dtdv​=−C1​iL​(t),=dtdiL​​=+L1​v(t).​ Physics used: capacitor iC=C v˙i_C=C\,\dot viC​=Cv˙, inductor vL=L i˙Lv_L=L\,\dot i_LvL​=Li˙L​, plus the parallel-node KCL (iC=−iLi_C=-i_LiC​=−iL​; the current the capacitor releases flows into the inductor). Unit check: [v˙]=[A]/[F]=[A]/[C/V]=V/s[\dot v]=[\text{A}]/[\text{F}]=[\text{A}]/[\text{C/V}]=\text{V/s}[v˙]=[A]/[F]=[A]/[C/V]=V/s ✓; [i˙L]=[V]/[H]=[V]/[Wb/A]=A/s[\dot i_L]=[\text{V}]/[\text{H}]=[\text{V}]/[\text{Wb/A}]=\text{A/s}[i˙L​]=[V]/[H]=[V]/[Wb/A]=A/s ✓ (both right-hand sides are "time rate of change of a state"). As a vector field: let the state be x=(v, iL)T\mathbf{x}=(v,\ i_L)^Tx=(v, iL​)T; then x˙=A0x\dot{\mathbf x}=A_0\mathbf xx˙=A0​x, where A0=(0−1/C1/L0).A_0=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1/C\\[2pt] 1/L & 0\end{pmatrix}.A0​=(01/L​−1/C0​). Solving it (confirming it really oscillates): the eigenvalues λ\lambdaλ of A0A_0A0​ satisfy λ2=−1LC\lambda^2=-\dfrac{1}{LC}λ2=−LC1​, i.e. λ=±jω0\lambda=\pm j\omega_0λ=±jω0​, ω0=1LC\omega_0=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}ω0​=LC​1​ (rad/s). Purely imaginary eigenvalues → the solution is an undamped sinusoid: v(t)=Vmaxcos⁡(ω0t),iL(t)=Vmaxω0Lsin⁡(ω0t).v(t)=V_{max}\cos(\omega_0 t),\qquad i_L(t)=\frac{V_{max}}{\omega_0 L}\sin(\omega_0 t).v(t)=Vmax​cos(ω0​t),iL​(t)=ω0​LVmax​​sin(ω0​t). Unit check (frequency): ω0=1/LC\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}ω0​=1/LC​, [H⋅F]=(V s/A)(A s/V)=s2=s[\sqrt{\text{H}\cdot\text{F}}]=\sqrt{(\text{V s/A})(\text{A s/V})}=\sqrt{\text{s}^2}=\text{s}[H⋅F​]=(V s/A)(A s/V)​=s2​=s, so ω0\omega_0ω0​ is 1/s=rad/s1/\text{s}=\text{rad/s}1/s=rad/s ✓. This is the marginally stable ideal limit: no loss → the eigenvalues sit on the imaginary axis → the amplitude is set by the initial energy, neither growing nor decaying. A real LC has finite QQQ; an active circuit (cross-coupled pair) replenishes the loss to sustain constant amplitude — but the essence of the phase dynamics (Station ② onward) is the same. Site cross-reference: full 2-D state geometry in isf_definition Step 2, numerical model in lab_02. Injecting noise: drive a noise current in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) into the capacitor node (it changes the current flowing into the capacitor, so it only touches v˙\dot vv˙): v˙=−1C iL+1C in(t),i˙L=1L v.\dot v=-\frac{1}{C}\,i_L+\frac{1}{C}\,i_n(t),\qquad \dot i_L=\frac{1}{L}\,v.v˙=−C1​iL​+C1​in​(t),i˙L​=L1​v. Write it in the standard perturbation form x˙=A0x+B in\dot{\mathbf x}=A_0\mathbf x+B\,i_nx˙=A0​x+Bin​, where the injection vector B=(1/C, 0)TB=(1/C,\ 0)^TB=(1/C, 0)T — the mathematical ID card of "a current through the capacitor becomes v˙\dot vv˙" (the differential version of [P1] Eq.(9), p.181, ΔV=Δq/C\Delta V=\Delta q/CΔV=Δq/C). Unit check (B): [B in]=[A]/[F]=V/s[B\,i_n]=[\text{A}]/[\text{F}]=\text{V/s}[Bin​]=[A]/[F]=V/s, same units as v˙\dot vv˙ ✓. This station delivers: a clean set of linear state equations + an explicit noise-injection vector B=(1/C,0)TB=(1/C,0)^TB=(1/C,0)T. Every later station grows out of here.
documents.s: Station ①: LC state equations (v˙, i˙L\dot v,\ \dot i_Lv˙, i˙L​)

documents.t: For the ideal LC, A0A_0A0​ is a constant matrix (a linear circuit), so the "linearization" step is trivial — it is linear to begin with. But the rigorous basis for permanent phase accumulation is Floquet theory (the solution structure of linear systems with periodic coefficients). Here we take only the conclusion and map it onto the LC; the full proof is in derivation_floquet_ppv (that page explicitly marks Floquet/adjoint/PPV as external literature, not among the 5 source PDFs; primary source [E2] Demir 2000). Key theorem (derivation_floquet_ppv Step 3): differentiate the steady-state solution xs(t)\mathbf x_s(t)xs​(t) with respect to time; x˙s\dot{\mathbf x}_sx˙s​ itself is automatically a solution of the homogeneous perturbation equation, and it is periodic, with no exponential factor — corresponding to Floquet exponent λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0. Physically, x˙s\dot{\mathbf x}_sx˙s​ is the tangential "walk along the trajectory" direction = the phase direction; λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0 mathematically guarantees that a phase perturbation neither grows nor decays — it is retained forever. Concrete verification for the LC: xs(t)=Vmax(cos⁡ω0t, 1ω0Lsin⁡ω0t)\mathbf x_s(t)=V_{max}\big(\cos\omega_0 t,\ \tfrac{1}{\omega_0 L}\sin\omega_0 t\big)xs​(t)=Vmax​(cosω0​t, ω0​L1​sinω0​t), x˙s(t)=Vmax ω0(−sin⁡ω0t, 1ω0Lcos⁡ω0t).\dot{\mathbf x}_s(t)=V_{max}\,\omega_0\Big(-\sin\omega_0 t,\ \tfrac{1}{\omega_0 L}\cos\omega_0 t\Big).x˙s​(t)=Vmax​ω0​(−sinω0​t, ω0​L1​cosω0​t). Substituting back into ( ⋅ )˙=A0(⋅)\dot{(\,\cdot\,)}=A_0(\cdot)(⋅)˙​=A0​(⋅) holds directly (that is exactly "it is itself a solution"), and it is purely periodic, λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0 ✓. The other direction (the amplitude direction) corresponds to λ2\lambda_2λ2​: for the ideal lossless LC, λ2\lambda_2λ2​ is also on the imaginary axis (Re λ2=0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_2=0Reλ2​=0), meaning the ideal LC does not even damp its amplitude; only real loss + amplitude restoring makes the amplitude direction Re λ2<0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_2<0Reλ2​<0 (decaying), so that "only phase persists forever" holds rigorously (see phase_vs_amplitude_noise). Why this station is needed: Station ③ will "project the perturbation onto the phase direction". Floquet tells us what that direction is (the x˙s\dot{\mathbf x}_sx˙s​ with λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0) and why the projected phase accumulates permanently (a neutral direction, no restoring force). Without this station, Station ③'s "projection" would be mere intuition. Unit check: the Floquet exponent λ\lambdaλ has units 1/s1/\text{s}1/s, λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0 (rad persists forever); λT\lambda TλT is dimensionless ✓. Rigorous correspondence: derivation_floquet_ppv proves that the ISF is the component of the PPV (perturbation projection vector) at the injection node: Γ(ω0τ)/qmax=v1T(τ) b\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)/q_{max}=v_1^T(\tau)\,\mathbf bΓ(ω0​τ)/qmax​=v1T​(τ)b, where b=B\mathbf b=Bb=B is Station ①'s injection vector. Station ③ of this page computes this projection by hand using geometry, consistent with the PPV result. This station delivers: the phase direction =x˙s=\dot{\mathbf x}_s=x˙s​ (λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0, never decays). The next station projects the noise onto it.
documents.s: Station ②: Linearization / Floquet — why there is a phase direction that "never decays"

documents.t: Now execute Station ②'s "project onto the phase direction" concretely for the LC. Normalize the state (take Vmax=1V_{max}=1Vmax​=1 and rescale the iLi_LiL​ axis to equal radius); the limit cycle is the unit circle z(θ)=(cos⁡θ, sin⁡θ)\mathbf z(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)z(θ)=(cosθ, sinθ), θ=ω0t\theta=\omega_0 tθ=ω0​t, and the first component v=cos⁡θv=\cos\thetav=cosθ is the tank voltage. Step A — state displacement caused by injection: Station ①'s noise current only moves the capacitor voltage, Δv=Δq/C\Delta v=\Delta q/CΔv=Δq/C, so the displacement is along the +v+v+v axis: Δz=(Δv, 0)=(ΔqC, 0).\Delta\mathbf z=(\Delta v,\ 0)=\big(\tfrac{\Delta q}{C},\ 0\big).Δz=(Δv, 0)=(CΔq​, 0). Step B — tangential projection. The tangent vector along the cycle is ∂z∂θ=(−sin⁡θ, cos⁡θ)\dfrac{\partial\mathbf z}{\partial\theta}=(-\sin\theta,\ \cos\theta)∂θ∂z​=(−sinθ, cosθ), with norm ∣∂z/∂θ∣=1\left|\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta\right|=1∣∂z/∂θ∣=1. Phase increment === "tangential displacement" ÷ "arc length per unit θ\thetaθ along the cycle": Δϕ=Δz⋅(∂z/∂θ)∣∂z/∂θ∣2=(Δv,0)⋅(−sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ)sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ=−sin⁡θ Δv1=−sin⁡θ Δv.\Delta\phi=\frac{\Delta\mathbf z\cdot(\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta)}{\lvert\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta\rvert^2} =\frac{(\Delta v,0)\cdot(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)}{\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta} =\frac{-\sin\theta\,\Delta v}{1}=-\sin\theta\,\Delta v.Δϕ=∣∂z/∂θ∣2Δz⋅(∂z/∂θ)​=sin2θ+cos2θ(Δv,0)⋅(−sinθ,cosθ)​=1−sinθΔv​=−sinθΔv. Step C — substitute Δv=Δq/C\Delta v=\Delta q/CΔv=Δq/C and use qmax=C⋅Vmax=Cq_{max}=C\cdot V_{max}=Cqmax​=C⋅Vmax​=C (normalized Vmax=1V_{max}=1Vmax​=1): Δϕ=−sin⁡θ ΔqC=−sin⁡θqmax Δq=Γ(θ)qmax Δq,Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ. \boxed{\ \Delta\phi=-\sin\theta\,\frac{\Delta q}{C}=\frac{-\sin\theta}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q=\frac{\Gamma(\theta)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q,\qquad \Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\theta.\ } Δϕ=−sinθCΔq​=qmax​−sinθ​Δq=qmax​Γ(θ)​Δq,Γ(θ)=−sinθ. ​ Dimension check: Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ in rad (dimensionless); Δq/qmax=C/C\Delta q/q_{max}=\text{C}/\text{C}Δq/qmax​=C/C dimensionless; hence Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless ✓ (this is exactly why [P1] normalizes by qmaxq_{max}qmax​: it turns Γ\GammaΓ into a pure shape describing "where the waveform is sensitive"). Physics check: θ=0\theta=0θ=0 (peak, v=1v=1v=1) → Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0; the kick becomes all amplitude (which gets pulled back). θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2 (rising zero crossing, v=0v=0v=0) → Γ=−1\Gamma=-1Γ=−1; the kick becomes all phase (∣Γ∣\vert\Gamma\vert∣Γ∣ maximal). Exactly as intuition demands. Site cross-reference: this expression is verbatim identical to the hands-on derivation in isf_definition, the numerical verification in lab_02 (error ∼\sim∼0.001), and the operational definition impulse_to_phase_shift. Rigorous correspondence: comparing with Station ②, Γ(θ)/qmax=v1T(θ) B\Gamma(\theta)/q_{max}=v_1^T(\theta)\,BΓ(θ)/qmax​=v1T​(θ)B — the −sin⁡θ/qmax-\sin\theta/q_{max}−sinθ/qmax​ computed here by geometric projection is precisely the component of the PPV v1v_1v1​ at the capacitor node (derivation_floquet_ppv Step 6). Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Panel titles read: "(a) LC 波形與其 ISF" = (a) LC waveform and its ISF; "(b) Δφ 與注入電荷成正比 (small-signal)" = (b) Δφ is proportional to the injected charge (small-signal); "(c) zero-crossing 注入 → 相位跳變" = (c) zero-crossing injection → a phase jump. This station delivers: the ideal LC's ISF Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ (analytic, dimensionless, 2π2\pi2π-periodic). Note it has only one harmonic (c1=1c_1=1c1​=1, all other cn=0c_n=0cn​=0, c0=0c_0=0c0​=0) — this cleanness lets every later step be done in your head.

documents.t: The phase-noise formula consumes only the ISF's rms value (no need for the individual cnc_ncn​). Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is defined as the root mean square over one period (see rms_isf): Γrms=12π∫02π∣Γ(x)∣2 dx.\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\lvert\Gamma(x)\rvert^2\,dx}.Γrms​=2π1​∫02π​∣Γ(x)∣2dx​. Substitute Γ(x)=−sin⁡x\Gamma(x)=-\sin xΓ(x)=−sinx, use the half-angle identity sin⁡2x=12(1−cos⁡2x)\sin^2 x=\tfrac12(1-\cos 2x)sin2x=21​(1−cos2x), and the fact that cos⁡2x\cos 2xcos2x integrates to 0 over a full period: Γrms2=12π∫02πsin⁡2x dx=12π∫02π1−cos⁡2x2 dx=12π⋅2π2=12,Γrms=12≈0.707.\begin{aligned} \Gamma_{rms}^2&=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2 x\,dx =\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}\,dx =\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{2\pi}{2}=\frac12,\\ \Gamma_{rms}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx0.707. \end{aligned}Γrms2​Γrms​​=2π1​∫02π​sin2xdx=2π1​∫02π​21−cos2x​dx=2π1​⋅22π​=21​,=2​1​≈0.707.​ Cross-check with Parseval ([P1] Eq.(20), p.185; ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​): the ideal LC has only c1=1c_1=1c1​=1, all others 0, so ∑n=0∞cn2=c12=1=2Γrms2 ⟹ Γrms2=12,Γrms=12.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=c_1^2=1=2\Gamma_{rms}^2\ \Longrightarrow\ \Gamma_{rms}^2=\tfrac12,\quad\Gamma_{rms}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}.n=0∑∞​cn2​=c12​=1=2Γrms2​ ⟹ Γrms2​=21​,Γrms​=2​1​. The two methods agree ✓. Dimension check: Γ\GammaΓ dimensionless → Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ dimensionless ✓. Physical meaning: the smaller Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, the lower the oscillator's "average efficiency" at converting noise into phase → the better the phase noise. −sin⁡-\sin−sin's Γrms=0.707\Gamma_{rms}=0.707Γrms​=0.707 is the LC's signature value; a ring concentrates its sensitivity at the transitions, and with Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 ([P2] Eq.(16), p.794; the radical covers only the constant, confirmed by the text's 4/N^1.5@η=0.75) the stage count can push it down, but the LC's high QQQ usually still wins (see lc_vs_ring). This station delivers: Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​. It is the only ISF input to Station ⑤'s formula.

documents.t: Station ⑤'s Sϕ∝1/Δω2S_\phi\propto1/\Delta\omega^2Sϕ​∝1/Δω2 diverges as Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0 — yet the total phase power cannot be infinite (carrier power is conserved). The contradiction comes from "linearization treating phase as a random walk that can accumulate without bound". The rigorous treatment (phase diffusion → carrier autocorrelation → Wiener–Khinchin) yields a Lorentzian with a finite linewidth. Full derivation in lorentzian_linewidth (with [E2] Demir 2000, not among the 5 source PDFs); here we take the result of spec sec. 11.2 and plug in the numbers. The phase diffusion coefficient DDD (rad²/s) is fixed by the coefficient of the 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt. Match the single-sided Sϕ=4D/Δω2S_\phi=4D/\Delta\omega^2Sϕ​=4D/Δω2 (double-sided 2D/Δω22D/\Delta\omega^22D/Δω2; spec sec. 11.2, v5 correction) against Station ⑤'s Sϕ=Γrms2qmax2SiΔω2S_\phi=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\dfrac{S_i}{\Delta\omega^2}Sϕ​=qmax2​Γrms2​​Δω2Si​​ (single-sided): D=Γrms24 qmax2 in2‾Δf=κ22.D=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{4\,q_{max}^2}\,\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=\frac{\kappa^2}{2}.D=4qmax2​Γrms2​​Δfin2​​​=2κ2​. Lorentzian spectrum and 3-dB linewidth (FWHM, full width at half maximum) (spec sec. 11.2, v5 correction): S(Δω)∝DD2+Δω2, Δf3dB=Dπ=Γrms24π qmax2 in2‾Δf=κ22π S(\Delta\omega)\propto\frac{D}{D^2+\Delta\omega^2},\qquad \boxed{\ \Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\frac{D}{\pi}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{4\pi\,q_{max}^2}\,\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=\frac{\kappa^2}{2\pi}\ }S(Δω)∝D2+Δω2D​, Δf3dB​=πD​=4πqmax2​Γrms2​​Δfin2​​​=2πκ2​ ​ Plug in the canonical numbers (Γrms2=0.5\Gamma_{rms}^2=0.5Γrms2​=0.5, qmax=10−12q_{max}=10^{-12}qmax​=10−12 C, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz): Step 1: compute DDD. D=0.54×(10−12)2×10−24=0.54×10−24×10−24=0.54=0.125 rad2/s.D=\frac{0.5}{4\times(10^{-12})^2}\times10^{-24} =\frac{0.5}{4\times10^{-24}}\times10^{-24} =\frac{0.5}{4}=0.125\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}.D=4×(10−12)20.5​×10−24=4×10−240.5​×10−24=40.5​=0.125 rad2/s. Step 2: compute the linewidth. Δf3dB=Dπ=0.1253.1416=0.0398 Hz≈40 mHz.\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\frac{D}{\pi}=\frac{0.125}{3.1416}=0.0398\ \text{Hz}\approx40\ \text{mHz}.Δf3dB​=πD​=3.14160.125​=0.0398 Hz≈40 mHz. Dimension check (DDD): (dimensionless)C2⋅A2Hz=A2⋅sA2s2=1s\dfrac{(\text{dimensionless})}{\text{C}^2}\cdot\dfrac{\text{A}^2}{\text{Hz}} =\dfrac{\text{A}^2\cdot\text{s}}{\text{A}^2\text{s}^2}=\dfrac{1}{\text{s}}C2(dimensionless)​⋅HzA2​=A2s2A2⋅s​=s1​ — and DDD is rad²/s; rad is dimensionless, so =1/s=1/\text{s}=1/s ✓. Δf3dB=D/π\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=D/\piΔf3dB​=D/π: [1/s]/(dimensionless)=Hz[1/\text{s}]/(\text{dimensionless})=\text{Hz}[1/s]/(dimensionless)=Hz ✓. Physical meaning (resolving the paradox): 1/f21/f^21/f2 is only the far-out asymptote; for Δω≲D\Delta\omega\lesssim DΔω≲D (here ≲0.125\lesssim0.125≲0.125 rad/s) the spectrum flattens into the Lorentzian top and no longer diverges. Integrating the Lorentzian over all frequencies === the carrier power (conserved). So the divergence in [P1] Eq.(21) is a "linearization artifact"; the real spectrum near the carrier is a Lorentzian of finite height. Do not confuse HWHM with FWHM (the 20/40 pair is not a contradiction): the corner where the spectrum flattens — the half-width at half maximum (HWHM) — occurs at Δω=D\Delta\omega=DΔω=D, i.e. a single-sided offset fHWHM=D/2π=0.125/6.283≈20f_{\mathrm{HWHM}}=D/2\pi=0.125/6.283\approx20fHWHM​=D/2π=0.125/6.283≈20 mHz; whereas the boxed linewidth is the full width at half maximum (FWHM) Δf3dB=D/π≈40\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=D/\pi\approx40Δf3dB​=D/π≈40 mHz, exactly twice the HWHM (FWHM=2×HWHM\text{FWHM}=2\times\text{HWHM}FWHM=2×HWHM). So "flattening starts around a 20 mHz offset" refers to the single-sided half-width, and "linewidth 40 mHz" refers to the full width — same Lorentzian, same DDD, merely half-width vs full width; both are correct and they do not conflict. Intuition: a 40 mHz linewidth against a 5 GHz carrier is Δf3dB/f0≈8.0×10−12\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}/f_0\approx8.0\times10^{-12}Δf3dB​/f0​≈8.0×10−12 — extremely narrow, the numerical face of the high-QQQ LC's "spectral purity". (This is the floor for a single ideal white-noise source; real circuits are wider.) Alignment with the 20 mHz of lorentzian_linewidth (the 2× is Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ bookkeeping, not an error): this page uses the true-LC Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​ (Γrms2=0.5\Gamma_{rms}^2=0.5Γrms2​=0.5), giving D=0.125D=0.125D=0.125 rad²/s and Δf3dB=D/π≈40\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=D/\pi\approx40Δf3dB​=D/π≈40 mHz; the example in lorentzian_linewidth uses the spec representative value Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5 (Γrms2=0.25\Gamma_{rms}^2=0.25Γrms2​=0.25), giving D=0.0625D=0.0625D=0.0625 rad²/s and ≈20\approx20≈20 mHz. The two pages differ by exactly 2×, entirely because Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ is taken as 0.50.50.5 vs 0.250.250.25 (D∝Γrms2D\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2D∝Γrms2​, so the linewidth also ×2\times2×2) — the very same origin as Station ⑤'s −145-145−145 vs −148-148−148 dBc/Hz 3 dB gap (10log⁡10210\log_{10}210log10​2). Both numbers are correct; the only difference is whether Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ takes the "ideal −sin⁡-\sin−sin value" or the "representative value" — not an error. This station delivers: a finite linewidth Δf3dB≈40\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}\approx40Δf3dB​≈40 mHz (v5, with the corrected mapping D=Γrms2Si/(4qmax2)D=\Gamma_{rms}^2S_i/(4q_{max}^2)D=Γrms2​Si​/(4qmax2​)), and the Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0 divergence paradox resolved. Station ⑦'s jitter integration starts from f1≫Δf3dBf_1\gg\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}f1​≫Δf3dB​, so the 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt remains safe to use. (v8 toolbox) This station's Lorentzian rests on the assumption that "the noise driving the phase is white"; for where that assumption breaks down (how flicker FM distorts the lineshape away from Lorentzian, and what an instrument actually measures), see beyond_lorentzian.

documents.t: Jitter is the phase noise summed over all offset frequencies. (This is far worse than Station ⑤'s −145-145−145 dBc/Hz — because Station ⑤ is the theoretical floor of "a single ideal white-noise source", while −100-100−100 dBc/Hz is a "real datasheet level" that includes multiple sources/cyclostationary/flicker; both sit on the spine, representing the "physical floor" and the "practical value" respectively. Jitter only carries engineering meaning with the practical value.) Step 1: L→Sϕ\mathcal{L}\to S_\phiL→Sϕ​ (small angle, ×2\times2×2 to restore both sidebands). Sϕ(1MHz)=2×10−100/10=2×10−10 rad2/Hz.S_\phi(1\text{MHz})=2\times10^{-100/10}=2\times10^{-10}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}.Sϕ​(1MHz)=2×10−100/10=2×10−10 rad2/Hz. Step 2: 1/f21/f^21/f2 shape + closed-form integral (∫f−2df=−1/f\int f^{-2}df=-1/f∫f−2df=−1/f, lower limit dominates). σϕ2=Sϕ(fref) fref2(1f1−1f2)=2×10−10 (106)2 (10−6−10−8)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2.\sigma_\phi^2=S_\phi(f_{ref})\,f_{ref}^2\Big(\frac{1}{f_1}-\frac{1}{f_2}\Big) =2\times10^{-10}\,(10^6)^2\,(10^{-6}-10^{-8}) =200\times9.9\times10^{-7}=1.98\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}^2.σϕ2​=Sϕ​(fref​)fref2​(f1​1​−f2​1​)=2×10−10(106)2(10−6−10−8)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2. Step 3: take the square root to get the rms phase. σϕ=1.98×10−4=1.407×10−2 rad=14.07 mrad.\sigma_\phi=\sqrt{1.98\times10^{-4}}=1.407\times10^{-2}\ \text{rad}=14.07\ \text{mrad}.σϕ​=1.98×10−4​=1.407×10−2 rad=14.07 mrad. documents.t: The last station: connect σt\sigma_tσt​ to the communications engineer's BER bathtub curve. The receiver samples at the center of each bit; the bit period is denoted UI (unit interval). For RJ (random jitter — Gaussian, unbounded) only, the BER when sampling at an offset ttt from the eye center is (spec sec. 10.2, standard SerDes model, not among the 5 source PDFs): BER(t)=12[Q ⁣(UI/2−tσt)+Q ⁣(UI/2+tσt)],Q(x)=12 erfc ⁣(x2).\text{BER}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left[Q\!\left(\frac{\text{UI}/2-t}{\sigma_t}\right)+Q\!\left(\frac{\text{UI}/2+t}{\sigma_t}\right)\right],\qquad Q(x)=\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt2}\right).BER(t)=21​[Q(σt​UI/2−t​)+Q(σt​UI/2+t​)],Q(x)=21​erfc(2​x​). How to read it: the two QQQ terms are the probabilities that the left/right edge jitters past the sampling point and causes an error. At the eye center t=0t=0t=0 the two terms are equal and the BER is lowest (the bathtub floor). Full eye/CDR high-pass discussion in serdes_clocking_connection; figure in lab_12. documents.t: Eight stations, one chain: LC state eqs → Floquet (λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0 phase direction) → Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ → Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​ → [P1] Eq.(21) gives L\mathcal{L}L → Lorentzian linewidth → integrate to σt\sigma_tσt​ → BER bathtub. Every step rigorous + numerical: ω0=1/LC\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}ω0​=1/LC​; Γrms2=0.5\Gamma_{rms}^2=0.5Γrms2​=0.5; L=−145\mathcal{L}=-145L=−145 dBc/Hz (true LC value, 3 dB above the spec's −148-148−148); D=0.125D=0.125D=0.125 rad²/s, Δf3dB=40\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=40Δf3dB​=40 mHz (v5-corrected mapping D=κ2/2D=\kappa^2/2D=κ2/2); σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs; at BER 10−1210^{-12}10−12 RJ eats 6.3% UI. Do not mix the three phase-noise numbers: −145-145−145/−148-148−148 are the ideal single-source floor; −100-100−100 is the real datasheet level (45 dB gap = all the imperfections). The design knob runs end to end: L∝Γrms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​/qmax2​ (Stations ④⑤) propagates through to jitter (Station ⑦) and the eye budget (Station ⑧); 20 dB better phase noise ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ jitter ÷10 ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ eye budget ÷10. The divergence paradox is resolved: Station ⑤'s 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 divergence is a linearization artifact; Station ⑥'s Lorentzian gives a finite linewidth with total power conserved. documents.t: The eight stations above are the "rigorous hand derivation"; this section wires the same chain into a single executable script built from the existing common utilities (simulations/lab_22_capstone_lc_end_to_end.py), running Γ→Γrms→Sϕ→\Gamma\to\Gamma_{rms}\to S_\phi\toΓ→Γrms​→Sϕ​→ Lorentzian linewidth →σt→\to\sigma_t\to→σt​→ BER in one pass, printing every intermediate value with its # -> expected value, so that scripts/verify_examples.py can automatically verify the entire spine (not just a single station). Why this script exists: a hand derivation can copy a constant wrong at some step without anyone noticing; running it through the same set of isf_utils/noise_utils/serdes_utils functions used by Stations ①–③ and matching the numbers proves that the "formula chain" and the "code chain" agree. This is also why every line carries # ->: without it, a silently broken call (wrong kwargs, missing argument) would slip past the check. The script reuses real functions (no re-implementing the physics): isf_utils.gamma_lc_ideal (Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ), isf_utils.gamma_rms (Parseval rms), noise_utils.leeson_one_over_f2 + noise_utils.integrate_rms_jitter (L→Sϕ→\mathcal{L}\to S_\phi\toL→Sϕ​→ integrate to σt\sigma_tσt​), serdes_utils.ber_bathtub (RJ bathtub). Convention alignment (factor-of-2): Station ⑤'s boxed phase PSD Sϕ=Γrms2qmax2Si(2πf)2S_\phi=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\dfrac{S_i}{(2\pi f)^2}Sϕ​=qmax2​Γrms2​​(2πf)2Si​​ is the clean time-domain version (L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​); it sits 3 dB above [P1] Eq.(21)'s SSB /4/4/4 version. Hence the L(1MHz) clean = -141.98 dBc/Hz printed in this section is exactly Station ⑤'s −145-145−145 dBc/Hz (/4/4/4 convention) +3+3+3 dB — two bookkeepings of the same number; both are correct, differing only in SSB /4/4/4 vs time-domain /2/2/2 (see the factor-of-2 section of white_noise_to_phase_noise). Station ⑦'s σt\sigma_tσt​ still follows canonical example C's datasheet anchor L(1MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz, giving 447.9447.9447.9 fs. import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, gamma_rms from simulations.common.noise_utils import integrate_rms_jitter, leeson_one_over_f2 from simulations.common.serdes_utils import ber_bathtub # --- canonical inputs (spec sec. 8 / 11.2) --- q_max, S_i, f0 = 1e-12, 1e-24, 5e9 # 1 pC, A^2/Hz, 5 GHz # --- station 3+4: Gamma = -sin(theta) -> Gamma_rms (Parseval) --- theta = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 4001, endpoint=True) Grms = gamma_rms(theta, gamma_lc_ideal(theta)) # = 1/sqrt(2) Grms2 = Grms ** 2 print("Gamma_rms =", round(float(Grms), 4)) # -> 0.7071 print("Gamma_rms^2 =", round(float(Grms2), 4)) # -> 0.5 # --- station 5: phase PSD S_phi(f) = Grms^2/q_max^2 * S_i/(2 pi f)^2 --- df = 1e6 S_phi = Grms2 / q_max ** 2 * S_i / (2 * np.pi * df) ** 2 print("S_phi(1MHz) =", "{:.4e}".format(S_phi)) # -> 1.2665e-14 L_clean = 10 * np.log10(0.5 * S_phi) # time-domain /2 convention print("L(1MHz) =", round(float(L_clean), 2)) # -> -141.98 # --- station 6: Lorentzian D = Grms^2/(4 q_max^2)*S_i ; Df_3dB = D/pi --- D = Grms2 / (4 * q_max ** 2) * S_i print("D =", round(float(D), 4)) # -> 0.125 print("Df_3dB [Hz] =", round(float(D / np.pi), 4)) # -> 0.0398 # --- station 7: integrate L(f) over 1..100 MHz (datasheet anchor) -> sigma_t --- f = np.logspace(6, 8, 20001) L_band = leeson_one_over_f2(f, L_ref_dbc=-100.0, f_ref=1e6) sigma_t, sigma_phi = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L_band, f0=f0, fmin=1e6, fmax=100e6) print("sigma_phi =", "{:.4e}".format(sigma_phi)) # -> 1.407e-02 print("sigma_t[fs] =", round(float(sigma_t * 1e15), 1)) # -> 447.9 # --- station 8: sigma_t -> BER bathtub (10 Gb/s, UI = 100 ps) --- ui = 100e-12 print("UI/2/sig_t =", round(float((ui / 2) / sigma_t), 1)) # -> 111.6 rj_pp = 2 * 7.03 * sigma_t # Q^-1(1e-12) ~ 7.03 print("RJ_pp [ps] =", round(float(rj_pp * 1e12), 3)) # -> 6.297 print("eye [% UI] =", round(float(rj_pp / ui * 100), 2)) # -> 6.3 ber0 = float(ber_bathtub(np.array([0.0]), sigma_t, ui)[0]) print("BER(center) =", "{:.1e}".format(ber0)) # -> 1.0e-300 How to run (from the repo root): PYTHONPATH=. python3 simulations/lab_22_capstone_lc_end_to_end.py Printed output (line-by-line aligned with the # -> expected values above): Gamma_rms = 0.7071 # -> 0.7071 Gamma_rms^2 = 0.5 # -> 0.5 S_phi(1MHz) = 1.2665e-14 rad^2/Hz # -> 1.2665e-14 L(1MHz) clean = -141.98 dBc/Hz # -> -141.98 D (diffusion) = 0.125 rad^2/s # -> 0.125 Df_3dB (FWHM) = 0.0398 Hz # -> 0.0398 sigma_phi = 1.4071e-02 rad # -> 1.407e-02 sigma_t = 4.4790e-13 s # -> 4.479e-13 sigma_t [fs] = 447.9 fs # -> 447.9 UI/2 / sigma_t = 111.6 # -> 111.6 RJ_pp [ps] = 6.297 ps # -> 6.297 eye closure = 6.3 % UI # -> 6.3 BER(center) = 1.0e-300 # -> 1.0e-300 How to read these numbers: lines 1–2 are Stations ③④ (Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​, Γrms2=0.5\Gamma_{rms}^2=0.5Γrms2​=0.5); lines 3–4 Station ⑤ (Sϕ=1.27×10−14S_\phi=1.27\times10^{-14}Sϕ​=1.27×10−14 rad²/Hz; time-domain /2/2/2 version L=−142\mathcal{L}=-142L=−142 dBc/Hz); lines 5–6 Station ⑥ (D=0.125D=0.125D=0.125 rad²/s, linewidth 404040 mHz); lines 7–9 Station ⑦ (σϕ=14.07\sigma_\phi=14.07σϕ​=14.07 mrad, σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs); the last four lines Station ⑧ (center sampling puts UI/2\text{UI}/2UI/2 at 111.6 σt111.6\,\sigma_t111.6σt​, so the center BER →0\to0→0; at BER 10−1210^{-12}10−12 RJ eats 6.3%6.3\%6.3% UI). Digit-for-digit agreement with the hand derivation: 0.50.50.5, 0.1250.1250.125, 404040 mHz, 447.9447.9447.9 fs, 6.3%6.3\%6.3% all match Stations ④–⑧'s hand-computed values, proving "formula chain = code chain". The only deliberate difference is L\mathcal{L}L: this section prints the time-domain /2/2/2 version −142-142−142, Station ⑤ prints the SSB /4/4/4 version −145-145−145; the 3 dB gap is 10log⁡10210\log_{10}210log10​2, rooted in the same factor-of-2 convention, flagged clearly above. This is a toy / ideal model: Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ is the analytic ISF of the lossless ideal LC, single white-noise source, pure RJ; real circuits are worse (see the −100-100−100 dBc/Hz and the 45 dB gap in "The roles of the three sets of numbers" table). BER/eye and the Lorentzian are external literature, not among the 5 source PDFs (standard SerDes, [E2] Demir 2000); the ISF core (Stations ③④⑤) comes from [P1].

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: isf_definition | Next: white_noise_to_phase_noise The previous page, isf_definition, gave the definition "one current impulse → one phase step". But the noise current in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) in a real circuit is injected continuously and persistently — it does not arrive as separate, isolated pulses. This page answers: What is the total excess phase ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) produced by a continuous noise current in(t)i_n(t)in​(t)? The answer is the single most central integral in ISF theory ([P1] Eq.(11), p.182): ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tauϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ Our job is to derive it, step by step, from the previous page's "single step" using the superposition principle — and to see clearly that although it looks like a convolution, it is an LTV (linear time-variant) convolution, not the LTI convolution of a signals-and-systems textbook. Physical intuition (conclusion first): slice the noise current into countless thin slivers, each a miniature impulse; each miniature impulse produces a miniature phase step weighted by the phase at that instant, Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ); because phase has no restoring force, every step, once it happens, stays forever; so the total phase ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) "now" = the accumulation of all past steps. Accumulating a continuum of infinitely many steps is an integral; "accumulate only the past" is why the upper limit is ttt. Γ\GammaΓ changes with the injection instant, so the weight is time-varying — that is LTV.
documents.s: From a Single Impulse to Arbitrary Noise: the Convolution Derivation

documents.t: Any continuous current can be approximated by a train of adjacent, very narrow rectangular pulses. The slice at time τ\tauτ of width dτd\taudτ deposits a charge dq(τ)=in(τ) dτ.dq(\tau)=i_n(\tau)\,d\tau .dq(τ)=in​(τ)dτ. Physics used: the definition of current, i=dq/dti=dq/dti=dq/dt, inverted: dq=i dτdq=i\,d\taudq=idτ. Unit check: [A]⋅[s]=[C][\text{A}]\cdot[\text{s}]=[\text{C}][A]⋅[s]=[C] ✓. Why this is legitimate: as long as each slice width dτ≪Td\tau\ll Tdτ≪T (one period), each slice can be treated as "a lump of charge injected instantaneously" — exactly the applicability condition of the impulse on the previous page.
documents.s: Step 1: slice the noise into small impulses

documents.t: Apply the previous page's operational definition to the slice of charge dq(τ)dq(\tau)dq(τ) at time τ\tauτ: dϕ(τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax dq(τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax in(τ) dτ.d\phi(\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,dq(\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau .dϕ(τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​dq(τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​in​(τ)dτ. Key point: the weight Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) is evaluated at the phase of the injection instant, ω0τ\omega_0\tauω0​τ — not at the observation time ttt. The same charge injected at a zero crossing (large Γ\GammaΓ) produces a large step; at the peak (Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0) it produces almost none. Unit check: dϕ=[dimensionless][C]⋅[C]=[dimensionless]=[rad]d\phi=\dfrac{[\text{dimensionless}]}{[\text{C}]}\cdot[\text{C}]=[\text{dimensionless}]=[\text{rad}]dϕ=[C][dimensionless]​⋅[C]=[dimensionless]=[rad] ✓.
documents.s: Step 2: each small charge produces a small phase step

documents.t: This is the soul of the whole derivation, and where an oscillator differs most from an ordinary RLC filter. Once a phase step dϕd\phidϕ occurs at time τ\tauτ, because there is no restoring force along the phase direction (claim C2, [P1] Sec. III-A; geometric reason in isf_definition, Step 2), it does not decay — it persists through every future t>τt>\taut>τ. Written as an impulse response, this brings a unit step u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) ([P1] Eq.(10), p.182): hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ).h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau).hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ). u(t−τ)=1u(t-\tau)=1u(t−τ)=1 (for t≥τt\ge\taut≥τ), =0=0=0 (for t<τt<\taut<τ). Its physical meaning: "visible only in the future, and never fades" — the phase integrator has infinite memory. Contrast: if this were an amplitude perturbation, the impulse response would carry a decaying term (e.g. e−(t−τ)/τAu(t−τ)e^{-(t-\tau)/\tau_A}u(t-\tau)e−(t−τ)/τA​u(t−τ)) — the perturbation gets pulled back. Phase gets a step, amplitude gets a decaying exponential — this is the mathematical face of "why phase noise accumulates and amplitude noise does not".
documents.s: Step 3: each step persists permanently into the "future"

documents.t: In a linear (small-signal) system, the total phase = the sum of all contributions. Step by step: discrete superposition → limit → integral (no skipped steps). First slice the time axis into cells of width Δτ\Delta\tauΔτ, with injection instants τk=k Δτ\tau_k=k\,\Delta\tauτk​=kΔτ (k=…,−2,−1,0,1,…k=\dots,-2,-1,0,1,\dotsk=…,−2,−1,0,1,…). Charge of the kkk-th slice (step: treat the continuous current as a train of small impulses): Δqk=in(τk) Δτ[A⋅s=C].\Delta q_k=i_n(\tau_k)\,\Delta\tau\quad[\text{A}\cdot\text{s}=\text{C}].Δqk​=in​(τk​)Δτ[A⋅s=C]. Phase step produced by the kkk-th slice (step: apply Step 2's operational definition, with the weight taken at the injection-instant phase ω0τk\omega_0\tau_kω0​τk​): Δϕk=Γ(ω0τk)qmax Δqk=Γ(ω0τk)qmax in(τk) Δτ.\Delta\phi_k=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau_k)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q_k=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau_k)}{q_{max}}\,i_n(\tau_k)\,\Delta\tau.Δϕk​=qmax​Γ(ω0​τk​)​Δqk​=qmax​Γ(ω0​τk​)​in​(τk​)Δτ. Each step persists permanently (step: phase has no restoring force): at the observation time ttt, only steps with τk≤t\tau_k\le tτk​≤t have already happened and are still present; their contribution is multiplied by u(t−τk)u(t-\tau_k)u(t−τk​) (equal to 1 when τk≤t\tau_k\le tτk​≤t, 0 otherwise). Add up all past steps (discrete superposition): ϕ(t)=∑k: τk≤tΔϕk=∑k=−∞∞Γ(ω0τk)qmax in(τk) u(t−τk) Δτ.\phi(t)=\sum_{k:\ \tau_k\le t}\Delta\phi_k=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau_k)}{q_{max}}\,i_n(\tau_k)\,u(t-\tau_k)\,\Delta\tau.ϕ(t)=k: τk​≤t∑​Δϕk​=k=−∞∑∞​qmax​Γ(ω0​τk​)​in​(τk​)u(t−τk​)Δτ. Take the limit Δτ→0\Delta\tau\to0Δτ→0 (step: Riemann sum → Riemann integral): as the cells become infinitely fine, the discrete injection instants τk\tau_kτk​ become a continuous variable τ\tauτ, Δτ→dτ\Delta\tau\to d\tauΔτ→dτ, and ∑k(⋯ )Δτ→∫(⋯ ) dτ\sum_k(\cdots)\Delta\tau\to\int(\cdots)\,d\tau∑k​(⋯)Δτ→∫(⋯)dτ. This step is legitimate provided Γ\GammaΓ and ini_nin​ are approximately constant within each cell (an integrable integrand), which for noise physically always holds: ϕ(t)=lim⁡Δτ→0∑kΓ(ω0τk)qmax in(τk) u(t−τk) Δτ=∫−∞∞Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ) in(τ) dτ.\phi(t)=\lim_{\Delta\tau\to0}\sum_{k}\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau_k)}{q_{max}}\,i_n(\tau_k)\,u(t-\tau_k)\,\Delta\tau =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau .ϕ(t)=Δτ→0lim​k∑​qmax​Γ(ω0​τk​)​in​(τk​)u(t−τk​)Δτ=∫−∞∞​qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ)in​(τ)dτ. Written in the superposition form with hϕ(t,τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)hϕ​(t,τ) ([P1] Eq.(11)): ϕ(t)=∫−∞∞hϕ(t,τ) in(τ) dτ=∫−∞∞Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ) in(τ) dτ.\phi(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h_\phi(t,\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau .ϕ(t)=∫−∞∞​hϕ​(t,τ)in​(τ)dτ=∫−∞∞​qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ)in​(τ)dτ. Why u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) appears naturally at the "adding" step: it is not inserted by hand — it is the mathematical notation for two facts, "a step persists forever" + "only steps that have already happened can be added". The τk≤t\tau_k\le tτk​≤t condition of item 3 becomes u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) in the continuum limit. Right below, you see it cut the upper integration limit to ttt. The role of u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) is to "cut" the upper integration limit at ttt: for τ>t\tau>tτ>t, u(t−τ)=0u(t-\tau)=0u(t−τ)=0 — future noise has not happened yet and cannot affect the present (causality). Hence ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ [P1] Eq.(11), p.182\boxed{\ \phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau\ }\qquad\text{[P1] Eq.(11), p.182} ϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ ​[P1] Eq.(11), p.182 Why the upper limit is ttt: causality + infinite phase memory. The lower limit −∞-\infty−∞ says "all noise since power-up is still remembered" — precisely the root of long-term jitter's random walk, drifting further the longer it runs (see σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ in [P2] Eq.(8)). Unit check: ϕ=1[C]⋅[dimensionless]⋅[A]⋅[s]=[A⋅s][C]=[C][C]=[dimensionless]=[rad]\phi=\dfrac{1}{[\text{C}]}\cdot[\text{dimensionless}]\cdot[\text{A}]\cdot[\text{s}]=\dfrac{[\text{A}\cdot\text{s}]}{[\text{C}]}=\dfrac{[\text{C}]}{[\text{C}]}=[\text{dimensionless}]=[\text{rad}]ϕ=[C]1​⋅[dimensionless]⋅[A]⋅[s]=[C][A⋅s]​=[C][C]​=[dimensionless]=[rad] ✓. Degeneration check: for in(τ)=Δq δ(τ−τ0)i_n(\tau)=\Delta q\,\delta(\tau-\tau_0)in​(τ)=Δqδ(τ−τ0​) (a single impulse), the integral picks out τ0\tau_0τ0​: ϕ(t)=Γ(ω0τ0)qmaxΔq\phi(t)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau_0)}{q_{max}}\Delta qϕ(t)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ0​)​Δq (for t>τ0t>\tau_0t>τ0​), recovering exactly the previous page's Δϕ=Γ Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=ΓΔq/qmax​ ✓.
documents.s: Step 4: superpose all past steps → an integral

documents.t: The LTI convolution taught in signals-and-systems is y(t)=∫h(t−τ)x(τ) dτy(t)=\int h(t-\tau)x(\tau)\,d\tauy(t)=∫h(t−τ)x(τ)dτ — the kernel depends only on the time difference t−τt-\taut−τ. Here the kernel is hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ),h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau),hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ), which depends explicitly on the absolute injection instant τ\tauτ (through Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ)) and cannot be written as just h(t−τ)h(t-\tau)h(t−τ). Physically: the same impulse, injected at different phases of the waveform, gives different responses (claim C1, [P1] Sec. III). LTI (time-invariant): delay the entire input by Δ\DeltaΔ and the output is merely delayed by Δ\DeltaΔ, shape unchanged. LTV (time-variant): delay the input by Δ\DeltaΔ, and because Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) takes different values at different phases, the output changes shape. But be careful: it is still linear (linear in ini_nin​, superposable) — it is just not time-invariant. Hence LTV (Linear Time-Variant). Slicing ini_nin​, weighting each slice, and superposing works precisely because of this "linearity"; the weight varying with time is the "time variance". For the graphical comparison see lti_vs_ltv. One-line mnemonic: ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) is in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) first multiplied pointwise by the periodic weight Γ(ω0t)/qmax\Gamma(\omega_0 t)/q_{max}Γ(ω0​t)/qmax​, then fed into an infinite-memory integrator. Multiplication (time-varying weight) + integration (memory) = the LTV phase response.
documents.s: Why this is LTV, not ordinary LTI convolution

documents.t: Draw Eq.(11) as two blocks: a time-varying multiplier and an integrator. Block B (multiplication) provides the "time variance": the weight varies periodically with the waveform phase ω0t\omega_0 tω0​t — the origin of LTV. Block C (integration) provides the "memory": it accumulates all past weighted noise — the origin of phase accumulation and of long-term jitter's random walk.
documents.s: Block diagram

documents.t: integrate_phase_from_noise is exactly block B (time-varying multiplication) followed by block C (cumulative integration) — an implementation of Eq.(11). Below we verify it with a single-tone injection: in theory, feeding in a single tone in(t)=I0cos⁡(Δωt)i_n(t)=I_0\cos(\Delta\omega t)in​(t)=I0​cos(Δωt) (very small offset, near DC), the excess phase should approach [P1] Eq.(15), p.183: ϕ(t)≈I0 c0sin⁡(Δωt)2qmax Δω.\phi(t)\approx\frac{I_0\,c_0\sin(\Delta\omega t)}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}.ϕ(t)≈2qmax​ΔωI0​c0​sin(Δωt)​. For the ideal LC (Γ=−sin⁡\Gamma=-\sinΓ=−sin) the DC coefficient is c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 and the response is suppressed; only with an asymmetric ISF carrying DC (Γ=cos⁡θ+α\Gamma=\cos\theta+\alphaΓ=cosθ+α, giving c0=2αc_0=2\alphac0​=2α) does the slow phase drift of the form above — proportional to sin⁡(Δωt)\sin(\Delta\omega t)sin(Δωt) with amplitude ∝1/Δω\propto1/\Delta\omega∝1/Δω — appear (site convention: here α\alphaα is the DC offset of the toy ISF, unrelated to [P1]'s NMF α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0t)α(ω0​t)). The code below runs both for comparison: import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import ( gamma_lc_ideal, gamma_asymmetric, integrate_phase_from_noise, ) # --- setup --- f0 = 1.0 # normalized carrier w0 = 2 * np.pi * f0 fs = 8000.0 # amply oversampled t = np.arange(0, 200.0, 1/fs) # run many periods to see the slow phase drift qmax = 1.0 I0 = 1e-3 d_omega = 2 * np.pi * 0.01 # offset 0.01 Hz (near DC, far below w0) i_n = I0 * np.cos(d_omega * t) # inject a single tone # --- blocks B×C: run Eq.(11) once for each ISF --- phi_lc = integrate_phase_from_noise(t, i_n, gamma_lc_ideal(w0 * t), qmax) # c0 = 0 alpha = 0.4 phi_asy = integrate_phase_from_noise(t, i_n, gamma_asymmetric(w0 * t, alpha), qmax) # c0 = 2*alpha # --- theory Eq.(15): phi ~ I0 c0 sin(d_omega t)/(2 qmax d_omega) --- c0_asy = 2 * alpha phi_theory = I0 * c0_asy * np.sin(d_omega * t) / (2 * qmax * d_omega) print("LC (c0=0) max|phi| =", np.max(np.abs(phi_lc))) # tiny: DC is suppressed print("asym sim max|phi| =", np.max(np.abs(phi_asy))) print("asym theory max|phi| =", np.max(np.abs(phi_theory))) # same order as sim, same 1/d_omega trend How to read it: phi_lc barely drifts because c0=0c_0=0c0​=0; phi_asy shows a slow phase drift ∝sin⁡(Δωt)\propto\sin(\Delta\omega t)∝sin(Δωt) with amplitude ∝1/Δω\propto1/\Delta\omega∝1/Δω, matching the analytic Eq.(15) in order of magnitude and in trend. This verifies "time-domain integration of Eq.(11) = the literature's frequency-domain result". Why compare only magnitude/trend: the toy ISF (gamma_asymmetric) is not transistor-level, and the numerical integration carries sampling and finite-length errors; the point is that the scaling (∝I0c0/Δω\propto I_0 c_0/\Delta\omega∝I0​c0​/Δω) matches, not point-by-point numbers. The full version, splitting this integral into "each ISF harmonic down-converting separately", is [P1] Eq.(13), p.183 — taught in fourier_series_of_isf. Implementation for reference (simulations/common/isf_utils.py, quoted verbatim from the real code): def integrate_phase_from_noise(t, i_noise, gamma_values, qmax): dt = np.mean(np.diff(t)) return np.cumsum(gamma_values * i_noise / qmax) * dt np.cumsum(...)*dt is the "infinite-memory integrator" (block C, accumulating all of the past); gamma_values * i_noise / qmax is the time-varying weighting (block B). Full library: simulations/common/isf_utils.py; noise utilities: simulations/common/noise_utils.py.

documents.t: Degenerating the continuous integral back to a single kick reproduces Example A of impulse_to_phase_shift: qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC, Γ=0.5\Gamma=0.5Γ=0.5, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz → Δϕ=5×10−4\Delta\phi=5\times10^{-4}Δϕ=5×10−4 rad → Δt=15.9\Delta t=15.9Δt=15.9 fs. What continuous noise means: every dτd\taudτ kicks like this, and the integrator remembers and accumulates all of it, so the rms phase grows with time (or with the lower limit of the integration bandwidth) — the starting point of the next stage, where the PSD of ini_nin​ is connected to the phase noise L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf).

documents.t: Format per spec 10.4: problem → step-by-step substitution (with units) → result → dimension check → one-line Python verification. We deliberately pick constant scenarios that can be hand-computed, dissecting integrate_phase_from_noise (the implementation of Eq.(11)) for verification.

documents.t: Problem: take a constant ISF Γ=0.5\Gamma=0.5Γ=0.5, a constant noise current in=I0=2 μAi_n=I_0=2\ \mu\text{A}in​=I0​=2 μA, and qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, injected over the window [0, 1 ns][0,\,1\ \text{ns}][0,1 ns]. Use Eq.(11) to find the final phase ϕ(T)\phi(T)ϕ(T) and compare with the hand calculation. Step-by-step substitution (by hand): the integrand is constant, so the integral degenerates into a multiplication. ϕ(T)=1qmax∫0TΓ in dτ=Γ I0 Tqmax=0.5×(2×10−6 A)×(1×10−9 s)1×10−12 C.\phi(T)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_0^{T}\Gamma\,i_n\,d\tau=\frac{\Gamma\,I_0\,T}{q_{max}}=\frac{0.5\times(2\times10^{-6}\,\text{A})\times(1\times10^{-9}\,\text{s})}{1\times10^{-12}\,\text{C}}.ϕ(T)=qmax​1​∫0T​Γin​dτ=qmax​ΓI0​T​=1×10−12C0.5×(2×10−6A)×(1×10−9s)​. Numerator first: 0.5×2×10−6×10−9=1×10−15 A⋅s=1×10−15 C0.5\times2\times10^{-6}\times10^{-9}=1\times10^{-15}\ \text{A}\cdot\text{s}=1\times10^{-15}\ \text{C}0.5×2×10−6×10−9=1×10−15 A⋅s=1×10−15 C. Then divide by qmaxq_{max}qmax​: ϕ(T)=1×10−15 C1×10−12 C=1×10−3 rad=1 mrad.\phi(T)=\frac{1\times10^{-15}\ \text{C}}{1\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}}=1\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad}=1\ \text{mrad}.ϕ(T)=1×10−12 C1×10−15 C​=1×10−3 rad=1 mrad. Cross-check from the "charge viewpoint" (degenerate back to a single impulse): the total injected charge is Δq=I0T=2×10−6×10−9=2×10−15\Delta q=I_0 T=2\times10^{-6}\times10^{-9}=2\times10^{-15}Δq=I0​T=2×10−6×10−9=2×10−15 C =2=2=2 fC; applying Δϕ=Γ Δq/qmax=0.5×2×10−15/10−12=1×10−3\Delta\phi=\Gamma\,\Delta q/q_{max}=0.5\times2\times10^{-15}/10^{-12}=1\times10^{-3}Δϕ=ΓΔq/qmax​=0.5×2×10−15/10−12=1×10−3 rad ✓ (consistent with the integral — with constant Γ\GammaΓ, the continuous integral equals injecting the total charge all at once). Result: ϕ(T)=1\phi(T)=1ϕ(T)=1 mrad; the numerical integration integrate_phase_from_noise gives 1.00001×10−31.00001\times10^{-3}1.00001×10−3 rad, matching the hand calculation (the difference comes from the endpoint effect of the discrete np.cumsum accumulation, ∼10−5\sim10^{-5}∼10−5 relative error). Dimension check: 1[C]⋅[dimensionless]⋅[A]⋅[s]=[A⋅s][C]=[C][C]=\dfrac{1}{[\text{C}]}\cdot[\text{dimensionless}]\cdot[\text{A}]\cdot[\text{s}]=\dfrac{[\text{A}\cdot\text{s}]}{[\text{C}]}=\dfrac{[\text{C}]}{[\text{C}]}=[C]1​⋅[dimensionless]⋅[A]⋅[s]=[C][A⋅s]​=[C][C]​= dimensionless (rad) ✓. import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import integrate_phase_from_noise qmax, I0, gamma = 1e-12, 2e-6, 0.5 t = np.linspace(0, 1e-9, 100001) # 0 -> 1 ns i = np.full_like(t, I0) # constant noise current gv = np.full_like(t, gamma) # constant ISF phi = integrate_phase_from_noise(t, i, gv, qmax) print(phi[-1], "rad") # -> 0.00100001 rad (hand calc = 1e-3 rad)

documents.t: Problem: now use the real, time-varying ISF Γ(ω0τ)=−sin⁡(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=-\sin(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ)=−sin(ω0​τ), constant in=I0=2 μAi_n=I_0=2\ \mu\text{A}in​=I0​=2 μA, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, f0=1f_0=1f0​=1 (normalized, so ω0=2π\omega_0=2\piω0​=2π), integrated over an integer number of periods. Find ϕ\phiϕ. Step-by-step substitution (by hand): ϕ=I0qmax∫0NT(−sin⁡ω0τ) dτ=I0qmax⋅cos⁡ω0τω0∣0NT.\phi=\frac{I_0}{q_{max}}\int_0^{NT}(-\sin\omega_0\tau)\,d\tau=\frac{I_0}{q_{max}}\cdot\frac{\cos\omega_0\tau}{\omega_0}\Big|_0^{NT}.ϕ=qmax​I0​​∫0NT​(−sinω0​τ)dτ=qmax​I0​​⋅ω0​cosω0​τ​​0NT​. Over an integer number of periods NTNTNT, cos⁡ω0(NT)=cos⁡(2πN)=1=cos⁡0\cos\omega_0(NT)=\cos(2\pi N)=1=\cos0cosω0​(NT)=cos(2πN)=1=cos0, so the integral = 0: ϕ(NT)=I0qmax⋅1−1ω0=0 rad.\phi(NT)=\frac{I_0}{q_{max}}\cdot\frac{1-1}{\omega_0}=0\ \text{rad}.ϕ(NT)=qmax​I0​​⋅ω0​1−1​=0 rad. Result: under Γ=−sin⁡\Gamma=-\sinΓ=−sin (zero DC, c0=0c_0=0c0​=0), constant (DC) noise produces zero net phase shift per full period — the positive and negative half cycles cancel. This is the time-domain face of "a symmetric ISF suppresses DC/near-DC injection" (echoing the single-tone example above: the LC has c0=0c_0=0c0​=0, so the Eq.(15) response is suppressed). If you stop at a half period (τ=T/2\tau=T/2τ=T/2), cos⁡π−cos⁡0=−2\cos\pi-\cos0=-2cosπ−cos0=−2 leaves a nonzero transient phase offset (the Python below prints ϕ(T/2)≈−636619.7\phi(T/2)\approx-636619.7ϕ(T/2)≈−636619.7 rad). (Note: here I0=2 μAI_0=2\ \mu\text{A}I0​=2 μA, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, and the half period t=0.5t=0.5t=0.5 s are all normalized numbers; I0/qmax=2×106I_0/q_{max}=2\times10^6I0​/qmax​=2×106, further divided by ω0=2π\omega_0=2\piω0​=2π, so the "rad count" of ϕ\phiϕ is enormous. This is purely a bookkeeping artifact of normalized units, not a physical phase of 10510^5105 rad — in fact, the small-signal/linear premises (Step 1's dτ≪Td\tau\ll Tdτ≪T; a single impulse charging only about 10% of the total charge, [P1] p.182) are badly violated long before that. The point is the sign structure — full periods cancel, half periods do not — not the magnitude of that rad number.) Dimension check: as in Example 1, the final ϕ\phiϕ is dimensionless (rad) ✓. import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, integrate_phase_from_noise f0, w0, qmax, I0 = 1.0, 2*np.pi, 1e-12, 2e-6 t = np.arange(0, 10.0, 1/8000.0) # 10 full periods i = np.full_like(t, I0) gv = gamma_lc_ideal(w0 * t) # Γ = -sin(w0 t) phi = integrate_phase_from_noise(t, i, gv, qmax) assert abs(phi[-1]) < 1e-6 # net phase cancels over full periods (residual ~6e-10, purely cumsum discretization) print(round(abs(phi[-1]), 6)) # -> 0.0 (net phase cancels over full periods) print(round(phi[len(t)//20], 1)) # -> -636619.7 (near the half period: nonzero transient) Full library: simulations/common/isf_utils.py.

documents.t: Prerequisites: white_noise_to_phase_noise · lorentzian_linewidth · allan_variance | Next: capstone_lc_end_to_end The white-noise phase diffusion of one and the same free-running oscillator goes by five "different" numbers in the mouths of five different communities: The ring / jitter crowd ([P2]) speaks in κ\kappaκ: "how many s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​ is the accumulated-jitter constant?" The theoretical-physics / Demir crowd speaks in DDD: "how many rad2/s\text{rad}^2/\text{s}rad2/s is the phase diffusion constant?" The laser / spectroscopy crowd speaks in linewidth: "how many Hz is the 3-dB linewidth?" The RF / IC crowd speaks in L\mathcal{L}L: "how many dBc/Hz is the 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt at 1 MHz offset?" The clock / metrology crowd speaks in ADEV: "what is the white-FM segment of σy(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)σy​(τ) at τ=1\tau=1τ=1 s?" This page proves that these five numbers are one physical quantity wearing five outfits, and gives the complete conversion chain with every single factor of 2 reconciled. In 40 years, the most common oscillator-spec error I have seen is not a miscalculated Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ or a mismeasured PSD — it is dropping a 2 while changing between these five outfits. So every step on this page states explicitly which convention each 2 comes from (single- or double-sided? Var=D∣t∣\mathrm{Var}=D|t|Var=D∣t∣ or 2D∣t∣2D|t|2D∣t∣? SSB /2/2/2 or /4/4/4?), and at the end lab_23 signs off with one simulation, five extraction paths, all recovering the same number. Physical intuition (conclusion first): white noise turns the phase into a random walk (a Wiener process), and a random walk has only one free parameter — how fast the variance grows per second. We write it κ2≡d Var[Δϕ]/dt\kappa^2\equiv d\,\mathrm{Var}[\Delta\phi]/dtκ2≡dVar[Δϕ]/dt (units rad2/s\text{rad}^2/\text{s}rad2/s). Everything you will ever measure — how jitter grows as Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​, how fat the carrier is, how high the skirt sits, how stable the clock is — is just the shadow of this one rate projected onto different instruments. The dictionary's job: given the number in any one outfit, hand you the other four immediately.
