documents.t: The literature carries two definitions of the "diffusion constant DDD", differing by a 2. This section is the head-on reconciliation between the spec (Spec 11.2) and [P2] Eq.(11) — with a single job: state exactly what κ2\kappa^2κ2 equals under each convention. (The CJK subscripts in the math below are kept from the original notation: 甲 = convention A, 乙 = convention B.) Convention A (the rate convention): define DDD directly as the variance growth rate — Var[Δϕ(t)]=D甲 ∣t∣⟹κ2=D甲.\mathrm{Var}[\Delta\phi(t)]=D_{\text{甲}}\,|t|\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \kappa^2=D_{\text{甲}}.Var[Δϕ(t)]=D甲​∣t∣⟹κ2=D甲​. Convention B (the Demir / laser convention, as written in [E2] Demir 2000 and the laser-linewidth literature): mimic Brownian motion ⟨x2⟩=2Dt\langle x^2\rangle=2Dt⟨x2⟩=2Dt and put the 2 out front — Var[Δϕ(t)]=2D乙 ∣t∣⟹κ2=2D乙,D乙=κ22.\mathrm{Var}[\Delta\phi(t)]=2D_{\text{乙}}\,|t|\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \kappa^2=2D_{\text{乙}},\qquad D_{\text{乙}}=\frac{\kappa^2}{2}.Var[Δϕ(t)]=2D乙​∣t∣⟹κ2=2D乙​,D乙​=2κ2​. The two differ only in naming; the physics (how fast the variance grows) is identical. Written in ISF quantities: D甲=Γrms22qmax2in2‾Δf=0.125 rad2/s,D乙=Γrms24qmax2in2‾Δf=0.0625 rad2/s(canonical).D_{\text{甲}}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{2q_{max}^2}\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=0.125\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s},\qquad D_{\text{乙}}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{4q_{max}^2}\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=0.0625\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}\quad(\text{canonical}).D甲​=2qmax2​Γrms2​​Δfin2​​​=0.125 rad2/s,D乙​=4qmax2​Γrms2​​Δfin2​​​=0.0625 rad2/s(canonical). Reconciliation with Spec 11.2 / lorentzian_linewidth (important; fixed in v5 per this page): Spec 11.2 v3 once wrote D=Γrms2Si/(2qmax2)D=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(2q_{max}^2)D=Γrms2​Si​/(2qmax2​) (canonical D=0.125D=0.125D=0.125, true LC 0.250.250.25) — that value is precisely κ2\kappa^2κ2, i.e. convention A's DDD (the variance growth rate itself). But the same paragraph of the spec also wrote Var[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣\mathrm{Var}[\Delta\phi]=2D|t|Var[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣ (convention B's variance law). The two statements cannot both hold: if D=0.125D=0.125D=0.125 and Var=2D∣t∣\mathrm{Var}=2D|t|Var=2D∣t∣, the variance would have to grow 0.25 rad20.25\ \text{rad}^20.25 rad2 per second, contradicting [P2] Eq.(11) (0.125 rad20.125\ \text{rad}^20.125 rad2 per second). Simulation verdict (lab_23, panel (a)): synthesizing ISF-weighted white-noise phase with the canonical constants yields Var[Δϕ(τ)]/τ=0.1252 rad2/s\mathrm{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]/\tau=0.1252\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}Var[Δϕ(τ)]/τ=0.1252 rad2/s — landing on the κ2τ\kappa^2\tauκ2τ line, not on the 2×0.125 τ2\times0.125\,\tau2×0.125τ line. Conclusion: the canonical value D=0.125D=0.125D=0.125 is correct, but it is convention A's DDD (=κ2=\kappa^2=κ2); the variance law that goes with it must be Var=D∣t∣\mathrm{Var}=D|t|Var=D∣t∣. If you insist on convention B's Var=2D∣t∣\mathrm{Var}=2D|t|Var=2D∣t∣, then DDD must be read as 0.06250.06250.0625. This affects no scaling — only the absolute value of the linewidth in the next section (see Outfit Three's honesty note). Units: both DDD's are rad2/s\text{rad}^2/\text{s}rad2/s (equivalently 1/s1/\text{s}1/s) ✓. One-line dictionary: κ2=D甲=2D乙\kappa^2=D_{\text{甲}}=2D_{\text{乙}}κ2=D甲​=2D乙​. Before quoting DDD to anyone, first ask whether their Var\mathrm{Var}Var expression carries that 2.

documents.t: Prerequisites: flicker_noise_upconversion | Next: capstone_lc_end_to_end So far we have assumed the noise sources are stationary — their statistics (e.g., mean-square power) do not change with time. Resistor thermal noise is like that. But the dominant noise sources in an oscillator are the transistors, and transistor noise power varies periodically with the operating point: strong when the device conducts a large current, weak when it is off. Noise whose statistics vary periodically with time is called cyclostationary noise. This page answers: how does ISF theory handle cyclostationary device noise? The answer is elegant and simple — fold the periodic "noise-intensity modulation" into the ISF, obtaining the effective ISF: Γeff(x)=Γ(x) α(x)\Gamma_{eff}(x)=\Gamma(x)\,\alpha(x)Γeff​(x)=Γ(x)α(x) From then on, every formula stays the same with Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ substituted for Γ\GammaΓ (the cyclostationary decomposition and the effective ISF come from [P1] Sec. II-D "Cyclostationary Noise Sources", Eq.(25)–(27), p.186; Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α is Eq.(27)). Try it yourself: the interactive explorer below keeps Γ(x)=−sin⁡x\Gamma(x)=-\sin xΓ(x)=−sinx fixed and lets you drag the NMF α(x)\alpha(x)α(x) window's center phase θc\theta_cθc​, width, and floor, watching Γ\GammaΓ, α\alphaα, and Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α overlaid live, along with Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​, c0effc_0^{eff}c0eff​, and the phase-noise change relative to the stationary case. Γ×α alignment explorer (cyclostationary gating) 00.25·2π0.5·2π0.75·2π2πΓ(x) = −sin xα(x) (NMF window)00.25·2π0.5·2π0.75·2π2πΓ_eff(x) = Γ(x)·α(x) Center phase θc90 ° Width (% of period)50 % Floor0.00 Bad (zero crossing, θc=90°)Good (peak, θc=0°, Colpitts-like) Γ_eff,rms 0.395 stationary Γ_rms = 0.707 c₀_eff (DC×2) -0.4244 ⟨Γα⟩ = -0.2122 L-degradation vs stationary -5.1 dB vs Γ_rms=0.5 ref: -2.0 dB The Colpitts aha: drag θ_c to 90° (device noisy right at the ISF zero crossing, where |Γ|=1) — Γ_eff,rms stays large (≈0.40 at width=50%, floor=0: the classic "bad" case). Now drag θ_c to 0° (device noisy at the waveform peak, where Γ≈0, Colpitts-like) — Γ_eff,rms collapses to ≈0.18, a further ≈7 dB better than the zero-crossing case even though the noise amount (window width, floor) is identical. Windowing at the ISF zero crossing hurts the most; windowing at the peak barely matters. (Anchor check at width=50%, floor=0: stationary 0.707, zero-crossing 0.395, peak 0.177 — matching lab_14.) Model: Γ(x) = −sin x fixed (ideal LC). α(x) is a raised-cosine-ish window, α(x) = floor + (1−floor)·0.5[1+cos(π·clip(d/(width/2),−1,1))] with d the wrapped distance to center θ_c (same family as nmf_window in simulations/lab_14_cyclostationary_isf.py). Γ_eff = Γ·α; Γ_eff,rms and c0_eff are computed with the trapezoidal rule (361 samples over one period), matching simulations/common/isf_utils.py's gamma_rms/compute_fourier_coefficients conventions. L-degradation uses 10·log₁₀(Γ_eff,rms²/0.5²) dB referencing the site's canonical stationary example B (Γ_rms=0.5, [P1] Eq.21); this ratio is independent of the well-known /2-vs-/4 SSB-accounting constant in Eq.(21) since that constant cancels between numerator and denominator (see white_noise_to_phase_noise.md). Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Keeping the explorer at its default settings (center phase θc = 90°, width 50%, floor = 0 — the 'bad' case at the ISF zero crossing / most-sensitive phase), what Γ_eff,rms does the panel read out? CheckShow answer Graded correct within ±2% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Verification: reproducing the panel's Γ_eff,rms (mirrors EffectiveIsfExplorer.js's gammaLc / alphaWindow / trapzRms) import numpy as np TWO_PI = 2 * np.pi N = 361 # EffectiveIsfExplorer.js sample count def wrap_pi(d): return np.arctan2(np.sin(d), np.cos(d)) def gamma_lc(x): return -np.sin(x) # .js gammaLc() def alpha_window(x, center_rad, width_frac, floor): # .js alphaWindow(), same formula width = width_frac * TWO_PI d = wrap_pi(x - center_rad) clipped = np.clip(d / (width / 2), -1, 1) raised = 0.5 * (1 + np.cos(np.pi * clipped)) return floor + (1 - floor) * raised def trapz_rms(xs, ys): # .js trapzRms() s = 0.0 for i in range(len(xs) - 1): s += 0.5 * (ys[i]**2 + ys[i+1]**2) * (xs[i+1] - xs[i]) return np.sqrt(s / TWO_PI) xs = np.array([TWO_PI * i / (N - 1) for i in range(N)]) # widget defaults: centerDeg=90, widthPct=50, floor=0 (EffectiveIsfExplorer.js:122-124) center_rad = 90.0 * np.pi / 180 width_frac = 50.0 / 100 floor = 0.0 gamma = gamma_lc(xs) alpha = alpha_window(xs, center_rad, width_frac, floor) gamma_eff = gamma * alpha grms_eff = trapz_rms(xs, gamma_eff) print("Gamma_eff,rms =", round(grms_eff, 3)) # -> 0.395 Physical intuition (conclusion first): two "time windows" open and close simultaneously in an oscillator: (1) the ISF Γ(x)\Gamma(x)Γ(x) — how sensitive the oscillator is to noise right now (where the waveform is easy to kick); (2) the NMF α(x)\alpha(x)α(x) — how much noise the device leaks right now (when the transistor is working). What actually enters the phase is the overlap of the two windows. If the device dumps most of its noise only at instants where the ISF is insensitive (like a good Colpitts: the current pulse lands at the voltage trough, where the ISF is small), most of the noise is simply wasted — this is why including α\alphaα matters; using the average noise power alone can badly over- or under-estimate.

documents.t: [P1] Sec. II-D "Cyclostationary Noise Sources" (p.186) decomposes a white cyclostationary current in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) as ([P1] Sec. II-D, Eq.(25), p.186): in(t)=in0(t) α(ω0t)i_n(t)=i_{n0}(t)\,\alpha(\omega_0 t)in​(t)=in0​(t)α(ω0​t) where: in0(t)i_{n0}(t)in0​(t) is a white stationary random process — fixed intensity, easy to handle. α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0 t)α(ω0​t) is a deterministic periodic function describing the modulation of the noise amplitude, called the noise-modulating function (NMF). [P1] normalizes α\alphaα to a maximum of 1 (0≤α≤10\le\alpha\le10≤α≤1, period 2π2\pi2π). Under this definition, the instantaneous mean-square noise power =α2(ω0t)⋅in02‾=\alpha^2(\omega_0 t)\cdot\overline{i_{n0}^2}=α2(ω0​t)⋅in02​​, where in02‾\overline{i_{n0}^2}in02​​ is the maximum mean-square power. Physics used: MOS channel noise ∝gm\propto g_m∝gm​ or ∝\propto∝ overdrive voltage, and these quantities vary periodically with the waveform, so the noise power is "gated" — the device only really leaks noise at certain phases ([P1] uses MOS channel noise as its example). Unit check: α\alphaα is dimensionless (000 to 111); in0i_{n0}in0​ and ini_nin​ are both currents (A) ✓.
documents.s: Step 1: decomposing cyclostationary noise

documents.t: The previous step took α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0 t)α(ω0​t) as a periodic modulation that fell from the sky. But for an analog designer with 40 years of experience, the real question is: where does α(t)\alpha(t)α(t) come from, and why does it have that shape? The answer is written entirely in the device's bias-dependent thermal noise. This section derives α(t)\alpha(t)α(t) by hand from the transistor's instantaneous bias, and works a switching-pair example to show how it changes the 1/f31/f^31/f3. Physical intuition (conclusion first): transistor thermal noise is not of fixed intensity — its mean-square noise current is proportional to some bias-dependent quantity (gmg_mgm​ or IDI_DID​ for a MOS, the collector current for a BJT). In an oscillator these quantities swing periodically with the large-signal waveform: noise is strongest when the device is fully on and nearly vanishes when it is off. Take the instantaneous noise power relative to its maximum, take the square root, normalize the peak to 1 — that is the NMF α(t)\alpha(t)α(t). So α(t)\alpha(t)α(t) is not an extra assumption; it is simply the instantaneous envelope of the device thermal noise.
documents.s: Deriving the NMF α(t)\alpha(t)α(t) from device thermal noise

documents.t: Start from the standard device thermal-noise expression (treated as white over the offset band of interest). For MOSFET channel thermal noise (standard external device model, not among the five source PDFs): in,d2‾Δf=4kT γ gm[A2/Hz],\frac{\overline{i_{n,d}^2}}{\Delta f}=4kT\,\gamma\,g_m \qquad[\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}],Δfin,d2​​​=4kTγgm​[A2/Hz], where γ\gammaγ is the noise coefficient (≈2/3\approx2/3≈2/3 long-channel, larger short-channel) and gmg_mgm​ is the instantaneous transconductance (units S = A/V). The key point is that gmg_mgm​ itself varies with the instantaneous bias — in an oscillator the device's gate-source voltage vGS(t)v_{GS}(t)vGS​(t) swings with the waveform, so gm=gm(vGS(t))⟹in,d2(t)‾Δf=4kTγ gm(vGS(t))g_m=g_m\big(v_{GS}(t)\big)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\overline{i_{n,d}^2(t)}}{\Delta f}=4kT\gamma\,g_m\big(v_{GS}(t)\big)gm​=gm​(vGS​(t))⟹Δfin,d2​(t)​​=4kTγgm​(vGS​(t)) is itself a periodic function of time. For a square-law MOS in saturation, gm=2μCox(W/L) ID(t)∝ID(t)g_m=\sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}(W/L)\,I_D(t)}\propto\sqrt{I_D(t)}gm​=2μCox​(W/L)ID​(t)​∝ID​(t)​; when the device is off (vGS<VTv_{GS}<V_TvGS​<VT​), ID→0I_D\to0ID​→0, gm→0g_m\to0gm​→0, and the noise switches off. Physics used: thermal-noise intensity is set by the channel conductance (proportional to gmg_mgm​ or IDI_DID​); the oscillator's large-signal waveform switches this conductance periodically. Same story for a BJT: collector shot noise ic2‾/Δf=2qIC(t)\overline{i_c^2}/\Delta f=2qI_C(t)ic2​​/Δf=2qIC​(t), with IC(t)I_C(t)IC​(t) pulsing along the waveform. Unit check: 4kT4kT4kT is J=V⋅A⋅s\text{J}=\text{V}\cdot\text{A}\cdot\text{s}J=V⋅A⋅s; multiplying by gmg_mgm​ (A/V) gives A2⋅s=A2/Hz\text{A}^2\cdot\text{s}=\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}A2⋅s=A2/Hz ✓.

documents.t: Write the instantaneous mean-square noise power as "maximum × a [0,1][0,1][0,1] shape". Define the maximum mean-square power in02‾/Δf≡max⁡t[4kTγ gm(vGS(t))]\overline{i_{n0}^2}/\Delta f\equiv\max_t\big[4kT\gamma\,g_m(v_{GS}(t))\big]in02​​/Δf≡maxt​[4kTγgm​(vGS​(t))] (the peak over one period); then in,d2(t)‾Δf=in02‾Δf⋅gm(vGS(t))max⁡tgm⏟≡ α2(ω0t).\frac{\overline{i_{n,d}^2(t)}}{\Delta f}=\frac{\overline{i_{n0}^2}}{\Delta f}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{g_m\big(v_{GS}(t)\big)}{\max_t g_m}}_{\equiv\,\alpha^2(\omega_0 t)} .Δfin,d2​(t)​​=Δfin02​​​⋅≡α2(ω0​t)maxt​gm​gm​(vGS​(t))​​​. Comparing term by term with [P1]'s decomposition in2(t)‾=α2(ω0t) in02‾\overline{i_n^2(t)}=\alpha^2(\omega_0 t)\,\overline{i_{n0}^2}in2​(t)​=α2(ω0​t)in02​​ (Step 1 above), read off immediately α(ω0t)=gm(vGS(t))max⁡tgm(vGS(t)) (0≤α≤1).\boxed{\ \alpha(\omega_0 t)=\sqrt{\frac{g_m\big(v_{GS}(t)\big)}{\max_t g_m\big(v_{GS}(t)\big)}}\ }\qquad(0\le\alpha\le1). α(ω0​t)=maxt​gm​(vGS​(t))gm​(vGS​(t))​​ ​(0≤α≤1). This is the microscopic origin of the NMF: α(t)\alpha(t)α(t) is the square root of the instantaneous transconductance relative to its peak (the square root because α\alphaα is defined on the amplitude side; noise power is α2\alpha^2α2). α=1\alpha=1α=1 at phases where the device conducts fully, α=0\alpha=0α=0 where it is off. For circuits that conduct only over a small slice of phase (switching pair, class-C, the Colpitts current pulse), α\alphaα is a narrow periodic gate. Unit check: a ratio is dimensionless, and so is its square root → α\alphaα is dimensionless, 0≤α≤10\le\alpha\le10≤α≤1 ✓, consistent with the convention. Interface to the ISF: substituting back into the previous step gives Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α. The shape of α\alphaα is set entirely by the device's gm(vGS(t))g_m(v_{GS}(t))gm​(vGS​(t)) — i.e., by circuit topology + bias + large-signal waveform — it is not a free parameter. Design takeaway (deeper): since α∝gm\alpha\propto\sqrt{g_m}α∝gm​​ and gmg_mgm​ switches with whether the device conducts, which slice of phase the device conducts in is a knob in the designer's hand. Push the conduction window (the α\alphaα peak) onto a zero of the ISF (Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0) and Γeff=Γα\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\alphaΓeff​=Γα collapses — this is exactly the physics behind the low phase noise of Colpitts/class-C. The switching-pair example below turns this into numbers.

The product of the two periodic functions in the middle is defined as the effective ISF (substituted back into (11) this is [P1] Sec. II-D, Eq.(26), p.186; Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α itself is [P1] Eq.(27), p.186): Γeff(x)=Γ(x) α(x) \boxed{\ \Gamma_{eff}(x)=\Gamma(x)\,\alpha(x)\ } Γeff​(x)=Γ(x)α(x) ​ So the form of the equation is entirely unchanged: the remaining in0i_{n0}in0​ is stationary white noise acting on a system whose ISF is Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​. [P1] says it plainly: "the cyclostationary noise can be treated as a stationary noise applied to a system with an effective ISF". Math used: move the deterministic periodic factor α\alphaα from the "random-process side" to the "system-weight side" — since α\alphaα is deterministic, this move is fully legal and changes no statistics. Unit check: Γ\GammaΓ dimensionless, α\alphaα dimensionless ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ dimensionless and still 2π2\pi2π-periodic ✓. Practical rule (claim C9): use Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ in every subsequent calculation — especially the Fourier coefficients cnc_ncn​, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, and c0c_0c0​. That is, in white_noise_to_phase_noise and flicker_noise_upconversion, Eq.(21), (23), (24) all take Γ→Γeff\Gamma\to\Gamma_{eff}Γ→Γeff​, c0→c0effc_0\to c_0^{eff}c0​→c0eff​, Γrms→Γrmseff\Gamma_{rms}\to\Gamma_{rms}^{eff}Γrms​→Γrmseff​.

documents.t: Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α is a pointwise product of two periodic functions, so phase alignment decides everything. [P1] (p.187, Fig. 14–15) illustrates with two classic examples, and the difference is dramatic: Colpitts LC oscillator: the transistor's collector current is a short, tall current pulse followed by a long quiet stretch. That current spike lands exactly at the minimum of the tank voltage — where the ISF Γ\GammaΓ is small (the trough is insensitive). So Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α is much smaller than Γ\GammaΓ alone: the device leaks noise only at the least sensitive instants, and most of the noise is wasted. [P1] verbatim: "Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ is quite different from Γ\GammaΓ, and hence the effect of cyclostationarity is very significant for the LC oscillator and cannot be neglected." — this is one key reason Colpitts phase noise is good. Ring oscillator: device current is largest during the transition — exactly where the ISF is largest (most sensitive). The α\alphaα peak overlaps the Γ\GammaΓ peak, so Γeff≈Γ\Gamma_{eff}\approx\GammaΓeff​≈Γ and cyclostationarity does not help. [P1]: the ring's Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ is nearly identical to Γ\GammaΓ — this "unfortunate coincidence" is one reason ring phase noise is usually worse (another is that a ring burns all its stored energy every period). Design takeaway: low phase noise takes more than small Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and large qmaxq_{max}qmax​ — you also want the device to leak noise only at ISF-insensitive phases (keep the α\alphaα peak misaligned from the Γ\GammaΓ peak). Colpitts does this by construction; it is a topology-level advantage.

documents.t: Continuing from the previous page: flicker upconversion depends only on the DC term c0c_0c0​ of the ISF. But the quantity to look at is really the DC value of Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​, i.e., c0eff/2=⟨Γ α⟩c_0^{eff}/2=\langle\Gamma\,\alpha\ranglec0eff​/2=⟨Γα⟩ (average over one period). [P1] states it explicitly in the design section (p.187–188, near Eq.(30)): the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner is set by the DC value of the (effective) ISF. Consequence: even if the main signal path's Γ\GammaΓ is very symmetric (c0≈0c_0\approx0c0​≈0), if some source's α\alphaα is asymmetric, the average of Γeff=Γα\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\alphaΓeff​=Γα can still be nonzero ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ the flicker gate reopens. The tail source's notoriety (echoing the flicker page): the ISF/NMF combination of the tail current source often gives Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ a large DC value, strongly upconverting the tail's flicker. Symmetrizing the main path cannot save it — check every source from the Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ (including α\alphaα) point of view.

documents.t: In [P1] the ISF is introduced via physical intuition plus impulse simulations. Behind it there is in fact a rigorous mathematical foundation, but that foundation is not among the five PDFs we downloaded — it comes from the broader nonlinear-oscillator/perturbation-theory literature (claim C13). So you can see the whole map, here is the intuition; formal citations have been added (see the honesty note below, [E2]/[E3]): Floquet theory: the mathematical framework for the solution structure of linear differential equations with periodic coefficients. An oscillator linearized around its limit cycle is exactly such a system. Floquet gives a set of periodically time-varying eigenvectors (Floquet eigenvectors) and exponents describing the growth/decay of perturbations along each direction. PPV (Perturbation Projection Vector): within the Floquet framework, the first principal vector v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) corresponding to the zero Floquet exponent (the neutral direction — the phase direction, because phase has no restoring force). Projecting any perturbation onto v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) yields the phase shift. The PPV is essentially the rigorous version of the ISF — Γ(ω0τ)/qmax\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)/q_{max}Γ(ω0​τ)/qmax​ corresponds to the component of v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) at the injection node. Demir et al. (2000) use the PPV to write the phase dynamics as the first-order equation ϕ˙(t)=v1T(t) B(t) ξ(t)\dot{\phi}(t)=v_1^T(t)\,B(t)\,\xi(t)ϕ˙​(t)=v1T​(t)B(t)ξ(t) (see the reference form collected in equation_index). Adjoint method: the standard practical method for extracting the ISF/PPV from simulation. It solves the periodic solution of the adjoint (transposed) problem of the system's monodromy matrix, obtaining the entire v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) (i.e., the entire ISF) in one shot — far more efficient than injecting impulses one phase at a time (the brute-force method of this site's lab_04). The PSS + Pnoise flow of commercial RF simulators uses this class of method internally. Honesty note: PPV / adjoint / Floquet belong to Demir–Mehrotra–Roychowdhury (2000), Kärtner, and other external literature — not among the five PDFs downloaded for this site; they are given here only as standard literature background for intuition. Formal citation added: Demir et al. 2000 (IEEE TCAS-I 47(5):655–674, DOI 10.1109/81.847872), see references [E2] (external literature). Scope note: the rigorous PPV definition and the ϕ˙=v1TBξ\dot\phi=v_1^T B\xiϕ˙​=v1T​Bξ form are the core result of [E2] Demir 2000 (the entire paper is on this topic, TCAS-I 47(5):655–674, DOI 10.1109/81.847872); the correspondence between v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) and Γ/qmax\Gamma/q_{max}Γ/qmax​ ("ISF = the PPV scalarized along the charge-injection direction") is in [E2] and Kärtner [E3]. This site only cites, and does not re-derive (external-literature scope).

documents.t: Toy problem: ideal LC with Γ(x)=−sin⁡x\Gamma(x)=-\sin xΓ(x)=−sinx. The device conducts only in a narrow window of duty don=0.1d_{on}=0.1don​=0.1 (10%10\%10% of the period) centered on the zero crossing (x=π/2x=\pi/2x=π/2, where ∣Γ∣=1|\Gamma|=1∣Γ∣=1, the most sensitive point), and leaks no noise the rest of the time. A bit more precisely: with the window centered at π/2\pi/2π/2 with half-width 0.1π0.1\pi0.1π, the average of sin⁡2x\sin^2 xsin2x inside the window is slightly below 1 (about 0.970.970.97), so Γeff,rms≈0.97×0.1≈0.311\Gamma_{eff,rms}\approx\sqrt{0.97\times0.1}\approx0.311Γeff,rms​≈0.97×0.1​≈0.311. Result: Γeff,rms≈0.31\Gamma_{eff,rms}\approx0.31Γeff,rms​≈0.31, much smaller than the ungated LC's Γrms=0.707\Gamma_{rms}=0.707Γrms​=0.707. (Note: here the device sits at the most sensitive phase — "bad" alignment; a Colpitts-like window at the trough Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0 gives an even smaller Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​ — see Worked example 2.) documents.t: This example applies the "derive α\alphaα from device thermal noise" result above to the skeleton of a real topology: the differential switching pair. It is the core shared by cross-coupled LC VCOs, Gilbert mixers, and CML logic, so this α\alphaα shape (conducting twice per period) is especially representative. We compute the c0c_0c0​ and c2c_2c2​ of Γeff=Γα\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\alphaΓeff​=Γα and see how they open/alter the close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3. Toy problem (gate shape is illustrative, not a transistor-level extraction): the two devices of a differential pair conduct alternately — the left device in the positive half-cycle, the right device in the negative half-cycle. Seen from a single device's noise, its α\alphaα is a narrow once-per-period pulse (duty don=0.1d_{on}=0.1don​=0.1); but treating the pair as a whole (both devices' noise counted) as one equivalent source injecting into the tank, conduction events occur twice per period (one narrow gate each at x=π/2x=\pi/2x=π/2 and x=3π/2x=3\pi/2x=3π/2), so the equivalent NMF is a 2-per-period gate α(x)\alpha(x)α(x): a window of half-width 0.1π0.1\pi0.1π and height 1 at each of x=π/2, 3π/2x=\pi/2,\,3\pi/2x=π/2,3π/2, and 0 elsewhere. Take the ideal-LC ISF Γ(x)=−sin⁡x\Gamma(x)=-\sin xΓ(x)=−sinx. Find c0effc_0^{eff}c0eff​ and c2effc_2^{eff}c2eff​ of Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​, and assess the 1/f31/f^31/f3. Step-by-step substitution: (1) Why a 2-per-period gate generates c2c_2c2​. α(x)\alpha(x)α(x) repeats twice per period (fundamental period π\piπ), so by itself it contains only even harmonics (2ω0,4ω0,…2\omega_0,4\omega_0,\dots2ω0​,4ω0​,…). Γ=−sin⁡x\Gamma=-\sin xΓ=−sinx is pure fundamental (odd). Their product Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α mixes "odd × even" into new harmonics — the point is that it generates a nonzero c2effc_2^{eff}c2eff​ (absent when looking at Γ\GammaΓ alone, which has c2=0c_2=0c2​=0), and possibly a nonzero c0effc_0^{eff}c0eff​. (2) Compute c0effc_0^{eff}c0eff​ (DC value = one-period average). c0eff/2=⟨Γα⟩c_0^{eff}/2=\langle\Gamma\alpha\ranglec0eff​/2=⟨Γα⟩. Inside the window at x=π/2x=\pi/2x=π/2, Γ=−sin⁡(π/2)=−1\Gamma=-\sin(\pi/2)=-1Γ=−sin(π/2)=−1; inside the window at x=3π/2x=3\pi/2x=3π/2, Γ=−sin⁡(3π/2)=+1\Gamma=-\sin(3\pi/2)=+1Γ=−sin(3π/2)=+1. The two windows carry equal and opposite Γ\GammaΓ; with equal width and height, the average cancels: c0eff/2=⟨Γα⟩≈12π[(−1)(0.2π)⏟x=π/2 window+(+1)(0.2π)⏟x=3π/2 window]=0 ⇒ c0eff≈0.c_0^{eff}/2=\langle\Gamma\alpha\rangle\approx\frac{1}{2\pi}\Big[\underbrace{(-1)(0.2\pi)}_{x=\pi/2\,\text{window}}+\underbrace{(+1)(0.2\pi)}_{x=3\pi/2\,\text{window}}\Big]=0\ \Rightarrow\ c_0^{eff}\approx0.c0eff​/2=⟨Γα⟩≈2π1​[x=π/2window(−1)(0.2π)​​+x=3π/2window(+1)(0.2π)​​]=0 ⇒ c0eff​≈0. (Each window has width 2×0.1π=0.2π2\times0.1\pi=0.2\pi2×0.1π=0.2π.) A symmetric 2-per-period gate → c0eff=0c_0^{eff}=0c0eff​=0 → in theory no 1/f31/f^31/f3 — this is the root of the "clean close-in" behavior of differential/push-pull structures (echoing fourier_series_of_isf Step 7 on half-wave symmetry suppressing even harmonics, and symmetry). (3) Compute c2effc_2^{eff}c2eff​. Even harmonics do not cancel. c2eff=1π∫02πΓαcos⁡2x dxc_2^{eff}=\dfrac1\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma\alpha\cos 2x\,dxc2eff​=π1​∫02π​Γαcos2xdx (take the magnitude together with the sin⁡\sinsin component). At x=π/2x=\pi/2x=π/2: Γ=−1\Gamma=-1Γ=−1, cos⁡2x=cos⁡π=−1\cos2x=\cos\pi=-1cos2x=cosπ=−1, product +1+1+1; at x=3π/2x=3\pi/2x=3π/2: Γ=+1\Gamma=+1Γ=+1, cos⁡3π=−1\cos3\pi=-1cos3π=−1, product −1-1−1 — huh, it cancels again? Check the sin⁡2x\sin2xsin2x component: sin⁡π=0\sin\pi=0sinπ=0 at x=π/2x=\pi/2x=π/2 and sin⁡3π=0\sin3\pi=0sin3π=0 at x=3π/2x=3\pi/2x=3π/2, also 0. So in this ideally symmetric arrangement c2effc_2^{eff}c2eff​ is also very small — an ideal differential pair suppresses the even harmonics too. What really generates c2effc_2^{eff}c2eff​ is mismatch: if the two conduction windows differ in width/height (rise/fall asymmetry, VTV_TVT​ mismatch), the cancellation fails, and c2effc_2^{eff}c2eff​ pops up together with c0effc_0^{eff}c0eff​. Below we quantify this "mismatch opens the door" effect. (4) Mismatch opens the door: set the right window's height to 1−δ1-\delta1−δ (δ=0.2\delta=0.2δ=0.2 mismatch). The two windows are no longer equal, and the average is no longer zero: c0eff/2≈12π[(−1)(0.2π)+(+1)(1−δ)(0.2π)]=0.2π2π[−1+(1−δ)]=0.1 (−δ)1=−0.02,c_0^{eff}/2\approx\frac{1}{2\pi}\big[(-1)(0.2\pi)+(+1)(1-\delta)(0.2\pi)\big] =\frac{0.2\pi}{2\pi}\big[-1+(1-\delta)\big]=\frac{0.1\,(-\delta)}{1}=-0.02,c0eff​/2≈2π1​[(−1)(0.2π)+(+1)(1−δ)(0.2π)]=2π0.2π​[−1+(1−δ)]=10.1(−δ)​=−0.02, so c0eff≈−0.04c_0^{eff}\approx-0.04c0eff​≈−0.04 (magnitude ∣c0eff∣≈0.04|c_0^{eff}|\approx0.04∣c0eff​∣≈0.04). A mismatch of δ=0.2\delta=0.2δ=0.2 pushes the formerly zero c0effc_0^{eff}c0eff​ up to ≈0.04\approx0.04≈0.04 — the 1/f31/f^31/f3 is reopened. (5) Consequence for the 1/f31/f^31/f3 (using [P1] Eq.(23),(24)). The amount of flicker-upconverted 1/f31/f^31/f3 is proportional to c0eff 2c_0^{eff\,2}c0eff2​ ([P1] Eq.(23)); the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ([P1] Eq.(24)): Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c0eff 22 Γrmseff 2.\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^{eff\,2}}{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^{eff\,2}}.Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2Γrmseff2​c0eff2​​. Γrmseff\Gamma_{rms}^{eff}Γrmseff​ from the 2-per-period gate (two windows, Γ2≈1\Gamma^2\approx1Γ2≈1 inside each, total duty 0.20.20.2): Γrmseff≈0.2≈0.447\Gamma_{rms}^{eff}\approx\sqrt{0.2}\approx0.447Γrmseff​≈0.2​≈0.447. Substituting: symmetric (c0eff=0c_0^{eff}=0c0eff​=0) → corner =0=0=0 (no 1/f31/f^31/f3); mismatched (c0eff=0.04c_0^{eff}=0.04c0eff​=0.04) → Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅0.0422×0.4472=ω1/f⋅1.6×10−30.4=4.0×10−3 ω1/f.\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{0.04^2}{2\times0.447^2}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{1.6\times10^{-3}}{0.4}=4.0\times10^{-3}\,\omega_{1/f}.Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2×0.44720.042​=ω1/f​⋅0.41.6×10−3​=4.0×10−3ω1/f​. Result: ideal symmetric switching pair: c0eff≈0c_0^{eff}\approx0c0eff​≈0, c2eff≈0c_2^{eff}\approx0c2eff​≈0, no 1/f31/f^31/f3. With 20%20\%20% mismatch: c0eff≈0.04c_0^{eff}\approx0.04c0eff​≈0.04, 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ≈4×10−3 ω1/f\approx4\times10^{-3}\,\omega_{1/f}≈4×10−3ω1/f​ (small but nonzero) — the device's bias-dependent gating combined with mismatch is the source of close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3; symmetry is the knob that closes this door. Dimension check: c0effc_0^{eff}c0eff​, c2effc_2^{eff}c2eff​, Γrmseff\Gamma_{rms}^{eff}Γrmseff​ are all dimensionless; in the corner formula, ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ (rad/s) × dimensionless ratio = rad/s ✓. import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, effective_isf, gamma_rms, compute_fourier_coefficients x = np.linspace(0.0, 2*np.pi, 200001, endpoint=True) gamma = gamma_lc_ideal(x) # -sin x half = 0.1*np.pi def gate_2pp(delta=0.0): # two windows per period: pi/2 and 3pi/2, right window height 1-delta w1 = (np.abs(((x-np.pi/2 + np.pi) % (2*np.pi)) - np.pi) <= half).astype(float) w2 = (np.abs(((x-3*np.pi/2 + np.pi) % (2*np.pi)) - np.pi) <= half).astype(float) return w1 + (1.0-delta)*w2 for delta, name in [(0.0, "symmetric"), (0.2, "mismatch 20%")]: g_eff = effective_isf(gamma, gate_2pp(delta)) a0, a, b, c, ph = compute_fourier_coefficients(x, g_eff, n_harmonics=4) grms = gamma_rms(x, g_eff) corner = (a0**2) / (2*grms**2) # Δω_{1/f3} / ω_{1/f} print(name, "c0_eff=", round(abs(a0),3), "c2_eff=", round(c[2],3), "Grms_eff=", round(grms,3), "corner/w1f=", round(corner,4)) # -> symmetric c0_eff≈0.000 c2_eff≈0.000 Grms_eff≈0.440 corner/w1f≈0.0 # -> mismatch 20% c0_eff≈0.039 c2_eff≈0.037 Grms_eff≈0.398 corner/w1f≈0.005 Intuition: this example quantifies the second knob — symmetry — beyond the main text's "phase alignment decides everything". The switching pair's 2-per-period gating by itself (when symmetric) forces c0effc_0^{eff}c0eff​ to zero and keeps close-in clean; once device mismatch breaks the symmetry, c0effc_0^{eff}c0eff​ comes back to life and the 1/f31/f^31/f3 reopens. This is why the flicker upconversion of differential VCOs is so sensitive to layout symmetry and VTV_TVT​ mismatch. Required caveat: the gate duty, half-width, and 20%20\%20% mismatch are all illustrative toy numbers (not transistor-level extractions). A real switching pair's α(x)\alpha(x)α(x) must come from device operating points/PSS simulation. documents.t: Device noise is mostly cyclostationary: the noise power is periodically "gated" by the operating point. Decompose in=in0 α(ω0t)i_n=i_{n0}\,\alpha(\omega_0 t)in​=in0​α(ω0​t) (α\alphaα = NMF, 0≤α≤10\le\alpha\le10≤α≤1) and absorb α\alphaα into the ISF: Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α; every formula afterwards uses Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ unchanged. Phase alignment decides everything: Colpitts (α\alphaα peak at the Γ\GammaΓ trough) → Γeff≪Γ\Gamma_{eff}\ll\GammaΓeff​≪Γ, noise is wasted (a good thing); ring (the two peaks overlap) → Γeff≈Γ\Gamma_{eff}\approx\GammaΓeff​≈Γ, cyclostationarity does not help. For flicker, look at the DC value of Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​, c0effc_0^{eff}c0eff​; the tail source often dominates the 1/f31/f^31/f3 through a large DC in its Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​. The rigorous foundation is PPV / adjoint / Floquet (ISF = the first Floquet vector v1v_1v1​ of the zero exponent), from Demir et al. and other external literature, not among the five PDFs; the adjoint method extracts the ISF efficiently from simulation.

documents.t: Prerequisites: lorentzian_linewidth | Next: effective_isf Hands-on verification: this page's "symmetric vs asymmetric waveforms decide close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3" simulation is in lab_07. The previous page white_noise_to_phase_noise explained how white noise turns into 1/f21/f^21/f2. But look at any real oscillator's phase-noise plot: the segment closest to the carrier is usually steeper — slope −30-30−30 dB/decade, i.e. 1/f31/f^31/f3. Where does this steep skirt come from? Answer: device flicker noise (1/f1/f1/f noise, the noise that is especially strong in transistors at low frequency) gets "upconverted" by the oscillator to the vicinity of the carrier. This page answers three things: (1) what flicker noise is, (2) why only the ISF's DC term c0c_0c0​ can upconvert it, (3) why the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner is not equal to the device's 1/f1/f1/f corner, and how waveform symmetry helps. Physical intuition (conclusion first): low-frequency flicker noise itself lives at baseband (near DC). For it to show up near the carrier, some mechanism must "move" it up to ω0\omega_0ω0​. The ISF is a periodic function, and in its Fourier series the only DC component is c0/2c_0/2c0​/2. Only this DC term multiplies the "flicker sitting right next to DC" and gets accumulated by the phase integrator into close-in phase jitter. In other words: c0c_0c0​ is flicker's only gate to the carrier. Push c0c_0c0​ to 0 (via waveform symmetry) and that gate closes — the 1/f31/f^31/f3 skirt drops dramatically.

documents.t: Flicker (1/f1/f1/f) noise is the transistor's intrinsic low-frequency noise; its PSD rises toward low frequency (∝1/f\propto 1/f∝1/f), usually attributed to carrier trapping/release at the channel–oxide interface. Below the device's 1/f1/f1/f corner ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​, flicker exceeds white noise; above it, white noise dominates. [P1] describes it with a compact model ([P1] Eq.(22), p.185): in,1/f2‾=in2‾⋅ω1/fΔω(Δω<ω1/f)\overline{i_{n,1/f}^2}=\overline{i_n^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}\qquad(\Delta\omega<\omega_{1/f})in,1/f2​​=in2​​⋅Δωω1/f​​(Δω<ω1/f​) How to read it: in2‾\overline{i_n^2}in2​​ is the white-noise floor (per-Hz); multiplied by ω1/f/Δω\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omegaω1/f​/Δω, it is amplified when Δω<ω1/f\Delta\omega<\omega_{1/f}Δω<ω1/f​ and rises as 1/Δω1/\Delta\omega1/Δω — exactly the 1/f1/f1/f shape. At Δω=ω1/f\Delta\omega=\omega_{1/f}Δω=ω1/f​ the two are equal (the definition of the corner). Unit check: ω1/f/Δω\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omegaω1/f​/Δω is dimensionless (rad/s divided by rad/s); multiplying in2‾\overline{i_n^2}in2​​ (A2/Hz\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}A2/Hz) still gives A2/Hz\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}A2/Hz ✓. Watch the notation: ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ is the device 1/f1/f1/f corner (rad/s), set by the transistor process — a different thing from the phase-noise 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner that appears later (see Step 4; the notation page warns about this explicitly).

documents.t: Return to the harmonic-decomposition phase response of [P1] Eq.(13), p.183: ϕ(t)=1qmax ⁣[c02 ⁣∫−∞t ⁣in dτ+∑n=1∞cn ⁣∫−∞t ⁣incos⁡(nω0τ+θn) dτ].\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\!\left[\frac{c_0}{2}\!\int_{-\infty}^{t}\!i_n\,d\tau+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\!\int_{-\infty}^{t}\!i_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\,d\tau\right].ϕ(t)=qmax​1​[2c0​​∫−∞t​in​dτ+n=1∑∞​cn​∫−∞t​in​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)dτ]. Flicker's energy is concentrated at low frequency (near DC). Look at each term in the sum: Every n≥1n\ge1n≥1 term carries cos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)cos(nω0​τ+θn​) — it downconverts noise sitting "right around nω0n\omega_0nω0​" to baseband. But flicker has almost no energy at nω0n\omega_0nω0​ (≥ω0\ge\omega_0≥ω0​, which is high), so these terms cannot capture flicker. Only the n=0n=0n=0 (DC) term c02∫in dτ\dfrac{c_0}{2}\int i_n\,d\tau2c0​​∫in​dτ has no cos⁡\coscos multiplier — it directly integrates baseband noise. Flicker's energy is exactly at baseband, so only this term accumulates flicker into phase. Math used: frequency translation (mixing). cos⁡(nω0t)×\cos(n\omega_0 t)\timescos(nω0​t)×noise moves noise to ±nω0\pm n\omega_0±nω0​; only the DC multiplier (=1=1=1) leaves baseband noise at baseband to be integrated. Physical meaning (claim C4): c0c_0c0​ (the ISF's DC Fourier coefficient) is the only channel from flicker to close-in. With c0=0c_0=0c0​=0, flicker simply never gets up there and the 1/f31/f^31/f3 skirt vanishes.

documents.t: This step "multiplies" three things together: (i) flicker injected via c0c_0c0​, (ii) the 1/f21/f^21/f2 mechanism (the integrator), (iii) and the product is 1/f31/f^31/f3. No skipped steps — we compute line by line. Step 3.1: the white-noise sum keeps only the DC term. The white-noise result (spec Section 3, formula 10; [P1] Eq.(19), p.185) is L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣((in2‾/Δf) ∑n=0∞cn28 qmax2 Δω2).\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)\,\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2}{8\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}\right).L{Δω}=10log10​(8qmax2​Δω2(in2​​/Δf)∑n=0∞​cn2​​). So for flicker, the sum ∑n=0∞cn2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2∑n=0∞​cn2​ collapses to the single term c02c_0^2c02​: ∑n=0∞cn2 → flicker 只剩 DC c02.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{flicker 只剩 DC}\ }\ c_0^2.n=0∑∞​cn2​ flicker 只剩 DC ​ c02​. Why this c02c_0^2c02​ pairs with the 888 in the denominator: Eq.(19)'s denominator is 8qmax2Δω28q_{max}^2\Delta\omega^28qmax2​Δω2 and its numerator carries ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​. The DC term of the ISF Fourier series ([P1] Eq.(12)) is written c02\tfrac{c_0}{2}2c0​​, but in Parseval ([P1] Eq.(20)) the DC power coefficient is recorded as c02c_0^2c02​ (the same convention as the other cn2c_n^2cn2​), so we substitute c02c_0^2c02​ directly and keep the 888 in the denominator. Substituting gives the "DC-only, still white-noise" intermediate form: L{Δω}∣1/f2, DC only=10log⁡10 ⁣(c02qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf8 Δω2).\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}\Big|_{1/f^2,\,\text{DC only}}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{8\,\Delta\omega^2}\right).L{Δω}​1/f2,DC only​=10log10​(qmax2​c02​​⋅8Δω2in2​​/Δf​). Step 3.2: replace the white-noise floor with flicker (multiply by the amplification factor of Eq.(22)). The in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf in the numerator above is still the white-noise floor. Device flicker ([P1] Eq.(22), p.185) says that for Δω<ω1/f\Delta\omega<\omega_{1/f}Δω<ω1/f​, the current noise is amplified by ω1/f/Δω\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omegaω1/f​/Δω: in,1/f2‾=in2‾⋅ω1/fΔω.\overline{i_{n,1/f}^2}=\overline{i_n^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}.in,1/f2​​=in2​​⋅Δωω1/f​​. Replacing the numerator's in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf with in,1/f2‾/Δf=(in2‾/Δf)⋅(ω1/f/Δω)\overline{i_{n,1/f}^2}/\Delta f=(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)\cdot(\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omega)in,1/f2​​/Δf=(in2​​/Δf)⋅(ω1/f​/Δω) is exactly the product "flicker mechanism × 1/f21/f^21/f2 mechanism": c02qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf8 Δω2⏟1/f2 機制（積分器） × ω1/fΔω⏟flicker 機制.\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{8\,\Delta\omega^2}}_{1/f^2\ \text{機制（積分器）}}\;\times\;\underbrace{\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}}_{\text{flicker 機制}}.qmax2​c02​​⋅1/f2 機制（積分器）8Δω2in2​​/Δf​​​×flicker 機制Δωω1/f​​​​. Step 3.3: combine to get [P1] Eq.(23). Multiplying the two brackets and putting back the 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ yields the flicker-upconverted 1/f31/f^31/f3 phase noise ([P1] Eq.(23), p.185): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(c02qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf8 Δω2⋅ω1/fΔω) \boxed{\ \mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{8\,\Delta\omega^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}\right)\ } L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​c02​​⋅8Δω2in2​​/Δf​⋅Δωω1/f​​) ​ See the 1/f31/f^31/f3? The denominator has Δω2\Delta\omega^2Δω2 (the integrator, 1/f21/f^21/f2) times one more Δω\Delta\omegaΔω (flicker's 1/Δω1/\Delta\omega1/Δω), together Δω3\Delta\omega^3Δω3. One decade up drops it 100010001000× ⇒30\Rightarrow 30⇒30 dB ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ slope −30-30−30 dB/decade ✓. This is the mathematical root of "symmetry can only save flicker, not white noise" — in Step 4, dividing these two numerators directly yields the corner. documents.t: On the phase-noise spectrum, the offset where the 1/f31/f^31/f3 segment meets the 1/f21/f^21/f2 segment is called the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner Δω1/f3\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}Δω1/f3​. Set the 1/f31/f^31/f3 expression (Eq.(23), with c02c_0^2c02​) equal to the 1/f21/f^21/f2 expression (Eq.(21), with Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​) and solve for the intersection ([P1] Eq.(24), p.185): Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c022 Γrms2≈ω1/f(c0c1)2 \boxed{\ \Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}\approx\omega_{1/f}\left(\frac{c_0}{c_1}\right)^2\ } Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​≈ω1/f​(c1​c0​​)2 ​ Step-by-step algebra (solving for the intersection, no skipped steps): the corner is defined as the Δω\Delta\omegaΔω where "1/f31/f^31/f3 segment = 1/f21/f^21/f2 segment". Set the two brackets inside the log⁡10\log_{10}log10​ equal (equal logs ⇔ equal arguments): c02qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf8 Δω2⋅ω1/fΔω⏟Eq.(23)：1/f3=Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2⏟Eq.(21)：1/f2.\underbrace{\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{8\,\Delta\omega^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}}_{\text{Eq.(23)：}1/f^3} =\underbrace{\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}}_{\text{Eq.(21)：}1/f^2}.Eq.(23)：1/f3qmax2​c02​​⋅8Δω2in2​​/Δf​⋅Δωω1/f​​​​=Eq.(21)：1/f2qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​​​. Step (a): cancel the common factors. Both sides carry 1qmax2\dfrac{1}{q_{max}^2}qmax2​1​ and in2‾/ΔfΔω2\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{\Delta\omega^2}Δω2in2​​/Δf​; divide them out: c028⋅ω1/fΔω=Γrms24.\frac{c_0^2}{8}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{4}.8c02​​⋅Δωω1/f​​=4Γrms2​​. Step (b): solve for Δω\Delta\omegaΔω. Multiply both sides by Δω\Delta\omegaΔω, then divide by Γrms2/4\Gamma_{rms}^2/4Γrms2​/4: c02 ω1/f8=Γrms24 Δω ⟹ Δω=c02 ω1/f8⋅4Γrms2=ω1/f⋅4c028 Γrms2=ω1/f⋅c022 Γrms2.\frac{c_0^2\,\omega_{1/f}}{8}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{4}\,\Delta\omega \;\Longrightarrow\; \Delta\omega=\frac{c_0^2\,\omega_{1/f}}{8}\cdot\frac{4}{\Gamma_{rms}^2}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{4c_0^2}{8\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}.8c02​ω1/f​​=4Γrms2​​Δω⟹Δω=8c02​ω1/f​​⋅Γrms2​4​=ω1/f​⋅8Γrms2​4c02​​=ω1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​. 4/8=1/24/8=1/24/8=1/2, giving exactly the boxed c022Γrms2\dfrac{c_0^2}{2\Gamma_{rms}^2}2Γrms2​c02​​ ✓. Note the factor here is 12\tfrac1221​ (not 14\tfrac1441​); it comes from the ratio of the 888 in Eq.(23)'s denominator to the 444 in Eq.(21)'s denominator. The most important concept on this page (claim C5): Δω1/f3≠ω1/f\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}\ne\omega_{1/f}Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​. The 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner equals the device's 1/f1/f1/f corner times the ratio c02/(2Γrms2)c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)c02​/(2Γrms2​). Because a symmetric waveform has c0≪Γrmsc_0\ll\Gamma_{rms}c0​≪Γrms​, this ratio is far below 1, so the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner is pushed far below the device's 1/f1/f1/f corner. This overturns the myth of the early empirical model "1/f31/f^31/f3 corner === device 1/f1/f1/f corner" — [P1]'s abstract and introduction emphasize that "contrary to widely held beliefs, the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner is smaller than the device 1/f1/f1/f corner by a factor determined by waveform symmetry". Where ≈ω1/f(c0/c1)2\approx\omega_{1/f}(c_0/c_1)^2≈ω1/f​(c0​/c1​)2 comes from: when the ISF is fundamental-dominated, Γrms2≈c12/2\Gamma_{rms}^2\approx c_1^2/2Γrms2​≈c12​/2 (Parseval keeps only the n=1n=1n=1 term); substituting gives the right-hand form. It lets you estimate the corner directly from "DC coefficient vs fundamental coefficient". Unit check: ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ (rad/s) times a dimensionless ratio → rad/s ✓, an angular frequency.
documents.s: Step 4: the 1/f³ corner (Eq.(24)) — it is not the device 1/f corner

documents.t: c0c_0c0​ is the ISF's DC Fourier coefficient; the ISF's DC value is c0/2c_0/2c0​/2 (the notation trap flagged on the notation page). The DC value is the ISF's average over one period. [P1] points out in the design section (p.187–188, Fig. 16): The DC value of the ISF is determined by the waveform's symmetry, in particular its rise/fall symmetry. If the rise time and fall time differ significantly, the ISF has a large DC value (large c0c_0c0​). Intuition: the ISF swings positive and negative in the "sensitive region" (near the waveform transitions). If the rising and falling segments are mirror-symmetric, the positive and negative swings cancel and the average ≈0\approx0≈0 (small c0c_0c0​); if they are asymmetric (e.g. fast rise, slow fall), they do not cancel, the average is nonzero (large c0c_0c0​), and flicker's gate opens wide. Odd-symmetric waveforms (odd-symmetric, e.g. an ideal −sin⁡-\sin−sin, antiphase over half a period) have c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 — an excellent special case; but [P1] clarifies explicitly: small c0c_0c0​ is not limited to odd-symmetric waveforms — rise/fall symmetry alone suffices, a much broader class. Toy contrast: lab_05 uses Γ=cos⁡θ\Gamma=\cos\thetaΓ=cosθ (symmetric, c0=0c_0=0c0​=0) against Γ=cos⁡θ+0.4\Gamma=\cos\theta+0.4Γ=cosθ+0.4 (deliberately added DC, c0=0.8c_0=0.8c0​=0.8) to show directly whether the DC term is present. documents.s: Step 5: why waveform symmetry determines c0c_0c0​

documents.t: In practice two tricks are commonly used to approach symmetry and suppress c0c_0c0​: Differential: use a pair of complementary nodes to cancel even harmonics and common-mode error, improving symmetry. Complementary (complementary CMOS, symmetric PMOS/NMOS arrangement): deliberately match pull-up/pull-down so that rise/fall times are equal → rise/fall symmetry → small c0c_0c0​. [P2] (the ring-oscillator paper) confirms this rule directly by experiment: phase noise varies with the "symmetry control voltage" and reaches a minimum at the symmetry point, and the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner drops sharply at the symmetry point ([P2] Fig. 17, p.802; corresponds to claim C4). Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Title reads: "Flicker upconversion: ISF 對稱性 (c0) 決定 close-in 1/f³" = Flicker upconversion: the ISF's symmetry (c0) determines the close-in 1/f³ term. Limits (honesty note) — [P2] makes the following three points in Sec. VII Design Implications (p.798, original text); the "more linear loads" point below is also independently made by [P1] (Sec. IV, p.189) — see below. Differential symmetry is not necessarily enough: [P2] states plainly that "differential symmetry is insufficient"; what is needed is rise/fall symmetry within each half period, not merely symmetry between the two differential branches. The tail / bias source is a major leak: the ISF of the tail current source often has a large DC value, strongly upconverting the tail's flicker, which frequently dominates close-in noise. Symmetrizing the main signal path does not help — the tail must be handled separately. More linear loads help: [P2]'s own text (p.798) states, in its own words, that using more linear loads (e.g. resistors or linearized MOS devices) reduces 1/f noise upconversion and substrate/supply coupling (citing [20] Maneatis & Horowitz 1993). [P1] (Sec. IV, p.189) independently traces this back to prior observations in the context of supply-noise rejection — [15] Maneatis 1993 and [16] Yang/Farjad-Rad/Horowitz 1997 (more linear loads reduce the effect of supply noise on timing jitter) — and then adds a new point on top of that: the same measure also makes the waveform more symmetric and lowers the corner for low-frequency-noise upconversion into phase noise. In short, both papers independently arrive at — and corroborate — the same design recommendation; it is not unique to either one. Even so, symmetry only suppresses flicker (1/f31/f^31/f3); it does not change the white-noise 1/f21/f^21/f2 region (that region is set by Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, not c0c_0c0​). Do not expect symmetry to rescue the whole curve.

Symmetric (c0=0.04c_0=0.04c0​=0.04, c02=1.6×10−3c_0^2=1.6\times10^{-3}c02​=1.6×10−3): f1/f3f1/f=1.6×10−30.5=3.2×10−3 ⇒ f1/f3=3.2×10−3×1 MHz=3.2 kHz.\frac{f_{1/f^3}}{f_{1/f}}=\frac{1.6\times10^{-3}}{0.5}=3.2\times10^{-3}\;\Rightarrow\;f_{1/f^3}=3.2\times10^{-3}\times1\,\text{MHz}=3.2\ \text{kHz}.f1/f​f1/f3​​=0.51.6×10−3​=3.2×10−3⇒f1/f3​=3.2×10−3×1MHz=3.2 kHz. Feel for it: the device 1/f1/f1/f corner is 1 MHz in both cases, but the phase-noise 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner drops from 320 kHz (asymmetric) to 3.2 kHz (symmetric) — a full 100× lower (because c02c_0^2c02​ differs by 100×). documents.t: lab_07 feeds flicker current into a symmetric (cos⁡\coscos, c0=0c_0=0c0​=0) and an asymmetric (cos⁡+0.5\cos+0.5cos+0.5) toy ISF and estimates the close-in phase PSD: the symmetric case shows almost no 1/f31/f^31/f3, while the asymmetric case shows a clear −30-30−30 dB/decade skirt. For a visualization of c0c_0c0​ see lab_05's symmetric_vs_asymmetric_isf_c0.png (table above). Core Python (full script: simulations/lab_07_flicker_noise.py; site convention: the alpha parameter of gamma_asymmetric below is the DC offset of the toy ISF Γ=cos⁡θ+α\Gamma=\cos\theta+\alphaΓ=cosθ+α (c0=2αc_0=2\alphac0​=2α), unrelated to [P1]'s NMF α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0t)α(ω0​t)): import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import flicker_noise, estimate_psd from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_symmetric, gamma_asymmetric fs, n, qmax = 256.0, 2**20, 1.0 t = np.arange(n) / fs theta = 2 * np.pi * 1.0 * t # f0 = 1 (toy normalized frequency) i_f = flicker_noise(n, fs, k_flicker=1e-4) # 1/f current # ISF weighting + integrator: phi = cumsum(Gamma * i_n / qmax) / fs def phase_from_isf(i_n, gamma_vals, q_max, fs): g = gamma_vals * i_n / q_max return np.cumsum(g) / fs gamma_sym = gamma_symmetric(theta) # c0 = 0 gamma_asym = gamma_asymmetric(theta, alpha=0.5) # c0 = 2*alpha = 1.0 (DC = 0.5) phi_sym = phase_from_isf(i_f, gamma_sym, qmax, fs) # symmetric -> close-in nearly flat phi_asym = phase_from_isf(i_f, gamma_asym, qmax, fs) # asymmetric -> 1/f^3 skirt

Step 1 (new ratio): c022Γrms2=0.0422×0.52=1.6×10−30.5=3.2×10−3\dfrac{c_0^2}{2\Gamma_{rms}^2}=\dfrac{0.04^2}{2\times0.5^2}=\dfrac{1.6\times10^{-3}}{0.5}=3.2\times10^{-3}2Γrms2​c02​​=2×0.520.042​=0.51.6×10−3​=3.2×10−3. How symmetry pushes it down (the point of this problem): corner ∝c02\propto c_0^2∝c02​, and c0/2c_0/2c0​/2 is the ISF's average over one period (the DC value). Make the waveform's rise/fall symmetric, and the ISF's positive and negative swings in the sensitive region cancel → c0c_0c0​ approaches 0 → the corner collapses at a quadratic rate. documents.t: Flicker is the device's low-frequency noise (∝1/f\propto1/f∝1/f); it must be "upconverted" to appear near the carrier. Only the ISF's DC term c0c_0c0​ can upconvert flicker → close-in becomes −30-30−30 dB/decade 1/f31/f^31/f3 (Eq.23). 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner =ω1/f⋅c02/(2Γrms2)≠=\omega_{1/f}\cdot c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)\ne=ω1/f​⋅c02​/(2Γrms2​)= device 1/f1/f1/f corner (Eq.24); a symmetric waveform (small c0c_0c0​) pushes the corner far below the device corner. Waveform rise/fall symmetry ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ ISF average (c0/2c_0/2c0​/2) ≈0\approx0≈0 ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ 1/f31/f^31/f3 drops dramatically. Differential/complementary designs help symmetry, but differential symmetry alone is not enough, the tail source's large c0c_0c0​ is a leak, and symmetry does not improve the white-noise 1/f21/f^21/f2 region. Numbers: with a 1 MHz device corner and canonical Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, moving c0c_0c0​ from 0.4→0.04 takes the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner from 320 kHz→3.2 kHz (a factor of 100).

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: white_noise_to_phase_noise | Next: rms_isf Hands-on verification: the Fourier-coefficient extraction, reconstruction, and Parseval numerical checks for this page are in lab_05. The previous chapter impulse_to_phase_shift derived the operational definition of the ISF, Δϕ=Γ(ω0τ) Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=Γ(ω0​τ)Δq/qmax​, and pointed out that Γ\GammaΓ is a dimensionless, 2π2\pi2π-periodic function. This page answers the next key question: Given that Γ\GammaΓ is periodic, once it is expanded as a Fourier series, what physics does each term represent? The answer is the most elegant piece of ISF theory — it spells out exactly which band of device noise the oscillator moves to the vicinity of the carrier. The core result ([P1] Eq.(12), p.183): Γ(ω0τ)=c02+∑n=1∞cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=\frac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)Γ(ω0​τ)=2c0​​+n=1∑∞​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​) Physical intuition (conclusion first): an oscillator is a time-varying mixer. Its phase sensitivity to noise, Γ\GammaΓ, varies periodically with the waveform phase — equivalent to multiplying the noise by a "periodic weight" with fundamental ω0\omega_0ω0​. Multiplying noise by a periodic function is, mathematically, shifting the noise spectrum to 0, ω0, 2ω0,…0,\ \omega_0,\ 2\omega_0,\dots0, ω0​, 2ω0​,… and summing. So device noise near each nω0n\omega_0nω0​ is weighted by the nnn-th Fourier coefficient cnc_ncn​ and then down-converted to the carrier vicinity as phase noise. The c0c_0c0​ (DC) term is especially important: it moves the 1/f flicker noise near DC straight up, producing the close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3 phase noise.
documents.s: Fourier Series of the ISF

documents.t: Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) describes "how far the phase is pushed by a kick at a given point of the waveform". The oscillator sits in periodic steady state (the output waveform repeats every T=1/f0T=1/f_0T=1/f0​), so "kicking at phase xxx" and "kicking at phase x+2πx+2\pix+2π" have exactly the same effect. In other words Γ\GammaΓ is 2π2\pi2π-periodic in its argument x≡ω0τx\equiv\omega_0\taux≡ω0​τ: Γ(x+2π)=Γ(x).\Gamma(x+2\pi)=\Gamma(x).Γ(x+2π)=Γ(x). Math used: any 2π2\pi2π-periodic function that is square-integrable over one period (∫02π∣Γ∣2dx<∞\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma|^2dx<\infty∫02π​∣Γ∣2dx<∞) admits a Fourier series (Dirichlet conditions). Real ISFs are continuous and piecewise smooth, so the conditions are easily satisfied. Physical basis: the periodicity comes from the oscillator's limit cycle — in steady state the state point goes around the cycle once per period, and the sensitivity depends only on the "position on the cycle (phase)", not on "which lap". Unit check: x=ω0τx=\omega_0\taux=ω0​τ is [rad/s]⋅[s]=[rad][\text{rad/s}]\cdot[\text{s}]=[\text{rad}][rad/s]⋅[s]=[rad] ✓, dimensionless; Γ\GammaΓ itself is dimensionless, and so are c0,cnc_0,c_nc0​,cn​ (see notation).
documents.s: Step 1: why Γ\GammaΓ can be expanded as a Fourier series

documents.t: First write the familiar real cos/sin Fourier series, then merge it into the amplitude–phase form of [P1]. For a 2π2\pi2π-periodic function: Γ(x)=a02+∑n=1∞[ancos⁡(nx)+bnsin⁡(nx)],\Gamma(x)=\frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big[a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big],Γ(x)=2a0​​+n=1∑∞​[an​cos(nx)+bn​sin(nx)], with the coefficients obtained by inner products (projections) over one period: a0=1π∫02πΓ(x) dx,an=1π∫02πΓ(x)cos⁡(nx) dx,bn=1π∫02πΓ(x)sin⁡(nx) dx.a_0=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma(x)\,dx,\qquad a_n=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma(x)\cos(nx)\,dx,\qquad b_n=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma(x)\sin(nx)\,dx.a0​=π1​∫02π​Γ(x)dx,an​=π1​∫02π​Γ(x)cos(nx)dx,bn​=π1​∫02π​Γ(x)sin(nx)dx. Math used: {cos⁡(nx),sin⁡(nx)}\{\cos(nx),\sin(nx)\}{cos(nx),sin(nx)} are orthogonal on [0,2π][0,2\pi][0,2π], ∫02πcos⁡(mx)cos⁡(nx) dx=π δmn\int_0^{2\pi}\cos(mx)\cos(nx)\,dx=\pi\,\delta_{mn}∫02π​cos(mx)cos(nx)dx=πδmn​ (m,n≥1m,n\ge1m,n≥1); this orthogonality "sifts" out the corresponding component. Watch the 1/π1/\pi1/π and the DC factor: a0=1π∫02πΓ dxa_0=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma\,dxa0​=π1​∫02π​Γdx, while the mean (DC value) of Γ\GammaΓ is 12π∫02πΓ dx=a02\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma\,dx=\frac{a_0}{2}2π1​∫02π​Γdx=2a0​​. So the first term of the series must be written a02\frac{a_0}{2}2a0​​ to equal the true mean. This 1/21/21/2 is not arbitrary; the definition of c0c_0c0​ below inherits it.

documents.t: Combine the same-frequency pair ancos⁡(nx)+bnsin⁡(nx)a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)an​cos(nx)+bn​sin(nx) into a single cosine via the trig identity: ancos⁡(nx)+bnsin⁡(nx)=cncos⁡(nx+θn),a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)=c_n\cos(nx+\theta_n),an​cos(nx)+bn​sin(nx)=cn​cos(nx+θn​), where cn=an2+bn2,θn=atan2⁡(−bn, an).c_n=\sqrt{a_n^2+b_n^2},\qquad \theta_n=\operatorname{atan2}(-b_n,\,a_n).cn​=an2​+bn2​​,θn​=atan2(−bn​,an​). Math used: cncos⁡(nx+θn)=cncos⁡θncos⁡(nx)−cnsin⁡θnsin⁡(nx)c_n\cos(nx+\theta_n)=c_n\cos\theta_n\cos(nx)-c_n\sin\theta_n\sin(nx)cn​cos(nx+θn​)=cn​cosθn​cos(nx)−cn​sinθn​sin(nx); matching coefficients gives an=cncos⁡θna_n=c_n\cos\theta_nan​=cn​cosθn​, bn=−cnsin⁡θnb_n=-c_n\sin\theta_nbn​=−cn​sinθn​; inverting yields the expressions above. DC correspondence: set c0≡a0c_0\equiv a_0c0​≡a0​ (the DC coefficient), so the constant term a02=c02\frac{a_0}{2}=\frac{c_0}{2}2a0​​=2c0​​. Substituting gives [P1] Eq.(12): Γ(ω0τ)=c02+∑n=1∞cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn) [P1] Eq.(12), p.183\boxed{\ \Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=\frac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\ }\qquad[\text{P1] Eq.(12), p.183} Γ(ω0​τ)=2c0​​+n=1∑∞​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​) ​[P1] Eq.(12), p.183 Notation trap (important): c0c_0c0​ is the Fourier coefficient, while the DC value of the ISF is c0/2c_0/2c0​/2. This factor is the easiest place to slip when computing the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner (Eq.(24)); later chapters will keep reminding you. The a0 returned by this site's Python compute_fourier_coefficients equals this c0c_0c0​ (see Step 8).

documents.t: Substitute the Fourier expansion of the ISF back into the LTV phase response ([P1] Eq.(11)→Eq.(13), p.183): ϕ(t)=1qmax ⁣[c02 ⁣∫−∞t ⁣in dτ+∑n=1∞cn ⁣∫−∞t ⁣incos⁡(nω0τ+θn) dτ][P1] Eq.(13), p.183\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\!\left[\frac{c_0}{2}\!\int_{-\infty}^{t}\!i_n\,d\tau+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\!\int_{-\infty}^{t}\!i_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\,d\tau\right]\qquad[\text{P1] Eq.(13), p.183}ϕ(t)=qmax​1​[2c0​​∫−∞t​in​dτ+n=1∑∞​cn​∫−∞t​in​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)dτ][P1] Eq.(13), p.183 The first term (the c0c_0c0​ term) integrates the noise current directly, without any cos⁡(nω0τ)\cos(n\omega_0\tau)cos(nω0​τ) modulation. Meaning: The c0c_0c0​ term responds to the DC / very-low-frequency components of the noise current — push the node slowly and the phase drifts slowly. Inject a small tone near DC, i(t)=I0cos⁡(Δωt)i(t)=I_0\cos(\Delta\omega t)i(t)=I0​cos(Δωt) (Δω≪ω0\Delta\omega\ll\omega_0Δω≪ω0​): only the c0c_0c0​ term responds (the other harmonics are averaged out by cos⁡(nω0τ)\cos(n\omega_0\tau)cos(nω0​τ)), giving ([P1] Eq.(15), p.183): ϕ(t)≈I0 c0sin⁡(Δωt)2qmax Δω.\phi(t)\approx\frac{I_0\,c_0\sin(\Delta\omega t)}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}.ϕ(t)≈2qmax​ΔωI0​c0​sin(Δωt)​. Why this is called "1/f1/f1/f upconversion": device flicker / 1/f1/f1/f noise is concentrated at low frequency (near DC). The c0c_0c0​ term moves (up-converts) this "noise living at baseband" next to the carrier, turning it into close-in phase noise. Later, flicker_noise_upconversion uses this to derive the 1/f31/f^31/f3 skirt ([P1] Eq.(23),(24)). Design implication: the smaller c0c_0c0​, the weaker the flicker upconversion. With c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 (a perfectly symmetric waveform), close-in theoretically has no 1/f31/f^31/f3 contribution. This is the mathematical root of the "waveform symmetry → close-in phase noise" design rule (experimentally supported by [P2] Fig. 17, p.802).

documents.t: Look at the nnn-th component of the second term of Eq.(13): it multiplies the noise current by cos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)cos(nω0​τ+θn​) and then integrates. Multiplying by cos⁡(nω0τ)\cos(n\omega_0\tau)cos(nω0​τ) is, in the frequency domain, shifting the noise spectrum by ±nω0\pm n\omega_0±nω0​ (modulation theorem). So: Device noise near nω0+Δωn\omega_0+\Delta\omeganω0​+Δω (and nω0−Δωn\omega_0-\Delta\omeganω0​−Δω) is weighted by cnc_ncn​ and down-converted to Δω\Delta\omegaΔω, becoming the phase noise at offset Δω\Delta\omegaΔω from the carrier. Inject a small tone near nω0n\omega_0nω0​, i(t)=I0cos⁡((nω0+Δω)t)i(t)=I_0\cos((n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)t)i(t)=I0​cos((nω0​+Δω)t), into Eq.(13): only the nnn-th harmonic responds, giving ([P1] Eq.(16)/(17), p.183): ϕ(t)≈I0 cnsin⁡(Δωt)2qmax Δω.\phi(t)\approx\frac{I_0\,c_n\sin(\Delta\omega t)}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}.ϕ(t)≈2qmax​ΔωI0​cn​sin(Δωt)​. Explicit algebra: using cos⁡Acos⁡B\cos A\cos BcosAcosB to move noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ to the carrier​ The line above is the "result"; now we work the frequency-translation algebra out in full, not just the intuition. Take the nnn-th component of the second term of Eq.(13) and substitute the single tone in(τ)=I0cos⁡((nω0+Δω)τ)i_n(\tau)=I_0\cos((n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau)in​(τ)=I0​cos((nω0​+Δω)τ): ϕn(t)=cnqmax∫−∞tcos⁡(nω0τ+θn) I0cos⁡((nω0+Δω)τ) dτ.\phi_n(t)=\frac{c_n}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\,I_0\cos\big((n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau\big)\,d\tau .ϕn​(t)=qmax​cn​​∫−∞t​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)I0​cos((nω0​+Δω)τ)dτ. Step (i): product-to-sum. The product of the two cosines uses the identity cos⁡Acos⁡B=12[cos⁡(A−B)+cos⁡(A+B)],\cos A\cos B=\tfrac12\big[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)\big],cosAcosB=21​[cos(A−B)+cos(A+B)], with A=nω0τ+θnA=n\omega_0\tau+\theta_nA=nω0​τ+θn​, B=(nω0+Δω)τB=(n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tauB=(nω0​+Δω)τ; compute the difference and sum frequencies: A−B=θn−Δωτ(frequency≈Δω),A+B=(2nω0+Δω)τ+θn(frequency≈2nω0).A-B=\theta_n-\Delta\omega\tau\quad(\text{frequency}\approx\Delta\omega),\qquad A+B=(2n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau+\theta_n\quad(\text{frequency}\approx 2n\omega_0).A−B=θn​−Δωτ(frequency≈Δω),A+B=(2nω0​+Δω)τ+θn​(frequency≈2nω0​). The integrand becomes two terms: cos⁡(nω0τ+θn)cos⁡((nω0+Δω)τ)=12[cos⁡(Δωτ−θn)+cos⁡((2nω0+Δω)τ+θn)].\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\cos\big((n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau\big)=\tfrac12\Big[\cos(\Delta\omega\tau-\theta_n)+\cos\big((2n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau+\theta_n\big)\Big].cos(nω0​τ+θn​)cos((nω0​+Δω)τ)=21​[cos(Δωτ−θn​)+cos((2nω0​+Δω)τ+θn​)]. This line is the core of "frequency translation": noise that originally lived at nω0+Δωn\omega_0+\Delta\omeganω0​+Δω, once multiplied by cos⁡(nω0τ)\cos(n\omega_0\tau)cos(nω0​τ), has its difference frequency collapse down to Δω\Delta\omegaΔω at baseband (moved down), while its sum frequency is pushed to 2nω02n\omega_02nω0​ (higher, useless). Step (ii): the integrator amplifies only the slow term and averages out the fast one. ∫tdτ\int^t d\tau∫tdτ is a low-pass: ∫tcos⁡(Δωτ−θn) dτ=sin⁡(Δωt−θn)Δω (slow; small denominator⇒amplified, survives),\int^{t}\cos(\Delta\omega\tau-\theta_n)\,d\tau=\frac{\sin(\Delta\omega t-\theta_n)}{\Delta\omega}\ (\text{slow; small denominator}\Rightarrow\text{amplified, survives}),∫tcos(Δωτ−θn​)dτ=Δωsin(Δωt−θn​)​ (slow; small denominator⇒amplified, survives),∫tcos⁡((2nω0+Δω)τ+θn) dτ=sin⁡(⋯ )2nω0+Δω (fast; denominator≈2nω0⇒suppressed to negligible).\int^{t}\cos\big((2n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau+\theta_n\big)\,d\tau=\frac{\sin(\cdots)}{2n\omega_0+\Delta\omega}\ (\text{fast; denominator}\approx2n\omega_0\Rightarrow\text{suppressed to negligible}).∫tcos((2nω0​+Δω)τ+θn​)dτ=2nω0​+Δωsin(⋯)​ (fast; denominator≈2nω0​⇒suppressed to negligible). Step (iii): keep only the slow term. ϕn(t)≈cnqmax⋅I02⋅sin⁡(Δωt−θn)Δω=I0 cnsin⁡(Δωt−θn)2qmax Δω,\phi_n(t)\approx\frac{c_n}{q_{max}}\cdot\frac{I_0}{2}\cdot\frac{\sin(\Delta\omega t-\theta_n)}{\Delta\omega}=\frac{I_0\,c_n\sin(\Delta\omega t-\theta_n)}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega},ϕn​(t)≈qmax​cn​​⋅2I0​​⋅Δωsin(Δωt−θn​)​=2qmax​ΔωI0​cn​sin(Δωt−θn​)​, Absorbing the fixed phase θn\theta_nθn​ into the origin recovers Eq.(16/17). Conclusion: the nnn-th Fourier coefficient cnc_ncn​ really does take the noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​, "multiply it by 12cn\tfrac12 c_n21​cn​ and collapse it to Δω\Delta\omegaΔω" — this is the algebraic proof of frequency translation, matching the mixer picture below. (The same downconversion integral is used again in white_noise_to_phase_noise to accumulate the 1/f21/f^21/f2 summation.) This is exactly the picture of [P1] Fig. 8 (p.183): noise is spread across the bands at 0,ω0,2ω0,…0,\omega_0,2\omega_0,\dots0,ω0​,2ω0​,…; the ISF's c0,c1,c2,…c_0,c_1,c_2,\dotsc0​,c1​,c2​,… act like a bank of mixer gains, each folding its band's noise back to the carrier vicinity, all superposing into the final phase-noise sideband. Unit/dimension check: in Eq.(15)/(16) the dimensions of I0 cn2qmax Δω\dfrac{I_0\,c_n}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}2qmax​ΔωI0​cn​​ are [A]⋅(dimensionless)[C]⋅[rad/s]=[A][C/s]⋅[rad]=[A][A]⋅1[rad]−1\dfrac{[\text{A}]\cdot(\text{dimensionless})}{[\text{C}]\cdot[\text{rad/s}]} =\dfrac{[\text{A}]}{[\text{C/s}]\cdot[\text{rad}]}=\dfrac{[\text{A}]}{[\text{A}]}\cdot\dfrac{1}{[\text{rad}]^{-1}}[C]⋅[rad/s][A]⋅(dimensionless)​=[C/s]⋅[rad][A]​=[A][A]​⋅[rad]−11​ — after simplification ϕ\phiϕ is rad (dimensionless), and sin⁡(Δωt)\sin(\Delta\omega t)sin(Δωt) is dimensionless ✓. (Remember C=A⋅sC=\text{A}\cdot\text{s}C=A⋅s.)

documents.t: Put the two steps above together into one "frequency map": Where the device noise lives Via which coefficient What it becomes next to the carrier 1/f1/f1/f flicker near DC c0/2c_0/2c0​/2 close-in, slope 1/f31/f^31/f3 (very steep) White noise near ω0\omega_0ω0​ c1c_1c1​ 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt (−20-20−20 dB/dec) White noise at 2ω0,3ω0,…2\omega_0,3\omega_0,\dots2ω0​,3ω0​,… c2,c3,…c_2,c_3,\dotsc2​,c3​,… also folds back, merged into 1/f21/f^21/f2 (counted via ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​) Why flicker becomes 1/f31/f^31/f3 through c0c_0c0​: flicker is already 1/f1/f1/f (power spectrum ∝1/Δω\propto1/\Delta\omega∝1/Δω). The c0c_0c0​ term moves it intact next to the carrier; the phase integrator (the ∫dτ\int d\tau∫dτ in Eq.(13)) then adds another 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 (integration divides by (jΔω)(j\Delta\omega)(jΔω) in frequency, i.e. by Δω2\Delta\omega^2Δω2 in power), 1Δω×1Δω2=1Δω3\dfrac{1}{\Delta\omega}\times\dfrac{1}{\Delta\omega^2}=\dfrac{1}{\Delta\omega^3}Δω1​×Δω21​=Δω31​ → 1/f31/f^31/f3. Why the higher-order cnc_ncn​ mainly feed 1/f21/f^21/f2: white noise is flat — flat wherever it is moved — and the integrator only adds 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 → 1/f21/f^21/f2. All harmonic contributions are summarized by a single number, ∑n=0∞cn2\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n^2∑n=0∞​cn2​, which is exactly the Parseval relation and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ of the next page rms_isf. The full 1/f31/f^31/f3 / 1/f21/f^21/f2 derivations are in flicker_noise_upconversion and white_noise_to_phase_noise respectively.

The parity of the Fourier coefficients follows directly from the symmetry of Γ(x)\Gamma(x)Γ(x), giving the designer a knob to "switch off certain upconversions via the waveform shape": Symmetry of Γ\GammaΓ Mathematical result Physical consequence Even function Γ(−x)=Γ(x)\Gamma(-x)=\Gamma(x)Γ(−x)=Γ(x) all bn=0b_n=0bn​=0 (pure cos) θn∈{0,π}	heta_n\in\{0,\pi\}θn​∈{0,π}, simple phases Odd function Γ(−x)=−Γ(x)\Gamma(-x)=-\Gamma(x)Γ(−x)=−Γ(x) all an=0a_n=0an​=0 and a0=0a_0=0a0​=0 ⟹ c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 no 1/f1/f1/f upconversion (the ideal-LC −sin⁡-\sin−sin is of this type) Half-wave symmetry Γ(x+π)=−Γ(x)\Gamma(x+\pi)=-\Gamma(x)Γ(x+π)=−Γ(x) even harmonics c2=c4=⋯=0c_2=c_4=\dots=0c2​=c4​=⋯=0 noise near 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ does not fold back DC offset cos⁡θ+α\cos	heta+\alphacosθ+α (toy gamma_asymmetric) c0=2α≠0c_0=2\alpha
eq0c0​=2α=0 1/f31/f^31/f3 appears (close-in degrades) Site convention: here α\alphaα is the DC offset of the toy ISF Γ=cos⁡θ+α\Gamma=\cos	heta+\alphaΓ=cosθ+α (c0=2αc_0=2\alphac0​=2α), unrelated to [P1]'s NMF α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0t)α(ω0​t) (the cyclostationary noise modulation function; see effective_isf). Example (ideal LC): ΓLC(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma_{LC}(	heta)=-\sin	hetaΓLC​(θ)=−sinθ is odd ⟹ c0=0c_0=0c0​=0. So the ideal LC has, to first order, no flicker upconversion; it is real-world asymmetry (hard switching, bias asymmetry) that props c0c_0c0​ up. Example (half-wave symmetry): differential / push-pull structures make the rising and falling edges mirror images ⟹ Γ(x+π)=−Γ(x)\Gamma(x+\pi)=-\Gamma(x)Γ(x+π)=−Γ(x) ⟹ the even harmonics are suppressed, and noise at 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ (often supply ripple and second-harmonic distortion) does not fold back to the carrier. Note (mechanism of the toy model): the gamma_asymmetric in the table props c0c_0c0​ up in the simplest possible way — adding a DC offset to the whole ISF (cos⁡θ+α\cos	heta+\alphacosθ+α); in real circuits, asymmetric rise/fall transition slopes are a different — and more common — mechanism that likewise makes c0≠0c_0

documents.t: Beyond the theory, here is code that runs. This site's compute_fourier_coefficients (read from simulations/common/isf_utils.py) simply carries out the Step-2 integrals with the trapezoidal rule: import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import ( gamma_lc_ideal, gamma_asymmetric, compute_fourier_coefficients, reconstruct_from_fourier, gamma_rms, ) # theta must span exactly one period [0, 2*pi] (endpoint included) for the trapezoidal rule to give the correct (1/pi)*∫ value theta = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 4096, endpoint=True) # Ideal LC ISF: Gamma(theta) = -sin(theta) (odd function) gamma = gamma_lc_ideal(theta) # a0 is c0 in Hajimiri's notation; a,b are the cos/sin coefficients; c_n = sqrt(a_n^2+b_n^2) a0, a, b, c, phase = compute_fourier_coefficients(theta, gamma, n_harmonics=8) print("c0 =", a0) # -> ~0.0 (odd function: no DC, no 1/f upconversion) print("c1 =", c[1]) # -> ~1.0 (fundamental component only) print("c2..c8 =", c[2:]) # -> ~0 (pure single tone) # Reconstruct the waveform to verify the Eq.(12) reconstruction gamma_hat = reconstruct_from_fourier(theta, a0, a, b) print("max reconstruction error =", np.max(np.abs(gamma_hat - gamma))) # -> ~1e-15 Why the trapezoidal rule suffices: the integrand is a smooth periodic function, and the trapezoidal rule converges exponentially for periodic functions (the endpoint errors cancel); a few thousand points reach machine precision. The endpoints must include 2π2\pi2π: the function docstring states explicitly that theta must span [0, 2*pi] (endpoint included), otherwise 1π∫\frac{1}{\pi}\intπ1​∫ misses one cell. This is the most common source of numerical off-by-one errors. Asymmetric toy-model comparison: plug in gamma = gamma_asymmetric(theta, alpha=0.3) (i.e. cos⁡θ+0.3\cos\theta+0.3cosθ+0.3) and you get c0≈2α=0.6c_0\approx2\alpha=0.6c0​≈2α=0.6, c1≈1c_1\approx1c1​≈1, and the rest ≈0\approx0≈0 — confirming that α\alphaα is exactly the knob that "props up the DC and turns on 1/f1/f1/f upconversion" (this is a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level).

documents.t: The figure below (fig_reconstruction from lab_05) takes a multi-harmonic toy ISF (Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ+0.35sin⁡2θ+0.18cos⁡3θ+0.25\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\theta+0.35\sin2\theta+0.18\cos3\theta+0.25Γ(θ)=−sinθ+0.35sin2θ+0.18cos3θ+0.25) and reconstructs it with N=1,2,4N=1,2,4N=1,2,4 terms, showing how the partial sums of Eq.(12) converge step by step to the original waveform. Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Title reads: "ISF Fourier reconstruction (越多 harmonic 越接近)" = ISF Fourier reconstruction (more harmonics → closer to the original). Corresponding formula: [P1] Eq.(12) (partial sum ΓN=c02+∑n=1Ncncos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\Gamma_N=\frac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)ΓN​=2c0​​+∑n=1N​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)). How to read it: N=1N=1N=1 captures only the fundamental and has the largest error; by N=4N=4N=4 the curves almost coincide. In practice the ISF's energy concentrates in the low-order harmonics, so a handful of terms is enough to compute phase noise accurately. Toy-model note: this ISF is a synthetic teaching waveform, not a transistor-level extraction. Full script: simulations/lab_05_fourier_isf.py.

documents.t: The figure below (fig_coefficients from lab_05, n_harmonics=8) plots cnc_ncn​ as a bar chart (the coefficient spectrum) and marks the Parseval check ∑n=0∞cn2=2Γrms2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑n=0∞​cn2​=2Γrms2​ ([P1] Eq.(20), derived in detail on the next page). Corresponding formulas: the cnc_ncn​ of [P1] Eq.(12); the ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ of [P1] Eq.(20). How to read it: each bar's height is that harmonic's "weight" in the phase noise. The c0c_0c0​ bar is critical — as soon as it is nonzero, close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3 appears. The low-order bars dominate; the high orders decay quickly. The detailed Parseval derivation and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ are in rms_isf.

documents.t: The figure below (fig_symmetric_vs_asymmetric from lab_05) contrasts two toy ISFs: the symmetric Γ=cos⁡θ\Gamma=\cos\thetaΓ=cosθ (c0=0c_0=0c0​=0) and the asymmetric Γ=cos⁡θ+0.4\Gamma=\cos\theta+0.4Γ=cosθ+0.4 (c0=0.8c_0=0.8c0​=0.8), highlighting that only c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0 upconverts 1/f1/f1/f noise. Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Title reads: "c0≠0 才會把 1/f noise upconvert 到 close-in phase noise" = only c0≠0 upconverts 1/f noise into close-in phase noise. Corresponding formulas: c0c_0c0​ ([P1] Eq.(12)); its consequence, the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner of [P1] Eq.(24). How to read it: on the left, the symmetric waveform has zero mean and the DC bar disappears → no 1/f31/f^31/f3; on the right, the whole curve is lifted and the DC bar pops out → close-in noise degrades. In design terms, "making the waveform symmetric" means "flattening this DC bar". Toy-model note: gamma_symmetric/gamma_asymmetric are pedagogical toy ISFs, not transistor-level (see the isf_utils.py docstring). Design-side extension: symmetry.

documents.t: Take the ideal-LC Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ and hand-compute the first few coefficients. View −sin⁡x-\sin x−sinx as a Fourier expansion of itself: −sin⁡x=c1cos⁡(x+θ1)-\sin x=c_1\cos(x+\theta_1)−sinx=c1​cos(x+θ1​), where cos⁡(x+θ1)=cos⁡xcos⁡θ1−sin⁡xsin⁡θ1\cos(x+\theta_1)=\cos x\cos\theta_1-\sin x\sin\theta_1cos(x+θ1​)=cosxcosθ1​−sinxsinθ1​; for this to equal −sin⁡x-\sin x−sinx requires θ1=π/2\theta_1=\pi/2θ1​=π/2 (then cos⁡(x+π/2)=−sin⁡x\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin xcos(x+π/2)=−sinx), hence c1=1c_1=1c1​=1, θ1=π/2\theta_1=\pi/2θ1​=π/2. c0=1π∫02π(−sin⁡x) dx=0c_0=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}(-\sin x)\,dx=0c0​=π1​∫02π​(−sinx)dx=0 (odd function, zero DC). c1=1c_1=1c1​=1, cn=0c_n=0cn​=0 (n≥2n\ge2n≥2). Feel: the ideal-LC ISF is a "clean single fundamental" — all the energy sits in c1c_1c1​. So it folds noise back mainly from near ω0\omega_0ω0​ (1/f21/f^21/f2), and since c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 there is, ideally, no 1/f31/f^31/f3. The next page shows ∑cn2=c12=1=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=c_1^2=1=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=c12​=1=2Γrms2​ ⟹ Γrms=1/2≈0.707\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt{2}\approx0.707Γrms​=1/2​≈0.707.

documents.t: Two problems in the strict format: problem → step-by-step substitution (with units) → result → dimension check → one-line Python verification. Problem 1 hand-computes c0,c1,c2c_0,c_1,c_2c0​,c1​,c2​ and cross-checks with compute_fourier_coefficients; Problem 2 computes one harmonic's contribution to the phase noise. documents.t: Γ\GammaΓ is a 2π2\pi2π-periodic function, expandable as Γ=c02+∑n≥1cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\Gamma=\dfrac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)Γ=2c0​​+∑n≥1​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​) ([P1] Eq.(12), p.183). The oscillator acts like a time-varying mixer: the nnn-th coefficient cnc_ncn​ down-converts device noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ to the carrier ([P1] Eq.(16), Fig. 8). c0c_0c0​ (the DC coefficient; the DC value =c0/2=c_0/2=c0​/2) upconverts baseband flicker noise into close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3 ([P1] Eq.(15),(23),(24)). Waveform symmetry sets the parity of the coefficients: odd function ⟹ c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 (no 1/f1/f1/f upconversion); half-wave symmetry ⟹ even harmonics vanish. Ideal LC: c0=0, c1=1c_0=0,\ c_1=1c0​=0, c1​=1, the rest zero; Γrms=1/2≈0.707\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2\approx0.707Γrms​=1/2​≈0.707.
