documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: oscillator_phase (limit-cycle and phase/amplitude geometry), lti_vs_ltv (why an oscillator is LTV with respect to noise) | Up next: isf_definition (the rigorous ISF definition and the multi-node picture) → convolution_derivation (superposing arbitrary noise by convolution) This page answers a very concrete question: when a current impulse is injected into some node of an oscillator, by how much does the oscillator's phase shift? The answer is the operational definition at the heart of ISF theory: Δϕ=Γ(ω0τ)qmax Δq\Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta qΔϕ=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​Δq We will not simply memorize this line — we will derive it from the capacitor relation q=Cvq=Cvq=Cv, one step at a time, stating at every step which physics is invoked, which approximation is made, what the units are, and how to run the dimension check. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the noise current first becomes a packet of charge Δq\Delta qΔq on the node; that charge nudges the oscillator's instantaneous state slightly off its steady orbit; how much of that nudge turns into phase and how much into amplitude depends on at which phase of the waveform you deliver the kick — and that conversion ratio is precisely the ISF Γ\GammaΓ. Kick where the waveform slope is large and the phase gets pushed a lot; kick at the peak and you mostly perturb the amplitude.
documents.s: From Impulse to Phase Shift — the Derivation

documents.t: Current integrated over time is charge. A very narrow, very short current pulse i(t)i(t)i(t) injected into the node deposits a total charge Δq=∫i(t) dt.\Delta q=\int i(t)\,dt .Δq=∫i(t)dt. Physics used: charge conservation / the definition of current, i=dq/dti=dq/dti=dq/dt. Unit check: [A]⋅[s]=[C][\text{A}]\cdot[\text{s}]=[\text{C}][A]⋅[s]=[C] ✓ (amperes times seconds are coulombs). Why this is legitimate: when the pulse width is far smaller than the period TTT, the injection can be treated as dumping Δq\Delta qΔq onto the node "instantaneously".
documents.s: Step 1: the current impulse becomes charge

documents.t: The node carries a total capacitance CnodeC_{node}Cnode​. Charge appearing instantaneously makes the node voltage jump by a step ([P1] Eq.(9), p.181): ΔV=ΔqCnode.\Delta V=\frac{\Delta q}{C_{node}} .ΔV=Cnode​Δq​. Physics used: the capacitor relation q=Cvq=Cvq=Cv; differentiate for a small change, Δq=C ΔV\Delta q=C\,\Delta VΔq=CΔV. Unit check: [C]/[F]=[C]/[C/V]=[V][\text{C}]/[\text{F}]=[\text{C}]/[\text{C/V}]=[\text{V}][C]/[F]=[C]/[C/V]=[V] ✓. Key observation: in a parallel LC, a current impulse changes only the capacitor voltage (instantaneously); it cannot change the inductor current (an inductor current cannot jump). In state space, the perturbation is therefore a horizontal displacement along the voltage axis.
documents.s: Step 2: charge becomes a voltage step

documents.t: Draw the oscillator's state in a 2-D plane (say, horizontal axis = capacitor voltage vvv, vertical axis = www, proportional to the inductor current). In steady state, the state point circulates along the limit cycle. The voltage jump from Step 2 shoves the state point sideways: The radial component, pushing away from the cycle → changes the amplitude AAA. But the oscillator has an amplitude-restoring mechanism, so this part is slowly pulled back and leaves no permanent residue. The tangential component, along the cycle → changes the phase ϕ\phiϕ. Phase has no restoring force, so this part stays forever. The same ΔV\Delta VΔV, kicked at a different phase τ\tauτ, splits differently between tangential and radial. Collect the "ΔV\Delta VΔV-to-Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ conversion ratio" into a periodic function that depends only on the injection phase — that is the ISF: Δϕ=(phase-conversion ratio)⏟depends only on ω0τ×ΔV.\Delta\phi=\underbrace{\big(\text{phase-conversion ratio}\big)}_{\text{depends only on }\omega_0\tau}\times\Delta V .Δϕ=depends only on ω0​τ(phase-conversion ratio)​​×ΔV. The figure below draws this decomposition on the state plane. The same packet of charge produces a horizontal ΔV=Δq/C\Delta V=\Delta q/CΔV=Δq/C (the current kicks only the capacitor-voltage axis; the inductor current cannot jump), which the dashed lines split into a tangential component along the cycle (green — permanent phase) and a radial component off the cycle (red — decays). Injected near the zero crossing, the horizontal kick lands almost entirely on the tangent (the phase gets pushed a lot); injected near the peak, it lands almost entirely on the radius (only the amplitude changes). The lower-left corner of each panel prints the value of Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ — the tangential fraction is exactly Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ), which makes the ideal-LC Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ geometrically inevitable (the algebraic derivation of Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ is in isf_definition). Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Axis labels read: "state v (電容電壓, normalized)" = state v (capacitor voltage, normalized); "state w (∝ 電感電流, normalized)" = state w (∝ inductor current, normalized). Math used: project the perturbation vector onto the tangent direction (the phase direction) of the limit cycle. Why only the tangential part is kept: see phase_vs_amplitude_noise and oscillator_phase — amplitude is pulled back by the restoring mechanism; phase is not.
documents.s: Step 3: the voltage step pushes the state off the limit cycle — but only the tangential component becomes phase

documents.t: Chain Steps 1–3 together: Δϕ∝ΔV=Δq/Cnode\Delta\phi\propto\Delta V=\Delta q/C_{node}Δϕ∝ΔV=Δq/Cnode​. Hajimiri–Lee chose to normalize by the node's maximum charge swing qmax=CnodeVmaxq_{max}=C_{node}V_{max}qmax​=Cnode​Vmax​, writing that "phase-conversion ratio" as the dimensionless function Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) ([P1] Eq.(10)–(11), p.182): Δϕ=Γ(ω0τ)qmax Δq \boxed{\ \Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q\ } Δϕ=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​Δq ​ Why the qmaxq_{max}qmax​ normalization: it turns Γ\GammaΓ into a dimensionless, amplitude-independent "shape" that describes only where the waveform is sensitive. The actual magnitude of the phase shift is set by Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ (the injected charge relative to the signal charge). Why Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless: Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is in rad (dimensionless) and Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ is dimensionless, so Γ\GammaΓ must be dimensionless. Dimension check: [rad]=Γ⋅[C]/[C][\text{rad}]=\Gamma\cdot[\text{C}]/[\text{C}][rad]=Γ⋅[C]/[C] ⇒Γ\Rightarrow\Gamma⇒Γ dimensionless ✓. Small-signal assumption: Step 3 treats the projection as linear, which requires Δq≪qmax\Delta q\ll q_{max}Δq≪qmax​ (the kick must not knock the oscillator over). [P1] Fig. 6 confirms, on an actual Colpitts and a 5-stage ring, that Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is proportional to Δq\Delta qΔq for small charge.
documents.s: Step 4: normalize by qmaxq_{max}qmax​ to get the dimensionless ISF

documents.t: Because the phase step is retained forever, writing it as an impulse response brings along a unit step u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) ([P1] Eq.(10)): hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ).h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau).hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ). Note that it depends on the absolute injection instant τ\tauτ (through Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ)), not merely on t−τt-\taut−τ — the very signature of an LTV (linear time-variant) system. The next chapter, convolution_derivation, uses it to superpose an arbitrary noise current. The complete ISF definition and the multi-node discussion are in isf_definition.

Phase step: Δϕ=Γ Δqqmax=0.5×(1×10−15 C)1×10−12 C=5×10−4 rad.\Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma\,\Delta q}{q_{max}}=\frac{0.5\times(1\times10^{-15}\,\text{C})}{1\times10^{-12}\,\text{C}}=5\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}.Δϕ=qmax​ΓΔq​=1×10−12C0.5×(1×10−15C)​=5×10−4 rad. In degrees: Δϕ=5×10−4×180π≈0.0286∘\Delta\phi=5\times10^{-4}\times\dfrac{180}{\pi}\approx0.0286^\circΔϕ=5×10−4×π180​≈0.0286∘. Converted to a timing error (using Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0)\Delta t=\Delta\phi/(2\pi f_0)Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0​)): Δt=5×10−4 rad2π×5×109 Hz=5×10−43.1416×1010 s≈1.59×10−14 s=15.9 fs.\Delta t=\frac{5\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{9}\ \text{Hz}}=\frac{5\times10^{-4}}{3.1416\times10^{10}}\ \text{s}\approx1.59\times10^{-14}\ \text{s}=15.9\ \text{fs}.Δt=2π×5×109 Hz5×10−4 rad​=3.1416×10105×10−4​ s≈1.59×10−14 s=15.9 fs. Dimension check: [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] ✓ (note that 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ carries units of rad/s). Feel for the numbers: at 5 GHz (a 200 ps period), a single 1 fC packet of charge (about 6240 electrons) causes only ~16 fs of timing error even at the most sensitive phase. One kick is tiny — but the noise kicks continuously, and the integral accumulates (next chapter). Quick verification with the built-in functions: from simulations.common.isf_utils import impulse_to_phase_step from simulations.common.noise_utils import phase_to_time_error dphi = impulse_to_phase_step(delta_q=1e-15, gamma_value=0.5, qmax=1e-12) dt = phase_to_time_error(dphi, f0=5e9) print(dphi, "rad", dt*1e15, "fs") # -> 0.0005 rad 15.92 fs (Full scripts: simulations/common/isf_utils.py, simulations/common/noise_utils.py.)

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: impulse_to_phase_shift | Next: convolution_derivation This page answers a question that sounds simple and runs deep: what exactly is the ISF (Impulse Sensitivity Function)? It is a function — but what is its argument, what does its value represent, what are its units, why is it periodic, and why does every node and every noise source get one of its own? The ISF is the central object of Hajimiri–Lee's 1998 LTV (Linear Time-Variant) phase-noise theory. Its operational definition: inject a packet of charge Δq\Delta qΔq at waveform phase ω0τ\omega_0\tauω0​τ, and the resulting permanent phase shift Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is ([P1] from Eq.(10)-(11), p.182): Δϕ=Γ(ω0τ)qmax Δq\Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta qΔϕ=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​Δq Written as an impulse response, this is [P1] Eq.(10), p.182: hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau)hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ) Physical intuition (conclusion first): in steady state, the oscillator's state point travels round and round a closed trajectory (the limit cycle). Poke it with a finger (a current impulse) — the resulting displacement splits into a component tangential to the trajectory and a component radial, perpendicular to it. The tangential part changes how far along the loop the state has turned — that is, the phase — and because phase has no restoring force, this shift stays forever. The radial part changes the amplitude and gets slowly pulled back by the oscillator's amplitude-restoring mechanism, leaving no trace. Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) is exactly the sensitivity weight answering "poke one unit of charge at phase ω0τ\omega_0\tauω0​τ — how much becomes permanent phase?" It is not the noise itself; it is the conversion coefficient that translates noise into phase. Go ahead and poke it yourself — the animation below is the interactive version of that intuition: Interactive "kick the limit cycle and watch the phase" animation (ideal LC toy model) θ=0° (peak)θ=90°zero crossing (falling)θ=180° (trough)θ=270°zero crossing (rising) actual dot (perturbed)ghost (unperturbed reference)▲θ_inj injection pointΔV kick (along vertical voltage axis)tangential component / Δφ arc (permanent)radial component (amplitude, exponential relaxation) Injection phase θ_inj90 ° Charge ratio Δq/q_max0.15 Inject!PauseReset Click "Inject!" — a packet of charge Δq fires once the dot reaches θ_inj. Γ(θ_inj) = −sin(θ_inj) -1.000 dimensionless Δφ = Γ·Δq/q_max (this prediction) -0.1500 rad (-8.59°) Accumulated Δφ (dot − ghost) 0.0000 rad (0.00°) Model: the unit-circle limit cycle of an ideal LC (a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level). Δφ = Γ(θ_inj)·Δq/q_max, Γ(θ) = −sinθ (derived in Steps A–D on this page; [P1] Eqs.(10),(11), p.182). Negative Δφ = phase lag, positive Δφ = phase lead. The radial (amplitude) component is shown relaxing exponentially with time constant ≈ 0.55 cycles (≈ 2.6% remaining after 2 cycles); all three arrows share the same 1.6× visual magnification, so the decomposition geometry stays correct. How to drive it: after you press "Inject!", the animation waits until the dot on the orbit reaches the phase θinj\theta_{inj}θinj​ you selected with the slider, then fires a packet of charge Δq\Delta qΔq, draws the vertical ΔV\Delta VΔV kick arrow, and decomposes it into a tangential component (orange, permanent) and a radial component (gray, relaxing exponentially). Try injecting at θinj=0∘\theta_{inj}=0^\circθinj​=0∘ (the peak): the kick is almost purely radial — the dot is pushed off the cycle and pulled right back, barely separating from the pale ghost (the unperturbed reference), so Δϕ≈0\Delta\phi\approx0Δϕ≈0. Now try θinj=90∘\theta_{inj}=90^\circθinj​=90∘ (the zero crossing): the kick is almost purely tangential, and the dot falls permanently behind the ghost by Δϕ=−Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=-\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=−Δq/qmax​ (readout Γ=−sin⁡90∘=−1\Gamma=-\sin 90^\circ=-1Γ=−sin90∘=−1). Crank up Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ and press "Inject!" a few more times — the phase offsets never recover, and they accumulate. That is the entire intuition behind Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ and LTV behavior. The complete step-by-step charge→voltage→phase derivation lives in impulse_to_phase_shift. This page concentrates on what Γ\GammaΓ is and what properties Γ\GammaΓ has, and computes the ideal-LC Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ from the geometry by hand.

documents.t: Run quickly through the chain from the previous page, because the definition of Γ\GammaΓ stands on it: current impulse → charge: a very narrow current pulse deposits a charge Δq=∫i(t) dt\Delta q=\int i(t)\,dtΔq=∫i(t)dt. Units [A]⋅[s]=[C][\text{A}]\cdot[\text{s}]=[\text{C}][A]⋅[s]=[C] ✓. charge → voltage step: on the node capacitance CnodeC_{node}Cnode​ the voltage jumps instantaneously by ΔV=Δq/Cnode\Delta V=\Delta q/C_{node}ΔV=Δq/Cnode​ ([P1] Eq.(9), p.181). Units [C]/[F]=[V][\text{C}]/[\text{F}]=[\text{V}][C]/[F]=[V] ✓. voltage step → state perturbation: in an LC, a current impulse can only change the capacitor voltage instantaneously (the inductor current cannot jump), so the perturbation is a horizontal displacement along the voltage axis in state space. At this point the state has been nudged slightly off the limit cycle. The key question: how much of that displacement becomes phase?
documents.s: Step 1: from impulse to state perturbation (recap of the key physics)

documents.t: Draw the oscillator state as a 2-D vector z=(v,w)\mathbf{z}=(v,w)z=(v,w), where vvv is the capacitor voltage and www is proportional to the inductor current. The steady-state trajectory is a closed loop, and the state moves along it at angular rate ω0\omega_0ω0​. Define the phase on the loop, θ=ω0t\theta=\omega_0 tθ=ω0​t, as "the angle you have turned to". A small displacement along the voltage axis, Δz=(ΔV,0)\Delta\mathbf{z}=(\Delta V,0)Δz=(ΔV,0), strikes the loop at some point. Decompose this displacement at that point into the tangential direction (the phase direction, i.e. the direction of ∂z/∂θ\partial\mathbf{z}/\partial\theta∂z/∂θ) and the normal direction (the amplitude direction): Δz=(Δz⋅t^)⏟tangential→phaset^+(Δz⋅n^)⏟normal→amplitude (decays)n^.\Delta\mathbf{z}=\underbrace{(\Delta\mathbf{z}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{t}})}_{\text{tangential→phase}}\hat{\mathbf{t}}+\underbrace{(\Delta\mathbf{z}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}})}_{\text{normal→amplitude (decays)}}\hat{\mathbf{n}}.Δz=tangential→phase(Δz⋅t^)​​t^+normal→amplitude (decays)(Δz⋅n^)​​n^. Math used: project the perturbation vector onto the unit tangent t^\hat{\mathbf{t}}t^ of the limit cycle. This is the embryo of the rigorous machinery behind it — the PPV (perturbation projection vector) / Floquet theory (PPV/adjoint/Floquet are not in the five downloaded PDFs; they belong to Demir et al., external literature — see effective_isf). Why only the tangential part is kept: the normal component changes "how far from the loop" — the amplitude; a stable oscillation always has amplitude restoring that pulls it back (see phase_vs_amplitude_noise). The tangential component changes "the angle along the loop" — the phase; phase is the neutral direction with no restoring force, so the shift is retained permanently and accumulates (claim C2, [P1] Sec. III-A). Divide the tangential projection by "how much state displacement corresponds to one unit of phase along the loop", and ΔV\Delta VΔV converts into Δθ=Δϕ\Delta\theta=\Delta\phiΔθ=Δϕ. The entire conversion depends only on at which angle of the loop you strike — and that is why Γ\GammaΓ is a function of ω0τ\omega_0\tauω0​τ alone.
documents.s: Step 2: projection onto the phase direction

documents.t: Chain Steps 1–2 together: Δϕ∝ΔV=Δq/Cnode\Delta\phi\propto\Delta V=\Delta q/C_{node}Δϕ∝ΔV=Δq/Cnode​, with a proportionality coefficient that depends only on the injection phase. Hajimiri–Lee normalize by the node's maximum charge swing qmax=CnodeVmaxq_{max}=C_{node}V_{max}qmax​=Cnode​Vmax​ and define the dimensionless function Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ): Δϕ=Γ(ω0τ)qmax Δq \boxed{\ \Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q\ } Δϕ=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​Δq ​ Why Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless: Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is in rad (dimensionless) and Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ is a charge ratio (dimensionless), so Γ\GammaΓ must be dimensionless. Dimension check: [rad]=Γ⋅[C]/[C]⇒Γ[\text{rad}]=\Gamma\cdot[\text{C}]/[\text{C}]\Rightarrow\Gamma[rad]=Γ⋅[C]/[C]⇒Γ dimensionless ✓. Why normalize by qmaxq_{max}qmax​: it lets Γ\GammaΓ describe only the shape of "where the waveform is sensitive", decoupled from the absolute amplitude; the actual size of the phase shift is set by Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ (the injected charge relative to the signal charge). This also yields the design conclusion C3 directly: phase noise ∝Γrms2/qmax2\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2∝Γrms2​/qmax2​ — to push it down, "raise qmaxq_{max}qmax​, shrink Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​" ([P1] Eq.(21)).

documents.t: Property Statement Why Dimensionless carries no units guaranteed by the dimension check (above) 2π2\pi2π-periodic Γ(x+2π)=Γ(x)\Gamma(x+2\pi)=\Gamma(x)Γ(x+2π)=Γ(x) the argument is the "waveform phase", and the waveform itself is 2π2\pi2π-periodic Not the noise itself it is a "phase sensitivity" weighting function the noise is in(τ)i_n(\tau)in​(τ); Γ\GammaΓ is the kernel that translates ini_nin​ into ϕ\phiϕ Set by the large-signal periodic operating point the full periodic steady-state waveform (including hard switching) must be known before Γ\GammaΓ can be determined the projection direction t^\hat{\mathbf{t}}t^ varies along the limit cycle — it is the geometry of the large-signal trajectory ([P1] assumptions) One per node / per noise source different injection points and different devices see different Γ\GammaΓ the projection direction depends on that node's capacitance and where the source injects "Not the noise itself" is the most common misconception. Γ\GammaΓ is a deterministic periodic function fixed by the circuit structure and its waveform — it has nothing to do with how large the noise is, or whether it is white or flicker. Swapping the noise source (changing ini_nin​) does not change Γ\GammaΓ; it changes the resulting ϕ\phiϕ. Only changing the injection node (changing the projection geometry) changes Γ\GammaΓ.

documents.t: A theory must not merely sound elegant. Here we compute Γ\GammaΓ end to end for a lossless parallel LC, the reference waveform for the entire site. Setup: the ideal LC state executes uniform circular motion (harmonic resonance); write it as z(θ)=A (cos⁡θ, sin⁡θ),θ=ω0t,\mathbf{z}(\theta)=A\,(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta),\qquad \theta=\omega_0 t,z(θ)=A(cosθ, sinθ),θ=ω0​t, where the first component v=Acos⁡θv=A\cos\thetav=Acosθ is the capacitor voltage (output waveform ∝cos⁡θ\propto\cos\theta∝cosθ). Step A — the state displacement caused by the injection: the current impulse changes only the capacitor voltage, Δv=Δq/C\Delta v=\Delta q/CΔv=Δq/C, so Δz=(Δv, 0)=(ΔqC, 0).\Delta\mathbf{z}=(\Delta v,\,0)=\Big(\tfrac{\Delta q}{C},\,0\Big).Δz=(Δv,0)=(CΔq​,0). Step B — project onto the tangent. The tangent vector along the loop: ∂z∂θ=A (−sin⁡θ, cos⁡θ),∣∂z∂θ∣=A.\frac{\partial\mathbf{z}}{\partial\theta}=A\,(-\sin\theta,\ \cos\theta),\qquad \left|\frac{\partial\mathbf{z}}{\partial\theta}\right|=A.∂θ∂z​=A(−sinθ, cosθ),​∂θ∂z​​=A. The phase increment Δθ\Delta\thetaΔθ obeys "tangential displacement = tangential speed × phase increment": dot Δz\Delta\mathbf{z}Δz into the unit tangent, then divide by ∣∂z/∂θ∣|\partial\mathbf{z}/\partial\theta|∣∂z/∂θ∣: Δϕ=Δθ=Δz⋅(∂z/∂θ)∣∂z/∂θ∣2=(Δv,0)⋅A(−sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ)A2=−Asin⁡θ ΔvA2=−sin⁡θA Δv.\Delta\phi=\Delta\theta=\frac{\Delta\mathbf{z}\cdot(\partial\mathbf{z}/\partial\theta)}{|\partial\mathbf{z}/\partial\theta|^2}=\frac{(\Delta v,0)\cdot A(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)}{A^2}=\frac{-A\sin\theta\,\Delta v}{A^2}=\frac{-\sin\theta}{A}\,\Delta v.Δϕ=Δθ=∣∂z/∂θ∣2Δz⋅(∂z/∂θ)​=A2(Δv,0)⋅A(−sinθ,cosθ)​=A2−AsinθΔv​=A−sinθ​Δv. Step-by-step algebra (every equals sign above unpacked — no skipped steps): numerator (dot product): (Δv, 0)⋅A(−sin⁡θ, cos⁡θ)=Δv⋅(−Asin⁡θ)+0⋅(Acos⁡θ)=−Asin⁡θ Δv,denominator: ∣∂z∂θ∣2=(A(−sin⁡θ))2+(Acos⁡θ)2=A2(sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ)=A2,divide: Δϕ=−Asin⁡θ ΔvA2=−sin⁡θA Δv.\begin{aligned} \text{numerator (dot product)}&:\ (\Delta v,\,0)\cdot A(-\sin\theta,\ \cos\theta) =\Delta v\cdot(-A\sin\theta)+0\cdot(A\cos\theta)=-A\sin\theta\,\Delta v,\\ \text{denominator}&:\ \left|\frac{\partial\mathbf{z}}{\partial\theta}\right|^2=\big(A(-\sin\theta)\big)^2+\big(A\cos\theta\big)^2=A^2(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta)=A^2,\\ \text{divide}&:\ \Delta\phi=\frac{-A\sin\theta\,\Delta v}{A^2}=\frac{-\sin\theta}{A}\,\Delta v. \end{aligned}numerator (dot product)denominatordivide​: (Δv,0)⋅A(−sinθ, cosθ)=Δv⋅(−Asinθ)+0⋅(Acosθ)=−AsinθΔv,: ​∂θ∂z​​2=(A(−sinθ))2+(Acosθ)2=A2(sin2θ+cos2θ)=A2,: Δϕ=A2−AsinθΔv​=A−sinθ​Δv.​ Why divide by ∣∂z/∂θ∣2|\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta|^2∣∂z/∂θ∣2 rather than ∣∂z/∂θ∣|\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta|∣∂z/∂θ∣: first dot into the unit tangent t^=∂z/∂θ∣∂z/∂θ∣\hat{\mathbf t}=\dfrac{\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta}{|\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta|}t^=∣∂z/∂θ∣∂z/∂θ​ to get the length of the tangential displacement, then divide by "the arc length per unit θ\thetaθ along the loop, ∣∂z/∂θ∣|\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta|∣∂z/∂θ∣" to convert into Δθ\Delta\thetaΔθ; the two factors of ∣∂z/∂θ∣|\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta|∣∂z/∂θ∣ combine into the squared denominator. sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ=1\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1sin2θ+cos2θ=1 is the identity that lets the denominator collapse cleanly to A2A^2A2 (the uniform speed of circular motion). Step C — substitute Δv=Δq/C\Delta v=\Delta q/CΔv=Δq/C: Δϕ=−sin⁡θA⋅ΔqC=−sin⁡θAC Δq.\Delta\phi=\frac{-\sin\theta}{A}\cdot\frac{\Delta q}{C}=\frac{-\sin\theta}{AC}\,\Delta q.Δϕ=A−sinθ​⋅CΔq​=AC−sinθ​Δq. Step D — recognize qmaxq_{max}qmax​: the node's maximum charge swing is qmax=C Vmax=CAq_{max}=C\,V_{max}=C Aqmax​=CVmax​=CA. Substituting: Δϕ=−sin⁡θqmax Δq⟹ Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ \Delta\phi=\frac{-\sin\theta}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\boxed{\ \Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\theta\ }Δϕ=qmax​−sinθ​Δq⟹ Γ(θ)=−sinθ ​ which lands exactly on the definition Δϕ=Γ(θ) Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma(\theta)\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=Γ(θ)Δq/qmax​. Dimension check: Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ dimensionless ✓; Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ dimensionless ✓; Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ rad ✓. How to read this −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ (matching the intuition of [P1] Fig. 4, p.181): Inject at the peak (θ=0\theta=0θ=0, where the output v=Acos⁡θv=A\cos\thetav=Acosθ is maximal): Γ(0)=0\Gamma(0)=0Γ(0)=0. The finger pokes along the voltage axis, almost perpendicular to the trajectory (purely radial) → it changes only the amplitude and barely touches the phase. The amplitude disturbance gets pulled back, so this poke "leaves no permanent trace". Inject at the zero crossing (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2, v=0v=0v=0, maximum waveform slope): ∣Γ∣=1|\Gamma|=1∣Γ∣=1 (maximal). The poke along the voltage axis is almost tangent to the trajectory (purely tangential) → nearly all of it becomes a permanent phase jump. In between: the tangential/radial split follows −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ continuously. This is the essence of LTV: the same Δq\Delta qΔq, injected at a different instant (different θ\thetaθ), produces a completely different effect. No LTI system exhibits this "it matters when you strike" behavior. See lti_vs_ltv.

This site consistently uses Δω≡ω0−ωinj\Delta\omega\equiv\omega_0-\omega_{inj}Δω≡ω0​−ωinj​, which differs from the Δω≡ωinj−ω0\Delta\omega\equiv\omega_{inj}-\omega_0Δω≡ωinj​−ω0​ of [P3] Fig. 5 by an overall sign) high (checked against the original PDF; v11 correction: the earlier version wrote a minus sign and claimed an "opposite sign convention") [P4] Hong–Hajimiri 2019 Part II Δ(ϕ)\Delta(\phi)Δ(ϕ) (APF) amplitude modulation (amplitude domain) the amplitude version: projects the impulse onto the radial rather than the tangential direction; units A−1\text{A}^{-1}A−1; in the ideal LC the ISF and APF are in quadrature ([P4] Eq.(26), p.2128) ✓ (APF=[P4] Eq.(19), Fig. 5, p.2126, verified) [P5] Hajimiri–Heald 1998 — sense amplifier unrelated to the ISF (a sense-amplifier paper, honestly flagged as mislabeled) high (clearly off-topic) Notation trap: [P3] writes Γ(θ+ϕ)\Gamma(\theta+\phi)Γ(θ+ϕ), taking "the injection waveform phase θ\thetaθ" plus "the oscillator's own excess phase ϕ\phiϕ" as the argument — in essence it is still the same Γ\GammaΓ, only with the argument recast as a relative phase. The APF Δ\DeltaΔ of [P4] is the amplitude sensitivity, complementary to Γ\GammaΓ (the phase sensitivity); in the ideal LC the two are orthogonal (one ∝sin⁡\propto\sin∝sin, the other ∝cos⁡\propto\cos∝cos). documents.t: Problem: the ideal LC has Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ. Inject the same packet of charge at three phases — θ=0\theta=0θ=0 (peak), θ=π/4\theta=\pi/4θ=π/4 (halfway), θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2 (zero crossing) — with the injected-charge ratio fixed at Δq/qmax=10−3\Delta q/q_{max}=10^{-3}Δq/qmax​=10−3. Find Γ\GammaΓ and the phase step Δϕ=Γ⋅Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma\cdot\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=Γ⋅Δq/qmax​ at each point. Step-by-step substitution: compute Γ\GammaΓ first, then multiply by Δq/qmax=10−3\Delta q/q_{max}=10^{-3}Δq/qmax​=10−3. θ=0:Γ=−sin⁡0=0,Δϕ=0×10−3=0 rad.θ=π4:Γ=−sin⁡π4=−12≈−0.7071,Δϕ=−0.7071×10−3=−7.07×10−4 rad.θ=π2:Γ=−sin⁡π2=−1,Δϕ=−1×10−3=−1.0×10−3 rad.\begin{aligned} \theta=0:\quad &\Gamma=-\sin0=0, &\Delta\phi&=0\times10^{-3}=0\ \text{rad}.\\ \theta=\tfrac{\pi}{4}:\quad &\Gamma=-\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx-0.7071, &\Delta\phi&=-0.7071\times10^{-3}=-7.07\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}.\\ \theta=\tfrac{\pi}{2}:\quad &\Gamma=-\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}=-1, &\Delta\phi&=-1\times10^{-3}=-1.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad}. \end{aligned}θ=0:θ=4π​:θ=2π​:​Γ=−sin0=0,Γ=−sin4π​=−2​1​≈−0.7071,Γ=−sin2π​=−1,​ΔϕΔϕΔϕ​=0×10−3=0 rad.=−0.7071×10−3=−7.07×10−4 rad.=−1×10−3=−1.0×10−3 rad.​ Result: the same packet of charge barely moves the phase at the peak (Δϕ=0\Delta\phi=0Δϕ=0), delivers the maximum phase step at the zero crossing (∣Δϕ∣=1|\Delta\phi|=1∣Δϕ∣=1 mrad), and lands in between at the halfway point (0.7070.7070.707 mrad). This is the core LTV phenomenon: the effect is decided by when you strike. Dimension check: Γ\GammaΓ dimensionless, Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ dimensionless → Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ dimensionless (rad) ✓. The minus sign means the phase is pushed backward (it lags); the order of magnitude is set by Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​, the same order as Example A's 5×10−45\times10^{-4}5×10−4 rad (Example A uses Γ=0.5\Gamma=0.5Γ=0.5). import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, impulse_to_phase_step theta = np.array([0.0, np.pi/4, np.pi/2]) g = gamma_lc_ideal(theta) # -> [ 0. -0.7071 -1. ] dphi = impulse_to_phase_step(delta_q=1e-3, gamma_value=g, qmax=1.0) # Δq/qmax = 1e-3 print(g) # ISF values print(dphi) # -> [ 0. -7.07e-04 -1.0e-03 ] rad

documents.t: Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) = the sensitivity weight answering "inject one unit of charge at waveform phase ω0τ\omega_0\tauω0​τ — how much becomes permanent phase?" The derivation chain: impulse → charge Δq\Delta qΔq → voltage step ΔV\Delta VΔV → state displacement → projection onto the tangent (the phase direction) → permanent phase Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ. Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless, 2π2\pi2π-periodic, not the noise itself, set by the large-signal periodic operating point, and there is one per node / per noise source. Ideal LC: Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ — peak injection gives Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0 (amplitude only), zero crossing gives ∣Γ∣=1|\Gamma|=1∣Γ∣=1 (maximum phase) — that is LTV. Across the papers: [P1][P2] use Γ\GammaΓ for phase noise; [P3] applies the same Γ\GammaΓ to injection; [P4]'s APF Δ\DeltaΔ is the amplitude counterpart; [P5] is unrelated to the ISF. Sources: [P1] Eqs.(10),(11), p.182; verification figures in lab_02 / lab_04.

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: isf_definition (the definition of Γ\GammaΓ and the tangential-projection intuition), waveform_slope (the 1/slope1/\text{slope}1/slope heuristic and its divergence at waveform peaks) | Next: derivation_floquet_ppv (the rigorous adjoint/PPV — the source of this page's "ground truth"), lab_32 (the impulse method implemented on an equation-level ring) The preceding pages define Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) very carefully, but they leave one intensely practical question open: given an actual oscillator in hand (a SPICE netlist, a set of equations, or a measured steady-state waveform), how do you actually COMPUTE Γ\GammaΓ? The appendix of [P1], "Calculation of the Impulse Sensitivity Function" ([P1] pp.192–193), gives three methods that form a spectrum from most accurate to fastest. This page transcribes all three verbatim, derives each step by step, and states each one's failure conditions clearly — then stages a three-way duel on a single van der Pol oscillator to turn "how far apart are they" into numbers. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the three methods are really three tiers of the same thing. Method A (impulse injection) is "just run the experiment": poke the oscillator, measure the phase shift, assume nothing — so it is the most accurate and the slowest. Method B (closed form) replaces the experiment with geometry: it assumes that of the displacement you poke into the state, only the component tangent to the trajectory survives as phase — the experiment collapses into one inner product, computable from a single period of the waveform. Method C (first derivative) cuts once more: it assumes the denominator (the squared "speed" along the trajectory) is roughly constant, so Γ\GammaΓ becomes directly proportional to the waveform slope. Every cut buys speed and costs one more assumption that can fail. The core lesson of this page: Method B's tangential projection quietly assumes that "decaying amplitude perturbations leave no phase behind" — the moment amplitude-to-phase coupling (AM→PM) appears, it starts leaking.
documents.s: Computing the ISF Directly from the Waveform — the Three Methods of [P1]'s Appendix

documents.t: [P1]'s description on p.192 (transcribed): inject an impulse at different relative phases of the oscillation waveform and let the oscillator run for a few cycles; by sweeping the impulse injection time across one cycle and measuring the resulting time shift Δt\Delta tΔt, you obtain hϕ(t,τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)hϕ​(t,τ), using the conversion Δϕ=2π ΔtT,\Delta\phi=2\pi\,\frac{\Delta t}{T},Δϕ=2πTΔt​, where TTT is the period of oscillation ([P1] p.192; this is exactly the phase–time conversion used in impulse_to_phase_shift). The paper adds that many SPICE implementations can perform the sweep automatically, and since each impulse needs only a few simulated cycles, it executes quickly; once hϕ(t,τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)hϕ​(t,τ) is found, "the ISF is calculated by multiplication with qmaxq_{max}qmax​" (compare [P1] Eq.(10): hϕ=Γ/qmax⋅u(t−τ)h_\phi=\Gamma/q_{max}\cdot u(t-\tau)hϕ​=Γ/qmax​⋅u(t−τ), so Γ=qmaxhϕ\Gamma=q_{max}h_\phiΓ=qmax​hϕ​ is the step height). [P1]'s own verdict (p.192, verbatim): "This method is the most accurate of the three methods presented." — the most accurate of the three. The price is NphaseN_{phase}Nphase​ transient runs (one per injection phase). Unit check: Δϕ=2π [s]/[s]=\Delta\phi=2\pi\,[\text{s}]/[\text{s}]=Δϕ=2π[s]/[s]= rad ✓; Γ=qmax⋅hϕ\Gamma=q_{max}\cdot h_\phiΓ=qmax​⋅hϕ​, [C]⋅[rad/C]=[C]\cdot[\text{rad/C}]=[C]⋅[rad/C]= dimensionless ✓. This site has implemented the method three times: a sinusoidal oscillator (lab_04, error ~0.001), a van der Pol (lab_15), and a MOS Level-1 equation-level ring (lab_32). Mind the wrap-around: fold Δt\Delta tΔt back into [−T/2, T/2)[-T/2,\,T/2)[−T/2,T/2) before converting, or you are off by a whole cycle (an implementation detail of lab_15/lab_32).
documents.s: Method A: direct measurement of the impulse response ([P1] Appendix A, p.192)

documents.t: Consider the state-space trajectory of an nnnth-order system ([P1] Fig. 29, p.192: "State-space trajectory of an nnnth-order oscillator"). The effect of a group of external impulses is a perturbation vector ΔX⃗\Delta\vec XΔX that instantly moves the state to X⃗+ΔX⃗\vec X+\Delta\vec XX+ΔX. The paper's key assumption sentence (p.192, verbatim): "As discussed earlier, amplitude variations eventually die away, but phase variations do not." To compute the equivalent time shift, project the perturbation onto the normalized velocity vector ([P1] Eq.(31), p.192): l=ΔX⃗⋅X⃗˙∣X⃗˙∣l=\Delta\vec X\cdot\frac{\dot{\vec X}}{\bigl|\dot{\vec X}\bigr|}l=ΔX⋅​X˙​X˙​ lll is the "equivalent displacement along the trajectory" (the paper's wording), and X⃗˙\dot{\vec X}X˙ is the first derivative of the state vector (the trajectory's "velocity"). Unit check: with all states as voltages, [ΔX⃗]=[\Delta\vec X]=[ΔX]= V and X⃗˙/∣X⃗˙∣\dot{\vec X}/|\dot{\vec X}|X˙/∣X˙∣ dimensionless → lll in V ✓ (a displacement carries the state's units). Hidden assumption #1: the inner product requires all state components to share one unit / one scale. If the state mixes V and A (e.g., an LC's vC,iLv_C,i_LvC​,iL​) you must normalize first — and the choice of normalization changes the answer (see "failure conditions"). The figure below replicates Fig. 29's state-space picture (left) and Fig. 30's three-method comparison (right — the Method C section refers back to it), computed on this site's van der Pol toy: Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Titles/labels read: "[P1] Fig. 29 概念復刻：n 階振盪器的 state-space 軌跡\n（van der Pol μ=2.0 實算：細線＝踢一下後真的重新收斂）" = [P1] Fig. 29 conceptual replica: state-space trajectory of an n-th order oscillator (an actually-integrated van der Pol μ=2.0: thin line = the genuinely re-converging trajectory after a kick); "x (radians)（θ=0 對齊波形谷值）" = x (radians) (θ=0 aligned to the waveform minimum); "[P1] Fig. 30 概念復刻：Calculation of Impulse Sensitivity Function\n（van der Pol μ=0.2；原圖振盪器未載明）" = [P1] Fig. 30 conceptual replica: Calculation of Impulse Sensitivity Function (van der Pol μ=0.2; the original figure does not specify the oscillator). Conceptual replica, not a digitization of the originals. Left: corresponds to [P1] Fig. 29 (p.192), original caption verbatim: "State-space trajectory of an nnnth-order oscillator." — the original is an nnn-dimensional schematic hand drawing (no specific system); the replica instead actually computes a van der Pol (μ=2.0): thick line = limit cycle, thin line = the genuinely integrated re-converging trajectory after a kick Δx=0.45\Delta x=0.45Δx=0.45 on the xxx axis (deliberately exaggerated for legibility), with Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ marked as the same-time gap between the two trajectories and measured from late zero crossings as −0.768-0.768−0.768 rad (−0.122-0.122−0.122 cycles). Right: corresponds to [P1] Fig. 30 (p.193), original caption verbatim: "ISF's obtained from different methods.", original plot title "Calculation of Impulse Sensitivity Function" — the original's oscillator is not specified; the replica uses the same μ=0.2 vdP (the same machinery as the duel below), with the original's line styles: solid = 1st Method (A), dotted = 2nd Method (B), dashed = 3rd Method (C), and phase zero at the waveform minimum so the positive lobe precedes the negative one (the original's ordering). Honest difference: in the paper the 1st and 2nd methods nearly coincide and the dashed 3rd deviates (an NNN-identical-stage ring keeps Eq.(36)'s denominator constant); on this single-node vdP it is Methods B and C that nearly coincide (rms gap 0.134), while the impulse truth A departs near the waveform extrema (AM→PM, see the duel below). Numbers: Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ A/B/C =0.7777=0.7777=0.7777/0.70970.70970.7097/0.67580.67580.6758; rms ∣B−A∣=0.2365|B-A|=0.2365∣B−A∣=0.2365, rms ∣C−A∣=0.3219|C-A|=0.3219∣C−A∣=0.3219. documents.s: Step 1: project the perturbation onto the direction of motion — Eq. (31)

documents.t: A displacement lll along the trajectory is equivalent to a time shift of "lll divided by the speed ∣X⃗˙∣|\dot{\vec X}|∣X˙∣" ([P1] Eq.(32), p.193): Δt=l∣X⃗˙∣=ΔX⃗⋅X⃗˙∣X⃗˙∣2\Delta t=\frac{l}{\bigl|\dot{\vec X}\bigr|}=\Delta\vec X\cdot\frac{\dot{\vec X}}{\bigl|\dot{\vec X}\bigr|^{2}}Δt=​X˙​l​=ΔX⋅​X˙​2X˙​ Unit check: [V]⋅[V/s]/[V/s]2=[V]/[V/s]=[\text{V}]\cdot[\text{V/s}]/[\text{V/s}]^2=[\text{V}]/[\text{V/s}]=[V]⋅[V/s]/[V/s]2=[V]/[V/s]= s ✓. Note the denominator becomes a square: one factor from normalizing the tangent vector, one from converting displacement to time. This is exactly the "divide by ∣∂z/∂θ∣2\vert\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta\vert^2∣∂z/∂θ∣2" step in the ideal-LC derivation of isf_definition.
documents.s: Step 2: displacement ÷ speed = time shift — Eq. (32)

documents.t: ([P1] Eq.(33), p.193): Δϕ=2π ΔtT=2πT(ΔX⃗⋅X⃗˙∣X⃗˙∣2).\Delta\phi=2\pi\,\frac{\Delta t}{T}=\frac{2\pi}{T}\left(\Delta\vec X\cdot\frac{\dot{\vec X}}{\bigl|\dot{\vec X}\bigr|^{2}}\right).Δϕ=2πTΔt​=T2π​​ΔX⋅​X˙​2X˙​​. Since 2π/T=ω02\pi/T=\omega_02π/T=ω0​, this is the "state-space projection" form often quoted: Δϕ=ω0 (ΔX⃗⋅X⃗˙)/∣X⃗˙∣2\Delta\phi=\omega_0\,(\Delta\vec X\cdot\dot{\vec X})/|\dot{\vec X}|^2Δϕ=ω0​(ΔX⋅X˙)/∣X˙∣2.

documents.t: If the state variables are node voltages and the impulse hits node iii, the voltage jump is given by [P1] Eq.(9) (ΔVi=Δqi/Ci\Delta V_i=\Delta q_i/C_iΔVi​=Δqi​/Ci​), and Eq.(33) reduces to ([P1] Eq.(34), p.193): Δϕi=2πT⋅ΔqiCi⋅v˙i∣v⃗˙∣2\Delta\phi_i=\frac{2\pi}{T}\cdot\frac{\Delta q_i}{C_i}\cdot\frac{\dot v_i}{\bigl|\dot{\vec v}\bigr|^{2}}Δϕi​=T2π​⋅Ci​Δqi​​⋅​v˙​2v˙i​​ where ∣v⃗˙∣2\vert\dot{\vec v}\vert^2∣v˙∣2 is the norm of the first derivative of the waveform vector and v˙i\dot v_iv˙i​ is the derivative of the iii-th node voltage (definitions verbatim from p.193). Step-by-step reading: ΔX⃗\Delta\vec XΔX has only its iii-th component nonzero (=Δqi/Ci=\Delta q_i/C_i=Δqi​/Ci​), so the inner product ΔX⃗⋅v⃗˙\Delta\vec X\cdot\dot{\vec v}ΔX⋅v˙ keeps only the v˙i\dot v_iv˙i​ term. Unit check: [rad/s]⋅[C]/[F]⋅[V/s][V/s]2=[rad/s]⋅[V][V/s]=\dfrac{[\text{rad/s}]\cdot[\text{C}]/[\text{F}]\cdot[\text{V/s}]}{[\text{V/s}]^2}=\dfrac{[\text{rad/s}]\cdot[\text{V}]}{[\text{V/s}]}=[V/s]2[rad/s]⋅[C]/[F]⋅[V/s]​=[V/s][rad/s]⋅[V]​= rad ✓.

documents.t: Substitute the normalized waveform fff of [P1] Eq.(1) (vi=Vmax fi(x)v_i=V_{max}\,f_i(x)vi​=Vmax​fi​(x), x=ω0τx=\omega_0\taux=ω0​τ, with fff's derivatives taken with respect to xxx). Step by step: v˙i=ddt[Vmaxfi(x)]=Vmax fi′(x) ω0(chain rule, dx/dt=ω0)∣v⃗˙∣2=∑j(Vmaxfj′ω0)2=ω02Vmax2 ∣f⃗ ′∣2(equal amplitudes Vmax: the identical-stage assumption)Δϕ=ω0⋅ΔqCi⋅Vmaxfi′ ω0ω02Vmax2∣f⃗ ′∣2=ΔqCiVmax⋅fi′∣f⃗ ′∣2(every ω0 cancels)\begin{aligned} \dot v_i&=\frac{d}{dt}\bigl[V_{max}f_i(x)\bigr]=V_{max}\,f_i'(x)\,\omega_0 &&(\text{chain rule},\ dx/dt=\omega_0)\\[4pt] \bigl|\dot{\vec v}\bigr|^{2}&=\sum_j\bigl(V_{max}f_j'\omega_0\bigr)^2=\omega_0^2V_{max}^2\,\bigl|\vec f\,'\bigr|^{2} &&(\text{equal amplitudes }V_{max}\text{: the identical-stage assumption})\\[4pt] \Delta\phi&=\omega_0\cdot\frac{\Delta q}{C_i}\cdot\frac{V_{max}f_i'\,\omega_0}{\omega_0^2V_{max}^2\bigl|\vec f\,'\bigr|^{2}} =\frac{\Delta q}{C_iV_{max}}\cdot\frac{f_i'}{\bigl|\vec f\,'\bigr|^{2}} &&(\text{every }\omega_0\text{ cancels}) \end{aligned}v˙i​​v˙​2Δϕ​=dtd​[Vmax​fi​(x)]=Vmax​fi′​(x)ω0​=j∑​(Vmax​fj′​ω0​)2=ω02​Vmax2​​f​′​2=ω0​⋅Ci​Δq​⋅ω02​Vmax2​​f​′​2Vmax​fi′​ω0​​=Ci​Vmax​Δq​⋅​f​′​2fi′​​​​(chain rule, dx/dt=ω0​)(equal amplitudes Vmax​: the identical-stage assumption)(every ω0​ cancels)​ Recognizing CiVmax=C_iV_{max}=Ci​Vmax​= the node's maximum charge swing gives ([P1] Eq.(35), p.193, transcribed verbatim): Δϕ=Δqqi⋅fi′∣f⃗ ′∣2\Delta\phi=\frac{\Delta q}{q_i}\cdot\frac{f_i'}{\bigl|\vec f\,'\bigr|^{2}}Δϕ=qi​Δq​⋅​f​′​2fi′​​ Notation note: [P1] Eq.(35) prints qiq_iqi​ — the maximum charge swing of node iii, i.e., the main text's (and this site's) qmaxq_{max}qmax​ for that node. fi′f_i'fi′​ is "the derivative of the normalized waveform on node iii" with respect to the phase xxx (p.193, verbatim). Comparing against the definition Δϕ=Γ Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=ΓΔq/qmax​, the ISF reads off directly ([P1] Eq.(36), p.193): Γi(x)=fi′∣f⃗ ′∣2=fi′∑j=1nfj′ 2\Gamma_i(x)=\frac{f_i'}{\bigl|\vec f\,'\bigr|^{2}}=\frac{f_i'}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}f_j'^{\,2}}Γi​(x)=​f​′​2fi′​​=j=1∑n​fj′2​fi′​​ Unit check: f′f'f′ is dimensionless (a dimensionless waveform differentiated with respect to rad) → Γ\GammaΓ dimensionless ✓. [P1]'s observation after Eq.(36) (p.193 — important; paraphrase plus the key sentence): this expression is maximum during transitions (where the derivative of fff is maximum), and that maximum value is inversely proportional to the maximum derivative — verbatim: "waveforms with larger slope show a smaller peak in the ISF function." This is the original source of the entire design intuition of waveform_slope.
documents.s: Step 5: rewrite with the normalized waveform — Eqs. (35), (36)

documents.t: For a second-order system one can use the normalized waveform fff and its derivative f′f'f′ as the state variables, so the denominator of Eq.(36) keeps only two terms ([P1] Eq.(37), p.193): Γ(x)=f′f′ 2+f′′ 2\Gamma(x)=\frac{f'}{f'^{\,2}+f''^{\,2}}Γ(x)=f′2+f′′2f′​ where f′′f''f′′ is the second derivative of fff (defined on p.193). Verify the ideal sinusoid by hand ([P1]'s own sanity check on p.193 — here with the algebra written out): take f(x)=cos⁡xf(x)=\cos xf(x)=cosx, f′(x)=−sin⁡x,f′′(x)=−cos⁡x,f′ 2+f′′ 2=sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1(Pythagorean identity: the denominator is identically 1),Γ(x)=−sin⁡x1=−sin⁡x.\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=-\sin x,\qquad f''(x)=-\cos x,\\[4pt] f'^{\,2}+f''^{\,2}&=\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\qquad(\text{Pythagorean identity: the denominator is identically }1),\\[4pt] \Gamma(x)&=\frac{-\sin x}{1}=-\sin x. \end{aligned}f′(x)f′2+f′′2Γ(x)​=−sinx,f′′(x)=−cosx,=sin2x+cos2x=1(Pythagorean identity: the denominator is identically 1),=1−sinx​=−sinx.​ The paper's conclusion (p.193, verbatim): "In the case of an ideal sinusoidal oscillator f=cos⁡(x)f=\cos(x)f=cos(x), so that Γ(ωt)=−sin⁡(ωt)\Gamma(\omega t)=-\sin(\omega t)Γ(ωt)=−sin(ωt), which is consistent with the argument of Section III." Numerically we verify this to machine precision (simulations/fig_isf_three_methods.py prints max |Eq.(37) on cos - (-sin)| = 2.2e-16). This step also resolves the "1/slope1/\text{slope}1/slope diverges at the peak" paradox left open by waveform_slope: On transitions (f′2≫f′′2f'^2\gg f''^2f′2≫f′′2): Γ≈f′/f′ 2=1/f′\Gamma\approx f'/f'^{\,2}=1/f'Γ≈f′/f′2=1/f′ — precisely the regime where the 1/slope1/\text{slope}1/slope heuristic applies. Near peaks (f′→0f'\to0f′→0): the numerator f′→0f'\to0f′→0 while the denominator is held up by f′′ 2f''^{\,2}f′′2, so Γ≈f′/f′′ 2→0\Gamma\approx f'/f''^{\,2}\to0Γ≈f′/f′′2→0 — bounded, and tending to 0, no divergence. So 1/slope1/\text{slope}1/slope is the shadow of Eq.(37) in its slope-dominated limit; Eq.(37) is its rigorous parent formula, interpolating continuously between the two limits. But beware: Eq.(37) has its own sick point — if at some phase f′f'f′ and f′′f''f′′ approach 0 simultaneously (the waveform has a dead zone where both slope and curvature are flat), the denominator collapses and Γ\GammaΓ spikes (the waveform of worked example 2 below shows a spurious peak of ∣Γ∣≈22.8\vert\Gamma\vert\approx22.8∣Γ∣≈22.8 at x≈2.81x\approx2.81x≈2.81). The higher-order form Eq.(36) is safer, its denominator being propped up by the other nodes' fj′ 2f_j'^{\,2}fj′2​.

documents.t: The paper (p.193, paraphrase): this is a simplified version of the second approach. In certain cases the denominator of Eq.(36) shows little variation and can be approximated by a constant — the concrete example being a ring oscillator with NNN identical stages (the stage transitions take turns, so ∑jfj′2\sum_j f_j'^2∑j​fj′2​ is nearly constant). The denominator may then be approximated by fmax′ 2f_{max}'^{\,2}fmax′2​ ([P1] Eq.(38), p.193): Γi(x)=fi′(x)fmax′ 2\Gamma_i(x)=\frac{f_i'(x)}{f_{max}'^{\,2}}Γi​(x)=fmax′2​fi′​(x)​ The ISF is directly proportional to the waveform slope (divided by one constant). [P1]'s honest verdict (p.193, verbatim): "Although this method is approximate, it is the easiest to use and allows a designer to rapidly develop important insights into the behavior of an oscillator." [P1] Fig. 30 (p.193, "ISF's obtained from different methods") plots the three methods together; Method C (dashed) deviates in lobe height and detail but gets the shape right (see the right half of the replica figure in Method B, Step 1, for its conceptual replica). It is the engine of this site's interactive tool: interactive tool 7, the IsfSandbox (draw a waveform → see its ISF) uses precisely the [P2]-appendix variant of this slope approximation (each edge normalized by its own maximum slope, which is what lets rise/fall asymmetry produce c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0); this page is that widget's rigorous pedigree. The ring closed form of [P2] App. B (Eqs.(52)–(55), Γrms=2π2/(3η3) N−1.5\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{2\pi^2/(3\eta^3)}\,N^{-1.5}Γrms​=2π2/(3η3)​N−1.5, see rms_isf) is essentially the result of integrating Method C's triangular ISF. Failure: if the denominator ∑jfj′2\sum_j f_j'^2∑j​fj′2​ varies strongly with phase (single-node view, few stages, badly distorted waveform), the constant-denominator approximation collapses — the μ=2 van der Pol in the duel below is exactly that case.

documents.t: Theory done; now numbers. On a van der Pol oscillator (x¨−μ(1−x2)x˙+x=0\ddot x-\mu(1-x^2)\dot x+x=0x¨−μ(1−x2)x˙+x=0; the same toy as lab_15 and derivation_floquet_ppv), we kick charge into the xxx axis (xxx is this toy's "node voltage" — the vdP rewrites as a parallel RLC plus a nonlinear conductance with x=vCx=v_Cx=vC​, and a current impulse instantaneously changes exactly xxx), and put the three methods on stage: Method A (ground truth): impulse measurement at 24 phases (reusing lab_25's extract_isf_impulse_axis, machinery already cross-verified against the adjoint/PPV to rms 0.0023). Method B: Eq.(37) with f=x/Af=x/Af=x/A, f′=y/(ω0A)f'=y/(\omega_0A)f′=y/(ω0​A), f′′=y˙/(ω02A)f''=\dot y/(\omega_0^2A)f′′=y˙​/(ω02​A), needing only one period of the waveform. Method C: Eq.(38), f′/fmax′ 2f'/f_{max}'^{\,2}f′/fmax′2​. References: the harmonic limit −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ (phase θ=0\theta=0θ=0 aligned to the waveform maximum, i.e., the f≈cos⁡θf\approx\cos\thetaf≈cosθ convention) and the rigorous adjoint/PPV curve (lab_25; the PPV is external literature, [E2] Demir 2000, not among the site's 5 PDFs). Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Axis labels/annotations read: "注入相位 θ/2π（θ=0 對齊波形峰值，無因次）" = injection phase θ/2π (θ=0 aligned to the waveform peak, dimensionless); "Γ(θ)（無因次，qmax=A）" = Γ(θ) (dimensionless, qmax=A); "近諧波：形狀吻合，但峰值附近差 O(μ)" = near-harmonic: shapes match, but they differ by O(μ) near the peak; "強非線性：closed form 失準" = strongly nonlinear: the closed form loses accuracy. Parameter table: μ∈{0.2, 2.0}\mu\in\{0.2,\,2.0\}μ∈{0.2,2.0}; impulse Δq=0.02\Delta q=0.02Δq=0.02 (Δq/qmax≈1%\Delta q/q_{max}\approx1\%Δq/qmax​≈1%, qmax ⁣= ⁣A≈2q_{max}\!=\!A\approx2qmax​=A≈2); 24 injection phases; RK4 step 2.5×10−32.5\times10^{-3}2.5×10−3 (impulse runs) / T/6000T/6000T/6000 (waveform grid); everything in normalized dimensionless units. Pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level. Full script: simulations/fig_isf_three_methods.py (run with PYTHONPATH=. python simulations/fig_isf_three_methods.py, about 3 s). Measured output: --- mu = 0.2 --- T = 6.2989 # -> 6.2989 (the 2π(1+μ²/16) prediction) A = 2.0004 # -> 2.0004 (harmonic limit A=2) Gamma_rms (Method B) = 0.7097 # -> 0.7097 (≈ the true-LC 1/√2=0.7071, not the representative 0.5) Gamma_rms (Method A points) = 0.7777 # -> 0.7777 (the truth sits 9% above Method B) peak |Gamma_B| = 0.9762 # -> 0.9762 peak |Gamma_A| = 1.0144 # -> 1.0144 rms |B - A(impulse)| = 0.2365 # -> 0.2365 (Method B's projection error) rms |C - A(impulse)| = 0.3219 # -> 0.3219 rms |B - (-sin)| = 0.078 # -> 0.078 (Method B essentially IS −sin) rms |A - (-sin)| = 0.28 # -> 0.28 (the truth left −sin long ago) --- mu = 2.0 --- Gamma_rms (Method B) = 1.9898 # -> 1.9898 Gamma_rms (Method A points) = 3.2151 # -> 3.2151 (Method B underestimates by 38%, ≈4.2 dB of phase noise) peak |Gamma_A| = 5.0011 # -> 5.0011 rms |B - A(impulse)| = 2.072 # -> 2.072 (off the rails) rms |C - A(impulse)| = 3.1803 # -> 3.1803 (collapse: one node, no N-stage sum to prop the denominator) rms |B - A(impulse)| at mu=0.05 = 0.0586 # -> 0.0586 (shrink μ 4×, error shrinks 4.0×: error ∝ O(μ)) rms |B - PPV| (mu=0.2) = 0.237 # -> 0.237 (impulse ≡ PPV to 0.002, so the whole gap is Method B's projection error) How to read the figure (and the numbers): Left panel (μ=0.2, near-harmonic): Method B (blue) and Method C (green) are essentially −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ (black dashed, rms gap 0.078), and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ lands on the true-LC 1/21/\sqrt21/2​ (0.7097 vs 0.7071 — note this is the true-LC value 1/21/\sqrt21/2​, not the site's representative value 0.5). But the measured impulse points (red circles) and the rigorous PPV (purple dash-dot) coincide with each other and systematically leave Method B near the waveform peaks: at the peak, Method B says Γ≈−0.11\Gamma\approx-0.11Γ≈−0.11; the truth is −0.59-0.59−0.59. That gap is not numerical noise — it is Method B's principled omission. Recall the assumption sentence of Step 1: "amplitude variations eventually die away, but phase variations do not" — it assumes that while an amplitude perturbation decays, it drags no phase along. The van der Pol's amplitude, however, back-modulates the instantaneous frequency (isochron twist, AM→PM): a radial offset Δr\Delta rΔr decays as e−μte^{-\mu t}e−μt, detunes the frequency by O(μΔr)O(\mu\Delta r)O(μΔr) while decaying, and accumulates a phase ∫O(μΔre−μt)dt=O(Δr)\int O(\mu\Delta r e^{-\mu t})dt=O(\Delta r)∫O(μΔre−μt)dt=O(Δr) — the μ\muμ of the decay rate and the μ\muμ of the modulation strength cancel, leaving a finite residual phase. Only the oblique adjoint/PPV projection books this entry; the orthogonal tangential projection cannot (see derivation_floquet_ppv; this criterion is external literature, [E2]). Numerical evidence: dropping μ\muμ from 0.2 to 0.05 (4× smaller) shrinks the rms gap from 0.2365 → 0.0586 (exactly 4.0× smaller) — error ∝O(μ)\propto O(\mu)∝O(μ), concentrated exactly where Method B predicts Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0 (the peaks; precisely the "high AM–PM leaves residual phase even for peak injection" cell of the failure table in isf_definition). Right panel (μ=2.0, strongly nonlinear): Method B's lobe height (3.85 vs the true 5.00), position, and width are all wrong, and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is underestimated by 38%; via L∝Γrms2\mathcal L\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2L∝Γrms2​ ([P1] Eq.(21) — its 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2 denominator is the SSB bookkeeping convention; the clean time-domain derivation gives 2Δω22\Delta\omega^22Δω2, see white_noise_to_phase_noise) that is an underestimate of about 4.2 dB of phase noise. Method C (green) fares worse: the relaxation waveform's huge fmax′f'_{max}fmax′​ squashes the whole ISF toward 0 (rms gap 3.18). Engineering conclusion: for sign-off numbers use Method A (or the adjoint/PPV); use Method B for a "one-period quick look at the shape", quantitatively trustworthy on near-harmonic, low-AM–PM oscillators (error ∼O(μ)\sim O(\mu)∼O(μ)); use Method C only in the "NNN identical ring stages" scenario it was invented for (the dual-lobe ISF of lab_32 is the equation-level validation of that scenario).

documents.t: Problem: a waveform with 30% second harmonic: f(x)=cos⁡x+0.3cos⁡2xf(x)=\cos x+0.3\cos 2xf(x)=cosx+0.3cos2x. Near the zero crossing, at x=π/2x=\pi/2x=π/2, compute Γ\GammaΓ with Method B (Eq.(37)) and Method C (Eq.(38)) and compare. Step-by-step substitution: first the derivatives, f′(x)=−sin⁡x−0.6sin⁡2x,f′′(x)=−cos⁡x−1.2cos⁡2x.f'(x)=-\sin x-0.6\sin 2x,\qquad f''(x)=-\cos x-1.2\cos 2x.f′(x)=−sinx−0.6sin2x,f′′(x)=−cosx−1.2cos2x. At x=π/2x=\pi/2x=π/2: sin⁡x=1\sin x=1sinx=1, sin⁡2x=0\sin 2x=0sin2x=0, cos⁡x=0\cos x=0cosx=0, cos⁡2x=−1\cos 2x=-1cos2x=−1, so f′=−1,f′′=+1.2,ΓB=f′f′ 2+f′′ 2=−11+1.44=−0.4098,fmax′ 2=1.9247(numerical extremum: fmax′=1.3873 at x≈58∘),ΓC=f′fmax′ 2=−11.9247=−0.5196,ΓCΓB=1.27.\begin{aligned} f'&=-1,\qquad f''=+1.2,\\[4pt] \Gamma_B&=\frac{f'}{f'^{\,2}+f''^{\,2}}=\frac{-1}{1+1.44}=-0.4098,\\[4pt] f_{max}'^{\,2}&=1.9247\quad(\text{numerical extremum: }f'_{max}=1.3873\text{ at }x\approx58^\circ),\\[4pt] \Gamma_C&=\frac{f'}{f_{max}'^{\,2}}=\frac{-1}{1.9247}=-0.5196,\qquad \frac{\Gamma_C}{\Gamma_B}=1.27. \end{aligned}f′ΓB​fmax′2​ΓC​​=−1,f′′=+1.2,=f′2+f′′2f′​=1+1.44−1​=−0.4098,=1.9247(numerical extremum: fmax′​=1.3873 at x≈58∘),=fmax′2​f′​=1.9247−1​=−0.5196,ΓB​ΓC​​=1.27.​ Result: with only 30% harmonic distortion, Method C already overshoots Method B by 27% at the ZC — because it forces "constant denominator" onto a waveform whose denominator does vary with phase. In Γ2\Gamma^2Γ2 terms that is roughly a 2 dB phase-noise error source. Bonus (Method B's own sick point): on this waveform, at x≈2.81x\approx2.81x≈2.81 both f′f'f′ and f′′f''f′′ pass near 0 simultaneously, and Eq.(37)'s ∣Γ∣\vert\Gamma\vert∣Γ∣ spikes to 22.8 (a spurious peak) — Method B "cures the 1/slope1/\text{slope}1/slope divergence at the peak", but its own denominator can also die; scan f′ 2+f′′ 2f'^{\,2}+f''^{\,2}f′2+f′′2 for near-zeros before trusting it. documents.t: [P1]'s appendix gives three ways to compute the ISF: A impulse injection (most accurate) → B closed form Γ=f′/(f′ 2+f′′ 2)\Gamma=f'/(f'^{\,2}+f''^{\,2})Γ=f′/(f′2+f′′2) (one period of waveform suffices) → C slope approximation Γ=f′/fmax′ 2\Gamma=f'/f_{max}'^{\,2}Γ=f′/fmax′2​ (fastest, ring-specific) ([P1] Eqs.(31)–(38), pp.192–193). Method B's chain: project onto the unit tangent (Eq.(31)) → divide by speed to get time (Eq.(32)) → multiply by 2π/T2\pi/T2π/T to get phase (Eq.(33)) → node-voltage special case (Eq.(34)) → normalized waveform (Eqs.(35)(36)) → second-order special case (Eq.(37)). Substituting f=cos⁡xf=\cos xf=cosx into Eq.(37): the denominator sin⁡2+cos⁡2=1\sin^2+\cos^2=1sin2+cos2=1, so Γ=−sin⁡x\Gamma=-\sin xΓ=−sinx exactly — at the peak the numerator vanishes and the result stays bounded, resolving the 1/slope1/\text{slope}1/slope heuristic's divergence; 1/slope1/\text{slope}1/slope is just its limit where f′2≫f′′2f'^2\gg f''^2f′2≫f′′2. Method B's original sin is the orthogonal projection: it assumes "decaying amplitude leaves no phase". Turn on AM→PM (a van der Pol suffices) and the truth departs from Method B, with error ∝O(μ)\propto O(\mu)∝O(μ) concentrated at the peaks; under strong nonlinearity (μ=2) Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is underestimated by 38% ≈ 4.2 dB of phase noise. The rigorous fix is the adjoint/PPV oblique projection (external literature). Method C is the engine of the IsfSandbox and of [P2]'s ring closed form; leave the "N identical stages" scenario and it collapses. Practical order: build intuition with C/B first; get sign-off numbers from A or the adjoint.

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: rms_isf | Next: flicker_noise_upconversion The previous page white_noise_to_phase_noise derived the signature result of oscillator phase noise, [P1] Eq.(21): the phase-noise skirt caused by white noise is L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2).\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right).L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​). The equation is beautiful, but it hides a disturbing mathematical pathology: the denominator contains Δω2\Delta\omega^2Δω2, so as the offset Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0 (infinitely close to the carrier), the bracket →∞\to\infty→∞ and L→+∞\mathcal{L}\to+\inftyL→+∞. Read literally, the noise power density at the exact center of the carrier is infinite — which is obviously wrong: a real oscillator has finite total power (namely its output power) and cannot pack infinite power density into any single frequency. This page resolves that paradox head-on. Conclusion first: 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 is the far-offset asymptote of the "phase linearization" approximation, not the truth near the carrier. Honestly account for the random-walk nature of the phase, and the carrier spectrum flattens near the carrier into a Lorentzian, with a finite peak, conserved total power, and a naturally defined finite 3-dB linewidth Δf3dB=D/π\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=D/\piΔf3dB​=D/π. Physical intuition (conclusion first): white noise keeps kicking the phase, so ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) does not settle at any value; like a drunkard's walk it random-walks without bound (a Wiener process). The phase variance grows linearly: Var[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣\mathrm{Var}[\Delta\phi]=2D|t|Var[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣. The carrier cos⁡(ω0t+ϕ)\cos(\omega_0t+\phi)cos(ω0​t+ϕ) therefore gradually loses memory: the longer the separation, the larger and less correlated the phase difference, so the autocorrelation Rx(τ)R_x(\tau)Rx​(τ) decays exponentially. The Fourier transform of an exponentially decaying autocorrelation is a Lorentzian — a bell-shaped line of finite height and finite width. 1/f21/f^21/f2 is merely the tail of this Lorentzian "far from center." Near the center it must flatten, because "complete phase amnesia" can at most spread the power flat — it can never make it diverge. This page follows the complete step-by-step Lorentzian derivation of spec 11.2 throughout. The mechanism used here — "phase diffusion → exponential autocorrelation → Lorentzian" — is external literature, corresponding mainly to [E2] A. Demir, A. Mehrotra, and J. Roychowdhury, "Phase Noise in Oscillators: A Unifying Theory and Numerical Methods for Characterization," IEEE Trans. Circuits Syst. I, vol. 47, no. 5, pp. 655–674, May 2000 (DOI: 10.1109/81.847872), not among the 5 source PDFs downloaded on this site (volume/issue/pages/DOI verified; see [E2] in references). [P1] itself obtains 1/f21/f^21/f2 by linearization but never addresses the Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0 divergence; the phase-diffusion model of Demir et al. is exactly the standard tool that fills that gap.
documents.s: Lorentzian Linewidth: Resolving the 1/f² Divergence Paradox at Δf→0

documents.t: Return to the phase integral of [P1] Eq.(11) (see convolution_derivation): ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ.\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau .ϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ. The integral of white noise ini_nin​ is a Wiener process — a Brownian-motion-style random walk. Its key property: no restoring force (the phase is the Floquet λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0 neutral direction, see derivation_floquet_ppv), so the phase never returns to some equilibrium value; it diffuses without bound. Mathematical signature: the variance of integrated white noise grows linearly with time (this is the defining property of a Wiener process). Write the proportionality constant as 2D2D2D: Var⁡[Δϕ(t)]=⟨(ϕ(t+t0)−ϕ(t0))2⟩=2D ∣t∣.\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(t)]=\big\langle(\phi(t+t_0)-\phi(t_0))^2\big\rangle=2D\,|t|.Var[Δϕ(t)]=⟨(ϕ(t+t0​)−ϕ(t0​))2⟩=2D∣t∣. Here DDD is called the phase diffusion constant, in units of rad2/s\text{rad}^2/\text{s}rad2/s (spec 11.2). ∣t∣|t|∣t∣ carries an absolute value because the variance is the same looking forward or backward (stationary increments). Unit check: [Var⁡Δϕ]=rad2[\operatorname{Var}\Delta\phi]=\text{rad}^2[VarΔϕ]=rad2; right-hand side [2D]⋅[t]=(rad2/s)⋅s=rad2[2D]\cdot[t]=(\text{rad}^2/\text{s})\cdot\text{s}=\text{rad}^2[2D]⋅[t]=(rad2/s)⋅s=rad2 ✓. Why linear and not something else: white noise is uncorrelated across time; integrating NNN independent increments makes the variances add linearly, like "summing NNN dice rolls" (N∝tN\propto tN∝t) — this is the origin of the t\sqrt{t}t​ walk and the ttt variance, and it is exactly the same thing as σΔt∝Δt\sigma_{\Delta t}\propto\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​∝Δt​ in numerical_feeling (accumulated jitter is the time-domain version of the phase walk). This step already exposes the seed of the paradox: the 1/f21/f^21/f2 derivation treats ϕ\phiϕ as "small, linearizable, bounded"; but the real ϕ\phiϕ is an unbounded walk. When you ask "what happens infinitely close to the carrier (Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0, i.e., observing infinitely long, t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞)", ϕ\phiϕ has long since wandered to ≫1\gg 1≫1 rad and the linearization has broken down. So the divergence is not physics — it is an approximation used where it fails.
documents.s: Step 0: The root of the problem — the phase is a random walk, not a fixed value

documents.t: Write the carrier as (the pure-phase version of [P1] Eq.(1); amplitude AAA held constant, phase only): x(t)=Acos⁡(ω0t+ϕ(t)).x(t)=A\cos\big(\omega_0 t+\phi(t)\big).x(t)=Acos(ω0​t+ϕ(t)). We want its autocorrelation function (the average product of the signal with itself delayed by τ\tauτ): Rx(τ)=⟨x(t) x(t+τ)⟩.R_x(\tau)=\big\langle x(t)\,x(t+\tau)\big\rangle .Rx​(τ)=⟨x(t)x(t+τ)⟩. Step (i): expand the two cosines with the product-to-sum identity. Let Δϕ≡ϕ(t+τ)−ϕ(t)\Delta\phi\equiv\phi(t+\tau)-\phi(t)Δϕ≡ϕ(t+τ)−ϕ(t): x(t)x(t+τ)=A2cos⁡(ω0t+ϕ(t))cos⁡(ω0(t+τ)+ϕ(t+τ)).x(t)x(t+\tau)=A^2\cos(\omega_0t+\phi(t))\cos(\omega_0(t+\tau)+\phi(t+\tau)).x(t)x(t+τ)=A2cos(ω0​t+ϕ(t))cos(ω0​(t+τ)+ϕ(t+τ)). Using cos⁡αcos⁡β=12[cos⁡(α−β)+cos⁡(α+β)]\cos\alpha\cos\beta=\tfrac12[\cos(\alpha-\beta)+\cos(\alpha+\beta)]cosαcosβ=21​[cos(α−β)+cos(α+β)]: x(t)x(t+τ)=A22[cos⁡(ω0τ+Δϕ)+cos⁡(2ω0t+ω0τ+ϕ(t)+ϕ(t+τ))].x(t)x(t+\tau)=\frac{A^2}{2}\Big[\cos\big(\omega_0\tau+\Delta\phi\big)+\cos\big(2\omega_0t+\omega_0\tau+\phi(t)+\phi(t+\tau)\big)\Big].x(t)x(t+τ)=2A2​[cos(ω0​τ+Δϕ)+cos(2ω0​t+ω0​τ+ϕ(t)+ϕ(t+τ))]. The slow term cos⁡(ω0τ+Δϕ)\cos(\omega_0\tau+\Delta\phi)cos(ω0​τ+Δϕ) is independent of absolute time ttt (it contains only τ\tauτ and the phase difference) and survives the averaging. The fast term contains 2ω0t2\omega_0t2ω0​t; time-averaging over ttt (or averaging over the random phase) kills it — it oscillates near 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ and is invisible to any long-term carrier average. Drop it. Hence Rx(τ)=A22⟨cos⁡(ω0τ+Δϕ)⟩.R_x(\tau)=\frac{A^2}{2}\big\langle\cos(\omega_0\tau+\Delta\phi)\big\rangle.Rx​(τ)=2A2​⟨cos(ω0​τ+Δϕ)⟩. Step (ii): move the average inside using the Gaussian characteristic function. Expand cos⁡(ω0τ+Δϕ)=cos⁡ω0τcos⁡Δϕ−sin⁡ω0τsin⁡Δϕ\cos(\omega_0\tau+\Delta\phi)= \cos\omega_0\tau\cos\Delta\phi-\sin\omega_0\tau\sin\Delta\phicos(ω0​τ+Δϕ)=cosω0​τcosΔϕ−sinω0​τsinΔϕ. Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is zero-mean Gaussian (integrated white noise → Gaussian; and the distribution is symmetric, so ⟨sin⁡Δϕ⟩=0\langle\sin\Delta\phi\rangle=0⟨sinΔϕ⟩=0): Rx(τ)=A22[cos⁡ω0τ ⟨cos⁡Δϕ⟩−sin⁡ω0τ ⟨sin⁡Δϕ⟩⏟=0]=A22cos⁡ω0τ ⟨cos⁡Δϕ⟩.R_x(\tau)=\frac{A^2}{2}\Big[\cos\omega_0\tau\,\langle\cos\Delta\phi\rangle-\sin\omega_0\tau\,\underbrace{\langle\sin\Delta\phi\rangle}_{=0}\Big]=\frac{A^2}{2}\cos\omega_0\tau\,\langle\cos\Delta\phi\rangle.Rx​(τ)=2A2​[cosω0​τ⟨cosΔϕ⟩−sinω0​τ=0⟨sinΔϕ⟩​​]=2A2​cosω0​τ⟨cosΔϕ⟩. The remaining ⟨cos⁡Δϕ⟩\langle\cos\Delta\phi\rangle⟨cosΔϕ⟩ uses the Gaussian characteristic function — for a zero-mean Gaussian variable Δϕ∼N(0,σ2)\Delta\phi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)Δϕ∼N(0,σ2), ⟨ejΔϕ⟩=e−σ2/2⟹⟨cos⁡Δϕ⟩=Re⁡⟨ejΔϕ⟩=e−σ2/2.\big\langle e^{j\Delta\phi}\big\rangle=e^{-\sigma^2/2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle\cos\Delta\phi\rangle=\operatorname{Re}\big\langle e^{j\Delta\phi}\big\rangle=e^{-\sigma^2/2}.⟨ejΔϕ⟩=e−σ2/2⟹⟨cosΔϕ⟩=Re⟨ejΔϕ⟩=e−σ2/2. This is the mathematical pivot of this page: for a Gaussian, "the average of a complex exponential" equals "e−12variancee^{-\tfrac12\text{variance}}e−21​variance". Substitute Step 0's σ2=Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]=2D∣τ∣\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]=2D|\tau|σ2=Var[Δϕ(τ)]=2D∣τ∣: ⟨cos⁡Δϕ⟩=e−12⋅2D∣τ∣=e−D∣τ∣.\langle\cos\Delta\phi\rangle=e^{-\tfrac12\cdot 2D|\tau|}=e^{-D|\tau|}.⟨cosΔϕ⟩=e−21​⋅2D∣τ∣=e−D∣τ∣. Step (iii): combine to get the carrier autocorrelation (spec 11.2). Absorb A2A^2A2 into the normalization (adopting the unit-power convention A2/2→12A^2/2\to\tfrac12A2/2→21​, consistent with lab_18): Rx(τ)=12cos⁡(ω0τ) e−D∣τ∣ \boxed{\ R_x(\tau)=\frac{1}{2}\cos(\omega_0\tau)\,e^{-D|\tau|}\ } Rx​(τ)=21​cos(ω0​τ)e−D∣τ∣ ​ Physical meaning: cos⁡(ω0τ)\cos(\omega_0\tau)cos(ω0​τ) is the carrier's own oscillation; e−D∣τ∣e^{-D|\tau|}e−D∣τ∣ is the memory-loss envelope — the longer the separation, the more phase difference accumulates and the smaller ⟨cos⁡Δϕ⟩\langle\cos\Delta\phi\rangle⟨cosΔϕ⟩ gets: the autocorrelation decays exponentially. Larger DDD (fiercer noise) means faster memory loss. Unit check: [D∣τ∣]=(rad2/s)⋅s=rad2[D|\tau|]=(\text{rad}^2/\text{s})\cdot\text{s}=\text{rad}^2[D∣τ∣]=(rad2/s)⋅s=rad2? — note that D∣τ∣D|\tau|D∣τ∣ appears in an exponent and must be dimensionless. The convention here treats the "rad2\text{rad}^2rad2" of DDD as dimensionless (phase is dimensionless radians to begin with), so DDD is effectively [1/s][1/\text{s}][1/s] and D∣τ∣D|\tau|D∣τ∣ is dimensionless ✓. RxR_xRx​ is dimensionless (power-normalized) ✓. Connection to [P1]: [P1] never wrote this e−D∣τ∣e^{-D|\tau|}e−D∣τ∣; it stops at "phase small, linear." Once you admit the phase is an unbounded walk, this exponential decay is the only self-consistent outcome (the core of [E2] Demir 2000).
documents.s: Step 1: Carrier autocorrelation — turning the phase walk into exponential decay via the Gaussian characteristic function

documents.t: Wiener-Khinchin theorem: the power spectral density Sx(ω)S_x(\omega)Sx​(ω) of a stationary random process is the Fourier transform of its autocorrelation Rx(τ)R_x(\tau)Rx​(τ): Sx(ω)=∫−∞∞Rx(τ) e−jωτ dτ.S_x(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}R_x(\tau)\,e^{-j\omega\tau}\,d\tau .Sx​(ω)=∫−∞∞​Rx​(τ)e−jωτdτ. Substitute Step 1's Rx(τ)=12cos⁡(ω0τ)e−D∣τ∣R_x(\tau)=\tfrac12\cos(\omega_0\tau)e^{-D|\tau|}Rx​(τ)=21​cos(ω0​τ)e−D∣τ∣. Splitting cos⁡(ω0τ)=12(ejω0τ+e−jω0τ)\cos(\omega_0\tau)= \tfrac12(e^{j\omega_0\tau}+e^{-j\omega_0\tau})cos(ω0​τ)=21​(ejω0​τ+e−jω0​τ) gives two identical two-sided-exponential transforms, shifted to ±ω0\pm\omega_0±ω0​. We only need the branch around +ω0+\omega_0+ω0​ (near the positive-frequency carrier). The standard transform used (Fourier transform of the two-sided exponential — the canonical Lorentzian pair): ∫−∞∞e−D∣τ∣ e−jΩτ dτ=2DD2+Ω2.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-D|\tau|}\,e^{-j\Omega\tau}\,d\tau=\frac{2D}{D^2+\Omega^2}.∫−∞∞​e−D∣τ∣e−jΩτdτ=D2+Ω22D​. Work it out by hand (split into the τ>0\tau>0τ>0 and τ<0\tau<0τ<0 halves): ∫−∞∞e−D∣τ∣e−jΩτdτ=∫0∞e−(D+jΩ)τdτ+∫0∞e−(D−jΩ)τdτ=1D+jΩ+1D−jΩ=(D−jΩ)+(D+jΩ)D2+Ω2=2DD2+Ω2.\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-D|\tau|}e^{-j\Omega\tau}d\tau &=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-(D+j\Omega)\tau}d\tau+\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-(D-j\Omega)\tau}d\tau\\ &=\frac{1}{D+j\Omega}+\frac{1}{D-j\Omega}=\frac{(D-j\Omega)+(D+j\Omega)}{D^2+\Omega^2}=\frac{2D}{D^2+\Omega^2}. \end{aligned}∫−∞∞​e−D∣τ∣e−jΩτdτ​=∫0∞​e−(D+jΩ)τdτ+∫0∞​e−(D−jΩ)τdτ=D+jΩ1​+D−jΩ1​=D2+Ω2(D−jΩ)+(D+jΩ)​=D2+Ω22D​.​ Let the offset angular frequency near the carrier be Ω=ω−ω0≡Δω\Omega=\omega-\omega_0\equiv\Delta\omegaΩ=ω−ω0​≡Δω (absorbing the ejω0τe^{j\omega_0\tau}ejω0​τ branch of the cos⁡\coscos, which amounts to shifting the frequency origin to the carrier), and carry the RxR_xRx​ prefactor 12⋅12=14\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac1421​⋅21​=41​: Sx(Δω)∝DD2+Δω2 (Lorentzian, spec 11.2).\boxed{\ S_x(\Delta\omega)\propto\frac{D}{D^2+\Delta\omega^2}\ }\qquad(\textbf{Lorentzian, spec 11.2}). Sx​(Δω)∝D2+Δω2D​ ​(Lorentzian, spec 11.2). This is the Lorentzian: a bell-shaped line centered on the carrier, with a finite peak, symmetric left and right. See how the divergence is gone: as Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0, Sx→D/D2=1/DS_x\to D/D^2=1/DSx​→D/D2=1/D — finite! The peak is 1/D1/D1/D, not infinity. The divergence is cured. Unit/shape check: the two denominator terms D2+Δω2D^2+\Delta\omega^2D2+Δω2 share the same dimension (both [s−2][\text{s}^{-2}][s−2]), so the shape of the ratio is correct; the overall constant is fixed by total-power normalization (see Step 4).
documents.s: Step 2: Wiener-Khinchin — exponentially decaying autocorrelation ⇒ Lorentzian spectrum

documents.t: When Δω≫D\Delta\omega\gg DΔω≫D (far enough from the carrier), the denominator D2+Δω2≈Δω2D^2+\Delta\omega^2\approx\Delta\omega^2D2+Δω2≈Δω2: Sx(Δω)→Δω≫DDΔω2∝1Δω2.S_x(\Delta\omega)\xrightarrow[\Delta\omega\gg D]{}\frac{D}{\Delta\omega^2}\propto\frac{1}{\Delta\omega^2}.Sx​(Δω)Δω≫D​Δω2D​∝Δω21​. The far-offset asymptote is exactly 1/f21/f^21/f2 — in full agreement with [P1] Eq.(21). So the Lorentzian does not overturn [P1]; it embeds [P1]'s 1/f21/f^21/f2 into a complete lineshape that flattens near the carrier: 1/f21/f^21/f2 far out, flat close in, with the corner at Δω≈D\Delta\omega\approx DΔω≈D. The figure below overlays all three (simulation / Lorentzian theory / 1/f21/f^21/f2 asymptote).
documents.s: Why the far offset returns to 1/f21/f^21/f2 (consistent with [P1])

documents.t: The Lorentzian's full width at half maximum (FWHM) is what engineers call the "3-dB linewidth" or simply the "linewidth." Find it: the peak at Δω=0\Delta\omega=0Δω=0 is D/D2=1/DD/D^2=1/DD/D2=1/D; at half maximum Sx=12⋅1DS_x=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac1DSx​=21​⋅D1​: DD2+Δω2=12D⟹D2+Δω2=2D2⟹Δω=±D.\frac{D}{D^2+\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{1}{2D}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D^2+\Delta\omega^2=2D^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Delta\omega=\pm D.D2+Δω2D​=2D1​⟹D2+Δω2=2D2⟹Δω=±D. So the half-maximum points sit at Δω=±D\Delta\omega=\pm DΔω=±D (rad/s). HWHM (half width): ΔωHWHM=D\Delta\omega_{\text{HWHM}}=DΔωHWHM​=D rad/s ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ ΔfHWHM=D2π\Delta f_{\text{HWHM}}=\dfrac{D}{2\pi}ΔfHWHM​=2πD​ Hz. FWHM (3-dB full width): twice the HWHM, ΔωFWHM=2D\Delta\omega_{\text{FWHM}}=2DΔωFWHM​=2D rad/s ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ Δf3dB=2D2π=Dπ Hz (spec 11.2).\boxed{\ \Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\frac{2D}{2\pi}=\frac{D}{\pi}\ \text{Hz}\ }\qquad(\textbf{spec 11.2}). Δf3dB​=2π2D​=πD​ Hz ​(spec 11.2). Physical meaning: larger DDD (fiercer noise, faster phase amnesia) means a wider linewidth and a "fatter" carrier. An ideal noiseless oscillator has D→0D\to0D→0 → linewidth →0\to0→0 → it degenerates into a delta line (pure carrier). Unit check: [D/π]=(1/s)/(dimensionless)=Hz[D/\pi]=(1/\text{s})/(\text{dimensionless})=\text{Hz}[D/π]=(1/s)/(dimensionless)=Hz ✓. Where "3 dB" comes from: half height === half power =10log⁡10(1/2)=−3.01=10\log_{10}(1/2)=-3.01=10log10​(1/2)=−3.01 dB, hence "3-dB linewidth."
documents.s: Step 3: 3-dB linewidth (FWHM) = D/π

documents.t: The most fatal consequence of the near-carrier 1/f21/f^21/f2 divergence: integrating 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 from 000 diverges (∫0d(Δω)/Δω2=∞\int_0 d(\Delta\omega)/\Delta\omega^2=\infty∫0​d(Δω)/Δω2=∞), which would say the phase-noise power is infinite. The Lorentzian cures this, because the Lorentzian's integral converges. Using the standard integral ∫−∞∞dΩD2+Ω2=πD\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\dfrac{d\Omega}{D^2+\Omega^2}=\dfrac{\pi}{D}∫−∞∞​D2+Ω2dΩ​=Dπ​: ∫−∞∞DD2+Δω2 d(Δω)=D⋅πD=π(finite).\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{D}{D^2+\Delta\omega^2}\,d(\Delta\omega)=D\cdot\frac{\pi}{D}=\pi\quad(\text{finite}).∫−∞∞​D2+Δω2D​d(Δω)=D⋅Dπ​=π(finite). Physical meaning: summing the power over all offsets gives a finite constant — exactly equal to the carrier's total power (after proper normalization). The phase walk merely smears the power originally concentrated in a delta line into a Lorentzian of finite width; no total power is lost (energy conservation). This is "total power conservation" (the key teaching point of spec 11.2). Compare with the delta line: as D→0D\to0D→0 the Lorentzian →π δ(Δω)\to\pi\,\delta(\Delta\omega)→πδ(Δω) (infinitely tall and thin), degenerating back into the ideal carrier; for D>0D > 0D>0 it is flattened into a finite peak. The power never diverged — it was only redistributed. The paradox resolved in one sentence: the 1/f21/f^21/f2 divergence is a "false divergence" — it comes from forcing the unbounded phase walk into a bounded linear approximation. The real spectrum must flatten into a Lorentzian near the carrier (peak =1/D=1/D=1/D, width =D/π=D/\pi=D/π, total power === carrier power, conserved). [P1] Eq.(21)'s 1/f21/f^21/f2 holds only for Δω≫D\Delta\omega\gg DΔω≫D; it is the Lorentzian's far tail.
documents.s: Step 4: Total power conservation — the Lorentzian flattens the infinity into a finite integral

documents.t: Now connect the abstract DDD back to [P1]'s ISF quantities. Matching "the two expressions for the near-carrier 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt" pins down DDD. From the Lorentzian side: far out, Sx→D/Δω2S_x\to D/\Delta\omega^2Sx​→D/Δω2. Write it as a phase PSD — the double-sided phase PSD of a Wiener phase (Var=2D∣t∣\mathrm{Var}=2D|t|Var=2D∣t∣) is 2D/Δω22D/\Delta\omega^22D/Δω2; this site keeps its books in single-sided PSD throughout (consistent with jitter_kernels), so Sϕ(Δω)=4DΔω2[rad2/Hz] (single-sided).S_\phi(\Delta\omega)=\frac{4D}{\Delta\omega^2}\qquad[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]\ (\text{single-sided}).Sϕ​(Δω)=Δω24D​[rad2/Hz] (single-sided). From the ISF side (the clean time-domain version from the previous page, Sϕ=Γrms2Si/(qmax2Δω2)S_\phi=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(q_{max}^2\Delta\omega^2)Sϕ​=Γrms2​Si​/(qmax2​Δω2), writing Si=in2‾/ΔfS_i=\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fSi​=in2​​/Δf): Sϕ(Δω)=Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/ΔfΔω2.S_\phi(\Delta\omega)=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{\Delta\omega^2}.Sϕ​(Δω)=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δω2in2​​/Δf​. Set them equal (same 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 skirt, so the coefficients must match): 4D=Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾Δf⟹ D=Γrms24qmax2⋅in2‾Δf=κ22 (spec 11.2, v5 corrected).4D=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\boxed{\ D=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{4q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=\frac{\kappa^2}{2}\ }\qquad(\textbf{spec 11.2, v5 corrected}).4D=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δfin2​​​⟹ D=4qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δfin2​​​=2κ2​ ​(spec 11.2, v5 corrected). Substituting into Step 3's linewidth formula gives the 3-dB linewidth directly in ISF quantities: Δf3dB=Dπ=Γrms24π qmax2⋅in2‾Δf=κ22π (spec 11.2, v5 corrected).\boxed{\ \Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\frac{D}{\pi}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{4\pi\,q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=\frac{\kappa^2}{2\pi}\ }\qquad(\textbf{spec 11.2, v5 corrected}). Δf3dB​=πD​=4πqmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δfin2​​​=2πκ2​ ​(spec 11.2, v5 corrected). Design message: linewidth ∝Γrms2/qmax2⋅Si\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2\cdot S_i∝Γrms2​/qmax2​⋅Si​ — the same set of knobs as [P1] Eq.(21)'s L\mathcal{L}L! For a narrow linewidth (a clean carrier), you still increase the charge swing qmaxq_{max}qmax​, suppress Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, and lower the noise PSD SiS_iSi​. The Lorentzian introduces no new knob; it merely repackages the same physical quantities into "linewidth," a directly measurable number. Unit check: [D]=1C2⋅A2Hz=A2A2s2⋅s=1s[D]=\dfrac{1}{\text{C}^2}\cdot\dfrac{\text{A}^2}{\text{Hz}}=\dfrac{\text{A}^2}{\text{A}^2\text{s}^2}\cdot\text{s}=\dfrac{1}{\text{s}}[D]=C21​⋅HzA2​=A2s2A2​⋅s=s1​ (using C=A⋅s\text{C}=\text{A}\cdot\text{s}C=A⋅s and Hz−1=s\text{Hz}^{-1}=\text{s}Hz−1=s) ✓, so D/πD/\piD/π is in Hz ✓. Factor-of-2 note (the clean version after the v5 correction): DDD is a physical quantity (the decay rate of RxR_xRx​, κ2/2\kappa^2/2κ2/2) and is independent of the bookkeeping convention for L\mathcal{L}L. Only L\mathcal{L}L changes: the clean time-domain version is L=2D/Δω2=κ2/Δω2\mathcal{L}=2D/\Delta\omega^2=\kappa^2/\Delta\omega^2L=2D/Δω2=κ2/Δω2; [P1] Eq.(21)'s SSB /4/4/4 version is L=D/Δω2\mathcal{L}=D/\Delta\omega^2L=D/Δω2 — the famous 3 dB lives in L\mathcal{L}L, not in DDD. (v3 had mistakenly stuffed κ2\kappa^2κ2 into D/πD/\piD/π as if it were DDD, making the linewidth 2× too large; fixed in v5 — MC adjudication in diffusion_dictionary and lab_23.) This page is consistent with lab_18 throughout (lab_18 generates directly with Var=2D dt\mathrm{Var}=2D\,dtVar=2Ddt, so the mechanism check is unaffected by the mapping).

documents.t: simulations/lab_18_lorentzian.py synthesizes a carrier x=cos⁡(2πf0t+ϕ)x=\cos(2\pi f_0t+\phi)x=cos(2πf0​t+ϕ) from a segment of Wiener phase (accumulated white noise, ϕ=cumsum⁡(N(0,2D dt))\phi=\operatorname{cumsum}(\text{N}(0,2D\,dt))ϕ=cumsum(N(0,2Ddt))), estimates its spectrum with Welch, and overlays the Lorentzian theory and the 1/f21/f^21/f2 asymptote; the right panel directly measures Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]Var[Δϕ(τ)] to verify its linear growth (=2Dτ=2D\tau=2Dτ). Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Titles read: "載波是 Lorentzian：近載波轉平（有限峰），1/f² 只是遠端漸近" = the carrier is Lorentzian: it flattens near the carrier (a finite peak), 1/f² is only the far-out asymptote; "相位是 random walk：方差線性成長 → 載波自相關指數衰減" = phase is a random walk: variance grows linearly → the carrier autocorrelation decays exponentially. Item Value (lab_18) Notes Model toy / illustrative (not transistor-level) Wiener phase synthesized directly, labeled in normalized units Carrier f0f_0f0​ 400400400 (normalized) Arbitrary carrier; only the relative offset matters Phase diffusion DDD 2.0 rad2/s2.0\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}2.0 rad2/s The single knob controlling the linewidth Phase increment dϕ∼N(0, 2D/fs)d\phi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\,2D/f_s)dϕ∼N(0,2D/fs​) Wiener: variance =2D dt=2D\,dt=2Ddt 3-dB linewidth Δf3dB=D/π≈0.64\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=D/\pi\approx0.64Δf3dB​=D/π≈0.64 Hz FWHM; HWHM =D/2π≈0.32=D/2\pi\approx0.32=D/2π≈0.32 Hz Near carrier Flattens into a finite peak ∝1/D\propto1/D∝1/D No longer diverges Far from carrier ∝1/Δf2\propto1/\Delta f^2∝1/Δf2 asymptote Consistent with [P1] Eq.(21) How to read the left panel: at large offsets, the blue curve (simulated spectrum) slides down along the red dotted line (1/Δf21/\Delta f^21/Δf2 asymptote); approaching the carrier, the blue curve departs from 1/f21/f^21/f2, hugs the black dashed line (Lorentzian), and flattens; the green dash-dot line marks the HWHM =D/2π=D/2\pi=D/2π position — exactly where the corner happens. One glance at this figure says it all: 1/f21/f^21/f2 is the tail; the Lorentzian is the whole picture. How to read the right panel: the measured Var⁡[Δϕ(τ)]\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi(\tau)]Var[Δϕ(τ)] (blue) lands precisely on the 2Dτ2D\tau2Dτ line (black dashed), confirming that the phase really is a linearly diffusing random walk — the very root of the exponential autocorrelation and hence the Lorentzian.
