documents.t: The figure above is the white-FM case; beyond_lorentzian proves that under flicker FM the same machinery yields a near-Gaussian line core instead of a Lorentzian, with linewidths that can differ by two orders of magnitude for the same spec point. The widget below overlays both lineshapes on the same axes and lets you sweep a spectrum analyzer's resolution bandwidth (RBW) — see for yourself how the "flattening" gets smeared away by the instrument's own resolution once the RBW is too wide: Lineshape explorer: same L(f_ref) spec, two noise colors, RBW smearing Dominant near-carrier noise: White FM (Lorentzian)Flicker FM (near-Gaussian, approx.) L(10 kHz)-71.0 dBc/Hz RBW (log)100 = 100 Hz -3.0k-1.5k01.5k3.0k00.51offset from carrier Δf (Hz)normalized powertrue lineshapemeasured (RBW-convolved) FWHM_true 49.9 Hz apparent width @ this RBW 130 Hz RBW 100 Hz Model: a single spec point, L at 10 kHz (time-domain "/2" convention), is mapped to the near-carrier lineshape two ways. White FM(lorentzian_linewidth.md): unilateral S_phi = 4D / Delta-omega^2 fixes the phase diffusion constant D, giving an exact Lorentzian with FWHM = D/pi. Flicker FM(beyond_lorentzian.md Part A): b_-3 = S_phi times f_ref^3 fixes the 1/f^3 level; with a low-frequency cutoff f_l = 1/32 Hz (an observation-time artifact, not a device parameter — the page shows the dependence on f_l is only logarithmic), the frozen-log Gaussian-envelope approximation gives FWHM ≈ 2·sqrt(2 ln 2)·sqrt(b_-3 · L*) — an approximation the page itself quotes as roughly 2% off the exact numeric Fourier transform, not an exact result. Both curves are then convolved (direct 512-point discrete convolution, no FFT) with a Gaussian resolution-bandwidth kernel of FWHM = RBW to produce the "measured" trace. Toy/illustrative: real spectrum analyzers, cross-correlation instruments, and residual white-FM skirts (see beyond_lorentzian.md) all modify this picture further. How to read it: fix a single spec point L(10 kHz)\mathcal{L}(10\,\text{kHz})L(10kHz) and toggle white FM / flicker FM to see how different FWHM_true is (tens-to-hundreds of Hz for white FM versus thousands of Hz for flicker FM — up to a hundredfold difference for the same number); then drag the RBW slider to the right and watch when the gray dashed curve (true lineshape) and the blue solid curve (RBW-convolved "measured" trace) part ways — once RBW is much larger than the linewidth, all you measure is a wide, featureless hump, and the flattening / near-Gaussian shoulder information is gone. Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Keeping the explorer at its default settings (L(10 kHz) = −71 dBc/Hz, white FM, RBW = 100 Hz), what FWHM does the panel measure (after RBW convolution)? HzCheckShow answer Graded correct within ±5% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Verification: reproducing the panel's measured FWHM (mirrors LineshapeExplorer.js's whiteLineshape / buildGrid / gaussKernel / convolveSame / fwhmOfCurve) import numpy as np TWO_PI = 2 * np.pi N_GRID = 512 F_REF = 10e3 # LineshapeExplorer.js F_REF def white_lineshape(Sphi_at_fref, fref): # .js whiteLineshape() dw = TWO_PI * fref D = Sphi_at_fref * dw * dw / 4 fwhm = D / np.pi return D, fwhm, (lambda df: D / (D**2 + (TWO_PI * df)**2)) def build_grid(fwhm_for_span, n_pts): # .js buildGrid() span = max(30 * fwhm_for_span, 5) df = (2 * span) / (n_pts - 1) freqs = np.array([-span + i * df for i in range(n_pts)]) return freqs, df def gauss_kernel(rbw_hz, df): # .js gaussKernel() sigma = rbw_hz / (2 * np.sqrt(2 * np.log(2))) half = max(1, round((4 * sigma) / df)) xs = (np.arange(2 * half + 1) - half) * df k = np.exp(-0.5 * (xs / sigma) ** 2) return k / k.sum() def convolve_same(sig, kernel): # .js convolveSame() n_ = len(sig) m_ = len(kernel) half = (m_ - 1) // 2 out = np.zeros(n_) for i in range(n_): acc = 0.0 for j in range(m_): idx = i + (j - half) if 0 <= idx < n_: acc += sig[idx] * kernel[j] out[i] = acc return out def fwhm_of_curve(freqs, curve): # .js fwhmOfCurve() i_peak = int(np.argmax(curve)) peak = curve[i_peak] half = peak / 2 i_l = 0 for i in range(i_peak, 0, -1): if curve[i] < half: i_l = i break i_r = len(curve) - 1 for i in range(i_peak, len(curve) - 1): if curve[i] < half: i_r = i break f_l = freqs[i_l] + (half - curve[i_l]) / (curve[i_l+1] - curve[i_l]) * (freqs[i_l+1] - freqs[i_l]) f_r = freqs[i_r-1] + (half - curve[i_r-1]) / (curve[i_r] - curve[i_r-1]) * (freqs[i_r] - freqs[i_r-1]) return f_r - f_l # widget defaults: L_dbc=-71.0, noiseType='white', logRbw=2.0 -> RBW=100 Hz (LineshapeExplorer.js:196-198) L_dbc = -71.0 rbw = 10 ** 2.0 Llin = 10 ** (L_dbc / 10) Sphi = 2 * Llin # time-domain /2 convention D, true_fwhm, curve_fn = white_lineshape(Sphi, F_REF) span_fwhm = max(true_fwhm, rbw) freqs, df = build_grid(span_fwhm, N_GRID) raw_true = np.array([curve_fn(f) for f in freqs]) true_curve = raw_true / raw_true.max() kernel = gauss_kernel(rbw, df) raw_measured = convolve_same(true_curve, kernel) measured_curve = raw_measured / raw_measured.max() apparent_fwhm = fwhm_of_curve(freqs, measured_curve) print("true FWHM =", round(true_fwhm, 1), "Hz") print("apparent (RBW-convolved) FWHM =", round(apparent_fwhm, 1), "Hz") # -> 130.0 Core Python (full script: simulations/lab_18_lorentzian.py): import numpy as np from scipy.signal import welch RNG = np.random.default_rng(18) fs, n, f0, D = 4096.0, 2**20, 400.0, 2.0 # D = phase diffusion [rad^2/s] t = np.arange(n) / fs # Wiener phase: increments ~ N(0, 2 D dt) -> Var[phi(t)] = 2 D t dphi = RNG.standard_normal(n) * np.sqrt(2 * D / fs) phi = np.cumsum(dphi) x = np.cos(2 * np.pi * f0 * t + phi) f, P = welch(x, fs=fs, nperseg=2**16, scaling="density") # spectrum: the carrier is a Lorentzian off = f - f0 lor = D / (D**2 + (2 * np.pi * off)**2) # Lorentzian theory fwhm = D / np.pi # 3-dB linewidth = D/pi Hz

documents.t: Both problems follow the strict format: problem → step-by-step substitution (with units) → result → dimension check → one-line Python verification. Example 1 works backward from a "real PN spec" to DDD and the linewidth (the most design-flavored calculation); Example 2 works forward from the ISF quantities. Intuition check: a 5 GHz oscillator at −100-100−100 dBc/Hz@1MHz actually has a carrier that is a Lorentzian about 0.63 kHz wide — a fractional linewidth of 1.26×10−71.26\times10^{-7}1.26×10−7 relative to the 5 GHz carrier (equivalent to a QQQ on the order of ∼8×106\sim 8\times10^6∼8×106). If the measurement resolution bandwidth (RBW) is far wider than 0.63 kHz, what you see is a "spike" smeared flat by the RBW, and the Lorentzian flattening is completely invisible; to see it you need ∼100\sim100∼100 Hz-class RBW or cross-correlation methods. This is why everyday PN plots show only 1/f21/f^21/f2 and never the Lorentzian plateau — the measurement resolution cannot get close enough to the carrier. documents.t: The 1/f21/f^21/f2 divergence at Δω→0\Delta\omega\to0Δω→0 is a false divergence: it comes from forcing an unbounded phase random walk into a linear approximation. The phase is a Wiener process: Var⁡[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\phi]=2D|t|Var[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣ (DDD = phase diffusion, rad2/s\text{rad}^2/\text{s}rad2/s). Gaussian characteristic function ⟨ejΔϕ⟩=e−σ2/2\langle e^{j\Delta\phi}\rangle=e^{-\sigma^2/2}⟨ejΔϕ⟩=e−σ2/2 → carrier autocorrelation Rx(τ)=12cos⁡(ω0τ)e−D∣τ∣R_x(\tau)=\tfrac12\cos(\omega_0\tau)e^{-D|\tau|}Rx​(τ)=21​cos(ω0​τ)e−D∣τ∣. Wiener-Khinchin → Lorentzian S∝DD2+Δω2S\propto\dfrac{D}{D^2+\Delta\omega^2}S∝D2+Δω2D​: flattens near the carrier (peak =1/D=1/D=1/D, no divergence), returns to 1/f21/f^21/f2 far out, total power conserved (integral =π=\pi=π, finite). 3-dB linewidth Δf3dB=Dπ\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\dfrac{D}{\pi}Δf3dB​=πD​ Hz; ISF link D=Γrms24qmax2in2‾Δf=κ22D=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{4q_{max}^2}\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=\dfrac{\kappa^2}{2}D=4qmax2​Γrms2​​Δfin2​​​=2κ2​, so linewidth =Γrms24πqmax2in2‾Δf=κ22π=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{4\pi q_{max}^2}\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=\dfrac{\kappa^2}{2\pi}=4πqmax2​Γrms2​​Δfin2​​​=2πκ2​ — the same knobs as L\mathcal{L}L (v5-corrected mapping). Canonical: 5 GHz, −100-100−100 dBc/Hz@1MHz → D≈1.97×103 rad2/sD\approx1.97\times10^3\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}D≈1.97×103 rad2/s, linewidth ≈628\approx628≈628 Hz; representative-value ISF example → D=0.0625D=0.0625D=0.0625, linewidth ≈20\approx20≈20 mHz (true LC: D=0.125D=0.125D=0.125, ≈40\approx40≈40 mHz). documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: fourier_series_of_isf | Next: lorentzian_linewidth The previous page, fourier_series_of_isf, decomposed the ISF into a set of Fourier coefficients c0,c1,c2,…c_0,c_1,c_2,\dotsc0​,c1​,c2​,… and showed that each cnc_ncn​ folds the noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ back onto the carrier. This page answers: When the device noise is flat white noise and the contributions of all bands must be summed, can a single number describe the entire ISF's contribution to phase noise? It can — that number is the rms value of the ISF, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, tied to the sum of squared coefficients by Parseval's theorem ([P1] Eq.(20), p.185): ∑n=0∞cn2=1π∫02π∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2 Γrms2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma(x)|^2dx=2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2n=0∑∞​cn2​=π1​∫02π​∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2Γrms2​ Physical intuition (conclusion first): white noise is equally strong in every nω0n\omega_0nω0​ band, so the "total folded-back power" is proportional to the sum of the squares of all coefficients, ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​. Parseval tells us this sum equals twice the mean square of the ISF over one period, i.e. 2Γrms22\Gamma_{rms}^22Γrms2​. The messy band-by-band summation thus collapses into one clean shape metric, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ — which (together with qmaxq_{max}qmax​) sets the level of the 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise. Intuitively: the "quieter" the ISF is overall (the smaller its rms), the less sensitive the oscillator is to white noise.
documents.s: The rms ISF and the Parseval Relation

documents.t: Parseval's theorem states: the mean square of a periodic function over one period equals the sum of the mean squares of its Fourier components. For the standard cos/sin expansion Γ(x)=a02+∑n≥1[ancos⁡nx+bnsin⁡nx]\Gamma(x)=\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n\ge1}[a_n\cos nx+b_n\sin nx]Γ(x)=2a0​​+∑n≥1​[an​cosnx+bn​sinnx]: 12π∫02π∣Γ(x)∣2 dx=(a02)2+12∑n=1∞(an2+bn2).\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma(x)|^2\,dx =\left(\frac{a_0}{2}\right)^2+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(a_n^2+b_n^2).2π1​∫02π​∣Γ(x)∣2dx=(2a0​​)2+21​n=1∑∞​(an2​+bn2​). Math used: the basis {1,cos⁡nx,sin⁡nx}\{1,\cos nx,\sin nx\}{1,cosnx,sinnx} is orthogonal. After expanding ∣Γ∣2|\Gamma|^2∣Γ∣2, all cross terms such as ∫cos⁡mxcos⁡nx dx\int\cos mx\cos nx\,dx∫cosmxcosnxdx (m≠nm\neq nm=n) integrate to 0; only the "self-with-self" terms survive. Where each term's coefficient comes from: 12π∫02πcos⁡2(nx) dx=12\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2(nx)\,dx=\dfrac122π1​∫02π​cos2(nx)dx=21​ (n≥1n\ge1n≥1), so each ancos⁡nxa_n\cos nxan​cosnx contributes 12an2\dfrac12 a_n^221​an2​ to the mean square; the constant term a02\dfrac{a_0}{2}2a0​​ has mean square (a02)2\left(\dfrac{a_0}{2}\right)^2(2a0​​)2 (the mean square of a constant is its own square — no 12\frac1221​). This factor difference between the DC and AC terms is the single most error-prone spot in the entire derivation; Step 4 is devoted to it. Step-by-step algebra (killing the cross terms one at a time, no skipped steps): first expand the square of Γ\GammaΓ in full, then integrate class by class. 12π∫02π∣Γ∣2dx=12π∫02π ⁣[a02+∑m≥1(amcos⁡mx+bmsin⁡mx)]2dx=12π∫02π(a02)2dx⏟(I) DC×DC+12π∫02π2⋅a02∑m≥1(amcos⁡mx+bmsin⁡mx) dx⏟(II) DC×AC+12π∫02π[∑m≥1(amcos⁡mx+bmsin⁡mx)]2dx⏟(III) AC×AC.\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma|^2dx &=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\left[\frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{m\ge1}(a_m\cos mx+b_m\sin mx)\right]^2 dx\\ &=\underbrace{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(\frac{a_0}{2}\right)^2 dx}_{\text{(I) DC×DC}} +\underbrace{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}2\cdot\frac{a_0}{2}\sum_{m\ge1}(a_m\cos mx+b_m\sin mx)\,dx}_{\text{(II) DC×AC}}\\ &\quad+\underbrace{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Big[\sum_{m\ge1}(a_m\cos mx+b_m\sin mx)\Big]^2 dx}_{\text{(III) AC×AC}}. \end{aligned}2π1​∫02π​∣Γ∣2dx​=2π1​∫02π​[2a0​​+m≥1∑​(am​cosmx+bm​sinmx)]2dx=(I) DC×DC2π1​∫02π​(2a0​​)2dx​​+(II) DC×AC2π1​∫02π​2⋅2a0​​m≥1∑​(am​cosmx+bm​sinmx)dx​​+(III) AC×AC2π1​∫02π​[m≥1∑​(am​cosmx+bm​sinmx)]2dx​​.​ Term by term (with the orthogonality used at each step called out): (I): the integrand is a constant, 12π∫02π(a02)2dx=(a02)2\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(\dfrac{a_0}{2}\right)^2dx=\left(\dfrac{a_0}{2}\right)^22π1​∫02π​(2a0​​)2dx=(2a0​​)2. (II): every ∫02πcos⁡mx dx=∫02πsin⁡mx dx=0\int_0^{2\pi}\cos mx\,dx=\int_0^{2\pi}\sin mx\,dx=0∫02π​cosmxdx=∫02π​sinmxdx=0 (m≥1m\ge1m≥1), so the whole block = 0. This is "the constant is orthogonal to every harmonic." (III): expanding the square produces three kinds of integrals. First, ∫02πcos⁡mxcos⁡nx dx=π δmn\int_0^{2\pi}\cos mx\cos nx\,dx=\pi\,\delta_{mn}∫02π​cosmxcosnxdx=πδmn​ and ∫02πsin⁡mxsin⁡nx dx=π δmn\int_0^{2\pi}\sin mx\sin nx\,dx=\pi\,\delta_{mn}∫02π​sinmxsinnxdx=πδmn​ (m,n≥1m,n\ge1m,n≥1); second, ∫02πcos⁡mxsin⁡nx dx=0\int_0^{2\pi}\cos mx\sin nx\,dx=0∫02π​cosmxsinnxdx=0 (all of these vanish — cos and sin are mutually orthogonal). Only the m=nm=nm=n "self-with-self" terms survive, each weighted 12π⋅π=12\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\pi=\dfrac122π1​⋅π=21​: (III)=12∑n≥1(an2+bn2).\text{(III)}=\frac12\sum_{n\ge1}(a_n^2+b_n^2).(III)=21​n≥1∑​(an2​+bn2​). Collecting (I)+(II)+(III) recovers the line above, (a02)2+12∑n≥1(an2+bn2)\left(\frac{a_0}{2}\right)^2+\frac12\sum_{n\ge1}(a_n^2+b_n^2)(2a0​​)2+21​∑n≥1​(an2​+bn2​). The soul of the whole passage is one sentence: the basis is orthogonal, so the squared integral keeps only the "diagonal" terms.
documents.s: Step 1: Parseval's theorem — time-domain energy = sum of squared frequency-domain coefficients

documents.t: Use the correspondence from the previous page: cn2=an2+bn2c_n^2=a_n^2+b_n^2cn2​=an2​+bn2​ (n≥1n\ge1n≥1), and the DC coefficient c0≡a0c_0\equiv a_0c0​≡a0​. Substituting into Step 1: 12π∫02π∣Γ∣2 dx=(c02)2+12∑n=1∞cn2=c024+12∑n=1∞cn2.\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma|^2\,dx =\left(\frac{c_0}{2}\right)^2+\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n^2 =\frac{c_0^2}{4}+\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n^2.2π1​∫02π​∣Γ∣2dx=(2c0​​)2+21​n=1∑∞​cn2​=4c02​​+21​n=1∑∞​cn2​. Simplification trick: note that c024=12⋅c022\dfrac{c_0^2}{4}=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{c_0^2}{2}4c02​​=21​⋅2c02​​. To fold DC into the same summation, Hajimiri–Lee adopt the bookkeeping "c0c_0c0​ carries half weight inside the sum" — i.e. the n=0n=0n=0 term contributes 12⋅c022\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{c_0^2}{2}21​⋅2c02​​. The next step shows this is exactly what lets the total be written in its cleanest form.
documents.s: Step 2: switching to the amplitude–phase coefficients cnc_ncn​

documents.t: Multiply both sides of Step 2 by 2: 1π∫02π∣Γ∣2 dx=c022+∑n=1∞cn2.\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma|^2\,dx =\frac{c_0^2}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n^2.π1​∫02π​∣Γ∣2dx=2c02​​+n=1∑∞​cn2​. In [P1] Eq.(20), Hajimiri–Lee define the left side as 2Γrms22\Gamma_{rms}^22Γrms2​ and write the right side as ∑n=0∞cn2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2∑n=0∞​cn2​ — i.e. by convention the n=0n=0n=0 term inside the sum stands for c022\dfrac{c_0^2}{2}2c02​​ (not c02c_0^2c02​). This yields the signature equation at the top of this page: ∑n=0∞cn2=1π∫02π∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2 Γrms2 [P1] Eq.(20), p.185\boxed{\ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma(x)|^2dx=2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2\ }\qquad[\text{P1] Eq.(20), p.185} n=0∑∞​cn2​=π1​∫02π​∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2Γrms2​ ​[P1] Eq.(20), p.185 where Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is simply the root-mean-square of the ISF: Γrms=12π∫02π∣Γ(x)∣2 dx.\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma(x)|^2\,dx}.Γrms​=2π1​∫02π​∣Γ(x)∣2dx​. Dimension check: Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless ⟹ ∣Γ∣2|\Gamma|^2∣Γ∣2 is dimensionless ⟹ dividing the integral by 2π2\pi2π (rad) and taking the square root leaves it dimensionless ✓. cnc_ncn​ is dimensionless too, so both sides agree. This site's Python: gamma_rms(theta, gamma) computes exactly 12π∫02πΓ2\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma^2}2π1​∫02π​Γ2​ (see the simulations/common/isf_utils.py docstring, explicitly matched to Eq.(20)).
documents.s: Step 3: arriving at [P1] Eq.(20) — defining Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​

documents.t: Read this section carefully — otherwise you will be off by a factor when computing the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ([P1] Eq.(24)). Keep the three flavors of "c0c_0c0​" straight: Name Expression Appears in the ISF's DC value (its mean) c02\dfrac{c_0}{2}2c0​​ the constant term in Eq.(12); the single-tone response in Eq.(15) the Fourier DC coefficient c0c_0c0​ (=a0=1π∫02πΓ dx=a_0=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma\,dx=a0​=π1​∫02π​Γdx) the bar chart; the n=0n=0n=0 term of Eq.(20) the n=0n=0n=0 contribution in the Parseval sum c022\dfrac{c_0^2}{2}2c02​​ (not c02c_0^2c02​!) the right side of Eq.(20), ∑n=0∞cn2\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n^2∑n=0∞​cn2​ Why DC enters the sum at "half weight": an AC harmonic cncos⁡(nx+θn)c_n\cos(nx+\theta_n)cn​cos(nx+θn​) has mean square 12cn2\dfrac12 c_n^221​cn2​ (the time average of cosine, ⟨cos⁡2⟩=12\langle\cos^2\rangle=\frac12⟨cos2⟩=21​); but DC is a constant, whose mean square is (c02)2=c024\left(\dfrac{c_0}{2}\right)^2 =\dfrac{c_0^2}{4}(2c0​​)2=4c02​​. For "multiply by 2 and write it as ∑n≥0cn2\sum_{n\ge0}c_n^2∑n≥0​cn2​" to be formally consistent for every nnn, the n=0n=0n=0 term must count only c022\dfrac{c_0^2}{2}2c02​​ (i.e. treat c0c_0c0​ as "half a coefficient" in the rms sum). Teaching reminder: many textbooks (and the notation traps in this site's notation) hammer this point — c0c_0c0​ is the "coefficient"; the DC "value" is c0/2c_0/2c0​/2. The constants in the phase-noise formulas (e.g. c02/8c_0^2/8c02​/8 in Eq.(23), c02/(2Γrms2)c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)c02​/(2Γrms2​) in Eq.(24)) are exactly this factor carried all the way through. Copy the equations from Section 3 of the spec verbatim — do not re-insert factors yourself — and you will not go wrong.

documents.t: Substitute Eq.(20) into the white-noise phase-noise summation ([P1] Eq.(19), p.185): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(in2‾/Δf ∑n=0∞cn28 qmax2 Δω2).\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f\;\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2}{8\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}\right).L{Δω}=10log10​(8qmax2​Δω2in2​​/Δf∑n=0∞​cn2​​). Using ∑n=0∞cn2=2Γrms2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑n=0∞​cn2​=2Γrms2​ to replace ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​, the 888 in the denominator and the 222 in the numerator reduce to 444, giving the signature result ([P1] Eq.(21), p.185): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2).\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right).L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​). How to read it: phase noise is proportional to Γrms2qmax2\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}qmax2​Γrms2​​ and falls with offset Δω\Delta\omegaΔω as 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 (i.e. −20-20−20 dB/dec, the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region). Two design knobs: increase qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (the signal charge swing) and shrink Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (keep the ISF quiet overall). Factor-of-2 teaching note: a clean time-domain "white noise × ISF → integrate" derivation gives Sϕ(f)=Γrms2Si/(qmax2(2πf)2)S_\phi(f)=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(q_{max}^2(2\pi f)^2)Sϕ​(f)=Γrms2​Si​/(qmax2​(2πf)2), corresponding to L=Γrms2Si/(2qmax2Δω2)\mathcal{L}=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(2q_{max}^2\Delta\omega^2)L=Γrms2​Si​/(2qmax2​Δω2); [P1] Eq.(21) writes /(4Δω2)/(4\Delta\omega^2)/(4Δω2). The factor of 2 comes from the SSB (single-sideband) bookkeeping convention — a well-known small dispute in the literature — and does not affect the Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ scaling or the −20-20−20 dB/dec slope. Full discussion in white_noise_to_phase_noise.

documents.t: Take Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ. Method A (integral): Γrms2=12π∫02πsin⁡2θ dθ=12π⋅π=12 ⇒ Γrms=12≈0.707.\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\pi=\frac12 \ \Rightarrow\ \Gamma_{rms}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx0.707.Γrms2​=2π1​∫02π​sin2θdθ=2π1​⋅π=21​ ⇒ Γrms​=2​1​≈0.707. Method B (coefficients): the previous page gave c0=0, c1=1c_0=0,\ c_1=1c0​=0, c1​=1, all others 0. By Eq.(20), ∑cn2=c12=1=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=c_1^2=1=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=c12​=1=2Γrms2​ ⟹ Γrms=1/2≈0.707\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2\approx0.707Γrms​=1/2​≈0.707. The two agree ✓. Feel: Γrms≈0.707\Gamma_{rms}\approx0.707Γrms​≈0.707 is the benchmark value for a "clean single-tone ISF". This site's canonical worked example (Example B) uses Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5 as the representative value — slightly below the ideal −sin⁡-\sin−sin, corresponding to an ISF somewhat flattened by factors other than qmaxq_{max}qmax​.

First compute Δω=2π×106=6.283×106\Delta\omega=2\pi\times10^6=6.283\times10^6Δω=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s, Δω2=3.948×1013\Delta\omega^2=3.948\times10^{13}Δω2=3.948×1013. The bracket =0.251.579×1014=1.583×10−15=\dfrac{0.25}{1.579\times10^{14}}=1.583\times10^{-15}=1.579×10140.25​=1.583×10−15, so L=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15)≈−148.0 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}(1.583\times10^{-15})\approx-148.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}.L=10log10​(1.583×10−15)≈−148.0 dBc/Hz. Dimension check: Γrms2qmax2⋅SiΔω2=1[C]2⋅[A2/Hz][rad/s]2\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\dfrac{S_i}{\Delta\omega^2} =\dfrac{1}{[\text{C}]^2}\cdot\dfrac{[\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}]}{[\text{rad/s}]^2}qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δω2Si​​=[C]21​⋅[rad/s]2[A2/Hz]​; since C=A⋅s\text{C}=\text{A}\cdot\text{s}C=A⋅s, Hz=1/s\text{Hz}=1/\text{s}Hz=1/s, and rad is dimensionless, this reduces to A2⋅sA2s2⋅s=\dfrac{\text{A}^2\cdot\text{s}}{\text{A}^2\text{s}^2}\cdot\text{s}=A2s2A2⋅s​⋅s= dimensionless (the per-Hz is already included); after the log⁡\loglog, dBc/Hz ✓. documents.t: The figure below (fig_coefficients from lab_05, n_harmonics=8) plots the cnc_ncn​ as a bar chart and compares, on the plot, "∑n=0∞cn2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2∑n=0∞​cn2​ (computed on the coefficient side)" against "2Γrms22\Gamma_{rms}^22Γrms2​ (computed on the integral side)" — they match, which is precisely the numerical verification of Parseval ([P1] Eq.(20)). Matching equation: [P1] Eq.(20). How to read it: square each bar's height and add them up (remember the n=0n=0n=0 bar counts at "half weight", c02/2c_0^2/2c02​/2) — the total equals 2Γrms22\Gamma_{rms}^22Γrms2​. This gives a practical sanity check: after computing the coefficients, reconcile once against Parseval and you immediately catch errors such as a misaligned numerical-integration window (endpoint 2π2\pi2π not included). Code verification: import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import ( gamma_lc_ideal, compute_fourier_coefficients, gamma_rms, ) theta = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 4096, endpoint=True) # must include endpoint 2*pi gamma = gamma_lc_ideal(theta) # -sin(theta) a0, a, b, c, phase = compute_fourier_coefficients(theta, gamma, n_harmonics=8) # Left side: sum c_n^2, with n=0 at half weight (c0^2 / 2) lhs = 0.5 * c[0] ** 2 + np.sum(c[1:] ** 2) # Right side: 2 * Gamma_rms^2 rhs = 2.0 * gamma_rms(theta, gamma) ** 2 print(lhs, rhs) # -> 1.0 , 1.0 (ideal LC: c1=1, the rest ≈0) print(gamma_rms(theta, gamma)) # -> 0.7071 (= 1/sqrt(2)) Toy-model note: the ISF used is a pedagogical toy / ideal-LC analytic form, not transistor-level. documents.t: The figure below (fig_lc_vs_ring_isf from lab_03) contrasts the ideal LC's −sin⁡-\sin−sin with the ring's toy triangular ISF (N=5,15N=5,15N=5,15). The ring's sensitivity is concentrated at the transitions; the more stages NNN, the flatter the overall ISF and the smaller Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Title reads: "LC vs ring ISF (toy)：敏感度集中在 transition，N 越大 rms 越小" = LC vs. ring ISF (toy): sensitivity concentrates at the transition; the larger N, the smaller the rms. Matching references: [P1] Fig. 7 (LC vs ring waveforms and ISFs); [P2] Fig. 8 (Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ vs NNN). How to read it: the LC ISF is a smooth single tone; the ring's energy is squeezed into narrow transitions — with more stages, each transition occupies a smaller fraction of the period, and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ drops. Toy-model note: this site's gamma_triangular is a pedagogical toy ISF with "energy concentrated at the transitions", not a transistor-level extraction (see the isf_utils.py docstring).

documents.t: [P2] quantifies the observation above into a scaling law ([P2] Eq.(16), p.794): Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 Intuition: as the stage count NNN increases, (i) each stage's transition becomes steeper and the ISF pulse narrower (rms drops), and (ii) the number of transitions per period grows but is diluted by the period length. Combined, this gives Γrms2∝N−3\Gamma_{rms}^2\propto N^{-3}Γrms2​∝N−3 (i.e. Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2). Full expression: [P2] Eq.(16) is Γrms=2π23η3 1N1.5,\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi^2}{3\eta^3}}\;\dfrac{1}{N^{1.5}},Γrms​=3η32π2​​N1.51​, where η\etaη is the stage-delay proportionality constant ([P2] Eq.(14), η≈1\eta\approx1η≈1 — not γ\gammaγ). The square root covers only the constant 2π2/(3η3)2\pi^2/(3\eta^3)2π2/(3η3); 1/N1.51/N^{1.5}1/N1.5 sits outside the radical, so Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 (at η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75, this is ≈4/N1.5\approx4/N^{1.5}≈4/N1.5, the solid line in [P2] Fig.8; [P2] Eq.(16), p.794 — re-verified in v7: the main text's statement "the 1/N1.51/N^{1.5}1/N1.5 dependence of Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​", the η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75 numerical anchor, and an independent algebraic derivation from App.B Eq.(52)+(54) all agree on N−3/2N^{-3/2}N−3/2. A v3 audit misread the radical's scope and mistakenly changed this to N−3/4N^{-3/4}N−3/4, mislabeling it "verified" — that was a misreading, not a formula-vs-text inconsistency; v7 corrects it back). Key conclusion: [P2] further shows that under the constraint of fixed f0f_0f0​ and power PPP, a single-ended ring's 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise/jitter is nearly independent of the stage count NNN ([P2] Sec.V, Eq.(23)/(25), p.796, L∣1/f2≈83η VDDVchar kTP(ω0/Δω)2\mathcal{L}\big|_{1/f^2}\approx\dfrac{8}{3\eta}\,\dfrac{V_{DD}}{V_{char}}\,\dfrac{kT}{P}(\omega_0/\Delta\omega)^2L​1/f2​≈3η8​Vchar​VDD​​PkT​(ω0​/Δω)2). Prefactor note: the prefactor of [P2] Eq.(23) is 83η\dfrac{8}{3\eta}3η8​ (η\etaη being the stage-delay proportionality constant of Eq.(14), ≈1\approx1≈1); γ\gammaγ enters only through Vchar=ΔV/γV_{char}=\Delta V/\gammaVchar​=ΔV/γ. Its VT=0V_T=0VT​=0 lower bound ([P2] Eq.(25)) is 16γ3η\dfrac{16\gamma}{3\eta}3η16γ​. (v2 mistakenly changed this to 8/(3γ)8/(3\gamma)8/(3γ) and mislabeled it "verified verbatim"; v3 corrected it against the original PDF, p.796.) Full LC-vs-ring discussion in lc_vs_ring; the random walk of accumulated jitter, σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ ([P2] Eq.(8)), is in lab_03_ring_oscillator_toy_model.

documents.t: Problem: for the ideal LC, Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ. Find Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. Step-by-step substitution: apply the definition directly, Γrms2=12π∫02πΓ2 dθ\Gamma_{rms}^2=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma^2\,d\thetaΓrms2​=2π1​∫02π​Γ2dθ. Γrms2=12π∫02π(−sin⁡θ)2 dθ=12π∫02πsin⁡2θ dθ=12π∫02π1−cos⁡2θ2 dθ=12π[θ2−sin⁡2θ4]02π=12π⋅2π2=12.\begin{aligned} \Gamma_{rms}^2 &=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}(-\sin\theta)^2\,d\theta =\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta\\ &=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}\,d\theta =\frac{1}{2\pi}\left[\frac{\theta}{2}-\frac{\sin2\theta}{4}\right]_0^{2\pi} =\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{2\pi}{2}=\frac12. \end{aligned}Γrms2​​=2π1​∫02π​(−sinθ)2dθ=2π1​∫02π​sin2θdθ=2π1​∫02π​21−cos2θ​dθ=2π1​[2θ​−4sin2θ​]02π​=2π1​⋅22π​=21​.​ Result: Γrms=1/2=12≈0.707\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{1/2}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx0.707Γrms​=1/2​=2​1​≈0.707. The second line uses the half-angle identity sin⁡2θ=12(1−cos⁡2θ)\sin^2\theta=\tfrac12(1-\cos2\theta)sin2θ=21​(1−cos2θ); cos⁡2θ\cos2\thetacos2θ integrates to 0 over a full period. documents.t: Problem: the ring's pedagogical toy ISF uses this site's gamma_triangular (N=5N=5N=5): a triangle wave with peak P=1/N=1/5P=1/\sqrt N=1/\sqrt5P=1/N​=1/5​, ramping linearly back and forth between [−P,P][-P,P][−P,P] (two transitions per period). Find Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. (Toy model, not transistor-level.) Step-by-step substitution: the triangle wave is linear on each basic ramp, so the mean square follows the standard result "mean square of a linear segment over [−P,P][-P,P][−P,P] =P2/3=P^2/3=P2/3". Reason: write the linear segment as Γ=P s\Gamma=P\,sΓ=Ps (with sss sweeping uniformly from −1-1−1 to 111), ⟨Γ2⟩=12∫−11(Ps)2 ds=P22⋅s33∣−11=P22⋅23=P23.\langle\Gamma^2\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}(P s)^2\,ds=\frac{P^2}{2}\cdot\frac{s^3}{3}\Big|_{-1}^{1}=\frac{P^2}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}=\frac{P^2}{3}.⟨Γ2⟩=21​∫−11​(Ps)2ds=2P2​⋅3s3​​−11​=2P2​⋅32​=3P2​. Substituting P=1/5P=1/\sqrt5P=1/5​: Γrms2=P23=1/53=115≈0.0667 ⇒ Γrms=115≈0.258.\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{P^2}{3}=\frac{1/5}{3}=\frac{1}{15}\approx0.0667 \ \Rightarrow\ \Gamma_{rms}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}}\approx0.258.Γrms2​=3P2​=31/5​=151​≈0.0667 ⇒ Γrms​=15​1​≈0.258. Result: Γrms≈0.258\Gamma_{rms}\approx0.258Γrms​≈0.258, far below the LC's 0.707 — consistent with the physics that "the ring squeezes its sensitivity into narrow transitions, the energy is flattened out, and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ shrinks with NNN" (echoing the Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 trend; the toy's NNN dependence here is 1/N1/\sqrt N1/N​, not the real scaling). Dimension check: PPP is dimensionless (the ISF is dimensionless) → Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ dimensionless ✓. import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_triangular, gamma_rms theta = np.linspace(0.0, 2*np.pi, 200001, endpoint=True) print(gamma_rms(theta, gamma_triangular(theta, n_stages=5))) # -> 0.2582 (= 1/sqrt(15))

Dimension check: cnc_ncn​ and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ are all dimensionless; both sides agree ✓. import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import ( gamma_triangular, compute_fourier_coefficients, gamma_rms, ) theta = np.linspace(0.0, 2*np.pi, 4096, endpoint=True) gamma = gamma_triangular(theta, n_stages=5) a0, a, b, c, ph = compute_fourier_coefficients(theta, gamma, n_harmonics=32) lhs = 0.5*c[0]**2 + np.sum(c[1:]**2) # half weight for n=0 rhs = 2.0*gamma_rms(theta, gamma)**2 print(lhs, rhs) # -> ~0.1333 , 0.1333 (more harmonics, closer match) Feel: a triangle wave carries "infinitely many odd harmonics", so the coefficient side needs enough n_harmonics (e.g. 32) to approach 2Γrms22\Gamma_{rms}^22Γrms2​; taking too few harmonics (e.g. 8) slightly undershoots the integral value — which is itself a numerical portrait of "the ring ISF's energy spread across high harmonics". documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: convolution_derivation | Next: fourier_series_of_isf · rms_isf Hands-on verification: see lab_06 for this page's "white noise → 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise" time-domain simulation matching theory. This page answers the most iconic result in oscillator phase-noise theory: why does a spectrally flat white current noise (a random current whose power spectral density is independent of frequency), after passing through an oscillator, turn into a phase-noise skirt with a slope of −20-20−20 dB/decade (i.e., 1/f21/f^21/f2)? We will derive all the way to L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​) and honestly account for the famous "off by a factor of 2" bookkeeping issue in the literature. Physical intuition (conclusion first): white noise is itself "flat" — it has no 1/f1/f1/f structure whatsoever. But the previous chapter convolution_derivation told us: the phase ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) is the time integral of the noise current ([P1] Eq.(11)). An integrator is a 1/(jω)1/(j\omega)1/(jω) filter: it multiplies the power spectrum by 1/ω21/\omega^21/ω2. Something flat goes in, gets multiplied by 1/ω21/\omega^21/ω2, and comes out — that is where 1/f21/f^21/f2 comes from. The ISF only decides "how large a weight to multiply by" (set by Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and qmaxq_{max}qmax​); it does not decide the slope. The slope always comes from the integrator.

documents.t: White noise is by definition noise whose PSD is independent of frequency (flat). Using the single-sided PSD, we write Si(f)=in2‾Δf[A2/Hz].S_i(f)=\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}\quad[\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}].Si​(f)=Δfin2​​​[A2/Hz]. Physics used: thermal noise and shot noise can both be treated as white within the offset band we care about (kHz–MHz) — their corner frequencies lie far higher. Order-of-magnitude feel: the thermal noise current of a conducting resistance RRR is in2‾/Δf=4kT/R\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=4kT/Rin2​​/Δf=4kT/R; at R=1 kΩR=1\,\text{k}\OmegaR=1kΩ and room temperature this is about 1.6×10−23 A2/Hz1.6\times10^{-23}\,\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}1.6×10−23A2/Hz. The canonical Example B on this page takes Si=10−24 A2/HzS_i=10^{-24}\,\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si​=10−24A2/Hz as a round-number "single equivalent white-noise source", convenient for mental arithmetic.

documents.t: Expand Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) in a Fourier series ([P1] Eq.(12), p.183): Γ(ω0τ)=c02+∑n=1∞cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn).\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=\frac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n).Γ(ω0​τ)=2c0​​+n=1∑∞​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​). Multiplying by the white noise in(τ)i_n(\tau)in​(τ) amounts to picking up the noise near each harmonic nω0n\omega_0nω0​ and "down-converting" it back to baseband (this is the frequency translation described in fourier_series_of_isf). The key point: for white noise, the noise power near every harmonic nω0n\omega_0nω0​ is equally large (because the spectrum is flat), so every cnc_ncn​ brings down white noise of the same strength. The harmonics are uncorrelated (white noise in different frequency bands is mutually independent), so powers add directly, and the total weight is ∑ncn2\sum_n c_n^2∑n​cn2​. Math used: white noise in different bands is uncorrelated → the harmonic contributions add in power (not in amplitude). Unit check: cnc_ncn​ is dimensionless, so ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ is dimensionless ✓.
documents.s: Step 2: ISF modulation — white noise "stirred" by the periodic weight

documents.t: [P1]'s strategy is clever: first compute how much sideband "one small single-tone current" produces, then treat white noise as a superposition of countless independent small tones. For a tone injected near nω0n\omega_0nω0​, i(t)=I0cos⁡(nω0+Δω)ti(t)=I_0\cos(n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)ti(t)=I0​cos(nω0​+Δω)t, the excess phase is a slow modulation ([P1] Eq.(16/17), p.183): ϕ(t)≈I0 cnsin⁡(Δωt)2qmax Δω.\phi(t)\approx\frac{I_0\,c_n\sin(\Delta\omega t)}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}.ϕ(t)≈2qmax​ΔωI0​cn​sin(Δωt)​. The single-sideband power it produces relative to the carrier ([P1] Eq.(18), p.183): PSBC(Δω)=10log⁡10 ⁣(I0 cn4qmax Δω)2.P_{SBC}(\Delta\omega)=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{I_0\,c_n}{4q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}\right)^2.PSBC​(Δω)=10log10​(4qmax​ΔωI0​cn​​)2.
documents.s: Step 3: from single-tone sidebands to the white-noise summation (Eq.(19))

documents.t: Eq.(16/17) above does not appear out of thin air; it is the algebraic result of "down-converting the noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ to baseband". We now work it out for you step by step — this is exactly the intermediate step that the authoring spec (§10.2) requires. Substitute the near-nω0n\omega_0nω0​ injected tone i(τ)=I0cos⁡((nω0+Δω)τ)i(\tau)=I_0\cos((n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau)i(τ)=I0​cos((nω0​+Δω)τ) into the nnn-th harmonic term of [P1] Eq.(13). The integral to evaluate for that term is "the ISF's nnn-th harmonic weight" times "the injected current", integrated: ϕn(t)=1qmax∫t ⁣ ⁣cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn) I0cos⁡((nω0+Δω)τ) dτ.\phi_n(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int^{t}\!\!c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\,I_0\cos\big((n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau\big)\,d\tau .ϕn​(t)=qmax​1​∫tcn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)I0​cos((nω0​+Δω)τ)dτ. Step (i): use the product-to-sum identity to split the product of the two cosines into a "sum" cosine and a "difference" cosine. The identity cos⁡Acos⁡B=12[cos⁡(A−B)+cos⁡(A+B)]\cos A\cos B=\tfrac12\big[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)\big]cosAcosB=21​[cos(A−B)+cos(A+B)] Let A=nω0τ+θnA=n\omega_0\tau+\theta_nA=nω0​τ+θn​ and B=(nω0+Δω)τB=(n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tauB=(nω0​+Δω)τ. Compute the difference and sum frequencies: A−B=(nω0τ+θn)−(nω0+Δω)τ=θn−Δωτ,A-B=(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)-(n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau=\theta_n-\Delta\omega\tau,A−B=(nω0​τ+θn​)−(nω0​+Δω)τ=θn​−Δωτ,A+B=(nω0τ+θn)+(nω0+Δω)τ=(2nω0+Δω)τ+θn.A+B=(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)+(n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau=(2n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau+\theta_n .A+B=(nω0​τ+θn​)+(nω0​+Δω)τ=(2nω0​+Δω)τ+θn​. So the integrand becomes cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn) I0cos⁡((nω0+Δω)τ)=I0cn2[cos⁡(Δωτ−θn)⏟slow term, ≈Δω+cos⁡((2nω0+Δω)τ+θn)⏟fast term, ≈2nω0].c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\,I_0\cos\big((n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau\big)=\frac{I_0c_n}{2}\Big[\underbrace{\cos(\Delta\omega\tau-\theta_n)}_{\text{slow term, }\approx\Delta\omega}+\underbrace{\cos\big((2n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau+\theta_n\big)}_{\text{fast term, }\approx 2n\omega_0}\Big].cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)I0​cos((nω0​+Δω)τ)=2I0​cn​​[slow term, ≈Δωcos(Δωτ−θn​)​​+fast term, ≈2nω0​cos((2nω0​+Δω)τ+θn​)​​]. (Using cos⁡(θn−Δωτ)=cos⁡(Δωτ−θn)\cos(\theta_n-\Delta\omega\tau)=\cos(\Delta\omega\tau-\theta_n)cos(θn​−Δωτ)=cos(Δωτ−θn​) — cosine is an even function.) Step (ii): the two terms meet completely different fates. The integrator (that ∫tdτ\int^t d\tau∫tdτ) is essentially a low-pass — it accumulates the signal over time; high-frequency components "cancel between positive and negative excursions and get averaged away", while low-frequency (slow) components keep accumulating. The slow term has frequency about Δω\Delta\omegaΔω (the offset, typically kHz–MHz, Δω≪ω0\Delta\omega\ll\omega_0Δω≪ω0​). Integrating a slow cosine gives ∫cos⁡(Δωτ−θn) dτ=sin⁡(Δωτ−θn)Δω\int\cos(\Delta\omega\tau-\theta_n)\,d\tau=\dfrac{\sin(\Delta\omega\tau-\theta_n)}{\Delta\omega}∫cos(Δωτ−θn​)dτ=Δωsin(Δωτ−θn​)​ — the denominator is only a tiny Δω\Delta\omegaΔω, so the term is amplified and survives. The fast term has frequency about 2nω02n\omega_02nω0​ (twice-the-carrier scale, GHz). The same integration gives sin⁡(⋯ )2nω0+Δω\dfrac{\sin(\cdots)}{2n\omega_0+\Delta\omega}2nω0​+Δωsin(⋯)​ — the denominator is the huge 2nω02n\omega_02nω0​, squeezing the amplitude down to a factor of ∼Δω/(2nω0)\sim\Delta\omega/(2n\omega_0)∼Δω/(2nω0​); negligible relative to the slow term, it is effectively averaged away by the integrator. Step (iii): keep only the slow term, obtaining Eq.(16/17). ϕn(t)≈1qmax⋅I0cn2⋅sin⁡(Δωt−θn)Δω=I0 cnsin⁡(Δωt−θn)2qmax Δω\phi_n(t)\approx\frac{1}{q_{max}}\cdot\frac{I_0c_n}{2}\cdot\frac{\sin(\Delta\omega t-\theta_n)}{\Delta\omega}=\frac{I_0\,c_n\sin(\Delta\omega t-\theta_n)}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}ϕn​(t)≈qmax​1​⋅2I0​cn​​⋅Δωsin(Δωt−θn​)​=2qmax​ΔωI0​cn​sin(Δωt−θn​)​ Absorbing the time-independent phase θn\theta_nθn​ into the time origin recovers [P1] Eq.(16/17) above, ϕ(t)≈I0cnsin⁡(Δωt)2qmaxΔω\phi(t)\approx\dfrac{I_0 c_n\sin(\Delta\omega t)}{2q_{max}\Delta\omega}ϕ(t)≈2qmax​ΔωI0​cn​sin(Δωt)​. This downconversion integral (spec §10.2) is the hard core of "the oscillator acting as a mixer": noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ is moved by the ISF's nnn-th harmonic to Δω\Delta\omegaΔω (the difference-frequency slow term survives), while the sum-frequency fast term at 2nω02n\omega_02nω0​ vanishes automatically. Unit check: [A]⋅(dimensionless)[C]⋅[rad/s]=AA⋅s⋅s⋅rad−1\dfrac{[\text{A}]\cdot(\text{dimensionless})}{[\text{C}]\cdot[\text{rad/s}]}=\dfrac{\text{A}}{\text{A}\cdot\text{s}}\cdot\text{s}\cdot\text{rad}^{-1}[C]⋅[rad/s][A]⋅(dimensionless)​=A⋅sA​⋅s⋅rad−1 — with C=A⋅sC=\text{A}\cdot\text{s}C=A⋅s and Δω\Delta\omegaΔω in rad/s, this simplifies so that ϕ\phiϕ is dimensionless (rad) ✓.

documents.t: Next, accumulate the "single-tone sideband powers" into the "white-noise summation". Three things hide in this step: both sidebands, the white-noise substitution I02/2→in2‾/ΔfI_0^2/2\to\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fI02​/2→in2​​/Δf, and the sum over nnn. Unpacked step by step: Step (i): the linear value of the single-sideband relative power. Square the quantity inside Eq.(18)'s parentheses (hold off on the 10log⁡10\log10log): (I0 cn4qmax Δω)2=I02 cn216 qmax2 Δω2.\left(\frac{I_0\,c_n}{4q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}\right)^2=\frac{I_0^2\,c_n^2}{16\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}.(4qmax​ΔωI0​cn​​)2=16qmax2​Δω2I02​cn2​​. (The 444 here comes from the 2qmaxΔω2q_{max}\Delta\omega2qmax​Δω of Eq.(16) plus taking a single sideband — the power of the slow modulation sin⁡(Δωt)\sin(\Delta\omega t)sin(Δωt) corresponds to 12\tfrac1221​ of the amplitude, 12×12=14\tfrac12\times\tfrac1{2}=\tfrac1421​×21​=41​, so the denominator goes from 222 to 444; hence 42=164^2=1642=16.) Step (ii): the white-noise substitution I02/2→in2‾/ΔfI_0^2/2\to\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fI02​/2→in2​​/Δf. A single tone of amplitude I0I_0I0​ has mean square (power) I02/2I_0^2/2I02​/2 (sinusoid rms² === amplitude²/2/2/2). View the white noise as "one equivalent small tone near each nω0n\omega_0nω0​, within bandwidth Δf\Delta fΔf"; its power is the PSD times the bandwidth =(in2‾/Δf)=(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)=(in2​​/Δf). Equate the two: I022 → in2‾Δf⟹I02 → 2 in2‾Δf.\frac{I_0^2}{2}\;\to\;\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad I_0^2\;\to\;2\,\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}.2I02​​→Δfin2​​​⟹I02​→2Δfin2​​​. Note that the extra piece here is exactly that factor 2: converting "peak amplitude" to "power" brings a 12\tfrac1221​, so substituting in the reverse direction brings a 222. Insert into step (i): I02 cn216 qmax2 Δω2 → 2(in2‾/Δf) cn216 qmax2 Δω2.\frac{I_0^2\,c_n^2}{16\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}\;\to\;\frac{2(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)\,c_n^2}{16\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}.16qmax2​Δω2I02​cn2​​→16qmax2​Δω22(in2​​/Δf)cn2​​. Step (iii): both sidebands + sum over nnn. Each harmonic nω0n\omega_0nω0​ folds one sideband back from each side of the carrier (both nω0+Δωn\omega_0+\Delta\omeganω0​+Δω and nω0−Δωn\omega_0-\Delta\omeganω0​−Δω down-convert to Δω\Delta\omegaΔω); the power above already contains both contributions. Then sum over all harmonics n=0,1,2,…n=0,1,2,\dotsn=0,1,2,… (the bands are uncorrelated, so powers add directly): L=∑n2(in2‾/Δf) cn216 qmax2 Δω2=(in2‾/Δf)∑ncn28 qmax2 Δω2.\mathcal{L}=\sum_n\frac{2(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)\,c_n^2}{16\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)\sum_n c_n^2}{8\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}.L=n∑​16qmax2​Δω22(in2​​/Δf)cn2​​=8qmax2​Δω2(in2​​/Δf)∑n​cn2​​. Step (iv): cancel to get the factor 8. Numerator 222, denominator 161616; cancelling leaves 888 — this is the origin of that famous 888 in Eq.(19)'s denominator: 8=162=(Eq.18 squared: 42)(white-noise substitution: 2).8=\frac{16}{2}=\frac{(\text{Eq.18 squared: }4^2)}{(\text{white-noise substitution: }2)} .8=216​=(white-noise substitution: 2)(Eq.18 squared: 42)​. Treating the white noise as countless independent tones near each nω0n\omega_0nω0​ within bandwidth Δf\Delta fΔf, letting I02/2→in2‾/ΔfI_0^2/2\to\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fI02​/2→in2​​/Δf, and summing over all harmonics n=0,1,2,…n=0,1,2,\dotsn=0,1,2,… gives the white-noise phase-noise summation ([P1] Eq.(19), p.185): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(in2‾/Δf ∑n=0∞cn28 qmax2 Δω2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f\;\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2}{8\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(8qmax2​Δω2in2​​/Δf∑n=0∞​cn2​​) See the 1/f21/f^21/f2 yet? The denominator carries Δω2\Delta\omega^2Δω2. For every decade up (Δω×10\Delta\omega\times10Δω×10), the bracketed quantity drops 100×100\times100× ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ 10log⁡10(100)=2010\log_{10}(100)=2010log10​(100)=20 dB. So the slope is −20-20−20 dB/decade — exactly 1/f21/f^21/f2. This Δω2\Delta\omega^2Δω2 comes entirely from the integrator (that ∫dt\int dt∫dt of Step 2). Unit check (the bracketed quantity should be dimensionless, since we take its log): [A2/Hz]⋅(dimensionless)[C2]⋅[rad/s]2\dfrac{[\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}]\cdot(\text{dimensionless})}{[\text{C}^2]\cdot[\text{rad/s}]^2}[C2]⋅[rad/s]2[A2/Hz]⋅(dimensionless)​. C=A⋅s\text{C}=\text{A}\cdot\text{s}C=A⋅s so C2=A2s2\text{C}^2=\text{A}^2\text{s}^2C2=A2s2; and Hz=1/s\text{Hz}=1/\text{s}Hz=1/s, (rad/s)2=1/s2(\text{rad/s})^2=1/\text{s}^2(rad/s)2=1/s2. Numerator A2/Hz=A2⋅s\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}=\text{A}^2\cdot\text{s}A2/Hz=A2⋅s; denominator A2s2⋅s−2=A2\text{A}^2\text{s}^2\cdot\text{s}^{-2}=\text{A}^2A2s2⋅s−2=A2. The ratio =s=\text{s}=s. Strictly speaking it carries a dimension of 1/Hz1/\text{Hz}1/Hz (this is exactly the per-Hz in dBc/Hz); after 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ it reads as dBc/Hz ✓.

documents.t: ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ is hard to measure directly, but it equals the "total energy" of the ISF. The Parseval relation ([P1] Eq.(20), p.185): ∑n=0∞cn2=1π∫02π∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2 Γrms2.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma(x)|^2dx=2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2.n=0∑∞​cn2​=π1​∫02π​∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2Γrms2​. Math used: the sum of squared Fourier coefficients = the mean square of the function (Parseval/Rayleigh); see rms_isf for details. Note the right-hand side is 2Γrms22\Gamma_{rms}^22Γrms2​ (not Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​), because Γrms2=12π∫02π∣Γ∣2dx\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma|^2dxΓrms2​=2π1​∫02π​∣Γ∣2dx — a factor of 222 apart. Physical meaning: you do not need to know every individual cnc_ncn​; knowing the ISF's rms value alone suffices to compute the white-noise phase noise.
documents.s: Step 4: use Parseval to replace the sum by Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (Eq.(20))

documents.t: Substitute ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ back into Eq.(19); the 888 in the denominator cancels by half, becoming 444: in2‾/Δf⋅2Γrms28 qmax2 Δω2=Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2.\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f\cdot 2\Gamma_{rms}^2}{8\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}.8qmax2​Δω2in2​​/Δf⋅2Γrms2​​=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​. This yields the white-noise 1/f² result ([P1] Eq.(21), p.185): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2) \boxed{\ \mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)\ } L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​) ​ Design message (claim C3): phase noise is proportional to Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​. To lower the 1/f21/f^21/f2 noise, increase the signal charge swing qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (squared in the denominator — a very strong lever) and reduce the ISF's rms value Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. These two are the fundamental knobs of all low-phase-noise oscillator design. Dimension check, same as Step 3: Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ carries 1/C21/\text{C}^21/C2; multiplying by Si/Δω2S_i/\Delta\omega^2Si​/Δω2, which carries A2s/s−2=A2s3=C2s\text{A}^2\text{s}/\text{s}^{-2}=\text{A}^2\text{s}^3=\text{C}^2\text{s}A2s/s−2=A2s3=C2s ✓ this reduces to s\text{s}s → per-Hz. Rigorous re-derivation from scratch: Step 3 above follows the "white noise === superposition of tones" heuristic route; if you want to see the same result re-derived from scratch with the rigorous machinery of signals and systems (the two-time autocorrelation of the LTV phase → period-averaging over absolute time to stationarize the cyclostationary process → the Wiener-Khinchin theorem for the spectrum) — letting ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ fall out of the autocorrelation by itself, with no hand-tallied factor-8 bookkeeping — see the appendix derivation_autocorrelation_wiener_khinchin.

documents.t: Engineering practice commonly uses two quantities to describe the same thing; you must be able to convert between them: phase PSD Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f): the power spectral density of phase fluctuations, in rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz; integrating over fff gives the phase variance σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​. SSB phase noise L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf): single-sideband noise power per Hz relative to the carrier, in dBc/Hz. Under the small-angle approximation (phase fluctuations far below 1 rad) the two are related by (spec Eq. 16): L(Δf)≈12Sϕ(Δf).\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\approx\tfrac12 S_\phi(\Delta f).L(Δf)≈21​Sϕ​(Δf). Writing the white-noise result in phase-PSD form (clean time-domain derivation, see the section below): Sϕ(f)=Γrms2qmax2⋅Si(2πf)2[rad2/Hz].S_\phi(f)=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{(2\pi f)^2}\quad[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}].Sϕ​(f)=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅(2πf)2Si​​[rad2/Hz]. dBc/Hz intuition: −100-100−100 dBc/Hz means "at that offset from the carrier, within a 1 Hz bandwidth, the noise power is 101010^{10}1010 times smaller than the carrier". The more negative the number, the cleaner. In the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region, every decade further out improves the dBc/Hz figure by 20 (20 more negative).
documents.s: The relation between Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) and L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) (dBc/Hz intuition)

documents.t: If you do the clean time-domain derivation yourself (white noise ×\times× ISF →\to→ integration), you get Sϕ(f)=Γrms2 Siqmax2(2πf)2,⇒L(Δf)≈12Sϕ=Γrms2qmax2⋅Si2 Δω2.S_\phi(f)=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2\,S_i}{q_{max}^2(2\pi f)^2},\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\approx\tfrac12 S_\phi=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{2\,\Delta\omega^2}.Sϕ​(f)=qmax2​(2πf)2Γrms2​Si​​,⇒L(Δf)≈21​Sϕ​=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅2Δω2Si​​. That is, the denominator is 2 Δω22\,\Delta\omega^22Δω2. But [P1] Eq.(21) has 4 Δω24\,\Delta\omega^24Δω2. They differ by a factor of 2. The gap comes from the SSB (single-sideband) bookkeeping convention: whether all of the phase-fluctuation power is charged to "a single sideband" or "split evenly across both sidebands", and whether in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf is a single-sided or two-sided PSD — any inconsistency in definitions produces a factor of 2. This is a famous minor controversy in the literature; the constant lands somewhere between /2/2/2 and /4/4/4 across textbooks/papers. The key point: it does not affect the Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ scaling at all, nor the −20-20−20 dB/decade slope. Design work looks at scaling and slope; that ±3\pm3±3 dB constant is naturally absorbed during measurement calibration. This site's lab_06 numerical simulation uses the clean time-domain version Sϕ=Γrms2Si/(qmax2(2πf)2)S_\phi=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(q_{max}^2(2\pi f)^2)Sϕ​=Γrms2​Si​/(qmax2​(2πf)2), so it differs from Eq.(21) by this factor of 2 — expected and taught, not a bug. One sentence to remember: slope and scaling are physics; the constant 2 is bookkeeping. Do not lose sleep over that 2.
documents.s: The important factor-of-2 teaching note (make sure you understand it)

documents.t: Example B: f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, Si=10−24 A2/HzS_i=10^{-24}\,\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si​=10−24A2/Hz. Use [P1] Eq.(21). Step 1: compute the offset angular frequency. Δω=2πΔf=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s,Δω2=3.948×1013 rad2/s2.\Delta\omega=2\pi\Delta f=2\pi\times10^{6}=6.283\times10^{6}\ \text{rad/s},\qquad\Delta\omega^2=3.948\times10^{13}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}^2.Δω=2πΔf=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s,Δω2=3.948×1013 rad2/s2. Step 2: compute Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​. Γrms2qmax2=0.25(10−12)2=0.2510−24=2.5×1023 C−2.\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}=\frac{0.25}{(10^{-12})^2}=\frac{0.25}{10^{-24}}=2.5\times10^{23}\ \text{C}^{-2}.qmax2​Γrms2​​=(10−12)20.25​=10−240.25​=2.5×1023 C−2. Step 3: compute Si/(4Δω2)S_i/(4\Delta\omega^2)Si​/(4Δω2). Si4 Δω2=10−244×3.948×1013=10−241.579×1014=6.332×10−39.\frac{S_i}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{10^{-24}}{4\times3.948\times10^{13}}=\frac{10^{-24}}{1.579\times10^{14}}=6.332\times10^{-39}.4Δω2Si​​=4×3.948×101310−24​=1.579×101410−24​=6.332×10−39. Step 4: multiply to get the linear value inside the parentheses. Γrms2qmax2⋅Si4 Δω2=2.5×1023×6.332×10−39=1.583×10−15.\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}=2.5\times10^{23}\times6.332\times10^{-39}=1.583\times10^{-15}.qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2Si​​=2.5×1023×6.332×10−39=1.583×10−15. Step 5: take 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​. L(1 MHz)=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15)=−148.0 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})=10\log_{10}(1.583\times10^{-15})=-148.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}.L(1MHz)=10log10​(1.583×10−15)=−148.0 dBc/Hz. Feel for the number: this is the theoretical floor for a "single ideal white-noise source", about −148-148−148 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz. Real circuits have multiple noise sources (several transistors, tail, load), cyclostationary gating (see effective_isf), and close-in flicker upconversion (see flicker_noise_upconversion); actual values are higher (closer to 0). Cross-page consistency: with the clean time-domain version (/2/2/2 instead of /4/4/4), the same parameters give ≈−145.0\approx-145.0≈−145.0 dBc/Hz — exactly 3 dB apart (10log⁡10210\log_{10}210log10​2) — the numerical face of the factor-of-2 above.

documents.t: The two problems below follow the strict format: problem → step-by-step substitution (with units) → result → dimension check → one-line Python verification. The first reuses the canonical Example B (spec §8); the second uses a different set of numbers for practice. Both apply [P1] Eq.(21). Example 1 (canonical Example B, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5): f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, Si=in2‾/Δf=10−24 A2/HzS_i=\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=10^{-24}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si​=in2​​/Δf=10−24 A2/Hz. documents.t: Prerequisites: capstone_lc_end_to_end (the site-wide spine, end to end) and the three chapter exercise sets — 02 Foundations, 03 Core Theory, 06 Design Insights (finish those first) | Next: none — this is the last page. Get all 11 right and you graduate. Passing criteria: Answer every question within the NumericQuiz tolerance — work it out yourself first, before opening the solution. For each question, be able to name which convention it uses (SSB /4/4/4 or time-domain /2/2/2) and whether it maps to [P1] Eq.(24) or [P2] Eq.(57). Be able to recite, in one breath, the formula and source page behind every link in the chain 15.915.915.9 fs → −148-148−148 dBc/Hz → 19.919.919.9 mHz → 447.9447.9447.9 fs → 7.307.307.30 ps. This is not yet another problem set. It is an exam: one design story, two warm-ups (0a/0b) plus 11 checkpoints, from the instant a single charge impulse hits the LC tank all the way to the eye opening of a SerDes link at BER =10−12=10^{-12}=10−12. Each question asks for exactly one "clean number", but every number requires cross-chapter dispatch — you will need [P1]'s ISF, [P2]'s κ and the App. B closed forms, the diffusion dictionary's wardrobe changes, the four clock-chain accounting rules, the PLL closed-loop algebra, and the dual-Dirac extrapolation. Work each one out yourself and type your answer first; only then expand the solution.

Ideal single-source-limit track (Questions 2, 3, 7): a single white-noise source and [P1] Eq.(21) give −148-148−148 dBc/Hz — a physical floor no real circuit reaches. Measured track (Questions 5, 6, 9, 10): the datasheet-grade −100-100−100 dBc/Hz — 48 dB above the ideal limit, reflecting the reality of multiple sources, cyclostationarity, flicker, and the buffer chain. documents.t: Learning-path step: Step 1 — What an oscillator's "phase" actually is Before the exam proper, a question that comes even before the "ISF". The VCO's LC tank has quality factor Q=20Q=20Q=20 and f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz. A single current impulse kicks both the amplitude and the phase ([P4] Sec. III-B's impulse-train thought experiment): the phase deviation persists forever because the oscillator is autonomous (no external time reference); the amplitude deviation recovers exponentially according to the LTI dynamics of a damped LC, d(t)=e−t/τ0d(t)=e^{-t/\tau_0}d(t)=e−t/τ0​ with τ0=2Q/ω0\tau_0=2Q/\omega_0τ0​=2Q/ω0​ ([P4] Sec. III-F, p.2128, the text immediately before Eq.(25); verified on this site in phase_vs_amplitude_noise). Find τ0\tau_0τ0​ (ns). Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Work it out first: for an LC tank with Q = 20 and f₀ = 5 GHz, the amplitude deviation caused by one impulse recovers exponentially with τ₀ = 2Q/ω₀; τ₀ = ? (answer in ns) nsCheckShow answer Graded correct within ±1% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Question 0a full solution (amplitude has a restoring force, phase does not: the root reason the ISF is about phase only) Step 1 (where τ0\tau_0τ0​ comes from — the free decay of a parallel RLC; RLC is standard circuit theory, external textbook material). Step 2 of tank_Q_and_energy_restoration derived Q=ω0RpCQ=\omega_0R_pCQ=ω0​Rp​C and showed the stored-energy envelope decays as e−ω0t/Qe^{-\omega_0t/Q}e−ω0​t/Q. Energy ∝\propto∝ amplitude squared, so the amplitude envelope decays at half the energy rate: A(t)∝e−ω0t/(2Q)=e−t/τ0,τ0=2Qω0=2RpC.A(t)\propto e^{-\omega_0t/(2Q)}=e^{-t/\tau_0},\qquad \tau_0=\frac{2Q}{\omega_0}=2R_pC.A(t)∝e−ω0​t/(2Q)=e−t/τ0​,τ0​=ω0​2Q​=2Rp​C. (The natural response of a parallel RLC is v(t)∝e−t/(2RpC)cos⁡(⋅)v(t)\propto e^{-t/(2R_pC)}\cos(\cdot)v(t)∝e−t/(2Rp​C)cos(⋅); substituting Q=ω0RpCQ=\omega_0R_pCQ=ω0​Rp​C gives the same expression.) [P4]'s physical premise: the transconductor only replenishes up to the free-running amplitude, so any excess energy dissipates along this damped-LC LTI dynamics. Step 2 (substitute step by step, with units): ω0=2πf0=2π×5×109=3.142×1010 rad/s,τ0=2Qω0=403.142×1010 rad/s=1.273×10−9 s=1.273 ns.\omega_0=2\pi f_0=2\pi\times5\times10^{9}=3.142\times10^{10}\ \text{rad/s},\qquad \tau_0=\frac{2Q}{\omega_0}=\frac{40}{3.142\times10^{10}\ \text{rad/s}}=1.273\times10^{-9}\ \text{s}=1.273\ \text{ns}.ω0​=2πf0​=2π×5×109=3.142×1010 rad/s,τ0​=ω0​2Q​=3.142×1010 rad/s40​=1.273×10−9 s=1.273 ns. In cycles: τ0f0=Q/π=6.37\tau_0f_0=Q/\pi=6.37τ0​f0​=Q/π=6.37 cycles — "the higher the QQQ, the slower the amplitude recovers, but it always does." The corresponding amplitude-noise corner is fc=1/(2πτ0)=f0/(2Q)=125f_c=1/(2\pi\tau_0)=f_0/(2Q)=125fc​=1/(2πτ0​)=f0​/(2Q)=125 MHz. Result: τ0=1.273\tau_0=1.273τ0​=1.273 ns (answer 1.27 ns). The contrast with phase (the real point of this question): the same impulse leaves a u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) step in the phase direction ([P1] Eq.(10), p.182) — no time constant, never recovers — because the limit cycle has no restoring force along its tangent (Floquet exponent 0), only along the radial direction (decay rate −1/τ0-1/\tau_0−1/τ0​). This is why the phase-noise variance diverges with time while the amplitude-noise variance converges to a finite value, and why this entire exam (and ISF theory) tracks phase only (oscillator_phase). Convention flag: the 2 in 2Q/ω02Q/\omega_02Q/ω0​ comes from "amplitude-envelope decay rate === half the energy decay rate"; mistaking the energy time constant Q/ω0Q/\omega_0Q/ω0​ for the amplitude time constant halves τ0\tau_0τ0​ (0.64 ns). Applicability and failure conditions: an LC tank with a single amplitude-decay mode, weak injection (linearized). Ring or multi-mode oscillators do not have a radial recovery rate of 2Q/ω02Q/\omega_02Q/ω0​ (the general case belongs to the Floquet framework, outside this site's 5 PDFs); under strong injection, nonlinear amplitude-restoring effects make [P4]'s theory deviate from simulation near the center of the amplitude curves of Fig. 8 on p.2128 — [P4] itself notes this. Dimension check: dimensionless ÷\div÷ (rad/s) === s ✓; Ω⋅F=\Omega\cdot\text{F}=Ω⋅F= s ✓; s ×\times× Hz === dimensionless (cycle count) ✓. import numpy as np f0, Q = 5e9, 20 w0 = 2*np.pi*f0 tau0 = 2*Q/w0 print(round(tau0*1e9, 3), round(tau0*f0, 2), round(1/(2*np.pi*tau0)/1e6, 1)) # -> 1.273 6.37 125.0

The only premise of this step is linear superposition (small injection, Δq≪qmax\Delta q\ll q_{max}Δq≪qmax​); the upper limit ttt says each term is permanent memory — phase is the integrator of noise. Step 2 (substitute step by step, with units): Γ(π/2)=−sin⁡π2=−1,Γ(3π/2)=−sin⁡3π2=+1,\Gamma(\pi/2)=-\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}=-1,\qquad \Gamma(3\pi/2)=-\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{2}=+1,Γ(π/2)=−sin2π​=−1,Γ(3π/2)=−sin23π​=+1,Δϕ1=(−1)(1×10−15 C)1×10−12 C=−1×10−3 rad,Δϕ2=(+1)(3×10−15 C)1×10−12 C=+3×10−3 rad,\Delta\phi_1=\frac{(-1)(1\times10^{-15}\ \text{C})}{1\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}}=-1\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad},\qquad \Delta\phi_2=\frac{(+1)(3\times10^{-15}\ \text{C})}{1\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}}=+3\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad},Δϕ1​=1×10−12 C(−1)(1×10−15 C)​=−1×10−3 rad,Δϕ2​=1×10−12 C(+1)(3×10−15 C)​=+3×10−3 rad,Δϕ=Δϕ1+Δϕ2=+2×10−3 rad,Δt=Δϕ2πf0=2×10−33.142×1010 rad/s=6.366×10−14 s=63.7 fs.\Delta\phi=\Delta\phi_1+\Delta\phi_2=+2\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad},\qquad \Delta t=\frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{2\times10^{-3}}{3.142\times10^{10}\ \text{rad/s}}=6.366\times10^{-14}\ \text{s}=63.7\ \text{fs}.Δϕ=Δϕ1​+Δϕ2​=+2×10−3 rad,Δt=2πf0​Δϕ​=3.142×1010 rad/s2×10−3​=6.366×10−14 s=63.7 fs. Result: Δϕ=+2\Delta\phi=+2Δϕ=+2 mrad, Δt=63.7\Delta t=63.7Δt=63.7 fs. The point: the total 4 fC, if all injected at θ=3π/2\theta=3\pi/2θ=3π/2, would give +4+4+4 mrad (127 fs); if both impulses land at the peak θ=0\theta=0θ=0, then Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0 and the net phase is zero. Phase adds the ISF-weighted charge — precisely the LTV-vs-LTI distinction (lti_vs_ltv), and the reason Eq.(11) keeps Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) inside the integral. The order of the two impulses does not affect the result (the integrator treats all of the past alike), but every term stays forever. Replace ini_nin​ with continuous white noise and the same expression integrates into Question 2's 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt. The v5-adjudicated mapping (settled by lab_23's Monte-Carlo variance slope 0.12520.12520.1252 and linewidth fit 20.020.020.0 mHz, see outfit three in diffusion_dictionary): Δf3dB=κ22π=0.1252π=1.99×10−2 Hz=19.9 mHz.\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\frac{\kappa^2}{2\pi}=\frac{0.125}{2\pi}=1.99\times10^{-2}\ \text{Hz}=19.9\ \text{mHz}.Δf3dB​=2πκ2​=2π0.125​=1.99×10−2 Hz=19.9 mHz. Result: κ2=0.125 rad2/s\kappa^2=0.125\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}κ2=0.125 rad2/s, Δf3dB=19.9\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=19.9Δf3dB​=19.9 mHz (a true LC with Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​ gives κ2=0.25\kappa^2=0.25κ2=0.25 and a 39.839.839.8 mHz linewidth). You answer the flicker-upconversion price on the spot with the [P2] Appendix B closed forms (asymmetric_isf_closed_form): N=5N=5N=5, η=1\eta=1η=1, waveform asymmetry ratio A=frise′/ffall′=1.5A=f'_{rise}/f'_{fall}=1.5A=frise′​/ffall′​=1.5, device 1/f corner f1/f=1f_{1/f}=1f1/f​=1 MHz. [P2] Eq.(57), p.803: f1/f3=f1/f⋅32ηN⋅(1−A)21−A+A2=106 Hz×32×1×5×(−0.5)21−1.5+2.25=106×0.3×0.251.75=42.86 kHz.f_{1/f^3}=f_{1/f}\cdot\frac{3}{2\eta N}\cdot\frac{(1-A)^2}{1-A+A^2} =10^6\ \text{Hz}\times\frac{3}{2\times1\times5}\times\frac{(-0.5)^2}{1-1.5+2.25} =10^6\times0.3\times\frac{0.25}{1.75}=42.86\ \text{kHz}.f1/f3​=f1/f​⋅2ηN3​⋅1−A+A2(1−A)2​=106 Hz×2×1×53​×1−1.5+2.25(−0.5)2​=106×0.3×1.750.25​=42.86 kHz. For completeness, the intermediate quantities ([P2] Eq.(55)/(56), triple-verified by lab_33 on that page): Γrms2=2π23η3N3[4 1+A3(1+A)3]=0.05895 ⇒ Γrms=0.2428,c0=2Γdc=2⋅2πη2N21−A1+A=−0.1005.\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{2\pi^2}{3\eta^3 N^3}\left[4\,\frac{1+A^3}{(1+A)^3}\right]=0.05895\;\Rightarrow\;\Gamma_{rms}=0.2428, \qquad c_0=2\Gamma_{dc}=2\cdot\frac{2\pi}{\eta^2N^2}\frac{1-A}{1+A}=-0.1005.Γrms2​=3η3N32π2​[4(1+A)31+A3​]=0.05895⇒Γrms​=0.2428,c0​=2Γdc​=2⋅η2N22π​1+A1−A​=−0.1005. Result: corner =42.86=42.86=42.86 kHz ([P2] Eq.(57) convention). Convention flag: substituting c0=2Γdcc_0=2\Gamma_{dc}c0​=2Γdc​ into [P1] Eq.(24) Δω1/f3=ω1/f c02/(2Γrms2)\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\,c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​c02​/(2Γrms2​) yields 85.71 kHz — exactly 2× (a DC-channel bookkeeping difference; each paper is internally self-consistent, and scalings and ratios are unaffected). Always state the convention when reporting the number. Design read: corner ∝(1−A)2/(1−A+A2)\propto(1-A)^2/(1-A+A^2)∝(1−A)2/(1−A+A2) and ∝1/N\propto1/N∝1/N — a 42.86 kHz close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3 would be mostly washed out by the SerDes PLL (loop BW far above 42.86 kHz), so flicker is not the reason to veto the ring; the ring's real price is the white-noise-region FOM (lc_vs_ring). This exam keeps the LC; this question archives Plan B quantitatively. Symmetrization (A→1A\to1A→1) sends the corner to zero quadratically — the closed-form version of symmetry. The integrated VCO measures L(1 MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz with a 1/f21/f^21/f2 slope (measured track — 48 dB above Question 2's ideal single-source limit: the reality of multiple sources, cyclostationarity, flicker, and the buffer chain). Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Work it out first: L(1 MHz) = −100 dBc/Hz, 1/f² slope, integrated 1→100 MHz, f₀ = 5 GHz — rms jitter σ_t = ? (answer in fs) fsCheckShow answer Graded correct within ±1% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Question 5 — full solution (jitter integration, canonical Example C) Step-by-step substitution (with units; the full four-step chain of lab_08): Sϕ(1 MHz)=2×10−100/10=2×10−10 rad2/Hz(L≈12Sϕ, small-angle SSB convention, canonical formula 16),σϕ2=Sϕ(fref) fref2(1f1−1f2)=2×10−10×(106)2×(10−6−10−8)=1.98×10−4 rad2,σϕ=1.407×10−2 rad=14.07 mrad,σt=σϕ2πf0=1.407×10−22π×5×109=4.479×10−13 s=447.9 fs.\begin{aligned} S_\phi(1\,\text{MHz})&=2\times10^{-100/10}=2\times10^{-10}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz} \quad(\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12 S_\phi\text{, small-angle SSB convention, canonical formula 16}),\\[2pt] \sigma_\phi^2&=S_\phi(f_{ref})\,f_{ref}^2\left(\frac{1}{f_1}-\frac{1}{f_2}\right) =2\times10^{-10}\times(10^6)^2\times(10^{-6}-10^{-8})=1.98\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}^2,\\[2pt] \sigma_\phi&=1.407\times10^{-2}\ \text{rad}=14.07\ \text{mrad},\\[2pt] \sigma_t&=\frac{\sigma_\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{1.407\times10^{-2}}{2\pi\times5\times10^9}=4.479\times10^{-13}\ \text{s}=447.9\ \text{fs}. \end{aligned}Sϕ​(1MHz)σϕ2​σϕ​σt​​=2×10−100/10=2×10−10 rad2/Hz(L≈21​Sϕ​, small-angle SSB convention, canonical formula 16),=Sϕ​(fref​)fref2​(f1​1​−f2​1​)=2×10−10×(106)2×(10−6−10−8)=1.98×10−4 rad2,=1.407×10−2 rad=14.07 mrad,=2πf0​σϕ​​=2π×5×1091.407×10−2​=4.479×10−13 s=447.9 fs.​ Result: σϕ=14.07\sigma_\phi=14.07σϕ​=14.07 mrad, σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs (canonical Example C). Convention flag: −100-100−100 is a measured SSB number; per the site rule it is restored to SϕS_\phiSϕ​ with L=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12S_\phiL=21​Sϕ​ (/2/2/2) — measured values never involve the /4/4/4 (that only enters when predicting from circuit noise, Questions 2/3). Feel: the 1/f21/f^21/f2 integral is dominated by the lower limit (the 1/f11/f_11/f1​ term carries 99%); "where the integration starts" is set by the PLL loop BW — the setup for Question 8. (This is exactly the "−100-100−100 dBc/Hz anchor" row of diffusion_dictionary: κ2=3.95×103\kappa^2=3.95\times10^3κ2=3.95×103, linewidth 628 Hz, κt=2.0×10−9s\kappa_t=2.0\times10^{-9}\sqrt{\text{s}}κt​=2.0×10−9s​.) Result: σP(1)≈28.3\sigma_P(1)\approx28.3σP​(1)≈28.3 fs (1.4×10−41.4\times10^{-4}1.4×10−4 of a period). Convention flags (two): (1) the inversion formula takes the /2/2/2-convention L\mathcal{L}L — measured values plug in as-is; plugging in a /4/4/4-convention predicted value here would come out 2\sqrt22​ low. (2) The kernel prefactor under the "single-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​, ∫0∞\int_0^\infty∫0∞​" convention is 1/ω021/\omega_0^21/ω02​ (not 2/ω022/\omega_0^22/ω02​ — that 2 belongs to double-sided-spectrum bookkeeping; adjudicated by the jitter_kernels Step 0 table plus Monte-Carlo). worked_examples Example C3's 27.6 fs is this same formula truncated to the 10310^3103–101010^{10}1010 Hz band — one physics. Against Question 5: same clock — accumulated jitter (TIE, 1–100 MHz band) 447.9 fs vs single-period 28.3 fs. TIE eats the low frequencies; the period kernel is a first-order high-pass that suppresses close-in. Both numbers are right; they measure different things (psd_phase_noise_jitter). Dimension check: rad2/s×s=rad2\text{rad}^2/\text{s}\times\text{s}=\text{rad}^2rad2/s×s=rad2 ✓; rad ÷ (rad/s) === s ✓. import numpy as np kappa2 = 10**(-100/10)*(2*np.pi*1e6)**2 print(round(kappa2, 1), round(np.sqrt(kappa2/5e9)/(2*np.pi*5e9)*1e15, 2)) # -> 3947.8 28.28

documents.t: Learning-path step: Step 12 — System integration and measurement The clock tree: 5 GHz through an ideal ÷2 to 2.5 GHz, then one output buffer with a flat −155-155−155 dBc/Hz floor. Look at 1 MHz offset (the same offset as Question 2's anchor — no extrapolation needed). Use the ideal single-source-limit track: the VCO skirt is just Question 2's −148-148−148 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz ([P1] Eq.(21)). Find the buffer output's L(1 MHz)\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})L(1MHz). Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Work it out first: VCO skirt −148 dBc/Hz@1 MHz (Question 2's anchor, no extrapolation needed), ideal ÷2, then power-summed with the −155 dBc/Hz buffer floor — L(1 MHz) = ? (answer in dBc/Hz, mind the sign) dBc/HzCheckShow answer Graded correct within ±1% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Question 7 — full solution (clock_chain rules 2 + 4: ÷N and the additive floor) (a) 1 MHz offset (this question's primary answer) Step 1 (rule 2: an ideal ÷2 is edge-picking, ϕout=ϕin/2\phi_{out}=\phi_{in}/2ϕout​=ϕin​/2 — use Question 2's −148-148−148 dBc/Hz anchor directly, no extrapolation needed): L(1 MHz)∣2.5 GHz=−148.00−20log⁡102=−154.02 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})\big|_{2.5\,\text{GHz}}=-148.00-20\log_{10}2=-154.02\ \text{dBc/Hz}.L(1MHz)​2.5GHz​=−148.00−20log10​2=−154.02 dBc/Hz. Step 2 (rule 4: the buffer floor is uncorrelated with the input — powers add): Lout(1 MHz)=10log⁡10 ⁣(10−154.02/10+10−155/10)=−151.47 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}_{out}(1\,\text{MHz})=10\log_{10}\!\big(10^{-154.02/10}+10^{-155/10}\big)=-151.47\ \text{dBc/Hz}.Lout​(1MHz)=10log10​(10−154.02/10+10−155/10)=−151.47 dBc/Hz. Result: −151.47-151.47−151.47 dBc/Hz — the signal (−154.02-154.02−154.02) and the floor (−155-155−155) are only 0.980.980.98 dB apart, so both are the same order of magnitude and both contribute (neither one dominates); the power sum pushes the output about 3 dB below either. This is deliberately built so you cannot just retype the given floor value −155-155−155 and get lucky: if the floor genuinely dominated (see (b)) the answer would land close to the floor itself, but here the two terms are comparable and the only way to get it right is to actually do the power addition. Convention flag: /2/2/2 vs /4/4/4 bookkeeping only shifts input and output together, and ±20log⁡10N\pm20\log_{10}N±20log10​N plus power addition are ratio/additive operations — the conclusion "both terms matter, powers must add" is unchanged. Dimension check: all dB operations act on dimensionless power ratios ✓. import numpy as np L_div = -148.0 - 20*np.log10(2) print(round(L_div, 2)) # -> -154.02 print(round(10*np.log10(10**(L_div/10) + 10**(-155.0/10)), 2)) # -> -151.47 (b) 10 MHz offset (the floor-dominated comparison case) Now look instead at 10 MHz offset (PLL out-of-band, where the VCO skirt must first be extrapolated at 1/f21/f^21/f2). Same procedure, but the signal is now far below the floor, so the power sum is essentially just the floor value — this is the pitfall case where the original version of this question could be beaten by simply typing −155-155−155. Kept here for contrast: Step 1 (1/f21/f^21/f2 extrapolation): Lvco(10 MHz)=−148−20log⁡10 ⁣10 MHz1 MHz=−168.00 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}_{vco}(10\,\text{MHz})=-148-20\log_{10}\!\frac{10\,\text{MHz}}{1\,\text{MHz}}=-168.00\ \text{dBc/Hz}.Lvco​(10MHz)=−148−20log10​1MHz10MHz​=−168.00 dBc/Hz. Step 2 (rule 2: an ideal ÷2): L(10 MHz)∣2.5 GHz=−168.00−20log⁡102=−174.02 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}(10\,\text{MHz})\big|_{2.5\,\text{GHz}}=-168.00-20\log_{10}2=-174.02\ \text{dBc/Hz}.L(10MHz)​2.5GHz​=−168.00−20log10​2=−174.02 dBc/Hz. Step 3 (rule 4: the buffer floor is uncorrelated with the input — powers add, never dB): Lout=10log⁡10 ⁣(10−174.02/10+10−155/10)=−154.95 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}_{out}=10\log_{10}\!\big(10^{-174.02/10}+10^{-155/10}\big)=-154.95\ \text{dBc/Hz}.Lout​=10log10​(10−174.02/10+10−155/10)=−154.95 dBc/Hz. Result: −154.95-154.95−154.95 dBc/Hz — the signal is 19 dB below the floor, so the floor takes over and the output is clamped at the buffer floor. However clean the source, one noisy buffer ruins it: those 19 dB of margin are voided outright — the core lesson of clock_chain_budget (same numbers as that page's worked chain: −168→−174.02→−154.95-168\to-174.02\to-154.95−168→−174.02→−154.95). Convention flag: ±20log⁡10N\pm20\log_{10}N±20log10​N and power addition are ratio/additive operations; the /2/2/2 vs /4/4/4 convention cancels between input and output — the only convention-sensitive item is the anchor itself (−148-148−148 = [P1] Eq.(21)'s /4/4/4; the /2/2/2 bookkeeping shifts the whole curve +3+3+3 dB, and the conclusion "floor takes over" stands, output still ≈−154.9\approx-154.9≈−154.9). Also note the conserved quantity: an ideal ÷2 improves L\mathcal{L}L by 6.02 dB, but the σt\sigma_tσt​ in seconds does not change by a single fs (needed in Question 9). Dimension check: all dB operations act on dimensionless power ratios ✓. import numpy as np L_div = (-148.0 - 20*np.log10(10)) - 20*np.log10(2) print(round(L_div, 2)) # -> -174.02 print(round(10*np.log10(10**(L_div/10) + 10**(-155.0/10)), 2)) # -> -154.95

documents.t: Learning-path step: Step 9 — Connect to SerDes clocking (jitter, eye, PLL/CDR) (PLL budget page: pll_noise_budget) The VCO goes into a type-II second-order PLL (ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707). The system spec asks: what is the jitter-transfer peaking (how far the peak exceeds 0 dB)? Use the closed form from pll_noise_budget. Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Work it out first: type-II second-order PLL, ζ = 0.707 — the |H_lp|² peaking = ? (answer in dB) dBCheckShow answer Graded correct within ±1% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Question 8 — full solution (peaking closed form: ζ=0.707→2.09\zeta=0.707\to2.09ζ=0.707→2.09 dB @ 0.786fn0.786f_n0.786fn​) Closed form (the result of that page's supplementary derivation, self-contained algebra). Let s=1+8ζ2s=\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}s=1+8ζ2​: ∣Hlp∣max2=(s+1)2(s−1)(s+3),fpk=fn2s+1.\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2_{max}=\frac{(s+1)^2}{(s-1)(s+3)},\qquad f_{pk}=f_n\sqrt{\frac{2}{s+1}}.∣Hlp​∣max2​=(s−1)(s+3)(s+1)2​,fpk​=fn​s+12​​. Step-by-step substitution (ζ=1/2\zeta=1/\sqrt2ζ=1/2​, ζ2=12\zeta^2=\tfrac12ζ2=21​): s=1+4=5=2.236s=\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt5=2.236s=1+4​=5​=2.236, ∣Hlp∣max2=(5+1)2(5−1)(5+3)=5+12=φ=1.618,fpk=fn25+1=0.786 fn.\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2_{max}=\frac{(\sqrt5+1)^2}{(\sqrt5-1)(\sqrt5+3)}=\frac{\sqrt5+1}{2}=\varphi=1.618, \qquad f_{pk}=f_n\sqrt{\frac{2}{\sqrt5+1}}=0.786\,f_n.∣Hlp​∣max2​=(5​−1)(5​+3)(5​+1)2​=25​+1​=φ=1.618,fpk​=fn​5​+12​​=0.786fn​.peaking=10log⁡101.618=2.09 dB.\text{peaking}=10\log_{10}1.618=2.09\ \text{dB}.peaking=10log10​1.618=2.09 dB. (The peak is exactly the golden ratio — that page's easter egg; a 4-million-point fine sweep of pll_utils.H_lowpass_mag2 numerically gives the same 0.7862/2.09030.7862/2.09030.7862/2.0903 dB.) Result: peaking =2.09=2.09=2.09 dB @ fpk=0.786fnf_{pk}=0.786f_nfpk​=0.786fn​ (phase margin 65.5∘65.5^\circ65.5∘). Convention flag: this is a power transfer's 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ (numerically equal to the magnitude's 20log⁡1020\log_{10}20log10​) — no SSB /2/2/2, /4/4/4 business here (that only appears in the Sϕ↔LS_\phi\leftrightarrow\mathcal{L}Sϕ​↔L conversion). A type-II loop with a zero must peak (the derivative at DC is always positive): it is the price of stability, not a design error; cascading MMM stages adds the dB directly — 20 regenerators make 41.841.841.8 dB, which is why telecom specs cap per-stage peaking at 0.1 dB (requiring ζ≈4.32\zeta\approx4.32ζ≈4.32). For this exam: reference/in-band noise near fpkf_{pk}fpk​ pays an extra 2.09 dB tax — do not miss it in the jitter budget. Dimension check: ζ,s,x\zeta,s,xζ,s,x all dimensionless; fpk=fn×f_{pk}=f_n\timesfpk​=fn​×dimensionless === Hz ✓. import numpy as np s = np.sqrt(1 + 8*0.707**2) print(round(np.sqrt(2/(s+1)), 4), round(10*np.log10((s+1)**2/((s-1)*(s+3))), 2)) # -> 0.7862 2.09

documents.t: Learning-path step: Step 12 — System integration and measurement The RX-side monitor ADC samples a full-scale 2.5 GHz calibration tone with the final 2.5 GHz clock. Clock RJ on the measured track: Question 5's σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs — an ideal ÷2 does not change σt\sigma_tσt​ in seconds (Question 7's conserved quantity; the buffer floor adds about 16 fs in the same band, +0.06%+0.06\%+0.06% after RSS, negligible). Find the jitter-limited SNR. Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Work it out first: a clock with σ_t = 447.9 fs samples a full-scale f_in = 2.5 GHz sine — SNR_jitter = ? (answer in dB) dBCheckShow answer Graded correct within ±1% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Question 9 — full solution (aperture SNR and ENOB) Step-by-step substitution (with units; derivation in adc_aperture_jitter). Sampling error === slope ×\times× timing error; after mean-squaring over sampling phase and jitter the two 12\tfrac1221​s cancel: σϕ,in=2πfin σt=2π×2.5×109 Hz×4.479×10−13 s=7.036×10−3 rad,\sigma_{\phi,in}=2\pi f_{in}\,\sigma_t=2\pi\times2.5\times10^9\ \text{Hz}\times4.479\times10^{-13}\ \text{s}=7.036\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad},σϕ,in​=2πfin​σt​=2π×2.5×109 Hz×4.479×10−13 s=7.036×10−3 rad,SNRjitter=−20log⁡10 ⁣(2πfinσt)=−20log⁡10(7.036×10−3)=43.05 dB,\text{SNR}_{jitter}=-20\log_{10}\!\big(2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t\big)=-20\log_{10}(7.036\times10^{-3})=43.05\ \text{dB},SNRjitter​=−20log10​(2πfin​σt​)=−20log10​(7.036×10−3)=43.05 dB,ENOB=43.05−1.766.02=6.86 bit.\text{ENOB}=\frac{43.05-1.76}{6.02}=6.86\ \text{bit}.ENOB=6.0243.05−1.76​=6.86 bit. Result: SNR =43.05=43.05=43.05 dB, ENOB =6.86=6.86=6.86 bit — word-for-word the 2.5 GHz row of the adc_aperture_jitter design table. Buying a 12-bit ADC would not help: the high-frequency SNR is pinned by the clock. Convention flag: the formula itself is independent of SSB/DSB or any L\mathcal{L}L convention (the 12\tfrac1221​ in PsigP_{sig}Psig​ cancels the 12\tfrac1221​ from ⟨cos⁡2⟩\langle\cos^2\rangle⟨cos2⟩); the convention hides upstream in σt\sigma_tσt​ — 447.9 fs was integrated from a measured L\mathcal{L}L via the /2/2/2 small-angle conversion (Question 5); keep the chain consistent and there is no ambiguity. Using the conserved quantity: σt\sigma_tσt​ (seconds) is invariant through an ideal ÷2 (clock_chain_budget, Step 5) — ÷2 saves dB of L\mathcal{L}L, not fs; so the 2.5 GHz clock inherits 447.9 fs directly. Honesty note: with the buffer floor, 447.92+16.02=448.2\sqrt{447.9^2+16.0^2}=448.2447.92+16.02​=448.2 fs (+0.06%+0.06\%+0.06%) — ignored in this question. Dimension check: Hz ×\times× s ×2π=\times2\pi=×2π= rad (dimensionless) ✓ — a legal log argument; dB and bit dimensionless ✓. import numpy as np snr = -20*np.log10(2*np.pi*2.5e9*447.9e-15) print(round(snr, 2), round((snr - 1.76)/6.02, 2)) # -> 43.05 6.86
