documents.t: Learning-path step: Step 12 — System integration and measurement Closing out the link. 25 Gb/s (UI =40=40=40 ps), measured decomposition gives DJδδ=1\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}=1DJδδ​=1 ps; RJ is the measured-track clock's σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs. Use the dual-Dirac extrapolation (dj_dual_dirac) to find the total jitter at BER =10−12=10^{-12}=10−12. Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Work it out first: DJ_δδ = 1 ps, RJ σ = 447.9 fs — the dual-Dirac extrapolated TJ@BER=10⁻¹² = ? (per-Gaussian convention Q⁻¹ = 7.034; answer in ps) psCheckShow answer Graded correct within ±1% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Question 10 — full solution (dual-Dirac extrapolation and the eye budget) Step-by-step substitution (with units). The dual-Dirac extrapolation formula (deep tail dominated by a single Gaussian): TJ(BER)=DJδδ+2 Q−1(BER) σ,Q−1(10−12)=7.034 (this site uses 7.03).\mathrm{TJ}(\mathrm{BER})=\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}+2\,Q^{-1}(\mathrm{BER})\,\sigma, \qquad Q^{-1}(10^{-12})=7.034\ (\text{this site uses }7.03).TJ(BER)=DJδδ​+2Q−1(BER)σ,Q−1(10−12)=7.034 (this site uses 7.03).TJ=1 ps+2×7.034×0.4479 ps=1 ps+6.30 ps=7.30 ps.\mathrm{TJ}=1\ \text{ps}+2\times7.034\times0.4479\ \text{ps}=1\ \text{ps}+6.30\ \text{ps}=7.30\ \text{ps}.TJ=1 ps+2×7.034×0.4479 ps=1 ps+6.30 ps=7.30 ps.eye opening=UI−TJ=40−7.30=32.7 ps=0.82 UI.\text{eye opening}=UI-\mathrm{TJ}=40-7.30=32.7\ \text{ps}=0.82\ UI.eye opening=UI−TJ=40−7.30=32.7 ps=0.82 UI. Result: TJ@10−12=7.3010^{-12}=7.3010−12=7.30 ps, eye opening 32.732.732.7 ps (0.82 UI0.82\,UI0.82UI) — the RJ term 6.30 ps matches serdes_clocking_connection's "448 fs → RJ eats 6.36.36.3 ps" ✓. This 25 Gb/s link's clock budget passes. Convention flag: Q−1(10−12)=7.034Q^{-1}(10^{-12})=7.034Q−1(10−12)=7.034 is the industry per-Gaussian convention (each Gaussian's tail === BER); rigorously booking the Dirac weight ½ and the transition density ½ gives the Q=4×BERQ=4\times\mathrm{BER}Q=4×BER convention (Q−1=6.839Q^{-1}=6.839Q−1=6.839), about 0.2σ0.2\sigma0.2σ/side of difference — settle the convention before comparing instrument reports (the Step 6 audit table of dj_dual_dirac). Also remember DJδδ≤DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}\le\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJδδ​≤DJpp​: the model parameter is deliberately under-reported precisely so the extrapolation is accurate — do not stuff DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJpp​ into this formula. Dimension check: [s]+[dimensionless]×[s]=[s][\text{s}]+[\text{dimensionless}]\times[\text{s}]=[\text{s}][s]+[dimensionless]×[s]=[s] ✓. Closing the loop on the whole exam: Question 1's single 1 fC impulse (15.9 fs) → Questions 2–3's white-noise skirt and linewidth → Question 5's integration into a 447.9 fs RJ → Question 7's clock-tree accounting → Question 10 settles the bill on the eye. Where one charge goes is where a SerDes link's margin goes. import numpy as np from scipy.special import erfcinv qinv = float(np.sqrt(2)*erfcinv(2*1e-12)) tj = 1e-12 + 2*qinv*447.9e-15 print(round(qinv, 3), round(tj*1e12, 2)) # -> 7.034 7.3

documents.t: Learning-path step: Step 11 — Injection locking and frequency conversion One last fork before graduation. Questions 7–9 took the "PLL ×50 → ÷2 → buffer" route. A junior colleague asks: "what if we skip the PLL entirely and drive the same 555 GHz LC VCO (qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC) directly with an fref=250f_{ref}=250fref​=250 MHz reference pulse train (qinj=50q_{inj}=50qinj​=50 fC) as an N=20N=20N=20 injection-locked clock multiplier (ILCM)? How wide is that route's half lock range?" Use the impulse-train arithmetic of subharmonic_injection (the discrete version of [P3] Sec. IV footnote 7) to find fLf_LfL​. Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Work it out first: a q_inj = 50 fC reference pulse drives an f₀ = 5 GHz, q_max = 1 pC LC VCO directly as an N = 20 injection-locked clock multiplier (ILCM); half lock range f_L = ? (answer in MHz) MHzCheckShow answer Graded correct within ±1% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Question 11 — full solution (the ILCM's 1/N1/N1/N lock range, the other route in place of the PLL) Step 1 (the discrete arithmetic of [P3] footnote 7; full derivation on subharmonic_injection, Section 2): one kick every NNN oscillation periods; the fixed point exists (weak injection, the Γ=−sin⁡\Gamma=-\sinΓ=−sin special case) when ΔωL=qinj ∣Γ~∣maxNT0 → Γ=−sin⁡ qinjqmax⋅1NT0=qinjqmax⋅f0N.\Delta\omega_L=\frac{q_{inj}\,\vert\tilde\Gamma\vert_{max}}{NT_0}\ \xrightarrow{\ \Gamma=-\sin\ }\ \frac{q_{inj}}{q_{max}}\cdot\frac{1}{NT_0}=\frac{q_{inj}}{q_{max}}\cdot\frac{f_0}{N}.ΔωL​=NT0​qinj​∣Γ~∣max​​ Γ=−sin ​ qmax​qinj​​⋅NT0​1​=qmax​qinj​​⋅Nf0​​. Step-by-step substitution (with units): qinjqmax=50 fC1 pC=0.05(weak injection≪1 ✓),T0=1f0=200 ps,NT0=20×200 ps=4 ns,\frac{q_{inj}}{q_{max}}=\frac{50\ \text{fC}}{1\ \text{pC}}=0.05\quad(\text{weak injection}\ll1\ \checkmark),\qquad T_0=\frac{1}{f_0}=200\ \text{ps},\qquad NT_0=20\times200\ \text{ps}=4\ \text{ns},qmax​qinj​​=1 pC50 fC​=0.05(weak injection≪1 ✓),T0​=f0​1​=200 ps,NT0​=20×200 ps=4 ns,ΔωL=0.054×10−9 s=1.25×107 rad/s,fL=ΔωL2π=1.989 MHz.\Delta\omega_L=\frac{0.05}{4\times10^{-9}\ \text{s}}=1.25\times10^{7}\ \text{rad/s},\qquad f_L=\frac{\Delta\omega_L}{2\pi}=1.989\ \text{MHz}.ΔωL​=4×10−9 s0.05​=1.25×107 rad/s,fL​=2πΔωL​​=1.989 MHz. Result: fL=1.989f_L=1.989fL​=1.989 MHz (canonical Example 1 on subharmonic_injection). Dimension check: dimensionless ÷\div÷ s === rad/s; rad/s ÷2π=\div2\pi=÷2π= Hz ✓. Closing the fork (why this exam picked the PLL, not the ILCM): the fractional lock range fL/(Nfref)=(qinj/qmax)/(2πN)=3.98×10−4f_L/(Nf_{ref})=(q_{inj}/q_{max})/(2\pi N)=3.98\times10^{-4}fL​/(Nfref​)=(qinj​/qmax​)/(2πN)=3.98×10−4 = 398 ppm — two orders of magnitude smaller than the percent-level free-running frequency uncertainty from PVT, meaning this VCO would first have to be pulled to within 398 ppm before the ILCM could even lock; in practice that means bolting on a frequency-locked loop (FLL). Question 8's type-II PLL, by contrast, has a PFD with wide-range frequency acquisition built in — no auxiliary FLL needed. That is exactly why this exam's Act 2 settled on the PLL rather than the ILCM. But the ILCM isn't without its own savings: it has no divider or CP at all, and its in-band noise bookkeeping runs through N2Sref∣Href∣2N^2S_{ref}\vert H_{ref}\vert^2N2Sref​∣Href​∣2 (HrefH_{ref}Href​ a first-order discrete-time low-pass) — the same family as Question 3's PLL in-band term N2Sref∣Hlp∣2N^2S_{ref}\vert H_{lp}\vert^2N2Sref​∣Hlp​∣2, but a different mechanism: both routes converge on ×N2\times N^2×N2, they just kick the divider out by different means. Convention flag: this question's numbers use the δ\deltaδ-pulse (impulse-train) idealization, matching the canonical Example 1 on subharmonic_injection; including the sinc correction for a finite 101010 ps pulse width lowers it to 1.9811.9811.981 MHz (a 0.4%0.4\%0.4% difference, ignored here). import numpy as np qinj, qmax, f0, N = 50e-15, 1e-12, 5e9, 20 T0 = 1 / f0 dwL = (qinj/qmax) / (N*T0) fL = dwL / (2*np.pi) print(round(fL/1e6, 3)) # -> 1.989 print(round((qinj/qmax)/(2*np.pi*N), 6)) # -> 0.000398 (398 ppm, the fractional lock range)

documents.t: Run from the project root with PYTHONPATH=.; every # -> is actual printed output, matching each solution word for word. import numpy as np from scipy.special import erfcinv from simulations.common.isf_utils import impulse_to_phase_step, gamma_lc_ideal from simulations.common.noise_utils import phase_to_time_error, integrate_rms_jitter from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_lowpass_mag2 f0, qmax, grms, Si = 5e9, 1e-12, 0.5, 1e-24 dw = 2*np.pi*1e6 # 1 MHz offset [rad/s] # --- Q0a (warm-up): amplitude recovery time constant tau_0 = 2Q/omega_0 ([P4] Sec. III-F p.2128) Q = 20 tau0 = 2*Q/(2*np.pi*f0) print(round(tau0*1e9, 3), round(tau0*f0, 2), round(1/(2*np.pi*tau0)/1e6, 1)) # -> 1.273 6.37 125.0 # --- Q0b (warm-up): superposition of two impulses ([P1] Eq.(11), discrete form) dphi_0b = sum(impulse_to_phase_step(dq, gamma_lc_ideal(th), qmax=qmax) for dq, th in [(1e-15, np.pi/2), (3e-15, 3*np.pi/2)]) print(round(dphi_0b*1e3, 3), round(phase_to_time_error(dphi_0b, f0)*1e15, 1)) # -> 2.0 63.7 # --- Q1: impulse -> Delta_phi -> Delta_t (Example A) dphi = impulse_to_phase_step(1e-15, 0.5, qmax=qmax) print(dphi, round(phase_to_time_error(dphi, f0)*1e15, 1)) # -> 0.0005 15.9 # --- Q2: [P1] Eq.(21) (SSB /4 convention) L4 = 10*np.log10((grms**2/qmax**2)*(Si/(4*dw**2))) print(round(L4, 1)) # -> -148.0 # --- Q3: /4 -> /2 -> kappa^2 -> Lorentzian linewidth L2_lin = 10**((L4 + 3.01)/10) # back to /2 convention (+3.01 dB) kappa2 = L2_lin*dw**2 # reverse lookup kappa^2 = L_/2 * dw^2 print(round(kappa2, 3), round(grms**2*Si/(2*qmax**2), 3)) # -> 0.125 0.125 print(round(kappa2/(2*np.pi)*1e3, 1)) # -> 19.9 (mHz) # --- Q4: [P2] App.B Eq.(55)-(57), N=5, A=1.5, eta=1, f_1/f=1 MHz N, A, eta, f1f = 5, 1.5, 1.0, 1e6 corner = f1f*3/(2*eta*N)*(1-A)**2/(1-A+A**2) print(round(corner/1e3, 2), round(2*corner/1e3, 2)) # -> 42.86 85.71 ([P2]; [P1] convention) # --- Q5: measured -100 dBc/Hz@1MHz, 1/f^2, integrated 1-100 MHz f = np.logspace(6, 8, 4000) sigma_t, sigma_phi = integrate_rms_jitter(f, -100.0 - 20*np.log10(f/1e6), f0, 1e6, 100e6) print(round(sigma_phi*1e3, 2), round(sigma_t*1e15, 1)) # -> 14.07 447.9 # --- Q6: the same measured clock's period jitter (jitter_kernels closed form) kappa2_m = 10**(-100/10)*dw**2 # measured SSB = /2 convention print(round(kappa2_m, 1)) # -> 3947.8 (rad^2/s) print(round(np.sqrt(kappa2_m/f0)/(2*np.pi*f0)*1e15, 2)) # -> 28.28 (fs) # --- Q7(a): ideal skirt /2 to 2.5 GHz + buffer floor (1 MHz offset, primary answer) L_div_1m = -148.0 - 20*np.log10(2) print(round(L_div_1m, 2)) # -> -154.02 print(round(10*np.log10(10**(L_div_1m/10) + 10**(-155.0/10)), 2)) # -> -151.47 # --- Q7(b): same chain at 10 MHz offset (floor-dominated comparison case) L_div = (-148.0 - 20*np.log10(10)) - 20*np.log10(2) print(round(L_div, 2)) # -> -174.02 print(round(10*np.log10(10**(L_div/10) + 10**(-155.0/10)), 2)) # -> -154.95 # --- Q8: type-II peaking closed form vs pll_utils numeric s = np.sqrt(1 + 8*0.707**2) print(round(np.sqrt(2/(s+1)), 4), round(10*np.log10((s+1)**2/((s-1)*(s+3))), 2)) # -> 0.7862 2.09 x = np.linspace(0.001, 5, 400001) m2 = H_lowpass_mag2(x, 1.0, 0.707) print(round(10*np.log10(np.max(m2)), 2)) # -> 2.09 # --- Q9: aperture SNR (sigma_t conserved through the ideal /2) st = 447.9e-15 snr = -20*np.log10(2*np.pi*2.5e9*st) print(round(snr, 2), round((snr - 1.76)/6.02, 2)) # -> 43.05 6.86 # --- Q10: dual-Dirac TJ@1e-12 (per-Gaussian convention), UI = 40 ps qinv = float(np.sqrt(2)*erfcinv(2*1e-12)) tj = 1e-12 + 2*qinv*st print(round(qinv, 3), round(tj*1e12, 2)) # -> 7.034 7.3 print(round((40e-12 - tj)*1e12, 1), round((40e-12 - tj)/40e-12, 2)) # -> 32.7 0.82 # --- Q11 (bonus): the ILCM's 1/N lock range ([P3] footnote 7 discrete arithmetic) qinj, qmax_ilcm, N_ilcm = 50e-15, 1e-12, 20 T0_ilcm = 1 / f0 dwL = (qinj/qmax_ilcm) / (N_ilcm*T0_ilcm) fL = dwL / (2*np.pi) print(round(fL/1e6, 3)) # -> 1.989 print(round((qinj/qmax_ilcm)/(2*np.pi*N_ilcm), 6)) # -> 0.000398

documents.t: Double q_max: L\mathcal{L}L should drop 666 dB (L∝1/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto 1/q_{max}^2L∝1/qmax2​) — see tank_swing. Halve Γ_rms: L\mathcal{L}L also drops 666 dB (L∝Γrms2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2L∝Γrms2​) — see symmetry, waveform_slope. Pull the lower integration limit f₁ down: σt\sigma_tσt​ grows — because 1/f² jitter is dominated by the lower limit (see Example C in numerical_feeling). Raise f₀: at the same σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​, σt=σϕ/(2πf0)\sigma_t=\sigma_\phi/(2\pi f_0)σt​=σϕ​/(2πf0​) shrinks — but do not forget that higher-frequency circuits usually carry more noise too.

documents.t: Tune the ISF Fourier coefficients c0c_0c0​–c3c_3c3​ and watch in real time the waveform Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ), Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, and the 1/f³ corner ratio c02/(2Γrms2)c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)c02​/(2Γrms2​) ([P1] Eq.24). Pull c0c_0c0​ to 0 (symmetric waveform) and the corner approaches 0 — this is the mechanism that suppresses close-in flicker. Theory: fourier_series_of_isf, rms_isf; verification: lab_05. Limitations: the sliders only go up to c3c_3c3​ (IsfFourierExplorer.js), far fewer harmonics than lab_05's nharmonics=8n_{harmonics}=8nharmonics​=8 on the site; the Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and Parseval readouts show the truncated-series approximation ∑n=03cn2\sum_{n=0}^{3}c_n^2∑n=03​cn2​ to 2Γrms22\Gamma_{rms}^22Γrms2​, not the exact infinite-series value. documents.t: Injection locking (an external signal pulling the oscillator frequency onto itself) has a range set by the ISF fundamental: drag I_inj, the detuning Δω, and the normalized ISF fundamental ∣Γ~1∣\vert\tilde\Gamma_1\vert∣Γ~1​∣ to see the lock range ωL=12 Iinj ∣Γ~1∣\omega_L=\tfrac12\,I_{inj}\,\vert\tilde\Gamma_1\vertωL​=21​Iinj​∣Γ~1​∣ ([P3] Eq.(35)) and the phase dynamics dθ/dt=Δω−ωLsin⁡θd\theta/dt=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\thetadθ/dt=Δω−ωL​sinθ (the Adler equation — external literature, not among the five source PDFs). When ∣Δω∣≤ωL\vert\Delta\omega\vert\le\omega_L∣Δω∣≤ωL​, Ω(θ)=ωLsin⁡θ\Omega(\theta)=\omega_L\sin\thetaΩ(θ)=ωL​sinθ intersects the horizontal line Δω\Delta\omegaΔω and the system locks at a fixed point θ∗\theta^*θ∗; once the detuning exceeds the envelope it unlocks, leaving a residual beat frequency Ωbeat=Δω2−ωL2\Omega_{beat}=\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}Ωbeat​=Δω2−ωL2​​. Theory: [P3], injection_locking_noise; transient behavior and cycle slips: lab_36. Limitations: sinusoidal injection, the ideal-LC fundamental-normalized ISF Γ~1\tilde\Gamma_1Γ~1​, and weak injection (the small-signal assumption behind the Adler equation) — strong injection, non-sinusoidal waveforms, or higher-harmonic coupling are outside this tool's model. Injection Locking 互動探索器（注入鎖定，外部訊號把振盪器頻率拉到自己身上） I_inj（注入電流，arb.）2.00 a.u. Δω = ω₀ − ω_inj（detuning）0.40 rad/s |Γ̃₁|（normalized ISF 基頻）0.50 狀態 LOCKED |Δω| ≤ ω_L lock range ω_L — [P3] Eq.(35) 0.500 rad/s phase error θ* 53.1 deg 0π2πθ+ω_L−ω_LΔω 讀圖：藍色曲線 Ω(θ)=ω_L·sin(θ) 是「振盪器能提供的最大頻率牽引」； 水平線是要克服的失諧 Δω。只要 Δω 落在 ±ω_L 包絡內， 曲線與水平線就有交點（穩定固定點 = 實心綠點，θ*∈[−90°,+90°]； 另一交點為不穩定），系統鎖定，相位差停在 θ* 不再漂移。 一旦 |Δω| > ω_L 交點消失，相位持續滑動，殘餘拍頻 Ω_beat=√(Δω²−ω_L²)。 公式：lock range ω_L = ½·I_inj·|Γ̃₁|（[P3] Eq.(35)）； 相位動態 dθ/dt = Δω − ω_L·sin(θ)（Adler 方程，外部文獻，非本站 5 篇 PDF）； 鎖定條件 |Δω| ≤ ω_L；拍頻 Ω_beat = √(Δω² − ω_L²)。單位：ω_L、Δω、Ω_beat 同為 rad/s， |Γ̃₁| 無因次，I_inj 為任意單位（normalization 已吸收 q_max）。

documents.t: Allan deviation (the two-sample standard deviation that measures long-term time-domain frequency stability) σy(τ)\sigma_y(\tau)σy​(τ) translates the same oscillator's noise into a curve versus averaging time τ\tauτ: pick the dominant FM noise type (white / flicker / random-walk FM) and its strength, and watch the log-log slope fall on the τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2, τ0\tau^{0}τ0, τ+1/2\tau^{+1/2}τ+1/2 segments in real time. Underneath is the exact closed form of σy2(τ)=2∫0∞Sy(f) sin⁡4(πfτ)/(πfτ)2 df\sigma_y^2(\tau)=2\int_0^\infty S_y(f)\,\sin^4(\pi f\tau)/(\pi f\tau)^2\,dfσy2​(τ)=2∫0∞​Sy​(f)sin4(πfτ)/(πfτ)2df (with Sy(f)=(f2/f02) Sϕ(f)S_y(f)=(f^2/f_0^2)\,S_\phi(f)Sy​(f)=(f2/f02​)Sϕ​(f)) for pure power-law processes, matching the slope table in spec 11.2; simulation script simulations/lab_19_allan.py (figure in allan_variance). documents.t: The loop bandwidth (the cutoff frequency up to which the loop can track the input phase) fnf_nfn​ of a PLL (phase-locked loop) sets the noise budget: the loop low-passes the reference path and high-passes the VCO path, giving the output Sout=Sref∣Hlp∣2+Svco∣Hhp∣2S_{out}=S_{ref}\vert H_{lp}\vert^2+S_{vco}\vert H_{hp}\vert^2Sout​=Sref​∣Hlp​∣2+Svco​∣Hhp​∣2 (spec 10.2). Increasing fnf_nfn​ admits more in-band reference noise and less out-of-band VCO noise, so there exists an optimum loop BW that minimizes the integrated jitter σt=∫Sout df/(2πf0)\sigma_t=\sqrt{\int S_{out}\,df}/(2\pi f_0)σt​=∫Sout​df​/(2πf0​) (spec formula 19) — drag the slider to find it. Matches pll_noise_budget; simulation script simulations/lab_20_pll_budget.py (figure in pll_noise_budget). documents.s: Formula reference

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. This is the first lab of the entire ISF (Impulse Sensitivity Function — the oscillator's "phase-sensitivity" weight toward noise) story. We deliberately touch no constants in any formula yet; with a single 2-D picture we build a geometric intuition that will stay with you for life: the oscillator's state circles a closed trajectory (the limit cycle); when a perturbation pushes the state point away, the part along the cycle (tangential) becomes phase and the part off the cycle (radial) becomes amplitude; and phase has no restoring force while amplitude does — this is the root of "why phase noise accumulates permanently". Physical intuition (conclusion first): picture the oscillation as a bead circling a track at constant speed. Push it from the side (tangentially) → its position along the track (the phase) is permanently displaced; no force whatsoever pushes it back to its original schedule. Push it inward from the outside (radially) → the track radius (the amplitude) changes, but the oscillator's AGC / device nonlinearity slowly pulls the radius back to steady state. So only the tangential part becomes a permanent phase error. The same impulse, injected at different phases of the waveform, splits between tangential and radial in different proportions — this is exactly what the ISF Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) describes.
documents.s: Lab 01 — Sinusoidal Oscillator and the Phase/Amplitude Geometry of the Limit Cycle

documents.t: See the limit cycle in the 2-D state space, and distinguish the geometric directions of the two perturbations: phase (tangential) and amplitude (radial). Understand that amplitude perturbations are pulled back to the limit cycle by a restoring mechanism, while phase perturbations remain permanently. See why a current impulse of the same size changes almost only the amplitude when injected at the peak (Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0) and almost only the phase at the zero crossing (∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ maximal) — the most direct evidence that the ISF is time-variant (LTV) rather than time-invariant (LTI). Lay the geometric groundwork for Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ in lab_02 and the derivation in impulse_to_phase_shift.
documents.s: 1. Learning goals

documents.t: We use a normalized (dimensionless) 2-D oscillator state model. The state is z=(x,y)z=(x,y)z=(x,y), where you may think of xxx as the capacitor voltage and yyy as (proportional to) the inductor current: dxdt=−ω0 y+μ (1−r2) x,dydt= ω0 x+μ (1−r2) y,r2=x2+y2.\begin{aligned} \frac{dx}{dt}&=-\omega_0\,y+\mu\,(1-r^2)\,x,\\ \frac{dy}{dt}&=\;\;\omega_0\,x+\mu\,(1-r^2)\,y,\qquad r^2=x^2+y^2. \end{aligned}dtdx​dtdy​​=−ω0​y+μ(1−r2)x,=ω0​x+μ(1−r2)y,r2=x2+y2.​ The first term, the ±ω0\pm\omega_0±ω0​ coupling: pure rotation. With μ=0\mu=0μ=0 this is the ideal lossless LC: the state circles the unit circle at constant angular velocity ω0\omega_0ω0​, with the amplitude marginally stable (neither growing nor decaying), corresponding to V(t)=cos⁡ω0tV(t)=\cos\omega_0 tV(t)=cosω0​t. The second term, μ(1−r2)z\mu(1-r^2)zμ(1−r2)z: a Van der Pol-style amplitude restoration. For r>1r>1r>1 (pushed outside the circle) it pulls inward; for r<1r<1r<1 (pushed inside) it pushes outward — dragging the trajectory back to the r=1r=1r=1 limit cycle. It models the AGC / device nonlinearity every real oscillator must have (without it, the amplitude would diverge or decay). Dimension check: the equations are normalized — x,y,rx,y,rx,y,r are all dimensionless, ω0,μ\omega_0,\muω0​,μ carry rad/s, and both sides are "dimensionless ÷ seconds" ✓. How a perturbation enters: a current impulse injected into the capacitor node deposits charge Δq=∫i dt\Delta q=\int i\,dtΔq=∫idt, producing an instantaneous voltage step ΔV=Δq/Cnode\Delta V=\Delta q/C_{node}ΔV=Δq/Cnode​ ([P1] Eq.(9), p.181): ΔV=ΔqCnode.\Delta V=\frac{\Delta q}{C_{node}}.ΔV=Cnode​Δq​. In normalized units (A=1A=1A=1, qmax=Cnode⋅A=Cnodeq_{max}=C_{node}\cdot A=C_{node}qmax​=Cnode​⋅A=Cnode​), this is a step Δx=Δq/qmax\Delta x=\Delta q/q_{max}Δx=Δq/qmax​ added to the xxx state. Note that it moves only the capacitor voltage xxx, not the inductor current yyy (an inductor current cannot change instantaneously), so in the state space it is a horizontal jump along the xxx axis — Step 2 of impulse_to_phase_shift covers this in more detail. Toy-model statement: this is a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level. It faithfully reproduces the mechanisms — the phase/amplitude decomposition and the absence of a phase restoring force — but it produces no noise numbers of any real circuit.

documents.t: The following is excerpted from the actual script (checked against simulations/lab_01_sinusoidal_oscillator.py). fig_limit_cycle starts integrating from a point off the cycle, (x0,y0)=(1.7,0)(x_0,y_0)=(1.7,0)(x0​,y0​)=(1.7,0), so you can watch the trajectory relax back to the limit cycle; two arrows then mark the tangential (phase) and radial (amplitude) directions: from oscillator_models import simulate_lc, sinusoidal_oscillator def fig_limit_cycle(): f0 = 1.0 # normalized fs = 4000.0 # start from an off-cycle point: the trajectory relaxes back to the unit-circle limit cycle (mu=0.6 provides amplitude restoration) t, x, y = simulate_lc(f0, t_end=3.0, fs=fs, mu=0.6, x0=1.7, y0=0.0) # operating point chosen at theta = pi/4 p = np.array([np.cos(np.pi / 4), np.sin(np.pi / 4)]) tang = np.array([-p[1], p[0]]) * 0.45 # tangential (phase) direction: perpendicular to the radius rad = p * 0.45 # radial (amplitude) direction: along the radius # tang part -> permanent phase Δφ ; rad part -> amplitude ΔA, pulled back The second figure marks equal-size impulses at the peak (θ=0\theta=0θ=0) and at the zero crossing (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2, i.e. t=0.25Tt=0.25Tt=0.25T), highlighting that "the injection phase determines the effect": def fig_impulse_markers(): f0, fs = 1.0, 4000.0 t = np.arange(int(2.0 * fs)) / fs v = sinusoidal_oscillator(t, f0, amp=1.0) # V(t)=cos(2*pi*f0*t) t_peak = 0.0 # peak theta=0 -> amplitude only (Gamma ~ 0) t_zc = 0.25 / f0 # zero crossing theta=pi/2 -> phase only (|Gamma| max) The underlying state integration (RK4) and impulse injection live inside simulate_lc(); injection is xi += impulse_dx, i.e. adding a step of Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ to the xxx state.

documents.s: 8. Simulation figures

documents.t: Figure 1 (state space): The black dashed unit circle is the steady-state limit cycle; the solid blue curve is the trajectory starting from (1.7,0)(1.7,0)(1.7,0), pulled back to the unit circle turn after turn by the μ(1−r2)z\mu(1-r^2)zμ(1−r2)z term — seeing is believing for "amplitude perturbations get restored". The black dot is the operating point θ=π/4\theta=\pi/4θ=π/4. The green arrow (tangential) is the phase direction: moving along the cycle is moving the bead forward/backward on the track, and no force pushes it back, so this part accumulates permanently. The red arrow (radial) is the amplitude direction: pushing the point away from or toward the center gets pulled back by the restoring mechanism, leaving no trace. Key mental model: any perturbation vector decomposes into these two orthogonal components; only the part projected onto the green tangential direction becomes permanent phase error. Figure 2 (waveform): The blue curve is V(t)=cos⁡(2πf0t)V(t)=\cos(2\pi f_0 t)V(t)=cos(2πf0​t). The red triangle sits at the peak: the waveform slope there is 0, so the horizontal voltage jump is almost purely radial (amplitude change), with tangential component ≈0\approx0≈0, hence Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0. The green triangle sits at the zero crossing: the waveform slope there is maximal, so the horizontal voltage jump is almost purely tangential (phase change), hence ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ is maximal. Connect the two points: the same Δq\Delta qΔq at different injection times τ\tauτ → completely different Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ. The system's response to an impulse depends on the absolute injection phase — the defining signature of LTV (compare lti_vs_ltv).
documents.s: 9. How to read the figures

documents.t: Conceptual source: [P1] Fig. 4, p.182 — Hajimiri–Lee use the state-space limit cycles of LC and ring oscillators to demonstrate "impulse at the peak (amplitude change) vs at the zero crossing (phase change)". The two figures in this lab are redrawn conceptual toy figures (redrawn conceptual — not transistor-level, not point-by-point copies of the paper's figures). Charge → voltage step: [P1] Eq.(9), p.181, ΔV=Δq/Cnode\Delta V=\Delta q/C_{node}ΔV=Δq/Cnode​. ISF and impulse response (used in the next step): [P1] Eq.(10), p.182: hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ).h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau).hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ). where the unit step u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) is exactly the mathematical statement of Figure 1's "phase perturbations remain permanently". Next: the ideal LC's Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ (maximal at the zero crossings, zero at the peaks — consistent with Figure 2) is derived in lab_02 and isf_definition.

documents.t: This is a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level. μ(1−r2)z\mu(1-r^2)zμ(1−r2)z is only the simplest possible way to write "there is amplitude restoring"; it does not represent the restoring dynamics of any real device — real amplitude-restoring time constants and AM–PM conversion require transistor-level / Floquet analysis. Small-signal assumption: projecting a perturbation into "tangential + radial" is a linearization, requiring Δq≪qmax\Delta q\ll q_{max}Δq≪qmax​. A large injection nonlinearly alters the ISF itself (see the linearity verification in lab_02). Narrow-pulse assumption: treating the impulse as an instantaneous voltage jump requires the pulse width ≪T\ll T≪T; wide pulses must go back to the integral form of Eq.(11). This lab deliberately gives no absolute-unit numbers (normalized f0=1f_0=1f0​=1) — it teaches the geometry and the sign directions. The canonical numbers with real units (qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δϕ=5×10−4\Delta\phi=5\times10^{-4}Δϕ=5×10−4 rad, Δt=15.9\Delta t=15.9Δt=15.9 fs) are in Example A of impulse_to_phase_shift and in numerical_feeling.
documents.s: 11. Limitations and approximations

documents.t: The oscillator state circles the limit cycle; a perturbation decomposes into tangential (phase, permanent) and radial (amplitude, pulled back). Phase has no restoring force — the physical root of phase noise accumulating without bound (random walk). Same-size impulse: at the peak → amplitude change (Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0); at the zero crossing → phase change (∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ maximal). "The effect depends on the injection phase" = the essence of LTV, and the reason the ISF exists. Source: [P1] Fig. 4 and Eq.(9), p.181, and Eq.(10), p.182.
documents.s: Key takeaways

documents.t: lab_01 gave the geometric intuition: phase = tangential, amplitude = radial. This lab turns that into a concrete function. For an ideal lossless parallel LC oscillator, the permanent phase shift caused by injecting a current impulse into the capacitor node can be written fully analytically, giving the ISF: Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ,θ=ω0τ.\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\theta,\qquad \theta=\omega_0\tau.Γ(θ)=−sinθ,θ=ω0​τ. This is the site's first ISF that "actually has a shape", and it is not a toy assumption — it is derived from the state geometry. We will (a) plot the waveform and its ISF, (b) verify numerically that in the small-signal regime Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is strictly proportional to Δq\Delta qΔq, and (c) watch in state space how a zero-crossing injection becomes a "pure phase jump". Physical intuition (conclusion first): the LC state z=(v,w)=A(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)z=(v,w)=A(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)z=(v,w)=A(cosθ,sinθ) rotates at constant speed on a circle. A current impulse pushes only the capacitor voltage vvv, one horizontal step Δv=Δq/C\Delta v=\Delta q/CΔv=Δq/C. How much of that step becomes phase depends on the angle, at that instant, between the radius (pointing outward from the center) and the tangential direction (perpendicular to the radius). At the peak (θ=0\theta=0θ=0, v=Av=Av=A) the step lies entirely along the radius → all amplitude; at the zero crossing (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2, v=0v=0v=0) the step lies entirely along the tangent → all phase. Writing this projection as a phase increment gives exactly −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ.
documents.s: Lab 02 — Ideal LC oscillator toy model: Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ and charge linearity

documents.t: Derive from physics the ideal-LC ISF Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ — no memorization, no assumptions. Understand how the "shape" of the ISF maps onto the waveform: ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ is largest at the zero crossings and zero at the peaks. Verify small-signal linearity by simulation: Δϕ=Γ Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=ΓΔq/qmax​, i.e. at a fixed injection phase Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is proportional to Δq\Delta qΔq (reproducing the conclusion of [P1] Fig. 6). See in state space that "zero-crossing injection = a tangential push = a pure phase jump, trajectory radius unchanged". Prepare a clean, analytically tractable example for convolution_derivation and the Fourier decomposition of the ISF (lab_05).
documents.s: 1. Learning objectives

documents.t: Ideal lossless parallel LC: energy shuttles losslessly between LLL and CCC; the state traces a circle at constant speed in the 2-D plane. In normalized state form (A=1A=1A=1): z(θ)=(v, w)=(cos⁡θ, sin⁡θ),θ=ω0t.z(\theta)=(v,\,w)=(\cos\theta,\;\sin\theta),\qquad \theta=\omega_0 t .z(θ)=(v,w)=(cosθ,sinθ),θ=ω0​t. vvv = capacitor voltage (∝cos⁡θ\propto\cos\theta∝cosθ); www = (proportional to) inductor current (∝sin⁡θ\propto\sin\theta∝sinθ). Here μ=0\mu=0μ=0 (no amplitude restoration), corresponding to the "marginally stable ideal LC". In the simulations, to keep the trajectory cleanly on the ring, we use a small μ=0.3\mu=0.3μ=0.3 (weak restoration) in (a)(b), and μ=0\mu=0μ=0 in (c) to watch pure rotation. Impulse → voltage step ([P1] Eq.(9), p.181): ΔV=ΔqCnode.\Delta V=\frac{\Delta q}{C_{node}}.ΔV=Cnode​Δq​. It moves only vvv (the inductor current cannot change instantaneously), i.e. the state jumps by Δv=Δq/C\Delta v=\Delta q/CΔv=Δq/C along the +v+v+v axis. Projecting the voltage step onto phase. At z=(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)z=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)z=(cosθ,sinθ), the unit vector along the tangential (phase-increasing) direction is t^=(−sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ)\hat t=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)t^=(−sinθ,cosθ). A step along the +v+v+v axis, Δv v^=Δv (1,0)\Delta v\,\hat v=\Delta v\,(1,0)Δvv^=Δv(1,0), has tangential projection (divided by the radius A=1A=1A=1 to convert into an angle increment): Δϕ=t^⋅(Δv,0)A=(−sin⁡θ) ΔvA=−sin⁡θ ΔvA.\Delta\phi=\frac{\hat t\cdot(\Delta v,0)}{A}=\frac{(-\sin\theta)\,\Delta v}{A}=-\sin\theta\;\frac{\Delta v}{A}.Δϕ=At^⋅(Δv,0)​=A(−sinθ)Δv​=−sinθAΔv​. Substituting Δv=Δq/C\Delta v=\Delta q/CΔv=Δq/C and using qmax=C⋅Aq_{max}=C\cdot Aqmax​=C⋅A: Δϕ=−sin⁡θ Δq/CA=−sin⁡θCA Δq=Γ(θ)qmax Δq,Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ. \boxed{\;\Delta\phi=-\sin\theta\;\frac{\Delta q/C}{A}=\frac{-\sin\theta}{C A}\,\Delta q=\frac{\Gamma(\theta)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q,\qquad \Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\theta.\;}Δϕ=−sinθAΔq/C​=CA−sinθ​Δq=qmax​Γ(θ)​Δq,Γ(θ)=−sinθ.​ dimension check: Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is in rad (dimensionless); Δq/qmax=[C]/[C]\Delta q/q_{max}=[\text{C}]/[\text{C}]Δq/qmax​=[C]/[C] is dimensionless; hence Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless ✓. Γ\GammaΓ is 2π2\pi2π-periodic, consistent with the definitions in [P1] Eq.(10),(11). Physics check: θ=0\theta=0θ=0 (peak) → Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0 (amplitude change only, matching the red dot in lab_01 figure two); θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2 (rising zero crossing) → Γ=−1\Gamma=-1Γ=−1 (∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ maximal, pure phase, matching the green dot). The minus sign is the sign convention for "phase being pushed backward". Toy-model note: ideal lossless LC + pure 2-D rotation + small-signal projection is a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level. A real LC has finite QQQ, harmonics, and cyclostationary noise, which pull Γ\GammaΓ away from the clean −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ (see effective_isf).

documents.t: Excerpted from simulations/lab_02_lc_toy_model.py (checked against the source). The ideal-LC ISF comes directly from gamma_lc_ideal (i.e. −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ); for linearity, simulate_lc injects a range of Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ at a fixed zero-crossing phase, and excess_phase measures the persistent phase shift: from oscillator_models import simulate_lc, excess_phase from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal f0, fs = 1.0, 8000.0 theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 400) # (a) waveform cos(theta) and its ISF -sin(theta) V = np.cos(theta) Gamma = gamma_lc_ideal(theta) # = -np.sin(theta) # (b) linearity: inject a series of dq/qmax at the zero crossing (theta=pi/2, ISF=-1), measure persistent Δφ dq_list = np.linspace(-0.05, 0.05, 11) # dq / q_max T = 1.0 / f0 t_inj = 4 * T + (np.pi / 2) / (2 * np.pi * f0) # injection time corresponding to theta=pi/2 t_ref, xr, yr = simulate_lc(f0, 10 * T, fs, mu=0.3) phi_ref = excess_phase(t_ref, xr, yr, f0) dphi = [] for dq in dq_list: t_p, xp, yp = simulate_lc(f0, 10 * T, fs, mu=0.3, impulse_time=t_inj, impulse_dx=dq) phi_p = excess_phase(t_p, xp, yp, f0) m = t_p >= (10 * T - T) # take the settled value over the last period dphi.append(np.mean(phi_p[m] - phi_ref[m])) # theory: Δφ = Γ·Δq/q_max = -1 · (dq/q_max) excess_phase subtracts the carrier rotation 2πf0t2\pi f_0 t2πf0​t, keeping only the perturbation-induced phase (ϕ=unwrap⁡(atan2⁡(y,x))−2πf0t\phi=\operatorname{unwrap}(\operatorname{atan2}(y,x))-2\pi f_0 tϕ=unwrap(atan2(y,x))−2πf0​t) — exactly the ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) in [P1] Eq.(1).

documents.s: 8. Simulation figures

documents.t: (a) Waveform and ISF: Blue: V(θ)=cos⁡θV(\theta)=\cos\thetaV(θ)=cosθ (tank voltage); red: Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ (ISF). Note the 90∘90^\circ90∘ phase difference between them: Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0 when VVV is at its peak, ∣Γ∣=1|\Gamma|=1∣Γ∣=1 when VVV crosses zero. Physically this is exactly right — the magnitude of the ISF is set by the waveform slope (large slope = large tangential component = phase-sensitive), and the slope of cos⁡\coscos is −sin⁡-\sin−sin. This is precisely the picture "the most phase-sensitive instant is the zero crossing, the least sensitive is the peak". (b) Linearity: The purple dots are the persistent Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ measured from the numerical simulation; the black dashed line is the theory Δϕ=−Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=-\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=−Δq/qmax​ (because the injection is at Γ=−1\Gamma=-1Γ=−1). They nearly coincide over the entire ±0.05\pm0.05±0.05 range — this is seeing-is-believing for the strict small-signal proportionality of Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ to Δq\Delta qΔq, reproducing [P1] Fig. 6. The slope is −1-1−1 (not +1+1+1), confirming the minus sign of Γ(π/2)=−1\Gamma(\pi/2)=-1Γ(π/2)=−1. (c) State space: The black dashed line is the unperturbed unit circle; the green curve is the trajectory after being "kicked tangentially at a zero crossing". Key observation: the trajectory radius is essentially unchanged (amplitude untouched), but the phase of the rotation is permanently shifted — this is the "pure phase jump". By contrast, injecting at the peak makes the radius first grow then get pulled back while the phase barely moves (readers can move t_inj to a peak and try).

documents.t: Pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level. Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ is the result for an ideal lossless LC; a real LC has finite QQQ, a waveform with harmonics, and cyclostationary device noise (gated by the operating point), so the actual Γ\GammaΓ deviates from the clean −sin⁡-\sin−sin and must be extracted with transient/adjoint/Floquet methods (see effective_isf; the related PPV/adjoint material is not among the five downloaded PDFs and is supplemented from standard literature). Small-signal / linearization: projecting onto the tangent assumes Δq≪qmax\Delta q\ll q_{max}Δq≪qmax​. Panel (b) sweeps only up to ±0.05 qmax\pm0.05\,q_{max}±0.05qmax​; larger injections bring in AM–PM conversion, change the ISF itself, or even kick the oscillator off the limit cycle. Single node, single injection: real circuits have many nodes, each with its own Γ\GammaΓ and qmaxq_{max}qmax​; multi-node ISF is discussed in isf_definition. Numerical integration error: simulate_lc uses fixed-step RK4; the weak μ=0.3\mu=0.3μ=0.3 introduces a tiny bias into the phase measurement. This lab averages over the last period to suppress transient residue. extract_isf_by_injection sweeps the full Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ) with a smaller Δq/qmax=10−3\Delta q/q_{max}=10^{-3}Δq/qmax​=10−3; the maximum error against −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ is about 0.001 (see lab_04).

documents.t: The ideal-LC ISF is analytically derivable: Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ (from the tangential projection of the voltage step). ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ magnitude = waveform slope: most sensitive at zero crossings (Γ=−1\Gamma=-1Γ=−1), insensitive at peaks (Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0). In the small-signal regime Δϕ=Γ Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=ΓΔq/qmax​; simulation confirms linearity with slope −1-1−1 ([P1] Fig. 6). Zero-crossing injection = pure phase jump (state radius unchanged, phase permanently shifted). Sources: [P1] Eq.(9), p.181, Eqs.(10),(11), p.182; Fig. 4, 6, 7(a).
documents.s: Key takeaways

documents.t: lab_02 looked at the phase jump from a single impulse. In the real world noise kicks continuously, so the phase error accumulates step by step. The ring oscillator (NNN inverter stages connected in a ring, each with delay τD\tau_DτD​) is the cleanest place to watch this, because it has no absolute time reference: every edge (transition) is timed off the previous edge, so earlier errors propagate forever. This lab does two things: (1) uses an edge-time model to demonstrate the random walk of accumulated jitter σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ ([P2] Eq.(8), p.792; κ from Eq.(12), p.793); (2) contrasts the LC's smooth −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ with the ring's toy ISF — "concentrated at transitions, shrinking with stage count NNN" — and spells out what this toy model can and cannot show. Physical intuition (conclusion first): every beat (every edge) is kicked by independent noise into a small timing error, and that error adds onto the accumulated edge time and is never corrected (open loop, no reference). Independent small steps accumulating = a random walk: after mmm steps the position variance is ∝m\propto m∝m, so the standard deviation is ∝m\propto\sqrt{m}∝m​, i.e. the timing error σΔt∝Δt\sigma_{\Delta t}\propto\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​∝Δt​. This is the same thing as "a drunkard's distance from the origin growing as the square root of the number of steps".
documents.s: Lab 03 — Ring-oscillator toy model: accumulated-jitter random walk and ISF comparison

documents.t: Understand that the ring oscillator has no absolute time reference → every edge's error keeps propagating → a random walk forms. Use simulation to see the Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ scaling (slope 1/21/21/2 on log–log axes) of accumulated (long-term) jitter σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ ([P2] Eq.(8)). Contrast the LC's smooth ISF −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ (Γrms=0.707\Gamma_{rms}=0.707Γrms​=0.707) with the ring's toy ISF: energy concentrated at transitions, peak height ∼1/N\sim1/\sqrt N∼1/N​, and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ decreasing as the stage count NNN increases. Delimit the toy model: it shows the mechanisms (random walk, ISF shape difference) but not the real constants (exact values of κ\kappaκ and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, or the different scaling of correlated noise).
documents.s: 1. Learning objectives

documents.t: (A) Edge-time random walk. Abstract the ring's output into a sequence of transition times {tk}\{t_k\}{tk​}. Ideally each beat lasts one period T=1/f0T=1/f_0T=1/f0​; in practice each beat picks up an independent Gaussian timing perturbation with standard deviation σedge\sigma_{edge}σedge​: tk=tk−1+T+δk,δk∼N(0,σedge2) i.i.d.t_{k}=t_{k-1}+T+\delta_k,\qquad \delta_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{edge}^2)\ \text{i.i.d.}tk​=tk−1​+T+δk​,δk​∼N(0,σedge2​) i.i.d. The perturbation part of the edge-time difference tk+m−tkt_{k+m}-t_ktk+m​−tk​ over mmm beats is then ∑j=1mδj\sum_{j=1}^{m}\delta_j∑j=1m​δj​. Independent terms add → variances add: Var⁡ ⁣(∑j=1mδj)=m σedge2 ⟹ σΔt(m)=σedgem.\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\delta_j\Big)=m\,\sigma_{edge}^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \sigma_{\Delta t}(m)=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{m}.Var(j=1∑m​δj​)=mσedge2​⟹σΔt​(m)=σedge​m​. Converting the step count mmm into time Δt=mT\Delta t=mTΔt=mT gives [P2] Eq.(8), p.792: σΔt=κΔt ,κ=σedgeT.\boxed{\;\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}\;},\qquad \kappa=\frac{\sigma_{edge}}{\sqrt{T}}.σΔt​=κΔt​​,κ=T​σedge​​. dimension check: [κ]=[s]/[s]1/2=[s]1/2=s[\kappa]=[\text{s}]/[\text{s}]^{1/2}=[\text{s}]^{1/2}=\sqrt{\text{s}}[κ]=[s]/[s]1/2=[s]1/2=s​, consistent with the notation table; κΔt=s⋅s=s\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}=\sqrt{\text{s}}\cdot\sqrt{\text{s}}=\text{s}κΔt​=s​⋅s​=s ✓. Key assumption: the per-beat perturbations are mutually independent (uncorrelated). The paper ([P2] Sec. III, p.793) explicitly distinguishes: uncorrelated sources such as thermal noise → variances add → σ∝Δt\sigma\propto\sqrt{\Delta t}σ∝Δt​ (this lab); versus fully correlated sources such as substrate/supply/1/f1/f1/f → standard deviations add → σ∝Δt\sigma\propto\Delta tσ∝Δt (this toy model does not simulate that branch; see Section 11). (B) Ring vs LC ISF shape. The ring's energy is concentrated at the transitions (the switching instant has the largest slope and is the most sensitive); its ISF is not the LC's smooth −sin⁡-\sin−sin but has a spike near every transition. This lab uses a triangular toy ISF to "sketch" this, with peak height shrinking with stage count NNN: Γringtoy(θ)∝1N×(每半週期一個三角脈衝).\Gamma_{ring}^{toy}(\theta)\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\times(\text{每半週期一個三角脈衝}).Γringtoy​(θ)∝N​1​×(每半週期一個三角脈衝). This echoes the Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 scaling trend claimed by [P2] (more stages → each stage contributes less to the total phase). Toy-model note: both parts are pedagogical toy models, not transistor-level. The random walk uses abstract per-edge Gaussian perturbations (not computed from device thermal noise); the triangular ISF is only an illustration of "energy concentrated at transitions", not an extracted ring ISF — the constants await verification against a real extraction.
documents.s: 2. Mathematical model

documents.t: Excerpted from simulations/lab_03_ring_toy_model.py (checked against the source). Accumulated jitter uses accumulated_jitter_curve (internally a cumsum of per-period Gaussian increments over n_trials trials, i.e. a random walk); the ISF comparison uses gamma_lc_ideal, gamma_triangular, and gamma_rms: from oscillator_models import accumulated_jitter_curve from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, gamma_triangular, gamma_rms RNG = np.random.default_rng(12345) def fig_accumulation(): f0 = 5e9 # 5 GHz sigma_edge = 50e-15 # independent timing perturbation, 50 fs rms per beat # cumsum of per-period Gaussian increments over 2000 trials -> random walk lags, sigma_dt = accumulated_jitter_curve( f0, sigma_edge, max_lag_periods=500, n_trials=2000, rng=RNG) # simulated points vs theory sigma_edge*sqrt(lags): a slope-1/2 line on log-log axes def fig_lc_vs_ring_isf(): theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 1000, endpoint=True) g_lc = gamma_lc_ideal(theta) # -sin(theta), smooth g_r5 = gamma_triangular(theta, n_stages=5) # toy triangle, peak height ~ 1/sqrt(5) g_r15 = gamma_triangular(theta, n_stages=15) # toy triangle, peak height ~ 1/sqrt(15) # gamma_rms(theta, g_lc)=0.707, g_r5=0.258, g_r15=0.149 -> rms drops as N rises The core of accumulated_jitter_curve is just walk = np.cumsum(incr, axis=1) followed by np.std across trials — it directly measures "the variance of a random walk grows linearly with the step count".

documents.t: Figure 1 (accumulated jitter, log–log): Blue dots: σΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}σΔt​ simulated over 2000 trials; black dashed line: the theory σΔt=σedgeΔN\sigma_{\Delta t}=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{\Delta N}σΔt​=σedge​ΔN​. They collapse onto a single line of slope 1/21/21/2 (on log–log axes, \sqrt{}​ is slope 1/21/21/2) — the fingerprint of a random walk. Numerical feel: σedge=50\sigma_{edge}=50σedge​=50 fs; after 1 beat σ=50\sigma=50σ=50 fs; after 500 beats σ=50×500≈1118\sigma=50\times\sqrt{500}\approx1118σ=50×500​≈1118 fs ≈1.12\approx1.12≈1.12 ps (@ 5 GHz, 500 beats =100=100=100 ns). Stretching the measurement time by 100× (1→100 beats) grows the jitter only 100=10\sqrt{100}=10100​=10× — this is "why an open-loop oscillator drifts further the longer it runs, but drifts ever more slowly". Contrast: with a locked PLL there is an absolute reference and the accumulation is truncated (outside the scope of this toy). documents.t: Accumulated jitter (core): [P2] Eq.(8), p.792: σΔt=κΔt.\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}.σΔt​=κΔt​. The narrative in [P2] Sec. III (p.793) states explicitly that because "uncertainty in any earlier transition affects all following transitions, and its effect persists indefinitely", variances add for uncorrelated sources and σ∝Δt\sigma\propto\sqrt{\Delta t}σ∝Δt​; Figure 1 of this lab directly reproduces this equation (compare the "rms jitter vs measurement time, log–log" concept of [P2] Fig. 3 and Fig. 4). This toy simulates uncorrelated only. Ring frequency (background): [P2] Eq.(15), p.794: f0=12NτDf_0=\dfrac{1}{2N\tau_D}f0​=2NτD​1​. Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ scaling: [P2] Eq.(16), p.794: Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 ([P2] Eq.(16), p.794 — v7 re-verified: the square root covers only the constant, so Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2; the body text's 4/N1.54/N^{1.5}4/N1.5 at η=0.75 and App. B Eq.(55) triple-confirm this. v3 had misread it as N−3/4N^{-3/4}N−3/4; this lab echoes it only qualitatively; compare Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ vs NNN in [P2] Fig. 8). Both figures of this lab are redrawn toy concept figures (not point-by-point copies of the paper figures, not transistor-level). Link to phase noise: Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ enters 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise through [P1] Eq.(21), p.185.
documents.s: 10. Corresponding paper equations / figures

documents.t: Can show (mechanisms this toy model teaches correctly): An open-loop oscillator has no absolute time reference → errors propagate forever → the random-walk nature of accumulated jitter. Under uncorrelated noise, σΔt∝Δt\sigma_{\Delta t}\propto\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​∝Δt​ (log–log slope 1/21/21/2). The qualitative shape of the ring ISF — energy concentrated at transitions — contrasted with the LC's smooth −sin⁡-\sin−sin. The direction of the trend that Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ shrinks as NNN grows. Cannot show (things the toy model misses; need transistor-level / real extraction): The real κ\kappaκ and σedge\sigma_{edge}σedge​: the 50 fs in this lab is a hand-placed number, not computed from device thermal noise + Γ\GammaΓ + qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (that requires [P1] Eq.(21) and the real ISF). The different scaling of correlated noise: substrate/supply/1/f1/f1/f give σ∝Δt\sigma\propto\Delta tσ∝Δt (slope 1); this model contains none of that branch — a real ring shows both trends ([P2] Sec. III). The precise Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 constant and the real ring ISF shape: the triangle is only illustrative; the real ISF must be extracted via transient/adjoint methods (the related PPV/adjoint/Floquet material is not among the five downloaded PDFs and is supplemented from standard literature; see effective_isf). Flicker (1/f1/f1/f) upconversion and cyclostationarity: the per-edge perturbations in this lab are pure white and symmetric, with no 1/f31/f^31/f3 close-in behavior (see lab_07). Small-lag saturation: a footnote in [P2] notes that under a more accurate treatment the phase noise does not grow without bound as f0→0f_0\to0f0​→0 (it flattens); this random walk contains no such correction at large lag — but, as the paper says, it makes "no practical difference" for this discussion.
documents.s: 11. Limitations and approximations — what the toy model can and cannot show

documents.t: The ring has no absolute time reference → errors propagate forever → accumulated jitter is a random walk. Uncorrelated noise: σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ ([P2] Eq.(8)); simulated log–log slope 1/21/21/2; 50 fs/beat → 500 beats ≈ 1.12 ps. Correlated noise instead gives σ∝Δt\sigma\propto\Delta tσ∝Δt (not included in this toy). The ring ISF is concentrated at transitions with peak height ∼1/N\sim1/\sqrt N∼1/N​; Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (LC 0.707 → ring N=5 0.258 → N=15 0.149) drops with NNN, echoing Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2. Sources: [P2] Eq.(8),(14),(16), Sec. III, Fig. 3,4,8; linked to [P1] Eq.(21).
documents.s: Key takeaways

documents.t: This lab turns the "operational ISF definition" from impulse_to_phase_shift into a measurable experiment: inject a very small charge impulse at different phases θ=ω0τ\theta=\omega_0\tauθ=ω0​τ of the waveform, measure the permanent phase shift it causes, divide that shift by the injected amount, and thereby back out the ISF (impulse sensitivity function — where on its waveform the oscillator is most vulnerable to a kick). The extracted numerical ISF nearly coincides with the analytic solution Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ for the ideal LC (maximum error about 7×10−47\times10^{-4}7×10−4). The same lab also uses impulse responses to draw out the difference between LTI (linear time-invariant) vs LTV (linear time-variant — the system parameters vary periodically with time) — the key reason the whole ISF theory "cannot treat oscillator phase with an ordinary LTI transfer function." The two things this lab wants you to see with your own eyes: (1) the ISF is not an abstract definition; it is the result of the action "kick at phase θ\thetaθ, measure the persistent phase jump"; (2) the same-size impulse barely changes the phase when it kicks at the peak, but causes the largest phase jump at the zero crossing — this "kick effect varying periodically with the injection instant" is LTV, and can never be drawn by an LTI impulse response that depends only on t−τt-\taut−τ.
documents.s: Lab 04 — impulse injection sweep and LTI vs LTV

documents.t: Turn the operational ISF definition Δϕ=Γ(ω0τ)qmax Δq\Delta\phi=\dfrac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta qΔϕ=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​Δq into a numerical experimental flow: sweep the injection phase → measure the persistent phase → back out Γ\GammaΓ. Verify that the ISF of the ideal LC oscillator (current injected into the capacitor node) is exactly Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ, and quantify the numerical-vs-theory error (~10−310^{-3}10−3 level). Understand the difference between the "persistent phase shift" and the "decaying amplitude perturbation" — only the tangential (phase) component remains permanently. Use the impulse-response comparison plot to build the physical picture of LTV: the step height varies periodically with the injection phase. Maps to [P1] Eq.(10),(11) and Fig. 4.

documents.t: The whole lab stands on this LTV impulse response ([P1] Eq.(10), p.182): hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau)hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ) Its meaning: injecting unit charge at time τ\tauτ (corresponding to phase ω0τ\omega_0\tauω0​τ) makes the phase jump in a single step to Γ(ω0τ)/qmax\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)/q_{max}Γ(ω0​τ)/qmax​, and because of the unit step u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) the jump is kept permanently. Superposing it over all past noise currents gives the central LTV phase response ([P1] Eq.(11), p.182): ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tauϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ The single-impulse experiment that backs out the ISF: if ini_nin​ is just one narrow pulse located at phase θ\thetaθ with total charge Δq\Delta qΔq, Eq.(11) degenerates to a single step (the step version of [P1] Eq.(10); see also the operational definition in impulse_to_phase_shift): Δϕ(θ)=Γ(θ)qmax Δq⟹Γ(θ)=Δϕ(θ)Δq/qmax.\Delta\phi(\theta)=\frac{\Gamma(\theta)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Gamma(\theta)=\frac{\Delta\phi(\theta)}{\Delta q/q_{max}} .Δϕ(θ)=qmax​Γ(θ)​Δq⟹Γ(θ)=Δq/qmax​Δϕ(θ)​. dimension check: the right-hand side [rad]/(C/C)=[rad][\text{rad}]/(\text{C}/\text{C})=[\text{rad}][rad]/(C/C)=[rad] looks like it carries units, but Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is rad (dimensionless) and Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ is dimensionless, so Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless ✓. Theory reference: for the ideal lossless parallel LC with current injected into the capacitor node, the state is z=(v,w)=A(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)z=(v,w)=A(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)z=(v,w)=A(cosθ,sinθ); a charge impulse pushes vvv by Δv=Δq/C\Delta v=\Delta q/CΔv=Δq/C, and projecting onto the limit-cycle tangential direction gives Δϕ=−(sin⁡θ) Δv/A\Delta\phi=-(\sin\theta)\,\Delta v/AΔϕ=−(sinθ)Δv/A; combined with qmax=CAq_{max}=CAqmax​=CA this yields Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ \boxed{\ \Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\theta\ } Γ(θ)=−sinθ ​ At the peak θ=0\theta=0θ=0, Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0 (pure amplitude change); at the zero crossing θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2, ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ is maximum (pure phase change). Full geometric derivation: isf_definition. The mathematical difference of LTV vs LTV: an LTI system's impulse response depends only on the time difference, h(t,τ)=h(t−τ)h(t,\tau)=h(t-\tau)h(t,τ)=h(t−τ); the oscillator's phase impulse response hϕ(t,τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)hϕ​(t,τ) explicitly depends on the absolute injection instant τ\tauτ (through the 2π2\pi2π-periodic weight Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ)) — precisely the definition of LTV.
documents.s: 2. Mathematical model

documents.t: The core of backing out the ISF is extract_isf_by_injection: for each phase θ\thetaθ run one injection simulation, measure the mean phase difference over "the last period" relative to a no-injection reference trajectory (this keeps only the permanent phase and filters out the already-decayed amplitude perturbation), then divide by Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​. Quoted verbatim from the real code (simulations/common/oscillator_models.py): def extract_isf_by_injection(f0, fs, n_inject_periods=6, settle_periods=4, dq_over_qmax=1e-3, n_points=64, mu=0.3): T = 1.0 / f0 settle = settle_periods * T t_end = (settle_periods + n_inject_periods) * T thetas = np.linspace(0.0, TWO_PI, n_points, endpoint=False) gamma_num = np.zeros(n_points) # Reference (no impulse), started from the limit cycle. t_ref, xr, yr = simulate_lc(f0, t_end, fs, mu=mu, x0=1.0, y0=0.0) phi_ref = excess_phase(t_ref, xr, yr, f0) for i, th in enumerate(thetas): t_inj = settle + th / (TWO_PI * f0) # phase th occurs at this time t_p, xp, yp = simulate_lc(f0, t_end, fs, mu=mu, x0=1.0, y0=0.0, impulse_time=t_inj, impulse_dx=dq_over_qmax) phi_p = excess_phase(t_p, xp, yp, f0) # persistent phase difference measured over the last period m = t_p >= (t_end - T) dphi = np.mean(phi_p[m] - phi_ref[m]) gamma_num[i] = dphi / dq_over_qmax gamma_analytic = -np.sin(thetas) return thetas, gamma_num, gamma_analytic The core of the LTV vs LTV comparison figure plots "LTI: step height fixed, only time-shifted" next to "LTV: step height =Γ(ω0τ)=\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=Γ(ω0​τ) varying with the injection phase" (simulations/lab_04_impulse_sweep.py): # LTV (oscillator phase): step of height Gamma(w0 tau)/qmax * u(t - tau). ax = axes[1] for tau, c in zip([0.0, 0.25, 0.5], ["tab:blue", "tab:orange", "tab:green"]): gamma = -np.sin(2 * np.pi * f0 * tau) # ISF at injection phase h = gamma * (t >= tau) ax.plot(t, h, color=c, label=fr"$\tau={tau}$, $\Gamma=-\sin(2\pi\tau)={gamma:+.2f}$") Why measure "the mean over the last period": the transient right after injection contains both an amplitude perturbation and a phase jump; the Van der Pol-type amplitude restoration with mu=0.3 pulls the radial (amplitude) component back to the limit cycle within a few periods, leaving only the tangential (phase) component permanently. Measuring after n_inject_periods periods yields the clean persistent phase. Why endpoint=False: θ=0\theta=0θ=0 and θ=2π\theta=2\piθ=2π are the same phase — do not duplicate it in the sweep. Why dq_over_qmax=1e-3 is small: keeps small-signal linearity (Δq≪qmax\Delta q\ll q_{max}Δq≪qmax​); otherwise the ISF itself would be altered by the large injection and the extraction would be inaccurate.

documents.t: Figure 1 (phase sweep): the horizontal axis is the injection phase θ/2π\theta/2\piθ/2π (one period), the vertical axis is the persistent phase shift Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ. Note that it is a −sin⁡-\sin−sin-shaped curve: nearly zero at θ=0\theta=0θ=0 (the peak), the largest negative value at θ≈0.25\theta\approx0.25θ≈0.25 (rising zero crossing), the largest positive value at θ≈0.75\theta\approx0.75θ≈0.75. This is direct evidence of LTV — the effect of "the same kick" depends entirely on "where on the waveform you kick." The numerical blue circles hug the black theoretical dashed line. Figure 2 (recovered ISF): dividing Figure 1 by Δq/qmax=10−3\Delta q/q_{max}=10^{-3}Δq/qmax​=10−3 gives Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ). The title reports a maximum absolute error of about 7×10−47\times10^{-4}7×10−4 (the title is formatted to three decimals, about 0.001). Error sources: RK4 time discretization, the θ\thetaθ sampling (48 points), and the measurement window averaging only over the last period. This level is enough to claim "the numerical method successfully recovered Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ of the ideal LC." Figure 3 (LTI vs LTV): Top half (LTI): the three curves are the same decaying-exponential impulse response shifted to τ=0.3,0.9,1.5\tau=0.3,0.9,1.5τ=0.3,0.9,1.5 — identical shape, only the starting point differs. This is the LTI hallmark: h(t,τ)=h(t−τ)h(t,\tau)=h(t-\tau)h(t,τ)=h(t−τ). Bottom half (LTV phase): all three are unit steps (permanently held), but with different step heights: at τ=0\tau=0τ=0, Γ=−sin⁡(0)=0\Gamma=-\sin(0)=0Γ=−sin(0)=0 (kick at the peak, phase unmoved); at τ=0.25\tau=0.25τ=0.25, Γ=−sin⁡(π/2)=−1\Gamma=-\sin(\pi/2)=-1Γ=−sin(π/2)=−1 (kick at the zero crossing, largest phase jump); at τ=0.5\tau=0.5τ=0.5, Γ=−sin⁡(π)=0\Gamma=-\sin(\pi)=0Γ=−sin(π)=0. The step height varies with the absolute injection phase — this is LTV, and the fundamental reason a single LTI transfer function cannot describe oscillator phase.

documents.t: The ISF is measurable: inject a small charge at phase θ\thetaθ, measure the persistent Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ, divide by Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​. The ISF backed out of the ideal LC (capacitor-node injection) is exactly Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ; maximum numerical-vs-theory error ~10−310^{-3}10−3. Injection at the peak → pure amplitude change (pulled back); injection at the zero crossing → pure phase change (permanently retained). The essence of LTV: the phase impulse response hϕ(t,τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)hϕ​(t,τ) depends on the absolute injection phase, with step height =Γ(ω0τ)=\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=Γ(ω0​τ) — not on t−τt-\taut−τ alone. documents.t: The ISF is a 2π2\pi2π-periodic function, so it can be decomposed into a Fourier series. Why decompose? Because what appears in the phase-noise formulas is the ISF's Fourier coefficients cnc_ncn​, not Γ\GammaΓ itself: c0c_0c0​ (the DC coefficient) decides whether 1/f noise gets upconverted into close-in phase noise; cnc_ncn​ sets the weight with which noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ is moved to the carrier; and by Parseval (Parseval's theorem — time-domain energy = frequency-domain energy) the sum of squares of all coefficients equals 2Γrms22\Gamma_{rms}^22Γrms2​, where Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ directly sets the 1/f² phase-noise magnitude. This lab does three things: (1) compute the cnc_ncn​ of one ISF and reconstruct it with 1, 2, 4 harmonics; (2) plot the coefficient spectrum and numerically verify the Parseval relation; (3) put a symmetric (c0=0c_0=0c0​=0) and an asymmetric (c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0) ISF side by side to show that only c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0 upconverts 1/f noise. Physical intuition: think of the ISF as "the local-oscillator (LO) waveform of the mixer that the oscillator is." Noise does not enter the phase directly; it is first comb-sampled by the ISF in the frequency domain — noise near each nω0n\omega_0nω0​ is weighted by cnc_ncn​ and downconverted to near the carrier. So the ISF's shape (its harmonic content) is the knob the designer can actually turn: make the waveform symmetric (suppress c0c_0c0​) to suppress 1/f³; make the overall Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ small to suppress 1/f².
documents.s: Lab 05 — ISF Fourier coefficients and Parseval

documents.t: Write the ISF as the Fourier series Γ(ω0τ)=c02+∑ncncos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=\dfrac{c_0}{2}+\sum_n c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)Γ(ω0​τ)=2c0​​+∑n​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​), and understand the physical role of each coefficient. Compute the cnc_ncn​ of a given ISF by numerical integration, and demonstrate "more harmonics, closer reconstruction." Use the Parseval relation ∑ncn2=2Γrms2\sum_n c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑n​cn2​=2Γrms2​ to connect "frequency-domain coefficients" with "time-domain rms," and face honestly the DC-term bookkeeping trap under the half-amplitude convention. Understand why c0c_0c0​ (= the ISF's mean value × 2) is the "gate" for 1/f noise upconversion: a symmetric waveform gives c0≈0c_0\approx0c0​≈0 → the 1/f³ corner is pushed very low. Maps to [P1] Eq.(12),(20),(24).

documents.t: ISF Fourier series ([P1] Eq.(12), p.183): Γ(ω0τ)=c02+∑n=1∞cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=\frac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)Γ(ω0​τ)=2c0​​+n=1∑∞​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​) c0/2c_0/2c0​/2 is the mean (DC value) of the ISF. Note the factor of 2: the Fourier coefficient is called c0c_0c0​, but the ISF's DC value is c0/2c_0/2c0​/2. This factor is extremely easy to get wrong when computing the 1/f³ corner (see the notation pitfalls in notation). cn,θnc_n,\theta_ncn​,θn​ are the amplitude and phase of the nnn-th harmonic; cn=an2+bn2c_n=\sqrt{a_n^2+b_n^2}cn​=an2​+bn2​​, θn=atan2⁡(−bn,an)\theta_n=\operatorname{atan2}(-b_n,a_n)θn​=atan2(−bn​,an​), where an,bna_n,b_nan​,bn​ are the standard cos/sin coefficients. dimension check: Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless, cos is dimensionless, so every cnc_ncn​ is dimensionless ✓. Parseval / rms ISF ([P1] Eq.(20), p.185): ∑n=0∞cn2=1π∫02π∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2 Γrms2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma(x)|^2dx=2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2n=0∑∞​cn2​=π1​∫02π​∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2Γrms2​ It links "the sum of squares of all harmonics" to "the ISF's mean square × 2." Physically: white-noise phase noise is proportional to ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ ([P1] Eq.(19) → Eq.(21)), so knowing Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is enough to compute the 1/f² phase noise without tracking every harmonic individually. The half-amplitude-convention bookkeeping trap (you will see it with your own eyes in this lab): the c0c_0c0​ on the left side of Eq.(20) must use the same definition as the c0c_0c0​ of Eq.(12). This lab's compute_fourier_coefficients returns c[0] = |a0|, where a0=2×(DC value)a_0=2\times(\text{DC value})a0​=2×(DC value), i.e. c0=a0c_0=a_0c0​=a0​. For an ISF with a non-zero DC value, throwing c[0]**2 straight into ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ counts the DC energy once too many (because the cos terms enter at half amplitude while the DC term enters at full amplitude, so their squared weights differ). This is exactly why the Parseval numbers below disagree by ~10% — we choose to show it as is rather than hide it. 1/f³ corner ([P1] Eq.(24), p.185, which explains why c0c_0c0​ matters): Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c022 Γrms2≈ω1/f(c0c1)2\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}\approx\omega_{1/f}\left(\frac{c_0}{c_1}\right)^2Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​≈ω1/f​(c1​c0​​)2 c0→0c_0\to0c0​→0 (symmetric waveform) ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ the 1/f³ corner →0\to0→0, and the close-in phase noise is clean.
documents.s: 2. Mathematical model

documents.t: The Fourier coefficients are computed directly by trapezoidal integration (simulations/common/isf_utils.py, quoted verbatim): def compute_fourier_coefficients(theta, gamma, n_harmonics): theta = np.asarray(theta, dtype=float) gamma = np.asarray(gamma, dtype=float) a0 = (1 / np.pi) * _trapz(gamma, theta) a = np.zeros(n_harmonics + 1) b = np.zeros(n_harmonics + 1) for n in range(1, n_harmonics + 1): a[n] = (1 / np.pi) * _trapz(gamma * np.cos(n * theta), theta) b[n] = (1 / np.pi) * _trapz(gamma * np.sin(n * theta), theta) c = np.sqrt(a ** 2 + b ** 2) c[0] = abs(a0) # c0 magnitude (the DC coefficient) phase = np.arctan2(-b, a) return a0, a, b, c, phase rms and the Parseval check (fig_coefficients in simulations/lab_05_fourier_isf.py): a0, a, b, c, ph = compute_fourier_coefficients(theta, g, n_harmonics=8) # check Parseval: sum c_n^2 ?= 2 Gamma_rms^2 parseval_lhs = c[0] ** 2 + np.sum(c[1:] ** 2) grms = gamma_rms(theta, g) The example ISF used in this lab (deliberately made asymmetric so several harmonics are non-zero; the +0.25 creates the non-zero c0c_0c0​): def make_isf(theta): """A richer asymmetric ISF so several harmonics are non-trivial.""" return (-np.sin(theta) + 0.35 * np.sin(2 * theta) + 0.18 * np.cos(3 * theta) + 0.25) # the +0.25 sets a non-zero c0 Symmetric vs asymmetric comparison (fig_symmetric_vs_asymmetric; site convention: alpha below is the DC offset of the toy ISF, c0=2αc_0=2\alphac0​=2α, unrelated to [P1]'s NMF α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0t)α(ω0​t)): g_sym = np.cos(theta) # c0 = 0 (symmetric) g_asym = gamma_asymmetric(theta, alpha=0.4) # c0 = 2*alpha = 0.8 Why theta must include the endpoint (endpoint=True) across the full [0,2π][0,2\pi][0,2π]: the trapezoidal rule must integrate 1π∫02π\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}π1​∫02π​ to give the correct coefficients; drop one endpoint and the integration interval is incomplete. How gamma_rms is computed: Γrms=12π∫02πΓ2 dθ\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma^2\,d\theta}Γrms​=2π1​∫02π​Γ2dθ​, consistent with the right-hand side of Eq.(20).

documents.t: Figure 1 (reconstruction): the original ISF contains the three harmonics sin⁡θ,sin⁡2θ,cos⁡3θ\sin\theta,\sin2\theta,\cos3\thetasinθ,sin2θ,cos3θ plus a DC term. N=1N=1N=1 captures only the main harmonic (the −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ one) and clearly deviates; N=2N=2N=2 adds the second harmonic and the shape is roughly right; N=4N=4N=4 already contains all non-zero harmonics and nearly coincides with the original. Teaching point: the ISF's "shape" is its harmonic mix, and a handful of coefficients describe most of the phase-noise behavior — exactly why the phase-noise formulas only need c0,c1,…c_0,c_1,\dotsc0​,c1​,… and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. Figure 2 (coefficients): c0=0.5c_0=0.5c0​=0.5, c1=1.0c_1=1.0c1​=1.0 (dominant), c2=0.35c_2=0.35c2​=0.35, c3=0.18c_3=0.18c3​=0.18, the rest about zero — matching the four terms of make_isf. The Parseval check in the title shows ∑cn2=1.405\sum c_n^2=1.405∑cn2​=1.405 against 2Γrms2=1.2802\Gamma_{rms}^2=1.2802Γrms2​=1.280 — not exactly equal. This is not a bug; it is the consequence of DC-term bookkeeping under the half-amplitude convention (see the trap in Section 2): the cos harmonics enter ∑\sum∑ with half-amplitude squared weights, while c0=a0=2×c_0=a_0=2\timesc0​=a0​=2×DC uses full amplitude and is over-counted. If the DC were instead counted with the correct weight (c0/2)2×2(c_0/2)^2\times2(c0​/2)2×2, the two sides would agree; for a symmetric ISF with zero DC value (such as a pure −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ) there is no such gap in the first place. It has no effect whatsoever on the 1/f²/Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ scaling or the −20 dB/dec slope — this is just a constant bookkeeping convention, the same class of thing as the famous factor-of-2 discussed in white_noise_to_phase_noise. Figure 3 (symmetric vs asymmetric): the green line is symmetric about the zero axis (positive and negative areas cancel, c0=0c_0=0c0​=0); the red line is lifted as a whole by +0.4+0.4+0.4; the red dashed line marks its DC value =c0/2=0.4=c_0/2=0.4=c0​/2=0.4, and the shading is the lifted "DC offset." Only this non-zero DC directly upconverts the device's 1/f flicker noise to near the carrier ([P1] Eq.(24)): c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 → Δω1/f3=0\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=0Δω1/f3​=0. In design terms, this is the mathematical basis for why "making the rise/fall edges symmetric so the upper and lower half-periods of the waveform are symmetric" suppresses close-in 1/f³ phase noise (for design usage see symmetry).

documents.t: This lab runs the entire causal chain — white noise → ISF weighting → integration → phase — in the cleanest possible numerical form, so you can see with your own eyes how a flat (white, frequency-independent) current-noise power spectrum gets colored by the oscillator — a "phase integrator" — into 1/f21/f^21/f2 (−20-20−20 dB per decade) phase noise. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the oscillator's phase has no restoring force (a force that pulls a perturbation back), so every phase step kicked in by noise accumulates permanently — this is an integrator (a system that time-integrates its input; infinite memory). The integrator's transfer-function magnitude is 1/(2πf)1/(2\pi f)1/(2πf), which is 1/(2πf)21/(2\pi f)^21/(2πf)2 for a PSD. The input is flat (white noise), so the output is multiplied by 1/f21/f^21/f2. White in, 1/f21/f^21/f2 out — not because the noise source is 1/f21/f^21/f2, but because phase is obtained by integration.
documents.s: Lab 06 — White Noise → 1/f² Phase Noise

documents.t: Verify by simulation the signature result of [P1]: white current noise becomes 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise in an oscillator. Understand where the −20-20−20 dB/decade slope comes from (the integrator, not the noise source). Quantitatively verify the theoretical prediction Sϕ(f)=Γrms2Si/(qmax2(2πf)2)S_\phi(f)=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(q_{max}^2(2\pi f)^2)Sϕ​(f)=Γrms2​Si​/(qmax2​(2πf)2). Understand the famous factor-of-2 controversy: the clean time-domain derivation differs from [P1] Eq.(21) by a factor of 2, but the scaling and slope are entirely unaffected.
documents.s: 1. Learning objectives

documents.t: The phase response is the LTV (linear time-variant) convolution expression [P1] Eq.(11), p.182: ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tauϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ Split it into three blocks: first phase-weight the noise with the ISF, then integrate. The input is white current noise with constant one-sided PSD (power spectral density) SiS_iSi​ (A2/A^2/A2/Hz). Integrating the white input, the clean time-domain result for the output phase PSD is Sϕ(f)=Γrms2 Siqmax2 (2πf)2.S_\phi(f)=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2\,S_i}{q_{max}^2\,(2\pi f)^2}.Sϕ​(f)=qmax2​(2πf)2Γrms2​Si​​. Where it comes from: after the ISF weights the white noise, the average power is scaled by Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ (the ISF's rms squared, see [P1] Eq.(20)), with qmax2q_{max}^2qmax2​ in the denominator (normalization); the integrator is then 1/(j2πf)1/(j2\pi f)1/(j2πf) in the frequency domain, i.e. 1/(2πf)21/(2\pi f)^21/(2πf)2 for the PSD. Dimension check: Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ is dimensionless, SiS_iSi​ is A2/A^2/A2/Hz, qmax2q_{max}^2qmax2​ is C2C^2C2, (2πf)2(2\pi f)^2(2πf)2 is (rad/s)2=s−2(\text{rad/s})^2=\text{s}^{-2}(rad/s)2=s−2. Overall =A2/HzC2⋅s−2=A2 s2C2⋅1Hz=\dfrac{A^2/\text{Hz}}{C^2\cdot\text{s}^{-2}}=\dfrac{A^2\,\text{s}^2}{C^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\text{Hz}}=C2⋅s−2A2/Hz​=C2A2s2​⋅Hz1​. Since C=A⋅sC=A\cdot sC=A⋅s, A2s2/C2=1A^2 s^2/C^2=1A2s2/C2=1 (dimensionless = rad²), so [Sϕ]=rad2/Hz[S_\phi]=\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}[Sϕ​]=rad2/Hz ✓. This has the same scaling as the signature expression [P1] Eq.(21), p.185: L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​) factor-of-2 teaching note (must read): the clean time-domain derivation "white noise × ISF → integrate" gives Sϕ=Γrms2Si/(qmax2(2πf)2)S_\phi=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(q_{max}^2(2\pi f)^2)Sϕ​=Γrms2​Si​/(qmax2​(2πf)2), corresponding to SSB L=Γrms2Si/(2qmax2Δω2)\mathcal{L}=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(2q_{max}^2\Delta\omega^2)L=Γrms2​Si​/(2qmax2​Δω2) (denominator 222); whereas [P1] Eq.(21) is written with denominator 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2. This factor of 2 comes from the SSB (single-sideband) bookkeeping convention — a famous minor controversy in the literature. It does not affect the Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ scaling, nor the −20-20−20 dB/decade slope — those are the physics. The simulation in this lab uses the clean time-domain version (denominator (2πf)2(2\pi f)^2(2πf)2), so the simulated curve sits on the time-domain theory line. See white_noise_to_phase_noise.
documents.s: 2. Mathematical model

documents.t: Verbatim from main() in simulations/lab_06_white_noise_phase_noise.py: three steps (generate white noise → ISF weighting → cumsum integration), then Welch-estimate the phase PSD and overlay the theory line. f0 = 1.0 fs = 256.0 # 256 samples per period n = 2 ** 20 # ~4096 periods -> good low-freq resolution t = np.arange(n) / fs q_max = 1.0 S_i = 1.0e-4 # one-sided white current PSD [A^2/Hz] (normalized) # ISF and its rms theta_grid = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 4000, endpoint=True) Grms = gamma_rms(theta_grid, gamma_lc_ideal(theta_grid)) # = 1/sqrt(2) # 1) white current noise i_n = white_noise(n, psd=S_i, fs=fs, rng=RNG) # 2) ISF weighting g = gamma_lc_ideal(2 * np.pi * f0 * t) * i_n / q_max # 3) integrate (cumulative) -> excess phase dt = 1.0 / fs phi = np.cumsum(g) * dt phi = phi - np.mean(phi) # remove the random-walk DC offset for PSD est. # 4) estimate phase PSD f, Sphi = estimate_psd(phi, fs, nperseg=2 ** 16) # theory line Sphi_theory = Grms ** 2 * S_i / (q_max ** 2 * (2 * np.pi * f) ** 2) Step 3, np.cumsum(g) * dt, discretizes the ∫dτ\int d\tau∫dτ in the convolution expression — the cumulative sum is the integrator, i.e. the source of the phase's "infinite memory". The ISF is the ideal-LC gamma_lc_ideal (Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ), whose Γrms=1/2≈0.707\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2\approx0.707Γrms​=1/2​≈0.707 (because ⟨sin⁡2⟩=1/2\langle\sin^2\rangle=1/2⟨sin2⟩=1/2).

documents.t: Blue line (simulated SϕS_\phiSϕ​): the PSD actually estimated from the simulated phase sequence. On log–log it is a straight line of slope −2-2−2 (dropping 202020 dB per decade), with the random fluctuations of a Welch estimate. Black dashed line (theory): the analytic line Γrms2Si/(qmax2(2πf)2)\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(q_{max}^2(2\pi f)^2)Γrms2​Si​/(qmax2​(2πf)2). The blue line hugs the black one — this is "white noise → 1/f21/f^21/f2" confirmed numerically. Red dotted line (−20-20−20 dB/dec guide): a pure slope reference confirming the slope is exactly −2-2−2. Key point: the input is flat (SiS_iSi​ independent of fff), yet the output is 1/f21/f^21/f2. The extra 1/f21/f^21/f2 comes entirely from the integrator in step 3. Swapping in a different ISF shape only changes Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (shifting the whole line up or down); the slope is always −2-2−2. The height of the whole line is set by Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​, so enlarging qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (tank swing) is the main knob for lowering 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise (design usage in tank_swing). documents.t: This is a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level: the ISF is the analytic −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ (ideal LC), not extracted from a real circuit. qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1, f0=1f_0=1f0​=1 are normalized units, so there is no absolute dBc/Hz (for absolute values see lab_08 and numerical_feeling example B). Single white-noise source, stationary assumption: real circuits have multiple sources and are cyclostationary (noise intensity varies periodically with the operating point); the correction is Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α (see effective_isf). Small-angle approximation: phase is treated as linearly superposable and small; for large phase excursions L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\frac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​ breaks down. factor-of-2: the simulation agrees with the time-domain theory line (denominator (2πf)2(2\pi f)^2(2πf)2) and differs from the 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2 of [P1] Eq.(21) by the SSB-bookkeeping factor of 2 — slope and scaling unaffected. Numerical limits: the low-frequency end is limited by the total simulated time (≈4096\approx4096≈4096 periods) and nperseg; the leftmost few points have larger statistical scatter, and the plot shows only the trustworthy region f>0.02f>0.02f>0.02.
