documents.t: This lab answers the most profitable question in oscillator design: why do some oscillators have terrible close-in phase noise (a steep 1/f31/f^31/f3) while others are clean? The answer lies not in the noise source but in the waveform's symmetry — specifically, in the ISF's DC Fourier coefficient c0c_0c0​. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the device's 1/f1/f1/f (flicker) noise is concentrated at very low frequencies (near DC). Whether it can "upconvert" (get moved next to the carrier and become phase noise) depends on whether the ISF has a DC component. The ISF's DC value is c0/2c_0/2c0​/2. If the waveform is perfectly symmetric (rise and fall mirror-symmetric), c0=0c_0=0c0​=0: near-DC 1/f1/f1/f noise, multiplied by an ISF that "averages to zero", cancels and does not upconvert; if the waveform is asymmetric, c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0: the near-DC noise survives, and the integrator then colors it into a steep, tall 1/f31/f^31/f3. Symmetry is a free lunch: making the waveform symmetric cuts 1/f31/f^31/f3 phase noise for free.
documents.s: Lab 07 — 1/f Noise Upconversion and ISF Symmetry

documents.t: Understand how device 1/f1/f1/f noise "upconverts" into close-in phase noise. Compare, by simulation, the close-in behavior of a symmetric ISF (c0=0c_0=0c0​=0) and an asymmetric ISF (c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0). Confirm with your own eyes: c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 → close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3 suppressed; c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0 → a steep 1/f31/f^31/f3 appears. Connect this phenomenon to [P1] Eq.(23) (the 1/f31/f^31/f3 expression) and Eq.(24) (the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner).
documents.s: 1. Learning objectives

documents.t: The one-sided PSD of device flicker current noise has a 1/f1/f1/f shape ([P1] Eq.(22), p.185): in,1/f2‾=in2‾⋅ω1/fΔω\overline{i_{n,1/f}^2}=\overline{i_n^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}in,1/f2​​=in2​​⋅Δωω1/f​​ Meaning: ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ is the device's 1/f1/f1/f corner (corner frequency); below it the noise goes as 1/f1/f1/f, above it the noise approaches white. Units: in2‾\overline{i_n^2}in2​​ is A2/A^2/A2/Hz; ω1/f/Δω\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omegaω1/f​/Δω is dimensionless, so the whole expression is still A2/A^2/A2/Hz ✓. Feeding this 1/f1/f1/f noise into the ISF's DC channel and integrating gives the close-in phase noise ([P1] Eq.(23), p.185): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(c02qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf8 Δω2⋅ω1/fΔω)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{8\,\Delta\omega^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​c02​​⋅8Δω2in2​​/Δf​⋅Δωω1/f​​) Where the slope comes from: 1Δω2\frac{1}{\Delta\omega^2}Δω21​ (integrator, −20-20−20 dB/dec) ×1Δω\times\frac{1}{\Delta\omega}×Δω1​ (1/f1/f1/f noise source, −10-10−10 dB/dec) =1Δω3=\frac{1}{\Delta\omega^3}=Δω31​, i.e. 1/f31/f^31/f3 (−30-30−30 dB/dec). c0c_0c0​ is the switch: the whole expression is multiplied by c02c_0^2c02​. c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 → this 1/f31/f^31/f3 term vanishes (is suppressed), and close-in falls back to white-noise-dominated 1/f21/f^21/f2; c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0 → 1/f31/f^31/f3 appears with height proportional to c02c_0^2c02​. The corner frequency where the 1/f31/f^31/f3 and 1/f21/f^21/f2 segments intersect ([P1] Eq.(24), p.185): Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c022 Γrms2≈ω1/f(c0c1)2\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}\approx\omega_{1/f}\left(\frac{c_0}{c_1}\right)^2Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​≈ω1/f​(c1​c0​​)2 Design implication: shrink c0c_0c0​ (waveform asymmetry) and the corner moves left — the close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3 region narrows. Notation trap: c0c_0c0​ is a Fourier coefficient; the ISF's DC value is c0/2c_0/2c0​/2 (see notation). In this lab's toy formulation, the asymmetric ISF is gamma_asym = cos(theta) + 0.5, DC value =0.5=0.5=0.5, corresponding to c0=1.0c_0=1.0c0​=1.0; the symmetric ISF is gamma_sym = cos(theta), DC value =0=0=0, c0=0c_0=0c0​=0. Using cos instead of the LC's −sin⁡-\sin−sin simply makes the "symmetric basis + DC shift" contrast more intuitive; both are toys.

documents.t: Verbatim from simulations/lab_07_flicker_noise.py: the same flicker-noise record passes separately through the symmetric and asymmetric ISFs, then each is integrated and its PSD estimated. Note that phase_from_isf is exactly "ISF weighting → cumsum integration". def phase_from_isf(i_n, gamma_vals, q_max, fs): g = gamma_vals * i_n / q_max phi = np.cumsum(g) / fs return phi - np.mean(phi) def main(): f0 = 1.0 fs = 256.0 n = 2 ** 20 t = np.arange(n) / fs q_max = 1.0 theta = 2 * np.pi * f0 * t gamma_sym = np.cos(theta) # c0 = 0 gamma_asym = np.cos(theta) + 0.5 # c0 = 1.0 (DC = 0.5) i_flicker = flicker_noise(n, fs, k_flicker=1e-4, rng=RNG) phi_sym = phase_from_isf(i_flicker, gamma_sym, q_max, fs) phi_asym = phase_from_isf(i_flicker, gamma_asym, q_max, fs) f, S_sym = estimate_psd(phi_sym, fs, nperseg=2 ** 16) _, S_asym = estimate_psd(phi_asym, fs, nperseg=2 ** 16) The only difference between the two ISFs is that + 0.5 (DC shift). Everything else is identical — so any difference between the two output PSDs can only come from c0c_0c0​. This turns "is c0c_0c0​ the switch for 1/f31/f^31/f3?" into a controlled experiment.

documents.s: 8. Simulation figure

documents.t: Red line (asymmetric, c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0): in the close-in (low-offset) region a tall, steep curve appears, with slope near −30-30−30 dB/dec (1/f31/f^31/f3). The black dotted line is a pure 1/f31/f^31/f3 slope reference; the red line hugs it. Green line (symmetric, c0=0c_0=0c0​=0): clearly much lower in the close-in region, with a gentler slope (near 1/f21/f^21/f2, gray dashed reference). 1/f31/f^31/f3 is suppressed — visual proof that "waveform symmetry cuts close-in noise for free". The two lines converge at higher offsets: far from the carrier, the gap between 1/f31/f^31/f3 and 1/f21/f^21/f2 shrinks, because flicker noise itself is already weak at high frequency. Key point: the only difference between the two ISFs is c0c_0c0​. The huge close-in gap between red and green is caused entirely by c0c_0c0​. As c0→0c_0\to0c0​→0, the red line collapses onto the green one.

documents.t: Pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level: the two ISFs (cos, cos+0.5) are teaching toys, not extracted from real circuits. The +0.5 is an artificially set c0c_0c0​, purely for a controlled comparison. Normalized units: f0=1f_0=1f0​=1, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1, k_flicker on an arbitrary scale — no absolute dBc/Hz. The relative shape of the curves (slopes, red–green gap) is the teaching point. Flicker generation is approximate: flicker_noise uses frequency-domain 1/f1/\sqrt f1/f​ shaping and relies on f_low to tame the divergent DC bin; accuracy at very low frequency is limited by f_low and the total record length. Stationary-noise assumption: real flicker upconversion also involves cyclostationary modulation (the device leaks noise only while conducting); the full treatment uses Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α (see effective_isf); this lab demonstrates only the c0c_0c0​ mechanism. Welch low-frequency scatter: the close-in region has few points and large statistical scatter; the plot shows only the trustworthy segment f>0.02f>0.02f>0.02.

documents.t: Device 1/f1/f1/f noise is concentrated near DC; whether it upconverts into phase noise is determined by the ISF's DC component (c0/2c_0/2c0​/2). c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0 → close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3 (−30-30−30 dB/dec); c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 → suppressed, falls back to 1/f21/f^21/f2. The 1/f31/f^31/f3 height is proportional to c02c_0^2c02​; the corner ∝c02/Γrms2\propto c_0^2/\Gamma_{rms}^2∝c02​/Γrms2​. Design lesson: making the waveform symmetric (suppressing c0c_0c0​) is a free way to lower close-in phase noise.

documents.t: This lab turns something you see on every datasheet — the single-sideband phase-noise curve L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) (dBc/Hz) — into the number designers actually care about: rms timing jitter σt\sigma_tσt​. We use a canonical scenario (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, L(1MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz, 1/f21/f^21/f2 slope, integrated 1→100 MHz) and make the numerical integration and the analytic closed form agree digit by digit: σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs. Physical intuition (conclusion first): phase noise is "how much phase power density sits at each offset frequency"; jitter is "add it all up, take the square root, convert to time". So going from L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) to σt\sigma_tσt​ is three things: (1) convert dBc/Hz back to linear and multiply by 2 to recover SϕS_\phiSϕ​; (2) integrate over offset frequency to get the phase variance; (3) take the square root and divide by 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ to convert to time. For a 1/f21/f^21/f2 shape, the integral is dominated by the lower limit f1f_1f1​ — "where you start integrating" matters far more than "how high you go".
documents.s: Lab 08 — rms Jitter by Integrating L(f)

documents.t: Convert L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) (dBc/Hz) step by step into rms phase σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ and rms jitter σt\sigma_tσt​. Build a feel for the 5 GHz conversion: −100-100−100 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, 1/f21/f^21/f2, integrated 1→100 MHz → about 448 fs. Verify numerical integration = analytic closed form (1/f21/f^21/f2 has a closed form). Understand why 1/f21/f^21/f2 jitter is dominated by the lower integration limit.

Under the small-angle / single-sideband approximation (canonical formula 16): L(Δf)≈12Sϕ(Δf) ⇒ Sϕ(f)=2⋅10L(f)/10.\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\approx\tfrac12 S_\phi(\Delta f)\;\Rightarrow\;S_\phi(f)=2\cdot10^{\mathcal{L}(f)/10}.L(Δf)≈21​Sϕ​(Δf)⇒Sϕ​(f)=2⋅10L(f)/10. Step 2: write the 1/f21/f^21/f2 shape (anchored at fref=1f_{ref}=1fref​=1 MHz, canonical example C): Sϕ(f)=Sϕ(fref)(freff)2.S_\phi(f)=S_\phi(f_{ref})\left(\frac{f_{ref}}{f}\right)^2.Sϕ​(f)=Sϕ​(fref​)(ffref​​)2. Step 3: integrate to get the phase variance (canonical formula 18): σϕ2=∫f1f2Sϕ(f) df.\sigma_\phi^2=\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_\phi(f)\,df.σϕ2​=∫f1​f2​​Sϕ​(f)df. Step 4: convert to rms jitter (canonical formula 19): σt=σϕ2πf0=12πf0∫f1f2Sϕ(f) df.\sigma_t=\frac{\sigma_\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{1}{2\pi f_0}\sqrt{\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_\phi(f)\,df}.σt​=2πf0​σϕ​​=2πf0​1​∫f1​f2​​Sϕ​(f)df​. Dimension check (step 4): σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ is rad, 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ is rad/s, [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] ✓. Substituting the canonical numbers digit by digit (identical to numerical_feeling example C): Sϕ(1MHz)=2×10−100/10=2×10−10 rad2/Hz,σϕ2=2×10−10 (106)2 (10−6−10−8)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2,σϕ=1.407×10−2 rad=14.07 mrad,σt=1.407×10−22π×5×109=4.479×10−13 s=447.9 fs.\begin{aligned} S_\phi(1\text{MHz})&=2\times10^{-100/10}=2\times10^{-10}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz},\\ \sigma_\phi^2&=2\times10^{-10}\,(10^6)^2\,(10^{-6}-10^{-8})=200\times9.9\times10^{-7}=1.98\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}^2,\\ \sigma_\phi&=1.407\times10^{-2}\ \text{rad}=14.07\ \text{mrad},\\ \sigma_t&=\frac{1.407\times10^{-2}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{9}}=4.479\times10^{-13}\ \text{s}=447.9\ \text{fs}. \end{aligned}Sϕ​(1MHz)σϕ2​σϕ​σt​​=2×10−100/10=2×10−10 rad2/Hz,=2×10−10(106)2(10−6−10−8)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2,=1.407×10−2 rad=14.07 mrad,=2π×5×1091.407×10−2​=4.479×10−13 s=447.9 fs.​

documents.t: Verbatim from main() in simulations/lab_08_jitter_integration.py: first build the 1/f21/f^21/f2 curve with leeson_one_over_f2, then integrate numerically with integrate_rms_jitter, and finally check against the hand-computed 1/f21/f^21/f2 closed form. import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import leeson_one_over_f2, integrate_rms_jitter f0 = 5e9 f_ref = 1e6 L_ref = -100.0 # dBc/Hz f1, f2 = 1e6, 100e6 f = np.logspace(np.log10(f1), np.log10(f2), 4000) L = leeson_one_over_f2(f, L_ref, f_ref) # numerical integration sigma_t, sigma_phi = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L, f0, f1, f2) # analytic closed form (1/f^2) L_ref_lin = 10 ** (L_ref / 10) sigma_phi2_analytic = 2 * L_ref_lin * f_ref ** 2 * (1 / f1 - 1 / f2) sigma_phi_analytic = np.sqrt(sigma_phi2_analytic) sigma_t_analytic = sigma_phi_analytic / (2 * np.pi * f0) print(round(sigma_t * 1e15, 1)) # -> 447.9 (sigma_t in fs) print(round(sigma_phi * 1e3, 2)) # -> 14.07 (sigma_phi in mrad) The underlying function integrate_rms_jitter (noise_utils.py) implements exactly steps 1, 3, and 4: l_linear = 10 ** (l_dbc_per_hz[mask] / 10) # dBc/Hz -> linear s_phi = 2 * l_linear # L ~= 0.5 * S_phi sigma_phi = np.sqrt(_trapz(s_phi, f[mask])) # integrate + square root sigma_t = sigma_phi / (2 * np.pi * f0) # convert to time The script prints sigma_phi (numeric) ≈ sigma_phi (analytic) and sigma_t ≈ 447.9 fs; the numerical and analytic values agree digit by digit (the only difference is the negligible discretization error of logspace sampling and trapezoidal integration).

documents.t: Small-angle approximation L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\frac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​: breaks down at large phase excursions; here σϕ=14\sigma_\phi=14σϕ​=14 mrad ≪1\ll1≪1 rad, so the approximation is excellent. This part is not a toy (the integration flow itself is real engineering practice), but the L(f)L(f)L(f) shape is idealized. Sensitivity to the integration range: with 1/f21/f^21/f2, the lower limit f1f_1f1​ dominates; changing f1f_1f1​ visibly changes σt\sigma_tσt​, while the upper limit matters little. In practice f1f_1f1​, f2f_2f2​ must be chosen per application (PLL loop bandwidth, data rate). Numerical = analytic: the two differ only by the discretization error (logspace + trapezoidal rule), negligible in this setup.

documents.t: Breadcrumb: Simulation labs › Noise & jitter › This page (design trade-offs intro). Upstream: lab_06, lab_08; advanced version: lab_17. The first eight labs exercised each mechanism one at a time. This synthesis lab introduces no new simulation; instead it treats [P1] Eq.(21) — the signature equation — as a map of design knobs: holding everything else fixed, separately sweep qmaxq_{max}qmax​, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, and the ring stage count NNN, and watch how the phase noise L\mathcal{L}L and the rms jitter σt\sigma_tσt​ move. Throughout we use the canonical numbers (spec Section 8) for back-of-envelope arithmetic, building the reflex of "turn this knob, gain that many dB". Physical intuition (conclusion first): 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise ∝Γrms2/qmax2\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2∝Γrms2​/qmax2​. There are only two broad roads to lower phase noise: make the signal charge qmaxq_{max}qmax​ larger (store more energy, so the noise is relatively smaller), or make the ISF Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ smaller (make the waveform insensitive to noise). Both are 20log⁡1020\log_{10}20log10​ relationships: doubling qmaxq_{max}qmax​ → phase noise −6-6−6 dB; halving Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ → also −6-6−6 dB. A ring oscillator's NNN moves two things at once — watch the net effect carefully.

documents.t: Read [P1] Eq.(21) as a scaling law and build design intuition for qmaxq_{max}qmax​, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, and NNN. Use the canonical numbers to compute "how many dB / how many fs one knob buys". Understand the two-sided nature of the ring oscillator's NNN (Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2, but power/area grow too). Connect the scaling conclusions to the design-insight pages.

documents.s: 2. Mathematical model

documents.t: This lab produces no new figure; the scaling comes straight from back-of-envelope use of [P1] Eq.(21). The snippet below (following the conventions of simulations/lab_08_jitter_integration.py) shows how to turn knob changes into dB and fs so you can sweep the parameters yourself: import math def L_dbc(Grms, qmax, Si, df): """Hajimiri-Lee Eq.(21): 1/f^2 SSB phase noise [dBc/Hz].""" dw = 2 * math.pi * df return 10 * math.log10((Grms**2 / qmax**2) * (Si / (4 * dw**2))) # canonical baseline (spec example B) f0, df, Si = 5e9, 1e6, 1e-24 base = L_dbc(Grms=0.5, qmax=1e-12, Si=Si, df=df) # -148.0 dBc/Hz print("baseline :", round(base, 1), "dBc/Hz") print("q_max x2 :", round(L_dbc(0.5, 2e-12, Si, df) - base, 1), "dB") # -6.0 print("Gamma_rms /2 :", round(L_dbc(0.25, 1e-12, Si, df) - base, 1), "dB") # -6.0 # ring N: Gamma_rms ~ N^-1.5 ([P2] Eq.(16), p.794, re-verified v7: sqrt covers only the constant); show isolated scaling for N in (5, 15, 45): rel = (N / 5.0) ** -1.5 print(f"N={N:2d} Gamma_rms rel={rel:.3f} dL={20*math.log10(rel):+.1f} dB") # jitter scales as Gamma_rms / q_max -> -6 dB phase noise = sigma_t / 2 L_dbc is not the same thing as lab_08's integrate_rms_jitter: lab_08 integrates jitter out of L\mathcal{L}L; here we go the other way — use Eq.(21) to generate L\mathcal{L}L, then infer jitter from the scaling. The two pages are forward and inverse operations of each other.

documents.t: Toy scaling, not transistor-level: the scaling assumes "turn one knob, hold everything else exactly fixed". In a real circuit qmaxq_{max}qmax​, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, NNN, power, area, and f0f_0f0​ are coupled and cannot be tuned in isolation. Ring NNN scaling ([P2] Eq.(16), p.794 — v7 re-verified: the square root covers only the constant, Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2; the body text's 4/N1.54/N^{1.5}4/N1.5 at η=0.75 and App. B Eq.(55) triple-confirm this. v3 had misread it as N−3/4N^{-3/4}N−3/4): the proportionality constant is Γrms=2π2/(3η3)⋅1N1.5\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{2\pi^2/(3\eta^3)}\cdot\dfrac{1}{N^{1.5}}Γrms​=2π2/(3η3)​⋅N1.51​ (η≈1\eta\approx1η≈1); adding stages also changes f0=1/(2NτD)f_0=1/(2N\tau_D)f0​=1/(2NτD​), power, and area — the net phase noise/jitter requires the full FOM, not Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ alone. Single white source: ignores multiple sources, cyclostationarity (Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α), and flicker upconversion (1/f31/f^31/f3, see lab_07). The table does not apply in the close-in region. Factor-of-2: uses Eq.(21)'s denominator 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2; it differs from the time-domain version by the factor-of-2 SSB bookkeeping, which affects none of the scaling conclusions (all dB changes are relative). Jitter scaling: σt∝Γrms/qmax\sigma_t\propto\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}σt​∝Γrms​/qmax​ assumes a fixed integration range and a 1/f21/f^21/f2 shape; if close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3 dominates, jitter is set by c0c_0c0​ and the lower integration limit and must be computed separately.

documents.t: Breadcrumb: Simulation labs › Noise & jitter › This page (RF spectrum skirt). Upstream: white_noise_to_phase_noise; downstream: lab_08. This lab connects the abstract phase-noise PSD Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) to what you actually see on a spectrum analyzer: an ideal carrier is a single line in the spectrum; with phase noise, that line gets "smeared" into a continuous skirt (sidebands sloping down on both sides of the carrier). We synthesize v(t)=cos⁡(ω0t+ϕ(t))v(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t+\phi(t))v(t)=cos(ω0​t+ϕ(t)) directly in the time domain, take an FFT, and see it with our own eyes — this is exactly the picture in [P1] Fig. 8, and it's where the unit dBc/Hz (decibels relative to carrier per Hz) comes from. Physical intuition (conclusion first): phase noise is not "an extra noise source sitting next to the carrier" — it is the carrier's own phase jittering. Stuff the jittering phase ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) into the cosine's phase argument (phase modulation, PM), and the carrier's energy "leaks" from that one clean spectral line into nearby offset frequencies. How far it leaks and how much depends on the spectral shape of ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t): 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise → a skirt that falls off at −20-20−20 dB/dec on either side of the carrier. Seeing the skirt means seeing Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) "moved" next to the carrier.
documents.s: Lab 10 — how phase noise smears the carrier into an RF skirt

documents.t: Start from the time-domain PM signal v(t)=cos⁡(ω0t+ϕ(t))v(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t+\phi(t))v(t)=cos(ω0​t+ϕ(t)) and use an FFT to see the sideband skirt caused by phase noise. Compare an "ideal carrier (nearly a single spectral line)" against "with phase noise (continuous skirt)" to understand the physical meaning of dBc/Hz. Map 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise (integrated white noise) to a −20-20−20 dB/dec skirt slope on either side of the carrier. Recognize this plot as the time-domain version of [P1] Fig. 8.

documents.t: Carrier + excess phase. An oscillator output corrupted by phase noise is written as (a special case of canonical formula 1, with A(t)A(t)A(t) treated as constant): v(t)=cos⁡ ⁣(ω0t+ϕ(t)),ω0=2πf0.v(t)=\cos\!\big(\omega_0 t+\phi(t)\big),\qquad \omega_0=2\pi f_0 .v(t)=cos(ω0​t+ϕ(t)),ω0​=2πf0​. ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) is 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise. White noise w(t)w(t)w(t) passed through a phase integrator (in the spirit of canonical formula 11: noise is first weighted by Γ/qmax\Gamma/q_{max}Γ/qmax​, then integrated by ∫dt\int dt∫dt) produces a random-walk-like phase: ϕ(t)=1fs∑k≤tfswk ⟹ Sϕ(f)∝1f2.\phi(t)=\frac{1}{f_s}\sum_{k\le t f_s} w_k\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; S_\phi(f)\propto\frac{1}{f^2}.ϕ(t)=fs​1​k≤tfs​∑​wk​⟹Sϕ​(f)∝f21​. Why integrating white noise gives 1/f21/f^21/f2: an integrator in the frequency domain is 1/(j2πf)1/(j2\pi f)1/(j2πf), so power transfers as 1/f21/f^21/f2; white noise (SwS_wSw​ flat) passing through this yields Sϕ(f)∝Sw/f2S_\phi(f)\propto S_w/f^2Sϕ​(f)∝Sw​/f2. This is exactly the signature 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt of a free-running oscillator (the spectral shape of canonical formula 21). RF spectrum = power spectrum of the PM signal. Window v(t)v(t)v(t) (Hanning), take the FFT, take the magnitude squared, and normalize to the carrier peak: P(f)=∣F{v(t) wwin(t)}∣2max⁡f∣⋯∣2,PdBc(Δf)=10log⁡10P(f0+Δf).P(f)=\frac{\lvert\mathcal{F}\{v(t)\,w_{\text{win}}(t)\}\rvert^2}{\max_f\lvert\cdots\rvert^2},\qquad P_{\text{dBc}}(\Delta f)=10\log_{10}P(f_0+\Delta f).P(f)=maxf​∣⋯∣2∣F{v(t)wwin​(t)}∣2​,PdBc​(Δf)=10log10​P(f0​+Δf). Sideband mechanism under the small-angle approximation (spec Section 10.2, "L≈12SϕL\approx\tfrac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​"): let ϕ(t)=ϕpsin⁡ωmt\phi(t)=\phi_p\sin\omega_m tϕ(t)=ϕp​sinωm​t; at small angle cos⁡(ω0t+ϕ)≈cos⁡ω0t−ϕp2[cos⁡(ω0−ωm)t−cos⁡(ω0+ωm)t].\cos(\omega_0 t+\phi)\approx\cos\omega_0 t-\frac{\phi_p}{2}\big[\cos(\omega_0-\omega_m)t-\cos(\omega_0+\omega_m)t\big].cos(ω0​t+ϕ)≈cosω0​t−2ϕp​​[cos(ω0​−ωm​)t−cos(ω0​+ωm​)t]. Each sideband's power relative to the carrier is (ϕp/2)2(\phi_p/2)^2(ϕp​/2)2; summing over the continuous spectrum of ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) produces the skirt. Dimension check: ϕ\phiϕ and ϕp\phi_pϕp​ are in rad (dimensionless), P/Pmax⁡P/P_{\max}P/Pmax​ is dimensionless, and 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ of that gives dBc ✓. The offset Δf\Delta fΔf and fff share units (this lab uses normalized units).

documents.t: Verbatim excerpt from main() in simulations/lab_10_rf_spectrum.py: cumsum white noise into 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase phi (scaled to ~0.03 rad rms to stay small-angle), then synthesize the clean carrier and the noisy carrier, and finally apply a Hanning window, take the rFFT, normalize to the peak, and convert to dB. fs = 8192.0 n = 2 ** 18 t = np.arange(n) / fs f0 = 512.0 # carrier (normalized units), 16 samples/cycle # 1/f^2 phase noise: integrate white noise, scale to a visible (small) rms white = RNG.standard_normal(n) phi = np.cumsum(white) / fs phi -= phi.mean() phi *= 0.03 / np.std(phi) # ~0.03 rad rms -> small-angle regime v_clean = np.cos(2 * np.pi * f0 * t) v_noisy = np.cos(2 * np.pi * f0 * t + phi) win = np.hanning(n) def spec(x): X = np.fft.rfft(x * win) P = np.abs(X) ** 2 return P / P.max() f = np.fft.rfftfreq(n, 1 / fs) Pc = spec(v_clean) Pn = spec(v_noisy) off = f - f0 # offset from carrier phi = np.cumsum(white) / fs is the discrete integrator (the source of 1/f21/f^21/f2). phi *= 0.03 / np.std(phi) compresses the rms to ~0.03 rad, keeping it in the small-angle regime (so the skirt stays proportional to SϕS_\phiSϕ​ without spawning strong higher-order harmonic sidebands). P / P.max() normalizes power to the carrier peak, so the y-axis is naturally dBc.

documents.s: 8. Simulation plot

documents.t: Blue line (ideal carrier): energy is almost entirely concentrated at the carrier itself and drops off sharply as offset increases — the spectrum looks "almost like a single line". The small residual skirt comes from finite FFT length and window leakage, not physical phase noise. Red line (with phase noise): a continuous skirt appears on both sides of the carrier, sloping down with increasing offset. On a log-offset axis it is nearly a straight-line falloff, matching −20-20−20 dB/dec for 1/f21/f^21/f2: this is the time-domain origin of the dBc/Hz curve. The single-line-vs-skirt contrast is the core message of this plot: the phase jitters → carrier energy leaks out → a spectral line becomes a skirt. "Lower and steeper skirt" means smaller phase noise. How to use it: the skirt height you measure on a spectrum analyzer (relative to the carrier, per Hz) is L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) (dBc/Hz). Integrate it (see lab_08) to get rms jitter. This lab lets you "see" how that curve grows out of time-domain PM.

documents.t: Core correspondence: [P1] A. Hajimiri and T. H. Lee, "A General Theory of Phase Noise in Electrical Oscillators," IEEE JSSC, 33(2), 1998, Fig. 8 — shows phase noise smearing the carrier into a sideband skirt. This lab is its time-domain synthesis version. [P1] Fig. 8 is on p.183 (checked against the original PDF). Carrier decomposition: canonical formula 1, Vout(t)=A(t)f(ω0t+ϕ(t))V_{out}(t)=A(t)f(\omega_0 t+\phi(t))Vout​(t)=A(t)f(ω0​t+ϕ(t)) (here AAA is taken constant, f=cos⁡f=\cosf=cos). Sideband mechanism (small-angle PM → L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​): spec Section 10.2, "L≈12SϕL\approx\tfrac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​ (small-angle PM)". Origin of the 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt: phase integration of white noise, consistent with the spectral shape of canonical formula 21 ([P1] Eq.(21), p.185). documents.t: This is a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level: we directly "inject" a 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise without actually simulating the full pipeline of transistor noise weighted by the ISF; the goal is to see "what the skirt looks like". Small-angle assumption: ϕ\phiϕ rms ≈0.03\approx0.03≈0.03 rad ≪1\ll1≪1, so the skirt is proportional to SϕS_\phiSϕ​ with no strong higher-order sidebands. At large phase excursions, PM produces carrier compression and higher-order sidebands, which this plot does not cover. Normalized units: fs and f0 have no physical dimension, and the x-axis offset is also normalized; the focus is on shape and contrast, not absolute Hz. Matching a real 5 GHz, dBc/Hz result requires setting a real sample rate and an absolute SϕS_\phiSϕ​ level. FFT artifacts: the blue line's residual skirt and the red line's far floor partly come from finite-length FFT and Hanning window leakage, not entirely physical phase noise. Increasing n or using a sharper window reduces this. Single random realization: the plot comes from one ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) trace with a fixed seed; a rigorous L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) requires ensemble averaging (Welch) over many realizations, see lab_06.

documents.t: Phase noise is not an extra source sitting beside the carrier — it is the carrier's own phase jittering → energy leaks from a single line into a sideband skirt. Taking the FFT of the time-domain v(t)=cos⁡(ω0t+ϕ(t))v(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t+\phi(t))v(t)=cos(ω0​t+ϕ(t)) lets you "see" the skirt of [P1] Fig. 8. 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise (integrated white noise) → a −20-20−20 dB/dec skirt on both sides of the carrier; skirt height is dBc/Hz. Under small-angle PM each sideband's relative power is (ϕp/2)2(\phi_p/2)^2(ϕp​/2)2, summing into a continuous spectrum (L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​).

documents.t: Breadcrumb: Simulation labs › Noise & jitter › This page (Monte Carlo accumulated jitter). Upstream: oscillator_phase, lab_03; downstream: lab_12, lab_13. This lab uses the most direct method — Monte Carlo (large-scale random sampling statistics) — to prove that the random jitter (RJ, Gaussian, unbounded) accumulated by a free-running (unlocked) oscillator has two key properties: its distribution is Gaussian; its standard deviation grows as the square root of the accumulated period count: σΔt=σedgeΔN\sigma_{\Delta t}=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{\Delta N}σΔt​=σedge​ΔN​. This is the junction between the "statistical (time-domain) view" and the "spectral view", and it is the microscopic origin of [P2] Eq.(8), σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​. Physical intuition (conclusion first): every period, noise pushes the oscillator's edge (zero-crossing/transition instant) by an independent small amount, mean 0, standard deviation σedge\sigma_{edge}σedge​. Phase has no restoring force (see oscillator_phase), so these small pushes are never pulled back — they simply accumulate. This is a one-dimensional random walk. After ΔN\Delta NΔN steps, a random walk's position still has mean 0, but its variance is ΔN\Delta NΔN times the single-step variance, so the standard deviation grows as ΔN\sqrt{\Delta N}ΔN​. And a sum of independent small increments tends to Gaussian by the central limit theorem.
documents.s: Lab 11 — Monte Carlo accumulated jitter — RJ is Gaussian, σ grows as √ΔN

documents.t: Use Monte Carlo to directly "see" the Gaussian distribution of accumulated jitter. Verify the random-walk law σΔt=σedgeΔN\sigma_{\Delta t}=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{\Delta N}σΔt​=σedge​ΔN​: a 4×4\times4× increase in ΔN\Delta NΔN gives only a 2×2\times2× increase in σ\sigmaσ. Link this time-domain result to [P2] Eq.(8), σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ (κ\kappaκ a proportionality constant). Understand why phase/jitter accumulates — because phase has no restoring force (unlike amplitude).
documents.s: 1. Learning objectives

documents.t: Per-period increment. The edge-timing error of the kkk-th period is an i.i.d. Gaussian increment: δk∼N(0, σedge2).\delta_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\;\sigma_{edge}^2).δk​∼N(0,σedge2​). Accumulated jitter = sum of increments (random walk). After accumulating ΔN\Delta NΔN periods, the timing error relative to the ideal edge is: ΔtΔN=∑k=1ΔNδk.\Delta t_{\Delta N}=\sum_{k=1}^{\Delta N}\delta_k .ΔtΔN​=k=1∑ΔN​δk​. Statistical properties (step by step). The increments are independent with zero mean: E[ΔtΔN]=∑k=1ΔNE[δk]=0,Var⁡[ΔtΔN]=∑k=1ΔNVar⁡[δk]=ΔN⋅σedge2,σΔt=Var⁡=σedgeΔN.\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[\Delta t_{\Delta N}]&=\sum_{k=1}^{\Delta N}\mathbb{E}[\delta_k]=0,\\ \operatorname{Var}[\Delta t_{\Delta N}]&=\sum_{k=1}^{\Delta N}\operatorname{Var}[\delta_k]=\Delta N\cdot\sigma_{edge}^2,\\ \sigma_{\Delta t}&=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}}=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{\Delta N}. \end{aligned}E[ΔtΔN​]Var[ΔtΔN​]σΔt​​=k=1∑ΔN​E[δk​]=0,=k=1∑ΔN​Var[δk​]=ΔN⋅σedge2​,=Var​=σedge​ΔN​.​ Why variances add: the variance of a sum of independent random variables equals the sum of the individual variances (zero covariance). This is the entire origin of the "ΔN\sqrt{\Delta N}ΔN​". Why it's Gaussian: a sum of ΔN\Delta NΔN independent increments tends to Gaussian by the central limit theorem (and since each increment is already Gaussian, the sum is exactly Gaussian). Dimension check: σedge\sigma_{edge}σedge​ is in s, ΔN\sqrt{\Delta N}ΔN​ is dimensionless (ΔN\Delta NΔN is a period count), so σΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}σΔt​ is in s ✓. Linking to [P2] Eq.(8). Convert the accumulated period count into accumulated time Δt=ΔN⋅T=ΔN/f0\Delta t=\Delta N\cdot T=\Delta N/f_0Δt=ΔN⋅T=ΔN/f0​: σΔt=σedgeΔN=σedgef0 Δt=(σedgef0)⏟κΔt,\sigma_{\Delta t}=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{\Delta N}=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{f_0\,\Delta t}=\underbrace{\big(\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{f_0}\big)}_{\kappa}\sqrt{\Delta t},σΔt​=σedge​ΔN​=σedge​f0​Δt​=κ(σedge​f0​​)​​Δt​, i.e., [P2] Eq.(8), p.792, σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​, with κ=σedgef0\kappa=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{f_0}κ=σedge​f0​​. Dimension check (κ\kappaκ): [s]⋅[Hz]1/2=[s]⋅[s−1/2]=[s1/2][\text{s}]\cdot[\text{Hz}]^{1/2}=[\text{s}]\cdot[\text{s}^{-1/2}]=[\text{s}^{1/2}][s]⋅[Hz]1/2=[s]⋅[s−1/2]=[s1/2], consistent with the unit s\sqrt{s}s​ given for κ\kappaκ in the canonical symbol table ✓.

documents.t: Verbatim excerpt from main() in simulations/lab_11_monte_carlo_jitter.py: for each accumulation length lag (=ΔN\Delta NΔN), draw n_trials × lag independent Gaussian increments, sum along the period axis to get the accumulated error acc, measure its std, then overlay the theoretical Gaussian. f0 = 5e9 sigma_edge = 50e-15 # 50 fs per period n_trials = 200000 lags = [25, 100, 400] # number of periods accumulated for lag, c in zip(lags, colors): incr = sigma_edge * RNG.standard_normal((n_trials, lag)) acc = incr.sum(axis=1) # accumulated timing error after `lag` periods sigma_meas = np.std(acc) sigma_theory = sigma_edge * np.sqrt(lag) # histogram (in fs) ax.hist(acc / 1e-15, bins=120, density=True, alpha=0.35, color=c, label=fr"$\Delta N$={lag}: 量得 $\sigma$={sigma_meas/1e-15:.0f} fs " fr"(理論 {sigma_theory/1e-15:.0f} fs)") # gaussian overlay xx = np.linspace(acc.min(), acc.max(), 300) g = np.exp(-xx ** 2 / (2 * sigma_theory ** 2)) / (sigma_theory * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)) ax.plot(xx / 1e-15, g * 1e-15, color=c, lw=1.6) incr.sum(axis=1) sums lag independent increments — a one-dimensional random walk. sigma_meas = np.std(acc) (measured) converges digit by digit to sigma_theory = sigma_edge*np.sqrt(lag) (theoretical), because n_trials=200000 is large enough. The Gaussian overlay g uses the theoretical σ\sigmaσ; its match to the histogram is the proof that the distribution is Gaussian. Expected numbers (σedge=50\sigma_{edge}=50σedge​=50 fs): ΔN=25→250\Delta N=25\to250ΔN=25→250 fs, ΔN=100→500\Delta N=100\to500ΔN=100→500 fs, ΔN=400→1000\Delta N=400\to1000ΔN=400→1000 fs (each ×4\times4×4 step in ΔN\Delta NΔN gives ×2\times2×2 in σ\sigmaσ).

documents.t: Three bell curves (blue/orange/red for ΔN=25/100/400\Delta N=25/100/400ΔN=25/100/400): the histogram (translucent) and the theoretical Gaussian curve (solid line) overlap almost perfectly — this is direct evidence that "RJ is Gaussian". Wider means longer accumulation: as ΔN\Delta NΔN grows, the bell gets shorter and wider. Note the width (σ\sigmaσ) grows only as ΔN\sqrt{\Delta N}ΔN​: from 25→10025\to10025→100 (×4\times4×4), σ\sigmaσ goes from 250 fs to 500 fs (only ×2\times2×2); from 100→400100\to400100→400 (another ×4\times4×4), 500 fs becomes 1000 fs (another ×2\times2×2). "Measured σ vs. theoretical" in the legend: the two numbers are nearly identical, quantitatively verifying σΔt=σedgeΔN\sigma_{\Delta t}=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{\Delta N}σΔt​=σedge​ΔN​. How to use it: this explains why a free-running oscillator's long-term stability cannot be described by "per-period jitter" alone — jitter grows with observation time. Stopping the accumulation requires a PLL/CDR to lock the phase back to a reference (see lab_13).

documents.t: Core correspondence: [P2] A. Hajimiri, S. Limotyrakis, and T. H. Lee, "Jitter and Phase Noise in Ring Oscillators," IEEE JSSC, 34(6), 1999, Eq.(8), p.792: σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​. This lab proves its microscopic origin is a random walk of per-edge Gaussian increments, and derives κ=σedgef0\kappa=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{f_0}κ=σedge​f0​​. Spec Section 10.2, "period / cycle-to-cycle jitter kernels": accumulated jitter "has no differencing (low-frequency dominated)", corresponding to the pure accumulation here (no high-pass differencing kernel). Phase has no restoring force (hence accumulates): [P1]'s LTV phase model (canonical formula 11), consistent with the geometry in oscillator_phase. Corresponds to site figure monte_carlo_jitter_histogram.png; echoes the time-domain accumulation plot ring_oscillator_timing_noise_accumulation.png in lab_03.

documents.t: This is a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level: we directly assume an independent Gaussian increment σedge\sigma_{edge}σedge​ per period, without deriving its numerical value from ISF + device noise (that requires [P2]'s κ\kappaκ/FOM formulas, canonical formulas 22–23, verified verbatim against [P2] Eq.(8)/(12) p.792-793, Eq.(16) p.794, Eq.(23) p.796). Pure RJ, independent increments: assumes period-to-period noise is uncorrelated (white at the period scale). Real 1/f1/f1/f (flicker) noise introduces correlated increments, causing long-term accumulation to deviate from pure ΔN\sqrt{\Delta N}ΔN​ (close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3, see lab_07). Only covers accumulated/long-term jitter: period jitter (single-period deviation) and cycle-to-cycle jitter (adjacent difference) are the first/second-order differences of phase and are outside the scope of this plot (spec Section 10.2). Gaussian, unbounded: RJ is described by σ\sigmaσ with tails extending to infinity — this is exactly why SerDes BER is always >0>0>0 (see lab_12). Deterministic jitter (DJ, bounded) is outside this model. Finite-sample error: the small difference between sigma_meas and sigma_theory comes from finite n_trials; increasing it improves convergence.

documents.t: Accumulated jitter is a random walk of per-edge Gaussian increments: mean 0, variance ∝ΔN\propto\Delta N∝ΔN, Gaussian distribution. σΔt=σedgeΔN\sigma_{\Delta t}=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{\Delta N}σΔt​=σedge​ΔN​: a 4×4\times4× increase in ΔN\Delta NΔN gives only a 2×2\times2× increase in σ\sigmaσ. Converting to time gives [P2] Eq.(8), σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​, with κ=σedgef0\kappa=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{f_0}κ=σedge​f0​​. No restoring force on phase → jitter accumulates → poor free-running long-term stability → needs a PLL/CDR to lock it back.

documents.t: Breadcrumb: Simulation labs › Noise & jitter › This page (eye / BER bathtub). Upstream: lab_08, lab_11; downstream: lab_13. This lab settles, once and for all, the "why care about jitter" question of the whole ISF course: the oscillator's phase noise integrates into rms timing jitter σt\sigma_tσt​ (see lab_08); this σt\sigma_tσt​ is the random jitter (RJ) of the SerDes sampling clock; RJ closes the eye diagram (the opening formed by overlaying many bits) and sets the BER (bit-error rate). We plot the eye diagram and the BER bathtub (a curve of BER versus sampling instant, shaped like a bathtub). Physical intuition (conclusion first): an ideal clock always samples at the exact center of the UI (unit interval, the time span of one bit), UI/2UI/2UI/2 away from either data edge — the safest spot. With jitter, the sampling instant wanders randomly left and right; whenever it wanders past either edge, the wrong bit is sampled. RJ is Gaussian and unbounded, so there is always a tail that crosses an edge — the BER is always >0>0>0; its size is set by "how many σ\sigmaσ you sit from the edge". The more σ\sigmaσ of margin, the error probability drops exponentially via Q(⋅)Q(\cdot)Q(⋅) (the Gaussian tail) — which is why the bathtub floor is deep and flat.

The larger xxx, the smaller Q(x)Q(x)Q(x) (exponential-like decay). BER bathtub (RJ only). The sampling instant is dithered by Gaussian jitter σt\sigma_tσt​; crossing either edge produces an error (spec section 10.2, "SerDes BER (RJ)"): BER(t)=12[ Q ⁣(UI/2−tσt)+Q ⁣(UI/2+tσt)].\text{BER}(t)=\frac12\Big[\,Q\!\Big(\frac{UI/2-t}{\sigma_t}\Big)+Q\!\Big(\frac{UI/2+t}{\sigma_t}\Big)\Big].BER(t)=21​[Q(σt​UI/2−t​)+Q(σt​UI/2+t​)]. documents.t: This is a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level: the eye approximates NRZ transitions with tanh-smoothed edges and has no real channel/equalizer; the BER uses the closed-form QQQ expression, not Monte-Carlo error counting. RJ-only (random jitter only): ignores DJ (deterministic jitter — bounded, from ISI, duty-cycle distortion, crosstalk, etc.). Real jitter is dual-Dirac (RJ ⊛ DJ); DJ pushes the bathtub walls inward and puts a plateau on the floor. This lab demonstrates only the Gaussian-tail RJ part. No amplitude noise / vertical eye closure: timing only (horizontal eye); vertical closure from voltage noise is not included. Ideal two-level signaling, no ISI: assumes clean transitions between adjacent bits and no inter-symbol interference; practical high-speed channels need CTLE/DFE equalization. The 12\tfrac1221​ bookkeeping: transition density taken as 0.5 (random-data average); specific patterns will differ.

documents.t: Integrated phase noise → σt\sigma_tσt​ → RJ of the SerDes sampling clock → eye closure → BER. The key quantity is the eye half-width in units of σ\sigmaσ, UI/(2σt)UI/(2\sigma_t)UI/(2σt​): double the jitter and the BER floor rises by dozens of orders of magnitude. Gaussian RJ is unbounded → the BER is always >0>0>0; the intersections of the bathtub with the target-BER line bound the usable sampling window.

documents.t: Breadcrumb: Simulation labs › System & advanced › This page (PLL/CDR jitter transfer). Upstream: lab_11; downstream: lab_12. This lab explains something practically crucial: how a PLL (phase-locked loop) / CDR (clock and data recovery) "filters" an oscillator's phase noise. The key conclusion — referred to the output phase, the VCO's (voltage-controlled oscillator's) own phase noise is high-pass shaped (close-in suppressed, far-out dominant), while the reference clock's phase noise is low-pass shaped. This is why a noisy ring VCO, once locked to a clean reference, can still deliver a usable clock. Physical intuition (conclusion first): a PLL is a negative-feedback loop that tracks the reference phase. Inside the loop bandwidth fnf_nfn​ (low offset, slow variation), the feedback reacts in time, so the output follows the reference — the reference's low-frequency noise passes straight to the output (reference low-pass), while the VCO's own low-frequency drift gets corrected away by the feedback (VCO high-pass). Beyond fnf_nfn​ (high offset, fast variation), the feedback cannot keep up and the output follows the VCO free-running — VCO noise passes through unchanged (the passband of the VCO high-pass) and the reference's high-frequency noise is filtered out (the stopband of the reference low-pass). The crossover sits at the loop bandwidth fnf_nfn​.

documents.t: Verbatim from main() in simulations/lab_13_pll_cdr_transfer.py: set the loop bandwidth fn and damping zeta, provide representative VCO and reference PSDs, then call shape_output_phase_noise to synthesize the output. f = np.logspace(3, 9, 2000) # 1 kHz .. 1 GHz offset fn = 1e6 # loop natural frequency ~ 1 MHz zeta = 0.707 # representative phase-noise PSDs (rad^2/Hz), anchored shapes S_vco = 1e-6 * (1e6 / f) ** 2 # ring VCO: strong 1/f^2 close-in S_ref = 1e-12 + 1e-14 * (1e6 / f) ** 2 # clean reference: low flat + slight 1/f^2 S_out, S_ref_sh, S_vco_sh = shape_output_phase_noise(f, S_ref, S_vco, fn, zeta) The underlying transfer functions (pll_utils.py) are a verbatim implementation of the spec section 10.2 PLL formulas: def H_lowpass_mag2(f, fn_hz, zeta=0.707): """|H_lp(j2*pi*f)|^2 for a type-II 2nd-order PLL (reference -> output).""" w = 2 * np.pi * np.asarray(f, dtype=float) wn = loop_natural_freq(fn_hz) num = (2 * zeta * wn * w) ** 2 + wn ** 4 den = (wn ** 2 - w ** 2) ** 2 + (2 * zeta * wn * w) ** 2 return num / den def H_highpass_mag2(f, fn_hz, zeta=0.707): """|H_hp(j2*pi*f)|^2 = |1 - H_lp|^2 for the VCO -> output path.""" w = 2 * np.pi * np.asarray(f, dtype=float) wn = loop_natural_freq(fn_hz) num = w ** 4 den = (wn ** 2 - w ** 2) ** 2 + (2 * zeta * wn * w) ** 2 return num / den Internally, shape_output_phase_noise is simply S_ref*lp + S_vco*hp, returning the output and the two shaped components. zeta=0.707 (Butterworth damping) gives a flat closed loop with no visible jitter peaking.

documents.t: Left panel (transfer functions): the blue curve ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 is 1 (0 dB) at low offsets and rolls off past fnf_nfn​ (low-pass); the red curve ∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hhp​∣2 approaches 0 at low offsets and rises to 1 past fnf_nfn​ (high-pass). The two cross near fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz (gray dashed line) — that is the loop bandwidth. Right panel (output PN synthesis): The black curve (locked output) close-in (<fn<f_n<fn​) hugs the blue reference — the VCO's strong 1/f21/f^21/f2 has been suppressed by the high-pass. Far-out (>fn>f_n>fn​) the black curve hugs the red VCO — the reference's high frequencies are low-pass filtered out and the VCO passes through unchanged. The crossover (where the two inputs are comparable) sits near fnf_nfn​. Core message: locking swaps "the noisy VCO's close-in" for "the clean reference's close-in", at the cost that far-out is still set by the VCO. The loop bandwidth fnf_nfn​ is the design knob: raising fnf_nfn​ → suppresses more VCO close-in but admits more reference far-out and possible jitter peaking; lowering fnf_nfn​ does the opposite. CDR view: think of the "reference" as the jitter of the incoming data — a CDR's low-pass tracks low-frequency input jitter; that is jitter transfer ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 (how much the recovered clock "follows" the input jitter), not jitter tolerance. How much input jitter the CDR can actually tolerate without erroring is a different question, set by the untracked error 1−Hlp=Hhp1-H_{lp}=H_{hp}1−Hlp​=Hhp​ (see the "CDR jitter tolerance" subsection of pll_noise_budget).

documents.t: This is a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level: ideal type-II second-order closed-loop expressions (the §2 design equations connect the four blocks charge-pump, RRR–CCC, VCO, divider, but still with an ideal CP); no CP up/down mismatch, leakage, dead-zone, divider delay, reference spurs, etc. Linear, time-invariant, small-phase assumption: phase-domain linearization (the small-signal model of a locked PLL); large loss of lock and cycle slips are out of scope. Second-order approximation: real loops often contain extra poles (third order and above) affecting high-frequency roll-off and stability; only the dominant second-order behavior is kept here (§2 gives the third-pole location fp3f_{p3}fp3​ and its PM cost, but the figure still uses the second-order form). Uncorrelated-noise assumption: Sout=Sref∣Hlp∣2+Svco∣Hhp∣2S_{out}=S_{ref}\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2+S_{vco}\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2Sout​=Sref​∣Hlp​∣2+Svco​∣Hhp​∣2 requires the reference and VCO noise to be uncorrelated (powers add). In practice, shared bias/supply can correlate them. Input PSD shapes are illustrative: the levels and shapes of SvcoS_{vco}Svco​, SrefS_{ref}Sref​ are anchored examples, not measurements of a specific silicon process; the point is the shaping mechanism and the crossover at fnf_nfn​, not absolute dBc/Hz. No jitter-peaking detail: ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707 is deliberately chosen flat; a smaller ζ\zetaζ produces peaking near fnf_nfn​ (a bump in the output PN), a case this figure does not sweep.

documents.t: Breadcrumb: Simulation labs › System & advanced › This page (cyclostationary / effective ISF). Upstream: lab_06, effective_isf; related: lab_09. The previous labs all assumed the noise source is "equally noisy over the entire cycle" (stationary). Real circuits are not like that: a tail current source or a switching transistor conducts — and injects noise — only during part of the cycle. Noise whose intensity itself varies periodically with the oscillation phase is called cyclostationary noise. This lab uses a noise-modulating function (NMF) α(θ)\alpha(\theta)α(θ), bounded between 0 and 1, to draw "when the device is noisy", then shows that what actually determines the phase noise is not the raw ISF but the effective ISF Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α. Physical intuition (conclusion first): phase noise depends not only on how noisy the device is (in2‾\overline{i_n^2}in2​​) but also on at which phase of the waveform it is noisy. For the same device, if its noisiest interval happens to land where the ISF is large (e.g. the zero crossing), it does a lot of damage; if it lands at the peak, where ISF≈0, little damage. Multiplying "when it is noisy", α(θ)\alpha(\theta)α(θ), into the ISF gives Γeff=Γα\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\alphaΓeff​=Γα; taking the rms of Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ then yields this cyclostationary source's true effective sensitivity Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​.
documents.s: Lab 14 — Cyclostationary noise and the effective ISF

documents.t: Understand the difference between stationary and cyclostationary noise. Model "the device is noisy only during part of the cycle" with the NMF α(θ)∈[0,1]\alpha(\theta)\in[0,1]α(θ)∈[0,1]. Derive the effective ISF Γeff(θ)=Γ(θ) α(θ)\Gamma_{eff}(\theta)=\Gamma(\theta)\,\alpha(\theta)Γeff​(θ)=Γ(θ)α(θ) and use it in place of Γ\GammaΓ when computing the rms. See that for the same device with the same amount of noise, the injection phase alone can change Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​ by severalfold.
documents.s: 1. Learning objectives

documents.t: Start from the white-noise phase-noise law of [P1] Eq.(21), p.185: L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​) This assumes in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf is constant (stationary). If the noise is cyclostationary, its instantaneous PSD can be written as "a stationary component times a periodic gate": in2(θ)‾/Δf=(in2‾/Δf)⋅α2(θ),α(θ)∈[0,1].\overline{i_n^2(\theta)}/\Delta f=\big(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f\big)\cdot\alpha^2(\theta),\qquad \alpha(\theta)\in[0,1].in2​(θ)​/Δf=(in2​​/Δf)⋅α2(θ),α(θ)∈[0,1]. Plugging this phase dependence back into the ISF integral kernel Γ(ω0τ) in(τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ) of [P1] Eq.(11), p.182 is equivalent to folding the noise's "α\alphaα" into the ISF. Define the effective ISF (spec section 10): Γeff(θ)=Γ(θ) α(θ).\Gamma_{eff}(\theta)=\Gamma(\theta)\,\alpha(\theta).Γeff​(θ)=Γ(θ)α(θ). The phase noise of a cyclostationary source is then obtained by replacing Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ with Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​: Γeff,rms=12π∫02π[Γ(θ) α(θ)]2 dθ,\Gamma_{eff,rms}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\big[\Gamma(\theta)\,\alpha(\theta)\big]^2\,d\theta},Γeff,rms​=2π1​∫02π​[Γ(θ)α(θ)]2dθ​, and substituting it into [P1] Eq.(21): L∝Γeff,rms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γeff,rms2​/qmax2​. Why multiplication is correct: α\alphaα describes "the fraction by which the noise amplitude is gated"; the ISF describes "how efficiently noise at that phase converts into phase". Both act on the same injection at the same instant, so their effects multiply. Dimension check: Γ\GammaΓ dimensionless, α\alphaα dimensionless (∈[0,1]\in[0,1]∈[0,1]) ⇒ Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ dimensionless ✓, same units as the raw ISF, directly substitutable into Eq.(21). This lab uses the ideal-LC Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ (derived in [P1]; maximum ∣Γ∣\vert\Gamma\vert∣Γ∣ at the zero crossing θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2, Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0 at the peak θ=0\theta=0θ=0), paired with two smooth gates of equal width π\piπ: one gate at the zero crossing (bad), one at the peak (good).
documents.s: 2. Mathematical model

documents.t: Below is the core of simulations/lab_14_cyclostationary_isf.py: use gamma_lc_ideal (−sin⁡-\sin−sin) as the ISF, a smooth periodic window nmf_window as α(θ)\alpha(\theta)α(θ), then effective_isf (i.e. Γ⋅α\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓ⋅α) and gamma_rms to compute each rms. import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, gamma_rms, effective_isf def nmf_window(theta, center, width): """Smooth periodic gate in [0,1], centered at `center`, of given width (rad).""" d = np.angle(np.exp(1j * (theta - center))) # wrapped distance return 0.5 * (1 + np.cos(np.pi * np.clip(d / (width / 2), -1, 1))) theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 2000, endpoint=True) gamma = gamma_lc_ideal(theta) # -sin(theta) # case 1: device noisy near the ZERO CROSSING (where |Gamma| is max) -> bad a_bad = nmf_window(theta, center=np.pi / 2, width=np.pi) # case 2: device noisy near the PEAK (where |Gamma|~0) -> good a_good = nmf_window(theta, center=0.0, width=np.pi) g_bad = effective_isf(gamma, a_bad) # Gamma * alpha g_good = effective_isf(gamma, a_good) grms = gamma_rms(theta, gamma) # stationary reference grms_bad = gamma_rms(theta, g_bad) grms_good = gamma_rms(theta, g_good) print(f"stationary={grms:.3f} bad={grms_bad:.3f} good={grms_good:.3f}") # -> stationary=0.707, bad=0.395, good=0.177 effective_isf(gamma_values, alpha_values) is a pointwise product (see simulations/common/isf_utils.py), and gamma_rms(theta, gamma) is 12π∫02πΓ2 dθ\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma^2\,d\theta}2π1​∫02π​Γ2dθ​, corresponding to [P1] Eq.(20).

documents.t: Breadcrumb: Simulation labs › System & advanced › This page (nonlinear ISF). Upstream: isf_definition, lab_04; related: lab_03. β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Earlier we derived Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ for an ideal LC — clean, but that is a special case of a weakly nonlinear, near-sinusoidal waveform. This lab dismantles a common misconception: the ISF is not always −sin⁡-\sin−sin. The ISF is set by the oscillator's large-signal steady-state waveform — whatever the waveform looks like, the ISF looks accordingly. We use the classic van der Pol oscillator, with a nonlinearity-strength knob μ\muμ that tunes the waveform continuously from "near-sinusoidal" to "relaxation oscillation with sharp transitions", and watch how the ISF deforms along with it. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the ISF measures "kick at which phase of the waveform pushes the phase the most". For a near-sinusoidal waveform (small μ\muμ), the most sensitive point is the zero crossing and the least sensitive is the peak, so the ISF is close to ±sin⁡\pm\sin±sin. But once μ\muμ grows and the waveform develops fast, steep transitions, the sensitivity concentrates and skews onto those steep edges — the ISF is no longer a symmetric sine but gets "pinched" by the waveform into an asymmetric shape. The waveform determines the ISF — exactly why ring (square-wave-like, steep edges) and LC (near-sinusoidal) ISF shapes differ so much.
documents.s: Lab 15 — ISF of a Nonlinear Oscillator (van der Pol)

documents.t: Meet the van der Pol oscillator and the nonlinearity strength μ\muμ: small μ\muμ → near-sinusoidal, large μ\muμ → relaxation. Internalize "the ISF is set by the large-signal waveform" — not always −sin⁡-\sin−sin. Learn to extract the ISF numerically: inject a small perturbation at different phases and measure the persistent steady-state time shift ⇒Δϕ\Rightarrow\Delta\phi⇒Δϕ. Connect to the LC vs ring ISF shape difference (lab_03).
documents.s: 1. Learning objectives

documents.t: Second-order ODE of the van der Pol oscillator (dimensionless form): x¨−μ (1−x2) x˙+x=0.\ddot{x}-\mu\,(1-x^2)\,\dot{x}+x=0.x¨−μ(1−x2)x˙+x=0. Rewritten in first-order state space (y=x˙y=\dot{x}y=x˙): x˙=y,y˙=μ (1−x2) y−x.\dot{x}=y,\qquad \dot{y}=\mu\,(1-x^2)\,y-x.x˙=y,y˙​=μ(1−x2)y−x. Physics of the nonlinear term μ(1−x2)x˙\mu(1-x^2)\dot{x}μ(1−x2)x˙: when ∣x∣<1\vert x\vert<1∣x∣<1, (1−x2)>0(1-x^2)>0(1−x2)>0 → negative damping (injects energy, grows small oscillations); when ∣x∣>1\vert x\vert>1∣x∣>1, (1−x2)<0(1-x^2)<0(1−x2)<0 → positive damping (dissipates, compresses large oscillations). The balance between the two forms a stable limit cycle. Role of μ\muμ: μ→0\mu\to0μ→0 degenerates to the simple harmonic oscillator x¨+x=0\ddot x+x=0x¨+x=0 (pure sine, ω=1\omega=1ω=1); for large μ\muμ the energy injection/dissipation is violent and the waveform becomes relaxation-type: slow charging plus abrupt flips with steep edges. Units: the equation is dimensionless (normalized); time and xxx are already normalized, ω≈1\omega\approx1ω≈1 (small μ\muμ). Principle of numerical ISF extraction (operational definition, matching [P1] Eq.(10)): at some injection phase θ\thetaθ, hit the velocity state yyy with a small impulse Δq\Delta qΔq; the oscillator steady state is permanently shifted by a time Δtshift\Delta t_{shift}Δtshift​. Convert the time shift to phase: Δϕ=−ω0 Δtshift,Γ(θ)≈ΔϕΔq=− ω0 ΔtshiftΔq.\Delta\phi=-\omega_0\,\Delta t_{shift},\qquad \Gamma(\theta)\approx\frac{\Delta\phi}{\Delta q}=-\,\frac{\omega_0\,\Delta t_{shift}}{\Delta q}.Δϕ=−ω0​Δtshift​,Γ(θ)≈ΔqΔϕ​=−Δqω0​Δtshift​​. Why measure the "persistent time shift": phase perturbations have no restoring force (they persist forever), while amplitude perturbations decay ([P1] assumption); so once the transient dies out, the remaining steady-state edge-timing offset is purely phase. The code measures the offset of the rising zero crossing many periods after injection relative to a reference, wrapped to [−T/2,T/2][-T/2,T/2][−T/2,T/2]. Dimension check: [rad/s]×[s]=[rad][\text{rad/s}]\times[\text{s}]=[\text{rad}][rad/s]×[s]=[rad]; after dividing by Δq\Delta qΔq we get the ISF (here normalized to max⁡∣Γ∣=1\max\vert\Gamma\vert=1max∣Γ∣=1 for shape comparison) ✓.

documents.t: simulations/lab_15_nonlinear_isf.py integrates the van der Pol equation with RK4 and extracts the ISF from the persistent shift of the rising zero crossings. Core integrator and extractor: import numpy as np def simulate_vdp(mu, t_end, fs, x0=2.0, y0=0.0, impulse_time=None, impulse_dy=0.0): dt = 1.0 / fs n = int(round(t_end * fs)) x = np.empty(n); y = np.empty(n) xi, yi = float(x0), float(y0) imp = int(round(impulse_time * fs)) if impulse_time is not None else -1 def deriv(xx, yy): return yy, mu * (1 - xx * xx) * yy - xx # van der Pol RHS for k in range(n): x[k] = xi; y[k] = yi if k == imp: yi += impulse_dy # inject small impulse on velocity k1x, k1y = deriv(xi, yi) k2x, k2y = deriv(xi + 0.5 * dt * k1x, yi + 0.5 * dt * k1y) k3x, k3y = deriv(xi + 0.5 * dt * k2x, yi + 0.5 * dt * k2y) k4x, k4y = deriv(xi + dt * k3x, yi + dt * k3y) xi += dt / 6 * (k1x + 2 * k2x + 2 * k3x + k4x) yi += dt / 6 * (k1y + 2 * k2y + 2 * k3y + k4y) return np.arange(n) * dt, x, y def extract_vdp_isf(mu, fs=400.0, n_points=36, dq=0.02): T, _ = measure_period(mu, fs, t_end=220.0, t_settle=80.0) t_settle = max(60.0, 10 * T); t_late = t_settle + 6 * T; t_end = t_late + 4 * T w0 = 2 * np.pi / T t_ref, xr, _ = simulate_vdp(mu, t_end, fs) # reference (no impulse) zr = rising_zero_crossings(t_ref, xr) t0 = zr[zr > t_settle][0]; zr_late = zr[zr > t_late][0] thetas = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, n_points, endpoint=False) isf = np.zeros(n_points) for i, th in enumerate(thetas): t_inj = t0 + (th / (2 * np.pi)) * T + T # inject at phase th t_p, xp, yp = simulate_vdp(mu, t_end, fs, impulse_time=t_inj, impulse_dy=dq) zp = rising_zero_crossings(t_p, xp); zp = zp[zp > t_late] dt_shift = (zp[0] - zr_late + T / 2) % T - T / 2 # wrap to [-T/2, T/2] isf[i] = -w0 * dt_shift / dq # Gamma(theta) ~ Dphi/Dq return thetas, isf, T (rising_zero_crossings uses linear interpolation to find where xxx crosses from negative to positive; measure_period takes the median zero-crossing spacing as the period TTT. See the script path below for the complete, runnable version — the excerpt above is for explanation.)

Titles read: "(a) van der Pol 波形：μ 越大越偏離正弦 (relaxation)" = (a) van der Pol waveform: larger μ deviates more from a sinusoid (relaxation); "(b) ISF 隨大訊號波形改變：大 μ 明顯非正弦" = (b) the ISF changes with the large-signal waveform: at large μ it is clearly non-sinusoidal.
documents.s: 8. Simulation figure

documents.t: Left panel (a), waveforms: μ=0.1\mu=0.1μ=0.1 (blue) is almost a sine; μ=1\mu=1μ=1 (orange) already shows visible asymmetry; μ=3\mu=3μ=3 (red) is classic relaxation — the rising segment is pushed fast and steep, the top flattens, the fall is abrupt too. The larger μ\muμ, the further the waveform departs from a sine. Right panel (b), extracted ISF: at μ=0.1\mu=0.1μ=0.1 (blue) the measured ISF nearly overlaps the sine reference (black dashed), confirming "weak nonlinearity ≈ ±sin⁡\pm\sin±sin"; at μ=3\mu=3μ=3 (red) the ISF is clearly deformed and asymmetric — the peak is shifted, rise/fall slopes are unequal, reflecting the steep edge in (a). The ISF changes with the large-signal waveform; it is not always −sin⁡-\sin−sin. Key reading: panel (b) deliberately normalizes each ISF to peak 1, comparing shape only. The point is not the amplitude but that "the shape is no longer a clean sine". The more nonlinear the waveform, the richer the ISF harmonics (cnc_ncn​ beyond just c1c_1c1​), and its Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and c0c_0c0​ (which sets 1/f31/f^31/f3) are likewise dictated by the waveform. Connection to rings: the ring's square-wave-like steep edges concentrate the ISF energy at the transitions, giving a shape close to a triangular pulse (lab_03) — another instance of "the large-signal waveform determines the ISF".

documents.t: Operational ISF definition (impulse → persistent phase step): [P1] Eq.(10), p.182, hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)/qmax⋅u(t−τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)=\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)/q_{max}\cdot u(t-\tau)hϕ​(t,τ)=Γ(ω0​τ)/qmax​⋅u(t−τ). "ISF is set by the waveform": [P1] Fig. 7, p.183 (LC vs ring waveforms with their ISFs); this lab uses van der Pol to display the waveform→ISF causality continuously. Linearity of excess phase vs injected charge (small perturbation): [P1] Fig. 6, p.182. ISF Fourier series (deformed ISF → more cnc_ncn​): [P1] Eq.(12), p.183. The van der Pol oscillator and the numerical ISF extraction method are external literature, not among the five source PDFs, supplemented from standard nonlinear-oscillation / oscillator perturbation literature (teaching toy). documents.t: Toy model, not transistor-level: van der Pol is a dimensionless nonlinear oscillator for teaching; it does not correspond to any specific circuit; xxx and time are normalized, with no physical V/A/s units. Approximations of the numerical extraction: measuring the persistent time shift with a single small impulse assumes (i) Δq\Delta qΔq is small enough for a linear response, (ii) the transient (amplitude perturbation) has decayed completely before tlatet_{late}tlate​, (iii) RK4 step size and zero-crossing interpolation errors are negligible. At large μ\muμ the time resolution at the steep edges gets strained, so the ISF is numerically more sensitive near the transitions. Phase definition: the rising zero crossing serves as the phase reference; "phase" of a non-sinusoidal waveform is itself a matter of choice, and different reference points shift the ISF along its horizontal axis. Phase only, no amplitude tracking: follows the [P1] first-order assumption (amplitude perturbations decay); AM–PM under strong nonlinearity is not fully captured. Normalized amplitude: dividing the ISF by its peak in the figure is only for shape comparison; the absolute values of Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and c0c_0c0​ require keeping the qmaxq_{max}qmax​ normalization before plugging into [P1] Eq.(21)/(24).
documents.s: 11. Limitations and approximations

documents.t: The ISF is set by the large-signal waveform, not always −sin⁡-\sin−sin: only near-sinusoidal oscillators approach ±sin⁡\pm\sin±sin. van der Pol: small μ\muμ → near-sinusoidal waveform, near-sinusoidal ISF; large μ\muμ → relaxation, deformed and asymmetric ISF. Numerical extraction: inject a small impulse, measure the persistent steady-state time shift Δtshift\Delta t_{shift}Δtshift​, Δϕ=−ω0Δtshift\Delta\phi=-\omega_0\Delta t_{shift}Δϕ=−ω0​Δtshift​, Γ≈Δϕ/Δq\Gamma\approx\Delta\phi/\Delta qΓ≈Δϕ/Δq. The more nonlinear the waveform → the more ISF harmonics → affecting Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and c0c_0c0​ (the latter sets 1/f31/f^31/f3 upconversion).

documents.t: Breadcrumb: Simulation labs › System & advanced › This page (Leeson vs ISF). Upstream: lab_06, lab_07; related: lab_09. β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. The phase-noise model designers see most often actually comes in two lineages. One is Leeson (1966), an empirical formula: it fits a measured curve after the fact into three regions — 1/f31/f^31/f3, 1/f21/f^21/f2, and a flat floor — with parameters (quality factor QQQ, noise figure FFF, flicker corner) mostly obtained by fitting. The other is the ISF model, the main thread of this site: from [P1] Hajimiri–Lee's LTV theory it derives from first principles the same three regions, and every parameter has a physical origin (Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, qmaxq_{max}qmax​, c0c_0c0​). This lab overlays the two curves on one plot so you can see clearly: they are two maps of the same mountain — Leeson describes "what it looks like", the ISF explains "why it looks that way". External-literature note: the Leeson model is external literature, not among the five source PDFs; it is supplemented from the standard reference (D. B. Leeson, "A simple model of feedback oscillator noise spectrum," Proc. IEEE, 1966). This site treats it as a comparison baseline and historical context; the ISF model is the main thread. Step-by-step Leeson derivation and term-by-term comparison: see the appendix derivation_leeson. Physical intuition (conclusion first): every free-running oscillator's phase noise looks the same from near to far — close to the carrier it is 1/f31/f^31/f3 (flicker upconversion, steepest, −30-30−30 dB/dec), the middle is 1/f21/f^21/f2 (white noise, −20-20−20 dB/dec), and the far end is a flat measurement/buffer floor. Leeson assembles the three regions with QQQ and a corner; the ISF tells you the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region's height is Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​, the 1/f31/f^31/f3 region is set by c02c_0^2c02​, and the corner does not equal the device 1/f1/f1/f corner.
documents.s: Lab 16 — Leeson Model vs ISF Model (Three-Region Comparison)

documents.t: Recognize the three-region structure of the empirical Leeson model and its fitting parameters (F,Q,F,Q,F,Q, flicker corner). Write the ISF model ([P1] Eq.(21) + Eq.(23) + floor) as the same three regions and overlay the plots. Understand the correspondence and differences of the two models in the 1/f31/f^31/f3, 1/f21/f^21/f2, and floor regions. Understand how the ISF gives Leeson's parameters physical meaning (and honestly flag Leeson as external literature).

documents.t: Leeson model (external literature, not among the five PDFs; verbatim per spec section 10.2): L(Δω)=10log⁡10 ⁣[2FkTPs(1+(ω02QΔω)2)(1+ω1/f3∣Δω∣)]\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega)=10\log_{10}\!\left[\frac{2FkT}{P_s}\left(1+\Big(\frac{\omega_0}{2Q\Delta\omega}\Big)^2\right)\left(1+\frac{\omega_{1/f^3}}{\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert}\right)\right]L(Δω)=10log10​[Ps​2FkT​(1+(2QΔωω0​​)2)(1+∣Δω∣ω1/f3​​)] First bracket (1+(ω0/2QΔω)2)\big(1+(\omega_0/2Q\Delta\omega)^2\big)(1+(ω0​/2QΔω)2): approaches 111 at large offset (floor), and gives the 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2-shaped 1/f21/f^21/f2 region at small offset; the corner is set by QQQ (tank quality factor). Second bracket (1+ω1/f3/∣Δω∣)\big(1+\omega_{1/f^3}/\vert\Delta\omega\vert\big)(1+ω1/f3​/∣Δω∣): inside the corner it multiplies in an extra 1/∣Δω∣1/\vert\Delta\omega\vert1/∣Δω∣, lifting 1/f21/f^21/f2 into 1/f31/f^31/f3. FFF is the noise figure, PsP_sPs​ the signal power, kTkTkT the thermal noise — in Leeson these are mostly fitted/estimated values. ISF model (derived from [P1] plus one white-noise floor): add the 1/f21/f^21/f2 ([P1] Eq.(21)) and 1/f31/f^31/f3 ([P1] Eq.(23)) regions on a linear scale, then add the floor: L(Δω)=10log⁡10 ⁣[Γrms2qmax2in2‾/Δf4 Δω2⏟1/f2, Eq.(21)+c02qmax2in2‾/Δf8 Δω2ω1/fΔω⏟1/f3, Eq.(23)+floor⏟flat]\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega)=10\log_{10}\!\left[\underbrace{\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}}_{1/f^2,\ \text{Eq.(21)}}+\underbrace{\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{8\,\Delta\omega^2}\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}}_{1/f^3,\ \text{Eq.(23)}}+\underbrace{\text{floor}}_{\text{flat}}\right]L(Δω)=10log10​​1/f2, Eq.(21)qmax2​Γrms2​​4Δω2in2​​/Δf​​​+1/f3, Eq.(23)qmax2​c02​​8Δω2in2​​/Δf​Δωω1/f​​​​+flatfloor​​​ Physical correspondence: the ISF's 1/f21/f^21/f2 region height =Γrms2/qmax2=\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2=Γrms2​/qmax2​ (Leeson's 2FkT/Ps2FkT/P_s2FkT/Ps​ maps to it), while the 1/f31/f^31/f3 region strength is set by c02c_0^2c02​ (the ISF DC coefficient, waveform asymmetry). Corners have different origins: the ISF's 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ([P1] Eq.(24)) is Δω1/f3=ω1/f c02/(2Γrms2)\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\,c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​c02​/(2Γrms2​), which is not equal to the device's ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​; Leeson simply inserts the corner as a fitting parameter ω1/f3\omega_{1/f^3}ω1/f3​. Dimension check: both bracketed terms are dimensionless power ratios (before taking 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ in dBc/Hz), so adding them is legitimate ✓; the 1/f21/f^21/f2 term ∝1/Δω2\propto1/\Delta\omega^2∝1/Δω2 and the 1/f31/f^31/f3 term carries one more 1/Δω1/\Delta\omega1/Δω ✓. Numbers for this lab (pedagogical, deliberately tuned so the two curves overlap in the middle region): f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Q=10Q=10Q=10, F=5F=5F=5, Ps=1P_s=1Ps​=1 mW, flicker corner fc=100f_c=100fc​=100 kHz; on the ISF side qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, c0=0.2c_0=0.2c0​=0.2, in2‾/Δf=10−20\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=10^{-20}in2​​/Δf=10−20 A²/Hz, floor =−160=-160=−160 dBc/Hz.

documents.t: Core of simulations/lab_16_leeson_vs_isf.py: each model computes dBc/Hz, overlaid on a semilogx plot. import numpy as np k = 1.380649e-23 T = 300.0 f = np.logspace(3, 8, 2000) # 1 kHz .. 100 MHz offset dw = 2 * np.pi * f f0 = 5e9 w0 = 2 * np.pi * f0 # --- Leeson (empirical; external literature) --- F = 5.0; Ps = 1e-3; Q = 10.0; fc = 1e5 # flicker corner 100 kHz leeson = (2 * F * k * T / Ps) * (1 + (w0 / (2 * Q * dw)) ** 2) * (1 + 2 * np.pi * fc / dw) L_leeson = 10 * np.log10(leeson) # --- ISF model ([P1] Eq.(21) 1/f^2 + Eq.(23) 1/f^3 + white floor) --- qmax = 1e-12 in2_df = 1e-20 Grms = 0.5 c0 = 0.2 w1f = 2 * np.pi * fc floor = 10 ** (-160 / 10) isf = (Grms ** 2 / qmax ** 2) * in2_df / (4 * dw ** 2) \ + (c0 ** 2 / qmax ** 2) * in2_df / (8 * dw ** 2) * (w1f / dw) \ + floor L_isf = 10 * np.log10(isf) How to read it: Leeson multiplies the three regions together (floor → ×1/f2\times1/f^2×1/f2 factor → ×1/f3\times1/f^3×1/f3 factor); the ISF adds the three regions in the linear power domain. Both bookkeeping styles produce a three-segment broken line on a log plot. Note on the constants: the ISF-side Γrms,c0,\Gamma_{rms},c_0,Γrms​,c0​, floor were deliberately picked so the two curves overlap in the middle region for the teaching overlay, not extracted from any specific circuit.

documents.s: 8. Simulation figure

documents.t: Three-segment broken line: both curves, from left (close to carrier) to right (far offset), show 1/f31/f^31/f3 (steepest) → 1/f21/f^21/f2 (middle) → flat floor. The gray dotted line is the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner (fc=100f_c=100fc​=100 kHz): to its left both curves are steeper (−30-30−30 dB/dec), to its right they turn to −20-20−20 dB/dec. Overlap in the middle, divergence at the ends: this lab deliberately tunes the parameters so the two curves nearly coincide in the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region (teaching overlay). Note the right end (large offset) where the curves separate: Leeson's (1+…)(1+\ldots)(1+…) factor has already flattened toward its constant floor, while the ISF model's floor is set lower at −160-160−160 dBc/Hz, so the red curve keeps following 1/f21/f^21/f2 a while longer at high offset before hitting the floor. This difference is not a bug — the two models book the floor differently — a reminder that "the curve shape is right; absolute values depend on each model's parameters". Key reading: Leeson's QQQ sets the mid-region corner, F/PsF/P_sF/Ps​ sets the floor; the ISF's Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ sets the mid-region height, c0c_0c0​ sets the 1/f31/f^31/f3 strength. One curve, two languages: to lower the middle region, lower Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ / raise qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (= raise QQQ, raise PsP_sPs​); to lower close-in noise, suppress c0c_0c0​ (= make the waveform symmetric).

documents.t: Leeson is an empirical model (external literature): FFF, QQQ, and the corner are mostly after-the-fact fits, unlike the ISF which derives them from circuit quantities (Γrms,qmax,c0\Gamma_{rms},q_{max},c_0Γrms​,qmax​,c0​); the Leeson parameters in this figure are illustrative. Parameters deliberately co-tuned: the ISF-side Γrms=0.5,c0=0.2,\Gamma_{rms}=0.5,c_0=0.2,Γrms​=0.5,c0​=0.2, floor=−160=-160=−160 dBc/Hz were chosen to make the curves coincide in the middle region, not extracted from any specific oscillator; do not read the absolute dBc/Hz as real device specs. Different floor bookkeeping: Leeson's floor is built into the (1+…)(1+\ldots)(1+…) factor, while the ISF model uses an added constant floor; hence the divergence at high offset (see figure reading) — a model-structure difference, not a physical one. Single white source, linear region summation: the ISF model directly adds 1/f21/f^21/f2 and 1/f31/f^31/f3 in the linear power domain, ignoring multiple sources, cyclostationarity (see lab_14), and AM–PM. Factor-of-2: 1/f21/f^21/f2 uses Eq.(21)'s 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2, 1/f31/f^31/f3 uses Eq.(23)'s 8Δω28\Delta\omega^28Δω2; the minor factor-of-2 SSB-bookkeeping dispute does not affect the three-region slopes or the comparison conclusions. Q=10Q=10Q=10 is low: illustrative; real LC tanks often have Q≳Q\gtrsimQ≳ several tens, moving Leeson's mid-region corner closer to the carrier.

documents.t: Free-running oscillator phase noise has three regions: 1/f31/f^31/f3 (close-in) → 1/f21/f^21/f2 (white noise) → flat floor. Leeson (empirical, external literature) and the ISF (derived in [P1]) describe the same three regions; the ISF gives Leeson's parameters physical meaning. 1/f21/f^21/f2 height =Γrms2/qmax2=\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2=Γrms2​/qmax2​ (↔ Leeson's 2FkT/Ps2FkT/P_s2FkT/Ps​ and QQQ); 1/f31/f^31/f3 strength =c02=c_0^2=c02​. The ISF's 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ([P1] Eq.(24)) scales with c02/Γrms2c_0^2/\Gamma_{rms}^2c02​/Γrms2​ and is not equal to the device 1/f1/f1/f corner.

Back-of-the-envelope intro version: lab_09; upstream: lab_06, lab_08. β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. lab_09 read [P1] Eq.(21) as a scaling law by mental arithmetic. This lab actually sweeps the same equation and plots it as three curves: holding everything else fixed, sweep the node charge swing qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (swing), the ISF rms Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, and the ring stage count NNN, and watch how the phase noise L\mathcal{L}L at 111 MHz offset moves. On the plots you will see with your own eyes the "−20-20−20 dB/decade" straight-line slope, the "2×2\times2× swing →−6\to-6→−6 dB" arrow, and the ring oscillator's nearly horizontal NNN curve (the famous NNN-independence). Physical intuition (conclusion first): 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise ∝Γrms2/qmax2\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2∝Γrms2​/qmax2​. Both knobs enter as 20log⁡1020\log_{10}20log10​: doubling qmaxq_{max}qmax​ → −6-6−6 dB; halving Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ → −6-6−6 dB. The ring's NNN is sneakier: adding stages shrinks Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2, but the per-node qmaxq_{max}qmax​ shrinks and there are more noisy devices — the three roughly cancel at fixed f0f_0f0​/power, so net phase noise is almost independent of NNN.

On the qmaxq_{max}qmax​ curve, quantify "−20-20−20 dB/decade" and "2×2\times2× swing →−6\to-6→−6 dB". On the Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ curve, see "symmetric waveform / low Γrms→\Gamma_{rms}\toΓrms​→ PN↓". On the ring NNN curve, see where NNN-independence comes from ([P2] Eq.(16), p.794 — v7 re-verified: Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2). documents.t: simulations/lab_17_design_sweep.py uses a shared L_dbc to evaluate [P1] Eq.(21) in dBc/Hz, then sweeps one curve per knob: import numpy as np def L_dbc(Grms, qmax, in2_df, dw): return 10 * np.log10(Grms ** 2 / qmax ** 2 * in2_df / (4 * dw ** 2)) dw = 2 * np.pi * 1e6 # evaluate at 1 MHz offset in2_df = 1e-22 # (a) sweep q_max: 0.1 pC .. 10 pC -> slope -20 dB/decade, 2x -> -6 dB q = np.logspace(-13, -11, 50) L_q = L_dbc(0.5, q, in2_df, dw) # baseline qmax=1pC -> -128 dBc/Hz # (b) sweep Gamma_rms: low Grms -> lower PN g = np.linspace(0.1, 1.5, 50) L_g = L_dbc(g, 1e-12, in2_df, dw) # (c) ring N: Gamma_rms ~ N^-3/2, per-node qmax ~ 1/N, more noisy devices ~ N N = np.arange(3, 31) Grms_N = 0.5 * (5.0 / N) ** 1.5 # scaling (illustrative; [P2]) qmax_N = 1e-12 * (5.0 / N) # lower per-node swing as N grows noise_N = in2_df * (N / 5.0) # more noisy devices L_N = 10 * np.log10(Grms_N ** 2 / qmax_N ** 2 * noise_N / (4 * dw ** 2)) print(round(L_N[0], 1), round(L_N[-1], 1)) # -> -128.0 -128.0 (essentially flat for all N: the famous N-independence) L_dbc vs lab_08: lab_08 integrates the measured L\mathcal{L}L into jitter; here we go the other way, using Eq.(21) to generate L\mathcal{L}L and then sweep the knobs. The two pages are inverse operations of each other (same note as in lab_09). The three scalings in (c) are illustrative: the constant in Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 and the exponents for per-node qmaxq_{max}qmax​ and device count are toy assumptions, meant to draw concretely "why NNN roughly cancels".

documents.s: 8. Simulation figure

documents.t: (a) swing sweep (blue): on a log horizontal axis, qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (0.1–10 pC) vs L\mathcal{L}L is a straight line with slope −20-20−20 dB/decade — as qmaxq_{max}qmax​ goes from 0.1 → 10 pC (two decades), L\mathcal{L}L drops from −108-108−108 → −148-148−148 dBc/Hz, exactly 404040 dB. The red arrow marks "2×2\times2× swing →−6\to-6→−6 dB" (1→21\to21→2 pC, −128→−134-128\to-134−128→−134 dBc/Hz). Mnemonic: double the swing, gain 6 dB of phase noise. (b) Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ sweep (green): linear horizontal axis, a logarithmic curve L=20log⁡10Γrms+\mathcal{L}=20\log_{10}\Gamma_{rms}+L=20log10​Γrms​+const — smaller Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ means lower phase noise, with the steepest descent at the small-Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ end (halving Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ from 0.5 to 0.25 → −6-6−6 dB). This is the payoff of "symmetric waveform / low sensitivity". (c) ring NNN sweep (purple): a nearly perfectly horizontal line (≈−128\approx-128≈−128 dBc/Hz, independent of NNN). Not a coincidence — it is the N0N^0N0 computed in Section 2: more stages shrink Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (good), but qmaxq_{max}qmax​ also shrinks and there are more devices (bad); the three cancel at fixed f0f_0f0​/power. Adding ring stages does not buy you phase noise for free ([P2]). Putting it together: (a)(b) are the "knobs that truly earn dB" (raise the swing, suppress Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​); (c) is the "looks tunable, actually cancels" knob — choose NNN based on f0f_0f0​, power, area, and phase-count requirements, not for phase noise.
