documents.t: Breadcrumb: Simulation labs › System & advanced › This page (MOS Level-1 equation-level ring ISF). Upstream: lab_03 (toy triangular ISF), lab_04 (impulse extraction method); related: waveform_slope, real_oscillator_topologies. Every ring ISF on this site so far has been a hand-placed shape: the triangle in lab_03 was only a sketch of "energy concentrated in the transitions" — its height, width, and sign were never computed. This page takes an honest step forward: model each inverter stage with the MOS Level-1 (Shichman-Hodges) square-law equations — cutoff/triode/saturation, real k′k'k′, VtV_tVt​, W/LW/LW/L, CLC_LCL​ — integrate the steady-state oscillation in numpy with a fixed small step, then assume nothing and directly measure node 1's Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ) phase by phase with the impulse method of [P1]. Model-level statement (applies to the whole page): this lab is MOS Level-1 equation-level (Shichman-Hodges), not SPICE/BSIM/PDK. It is one level more honest than a toy model (the currents really come from device equations, and the ISF really is measured), but it is still not transistor-level sign-off: no velocity saturation, no subthreshold, no parasitic RC, and no noise sources (see Section 11). ngspice is not installed in this environment — this is precisely a demonstration of the upper limit of "how honest you can be without SPICE." Physical intuition (conclusion first): a ring node only fears a kick while it (or the gate driving it) is switching. When pinned to a rail, the low output impedance of the driving stage swallows the injected charge within tens of ps (τ≈CL/g\tau\approx C_L/gτ≈CL​/g) and no phase trace remains; during a transition, ΔV=Δq/CL\Delta V=\Delta q/C_LΔV=Δq/CL​ directly shifts the edge in time, and that shift propagates permanently. So the measured Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ) is dual-lobe: a positive lobe around the rising edge (advance) and a negative lobe around the falling edge (delay) — exactly the signature of [P2] Fig. 5/Fig. 6 (p.793). Three rungs on the model ladder; this page stands on the middle one: Level Where the current comes from Where the ISF comes from Site counterpart toy model no current, waveform drawn directly hand-placed shape (−sin⁡-\sin−sin, triangle) lab_02, lab_03 equation-level (this page) Level-1 square-law device equations measured with the impulse method lab_32 SPICE + PDK BSIM4/PSP + extracted parasitics measured via transient/PSS+adjoint not on this site (honesty note) The SPICE/PDK rung would further add: velocity saturation and mobility degradation (short-channel IDI_DID​ no longer ∝Vov2\propto V_{ov}^2∝Vov2​), subthreshold conduction (exponential tail when VGSV_{GS}VGS​ is below VtV_tVt​), channel-length modulation (λ\lambdaλ), gate capacitances Cgs/CgdC_{gs}/C_{gd}Cgs​/Cgd​ (Miller coupling), layout parasitic RC, corners/mismatch, and the noise models (thermal + flicker). All of these change the numbers, but they do not change the mechanism this page teaches: the ISF is a physical quantity that can be measured directly from device equations.
documents.s: Lab 32 — MOS Level-1 Equation-Level Ring: Extracting the ISF from Transistor Equations

documents.t: Write the MOS Level-1 (Shichman-Hodges) three-region IV equations as integrable node equations and integrate the 3-stage ring to a steady-state oscillation (f0=1.2252f_0=1.2252f0​=1.2252 GHz, measured, not computed by formula). Extract node 1's Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ) with the impulse method of [P1]: 24 injection phases, Δq=0.5\Delta q=0.5Δq=0.5 fC, wait ≥20\ge20≥20 periods, then read the permanent phase shift by threshold-crossing time comparison. Verify the [P2] signatures: dual-lobe shape, energy concentrated near the node's own transitions, sensitivity approaching 0 while pinned to the rails. Compare against the triangular approximation of [P2] Fig. 6 (p.793) and the Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ of Eq.(16) (p.794) — which parts hold, and which distort at N=3N=3N=3. Honest scoping: this level extracts only the deterministic ISF; getting to phase noise still requires noise sources ([P1] Eq.(21), see device_noise_mapping).

documents.s: 2.3 ISF extraction: impulse injection + threshold-crossing comparison

documents.t: Excerpt from simulations/lab_32_mos_level1_ring.py (checked against the source). Device three-region single expression, ring derivative, and the extraction main loop: def _sq_v(vgs, vds, beta, vt): """Level-1 square law (vds>=0): cutoff/triode/saturation in one clamped expression.""" vov = np.maximum(vgs - vt, 0.0) # cutoff -> vov = 0 vde = np.minimum(vds, vov) # saturation -> vde = vov return beta * (vov - 0.5 * vde) * vde def ring_dvdt_v(v): """dV/dt [V/s]; v shape (..., 3), stage-i input = node i-1 (np.roll).""" vin = np.roll(v, 1, axis=-1) i_n = (_sq_v(vin, np.maximum(v, 0.0), BETA_N, VTN) - _sq_v(vin - v, np.maximum(-v, 0.0), BETA_N, VTN)) # reverse-conduction term i_p = (_sq_v(VDD - vin, np.maximum(VDD - v, 0.0), BETA_P, VTP_ABS) - _sq_v(v - vin, np.maximum(v - VDD, 0.0), BETA_P, VTP_ABS)) return (i_p - i_n) / CL # 26 rings run in lockstep: run 0 = unperturbed reference, runs 1..24 = the 24 phases, run 25 = linearity check for k in range(n): r = inj.get(k) if r is not None: V[r + 1, 0] += DV # dV = dq/CL ([P1] Eq.(9)) V += dt * ring_dvdt_v(V) # fixed small-step Euler rec[k + 1] = V[:, 0] # record node 1 for threshold-crossing comparison tc = first_after(rising_crossings(x[:, r], dt), t_late) # after >= 20 periods dts = (tc - tc_ref + 0.5 * T) % T - 0.5 * T # fold back into [-T/2, T/2) gamma = -w0 * dts * QMAX / DQ # Δφ·q_max/Δq The reference run and the perturbed runs share the same integrator and initial condition, so Euler's (first-order) period bias cancels exactly — the same differential-measurement trick used in the numerical verification of derivation_floquet_ppv (lab_25).

documents.t: (a) Waveforms (one period): the three nodes toggle in turn, spaced T/6=136T/6=136T/6=136 ps apart (a 3-stage ring has 3 edges per half period). f0=1.2252f_0=1.2252f0​=1.2252 GHz and T=816.186T=816.186T=816.186 ps are measured; inverting [P2] Eq.(15) gives a per-stage delay τD=136.03\tau_D=136.03τD​=136.03 ps. Note that at N=3N=3N=3 the waveform is far from square — each transition's 10%–90% window occupies roughly a fifth of the period, and the flat tops on the rails are not actually long. (b) Extracted Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ) (the star of this page): the 24 purple dots are 24 independent impulse experiments. The structure they read out: θ\thetaθ 0∘0^\circ0∘ 45∘45^\circ45∘ 75∘75^\circ75∘ 90∘90^\circ90∘ 135∘135^\circ135∘ 180∘180^\circ180∘ 225∘225^\circ225∘ 255∘255^\circ255∘ 315∘315^\circ315∘ Γ\GammaΓ +1.128+1.128+1.128 +0.786+0.786+0.786 +0.038+0.038+0.038 −0.356-0.356−0.356 −1.155-1.155−1.155 −1.132-1.132−1.132 −0.844-0.844−0.844 −0.059-0.059−0.059 +1.173+1.173+1.173 Dual-lobe, correctly registered: the positive lobe sits around node 1's own rising edge (θ=0\theta=0θ=0, Γ=+1.128\Gamma=+1.128Γ=+1.128), the negative lobe around its own falling edge (θ=180∘\theta=180^\circθ=180∘, Γ=−1.132\Gamma=-1.132Γ=−1.132). Positive charge advances the phase at the rising edge and delays it at the falling edge — the signs are not postulated, they are measured. Peak at the onset of a transition: max⁡∣Γ∣=1.1734\max\lvert\Gamma\rvert=1.1734max∣Γ∣=1.1734 occurs at θ=315∘\theta=315^\circθ=315∘, i.e. 45∘45^\circ45∘ before the rising edge; the deepest point of the negative lobe, −1.1555-1.1555−1.1555, is at 135∘135^\circ135∘, i.e. 45∘45^\circ45∘ before the falling edge — mirror symmetric. The physics: the driving gate (node 3) is starting to flip and the transistor holding the rail is letting go; charge injected at that moment is neither swallowed nor wasted — it directly shifts the imminent edge. That hurts the most. Energy concentrated in the transitions: the 10%–90% transition windows (shaded) take 40.7% of the period yet contain 58.7% of the Γ2\Gamma^2Γ2 energy. At N=3N=3N=3 the concentration looks "not dramatic enough," and the honest reason is: one stage switches every T/6T/6T/6, and each transition takes ≈0.2T\approx0.2T≈0.2T — the ring has almost no quiet moment; the quietest phases (Γ\GammaΓ zero crossings) are at 75∘/255∘75^\circ/255^\circ75∘/255∘ (+0.038/−0.059+0.038/-0.059+0.038/−0.059). The [P2] picture is: as NNN grows, the transition fraction shrinks, the lobes narrow, and the quiet zones widen — a single-NNN lab like this one can only demonstrate the mechanism, not verify the scaling (see below). Against the lab_03 toy triangle (black dashed): the toy guessed the right direction ("concentrated in the transitions"), but (i) its peak height 1/3=0.5771/\sqrt3=0.5771/3​=0.577 is half the measured 1.171.171.17; (ii) the toy puts a positive peak on both edges, while the measurement gives one positive, one negative; (iii) at N=3N=3N=3 the measured lobes are wide flat-tops, not sharp triangles. That is the gap between a hand-placed shape and a measured one. Against Γ∝1/V˙\Gamma\propto1/\dot VΓ∝1/V˙ from waveform_slope: inside a lobe, Γ(0)=1.128\Gamma(0)=1.128Γ(0)=1.128 corresponds to V˙=ω0VDD/Γ≈6.8×109\dot V=\omega_0V_{DD}/\Gamma\approx6.8\times10^9V˙=ω0​VDD​/Γ≈6.8×109 V/s, consistent with the waveform slope; but on the rails the slope goes to 0 while Γ\GammaΓ also goes to 0 — because the inverse-proportionality assumes the perturbation stays on the orbit, whereas on the rail the driving stage is a low-impedance termination that simply swallows the charge. The two pages are complementary, not contradictory. (c) ∣cn∣\lvert c_n\rvert∣cn​∣ stems: c1=1.3047c_1=1.3047c1​=1.3047 dominates, c3=0.1633c_3=0.1633c3​=0.1633 is second, and the even harmonics are nearly 0 — a wide flat-top, odd-symmetric dual lobe is naturally dominated by odd harmonics. The most important stem is the one you can barely see: c0=0.0014≈0c_0=0.0014\approx0c0​=0.0014≈0. Because rise/fall were designed symmetric via βn=βp\beta_n=\beta_pβn​=βp​, flicker upconversion (1/f31/f^31/f3, [P1] Eq.(23)(24), ∝c02\propto c_0^2∝c02​) would be suppressed to almost nothing — if a flicker source had been modeled (this lab has none, see Section 11). Parseval ([P1] Eq.(20)): ∑cn2=1.7308\sum c_n^2=1.7308∑cn2​=1.7308 vs 2Γrms2=1.73092\Gamma_{rms}^2=1.73092Γrms2​=1.7309, consistent. Three measurement-quality checks (printed by the actual run): halving dtdtdt moves f0f_0f0​ by only 1.22×10−51.22\times10^{-5}1.22×10−5; halving Δq\Delta qΔq moves Γ\GammaΓ by only 0.1%; period spread 10−810^{-8}10−8 ps. The numbers are trustworthy.

documents.t: Operational ISF definition: [P1] Eq.(10)–(11), p.182 together with ΔV=Δq/C\Delta V=\Delta q/CΔV=Δq/C (Eq.(9), p.181) — this lab's extraction procedure uses these two equations as the measurement instrument. Linearity premise: [P1] Fig. 6, p.182 (Δϕ∝Δq\Delta\phi\propto\Delta qΔϕ∝Δq for small charge; this lab verifies by halving Δq\Delta qΔq, 0.1% difference). Ring ISF shape: [P2] Fig. 5, p.793 (simulation-extracted ring ISF, energy concentrated in the transitions), Fig. 6, p.793 (approximate waveform + triangular ISF approximation). This lab's N=3N=3N=3 measurement: dual lobes, peaks at the transition onsets ✓; but the lobes are wide flat-tops rather than narrow triangles — the triangular approximation only becomes accurate at large NNN (small transition fraction). Frequency: [P2] Eq.(15), p.794: f0=1/(2NτD)f_0=1/(2N\tau_D)f0​=1/(2NτD​); this lab back-solves τD=136.03\tau_D=136.03τD​=136.03 ps. Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​: the correct reading of [P2] Eq.(16), p.794 is that the square root covers only the constant: Γrms=2π23η3 1N1.5\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\pi^2}{3\eta^3}}\;\dfrac{1}{N^{1.5}}Γrms​=3η32π2​​N1.51​ (at η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75 this is ≈4/N1.5\approx4/N^{1.5}≈4/N1.5, the solid line in [P2] Fig.8). Plugging in N=3N=3N=3: η=1\eta=1η=1 gives 0.49370.49370.4937, the η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75 anchor gives 0.7600.7600.760. The measured Γrms=0.9303\Gamma_{rms}=0.9303Γrms​=0.9303 is 88% above the η=1\eta=1η=1 reference and 22% above the η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75 anchor — same order of magnitude, but no single η\etaη lines up exactly (η\etaη was not fitted to this circuit, and at N=3N=3N=3 the triode/saturation mix and the symmetric inverter's actual waveform naturally deviate from the triangular/exponential approximation used in the paper's derivation). A single NNN cannot verify the Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 scaling — it can only serve as a ballpark magnitude check; verifying the scaling requires sweeping N=3,5,7,…N=3,5,7,\dotsN=3,5,7,… (this script's vectorized derivative supports any stage count; the NNN sweep is left as an extension exercise). Next step toward phase noise (not done in this lab): plugging the measured Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and c0c_0c0​ into [P1] Eq.(21) (1/f21/f^21/f2) and Eq.(23)(24) (1/f31/f^31/f3) still requires the device noise PSD in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf and cyclostationary weighting (effective_isf).

documents.t: What we see beyond the toy model: f0f_0f0​, the waveforms, and the shape/sign/magnitude of Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ) are all measured from device equations; symmetric design ⇒ c0≈0c_0\approx0c0​≈0 can be engineered, not merely declared. What remains invisible (needs SPICE/BSIM/PDK or more modeling): Level-1 physics gaps: no velocity saturation/mobility degradation (in advanced nodes ID∝VovI_D\propto V_{ov}ID​∝Vov​ rather than Vov2V_{ov}^2Vov2​, which changes transition slopes and lobe shapes); no subthreshold conduction (real devices still carry an exponential tail current for VGSV_{GS}VGS​ below VtV_tVt​, softening the lobe edges); λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 (no channel-length modulation). Lumped CLC_LCL​ only: no Cgs/CgdC_{gs}/C_{gd}Cgs​/Cgd​ (Miller coupling would make edges tug at each other), no layout parasitic RC. qmax=CLVDD=10q_{max}=C_LV_{DD}=10qmax​=CL​VDD​=10 fC uses the nominal value (measured swing 99.2% of VDDV_{DD}VDD​, 0.8% off). No noise model at all: this lab is deterministic — it extracts the ISF itself and produces no phase noise. Thermal (4kTγgm4kT\gamma g_m4kTγgm​) and flicker sources, and their cyclostationary modulation, are not at this level. Single NNN, single corner: does not verify N−3/2N^{-3/2}N−3/2, does not look at PVT. Numerics: fixed-step first-order Euler (convergence measured at 1.22×10−51.22\times10^{-5}1.22×10−5); injection-phase quantization ≤0.011∘\le0.011^\circ≤0.011∘; threshold crossing via linear interpolation.

documents.t: Prerequisites: lab_03 (ring toy and accumulated jitter), lab_05 (numerical extraction of cnc_ncn​), fourier_series_of_isf (cnc_ncn​ as "receive channels") | Next: varactor_tuning_supply_pushing (the quasi-static KpushK_{push}Kpush​ door for supply noise), device_noise_mapping (the full harmonics-equal-channels map) Every phase-noise computation so far carried an unstated assumption: each noise source injects into ONE node, and the sources on different nodes are independent (uncorrelated). For device thermal / flicker noise that is indeed the case — [P2] p.792 says it explicitly: with uncorrelated sources on the nodes, the total phase noise of NNN sources is NNN times the single-source result ([P2] Eq.(6)) (2N2N2N times for a differential ring) — powers simply add, with no frequency selection whatsoever. But supply and substrate noise are not like that. [P2] Sec. VI (p.797) points out two key differences from internal device noise: their PSD is usually nonwhite, often with strong peaks at specific frequencies (switching-regulator harmonics, digital-block switching harmonics); the same supply line / the same substrate hits every node of the ring with a nearly identical disturbance — the nodes see strongly correlated (nearly identical) noise. This page turns point 2 into a selection rule you can measure: the effective ISF for correlated noise is the SUM of NNN per-stage ISFs shifted by 2π/N2\pi/N2π/N, and its Fourier components — except those with n≡0 (mod N)n\equiv0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ N)n≡0 (mod N) — all cancel as phasors. Hence correlated noise converts into phase only from bands near DC and near k⋅N⋅f0k\cdot N\cdot f_0k⋅N⋅f0​. Physical intuition (conclusion first): think of the NNN-stage ring as NNN antennas pointing in different directions — every stage's ISF has the same shape, offset only by a 2π/N2\pi/N2π/N phase ([P2] Fig. 10 draws them as five phasors ej2πn/5e^{j2\pi n/5}ej2πn/5). When the same disturbance hits all NNN antennas, the mmm-th harmonic channel receives the sum of NNN phasors: only when mmm is an integer multiple of NNN do the five phasors add in phase (gain NNN); otherwise they walk a full circle in the complex plane and their vector sum is exactly zero. This is not an approximation — it is a finite-geometric-series identity, and this lab computes it down to machine precision for you. Model-level statement: the per-stage ISF in this lab is a pedagogical toy model (dual triangular lobes, deliberately rise/fall-asymmetric), not transistor-level (for a measured ring ISF go to lab_32). The selection rule itself does not depend on the ISF shape — the derivation holds for any 2π2\pi2π-periodic Γ\GammaΓ, which is exactly what makes it powerful. The phase model is linear LTV ([P1] Eq.(11)) with no amplitude dynamics; a real oscillator's amplitude response leaves residual sidebands ([P2] Fig. 11 measured them; see Section 11).
documents.s: Lab 34 — The N·f0 Selection Rule for Correlated Supply/Substrate Noise

documents.t: Transcribe verbatim and explain [P2] Eq.(37)–(38) (p.797): with identical noise sources on all NNN nodes, the total phase is the superposition of NNN phase-shifted ISFs. Prove, with a finite geometric sum and no skipped steps, that the summed ISF keeps only the Fourier components with n≡0 (mod N)n\equiv0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ N)n≡0 (mod N), and that the survivors are amplified by NNN. Numerical verification on an N=5N=5N=5 toy ring (frequency domain): the summed ISF's ∣cn∣\lvert c_n\rvert∣cn​∣ comb keeps only n=0,5,10,15n=0,5,10,15n=0,5,10,15; forbidden components drop to the numeric floor (165.8 dB selection ratio). Time-domain verification (after [P2] Fig. 11's 10 µA experiment): sweep a common sinusoidal disturbance across nf0+Δfn f_0+\Delta fnf0​+Δf; the phase response peaks only at n=0,5,10n=0,5,10n=0,5,10 (66 dB selection, coherent gain 4.998≈N4.998\approx N4.998≈N, matching the [P1] Eq.(15)/(16) theory to 10−510^{-5}10−5 relative error). Translate into design language: the N⋅f0N\cdot f_0N⋅f0​ selection rule — keep supply peaks away from k⋅N⋅f0k\cdot N\cdot f_0k⋅N⋅f0​; rise/fall symmetry closes the DC door; stage mismatch makes the cancellation incomplete.

Therefore: Correlated noise: cΣ,m=0c_{\Sigma,m}=0cΣ,m​=0 unless m≡0 (mod N)m\equiv0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ N)m≡0 (mod N) ⇒ only noise near DC (through ΓΣ,dc=Nc0/2\Gamma_{\Sigma,dc}=Nc_0/2ΓΣ,dc​=Nc0​/2, upconverted to close-in) and near k⋅N⋅f0k\cdot N\cdot f_0k⋅N⋅f0​ (downconverted) becomes phase; within each surviving band the integrator behaviour 1/Δω1/\Delta\omega1/Δω still applies ⇒ sidebands fall at −20-20−20 dB/dec of offset ([P2] Fig. 11 measured this slope). Uncorrelated noise (the control): independent per-node sources ⇒ powers add; total phase noise is NNN times a single source ([P2] p.792, NNN times Eq.(6)); every harmonic channel stays open — no selection rule. The difference on the surviving bands: a correlated source gets amplitude gain NNN ⇒ power N2N^2N2; NNN uncorrelated sources get power NNN ⇒ correlated is worse by 10log⁡10N10\log_{10}N10log10​N dB (N=5N=5N=5: 7.0 dB). Coherent addition cuts both ways: it saves you on the forbidden bands (total kill) and punishes you on the surviving ones (N2N^2N2).

documents.t: Supply-noise power is concentrated at low frequency (regulator ripple, load transients, 1/f1/f1/f) — exactly aligned with the DC channel of ΓΣ\Gamma_\SigmaΓΣ​. How wide that channel opens is set by the single-stage c0c_0c0​, and c0c_0c0​ is set by rise/fall asymmetry ([P2] App. B, p.803): Eq.(53) defines A=frise′/ffall′A=f_{rise}'/f_{fall}'A=frise′​/ffall′​ (rise/fall slope ratio) and Eq.(56) gives Γdc=2πη2N2⋅1−A1+A\Gamma_{dc}=\frac{2\pi}{\eta^2N^2}\cdot\frac{1-A}{1+A}Γdc​=η2N22π​⋅1+A1−A​ — perfect symmetry (A=1A=1A=1) slams the DC door shut; the more asymmetric, the wider it opens, raising the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner through Eq.(57). This lab's toy ISF is deliberately asymmetric (positive-lobe peak 1.0, negative-lobe peak 0.6), so that c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0 and the DC channel is open — letting you see both stories, "the DC door" and "the Nf0N f_0Nf0​ comb", in one figure. Design language (the N⋅f0N\cdot f_0N⋅f0​ selection rule): to correlated supply/substrate noise, the ring is a comb receiver — it only listens at DC and at k⋅N⋅f0k\cdot N\cdot f_0k⋅N⋅f0​. Hence: (i) if the supply has a known switching spur at fswf_{sw}fsw​ and harmonics, choose NNN and f0f_0f0​ so that k⋅N⋅f0k\cdot N\cdot f_0k⋅N⋅f0​ avoids the spurs (or choose fswf_{sw}fsw​ the other way around); (ii) larger NNN pushes the first high-frequency sensitive band Nf0N f_0Nf0​ higher, where package/decoupling attenuation is usually better; (iii) rise/fall symmetry (A→1A\to1A→1) narrows the DC door — the same knob as the device-flicker c0c_0c0​ counter-measure (symmetry); (iv) stage mismatch makes the phasor cancellation incomplete, leaking residue into the forbidden bands (Section 11).

documents.t: Excerpts from simulations/lab_34_correlated_supply.py (checked against the source). Toy per-stage ISF, summed ISF, and the time-domain injection measurement: def gamma_stage(theta): """Per-stage toy ring ISF: +1.0 triangular lobe at the rising edge (θ=0), −0.6 triangular lobe at the falling edge (θ=π). Deliberately asymmetric (1.0 vs 0.6) → c0 ≠ 0 ([P2] App.B: A≠1 ⇒ Γdc≠0).""" th = wrap_phase(theta) d_rise = np.minimum(th, 2 * np.pi - th) d_fall = np.abs(th - np.pi) return H_RISE * _tri(d_rise, W_LOBE) - H_FALL * _tri(d_fall, W_LOBE) def gamma_summed(theta): """Sum of N per-stage ISFs shifted by 2π/N (the bracket of [P2] Eq.(37)).""" acc = np.zeros_like(np.asarray(theta, dtype=float)) for n in range(N_STAGES): acc += gamma_stage(theta + 2 * np.pi * n / N_STAGES) return acc def response(n_h, g_t): """Common injection i(t)=I0·cos(2π(n_h·f0+Δf)t); return the amplitude of φ at Δf [rad].""" i_inj = I0 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * (n_h * F0 + DF) * t) phi = np.cumsum(i_inj * g_t) * dt / QMAX # discrete version of [P1] Eq.(11) return 2.0 * np.abs(np.mean(phi * proj)) # project onto the Δf bin (integer slow periods) The frequency-domain part uses compute_fourier_coefficients (the same ruler as lab_05) to compute c0…c15c_0\dots c_{15}c0​…c15​ of both the single-stage and the summed ISF; the phasor identity is evaluated directly as ∣Sm∣=∣∑nej2πmn/5∣\lvert S_m\rvert=\lvert\sum_n e^{j2\pi mn/5}\rvert∣Sm​∣=∣∑n​ej2πmn/5∣.

documents.s: 10. Corresponding paper equations / figures

documents.t: Pure-phase linear LTV: this lab has only the phase integral of [P1] Eq.(11), no amplitude dynamics. [P2] Fig. 11's measurement shows residual sidebands from the amplitude response at non-multiples of NNN — that path (AM, and AM-PM back into phase) does not exist in this model; our forbidden-band residue (−66-66−66 dB) is purely numerical (sampling leakage). Do not use it to predict the forbidden-band depth of a real circuit. Identical stages: exact cancellation relies on every stage's ISF having the same shape at exactly 2π/N2\pi/N2π/N spacing. Real mismatch (load, drive strength, layout) leaves a phasor residue ∝\propto∝ mismatch — to first order, a relative mismatch ε\varepsilonε leaks an amplitude ∼ε\sim\varepsilon∼ε into the forbidden channels (20log⁡10ε20\log_{10}\varepsilon20log10​ε dB). 1% mismatch ⇒ the forbidden bands are only suppressed by 40 dB, not infinitely deep. "Fully correlated, equal-strength, same-sign" injection: real supply/substrate coupling coefficients differ from node to node (IR drop, layout distance), landing between "fully correlated" and "uncorrelated"; the two extremes on this page bracket the answer. Toy ISF: the dual triangular lobes are hand-placed (lab_03-style, plus asymmetry); for the real single-ended ring ISF shape see lab_32. But the selection rule does not depend on shape — the proof of 2.2 holds for any 2π2\pi2π-periodic Γ\GammaΓ; changing the ISF changes the cnc_ncn​ values of each channel, not which channels exist. Supply noise is modeled here as node-current injection: low-frequency supply noise also has a quasi-static FM path (KpushK_{push}Kpush​, shifting f0f_0f0​ through the operating point) — the subject of varactor_tuning_supply_pushing; both paths coexist, the KpushK_{push}Kpush​ door usually dominating at low offsets while the kNf0k N f_0kNf0​ comb is the dedicated entrance for high-frequency supply spurs. Cyclostationary weighting not included: strictly each stage's injection should also be multiplied by the NMF α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0t)α(ω0​t) (effective_isf); for identical stages the α\alphaα's are the same phase-shifted family, so the selection rule holds unchanged for Γeff=Γα\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\alphaΓeff​=Γα (the product is still 2π2\pi2π-periodic).
documents.s: 11. Limitations and approximations

documents.t: The essential difference between supply/substrate noise and device noise: nonwhite PSD (with spurs) + strong cross-node correlation ([P2] Sec. VI, p.797). The effective ISF of a correlated source is the SUM of NNN per-stage ISFs shifted by 2π/N2\pi/N2π/N ([P2] Eq.(37)); the finite geometric sum gives Sm=NS_m=NSm​=N (m≡0 mod Nm\equiv0\ \mathrm{mod}\ Nm≡0 mod N) or 000 (otherwise) ⇒ only the n≡0 (mod N)n\equiv0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ N)n≡0 (mod N) channels remain, with gain NNN ([P2] Eq.(38)). Numerical verification (N=5N=5N=5 toy): ∣Sm∣\lvert S_m\rvert∣Sm​∣ to machine precision; cΣ,n/cn=5.000000c_{\Sigma,n}/c_n=5.000000cΣ,n​/cn​=5.000000; 165.8 dB frequency-domain selection; the time-domain sweep peaks only at n=0,5,10n=0,5,10n=0,5,10 (66.0 dB, coherent gain 4.9978, theory match 10−510^{-5}10−5). The N⋅f0N\cdot f_0N⋅f0​ selection rule: correlated noise enters only from DC (door size =Nc0/2=Nc_0/2=Nc0​/2, set by the rise/fall asymmetry AAA, [P2] Eq.(56)) and from near k⋅N⋅f0k\cdot N\cdot f_0k⋅N⋅f0​. In design: keep kNf0kNf_0kNf0​ away from supply spurs, symmetrize to close the DC door, and watch mismatch, which makes the cancellation incomplete. On the surviving bands, correlated is worse than uncorrelated by 10log⁡10N10\log_{10}N10log10​N dB (coherent N2N^2N2 vs power NNN); on the forbidden bands, correlated is better all the way down to the mismatch/amplitude residue. Get the correlation wrong and both numbers are wrong.

documents.t: Prerequisites: injection_locking_noise (reduction of the [P3] generalized Adler equation to θ˙=Δω−ωLsin⁡θ\dot\theta=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\thetaθ˙=Δω−ωL​sinθ, in-lock noise shaping lab_26, out-of-lock pulling lab_27), paper_003 (origin of the lock characteristic), diffusion_dictionary (bookkeeping of the DDD conventions) | Next: paper_004 (original source of the pull-in transient, [P4] Sec. V), quadrature_and_coupled_oscillators. injection_locking_noise already answered the two steady-state questions — "after lock" (noise shaping) and "cannot lock" (pulling comb). This page fills in the two missing transient pieces: What this page answers: The moment the injection turns on, how long does the phase take to climb into the locked point? What is the settle rate? Why is it that near the lock-range edge you can "lock, but lock extremely slowly"? (Part a: the acquisition transient) Once locked, what is the probability that noise occasionally kicks the phase over a whole cycle (a cycle slip — the phase slides by 2π2\pi2π in one event)? How does it scale with detuning and noise strength? At the canonical numbers, how often does it slip? (Part b) Physical intuition (conclusion first): rewrite the Adler equation as an overdamped particle rolling in a tilted washboard potential and everything becomes obvious. Acquisition = the particle rolls down the slope into the nearest well: the potential curvature near the well is ωc=ωL2−Δω2\omega_c=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωc​=ωL2​−Δω2​, so settling is an exponential with rate ωc\omega_cωc​; as the detuning ratio r=Δω/ωL→1r=\Delta\omega/\omega_L\to1r=Δω/ωL​→1 the well and the saddle merge, the curvature vanishes, and the acquisition time diverges as 1/1−r1/\sqrt{1-r}1/1−r​ (critical slowing down). A cycle slip = thermal noise kicks the particle over the barrier of height ΔU\Delta UΔU next to the well and it slides down one washboard period (2π2\pi2π): the rate is Arrhenius-like, e−ΔU/De^{-\Delta U/D}e−ΔU/D, and the "attempt frequency" is again the same ωc/2π\omega_c/2\piωc​/2π — the third appearance of that Pythagorean square root (first: settle rate; second: the noise-shaping corner of lab_26; outside lock it turns into the beat frequency ωb\omega_bωb​). Positioning of this page: an advanced lab page with the theory derived in full on the page. The phase equation itself and the pull-in frequency are native results of [P3]/[P4] ([P3] Eq.(38)–(40), p.2115; [P4] Eq.(31)–(32) and Table I, p.2130, all verified against the original PDFs); the escape rate of noise over a barrier (Kramers/MFPT) is standard stochastic-process theory, not contained in the site's 5 PDFs (external references: Kramers 1940, Risken 1989, Ambegaokar–Halperin 1969, see the end of the page). This page honestly derives the barrier itself, quotes the escape-rate formula, and then checks everything against an SDE simulation term by term.

Exact closed form, barrier, and the slip-counting main loop: def barrier(r): # ΔU/ω_L = 2(√(1−r²) − r·arccos r) return 2.0 * (np.sqrt(1.0 - r**2) - r * np.arccos(r)) def acquisition_exact(r, theta0=0.0, eps=0.01): wc = np.sqrt(1.0 - r**2) # ω_c/ω_L (dimensionless pull-in rate) um = (1.0 - wc) / r # tan(θ_ss/2) (stable root) up = (1.0 + wc) / r # tan(θ_u/2) (unstable root; um·up = 1) R = lambda u: (u - um) / (u - up) # R(θ(t)) = R(θ₀)·e^(−ω_c t) u0, uthr = np.tan(theta0 / 2), np.tan((np.arcsin(r) - eps) / 2) return (1.0 / wc) * np.log(R(u0) / R(uthr)) # exact acquisition time [1/ω_L] # --- slips: Euler–Maruyama (dimensionless τ=ω_L t; n supplied by the site's white_noise) --- # white_noise one-sided PSD = 4D ⇒ increment variance 2·D·dτ (convention B ⟨nn'⟩=2Dδ) [checked] nz = white_noise(nb * m, 4.0 * D, 1.0 / dtau, rng).reshape(nb, m) for i in range(nb): theta += (r - np.sin(theta) + nz[i]) * dtau # integer slip count: floor((θ−θ_u)/2π) is constant inside one well, jumps ±1 on a slip slips = int(np.sum(np.floor((th_end - th_u) / (2*np.pi)) - np.floor((th_start - th_u) / (2*np.pi)))) Verification numbers as printed (PYTHONPATH=. python3 simulations/lab_36_lock_acquisition.py): print(ratio_min, ratio_max) # -> 1.0000 1.0000 RK4 acquisition time / exact closed form (all 12 r values) print(T_r050) # -> 4.435 ω_L·T_acq @ r=0.5 (ε=0.01 rad, θ₀=0) print(T_r090) # -> 9.202 ω_L·T_acq @ r=0.9 print(T_r099) # -> 22.913 ω_L·T_acq @ r=0.99 (critical slowing) print(wc_T_range) # -> 2.30 .. 4.10 ω_c·T_acq barely moves (the divergence is all in 1/ω_c) print(max_traj_dev) # -> 2.90e-14 rad, max deviation closed form vs RK4 whole trajectory (r=0.8) print(T_r05_real) # -> 141.2 ns (=706 carrier periods at 5 GHz; f_L=5 MHz) print(dU_over_wL) # -> 0.1704 barrier ΔU/ω_L @ r=0.8 print(slips_x6, ratio_x6) # -> 1350, 0.93 slips and (measured/Kramers) @ ΔU/D=6 print(dU_fit_over_theory) # -> 0.993 fitted barrier / analytic barrier (log-linear slope) print(prefac_fit_over_kramers) # -> 0.88 fitted prefactor / (ω_c/2π) (Kramers asymptote) print(dt_halving) # -> 1.053 slip-rate ratio after halving dτ (step-size bias ~5%) print(log10_nu_canonical) # -> -1.860e7 log10(ν·s) @ true-LC D=0.125, r=0.8 print(one_minus_rstar) # -> 7.573e-06 1−r*: distance to the edge for ν=1 slip/s (true LC)

documents.t: (a) Acquisition time (left): the blue line is the exact closed form Tacq=ωc−1ln⁡[R(θ0)/R(θss−ε)]T_{acq}=\omega_c^{-1}\ln[R(\theta_0)/R(\theta_{ss}-\varepsilon)]Tacq​=ωc−1​ln[R(θ0​)/R(θss​−ε)], the red circles are the first-crossing times measured by direct RK4 integration — all 12 values of rrr agree to a ratio of 1.0000 (maximum deviation over the whole trajectory 2.9×10−142.9\times10^{-14}2.9×10−14 rad, machine-precision level: the closed form is the solution). The gray dashed line is the pure 1/ωc1/\omega_c1/ωc​ scaling (anchored at r=0.99r=0.99r=0.99): beyond r≳0.5r\gtrsim0.5r≳0.5 the measured points ride it exactly — every bit of the divergence comes from ωc→0\omega_c\to0ωc​→0, while the start point and threshold enter only through the log (ωcTacq\omega_c T_{acq}ωc​Tacq​ stays within 2.30–4.10 throughout, while TacqT_{acq}Tacq​ itself spans an order of magnitude). The design reading: the acquisition bandwidth and the noise-suppression bandwidth are the same number — pulling the detuning back from the edge (r=0.99r=0.99r=0.99) to mid-range (r=0.5r=0.5r=0.5) not only drops the noise plateau (the 1/cos⁡2θss1/\cos^2\theta_{ss}1/cos2θss​ accounting of lab_26) but also makes acquisition 5.2× faster. (b) Slip rate (right): on the log-linear axis the measured points fall on a straight line — the signature of an Arrhenius-type e−ΔU/De^{-\Delta U/D}e−ΔU/D. The weighted fit of the slope gives ΔUfit=0.993 ΔUtheory\Delta U_{fit}=0.993\,\Delta U_{theory}ΔUfit​=0.993ΔUtheory​: the barrier height is measured by the simulation itself, matching 2ωL[1−r2−rarccos⁡r]=0.1704 ωL2\omega_L[\sqrt{1-r^2}-r\arccos r]=0.1704\,\omega_L2ωL​[1−r2​−rarccosr]=0.1704ωL​. The prefactor, honestly: the fit gives 0.88 of the Kramers ωc/2π\omega_c/2\piωc​/2π, with point-by-point ratios 0.77–0.94 — three sources: Kramers is the ΔU/D≫1\Delta U/D\gg1ΔU/D≫1 asymptote (x=4x=4x=4 is only a moderate barrier), Euler step-size bias (halving dτd\taudτ moves the slip rate by 5.3%, dt_halving = 1.053), and statistics at x=9x=9x=9 with only 56 events (error bar ±13%). The exponent (the physics) is accurate to 0.7%; the prefactor (asymptotics + numerics) is off by a tenth — exactly what Kramers theory should look like. The inset shows a single walker's θ/2π\theta/2\piθ/2π at ΔU/D=5\Delta U/D=5ΔU/D=5: long plateaus (dithering inside a well) plus integer stair steps (one 2π2\pi2π slide per slip) — a slip is a discrete event, not a continuous drift; the plateau lengths are exponentially distributed, which is also why counting integer jumps of floor((θ−θu)/2π)\mathrm{floor}((\theta-\theta_u)/2\pi)floor((θ−θu​)/2π) is the cleanest method (constant inside a well, ±1 across the barrier, zero fractional noise).

documents.t: Phase-domain toy model: what is integrated is the time-averaged Adler equation (the sinusoidal reduction of [P3] Eq.(30)), not a transistor-level circuit — no amplitude dynamics (APF), no harmonics, no cyclostationary weighting (the latter is already absorbed into SnS_nSn​ through Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, see effective_isf). Kramers asymptotics: ν=(ωc/2π)e−ΔU/D\nu=(\omega_c/2\pi)e^{-\Delta U/D}ν=(ωc​/2π)e−ΔU/D holds only for ΔU≫D\Delta U\gg DΔU≫D; this lab sweeps ΔU/D=4\Delta U/D=4ΔU/D=4–999, medium-to-high barriers, so the exponential slope is accurate (0.993) while the prefactor is off by 12%. Higher accuracy needs the closed-form MFPT double integral (Risken Ch. 11), not expanded here. Euler–Maruyama, first-order weak convergence: at dτ=0.02d\tau=0.02dτ=0.02 the slip-rate step-size bias is ~5% (measured dt_halving = 1.053); the barrier fit is insensitive to it (the slope is a difference between ratios). One-directional counting assumption: at r=0.8r=0.8r=0.8 the backward barrier is higher by 2πr ωL2\pi r\,\omega_L2πrωL​, suppressing the backward rate by e−2πrωL/De^{-2\pi r\omega_L/D}e−2πrωL​/D (≲e−100\lesssim e^{-100}≲e−100 at this page's parameters); at small rrr or large DDD forward and backward slips must be counted separately. White-noise assumption: under flicker FM, DDD is not constant and slips are non-Poissonian; long-gate slip statistics in measurements then deviate from exponential. TacqT_{acq}Tacq​ depends on the start point: θ0=0\theta_0=0θ0​=0 is a representative choice; changing it only moves the log factor (the 2.30–4.10 range of ωcT\omega_c Tωc​T), never the 1/ωc1/\omega_c1/ωc​ divergence. Starting exactly at θu\theta_uθu​ (measure zero) never acquires, in theory.
documents.s: 11. Limitations and approximations

documents.t: The in-lock Adler equation has an exact closed-form solution: R(θ)≡tan⁡θ2−tan⁡θss2tan⁡θ2−tan⁡θu2R(\theta)\equiv\dfrac{\tan\frac{\theta}{2}-\tan\frac{\theta_{ss}}{2}}{\tan\frac{\theta}{2}-\tan\frac{\theta_u}{2}}R(θ)≡tan2θ​−tan2θu​​tan2θ​−tan2θss​​​ decays strictly as e−ωcte^{-\omega_c t}e−ωc​t, so the settle rate is globally the pull-in frequency ωc=ωL2−Δω2\omega_c=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωc​=ωL2​−Δω2​ ([P3] Eq.(40); equivalent to the tanh form of [P4] Eq.(31)–(32)). Critical slowing: as r→1r\to1r→1 the two equilibria merge in a saddle-node, Tacq∝(1−r)−1/2T_{acq}\propto(1-r)^{-1/2}Tacq​∝(1−r)−1/2; simulation: ωLTacq\omega_L T_{acq}ωL​Tacq​ grows from 4.435 (r=0.5r=0.5r=0.5) to 22.913 (r=0.99r=0.99r=0.99), all riding the 1/ωc1/\omega_c1/ωc​ line (RK4/closed-form ratio 1.0000). Canonical scale: 141.2 ns → 729.3 ns. With white FM noise the Adler equation = an overdamped particle in the tilted washboard U=−Δωθ−ωLcos⁡θU=-\Delta\omega\theta-\omega_L\cos\thetaU=−Δωθ−ωL​cosθ; forward barrier ΔU+=2ωL[1−r2−rarccos⁡r]\Delta U_+=2\omega_L[\sqrt{1-r^2}-r\arccos r]ΔU+​=2ωL​[1−r2​−rarccosr] (r=0.8r{=}0.8r=0.8: 0.1704 ωL0.1704\,\omega_L0.1704ωL​; r→1r\to1r→1: ∝(1−r)3/2\propto(1-r)^{3/2}∝(1−r)3/2). Kramers slip rate ν≈(ωc/2π)e−ΔU+/D\nu\approx(\omega_c/2\pi)e^{-\Delta U_+/D}ν≈(ωc​/2π)e−ΔU+​/D (external reference), D=Sn/4D=S_n/4D=Sn​/4 (convention B): the simulated log-linear slope = 0.993 of the barrier, prefactor 0.88 (asymptotics + Euler, honestly accounted). Canonical numbers (fL=5f_L=5fL​=5 MHz, true-LC D=0.125D=0.125D=0.125 rad²/s, r=0.8r=0.8r=0.8): log⁡10ν≈−1.86×107\log_{10}\nu\approx-1.86\times10^7log10​ν≈−1.86×107 — thermal slips never happen; one slip per second requires pushing the detuning to the cliff edge 1−r=7.6×10−61-r=7.6\times10^{-6}1−r=7.6×10−6. One slip = one whole carrier period — a dropped-bit-class event. The four identities of the same square root ∣ωL2−Δω2∣\sqrt{\lvert\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2\rvert}∣ωL2​−Δω2∣​: in lock, settle rate = noise-shaping corner = Kramers attempt frequency; out of lock, the beat frequency ωb\omega_bωb​.

documents.t: [E-Kramers] H. A. Kramers, "Brownian motion in a field of force and the diffusion model of chemical reactions," Physica, vol. 7, no. 4, pp. 284–304, 1940. (Original source of the overdamped escape rate ∝e−ΔU/D\propto e^{-\Delta U/D}∝e−ΔU/D with the curvature prefactor.) [E-Risken] H. Risken, The Fokker–Planck Equation: Methods of Solution and Applications, 2nd ed., Springer, 1989, Ch. 11. (Complete MFPT theory of tilted periodic potentials.) [E-AH] V. Ambegaokar and B. I. Halperin, "Voltage due to thermal noise in the dc Josephson effect," Phys. Rev. Lett., vol. 22, no. 25, pp. 1364–1366, 1969. (The classic application of the same tilted-washboard + thermal-escape mathematics to Josephson junctions.) [E-Strogatz] S. H. Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos, 2nd ed., Westview, 2015. (The standard textbook for saddle-node bifurcations and critical slowing ∝1/distance\propto1/\sqrt{\text{distance}}∝1/distance​.) [E-Adler] R. Adler, "A Study of Locking Phenomena in Oscillators," Proc. IRE, vol. 34, no. 6, pp. 351–357, Jun. 1946. (The classic Adler equation.)

documents.t: Prerequisites: subharmonic_injection (every closed form this lab verifies — the lock range, the realignment factor β\betaβ, discrete-time noise shaping, output jitter, and the reference spur), paper_003 ([P3] Sec. IV's impulse train and footnote 7's subharmonic arithmetic), paper_004 ([P4] Eq.(28)–(30)'s M:N averaging equation) | Next: injection_locked_division (the dual, divider direction), sampling_pll, clock_chain_budget The subharmonic_injection page has already derived every formula for the injection-locked clock multiplier (ILCM) step by step: the multiplier closed form ωL=12∣IN∣∣Γ~1∣\omega_L=\tfrac12\vert I_N\vert\vert\tilde\Gamma_1\vertωL​=21​∣IN​∣∣Γ~1​∣ from [P4] Eq.(29), the ΔωL∝1/N\Delta\omega_L\propto1/NΔωL​∝1/N scaling from the discrete arithmetic of [P3] footnote 7, the realignment factor β\betaβ from the linearized per-pulse map, and the output-jitter closed form from putting noise on a first-order discrete loop. This page does not re-derive any of it — it uses two independent numerical engines to score every one of those closed forms term by term. What this lab verifies: Does the lock range really go as 1/N1/N1/N (Engine 2: sweep NNN with the unaveraged ODE)? How does a finite pulse width eat into the lock range — a clean sinc for LC, and what about the ring (Engine 2: sweep the pulse width)? At the same rms current, does the pulse train really lock while a pure sine really doesn't (Engine 2: pulse-train vs. sine comparison)? How accurate is the first-order prediction −qinjΓ~′(θss)-q_{inj}\tilde\Gamma'(\theta_{ss})−qinj​Γ~′(θss​) for the realignment factor β\betaβ (Engine 2: step response)? Is the locked phase noise really a first-order discrete high-pass, with corner ≈βfref/2π\approx\beta f_{ref}/2\pi≈βfref​/2π (Engine 1: map + white FM noise)? Does output jitter really go as N\sqrt NN​, and is the reference spur really independent of β\betaβ (Engine 1: edge-level simulation)? Physical intuition: the two engines measure the same physics at different resolutions. Engine 1 (the map) compresses one pulse's effect into an instantaneous jump θk+1=θk+Δω0NT0+qinjΓ~(θk)+nk\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\Delta\omega_0NT_0+q_{inj}\tilde\Gamma(\theta_k)+n_kθk+1​=θk​+Δω0​NT0​+qinj​Γ~(θk​)+nk​ — fast, well suited to long-horizon noise statistics (PSD, jitter), but assumes the pulse is narrow. Engine 2 (the unaveraged ODE) honestly integrates the instantaneous equation θ˙=Δω+Γ~(Nωinjt+θ)(qinj/τp)\dot\theta=\Delta\omega+\tilde\Gamma(N\omega_{inj}t+\theta)(q_{inj}/\tau_p)θ˙=Δω+Γ~(Nωinj​t+θ)(qinj​/τp​) through the pulse with RK4 — it sees pulse-width effects and β\betaβ's second-order correction (the phase is already moving during the pulse), but each data point costs thousands of periods of integration, so it is best suited to "does it lock or not" edge sweeps. The two engines agree to within 0.1%–1% at the canonical parameters — that agreement is this lab's acceptance criterion. Where this page sits: an independent verification lab. All the theory has already been derived step by step, with sources flagged ([P3]/[P4] verified portions vs. this site's own derivations vs. external literature), on subharmonic_injection; this page lists only the verification core code and the resulting numbers. Pedagogical toy model: phase-only, weak injection, no transistors.
documents.s: Lab 40 — Subharmonic (×N) Pulse Injection: Impulse-Train Map vs. Unaveraged Time-Synchronous ODE

documents.t: Independently verify lock range∝1/N\text{lock range}\propto1/Nlock range∝1/N using the unaveraged time-synchronous ODE (not the already-averaged map) — this avoids the circular-reasoning trap of "verifying an averaged formula with the same averaged formula" (log-log slope −1.000-1.000−1.000, for both LC and ring). Sweep the pulse width τp\tau_pτp​: LC's lock range follows sinc(τp/T0)\mathrm{sinc}(\tau_p/T_0)sinc(τp​/T0​) exactly (a single harmonic, max deviation 10−410^{-4}10−4); the ring's sharp ISF spreads its energy across multiple harmonics, so a plain sinc is not enough (deviation up to 0.74) — only a "box-averaged whole ISF" matches (deviation ≤0.0074\le0.0074≤0.0074). At equal rms current, the pulse train locks throughout the lock range (15/15 grid points) while a pure sine cannot lock at first order anywhere (0/15) — pinning down numerically what subharmonic_injection Section 1 states in words: "a pure sine cannot lock." The realignment factor β\betaβ's ODE step response against the first-order prediction −qinjΓ~′(θss)/qmax-q_{inj}\tilde\Gamma'(\theta_{ss})/q_{max}−qinj​Γ~′(θss​)/qmax​: ratio 0.980.980.98–1.031.031.03 (qinj/qmax=0.05q_{inj}/q_{max}=0.05qinj​/qmax​=0.05), tightening to 0.9950.9950.995–1.031.031.03 at qinj/qmax=0.01q_{inj}/q_{max}=0.01qinj​/qmax​=0.01 — the deviation is a second-order, O(qinj/qmax)O(q_{inj}/q_{max})O(qinj​/qmax​) effect (the phase is already moving during the pulse), matching the precision the linear theory promises. Put white FM noise on the map and measure the locked phase's PSD: the low-frequency plateau matches theory to a ratio of 0.9910.9910.991, and the corner measures 1.9341.9341.934 MHz (simplified theory 1.9811.9811.981 MHz; the exact discrete closed form gives 1.9341.9341.934 MHz — the measurement rides right on the exact form). Edge-level simulation of the output jitter's power law in NNN: fitted slope 0.4970.4970.497 (theory 0.50.50.5); the canonical N=20N=20N=20 gives 2.2262.2262.226 fs (closed form 2.2282.2282.228 fs). The reference spur at a detuned lock: k=1k=1k=1 error 0.000.000.00 dB, k=2k=2k=2 error 0.010.010.01 dB — the first-order sawtooth approximation is nearly exact at the canonical parameters.

documents.t: Excerpted from simulations/lab_40_subharmonic_injection.py (checked against the source). The box-averaged table, the per-pulse map, and one pulse period of the unaveraged ODE (RK4): def isf_tables(gamma_func, tp): """Gbar(theta) = ISF box-averaged over the pulse (width tp/T0), via FFT: k-th harmonic multiplied by sinc(k*tp/T0).""" g = gamma_func(XG) G = np.fft.rfft(g) k = np.arange(G.size) Gb = G * np.sinc(k * tp) gbar = np.fft.irfft(Gb, NG) gbar_p = np.fft.irfft(1j * k * Gb, NG) # d Gbar / d theta return gbar, gbar_p def pulse_period_step(theta, dw, n_div, qt, gamma_func, tp, nsub): """ENGINE 2: one injection period T_inj = n_div*T0 of the UNAVERAGED ODE — RK4 through the rectangular pulse (width tp), analytic free-run in between.""" h = tp / nsub amp = qt / tp t = -tp / 2.0 for _ in range(nsub): k1 = dw + amp * gamma_func(TWO_PI * t + theta) k2 = dw + amp * gamma_func(TWO_PI * (t + 0.5 * h) + theta + 0.5 * h * k1) k3 = dw + amp * gamma_func(TWO_PI * (t + 0.5 * h) + theta + 0.5 * h * k2) k4 = dw + amp * gamma_func(TWO_PI * (t + h) + theta + h * k3) theta = theta + (h / 6.0) * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4) t += h return theta + dw * (n_div - tp) def gbar_prime_exact(gamma_func, theta, tp): """Exact derivative of the box-averaged ISF (difference of raw Gamma at the two box ends over the box width) -- used for beta = -q_t * Gbar'(theta*).""" half_w = np.pi * tp return (gamma_func(theta + half_w) - gamma_func(theta - half_w)) / (2.0 * half_w) Numbers printed by the script (PYTHONPATH=. python3 simulations/lab_40_subharmonic_injection.py, about 35 s single core; seed fixed with default_rng(40), results reproducible): print(A_edge_pred['LC']) # -> 0.04979 rad/period (qt*max|Gbar|, N=20) print(fL_pred['LC']/1e6) # -> 1.9813 MHz (with the 10 ps pulse-width sinc correction) print(slope_N['LC'], slope_N['ring']) # -> -1.000 -1.000 ((a) log-log slope, theory -1) print(ratio_N['LC'].min(), ratio_N['LC'].max()) # -> 1.0000 1.0000 (LC measured/theory) print(dev_lc_sinc) # -> 0.0001 ((b) LC: max deviation of ODE/f_L(0) from sinc) print(dev_ring_box, dev_ring_sinc) # -> 0.0074 0.7434 (ring: box average correct, plain sinc wrong) print(n_lock_pulse, n_plateau_sine) # -> 15 0 ((c): 15/15 grid points lock for the LC pulse train, 0 for the pure sine) print(beta_c_lc[5], beta_c_lc[4]) # -> 0.04858 0.04979 ((d) headline beta: ODE vs. first order) print(r_plateau, fc_meas/1e6, fc_pred/1e6) # -> 0.991 1.9343 1.9813 ((e) plateau ratio, measured/theory corner) print(slope_j, sig_all[10]/(2*np.pi*5e9)*1e15) # -> 0.497 2.226 ((f1) jitter's power law in N, N=20 output in fs) print(round(spur1[0], 2)) # -> -67.96 ((f2) reference spur at 100 kHz detuning, dBc)

documents.t: (a) Lock range vs. NNN: the two theory dashed lines (LC, ring) are fL=qinj2πqmaxmax⁡∣Γˉ∣NT0f_L=\dfrac{q_{inj}}{2\pi q_{max}}\dfrac{\max\vert\bar\Gamma\vert}{NT_0}fL​=2πqmax​qinj​​NT0​max∣Γˉ∣​; the circles/squares are the unaveraged-ODE measurements at N=2,4,8,16,20N=2,4,8,16,20N=2,4,8,16,20 — LC lies exactly on the theory line (ratio 1.00001.00001.0000), the ring runs 0.30%0.30\%0.30% high (a slightly larger finite-pulse effect at the triangle's sharp corner). Both log-log slopes are −1.000-1.000−1.000: the same pulse has to pay for NNN-times-longer drift, no exceptions to the 1/N1/N1/N law. (b) Lock range vs. pulse width: the black dashed line is the "plain sinc" reference (the decay of the single k=Nk=Nk=N harmonic). LC's blue measured points lie exactly on that line (max deviation 10−410^{-4}10−4) — because LC's ISF has only one harmonic (−sin⁡-\sin−sin), and locking taps only the NNN-th harmonic. The ring's green measured points fall off much faster and clearly deviate from the plain sinc (deviation up to 0.740.740.74): the ring's triangular pulse spreads its energy across many harmonics (m=1,2,3,…m=1,2,3,\dotsm=1,2,3,…, each paired with mNmNmN), and the pulse's box window shaves all of them at once — so only "box-average the whole ISF, then take the extremum" (the green solid line) matches the measurement (deviation ≤0.0074\le0.0074≤0.0074). This is direct numerical evidence that a plain sinc is not enough for the ring. (c) Pulse train vs. pure sine: the horizontal axis is the normalized detuning Δω/ωL\Delta\omega/\omega_LΔω/ωL​. The pulse train (circles/squares) has its drift rate pinned at zero for ∣x∣<1\vert x\vert<1∣x∣<1 (the locked plateau); the pure sine at the same rms current (crosses) has no plateau at all, only a line lightly offset by a second-order pushing effect (LC's fitted intercept −0.0801 ωL=−158.7-0.0801\,\omega_L=-158.7−0.0801ωL​=−158.7 kHz matches the analytic pushing formula −(I/qmax)2ω0/(4(ω02−ωinj2))-(I/q_{max})^2\omega_0/(4(\omega_0^2-\omega_{inj}^2))−(I/qmax​)2ω0​/(4(ω02​−ωinj2​)) to a ratio of 1.0001.0001.000). documents.t: [P3] Sec. IV footnote 7, p.2112 (verified): the injection can also land once every MMM periods — this lab's impulse-train map (Engine 1) and the (a)(b) unaveraged-ODE lock-range sweeps are exactly this sentence's discrete arithmetic and its numerical verification. [P4] Eq.(28)–(30), p.2129 (verified): the M:NM{:}NM:N time-synchronous averaging equation; this lab takes (M,N)[P4]=(N,1)(M,N)_{[P4]}=(N,1)(M,N)[P4]​=(N,1), whose term-by-term derivation into the multiplier closed form is written out in full on subharmonic_injection, Section 1 — this lab independently verifies that conclusion with Engine 2's unaveraged ODE (avoiding circular reasoning). [P4] footnote 10, p.2129 (verified): the injection harmonics needed for M≠1M\neq1M=1 are "not explicitly captured by our framework" — this lab's (c) "pure sine 0/15 vs. pulse train 15/15" is exactly the numerical demonstration of that sentence: assuming the injection already carries the NNN-th harmonic (a pulse), the first-order theory applies directly. Noise shaping and the closed-form output jitter: derived on this site (not in the 5 PDFs); the full derivation is in Section 4 of subharmonic_injection, and this lab's (e)(f1) are that derivation's independent numerical adjudication. The first-order sawtooth reference-spur formula: derived on this site (subharmonic_injection, Section 4.4); this lab's (f2) verifies it via an FFT of the deterministic sawtooth phase modulation.

documents.t: Phase-only toy model: amplitude dynamics (the APF) are ignored; at zero detuning the LC's lock point sits at the voltage peak, where a pulse also kicks the amplitude ([P4]'s APF), a second-order effect when qinj≪qmaxq_{inj}\ll q_{max}qinj​≪qmax​ — not covered by this lab. Weak injection: qinj/qmax=0.05q_{inj}/q_{max}=0.05qinj​/qmax​=0.05 or 0.010.010.01; (d) already measures the first-order theory's O(qinj/qmax)O(q_{inj}/q_{max})O(qinj​/qmax​) deviation; stronger injection needs the APF correction from paper_004_large_injection_transient. White-FM noise assumption (Engine 1's noise part): σw2=κ2Tinj\sigma_w^2=\kappa^2T_{inj}σw2​=κ2Tinj​ is the exact result for white FM noise; under flicker FM the variance is no longer ∝t\propto t∝t — not covered by this lab. The ring toy is a triangular construction: a real ring's ISF flank is not a strict triangle, and its dead zone is not strictly zero; the order-of-magnitude conclusion driven by qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (the ring's β\betaβ wins on small qmaxq_{max}qmax​, not on slope) is unaffected by this simplification — see the ring-vs-LC table in Section 3 of subharmonic_injection. f≪fref/2f\ll f_{ref}/2f≪fref​/2: (e)'s discrete ∣H∣2\vert H\vert^2∣H∣2 equals the continuous first-order PLL only well below fref/2f_{ref}/2fref​/2; sampling effects start to show up near fref/2f_{ref}/2fref​/2 (this lab logs only near f<fref/8f<f_{ref}/8f<fref​/8). First-order spur: (f2)'s sawtooth approximation ignores direct pulse feedthrough, AM caused by the APF, and pulse-width effects — none of these are in the phase-only model, and are honestly left out (see Section 4.4 of subharmonic_injection).
documents.s: 11. Limitations and approximations

documents.t: (a) Lock range ∝1/N\propto1/N∝1/N: the unaveraged-ODE sweep over N=2N=2N=2–202020 gives a log-log slope of −1.000-1.000−1.000 (LC and ring alike), with measured/theory ratios of 1.00001.00001.0000 (LC) and 1.00301.00301.0030 (ring). (b) Pulse-width effect: LC follows sinc(τp/T0)\mathrm{sinc}(\tau_p/T_0)sinc(τp​/T0​) exactly (deviation 10−410^{-4}10−4); the ring's multi-harmonic energy makes the plain sinc fail (deviation 0.740.740.74), requiring the extremum of the box-averaged ISF to match (deviation 0.00740.00740.0074). (c) A pure sine cannot lock: at the same Irms=250 μI_{rms}=250\ \muIrms​=250 μA, the pulse train locks at 15/15 grid points while the pure sine locks at 0/15 — completely unable to lock at first order, with only the second-order pushing effect left (LC: −158.7-158.7−158.7 kHz, matching the analytic formula at a ratio of 1.0001.0001.000). (d) β\betaβ's first-order precision: the ODE step response against the first-order prediction has ratio 0.980.980.98–1.031.031.03 (qinj/qmax=0.05q_{inj}/q_{max}=0.05qinj​/qmax​=0.05), tightening at 0.010.010.01; the deviation is essentially the second-order term 1−e−β1-e^{-\beta}1−e−β, with headline βODE=0.04858\beta_{ODE}=0.04858βODE​=0.04858 against the first-order 0.049790.049790.04979. (e) Noise shaping: the locked PSD's low-frequency plateau matches theory to a ratio of 0.9910.9910.991, and the corner measures 1.9341.9341.934 MHz — an almost exact match (ratio 1.00021.00021.0002) against the exact discrete closed form (not the simplified βfref/2π\beta f_{ref}/2\piβfref​/2π). (f) Jitter and spur: the output jitter's fitted power-law slope is 0.497≈1/20.497\approx1/20.497≈1/2, giving 2.2262.2262.226 fs at N=20N=20N=20 (closed form 2.2282.2282.228 fs); the reference spur matches the first-order sawtooth formula to within 0.010.010.01 dB. The two independent engines (the linearized map and the unaveraged ODE) agree with each other to within 0.10.10.1–1%1\%1% at the canonical parameters — every closed form on subharmonic_injection has passed this lab's numerical adjudication.

documents.t: However beautiful the theory, without numbers there is no feel. This page uses three small examples to turn the conversions among phase, time, dBc/Hz, and jitter into reflexes. Each example comes with a Python check; the full library lives in simulations/common/. Formula sources: the phase/time/jitter conversions and the 1/f² integral are all standard results, consistent with [P1] A. Hajimiri and T. H. Lee, "A General Theory of Phase Noise in Electrical Oscillators," IEEE JSSC, 33(2), 1998 (especially Eq.(21)); step-by-step derivations in impulse_to_phase_shift and psd_phase_noise_jitter. Why drill the numbers first: an analog designer's ability to estimate orders of magnitude at the whiteboard matters more than memorizing formulas. Given "−100-100−100 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, 5 GHz," you should be able to estimate "a few hundred fs of jitter" within 30 seconds.

Phase step: Δϕ=Γ Δqqmax=0.5×10−1510−12=5×10−4 rad (≈0.0286∘).\Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma\,\Delta q}{q_{max}}=\frac{0.5\times10^{-15}}{10^{-12}}=5\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}\;(\approx0.0286^\circ).Δϕ=qmax​ΓΔq​=10−120.5×10−15​=5×10−4 rad(≈0.0286∘). Timing error (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz): Δt=5×10−42π×5×109≈15.9 fs.\Delta t=\frac{5\times10^{-4}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{9}}\approx15.9\ \text{fs}.Δt=2π×5×1095×10−4​≈15.9 fs. documents.t: Given L(1 MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz, assuming a 1/f² slope, integrating from 1 MHz to 100 MHz, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, estimate the rms jitter. Step 1: convert dBc/Hz to linear and recover the phase PSD. Under the single-tone small-angle approximation L(f)≈12Sϕ(f)\mathcal{L}(f)\approx\frac12 S_\phi(f)L(f)≈21​Sϕ​(f), so Sϕ(f)=2⋅10L(f)/10S_\phi(f)=2\cdot10^{\mathcal{L}(f)/10}Sϕ​(f)=2⋅10L(f)/10. At 1 MHz: L=−100\mathcal{L}=-100L=−100 dBc/Hz ⇒10−10\Rightarrow 10^{-10}⇒10−10, Sϕ(1MHz)=2×10−10S_\phi(1\text{MHz})=2\times10^{-10}Sϕ​(1MHz)=2×10−10 rad²/Hz. Step 2: write down the 1/f² shape. Anchored at fref=1f_{ref}=1fref​=1 MHz: Sϕ(f)=Sϕ(fref)(freff)2=2×10−10(106f)2.S_\phi(f)=S_\phi(f_{ref})\left(\frac{f_{ref}}{f}\right)^2=2\times10^{-10}\left(\frac{10^6}{f}\right)^2.Sϕ​(f)=Sϕ​(fref​)(ffref​​)2=2×10−10(f106​)2. Step 3: integrate to get the phase variance. σϕ2=∫f1f2Sϕ(f) df=2×10−10 (106)2 ⁣∫106108dff2=2×102(1106−1108).\sigma_\phi^2=\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_\phi(f)\,df=2\times10^{-10}\,(10^6)^2\!\int_{10^6}^{10^8}\frac{df}{f^2}=2\times10^{2}\left(\frac{1}{10^6}-\frac{1}{10^8}\right).σϕ2​=∫f1​f2​​Sϕ​(f)df=2×10−10(106)2∫106108​f2df​=2×102(1061​−1081​).σϕ2=200×(10−6−10−8)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2⇒σϕ=1.407×10−2 rad=14.07 mrad.\sigma_\phi^2=200\times(10^{-6}-10^{-8})=200\times9.9\times10^{-7}=1.98\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}^2\Rightarrow\sigma_\phi=1.407\times10^{-2}\ \text{rad}=14.07\ \text{mrad}.σϕ2​=200×(10−6−10−8)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2⇒σϕ​=1.407×10−2 rad=14.07 mrad. Step 4: convert to rms jitter. σt=σϕ2πf0=1.407×10−22π×5×109≈4.48×10−13 s=447.9 fs.\sigma_t=\frac{\sigma_\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{1.407\times10^{-2}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{9}}\approx4.48\times10^{-13}\ \text{s}=447.9\ \text{fs}.σt​=2πf0​σϕ​​=2π×5×1091.407×10−2​≈4.48×10−13 s=447.9 fs. Feel: the integral is dominated by the lower limit f1f_1f1​ (the 1/f11/f_11/f1​ term is largest) — so "where you start integrating" is critical for 1/f². Reference point: if this part were −120-120−120 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz (10× better in power, 102=10\sqrt{10^2}=10102​=10× in voltage), the jitter shrinks to roughly ~45 fs. This is exactly the figure of lab_08; the numerical integration matches the analytic expression exactly. import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import leeson_one_over_f2, integrate_rms_jitter f = np.logspace(6, 8, 4000) # 1 MHz -> 100 MHz L = leeson_one_over_f2(f, L_ref_dbc=-100, f_ref=1e6) # 1/f^2 skirt sigma_t, sigma_phi = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L, f0=5e9, fmin=1e6, fmax=100e6) print(sigma_phi*1e3, "mrad ;", sigma_t*1e15, "fs") # -> 14.07 mrad ; 447.9 fs Full script: simulations/lab_08_jitter_integration.py.

documents.t: This page is the hands-on worked-example bank for ISF / phase noise / jitter. The theory pages show where the formulas come from; here you learn to plug in the numbers, compute all the way through, check the units, and verify with one line of Python. All formulas are carried over verbatim from [the AUTHORING_SPEC authoritative formula table]; numbers follow numerical_feeling and the spec Section 8 canonical values (qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, L(1MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz). How to use this page: cover the step-by-step solution, work each problem yourself, then check. The core skill of an analog designer is order-of-magnitude estimation at the whiteboard — seeing "−100-100−100 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, 5 GHz" you should call out "a few hundred fs of jitter" within 30 seconds. The one-line Python at the end of each problem is only for checking, never a substitute for the hand calculation. Four levels: (A) Basic conversions: rad ↔ fs, dBc ↔ linear, phase PSD ↔ L\mathcal{L}L. Drill until they become reflexes. (B) ISF → phase noise: Eq.(21)/(23)/(24) algebra — turn Γrms,c0,qmax\Gamma_{rms},c_0,q_{max}Γrms​,c0​,qmax​ into dBc/Hz. (C) jitter integration: integrate L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) to get σt\sigma_tσt​; the high-pass kernel of period jitter. (D) design back-calculation: how large a qmax/Γrmsq_{max}/\Gamma_{rms}qmax​/Γrms​ for −120-120−120 dBc/Hz; how to choose the ring stage count NNN. Every problem follows a fixed format: Problem → step-by-step solution (with units) → Result → dimension check → one-line Python verification. All Python calls real functions from simulations/common/ (see the spec Section 5 API) and runs as-is.

documents.t: Problem: f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δϕ=1\Delta\phi=1Δϕ=1 mrad; find the timing error Δt\Delta tΔt. Step-by-step solution Step 1: write the phase→time conversion (spec formula 17, Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0)\Delta t=\Delta\phi/(2\pi f_0)Δt=Δϕ/(2πf0​)). The unit of 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ is rad/s (angular frequency) and Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is rad; the quotient is seconds: Δt=Δϕ2πf0=1×10−3 rad2π×5×109 rad/s.\Delta t=\frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{1\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{9}\ \text{rad/s}} .Δt=2πf0​Δϕ​=2π×5×109 rad/s1×10−3 rad​. Step 2: evaluate the denominator: 2π×5×109=3.1416×10102\pi\times5\times10^{9}=3.1416\times10^{10}2π×5×109=3.1416×1010 rad/s. Δt=10−33.1416×1010 s=3.183×10−14 s=31.8 fs.\Delta t=\frac{10^{-3}}{3.1416\times10^{10}}\ \text{s}=3.183\times10^{-14}\ \text{s}=31.8\ \text{fs} .Δt=3.1416×101010−3​ s=3.183×10−14 s=31.8 fs. Result: Δt≈31.8\Delta t\approx31.8Δt≈31.8 fs. Dimension check: [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] ✓. Intuition anchor: at 5 GHz, "1 mrad ≈ 32 fs"; conversely "1 rad ≈ 31.8 ps" (the very same 31.8331.8331.83 digits, offset by 10310^3103). The period is T=200T=200T=200 ps, so 1 mrad is about 1.6×10−41.6\times10^{-4}1.6×10−4 of a period. documents.t: Problem: L=−100\mathcal{L}=-100L=−100 dBc/Hz. Convert to linear (power ratio relative to the carrier, per Hz), then recover the phase PSD SϕS_\phiSϕ​. Step-by-step solution Step 1: dBc/Hz is the "decibels relative to carrier" unit of 10log⁡10(⋅)10\log_{10}(\cdot)10log10​(⋅); invert by dividing by 10 and raising 10 to that power: Llinear=10L/10=10−100/10=10−10 [1/Hz].\mathcal{L}_{\text{linear}}=10^{\mathcal{L}/10}=10^{-100/10}=10^{-10}\ [\text{1/Hz}] .Llinear​=10L/10=10−100/10=10−10 [1/Hz]. Step 2: under the small-angle single-tone PM approximation, L(f)≈12Sϕ(f)\mathcal{L}(f)\approx\tfrac12 S_\phi(f)L(f)≈21​Sϕ​(f) (spec formula 16 and the Section 10.2 "L≈12SϕL\approx\tfrac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​" derivation), so back out the phase PSD: Sϕ=2 Llinear=2×10−10 rad2/Hz.S_\phi=2\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{linear}}=2\times10^{-10}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz} .Sϕ​=2Llinear​=2×10−10 rad2/Hz. Result: Llinear=10−10\mathcal{L}_{\text{linear}}=10^{-10}Llinear​=10−10/Hz, Sϕ=2×10−10S_\phi=2\times10^{-10}Sϕ​=2×10−10 rad²/Hz. Dimension check: dBc/Hz is a dimensionless power ratio per Hz; Llinear\mathcal{L}_{\text{linear}}Llinear​ is likewise 1/Hz; after the ×2 it reads as a phase PSD in rad²/Hz (rad² is the unit of phase variance; integrating the variance density over fff gives rad²) ✓. Mnemonic: every −10-10−10 dB = one decade less in linear power; every −20-20−20 dB = one decade less in voltage/phase amplitude. Python verification import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import phase_psd_to_l_dbc_per_hz s_phi = 2 * 10**(-100/10) print(s_phi, "rad^2/Hz") # -> 2e-10 print(phase_psd_to_l_dbc_per_hz(s_phi), "dBc/Hz") # -> -100.0 (round trip consistent)

Result: Δϕ=5×10−4\Delta\phi=5\times10^{-4}Δϕ=5×10−4 rad (0.0286∘0.0286^\circ0.0286∘), Δt≈15.9\Delta t\approx15.9Δt≈15.9 fs. Dimension check: Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ: [C]/[C]=[\text{C}]/[\text{C}]=[C]/[C]= dimensionless ✓; Δt\Delta tΔt: [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] ✓. Python verification from simulations.common.isf_utils import impulse_to_phase_step from simulations.common.noise_utils import phase_to_time_error dphi = impulse_to_phase_step(delta_q=1e-15, gamma_value=0.5, qmax=1e-12) print(dphi, "rad ->", phase_to_time_error(dphi, 5e9)*1e15, "fs") # 0.0005 rad -> 15.92 fs

documents.t: Problem: an ideal LC oscillator has ISF Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ. With the same Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC and qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, inject at the zero crossing (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2, maximum waveform slope) and at the peak (θ=0\theta=0θ=0, waveform top), and find Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ in each case. Step-by-step solution Step 1: read off the ISF at both points. Note the phase convention here: with V∝cos⁡θV\propto\cos\thetaV∝cosθ the peak is at θ=0\theta=0θ=0 and the (falling-edge) zero crossing at θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2; the ideal LC has Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ: Γ(θ=π/2)=−sin⁡π2=−1,Γ(θ=0)=−sin⁡0=0.\Gamma(\theta=\pi/2)=-\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}=-1,\qquad \Gamma(\theta=0)=-\sin 0=0 .Γ(θ=π/2)=−sin2π​=−1,Γ(θ=0)=−sin0=0. Step 2: substitute each into Δϕ=Γ Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=ΓΔq/qmax​ (Δq/qmax=10−15/10−12=10−3\Delta q/q_{max}=10^{-15}/10^{-12}=10^{-3}Δq/qmax​=10−15/10−12=10−3): ΔϕZC=(−1)(10−3)=−1×10−3 rad,Δϕpeak=(0)(10−3)=0 rad.\Delta\phi_{\text{ZC}}=(-1)(10^{-3})=-1\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad},\qquad \Delta\phi_{\text{peak}}=(0)(10^{-3})=0\ \text{rad}.ΔϕZC​=(−1)(10−3)=−1×10−3 rad,Δϕpeak​=(0)(10−3)=0 rad. Result: injection at the zero crossing → −1-1−1 mrad (maximum phase effect); injection at the peak → 0 rad (pure amplitude change, no phase change). Dimension check: both are [ ]⋅[C]/[C]=[\,]\cdot[\text{C}]/[\text{C}]=[]⋅[C]/[C]= rad ✓. This is the essence of LTV (linear time-variant) behavior: the effect of the same impulse depends on which phase of the waveform it kicks. Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0 at the peak because the perturbation there is purely radial (amplitude) with no tangential (phase) component, and amplitude is pulled back by the restoring mechanism. See impulse_to_phase_shift. Python verification import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, impulse_to_phase_step for name, th in [("ZC", np.pi/2), ("peak", 0.0)]: g = gamma_lc_ideal(th) # = -sin(theta) print(name, impulse_to_phase_step(1e-15, g, 1e-12), "rad") # ZC -0.001 rad ; peak 0.0 rad

documents.t: This level repeatedly uses three signature formulas (all [P1], carried verbatim from spec Section 3): White noise 1/f² [P1] Eq.(21), p.185: L=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4Δω2)\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}\!\big(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\Delta\omega^2}\big)L=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​) flicker 1/f³ [P1] Eq.(23), p.185: contains the c02c_0^2c02​ and ω1/f/Δω\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omegaω1/f​/Δω factors. 1/f³ corner [P1] Eq.(24), p.185: Δω1/f3=ω1/f c02/(2Γrms2)\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\,c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​c02​/(2Γrms2​). Reminder: the denominator of Eq.(21) is 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2 (SSB bookkeeping convention). A clean time-domain derivation gives 2Δω22\Delta\omega^22Δω2; the factor of 2 is a well-known minor dispute in the literature and does not affect the Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ scaling or the −20-20−20 dB/dec slope. See white_noise_to_phase_noise. This page uses the 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2 of the original [P1] expression throughout.

documents.t: Problem: f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz offset, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, white noise in2‾/Δf=Si=10−24\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=S_i=10^{-24}in2​​/Δf=Si​=10−24 A²/Hz. Use Eq.(21) to find L(1MHz)\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})L(1MHz). Step-by-step solution Step 1: convert the offset frequency to angular frequency: Δω=2πΔf=2π×106=6.283×106\Delta\omega=2\pi\Delta f=2\pi\times10^{6}=6.283\times10^{6}Δω=2πΔf=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s, Δω2=3.948×1013 (rad/s)2\Delta\omega^2=3.948\times10^{13}\ (\text{rad/s})^2Δω2=3.948×1013 (rad/s)2. Step 2: evaluate the bracket of Eq.(21) (separate the dimensionless part from the part carrying units first): Γrms2qmax2=0.25(10−12)2=0.25×1024=2.5×1023 C−2.\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}=\frac{0.25}{(10^{-12})^2}=0.25\times10^{24}=2.5\times10^{23}\ \text{C}^{-2} .qmax2​Γrms2​​=(10−12)20.25​=0.25×1024=2.5×1023 C−2.Si4Δω2=10−244×3.948×1013=10−241.579×1014=6.333×10−39 A2/Hz⋅s2.\frac{S_i}{4\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{10^{-24}}{4\times3.948\times10^{13}}=\frac{10^{-24}}{1.579\times10^{14}}=6.333\times10^{-39}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz}\cdot\text{s}^2 .4Δω2Si​​=4×3.948×101310−24​=1.579×101410−24​=6.333×10−39 A2/Hz⋅s2. Step 3: multiply (units checked below): 2.5×1023×6.333×10−39=1.583×10−15.2.5\times10^{23}\times6.333\times10^{-39}=1.583\times10^{-15} .2.5×1023×6.333×10−39=1.583×10−15. Step 4: take 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​: L=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15)=−148.0 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}(1.583\times10^{-15})=-148.0\ \text{dBc/Hz} .L=10log10​(1.583×10−15)=−148.0 dBc/Hz. Result: L(1MHz)=−148.0\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-148.0L(1MHz)=−148.0 dBc/Hz. Dimension check: the bracket must be dimensionless (argument of a log). [C−2]⋅[A2 Hz−1 s2][\text{C}^{-2}]\cdot[\text{A}^2\,\text{Hz}^{-1}\,\text{s}^2][C−2]⋅[A2Hz−1s2]; with A=C/s\text{A}=\text{C/s}A=C/s ⇒ A2=C2/s2\text{A}^2=\text{C}^2/\text{s}^2A2=C2/s2, Hz−1=s\text{Hz}^{-1}=\text{s}Hz−1=s, collect C−2⋅(C2/s2)⋅s⋅s2=C−2⋅C2⋅s−2⋅s3=s\text{C}^{-2}\cdot(\text{C}^2/\text{s}^2)\cdot\text{s}\cdot\text{s}^2=\text{C}^{-2}\cdot\text{C}^2\cdot\text{s}^{-2}\cdot\text{s}^{3}=\text{s}C−2⋅(C2/s2)⋅s⋅s2=C−2⋅C2⋅s−2⋅s3=s. One 1/s1/\text{s}1/s is still missing — it comes from the per-Hz nature of a PSD: the result is "relative power per Hz", so the argument is really 1/Hz, and after the log it is dBc/Hz ✓. (This is exactly why the units are easy to misread; just remember "the final answer is dBc/Hz".) Intuition: this is the floor set by a single ideal white-noise source. Real circuits have multiple noise sources, cyclostationarity, and flicker; measurements come in tens of dB higher. Python verification import numpy as np Grms, qmax, Si = 0.5, 1e-12, 1e-24 dw = 2*np.pi*1e6 L = 10*np.log10((Grms**2/qmax**2) * (Si/(4*dw**2))) print(round(L, 2), "dBc/Hz") # -> -148.0

documents.t: Problem: the ideal-LC ISF is purely Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ, i.e. only the first harmonic c1=1c_1=1c1​=1 and all other cn=0c_n=0cn​=0. (a) Use Parseval (Eq.(20)) to find Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​; (b) with qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, find L. Step-by-step solution Step 1 (a): Parseval ([P1] Eq.(20)): ∑ncn2=2Γrms2\sum_n c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑n​cn2​=2Γrms2​. Here ∑ncn2=c12=1\sum_n c_n^2=c_1^2=1∑n​cn2​=c12​=1, so 2Γrms2=1 ⇒ Γrms=12≈0.707.2\Gamma_{rms}^2=1\ \Rightarrow\ \Gamma_{rms}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx0.707 .2Γrms2​=1 ⇒ Γrms​=2​1​≈0.707. (Direct check: Γrms2=12π∫02πsin⁡2θ dθ=12\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=\tfrac12Γrms2​=2π1​∫02π​sin2θdθ=21​, which also gives Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​ ✓.) Step 2 (b): substitute into Eq.(21) with Γrms2=0.5\Gamma_{rms}^2=0.5Γrms2​=0.5: L=10log⁡10 ⁣(0.5(10−12)2⋅10−244×3.948×1013)=10log⁡10(3.166×10−15)=−145.0 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{0.5}{(10^{-12})^2}\cdot\frac{10^{-24}}{4\times3.948\times10^{13}}\right) =10\log_{10}(3.166\times10^{-15})=-145.0\ \text{dBc/Hz} .L=10log10​((10−12)20.5​⋅4×3.948×101310−24​)=10log10​(3.166×10−15)=−145.0 dBc/Hz. Result: Γrms=0.707\Gamma_{rms}=0.707Γrms​=0.707; L(1MHz)=−145.0\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-145.0L(1MHz)=−145.0 dBc/Hz. Dimension check: Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is dimensionless (the cnc_ncn​ are dimensionless) ✓; L same as Example B1, dBc/Hz ✓. Note Γrms=0.707\Gamma_{rms}=0.707Γrms​=0.707 is larger than the canonical 0.50.50.5, so L comes out about 333 dB above B1 (10log⁡10(0.5/0.25)=310\log_{10}(0.5/0.25)=310log10​(0.5/0.25)=3 dB) — consistent. Python verification import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, gamma_rms theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 100000, endpoint=False) Grms = gamma_rms(theta, gamma_lc_ideal(theta)) print("Grms =", round(Grms, 4)) # -> 0.7071 L = 10*np.log10((Grms**2/(1e-12)**2)*(1e-24/(4*(2*np.pi*1e6)**2))) print(round(L, 2), "dBc/Hz") # -> -145.0
documents.s: Example B2: use Parseval to get Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ from cnc_ncn​, then compute L

documents.t: Problem: two oscillators with identical white noise and qmaxq_{max}qmax​, ω1/f=2π×1\omega_{1/f}=2\pi\times1ω1/f​=2π×1 MHz. A has a fully symmetric waveform (c0=0c_0=0c0​=0); B is slightly asymmetric (c0=0.2c_0=0.2c0​=0.2, c1=1c_1=1c1​=1). Which one shows close-in 1/f³ upconversion? What is each 1/f³ contribution at Δf=10\Delta f=10Δf=10 kHz? Step-by-step solution Step 1: look at Eq.(23) — phase noise in the 1/f³ region is proportional to c02c_0^2c02​. L1/f3=10log⁡10 ⁣(c02qmax2⋅Si8Δω2⋅ω1/fΔω).\mathcal{L}_{1/f^3}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{8\Delta\omega^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}\right) .L1/f3​=10log10​(qmax2​c02​​⋅8Δω2Si​​⋅Δωω1/f​​). Step 2, for A: c0=0⇒c_0=0\Rightarrowc0​=0⇒ the bracket =0⇒L1/f3→−∞=0\Rightarrow \mathcal{L}_{1/f^3}\to-\infty=0⇒L1/f3​→−∞ dBc/Hz (no flicker upconversion; the 1/f³ region is fully suppressed). In practice it never truly reaches −∞-\infty−∞ (other mechanisms take over), but it can sit far below B. Step 3, for B: c0=0.2c_0=0.2c0​=0.2, a finite value. Use Eq.(24) to compare the two 1/f³ corners: Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c022Γrms2.\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\Gamma_{rms}^2} .Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​. For B, ∑cn2=c02+c12=0.04+1=1.04⇒Γrms2=0.52\sum c_n^2=c_0^2+c_1^2=0.04+1=1.04\Rightarrow\Gamma_{rms}^2=0.52∑cn2​=c02​+c12​=0.04+1=1.04⇒Γrms2​=0.52, so Δω1/f3,B=ω1/f⋅0.042×0.52=ω1/f×0.0385.\Delta\omega_{1/f^3,B}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{0.04}{2\times0.52}=\omega_{1/f}\times0.0385 .Δω1/f3,B​=ω1/f​⋅2×0.520.04​=ω1/f​×0.0385. That is, B's 1/f³ corner sits at ≈0.0385 ω1/f=2π×38.5\approx0.0385\,\omega_{1/f}=2\pi\times38.5≈0.0385ω1/f​=2π×38.5 kHz. For A, the corner →0\to0→0. Result: A (symmetric, c0=0c_0=0c0​=0) has no 1/f³ upconversion; B (c0=0.2c_0=0.2c0​=0.2) does, with a corner near 38.538.538.5 kHz. Design rule: suppress c0c_0c0​ through waveform symmetry and the 1/f³ corner can be pushed far below the device ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​. Dimension check: in Eq.(24), c02/Γrms2c_0^2/\Gamma_{rms}^2c02​/Γrms2​ is dimensionless; multiplying by ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ (rad/s) gives rad/s ✓. Python verification import numpy as np w_1f = 2*np.pi*1e6 for name, c0, c1 in [("A", 0.0, 1.0), ("B", 0.2, 1.0)]: Grms2 = 0.5*(c0**2 + c1**2) # Parseval: sum cn^2 = 2 Grms^2 corner = w_1f * c0**2/(2*Grms2) print(name, "1/f^3 corner =", corner/(2*np.pi)*1e-3, "kHz") # A 0.0 kHz ; B 38.46 kHz

documents.t: Problem: reuse the B1 oscillator (L(1MHz)=−148\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-148L(1MHz)=−148 dBc/Hz, 1/f² region). What is L at Δf=10\Delta f=10Δf=10 MHz? (I.e. push the offset out by 10×.) Step-by-step solution Step 1: in Eq.(21), L∝1/Δω2\mathcal{L}\propto1/\Delta\omega^2L∝1/Δω2; after the log this is −20log⁡10Δω+-20\log_{10}\Delta\omega+−20log10​Δω+const, i.e. every 10× in offset drops L by 20 dB (−20-20−20 dB/decade). Step 2: Δf\Delta fΔf goes from 1 MHz → 10 MHz (×10): L(10MHz)=L(1MHz)−20log⁡10(10)=−148−20=−168 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}(10\text{MHz})=\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})-20\log_{10}(10)=-148-20=-168\ \text{dBc/Hz} .L(10MHz)=L(1MHz)−20log10​(10)=−148−20=−168 dBc/Hz. Result: L(10MHz)=−168\mathcal{L}(10\text{MHz})=-168L(10MHz)=−168 dBc/Hz. Dimension check: the argument of −20log⁡10(Δf2/Δf1)-20\log_{10}(\Delta f_2/\Delta f_1)−20log10​(Δf2​/Δf1​) is dimensionless (a frequency ratio) ✓; the result is a dB difference, and adding it to dBc/Hz still gives dBc/Hz ✓. Intuition: "20 dB per decade" in the 1/f² region is the most-used visual slope on a phase-noise plot; compare −30-30−30 dB/dec in the 1/f³ region. Python verification import numpy as np Grms, qmax, Si = 0.5, 1e-12, 1e-24 def L(df): return 10*np.log10((Grms**2/qmax**2)*(Si/(4*(2*np.pi*df)**2))) print(round(L(1e6),2), round(L(10e6),2), "dBc/Hz", "slope =", round(L(10e6)-L(1e6),1), "dB/dec") # -148.0 -168.0 ; -20.0

documents.t: Core idea: phase noise is a frequency-domain density, jitter is a time-domain rms; they connect via "integrate + square root + ÷(2πf0)\div(2\pi f_0)÷(2πf0​)" (spec formulas 18, 19): σϕ2=∫f1f2Sϕ(f) df,σt=σϕ2πf0.\sigma_\phi^2=\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_\phi(f)\,df,\qquad \sigma_t=\frac{\sigma_\phi}{2\pi f_0} .σϕ2​=∫f1​f2​​Sϕ​(f)df,σt​=2πf0​σϕ​​.
documents.s: Level C: jitter integration

documents.t: Problem: L(1MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz, 1/f² slope, integrate from f1=1f_1=1f1​=1 MHz to f2=100f_2=100f2​=100 MHz, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz. Find σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ and σt\sigma_tσt​. Step-by-step solution Step 1: convert the datasheet point to a phase PSD (using A2): Sϕ(fref)=2×10−10S_\phi(f_{ref})=2\times10^{-10}Sϕ​(fref​)=2×10−10 rad²/Hz, fref=1f_{ref}=1fref​=1 MHz. Step 2: write the 1/f² shape (anchored at freff_{ref}fref​): Sϕ(f)=Sϕ(fref)(freff)2=2×10−10 (106)2 1f2.S_\phi(f)=S_\phi(f_{ref})\left(\frac{f_{ref}}{f}\right)^2=2\times10^{-10}\,(10^6)^2\,\frac1{f^2} .Sϕ​(f)=Sϕ​(fref​)(ffref​​)2=2×10−10(106)2f21​. Step 3: integrate (∫f−2df=−1/f\int f^{-2}df=-1/f∫f−2df=−1/f): σϕ2=2×10−10(106)2 ⁣∫106108 ⁣dff2=2×102(1106−1108)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2.\sigma_\phi^2=2\times10^{-10}(10^6)^2\!\int_{10^6}^{10^8}\!\frac{df}{f^2} =2\times10^{2}\left(\frac1{10^6}-\frac1{10^8}\right)=200\times9.9\times10^{-7}=1.98\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}^2 .σϕ2​=2×10−10(106)2∫106108​f2df​=2×102(1061​−1081​)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2. So σϕ=1.98×10−4=1.407×10−2\sigma_\phi=\sqrt{1.98\times10^{-4}}=1.407\times10^{-2}σϕ​=1.98×10−4​=1.407×10−2 rad =14.07=14.07=14.07 mrad. Step 4: convert to rms jitter (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz): σt=σϕ2πf0=1.407×10−22π×5×109≈4.48×10−13 s=447.9 fs.\sigma_t=\frac{\sigma_\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{1.407\times10^{-2}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{9}}\approx4.48\times10^{-13}\ \text{s}=447.9\ \text{fs} .σt​=2πf0​σϕ​​=2π×5×1091.407×10−2​≈4.48×10−13 s=447.9 fs. Result: σϕ=14.07\sigma_\phi=14.07σϕ​=14.07 mrad, σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs. Dimension check: σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​: [rad2/Hz]⋅[Hz]=rad2[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]\cdot[\text{Hz}]=\text{rad}^2[rad2/Hz]⋅[Hz]=rad2 ✓; σt\sigma_tσt​: [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] ✓. Intuition: the 1/f² integral is dominated by the lower limit f1f_1f1​ (1/f1≫1/f21/f_1\gg1/f_21/f1​≫1/f2​) — where you start integrating matters most. With −120-120−120 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz instead (20 dB better = 1/100 the power, 1/10 the amplitude), the jitter shrinks to ~45 fs. Python verification import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import leeson_one_over_f2, integrate_rms_jitter f = np.logspace(6, 8, 4000) # 1 MHz -> 100 MHz L = leeson_one_over_f2(f, L_ref_dbc=-100, f_ref=1e6) # 1/f^2 skirt sigma_t, sigma_phi = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L, f0=5e9, fmin=1e6, fmax=100e6) print(round(sigma_phi*1e3,2), "mrad ;", round(sigma_t*1e15,1), "fs") # 14.07 mrad ; 447.9 fs
