documents.t: Problem: same spectrum as C1 (−100-100−100 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, 1/f², f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz), but integrate from f1=100f_1=100f1​=100 kHz to 100 MHz. Estimate σt\sigma_tσt​ and compare with C1. Step-by-step solution Step 1: for 1/f², σϕ2∝(1/f1−1/f2)≈1/f1\sigma_\phi^2\propto(1/f_1-1/f_2)\approx1/f_1σϕ2​∝(1/f1​−1/f2​)≈1/f1​ (lower-limit dominated). The lower limit moves from 10610^6106 to 10510^5105 (10× smaller), so 1/f11/f_11/f1​ is 10× larger: σϕ2≈2×102(1105−1108)=200×(10−5−10−8)≈2.0×10−3 rad2.\sigma_\phi^2\approx2\times10^{2}\left(\frac1{10^5}-\frac1{10^8}\right)=200\times(10^{-5}-10^{-8})\approx2.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad}^2 .σϕ2​≈2×102(1051​−1081​)=200×(10−5−10−8)≈2.0×10−3 rad2. Step 2: σϕ=2.0×10−3=4.47×10−2\sigma_\phi=\sqrt{2.0\times10^{-3}}=4.47\times10^{-2}σϕ​=2.0×10−3​=4.47×10−2 rad =44.7=44.7=44.7 mrad (about 10≈3.16\sqrt{10}\approx3.1610​≈3.16× C1). Step 3: σt=4.47×10−22π×5×109≈1.42×10−12\sigma_t=\dfrac{4.47\times10^{-2}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{9}}\approx1.42\times10^{-12}σt​=2π×5×1094.47×10−2​≈1.42×10−12 s =1.42=1.42=1.42 ps. Result: σt≈1.42\sigma_t\approx1.42σt​≈1.42 ps (C1 was 448 fs). Lowering the limit by 10× → jitter grows by about 10≈3.16\sqrt{10}\approx3.1610​≈3.16×. Dimension check: same as C1 ✓. Intuition: this is why an "rms jitter" number is only meaningful with its integration band attached; the instrument's lower limit (or the PLL loop bandwidth) determines how much accumulated jitter you get to see. Python verification import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import leeson_one_over_f2, integrate_rms_jitter f = np.logspace(5, 8, 6000) # 100 kHz -> 100 MHz L = leeson_one_over_f2(f, L_ref_dbc=-100, f_ref=1e6) sigma_t, sigma_phi = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L, f0=5e9, fmin=1e5, fmax=100e6) print(round(sigma_phi*1e3,1), "mrad ;", round(sigma_t*1e12,2), "ps") # ~44.7 mrad ; ~1.42 ps

documents.t: Problem: period jitter (the deviation of a single period, Tk−TT_k-TTk​−T) is the first difference of phase. Using the spec Section 10.2 kernel ∣1−e−j2πfT∣2\lvert1-e^{-j2\pi fT}\rvert^2∣1−e−j2πfT∣2, estimate the period jitter σT\sigma_TσT​ for the C1 spectrum (−100-100−100 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, 1/f², f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, T=200T=200T=200 ps). Step-by-step solution Step 1: write the period-jitter formula (spec Section 10.2 period/cycle-to-cycle kernel): σT2=1(2πf0)2∫0∞Sϕ(f) ∣1−e−j2πfT∣2 df.\sigma_T^2=\frac1{(2\pi f_0)^2}\int_0^{\infty}S_\phi(f)\,\lvert1-e^{-j2\pi fT}\rvert^2\,df .σT2​=(2πf0​)21​∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)∣1−e−j2πfT∣2df. Step 2: understand what the kernel does: ∣1−e−j2πfT∣2=2(1−cos⁡2πfT)=4sin⁡2(πfT)\lvert1-e^{-j2\pi fT}\rvert^2=2(1-\cos2\pi fT)=4\sin^2(\pi fT)∣1−e−j2πfT∣2=2(1−cos2πfT)=4sin2(πfT) is high-pass — low frequencies (fT≪1fT\ll1fT≪1) are suppressed (∝f2\propto f^2∝f2), so period jitter is not dominated by the low-frequency 1/f² lower limit (opposite to the accumulated jitter of C1/C2). This is why period jitter is usually much smaller than the "accumulated jitter" of the same spectrum. Step 3: numerical integration (not feasible by hand — hand it to the computer; constants aligned with the spec kernel). See the Python below: σT≈27.6\sigma_T\approx27.6σT​≈27.6 fs. Result: σT≈27.6\sigma_T\approx27.6σT​≈27.6 fs (versus the C1 accumulated σt=448\sigma_t=448σt​=448 fs — more than an order of magnitude smaller). Dimension check: the kernel ∣1−e−j2πfT∣2\lvert1-e^{-j2\pi fT}\rvert^2∣1−e−j2πfT∣2 is dimensionless; ∫Sϕ (kernel) df\int S_\phi\,(\text{kernel})\,df∫Sϕ​(kernel)df gives rad²; dividing by the (rad/s)2(\text{rad/s})^2(rad/s)2 of (2πf0)2(2\pi f_0)^2(2πf0​)2… note the order: first rad², then dividing by (2πf0)2(2\pi f_0)^2(2πf0​)2 gives s², and the square root gives s ✓. Resolved (v5): the exact prefactor for period/cycle-to-cycle jitter has been derived from first principles + Monte-Carlo verified in jitter_kernels (under the single-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​ convention the kernel is 4sin⁡24\sin^24sin2 with prefactor 1/ω021/\omega_0^21/ω02​; the 27.6 fs here is the band-limited version of that page's closed-form 28.28 fs) Cross-check against standard references; here we use the kernel given in spec Section 10.2, and the number is for order-of-magnitude feel only. Python verification import numpy as np T, f0, fref, Lref = 1/5e9, 5e9, 1e6, -100 f = np.logspace(3, 10, 2_000_000) # wide band: the high-pass kernel suppresses low f S_phi = 2 * 10**((Lref + 20*np.log10(fref/f))/10) # 1/f^2 phase PSD kernel = np.abs(1 - np.exp(-1j*2*np.pi*f*T))**2 # first-difference high-pass kernel trapz = getattr(np, "trapezoid", np.trapz) sigma_T = np.sqrt(trapz(S_phi*kernel, f)) / (2*np.pi*f0) print(round(sigma_T*1e15, 1), "fs") # ~27.6 fs

documents.t: Problem ([P2] Eq.(8)): a ring has jitter proportionality constant κ=1×10−8 s\kappa=1\times10^{-8}\ \sqrt{\text{s}}κ=1×10−8 s​ (toy value). Find the accumulated rms jitter for measurement intervals Δt=1 μ\Delta t=1\ \muΔt=1 μs and Δt=1\Delta t=1Δt=1 ms. Step-by-step solution Step 1: the random-walk law ([P2] Eq.(8), the signature of an oscillator with no absolute time reference): σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​. Step 2: Δt=10−6\Delta t=10^{-6}Δt=10−6 s: σΔt=10−810−6=10−8×10−3=10−11 s=10 ps.\sigma_{\Delta t}=10^{-8}\sqrt{10^{-6}}=10^{-8}\times10^{-3}=10^{-11}\ \text{s}=10\ \text{ps} .σΔt​=10−810−6​=10−8×10−3=10−11 s=10 ps. Step 3: Δt=10−3\Delta t=10^{-3}Δt=10−3 s: σΔt=10−810−3=10−8×3.162×10−2=3.16×10−10 s=316 ps.\sigma_{\Delta t}=10^{-8}\sqrt{10^{-3}}=10^{-8}\times3.162\times10^{-2}=3.16\times10^{-10}\ \text{s}=316\ \text{ps} .σΔt​=10−810−3​=10−8×3.162×10−2=3.16×10−10 s=316 ps. Result: 1 μs → 10 ps; 1 ms → 316 ps. Interval ×1000, jitter ×1000≈31.6\sqrt{1000}\approx31.61000​≈31.6. Dimension check: κ\kappaκ has units of s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​, Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ is s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​, and their product is s ✓ (which is also why κ\kappaκ carries that odd unit). Intuition: the phase of a ring (no high-Q tank) is a pure random walk — the longer you wait, the larger the error, and it never converges. This is exactly the time-domain picture of why rings are noisier than LC. Companion figure: Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image (the same script as lc_vs_ring_isf_comparison.png; see its Translator's note above/below on this page for the printed terms). Python verification import numpy as np kappa = 1e-8 # sqrt(s) for dt in [1e-6, 1e-3]: print(dt, "s ->", kappa*np.sqrt(dt)*1e12, "ps") # 1e-06 s -> 10.0 ps ; 0.001 s -> 316.2 ps

documents.t: Problem: spec L(1MHz)=−120\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-120L(1MHz)=−120 dBc/Hz, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz. Assume a single white-noise source Si=1×10−21S_i=1\times10^{-21}Si​=1×10−21 A²/Hz (1000× the canonical value, closer to a real node injection) and Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5. Back-solve the required qmaxq_{max}qmax​. Step-by-step solution Step 1: solve Eq.(21) for qmaxq_{max}qmax​. First convert the spec to linear: Llin=10−120/10=10−12\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}=10^{-120/10}=10^{-12}Llin​=10−120/10=10−12. 10−12=Γrms2qmax2⋅Si4Δω2 ⇒ qmax2=Γrms2 Si4Δω2 Llin.10^{-12}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{4\Delta\omega^2} \ \Rightarrow\ q_{max}^2=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2\,S_i}{4\Delta\omega^2\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}} .10−12=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2Si​​ ⇒ qmax2​=4Δω2Llin​Γrms2​Si​​. Step 2: plug in numbers (Δω2=3.948×1013\Delta\omega^2=3.948\times10^{13}Δω2=3.948×1013, Γrms2=0.25\Gamma_{rms}^2=0.25Γrms2​=0.25): qmax2=0.25×10−214×3.948×1013×10−12=0.25×10−211.579×102=1.583×10−24 C2.q_{max}^2=\frac{0.25\times10^{-21}}{4\times3.948\times10^{13}\times10^{-12}} =\frac{0.25\times10^{-21}}{1.579\times10^{2}}=1.583\times10^{-24}\ \text{C}^2 .qmax2​=4×3.948×1013×10−120.25×10−21​=1.579×1020.25×10−21​=1.583×10−24 C2. Step 3: take the square root: qmax=1.583×10−24=1.258×10−12q_{max}=\sqrt{1.583\times10^{-24}}=1.258\times10^{-12}qmax​=1.583×10−24​=1.258×10−12 C =1.26=1.26=1.26 pC. Result: qmax≈1.26q_{max}\approx1.26qmax​≈1.26 pC (i.e. raise the canonical 1 pC by about 26%; at this noise level the spec is met). Dimension check: qmax2q_{max}^2qmax2​: [ ]⋅[A2Hz−1]/([rad/s]2⋅[ ])[\,]\cdot[\text{A}^2\text{Hz}^{-1}]/([\text{rad/s}]^2\cdot[\,])[]⋅[A2Hz−1]/([rad/s]2⋅[]); with A2Hz−1=C2s−2⋅s=C2s−1\text{A}^2\text{Hz}^{-1}=\text{C}^2\text{s}^{-2}\cdot\text{s}=\text{C}^2\text{s}^{-1}A2Hz−1=C2s−2⋅s=C2s−1, dividing by s−2\text{s}^{-2}s−2 gives C2s\text{C}^2\text{s}C2s, and after absorbing the PSD's per-Hz it is C2\text{C}^2C2 ✓. Design intuition: L∝1/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto1/q_{max}^2L∝1/qmax2​, so doubling qmaxq_{max}qmax​ → 6 dB lower phase noise. Ways to increase qmax=CnodeVmaxq_{max}=C_{node}V_{max}qmax​=Cnode​Vmax​: raise the swing VmaxV_{max}Vmax​ or the node capacitance/current. Python verification import numpy as np Grms, Si, dw, Llin = 0.5, 1e-21, 2*np.pi*1e6, 10**(-120/10) qmax = np.sqrt(Grms**2 * Si / (4*dw**2 * Llin)) print(round(qmax*1e12, 3), "pC") # -> 1.258 pC

documents.t: Problem: same spec and noise as D1 (−120-120−120 dBc/Hz, Si=10−21S_i=10^{-21}Si​=10−21, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz), but this time qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC is fixed (the swing cannot be raised further). Back-solve the required Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. Step-by-step solution Step 1: solve Eq.(21) for Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​: Γrms2=Llin qmax2 4Δω2Si=10−12×(10−12)2×4×3.948×101310−21.\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}\,q_{max}^2\,4\Delta\omega^2}{S_i} =\frac{10^{-12}\times(10^{-12})^2\times4\times3.948\times10^{13}}{10^{-21}} .Γrms2​=Si​Llin​qmax2​4Δω2​=10−2110−12×(10−12)2×4×3.948×1013​. Step 2: evaluate the numerator term by term: 10−12×10−24=10−3610^{-12}\times10^{-24}=10^{-36}10−12×10−24=10−36; ×1.579×1014=1.579×10−22\times1.579\times10^{14}=1.579\times10^{-22}×1.579×1014=1.579×10−22. Divide by 10−2110^{-21}10−21: Γrms2=0.1579\Gamma_{rms}^2=0.1579Γrms2​=0.1579. Step 3: Γrms=0.1579=0.397\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{0.1579}=0.397Γrms​=0.1579​=0.397. Result: Γrms≈0.40\Gamma_{rms}\approx0.40Γrms​≈0.40 (the ISF rms must drop from 0.5 to 0.40, about a 20% reduction). Dimension check: Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ is dimensionless (same argument analysis as B1; all unit-bearing terms cancel) ✓. Design intuition: L∝Γrms2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2L∝Γrms2​, so halving Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ → 6 dB lower phase noise. Ways to lower Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​: waveform symmetry (suppress c0c_0c0​), schedule noise injection at phases where the ISF is small, more ring stages (see D3). D1 (tune qmaxq_{max}qmax​) and D2 (tune Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​) are two independent knobs toward the same spec. Python verification import numpy as np qmax, Si, dw, Llin = 1e-12, 1e-21, 2*np.pi*1e6, 10**(-120/10) Grms = np.sqrt(Llin * qmax**2 * 4*dw**2 / Si) print(round(Grms, 3)) # -> 0.397

documents.t: Problem: build an f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz single-ended ring. (a) With per-stage delay τD=20\tau_D=20τD​=20 ps, how many stages NNN? (b) Going from N=5N=5N=5 to N=15N=15N=15 stages (adjusting τD\tau_DτD​ to hold f0f_0f0​), use Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 to estimate the phase-noise change in dB (looking at the Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ factor only). Step-by-step solution Step 1 (a): ring frequency ([P2] Eq.(15)): f0=12NτD⇒N=12f0τDf_0=\dfrac1{2N\tau_D}\Rightarrow N=\dfrac1{2f_0\tau_D}f0​=2NτD​1​⇒N=2f0​τD​1​. N=12×5×109×20×10−12=10.2=5.N=\frac1{2\times5\times10^{9}\times20\times10^{-12}}=\frac1{0.2}=5 .N=2×5×109×20×10−121​=0.21​=5. Step 2 (b): Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 ([P2] Eq.(16), p.794, re-verified in v7: the square root covers only the constant; the body text's 4/N1.54/N^{1.5}4/N1.5@η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75 and App.B Eq.(55) triple-confirm this. v3 had misread it as N−3/4N^{-3/4}N−3/4; scaling-level statement). Ratio: Γrms(15)Γrms(5)=(155)−3/2=3−1.5=0.1925.\frac{\Gamma_{rms}(15)}{\Gamma_{rms}(5)}=\left(\frac{15}{5}\right)^{-3/2}=3^{-1.5}=0.1925 .Γrms​(5)Γrms​(15)​=(515​)−3/2=3−1.5=0.1925. Step 3: phase noise ∝Γrms2\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2∝Γrms2​, so the change (dB): ΔL=10log⁡10 ⁣(0.19252)=10log⁡10(0.0370)=−14.3 dB.\Delta\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}\!\big(0.1925^2\big)=10\log_{10}(0.0370)=-14.3\ \text{dB} .ΔL=10log10​(0.19252)=10log10​(0.0370)=−14.3 dB. Result: (a) N=5N=5N=5 stages. (b) Looking at the Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ term alone, going from N=5N=5N=5 to 15 lowers phase noise by about 14.3 dB. Dimension check: N=1/(2f0τD)N=1/(2f_0\tau_D)N=1/(2f0​τD​): 1/([Hz][s])=1/([s−1][s])=1/([\text{Hz}][\text{s}])=1/([\text{s}^{-1}][\text{s}])=1/([Hz][s])=1/([s−1][s])= dimensionless ✓ (NNN must be an integer; here it comes out exact). ΔL\Delta\mathcal{L}ΔL: the argument of 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ is a dimensionless ratio ✓. Important caveat: the above isolates Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ only. The full [P2] conclusion is — at fixed f0f_0f0​ and total power PPP, the phase noise / jitter of a single-ended ring is nearly independent of NNN (see the FOM in [P2] Eq.(23), p.796, verified). Increasing NNN does lower Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, but the noise sources multiply and the per-stage swing/power allocation changes, and these cancel. So the "14.3 dB" of D3(b) is a single-factor teaching illustration, not a gain a real design gets for free. See lc_vs_ring and lab_03. This is pedagogical toy scaling, not transistor-level. Python verification import numpy as np f0, tauD = 5e9, 20e-12 N = 1/(2*f0*tauD) print("N =", N) # -> 5.0 ratio = (15/5)**-1.5 # Grms scaling print("dPN =", round(10*np.log10(ratio**2), 1), "dB") # -> -14.3 dB (Grms factor only)

documents.t: Problem: a 5 GHz clock requires integrated rms jitter σt≤100\sigma_t\le100σt​≤100 fs (integrated 1 MHz→100 MHz, 1/f² spectrum). Back-solve how low L\mathcal{L}L must be at 1 MHz. Step-by-step solution Step 1: C1 already established the mapping — for the same integration band and 1/f² shape, σt∝Llin(fref)\sigma_t\propto\sqrt{\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}(f_{ref})}σt​∝Llin​(fref​)​ (since σϕ2∝Sϕ(fref)∝Llin\sigma_\phi^2\propto S_\phi(f_{ref})\propto\mathcal{L}_{\text{lin}}σϕ2​∝Sϕ​(fref​)∝Llin​, then take the square root). C1 baseline: L=−100\mathcal{L}=-100L=−100 dBc/Hz → σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs. Step 2: getting from 447.9 fs down to 100 fs is a factor of 447.9/100=4.479447.9/100=4.479447.9/100=4.479. Jitter is a voltage/amplitude-like quantity, so reducing it by kkk corresponds to reducing phase-noise power by k2k^2k2: ΔL=−20log⁡10(4.479)=−13.0 dB.\Delta\mathcal{L}=-20\log_{10}(4.479)=-13.0\ \text{dB} .ΔL=−20log10​(4.479)=−13.0 dB. Step 3: required level: −100−13.0=−113.0-100-13.0=-113.0−100−13.0=−113.0 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz. Result: L(1MHz)≈−113\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})\approx-113L(1MHz)≈−113 dBc/Hz is needed (1/f², integrated 1→100 MHz) to reach σt≤100\sigma_t\le100σt​≤100 fs. Dimension check: the argument of −20log⁡10(ratio)-20\log_{10}(\text{ratio})−20log10​(ratio) is dimensionless ✓; the dB difference added to dBc/Hz is still dBc/Hz ✓. SerDes link: 100 fs RJ in a high-speed SerDes (e.g. UI = 1/(28 Gbps) ≈ 35.7 ps) directly determines eye closure and BER; see lab_12 and serdes_clocking_connection. Python verification import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import leeson_one_over_f2, integrate_rms_jitter target_fs = 100.0 # measure sigma_t from the -100 baseline, then back-solve the required dBc/Hz via the square law f = np.logspace(6, 8, 4000) L0 = leeson_one_over_f2(f, L_ref_dbc=-100, f_ref=1e6) st0, _ = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L0, f0=5e9, fmin=1e6, fmax=100e6) L_req = -100 - 20*np.log10((st0*1e15)/target_fs) print(round(L_req, 1), "dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz") # -> -113.0 dBc/Hz

documents.t: Problem: UI = 35.7 ps (28 Gbps), RJ-only σt=2\sigma_t=2σt​=2 ps. What is the BER at eye center (sampling offset t=0t=0t=0)? And if σt\sigma_tσt​ degrades to 4 ps, what does the BER become? Step-by-step solution Step 1: RJ-only BER bathtub (spec Section 10.2 SerDes BER): BER(t)=12[Q(UI/2−tσt)+Q(UI/2+tσt)]\text{BER}(t)=\tfrac12[Q(\tfrac{UI/2-t}{\sigma_t})+Q(\tfrac{UI/2+t}{\sigma_t})]BER(t)=21​[Q(σt​UI/2−t​)+Q(σt​UI/2+t​)], Q(x)=12erfc(x/2)Q(x)=\tfrac12\mathrm{erfc}(x/\sqrt2)Q(x)=21​erfc(x/2​). Step 2: at eye center t=0t=0t=0 the two terms are equal: BER=Q ⁣(UI/2σt)\text{BER}=Q\!\big(\tfrac{UI/2}{\sigma_t}\big)BER=Q(σt​UI/2​). Step 3: for σt=2\sigma_t=2σt​=2 ps: UI/2σt=17.852=8.93\dfrac{UI/2}{\sigma_t}=\dfrac{17.85}{2}=8.93σt​UI/2​=217.85​=8.93. Q(8.93)Q(8.93)Q(8.93) is a vanishingly small number (Gaussian tail), ≈2×10−19\approx2\times10^{-19}≈2×10−19. For σt=4\sigma_t=4σt​=4 ps: 17.854=4.46\dfrac{17.85}{4}=4.46417.85​=4.46, Q(4.46)≈4×10−6Q(4.46)\approx4\times10^{-6}Q(4.46)≈4×10−6. Result: σt=2\sigma_t=2σt​=2 ps → BER ≈2×10−19\approx2\times10^{-19}≈2×10−19; σt=4\sigma_t=4σt​=4 ps → BER ≈4×10−6\approx4\times10^{-6}≈4×10−6. Doubling the jitter → BER degrades by 13 orders of magnitude (the Gaussian tail is extremely sensitive to σ\sigmaσ). Dimension check: the argument of QQQ, UI/2σt=[s][s]\dfrac{UI/2}{\sigma_t}=\dfrac{[\text{s}]}{[\text{s}]}σt​UI/2​=[s][s]​, is dimensionless ✓; BER is dimensionless (a probability) ✓. Intuition: this is why SerDes specs quote σt\sigma_tσt​ (rms) while BER depends on the multiple of σ\sigmaσ (the QQQ function); a modest jitter saving buys a huge BER improvement. Companion figure: Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Panel (b) title reads: "(b) BER bathtub：jitter 越大，可用取樣窗（eye）越窄" = (b) BER bathtub: the larger the jitter, the narrower the usable sampling window (eye). Python verification import numpy as np from simulations.common.serdes_utils import ber_bathtub ui = 1/28e9 for st in [2e-12, 4e-12]: ber = ber_bathtub(np.array([0.0]), sigma_t=st, ui=ui)[0] print(st*1e12, "ps -> BER =", f"{ber:.2e}") # 2.0 ps -> BER ~ 2e-19 ; 4.0 ps -> BER ~ 4e-06

documents.t: After finishing the 15 problems above, cover the answers and quiz yourself — every item should get an instant "direction" answer in your head: Level A (conversion reflexes) Given a phase error (rad), immediately convert to time (s) via ÷(2πf0)\div(2\pi f_0)÷(2πf0​) and run the [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] check. Remember "at 5 GHz: 1 mrad ≈ 32 fs, 1 rad ≈ 31.8 ps". dBc/Hz → linear (10L/1010^{\mathcal{L}/10}10L/10) → phase PSD (×2\times2×2) in one breath. Understand why Δϕ=Γ Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=ΓΔq/qmax​ is dimensionless, and that the ISF varies with injection phase (LTV). Level B (ISF → phase noise) Can write Eq.(21) from memory and plug in numbers to get dBc/Hz; know the denominator is 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2 (SSB convention). Can use Parseval (∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​) to get Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ from the cnc_ncn​. Know that 1/f³ upconversion exists only when c0≠0c_0\ne0c0​=0, with corner =ω1/fc02/(2Γrms2)=\omega_{1/f}c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)=ω1/f​c02​/(2Γrms2​). 1/f² is −20-20−20 dB/dec, 1/f³ is −30-30−30 dB/dec — read them off a plot by eye. Level C (jitter integration) Can run the full chain dBc/Hz → (integrate) → σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ → (÷2πf0\div2\pi f_0÷2πf0​) → σt\sigma_tσt​. Know that 1/f² accumulated jitter is dominated by the lower integration limit; an rms-jitter number must always come with its band. Understand that period jitter uses a high-pass kernel and is not dominated by low frequencies; distinguish it from accumulated jitter. Remember ring accumulated jitter σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ (random walk, never converges). Level D (design back-calculation) Given a dBc/Hz spec, can back-solve qmaxq_{max}qmax​ or Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (doubling qmaxq_{max}qmax​ or halving Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ each gives −6-6−6 dB). Can compute the ring stage count from f0=1/(2NτD)f_0=1/(2N\tau_D)f0​=1/(2NτD​), and remember the caveat "at fixed f0,Pf_0,Pf0​,P, ring PN is nearly independent of NNN". Can translate a jitter spec (fs) back into dBc/Hz at 1 MHz (reducing σt\sigma_tσt​ by kkk ⇒ L\mathcal{L}L drops by 20log⁡10k20\log_{10}k20log10​k dB). Know that RJ-limited BER is extremely sensitive to σt\sigma_tσt​ (Gaussian tail); a small jitter improvement → a large BER improvement. Honesty notes The period-jitter prefactor in Example C3 carries TODO: manual verification needed (tied to the single-/double-sided spectrum convention). The ring Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 in Example D3 ([P2] Eq.(16), p.794; re-verified in v7: the square root covers only the constant; the body text's 4/N1.54/N^{1.5}4/N1.5@η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75 and App.B Eq.(55) triple-confirm this; v3 had misread it as N−3/4N^{-3/4}N−3/4). The "14.3 dB" is the correct dB conversion of the Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ ratio (15/5)−3=1/27(15/5)^{-3}=1/27(15/5)−3=1/27 for N=5→15N=5\to15N=5→15 (10log⁡10(1/27)=−14.310\log_{10}(1/27)=-14.310log10​(1/27)=−14.3 dB), but it remains a single-factor illustration only, not a real design gain (toy scaling, not transistor-level; see the FOM N-independence caveat in D3).

documents.t: Think of the four related papers as a tree: [P1] is the trunk (ISF and phase noise), [P2] is the main branch that applies the trunk to ring oscillators, and [P3]/[P4] are the two new 2019 branches where Hong–Hajimiri extend the same ISF from "free-running phase noise" to "locking/pulling under an external injected signal." One main thread runs through all of them: "An oscillator's phase response to any perturbation = the perturbation weighted by the ISF Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ), then integrated." Phase noise ([P1][P2]) makes the perturbation a random noise current; injection locking ([P3][P4]) makes it a deterministic, periodic injected current. Same mathematical skeleton, different input.
documents.s: Their role in the course

documents.t: Read [P1] first (paper_001). It defines the ISF, derives the 1/f² (Eq.(21)) and 1/f³ (Eq.(23)–(24)) phase noise, and gives the three design rules (raise qmaxq_{max}qmax​, lower Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, use symmetry to suppress c0c_0c0​). If you have not understood it, nothing downstream will move. Then [P2] (paper_002). It applies [P1] to rings: accumulated jitter σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​, Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2, and the conclusion that "at fixed power and frequency, ring phase noise is almost independent of NNN" (verified). For injection, read [P3]→[P4]. [P3] is the phase-only generalized Adler equation; [P4] adds amplitude (APF) and frequency division. These two are advanced; their core equations have been verified against the original PDFs ([P3] generalized Adler Eq.(30)/(35), pp.2113–2114; [P4] APF Eq.(18)–(22), Fig. 5, p.2126). [P5] last, and only as an aside. See below.
documents.s: Suggested reading order

documents.t: The source folder holds 5 PDFs, but Hajimiri_ISCS_98.pdf ([P5]) is not an oscillator phase noise/ISF paper. It is a 4-page ISCAS 1998 paper on the design of a cross-coupled inverter sense amplifier. It discusses regeneration speed, the offset voltage caused by device mismatch, and a figure of merit for offset — entirely outside the scope of ISF/phase noise/jitter. It appears in this list purely because it sits in the source folder and shares the author Hajimiri. We do not pretend it is related to the ISF. Its only conceptual bridge to this course: the heart of a sense amp is the positive feedback/regeneration of a cross-coupled pair, and that same positive-feedback mechanism is what lets latch-based and LC oscillators "self-start and sustain a limit cycle." Beyond that, treat [P5] as a marginal note. See paper_005 (claim C12).
documents.s: Honesty note: [P5] is unrelated to the ISF

documents.t: Four related papers, one main thread: phase response = ISF-weighted perturbation, integrated; phase noise and injection differ only in the input. Reading order: [P1] → [P2] → (advanced) [P3] → [P4]; [P5] only as an aside. [P5] is a sense-amplifier paper, unrelated to the ISF; the only bridge is regeneration/positive feedback. documents.t: Prerequisites (recommended reading order): oscillator_phase (the geometry of the limit cycle and excess phase) → lti_vs_ltv (why an oscillator is LTV, not LTI) → stochastic_noise_basics (white/flicker noise PSD). This page is the foundation of the entire site — the other four deep dives all build on it. This is the foundation of the whole course. It is the first work to model an oscillator's response to noise correctly as an LTV (linear time-variant) system, introducing the ISF (Impulse Sensitivity Function) Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) and using it to derive, in one stroke, closed-form expressions for 1/f² and 1/f³ phase noise together with three design rules still in use today. The remaining four papers ([P2][P3][P4]) all build on the concepts on this page.
documents.s: A General Theory of Phase Noise in Electrical Oscillators

documents.t: [P1] A. Hajimiri and T. H. Lee, "A General Theory of Phase Noise in Electrical Oscillators," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 33, no. 2, pp. 179–194, Feb. 1998. (file general.pdf, paper_001)
documents.s: Citation

documents.t: An oscillator's response to noise is not LTI but LTV: the same noise impulse injected at different phases of the waveform produces different phase shifts; this "phase sensitivity" is the ISF Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ). With it, arbitrary noise can be propagated into phase noise, yielding the design rule L∝Γrms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​/qmax2​ (claim C1, C3).
documents.s: One-sentence contribution

documents.t: Before [P1], engineering practice relied mainly on the Leeson model (1966, semi-empirical) — it draws the 1/f³, 1/f², and flat slope regions, but cannot explain why the 1/f³ corner does not equal the device's 1/f corner, or why some waveforms upconvert less flicker noise into close-in phase noise. [P1] supplies the physical answers: LTV, not LTI (claim C1): an oscillator is an autonomous system with no absolute time reference. A noise impulse landing on the waveform peak changes almost only the amplitude; one landing at a zero crossing converts almost entirely into phase. So "same impulse, different injection instant, different effect" — that is time variance. The LTI convolution h(t−τ)h(t-\tau)h(t−τ) cannot capture it. Phase accumulates permanently, amplitude is pulled back (claim C2): an oscillator has an amplitude-restoring mechanism that pulls amplitude perturbations back onto the limit cycle, but phase has no restoring force — every kick is kept forever. Phase noise lives in this accumulating phase. Quantify both points in a single function Γ\GammaΓ: phase noise is no longer fitted — it can be computed from the waveform and the noise PSD, and the computation points at the design knobs. It also subsumes Leeson and cyclostationary noise as its own special cases (claim C9).
documents.s: Why this paper matters

documents.t: Per paper_metadata (paper_001.assumptions): Noise is a small perturbation — the phase response can be linearized (requires Δq≪qmax\Delta q\ll q_{max}Δq≪qmax​). Amplitude perturbations decay (stable limit cycle); only phase persists, so "tracking phase alone" suffices. The ISF is known, periodic, and frequency-independent — Γ\GammaΓ is a 2π2\pi2π-periodic function determined solely by the steady-state waveform. Hard-switching / large-signal cyclostationary operation defines the ISF — Γ\GammaΓ is the sensitivity measured on that steady-state trajectory. Physical intuition: draw the oscillator state in a 2-D plane; the steady state circulates along the limit cycle. A current impulse nudges the state point; the tangential component along the cycle becomes phase (kept forever), the radial component off the cycle becomes amplitude (pulled back). The same impulse kicked at different phases splits differently between tangential and radial — collect that ratio into a periodic function of the injection phase alone, and you have the ISF. Full geometry in oscillator_phase.

documents.t: Below are the most critical equations of [P1] (Eq.(1) and Eq.(9)–(24)). The LaTeX of each is taken verbatim from Section 3 of the specification, with [P1] Eq.(n) page citations; constants are never altered.

documents.t: Original formula ([P1] Eq.(1), p.180): Vout(t)=A(t) f ⁣(ω0t+ϕ(t))V_{out}(t)=A(t)\,f\!\big(\omega_0 t+\phi(t)\big)Vout​(t)=A(t)f(ω0​t+ϕ(t)) Meaning: any oscillator output can be decomposed into an "instantaneous amplitude A(t)A(t)A(t)" times "the periodic waveform fff evaluated at ω0t+ϕ(t)\omega_0 t+\phi(t)ω0​t+ϕ(t)". fff is the steady-state waveform (not necessarily a sinusoid). Phase noise lives in the excess phase ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t); amplitude noise lives in A(t)A(t)A(t). Step-by-step: the ideal oscillation is f(ω0t)f(\omega_0 t)f(ω0​t); once noise enters, the amplitude is perturbed into A(t)A(t)A(t) and the phase gains ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t). Because amplitude has a restoring force (assumption 2), A(t)→A0A(t)\to A_0A(t)→A0​, so for phase-noise analysis A(t)A(t)A(t) can be treated as a constant and only ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) tracked. This step collapses the problem from a "2-D state" to a "1-D phase".
documents.s: Eq.(1): output decomposition (where phase noise lives)

documents.t: Original formula ([P1] Eq.(9), p.181): ΔV=ΔqCnode\Delta V=\frac{\Delta q}{C_{node}}ΔV=Cnode​Δq​ Meaning: a current impulse deposits charge Δq=∫i dt\Delta q=\int i\,dtΔq=∫idt on the node capacitance, instantly stepping the node voltage by ΔV\Delta VΔV. This is the physical entry point through which noise enters the oscillator state. Dimension check: [C]/[F]=[C]/[C/V]=[V][\text{C}]/[\text{F}]=[\text{C}]/[\text{C/V}]=[\text{V}][C]/[F]=[C]/[C/V]=[V] ✓.

documents.t: Original formula ([P1] Eq.(10), p.182, excess-phase impulse response): hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau)hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ) Original formula ([P1] Eq.(11), p.182, convolution form): ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tauϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ Meaning: Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) is the dimensionless, 2π2\pi2π-periodic ISF; qmax=CnodeVmaxq_{max}=C_{node}V_{max}qmax​=Cnode​Vmax​ is the maximum charge swing on the node. The u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) (unit step) is crucial: once a phase step is created it persists forever (phase has no restoring force), so the impulse response carries a step rather than a decaying term. Eq.(11) is the superposition integral over all past noise. Step-by-step derivation (no skipped steps): (i) current impulse deposits charge:Δq=∫in(τ) dτ(ii) charge raises the node voltage (Eq.9):ΔV=ΔqCnode(iii) project onto the limit-cycle tangent to get the phase step:Δϕ=Γ(ω0τ)qmax Δq(iv) the step persists forever; write the impulse response:hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ)(v) linear superposition (convolution) over arbitrary in:ϕ(t)=∫−∞∞hϕ(t,τ) in(τ) dτ=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ\begin{aligned} &\text{(i) current impulse deposits charge:}\quad \Delta q=\int i_n(\tau)\,d\tau \\ &\text{(ii) charge raises the node voltage (Eq.9):}\quad \Delta V=\frac{\Delta q}{C_{node}} \\ &\text{(iii) project onto the limit-cycle tangent to get the phase step:}\quad \Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q \\ &\text{(iv) the step persists forever; write the impulse response:}\quad h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau) \\ &\text{(v) linear superposition (convolution) over arbitrary }i_n\text{:}\quad \phi(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h_\phi(t,\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau \end{aligned}​(i) current impulse deposits charge:Δq=∫in​(τ)dτ(ii) charge raises the node voltage (Eq.9):ΔV=Cnode​Δq​(iii) project onto the limit-cycle tangent to get the phase step:Δϕ=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​Δq(iv) the step persists forever; write the impulse response:hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ)(v) linear superposition (convolution) over arbitrary in​:ϕ(t)=∫−∞∞​hϕ​(t,τ)in​(τ)dτ=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ​ Why Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless: Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is in rad (dimensionless) and Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ is also dimensionless, so Γ\GammaΓ must be dimensionless ✓. Note that hϕh_\phihϕ​ depends on the absolute injection instant τ\tauτ (through Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ)), not merely on t−τt-\taut−τ — exactly the fingerprint of an LTV system (claim C1). The full step-by-step derivations are in impulse_to_phase_shift and convolution_derivation. Numerical example (Example A): qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC, Γ=0.5\Gamma=0.5Γ=0.5, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz. Δϕ=0.5×(1×10−15)1×10−12=5×10−4 rad (≈0.0286∘),Δt=Δϕ2πf0=15.9 fs.\Delta\phi=\frac{0.5\times(1\times10^{-15})}{1\times10^{-12}}=5\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}\;(\approx0.0286^\circ),\quad \Delta t=\frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi f_0}=15.9\ \text{fs}.Δϕ=1×10−120.5×(1×10−15)​=5×10−4 rad(≈0.0286∘),Δt=2πf0​Δϕ​=15.9 fs. Python verification: from simulations.common.isf_utils import impulse_to_phase_step from simulations.common.noise_utils import phase_to_time_error dphi = impulse_to_phase_step(delta_q=1e-15, gamma_value=0.5, qmax=1e-12) dt = phase_to_time_error(dphi, f0=5e9) print(dphi, "rad", dt*1e15, "fs") # -> 0.0005 rad 15.92 fs
documents.s: Eq.(10)–(11): the ISF and the LTV phase response (the core)

documents.t: Original formula ([P1] Eq.(12), p.183): Γ(ω0τ)=c02+∑n=1∞cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=\frac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)Γ(ω0​τ)=2c0​​+n=1∑∞​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​) Original formula ([P1] Eq.(13), p.183): ϕ(t)=1qmax ⁣[c02 ⁣∫−∞t ⁣in dτ+∑n=1∞cn ⁣∫−∞t ⁣incos⁡(nω0τ+θn) dτ]\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\!\left[\frac{c_0}{2}\!\int_{-\infty}^{t}\!i_n\,d\tau+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\!\int_{-\infty}^{t}\!i_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\,d\tau\right]ϕ(t)=qmax​1​[2c0​​∫−∞t​in​dτ+n=1∑∞​cn​∫−∞t​in​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)dτ] Meaning: expand the ISF in a Fourier series; each harmonic coefficient cnc_ncn​ tells you "how strongly the oscillator moves noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ onto the carrier". c0c_0c0​ (the DC term — the DC value of the ISF is c0/2c_0/2c0​/2) is especially important — it is the only channel that upconverts the device's low-frequency 1/f noise into close-in 1/f³ phase noise (see Eq.(23)–(24)). Step-by-step: substitute Eq.(12) into Eq.(11) and expand term by term to get Eq.(13). Physically this is a frequency-translation map ([P1] Fig. 8): noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ is down-converted by the nnn-th harmonic into slow phase modulation at baseband. The full derivation and the notation trap (c0c_0c0​ vs c0/2c_0/2c0​/2) are in fourier_series_of_isf.
documents.s: Eq.(12)–(13): Fourier series of the ISF and its harmonics

documents.t: Original formula ([P1] Eq.(20), p.185): ∑n=0∞cn2=1π∫02π∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2 Γrms2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma(x)|^2dx=2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2n=0∑∞​cn2​=π1​∫02π​∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2Γrms2​ Meaning: summing the energy of all harmonics (Parseval) gives 2Γrms22\Gamma_{rms}^22Γrms2​. This is what lets the "sum over all harmonics" of Eq.(19) collapse into a single clean Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​. Step-by-step: square both sides of Eq.(12), integrate over one period [0,2π][0,2\pi][0,2π], and use trigonometric orthogonality (cross terms between different harmonics integrate to 0). Details in rms_isf.
documents.s: Eq.(20): Parseval / rms ISF

documents.t: Original formula ([P1] Eq.(21), p.185): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​) Meaning: the SSB phase noise produced by a white-noise current source, in the 1/f² region (−20-20−20 dB/dec). Phase noise is proportional to Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ (claim C3) — the most important of the three design rules: enlarge qmaxq_{max}qmax​, shrink Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. Step-by-step: from Eq.(16)/(17) obtain the phase modulation for a single injected tone (∝cn/Δω\propto c_n/\Delta\omega∝cn​/Δω), from Eq.(18) the single-sideband power, then sum over all harmonics for white noise (Eq.(19)) and use Eq.(20) to collapse the sum into Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​. Numerical example (Example B): f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz. Δω=2π×106=6.283×106\Delta\omega=2\pi\times10^6=6.283\times10^6Δω=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s, Δω2=3.948×1013\Delta\omega^2=3.948\times10^{13}Δω2=3.948×1013. L=10log⁡10 ⁣(0.2510−24⋅10−244×3.948×1013)=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15)=−148.0 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{0.25}{10^{-24}}\cdot\frac{10^{-24}}{4\times3.948\times10^{13}}\right)=10\log_{10}(1.583\times10^{-15})=-148.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}.L=10log10​(10−240.25​⋅4×3.948×101310−24​)=10log10​(1.583×10−15)=−148.0 dBc/Hz. This is the ideal value for a single white-noise source; a real circuit has multiple sources, cyclostationarity, and flicker, so it sits higher. The full step-by-step account, including the famous factor-of-2 (SSB bookkeeping convention) discussion, is in white_noise_to_phase_noise.
documents.s: Eq.(21): 1/f² phase noise (the signature result)

documents.t: Original formula ([P1] Eq.(22), p.185, device flicker): in,1/f2‾=in2‾⋅ω1/fΔω\overline{i_{n,1/f}^2}=\overline{i_n^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}in,1/f2​​=in2​​⋅Δωω1/f​​ Original formula ([P1] Eq.(23), p.185, 1/f³ phase noise): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(c02qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf8 Δω2⋅ω1/fΔω)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{8\,\Delta\omega^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​c02​​⋅8Δω2in2​​/Δf​⋅Δωω1/f​​) Original formula ([P1] Eq.(24), p.185, 1/f³ corner): Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c022 Γrms2≈ω1/f(c0c1)2\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}\approx\omega_{1/f}\left(\frac{c_0}{c_1}\right)^2Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​≈ω1/f​(c1​c0​​)2 Meaning: the device's 1/f noise can be upconverted into close-in 1/f³ phase noise only through the DC term c0c_0c0​ of the ISF (claim C4). The most counter-intuitive and most important point (claim C5): the 1/f³ corner ≠\ne= the device 1/f corner — it is scaled by (c0/Γrms)2/2(c_0/\Gamma_{rms})^2/2(c0​/Γrms​)2/2. If the waveform is symmetric and c0c_0c0​ is small, the 1/f³ corner can be pushed far below ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​. This is the mathematical basis of the "symmetry design rule". Step-by-step: substitute the 1/f noise of Eq.(22) into Eq.(19); because only the DC coefficient c0c_0c0​ has a DC response at baseband, only the c02c_0^2c02​ term survives the sum, giving Eq.(23) (note the denominator is 888, not 444). Setting the 1/f² of Eq.(21) equal to the 1/f³ of Eq.(23) and solving for the crossover frequency gives Eq.(24). The approximation c0/c1≈c0/Γrms2c_0/c_1\approx \dfrac{c_0/\Gamma_{rms}}{\sqrt2}c0​/c1​≈2​c0​/Γrms​​ comes from "a symmetric waveform is dominated by c1c_1c1​, so Γrms2≈c12/2\Gamma_{rms}^2\approx c_1^2/2Γrms2​≈c12​/2" (i.e. c1≈2 Γrmsc_1\approx\sqrt2\,\Gamma_{rms}c1​≈2​Γrms​, hence c0/c1=(c0/Γrms)/2c_0/c_1=(c_0/\Gamma_{rms})/\sqrt2c0​/c1​=(c0​/Γrms​)/2​, consistent with c02/(2Γrms2)=(c0/c1)2c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)=(c_0/c_1)^2c02​/(2Γrms2​)=(c0​/c1​)2). Numerical example: if ω1/f=2π×1\omega_{1/f}=2\pi\times1ω1/f​=2π×1 MHz and the waveform is symmetric enough that c0/Γrms=0.1c_0/\Gamma_{rms}=0.1c0​/Γrms​=0.1, then Δω1/f3=ω1/f×(0.1)2/2=ω1/f×5×10−3\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\times(0.1)^2/2=\omega_{1/f}\times5\times10^{-3}Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​×(0.1)2/2=ω1/f​×5×10−3, i.e. a 1/f³ corner of ≈5\approx5≈5 kHz — far below the device's 1 MHz corner. Symmetry has pushed the close-in noise away by a factor of 200 in frequency. Full derivation in flicker_noise_upconversion.

documents.t: [P1] distills phase-noise design into three knobs (all read directly off Eq.(21) and Eq.(24)): Enlarge qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (node charge swing): L∝1/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto1/q_{max}^2L∝1/qmax2​; every doubling of qmaxq_{max}qmax​ buys 6 dB. Larger capacitance, larger voltage swing, and higher power all push this way. Shrink Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​: make the noise injection instants land where the ISF is small. The LC's Γ=−sin⁡\Gamma=-\sinΓ=−sin is zero at the waveform peak, so "replenishing energy near the peak" hurts phase noise the least. Use symmetry to suppress c0c_0c0​: a waveform with symmetric rise/fall has c0≈0c_0\approx0c0​≈0, pushing the 1/f³ corner (Eq.(24)) very low and cutting close-in phase noise sharply. This rule is directly verified in the ring experiment of [P2] (Fig. 17). Design-side summaries in symmetry and lc_vs_ring.

documents.t: What this section answers: this site's numeric chain (Example B's −148.0-148.0−148.0 dBc/Hz) uses clean pedagogical numbers; the very same "process data → CnodeC_{node}Cnode​ → qmaxq_{max}qmax​ → in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf → Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ → Eq.(21) → L\mathcal{L}L" pipeline was validated by [P1] Sec. V (pp.189–191) on real silicon with eight experiments, with prediction–measurement gaps of 0.2–0.7 dB — and every input is available a priori (process parameters, geometry, swing, extracted ISF); nothing is fitted after the fact. Below we first survey the eight experiments, then replay the chain with the most complete numbers step by step. (In other words the prefactor 0.84 carries the unit Hz.) Step 5 — prediction vs measurement: substituting Δf=500\Delta f=500Δf=500 kHz: L=10log⁡10 ⁣(0.839 Hz(5×105 Hz)2)=10log⁡10 ⁣(3.35×10−12 Hz−1)=−114.7 dBc/Hz\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{0.839\ \text{Hz}}{(5\times10^5\ \text{Hz})^2}\right)=10\log_{10}\!\left(3.35\times10^{-12}\ \text{Hz}^{-1}\right)=-114.7\ \text{dBc/Hz}L=10log10​((5×105 Hz)20.839 Hz​)=10log10​(3.35×10−12 Hz−1)=−114.7 dBc/Hz The paper measures −114.5-114.5−114.5 dBc/Hz — a 0.2 dB gap. factor-of-2/4 flag (called out every time it appears): the 4 in the denominator is [P1] Eq.(21)'s SSB bookkeeping, the same convention as this site's Example B (−148.0-148.0−148.0 dBc/Hz). With the clean time-domain /2 bookkeeping instead, the same inputs would predict −111.7-111.7−111.7 dBc/Hz (3 dB higher), i.e. 3.0 dB away from the measurement. This experiment is therefore often cited as empirical support for the /4 version; note, however, that the 0.2 dB agreement also absorbs estimation errors in Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and CtotalC_{total}Ctotal​, so reading it as "the magnitude and scaling are right" is more robust than reading it as a definitive verdict on the factor of 2. See white_noise_to_phase_noise. Step 6 — the 1/f³ corner (Eq.(24) divided through by 2π2\pi2π): an isolated inverter on the same die (input and output shorted) measures a device 1/f corner of f1/f=250f_{1/f}=250f1/f​=250 kHz; from the extracted ISF, c02/2Γrms2=0.3c_0^2/2\Gamma_{rms}^2=0.3c02​/2Γrms2​=0.3: f1/f3=f1/f⋅c022 Γrms2=250 kHz×0.3=75 kHzf_{1/f^3}=f_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}=250\ \text{kHz}\times0.3=75\ \text{kHz}f1/f3​=f1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​=250 kHz×0.3=75 kHz Measured: 80 kHz. This is the most direct silicon evidence for claim C5, "the 1/f³ corner ≠\ne= the device 1/f corner": the corner is pushed from 250 kHz down to 80 kHz by the (partial) symmetry of the waveform. Python verification (pure-algebra recomputation; all inputs from [P1] p.190–191): import math # [P1] Sec. V, fourth experiment: 5-stage 232 MHz single-ended ring (2-µm 5-V CMOS, p.190) N = 5 # number of stages qmax = 179e-15 # C (= C_total 35.7 fF × V_swing 5 V) Si_nmos = 4.44e-24 # A²/Hz (given by the paper, p.190, at the transition point) Si_pmos = 2.19e-24 # A²/Hz (given by the paper, p.190) G2rms = 16 / N**3 # Γ²_rms ≈ 16/N³ (paper, p.190) print(round(G2rms, 3)) # -> 0.128 Si_total = N * (Si_nmos + Si_pmos) # powers of N uncorrelated sources add prefac = G2rms * Si_total / (4 * qmax**2 * (2*math.pi)**2) print(round(prefac, 3)) # -> 0.839 (paper prints 0.84) df = 500e3 # Hz print(round(10*math.log10(prefac/df**2), 2)) # -> -114.74 (paper predicts -114.7; measured -114.5) print(round(10*math.log10(2*prefac/df**2), 2)) # -> -111.73 (with the time-domain /2 bookkeeping: 3 dB off the measurement) print(round(250e3*0.3/1e3, 1)) # -> 75.0 (kHz, Eq.(24); measured 80 kHz) # Fifth experiment: 11-stage 115 MHz (same die; noise scales with W: NMOS×4/3, PMOS×6/5, same L) N2, qmax2 = 11, 217e-15 Si_stage2 = Si_nmos*(4/3) + Si_pmos*(6/5) prefac2 = (16/N2**3) * N2 * Si_stage2 / (4 * qmax2**2 * (2*math.pi)**2) print(round(prefac2, 3)) # -> 0.152 (paper prints 0.152, digit-for-digit) print(round(10*math.log10(prefac2/df**2), 2)) # -> -122.16 (paper predicts -122.1; measured -122.5) print(round(250e3*0.17/1e3, 1)) # -> 42.5 (kHz, paper rounds to 43; measured 45 kHz) # Seventh experiment: 4-stage differential 200 MHz (0.5-µm; q_max = 49 fF × 1.2 V = 58.8 fC) prefac3 = (16/4**3) * 4 * 2.63e-23 / (4 * (58.8e-15)**2 * (2*math.pi)**2) print(round(prefac3, 1)) # -> 48.2 (paper prints 48.1, trailing-digit rounding) print(round(10*math.log10(prefac3/(1e6)**2), 2)) # -> -103.17 (paper predicts -103.2; measured -103.9)

The paper states the phase noise is "calculated in exactly the same manner as the previous experiment", giving L{Δf}=10log⁡(0.152/Δf2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta f\}=10\log(0.152/\Delta f^2)L{Δf}=10log(0.152/Δf2), i.e. −122.1-122.1−122.1 dBc/Hz at 500 kHz; measured −122.5-122.5−122.5 dBc/Hz (0.4 dB gap). c02/2Γrms2=0.17c_0^2/2\Gamma_{rms}^2=0.17c02​/2Γrms2​=0.17 predicts a 1/f³ corner of 43 kHz; measured 45 kHz. The paper does not list the device PSDs of the 11-stage inverters; the Python above recomputes them by scaling the noise linearly with WWW (same LLL) and lands on a prefactor of 0.152, digit-for-digit identical to the paper — reverse-confirming that this is exactly the paper's internal calculation. documents.t: The seventh experiment ([P1] p.191): tail current 108 µA, total capacitance on each differential node Ctotal=49C_{total}=49Ctotal​=49 fF, Vswing=1.2V_{swing}=1.2Vswing​=1.2 V, hence qmax=58.8q_{max}=58.8qmax​=58.8 fC (the paper's text prints "58.8 fF" — dimensionally 49 fF×1.2 V49\ \text{fF}\times1.2\ \text{V}49 fF×1.2 V can only be fC; this is a typo in the paper, which we transcribe faithfully and flag). Total channel noise per node (in2‾/Δf)total=2.63×10−23(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)_{total}=2.63\times10^{-23}(in2​​/Δf)total​=2.63×10−23 A²/Hz; with N=4N=4N=4 the same chain gives L{Δf}=10log⁡(48.1/Δf2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta f\}=10\log(48.1/\Delta f^2)L{Δf}=10log(48.1/Δf2) (our recomputation gives 48.2, a trailing-digit rounding difference), predicting −103.2-103.2−103.2 at 1 MHz; measured −103.9-103.9−103.9 dBc/Hz (0.7 dB gap). The same experiment carries a symmetry lesson: although the differential signal is perfectly symmetric, the single-ended waveform of each half-circuit is not, so Fig. 27 still shows a distinct 1/f³ region — "differential signaling does not rescue c0c_0c0​; what counts is half-circuit symmetry" (echoing p.188 and symmetry).

documents.t: The predictions are a priori: the three full chains (232 MHz / 115 MHz / 200 MHz differential) miss by 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.7 dB, with inputs limited to process parameters, geometry, VswingV_{swing}Vswing​, and the extracted ISF. This site's Example B toy chain (qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz → −148.0-148.0−148.0 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, SSB /4 bookkeeping) runs the very same pipeline, just with clean numbers. Applicable when: noise is concentrated at the transitions (true for single-ended CMOS rings); Γrms2≈16/N3\Gamma_{rms}^2\approx16/N^3Γrms2​≈16/N3 is a ring-specific approximation for "identical inverters with standard rise/fall" (corresponding to [P2]'s η≈0.75\eta\approx0.75η≈0.75); the noise of different stages is uncorrelated (only then may powers be added). Fails when: the waveform is asymmetric (experiments 3/6/7) so that close-in noise is dominated by the c0c_0c0​-driven 1/f³ — Eq.(21) covers only the 1/f² region; very close to the carrier the linearization breaks down (see lorentzian_linewidth); strong spurs or injection pulling require separate treatment ([P3]/[P4]). Dimensions: the argument of every 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ is 1/Hz — the hallmark of dBc/Hz.
documents.s: What this set of experiments establishes (applicability and failure conditions)

documents.t: Per paper_metadata (paper_001.limitations): The 1/f³ region was historically linked empirically; this theory clarifies that it is set by c0c_0c0​, but the exact c0c_0c0​ still has to be extracted. In real circuits Γ\GammaΓ must be extracted via transient impulse simulation or adjoint/PSS methods; the closed forms are first-order approximations. AM–PM conversion and strong nonlinearity are not fully covered by the first-order phase-only model (exactly the hole [P4] patches with the APF). The rigorous mathematical foundation (PPV / adjoint / Floquet) is not among the five source PDFs; it belongs to external literature (claim C13) — see effective_isf.

documents.t: [P2] applies this page's ISF to the ring oscillator: it derives the jitter κ\kappaκ from the same Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ ratio and studies the Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 scaling (claim C8). [P3]/[P4] extend the same ISF from "random noise" to "deterministic injection": [P3] uses Γ\GammaΓ to write the generalized Adler equation (claim C10); [P4] adds the amplitude counterpart, the APF (claim C11). [P5] is unrelated to this page (sense amplifier, claim C12); the only conceptual bridge is regeneration / positive feedback. The Leeson model is a special case of this theory (claim C9); the Leeson formula is entry 19 in equation_index, marked as reference (not in the 5 PDFs).

documents.t: LTV, not LTI: same impulse, different injection phase, different effect — that is the ISF Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ). Phase accumulates, amplitude is pulled back: phase noise lives in the accumulating phase (Eq.(1); the upper limit of the integral in Eq.(11) is ttt). Signature formula: L∝Γrms2qmax2⋅SiΔω2\mathcal{L}\propto\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\dfrac{S_i}{\Delta\omega^2}L∝qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δω2Si​​ (Eq.(21)). Three design rules: enlarge qmaxq_{max}qmax​, shrink Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, use symmetry to suppress c0c_0c0​. 1/f³ corner ≠\ne= device 1/f corner (Eq.(24)) — symmetry can push it very low. All core derivations are in 03_isf_core_theory; numerical feel is in numerical_feeling.

documents.t: Prerequisites (recommended reading order): first digest paper_001 (ISF, Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​, the symmetry rule) — every conclusion on this page is [P1]'s ISF applied to the ring. For the time-/frequency-domain language of jitter see psd_phase_noise_jitter. [P2] applies the ISF framework of [P1] to the ring oscillator. It answers three very practical questions: (1) how does the long-term jitter of a free-running ring grow with time? (2) what effect does the number of stages NNN have on phase noise? (3) why does waveform symmetry suppress close-in noise? The answers are, respectively, σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​, Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 (with "nearly NNN-independent at fixed power and frequency"), and the symmetry experiment of Fig. 17.

documents.t: Applying [P1]'s ISF to the ring oscillator yields closed forms for jitter and phase noise, the Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 scaling, and the counter-intuitive conclusion that "at fixed f0f_0f0​ and power, the phase noise/jitter of a single-ended ring is nearly independent of the number of stages NNN" (claim C7, C8).
documents.s: One-sentence contribution

documents.t: An LC oscillator needs an inductor — large area, hard to integrate; a ring oscillator is all inverters: small area, easy to integrate, wide tuning range — the most common VCO in PLLs/CDRs. But a ring's phase noise is usually much worse than an LC's — [P2] uses the ISF to explain why, and gives actionable design rules: It ties the ring's jitter to the same Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ ratio as phase noise (claim C6), unifying "time-domain jitter" and "frequency-domain phase noise" under the ISF framework. It settles a commonly misunderstood question: "does adding more stages NNN to a ring make it better?" Under the constraint of fixed power and frequency the answer is "almost no difference" (claim C7) — more stages shrink Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, but each stage's swing shrinks and there are more devices; the effects cancel. It confirms [P1]'s symmetry rule with measurements (Fig. 17): tuning the control voltage to the point of symmetric rise/fall produces a minimum in phase noise (claim C4).
documents.s: Why this paper matters

documents.t: Per paper_metadata (paper_002.assumptions): The same LTV/ISF small-perturbation assumptions as [P1]. Per-stage device noise is white (plus a 1/f component handled via symmetry). Identical stages; delay and noise add independently at every transition. Physical intuition: nearly all of a ring's energy is injected in the instant of a transition (edge flip), so its ISF is not the smooth −sin⁡-\sin−sin of an LC but a set of sharp peaks concentrated at the transitions ([P2] Fig. 5). The sensitive spots — where a kick hurts phase the most — sit on those peaks. The more stages, the smaller the fraction of the full period a single transition occupies, and the smaller the rms ISF.
documents.s: Main assumptions

documents.t: Original formula ([P2] Eq.(8), p.792; κ from Eq.(12), p.793): σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ Meaning: for two edges of a free-running oscillator separated by Δt\Delta tΔt, the standard deviation of the timing error is proportional to Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ — the random-walk fingerprint of an oscillator with "no absolute time reference" (claim C6). κ\kappaκ is a device-dependent proportionality constant with units of s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​. Step-by-step derivation: each transition injects an independent, zero-mean timing perturbation with variance σstep2\sigma_{step}^2σstep2​. Over Δt\Delta tΔt there are about M=Δt/TM=\Delta t/TM=Δt/T transitions; independent quantities add in variance: σΔt2=M σstep2=ΔtT σstep2⇒σΔt=σstepT⏟≡ κΔt=κΔt.\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\Delta t}^2 &= M\,\sigma_{step}^2 = \frac{\Delta t}{T}\,\sigma_{step}^2 \\ \Rightarrow\quad \sigma_{\Delta t} &= \underbrace{\frac{\sigma_{step}}{\sqrt{T}}}_{\equiv\,\kappa}\sqrt{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}. \end{aligned}σΔt2​⇒σΔt​​=Mσstep2​=TΔt​σstep2​=≡κT​σstep​​​​Δt​=κΔt​.​ Dimension check: κ\kappaκ is s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​ and Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ is s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​; their product is s\text{s}s ✓. Cross-check against [P1] in the frequency domain: σΔt∝Δt\sigma_{\Delta t}\propto\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​∝Δt​ corresponds to 1/f² phase noise (the two are the time-/frequency-domain faces of the same thing). Numerical example: the toy ring sets per-edge σstep=50\sigma_{step}=50σstep​=50 fs (see the parameters of ring_oscillator_timing_noise_accumulation.png). Accumulated jitter over Δt=1\Delta t=1Δt=1 µs (about 5000 periods at f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz): first find κ\kappaκ. With T=200T=200T=200 ps, κ=50fs/200ps=50×10−15/2×10−10=3.54×10−9 s\kappa=50\text{fs}/\sqrt{200\text{ps}}=50\times10^{-15}/\sqrt{2\times10^{-10}}=3.54\times10^{-9}\ \sqrt{\text{s}}κ=50fs/200ps​=50×10−15/2×10−10​=3.54×10−9 s​, so σΔt=3.54×10−9×10−6=3.54 ps\sigma_{\Delta t}=3.54\times10^{-9}\times\sqrt{10^{-6}}=3.54\ \text{ps}σΔt​=3.54×10−9×10−6​=3.54 ps. Intuition: the longer the separation, the larger the drift — but it grows only slowly, as Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​. Python verification: import numpy as np from simulations.common.oscillator_models import accumulated_jitter_curve # toy random walk: each edge adds an independent 50 fs timing perturbation lags, sigma = accumulated_jitter_curve(f0=5e9, sigma_edge=50e-15, max_lag_periods=500, n_trials=2000) # expect sigma(lag) ~ sigma_edge * sqrt(lag) -> log-log slope 0.5 slope = np.polyfit(np.log(lags[1:]), np.log(sigma[1:]), 1)[0] print(round(slope, 2)) # -> 0.50 The full toy derivation is in lab_03_ring_oscillator_toy_model (pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level).

documents.t: Original formula ([P2] Eq.(11)–(12), p.793, proportionality): κ2 ∝ Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾Δf\kappa^2\;\propto\;\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}κ2∝qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δfin2​​​ Meaning: the jitter proportionality constant κ\kappaκ is set by exactly the same Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ ratio as phase noise (claim C6). This ties time-domain jitter and frequency-domain phase noise to the same ISF quantity: the knobs that lower phase noise lower jitter as well. Verified (corrected in v11 after re-reading the PDF): [P2] Eq.(12), p.793 as printed is κ=Γrmsqmax ω012in2‾Δf\kappa=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}}{q_{max}\,\omega_0}\sqrt{\tfrac12\tfrac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}}κ=qmax​ω0​Γrms​​21​Δfin2​​​​ — the denominator contains ω0\omega_0ω0​, the units are s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​, and it is the timing jitter constant κt\kappa_tκt​ of Eq.(8) σΔT=κΔT\sigma_{\Delta T}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta T}σΔT​=κΔT​ (assembled from Eq.(10) σΔϕ=ω0σΔT\sigma_{\Delta\phi}=\omega_0\sigma_{\Delta T}σΔϕ​=ω0​σΔT​ and Eq.(11) σΔϕ2=Γrms2(in2‾/Δf) ΔT/(2qmax2)\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=\Gamma_{rms}^2(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)\,\Delta T/(2q_{max}^2)σΔϕ2​=Γrms2​(in2​​/Δf)ΔT/(2qmax2​); verified verbatim against the original PDF rendering). The κϕ=Γrmsqmax12in2‾Δf\kappa_\phi=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}}{q_{max}}\sqrt{\tfrac12\tfrac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}}κϕ​=qmax​Γrms​​21​Δfin2​​​​ (rad/s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​) of this site's diffusion_dictionary is the phase version of the same thing: κϕ=ω0κt\kappa_\phi=\omega_0\kappa_tκϕ​=ω0​κt​, numerically κt=κϕ/(2πf0)\kappa_t=\kappa_\phi/(2\pi f_0)κt​=κϕ​/(2πf0​). v4–v5 had recorded "Eq.(12) has no ω0\omega_0ω0​" as verified; corrected in v11, with every number on this site unchanged. Both versions share the same Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ ratio with phase noise (claim C6).

documents.t: Original formula ([P2] Eq.(14), p.794): f0=12NτDf_0=\frac{1}{2N\tau_D}f0​=2NτD​1​ Meaning: an NNN-stage ring with per-stage delay τD\tau_DτD​ oscillates at this frequency. The factor of 2 comes from the signal having to travel around the ring twice per period (one lap inverts; a second lap returns it in phase) to complete one full cycle. Dimension check: 1/(N⋅s)=Hz1/(N\cdot\text{s})=\text{Hz}1/(N⋅s)=Hz ✓ (NNN dimensionless). Numerical example: for a 5-stage ring at f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, the per-stage delay is τD=1/(2×5×5×109)=2×10−11 s=20\tau_D=1/(2\times5\times5\times10^9)=2\times10^{-11}\ \text{s}=20τD​=1/(2×5×5×109)=2×10−11 s=20 ps. Doubling to N=10N=10N=10 while keeping 5 GHz halves the per-stage delay to 10 ps — this is exactly where "at fixed frequency, larger NNN forces faster, smaller-swing stages" comes from, leading into the N-independence below.

documents.t: Original formula ([P2] Eq.(16), p.794; the radical covers only the constant term): Γrms=2π23η3 1N1.5\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\pi^2}{3\eta^3}}\;\dfrac{1}{N^{1.5}}Γrms​=3η32π2​​N1.51​ where η\etaη is the frequency proportionality constant (Eq.(14)–(15): t^D=η/fmax\hat t_D=\eta/f_{max}t^D​=η/fmax​, 2π=2Nη/fmax2\pi=2N\eta/f_{max}2π=2Nη/fmax​); at η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75, 2π2/(3×0.753)≈3.95≈4\sqrt{2\pi^2/(3\times0.75^3)}\approx3.95\approx42π2/(3×0.753)​≈3.95≈4, i.e. Γrms≈4/N1.5\Gamma_{rms}\approx4/N^{1.5}Γrms​≈4/N1.5, which is the solid line in [P2] Fig. 8 — the radical covers only the constant, and 1/N1.51/N^{1.5}1/N1.5 sits outside it. Meaning: Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 (i.e. Γrms2∝N−3\Gamma_{rms}^2\propto N^{-3}Γrms2​∝N−3). Intuition: with more stages, each transition occupies a narrower "sensitive window" of the 2π2\pi2π period and the peaks get shorter, so the rms naturally shrinks. [P2] Eq.(16), p.794 (re-verified in v7: the radical covers only the constant, Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2; triple-confirmed by the prose's 4/N1.54/N^{1.5}4/N1.5@η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75 and App.B Eq.(55). v3 had misread this as N−3/4N^{-3/4}N−3/4): three independent lines of evidence — (1) the paper's own text (p.794, the paragraph after Eq.16) states "the 1/N1.51/N^{1.5}1/N1.5 dependence of Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​"; (2) the η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75 numerical anchor: the text says "solid line = Γrms≈4/N1.5\Gamma_{rms}\approx4/N^{1.5}Γrms​≈4/N1.5, obtained from (16) for η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75", and 2π2/(3×0.753)=3.95≈4\sqrt{2\pi^2/(3\times0.75^3)}=3.95\approx42π2/(3×0.753)​=3.95≈4 ✓ (if N1.5N^{1.5}N1.5 were inside the radical this would give 4/N0.754/N^{0.75}4/N0.75, contradicting the text); (3) independent algebra in App.B Eq.(52)+(54) (p.803): Γrms2=(1/3π)(1/frise′)3(1+A3)\Gamma_{rms}^2=(1/3\pi)(1/f'_{rise})^3(1+A^3)Γrms2​=(1/3π)(1/frise′​)3(1+A3), 2π=ηN(1+A)/frise′2\pi=\eta N(1+A)/f'_{rise}2π=ηN(1+A)/frise′​, which combine to give Γrms2=(2π2/3η3)⋅[4(1+A3)/(1+A)3]⋅N−3\Gamma_{rms}^2=(2\pi^2/3\eta^3)\cdot[4(1+A^3)/(1+A)^3]\cdot N^{-3}Γrms2​=(2π2/3η3)⋅[4(1+A3)/(1+A)3]⋅N−3; at A=1A=1A=1 the bracket equals 1, so Γrms2∝N−3⇒Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}^2\propto N^{-3}\Rightarrow\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms2​∝N−3⇒Γrms​∝N−3/2 ✓. documents.t: Original formula ([P2] Eq.(23), p.796; the VT=0V_T=0VT​=0 lower bound is Eq.(25)): L{Δf}=83η⋅kTP⋅VDDVchar⋅(f0Δf)2(min⁡VT=0: 16γ3η⋅kTP⋅f02Δf2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta f\}=\frac{8}{3\eta}\cdot\frac{kT}{P}\cdot\frac{V_{DD}}{V_{char}}\cdot\left(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\right)^2 \qquad\Big(\min_{V_T=0}:\ \frac{16\gamma}{3\eta}\cdot\frac{kT}{P}\cdot\frac{f_0^2}{\Delta f^2}\Big)L{Δf}=3η8​⋅PkT​⋅Vchar​VDD​​⋅(Δff0​​)2(VT​=0min​: 3η16γ​⋅PkT​⋅Δf2f02​​) where γ\gammaγ is the MOSFET channel thermal-noise coefficient (2/32/32/3 long-channel, larger for short-channel), VcharV_{char}Vchar​ is the device's characteristic voltage (long-channel ≈ΔV/γ\approx\Delta V/\gamma≈ΔV/γ), PPP is the power dissipation (Eq.(21): P=2ηNVDDqmaxf0P=2\eta N V_{DD}q_{max}f_0P=2ηNVDD​qmax​f0​), and the per-stage noise is given by Eq.(17),(18) in2‾/Δf=4kTγμCox(W/L)ΔV\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=4kT\gamma\mu C_{ox}(W/L)\Delta Vin2​​/Δf=4kTγμCox​(W/L)ΔV. Meaning: ring white-noise phase noise collapses into a figure of merit — only kT/PkT/PkT/P, the voltage ratio VDD/VcharV_{DD}/V_{char}VDD​/Vchar​, and (f0/Δf)2(f_0/\Delta f)^2(f0​/Δf)2 appear. Key conclusion (claim C7): NNN is entirely absent from Eq.(23) — at fixed f0f_0f0​ and power PPP, the phase noise of a single-ended ring is independent of the number of stages NNN. Why N-independent: microscopically, raising NNN lowers Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (Eq.16) but simultaneously lowers each stage's swing qmaxq_{max}qmax​ and adds more noisy stages; [P2] shows these effects cancel exactly at fixed PPP, f0f_0f0​, so Eq.(23) contains no NNN. Hence "how many stages should my ring have" is not decided by phase noise, but by phase margin, tuning range, area, quadrature needs, and other considerations. Correction note (v3): the prefactor of [P2] Eq.(23) is 8/(3η)8/(3\eta)8/(3η) (η\etaη being the stage-delay proportionality constant of Eq.14, ≈1\approx1≈1); γ\gammaγ enters only through Vchar=ΔV/γV_{char}=\Delta V/\gammaVchar​=ΔV/γ. (v2 mistakenly changed it to 8/(3γ)8/(3\gamma)8/(3γ) and mislabeled it "verified verbatim"; v3 corrected it against the original PDF p.796.) The VT=0V_T=0VT​=0 lower bound is accordingly corrected to 16γ/(3η)16\gamma/(3\eta)16γ/(3η). γ\gammaγ (noise coefficient) and η\etaη (frequency proportionality constant, Eq.14) are different quantities — do not confuse them.

Python verification: import numpy as np k, T = 1.380649e-23, 300.0 kT = k*T # J Ec, L, gam_s, gam_l = 4e6, 0.25e-6, 2.5, 2/3 # [P2] p.799 numbers for oscillator #3; long-channel gamma = 2/3 ID = 3.47e-3 # A, simulated mid-transition drain current (#3) Si_28 = 8*kT*gam_s*ID/(Ec*L) # [P2] Eq.(28) Vchar_s = Ec*L/gam_s # [P2] Eq.(30) print(f"{Si_28:.2e}") # -> 2.87e-22 A^2/Hz (paper prints 2.87e-22) print(round(Vchar_s, 3)) # -> 0.4 V # short vs long channel: paper prints the factor gamma*dV/(Ec*L) (p.796); the site reads it with two gammas VT = 0.5 # V, ASSUMED (the paper does not print V_T for the 0.25 um process) dV = 2.5/2 - VT # gate overdrive at mid-transition, [P2] p.795 Vchar_l = dV/gam_l ratio = Vchar_l/Vchar_s # = (gam_s/gam_l)*dV/(Ec*L) print(round(Vchar_l,3), round(ratio,2), round(10*np.log10(ratio),1)) # -> 1.125 2.81 4.5 print(round(dV/(Ec*L),2)) # -> 0.75 same-gamma ratio dV/(Ec L) # N-independence check: N x Eq.(6) with Eq.(16),(28) under P = 2*eta*N*VDD*qmax*f0 and f0 = ID/(2*eta*N*qmax) def L_short(N, P=25e-3, f0=1.33e9, VDD=2.5, eta=0.75, df=1e6): qmax = P/(2*eta*N*VDD*f0); ID = 2*eta*N*qmax*f0 G2 = 2*np.pi**2/(3*eta**3*N**3) Si = 8*kT*gam_s*ID/(Ec*L) return 10*np.log10(N*G2*Si/(8*np.pi**2*df**2*qmax**2)) Ls = [round(float(L_short(N)),2) for N in (3,5,7,11,19)] L23 = 10*np.log10(8/(3*0.75)*kT/25e-3*2.5/Vchar_s*(1.33e9/1e6)**2) print(Ls, round(L23,2)) # -> [-111.86, -111.86, -111.86, -111.86, -111.86] -111.86 dBc/Hz (identical for N = 3..19 and equal to Eq.(23)) Applicability and failure conditions: Eq.(27) is a first-order fully-velocity-saturated model (valid only for ΔV≫EcL\Delta V\gg E_cLΔV≫Ec​L; oscillator number 3 has ΔV≈0.75\Delta V\approx0.75ΔV≈0.75 V against EcL=1.0E_cL=1.0Ec​L=1.0 V, which is really only the transition region, yet the paper applies it directly); the value of γ\gammaγ (2–3) is itself empirical and bias-dependent; Eq.(28) counts channel thermal noise only — no gate resistance, substrate, or induced-gate noise. For the measured comparison see "Measured validation" below.

documents.t: Original formulas ([P2] Sec. V-B, p.796, verified verbatim against a render of the original PDF): Power (Eq.(31)) and frequency (Eq.(32)): P=N Itail VDDf0=12NtD≈12ηNtr≈Itail2ηNqmaxP=N\,I_{tail}\,V_{DD} \qquad\qquad f_0=\frac{1}{2Nt_D}\approx\frac{1}{2\eta N t_r}\approx\frac{I_{tail}}{2\eta N q_{max}}P=NItail​VDD​f0​=2NtD​1​≈2ηNtr​1​≈2ηNqmax​Itail​​ Noise on each single-ended node (Eq.(33); two shares — differential transistor + load resistor RLR_LRL​ — with Vchar=(VGS−VT)/γV_{char}=(V_{GS}-V_T)/\gammaVchar​=(VGS​−VT​)/γ for a balanced long-channel stage, EcL/γE_cL/\gammaEc​L/γ short-channel): in2‾Δf=(in2‾Δf)N+(in2‾Δf)Load=4kT Itail(1Vchar+1RLItail)\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=\left(\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}\right)_{N}+\left(\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}\right)_{Load}=4kT\,I_{tail}\left(\frac{1}{V_{char}}+\frac{1}{R_L I_{tail}}\right)Δfin2​​​=(Δfin2​​​)N​+(Δfin2​​​)Load​=4kTItail​(Vchar​1​+RL​Itail​1​) The ring has 2N2N2N nodes (two outputs per stage), and the total phase noise is 2N2N2N times the single-source value (p.796, verbatim: "The phase noise and jitter due to all 2N2N2N noise sources is 2N2N2N times the value given by (6) and (12)." — this 2 is a node count, not the SSB convention's 2). Combined with the Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ of Eq.(16), it collapses into (Eq.(34)/(35); L\mathcal{L}L is the paper's L{Δf}L\{\Delta f\}L{Δf}): Lmin{Δf}=83η⋅N⋅kTP⋅(VDDVchar+VDDRLItail)⋅f02Δf2\mathcal{L}_{min}\{\Delta f\}=\frac{8}{3\eta}\cdot N\cdot\frac{kT}{P}\cdot\left(\frac{V_{DD}}{V_{char}}+\frac{V_{DD}}{R_L I_{tail}}\right)\cdot\frac{f_0^2}{\Delta f^2}Lmin​{Δf}=3η8​⋅N⋅PkT​⋅(Vchar​VDD​​+RL​Itail​VDD​​)⋅Δf2f02​​κmin=83η⋅N⋅kTP⋅(VDDVchar+VDDRLItail)\kappa_{min}=\sqrt{\frac{8}{3\eta}}\cdot\sqrt{N\cdot\frac{kT}{P}\cdot\left(\frac{V_{DD}}{V_{char}}+\frac{V_{DD}}{R_L I_{tail}}\right)}κmin​=3η8​​⋅N⋅PkT​⋅(Vchar​VDD​​+RL​Itail​VDD​​)​ The paper states verbatim that both are "valid in both long- and short-channel regimes of operation with the right choice of VcharV_{char}Vchar​"; a bipolar differential ring's shot + load noise (Eq.(36), p.797) folds back into the same two equations with Vchar=4kT/qeV_{char}=4kT/q_eVchar​=4kT/qe​. Meaning: only two differences from single-ended Eq.(23) — an explicit NNN, and an extra load share VDD/(RLItail)V_{DD}/(R_L I_{tail})VDD​/(RL​Itail​) in the bracket. At fixed f0f_0f0​ and PPP, a differential ring's phase noise degrades with NNN (ΔL=10log⁡10(N2/N1)\Delta\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}(N_2/N_1)ΔL=10log10​(N2​/N1​); for jitter, κmin∝N\kappa_{min}\propto\sqrt Nκmin​∝N​) — the lost other half of N-independence. Why the NNN appears (exponent bookkeeping, fixed PPP, f0f_0f0​, fixed swing): P=NItailVDDP=NI_{tail}V_{DD}P=NItail​VDD​ is a static bookkeeping (unlike Eq.(21), it is not tied to f0f_0f0​), so fixed PPP forces Itail∝1/NI_{tail}\propto1/NItail​∝1/N; Eq.(32) then forces qmax=Itail/(2ηNf0)∝1/N2q_{max}=I_{tail}/(2\eta Nf_0)\propto1/N^2qmax​=Itail​/(2ηNf0​)∝1/N2 (p.797, verbatim: "…reduce the swing, and hence qmaxq_{max}qmax​, by a factor of 1/N21/N^21/N2"). Hence 2N⋅Γrms2⋅Si/qmax2∝N⋅N−3⋅N−1⋅N4=N+12N\cdot\Gamma_{rms}^2\cdot S_i/q_{max}^2\propto N\cdot N^{-3}\cdot N^{-1}\cdot N^{4}=N^{+1}2N⋅Γrms2​⋅Si​/qmax2​∝N⋅N−3⋅N−1⋅N4=N+1. Full term-by-term table and worked example: lc_vs_ring Step 2b. [P2]'s conclusion sentence (pp.796–797, verbatim): "Note that, in contrast with the single-ended ring oscillator, a differential oscillator does exhibit a phase noise and jitter dependency on the number of stages, with the phase noise degrading as the number of stages increases for a given frequency and power dissipation." Numerical example: f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, kT=4.0×10−21kT=4.0\times10^{-21}kT=4.0×10−21 J, P=1P=1P=1 mW, η≈1\eta\approx1η≈1, VDD/Vchar=3V_{DD}/V_{char}=3VDD​/Vchar​=3, VDD/(RLItail)=2V_{DD}/(R_LI_{tail})=2VDD​/(RL​Itail​)=2 (fixed swing): N=4N=4N=4 gives −82.7-82.7−82.7 dBc/Hz, N=12N=12N=12 gives −78.0-78.0−78.0 dBc/Hz, ΔL=10log⁡103=+4.77\Delta\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}3=+4.77ΔL=10log10​3=+4.77 dB; and κmin\kappa_{min}κmin​ grows by ×3≈1.732\times\sqrt3\approx1.732×3​≈1.732. (Convention flag (corrected in v11): Eq.(34) is collected from 2N×2N\times2N×Eq.(6), and the printed [P2] Eq.(6), p.792 has denominator 8π2foff2=2Δω28\pi^2f_{off}^2=2\Delta\omega^28π2foff2​=2Δω2 — this site's L/2\mathcal{L}_{/2}L/2​ family, 3 dB above the /4/4/4 SSB family of [P1] Eq.(21) with its 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2. So the absolute values −82.7-82.7−82.7/−78.0-78.0−78.0 dBc/Hz are /2/2/2-family numbers; in the [P1] Eq.(21) bookkeeping they read −85.7-85.7−85.7/−81.0-81.0−81.0 dBc/Hz. ΔL\Delta\mathcal{L}ΔL is a difference, identical under both conventions.) Python verification: import numpy as np def L_ring_diff(N, kT, P, f0, df, eta=1.0, vdd_vchar=3.0, vdd_swing=2.0): # [P2] Eq.(34) return 10*np.log10(8/(3*eta) * N * (kT/P) * (vdd_vchar + vdd_swing) * (f0/df)**2) L4 = L_ring_diff(4, 4.0e-21, 1e-3, 5e9, 1e6) L12 = L_ring_diff(12, 4.0e-21, 1e-3, 5e9, 1e6) print(round(L4,1), round(L12,1), round(L12-L4,2)) # -> -82.7 -78.0 4.77 # Eq.(34) = 2N x Eq.(6); Eq.(6) denominator 8*pi^2*f^2 = 2*dw^2 -> these are /2-family values; [P1] Eq.(21) /4 family is 3.01 dB lower print(round(L4-10*np.log10(2),1), round(L12-10*np.log10(2),1)) # -> -85.7 -81.0 One-line design rule: single-ended = NNN-free (Eq.23); differential = fewest stages wins (Eq.34, +3.01+3.01+3.01 dB per doubling) — the lower bound on NNN is set by phase margin / quadrature / multiphase needs, so do not add more. Tail-source noise near f0f_0f0​ "surprisingly" does not enter the phase noise (p.796); what enters is its low-frequency noise (the symmetry path) and its noise near even harmonics (filterable with an LC).

documents.t: The most underrated section of [P2]: it uses 26 fabricated rings (three topologies, two processes — 2 µm 5 V and 0.25 µm 2.5 V — from 115 MHz to 5.5 GHz) to compare Eq.(6)/(23)/(34) with the measured L(1 MHz)\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})L(1MHz) device by device, and Fig. 16 to compare Eq.(8)/(12)/(35) with measured jitter. Measurement systems (p.798): HP 8563E, RDL NTS-1000A, HP E5500 (phase noise); Tektronix CSA 803A (jitter). The offset is fixed at 1 MHz to maximize the measurement dynamic range. documents.t: import numpy as np # [P2] Table II (current-starved single-ended, all 0.25 um / 2.5 V, p.799): N -> (I_sup mA, f0 MHz, measured L(1 MHz) dBc/Hz) tab2 = {3:(2.34,751,-114.0), 5:(2.51,850,-112.6), 7:(2.49,931,-111.7), 9:(2.73,932,-112.5), 11:(2.65,869,-112.2), 15:(2.8,929,-112.3), 17:(3.8,898,-112.0), 19:(3.9,959,-110.9)} # normalise each row to f0 = 900 MHz, P = 2.5 V x 2.5 mA = 6.25 mW with L ~ f0^2/P (Eq.23) norm = np.array([L - 20*np.log10(f/900) + 10*np.log10(2.5*I/6.25) for N,(I,f,L) in tab2.items()]) print(round(norm.min(),1), round(norm.max(),1), round(norm.max()-norm.min(),1)) # -> -112.7 -109.5 3.2 dBc/Hz (total spread after normalisation, N = 3..19, only 3.2 dB) print(round(10*np.log10(19**3/3**3),1)) # -> 24.0 dB (what Gamma_rms^2 ~ N^-3 alone would predict for N = 3 -> 19) # [P2] Table III rows 12/24/25/26 (p.800): P = 10 mW and R_L*I_tail = 2 V for all four -> Eq.(34) bracket fixed tab3 = {4:(2810,-95.4,-95.2), 6:(859,-103.9,-104.3), 8:(731,-104.1,-106.2), 12:(447,-106.6,-109.5)} # N: (f_max MHz, Pred.(34), Meas.) for N,(f,Lp,Lm) in tab3.items(): s = 20*np.log10(2810/f) print(N, round(Lp+s,1), round(Lm+s,1), round(10*np.log10(N/4),1)) # -> 4 -95.4 -95.2 0.0 # -> 6 -93.6 -94.0 1.8 # -> 8 -92.4 -94.5 3.0 # -> 12 -90.6 -93.5 4.8 (N, normalised Pred.(34), normalised Meas., Eq.(34)'s 10log(N/4); units dBc/Hz, dB) Applicability and failure conditions (when reading the three tables): (i) the predictions count white noise only (Eq.(6)/(23)/(34)); at 1 MHz offset these rings are already in the 1/f² region, hence the agreement; close-in (1/f³) belongs to Fig. 17 and symmetry. (ii) Eq.(23)/(34) assume symmetric waveforms and ignore supply/substrate and tail-source noise, so they are lower bounds (p.796); most measurements land within ±2 dB of the prediction, a few (the low-frequency Table III devices, oscillators 19–23) measure 4–6 dB above it. (iii) η\etaη, IDI_DID​, CtotalC_{total}Ctotal​ and the swing all come from circuit simulation and the paper does not print all of them (this site back-fits η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75 for oscillator 3). (iv) The ΔT\sqrt{\Delta T}ΔT​ segment of the jitter only lasts to roughly 10−810^{-8}10−8–10−710^{-7}10−7 s, after which 1/f takes over with slope 1; a SerDes integration that crosses that point needs the two-segment treatment (see jitter_kernels).

documents.t: Jitter and phase noise share one origin: lowering Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ lowers both; do not treat long-term jitter and close-in phase noise as two separate problems. Adding stages is not a phase-noise cure: for single-ended rings at fixed f0f_0f0​, PPP the phase noise is nearly independent of NNN (conclusion verified); differential rings want even fewer stages — Eq.(34) contains an explicit NNN, costing +3.01+3.01+3.01 dB per doubling at fixed f0f_0f0​, PPP. The real reasons to add stages are quadrature/multi-phase outputs, tuning range, and phase margin. Symmetry is the master knob for close-in noise: tune the rise/fall to be symmetric (e.g. the control voltage of Fig. 17) to suppress c0c_0c0​ and push the 1/f³ corner far out. Differential rings are usually more symmetric than single-ended ones. The steeper the transition, the better: the energy is concentrated at the transitions; the higher the slope, the larger qmaxq_{max}qmax​ and the relatively smaller Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. Design-side summaries in lc_vs_ring and symmetry; the SerDes view is in serdes_clocking_connection.

documents.t: Per paper_metadata (paper_002.limitations): Toy/first-order: short-channel effects and detailed device noise are approximate. The N-independence conclusion holds only for single-ended rings, at fixed power, fixed frequency, and for the specific noise model ([P2] Sec.V, Eq.(23)/(25), p.796, verified, claim C7); a differential ring instead contains an explicit NNN (Eq.(34), p.796, verified). Substrate/supply noise is treated separately and qualitatively.
documents.s: Limitations

documents.t: [P1] is the foundation: this page's jitter κ\kappaκ, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, and symmetry all use [P1]'s ISF and Eq.(21)/(24). [P3]/[P4] also use the ring as a vehicle ([P4]'s ILFD/prescaler is an inverter-chain ring), extending the ISF from phase noise to injection. [P5] is unrelated to this page; but latch-based/differential ring start-up also relies on cross-coupled positive feedback (the corner-case bridge of claim C12).

documents.t: Prerequisites: paper_001 (the ISF definition and the Eq.(11) phase kick from [P1]), fourier_series_of_isf (the Fourier harmonics cnc_ncn​ of the ISF) | Next: paper_004 (Part II: APF amplitude, transient, frequency division). This is an advanced deep dive. It extends the ISF of [P1] from "phase noise of a free-running oscillator" to "injection locking / pulling of an oscillator driven by an external signal." Core result: a single first-order differential equation written in terms of the ISF (the generalized Adler equation) predicts the lock range, the locked phase, and stability, for any oscillator topology and any injection waveform — and from it follows a recipe for designing the injection waveform that maximizes the lock range. Scope of this page: advanced deep-dive, not a core teaching chapter. The core equations (impulse-train Eq.(19)–(23), generalized Adler Eq.(26), (28)–(30), (33), (35)) have been verified against the original [P3] PDF. Make sure you have digested the ISF from [P1] (paper_001) before reading this.

documents.s: Citation

documents.t: The same ISF Γ\GammaΓ that computes phase noise also yields a topology-independent generalized Adler equation that predicts the lock range, locked phase, and stability for any oscillator and any injection waveform, and shows how to design the injection waveform to enlarge the lock range (claim C10).
documents.s: One-sentence contribution

documents.t: Injection locking means: when an oscillator is injected with an external signal whose frequency is close to its own, it "synchronizes to the external signal" — its phase and frequency get captured. When the frequency offset is too large to follow, the phase slips periodically and produces unwanted spurs; this is injection pulling. The phenomenon is everywhere — PLLs, clock distribution, quadrature generation, frequency division — both exploited and feared. In 1946 Adler described the behavior of an LC oscillator under weak, sinusoidal, near-free-running injection with a single first-order phase equation. [P3] identifies five major limitations of the Adler equation (weak injection only, LC only, sinusoidal injection assumed, requires hard-to-measure QQQ and IoscI_{osc}Iosc​, and predicts a symmetric lock range), then fully generalizes it using the ISF: Replace the LC-only parameters QQQ / IoscI_{osc}Iosc​ with Γ\GammaΓ — any oscillator whose ISF can be extracted qualifies. Allow arbitrary injection waveforms (not just sinusoids), so the injection waveform can be designed to maximize the lock range. Naturally produces an asymmetric lock range (common in real circuits, missed by Adler). Covers subharmonic / superharmonic locking (injection frequency near ω0/m\omega_0/mω0​/m or mω0m\omega_0mω0​).
documents.s: Why this paper matters

documents.t: Per paper_metadata (paper_003.assumptions): Oscillator autonomy and periodic time variance (same foundation as the ISF). Injection (perturbation) maps to phase through the ISF; amplitude is deferred to Part II (APF). Time-synchronous averaging: time-synchronous averaging over one period. Physical intuition: phase noise feeds the perturbation machine random noise; injection feeds it a deterministic, periodic injection current iinji_{inj}iinj​. Same "ISF-weight-then-integrate" machine — when the input changes from random to deterministic, the output changes from statistics (Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, PSD) to deterministic phase dynamics (locking / slipping).
