documents.t: Between classical Adler (Sec. III) and the time-synchronous model (Sec. V), [P3] inserts a purely arithmetic thought experiment (Sec. IV Locking to an Impulse Train, p.2112): feed an ideal LC oscillator a train of current impulses. Its value: not a drop of calculus is needed — using only the discrete bookkeeping "one impulse = one phase kick," it reproduces the lock range of classical Adler's Eq.(18) to the letter. And "one impulse = one kick" is exactly the interactive animation ImpulseAnimation you played with on isf_definition: one press of "Inject!" = one Δϕ=Γ(θ) Δqqmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma(\theta)\,\frac{\Delta q}{q_{max}}Δϕ=Γ(θ)qmax​Δq​ This section merely replaces "press once by hand" with "press automatically every TinjT_{inj}Tinj​ seconds" — the same physics, made periodic. (The animation kicks along the voltage axis with ΔV=Δq/C\Delta V=\Delta q/CΔV=Δq/C; [P3] Fig. 3 kicks along the charge axis with qinjq_{inj}qinj​ — the same thing, since V=q/CV=q/CV=q/C.) Setup ([P3] Fig. 3(a), p.2112): an ideal parallel LC (CCC, LLL, RPR_PRP​, −Gm-G_m−Gm​) with a periodic impulse-train injection current iinj(t)=± qinj∑n=−∞∞δ(t−nTinj),Tinj≡2πωinji_{inj}(t)=\pm\,q_{inj}\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t-nT_{inj}),\qquad T_{inj}\equiv\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{inj}}iinj​(t)=±qinj​n=−∞∑∞​δ(t−nTinj​),Tinj​≡ωinj​2π​ ([P3] adopts the convention qinj≥0q_{inj}\ge0qinj​≥0; the sign selects Fig. 3(b), speeding up, or Fig. 3(c), slowing down). Each impulse dumps a fixed charge qinjq_{inj}qinj​ [C] onto the capacitor in one shot. The key arrangement: the impulse lands at the zero crossing of the capacitor charge q(t)q(t)q(t) — it moves the capacitor voltage "to the opposite side of the zero-crossing" ([P3]'s words: "moving the capacitor voltage to the opposite side of the zero-crossing"), shifting the state-space point horizontally from q=−qinj/2q=-q_{inj}/2q=−qinj​/2 to q=+qinj/2q=+q_{inj}/2q=+qinj​/2. Half lock range: fL=qinjqmaxTinj⋅12π=0.01×5.005×1092π=7.97f_L=\dfrac{q_{inj}}{q_{max}T_{inj}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\pi}=\dfrac{0.01\times5.005\times10^{9}}{2\pi}=7.97fL​=qmax​Tinj​qinj​​⋅2π1​=2π0.01×5.005×109​=7.97 MHz; the 5 MHz detuning is inside the range ✓. Feel for the convergence: multiplier 1−0.01cos⁡θ\*=0.99221-0.01\cos\theta^\*=0.99221−0.01cosθ\*=0.9922, so 1/e1/e1/e convergence takes about 128 periods (≈25.7\approx25.7≈25.7 ns) — weak-injection locking is a "hundreds of periods" slow dynamic, which is precisely what justifies treating θ\thetaθ as a slow variable in the time-averaging. import numpy as np q_max, q_inj = 1e-12, 10e-15 # C f0, f_inj = 5e9, 5.005e9 # Hz T_inj = 1/f_inj # s drift = 2*np.pi*(f0 - f_inj)*T_inj # rad per period print(q_inj/q_max) # -> 0.01 print(drift) # -> -0.0062769083987808056 theta = 0.0 for n in range(3000): # discrete map theta += drift + (-np.sin(theta))*q_inj/q_max print(theta, np.degrees(theta)) # -> -0.6785833433413406 -38.879961621335696 print((q_inj/(q_max*T_inj))/(2*np.pi)/1e6) # -> 7.965704901749362 I_inj = 2*q_inj/T_inj print(I_inj, I_inj/(2*q_max)) # -> 0.0001001 50050000.0 print(1 - (q_inj/q_max)*np.cos(theta)) # -> 0.9922153727798411 print(1/((q_inj/q_max)*np.cos(theta))) # -> 128.45830271877517 (The 3000 steps are just conservative convergence; the fixed point θ\*\theta^\*θ\*, the lock range, and the Adler cross-check all agree with the hand calculation.) Slow phase: the net phase change per period must be ≪2π\ll2\pi≪2π rad for the map→ODE continuum limit (also the premise of Eq.(30)'s time-averaging) to hold. Amplitude assumption: "the amplitude never moves" holds only for an ideal LC with a charge kick across the zero crossing; a general oscillator relies on its amplitude-restoration mechanism to pull back to the limit cycle — that is the subject of Part II's APF ([P4]). Subharmonic: the impulse may also land once every MMM periods ([P3] footnote 7, p.2112) — the same arithmetic with the drift accumulated over MMM periods; this is the discrete picture of subharmonic locking. [P3] footnote 7, verbatim (p.2112): "...injection could also occur every MMM periods (MMM a positive integer), corresponding to subharmonic locking." In other words: when Tinj=N⋅T0T_{inj}=N\cdot T_0Tinj​=N⋅T0​ (injecting once every NNN oscillation periods) that is exactly subharmonic locking — swap the paper's MMM for the site's usual multiplication ratio NNN and expand term by term; the closed-form lock range lives on the subharmonic_injection page. documents.t: [P3] first converts Hajimiri's dimensionless ISF Γ\GammaΓ into a unit-bearing version ([P3] Eq.(26), p.2113): Γ~(x)≡Γ(x)qmax[units: rad/C]\tilde\Gamma(x)\equiv\frac{\Gamma(x)}{q_{max}}\qquad[\text{units: rad/C}]Γ~(x)≡qmax​Γ(x)​[units: rad/C] Then the instantaneous phase kick of the injection current, and the change of coordinates to the relative phase θ=ϕ−ωinjt\theta=\phi-\omega_{inj}tθ=ϕ−ωinj​t ([P3] Eq.(28)–(29), p.2113): dϕdt=Γ~(ϕ) iinj(t) → θ=ϕ−ωinjt dθdt=(ω0−ωinj)+Γ~(ωinjt+θ) iinj(t)\frac{d\phi}{dt}=\tilde\Gamma(\phi)\,i_{inj}(t) \;\xrightarrow{\ \theta=\phi-\omega_{inj}t\ }\; \frac{d\theta}{dt}=(\omega_0-\omega_{inj})+\tilde\Gamma(\omega_{inj}t+\theta)\,i_{inj}(t)dtdϕ​=Γ~(ϕ)iinj​(t) θ=ϕ−ωinj​t ​dtdθ​=(ω0​−ωinj​)+Γ~(ωinj​t+θ)iinj​(t) Time-synchronous averaging over "one fast injection period" (treating the slowly varying θ\thetaθ as constant) gives the time-averaged generalized Adler equation ([P3] Eq.(30), p.2113): dθdt=(ω0−ωinj)+1Tinj∫TinjΓ~(ωinjt+θ) iinj(t) dt\frac{d\theta}{dt}=(\omega_0-\omega_{inj})+\frac{1}{T_{inj}}\int_{T_{inj}}\tilde\Gamma(\omega_{inj}t+\theta)\,i_{inj}(t)\,dtdtdθ​=(ω0​−ωinj​)+Tinj​1​∫Tinj​​Γ~(ωinj​t+θ)iinj​(t)dt Rearranged into lock-characteristic form ([P3] Eq.(33), p.2114): dθdt=(ω0−ωinj)+Ω(θ), Ω(θ)=1Tinj∫TinjΓ~(ωinjt+θ) iinj(t) dt \frac{d\theta}{dt}=(\omega_0-\omega_{inj})+\Omega(\theta),\qquad \boxed{\ \Omega(\theta)=\frac{1}{T_{inj}}\int_{T_{inj}}\tilde\Gamma(\omega_{inj}t+\theta)\,i_{inj}(t)\,dt\ }dtdθ​=(ω0​−ωinj​)+Ω(θ), Ω(θ)=Tinj​1​∫Tinj​​Γ~(ωinj​t+θ)iinj​(t)dt ​ where Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ) is called the lock characteristic ([P3] Eq.(33), p.2114): the injection-induced average frequency shift as a function of the phase difference θ\thetaθ. Note the plus sign in front of the averaged term (same sign convention as [P3] Eq.(30)). It is not invented in Sec. V: as early as Sec. II-B (p.2110), [P3] uses "locked ⇔ dθ/dt=0d\theta/dt=0dθ/dt=0" (Eq.(8)) to formally define Ω(θ):=Δω∣dθ/dt=0\Omega(\theta):=\Delta\omega\big|_{d\theta/dt=0}Ω(θ):=Δω​dθ/dt=0​ with Δω:=ωinj−ω0\Delta\omega:=\omega_{inj}-\omega_0Δω:=ωinj​−ω0​ (Eq.(9)), and defines the upper/lower lock ranges as ωL+=max⁡θΩ(θ)\omega_L^+=\max_\theta\Omega(\theta)ωL+​=maxθ​Ω(θ), ωL−=min⁡θΩ(θ)\omega_L^-=\min_\theta\Omega(\theta)ωL−​=minθ​Ω(θ) (Eq.(10)); what Sec. V does is use time-synchronous averaging to re-derive this abstract definition as an explicit integral of the ISF and the injection waveform (Eq.(33)). So "lock range = width of the range of Ω\OmegaΩ" is a definition, while "Ω\OmegaΩ = the period-average of ISF × injection" is the physical content of this paper. Meaning: a single first-order ODE built from the unit-bearing ISF Γ~=Γ/qmax\tilde\Gamma=\Gamma/q_{max}Γ~=Γ/qmax​ and the injection waveform iinji_{inj}iinj​, predicting the behavior of any oscillator under any injection waveform (claim C10). Locking = existence of a θ\*\theta^\*θ\* with ωinj−ω0=Ω(θ\*)\omega_{inj}-\omega_0=\Omega(\theta^\*)ωinj​−ω0​=Ω(θ\*); lock range = the width of the range of Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ); stability is set by the sign of dΩ/dθd\Omega/d\thetadΩ/dθ. Sinusoidal injection reduces to classical Adler ([P3] Eq.(34)–(35)): for a single tone iinj=Iinjcos⁡ωinjti_{inj}=I_{inj}\cos\omega_{inj}tiinj​=Iinj​cosωinj​t, only the ISF fundamental Γ~1\tilde\Gamma_1Γ~1​ survives: Ω(θ)=12Iinj ∣Γ~1∣cos⁡(θ+∠Γ~1),ωL=12Iinj ∣Γ~1∣\Omega(\theta)=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\,\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvert\cos(\theta+\angle\tilde\Gamma_1), \qquad \omega_L=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\,\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvertΩ(θ)=21​Iinj​∣Γ~1​∣cos(θ+∠Γ~1​),ωL​=21​Iinj​∣Γ~1​∣ Half lock range ωL=12Iinj∣Γ~1∣\omega_L=\frac12 I_{inj}\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvertωL​=21​Iinj​∣Γ~1​∣ ([P3] Eq.(35)) — Ω∝cos⁡θ\Omega\propto\cos\thetaΩ∝cosθ is symmetric about 0, exactly classical Adler. Why it is asymmetric in general: for an arbitrary injection, Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ) contains multiple harmonics, its range is no longer symmetric about 0, so ωL+≠−ωL−\omega_L^+\ne-\omega_L^-ωL+​=−ωL−​ — the asymmetry common in real circuits that Adler cannot capture. Injection waveform design: lock range = the width of the range of Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ). Aligning the harmonics of the injection waveform iinji_{inj}iinj​ with the harmonics of the ISF Γ~\tilde\GammaΓ~ (making the inner product larger) enlarges the lock range — one more degree of freedom (waveform shape) beyond "just increase the injection current." Verified: Γ~=Γ/qmax\tilde\Gamma=\Gamma/q_{max}Γ~=Γ/qmax​ (Eq.26), the pulling equations Eq.(28)–(30), the lock characteristic Eq.(33), the sinusoidal reduction Eq.(34), and the lock range Eq.(35) have all been confirmed verbatim against the rendered original [P3] PDF, p.2113–2114.

documents.t: The generalized Adler equation is not just pretty on paper — [P3] closes with two layers of evidence, paraphrased here from the original (not a transistor-level simulation by this site; every number is a transcription of the paper's published figures, with page numbers checked against the rendered pages): (1) Transient simulation vs. theory (Sec. V-H, p.2116–2117). Two oscillators free-running at roughly f0=1f_0=1f0​=1 GHz: the 6-stage differential ring of Fig. 12 (each stage a differential pair with resistive load, Imax=3.0I_{max}=3.0Imax​=3.0 mA) and the Bose relaxation oscillator of Fig. 13 (Schmitt trigger + RC, Vmax±=±1V_{max}^\pm=\pm1Vmax±​=±1 V, VT±=±0.5V_T^\pm=\pm0.5VT±​=±0.5 V, R=50 ΩR=50\ \OmegaR=50 Ω, C=9.1C=9.1C=9.1 pF, Imax=29I_{max}=29Imax​=29 mA). The ISFs were obtained by direct impulse-response simulation (the method of [P1]); the simulated lock characteristic was obtained by "first find the lock range by inspection (1 MHz resolution), then sweep finjf_{inj}finj​ across it and read θ\thetaθ at each point," overlaid on the theoretical curve of Eq.(34) (unstable branch dashed). documents.t: The lock range is designable: lock range = the width of the range of ⟨Γ iinj⟩\langle\Gamma\,i_{inj}\rangle⟨Γiinj​⟩ over ϕ\phiϕ. Aligning the harmonics of the injection waveform iinji_{inj}iinj​ with the harmonics of the ISF Γ\GammaΓ (making the inner product larger) enlarges the lock range — one more degree of freedom (waveform shape) beyond "just increase the injection current." Topology-independent: as long as the ISF can be extracted, the same equation applies to ring, LC, and relaxation oscillators; no need to measure the hard-to-measure QQQ and IoscI_{osc}Iosc​. Subharmonic / superharmonic locking: when the injection frequency is near ω0/m\omega_0/mω0​/m or mω0m\omega_0mω0​, it is the corresponding harmonic of Γ\GammaΓ that does the averaging — this connects directly to frequency division (ILFD) in [P4]. Pulling is the other face of the same equation: when ∣Δω∣>|\Delta\omega| > ∣Δω∣> lock range, dϕ/dtd\phi/dtdϕ/dt is nonzero and the phase slips periodically, producing pulling spurs. In design, make sure the operating frequency falls inside the lock range.

documents.t: Per paper_metadata (paper_003.limitations): Part I covers phase only; amplitude modulation is deferred to Part II (APF, [P4]). Relies on an accurately extracted ISF — if the ISF is off, the predictions are off. "Injection Locked ⇔ dθ/dt=0d\theta/dt=0dθ/dt=0" is only a special case ([P3] Eq.(8), p.2110): the general definition is θ(t)=θ(t+Tinj)\theta(t)=\theta(t+T_{inj})θ(t)=θ(t+Tinj​) (Eq.(6)), equivalently 1Tinj∫Tinjdθdtdt=0\frac{1}{T_{inj}}\int_{T_{inj}}\frac{d\theta}{dt}dt=0Tinj​1​∫Tinj​​dtdθ​dt=0 (Eq.(7)) — it only requires zero net change of θ\thetaθ per period and allows intra-period variation (Fig. 1(c)). Eq.(8) throws the intra-period variation away in exchange for the simplicity of a first-order ODE (justified by time-averaging). [P3] footnote 3 (p.2110) states plainly that these intra-period variations could have a significant impact on higher-order locking properties, and lists it as an open question. Every result on this page and on injection_locking_noise rests on Eq.(8). This site treats it as an advanced deep-dive, not a core teaching chapter; the core generalized-Adler equations have been verified against the [P3] original.

This page is advanced; the APF is the radial dual of the ISF. [P3] covered phase only; this paper (Part II, advanced) adds the amplitude dimension. It introduces the APF (Amplitude Perturbation Function) Δ(ϕ)\Delta(\phi)Δ(ϕ) — the "amplitude version of the ISF" Λ~(ϕ)\tilde\Lambda(\phi)Λ~(ϕ) (amplitude ISF, units 1/C1/\text{C}1/C) multiplied by the amplitude memory time, units 1/A1/\text{A}1/A — and uses it to explain amplitude modulation of LC oscillators under injection, transient locking behavior, and injection-locked frequency division (ILFD). documents.t: Defines the amplitude version of the ISF — the amplitude ISF Λ~(ϕ)\tilde\Lambda(\phi)Λ~(ϕ) (units 1/C1/\text{C}1/C) and the APF Δ(ϕ)\Delta(\phi)Δ(ϕ) (units 1/A1/\text{A}1/A) — completing the phase framework of [P3] into a full phase + amplitude model, explaining amplitude modulation under injection, transient locking, and ILFD frequency division; for an ideal LC, the ISF and APF are in quadrature (claim C11).
documents.s: One-sentence contribution

documents.t: Both [P1] and [P3] assume "amplitude perturbations are pulled back and can be ignored." That assumption is fine for phase noise and weak injection, but not for strong injection, transients, or frequency division — there the amplitude is visibly modulated, and phase and amplitude couple. Part II adds this dimension: The APF is the ISF of amplitude: the ISF Γ\GammaΓ projects injected charge onto the tangential (phase) direction of the limit cycle; the amplitude ISF Λ~\tilde\LambdaΛ~ projects it onto the radial (amplitude) direction, and the APF Δ\DeltaΔ multiplies that radial projection by its decay time. Only together do they form the complete projection of a perturbation. In an ideal LC, the ISF and APF are in quadrature (90° apart): at the moment of maximum phase sensitivity (the zero-crossing), amplitude sensitivity is minimal; at the moment of maximum amplitude sensitivity (the peak), phase sensitivity is minimal. This is the mathematical version of what phase_vs_amplitude_noise says about "why amplitude noise decays." Frequency division (ILFD): inject a signal at NNN times the frequency into an oscillator so it locks at the 1/N1/N1/N subharmonic — a low-power frequency divider. Part II designs such dividers within the ISF/APF framework and builds a dual-modulus prescaler with switchable division ratio.
documents.s: Why this paper matters

documents.t: Per paper_metadata (paper_004.assumptions): Built on top of the time-synchronous ISF model of Part I. Amplitude dynamics are captured to first order via the APF and the amplitude decay function. The amplitude-modulation results focus on LC oscillators. Physical intuition (2-D projection): an injected charge Δq\Delta qΔq nudges the state point. Decompose the nudge along the two orthogonal directions of the limit cycle — tangential (phase, permanent) measured by Γ\GammaΓ, radial (amplitude, pulled back) measured by the amplitude ISF Λ~\tilde\LambdaΛ~. Phase noise cares only about the tangential part; the full dynamics of injection need both.

documents.t: The amplitude ISF Λ~(ϕ):=D(0,ϕ)\tilde\Lambda(\phi):=D(0,\phi)Λ~(ϕ):=D(0,ϕ) (units 1/C1/\text{C}1/C) is the amplitude analog of Part I's unit-bearing ISF Γ~=Γ/qmax\tilde\Gamma=\Gamma/q_{max}Γ~=Γ/qmax​ (units rad/C): the weight with which an injected current impulse projects onto the radial (amplitude) direction of the limit cycle. [P4] factors the amplitude perturbation into the product of the amplitude ISF and a decay, D(τ,ϕ)=Λ~(ϕ) d(τ,ϕ)D(\tau,\phi)=\tilde\Lambda(\phi)\,d(\tau,\phi)D(τ,ϕ)=Λ~(ϕ)d(τ,ϕ) ([P4] Eq.(18), p.2126), and defines the APF Δ(ϕ):=∫0∞D(τ,ϕ) dτ\Delta(\phi):=\int_0^\infty D(\tau,\phi)\,d\tauΔ(ϕ):=∫0∞​D(τ,ϕ)dτ ([P4] Eq.(19), p.2126, units 1/A1/\text{A}1/A; dimension check: [1/C]×[s]=1/A[1/\text{C}]\times[\text{s}]=1/\text{A}[1/C]×[s]=1/A ✓). Site convention (symbols, cf. [P4] footnote 6, p.2126): the tilde denotes "charge normalization" — Γ~=Γ/qmax\tilde\Gamma=\Gamma/q_{max}Γ~=Γ/qmax​, Λ~=Λ/qmax\tilde\Lambda=\Lambda/q_{max}Λ~=Λ/qmax​ ([P4] footnote 6 writes Λ≡qmax⋅Λ~\Lambda\equiv q_{max}\cdot\tilde\LambdaΛ≡qmax​⋅Λ~, where Λ\LambdaΛ is the dimensionless amplitude ISF of its ref. [28]); the APF Δ\DeltaΔ itself carries no tilde, because it is already Λ~\tilde\LambdaΛ~ times the time integral of the decay function (units 1/A1/\text{A}1/A), and its fundamental is written Δ1\Delta_1Δ1​ ([P4] Eq.(26)). This site always writes Λ~\tilde\LambdaΛ~ (amplitude ISF) and Δ(ϕ)\Delta(\phi)Δ(ϕ) (APF), and never uses Λ\LambdaΛ or Λ~\tilde\LambdaΛ~ to denote the APF. Unlike phase, amplitude perturbations decay — the ideal-LC amplitude decay function (in the ideal-LC section, [P4] p.2127–2128) is: d(t,ϕ)=e−t/τ0,∫0∞d(t,ϕ) dt=τ0=2Qωoscd(t,\phi)=e^{-t/\tau_0},\qquad \int_0^\infty d(t,\phi)\,dt=\tau_0=\frac{2Q}{\omega_{osc}}d(t,ϕ)=e−t/τ0​,∫0∞​d(t,ϕ)dt=τ0​=ωosc​2Q​ Key physics (gem): the "memory time" of the amplitude is τ0=2Q/ωosc\tau_0=2Q/\omega_{osc}τ0​=2Q/ωosc​ — a high-QQQ LC recovers its amplitude slowly (τ0\tau_0τ0​ is large), but it does recover (exponential decay back to the limit cycle); the phase has no such restoring force (its impulse response is a unit step — infinite memory). This is the quantitative version of "why amplitude noise is suppressed while phase noise accumulates" (claim C2). For an ideal LC, the APF and the decay are related by Δ(ϕ)=τ0 Λ~(ϕ)\Delta(\phi)=\tau_0\,\tilde\Lambda(\phi)Δ(ϕ)=τ0​Λ~(ϕ). documents.t: In its design section [P4] turns "half-wave symmetry cannot divide by 2" around: make the waveform asymmetric on purpose to manufacture the even harmonics. The key points (the full teaching version — time-domain proof, this site's toy reproduction figure /figures/isf_shaping_division.png, the Table IV worked example and the Python recomputation — is the "[P4] Sec. VII-A: ISF shaping" section of injection_locked_division): footnote 14, p.2132: the mathematical definition of half-wave symmetry, Γ~(x)=−Γ~(x+π)\tilde\Gamma(x)=-\tilde\Gamma(x+\pi)Γ~(x)=−Γ~(x+π). Fig. 15(a), p.2133 shows in the time domain that the phase kicks a second-harmonic injection delivers in two consecutive injection cycles (= two consecutive oscillation half-cycles) cancel exactly, independent of the relative phase θ\thetaθ — the time-domain version of ∣Γ~2∣=0\vert\tilde\Gamma_2\vert=0∣Γ~2​∣=0 in Eq.(30). footnote 15, p.2133: the general definition of the upper lock-range edge ωL+:=max⁡θ⟨Γ~(ωinjNt+θ) iinj(t)⟩NTinj\omega_L^{+}:=\max_\theta\big\langle\tilde\Gamma(\tfrac{\omega_{inj}}{N}t+\theta)\,i_{inj}(t)\big\rangle_{NT_{inj}}ωL+​:=maxθ​⟨Γ~(Nωinj​​t+θ)iinj​(t)⟩NTinj​​ (the maximum over θ\thetaθ of the injection term of Eq.(29); for sinusoidal injection in the linear regime it reduces to Eq.(30)'s 12Iinj∣Γ~N∣\tfrac12I_{inj}\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vert21​Iinj​∣Γ~N​∣); Fig. 15(b) shows unequal kicks in consecutive injection cycles and a net phase accrual once the waveform is asymmetric. footnote 16: the ISF amplitude scales roughly as 1/(charge swing of the injection node). Fig. 16 / Table IV, p.2134: a 1-GHz 17-stage single-ended inverter-chain ring with only WP/WNW_P/W_NWP​/WN​ changed (1.371.371.37 fairly symmetric → 8.338.338.33 PFET-dominant → 0.1750.1750.175 NFET-dominant; tF/tRt_F/t_RtF​/tR​ 0.74 → 1.92 → 0.30): ∣Γ~2∣/Γ~rms\vert\tilde\Gamma_2\vert/\tilde\Gamma_{rms}∣Γ~2​∣/Γ~rms​ 0.0927 → 0.301 → 0.371, Γ~rms\tilde\Gamma_{rms}Γ~rms​ 0.282 → 1.33 → 1.64 rad/pC (the overall ISF grows too, the "added benefit"), second-harmonic compliance η2\eta_2η2​ (Sec. VI Eq.(35)–(36), p.2132) 2.98×10−32.98\times10^{-3}2.98×10−3 → 0.0104 → 0.0130, and the simulated ÷2 lock range 2fL2f_L2fL​ for a 1.5 mA sinusoidal injection 16 → 560 → 710 MHz. footnote 17: nonlinear behavior is already prevalent at this injection strength, so the simulated lock range is much wider than Iinj∣Γ~2∣/2I_{inj}\vert\tilde\Gamma_2\vert/2Iinj​∣Γ~2​∣/2 (this site's recomputed linear values 2fL=Iinj∣Γ~2∣/2π=6.2/95.6/145.32f_L=I_{inj}\vert\tilde\Gamma_2\vert/2\pi=6.2/95.6/145.32fL​=Iinj​∣Γ~2​∣/2π=6.2/95.6/145.3 MHz; the simulations are 2.6/5.9/4.9× larger). Fig. 16 caption: because of the electron's higher mobility, strengthening the NMOS is more efficient than strengthening the PMOS. Why the worse 1/f1/f1/f is no concern (p.2134): asymmetric inverters up-convert 1/f1/f1/f noise more (the symmetry rule of [P2]; [P4] cites its [27]), but the close-in phase noise of an injection-locked oscillator is dominated by the injection, not by the free-running oscillator ([P4] cites its [29]). Table III, p.2133 (the compliance summary of Sec. VI for the oscillators measured in this paper and [P3]): the 17-stage ring measures η1=0.0192\eta_1=0.0192η1​=0.0192, η2=3.08×10−3\eta_2=3.08\times10^{-3}η2​=3.08×10−3, η3=0.0175\eta_3=0.0175η3​=0.0175, η5=0.0148\eta_5=0.0148η5​=0.0148; the LC ηLC\eta_{LC}ηLC​ (Eq.(38)) is covered in paper_004_large_injection_transient §1.7. Trends (p.2132): LC oscillators that convert bias current to swing more efficiently are less compliant, rings become less compliant as they grow longer, relaxation oscillators are the most compliant, and higher-harmonic compliances are typically lower.

documents.t: Strong injection / transients require the amplitude: ignoring the APF is fine for weak injection; for strong injection, transient locking, and frequency division, amplitude modulation cannot be ignored — compute with ISF + APF together. Quadrature is a design tool: to modulate phase purely, inject at the phase-sensitive point (ISF extremum); for amplitude keying / AM, inject at the amplitude-sensitive point (APF extremum). The ILFD is a low-power divider: compared with latch-based / CML dividers, which burn power at high frequency, the ILFD divides via injection locking at low power; use the NNN-th harmonic of the ISF/APF to design the division ratio and lock range. Dual-modulus prescaler: switch the division ratio on the same inverter-chain ring via a quadrature injection scheme, saving power. The large-injection / transient leftovers: Mirzaei's generalized Adler (Eq.(8)–(9)), the exact pull-in/pulling closed-form solutions (Eq.(31)–(34)), the APF-driven amplitude transient (dip→overshoot), and the full derivation and numerical verification of the large-injection pulling spectrum live in paper_004_large_injection_transient.

documents.t: Per paper_metadata (paper_004.limitations): Strongly nonlinear effects beyond the first-order APF are only partially captured; the injection harmonics required when M≠1M\neq1M=1 are generated by internal mixing, which is outside the framework ([P4] footnote 10, p.2129). Relative to this site's core ISF phase-noise goal, it is advanced / peripheral. The exact APF equations ([P4] Eq.(18)–(22), p.2126; quadrature Eq.(26), p.2128) and the M:N locking (Eq.(28)–(30), p.2129; ωL\omega_LωL​, p.2130) have been verified against the original (claim C11).

documents.t: [P3] is the direct prequel: this paper uses Part I's time-synchronous ISF model and adds amplitude (APF). [P1] provides the ISF Γ\GammaΓ; the APF is its radial dual. The ideal-LC Γ=−sin⁡\Gamma=-\sinΓ=−sin also appears in this site's isf_definition. [P2] provides the ring ISF; the ILFD/prescaler in this paper is implemented with an inverter-chain ring. [P5] is unrelated to this page (sense amplifier); but the start-up of LC / latch oscillators likewise relies on cross-coupled positive feedback (the corner-case bridge of claim C12). The APF is entry 21 in equation_index (verified on this page against [P4] Eq.(18)–(22)); the phase/amplitude geometry is in phase_vs_amplitude_noise.

documents.t: Amplitude ISF Λ~\tilde\LambdaΛ~ (1/C) = the amplitude version of the ISF; APF Δ=∫Λ~ d dτ\Delta=\int\tilde\Lambda\,d\,d\tauΔ=∫Λ~ddτ (1/A, no tilde); the ISF projects onto the tangential direction (phase), the amplitude ISF / APF onto the radial direction (amplitude). Ideal LC: the ISF and APF are in quadrature (90°90°90° apart) — when phase is most sensitive, amplitude is least sensitive, and vice versa (claim C11). Phase accumulates permanently; amplitude is pulled back by the decay function — this is the justification for "tracking only phase" in phase noise. ILFD: inject at ωinj≈Nω0\omega_{inj}\approx N\omega_0ωinj​≈Nω0​ and lock to ωinj/N\omega_{inj}/Nωinj​/N via the NNN-th ISF harmonic; the half lock range is ωL=12Iinj∣Γ~N∣=IinjcN/(2qmax)\omega_L=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vert=I_{inj}c_N/(2q_{max})ωL​=21​Iinj​∣Γ~N​∣=Iinj​cN​/(2qmax​) ([P4] Eq.(30) p.2129 and p.2130); NNN only selects the harmonic and does not enter the formula; the output has NNN indistinguishable locked phases spaced 2π/N2\pi/N2π/N apart. A half-wave-symmetric ISF (c2=0c_2=0c2​=0) cannot divide by 2 to first order — the symmetry that is good for phase noise is bad news for the ILFD; [P4]'s ÷2 experiments inject 2f02f_02f0​ into the tail of a differential LC to get around it. ISF shaping (Sec. VII-A, p.2132–2134): deliberately asymmetric single-ended inverter rings (WP/WNW_P/W_NWP​/WN​) enlarge ∣Γ~2∣\vert\tilde\Gamma_2\vert∣Γ~2​∣ by 15–23× (Table IV), and the simulated 1.5 mA ÷2 lock range goes 16 → 560 / 710 MHz; in the time domain half-wave symmetry = the phase kicks of consecutive injection cycles cancel exactly (footnote 14); the upper lock-range edge is ωL+=max⁡θ⟨Γ~ iinj⟩NTinj\omega_L^{+}=\max_\theta\langle\tilde\Gamma\,i_{inj}\rangle_{NT_{inj}}ωL+​=maxθ​⟨Γ~iinj​⟩NTinj​​ (footnote 15). This page is advanced; the exact APF equations ([P4] Eq.(18)–(22), p.2126; quadrature Eq.(26), p.2128) and the M:N locking (Eq.(28)–(30), p.2129; ωL\omega_LωL​, p.2130) have been verified against the original.

documents.t: Prerequisites: paper_004 (APF definition [P4] Eq.(18)–(22), ISF/APF quadrature Eq.(26), augmented Adler Eq.(27)), lab_36 (the RRR-form exact solution of the in-lock Adler equation, critical slowing, cycle slips), injection_locking_noise (Part A first-order PLL, Part B beat frequency ωb\omega_bωb​ and the one-sided comb), phase_vs_amplitude_noise (amplitude recovery with τ0=2Q/ω0\tau_0=2Q/\omega_0τ0​=2Q/ω0​, OU process) | Next: the M:N / ILFD part of paper_004, lab_37 (simulations/lab_37_ilfd_lock.py, documented inside the paper_004 page), quadrature_and_coupled_oscillators. paper_004 already covered the APF (amplitude perturbation function) definition of [P4], the ideal-LC ISF/APF quadrature, and M:N sub-/super-harmonic locking. This page collects what is left of [P4] Sec. III-E/F (the large-injection LC model) and Sec. V (transient behavior) and teaches it: What this page answers: Why is the "amplitude-aware Adler" — Mirzaei's Generalized Adler's equation ([P4] Eq.(8)) — exactly the Γ~/(1+A)\tilde\Gamma/(1+A)Γ~/(1+A) model of [P4] (Eq.(13), (27))? In the large-injection lock range ωL=ωL0/1−a2\omega_L=\omega_{L0}/\sqrt{1-a^2}ωL​=ωL0​/1−a2​ (Eq.(9), (23)), is aaa equal to Iinj/IoscI_{inj}/I_{osc}Iinj​/Iosc​ or to Iinj/ImaxI_{inj}/I_{max}Iinj​/Imax​? Why does the model become "unbounded" for a≥1a\ge1a≥1? Where does the exact transient solution of the sinusoidal Adler equation come from? Why do the tanh⁡\tanhtanh of [P4] Eq.(31) (in lock) and the tan⁡\tantan of Eq.(33) (out of lock) look alike? How long does locking take? Is there a closed form? Why does an oscillator near the lock-range edge lock, but extremely slowly? What is the recipe behind the asterisk in [P4] Table I, "τp\tau_pτp​ from the slope of the lock characteristic"? What does the amplitude do during acquisition? How does the APF turn the phase transient into an amplitude dip/overshoot? When does the quasi-static assumption fail? Out of lock (pulling), is the large-injection beat frequency still Δω2−ωL2\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}Δω2−ωL2​​? What does AM do to the pulling spectrum ("ISF + APF" vs "ISF Only" in [P4] Fig. 14(c))? Physical intuition (conclusions first): the injected current simultaneously "pushes the phase" (ISF, tangential) and "changes the amplitude" (APF, radial). Once the amplitude changes, the ISF scales inversely with it (Γ~LC=Γ~/(1+A)\tilde\Gamma_{LC}=\tilde\Gamma/(1+A)Γ~LC​=Γ~/(1+A): a larger swing means the same charge pushes the phase less). That single feedback turns Adler's sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ into sin⁡θ/(1+acos⁡θ)\sin\theta/(1+a\cos\theta)sinθ/(1+acosθ) — when the injection is in phase with the oscillation (θ≈0\theta\approx0θ≈0) the amplitude is inflated, the restoring force weakens, and locking is slow; in anti-phase (θ≈±π\theta\approx\pm\piθ≈±π) the amplitude is drained, the restoring force strengthens, and the lock characteristic is pulled up — so the lock range is stretched from ωL0\omega_{L0}ωL0​ to ωL0/1−a2\omega_{L0}/\sqrt{1-a^2}ωL0​/1−a2​, and diverges as a→1a\to1a→1 through the nonphysical "zero amplitude" solution. As for the transient: after the tan half-angle substitution the sinusoidal Adler equation leaves a single quadratic; flipping the sign of its discriminant turns the in-lock tanh⁡\tanhtanh (exponential convergence at rate ωp\omega_pωp​) into the out-of-lock tan⁡\tantan (periodic slipping at the beat frequency ωb\omega_bωb​) — the same Pythagorean root ∣ωL2−Δω2∣\sqrt{\lvert\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2\rvert}∣ωL2​−Δω2∣​. Scope of this page: advanced deep-dive ([P4] leftovers), not a core teaching chapter. III-B τ0=2Q/ω0\tau_0=2Q/\omega_0τ0​=2Q/ω0​ (p.2123), Eq.(13) (p.2124), Eq.(20)–(22) and footnote 7 (p.2126), Eq.(23) and the empirical θ∈[−110∘,110∘]\theta\in[-110^\circ,110^\circ]θ∈[−110∘,110∘] restriction (p.2127), Eq.(24)–(27) and the Fig. 8 caption (p.2128), Eq.(31)–(34), Table I and its asterisk note (p.2130), the Fig. 13 / Fig. 14 captions, Table II and the amplitude-conscious waveform (p.2131–2132), Eq.(35)–(38) (p.2132). Parts that are derived on this site and not in [P4] are labeled explicitly: the step-by-step derivation of Eq.(31)/(33) ([P4] only writes "one can show that [29]"), the closed-form beat frequency for large-injection pulling (Sec. 5.2), and the first-order amplitude-lag model (Sec. 4.3). III-B, p.2123 print(round(tau0 * 1e9, 4), round(tau0 * wL0, 4)) # -> 0.6366 0.4775 # (i) pull-in at Dw = 0.5*wL0: ISF-only [P4] Eq.(32) vs augmented slope recipe ([P4] Table I footnote) r0 = 0.5 th_ss = np.arcsin(r0) # [rad] ISF-only locked phase wp_isf = np.sqrt(1 - r0 ** 2) # [wL0] Eq.(32), N = 1 g = lambda th: np.sin(th) / (1 + a * np.cos(th)) - r0 th0 = brentq(g, -np.arccos(-a), np.arccos(-a)) # [rad] augmented locked phase (stable branch cos th + a > 0) wp_apf = (np.cos(th0) + a) / (1 + a * np.cos(th0)) ** 2 # [wL0] -Omega'(theta_0)/wL0 print(round(np.degrees(th_ss), 2), round(wp_isf, 4), round(np.degrees(th0), 2), round(wp_apf, 4)) # -> 30.0 0.866 42.53 0.6645 # (ii) lock time theta(0)=0 -> theta_ss - 0.01 rad from [P4] Eq.(31) (psi = theta + pi/2, alpha = tan(psi0/2)) eps = 0.01 psi0 = th_ss + np.pi / 2 alpha = np.tan(psi0 / 2) T = (2 / wp_isf) * (np.arctanh(np.tan((psi0 - eps) / 2) / alpha) - np.arctanh(np.tan(np.pi / 4) / alpha)) print(round(T, 3), round(T / wL0 * 1e9, 3), round(T / wL0 * f0, 1)) # -> 4.435 5.913 29.6 print(round(1 / wL0 * 1e9, 3), round((1 + a) / wL0 * 1e9, 3)) # -> 1.333 1.97 # (iii) pulled at Dw = 2*wL: beat frequency, ISF-only Eq.(34) vs augmented closed form vs naive r = 2 * wL / wL0 wb_isf = np.sqrt(r ** 2 - 1) # [wL0] [P4] Eq.(34), N = 1 R2 = 1 + (r * a) ** 2 # [-] S = np.sqrt(r ** 2 * (1 - a ** 2) - 1) # [-] -> 0 exactly at the augmented lock edge Dw = wL wb_apf = R2 * S / (1 + r * a ** 2 * S) # [wL0] site derivation (Sec. 5.2) wb_naive = np.sqrt(r ** 2 - (wL / wL0) ** 2) # [wL0] Eq.(34) with Eq.(9)'s wL plugged in print(round(wb_isf * wL0 / 2 / np.pi / 1e6, 1), round(wb_apf * wL0 / 2 / np.pi / 1e6, 1), round(wb_naive * wL0 / 2 / np.pi / 1e6, 1)) # -> 244.1 237.5 235.3

documents.t: Prerequisites (recommended reading): this page is not a prerequisite for the ISF. Its only connection to this course is the regeneration / positive feedback of the cross-coupled pair; to see how that mechanism becomes "oscillator start-up," first read oscillator_phase (limit-cycle start-up) and tank_Q_and_energy_restoration (negative resistance compensating losses). To learn the ISF itself, go straight to paper_001. Let's be clear up front: this paper has nothing to do with ISF / phase noise / jitter. It is an ISCAS 1998 short paper (4 pages) on the design of a cross-coupled inverter sense amplifier, covering regeneration speed, offset voltage caused by device mismatch, and a figure of merit for offset. It appears in this list purely because it is in the source folder and shares the author Hajimiri. This page honestly flags that mismatch (claim C12) and offers only one conceptual bridge. Why write a page anyway: Section 9 of the authoring conventions requires "[P5] must always be honestly described as a sense-amplifier paper unrelated to ISF." We do not pretend it relates to the ISF, nor force equations onto it; we simply state its actual content and point out its only legitimate connection to this course. Once you have read all five deep-dive papers, come back to the design layer: symmetry (learning-path step 8).

documents.t: Analytic design of a CMOS cross-coupled-inverter sense amplifier: analyzes the effect of the equilibrating transistors and the tail current source on sensing speed, the offset caused by mismatch, and proposes a figure of merit for offset — unrelated to oscillator phase noise / ISF (claim C12).
documents.s: One-sentence contribution

documents.t: For the ISF course, this paper's importance is ≈ zero. It solves problems in memory and datapath circuits: a sense amplifier must quickly and reliably amplify the tiny voltage difference appearing on the bitline into a full-swing digital 0/1. Its concerns are: Regeneration speed: the cross-coupled pair uses positive feedback to exponentially separate the two node voltages from the metastable point — the faster the separation, the faster the sensing. Offset: the two sides' transistors can never be identical (mismatch); this asymmetry makes the sense amp favor one side even at zero input difference, causing read errors. The paper analyzes the mismatch sources and gives a figure of merit. How the gradual switching of the equilibrating device and the tail current source degrades the above performance. These are digital/memory circuit topics — no limit cycle, no excess phase, no ISF, no phase noise spectrum.
documents.s: Why this paper matters (for this course: essentially not at all)

documents.t: Per paper_metadata (paper_005.assumptions): Small-signal regeneration analysis around the metastable point; mismatch-based offset model. (As stated in the paper) current has flowed through the transistors long enough, and the equilibrating device can be treated as an ideal switch — two simplifying assumptions that are challenged one by one in the later sections.

Meaning: as long as the effective transconductance GmG_mGm​ exceeds the node leakage conductance G0G_0G0​, the differential voltage grows exponentially (positive feedback), rapidly amplifying a tiny input difference to full swing — this is regeneration. The smaller τregen\tau_{regen}τregen​, the faster the sensing. documents.t: At the regenerative node, the design goal is to minimize the time constant τregen\tau_{regen}τregen​, not to blindly enlarge the initial voltage difference (the paper explicitly points out this trade-off). A complete offset analysis must consider the cell and bitline structure together, not just the cross-coupled pair itself. The gradual switching of the equilibrating device and the tail current source significantly degrades speed and offset and must be included in the analysis. These are useful to SRAM / sense-amp designers, but carry no transferable design rules for ISF / phase noise.

documents.t: [P5] has no theoretical continuity with [P1]–[P4]. The only legitimate connection is one mechanism: The regeneration (positive feedback) of the cross-coupled pair is also the foundation on which latch-based and LC oscillators "start up on their own and sustain a limit cycle." In a sense amp: positive feedback amplifies a tiny input difference once to full swing, then settles into a steady state (the latch locks). In an oscillator: the same negative resistance / positive feedback supplies energy to compensate the tank's losses, letting the oscillation persist without decaying — this is exactly the physical origin of a stable limit cycle ([P1] assumption 2). The −Gm-G_m−Gm​ pair of a differential LC-VCO and the cross-coupled stage of a latch-based ring share the same start-up mechanism as this paper's cross-coupled pair. So remember it this way: the same cross-coupled positive feedback, when it stops, is a latch/sense amp; when it cannot stop (keeps oscillating), it is an oscillator. But the moment we get to "the oscillator's phase response to noise," that is ISF territory — unrelated to this paper. For the details of oscillator start-up and limit-cycle geometry, see oscillator_phase; for the ISF itself, see paper_001.

documents.s: ADC aperture jitter: how clock jitter eats SNR and ENOB

documents.t: A high-speed ADC (analog-to-digital converter) "freezes" the input voltage at the sampling instant. But the sampling instant itself is not ideal: the sampling clock has jitter, and the trigger instant of the sampling switch carries its own random uncertainty — the two combined are called aperture jitter (the rms random error of the sampling instant, σt\sigma_tσt​, in s). As the input frequency rises, the waveform slope steepens, and the same timing error is amplified by that slope into an ever larger voltage error — beyond some input frequency the SNR is completely pinned by clock quality, regardless of how many bits of ADC you bought. This page does four things: Derive the signature formula SNRjitter=−20log⁡10(2πfinσt)\text{SNR}_{jitter}=-20\log_{10}(2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t)SNRjitter​=−20log10​(2πfin​σt​) step by step from first principles; Derive the ENOB (effective number of bits) conversion ENOB=(SNR−1.76)/6.02\text{ENOB}=(\text{SNR}-1.76)/6.02ENOB=(SNR−1.76)/6.02; Use this site's canonical Example C value σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs to compute an honest design table (1 / 2.5 / 5 / 10 GHz), and back-solve "how clean a clock does 10 ENOB @ 5 GHz require"; Connect it back to this site's main thread: L(Δf)→\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\toL(Δf)→ integrate →σt→\to\sigma_t\to→σt​→ SNR — the oscillator's phase noise plot directly sets the data converter's effective number of bits. External-literature note: the aperture-jitter SNR formula is a standard data-converter textbook result (external literature, not among the five source PDFs); e.g. W. Kester, "MT-007: Aperture Time, Aperture Jitter, Aperture Delay Time—Removing the Confusion," Analog Devices Tutorial MT-007, 2008; R. H. Walden, "Analog-to-digital converter survey and analysis," IEEE J. Sel. Areas Commun., vol. 17, no. 4, pp. 539–550, Apr. 1999. The input number σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs on this page, however, is this site's own verified canonical Example C (lab_08). Physical intuition (conclusion first): sampling error = slope × timing error. The steepest slope of a sine is A⋅2πfinA\cdot2\pi f_{in}A⋅2πfin​ (V/s), so the same clock (the same σt\sigma_tσt​) hitting an input at twice the frequency gives twice the voltage error and 4× the noise power — SNR drops 6 dB per octave, i.e. 1 bit per octave. This is why in direct RF-sampling systems the most expensive part is often not the ADC itself, but the low-noise clock that feeds it.

Extract the error with a first-order Taylor expansion. Because δtn\delta t_nδtn​ is tiny (fs scale), expand VVV around tnt_ntn​, keeping only the first order: V^n≈V(nTs)+dVdt∣t=nTs ⁣⋅δtn⟹en≡V^n−V(nTs)=A 2πfincos⁡(2πfinnTs) δtn.\hat V_n\approx V(nT_s)+\left.\frac{dV}{dt}\right|_{t=nT_s}\!\cdot\delta t_n \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e_n\equiv\hat V_n-V(nT_s)=A\,2\pi f_{in}\cos(2\pi f_{in}nT_s)\,\delta t_n.V^n​≈V(nTs​)+dtdV​​t=nTs​​⋅δtn​⟹en​≡V^n​−V(nTs​)=A2πfin​cos(2πfin​nTs​)δtn​. Math used: ddtAsin⁡(2πfint)=A⋅2πfincos⁡(2πfint)\frac{d}{dt}A\sin(2\pi f_{in}t)=A\cdot2\pi f_{in}\cos(2\pi f_{in}t)dtd​Asin(2πfin​t)=A⋅2πfin​cos(2πfin​t). Unit check (term by term): AAA (V) × 2πfin\times\,2\pi f_{in}×2πfin​ (rad/s) × δtn\times\,\delta t_n×δtn​ (s) === V·rad; rad is dimensionless, so ene_nen​ is in V ✓. The slope A⋅2πfinA\cdot2\pi f_{in}A⋅2πfin​ has units of V/s — "how many volts of change per second"; multiplied by "how many seconds off", you naturally get volts. Validity condition of the first-order approximation: the second-order Taylor term relative to the first is O(2πfinδtn)O(2\pi f_{in}\delta t_n)O(2πfin​δtn​), so we need 2πfinσt≪12\pi f_{in}\sigma_t\ll12πfin​σt​≪1 rad. The worst case on this page (10 GHz, 447.9 fs) is 2π×1010×4.479×10−13=2.81×10−22\pi\times10^{10}\times4.479\times10^{-13}=2.81\times10^{-2}2π×1010×4.479×10−13=2.81×10−2 rad ✓, far below 1. Physical meaning: this step is the core of the whole page — a timing error is amplified by the waveform slope into a voltage error. The slope is proportional to finf_{in}fin​, so the damage is proportional to finf_{in}fin​. This is the same physical quantity, seen from the other side, as waveform_slope's point that inside an oscillator "the steeper the slope, the less sensitive to noise": inside the oscillator, a steep slope is good (voltage noise converted to phase noise gets divided by the slope); at the sampling interface, a steep slope is bad (the timing error gets multiplied by it).
documents.s: Step 1: the voltage error of jittered sampling (error = slope × timing error)

documents.t: Now turn the single-sample error ene_nen​ into a statistical noise power. Assume (Section 5 below audits each item): δtn\delta t_nδtn​ is zero-mean Gaussian, independent between samples (white RJ), with variance E[δtn2]=σt2\mathrm{E}[\delta t_n^2]=\sigma_t^2E[δtn2​]=σt2​ (s²); δtn\delta t_nδtn​ is independent of the signal phase (the jitter does not know where the waveform currently is). Take the expectation of en2e_n^2en2​; because δtn\delta t_nδtn​ and cos⁡(⋅)\cos(\cdot)cos(⋅) are independent, the expectation factorizes: E[en2]=A2(2πfin)2 E[cos⁡2(2πfinnTs)]⏟= 1/2 E[δtn2]⏟= σt2.\mathrm{E}[e_n^2]=A^2(2\pi f_{in})^2\,\underbrace{\mathrm{E}\big[\cos^2(2\pi f_{in}nT_s)\big]}_{=\ 1/2}\;\underbrace{\mathrm{E}[\delta t_n^2]}_{=\ \sigma_t^2}.E[en2​]=A2(2πfin​)2= 1/2E[cos2(2πfin​nTs​)]​​= σt2​E[δtn2​]​​. Where that 12\tfrac1221​ comes from: the sampling phase 2πfinnTs2\pi f_{in}nT_s2πfin​nTs​ sweeps uniformly over a full period (coherent sampling over an integer number of periods, or treating the phase as uniformly distributed), and the average of cos⁡2\cos^2cos2 is 12\tfrac1221​ — the same fact as "the power of a sine is half the amplitude squared". So the noise power (V²) is: Pe=A2(2πfin)2σt22[V2].P_e=\frac{A^2(2\pi f_{in})^2\sigma_t^2}{2}\quad[\mathrm{V}^2].Pe​=2A2(2πfin​)2σt2​​[V2]. Dimension check: V2×(rad/s)2×s2=V2\mathrm{V}^2\times(\mathrm{rad/s})^2\times\mathrm{s}^2=\mathrm{V}^2V2×(rad/s)2×s2=V2 (rad dimensionless) ✓. Physical meaning: the error is largest at the zero crossings (steepest slope, cos⁡2=1\cos^2=1cos2=1), and at the peaks (zero slope, cos⁡2=0\cos^2=0cos2=0) jitter is completely harmless — this is exactly the LTV sensitivity idea of [P1] replayed at the sampling interface: "when you get hit" determines how much it hurts (compare lab_02's LC ISF: an oscillator is most sensitive to charge perturbations at the zero crossings — the same cos⁡\coscos/sin⁡\sinsin geometry). The 12\tfrac1221​ is just the average of "sometimes hit on the steep part, sometimes on the flat part".
documents.s: Step 2: mean-square over jitter and sampling phase → noise power

documents.t: The power of the sine signal itself is Psig=A22[V2].P_{sig}=\frac{A^2}{2}\quad[\mathrm{V}^2].Psig​=2A2​[V2]. SNR (signal-to-noise ratio) is the ratio of the two. Note that A2A^2A2 and the two 12\tfrac1221​'s all cancel: SNR=PsigPe=A2/2A2(2πfin)2σt2/2=1(2πfinσt)2.\text{SNR}=\frac{P_{sig}}{P_e}=\frac{A^2/2}{A^2(2\pi f_{in})^2\sigma_t^2/2}=\frac{1}{(2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t)^2}.SNR=Pe​Psig​​=A2(2πfin​)2σt2​/2A2/2​=(2πfin​σt​)21​. In dB (a 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ power ratio; the square comes out as 20): SNRjitter=−20log⁡10 ⁣(2πfin σt) [dB] \boxed{\ \text{SNR}_{jitter}=-20\log_{10}\!\big(2\pi f_{in}\,\sigma_t\big)\ \ [\mathrm{dB}]\ } SNRjitter​=−20log10​(2πfin​σt​) [dB] ​ Dimension check: 2πfinσt=2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t=2πfin​σt​= (rad/s) × (s) === rad, dimensionless ✓ — the argument of a log must be dimensionless, automatically satisfied here. SNR itself is a power ratio, dimensionless ✓. Physical reading (the single most important sentence): 2πfinσt2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t2πfin​σt​ is the "timing jitter converted to an equivalent rms phase error on the input sine", σϕ,in\sigma_{\phi,in}σϕ,in​ (rad). So this formula is really saying: SNR=1/σϕ,in2\text{SNR}=1/\sigma_{\phi,in}^2SNR=1/σϕ,in2​ — when sampling a sine, the SNR is the inverse square of the equivalent phase jitter. The elegant connection to this site's main thread: the clock's own rms phase at f0f_0f0​ is σϕ=2πf0σt\sigma_\phi=2\pi f_0\sigma_tσϕ​=2πf0​σt​; applied to an input at frequency finf_{in}fin​, the equivalent phase scales as σϕ,in=2πfinσt=(fin/f0) σϕ\sigma_{\phi,in}=2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t=(f_{in}/f_0)\,\sigma_\phiσϕ,in​=2πfin​σt​=(fin​/f0​)σϕ​. When fin=f0=5f_{in}=f_0=5fin​=f0​=5 GHz, the SNR is directly −20log⁡10(σϕ)=−20log⁡10(0.01407)=37.0-20\log_{10}(\sigma_\phi)=-20\log_{10}(0.01407)=37.0−20log10​(σϕ​)=−20log10​(0.01407)=37.0 dB — Example C's 14.07 mrad becomes the ADC's SNR unchanged. The same σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ read from a communications-receiver perspective is EVM[dB]: EVMrms≈σϕ\text{EVM}_{rms}\approx\sigma_\phiEVMrms​≈σϕ​, EVM[dB]=20log⁡10σϕ=20log⁡10(0.01407)=−37.0\text{EVM}[\text{dB}]=20\log_{10}\sigma_\phi=20\log_{10}(0.01407)=-37.0EVM[dB]=20log10​σϕ​=20log10​(0.01407)=−37.0 dB — equal in magnitude, opposite in sign to this SNRjitter=+37.0\text{SNR}_{jitter}=+37.0SNRjitter​=+37.0 dB (SNR is a power ratio, bigger is better; EVM is an error fraction, more negative is better). Two readings of the same σϕ=14.07\sigma_\phi=14.07σϕ​=14.07 mrad; see the "Receiver perspective" subsection of phase_vs_amplitude_noise. Validity/failure: holds only when 2πfinσt≪12\pi f_{in}\sigma_t\ll12πfin​σt​≪1 rad (the first-order Taylor of Step 1) and jitter is the only noise term; full conditions in Section 5.
documents.s: Step 3: SNR — the signature formula

documents.t: To phrase SNR in the language of ADC designers, first derive the SNR of an ideal N-bit quantizer (an external standard result: W. R. Bennett, "Spectra of quantized signals," Bell Syst. Tech. J., vol. 27, pp. 446–472, Jul. 1948 (external literature, not among the five source PDFs); derived self-contained here). (a) Quantization noise power q2/12q^2/12q2/12. Let the LSB (least significant bit, the smallest quantization step) be qqq (V). The quantization error eee is approximately uniformly distributed over [−q/2,+q/2][-q/2,+q/2][−q/2,+q/2], with power (variance): E[e2]=∫−q/2q/2e2 deq=1q⋅e33∣−q/2q/2=1q⋅2(q/2)33=q212[V2].\mathrm{E}[e^2]=\int_{-q/2}^{q/2}e^2\,\frac{de}{q}=\frac{1}{q}\cdot\frac{e^3}{3}\Big|_{-q/2}^{q/2}=\frac{1}{q}\cdot\frac{2(q/2)^3}{3}=\frac{q^2}{12}\quad[\mathrm{V}^2].E[e2]=∫−q/2q/2​e2qde​=q1​⋅3e3​​−q/2q/2​=q1​⋅32(q/2)3​=12q2​[V2]. (b) Full-scale sine power. The full-scale range of N bits is 2Nq2^N q2Nq (V), so the sine amplitude is A=2Nq/2=2N−1qA=2^N q/2=2^{N-1}qA=2Nq/2=2N−1q, with power: Psig=A22=22N−2q22=22Nq28[V2].P_{sig}=\frac{A^2}{2}=\frac{2^{2N-2}q^2}{2}=\frac{2^{2N}q^2}{8}\quad[\mathrm{V}^2].Psig​=2A2​=222N−2q2​=822Nq2​[V2]. (c) Divide and take dB. SNRq=22Nq2/8q2/12=128 22N=32⋅22N\text{SNR}_q=\frac{2^{2N}q^2/8}{q^2/12}=\frac{12}{8}\,2^{2N}=\frac{3}{2}\cdot2^{2N}SNRq​=q2/1222Nq2/8​=812​22N=23​⋅22NSNRq[dB]=10log⁡10 ⁣32+2N⋅10log⁡102=1.76+6.02 N.\text{SNR}_q[\mathrm{dB}]=10\log_{10}\!\tfrac32+2N\cdot10\log_{10}2=1.76+6.02\,N.SNRq​[dB]=10log10​23​+2N⋅10log10​2=1.76+6.02N. Dimension check: q2q^2q2 cancels top and bottom, SNR dimensionless ✓; NNN is a bit count (dimensionless). (d) Invert to define ENOB. Plug any SNR (here the jitter-limited one) back into this formula and solve for NNN: that is "how many bits of ideal quantizer this ADC is equivalent to": ENOB=SNR[dB]−1.766.02 [bit] \boxed{\ \text{ENOB}=\frac{\text{SNR}[\mathrm{dB}]-1.76}{6.02}\ \ [\mathrm{bit}]\ } ENOB=6.02SNR[dB]−1.76​ [bit] ​ Validity/failure: q2/12q^2/12q2/12 assumes the quantization error is uniform and signal-independent (true only for a busy signal; for very small or DC inputs it becomes a deterministic error and requires dither); ENOB is defined against a full-scale sine — back off the input by some dB and the SNR drops by the same dB. Composition rule: in a real ADC, jitter, quantization, and thermal noise add in power: SNRtot=−10log⁡10(10−SNRj/10+10−SNRq/10+10−SNRth/10)\text{SNR}_{tot}=-10\log_{10}\big(10^{-\text{SNR}_j/10}+10^{-\text{SNR}_q/10}+10^{-\text{SNR}_{th}/10}\big)SNRtot​=−10log10​(10−SNRj​/10+10−SNRq​/10+10−SNRth​/10). At low frequency quantization/thermal noise dominates and SNR is flat versus finf_{in}fin​; at high frequency the jitter term comes down at −20-20−20 dB/dec and takes over — the crossover is the boundary of "how many ADC bits this clock deserves".
documents.s: Step 4: ENOB — converting to an "effective number of bits"

documents.t: This site asks of every 2: "where does it come from, and which convention is it?" This formula has three places to check: The formula itself hides no 2. The 12\tfrac1221​ in the numerator Psig=A2/2P_{sig}=A^2/2Psig​=A2/2 (sine power) and the ⟨cos⁡2⟩=12\langle\cos^2\rangle=\tfrac12⟨cos2⟩=21​ in the denominator (sampling-phase average) cancel each other; the 2π2\pi2π is a genuine angular-frequency conversion (Hz→rad/s), not a bookkeeping convention. So SNR=1/(2πfinσt)2\text{SNR}=1/(2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t)^2SNR=1/(2πfin​σt​)2 does not depend on SSB/DSB or any convention of L\mathcal{L}L. The convention hides upstream of σt\sigma_tσt​. This site's σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs is integrated from the measured L(1 MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\,\mathrm{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz using Sϕ=2⋅10L/10S_\phi=2\cdot10^{\mathcal{L}/10}Sϕ​=2⋅10L/10 (the small-angle SSB convention L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​) (psd_phase_noise_jitter, Step 2). As long as L\mathcal{L}L is a measured quantity, this conversion is site-wide consistent and unambiguous. If L\mathcal{L}L is "predicted" from circuit noise, /2-vs-/4 enters. This site's Example B (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz) with [P1] Eq. (21), p.185 (SSB, /4Δω2/4\Delta\omega^2/4Δω2 convention) gives L(1 MHz)=−148.0\mathcal{L}(1\,\mathrm{MHz})=-148.0L(1MHz)=−148.0 dBc/Hz; with the time-domain /2Δω2/2\Delta\omega^2/2Δω2 bookkeeping it is −145.0-145.0−145.0 dBc/Hz (see white_noise_to_phase_noise). Numerical cross-check: a 3 dB difference in L\mathcal{L}L → σt∝10L/20\sigma_t\propto10^{\mathcal{L}/20}σt​∝10L/20 differs by 103/20=1.41≈210^{3/20}=1.41\approx\sqrt2103/20=1.41≈2​ → SNRjitter\text{SNR}_{jitter}SNRjitter​ differs by 20log⁡102=3.020\log_{10}\sqrt2=3.020log10​2​=3.0 dB. However many dB the convention shifts, that shift propagates unchanged into the SNR — pick a convention and stay consistent along the whole chain, or the numbers are meaningless.
documents.s: Step 5: factor-of-2 bookkeeping check (against this site's conventions)

documents.t: Assumption Why it is needed What happens when it fails White RJ (δtn\delta t_nδtn​ i.i.d. Gaussian) Noise power spreads uniformly across the Nyquist band (a flat floor in the FFT) A free-running clock's jitter is colored (1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt, σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ accumulation, [P2] Eq. (8), p.792): the total-SNR formula still holds (as long as σt\sigma_tσt​ is the total rms over the same integration bandwidth), but the noise concentrates into a skirt beside the signal instead of a flat floor; which close-in components "count" depends on whether the system tracks them out (see design knobs) First-order Taylor (2πfinσt≪12\pi f_{in}\sigma_t\ll12πfin​σt​≪1 rad) Error linear in δt\delta tδt Higher-order terms appear; carrier power leaks away as e−σϕ,in2e^{-\sigma_{\phi,in}^2}e−σϕ,in2​; at 447.9 fs, fin∼35f_{in}\sim35fin​∼35 GHz is needed to reach σϕ,in=0.1\sigma_{\phi,in}=0.1σϕ,in​=0.1 rad Jitter independent of the signal Expectation factorizes If the clock and the signal share a source (signal derived from the clock), part of the jitter is common-mode and cancels — measured SNR is actually better Full-scale sine, coherent sampling The standard reference for SNR/ENOB definitions Back off the input by x dB → SNR drops x dB; a non-coherent FFT needs windowing, with leakage accounted separately No quantization/thermal noise (jitter only) Isolates a single mechanism Real ADCs combine powers per Step 4 (d) σt\sigma_tσt​ = RSS of clock RJ + the ADC's internal aperture jitter Variances of two independent Gaussian sources add Counting only the clock and forgetting the ADC's internal contribution (the aperture-jitter line item in the datasheet) overestimates SNR

documents.t: Use this site's canonical Example C value σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs (5 GHz, −100-100−100 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, 1/f21/f^21/f2, integrated 1→100 MHz; lab_08). The table below is printed by simulations/lab_30_aperture_jitter.py (simulation verification in the next section): finf_{in}fin​ σϕ,in=2πfinσt\sigma_{\phi,in}=2\pi f_{in}\sigma_tσϕ,in​=2πfin​σt​ [rad] SNRjitter\text{SNR}_{jitter}SNRjitter​ [dB] ENOB [bit] 500 MHz 1.407×10−31.407\times10^{-3}1.407×10−3 57.03 9.18 1 GHz 2.814×10−32.814\times10^{-3}2.814×10−3 51.01 8.18 2.5 GHz 7.036×10−37.036\times10^{-3}7.036×10−3 43.05 6.86 5 GHz 1.407×10−21.407\times10^{-2}1.407×10−2 37.03 5.86 10 GHz 2.814×10−22.814\times10^{-2}2.814×10−2 31.01 4.86 Why add 500 MHz: it is the Nyquist frequency (fs/2f_s/2fs​/2) of a 1 GS/s sampling clock — the most common spec point for a 12-bit, 1 GS/s data converter. The "Second inverse design" section below answers directly: "what does the 12-bit @ 1 GS/s combination demand from clock cleanliness?" One row worked by hand (5 GHz) as a worked example: 2πfinσt=2π×5×109 Hz×4.479×10−13 s=3.1416×1010×4.479×10−13=1.407×10−2 rad.2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t=2\pi\times5\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{Hz}\times4.479\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{s} =3.1416\times10^{10}\times4.479\times10^{-13}=1.407\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}.2πfin​σt​=2π×5×109 Hz×4.479×10−13 s=3.1416×1010×4.479×10−13=1.407×10−2 rad.SNR=−20log⁡10(1.407×10−2)=−20×(−1.8517)=37.03 dB,\text{SNR}=-20\log_{10}(1.407\times10^{-2})=-20\times(-1.8517)=37.03\ \mathrm{dB},SNR=−20log10​(1.407×10−2)=−20×(−1.8517)=37.03 dB,ENOB=37.03−1.766.02=35.276.02=5.86 bit.\text{ENOB}=\frac{37.03-1.76}{6.02}=\frac{35.27}{6.02}=5.86\ \mathrm{bit}.ENOB=6.0237.03−1.76​=6.0235.27​=5.86 bit. Dimension check: Hz×s = dimensionless (rad once the 2π2\pi2π is attached) ✓; dB and bit are both dimensionless ✓. One-line Python verification: import numpy as np print(-20*np.log10(2*np.pi*5e9*447.9e-15)) # -> 37.03 print((-20*np.log10(2*np.pi*5e9*447.9e-15)-1.76)/6.02) # -> 5.86 # 500 MHz row (1 GS/s Nyquist, new table row): print(2*np.pi*5e8*447.9e-15) # -> 1.407e-03 print(-20*np.log10(2*np.pi*5e8*447.9e-15)) # -> 57.03 print((-20*np.log10(2*np.pi*5e8*447.9e-15)-1.76)/6.02) # -> 9.18 Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Try it yourself first: the same σ_t = 447.9 fs clock, now hitting f_in = 2 GHz (not one of the rows in the table above) — SNR_jitter = ? (answer in dB) dBCheckShow answer Graded correct within ±1% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Scaling intuition (reading the table as one straight line): Each octave of finf_{in}fin​: SNR −6.02-6.02−6.02 dB, ENOB −1-1−1 bit — in the table, 5→10 GHz is exactly 37.03→31.0137.03\to31.0137.03→31.01 (6.02 dB apart) and 5.86→4.865.86\to4.865.86→4.86 (1.00 bit apart) ✓. 1→10 GHz is log⁡210=3.32\log_2 10=3.32log2​10=3.32 octaves: 8.18−3.32=4.868.18-3.32=4.868.18−3.32=4.86 bit ✓, fully self-consistent. Every 10× improvement in σt\sigma_tσt​: SNR +20+20+20 dB, ENOB +3.32+3.32+3.32 bit. The clock and the input frequency are perfectly dual knobs (both enter through −20log⁡10-20\log_{10}−20log10​). Intuition cross-check (Example B's ideal limit): if the clock were Example B's "single-white-noise-source ideal LC" (L(1 MHz)=−148\mathcal{L}(1\,\mathrm{MHz})=-148L(1MHz)=−148 dBc/Hz, [P1] Eq. (21) SSB /4 convention), over the same integration bandwidth σt\sigma_tσt​ shrinks by 1048/20=25110^{48/20}=2511048/20=251× → about 1.8 fs → 5 GHz input SNR =37.0+48=85.0=37.0+48=85.0=37.0+48=85.0 dB, ENOB =13.8=13.8=13.8 bit (with the /2 convention, −145-145−145 dBc/Hz gives 82.0 dB, 13.3 bit — Section 5's 3 dB again). documents.t: Problem: the system must retain 10 effective bits on an fin=5f_{in}=5fin​=5 GHz input (jitter as the only contributor); find the aperture-jitter ceiling σt\sigma_tσt​. Step 1 (ENOB→SNR): SNRreq=6.02×10+1.76=61.96 dB.\text{SNR}_{req}=6.02\times10+1.76=61.96\ \mathrm{dB}.SNRreq​=6.02×10+1.76=61.96 dB. Step 3 (evaluate): σt=2.540×10−14 s=25.4 fs \boxed{\ \sigma_t=2.540\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s}=25.4\ \mathrm{fs}\ } σt​=2.540×10−14 s=25.4 fs ​ Dimension check: numerator dimensionless (rad), denominator rad/s → quotient is s ✓. One-line Python verification: import numpy as np print(10**(-(6.02*10+1.76)/20)/(2*np.pi*5e9)*1e15) # -> 25.40 Translating the requirement back into phase-noise language (which is how you talk to the oscillator designer): σt\sigma_tσt​ must be squeezed from 447.9 fs to 25.4 fs, a factor of 447.9/25.4=17.6447.9/25.4=17.6447.9/25.4=17.6, i.e. the entire 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt shifted down by 20log⁡1017.6=24.920\log_{10}17.6=24.920log10​17.6=24.9 dB — over the same integration bandwidth (1→100 MHz) this requires L(1 MHz) ≤ −100−24.9=−124.9 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}(1\,\mathrm{MHz})\ \le\ -100-24.9=-124.9\ \mathrm{dBc/Hz}.L(1MHz) ≤ −100−24.9=−124.9 dBc/Hz. Read through the scaling of [P1] Eq. (21), p.185, L∝Γrms2Si/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2S_i/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​Si​/qmax2​: 24.9 dB =310=310=310× in power ratio, to be pieced together from all three knobs — qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (swing × capacitance, see tank_swing), Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (waveform symmetry/topology, see lc_vs_ring), and the noise source SiS_iSi​ — or by using a PLL to filter out the close-in part (see design knobs). Honesty note: 25.4 fs is already an "excellent" clock — in order of magnitude, the best commercial RF-sampling clock chains land at integrated jitter of a few tens of fs (an order-of-magnitude statement, not a precise citation), so "10 ENOB @ 5 GHz" is a spec that hugs the practical limit.

documents.t: Problem: a common industry spec combination is a 12-bit, 1 GS/s data converter. At a sample rate fs=1f_s=1fs​=1 GS/s, the Nyquist frequency is fin=500f_{in}=500fin​=500 MHz (the row just added to the table above). With jitter as the only contributor, find the aperture-jitter ceiling σt\sigma_tσt​ needed to hold 12 ENOB; then check that requirement against two clocks this site has already verified — canonical Example C (447.9 fs) and the PLL output of clock_chain_budget (27.6 fs) — to see whether 12-bit @ 1 GS/s is actually achievable. Step 1 (ENOB→SNR): SNRreq=6.02×12+1.76=74.00 dB.\text{SNR}_{req}=6.02\times12+1.76=74.00\ \mathrm{dB}.SNRreq​=6.02×12+1.76=74.00 dB. Step 2 (invert the formula, fin=500f_{in}=500fin​=500 MHz): σt=10−SNRreq/202π×5×108=10−74.00/203.1416×109 s\sigma_t=\frac{10^{-\text{SNR}_{req}/20}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{8}} =\frac{10^{-74.00/20}}{3.1416\times10^{9}}\ \mathrm{s}σt​=2π×5×10810−SNRreq​/20​=3.1416×10910−74.00/20​ s σt ≤ 6.350×10−14 s=63.5 fs \boxed{\ \sigma_t\ \le\ 6.350\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s}=63.5\ \mathrm{fs}\ } σt​ ≤ 6.350×10−14 s=63.5 fs ​ Compare to 11 ENOB: the same method gives SNRreq=6.02×11+1.76=67.98\text{SNR}_{req}=6.02\times11+1.76=67.98SNRreq​=6.02×11+1.76=67.98 dB → σt≤127.0\sigma_t\le127.0σt​≤127.0 fs — one more bit of requirement tightens the clock budget by roughly half (127.0/63.5≈2127.0/63.5\approx2127.0/63.5≈2, matching the usual 6.02 dB/1 bit rule). Dimension check: numerator 10−SNR/2010^{-\text{SNR}/20}10−SNR/20 is rad (dimensionless), denominator 2πfin2\pi f_{in}2πfin​ is rad/s, quotient is s ✓. One-line Python verification: import numpy as np for N in (11, 12): snr_req = 6.02*N + 1.76 sigma_req = 10**(-snr_req/20) / (2*np.pi*5e8) print(N, snr_req, sigma_req*1e15) # -> 11 67.98 127.0 # -> 12 74.00 63.5 Step 3 (translate 63.5 fs back into phase-noise language, same 1/f21/f^21/f2 shape as Example C, 1→100 MHz integration bandwidth): σt\sigma_tσt​ must be squeezed from 447.9 fs to 63.5 fs, a factor of 447.9/63.5=7.05447.9/63.5=7.05447.9/63.5=7.05, i.e. the entire 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt shifted down by 20log⁡10(447.9/63.5)=20log⁡107.05=17.0 dB⟹L(1 MHz) ≤ −100−17.0=−117.0 dBc/Hz.20\log_{10}(447.9/63.5)=20\log_{10}7.05=17.0\ \mathrm{dB} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal{L}(1\,\mathrm{MHz})\ \le\ -100-17.0=-117.0\ \mathrm{dBc/Hz}.20log10​(447.9/63.5)=20log10​7.05=17.0 dB⟹L(1MHz) ≤ −100−17.0=−117.0 dBc/Hz. (11 ENOB only needs −100−20log⁡10(447.9/127.0)=−100−11.0≈−111.0-100-20\log_{10}(447.9/127.0)=-100-11.0\approx-111.0−100−20log10​(447.9/127.0)=−100−11.0≈−111.0 dBc/Hz — clearly looser.) One-line Python verification (reusing the real integration functions from simulations/common/noise_utils.py, sweeping L(1 MHz)\mathcal{L}(1\,\mathrm{MHz})L(1MHz) until σt≈63.5\sigma_t\approx63.5σt​≈63.5 fs): import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import leeson_one_over_f2, integrate_rms_jitter L_ref = -100 + 20*np.log10(63.5e-15/447.9e-15) # scaling law, sigma_t ∝ 10^(L/20) f = np.logspace(6, 8, 8000) L = leeson_one_over_f2(f, L_ref_dbc=L_ref, f_ref=1e6) sigma_t, _ = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L, f0=5e9, fmin=1e6, fmax=100e6) print(L_ref) # -> -117.0 print(sigma_t*1e15) # -> 63.5 Step 4 (feasibility check: two clocks this site has already verified, hitting 500 MHz): bare VCO (Example C, σt=447.9 fs):SNR=57.03 dB ⇒ ENOB=9.18 bit(the 500 MHz table row above, short of 12-bit),PLL-cleaned (σt=27.6 fs, the integrated-jitter magnitude from clock_chain_budget):SNR=−20log⁡10(2π×5×108×27.6×10−15)=81.2 dB⇒ ENOB=(81.2−1.76)/6.02=13.2 bit(exceeds the 12-bit requirement).\begin{aligned} \text{bare VCO (Example C, }\sigma_t=447.9\ \text{fs)}:\quad \text{SNR}&=57.03\ \text{dB}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{ENOB}=9.18\ \text{bit}\quad(\text{the 500 MHz table row above, short of 12-bit}), \\[4pt] \text{PLL-cleaned (}\sigma_t=27.6\ \text{fs, the integrated-jitter magnitude from clock\_chain\_budget)}:\quad \text{SNR}&=-20\log_{10}(2\pi\times5\times10^8\times27.6\times10^{-15})=81.2\ \text{dB} \\ &\Rightarrow\ \text{ENOB}=(81.2-1.76)/6.02=13.2\ \text{bit}\quad(\text{exceeds the 12-bit requirement}). \end{aligned}bare VCO (Example C, σt​=447.9 fs):SNRPLL-cleaned (σt​=27.6 fs, the integrated-jitter magnitude from clock_chain_budget):SNR​=57.03 dB ⇒ ENOB=9.18 bit(the 500 MHz table row above, short of 12-bit),=−20log10​(2π×5×108×27.6×10−15)=81.2 dB⇒ ENOB=(81.2−1.76)/6.02=13.2 bit(exceeds the 12-bit requirement).​ One-line Python verification: import numpy as np snr = -20*np.log10(2*np.pi*5e8*27.6e-15) print(snr) # -> 81.2 print((snr-1.76)/6.02) # -> 13.2 Conclusion: the bare VCO (447.9 fs, Example C's 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt) delivers only 9.18 ENOB at the 500 MHz Nyquist point — not enough to feed a 12-bit ADC. But the same VCO, run through the clock_chain_budget PLL chain down to 27.6 fs, delivers 13.2 ENOB — more than enough. 12-bit @ 1 GS/s is an achievable spec, but only if the clock feeding it has first been cleaned up by a PLL-purified LC VCO (a bare oscillator does not qualify). This echoes Step 4's conclusion that "the clock is the most expensive part," and is consistent with the gating logic of design_recipe: set the target ENOB/BER first, back-solve the σt\sigma_tσt​ ceiling, then pick the oscillator topology and loop design. Honesty note: 27.6 fs is the same canonical number computed in clock_chain_budget for that page's 2.5 GHz output chain (10 kHz–100 MHz integration); it is borrowed here as an order-of-magnitude benchmark for "what a PLL-cleaned clock can achieve," not a freshly derived 1-GS/s-specific clock chain.

documents.t: The first four boxes are exactly the four-step chain of psd_phase_noise_jitter (Example C); this page merely appends the last two. The whole chain in a few lines of Python (reusing lab_08's library): import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import leeson_one_over_f2, integrate_rms_jitter f = np.logspace(6, 8, 4000) # 1 MHz -> 100 MHz L = leeson_one_over_f2(f, L_ref_dbc=-100, f_ref=1e6) # 1/f^2 skirt (Example C) sigma_t, _ = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L, f0=5e9, fmin=1e6, fmax=100e6) print(sigma_t*1e15) # -> 447.9 print(-20*np.log10(2*np.pi*5e9*sigma_t)) # -> 37.03 An honest warning about integration bandwidth (continuing the psd page's "the lower limit dominates"): Example C's 447.9 fs is the "integrated 1→100 MHz" number. For an ADC, "which offset frequencies count as jitter" depends on observation length and system architecture: an FFT record lasts TrecT_{rec}Trec​, and phase drift slower than 1/Trec1/T_{rec}1/Trec​ looks like a frequency offset rather than a noise floor; if the clock is cleaned by a PLL, the close-in part is taken over by the reference. Change the integration bandwidth and σt\sigma_tσt​ changes, and the SNR with it — when reporting a jitter-limited SNR, the integration bandwidth of σt\sigma_tσt​ must be reported with it.

documents.t: Theory only counts once it has sparred with a "method that does not know the answer". simulations/lab_30_aperture_jitter.py runs exactly this experiment: sample a unit sine at tn=n/fs+δtnt_n=n/f_s+\delta t_ntn​=n/fs​+δtn​ (δtn\delta t_nδtn​ white Gaussian, σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs), rectangular-window coherent FFT (signal placed on an odd bin, coprime with the 2142^{14}214-point record, so every sample hits a distinct phase), measure SNRmeas=P(signal bin)∑P(all other bins, DC excluded),\text{SNR}_{meas}=\frac{P(\text{signal bin})}{\sum P(\text{all other bins, DC excluded})},SNRmeas​=∑P(all other bins, DC excluded)P(signal bin)​, then overlay it with −20log⁡10(2πfinσt)-20\log_{10}(2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t)−20log10​(2πfin​σt​). Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Annotation/labels/titles read: "10 ENOB 目標\n(5 GHz, 61.96 dB)" = 10-ENOB target (5 GHz, 61.96 dB); "輸入頻率 fin [GHz]" = input frequency fin [GHz]; "(a) aperture-jitter SNR：−6 dB/octave（每倍頻掉 1 bit）" = (a) aperture-jitter SNR: −6 dB/octave (loses 1 bit per octave); "頻率 [GHz]" / "相對載波功率 [dBc]" = frequency [GHz] / power relative to the carrier [dBc]; "(b) FFT 頻譜：fin=…GHz, σt=447.9 fs ⇒ SNR=…dB" = (b) FFT spectrum: fin=…GHz, σt=447.9 fs ⇒ SNR=…dB. How to read this figure: (a): the solid blue line is the formula (σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs), blue circles the FFT measurement — all 10 sweep points fall on the line; the green dashed line/green squares are the same experiment at σt=25.4\sigma_t=25.4σt​=25.4 fs, and the red star is the "10 ENOB @ 5 GHz (61.96 dB)" spec point, which lands exactly on the green line — the inverse design verified closed-loop. The right axis is graduated directly in ENOB: −6-6−6 dB/octave reads as "1 bit lost per octave". (b): a single spectrum at fin=5f_{in}=5fin​=5 GHz. The jitter noise is a flat floor (visual evidence of the white-RJ assumption), at about −76-76−76 dBc/bin — i.e. the total noise −37-37−37 dBc spread over NFFT/2=8192N_{FFT}/2=8192NFFT​/2=8192 bins (−37−10log⁡108192=−76-37-10\log_{10}8192=-76−37−10log10​8192=−76) ✓. If the jitter were colored (a real free-running clock), this floor would become a skirt beside the signal, with the total power unchanged. Actual output (run PYTHONPATH=. python3 simulations/lab_30_aperture_jitter.py): Monte-Carlo vs formula (same actual coherent f_in): f_in = 1.0016 GHz : measured 51.00 dB, formula 51.00 dB, diff -0.00 dB f_in = 5.0016 GHz : measured 37.03 dB, formula 37.03 dB, diff +0.00 dB Core code (full script in simulations/lab_30_aperture_jitter.py): m = int(round(f_in_target * n / fs)) if m % 2 == 0: m += 1 # odd bin -> coherent and coprime with 2^14 f_in = m * fs / n dt = rng.standard_normal(n) * sigma_t # white Gaussian RJ [s] x = np.sin(2*np.pi*f_in*(np.arange(n)/fs + dt)) # jittered sampling p = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)/n)**2 snr_db = 10*np.log10(p[m] / (p[1:].sum() - p[m])) Parameter Value Unit Notes σt\sigma_tσt​ 447.9 (second set: 25.4) fs canonical Example C; inverse-design spec point fsf_sfs​ 25.6 GS/s Nyquist 12.8 GHz covers fin≤10f_{in}\le10fin​≤10 GHz NFFTN_{FFT}NFFT​ 214=163842^{14}=16384214=16384 samples coherent record length finf_{in}fin​ 0.5–10 (10 sweep points) GHz placed on odd bins Averages 10–20 runs pushes the statistical error of the noise-power estimate down to ~0.02 dB AAA 1 V (normalized) full-scale sine; SNR independent of AAA Limitations of the simulation (honesty note): this is a pedagogical model — no quantizer (infinite bits), no thermal noise, jitter is white i.i.d. (real clocks are colored; total SNR unchanged, spectral shape changes), and sampling is ideal and instantaneous (no track-and-hold bandwidth roll-off). It verifies the formula itself, not any specific real ADC. Also, the simulation samples the exact value of sin⁡\sinsin (not the first-order Taylor), so "measurement = formula to 0.01 dB" simultaneously validates the first-order approximation for σϕ,in≤0.028\sigma_{\phi,in}\le0.028σϕ,in​≤0.028 rad.

documents.t: The clock source itself: L∝Γrms2Si/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2S_i/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​Si​/qmax2​ ([P1] Eq. (21), p.185) — raise qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (swing, tank capacitance), pick symmetric waveforms to suppress Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, replace the ring with an LC (representative value Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5; true LC 1/21/\sqrt21/2​; rings worse, see lc_vs_ring). PLL loop bandwidth: inside the loop, close-in noise is taken over by the reference; outside the loop it belongs to the VCO — the optimum bandwidth minimizes the integrated jitter (pll_noise_budget). Every stage of the clock chain: buffers, dividers, distribution all add jitter into the RSS; the ADC datasheet's internal aperture jitter is one more term. The budget must be apportioned from σt,tot2=∑σt,i2\sigma_{t,tot}^2=\sum\sigma_{t,i}^2σt,tot2​=∑σt,i2​. Lower the finf_{in}fin​ seen at the sampling interface: mixing down before sampling (IF sampling) trades mixer complexity for clock spec — every octave down buys 1 bit. Oversampling + digital filtering: white jitter noise spreads flat across the Nyquist band; filtering out the out-of-band part buys 10log⁡10(OSR)10\log_{10}(\mathrm{OSR})10log10​(OSR) of processing gain. But colored (close-in skirt) jitter hugs the signal and cannot be filtered — one more example of "the white/colored assumption decides the answer". Waveform slope: sharpening the clock edges (limiting, buffering) suppresses the clock chain's own additive-noise-to-jitter conversion (waveform_slope), but is powerless against phase noise that is "already σt\sigma_tσt​" — the slope knob works only on additive voltage noise.

documents.t: serdes_clocking_connection takes the same 447.9 fs and computes eye closure and BER (Q−1(10−12)=7.03Q^{-1}(10^{-12})=7.03Q−1(10−12)=7.03, consuming ±7.03σt=±3.1\pm7.03\sigma_t=\pm3.1±7.03σt​=±3.1 ps of eye width); this page uses it for SNR/ENOB. Both are "the time-domain bill for the oscillator's phase noise": SerDes cares about the tail probability (7σ7\sigma7σ events causing bit errors); the ADC cares about the mean-square power (σ2\sigma^2σ2 goes straight into the SNR). The same clock, the same L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) curve, starting from [P1]'s Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​, ends up setting the spec ceiling at both ends of a communication system (the sampler and the transceiver).

documents.t: Signature formula: SNRjitter=−20log⁡10(2πfinσt)\text{SNR}_{jitter}=-20\log_{10}(2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t)SNRjitter​=−20log10​(2πfin​σt​); the derivation's core is "error = slope × timing error"; the two 12\tfrac1221​'s (sine power, cos⁡2\cos^2cos2 average) cancel, and the formula contains no SSB bookkeeping convention whatsoever. 2πfinσt=σϕ,in2\pi f_{in}\sigma_t=\sigma_{\phi,in}2πfin​σt​=σϕ,in​: the SNR is just −20log⁡10-20\log_{10}−20log10​ of the equivalent input phase jitter; at fin=f0f_{in}=f_0fin​=f0​ it directly recycles Example C's σϕ=14.07\sigma_\phi=14.07σϕ​=14.07 mrad → 37.0 dB. ENOB =(SNR−1.76)/6.02=(\text{SNR}-1.76)/6.02=(SNR−1.76)/6.02: obtained by deriving SNRq=6.02N+1.76\text{SNR}_q=6.02N+1.76SNRq​=6.02N+1.76 from q2/12q^2/12q2/12 and the full-scale sine power, then inverting. Design table (σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs): 500 MHz / 1 / 2.5 / 5 / 10 GHz → 57.0 / 51.0 / 43.1 / 37.0 / 31.0 dB → 9.18 / 8.18 / 6.86 / 5.86 / 4.86 bit; 6.02 dB = 1 bit lost per octave. Inverse design one: 10 ENOB @ 5 GHz → SNR ≥61.96\ge61.96≥61.96 dB → σt≤25.4\sigma_t\le25.4σt​≤25.4 fs (17.6× cleaner than 447.9 fs = the whole skirt down −24.9-24.9−24.9 dB → L(1 MHz)≤−124.9\mathcal{L}(1\,\mathrm{MHz})\le-124.9L(1MHz)≤−124.9 dBc/Hz). Inverse design two (12-bit @ 1 GS/s, 500 MHz Nyquist): 12 ENOB → SNR ≥74.00\ge74.00≥74.00 dB → σt≤63.5\sigma_t\le63.5σt​≤63.5 fs → L(1 MHz)≤−117.0\mathcal{L}(1\,\mathrm{MHz})\le-117.0L(1MHz)≤−117.0 dBc/Hz; the bare VCO (447.9 fs, 9.18 ENOB) falls short, while the PLL-cleaned clock (27.6 fs, 13.2 ENOB) is sufficient — 12-bit @ 1 GS/s is achievable, but only with a PLL-purified LC clock. Convention discipline: upstream of σt\sigma_tσt​, [P1] Eq. (21)'s /4 (SSB) vs the time-domain /2 bookkeeping makes L\mathcal{L}L differ by 3 dB → σt\sigma_tσt​ by 2\sqrt22​ → SNR by 3 dB; only a chain-consistent choice is meaningful; a jitter-limited SNR must always be reported with the integration bandwidth of σt\sigma_tσt​. Simulation verification (lab_30): Monte-Carlo sampling + FFT matches the formula at 1 GHz and 5 GHz to within 0.01 dB; white-RJ noise is a flat floor (−76-76−76 dBc/bin @ NFFT=16384N_{FFT}=16384NFFT​=16384).

documents.s: All-digital PLL: TDC and DCO quantization noise are the same ISF bookkeeping

documents.t: The budget table in pll_noise_budget has five analog noise sources: reference, PFD/charge-pump, divider, loop filter, VCO. Over the past two decades, however, the mainstream has increasingly become the ADPLL (all-digital PLL): the "PFD + charge-pump + analog loop filter" is replaced by a TDC (time-to-digital converter — a circuit that measures the time difference between two edges as an integer) plus a digital loop filter, and the VCO is replaced by a DCO (digitally controlled oscillator — tuned by a bank of switched capacitors instead of a continuous varactor voltage). This page answers: How much in-band phase noise does the TDC's finite time resolution Δtres\Delta t_{res}Δtres​ become? It is the digital stand-in for the charge-pump's ScpS_{cp}Scp​, sits in the same slot of the budget table, but its magnitude is set by "quantization" rather than by electronic noise. How much out-of-band phase noise does the DCO's finite frequency resolution Δfres\Delta f_{res}Δfres​ become? It is the digital stand-in for the VCO and follows the varactor page pipeline "frequency error → integrate to phase → 1/Δf21/\Delta f^21/Δf2". How does ΔΣ dithering shape the DCO LSB away? This is the (1−z−1)m(1-z^{-1})^m(1−z−1)m shaping already derived in pll_noise_budget, reused in a new place. How the budget equation is rewritten: Sout=(SrefN2+STDC)∣Hlp∣2+(SDCO+Svco)∣Hhp∣2S_{out}=(S_{ref}N^2+S_{TDC})\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2+(S_{DCO}+S_{vco})\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2Sout​=(Sref​N2+STDC​)∣Hlp​∣2+(SDCO​+Svco​)∣Hhp​∣2, and why a 10 ps TDC makes the whole in-band budget lose to an ordinary charge-pump. External-literature statement: the ADPLL architecture and the two standard formulas for TDC and DCO quantization noise are not in the 5 PDFs downloaded for this site (external literature, not among this site's 5 PDFs). Classic sources: R. B. Staszewski, J. L. Wallberg, S. Rezeq, C.-M. Hung, O. E. Eliezer, S. K. Vemulapalli, C. Fernando, K. Maggio, R. Staszewski, N. Barton, M.-C. Lee, P. Cruise, M. Entezari, K. Muhammad, and D. Leipold, "All-Digital PLL and Transmitter for Mobile Phones," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 39, no. 12, pp. 2278–2291, Dec. 2004; R. B. Staszewski and P. T. Balsara, All-Digital Frequency Synthesizer in Deep-Submicron CMOS, Wiley, 2006 (equation numbers in both to be verified). The derivations on this page are fully self-contained: both formulas are derived step by step from "uniform quantization error → whitening → into the same integrator", identical to the site's existing ΔΣ four steps and the varactor pipeline; all numbers are marked illustrative. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the TDC "rounds" the phase error to the nearest Δtres\Delta t_{res}Δtres​ and rolls that die once per reference period — this is a white phase-error source sampled at fRf_RfR​, sitting exactly in the PFD's seat, low-passed by the loop and, like the reference, an in-band floor; its magnitude depends only on Δtres/TV\Delta t_{res}/T_VΔtres​/TV​ (the quantization step as a fraction of one output period), independent of NNN. The DCO rounds the control word to the nearest Δfres\Delta f_{res}Δfres​ — a white frequency-error source sitting in the VCO's seat, high-passed by the loop; frequency error must be integrated once to become phase, so it looks like the VCO's 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt but is set by the "quantization step" rather than by device noise. Neither newcomer is "electronic noise" — both are bit counts the designer chooses. The term that ISF theory is responsible for (the DCO's own device noise Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​) is unchanged; it simply gains two quantized neighbours.
documents.s: What this page answers

documents.t: Three things first, because the "no N2N^2N2" below depends entirely on them: Phase in an ADPLL is counted in "VCO cycles". Every reference period adds the "cycles that should have accumulated" RRR_RRR​ (the running sum of the frequency command word, which may be fractional); a counter counts how many cycles the DCO actually ran, RVR_VRV​ (an integer); the TDC supplies the sub-cycle fraction ε=Δt/TV\varepsilon=\Delta t/T_Vε=Δt/TV​ (Δt\Delta tΔt is the time from the reference edge to the next CKV edge, TV=1/f0T_V=1/f_0TV​=1/f0​ is the DCO period). The phase error ϕE=RR−RV−ε\phi_E=R_R-R_V-\varepsilonϕE​=RR​−RV​−ε is in output cycles; times 2π2\pi2π it is rad of output phase — this is the same fact as "the error is counted in VCO cycles to begin with" in the ΔΣ third term of pll_noise_budget, so TDC noise is likewise not multiplied by N2N^2N2. No charge-pump, no analog loop filter. The ScpS_{cp}Scp​ and SlfS_{lf}Slf​ terms disappear, replaced by the TDC quantization STDCS_{TDC}STDC​. The digital loop filter itself adds no noise (finite-word-length effects are a separate matter). The DCO is controlled by a bank of switched unit capacitors. The frequency step of the finest bank, Δfres\Delta f_{res}Δfres​, is the "quantization step"; the DCO's device noise (tank loss, active devices) is exactly the VCO's and is still set by the ISF: Svco∝Γrms2/qmax2⋅Si/f2S_{vco}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2\cdot S_i/f^2Svco​∝Γrms2​/qmax2​⋅Si​/f2.
