Verified with noise_utils (same convention Sϕ=2LS_\phi=2\mathcal{L}Sϕ​=2L): import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import integrate_rms_jitter f = np.logspace(4, 8, 20001) L_core = np.where(f <= 1e6, -132.04, -154.02 - 20*np.log10(f/1e6)) L_tot = 10*np.log10(10**(L_core/10) + 10**(-155.0/10)) st, sp = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L_tot, f0=2.5e9, fmin=1e4, fmax=1e8) print(round(st*1e15, 1)) # -> 27.6 print(round(sp*1e6, 1)) # -> 433.4 Who contributed these 27.6 fs? (breakdown from an actual run of simulations/fig_clock_chain.py, power ratios) Source Standalone σt\sigma_tσt​ Share of σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​ in-band floor (reference ×N2\times N^2×N2) 22.4 fs 65.9 % buffer floor 16.0 fs 33.7 % VCO skirt 1.78 fs 0.42 % RSS total 27.6 fs 100 % This table is the most important design message on this page: this chain's jitter is split between "the in-band floor raised by ×N2\times N^2×N2" and "the unremarkable buffer floor"; that beautiful −148-148−148 dBc/Hz VCO is nearly invisible (0.42 %). Spending effort improving the VCO further is wasted work — do the accounting first, so the effort goes where it counts. (The buffer's 16.0 fs is exactly the number from Rule 4's Step-5 formula.)

documents.t: Full script: simulations/fig_clock_chain.py (to run: from the project root, PYTHONPATH=. python3 simulations/fig_clock_chain.py — it prints every # -> number on this page and produces the figure). Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Axis labels/titles read: "offset 頻率 f [Hz]" = offset frequency f [Hz]; "時脈鏈各級的 SSB phase noise（記帳）" = the SSB phase noise of each stage in the clock chain (bookkeeping convention); "積分上限 f [Hz]（從 10 kHz 積起）" = integration upper limit f [Hz] (integrating from 10 kHz); "累積 rms jitter σt [fs]" = accumulated rms jitter σt [fs]; "最終 2.5 GHz 時脈：jitter 從哪裡累積" = the final 2.5 GHz clock: where the jitter accumulates from. How to read it: in the left panel, the blue line is the 5 GHz brick-wall (in-band −126-126−126 plateau + VCO skirt past 1 MHz), the green line is the same curve shifted down 6.02 dB (÷2), the orange dotted line is the −155-155−155 buffer floor, and the thick black line is the final output — −132.0-132.0−132.0 at 100 kHz, clamped by the floor at −154.9-154.9−154.9 at 10 MHz. The right panel is the cumulative jitter "integrated from 10 kHz to fff": the in-band floor accumulates 22 fs before 1 MHz, after which the buffer floor slowly pushes the total to 27.6 fs; the dashed red line (full type-II shaping) stays above the brick-wall around and beyond fnf_nfn​ — that is the trap the next step lays open.

documents.t: Brick-wall is lookup-table-grade approximation. Computing with pll_noise_budget's actual ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 (pll_utils, fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz, ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707), the difference at the two offsets is plain: in-band (100 kHz): shaped −131.9-131.9−131.9 vs brick-wall −132.0-132.0−132.0 — only 0.1 dB apart (slight peaking of ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 at fn/10f_n/10fn​/10). The lookup table is reliable ✓. out-of-band (10 MHz): shaped −148.0-148.0−148.0 vs brick-wall −154.9-154.9−154.9 — 7 dB apart! The reason: the type-II second-order closed loop's zero makes ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 roll off at only −20-20−20 dB/dec for f≫fnf\gg f_nf≫fn​ (∣Hlp∣2≈(2ζfn/f)2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx(2\zeta f_n/f)^2∣Hlp​∣2≈(2ζfn​/f)2), so the reference floor raised by ×N2\times N^2×N2 leaks a −20-20−20 dB/dec tail into the out-of-band region; and the VCO skirt is also −20-20−20 dB/dec — the two lines are parallel, the gap is constant and can never be closed: import numpy as np from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_lowpass_mag2 S_refN2 = 2 * 10**(-126.02/10) # N²·S_ref (S_phi of the in-band floor) [rad²/Hz] lp = H_lowpass_mag2(10e6, 1e6) # |H_lp|² @ 10 MHz, fn = 1 MHz L_refpath = 10*np.log10(0.5 * S_refN2 * lp) print(round(L_refpath, 1)) # -> -143.0 print(round(L_refpath - (-168.0), 1)) # -> 25.0 The reference tail at 10 MHz is −143.0-143.0−143.0 dBc/Hz (5 GHz carrier), 25 dB above the VCO's −168-168−168 — and because both have the same slope, these 25 dB hold at every out-of-band offset. The lookup-table cell "out-of-band = VCO" is, for a pure second-order loop, simply unreachable. The consequence for integrated jitter (actual run of fig_clock_chain.py): Model Final σt\sigma_tσt​ (10 kHz–100 MHz) brick-wall lookup 27.6 fs type-II second-order full shaping 44.0 fs (+59%+59\%+59%) second order + 3rd pole @ 3 MHz (illustrative) 38.6 fs How to fix it: real synthesizers add a third pole to the loop filter (plus higher-order post-filters) precisely for this, turning the ref tail into −40-40−40 dB/dec or steeper; the third row above shows one 3 MHz pole cutting the damage by a third (the pole-placement vs loop-stability trade-off belongs to the standard PLL literature — external literature, not among the five source PDFs). One level more honest: this chain's fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz was never the jitter-optimal choice to begin with — the crossover of the in-band floor (−126-126−126) and the VCO skirt sits at 79.679.679.6 kHz, far below 1 MHz. Sweeping fnf_nfn​ for this chain with pll_noise_budget's U-curve method (shaped model, 3rd pole tracking at 3fn3f_n3fn​): the minimum is at fn\*≈53f_n^\*\approx53fn\*​≈53 kHz, σt≈19.6\sigma_t\approx19.6σt​≈19.6 fs. Lookup accounting (this page) tells you each stage's bill; loop optimization (that page) tells you how to change the bill — two different things, don't mix them.

documents.t: The final 2.5 GHz clock's σt=27.6\sigma_t=27.6σt​=27.6 fs feeds directly into serdes_clocking_connection's eye/BER machinery: if this clock drives a 5 Gb/s half-rate link (UI =200=200=200 ps), the RJ overhead at BER =10−12=10^{-12}=10−12 (Q−1≈7.03Q^{-1}\approx7.03Q−1≈7.03, site canonical) is 2×7.03×27.6 fs=0.392\times7.03\times27.6\ \text{fs}=0.392×7.03×27.6 fs=0.39 ps =0.19%=0.19\%=0.19% UI — quite healthy; but note every extra buffer stage in the clock tree adds another Rule-4 floor (power addition) — in a high-fan-out tree the buffers alone can eat the whole budget. Accumulated jitter of the free-running segment ([P2] Eq.(8), p.792, σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​) is high-pass truncated once it enters the PLL/CDR loop — in this chain, "who free-runs and who is locked" determines which noise accumulates and which does not (Step 6 of that page).

documents.t: The five rules: ×N adds 20log⁡10N20\log_{10}N20log10​N (ϕout=Nϕin\phi_{out}=N\phi_{in}ϕout​=Nϕin​, offset axis unchanged); ÷N subtracts 20log⁡10N20\log_{10}N20log10​N (edge-picking, time error intact, angle divided by NNN); PLL = reference through N2∣Hlp∣2N^2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2N2∣Hlp​∣2, VCO through ∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hhp​∣2 (transfer functions reused from pll_noise_budget); buffer/divider floor = power addition, Lout=10log⁡10(10Lin/10+10Lbuf/10)\mathcal{L}_{out}=10\log_{10}(10^{\mathcal{L}_{in}/10}+10^{\mathcal{L}_{buf}/10})Lout​=10log10​(10Lin​/10+10Lbuf​/10); DLL = no oscillator, no random walk, σt,out2=σref2+Nσstage2\sigma_{t,out}^2=\sigma_{ref}^2+N\sigma_{stage}^2σt,out2​=σref2​+Nσstage2​ (bounded; 4 stages at σstage=50\sigma_{stage}=50σstage​=50 fs → 100.0 fs, does not grow with Δt\Delta tΔt; contrast the free-running VCO's κ2=0.125 rad2/s\kappa^2=0.125\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}κ2=0.125 rad2/s, only 11.311.311.3 fs at 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs but 355.9355.9355.9 fs by 1 ms), and phase-interpolator quantization DJpp=UI/2b\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}=UI/2^bDJpp​=UI/2b (UI=40UI=40UI=40 ps, 6-bit → 0.6250.6250.625 ps ≈0.0156 UI\approx0.0156\ UI≈0.0156 UI, uniformly distributed DJ, independent of BER). Conserved quantity: under ideal ×N/÷N, σt\sigma_tσt​ (seconds) is unchanged (both ends 22.5 fs in this example); ÷N saves "fraction of a UI", not seconds. Worked chain (100 MHz→×50→5 GHz→÷2→2.5 GHz→buffer): at 100 kHz, −160→−126.02→−132.04→−132.02-160\to-126.02\to-132.04\to-132.02−160→−126.02→−132.04→−132.02; at 10 MHz, −160→−168.00→−174.02→−154.95-160\to-168.00\to-174.02\to-154.95−160→−168.00→−174.02→−154.95 (floor dominates). Final integrated jitter (10 kHz–100 MHz) = 27.6 fs; breakdown = ref×N2\times N^2×N2 floor 65.9% + buffer floor 33.7% + VCO 0.42% — accounting first, don't blindly upgrade the VCO. Honest comparison: the pure type-II second-order loop's ref tail runs parallel to the VCO skirt (a constant +25+25+25 dB here), shaped σt=44.0\sigma_t=44.0σt​=44.0 fs (59% above the lookup); adding a 3rd pole (3 MHz) → 38.6 fs; this chain's jitter-optimal loop BW is actually fn\*≈53f_n^\*\approx53fn\*​≈53 kHz (σt≈19.6\sigma_t\approx19.6σt​≈19.6 fs). Convention discipline: the rules are all ratio/addition operations, /2-vs-/4 cancels; the only convention-sensitive item is the VCO anchor (−148-148−148 = [P1] Eq.(21)'s /4 SSB; the time-domain /2 gives −145-145−145).

Why a DLL does not accumulate jitter without an oscillator (Rule 5) (external literature, not among the five source PDFs): J. G. Maneatis, "Low-Jitter Process-Independent DLL and PLL Based on Self-Biased Techniques," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 31, no. 11, pp. 1723–1732, Nov. 1996. What the site's five PDFs provide is the physics of the chain's "sources": [P1] (the VCO's L\mathcal{L}L and the ISF), [P2] (the ring's κΔt\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}κΔt​ accumulation), [P3]/[P4] (injection locking and the ILFD division mechanism).

documents.t: Prerequisites: white_noise_to_phase_noise · psd_phase_noise_jitter | Next: exercises · cheat_sheet This page does not teach new formulas. It lays out 13 mistakes that actually happen in phase noise / jitter work and that cost you a factor of 2, 3 dB, or 2\sqrt22​ when they do — several of which this site itself made during drafting and review, then fixed by simulation adjudication (we leave the correction record honestly on each page). Every entry follows the same format: ❌ Wrong claim/practice → 💥 Why it's wrong (physics) → ✅ Correct version → 📍 On-site reference. 40 years of hard-won lesson: the most expensive mistakes in this line of work are not failures to derive something, but dropping a factor of 2 when swapping conventions, or forcing LTI intuition onto an LTV system. Look at the summary table first, then work through each entry. # Landmine Error size Antidote page 1 Treating κ2\kappa^2κ2 as Demir's convention DDD Linewidth ×2\times2×2 diffusion_dictionary 2 Mixing SSB /4/4/4 with time-domain /2/2/2 (−148-148−148 vs −145-145−145) 3 dB; back-solved κ\kappaκ off by 2\sqrt22​ white_noise_to_phase_noise 3 Single-sideband SϕS_\phiSϕ​ plugged into the coefficient-8 jitter kernel Variance ×2\times2×2, jitter ×2\times\sqrt2×2​ jitter_kernels 4 Using ΔV/\Delta V/ΔV/slope intuition to infer ISF direction Sign flipped, false divergence at the peak lti_vs_ltv 5 Treating the device 1/f1/f1/f corner as the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner Off by 3–300× in frequency in this example flicker_noise_upconversion 6 Ring FOM misremembered as 8/(3γ)8/(3\gamma)8/(3γ) 1.76 dB (long channel) fom_limit 7 Forgetting ×2\times2×2 in the dBc/Hz integral, or shifting f1f_1f1​ carelessly 2\sqrt22​; 10\sqrt{10}10​ per decade of f1f_1f1​ psd_phase_noise_jitter 8 Treating the Δf→0\Delta f\to0Δf→0 divergence as physical Qualitatively wrong (reality is Lorentzian) lorentzian_linewidth 9 Feeding DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJpp​ directly into the TJ formula Pessimistic by 0.84 ps in this example dj_dual_dirac 10 RBW too wide when measuring close-in High by 2.5 dB in this example (and can be worse) measurement_and_spurs 11 Assuming jitter (in seconds) also halves after ÷2 The time value does not change by a single fs clock_chain_budget 12 Applying the white-noise N\sqrt NN​ accumulation law to flicker Underestimates by ~3× at N=10N=10N=10 jitter_kernels 13 Assuming a pure-sine subharmonic injection would lock Lock range =0=0=0 at first order (not just narrower) subharmonic_injection

documents.t: ❌ Wrong practice: compute the phase-variance growth rate κ2=Γrms22qmax2in2‾Δf\kappa^2=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{2q_{max}^2}\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}κ2=2qmax2​Γrms2​​Δfin2​​​ ([P2] Eq.(11)/(12), p.793), call this number directly the diffusion constant DDD, then plug it into Demir's linewidth formula Δf3dB=D/π\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=D/\piΔf3dB​=D/π. (This site's v3 spec made exactly this mistake; v5 fixed it by Monte-Carlo adjudication.) 💥 Why it's wrong: the literature has two definitions of DDD — the rate convention Var[Δϕ]=D∣t∣\mathrm{Var}[\Delta\phi]=D\vert t\vertVar[Δϕ]=D∣t∣ (in which D=κ2D=\kappa^2D=κ2), and the Demir/laser convention Var[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣\mathrm{Var}[\Delta\phi]=2D\vert t\vertVar[Δϕ]=2D∣t∣ (in which D=κ2/2D=\kappa^2/2D=κ2/2). Δf3dB=D/π\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=D/\piΔf3dB​=D/π is the formula for the latter; plugging in the former's value overstates the linewidth by 2×2\times2×. ✅ Correct version: first ask whether the other party's Var\mathrm{Var}Var expression has that factor of 2 before converting conventions. The unambiguous way to write it is entirely in terms of κ2\kappa^2κ2: Δf3dB=κ22π[Hz]\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\frac{\kappa^2}{2\pi}\qquad[\text{Hz}]Δf3dB​=2πκ2​[Hz] Canonical Example B (Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz): κ2=0.125\kappa^2=0.125κ2=0.125 rad²/s → correct linewidth 19.9 mHz; the wrong version gives 39.8 mHz. A single lab_23 simulation extracting all four channels (variance slope 0.1252 rad²/s, linewidth fit 20.0 mHz) sides with 19.9 mHz. Dimension check: rad2/s÷2π=Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{s}\div2\pi=\text{Hz}rad2/s÷2π=Hz ✓ (rad is dimensionless). 📍 On-site reference: diffusion_dictionary (item-by-item reconciliation of Suits 2/3 and the lab_23 adjudication), lorentzian_linewidth.

documents.t: ❌ Wrong practice: for the same oscillator, one page states L(1 MHz)=−148\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})=-148L(1MHz)=−148 dBc/Hz, another states −145-145−145, and they cross-reference each other without labeling the convention; or the /4/4/4-convention number from [P1] Eq.(21) is plugged into the back-solving formula κ=2πΔfLlin\kappa=2\pi\Delta f\sqrt{\mathcal{L}_{lin}}κ=2πΔfLlin​​, which expects the /2/2/2 convention. 💥 Why it's wrong: [P1] Eq.(21), p.185 uses SSB (single-sideband) bookkeeping, with denominator 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2 (its summation form, Eq.(19), corresponds to 8qmax2Δω28q_{max}^2\Delta\omega^28qmax2​Δω2); the clean time-domain derivation for small-angle PM gives L=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12S_\phiL=21​Sϕ​, with denominator 2Δω22\Delta\omega^22Δω2 — the two differ by 10log⁡102≈310\log_{10}2\approx310log10​2≈3 dB, a well-known convention dispute in the literature, not an arithmetic error by either side. ✅ Correct version: know both faces of Example B: /4/4/4 gives −148.0-148.0−148.0, /2/2/2 gives −145.0-145.0−145.0 dBc/Hz. Any reported number must be labeled with its convention; back-solving κ\kappaκ ([P2] Eq.(50), p.803 route) expects the /2/2/2 convention — substituting −145-145−145 gives κ=0.354\kappa=0.354κ=0.354 rad/s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​ ✓, mistakenly substituting −148-148−148 gives only 0.250.250.25 (short by 2\sqrt22​). Scaling (Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​, −20-20−20 dB/dec) is identical between the two conventions. 📍 On-site reference: white_noise_to_phase_noise (factor-of-2 teaching note), diffusion_dictionary (Suit 4), jitter_kernels (Section 4.5's back-solving trap).

documents.t: ❌ Wrong practice: take the single-sideband spectrum Sϕ=2×10L/10S_\phi=2\times10^{\mathcal{L}/10}Sϕ​=2×10L/10 from a measured L\mathcal{L}L, then plug it into the literature's period-jitter formula σΔϕ2=8ω02∫0∞Sϕsin⁡2(πfτ) df\sigma^2_{\Delta\phi}=\dfrac{8}{\omega_0^2}\displaystyle\int_0^\infty S_\phi\sin^2(\pi f\tau)\,dfσΔϕ2​=ω02​8​∫0∞​Sϕ​sin2(πfτ)df ([P2] Eq.(49), p.803, taken literally). 💥 Why it's wrong: the Rϕ(τ)=∫−∞∞Sϕej2πfτdfR_\phi(\tau)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_\phi e^{j2\pi f\tau}dfRϕ​(τ)=∫−∞∞​Sϕ​ej2πfτdf defined in [P2] Eq.(48) is a double-sided spectrum; the coefficient-8 formula is matched to a double-sided spectrum. A single-sideband spectrum (the kind you get from a datasheet or from L\mathcal{L}L) has already folded the double-sided power into 2× the density, so pairing it with the coefficient-8 formula double-counts a factor of 2 — variance ×2\times2×2, jitter ×2\times\sqrt2×2​. ✅ Correct version: pick one convention and stay with it end to end. With a single-sideband SϕS_\phiSϕ​ and ∫0∞\int_0^\infty∫0∞​, the N-period kernel is σP2(N)=1ω02∫0∞Sϕ(f) 4sin⁡2(πfNT) df\sigma_P^2(N)=\frac{1}{\omega_0^2}\int_0^\infty S_\phi(f)\,4\sin^2(\pi fNT)\,dfσP2​(N)=ω02​1​∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)4sin2(πfNT)df (8SϕDSsin⁡2=4SϕOSsin⁡28S_\phi^{DS}\sin^2=4S_\phi^{OS}\sin^28SϕDS​sin2=4SϕOS​sin2 — numerically identical). For the canonical white-noise oscillator (κ2=0.125\kappa^2=0.125κ2=0.125 rad²/s, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz): correct σP=0.1592\sigma_P=0.1592σP​=0.1592 fs; the wrong version gives 0.2251 fs. lab_24 computes it three different ways with three different bookkeeping conventions and all three print 0.1592 fs. 📍 On-site reference: jitter_kernels (Step 0 comparison table, [P2] Eq.(48)/(49) verified-verbatim note, lab_24 Monte-Carlo).

documents.t: ❌ Wrong practice: apply the comparator intuition Δt=ΔV/(dV/dt)\Delta t=\Delta V/(\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}t)Δt=ΔV/(dV/dt) and claim that "injecting positive charge pushes the voltage up, so the phase always leads (or always lags)"; or extend this to "the smaller the slope, the more sensitive, so a sinusoidal oscillator is most vulnerable to noise at its peak." (An early version of this site's lti_vs_ltv page had the direction backwards; it has since been corrected.) 💥 Why it's wrong: an oscillator is an LTV (linear time-variant) system. The sign of Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is set by the tangential projection of the voltage jump onto the limit cycle, which flips sign with injection phase; at the peak, ΔV\Delta VΔV is almost entirely a radial (amplitude) component, which the amplitude restoring force absorbs — the true sensitivity there is 0, not the infinity that 1/1/1/slope suggests. ✅ Correct version: for an ideal LC oscillator (V=Vmaxcos⁡θV=V_{max}\cos\thetaV=Vmax​cosθ), the ISF is Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ ([P1] Sec. III; Δϕ=Γ Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=ΓΔq/qmax​). Look up the direction directly: rising zero-crossing (θ=3π/2\theta=3\pi/2θ=3π/2) Γ=+1\Gamma=+1Γ=+1 → phase leads; falling zero-crossing (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2) Γ=−1\Gamma=-1Γ=−1 → phase lags; peak/trough Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0 → pure amplitude change. Numerical feel (Example A): a 1 fC injection with qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz gives ∣Δϕ∣=10−3\vert\Delta\phi\vert=10^{-3}∣Δϕ∣=10−3 rad =31.8=31.8=31.8 fs at the zero-crossing, and 0 fs at the peak. The 1-D waveform-shift check δ=ΔV/(dV/dt)\delta=\Delta V/(\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}t)δ=ΔV/(dV/dt) agrees with the ISF only at the zero-crossing; it breaks down moving toward the peak — exactly where the amplitude channel takes over. 📍 On-site reference: lti_vs_ltv (direction table and projection argument), impulse_to_phase_shift, waveform_slope (where slope intuition does apply: driven threshold-crossing circuits).

documents.t: ❌ Wrong claim: "This transistor's flicker corner is at 1 MHz, so the phase noise's 1/f31/f^31/f3 region also extends out to 1 MHz offset." 💥 Why it's wrong: the efficiency of flicker upconversion is set by the DC term c0c_0c0​ of the ISF, while the white-noise floor is set by Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ — so the intersection of the two regions (the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner) is rescaled by waveform symmetry, not a copy of the device corner. [P1] specifically emphasizes that this overturns the old myth that "the two corners are equal." ✅ Correct version: [P1] Eq.(24), p.185: Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c022Γrms2≈ω1/f(c0c1)2\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\Gamma_{rms}^2}\approx\omega_{1/f}\left(\frac{c_0}{c_1}\right)^2Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​≈ω1/f​(c1​c0​​)2 With a device corner at 1 MHz and Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5: an asymmetric waveform (c0=0.4c_0=0.4c0​=0.4) → corner at 320 kHz; symmetrizing to c0=0.04c_0=0.04c0​=0.04 → 3.2 kHz. Same device, corner differs by 100× — the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner is a design variable (symmetry), not a process constant. Dimension check: frequency × dimensionless ratio = frequency ✓. 📍 On-site reference: flicker_noise_upconversion (Examples E/F are exactly these two numbers), symmetry.

documents.t: ❌ Wrong practice: write [P2]'s white-noise phase-noise limit for a ring as L=83γkTPVDDVchar(f0Δf)2\mathcal{L}=\dfrac{8}{3\gamma}\dfrac{kT}{P}\dfrac{V_{DD}}{V_{char}}\Big(\dfrac{f_0}{\Delta f}\Big)^2L=3γ8​PkT​Vchar​VDD​​(Δff0​​)2 (putting the channel thermal-noise coefficient γ\gammaγ in the denominator). 💥 Why it's wrong: the prefactor in [P2] Eq.(23), p.796 is 8/(3η)8/(3\eta)8/(3η), where η\etaη is the stage-delay proportionality constant ([P2] Eq.(14), ≈1\approx1≈1, waveform/delay bookkeeping) and has nothing to do with noise; γ\gammaγ only enters through Vchar=ΔV/γV_{char}=\Delta V/\gammaVchar​=ΔV/γ. Writing 8/(3γ)8/(3\gamma)8/(3γ) counts γ\gammaγ twice. ✅ Correct version: Llin=83η⋅kTP⋅VDDVchar⋅(f0Δf)2,Vchar=ΔVγ\mathcal{L}_{lin}=\frac{8}{3\eta}\cdot\frac{kT}{P}\cdot\frac{V_{DD}}{V_{char}}\cdot\left(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\right)^{2},\qquad V_{char}=\frac{\Delta V}{\gamma}Llin​=3η8​⋅PkT​⋅Vchar​VDD​​⋅(Δff0​​)2,Vchar​=γΔV​ For a long-channel device with γ=2/3\gamma=2/3γ=2/3, η=1\eta=1η=1, the misremembered formula overstates the noise by 10log⁡10 ⁣(4/(8/3))=1.7610\log_{10}\!\big(4/(8/3)\big)=1.7610log10​(4/(8/3))=1.76 dB; more insidiously, when γ=1\gamma=1γ=1 the two formulas coincide exactly, hiding the error. The VT=0V_T=0VT​=0 ceiling Feff≥16γ/(3η)F_{eff}\ge16\gamma/(3\eta)Feff​≥16γ/(3η) ([P2] Eq.(25)) is where the γ\gammaγ that genuinely comes from VcharV_{char}Vchar​ shows up. (This site's v3 spec corrected this coefficient against the original [P2] PDF, p.796.) 📍 On-site reference: fom_limit (Step 2, with a step-by-step derivation and the ceiling), paper_002 deep dive.

documents.t: ❌ Wrong practice: compute rms jitter directly as σϕ2=∫10L/10df\sigma_\phi^2=\int10^{\mathcal{L}/10}dfσϕ2​=∫10L/10df (forgetting the ×2\times2×2 in Sϕ=2×10L/10S_\phi=2\times10^{\mathcal{L}/10}Sϕ​=2×10L/10); or report "jitter = xx fs" without stating the integration band, so others using a different f1f_1f1​ can't reconcile the numbers. 💥 Why it's wrong: L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​ (small-angle PM: each sideband only carries half the power), so missing the ×2 → half the variance, jitter low by 2\sqrt22​. And the integral of a 1/f21/f^21/f2 spectrum is dominated by the lower limit f1f_1f1​ (∫f1df/f2∝1/f1\int_{f_1} df/f^2\propto1/f_1∫f1​​df/f2∝1/f1​) — every decade f1f_1f1​ drops, jitter rises by 10\sqrt{10}10​. ✅ Correct version: the four-step chain L→×2, de-dBSϕ→∫f1f2σϕ2→ σϕ→÷ 2πf0σt\mathcal{L}\xrightarrow{\times2,\ \text{de-dB}}S_\phi\xrightarrow{\int_{f_1}^{f_2}}\sigma_\phi^2\xrightarrow{\sqrt{\ }}\sigma_\phi\xrightarrow{\div\,2\pi f_0}\sigma_tL×2, de-dB​Sϕ​∫f1​f2​​​σϕ2​ ​​σϕ​÷2πf0​​σt​, and always attach [f1,f2][f_1,f_2][f1​,f2​]. Canonical Example C (5 GHz, −100-100−100 dBc/Hz@1 MHz, 1/f21/f^21/f2, integrated 1–100 MHz): correct 447.9 fs; forgetting ×2\times2×2 → 316.7 fs; moving f1f_1f1​ to 100 kHz → 1422.8 fs (×10\times\sqrt{10}×10​). Dimension check: rad÷(rad/s)=s\text{rad}\div(\text{rad/s})=\text{s}rad÷(rad/s)=s ✓. 📍 On-site reference: psd_phase_noise_jitter (Example C step-by-step), lab_08.

documents.t: ❌ Wrong claim: "Eq.(21) is 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2, so phase noise grows without bound as offset shrinks — power is infinite at Δf→0\Delta f\to0Δf→0"; or seeing an instrument fail to show the −20-20−20 dB/dec slope at very small offsets and suspecting the measurement is broken. 💥 Why it's wrong: 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 comes from linearization (small-angle approximation), and Δf→0\Delta f\to0Δf→0 corresponds to long time intervals, where the random phase walk has already gone far beyond ≫1\gg1≫1 rad — exactly where the approximation breaks down. The real carrier spectrum is Lorentzian: it flattens near the carrier, has a finite peak, and conserves total power (equal to the carrier power). ✅ Correct version: 1/f21/f^21/f2 is just the far asymptote of a Lorentzian at Δf≫Δf3dB\Delta f\gg\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}Δf≫Δf3dB​; the knee is at Δf3dB=κ2/2π\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\kappa^2/2\piΔf3dB​=κ2/2π. Canonical Example B: 19.9 mHz (almost unmeasurable, so in practice the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region "looks like" it goes all the way down); a datasheet-grade −100-100−100 dBc/Hz@1 MHz oscillator has a knee at 628 Hz — genuinely visible when measuring at low offset. Divergence is not physics; it's a signal that the approximation has failed. 📍 On-site reference: lorentzian_linewidth (full mechanism and power conservation), beyond_lorentzian, diffusion_dictionary (Suit 3).
documents.s: 8. Treating L's divergence at Δf→0 as physical — "infinite power near the carrier" does not exist

documents.t: ❌ Wrong practice: measure (or compute) the actual peak-to-peak value of deterministic jitter, DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJpp​, and substitute it directly into the industry extrapolation formula TJ(BER)=DJ+2Q−1(BER) σ\mathrm{TJ}(\mathrm{BER})=\mathrm{DJ}+2Q^{-1}(\mathrm{BER})\,\sigmaTJ(BER)=DJ+2Q−1(BER)σ. 💥 Why it's wrong: the dual-Dirac model's DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​ is a model parameter fitted from the Q-scale tail, and mathematically it must satisfy DJδδ≤DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}\le\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJδδ​≤DJpp​ (near its extremes the DJ distribution has only finite probability mass, so the deep tail is a "discounted Gaussian"); this "intentional underreporting" is precisely the mechanism that makes the BER extrapolation fit the true tail. ✅ Correct version: TJ(BER)=DJδδ+2Q−1(BER)σ\mathrm{TJ}(\mathrm{BER})=\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}+2Q^{-1}(\mathrm{BER})\sigmaTJ(BER)=DJδδ​+2Q−1(BER)σ, where 2Q−1=14.072Q^{-1}=14.072Q−1=14.07 at BER =10−12=10^{-12}=10−12. lab_31 (sinusoidal DJ, A=2A=2A=2 ps, RJ σ=1\sigma=1σ=1 ps): DJpp=4.0\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}=4.0DJpp​=4.0 ps but the fitted DJδδ=3.16\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}=3.16DJδδ​=3.16 ps; forcing in DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJpp​ gives TJ =18.07=18.07=18.07 ps, 0.84 ps more pessimistic than the exact bathtub value of 17.23 ps — throwing away margin for nothing. The reverse direction is also wrong: DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​ is not a physical peak-to-peak value, so don't use it to plot waveform extrema. Always state the fit window when reporting (lab_31: the deeper the fit window, the closer DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​ gets to, but never exceeds, DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJpp​: 3.07/3.16/3.27 ps). 📍 On-site reference: dj_dual_dirac (Steps 6/7: derivation plus the proof that "underreporting is intentional"), serdes_clocking_connection.
documents.s: 9. Plugging DJ_pp directly into the TJ formula — you should use DJ_δδ

documents.t: ❌ Wrong practice: when measuring near-carrier phase noise with a spectrum analyzer direct method, use a filter with RBW (resolution bandwidth) =1=1=1 kHz at 1 kHz offset to read dBc/Hz quickly; or normalize per-Hz using the nominal RBW instead of the ENBW. 💥 Why it's wrong: a dBc/Hz reading is "the average density inside the RBW filter window." In the 1/f31/f^31/f3 region, the density varies by tens of dB within one window, and the average is dominated by the side closer to the carrier — the reading is biased high, and the steep skirt gets smeared out; when the RBW is large enough that the window edge touches the carrier, carrier power leaks straight in and you read the filter shape, not the DUT. ✅ Correct version: for close-in measurements, keep RBW ≪Δf\ll\Delta f≪Δf (conservatively below Δf/10\Delta f/10Δf/10). An honest numerical feel (averaging the 1/f31/f^31/f3 density across the window and comparing to the true value at Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 kHz): RBW =1=1=1 kHz reads 2.5 dB high, RBW =100=100=100 Hz only 0.02 dB (see the code at the end of this page; this doesn't even account for carrier leakage — real conditions are only worse). Normalize per-Hz using ENBW (equivalent noise bandwidth), not the nominal RBW, and remember the log-detector's +2.5+2.5+2.5 dB correction (a different mechanism from the 2.5 dB window-averaging bias above — the matching numeric value is pure coincidence) — this is standard spectrum-analyzer measurement knowledge (external literature, not among the five source PDFs; see the measurement page's Method A, which cites Keysight/Agilent AN-1303). The true near-carrier flattening is the Lorentzian (Mistake 8) — you must rule out the RBW artifact before claiming to have seen it. 📍 On-site reference: measurement_and_spurs (Method A's ENBW normalization, the "re-weight by changing RBW" spur-identification test).
documents.s: 10. RBW set too wide when measuring close-in — smearing out the −30 dB/dec skirt

documents.t: ❌ Wrong claim: "A ÷2 frequency divider improves phase noise by 6 dB, so rms jitter (in fs) also halves (or shrinks by 2\sqrt22​)." 💥 Why it's wrong: an ideal divider is edge-picking — it copies the input edge's time position verbatim, without moving it by a single fs. What changes is the "exchange rate": the same time-domain error, spread over a period that is now NNN times longer, converts to a smaller phase angle (rad), which is why L\mathcal{L}L drops by 20log⁡10N20\log_{10}N20log10​N. ✅ Correct version: work it through honestly. ϕout=ϕin/N\phi_{out}=\phi_{in}/Nϕout​=ϕin​/N (the phase definition of division), so σϕ,out=σϕ,in/N\sigma_{\phi,out}=\sigma_{\phi,in}/Nσϕ,out​=σϕ,in​/N (the rad value truly shrinks); but f0,out=f0,in/Nf_{0,out}=f_{0,in}/Nf0,out​=f0,in​/N, and substituting into spec formula 17: σt,out=σϕ,out2πf0,out=σϕ,in/N2πf0,in/N=σϕ,in2πf0,in=σt,in\sigma_{t,out}=\frac{\sigma_{\phi,out}}{2\pi f_{0,out}}=\frac{\sigma_{\phi,in}/N}{2\pi f_{0,in}/N}=\frac{\sigma_{\phi,in}}{2\pi f_{0,in}}=\sigma_{t,in}σt,out​=2πf0,out​σϕ,out​​=2πf0,in​/Nσϕ,in​/N​=2πf0,in​σϕ,in​​=σt,in​ The two NNN's cancel — jitter measured in seconds is an invariant under ideal ×N/÷N. A worked chain (5 GHz divided by 2 to 2.5 GHz, same integration band): 22.5 fs → 22.5 fs, while σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ does halve (0.706 → 0.353 mrad). What ÷2 saves is "fraction of the UI" (the UI got longer), not the time value; an ADC aperture or an absolute timing budget cares about seconds, and gains nothing at all. Dimension check: rad÷(rad/s)=s\text{rad}\div(\text{rad/s})=\text{s}rad÷(rad/s)=s, independent of NNN ✓. 📍 On-site reference: clock_chain_budget (Rule 2 and Step 5's "conserved quantity"), adc_aperture_jitter.
documents.s: 11. Assuming jitter (in seconds) also halves after ÷2 — confusing phase in dB with absolute time

documents.t: ❌ Wrong practice: measure the period jitter σP(1)\sigma_P(1)σP​(1), then extrapolate the accumulated jitter after NNN periods using σ(N)=σP(1)N\sigma(N)=\sigma_P(1)\sqrt Nσ(N)=σP​(1)N​ — regardless of what the spectrum actually looks like. 💥 Why it's wrong: the N\sqrt NN​ law is a property of white-FM random walks (independent increments, [P2] Eq.(8)). When flicker (1/f31/f^31/f3) dominates, adjacent increments are strongly correlated, and the growth law is approximately ∝N\propto N∝N ([P2] Eq.(9) and the slope-1 region of Fig. 4) — extrapolating with N\sqrt NN​ systematically underestimates jitter over long intervals. ✅ Correct version: first check which mechanism dominates near f∼1/(2NT)f\sim1/(2NT)f∼1/(2NT). White-noise region: σΔϕ=κNT\sigma_{\Delta\phi}=\kappa\sqrt{NT}σΔϕ​=κNT​; flicker region: σΔϕ2=4π2b3(NT)2[32−γE−ln⁡(2πNTfl)]\sigma^2_{\Delta\phi}=4\pi^2b_3(NT)^2\big[\tfrac32-\gamma_E-\ln(2\pi NTf_l)\big]σΔϕ2​=4π2b3​(NT)2[23​−γE​−ln(2πNTfl​)] (γE=0.5772\gamma_E=0.5772γE​=0.5772 is the Euler–Mascheroni constant; nearly ∝N\propto N∝N, and with a logarithmic dependence on the low-frequency cutoff flf_lfl​ — always attach flf_lfl​ when reporting a number). Numerical picture (lab_24, T=200T=200T=200 ps, fl=100f_l=100fl​=100 Hz): σ(N=10)/σ(N=1)\sigma(N{=}10)/\sigma(N{=}1)σ(N=10)/σ(N=1) is 10=3.16\sqrt{10}=3.1610​=3.16 for white noise vs 9.299.299.29 for flicker — nearly 3× apart. Quick sanity check: only the white-noise region satisfies σc2c=2 σP\sigma_{c2c}=\sqrt2\,\sigma_Pσc2c​=2​σP​; if that relation doesn't hold, don't use N\sqrt NN​. 📍 On-site reference: jitter_kernels (Step 5's closed-form flicker expression and the log-band caveat), lab_03, allan_variance (the ADEV version of the same story: white FM τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2}τ−1/2 vs flicker FM τ0\tau^0τ0).

documents.t: ❌ Wrong claim: "I inject a clean sine at fref=f0/Nf_{ref}=f_0/Nfref​=f0​/N into the oscillator; it's the same generalized-Adler restoring force as fundamental injection locking, so it should lock to f0=Nfreff_0=Nf_{ref}f0​=Nfref​." — treating an injection-locked clock multiplier (ILCM, the multiplier direction) as fundamental locking with just a different injection frequency. 💥 Why it's wrong: term-by-term averaging of [P4] Eq.(29)–(30) gives the selection rule k=mNk=mNk=mN — the multiplier (M=1M=1M=1, N≥2N\ge2N≥2) restoring force Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ) is supplied only by "the injection waveform's NNN-th harmonic" times "the ISF's fundamental" (see subharmonic_injection, Section 1). A pure sine iinj=Iinjcos⁡(ωinjt)i_{inj}=I_{inj}\cos(\omega_{inj}t)iinj​=Iinj​cos(ωinj​t) has only the k=1k=1k=1 harmonic; for N≥2N\ge2N≥2, ∣IN∣=0\vert I_N\vert=0∣IN​∣=0, so after first-order averaging Ω(θ)≡0\Omega(\theta)\equiv0Ω(θ)≡0 — there is no restoring force at all, and the lock range is identically zero, not just narrow. (If a real circuit occasionally still locks, that's the oscillator's own nonlinearity mixing up an NNN-th harmonic of freff_{ref}fref​ — [P4] footnote 10 states explicitly that this is outside the Eq.(28)–(30) framework and cannot be relied on by design.) ✅ Correct version: to build the multiplier direction (ILCM), the injection waveform itself must carry the NNN-th harmonic — use a pulse generator (a narrow pulse), not a clean sine; the pulse width τp≪T0\tau_p\ll T_0τp​≪T0​ (the output period, not the reference period) is needed to keep enough ∣IN∣∝sinc(f0τp)\vert I_N\vert\propto\mathrm{sinc}(f_0\tau_p)∣IN​∣∝sinc(f0​τp​). Canonical example (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, N=20N=20N=20, qinj=50q_{inj}=50qinj​=50 fC, τp=10\tau_p=10τp​=10 ps) gives fL=1.981f_L=1.981fL​=1.981 MHz; lab_40's numerical check at the same rms current: the pulse train locks at 15/15 grid points, a pure sine locks at 0/15 — completely unable to lock at first order, not merely less efficient. 📍 On-site reference: subharmonic_injection (Section 1, Step 4, "a pure sine cannot lock"), lab_40_subharmonic_injection (experiment (c)'s numerical verification).

documents.t: Of the 13 landmines, 7 (1, 2, 3, 7, 9's 2Q−12Q^{-1}2Q−1, 11, 12) are fundamentally bookkeeping-convention issues, grouped into three families (see diffusion_dictionary for details): Single-sided vs double-sided PSD: the δ\deltaδ-strength Si/2S_i/2Si​/2, the single-sideband 2κ22\kappa^22κ2, the 8 vs 4 in the jitter kernel. Var=D∣t∣\mathrm{Var}=D\vert t\vertVar=D∣t∣ vs 2D∣t∣2D\vert t\vert2D∣t∣: κ2=DA=2DB\kappa^2=D_{\text{A}}=2D_{\text{B}}κ2=DA​=2DB​. SSB /2/2/2 vs /4/4/4: the 3 dB between −145-145−145 and −148-148−148. The other 4 (4, 5, 8, and part of 10) are cases of applying LTI/linearization intuition where it no longer holds: slope intuition colliding with amplitude restoration, device-corner intuition colliding with c0c_0c0​ upconversion, the 1/f21/f^21/f2 line colliding with the large-angle regime of a random walk, narrowband-density intuition colliding with wide-RBW averaging. There is only one defense: ask, for every number, "which convention is this? does the approximation still hold here?" — then reconcile it with a one-line Python check.
documents.s: Common root cause: three factor-of-2 families + one LTI habit

documents.t: Below, every number from the 13 landmines that can be verified in one line is recomputed (run with PYTHONPATH=. python3 <this-file> from the project root; the DJ numbers in Mistake 9 are produced by simulations/lab_31_dual_dirac.py, see dj_dual_dirac): import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import leeson_one_over_f2, integrate_rms_jitter # --- Mistake 1: κ² mistaken for D (linewidth 2×) --- GRMS, QMAX, SI = 0.5, 1e-12, 1e-24 k2 = GRMS**2 * SI / (2 * QMAX**2) # [P2] Eq.(11)/(12) print(round(k2, 3)) # -> 0.125 (κ², rad²/s) print(round(k2 / (2*np.pi) * 1e3, 1)) # -> 19.9 (correct FWHM, mHz) print(round(k2 / np.pi * 1e3, 1)) # -> 39.8 (κ² plugged into D/π, the 2x wrong value) # --- Mistake 2: SSB /4 vs time-domain /2 (3 dB) --- dw = 2 * np.pi * 1e6 print(round(10*np.log10(GRMS**2/QMAX**2 * SI/(4*dw**2)), 1)) # -> -148.0 ([P1] Eq.(21) /4) print(round(10*np.log10(GRMS**2/QMAX**2 * SI/(2*dw**2)), 1)) # -> -145.0 (time-domain /2) # --- Mistake 3: single-sideband spectrum plugged into coefficient-8 kernel (x√2) --- f0, T = 5e9, 2e-10 sigP = np.sqrt(k2 * T) / (2*np.pi*f0) print(round(sigP*1e15, 4)) # -> 0.1592 (correct period jitter, fs) print(round(sigP*np.sqrt(2)*1e15, 4)) # -> 0.2251 (x√2 wrong value, fs) # --- Mistake 5: 1/f³ corner != device corner (Eq.24, device corner=1 MHz) --- print(round(1e6 * 0.4**2 / (2*GRMS**2) / 1e3, 1)) # -> 320.0 (c0=0.4, kHz) print(round(1e6 * 0.04**2 / (2*GRMS**2) / 1e3, 1)) # -> 3.2 (c0=0.04, kHz) # --- Mistake 6: 8/(3γ) vs 8/(3η) (γ=2/3, η=1) --- print(round(10*np.log10((8/(3*(2/3))) / (8/3)), 2)) # -> 1.76 (dB, excess from misremembering) # --- Mistake 7: forgetting integral x2, or shifting f1 carelessly --- f = np.logspace(3, 9, 400001) L = leeson_one_over_f2(f, L_ref_dbc=-100.0, f_ref=1e6) st, _ = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L, f0=5e9, fmin=1e6, fmax=1e8) print(round(st*1e15, 1)) # -> 447.9 (correct, fs; Example C) print(round(st/np.sqrt(2)*1e15, 1)) # -> 316.7 (forgot x2, fs) st2, _ = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L, f0=5e9, fmin=1e5, fmax=1e8) print(round(st2*1e15, 1)) # -> 1422.8 (f1 moved to 100 kHz, fs) # --- Mistake 10: RBW bias on the 1/f³ skirt reading at offset=1 kHz --- d = 1e3 bias = lambda rbw: 10*np.log10(d**3/(2*rbw)*(1/(d-rbw/2)**2 - 1/(d+rbw/2)**2)) print(round(bias(1e3), 2)) # -> 2.5 (RBW=1 kHz, dB high) print(round(bias(1e2), 2)) # -> 0.02 (RBW=100 Hz, dB) # --- Mistake 11: dB improves by 6 dB after ÷2, time value unchanged --- f = np.logspace(4, 8, 20001) L5G = np.where(f <= 1e6, -126.02, -148.0 - 20*np.log10(f/1e6)) st5, sp5 = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L5G, f0=5e9, fmin=1e4, fmax=1e8) st25, sp25 = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L5G - 6.02, f0=2.5e9, fmin=1e4, fmax=1e8) print(round(st5*1e15, 1), round(st25*1e15, 1)) # -> 22.5 22.5 (fs, before/after division) print(round(sp5/sp25, 2)) # -> 2.0 (phase in rad does halve) # --- Mistake 12: flicker's N growth law ≈ N (not √N) --- gEM, fl = 0.5772156649, 100.0 br = lambda N: 1.5 - gEM - np.log(2*np.pi*N*T*fl) print(round(10*np.sqrt(br(10)/br(1)), 2)) # -> 9.29 (white noise should be √10=3.16) (In Mistake 10, bias is the closed form for "the average of the 1/f31/f^31/f3 density across the RBW window, divided by the true value at the window center": S‾=1RBW∫b/f3 df=b2 RBW(flo−2−fhi−2)\overline{S}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{RBW}}\int b/f^3\,df=\frac{b}{2\,\mathrm{RBW}}\big(f_{lo}^{-2}-f_{hi}^{-2}\big)S=RBW1​∫b/f3df=2RBWb​(flo−2​−fhi−2​), a teaching toy calculation that does not include carrier leakage or detector effects.)

documents.t: Reconcile before switching conventions: single-sided vs double-sided, Var=D∣t∣\mathrm{Var}=D\vert t\vertVar=D∣t∣ vs 2D∣t∣2D\vert t\vert2D∣t∣, SSB /2/2/2 vs /4/4/4 — these three factor-of-2 families account for most of the landmines. The ISF's direction and magnitude come from the tangential projection on the limit cycle, not ΔV/\Delta V/ΔV/slope; the peak belongs to the amplitude channel (Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0). The two corners are different things: the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner =ω1/f c02/(2Γrms2)=\omega_{1/f}\,c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)=ω1/f​c02​/(2Γrms2​) can be pushed far below the device corner by symmetry (300× lower in this example at c0=0.04c_0=0.04c0​=0.04: 1 MHz → 3.2 kHz). The ring FOM prefactor is 8/(3η)8/(3\eta)8/(3η); γ\gammaγ only lives inside Vchar=ΔV/γV_{char}=\Delta V/\gammaVchar​=ΔV/γ. Jitter integration: ×2\times2×2, label the band (f1f_1f1​ dominates), ÷ 2πf0\div\,2\pi f_0÷2πf0​; under ideal ×N/÷N, the time value is unchanged — only the dB exchange rate changes. The Δf→0\Delta f\to0Δf→0 divergence is a linearization artifact — the real spectrum is Lorentzian, and total power is conserved. TJ extrapolation uses DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​ (a model parameter, intentionally underreported), not DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJpp​. Close-in measurement: RBW ≪Δf\ll\Delta f≪Δf, normalize with ENBW, rule out instrument artifacts before discussing physics. When flicker dominates, the accumulation law is ≈N\approx N≈N (not N\sqrt NN​), with a logarithmic dependence on flf_lfl​ — always state the condition when reporting a number.

documents.t: Prerequisites: fom_limit (the FOM=173.8−10log⁡10Feff\mathrm{FOM}=173.8-10\log_{10}F_{eff}FOM=173.8−10log10​Feff​ ceiling family), tank_Q_and_energy_restoration (the three forms of QQQ, 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​), tank_swing (qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=CV_{max}qmax​=CVmax​, current/voltage-limited regimes, 4πIbiasRp\tfrac{4}{\pi}I_{bias}R_pπ4​Ibias​Rp​), white_noise_to_phase_noise ([P1] Eq.(21) and the /2 vs /4 convention) | Next: pll_noise_budget, clock_chain_budget, lab_09_design_tradeoffs Every other design page on this site runs forward: given qmaxq_{max}qmax​, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, SiS_iSi​, compute L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf); or it does a single-knob inversion: how much must qmaxq_{max}qmax​ grow (exercises problem 1), how high must QQQ be (fom_limit example 2). Real design work runs the other way: all you have is a spec sheet (phase noise, power, tuning range), and you must decide, in order, the topology, the tank element values, the swing and the bias current, then loop back to verify the spec and convert the result into the jitter the system asks for. This page writes that path down as a reusable recipe: 7 steps, one set of numbers carried from start to finish, each step naming the formula it uses, checking units, and stating when it fails; and at the end, iteration rules — which knob to turn when the margin is short, how many dB each turn buys, and what it costs in power. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the three numbers on the spec sheet, L\mathcal{L}L, PPP and f0/Δff_0/\Delta ff0​/Δf, collapse into one number — the required FOM. Compare that number with the ceiling family of fom_limit and the topology is decided (the ring ceiling of 168.3 dB is a hard wall). Once the topology is fixed, an LC oscillator's L\mathcal{L}L is set by exactly four things: QQQ (how small the 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​ noise source is), qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=CV_{max}qmax​=CVmax​ (how much signal charge there is), FFF (who else besides the tank is making noise), and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (the waveform shape) — precisely the four factors of [P1] Eq.(21). The recipe's job is to pin each of those four factors to an element value or a bias, then sign off with Eq.(21).

documents.t: Suppose the system engineer hands over this spec (used throughout the page): Spec item Value Reading Carrier f0f_0f0​ 555 GHz The site's canonical frequency SSB phase noise L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) ≤−120\le-120≤−120 dBc/Hz @ Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz One point in the white-noise 1/f21/f^21/f2 region (assumes 1 MHz is already beyond the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner) Total DC power PPP ≤5\le5≤5 mW Core plus bias, excluding buffers (see failure conditions) Tuning range TR 10%10\%10% (4.75∼5.254.75\sim5.254.75∼5.25 GHz) Affects the varactor fraction and FOMT_TT​ (end of page) Temperature 300300300 K kT=4.142×10−21kT=4.142\times10^{-21}kT=4.142×10−21 J Why one point of L\mathcal{L}L suffices: in the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region L\mathcal{L}L versus Δf\Delta fΔf is a −20-20−20 dB/dec straight line (the 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 of [P1] Eq.(21)), so one point fixes the whole segment. If the spec point lies in the 1/f31/f^31/f3 (close-in) region, first use symmetry to push the corner below the spec point, then come back to this recipe. The three spec numbers are not independent: a tighter L\mathcal{L}L can be bought with PPP (the "L×P≈\mathcal{L}\times P\approxL×P≈ constant" of tank_swing step 4), so the next step first merges them into a single power-independent number.

documents.t: Using the positive-valued convention of fom_limit step 0 (larger is better), merge the three spec numbers into the required FOM: FOMreq=−Lspec+20log⁡10 ⁣(f0Δf)−10log⁡10 ⁣(Pmax1 mW)\mathrm{FOM}_{req}=-\mathcal{L}_{spec}+20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\right)-10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P_{max}}{1\ \text{mW}}\right)FOMreq​=−Lspec​+20log10​(Δff0​​)−10log10​(1 mWPmax​​) Term by term (with units): 20log⁡10 ⁣(f0Δf)=20log⁡10 ⁣(5×109 Hz106 Hz)=20log⁡10(5000)=73.98 dB,10log⁡10 ⁣(Pmax1 mW)=10log⁡10 ⁣(5 mW1 mW)=6.99 dB,FOMreq=120+73.98−6.99=186.99≈187.0 dB.\begin{aligned} 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\right)&=20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{5\times10^{9}\ \text{Hz}}{10^{6}\ \text{Hz}}\right)=20\log_{10}(5000)=73.98\ \text{dB},\\[4pt] 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P_{max}}{1\ \text{mW}}\right)&=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{5\ \text{mW}}{1\ \text{mW}}\right)=6.99\ \text{dB},\\[4pt] \mathrm{FOM}_{req}&=120+73.98-6.99=186.99\approx187.0\ \text{dB}. \end{aligned}20log10​(Δff0​​)10log10​(1 mWPmax​​)FOMreq​​=20log10​(106 Hz5×109 Hz​)=20log10​(5000)=73.98 dB,=10log10​(1 mW5 mW​)=6.99 dB,=120+73.98−6.99=186.99≈187.0 dB.​ Reading: this is the minimum FOM needed to reach −120-120−120 dBc/Hz within a 5 mW budget. Using less than 5 mW, or doing better than −120-120−120, both require an actual FOM above 187.0. Dimension check: all three terms are log⁡10\log_{10}log10​ of dimensionless ratios (Hz/Hz\text{Hz}/\text{Hz}Hz/Hz, W/W\text{W}/\text{W}W/W, and L\mathcal{L}L normalized to a 1 Hz bandwidth) → dB ✓. Why PmaxP_{max}Pmax​: FOM carries PPP with a negative sign — the power ceiling gives the most lenient FOM requirement; if the implementation later burns only 2.5 mW, the required FOM automatically rises by 3 dB (Step 6 shows this). import numpy as np f0, df, L_spec, P_max = 5e9, 1e6, -120.0, 5e-3 print(round(20*np.log10(f0/df), 2)) # -> 73.98 print(round(10*np.log10(P_max/1e-3), 2)) # -> 6.99 FOM_req = -L_spec + 20*np.log10(f0/df) - 10*np.log10(P_max/1e-3) print(round(FOM_req, 2)) # -> 186.99 (required FOM, dB) Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Try it yourself: if the spec changes to L(1 MHz) ≤ −125 dBc/Hz and P ≤ 2 mW (f0 still 5 GHz), what is FOM_req? (dB) dBCheckShow answer Graded correct within ±1% relative error; scientific notation is accepted.

documents.t: Compare FOMreq\mathrm{FOM}_{req}FOMreq​ with the ceiling family of fom_limit step 4 (FOMmax=173.83−10log⁡10Feff\mathrm{FOM}_{max}=173.83-10\log_{10}F_{eff}FOMmax​=173.83−10log10​Feff​, 300 K): Candidate topology FeffF_{eff}Feff​ FOMmax\mathrm{FOM}_{max}FOMmax​ vs FOMreq=187.0\mathrm{FOM}_{req}=187.0FOMreq​=187.0 Verdict ring ([P2] Eq.(25) bound: VT=0V_T=0VT​=0, γ=2/3\gamma=2/3γ=2/3, η=1\eta=1η=1) 16γ/(3η)=3.5616\gamma/(3\eta)=3.5616γ/(3η)=3.56 168.32168.32168.32 dB 168.32−186.99=−18.67168.32-186.99=-18.67168.32−186.99=−18.67 dB Infeasible — even the ideal limit falls 18.7 dB short LC, Q=10Q=10Q=10 ([P1] Eq.(21) SSB /4; F=1+γF=1+\gammaF=1+γ, γ=2/3\gamma=2/3γ=2/3, Γrms2=12\Gamma_{rms}^2=\tfrac12Γrms2​=21​, ηP=1\eta_P=1ηP​=1) 4.17×10−34.17\times10^{-3}4.17×10−3 197.63197.63197.63 dB 197.63−186.99=+10.64197.63-186.99=+10.64197.63−186.99=+10.64 dB Feasible, ideal margin 10.6 dB Same, time-domain /2 convention 8.33×10−38.33\times10^{-3}8.33×10−3 194.62194.62194.62 dB +7.63+7.63+7.63 dB Same physics, 3.01 dB more conservative bookkeeping Decision rule: FOMmax−FOMreq\mathrm{FOM}_{max}-\mathrm{FOM}_{req}FOMmax​−FOMreq​ is the "ideal margin". fom_limit notes that good published LC designs sit about 5∼105\sim105∼10 dB below their own QQQ ceiling (ηP<1\eta_P\lt1ηP​<1, F>1+γF\gt1+\gammaF>1+γ, varactor loss), so an ideal margin of at least 5 dB is needed before going further; 10.6 dB is comfortable. The ring is 18.7 dB short — no choice of NNN, swing or power can recover that ([P2] N-independence; FOM is already normalized to PPP). Conclusion: choose LC, and the process must deliver a tank with Q≈10Q\approx10Q≈10. If the process only gives Q=5Q=5Q=5, the ceiling drops 666 dB to 191.6191.6191.6 dB and the margin shrinks to 4.6 dB — which lands you in the iteration at the end of this page. import numpy as np kB, T = 1.380649e-23, 300.0 Cref = -10*np.log10(kB*T*1.0/1e-3) # 173.83 dB (fom_limit step 1) FOM_req = 186.99 gamma = 2/3 FOM_ring = Cref - 10*np.log10(16*gamma/3) # [P2] Eq.(25) bound print(round(FOM_ring, 2), round(FOM_ring - FOM_req, 2)) # -> 168.32 -18.67 (ring ceiling, gap: infeasible) FOM_lc10 = Cref - 10*np.log10((1+gamma)*0.5/(2*10**2)) # [P1] Eq.(21) /4 convention, Q=10 print(round(FOM_lc10, 2), round(FOM_lc10 - FOM_req, 2)) # -> 197.63 10.64 (LC Q=10 ceiling, ideal margin) print(round(FOM_lc10 - 10*np.log10(2) - FOM_req, 2)) # -> 7.63 (margin under the time-domain /2 convention) FOM_lc5 = Cref - 10*np.log10((1+gamma)*0.5/(2*5**2)) print(round(FOM_lc5, 2), round(FOM_lc5 - FOM_req, 2)) # -> 191.61 4.62 (Q=5 ceiling, ideal margin) print(round(-10*np.log10(310/300), 2)) # -> -0.14 (change of C_ref per +10 K, dB)
documents.s: Step 2: Against the ceilings — ring or LC?

documents.t: The three tank quantities have only two degrees of freedom (f0f_0f0​ ties LCLCLC together); add the process-given QQQ and everything is fixed. Choose CCC first (not LLL) — CCC enters qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=CV_{max}qmax​=CVmax​ directly and sets the varactor and parasitic fractions: Lower bound on CCC: device, varactor and routing parasitics at 5 GHz already amount to a few hundred fF; too small a CCC lets the parasitics eat the tuning range. Upper bound on CCC: larger CCC → smaller LLL, smaller Rp=Qω0LR_p=Q\omega_0LRp​=Qω0​L → more current for the same swing (Step 4). Take C=1C=1C=1 pF (the site's canonical value, and the same order as the example in tank_Q_and_energy_restoration): ω0=2πf0=2π×5×109=3.1416×1010 rad/s,L=1ω02C=1(3.1416×1010)2×10−12=19.870×1020×10−12=1.013×10−9 H=1.013 nH,Rp=Q ω0L=10×3.1416×1010×1.013×10−9=318.3 Ω.\begin{aligned} \omega_0&=2\pi f_0=2\pi\times5\times10^{9}=3.1416\times10^{10}\ \text{rad/s},\\[4pt] L&=\frac{1}{\omega_0^2C}=\frac{1}{(3.1416\times10^{10})^2\times10^{-12}} =\frac{1}{9.870\times10^{20}\times10^{-12}}=1.013\times10^{-9}\ \text{H}=1.013\ \text{nH},\\[4pt] R_p&=Q\,\omega_0L=10\times3.1416\times10^{10}\times1.013\times10^{-9}=318.3\ \Omega . \end{aligned}ω0​LRp​​=2πf0​=2π×5×109=3.1416×1010 rad/s,=ω02​C1​=(3.1416×1010)2×10−121​=9.870×1020×10−121​=1.013×10−9 H=1.013 nH,=Qω0​L=10×3.1416×1010×1.013×10−9=318.3 Ω.​ Formulas used: ω0=1/LC\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}ω0​=1/LC​ and Q=Rp/(ω0L)=ω0RpC=RpC/LQ=R_p/(\omega_0L)=\omega_0R_pC=R_p\sqrt{C/L}Q=Rp​/(ω0​L)=ω0​Rp​C=Rp​C/L​ (the three equivalent forms from tank_Q_and_energy_restoration step 1; standard textbook material, external to the site's 5 PDFs). The three forms cross-check: Q=ω0RpC=3.1416×1010×318.3×10−12=10.0Q=\omega_0R_pC=3.1416\times10^{10}\times318.3\times10^{-12}=10.0Q=ω0​Rp​C=3.1416×1010×318.3×10−12=10.0 ✓; R0=L/C=1.013×10−9/10−12=31.83 ΩR_0=\sqrt{L/C}=\sqrt{1.013\times10^{-9}/10^{-12}}=31.83\ \OmegaR0​=L/C​=1.013×10−9/10−12​=31.83 Ω, Rp/R0=10.0R_p/R_0=10.0Rp​/R0​=10.0 ✓. Dimension check: [1/(ω02C)]=1/[(s−2)(F)]=s2/F=H[1/(\omega_0^2C)]=1/[(\text{s}^{-2})(\text{F})]=\text{s}^2/\text{F}=\text{H}[1/(ω02​C)]=1/[(s−2)(F)]=s2/F=H ✓ (H⋅F=s2\text{H}\cdot\text{F}=\text{s}^2H⋅F=s2); [Qω0L]=(s−1)(H)=Ω[Q\omega_0L]=(\text{s}^{-1})(\text{H})=\Omega[Qω0​L]=(s−1)(H)=Ω ✓. Physical reading: Rp=318 ΩR_p=318\ \OmegaRp​=318 Ω is where the tank leaks its energy every cycle — it simultaneously sets the Step 4 bias current (needed to "drive" this resistor to 1 V) and the Step 5 noise current 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​. Q=10Q=10Q=10 means a 3-dB bandwidth of f0/Q=500f_0/Q=500f0​/Q=500 MHz; the resonance is not sharp at all. What the tuning range costs at this step: f0∝1/Cf_0\propto1/\sqrt{C}f0​∝1/C​, so 4.75∼5.254.75\sim5.254.75∼5.25 GHz requires Cmax/Cmin=(fmax/fmin)2=(5.25/4.75)2=1.222C_{max}/C_{min}=(f_{max}/f_{min})^2=(5.25/4.75)^2=1.222Cmax​/Cmin​=(fmax​/fmin​)2=(5.25/4.75)2=1.222 — the total tank capacitance must vary by 22%, and the finite QQQ of that varactor (or switched-capacitor array) portion drags down the effective QQQ (varactor_tuning_supply_pushing; tank_Q_and_energy_restoration step 5). This page assumes Q=10Q=10Q=10 is already the loaded QQQ including the varactor. import numpy as np f0, Q, C = 5e9, 10.0, 1e-12 w0 = 2*np.pi*f0 L = 1/(w0**2*C) Rp = Q*w0*L print(round(L*1e9, 3)) # -> 1.013 (nH) print(round(Rp, 1)) # -> 318.3 (Ω) print(round(w0*Rp*C, 2), round(Rp/np.sqrt(L/C), 2)) # -> 10.0 10.0 (cross-check of the three forms of Q) print(round((5.25/4.75)**2, 3)) # -> 1.222 (C_max/C_min required by 10% TR) print(round(np.sqrt(L/C), 2), round(f0/Q/1e6, 0)) # -> 31.83 500.0 (R_0 Ω, 3-dB bandwidth MHz)

documents.t: Now pin the denominator of [P1] Eq.(21), qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=CV_{max}qmax​=CVmax​. The swing ceiling is set by headroom: tank_swing step 4 — the single-ended swing of a differential LC oscillator in the current-limited regime is about 4πIbiasRp\tfrac{4}{\pi}I_{bias}R_pπ4​Ibias​Rp​, capped near the supply VDDV_{DD}VDD​ (voltage-limited). The recipe's choice is to push the bias exactly to the voltage-limited boundary: any further current is wasted (the swing stops growing, L\mathcal{L}L stops falling). Take VDD=1V_{DD}=1VDD​=1 V and Vmax=1V_{max}=1Vmax​=1 V (single-ended peak): qmax=C Vmax=10−12 F×1 V=10−12 C=1 pC,Ibias=π4⋅VmaxRp=π4⋅1 V318.3 Ω=0.7854×3.142×10−3 A=2.467 mA,PDC=VDD Ibias=1 V×2.467 mA=2.467 mW ≤ 5 mW,Ptank=Vmax22Rp=12×318.3=1.571 mW,ηP=PtankPDC=1/(2Rp)(π/4)/Rp=2π=0.637.\begin{aligned} q_{max}&=C\,V_{max}=10^{-12}\ \text{F}\times1\ \text{V}=10^{-12}\ \text{C}=1\ \text{pC},\\[4pt] I_{bias}&=\frac{\pi}{4}\cdot\frac{V_{max}}{R_p}=\frac{\pi}{4}\cdot\frac{1\ \text{V}}{318.3\ \Omega}=0.7854\times3.142\times10^{-3}\ \text{A}=2.467\ \text{mA},\\[4pt] P_{DC}&=V_{DD}\,I_{bias}=1\ \text{V}\times2.467\ \text{mA}=2.467\ \text{mW}\ \le\ 5\ \text{mW},\\[4pt] P_{tank}&=\frac{V_{max}^2}{2R_p}=\frac{1}{2\times318.3}=1.571\ \text{mW},\qquad \eta_P=\frac{P_{tank}}{P_{DC}}=\frac{1/(2R_p)}{(\pi/4)/R_p}=\frac{2}{\pi}=0.637 . \end{aligned}qmax​Ibias​PDC​Ptank​​=CVmax​=10−12 F×1 V=10−12 C=1 pC,=4π​⋅Rp​Vmax​​=4π​⋅318.3 Ω1 V​=0.7854×3.142×10−3 A=2.467 mA,=VDD​Ibias​=1 V×2.467 mA=2.467 mW ≤ 5 mW,=2Rp​Vmax2​​=2×318.31​=1.571 mW,ηP​=PDC​Ptank​​=(π/4)/Rp​1/(2Rp​)​=π2​=0.637.​ The site's canonical value falls out naturally: C=1C=1C=1 pF and Vmax=1V_{max}=1Vmax​=1 V give qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC — the number examples A/B have used all along was always "a 1 pF tank at 1 V swing". Dimension check: [F][V]=[C][\text{F}][\text{V}]=[\text{C}][F][V]=[C] ✓; [V]/[Ω]=[A][\text{V}]/[\Omega]=[\text{A}][V]/[Ω]=[A] ✓; [V][A]=[W][\text{V}][\text{A}]=[\text{W}][V][A]=[W] ✓; ηP\eta_PηP​ dimensionless ✓. The physics of ηP=2/π\eta_P=2/\piηP​=2/π: at the voltage-limited boundary the tank receives Vmax2/(2Rp)V_{max}^2/(2R_p)Vmax2​/(2Rp​) while the supply pays VDD×IbiasV_{DD}\times I_{bias}VDD​×Ibias​; with VDD=VmaxV_{DD}=V_{max}VDD​=Vmax​ their ratio is exactly 12/π4=2/π\tfrac{1}{2}\big/\tfrac{\pi}{4}=2/\pi21​/4π​=2/π. This ηP<1\eta_P\lt1ηP​<1 will cost −10log⁡10(2/π)=1.96-10\log_{10}(2/\pi)=1.96−10log10​(2/π)=1.96 dB in the FOM bookkeeping of Step 6. ⚠️ Convention warning (the 4/π4/\pi4/π coefficient): this swing–current relation is standard LC design knowledge (external textbooks, not the site's 5 PDFs; Razavi, RF Microelectronics; the Hajimiri–Lee textbook), and this page follows the form used in tank_swing. Textbooks differ on "single-ended vs differential swing" and on whether RpR_pRp​ is the single-ended or differential equivalent, so the coefficient can differ by 2×2\times2×; treat IbiasI_{bias}Ibias​ and PDCP_{DC}PDC​ as order-of-magnitude estimates (2.5∼52.5\sim52.5∼5 mW) — note that even a 2×2\times2× error stays within the 5 mW budget, which is one reason Step 2 insists on margin. Exact values need transistor-level simulation (this site does not run SPICE; see python_environment). import numpy as np C, Vmax, VDD, Rp = 1e-12, 1.0, 1.0, 318.3 qmax = C*Vmax Ibias = (np.pi/4)*Vmax/Rp P_dc = VDD*Ibias P_tank = Vmax**2/(2*Rp) print(qmax*1e12) # -> 1.0 (pC: the site's canonical value) print(round(Ibias*1e3, 3), round(P_dc*1e3, 3)) # -> 2.467 2.467 (mA, mW; P≤5 mW ✓) print(round(P_tank*1e3, 3), round(P_tank/P_dc, 3)) # -> 1.571 0.637 (P_tank mW, η_P=2/π)

documents.t: The numerator of [P1] Eq.(21) needs "the total white-noise current PSD referred to the tank node". The tank loss itself contributes 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​ (tank_Q_and_energy_restoration step 3); the active core's device noise, weighted by its own Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​, is collected through the noise factor FFF as F⋅4kT/RpF\cdot4kT/R_pF⋅4kT/Rp​ (fom_limit step 3). The bound for an ideal class-B cross-coupled pair (tail noise filtered out) is F=1+γF=1+\gammaF=1+γ — the standard result of Hegazi–Sjöland–Abidi 2001 (external literature, not the site's 5 PDFs; see the end of the page). This recipe takes the short-channel γ=1\gamma=1γ=1 (more conservative than the long-channel 2/32/32/3 used for the Step 2 ceiling), so F=2F=2F=2: 4kTRp=4×1.380649×10−23 J/K×300 K318.3 Ω=1.6568×10−20 J318.3 Ω=5.205×10−23 A2/Hz,Si=F⋅4kTRp=2×5.205×10−23=1.041×10−22 A2/Hz.\begin{aligned} \frac{4kT}{R_p}&=\frac{4\times1.380649\times10^{-23}\ \text{J/K}\times300\ \text{K}}{318.3\ \Omega} =\frac{1.6568\times10^{-20}\ \text{J}}{318.3\ \Omega}=5.205\times10^{-23}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz},\\[4pt] S_i&=F\cdot\frac{4kT}{R_p}=2\times5.205\times10^{-23}=1.041\times10^{-22}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz}. \end{aligned}Rp​4kT​Si​​=318.3 Ω4×1.380649×10−23 J/K×300 K​=318.3 Ω1.6568×10−20 J​=5.205×10−23 A2/Hz,=F⋅Rp​4kT​=2×5.205×10−23=1.041×10−22 A2/Hz.​ Dimension check: J/Ω=(V⋅A⋅s)/(V/A)=A2s=A2/Hz\text{J}/\Omega=(\text{V}\cdot\text{A}\cdot\text{s})/(\text{V}/\text{A})=\text{A}^2\text{s}=\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}J/Ω=(V⋅A⋅s)/(V/A)=A2s=A2/Hz ✓ (single-sided PSD, consistent with the site's notation). Compared with the canonical example B, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24: this is 100 times larger (+20+20+20 dB). Example B's 10−2410^{-24}10−24 corresponds to Rp=16.6R_p=16.6Rp​=16.6 kΩ, Q≈521Q\approx521Q≈521 (the "FOM catches it" point in fom_limit step 3); the noise current of a real Q=10Q=10Q=10 tank is of order 10−2210^{-22}10−22 — the biggest difference between this page and the teaching examples. Where FFF fails: an unfiltered tail (2× upconversion through c0c_0c0​, c2c_2c2​; real_oscillator_topologies), flicker in the bias current source, and AM-PM on the varactor all push FFF above 1+γ1+\gamma1+γ; late in the design, account for each source with the method of device_noise_mapping. kB, T, Rp, gamma = 1.380649e-23, 300.0, 318.3, 1.0 Si_tank = 4*kB*T/Rp Si = (1+gamma)*Si_tank print(f"{Si_tank:.3e}") # -> 5.205e-23 (the tank's own 4kT/Rp, A²/Hz) print(f"{Si:.3e}") # -> 1.041e-22 (total S_i after F=1+γ=2) Rp_B = 4*kB*T/1e-24 print(round(Rp_B/1e3, 1), round(Rp_B/31.83)) # -> 16.6 521 (R_p in kΩ and Q implied by example B's S_i=1e-24)

documents.t: All four factors are pinned: Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​ (true LC, Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ; lab_02), qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Si=1.041×10−22S_i=1.041\times10^{-22}Si​=1.041×10−22 A²/Hz, Δω=2π×106\Delta\omega=2\pi\times10^6Δω=2π×106 rad/s. Substitute into [P1] Eq.(21), p.185 (checked against the rendered PDF page): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​)Δω2=(6.2832×106)2=3.948×1013 (rad/s)2,Γrms2qmax2=0.5(10−12)2=5×1023 C−2,Si4Δω2=1.041×10−224×3.948×1013=6.592×10−37,bracket=5×1023×6.592×10−37=3.296×10−13,L(1 MHz)=10log⁡10(3.296×10−13)=−124.8 dBc/Hz.\begin{aligned} \Delta\omega^2&=(6.2832\times10^{6})^2=3.948\times10^{13}\ (\text{rad/s})^2,\\[4pt] \frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}&=\frac{0.5}{(10^{-12})^2}=5\times10^{23}\ \text{C}^{-2},\\[4pt] \frac{S_i}{4\Delta\omega^2}&=\frac{1.041\times10^{-22}}{4\times3.948\times10^{13}}=6.592\times10^{-37},\\[4pt] \text{bracket}&=5\times10^{23}\times6.592\times10^{-37}=3.296\times10^{-13},\\[4pt] \mathcal{L}(1\ \text{MHz})&=10\log_{10}(3.296\times10^{-13})=-124.8\ \text{dBc/Hz}. \end{aligned}Δω2qmax2​Γrms2​​4Δω2Si​​bracketL(1 MHz)​=(6.2832×106)2=3.948×1013 (rad/s)2,=(10−12)20.5​=5×1023 C−2,=4×3.948×10131.041×10−22​=6.592×10−37,=5×1023×6.592×10−37=3.296×10−13,=10log10​(3.296×10−13)=−124.8 dBc/Hz.​ Sign-off: −124.8≤−120-124.8\le-120−124.8≤−120 ✓, margin 4.8 dB; power 2.47≤52.47\le52.47≤5 mW ✓. The same thing in FOM bookkeeping: the implementation burns only PDC=2.467P_{DC}=2.467PDC​=2.467 mW, so the required FOM rises from Step 1's 187.0 to 120+73.98−10log⁡10(2.467)=190.06120+73.98-10\log_{10}(2.467)=190.06120+73.98−10log10​(2.467)=190.06 dB (up by 10log⁡10(5/2.467)=3.0710\log_{10}(5/2.467)=3.0710log10​(5/2.467)=3.07 dB — the 3 dB Step 1 announced); 194.88−190.06=4.82194.88-190.06=4.82194.88−190.06=4.82 dB, identical to the margin obtained by comparing L\mathcal{L}L directly — the two bookkeepings confirm each other. Dimension check (as in tank_swing): 1[C]2⋅[A2/Hz][s−2]\dfrac{1}{[\text{C}]^2}\cdot\dfrac{[\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}]}{[\text{s}^{-2}]}[C]21​⋅[s−2][A2/Hz]​; with A=C/s\text{A}=\text{C/s}A=C/s → C2s−2/HzC2s−2=1/Hz\dfrac{\text{C}^2\text{s}^{-2}/\text{Hz}}{\text{C}^2\text{s}^{-2}}=1/\text{Hz}C2s−2C2s−2/Hz​=1/Hz, normalized to 1 Hz → dimensionless → dBc/Hz ✓. Actual FOM and distance to the ceiling: FOM=124.82+73.98−10log⁡10(2.467)=124.82+73.98−3.92=194.88\mathrm{FOM}=124.82+73.98-10\log_{10}(2.467)=124.82+73.98-3.92=194.88FOM=124.82+73.98−10log10​(2.467)=124.82+73.98−3.92=194.88 dB. Distance to the Q=10Q=10Q=10 ceiling: 197.63−194.88=2.75197.63-194.88=2.75197.63−194.88=2.75 dB, and it can be accounted for term by term: F=2F=2F=2 instead of 5/35/35/3 → 10log⁡10(2/(5/3))=0.7910\log_{10}(2/(5/3))=0.7910log10​(2/(5/3))=0.79 dB; ηP=2/π\eta_P=2/\piηP​=2/π instead of 1 → −10log⁡10(2/π)=1.96-10\log_{10}(2/\pi)=1.96−10log10​(2/π)=1.96 dB; total 2.752.752.75 dB ✓ (Γrms2=12\Gamma_{rms}^2=\tfrac12Γrms2​=21​ on both sides). The same thing through the universal form of fom_limit: Feff=FΓrms2/(2Q2ηP)=7.85×10−3F_{eff}=F\Gamma_{rms}^2/(2Q^2\eta_P)=7.85\times10^{-3}Feff​=FΓrms2​/(2Q2ηP​)=7.85×10−3, L=10log⁡10[Feff(kT/PDC)(f0/Δf)2]=−124.8\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}[F_{eff}(kT/P_{DC})(f_0/\Delta f)^2]=-124.8L=10log10​[Feff​(kT/PDC​)(f0​/Δf)2]=−124.8 dBc/Hz — identical digit for digit with the direct Eq.(21) substitution. ⚠️ Factor-of-2 convention: the formula above is [P1]'s SSB "/4" bookkeeping; the clean time-domain "/2" derivation gives −121.8-121.8−121.8 dBc/Hz and only 1.8 dB of margin (white_noise_to_phase_noise). Sign off with the conservative one, or at least confirm that the instrument's definition of L\mathcal{L}L belongs to the same family as your formula. import numpy as np kB, T, f0, df = 1.380649e-23, 300.0, 5e9, 1e6 grms2, qmax, Si, Q, P_dc = 0.5, 1e-12, 1.041e-22, 10.0, 2.467e-3 dw = 2*np.pi*df L_db = 10*np.log10(grms2/qmax**2 * Si/(4*dw**2)) # [P1] Eq.(21), p.185 (SSB /4) print(round(L_db, 2), round(-120.0 - L_db, 2)) # -> -124.82 4.82 (dBc/Hz, margin to spec in dB) print(round(10*np.log10(grms2/qmax**2 * Si/(2*dw**2)), 2)) # -> -121.81 (time-domain /2 convention) FOM = -L_db + 20*np.log10(f0/df) - 10*np.log10(P_dc/1e-3) print(round(FOM, 2)) # -> 194.88 (actual FOM, dB) FOM_req_actual = 120.0 + 20*np.log10(f0/df) - 10*np.log10(P_dc/1e-3) print(round(FOM_req_actual, 2), round(FOM - FOM_req_actual, 2)) # -> 190.06 4.82 (required FOM at 2.467 mW, margin: consistent with above) print(round(10*np.log10(5.0/2.467), 2)) # -> 3.07 (dB by which burning less power raises the required FOM) Cref = -10*np.log10(kB*T/1e-3) FOM_lc10 = Cref - 10*np.log10((5/3)*0.5/(2*Q**2)) print(round(FOM_lc10 - FOM, 2)) # -> 2.75 (distance to the Q=10 ceiling) print(round(10*np.log10(2/(5/3)), 2), round(-10*np.log10(2/np.pi), 2)) # -> 0.79 1.96 (F term, η_P term; sum = 2.75) Feff = 2.0*grms2/(2*Q**2*(2/np.pi)) print(round(10*np.log10(Feff*(kB*T/P_dc)*(f0/df)**2), 2)) # -> -124.82 (cross-check through the universal form)

documents.t: The system side wants jitter, not dBc/Hz. Use the 1/f21/f^21/f2 closed form (lab_08, serdes_clocking_connection step 2), integrating from f1=1f_1=1f1​=1 MHz to f2=100f_2=100f2​=100 MHz: Sϕ(1 MHz)=2×10L/10=2×10−12.482=6.59×10−13 rad2/Hz,σϕ2=Sϕ(fref) fref2(1f1−1f2)=6.59×10−13×(106)2×(10−6−10−8)=6.53×10−7 rad2,σϕ=8.08×10−4 rad=0.808 mrad,σt=σϕ2πf0=8.08×10−43.1416×1010=2.57×10−14 s=25.7 fs.\begin{aligned} S_\phi(1\ \text{MHz})&=2\times10^{\mathcal{L}/10}=2\times10^{-12.482}=6.59\times10^{-13}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz},\\[4pt] \sigma_\phi^2&=S_\phi(f_{ref})\,f_{ref}^2\left(\frac{1}{f_1}-\frac{1}{f_2}\right) =6.59\times10^{-13}\times(10^{6})^2\times(10^{-6}-10^{-8})=6.53\times10^{-7}\ \text{rad}^2,\\[4pt] \sigma_\phi&=8.08\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}=0.808\ \text{mrad},\\[4pt] \sigma_t&=\frac{\sigma_\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{8.08\times10^{-4}}{3.1416\times10^{10}}=2.57\times10^{-14}\ \text{s}=25.7\ \text{fs}. \end{aligned}Sϕ​(1 MHz)σϕ2​σϕ​σt​​=2×10L/10=2×10−12.482=6.59×10−13 rad2/Hz,=Sϕ​(fref​)fref2​(f1​1​−f2​1​)=6.59×10−13×(106)2×(10−6−10−8)=6.53×10−7 rad2,=8.08×10−4 rad=0.808 mrad,=2πf0​σϕ​​=3.1416×10108.08×10−4​=2.57×10−14 s=25.7 fs.​ Dimension check: [rad2/Hz][Hz2][1/Hz]=rad2[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}][\text{Hz}^2][1/\text{Hz}]=\text{rad}^2[rad2/Hz][Hz2][1/Hz]=rad2 ✓; rad÷(rad/s)=s\text{rad}\div(\text{rad/s})=\text{s}rad÷(rad/s)=s ✓. Against example C: example C is −100-100−100 dBc/Hz → 447.9447.9447.9 fs; this design is 24.8 dB better, so σt\sigma_tσt​ shrinks by 10−24.82/20=0.057410^{-24.82/20}=0.057410−24.82/20=0.0574 → 25.725.725.7 fs ✓ (for the same integration band and 1/f21/f^21/f2 slope, σt∝10ΔL/20\sigma_t\propto10^{\Delta\mathcal{L}/20}σt​∝10ΔL/20; lab_09). The spec point −120-120−120 dBc/Hz itself corresponds to 44.844.844.8 fs — jitter margin and dB margin are the same thing written two ways. documents.t: So far the TR of Step 0 has only appeared in Step 3 as "the varactor drags QQQ down". When comparing wide-tuning VCOs the literature commonly uses a tuning-range-normalized FOM (an external convention, not the site's 5 PDFs; its first appearance is yet to be verified, and the form is widely used in recent JSSC VCO papers): FOMT=FOM+20log⁡10 ⁣(TR [%]10)\mathrm{FOM}_T=\mathrm{FOM}+20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{TR}\,[\%]}{10}\right)FOMT​=FOM+20log10​(10TR[%]​) Reading: 10% tuning range is the reference; every doubling of TR adds 666 dB — the rationale is that at a given QQQ, tuning wider raises the varactor fraction and lowers the attainable effective QQQ, so "same FOM, wider TR" deserves credit. This is an empirical convention, not an identity derived from Eq.(21) the way FOM is; always confirm the other side uses the same definition when comparing. This design: TR =10%=10\%=10% → FOMT=194.88+20log⁡10(1)=194.88\mathrm{FOM}_T=194.88+20\log_{10}(1)=194.88FOMT​=194.88+20log10​(1)=194.88 dB (the reference point, zero credit). If the same oscillator reached TR =20%=20\%=20% without losing QQQ, FOMT=200.9\mathrm{FOM}_T=200.9FOMT​=200.9 dB. import numpy as np FOM = 194.88 print(round(FOM + 20*np.log10(10/10), 2), round(FOM + 20*np.log10(20/10), 2)) # -> 194.88 200.9 (TR=10%, 20%)

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: white_noise_to_phase_noise (white → 1/f²), flicker_noise_upconversion (flicker → 1/f³), fourier_series_of_isf (c0c_0c0​, cnc_ncn​) | Next: symmetry, tank_swing, serdes_clocking_connection This page collects the scattered design intuition from earlier pages into a single map: how does the noise (white and flicker) of one transistor end up as the oscillator's phase noise? The key is two things — which frequency band of device noise is picked up by which ISF harmonic, and the device does not leak noise throughout the entire period (cyclostationary), so what actually matters is the effective ISF Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α. Physical intuition (conclusion first): think of the ISF as a multi-channel radio. Its Fourier coefficients cnc_ncn​ are the antenna gains of each channel: c0c_0c0​ picks up device flicker "near DC" (upconverted to 1/f³); c1c_1c1​ picks up device white noise "near ω0\omega_0ω0​", c2c_2c2​ "near 2ω02\omega_02ω0​", and so on (downconverted to 1/f²). But the device only actually conducts — only actually leaks noise — during certain phases of the waveform. This "when does it leak" switching function α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0 t)α(ω0​t) must be multiplied into Γ\GammaΓ first, becoming the effective ISF, before it is the radio's true antenna.

documents.t: The drain current noise of a MOS device (referred to the injection node) splits roughly into two bands ([P1] Eqs.(19),(22), p.185): Si(f)=in2‾Δf⏟white (flat) + in2‾Δf⋅ω1/f2πf⏟flicker (1/f)S_i(f)=\underbrace{\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}}_{\text{white (flat)}}\;+\;\underbrace{\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{2\pi f}}_{\text{flicker (1/f)}}Si​(f)=white (flat)Δfin2​​​​​+flicker (1/f)Δfin2​​​⋅2πfω1/f​​​​ White noise: thermal (4kTγgm4kT\gamma g_m4kTγgm​-type) + shot, flat with frequency, energy spread over all frequencies, including near ω0,2ω0,…\omega_0,2\omega_0,\dotsω0​,2ω0​,…. Flicker (1/f) noise: slow trap/release processes in the channel, energy concentrated at low frequency (Δω≪ω0\Delta\omega\ll\omega_0Δω≪ω0​), significant below the device's 1/f corner ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​. Units: both bands are A²/Hz.

documents.t: Substitute the ISF Fourier expansion ([P1] Eq.(12)) into the phase response ([P1] Eq.(13)): each cnc_ncn​ term is a mixer that shifts "noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​" down to baseband phase: ISF harmonic Device-noise band received Shifted to Resulting phase-noise region c0c_0c0​ (DC term, value c0/2c_0/2c0​/2) Low-frequency flicker (near DC) Pure integration, no shift close-in 1/f³ ([P1] Eq.(23)) c1c_1c1​ White at ω0±Δω\omega_0\pm\Delta\omegaω0​±Δω Downconverted to Δω\Delta\omegaΔω Main 1/f² contribution c2,c3,…c_2,c_3,\dotsc2​,c3​,… White at nω0±Δωn\omega_0\pm\Delta\omeganω0​±Δω Downconverted to Δω\Delta\omegaΔω Also feeds 1/f² (via ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​) White noise → 1/f²: all cnc_ncn​ (the white part, n≥0n\ge0n≥0) contribute together, and via Parseval collapse to ∑n=0∞cn2=2Γrms2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑n=0∞​cn2​=2Γrms2​ ([P1] Eq.(20), p.185), giving L∝Γrms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​/qmax2​ ([P1] Eq.(21)). So 1/f² is set by Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. Flicker → 1/f³: only the DC channel c0c_0c0​ receives it, giving L∝c02/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto c_0^2/q_{max}^2L∝c02​/qmax2​ ([P1] Eq.(23)). So 1/f³ is set by c0c_0c0​. One-line summary: Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ governs white (1/f²); c0c_0c0​ governs flicker (1/f³). This is the skeleton of the whole map. The clearest way to see this "multi-channel radio" is a figure: the top half is the device's current-noise PSD Si(f)S_i(f)Si​(f) (a near-DC flicker bump plus a flat white plateau); three shaded bands mark the frequency ranges the ISF actually "listens to" (DC, f0f_0f0​, 2f02f_02f0​); the bottom half is the same ISF's Fourier coefficients ∣cn∣|c_n|∣cn​∣ as a stem plot, aligned under the bands above, with arrows showing each band folding back to the carrier weighted by that harmonic's cnc_ncn​ — c0c_0c0​ upconverts near-DC flicker into close-in 1/f³, while c1,c2c_1,c_2c1​,c2​ downconvert white noise near f0,2f0f_0,2f_0f0​,2f0​ into 1/f². Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Axis labels/title/annotation read: "電流雜訊 PSD Si(f) [A²/Hz, arb.]" = current-noise PSD Si(f) [A²/Hz, arb.]; "Device noise 的頻譜，與 ISF 諧波接收的三個頻段 (DC, f0, 2f0)" = the device-noise spectrum, and the three frequency bands the ISF's harmonics receive from (DC, f0, 2f0); "頻率 f / f0（下面 stem 的 n 對齊 n f0）" = frequency f / f0 (the stems below have n aligned to n·f0); "ISF 諧波增益 |cn|" = ISF harmonic gain |cn|; "載波 (carrier)" = carrier. The ∣cn∣|c_n|∣cn​∣ in the figure are computed by simulations/fig_device_noise_bands.py using compute_fourier_coefficients on a toy asymmetric ISF (Γ=−sin⁡θ+0.35sin⁡2θ+0.25\Gamma=-\sin\theta+0.35\sin2\theta+0.25Γ=−sinθ+0.35sin2θ+0.25), giving c0=0.50c_0=0.50c0​=0.50, c1=1.00c_1=1.00c1​=1.00, c2=0.35c_2=0.35c2​=0.35. This is a pedagogical toy model (not transistor-level): it only illustrates the "harmonic = channel" mapping structure; the Si(f)S_i(f)Si​(f) vertical axis is in arb. units. Corresponds to [P1] Eq.(12),(13) (Fourier expansion → per-harmonic phase response) and Eq.(19),(23) (white/flicker summation). Turning this map's "radio gain" into concrete algebra (this page has had relatively few equations so far; here we fill in the three core relations, all from [P1] and consistent with the site's formula table): (M1) White → 1/f² phase noise ([P1] Eq.(21), p.185; numerator is Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​): L1/f2{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2)\mathcal{L}_{1/f^2}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L1/f2​{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​) (M2) Flicker → 1/f³ phase noise ([P1] Eq.(23), p.185; numerator is c0c_0c0​): L1/f3{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(c02qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf8 Δω2⋅ω1/fΔω)\mathcal{L}_{1/f^3}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{8\,\Delta\omega^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}\right)L1/f3​{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​c02​​⋅8Δω2in2​​/Δf​⋅Δωω1/f​​) (M3) Relative height of the two regions (same offset, divide the linear bracket of (M2) by (M1)): L1/f3L1/f2∣linear=c02/(8 Δω2)Γrms2/(4 Δω2)⋅ω1/fΔω=c022 Γrms2⋅ω1/fΔω\frac{\mathcal{L}_{1/f^3}}{\mathcal{L}_{1/f^2}}\bigg|_{\text{linear}} =\frac{c_0^2/(8\,\Delta\omega^2)}{\Gamma_{rms}^2/(4\,\Delta\omega^2)}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega} =\frac{c_0^2}{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}L1/f2​L1/f3​​​linear​=Γrms2​/(4Δω2)c02​/(8Δω2)​⋅Δωω1/f​​=2Γrms2​c02​​⋅Δωω1/f​​ Use of (M3): at any given offset, this ratio >1> 1>1 means flicker (1/f³) dominates, <1< 1<1 means white (1/f²) dominates; setting it =1=1=1 solves for the 1/f³ corner Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c02/(2Γrms2)\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅c02​/(2Γrms2​) ([P1] Eq.(24), derivation in symmetry). documents.s: Step 2: ISF harmonics are "receive channels" — who picks up what

documents.t: The Γ\GammaΓ above is the "bare ISF" — it assumes the noise is equally large at every instant. But a real device's noise strength is periodically varying (cyclostationary): e.g. a tail current source conducts only during part of the cycle, and a switching pair's gmg_mgm​ peaks only during transitions. Hajimiri–Lee describe "when the device is leaking noise" with a noise-modulating function (NMF) α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0 t)α(ω0​t) (0≤α≤10\le\alpha\le10≤α≤1, periodic), folded into the ISF ([P1] Sec. II-D, Eq.(25)–(27), p.186; in(t)=in0(t)⋅α(ω0t)i_n(t)=i_{n0}(t)\cdot\alpha(\omega_0 t)in​(t)=in0​(t)⋅α(ω0​t) is Eq.(25), Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α is Eq.(27)): Γeff(ω0τ)=Γ(ω0τ)⋅α(ω0τ) \boxed{\ \Gamma_{eff}(\omega_0\tau)=\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\cdot\alpha(\omega_0\tau)\ } Γeff​(ω0​τ)=Γ(ω0​τ)⋅α(ω0​τ) ​ Meaning: what actually enters the phase-noise formulas is not Γ\GammaΓ but Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​. All of cnc_ncn​, c0c_0c0​, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ must be recomputed using Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​. A design-critical consequence: even if waveform symmetry makes the bare Γ\GammaΓ's c0=0c_0=0c0​=0, if the device leaks noise only during half the cycle (α\alphaα asymmetric), Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α can regrow a nonzero c0c_0c0​ → flicker gets upconverted again. Conversely, aligning the device's "conduction window α\alphaα" with the low-value phase of the bare Γ\GammaΓ can simultaneously lower c0c_0c0​ and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. A more rigorous mathematical foundation (PPV / adjoint / Floquet) is not in the five downloaded PDFs and is supplemented from standard literature (Demir–Mehrotra–Roychowdhury 2000, etc.); see effective_isf. A toy calculation using the built-in functions (pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level): import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import ( gamma_lc_ideal, effective_isf, compute_fourier_coefficients, gamma_rms) theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 2048, endpoint=False) gamma = gamma_lc_ideal(theta) # bare ISF = -sin(theta), c0 = 0 # Asymmetric NMF: device conducts only in the first half-cycle (alpha=1 for theta<pi, else 0) alpha = np.where(theta < np.pi, 1.0, 0.0) gamma_eff = effective_isf(gamma, alpha) # multiply by NMF (positional: gamma_values, alpha_values) a0, a, b, c, ph = compute_fourier_coefficients(theta, gamma_eff, n_harmonics=8) print("c0 =", a0, " Gamma_rms =", gamma_rms(theta, gamma_eff)) # -> c0 ≈ -0.637 (bare Γ had c0=0; regrown by the asymmetric α), Gamma_rms ≈ 0.500 (Full API in simulations/common/isf_utils.py; effective_isf and gamma_rms are real functions.)

documents.t: The core phase-noise ratios are Γrms2qmax2\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}qmax2​Γrms2​​ (white, [P1] Eq.(21)) and c02qmax2\dfrac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}qmax2​c02​​ (flicker, [P1] Eq.(23)). The numerator (ISF shape) and denominator (charge swing) are two mutually independent knobs. Classifying every design knob by "which quantity it moves": Move Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ / c0c_0c0​ (ISF shape) Move qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (charge swing) Waveform symmetry (matched rise/fall) → lowers c0c_0c0​ Increase voltage swing VmaxV_{max}Vmax​ Fast transitions (steep edges) → lowers Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ Raise tank QQQ/RpR_pRp​ (larger swing at the same current) Ring stage count N↑N\uparrowN↑ → Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 (below) Increase node capacitance CCC (ties to f0f_0f0​; use with care) Symmetric load, differential → lowers even harmonics, lowers c0c_0c0​ Differential → 2× effective swing Align device conduction window α\alphaα with low-Γ\GammaΓ phase (cyclostationary) → lowers effective Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, c0c_0c0​ Push bias to the headroom limit (current/voltage limited) Lower device ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ (larger area, PMOS) → lowers 1/f³ height (does not change c0c_0c0​) — The ring's Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 comes from [P2] Eq.(16), p.794 (re-verified in v7: the square root covers only the constant, Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms} \propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2; triple-checked against the main text's 4/N^1.5@η=0.75 and Appendix B Eq.(55). v3 had misread this as N^-0.75): Γrms=2π23η3⋅1N1.5\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\pi^2}{3\eta^3}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{N^{1.5}}Γrms​=3η32π2​​⋅N1.51​ (η≈1\eta\approx1η≈1 is the stage-delay proportionality constant), and at fixed f0f_0f0​ and fixed power ring phase noise is roughly independent of NNN (the device count growing with NNN offsets the drop in Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​) — see lc_vs_ring.
