Take canonical values: f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz, asymmetric c0=0.4c_0=0.4c0​=0.4, device f1/f=1f_{1/f}=1f1/f​=1 MHz. White → 1/f² (@ Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, [P1] Eq.(21)): as in Example B, L=−148.0\mathcal{L}=-148.0L=−148.0 dBc/Hz. Flicker → 1/f³ (@ Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, [P1] Eq.(23)): relative to 1/f² there is an extra factor c022Γrms2⋅ω1/fΔω\dfrac{c_0^2}{2\Gamma_{rms}^2}\cdot\dfrac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}2Γrms2​c02​​⋅Δωω1/f​​. At Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz =f1/f=f_{1/f}=f1/f​ the two regions cross (ω1/f/Δω=1\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omega=1ω1/f​/Δω=1); 1/f³ is 10log⁡10(c02/(2Γrms2))=10log⁡10(0.32)=−4.910\log_{10}(c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2))=10\log_{10}(0.32)=-4.910log10​(c02​/(2Γrms2​))=10log10​(0.32)=−4.9 dB relative to 1/f² — i.e. at this offset the flicker contribution is still slightly below white; the crossover point (1/f³ corner) falls at f1/f3=f1/f⋅c02/(2Γrms2)=320f_{1/f^3}=f_{1/f}\cdot c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)=320f1/f3​=f1/f​⋅c02​/(2Γrms2​)=320 kHz (see symmetry). Only below 320 kHz does flicker dominate. Intuition: at 1 MHz offset flicker is barely visible (masked by white); to see 1/f³ you need to look below 100 kHz. If a SerDes loop bandwidth filters out the close-in region, the 1/f³ impact shrinks (see serdes_clocking_connection).

documents.t: The following two problems map white and flicker device noise onto phase noise respectively, demonstrating the two independent knobs Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (governing white) and c0c_0c0​ (governing flicker). Using canonical values: f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, Si=in2‾/Δf=10−24S_i=\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=10^{-24}Si​=in2​​/Δf=10−24 A²/Hz, asymmetric c0=0.4c_0=0.4c0​=0.4, device f1/f=1f_{1/f}=1f1/f​=1 MHz. Example 1 (mapping white noise onto Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ → 1/f² height) Use (M1) to compute the 1/f² phase noise at Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz; then ask how much it drops (in dB) if Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is halved (0.5→0.250.5\to0.250.5→0.25). Result: white noise's 1/f² height =−148.0=-148.0=−148.0 dBc/Hz; halving Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ → 6 dB improvement. White depends only on Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, not on c0c_0c0​ at all. Dimension check: same as tank_swing Example 1 — the bracket reduces to a dimensionless per-Hz power ratio → dBc/Hz ✓. One-line Python check: import numpy as np def L_white(grms, qmax, Si, dw): return 10*np.log10(grms**2/qmax**2 * Si/(4*dw**2)) dw = 2*np.pi*1e6 print(round(L_white(0.5,1e-12,1e-24,dw),1), round(L_white(0.25,1e-12,1e-24,dw)-L_white(0.5,1e-12,1e-24,dw),2)) # -> -148.0 -6.02 Example 2 (mapping flicker noise onto c0c_0c0​ → 1/f³ height, using (M3) to determine which region dominates) Use (M2) to compute the 1/f³ phase noise at Δf=100\Delta f=100Δf=100 kHz, and use (M3) to determine whether that offset is dominated by flicker or white. Step-by-step substitution (with units), first computing the (M3) ratio to determine which dominates (Δf=100\Delta f=100Δf=100 kHz ⇒ω1/f/Δω=f1/f/Δf=10\Rightarrow\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omega=f_{1/f}/\Delta f=10⇒ω1/f​/Δω=f1/f​/Δf=10): L1/f3L1/f2∣linear=c022Γrms2⋅f1/fΔf=0.422×0.52⋅106105=0.32×10=3.2 (>1).\frac{\mathcal{L}_{1/f^3}}{\mathcal{L}_{1/f^2}}\bigg|_{\text{linear}} =\frac{c_0^2}{2\Gamma_{rms}^2}\cdot\frac{f_{1/f}}{\Delta f} =\frac{0.4^2}{2\times0.5^2}\cdot\frac{10^6}{10^5} =0.32\times10=3.2\;(>1).L1/f2​L1/f3​​​linear​=2Γrms2​c02​​⋅Δff1/f​​=2×0.520.42​⋅105106​=0.32×10=3.2(>1). Ratio 3.2>13.2 > 13.2>1 → at 100 kHz flicker already dominates (consistent with the corner f1/f3=320f_{1/f^3}=320f1/f3​=320 kHz >100>100>100 kHz). The flicker height itself: Δω=2π×105=6.283×105 rad/s,Δω2=3.948×1011,bracket=(0.4)2(10−12)2⋅10−248×3.948×1011⋅2π×1062π×105=0.1610−24⋅10−243.158×1012⋅10=0.16×103.158×1012=5.066×10−13,L1/f3=10log⁡10(5.066×10−13)=−122.95≈−123.0 dBc/Hz.\begin{aligned} \Delta\omega&=2\pi\times10^{5}=6.283\times10^{5}\ \text{rad/s},\quad\Delta\omega^2=3.948\times10^{11}, \\[4pt] \text{bracket}&=\frac{(0.4)^2}{(10^{-12})^2}\cdot\frac{10^{-24}}{8\times3.948\times10^{11}}\cdot\frac{2\pi\times10^6}{2\pi\times10^5} \\[4pt] &=\frac{0.16}{10^{-24}}\cdot\frac{10^{-24}}{3.158\times10^{12}}\cdot 10 =\frac{0.16\times10}{3.158\times10^{12}}=5.066\times10^{-13}, \\[4pt] \mathcal{L}_{1/f^3}&=10\log_{10}(5.066\times10^{-13})=-122.95\approx-123.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}. \end{aligned}ΔωbracketL1/f3​​=2π×105=6.283×105 rad/s,Δω2=3.948×1011,=(10−12)2(0.4)2​⋅8×3.948×101110−24​⋅2π×1052π×106​=10−240.16​⋅3.158×101210−24​⋅10=3.158×10120.16×10​=5.066×10−13,=10log10​(5.066×10−13)=−122.95≈−123.0 dBc/Hz.​ Result: at 100 kHz, 1/f³ (flicker) is about −123.0-123.0−123.0 dBc/Hz and dominant (ratio 3.2). Flicker depends only on c0c_0c0​: if symmetrizing the waveform brings c0→0.04c_0\to0.04c0​→0.04 (10× smaller), this 1/f³ curve drops by 10log⁡10(0.042/0.42)=−2010\log_{10}(0.04^2/0.4^2)=-2010log10​(0.042/0.42)=−20 dB overall. Dimension check: the (M3) ratio is dimensionless ✓; (M2)'s bracket has an extra dimensionless factor ω1/f/Δω\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omegaω1/f​/Δω, changing the slope to 1/Δω31/\Delta\omega^31/Δω3 (1/f³) ✓. One-line Python check: import numpy as np c0, grms, qmax, Si, f1f = 0.4, 0.5, 1e-12, 1e-24, 1e6 df = 1e5; dw = 2*np.pi*df ratio = c0**2/(2*grms**2) * (f1f/df) L_1f3 = 10*np.log10(c0**2/qmax**2 * Si/(8*dw**2) * (f1f/df)) print(round(ratio,2), round(L_1f3,1)) # -> 3.2 -123.0 (ratio>1 => flicker dominates) Both problems are pedagogical toys (not transistor-level): c0c_0c0​ and Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ use assumed values. A real circuit must recompute c0c_0c0​, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ using the effective ISF Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α (see Step 3 and effective_isf).

documents.t: Device noise has two bands: white (spread over all frequencies), flicker (concentrated at low frequency). ISF harmonics are receive channels: c0c_0c0​ receives flicker → 1/f³; c1,c2,…c_1,c_2,\dotsc1​,c2​,… receive white → 1/f² (collapsed to Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ via Parseval). What actually matters is the effective ISF Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α (cyclostationary); a symmetric bare Γ\GammaΓ can regrow c0c_0c0​ because of an asymmetric α\alphaα. Two independent levers: move Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​/c0c_0c0​ (waveform symmetry, fast edges, differential, α\alphaα alignment) vs. move qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (swing, QQQ, differential). Ring Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 ([P2] Eq.(16), p.794, re-verified in v7: the square root covers only the constant); at fixed f0f_0f0​/power, phase noise is roughly independent of NNN.

documents.t: Prerequisites: serdes_clocking_connection (first appearance of RJ/DJ/TJ, eye and BER), lab_12 (RJ-only bathtub), lab_08 (σt\sigma_tσt​ integrated from phase noise) | Next: exercises, lab_13 serdes_clocking_connection already gave the shorthand "TJ === DJ + 2Q⋅+\,2Q\cdot+2Q⋅RJ". This page builds that formula rigorously from scratch: what RJ is, what DJ is, which integral QQQ comes from, how the bathtub curve is derived from the CDF (cumulative distribution function) of jitter, and the dual-Dirac model the industry actually uses (SerDes specs from Fibre Channel MJSQ onward) — including its most misunderstood and most important honesty note: the model parameter DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​ is inherently less than or equal to the actual peak-to-peak DJ, and this "under-report" is deliberate — it is precisely what makes the TJ extrapolation accurate. Physical intuition (conclusion first): jitter has two fundamentally different components. RJ (random jitter) is the time-domain incarnation of oscillator phase noise — Gaussian, unbounded; the longer you wait (the tighter the BER target), the larger it "grows", so it must be booked as σ\sigmaσ times a multiplier that increases with the BER target. DJ (deterministic jitter) is driven by deterministic physical mechanisms (inter-symbol interference, duty-cycle distortion, supply ripple); its amplitude has a physical upper bound, so it is booked peak-to-peak and does not grow with BER. The dual-Dirac model compresses "bounded DJ of arbitrary shape" into two Diracs and keeps RJ as a Gaussian, in exchange for a straight line that can be extrapolated to 10−1210^{-12}10−12. Measuring a BER of 10−1210^{-12}10−12 requires waiting for 101210^{12}1012 bits — even at 10 Gb/s that is 100 s just to "see one error on average", and statistical confidence takes hours; extrapolation is not laziness, it is an engineering necessity.

See lab_08. Time-domain view — random walk: [P2] Eq.(8), p.792 gives the accumulated phase jitter σΔϕ=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta\phi}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔϕ​=κΔt​ (κ\kappaκ in 1/s1/\sqrt{\text{s}}1/s​, from [P2] Eq.(11)/(12), p.793 κ=Γrmsqmax12in2‾/Δf\kappa=\tfrac{\Gamma_{rms}}{q_{max}}\sqrt{\tfrac12\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}κ=qmax​Γrms​​21​in2​​/Δf​; note the expression contains no ω0\omega_0ω0​ — converting to the time version requires dividing by ω0\omega_0ω0​ once more). Why Gaussian: every period the oscillator absorbs a large number of mutually independent tiny noise kicks; the total phase error is a sum of independent increments → central limit theorem → Gaussian. lab_11 verified directly by Monte Carlo that the histogram is Gaussian and σ∝ΔN\sigma\propto\sqrt{\Delta N}σ∝ΔN​. RJ's key property: no upper bound. The Gaussian tail is never zero — there is no "guaranteed never to cross" margin; you can only ask "how small is the crossing probability". This is why RJ must be booked as σ\sigmaσ paired with a target BER (the QQQ function of Step 3).

documents.t: DJ is the half that ISF theory "cannot see" (it does not come from the oscillator's random noise), yet it is often the largest component of the TJ measured in a SerDes. Three main sources, each with clear physics and a clear upper bound: DJ type Physical mechanism PDF shape Why bounded ISI (inter-symbol interference) Finite channel bandwidth with memory: edge position depends on the preceding bit pattern Multiple discrete spikes (one per pattern) Channel impulse response has finite length DCD (duty-cycle distortion) Rise/fall asymmetry, threshold offset: rising edges systematically early, falling edges late Exactly two Diracs The asymmetry is a fixed amount PJ/SJ (periodic/sinusoidal jitter; supply spurs, crosstalk) Supply ripple modulates the VCO via supply pushing (see varactor_tuning_supply_pushing); coupling from adjacent clocks arcsine (double-horn) distribution Sinusoid amplitude is fixed PI quantization (phase interpolator quantization) A bbb-bit phase interpolator slices one UI into 2b2^b2b grid points; the sampled/output phase can only land on a grid point (derivation: clock_chain_budget Rule 5) Uniform distribution (width UI/2bUI/2^bUI/2b) Grid count is fixed, DJpp=UI/2b\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}=UI/2^bDJpp​=UI/2b (nominal lower bound; real DNL makes it larger) Note that DCD's PDF is inherently two Diracs — the dual-Dirac model is exact for it; the model's name and shape come precisely from this "worst-case shape". PI quantization's PDF is a uniform distribution — neither the sinusoid's double horn nor DCD's two points — a third common DJ shape; at b=6b=6b=6, UI=40UI=40UI=40 ps, DJpp=UI/26=0.625\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}=UI/2^6=0.625DJpp​=UI/26=0.625 ps (full derivation and # -> verification in clock_chain_budget Rule 5). PDF of sinusoidal DJ (the arcsine distribution), derived step by step. This is the DJ used in lab_31 and the standard model for supply spurs. Let the edge's time offset be x=Asin⁡θx=A\sin\thetax=Asinθ, with AAA the amplitude (unit: s); the spur is asynchronous with the data, so the sampled phase θ\thetaθ is uniform on [0,2π)[0,2\pi)[0,2π), pΘ(θ)=12πp_\Theta(\theta)=\tfrac{1}{2\pi}pΘ​(θ)=2π1​ (unit: 1/rad). Change of variables: within one period each x∈(−A,A)x\in(-A,A)x∈(−A,A) corresponds to two θ\thetaθ branches, each contributing pΘ/∣dx/dθ∣p_\Theta/\vert dx/d\theta\vertpΘ​/∣dx/dθ∣, and ∣dx/dθ∣=A∣cos⁡θ∣=A2−x2\vert dx/d\theta\vert=A\vert\cos\theta\vert=\sqrt{A^2-x^2}∣dx/dθ∣=A∣cosθ∣=A2−x2​: pDJ(x)=2⋅12π⋅1A2−x2=1πA2−x2,∣x∣<Ap_{DJ}(x)=2\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{A^2-x^2}}=\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{A^2-x^2}},\qquad \vert x\vert\lt ApDJ​(x)=2⋅2π1​⋅A2−x2​1​=πA2−x2​1​,∣x∣<A Units: 1/[s2]=1/[s]1/\sqrt{[\text{s}^2]}=1/[\text{s}]1/[s2]​=1/[s] ✓ (the PDF integrated over xxx is dimensionless). Normalization check: ∫−AAdxπA2−x2=1π[arcsin⁡xA]−AA=1π(π2+π2)=1\int_{-A}^{A}\frac{dx}{\pi\sqrt{A^2-x^2}}=\frac{1}{\pi}\big[\arcsin\tfrac{x}{A}\big]_{-A}^{A}=\frac{1}{\pi}\big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\big)=1∫−AA​πA2−x2​dx​=π1​[arcsinAx​]−AA​=π1​(2π​+2π​)=1 ✓. Physics: the sinusoid dwells longest near its turning points → the probability density diverges at the two ends ±A\pm A±A (an integrable "double horn"). Both horns are clearly visible in the histogram of lab_31 panel (a). Bounded: DJpp=2A\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}=2ADJpp​=2A (peak-to-peak, unit: s). Applicability: the spur is asynchronous with the data (uniform phase); if the spur is locked to the data (synchronous), the PDF degenerates into discrete spikes — still bounded.

documents.t: RJ's bookkeeping tool is the Gaussian tail probability. For a standard normal X∼N(0,1)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)X∼N(0,1) (dimensionless): Q(x)≡P(X>x)=∫x∞12π e−u2/2 duQ(x)\equiv P(X\gt x)=\int_x^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-u^2/2}\,duQ(x)≡P(X>x)=∫x∞​2π​1​e−u2/2du Step-by-step reduction to erfc (this is what connects it to scipy and this site's serdes_utils.Q). Substitute u=2 su=\sqrt2\,su=2​s, du=2 dsdu=\sqrt2\,dsdu=2​ds; the lower limit becomes x/2x/\sqrt2x/2​: Q(x)=22π∫x/2∞e−s2 ds=1π∫x/2∞e−s2 ds=12 erfc ⁣(x2)Q(x)=\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{x/\sqrt2}^{\infty}e^{-s^2}\,ds=\frac{1}{\sqrt\pi}\int_{x/\sqrt2}^{\infty}e^{-s^2}\,ds=\frac12\,\mathrm{erfc}\!\Big(\frac{x}{\sqrt2}\Big)Q(x)=2π​2​​∫x/2​∞​e−s2ds=π​1​∫x/2​∞​e−s2ds=21​erfc(2​x​) The last step used the definition erfc(z)=2π∫z∞e−s2ds\mathrm{erfc}(z)=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_z^\infty e^{-s^2}dserfc(z)=π​2​∫z∞​e−s2ds. For a general Gaussian (mean μ\muμ, standard deviation σ\sigmaσ, both in s), substitute once more with u=(v−μ)/σu=(v-\mu)/\sigmau=(v−μ)/σ to get P(V>v)=Q ⁣(v−μσ)P(V\gt v)=Q\!\big(\tfrac{v-\mu}{\sigma}\big)P(V>v)=Q(σv−μ​) — the argument of QQQ is always "how many σ\sigmaσ from the mean", dimensionless ✓. Deep-tail asymptotic form (one integration by parts): Q(x)≈e−x2/2x2π(x≫1, relative error ∼1/x2)Q(x)\approx\frac{e^{-x^2/2}}{x\sqrt{2\pi}}\quad(x\gg1,\ \text{relative error}\ \sim 1/x^2)Q(x)≈x2π​e−x2/2​(x≫1, relative error ∼1/x2) Use it to estimate Q(7.03)Q(7.03)Q(7.03) by hand: exponent 7.0342/2=24.77.034^2/2=24.77.0342/2=24.7, e−24.7≈1.8×10−11e^{-24.7}\approx1.8\times10^{-11}e−24.7≈1.8×10−11, divide by 7.03×2.507≈17.67.03\times2.507\approx17.67.03×2.507≈17.6 → ≈1.0×10−12\approx1.0\times10^{-12}≈1.0×10−12 ✓. This is the "BER 10−1210^{-12}10−12 ↔ 7.03σ7.03\sigma7.03σ" correspondence used throughout this site's jitter chapters (consistent with the QQQ table in 06 exercises): Target BER Q−1(BER)Q^{-1}(\text{BER})Q−1(BER) RJ peak-to-peak =2Q−1σ=2Q^{-1}\sigma=2Q−1σ 10−910^{-9}10−9 5.9985.9985.998 12.0 σ12.0\,\sigma12.0σ 10−1210^{-12}10−12 7.0347.0347.034 (written 7.03 on this site) 14.07 σ14.07\,\sigma14.07σ 10−1510^{-15}10−15 7.9417.9417.941 (written 7.94 on this site) 15.88 σ15.88\,\sigma15.88σ One-line Python verification (using this site's real API; Q−1Q^{-1}Q−1 inverts the tail integral above via erfcinv): import numpy as np from scipy.special import erfcinv from simulations.common.serdes_utils import Q q = np.sqrt(2) * erfcinv(2 * 1e-12) # inverse of Q (inverting the tail integral) print("Qinv(1e-12) =", round(float(q), 3)) # -> 7.034 print("Q(7.034) =", float(Q(7.034))) # -> 1.0e-12

documents.t: The model does two things (external literature, not among the five source PDFs; methodology references at the bottom of the page): The TJ PDF is the convolution of the DJ PDF with the Gaussian RJ (RJ and DJ statistically independent): pTJ=pDJ∗gσp_{TJ}=p_{DJ}*g_\sigmapTJ​=pDJ​∗gσ​, where gσ(x)=1σ2πe−x2/2σ2g_\sigma(x)=\tfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}gσ​(x)=σ2π​1​e−x2/2σ2 (unit: 1/s). Compress the bounded pDJp_{DJ}pDJ​ of arbitrary shape into two equal-weight Diracs, with spacing denoted DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​: pDJ(x) ⟶ 12 δ(x−μR)+12 δ(x−μL),DJδδ≡μR−μLp_{DJ}(x)\ \longrightarrow\ \frac12\,\delta(x-\mu_R)+\frac12\,\delta(x-\mu_L),\qquad \mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}\equiv\mu_R-\mu_LpDJ​(x) ⟶ 21​δ(x−μR​)+21​δ(x−μL​),DJδδ​≡μR​−μL​ The convolution uses the Dirac sampling property ∫δ(v−μ)gσ(x−v)dv=gσ(x−μ)\int\delta(v-\mu)g_\sigma(x-v)dv=g_\sigma(x-\mu)∫δ(v−μ)gσ​(x−v)dv=gσ​(x−μ), giving the model PDF in one step: pδδ(x)=12 gσ(x−μR)+12 gσ(x−μL)p_{\delta\delta}(x)=\frac12\,g_\sigma(x-\mu_R)+\frac12\,g_\sigma(x-\mu_L)pδδ​(x)=21​gσ​(x−μR​)+21​gσ​(x−μL​) — two Gaussians with the same σ\sigmaσ, each carrying half the probability. In the symmetric case (this page and lab_31), μR=−μL=μ=DJδδ/2\mu_R=-\mu_L=\mu=\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}/2μR​=−μL​=μ=DJδδ​/2. The tail function, integrated step by step. Define T(x)≡P(jitter>x)=1−F(x)T(x)\equiv P(\text{jitter}\gt x)=1-F(x)T(x)≡P(jitter>x)=1−F(x) (FFF is the CDF). Apply Step 3's result term by term to the model PDF, ∫x∞gσ(v−μ) dv=Q(x−μσ)\int_x^\infty g_\sigma(v-\mu)\,dv=Q\big(\tfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\big)∫x∞​gσ​(v−μ)dv=Q(σx−μ​): Tδδ(x)=12 Q ⁣(x−μRσ)+12 Q ⁣(x−μLσ)T_{\delta\delta}(x)=\frac12\,Q\!\Big(\frac{x-\mu_R}{\sigma}\Big)+\frac12\,Q\!\Big(\frac{x-\mu_L}{\sigma}\Big)Tδδ​(x)=21​Q(σx−μR​​)+21​Q(σx−μL​​) Only one term survives in the deep tail. The ratio of the two terms (asymptotic form, symmetric case): Q(x+μσ)Q(x−μσ)≈exp⁡ ⁣(−(x+μ)2−(x−μ)22σ2)=exp⁡ ⁣(−2μxσ2)=exp⁡ ⁣(−DJδδ xσ2)\frac{Q\big(\tfrac{x+\mu}{\sigma}\big)}{Q\big(\tfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\big)}\approx\exp\!\Big(-\frac{(x+\mu)^2-(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)=\exp\!\Big(-\frac{2\mu x}{\sigma^2}\Big)=\exp\!\Big(-\frac{\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}\,x}{\sigma^2}\Big)Q(σx−μ​)Q(σx+μ​)​≈exp(−2σ2(x+μ)2−(x−μ)2​)=exp(−σ22μx​)=exp(−σ2DJδδ​x​) With lab_31's numbers (DJδδ=3.16\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}=3.16DJδδ​=3.16 ps, σ=1.03\sigma=1.03σ=1.03 ps, region of interest x≈8.6x\approx8.6x≈8.6 ps), this ratio is ≈e−25.6≈8×10−12\approx e^{-25.6}\approx8\times10^{-12}≈e−25.6≈8×10−12 — completely negligible. So the deep tail is just a single Gaussian with weight ½: Tδδ(x)≈12 Q ⁣(x−μσ)(x in the deep right tail)T_{\delta\delta}(x)\approx\frac12\,Q\!\Big(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\Big)\qquad(x\ \text{in the deep right tail})Tδδ​(x)≈21​Q(σx−μ​)(x in the deep right tail) The Q-scale straight line — the principle behind extracting (DJδδ,σ)(\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta},\sigma)(DJδδ​,σ). Invert the expression above: Q−1(2 T(x))=x−μσQ^{-1}\big(2\,T(x)\big)=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}Q−1(2T(x))=σx−μ​ — on the "Q-scale" (vertical axis Q−1(2T)Q^{-1}(2T)Q−1(2T), horizontal axis xxx), the deep tail is a straight line: slope 1/σ1/\sigma1/σ, horizontal-axis intercept μ=DJδδ/2\mu=\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}/2μ=DJδδ​/2. Instruments (a BERT scan or an oscilloscope's TIE histogram) perform exactly this straight-line fit to the measured tail. Note the factor 2 inside Q−1Q^{-1}Q−1: it books the fact that "each Dirac carries only half the probability" — the first factor-of-2 to keep an eye on in this page (Step 7 has two more).

documents.t: Assume NRZ data with UI (unit interval) =Tb=T_b=Tb​ (unit: s). Take the eye center as the time origin and let the sampling-instant offset be ttt; the left data edge sits nominally at −UI/2-UI/2−UI/2, the right edge at +UI/2+UI/2+UI/2, each carrying jitter xxx (identically distributed, tail TTT, CDF FFF). Error event one (left edge late): the left edge actually lands at −UI/2+x-UI/2+x−UI/2+x; if it arrives later than the sampling instant, i.e. −UI/2+x>t⇔x>UI/2+t-UI/2+x\gt t\Leftrightarrow x\gt UI/2+t−UI/2+x>t⇔x>UI/2+t, the sampler reads the previous bit. Probability =T(UI/2+t)=T(UI/2+t)=T(UI/2+t). Error event two (right edge early): the right edge actually lands at +UI/2+x+UI/2+x+UI/2+x; if it arrives earlier than the sampling instant, i.e. UI/2+x<t⇔x<−(UI/2−t)UI/2+x\lt t\Leftrightarrow x\lt-(UI/2-t)UI/2+x<t⇔x<−(UI/2−t), probability =F(−(UI/2−t))=F(-(UI/2-t))=F(−(UI/2−t)), which for a symmetric distribution =T(UI/2−t)=T(UI/2-t)=T(UI/2−t). Only a transition can produce an error: for random data the probability that adjacent bits differ is 12\tfrac1221​ (transition density ρT=12\rho_T=\tfrac12ρT​=21​). Both events are rare, so the probability of the union ≈\approx≈ the sum (the intersection is second-order small): BER(t)=12[T ⁣(UI2−t)+T ⁣(UI2+t)] \boxed{\ \mathrm{BER}(t)=\frac12\Big[T\!\Big(\frac{UI}{2}-t\Big)+T\!\Big(\frac{UI}{2}+t\Big)\Big]\ } BER(t)=21​[T(2UI​−t)+T(2UI​+t)] ​ Consistency check: for pure RJ, T(x)=Q(x/σt)T(x)=Q(x/\sigma_t)T(x)=Q(x/σt​) and the expression reduces to BER(t)=12[Q(UI/2−tσt)+Q(UI/2+tσt)]\mathrm{BER}(t)=\tfrac12[Q(\tfrac{UI/2-t}{\sigma_t})+Q(\tfrac{UI/2+t}{\sigma_t})]BER(t)=21​[Q(σt​UI/2−t​)+Q(σt​UI/2+t​)] — exactly the formula of lab_12 and serdes_utils.ber_bathtub ✓. The bathtub's two "walls" are just the left and right tails of the jitter CDF, replotted with the horizontal axis changed from "jitter magnitude" to "sampling position". DJ's effect is immediately visible: it shifts the entire tail by ≈μ\approx\mu≈μ → both walls move inward; RJ sets the walls' slope (on a log-BER axis, the slope is set by σ\sigmaσ). Dimension check: the argument of TTT is [s][\text{s}][s], its output a probability (dimensionless); BER dimensionless ✓. Applicability: rare events (BER≪1\mathrm{BER}\ll1BER≪1); edge jitter stationary and data-independent (strictly speaking, ISI is data-correlated — see the failure conditions in Step 8).

documents.t: Derivation. Goal: at a specified BER, how much eye width does jitter "eat"? Define the right-wall position xRx_RxR​ as the point where the dominant Gaussian of the right deep tail drops to the target BER (industry convention books the per-Gaussian tail === BER directly; audit below): Q ⁣(xR−μσ)=BER ⟹ xR=μ+σ Q−1(BER)Q\!\Big(\frac{x_R-\mu}{\sigma}\Big)=\mathrm{BER}\ \Longrightarrow\ x_R=\mu+\sigma\,Q^{-1}(\mathrm{BER})Q(σxR​−μ​)=BER ⟹ xR​=μ+σQ−1(BER) Symmetrically, the left wall xL=−μ−σQ−1(BER)x_L=-\mu-\sigma Q^{-1}(\mathrm{BER})xL​=−μ−σQ−1(BER). Total jitter is defined as the total width eaten by the two walls: TJ(BER)=xR−xL=DJδδ+2 Q−1(BER) σ \boxed{\ \mathrm{TJ}(\mathrm{BER})=x_R-x_L=\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}+2\,Q^{-1}(\mathrm{BER})\,\sigma\ } TJ(BER)=xR​−xL​=DJδδ​+2Q−1(BER)σ ​ At BER =10−12=10^{-12}=10−12, TJ=DJδδ+14.07 σ\mathrm{TJ}=\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}+14.07\,\sigmaTJ=DJδδ​+14.07σ. Horizontal eye opening =UI−TJ(BER)=UI-\mathrm{TJ}(\mathrm{BER})=UI−TJ(BER). Dimension check: [s]+[dimensionless]×[s]=[s][\text{s}]+[\text{dimensionless}]\times[\text{s}]=[\text{s}][s]+[dimensionless]×[s]=[s] ✓. Physical meaning: the DJ part does not change with BER (bounded, eaten once); the RJ part grows slowly as Q−1Q^{-1}Q−1 while the BER tightens (10−12→10−1510^{-12}\to10^{-15}10−12→10−15 only moves from 14.07σ14.07\sigma14.07σ to 15.88σ15.88\sigma15.88σ — the logarithmic growth of the Gaussian tail). Factor-of-2 audit (site convention: spell out every 2). The formula above uses Q−1(BER)=7.034Q^{-1}(\mathrm{BER})=7.034Q−1(BER)=7.034, which implicitly books "the tail of each Gaussian === BER". Strictly following the bookkeeping of Steps 4 and 5 there are two more ½'s: the Dirac weight ½ (per-side tail T=12QT=\tfrac12QT=21​Q) and the transition density ρT=12\rho_T=\tfrac12ρT​=21​ (the bathtub multiplies by ½ again). With everything counted, the wall position is set by Q=4×BERQ=4\times\mathrm{BER}Q=4×BER: Convention Wall condition Multiplier (BER =10−12=10^{-12}=10−12) lab_31 resulting TJ per-Gaussian (industry formula) Q=BERQ=\mathrm{BER}Q=BER 7.0347.0347.034 17.6517.6517.65 ps per-side tail T=BERT=\mathrm{BER}T=BER Q=2 BERQ=2\,\mathrm{BER}Q=2BER 6.9376.9376.937 17.4317.4317.43 ps bathtub (ρT=12\rho_T=\tfrac12ρT​=21​, this site's lab_12 convention) Q=4 BERQ=4\,\mathrm{BER}Q=4BER 6.8396.8396.839 17.2317.2317.23 ps The three differ by Q−1(10−12)−Q−1(4×10−12)=0.196 σQ^{-1}(10^{-12})-Q^{-1}(4\times10^{-12})=0.196\,\sigmaQ−1(10−12)−Q−1(4×10−12)=0.196σ/side — 0.400.400.40 ps total in this example, about 2% of TJ; the industry formula is conservative. In practice this is not a problem, because (DJδδ,σ)(\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta},\sigma)(DJδδ​,σ) are fitted from the tail and substituted back for extrapolation under one and the same convention — with a consistent convention the errors nearly cancel; but when comparing DJ/RJ reports from different instruments, always first ask which convention each one uses. (lab_31 prints all three numbers.)
documents.s: Step 6: The TJ(BER) extrapolation formula — derivation and factor audit

documents.t: This is the most commonly misunderstood point about dual-Dirac: DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​ is a model parameter, not the actual peak-to-peak DJ. lab_31's numbers: the true sinusoidal DJ has DJpp=4.0\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}=4.0DJpp​=4.0 ps, while the fit gives DJδδ=3.16\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}=3.16DJδδ​=3.16 ps. Why it is necessarily smaller (derivation). The total jitter tail is the average of the Gaussian tail over the DJ distribution (obtained by swapping the order of integration in the convolution once): T(x)=P(u+n>x)=∫−AApDJ(u) Q ⁣(x−uσ) duT(x)=P(u+n\gt x)=\int_{-A}^{A}p_{DJ}(u)\,Q\!\Big(\frac{x-u}{\sigma}\Big)\,duT(x)=P(u+n>x)=∫−AA​pDJ​(u)Q(σx−u​)du Because u≤Au\le Au≤A and QQQ is strictly decreasing, the integrand satisfies pointwise Q(x−uσ)≤Q(x−Aσ)Q\big(\tfrac{x-u}{\sigma}\big)\le Q\big(\tfrac{x-A}{\sigma}\big)Q(σx−u​)≤Q(σx−A​). Split the integral into the right half (u>0u\gt0u>0, total mass ½) and the left half (u≤0u\le0u≤0, whose deep-tail contribution is smaller by another factor of e−Ax/σ2e^{-Ax/\sigma^2}e−Ax/σ2): T(x) ≤ 12 Q ⁣(x−Aσ)+12 Q ⁣(xσ)⏟exponentially smallT(x)\ \le\ \frac12\,Q\!\Big(\frac{x-A}{\sigma}\Big)+\underbrace{\frac12\,Q\!\Big(\frac{x}{\sigma}\Big)}_{\text{exponentially small}}T(x) ≤ 21​Q(σx−A​)+exponentially small21​Q(σx​)​​ Equality holds only when the entire right-half mass is concentrated at u=Au=Au=A (i.e. a two-point distribution like DCD). Flip to the Q-scale: Q−1(2T(x)) ≥ x−AσQ^{-1}(2T(x))\ \ge\ \tfrac{x-A}{\sigma}Q−1(2T(x)) ≥ σx−A​ — the true tail curve always lies above the line with "Diracs placed at the true extreme AAA" (blue line vs gray dashed line in lab_31 panel (b)). A straight-line fit to the true curve therefore necessarily has intercept μ≤A\mu\le Aμ≤A, i.e.: DJδδ=2μ ≤ 2A=DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}=2\mu\ \le\ 2A=\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJδδ​=2μ ≤ 2A=DJpp​ Why the under-report actually makes TJ accurate. For the extrapolation to be accurate, what is needed is that "over the few decades around the target BER, the line hugs the true tail height" — and the fit is anchored exactly that way (lab_31: the dual-Dirac extrapolated eye opening is 82.7682.7682.76 ps vs 82.7782.7782.77 ps for the exact composite — a 0.010.010.01 ps difference). Conversely, forcing the Diracs onto the true extremes ±A\pm A±A (using DJpp=4.0\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}=4.0DJpp​=4.0 ps as DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​) over-reports the DJ term alone by 4.0−3.16=0.844.0-3.16=0.844.0−3.16=0.84 ps: plugging into the formula (true σ=1.0\sigma=1.0σ=1.0 ps) gives TJ=4.0+14.07×1.0=18.07\mathrm{TJ}=4.0+14.07\times1.0=18.07TJ=4.0+14.07×1.0=18.07 ps, pessimistic by 0.840.840.84 ps compared with the exact bathtub's 17.2317.2317.23 ps — margin thrown away for nothing. Intuition: the DJ distribution carries only finite probability mass near its extremes (the sinusoid's double horns are still integrable singularities), so the deep tail is effectively a "discounted Gaussian" and the equivalent center naturally pulls inward. The costs (also stated honestly): DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​ depends on the fit depth. lab_31 sweeps three fit windows: T∈[10−8,10−4]→3.07T\in[10^{-8},10^{-4}]\to3.07T∈[10−8,10−4]→3.07 ps, [10−10,10−6]→3.16[10^{-10},10^{-6}]\to3.16[10−10,10−6]→3.16 ps, [10−14,10−10]→3.27[10^{-14},10^{-10}]\to3.27[10−14,10−10]→3.27 ps — the deeper the window, the closer to (but never exceeding) DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJpp​. A DJ/RJ decomposition report should state its fit window; the spec documents (the MJSQ family) provide explicit methodology for this. DJ "leaks" into σ\sigmaσ: the fit gives σ=1.03\sigma=1.03σ=1.03 ps, slightly larger than the true RJ's 1.001.001.00 ps — the residual curvature of the DJ tail is absorbed by the straight line into its slope. So do not take the instrument-reported RJ directly as the integral of the oscillator's phase noise when cross-checking (a few % discrepancy is normal); to cross-check, isolate DJ with a clean clock pattern.

documents.t: Full script: simulations/lab_31_dual_dirac.py (dependencies: Q from simulations/common/serdes_utils.py, savefig from simulations/common/plot_utils.py; running python scripts/run_all_sims.py re-runs it along with everything else). Synthesize RJ (σ=1\sigma=1σ=1 ps Gaussian) +++ sinusoidal DJ (A=2A=2A=2 ps → DJpp=4\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}=4DJpp​=4 ps) at UI=100UI=100UI=100 ps (10 Gb/s, same as lab_12). The tail T(x)T(x)T(x) is computed semi-analytically ("averaging over the sinusoid's phase") down to a depth of 10−1510^{-15}10−15 (no Monte-Carlo noise); the fit follows Step 4's Q-scale straight line. Parameter Variable Value Unit Notes RJ rms sigma_rj 1×10−121\times10^{-12}1×10−12 s Gaussian, unbounded (exaggerated for teaching; the canonical example-C clock is 447.9 fs) DJ amplitude a_dj 2×10−122\times10^{-12}2×10−12 s Sinusoidal (supply-spur type), DJpp=2A=4\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}=2A=4DJpp​=2A=4 ps Unit interval ui 100×10−12100\times10^{-12}100×10−12 s 10 Gb/s NRZ Target BER ber_target 10−1210^{-12}10−12 — Common SerDes spec Fit window t_deep, t_shallow [10−10,10−6][10^{-10},10^{-6}][10−10,10−6] — (tail probability) Q-scale line-fit region MC sample count n_mc 2×1062\times10^62×106 — Used for the histogram only Run output (excerpt; # -> marks verifiable numbers): extracted DJ_dd = 3.16 ps # -> 3.16 (< DJ_pp = 4.0) extracted sigma = 1.03 ps # -> 1.03 (true RJ rms 1.0) TJ@1e-12 (formula) = 17.65 ps # -> 17.65 TJ@1e-12 (bathtub) = 17.23 ps # -> 17.23 eye opening @1e-12: composite 82.77 ps vs dual-Dirac 82.76 ps Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Titles read: "(a) TJ 的 PDF：dual-Dirac 的 Dirac 在真極值內側" = (a) the PDF of TJ: the dual-Dirac's Diracs sit inside the true extreme values; "(b) Q-scale 尾巴擬合 → 取出 μ 與 σ" = (b) a Q-scale tail fit extracts μ and σ; "(c) BER bathtub：DJ 把兩壁往內推，RJ 決定壁的斜率" = (c) BER bathtub: DJ pushes both walls inward, RJ sets the walls' slope. How to read this figure: (a) PDF: the blue (true) curve has arcsine double horns smeared round by the Gaussian; the red dashed curve (dual-Dirac) visibly does not fit in the mid-section — the model never claims to fit the PDF; it is responsible only for the deep tail. The red dash-dot lines (Dirac positions ±μ=±1.58\pm\mu=\pm1.58±μ=±1.58 ps) sit inside the gray dotted lines (true extremes ±2\pm2±2 ps): this is DJδδ<DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}\lt\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJδδ​<DJpp​. (b) Q-scale: in the deep-tail region the blue curve is dead straight → Gaussian dominated; the red dashed line is the fitted line (slope 1/σ1/\sigma1/σ, intercept μ\muμ); the gray dotted line is the pessimistic prediction with "Diracs forced at ±A\pm A±A", lying below the true curve (a larger tail probability at the same xxx). (c) bathtub: blue (exact) and red dashed (dual-Dirac extrapolation) nearly coincide at 10−1210^{-12}10−12 (0.01 ps difference in opening) — the model doing its proper job; the green dotted line (RJ-only, no DJ) opens far wider: DJ shifts the walls, RJ sets the slope. Interactive: fit one yourself. The widget below lets you directly control the RJ σ and the sinusoidal DJ amplitude AAA (synthesized population, seeded PRNG, N=20,000N=20{,}000N=20,000), and switch between two BER-decade fit windows (shallow: [10−3,10−6][10^{-3},10^{-6}][10−3,10−6]; deep: [10−6,10−9][10^{-6},10^{-9}][10−6,10−9]) to watch DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​, σfit\sigma_{fit}σfit​, their difference Δ=DJpp−DJδδ\Delta=\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}-\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}Δ=DJpp​−DJδδ​, and the extrapolated TJ@10−12\mathrm{TJ}@10^{-12}TJ@10−12 move in real time as the fit depth changes — this is the quantitative version of Step 7's "the deeper the fit, the closer DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​ gets to (but never exceeds) DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJpp​", and it holds for whatever σ,A\sigma,Aσ,A you pick yourself. Dual-Dirac Q-scale fitter — extract DJ_δδ and σ_fit, compare fit depths RJ σ (true)1.00 ps Sinusoidal DJ amplitude A2.0 ps (a) TJ histogram (N=20,000, seeded) — double horn + Gaussian smear -8 ps8 psTJ (ps) (b) Q-scale bathtub tail — drag the fit-region buttons below 1e-31e-61e-91e-12x (ps)Q⁻¹(2T) shallow: 1e-3 .. 1e-6deep: 1e-6 .. 1e-9 ― shallow fit region (orange)― deep fit region (blue)― true tail (semi-analytic, exact — same method as lab_31; the bold line is the currently-selected fit depth). DJ_δδ (fitted) 3.15 ps DJ_pp (true) 4.00 ps Δ = DJ_pp − DJ_δδ 0.85 ps σ_fit / σ_true 1.03 / 1.00 ps TJ@10⁻¹² (extrapolated) 17.65 ps Shallow ([10⁻³, 10⁻⁶]): DJ_δδ = 2.99 ps, σ_fit = 1.05 ps, TJ@10⁻¹² = 17.74 ps. Deep ([10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁹]): DJ_δδ = 3.15 ps, σ_fit = 1.03 ps, TJ@10⁻¹² = 17.65 ps. The lesson: DJ_δδ < DJ_pp always, and the deeper fit pulls DJ_δδ closer to (but never past) DJ_pp — because the deep tail is dominated by the sinusoid's turning points, where nearly all of the DJ probability mass actually sits. Model: RJ ~ N(0, σ²) ⊛ sinusoidal DJ = A·sin(θ), θ ~ U[0, 2π) (arcsine "double horn"; see this page's Step 2). Histogram/CDF panel uses N = 20,000 seeded samples (mulberry32) purely for illustration; the fit itself uses the semi-analytic tail T(x) = ⟨Q((x−A sinθ)/σ)⟩_θ (same method as simulations/lab_31_dual_dirac.py), since BER windows this deep cannot be resolved honestly from any finite sample. Q(x) via the Numerical Recipes erfc approximation; Q⁻¹ via Acklam's rational approximation to the inverse normal CDF. Pedagogical toy model — real links superpose ISI+DCD+PJ and ISI is data-correlated (this page's Step 8 / Applicability table). Quick check (work it out yourself, then check) Keeping the explorer at its default settings (σ = 1.0 ps, A = 2.0 ps), if you plug the 'true' peak-to-peak DJ_pp = 2A directly into the TJ(BER) extrapolation formula (instead of the more conservative fitted DJ_δδ), what is TJ@10⁻¹² roughly? psCheckShow answer Graded correct within ±1% relative error; scientific notation is accepted. Verification: the peak-value TJ@1e-12 estimate (mirrors DualDiracFitter.js's defaults and the Q_INV_1E12 constant) # widget defaults: sigma_ps=1.0, A_ps=2.0 (DualDiracFitter.js:201-203); # Q_INV_1E12 = 7.034 (DualDiracFitter.js constant, matches this page's Step 3). sigma_ps = 1.0 A_ps = 2.0 Q_INV_1E12 = 7.034 DJ_pp_ps = 2 * A_ps # true peak-to-peak DJ (not the fitted DJ_dd) tj_ps = DJ_pp_ps + 2 * Q_INV_1E12 * sigma_ps # TJ(BER) formula (Step 6), with DJ_pp in place of DJ_dd print("DJ_pp =", DJ_pp_ps, "ps") print("TJ@1e-12 =", round(tj_ps, 2), "ps") # -> 18.07 One-liner verification (uses lab_31's real functions; a run takes a few seconds): from simulations.lab_31_dual_dirac import fit_dual_dirac, q_inv dj_dd, sigma_fit, _ = fit_dual_dirac(a_dj=2e-12, sigma_rj=1e-12) print("DJ_dd =", round(dj_dd * 1e12, 2), "ps") # -> 3.16 print("sigma =", round(sigma_fit * 1e12, 2), "ps") # -> 1.03 tj = dj_dd + 2 * q_inv(1e-12) * sigma_fit print("TJ@1e-12 =", round(float(tj) * 1e12, 2), "ps") # -> 17.65 This is a pedagogical model (not transistor-level): DJ is a single sinusoid only, and RJ is the equivalent Gaussian after integrating white noise; a real link's DJ is a superposition of ISI+DCD+PJ, and ISI is correlated with the data pattern.

documents.t: Example 1 (TJ budget: canonical clock + given DJ) 10 Gb/s (UI=100UI=100UI=100 ps). Clock RJ from canonical example C: σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, L(1MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz, 1/f², integrated 1→100 MHz). The link measures DJδδ=3\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}=3DJδδ​=3 ps. Find the TJ and eye opening at BER =10−12=10^{-12}=10−12. And converted back into an L(1MHz)\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})L(1MHz) spec (assuming example C's 1/f² shape and 1→100 MHz integration bandwidth), what does that become? Step-by-step substitution (with units): σt,max=TJ−DJδδ2 Q−1(10−12)=30−20 ps14.07=0.7107 ps=710.7 fs\sigma_{t,max}=\frac{\mathrm{TJ}-\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}}{2\,Q^{-1}(10^{-12})}=\frac{30-20\ \text{ps}}{14.07}=0.7107\ \text{ps}=710.7\ \text{fs}σt,max​=2Q−1(10−12)TJ−DJδδ​​=14.0730−20 ps​=0.7107 ps=710.7 fs With the 1/f² shape fixed, σt∝10L(1MHz)/20\sigma_t\propto10^{\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})/20}σt​∝10L(1MHz)/20 (proportional to amplitude), and example C's anchor is −100-100−100 dBc/Hz →447.9\to447.9→447.9 fs, so the allowed relaxation is: ΔL=20log⁡10710.7447.9=+4.0 dB ⟹ L(1MHz)≤−96.0 dBc/Hz\Delta\mathcal{L}=20\log_{10}\frac{710.7}{447.9}=+4.0\ \text{dB}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})\le-96.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}ΔL=20log10​447.9710.7​=+4.0 dB ⟹ L(1MHz)≤−96.0 dBc/Hz Dimension check: [s]/[−]=[s][\text{s}]/[-]=[\text{s}][s]/[−]=[s] ✓; the dB conversion acts on a dimensionless ratio ✓. Design message: once DJ eats two-thirds of the budget, the RJ spec immediately drops to sub-ps — this is why SerDes teams track DJ (layout/supply/equalization) and RJ (oscillator phase noise — ISF's territory) separately. import numpy as np ui, tj_budget, dj_dd = 100e-12, 30e-12, 20e-12 sigma_max = (tj_budget - dj_dd) / 14.07 print("sigma_max =", round(sigma_max * 1e15, 1), "fs") # -> 710.7 dL = 20 * np.log10(sigma_max / 447.9e-15) print("L(1MHz) max =", round(-100 + dL, 1), "dBc/Hz") # -> -96.0

documents.t: ISF owns RJ: every knob for σt\sigma_tσt​ lives in the earlier chapters — lower Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (waveform symmetry, symmetry), raise qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (tank_swing), lower SiS_iSi​, use the loop high-pass to cut the lower integration limit (serdes_clocking_connection Step 6). ISF cannot see DJ: DJ's knobs are power integrity (LDO/decoupling, against PJ), equalization (CTLE/DFE, against ISI), and duty-cycle correction (against DCD). For how spurs are distinguished from random phase noise in the spectrum, see measurement_and_spurs. Making the shorthand precise: the serdes page's TJ=DJpp+2Q⋅RJrms\mathrm{TJ}=\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}+2Q\cdot\mathrm{RJ}_{rms}TJ=DJpp​+2Q⋅RJrms​ is engineering shorthand (conservative); the strict version replaces DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJpp​ with the fitted DJδδ\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}DJδδ​, and Step 7 of this page quantifies the difference between the two (here 4.0 vs 3.16 ps → TJ over-reported by 0.84 ps).

DJ: bounded (ISI/DCD/PJ); booked peak-to-peak. Q(x)=12erfc(x/2)Q(x)=\tfrac12\mathrm{erfc}(x/\sqrt2)Q(x)=21​erfc(x/2​) comes from the Gaussian tail integral; Q−1(10−12)=7.03Q^{-1}(10^{-12})=7.03Q−1(10−12)=7.03, Q−1(10−15)=7.94Q^{-1}(10^{-15})=7.94Q−1(10−15)=7.94. dual-Dirac: pδδ=12gσ(x−μ)+12gσ(x+μ)p_{\delta\delta}=\tfrac12 g_\sigma(x-\mu)+\tfrac12 g_\sigma(x+\mu)pδδ​=21​gσ​(x−μ)+21​gσ​(x+μ); deep tail T≈12Q(x−μσ)T\approx\tfrac12Q(\tfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma})T≈21​Q(σx−μ​) → Q-scale straight-line fit yields (DJδδ,σ)(\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta},\sigma)(DJδδ​,σ). The bathtub BER(t)=12[T(UI2−t)+T(UI2+t)]\mathrm{BER}(t)=\tfrac12[T(\tfrac{UI}{2}-t)+T(\tfrac{UI}{2}+t)]BER(t)=21​[T(2UI​−t)+T(2UI​+t)] is just the two tails of the jitter CDF replotted. TJ(BER)=DJδδ+2Q−1(BER)σ\mathrm{TJ}(\mathrm{BER})=\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}+2Q^{-1}(\mathrm{BER})\sigmaTJ(BER)=DJδδ​+2Q−1(BER)σ; the conventions (per-Gaussian / per-side / ρT\rho_TρT​) differ by ≈0.2σ\approx0.2\sigma≈0.2σ/side — align conventions before comparing instrument numbers. DJδδ≤DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}\le\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJδδ​≤DJpp​, and the under-report is deliberate: the fit is anchored to the true deep tail → accurate extrapolation (lab_31: 0.01 ps difference in opening); forcing DJpp\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}DJpp​ in is pessimistic instead and wastes margin. lab_31: DJpp=4.0\mathrm{DJ}_{pp}=4.0DJpp​=4.0 ps → DJδδ=3.16\mathrm{DJ}_{\delta\delta}=3.16DJδδ​=3.16 ps, σ=1.03\sigma=1.03σ=1.03 ps, TJ@10−12=17.6510^{-12}=17.6510−12=17.65 ps. Methodology references (external literature, not among the five source PDFs): dual-Dirac is the industry-standard method; see INCITS T11.2, Fibre Channel — Methodologies for Jitter and Signal Quality Specification (MJSQ), Technical Report Rev 14.0, June 2005; and R. Stephens, "Jitter Analysis: The Dual-Dirac Model, RJ/DJ, and Q-Scale," Agilent Technologies Whitepaper, Dec. 2004. The jitter clauses of modern SerDes specs (PCIe, the OIF-CEI family) all inherit this model. The theory of phase noise / RJ itself comes from [P1]/[P2].

[P2] Eq.(16) (re-verified in v7: the square root covers only the constant, Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2; triple-checked against the body text's 4/N^1.5@η=0.75 and App. B Eq.(55). v3 had misread this as N−3/4N^{-3/4}N−3/4): N:5→15N:5\to15N:5→15 (×3\times3×3): Γrms(15)Γrms(5)=(155)−3/2=3−1.5=0.1925.\frac{\Gamma_{rms}(15)}{\Gamma_{rms}(5)}=\left(\frac{15}{5}\right)^{-3/2}=3^{-1.5}=0.1925.Γrms​(5)Γrms​(15)​=(515​)−3/2=3−1.5=0.1925. Phase noise ∝Γrms2\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2∝Γrms2​, so the improvement is: ΔL=10log⁡10(0.19252)=10log⁡10(0.03704)=−14.31 dB.\Delta\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}\big(0.1925^2\big)=10\log_{10}(0.03704)=-14.31\ \text{dB}.ΔL=10log10​(0.19252)=10log10​(0.03704)=−14.31 dB. (b) Why LC stays cleaner. Both knobs favor LC: Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​: the LC waveform is a smooth sinusoid (Γ=−sin⁡\Gamma=-\sinΓ=−sin, Γrms=0.707\Gamma_{rms}=0.707Γrms​=0.707, low sensitivity spread out evenly); the ring's ISF is concentrated at the transition (steep edge), giving higher rms and concentrating energy at the most sensitive point. qmaxq_{max}qmax​: the LC tank's high QQQ permits a large voltage swing → large qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=C V_{max}qmax​=CVmax​; each ring stage has swing limited by VDDV_{DD}VDD​ and small capacitance, so qmaxq_{max}qmax​ is usually much smaller. Since L∝Γrms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​/qmax2​, LC wins on both ends — smaller numerator, larger denominator. Result: (a) N:5→15N:5\to15N:5→15 drops Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ by ≈0.19×\approx0.19\times≈0.19× and improves phase noise by ≈14.3\approx14.3≈14.3 dB; (b) LC beats ring on both knobs — Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (small and spread out) and qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (high Q, large swing). Note: increasing NNN simultaneously lowers frequency (f0=1/(2NτD)f_0=1/(2N\tau_D)f0​=1/(2NτD​)) and raises power; ring's real appeal is area/tunability/no inductor, not low phase noise. See lc_vs_ring. Dimension check: NNN is dimensionless, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is dimensionless; the ratio and the dB value are both dimensionless ✓. import numpy as np ratio = (15/5)**(-1.5) print("Grms ratio", round(ratio,4), "; dPN", round(10*np.log10(ratio**2),2), "dB") # -> Grms ratio 0.1925 ; dPN -14.31 dB Exercise 4 solution (PLL optimal loop BW) Intuition. The PLL low-pass filters the ref and high-pass filters the VCO (spec Section 10.2). If loop BW fnf_nfn​ is too small → the VCO's close-in 1/f21/f^21/f2 noise isn't suppressed by the loop, so in-band noise is dominated by the VCO → large jitter. If loop BW fnf_nfn​ is too large → a large amount of ref noise (and CP noise) is let through, and the VCO high-pass corner is pushed too high, so out-of-band VCO noise is also large → large jitter. The optimal fn\*f_n^\*fn\*​ sits near the crossover point of the "rising ref+CP curve" and the "falling VCO curve" — where the two shaped curves intersect near fnf_nfn​, minimizing the total integrated area. Numerical (sweeping fnf_nfn​). Using shape_output_phase_noise and trapezoidal integration, sweep fn=104→107f_n=10^4\to10^7fn​=104→107 Hz, and find the one minimizing ∫Soutdf\int S_{out}df∫Sout​df (1 kHz→100 MHz): Result: the optimal fn\*≈f_n^\*\approxfn\*​≈ a few hundred kHz to ~1 MHz (near the crossover of the ref white-floor curve and the VCO 1/f21/f^21/f2 curve). For this problem's parameters, the grid sweep gives fn\*≈3×105f_n^\*\approx3\times10^5fn\*​≈3×105 Hz order of magnitude (shifts with Sref,KvS_{ref},K_vSref​,Kv​). This is the core trade-off in PLL noise budgeting: loop BW is neither best maximized nor minimized — an optimum exists. Dimension check: SoutS_{out}Sout​ is in rad²/Hz, ∫Soutdf\int S_{out}df∫Sout​df is in rad² (phase variance); σt=⋅/(2πf0)\sigma_t=\sqrt{\cdot}/(2\pi f_0)σt​=⋅​/(2πf0​) is in s ✓. import numpy as np from simulations.common.pll_utils import shape_output_phase_noise f = np.logspace(3, 8, 4000) S_ref = np.full_like(f, 1e-9) # white-floor reference (tuned so the optimal BW falls within the sweep range) S_vco = 1e2 / f**2 # VCO 1/f^2 fn_grid = np.logspace(4, 7, 60) var = [] for fn in fn_grid: S_out, _, _ = shape_output_phase_noise(f, S_ref, S_vco, fn_hz=fn) var.append(np.trapezoid(S_out, f)) # rad^2 fn_opt = fn_grid[int(np.argmin(var))] print("optimal f_n ~", f"{fn_opt:.2e}", "Hz") # -> ~1.9e5 Hz (order 10^5; slightly below 10/√S_ref≈3e5 due to non-ideal brick-wall rolloff) (See pll_noise_budget for the full plot.) Dimension check: psdimensionless=ps\dfrac{\text{ps}}{\text{dimensionless}}=\text{ps}dimensionlessps​=ps ✓. import numpy as np from scipy.special import erfcinv ui = 40e-12 qinv = np.sqrt(2)*erfcinv(2*1e-15) # Q^-1(1e-15) ~ 7.94 sigma_max = (ui/2)/qinv print(round(sigma_max*1e12,3), "ps ; UI/sigma =", round(ui/sigma_max,1)) # -> 2.519 ps ; UI/sigma = 15.9 Exercise 7 solution (tail-noise countermeasures, illustrative) Marked illustrative: the following cross-coupled LC VCO tail mechanism is a qualitative teaching model; the constants/specific cnc_ncn​ depend on topology, and rigorous values require transient/adjoint extraction (see real_oscillator_topologies). Mechanism review. The tail current source's low-frequency (including flicker) noise is upconverted by 2×2\times2× via the differential-pair switching, landing near 2ω02\omega_02ω0​; it then folds back close-in via the effective ISF's c2c_2c2​ (second harmonic) and its DC component c0c_0c0​, forming a 1/f31/f^31/f3/1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt. So "tail-noise trouble" is primarily written into the ISF's c0c_0c0​ and c2c_2c2​. Three countermeasures (each paired with one ISF quantity): Countermeasure Why it works (ISF quantity) Tail filter (add a 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ notch/large capacitor at the tail) Directly blocks tail noise near 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ in the frequency domain → equivalently reduces the energy folded back by c2c_2c2​, suppressing close-in 1/f21/f^21/f2. Waveform symmetrization (balance upper/lower half-cycles, reduce rise/fall asymmetry) Suppresses the effective ISF's c0c_0c0​; the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ∝c02\propto c_0^2∝c02​ (Eq.(24)), so c0↓c_0\downarrowc0​↓ directly pushes the flicker-upconversion corner away from the carrier. Increase tank swing / raise qmaxq_{max}qmax​ L∝Γrms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​/qmax2​; qmax↑q_{max}\uparrowqmax​↑ suppresses the contribution of every source (including the tail) together (claim C3). (A fourth measure as a supplement: use a device with lower noise and a lower 1/f1/f1/f corner for the tail, or use resistive degeneration to reduce tail gmg_mgm​ noise — equivalently reducing the in2‾\overline{i_n^2}in2​​ injected into c0,c2c_0,c_2c0​,c2​.) Result: tail noise is best addressed with three combined measures — "tail filter to block 2ω02\omega_02ω0​," "symmetrization to suppress c0c_0c0​," and "increase qmaxq_{max}qmax​"; the corresponding quantitative knobs are c2c_2c2​ (folded-back energy), c0c_0c0​ (the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ∝c02\propto c_0^2∝c02​), and qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (L∝1/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto1/q_{max}^2L∝1/qmax2​). Python verification (quantifying the effect of "symmetrization to suppress c0c_0c0​" on the corner): import numpy as np # Use Eq.(24) to quantify the benefit of symmetrizing to suppress c0 (f1f=2 MHz, Grms=0.9 toy values) def f3_corner(c0, Grms=0.9, f1f=2e6): return f1f*c0**2/(2*Grms**2) print("c0=0.3 ->", round(f3_corner(0.3)/1e3,1), "kHz ; c0=0.05 ->", round(f3_corner(0.05)/1e3,2), "kHz") # -> c0=0.3 -> 111.1 kHz ; c0=0.05 -> 3.09 kHz (symmetrization suppresses the corner by ~36x) Exercise 8 solution (allocating a jitter budget across PLL bands) Design back-calculation strategy. RJ sources are uncorrelated → variances (not rms values) add: σt,tot2=σt,ref2+σt,vco2⟹σt,vco=σt,tot2−σt,ref2.\sigma_{t,\text{tot}}^2=\sigma_{t,\text{ref}}^2+\sigma_{t,\text{vco}}^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sigma_{t,\text{vco}}=\sqrt{\sigma_{t,\text{tot}}^2-\sigma_{t,\text{ref}}^2}.σt,tot2​=σt,ref2​+σt,vco2​⟹σt,vco​=σt,tot2​−σt,ref2​​. Step-by-step substitution (with units). σt,vco=(300 fs)2−(180 fs)2=90000−32400 fs=57600 fs=240 fs.\sigma_{t,\text{vco}}=\sqrt{(300\ \text{fs})^2-(180\ \text{fs})^2}=\sqrt{90000-32400}\ \text{fs}=\sqrt{57600}\ \text{fs}=240\ \text{fs}.σt,vco​=(300 fs)2−(180 fs)2​=90000−32400​ fs=57600​ fs=240 fs. Corresponding phase variance (using σϕ=2πf0 σt\sigma_\phi=2\pi f_0\,\sigma_tσϕ​=2πf0​σt​, spec formula 19 reversed): σϕ,vco=2πf0 σt,vco=2π×1010×240×10−15=1.508×10−2 rad,\sigma_{\phi,\text{vco}}=2\pi f_0\,\sigma_{t,\text{vco}}=2\pi\times10^{10}\times240\times10^{-15}=1.508\times10^{-2}\ \text{rad},σϕ,vco​=2πf0​σt,vco​=2π×1010×240×10−15=1.508×10−2 rad,σϕ,vco2=(1.508×10−2)2=2.274×10−4 rad2.\sigma_{\phi,\text{vco}}^2=(1.508\times10^{-2})^2=2.274\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}^2.σϕ,vco2​=(1.508×10−2)2=2.274×10−4 rad2. Result: VCO budget σt,vco=240\sigma_{t,\text{vco}}=240σt,vco​=240 fs; corresponding σϕ,vco2≈2.27×10−4\sigma_{\phi,\text{vco}}^2\approx2.27\times10^{-4}σϕ,vco2​≈2.27×10−4 rad². Intuition: because variances add, 180 fs + 240 fs (rms) combine to 300 fs (not 420 fs) — RJ budgets must be allocated by sum of squares. This 240 fs is exactly the integrated jitter allowed for the PLL's out-of-band VCO segment, which feeds back into loop BW and VCO spec (connects to Exercise 4's optimal BW, pll_noise_budget). Dimension check: fs2−fs2=fs\sqrt{\text{fs}^2-\text{fs}^2}=\text{fs}fs2−fs2​=fs ✓; 2πf0 σt2\pi f_0\,\sigma_t2πf0​σt​ is rad/s⋅s=rad\text{rad/s}\cdot\text{s}=\text{rad}rad/s⋅s=rad ✓. import numpy as np sigma_tot, sigma_ref, f0 = 300e-15, 180e-15, 10e9 sigma_vco = np.sqrt(sigma_tot**2 - sigma_ref**2) sigma_phi = 2*np.pi*f0*sigma_vco print(sigma_vco*1e15, "fs ;", sigma_phi**2, "rad^2") # -> 240.0 fs ; 2.27e-4 rad^2

documents.t: Prerequisites: tank_swing (FOM definition and the phase-noise × power trade-off), white_noise_to_phase_noise ([P1] Eq.(21) and the factor-of-2 convention), lc_vs_ring ([P2] Eq.(23) ring FOM, the −91-91−91 dBc/Hz example) | Next: real_oscillator_topologies, pll_noise_budget This page answers three questions every VCO designer eventually asks: Does FOM (figure of merit — the oscillator quality metric) have a physical upper bound? What is it, and what sets it? The best published LC designs sit around FOM ≈190\approx190≈190 dB — how many dB below the ceiling are they? Why does the ring oscillator inherently trail LC by about 25 dB? Which term eats each dB of that gap? Physical intuition (conclusion first): FOM is constructed to exactly cancel (f0/Δf)2(f_0/\Delta f)^2(f0​/Δf)2 and power PPP. What's left are only two things: nature's price list, kTkTkT (thermal-noise energy in a 1 Hz bandwidth vs. 1 mW), which comes to 173.8 dB at 300 K; and the topology noise factor FeffF_{eff}Feff​ — how much your circuit amplifies kTkTkT (ring: Feff≥3.6F_{eff}\ge3.6Feff​≥3.6, ceiling 168.3 dB) or beats it down with high-QQQ energy storage (LC: Feff∝1/Q2F_{eff}\propto 1/Q^2Feff​∝1/Q2, ceiling rises 20 dB per decade of QQQ). So there is no single magic number: the ceiling is a "family," and which member you land on is set by what physics you allow into FeffF_{eff}Feff​.
documents.s: The Theoretical Ceiling of FOM

documents.t: This page uses the positive-value convention (bigger is better, the most common form in survey tables): FOM = −L(Δf) + 20log⁡10 ⁣(f0Δf) − 10log⁡10 ⁣(P1 mW)[dB]\mathrm{FOM}\;=\;-\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\;+\;20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\right)\;-\;10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P}{1\ \text{mW}}\right)\qquad[\text{dB}]FOM=−L(Δf)+20log10​(Δff0​​)−10log10​(1 mWP​)[dB] L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf): SSB phase noise at offset Δf\Delta fΔf, in dBc/Hz (negative, so −L-\mathcal{L}−L is positive). f0f_0f0​: carrier frequency [Hz]; Δf\Delta fΔf: offset frequency [Hz]; PPP: total DC power dissipation [W], normalized to 1 mW. Comparison with tank_swing: that page writes FOM′=L−20log⁡10(f0/Δf)+10log⁡10(P/1mW)\mathrm{FOM}'=\mathcal{L}-20\log_{10}(f_0/\Delta f)+10\log_{10}(P/1\text{mW})FOM′=L−20log10​(f0​/Δf)+10log10​(P/1mW) — the same quantity with the sign flipped (FOM=−FOM′\mathrm{FOM}=-\mathrm{FOM}'FOM=−FOM′; under that convention more negative is better). Both forms appear in the literature; this page uses the positive convention, so numerically the ring example's FOM=165.0\mathrm{FOM}=165.0FOM=165.0 dB here is that page's FOM′=−165.0\mathrm{FOM}'=-165.0FOM′=−165.0 dB. A hidden reference unit: the "per Hz" in L\mathcal{L}L is really "sideband power in a 1 Hz measurement bandwidth ÷ carrier power." Writing out this Bref=1B_{ref}=1Bref​=1 Hz explicitly is what makes FOM's log argument strictly dimensionless; FOM's full reference basis is "1 Hz bandwidth, 1 mW power." The next step shows this isn't pedantry — it's exactly what lets kTkTkT appear cleanly. Dimension check: all three terms are 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ of dimensionless ratios (LlinBref\mathcal{L}_{lin}B_{ref}Llin​Bref​, (f0/Δf)2(f_0/\Delta f)^2(f0​/Δf)2, P/PrefP/P_{ref}P/Pref​) → dB ✓. Do not confuse it with the PLL jitter–power FOM: for a whole PLL the common metric is FOMjitter=20log⁡10(σt/1 s)+10log⁡10(P/1 mW)\mathrm{FOM}_{jitter}=20\log_{10}(\sigma_t/1\ \text{s})+10\log_{10}(P/1\ \text{mW})FOMjitter​=20log10​(σt​/1 s)+10log10​(P/1 mW) (always negative, more negative is better; σt2P\sigma_t^2Pσt2​P is the invariant — halving the jitter gives −6-6−6 dB, halving the power −3-3−3 dB; e.g. σt=259\sigma_t=259σt​=259 fs, P=10P=10P=10 mW → −241.7-241.7−241.7 dB). It normalizes integrated jitter and power, not f0/Δff_0/\Delta ff0​/Δf, so it is a different quantity from this page's oscillator FOM — never swap or add the two; definition and worked example in the section "The PLL jitter–power FOM" of pll_noise_budget.

documents.t: Suppose some topology's phase noise in the 1/f21/f^21/f2 (white-noise) region can be arranged into the following universal form (the next two steps show both ring and LC reduce to this): Llin(Δf) = Feff⋅kTP⋅(f0Δf)2[1Hz]\mathcal{L}_{lin}(\Delta f)\;=\;F_{eff}\cdot\frac{kT}{P}\cdot\left(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\right)^2\qquad\left[\tfrac{1}{\text{Hz}}\right]Llin​(Δf)=Feff​⋅PkT​⋅(Δff0​​)2[Hz1​] where FeffF_{eff}Feff​ is the dimensionless topology noise factor (this equation is its definition). Unit check: kTP=[J][W]=[s]=1[Hz]\dfrac{kT}{P}=\dfrac{[\text{J}]}{[\text{W}]}=[\text{s}]=\dfrac{1}{[\text{Hz}]}PkT​=[W][J]​=[s]=[Hz]1​, multiplied by the dimensionless Feff(f0/Δf)2F_{eff}(f_0/\Delta f)^2Feff​(f0​/Δf)2 this gives exactly the per-Hz units Llin\mathcal{L}_{lin}Llin​ needs ✓. Substitute into the FOM definition and cancel step by step: FOM=−10log⁡10 ⁣(Feff kT BrefP(f0Δf)2)+10log⁡10 ⁣((f0Δf)2)−10log⁡10 ⁣(PPref)=−10log⁡10 ⁣(Feff⋅kT BrefP⋅PPref)(the two (f0/Δf)2 terms cancel)=−10log⁡10 ⁣(kT BrefPref)⏟≡ Cref(T), temperature-only − 10log⁡10Feff.\begin{aligned} \mathrm{FOM} &=-10\log_{10}\!\left(F_{eff}\,\frac{kT\,B_{ref}}{P}\Big(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\Big)^{2}\right) +10\log_{10}\!\left(\Big(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\Big)^{2}\right) -10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P}{P_{ref}}\right)\\[4pt] &=-10\log_{10}\!\left(F_{eff}\cdot\frac{kT\,B_{ref}}{P}\cdot\frac{P}{P_{ref}}\right) \qquad\text{(the two }(f_0/\Delta f)^{2}\text{ terms cancel)}\\[4pt] &=\underbrace{-10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{kT\,B_{ref}}{P_{ref}}\right)}_{\equiv\,C_{ref}(T)\text{, temperature-only}}\;-\;10\log_{10}F_{eff}. \end{aligned}FOM​=−10log10​(Feff​PkTBref​​(Δff0​​)2)+10log10​((Δff0​​)2)−10log10​(Pref​P​)=−10log10​(Feff​⋅PkTBref​​⋅Pref​P​)(the two (f0​/Δf)2 terms cancel)=≡Cref​(T), temperature-only−10log10​(Pref​kTBref​​)​​−10log10​Feff​.​ What each step uses: going from line 1→2, (f0/Δf)2(f_0/\Delta f)^2(f0​/Δf)2 cancels exactly between −L-\mathcal{L}−L and +20log⁡10(f0/Δf)+20\log_{10}(f_0/\Delta f)+20log10​(f0​/Δf); going from line 2→3, PPP cancels exactly between kT/PkT/PkT/P and P/PrefP/P_{ref}P/Pref​. These two cancellations are precisely the reason FOM was invented (to normalize away the "L×P≈\mathcal{L}\times P\approxL×P≈ constant" trade-off — see tank_swing step 4). Dimension check: kT BrefPref=[J][Hz][W]=[W][W]\dfrac{kT\,B_{ref}}{P_{ref}}=\dfrac{[\text{J}][\text{Hz}]}{[\text{W}]}=\dfrac{[\text{W}]}{[\text{W}]}Pref​kTBref​​=[W][J][Hz]​=[W][W]​, dimensionless ✓ — the Bref=1B_{ref}=1Bref​=1 Hz hidden in step 0 is exactly what completes kTkTkT's dimensions here. Physical meaning: kT⋅(1 Hz)kT\cdot(1\ \text{Hz})kT⋅(1 Hz) is the available thermal-noise power a resistor can deliver in a 1 Hz bandwidth (kT≈4.14×10−21kT\approx4.14\times10^{-21}kT≈4.14×10−21 J @ 300 K); CrefC_{ref}Cref​ is simply "how many dB is 1 mW above the thermal-noise floor." Numerically (k=1.380649×10−23k=1.380649\times10^{-23}k=1.380649×10−23 J/K, T=300T=300T=300 K): kT=4.142×10−21kT=4.142\times10^{-21}kT=4.142×10−21 J, kT⋅1 Hz/1 mW=4.142×10−18kT\cdot1\,\text{Hz}/1\,\text{mW}=4.142\times10^{-18}kT⋅1Hz/1mW=4.142×10−18, Cref=−10log⁡10(4.142×10−18)=173.83C_{ref}=-10\log_{10}(4.142\times10^{-18})=173.83Cref​=−10log10​(4.142×10−18)=173.83 dB. FOM = 173.8 dB − 10log⁡10Feff(T=300 K) \boxed{\;\mathrm{FOM}\;=\;173.8\ \text{dB}\;-\;10\log_{10}F_{eff}\qquad(T=300\ \text{K})\;}FOM=173.8 dB−10log10​Feff​(T=300 K)​ ⚠️ A memorization trap (worked out on this site — don't get it wrong): quick notes often write this constant as "−10log⁡10(2kT/1mW)=173.8-10\log_{10}(2kT/1\text{mW})=173.8−10log10​(2kT/1mW)=173.8" — wrong. 2kT2kT2kT pairs with 170.8170.8170.8 dB; 173.8173.8173.8 dB pairs with 1⋅kT1\cdot kT1⋅kT. This page's derivation naturally lands on 1⋅kT1\cdot kT1⋅kT: because [P2] Eq.(23) is printed in exactly the kT/PkT/PkT/P form (step 2), while the LC reduction (step 3) folds all factors of 2 and 4 into FeffF_{eff}Feff​. Every factor-of-2 convention (SSB's /4 vs. the time-domain /2) lives inside FeffF_{eff}Feff​ and only shifts FOM by 3.01 dB total; CrefC_{ref}Cref​ itself is convention-free. import numpy as np kB, T = 1.380649e-23, 300.0 print(round(-10*np.log10(kB*T*1.0/1e-3), 2)) # -> 173.83 print(round(-10*np.log10(2*kB*T/1e-3), 2)) # -> 170.82 (the 2kT pairing, often misremembered as 173.8) print(round(10*np.log10(kB*290.0/1e-3), 2)) # -> -173.98 (the RF world's famous -174 dBm/Hz thermal-noise floor) Bonus: converting kTkTkT using T0=290T_0=290T0​=290 K (the IEEE noise-figure reference temperature, from Friis 1944, external literature, not among the five source PDFs, full citation at page bottom) to dBm/Hz gives the famous −174-174−174 dBm/Hz; 300 K gives −173.83-173.83−173.83, both round to −174-174−174. Temperature effect: CrefC_{ref}Cref​ drops about 0.140.140.14 dB per 10 K rise (Cref(310 K)−Cref(300 K)=−0.142C_{ref}(310\,\text{K})-C_{ref}(300\,\text{K})=-0.142Cref​(310K)−Cref​(300K)=−0.142 dB) — remember this slope when comparing FOM measured at different temperatures.

documents.t: [P2] Eq.(23), p.796 (verified against the original PDF, leading coefficient 8/(3η)8/(3\eta)8/(3η)) is already in universal form: Llin{Δf}=83η⋅kTP⋅VDDVchar⋅(f0Δf)2 ⟹ Feffring=83η⋅VDDVchar\mathcal{L}_{lin}\{\Delta f\}=\frac{8}{3\eta}\cdot\frac{kT}{P}\cdot\frac{V_{DD}}{V_{char}}\cdot\left(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\right)^{2} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; F_{eff}^{ring}=\frac{8}{3\eta}\cdot\frac{V_{DD}}{V_{char}}Llin​{Δf}=3η8​⋅PkT​⋅Vchar​VDD​​⋅(Δff0​​)2⟹Feffring​=3η8​⋅Vchar​VDD​​ η\etaη: per-stage delay proportionality constant ([P2] Eq.(14)), ≈1\approx1≈1, dimensionless); VDDV_{DD}VDD​: supply voltage [V]; Vchar=ΔV/γV_{char}=\Delta V/\gammaVchar​=ΔV/γ: the device's characteristic voltage [V] (ΔV\Delta VΔV = gate overdrive [V], γ\gammaγ = channel thermal-noise coefficient, dimensionless). Why PPP appears naturally: [P2] Eq.(21) gives P=2ηNVDDqmaxf0P=2\eta N V_{DD}q_{max}f_0P=2ηNVDD​qmax​f0​ — power absorbs NNN, qmaxq_{max}qmax​, and f0f_0f0​ entirely, which is exactly lc_vs_ring's N-independence as seen in FOM language. Ceiling: Vchar=ΔV/γV_{char}=\Delta V/\gammaVchar​=ΔV/γ, and overdrive is bounded by supply, ΔV≤VDD/2\Delta V\le V_{DD}/2ΔV≤VDD​/2 (equality at VT=0V_T=0VT​=0), so VDDVchar=γ VDDΔV ≥ 2γ ⟹ Feffring ≥ 16γ3η\frac{V_{DD}}{V_{char}}=\gamma\,\frac{V_{DD}}{\Delta V}\;\ge\;2\gamma \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; F_{eff}^{ring}\;\ge\;\frac{16\gamma}{3\eta}Vchar​VDD​​=γΔVVDD​​≥2γ⟹Feffring​≥3η16γ​ This is the lower bound from [P2] Eq.(25), p.796. Taking long-channel γ=2/3\gamma=2/3γ=2/3, η=1\eta=1η=1: Feff,minring=32/9=3.556F_{eff,min}^{ring}=32/9=3.556Feff,minring​=32/9=3.556, 10log⁡10(3.556)=5.5110\log_{10}(3.556)=5.5110log10​(3.556)=5.51 dB, FOMmaxring=173.83−5.51=168.32 dB(300 K)\mathrm{FOM}_{max}^{ring}=173.83-5.51=168.32\ \text{dB}\quad(300\ \text{K})FOMmaxring​=173.83−5.51=168.32 dB(300 K) Verification against this site's ring worked example (lc_vs_ring example 1: L=−91.0\mathcal{L}=-91.0L=−91.0 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, P=1P=1P=1 mW, VDD/Vchar=3V_{DD}/V_{char}=3VDD​/Vchar​=3): FOM=91.0+20log⁡10(5000)−0=91.0+73.98=165.0 dB\mathrm{FOM}=91.0+20\log_{10}(5000)-0=91.0+73.98=165.0\ \text{dB}FOM=91.0+20log10​(5000)−0=91.0+73.98=165.0 dB import numpy as np kB, f0, df = 1.380649e-23, 5e9, 1e6 Cref = -10*np.log10(kB*300/1e-3) Feff_ring = 8/3 * 3 # [P2] Eq.(23): (8/(3η))·(V_DD/V_char), η=1, V_DD/V_char=3 print(round(Cref - 10*np.log10(Feff_ring), 2)) # -> 164.8 (F_eff path, kT using the exact 300 K value) print(round(91.0 + 20*np.log10(f0/df) - 0.0, 2)) # -> 164.98 (directly from this page's -91.0 dBc/Hz, P=1 mW) Feff_min = 16*(2/3)/3 # [P2] Eq.(25): V_T=0 lower bound, γ=2/3 print(round(Cref - 10*np.log10(Feff_min), 2)) # -> 168.32 (ring ceiling) Source of the 0.2 dB gap between the two paths (honest bookkeeping): the FeffF_{eff}Feff​ path uses the exact kT(300 K)=4.142×10−21kT(300\,\text{K})=4.142\times10^{-21}kT(300K)=4.142×10−21 J, giving 164.80164.80164.80; the lc_vs_ring chain used a rounded kT=4.0×10−21kT=4.0\times10^{-21}kT=4.0×10−21 J (which is actually the 290290290 K value), giving L=−91.0\mathcal{L}=-91.0L=−91.0, FOM=165.0\mathrm{FOM}=165.0FOM=165.0. The two are identical bit-for-bit once kTkTkT is taken consistently (simulations/fig_fom_limit.py prints an identity check =0.00=0.00=0.00). This page consistently quotes it as "≈165\approx165≈165 dB." This example sits only 168.32−164.80=3.52168.32-164.80=3.52168.32−164.80=3.52 dB below the ring ceiling (exactly the VDD/Vchar=3V_{DD}/V_{char}=3VDD​/Vchar​=3 vs. lower-bound 2γ=4/32\gamma=4/32γ=4/3 ratio of 2.25→3.522.25\to3.522.25→3.52 dB) — the ring's universal form leaves almost no room to maneuver, which is the key point. Applicability/breakdown: single-ended CMOS inverter ring, white noise, long-channel γ=2/3\gamma=2/3γ=2/3. Shorter channels give larger γ\gammaγ → lower ceiling (γ=1\gamma=1γ=1 gives 16γ/3=5.33→166.616\gamma/3=5.33\to166.616γ/3=5.33→166.6 dB); flicker noise and supply/substrate coupling only push it lower still.

documents.t: LC has no ready-made kT/PkT/PkT/P form — we have to build it. Starting from [P1] Eq.(21), p.185 (SSB, denominator 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2 convention): Llin{Δω}=Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2\mathcal{L}_{lin}\{\Delta\omega\}=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}Llin​{Δω}=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​ Introduce four standard circuit relations (checking units for each first): Noise source: thermal noise of the tank loss resistance RpR_pRp​, in2‾/Δf=4kT/Rp\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=4kT/R_pin2​​/Δf=4kT/Rp​ ([J]/[Ω]=[A2s]=[A2/Hz][\text{J}]/[\Omega]=[\text{A}^2\text{s}]=[\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}][J]/[Ω]=[A2s]=[A2/Hz] ✓; see tank_Q_and_energy_restoration). With multiple noise sources, define the noise factor FFF (dimensionless): weight each source by its own Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ and refer it back to the tank source, in2‾/Δf∣tot=F⋅4kT/Rp\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f\big|_{tot}=F\cdot4kT/R_pin2​​/Δf​tot​=F⋅4kT/Rp​, F≥1F\ge1F≥1 (the tank itself contributes 1). For an ideal class-B cross-coupled pair (ideally filtered tail), F=1+γF=1+\gammaF=1+γ — this is an external-literature standard result (Hegazi–Sjöland–Abidi 2001; Andreani et al. 2005, full citations at page bottom), not among the five PDFs. Charge swing: qmax=C Vmaxq_{max}=C\,V_{max}qmax​=CVmax​ ([F][V]=[C][\text{F}][\text{V}]=[\text{C}][F][V]=[C] ✓, [P1] definition). Power: average dissipation of the sinusoidal swing VmaxV_{max}Vmax​ across RpR_pRp​, Ptank=Vmax2/(2Rp)P_{tank}=V_{max}^2/(2R_p)Ptank​=Vmax2​/(2Rp​) ([V2/Ω]=[W][\text{V}^2/\Omega]=[\text{W}][V2/Ω]=[W] ✓); total DC power dissipation PDC=Ptank/ηPP_{DC}=P_{tank}/\eta_PPDC​=Ptank​/ηP​, ηP≤1\eta_P\le1ηP​≤1 being power efficiency (dimensionless). Quality factor: for a parallel RLC, Q=ω0RpCQ=\omega_0 R_p CQ=ω0​Rp​C ([s−1][Ω][F][\text{s}^{-1}][\Omega][\text{F}][s−1][Ω][F], Ω⋅F=s\Omega\cdot\text{F}=\text{s}Ω⋅F=s → dimensionless ✓). Substitute step by step (no steps skipped): Llin=Γrms2(CVmax)2⋅F⋅4kT/Rp4Δω2=F Γrms2 kTRp C2Vmax2 Δω2(sub 1, 2; cancel the 4)=F Γrms2 kTRp C2⋅2PtankRp⋅Δω2=F Γrms2 kT2Ptank (RpC)2 Δω2(sub 3: Vmax2=2PtankRp)=F Γrms22Q2⋅kTPtank⋅(ω0Δω)2(sub 4: RpC=Q/ω0)\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{lin} &=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{(CV_{max})^2}\cdot\frac{F\cdot4kT/R_p}{4\Delta\omega^2} =\frac{F\,\Gamma_{rms}^2\,kT}{R_p\,C^2V_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2} &&\text{(sub 1, 2; cancel the }4\text{)}\\[4pt] &=\frac{F\,\Gamma_{rms}^2\,kT}{R_p\,C^2\cdot 2P_{tank}R_p\cdot\Delta\omega^2} =\frac{F\,\Gamma_{rms}^2\,kT}{2P_{tank}\,(R_pC)^2\,\Delta\omega^2} &&\text{(sub 3: }V_{max}^2=2P_{tank}R_p\text{)}\\[4pt] &=\frac{F\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}{2Q^2}\cdot\frac{kT}{P_{tank}}\cdot\left(\frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}\right)^{2} &&\text{(sub 4: }R_pC=Q/\omega_0\text{)} \end{aligned}Llin​​=(CVmax​)2Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2F⋅4kT/Rp​​=Rp​C2Vmax2​Δω2FΓrms2​kT​=Rp​C2⋅2Ptank​Rp​⋅Δω2FΓrms2​kT​=2Ptank​(Rp​C)2Δω2FΓrms2​kT​=2Q2FΓrms2​​⋅Ptank​kT​⋅(Δωω0​​)2​​(sub 1, 2; cancel the 4)(sub 3: Vmax2​=2Ptank​Rp​)(sub 4: Rp​C=Q/ω0​)​ ω0/Δω=f0/Δf\omega_0/\Delta\omega=f_0/\Delta fω0​/Δω=f0​/Δf (the 2π2\pi2π factors cancel top and bottom), then convert Ptank=ηPPDCP_{tank}=\eta_P P_{DC}Ptank​=ηP​PDC​ to total power dissipation, giving the universal form and FeffLC=F Γrms22 Q2 ηP \boxed{\;F_{eff}^{LC}=\frac{F\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}{2\,Q^2\,\eta_P}\;}FeffLC​=2Q2ηP​FΓrms2​​​ Dimension check (whole chain): FeffLCF_{eff}^{LC}FeffLC​ is built entirely of dimensionless quantities ✓; kT/Ptank=[s]kT/P_{tank}=[\text{s}]kT/Ptank​=[s] gives per-Hz ✓. Physical meaning (the single most important sentence on this page): the Q2Q^2Q2 in the denominator is how LC punches through the 173.8 dB "reference line" — the resonant tank stores signal energy without adding noise; each watt of loss only buys kTkTkT worth of noise once, through RpR_pRp​. The higher QQQ, the larger "stored signal ÷ purchased noise" becomes, and Feff<1F_{eff}\lt1Feff​<1 is perfectly legitimate. The reference line is not LC's ceiling; LC's ceiling is set by whatever QQQ the process can provide (on-chip spiral inductors at GHz frequencies typically give Q≈8∼15Q\approx8\sim15Q≈8∼15). Breakdown conditions: swing large enough to distort the waveform (changing Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, FFF), ηP\eta_PηP​ collapsing once voltage-limited, varactor/switch loss eating into QQQ, flicker-dominated offsets (the universal form only covers the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region). Numerical consistency check (reverse-engineering canonical example B into an actual tank): example B (Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz → L=−148.0\mathcal{L}=-148.0L=−148.0 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz), if SiS_iSi​ is interpreted as a single tank source and Vmax=1V_{max}=1Vmax​=1 V is assumed, gives Rp=4kT/Si=16.6R_p=4kT/S_i=16.6Rp​=4kT/Si​=16.6 kΩ, C=1C=1C=1 pF, Q=ω0RpC=520.5Q=\omega_0R_pC=520.5Q=ω0​Rp​C=520.5, Ptank=30.2P_{tank}=30.2Ptank​=30.2 µW — the two paths (Eq.(21) computed directly vs. the FeffF_{eff}Feff​ universal form) must give the same L\mathcal{L}L: import numpy as np kB, T, f0, df = 1.380649e-23, 300.0, 5e9, 1e6 grms, qmax, Si = 0.5, 1e-12, 1e-24 dw = 2*np.pi*df L_direct = 10*np.log10(grms**2/qmax**2 * Si/(4*dw**2)) # [P1] Eq.(21) Rp = 4*kB*T/Si; C = qmax/1.0; Q = 2*np.pi*f0*Rp*C; Pt = 1.0**2/(2*Rp) Feff = 1.0*grms**2/(2*Q**2) # F=1, η_P=1 L_feff = 10*np.log10(Feff*(kB*T/Pt)*(f0/df)**2) print(round(L_direct, 2), round(L_feff, 2)) # -> -148.0 -148.0 (both paths agree bit-for-bit: the algebraic chain is correct) print(round(Q, 1), round(Pt*1e6, 2)) # -> 520.5 30.18 (Q≈520: no such tank exists on chip) FOM = -L_direct + 20*np.log10(f0/df) - 10*np.log10(Pt/1e-3) print(round(FOM, 1)) # -> 237.2 Teaching point (FOM catches you out): example B's −148-148−148 dBc/Hz is unremarkable on its own, but converted to FOM it comes out to 237 dB, equivalent to a Q≈520Q\approx520Q≈520 tank — instantly exposing that "Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz with 1 pC" is a deliberately idealized single-source teaching parameter, not a realizable design point. dBc/Hz can lie (it says nothing about power); FOM cannot.

Factor-of-2 discipline (which "2," which convention): this site records, in white_noise_to_phase_noise, that for the same example-B parameters, [P1] Eq.(21)'s SSB "/4" gives −148.0-148.0−148.0 dBc/Hz, while the clean time-domain derivation's "/2" gives −145.0-145.0−145.0 dBc/Hz. In FOM language this factor of 2 moves entirely into FeffF_{eff}Feff​: the /2 convention's FeffF_{eff}Feff​ is twice the /4 convention's, so FOM is lower by 10log⁡102=3.0110\log_{10}2=3.0110log10​2=3.01 dB (the two rows above). Leeson's 2FkT/Ps2FkT/P_s2FkT/Ps​ form (see derivation_leeson) reduces to Feff=F/(2Q2)F_{eff}=F/(2Q^2)Feff​=F/(2Q2), belonging to the /2 family — which differs by exactly this factor of 2 from this page's [P1]-based FΓrms2/(2Q2)=F/(4Q2)F\Gamma_{rms}^2/(2Q^2)=F/(4Q^2)FΓrms2​/(2Q2)=F/(4Q2) (Γrms2=12\Gamma_{rms}^2=\tfrac12Γrms2​=21​) ✓. documents.s: Step 4: the ceiling is a "family," not a single number

documents.t: Good published LC designs: survey-table standouts commonly fall in the 188∼195188\sim195188∼195 dB range (order-of-magnitude statement; corresponding to Feff≈0.008∼0.03F_{eff}\approx0.008\sim0.03Feff​≈0.008∼0.03, which can be back-derived from this page's bound family, e.g. worked example 2's 189189189 dB → an equivalent Q≈5.7Q\approx5.7Q≈5.7). Against their own QQQ-based ceiling (Q=10∼15Q=10\sim15Q=10∼15 → 197.6∼201.2197.6\sim201.2197.6∼201.2 dB, /4 convention), the typical gap is about 5∼105\sim105∼10 dB — eaten by ηP<1\eta_P\lt1ηP​<1, tail/bias noise (F>1+γF\gt1+\gammaF>1+γ), varactor/switch loss (lowering effective QQQ), and layout parasitics. In other words: the LC problem has already been solved to within arm's reach of the physical limit, and every remaining dB costs more than the last. Colpitts vs. LC-tank (Andreani et al., JSSC 2005; external literature, not among the five source PDFs, full citation at page bottom): this paper gives closed-form noise factors for CMOS Colpitts and differential LC-tank oscillators and validates them experimentally, with the well-known conclusion that in CMOS, LC-tank phase-noise performance is at least as good as Colpitts's — Colpitts's cyclostationary advantage (current pulse aligned to the ISF trough; this site's real_oscillator_topologies example 2 estimates roughly a 7 dB reduction in Γeff,rms2\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2Γeff,rms2​) is offset by its bias-efficiency and startup-margin cost. Both topologies sit under the same LC ceiling family (both have an FFF from the 1+γ1+\gamma1+γ family and a 1/Q21/Q^21/Q2 term) — neither can bypass the wall set by QQQ. Ring: this site's example sits only 3.53.53.5 dB below the ring ceiling — the ring's universal form has no QQQ to buy with, and the ceiling itself (168.3 dB) is already about 30 dB below LC's. Turn this "how many dB below the ceiling" question around — compute the FOM a spec needs, pick a topology against the ceiling, then pin it all the way down to component values and bias — see design_recipe. Ring's dB deficit vs. LC, itemized (this site's ring example at 164.8 dB against the LC ideal ceiling at Q=10Q=10Q=10, 197.63 dB, a gap of 32.8332.8332.83 dB; fig_fom_limit.py verifies the itemized terms sum exactly to the total gap): Term Ratio dB Physics No energy storage vs. 2Q22Q^22Q2 (Q=10Q=10Q=10) 200200200 23.023.023.0 LC's high-QQQ storage beats down kTkTkT; the ring discards all its energy and recharges every cycle VDD/Vchar=3V_{DD}/V_{char}=3VDD​/Vchar​=3 333 4.84.84.8 Overdrive/headroom: smaller VcharV_{char}Vchar​ amplifies more noise Leading coefficient 8/38/38/3 8/38/38/3 4.34.34.3 Ring waveform/transition bookkeeping ([P2] Eq.(23)'s 8/(3η)8/(3\eta)8/(3η)) LC waveform term (1+γ)Γrms2(1+\gamma)\Gamma_{rms}^2(1+γ)Γrms2​ 5/65/65/6 0.80.80.8 LC's own FFF and −sin⁡-\sin−sin ISF claw back only a little Total 192019201920 32.832.832.8 =197.63−164.80=197.63-164.80=197.63−164.80 ✓ Actual published LC designs don't hit their ideal ceiling (they give back 5∼105\sim105∼10 dB), so the observed real-world gap is about 25 dB — consistent with "good LC ≈190\approx190≈190, good ring ≈165\approx165≈165." Conclusion: the ring's deficit is not a lack of design effort — it's a structural gap made of QQQ (the 23 dB term) plus VcharV_{char}Vchar​/waveform (about 9 dB); the ring's selling points are area, tuning range, and multi-phase output (see lc_vs_ring).

documents.t: Example 1 (converting this site's ring example to FOM, and locating it relative to the ceiling) Given lc_vs_ring example 1: L=−91.0\mathcal{L}=-91.0L=−91.0 dBc/Hz @ Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, P=1P=1P=1 mW. Find FOM and the distance to the ring ceiling. Step-by-step substitution (with units): 20log⁡10 ⁣(f0Δf)=20log⁡10 ⁣(5×109 Hz106 Hz)=20log⁡10(5000)=73.98 dB,10log⁡10 ⁣(P1 mW)=10log⁡10(1)=0 dB,FOM=−(−91.0)+73.98−0=164.98≈165.0 dB.\begin{aligned} 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\right)&=20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{5\times10^9\ \text{Hz}}{10^6\ \text{Hz}}\right)=20\log_{10}(5000)=73.98\ \text{dB},\\[4pt] 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P}{1\ \text{mW}}\right)&=10\log_{10}(1)=0\ \text{dB},\\[4pt] \mathrm{FOM}&=-(-91.0)+73.98-0=164.98\approx165.0\ \text{dB}. \end{aligned}20log10​(Δff0​​)10log10​(1 mWP​)FOM​=20log10​(106 Hz5×109 Hz​)=20log10​(5000)=73.98 dB,=10log10​(1)=0 dB,=−(−91.0)+73.98−0=164.98≈165.0 dB.​ Result: FOM≈165\mathrm{FOM}\approx165FOM≈165 dB; about 3.53.53.5 dB below the ring ceiling at 168.3168.3168.3 dB (entirely from VDD/Vchar=3V_{DD}/V_{char}=3VDD​/Vchar​=3 vs. the lower bound 2γ=4/32\gamma=4/32γ=4/3), and 9.09.09.0 dB below the reference line at 173.8173.8173.8 dB (Feff=8F_{eff}=8Feff​=8). One-line Python check: import numpy as np print(round(91.0 + 20*np.log10(5e9/1e6) - 10*np.log10(1e-3/1e-3), 2)) # -> 164.98 Example 2 (design back-derivation: reading an "equivalent QQQ" off a measured FOM) An f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz LC VCO burns P=10P=10P=10 mW and measures L(1 MHz)=−125\mathcal{L}(1\ \text{MHz})=-125L(1 MHz)=−125 dBc/Hz. Find FOM, the implied FeffF_{eff}Feff​, and, assuming F=2F=2F=2, Γrms2=12\Gamma_{rms}^2=\tfrac12Γrms2​=21​, ηP=0.5\eta_P=0.5ηP​=0.5 (a more realistic loss assumption), the implied tank QQQ. Step-by-step substitution (with units): FOM=125+20log⁡10(5000)−10log⁡10(10)=125+73.98−10=188.98 dB,Feff=10(Cref−FOM)/10=10(173.83−188.98)/10=10−1.515=0.0305,Q=F Γrms22 Feff ηP=2×0.52×0.0305×0.5=32.7=5.72.\begin{aligned} \mathrm{FOM}&=125+20\log_{10}(5000)-10\log_{10}(10)=125+73.98-10=188.98\ \text{dB},\\[4pt] F_{eff}&=10^{(C_{ref}-\mathrm{FOM})/10}=10^{(173.83-188.98)/10}=10^{-1.515}=0.0305,\\[4pt] Q&=\sqrt{\frac{F\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}{2\,F_{eff}\,\eta_P}} =\sqrt{\frac{2\times0.5}{2\times0.0305\times0.5}}=\sqrt{32.7}=5.72 . \end{aligned}FOMFeff​Q​=125+20log10​(5000)−10log10​(10)=125+73.98−10=188.98 dB,=10(Cref​−FOM)/10=10(173.83−188.98)/10=10−1.515=0.0305,=2Feff​ηP​FΓrms2​​​=2×0.0305×0.52×0.5​​=32.7​=5.72.​ Result: FOM=189.0\mathrm{FOM}=189.0FOM=189.0 dB — a "good design" figure; the implied Q≈5.7Q\approx5.7Q≈5.7 is entirely reasonable on-chip. If the process could give Q=10Q=10Q=10 (ideal ceiling 197.6197.6197.6 dB, /4 convention), this design would sit about 8.78.78.7 dB below its own ceiling — the next thing to check is ηP\eta_PηP​ (class efficiency), tail noise (FFF), and varactor loss, not piling on more current. Dimension check: FeffF_{eff}Feff​ dimensionless (dB difference ÷10 then exponentiated) ✓; everything under the square root is dimensionless → QQQ dimensionless ✓.
