documents.t: Prerequisites: paper_004 (the original, fully worked derivation of [P4] Eq.(28)-(30), p.2129 — this page is a teaching summary and extension of it), fourier_series_of_isf (the ISF's Fourier coefficients and symmetry table, the skeleton for this page's payoff) | Next: subharmonic_injection (the dual story: sub-harmonic injection / multipliers), injection_locking_noise (noise shaping of a locked oscillator, whose framework this page's last section borrows) What this page answers: Why use an injection-locked frequency divider (ILFD) instead of a digital divider? Where does the ÷NNN lock-range formula come from, and which ISF harmonic sets it? Why can a differential, half-wave-symmetric oscillator not divide by 2 in the first place? How do you design around it? How should you account for the phase noise of a divided output — a clean −20log⁡10N-20\log_{10}N−20log10​N, or something else? Physical intuition (the punchline first): an ILFD is not a "division circuit" — it is an oscillator that already runs at f0=finj/Nf_0=f_{inj}/Nf0​=finj​/N, and the injection current gives its phase a small tug once per oscillation cycle, locking it to exactly 1/N1/N1/N of the input. How hard that tug pulls depends on how much content the oscillator's own ISF has at its NNN-th harmonic — this is the first place on this site where [P1] Eq.(12)'s Fourier expansion is genuinely used as a design knob: the ISF's harmonics don't just decide how noise folds back onto the carrier — they also decide whether the divider locks at all.
documents.s: Injection-Locked Frequency Division (ILFD): M:N Sub-/Super-Harmonic Locking and Design

documents.t: High-speed local-oscillator chains (e.g., the first divider stage in an mm-wave PLL) typically choose between: A static digital divider (CML latches, TSPC/D-flip-flop chains; the ÷2 section of quadrature_and_coupled_oscillators already covers this route): every stage must toggle correctly at the full input rate, so dynamic power scales up with input frequency and the process needs comfortable switching margin at that frequency — the closer the input frequency sits to the process limit, the steeper the power and reliability cost. An ILFD (this page's subject): fundamentally an oscillator that runs at its own f0f_0f0​ (not finjf_{inj}finj​); it only needs an injection current, much smaller than its own oscillation amplitude, to "hold" its phase — it never has to toggle logic at the full finjf_{inj}finj​ rate, only oscillate at its own native f0f_0f0​ and let the injection path (often just a capacitor or a small transistor window, not a full toggling stage) tolerate finjf_{inj}finj​. This typically lets an ILFD run cheaper on power and reach higher frequencies as the input approaches the process limit — which is why it is popular as the front divider stage in mm-wave PLLs. Honesty note: the above is standard analog/RF design lore (external knowledge, not a quantitative result from any of the 5 site PDFs); [P4] never gives a power comparison between an ILFD and a static divider. This section is qualitative reasoning only. A quantitative comparison would need to cite a specific process/topology paper (TODO: unverified). What follows is the rigorous math [P4] does give: whether an ILFD locks, and how wide.
documents.s: Why injection-locked division instead of a static divider

documents.t: [P3]'s generalized Adler equation only handles an injection frequency ωinj≈ω0\omega_{inj}\approx\omega_0ωinj​≈ω0​ (fundamental locking). [P4] Sec. IV (Eq.(28)-(30), p.2129, verified against the original PDF on this site; see paper_004 for the complete step-by-step version) generalizes this to an arbitrary rational frequency ratio: under lock, Mωinj=NωoscM\omega_{inj}=N\omega_{osc}Mωinj​=Nωosc​ (M,NM,NM,N coprime positive integers). ILFD is the M=1M=1M=1 special case (output =ωinj/N=\omega_{inj}/N=ωinj​/N, i.e., division); N=1N=1N=1 is the injection-locked frequency multiplier (multiplication). The derivation below is compressed to three steps; see [paper_004] for the full version. Step 1 (re-define the relative phase, Eq.(28)): φ(t)≡MN ωinjt+θ(t)\varphi(t)\equiv\frac{M}{N}\,\omega_{inj}t+\theta(t)φ(t)≡NM​ωinj​t+θ(t) φ\varphiφ is the oscillator's total phase [rad], and θ\thetaθ is the slowly varying phase relative to the injection clock [rad]. A ÷2 ILFD takes M=1,N=2M=1,N=2M=1,N=2: inject at ωinj≈2ω0\omega_{inj}\approx2\omega_0ωinj​≈2ω0​, and the oscillator runs at ωinj/2\omega_{inj}/2ωinj​/2. Step 2 (time-synchronous average over an NTinjNT_{inj}NTinj​ window, Eq.(29)): dθdt=ω0−MNωinj+1NTinj∫NTinjΓ~ ⁣(MNωinjt+θ)iinj(t) dt\frac{d\theta}{dt}=\omega_0-\frac{M}{N}\omega_{inj}+\frac{1}{NT_{inj}}\int_{NT_{inj}}\tilde\Gamma\!\left(\frac{M}{N}\omega_{inj}t+\theta\right)i_{inj}(t)\,dtdtdθ​=ω0​−NM​ωinj​+NTinj​1​∫NTinj​​Γ~(NM​ωinj​t+θ)iinj​(t)dt The window is NTinjNT_{inj}NTinj​ (not TinjT_{inj}Tinj​) because: within the window the injection waveform completes NNN full cycles, and the ISF's argument advances by (M/N) ωinj⋅NTinj=2πM(M/N)\,\omega_{inj}\cdot NT_{inj}=2\pi M(M/N)ωinj​⋅NTinj​=2πM, i.e., MMM full cycles — both are integer numbers of cycles, which is exactly what makes the averaging clean. Step 3 (term-by-term averaging — only the resonant harmonic survives, giving Eq.(30)): take M=1M=1M=1 and a sinusoidal injection iinj=Iinjcos⁡(ωinjt)i_{inj}=I_{inj}\cos(\omega_{inj}t)iinj​=Iinj​cos(ωinj​t), and expand Γ~\tilde\GammaΓ~ as a phasor Fourier series (matching [P1] Eq.(12): ∣Γ~n∣=cn/qmax\vert\tilde\Gamma_n\vert=c_n/q_{max}∣Γ~n​∣=cn​/qmax​, units rad/C). Multiplying term by term and applying the product-to-sum identity, every term except the n=Nn=Nn=N difference-frequency term (whose frequency is exactly 0) completes an integer number of cycles over the NTinjNT_{inj}NTinj​ window and averages exactly to zero — this is an identity, not "approximately small" (lab_37 below verifies it numerically to 10−1510^{-15}10−15). The one surviving term: Ω(θ)=12 Iinj ∣Γ~N∣cos⁡ ⁣(Nθ+∠Γ~N)\Omega(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\,I_{inj}\,\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vert\cos\!\big(N\theta+\angle\tilde\Gamma_N\big)Ω(θ)=21​Iinj​∣Γ~N​∣cos(Nθ+∠Γ~N​) Reading it: only the oscillator's ISF NNN-th harmonic ∣Γ~N∣\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vert∣Γ~N​∣ responds to injection at the NNN-th superharmonic — not the fundamental ∣Γ~1∣\vert\tilde\Gamma_1\vert∣Γ~1​∣, and not any other harmonic. ÷2 uses ∣Γ~2∣\vert\tilde\Gamma_2\vert∣Γ~2​∣ (i.e., c2c_2c2​); ÷3 uses ∣Γ~3∣\vert\tilde\Gamma_3\vert∣Γ~3​∣ (i.e., c3c_3c3​).

documents.t: Look back at the symmetry table in Step 7 of fourier_series_of_isf: half-wave symmetry Γ(x+π)=−Γ(x)\Gamma(x+\pi)=-\Gamma(x)Γ(x+π)=−Γ(x) ⟹ the even harmonics c2=c4=⋯=0c_2=c_4=\dots=0c2​=c4​=⋯=0. Substitute into ωL=Iinjc2/(2qmax)\omega_L=I_{inj}c_2/(2q_{max})ωL​=Iinj​c2​/(2qmax​): the ÷2 lock range is identically zero — to first order, no matter how large you make IinjI_{inj}Iinj​, an injection at 2f02f_02f0​ simply will not lock. This is the same symmetry table telling two different stories: on the phase-noise side (white_noise_to_phase_noise) it's good news — noise near 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ does not fold back onto the carrier; on the ILFD side it's bad news — symmetry is a double-edged sword. An ideal differential LC VCO's differential output nodes are exactly this case (c2≈0c_2\approx0c2​≈0). The design way out is to change the injection node — the ISF is "one curve per injection node" (as in [P1]); differential outputs are symmetric, but certain internal nodes are naturally asymmetric — the next section covers this in detail.

documents.t: "Half-wave symmetry can't divide by 2" is not a death sentence — it's a hint that the injection node needs to change. Two routes: Break the half-wave symmetry itself: half-wave symmetry Γ(x+π)=−Γ(x)\Gamma(x+\pi)=-\Gamma(x)Γ(x+π)=−Γ(x) requires that the "rising half-cycle" and "falling half-cycle" of the waveform be mirror-image, opposite-sign copies of each other — a differential, push-pull node naturally satisfies this (two complementary switching events, opposite polarity, half a period apart). A single-ended node typically does not: a period often contains only one dominant sensitivity event (e.g., the CMOS ring-inverter stage derived in real_oscillator_topologies section (c): the ISF concentrates in a single transition window, not two mirror-image windows), or the rise and fall edges' slope and timing are simply not symmetric to begin with (the Colpitts case in the same page's section (b)). Such topologies do not automatically satisfy Γ(x+π)=−Γ(x)\Gamma(x+\pi)=-\Gamma(x)Γ(x+π)=−Γ(x), and c2c_2c2​ is naturally nonzero — this is the mechanism behind "asymmetric/single-ended topologies are easier to divide by 2." Move to a node that is naturally asymmetric — tail injection at 2f02f_02f0​: a differential LC VCO's differential output is symmetric with c2≈0c_2\approx0c2​≈0, but section (a) of real_oscillator_topologies already works out that the tail node's effective ISF is rich in c2c_2c2​: because the switching pair "flips" the tail current twice per cycle, the tail node voltage naturally swings at 2ω02\omega_02ω0​, and Γtail(θ)=c02+c1,rescos⁡θ+c2cos⁡2θ\Gamma_{tail}(\theta)=\tfrac{c_0}{2}+c_{1,res}\cos\theta+c_2\cos2\thetaΓtail​(θ)=2c0​​+c1,res​cosθ+c2​cos2θ takes c2=0.55c_2=0.55c2​=0.55 in that page's illustrative model — much larger c2c_2c2​ content than the tank's c1=1,c2=0c_1=1,c_2=0c1​=1,c2​=0. [P4]'s own ÷2 experiments inject 2f02f_02f0​ precisely into the tail of a differential LC (Fig. 11(a)(b) caption and Fig. 12(d), p.2130-2131, verified) — matching, independently, what real_oscillator_topologies already establishes as "the tail is where c2c_2c2​ lives": that page discusses the same c2c_2c2​ folding back tail noise; this page uses the very same c2c_2c2​ for active injection locking — two sides of one coin. Design-knob summary: To make ÷2 lock, find a node not protected by differential symmetry to inject into (the tail, or an auxiliary single-ended node). If that node is also the source of c2c_2c2​ fold-back noise (as the tail is), you're "borrowing the same weakness" — injection locking uses it to help divide, but during normal operation it is also folding 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ noise back; the frequency a tail filter (see real_oscillator_topologies) normally wants to filter out is exactly the frequency you want to inject for locking — these two need to be designed with time- or frequency-domain separation, not left to fight each other. Single-ended topologies (ring inverters, Colpitts) already have nonzero c2c_2c2​, making ÷2 ILFD relatively easy — but note that their Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and c0c_0c0​ characteristics (sections (b)(c) of real_oscillator_topologies) come along for the ride too; you don't get to cherry-pick only the c2c_2c2​ term.
documents.s: Design notes: how to create c2c_2c2​ so ÷2 can lock

documents.t: The previous section said "single-ended topologies naturally have nonzero c2c_2c2​"; [P4] Sec. VII-A (p.2132–2134) upgrades that remark into a knob you can design on purpose: in a single-ended inverter-chain ring the rising and falling edges can be set independently through the PMOS/NMOS widths, so deliberately making them asymmetric enlarges the ISF's even harmonics (above all c2c_2c2​) and widens the ÷2 lock range dramatically. Three steps: first prove "why half-wave symmetry cancels exactly" once more, in the time domain (footnote 14 ⟹ Fig. 15(a)); then state the formal definition of the upper lock-range edge (footnote 15 ⟹ Fig. 15(b)); finally use the three 17-stage ring designs of Table IV as a worked example.
documents.s: [P4] Sec. VII-A: ISF shaping — "manufacturing" c2c_2c2​ with waveform asymmetry (Fig. 15–16, Table IV, p.2132–2134)

documents.t: [P4] footnote 14, p.2132 writes the mathematical definition of "rise/fall symmetry of the waveform" as Γ~(x)=−Γ~(x+π)\tilde\Gamma(x)=-\tilde\Gamma(x+\pi)Γ~(x)=−Γ~(x+π) (for all xxx). So two consecutive injection cycles = two consecutive oscillation half-cycles deliver phase kicks of equal size and opposite sign, and the average over the NTinj=ToscNT_{inj}=T_{osc}NTinj​=Tosc​ window is exactly 0 — for every θ\thetaθ (θ\thetaθ is only a shift and does not alter the relation p(t+Tinj)=−p(t)p(t+T_{inj})=-p(t)p(t+Tinj​)=−p(t)). This is the bottom panel of Fig. 15(a): the red positive lobe and the blue negative lobe have equal area and the green average line sits on 0. It is the time-domain twin of the "c2=0c_2=0c2​=0" payoff section above: the frequency domain says "the even harmonics vanish," the time domain says "the half-cycles cancel" — one and the same statement. Generalization: every even NNN behaves the same way — shift time by half an oscillation period Tosc/2=(N/2) TinjT_{osc}/2=(N/2)\,T_{inj}Tosc​/2=(N/2)Tinj​: iinji_{inj}iinj​ (period TinjT_{inj}Tinj​) is unchanged while the ISF argument advances by π\piπ and flips sign, so to first order the ÷2, ÷4, ÷6, … lock ranges all vanish under half-wave symmetry; odd NNN is not constrained (Tosc/2T_{osc}/2Tosc​/2 is not an integer multiple of TinjT_{inj}Tinj​, so iinji_{inj}iinj​ also flips sign under the shift and the product does not).

documents.t: [P4] footnote 15, p.2133 defines the upper edge of the lock range as the maximum over θ\thetaθ of the averaged term of Eq.(29): ωL+:=max⁡θ⟨Γ~ ⁣(ωinjNt+θ) iinj(t)⟩NTinj≡⟨Γ~ ⁣(ωinjNt+θu) iinj(t)⟩NTinj\omega_L^{+}:=\max_{\theta}\Big\langle\tilde\Gamma\!\Big(\frac{\omega_{inj}}{N}t+\theta\Big)\,i_{inj}(t)\Big\rangle_{NT_{inj}} \equiv\Big\langle\tilde\Gamma\!\Big(\frac{\omega_{inj}}{N}t+\theta_u\Big)\,i_{inj}(t)\Big\rangle_{NT_{inj}}ωL+​:=θmax​⟨Γ~(Nωinj​​t+θ)iinj​(t)⟩NTinj​​≡⟨Γ~(Nωinj​​t+θu​)iinj​(t)⟩NTinj​​ θu\theta_uθu​ is the relative phase that attains the maximum; ⟨⋅⟩NTinj\langle\cdot\rangle_{NT_{inj}}⟨⋅⟩NTinj​​ is the time average over an NTinjNT_{inj}NTinj​ window. This definition assumes neither a sinusoidal injection nor the linear regime — it is simply "take the injection term of Eq.(29) and maximize over θ\thetaθ." For a sinusoidal injection in the linear regime it reduces to this page's Eq.(30) result ωL+=12Iinj∣Γ~N∣\omega_L^{+}=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vertωL+​=21​Iinj​∣Γ~N​∣ (dimension check: rad/C × A = rad/s ✓). The picture in Fig. 15(b): once the waveform is asymmetric, the two injection cycles inside one oscillation period deliver kicks of unequal size (red lobe larger than blue lobe), the net phase no longer cancels and the green line leaves 0 — that offset is ωL+\omega_L^{+}ωL+​. [P4] p.2133 adds: for a fixed ISF amplitude (footnote 16: the ISF amplitude scales roughly inversely with the injection node's charge swing), the more pronounced the asymmetry, the larger the frequency deviation a given injection produces at a given θ\thetaθ, and hence the wider the lock range; the logic extends directly to higher even harmonics. This site's toy reproduction (pedagogical toy, not transistor-level): simulations/fig_isf_shaping_division.py caricatures a single-ended inverter-stage ISF as "two Gaussian pulses per period" (a negative pulse at the falling edge, a positive pulse at the rising edge; pulse height and width are both taken proportional to that edge's transition time — ISF peak ∝ 1/slope, width ∝ transition time, i.e. the ring picture of [P2] Sec. documents.t: [P4] Eq.(28)'s general M:NM:NM:N form actually describes a pair of mirror-image relationships; this site has only fully verified and derived the M=1M=1M=1 (division) half. Swapping the roles of MMM and NNN reveals the duality: ÷NNN (ILFD, this page, M=1M=1M=1) ×MMM (injection-locked multiplier, N=1N=1N=1) Lock condition M=1⇒ωosc=ωinj/NM=1\Rightarrow\omega_{osc}=\omega_{inj}/NM=1⇒ωosc​=ωinj​/N N=1⇒ωosc=M ωinjN=1\Rightarrow\omega_{osc}=M\,\omega_{inj}N=1⇒ωosc​=Mωinj​ Who must supply the harmonic The oscillator's ISF supplies the NNN-th harmonic ∣Γ~N∣\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vert∣Γ~N​∣; the injection itself only needs its fundamental cos⁡(ωinjt)\cos(\omega_{inj}t)cos(ωinj​t) The injection waveform must supply its own MMM-th harmonic; the ISF only needs its fundamental ∣Γ~1∣\vert\tilde\Gamma_1\vert∣Γ~1​∣ How it's built A plain sinusoidal current injection is enough (NNN-th-order content all comes from the ISF's own Fourier expansion) A pure sinusoid has no M≥2M\ge2M≥2 harmonics, so in practice they must be generated by mixing inside the oscillator — [P4] footnote 10, p.2129 explicitly states this is not captured by the Eq.(28)-(30) framework (partially handled by its reference [25]) Lock-range formula ωL=12Iinj∣Γ~N∣\omega_L=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vertωL​=21​Iinj​∣Γ~N​∣ (this page's Eq.(30), verified) Depends on the internal mixing gain; no closed form of this kind (beyond what this site has verified) Duality in one line: a divider outsources the work to the oscillator's own spectral content (ISF harmonics); a multiplier instead needs the injection signal to already have high-order harmonics — and "making a sinusoid grow harmonics" is exactly the problem subharmonic_injection works through (sub-harmonic injection / multipliers, and how they generate the needed MMM-th harmonic drive in practice). Both pages share the same formula skeleton ([P4] Eq.(28)) — the only difference is which side the harmonic content lives on.

documents.t: clock_chain_budget Rule 2 rigorously derives the phase accounting for an ideal ÷NNN (edge-picking — the divider only discards edges, it never moves them): ϕout=ϕin/N⇒Lout=Lin−20log⁡10N\phi_{out}=\phi_{in}/N\Rightarrow\mathcal{L}_{out}=\mathcal{L}_{in}-20\log_{10}Nϕout​=ϕin​/N⇒Lout​=Lin​−20log10​N. That page's "Relationship to [P4]" callout already points out that the ÷NNN phase accounting (ϕ/N\phi/Nϕ/N) also holds for the ILFD's carrier path — and the reason lies right here, in this page's Eq.(28): with M=1M=1M=1, φ(t)=ωinjt/N+θ(t)\varphi(t)=\omega_{inj}t/N+\theta(t)φ(t)=ωinj​t/N+θ(t), and θ\thetaθ is a bounded, slowly varying quantity within the lock range, so the deterministic carrier-frequency relationship ωout=ωinj/N\omega_{out}=\omega_{inj}/Nωout​=ωinj​/N is itself an exact 1/N1/N1/N scaling — the same statement as clock_chain_budget Rule 2's ϕout=ϕin/N\phi_{out}=\phi_{in}/Nϕout​=ϕin​/N, just with a whole locked oscillator standing in for the logic gate. But an ILFD is not a pure edge-picking machine — it is a locked oscillator — which is exactly the part clock_chain_budget honestly leaves open: "near the edge of the lock range, an ILFD has its own noise behavior." That other half connects to the framework of injection_locking_noise, which proves, for fundamental locking (M=N=1M=N=1M=N=1), that a locked oscillator's own noise is high-pass shaped, with corner defined as ωc≡−Ω′(θss)\omega_c\equiv-\Omega'(\theta_{ss})ωc​≡−Ω′(θss​) (the slope of the lock characteristic at the stable point). Applying that same definition to this page's M:NM:NM:N version, Ω(θ)=12Iinj∣Γ~N∣cos⁡(Nθ+∠Γ~N)\Omega(\theta)=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vert\cos(N\theta+\angle\tilde\Gamma_N)Ω(θ)=21​Iinj​∣Γ~N​∣cos(Nθ+∠Γ~N​): Ω′(θ)=−N ωLsin⁡ ⁣(Nθ+∠Γ~N)⟹ωc=∣Ω′(θss)∣=N ωL1−(ΔωωL)2=NωL2−Δω2\Omega'(\theta)=-N\,\omega_L\sin\!\big(N\theta+\angle\tilde\Gamma_N\big) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \omega_c=\big\vert\Omega'(\theta_{ss})\big\vert=N\,\omega_L\sqrt{1-\Big(\frac{\Delta\omega}{\omega_L}\Big)^{2}}=N\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}Ω′(θ)=−NωL​sin(Nθ+∠Γ~N​)⟹ωc​=​Ω′(θss​)​=NωL​1−(ωL​Δω​)2​=NωL2​−Δω2​ (using the lock condition cos⁡(Nθss+∠Γ~N)=Δω/ωL\cos(N\theta_{ss}+\angle\tilde\Gamma_N)=\Delta\omega/\omega_Lcos(Nθss​+∠Γ~N​)=Δω/ωL​. Dimension check: ωL\omega_LωL​ is rad/s, NNN is dimensionless ⟹ ωc\omega_cωc​ is rad/s ✓.) This ωc\omega_cωc​ is exactly the already-verified pull-in frequency ωp=NωL2−Δω2\omega_p=N\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωp​=NωL2​−Δω2​ of [P4] Eq.(32) — not a coincidence, but the same fact: applying injection_locking_noise's general principle "the noise corner is the restoring force of the lock characteristic" to the M:NM:NM:N version of Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ) automatically reproduces the paper's own already-verified transient time constant. The design picture that joins the two halves: Offset frequency ≪ωc\ll\omega_c≪ωc​ (inside the loop bandwidth): θ\thetaθ tracks the injection source closely, and the carrier-path accounting ϕout=ϕin/N\phi_{out}=\phi_{in}/Nϕout​=ϕin​/N holds — the output inherits the phase noise of the injection source (the upstream finjf_{inj}finj​ clock), echoing, in magnitude, the −20log⁡10N-20\log_{10}N−20log10​N intuition of clock_chain_budget Rule 2 (think of "−20log⁡10N-20\log_{10}N−20log10​N" as "the carrier is deterministically divided by NNN," not as "the divider actively suppresses noise"). Offset frequency ≫ωc\gg\omega_c≫ωc​ (outside the loop bandwidth): θ\thetaθ can no longer keep up, and the ILFD's own free-running phase noise (its own Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​, the familiar [P1] Eq.(21)) dominates the output through the high-pass Sn/(ωc2+ω2)S_n/(\omega_c^2+\omega^2)Sn​/(ωc2​+ω2) — here −20log⁡10N-20\log_{10}N−20log10​N no longer applies, and the output noise is set by the quality of the ILFD oscillator itself. The closer to the edge of the lock range (Δω→ωL\Delta\omega\to\omega_LΔω→ωL​), the smaller ωc→0\omega_c\to0ωc​→0 becomes — the high-pass corner retreats to lower frequency and the suppression bandwidth shrinks. This is the same honest reminder as clock_chain_budget Rule 4's "the divider's own noise floor": a real ILFD has its own noise floor too, and the output can never be better than the ILFD's own noise behavior at that offset frequency.

documents.t: An ILFD is a locked oscillator, not a logic divider: it locks its phase to ωinj/N\omega_{inj}/Nωinj​/N via injection current, without needing to switch logic at the full finjf_{inj}finj​ rate — the qualitative reason it saves power as a high-frequency front-end stage. The math of locking ([P4] Eq.(28)-(30), p.2129, verified): time-synchronous averaging over an NTinjNT_{inj}NTinj​ window keeps only the ISF's NNN-th harmonic, giving Ω(θ)=12Iinj∣Γ~N∣cos⁡(Nθ+∠Γ~N)\Omega(\theta)=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vert\cos(N\theta+\angle\tilde\Gamma_N)Ω(θ)=21​Iinj​∣Γ~N​∣cos(Nθ+∠Γ~N​), with lock range ωL=12Iinj∣Γ~N∣=IinjcN/(2qmax)\omega_L=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vert=I_{inj}c_N/(2q_{max})ωL​=21​Iinj​∣Γ~N​∣=Iinj​cN​/(2qmax​) — the division ratio NNN only picks the harmonic, it does not enter the formula; there are NNN locked phases spaced 2π/N2\pi/N2π/N apart that are mutually indistinguishable. The payoff: half-wave symmetry ⇒c2=c4=⋯=0⇒\Rightarrow c_2=c_4=\dots=0\Rightarrow⇒c2​=c4​=⋯=0⇒ the ÷2/÷4 lock range is identically zero to first order — a differential output node cannot divide by 2; the way out is to inject into an asymmetric node (the tail, or an auxiliary single-ended node) instead. lab_37: the unaveraged ODE directly verifies the averaging identity to 10−1510^{-15}10−15, measured lock ranges match theory at a ratio of 1.00-1.03, the c2=0c_2=0c2​=0 case locks at 0/61 grid points, and the 2π/N2\pi/N2π/N degeneracy is visible to the naked eye. Creating c2c_2c2​ by design: break half-wave symmetry (single-ended/asymmetric topologies naturally have nonzero c2c_2c2​) or move the injection node (a differential LC VCO's tail is naturally rich in c2c_2c2​ — the same mechanism as tail-noise fold-back, seen from the other side). ISF shaping ([P4] Sec. VII-A, p.2132–2134): in the time domain, half-wave symmetry = the phase kicks of consecutive injection cycles cancel exactly, independent of θ\thetaθ (footnote 14); once symmetry is broken a net phase accrues, with upper lock-range edge ωL+=max⁡θ⟨Γ~ iinj⟩NTinj\omega_L^{+}=\max_\theta\langle\tilde\Gamma\,i_{inj}\rangle_{NT_{inj}}ωL+​=maxθ​⟨Γ~iinj​⟩NTinj​​ (footnote 15); Table IV: changing WP/WNW_P/W_NWP​/WN​ of a 17-stage single-ended ring enlarges ∣Γ~2∣\vert\tilde\Gamma_2\vert∣Γ~2​∣ by 15–23× (two factors: harmonic fraction × overall Γ~rms\tilde\Gamma_{rms}Γ~rms​), and the simulated 1.5 mA ÷2 lock range goes 16 → 560 / 710 MHz (strong injection, 2.6–5.9× above linear); c0c_0c0​ grows too, but inside lock the close-in noise is dominated by the injection, so the price is acceptable. Duality: division (M=1M=1M=1) spends the oscillator's own ISF harmonics; multiplication (N=1N=1N=1) needs the injection signal's own harmonics — a sinusoidal injection has none, so internal mixing is required, which is outside this framework (see subharmonic_injection). Noise: the carrier-path accounting ϕout=ϕin/N\phi_{out}=\phi_{in}/Nϕout​=ϕin​/N holds for an ILFD (echoing clock_chain_budget Rule 2's −20log⁡10N-20\log_{10}N−20log10​N); but beyond the loop bandwidth ωc=NωL2−Δω2\omega_c=N\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωc​=NωL2​−Δω2​ (exactly [P4] Eq.(32)'s pull-in frequency), the output noise is set by the ILFD's own free-running phase noise, high-pass shaped — not a simple −20log⁡10N-20\log_{10}N−20log10​N.

documents.t: Prerequisites: paper_003 ([P3] generalized Adler, lock characteristic), white_noise_to_phase_noise (the machine that turns white noise into 1/f21/f^21/f2), lorentzian_linewidth (what a free-running oscillator is doing near the carrier) | Next: quadrature_and_coupled_oscillators (mutual injection = two coupled Adler equations), pll_noise_budget (how a second-order loop keeps the books). paper_003 covered "whether it locks at all" (lock range, stability). This page covers the other two dividends left in that [P3] equation: What this page answers: Once locked, where does the oscillator's own phase noise go? How much is it suppressed, and up to what frequency? (Part A) Why does "still locked" not mean "still clean" — what is this vanishing suppression at the lock edge? (Part A) When it does not lock (∣Δω∣>ωL\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert \gt \omega_L∣Δω∣>ωL​), what does the spectrum look like? Why a comb of spacing ωb\omega_bωb​, growing on only one side? Where does ωb=Δω2−ωL2\omega_b=\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}ωb​=Δω2−ωL2​​ come from? (Part B) Physical intuition (conclusion first): an injection-locked oscillator is a first-order PLL — the injection supplies a restoring force that pulls the phase back to the lock point, and the strength of that restoring force (units rad/s) is the loop bandwidth. So: self-noise below the frequency the restoring force can track gets flattened (high-pass shaping), reference noise below that same frequency is copied through wholesale (low-pass); the restoring force ωc=ωLcos⁡θss\omega_c=\omega_L\cos\theta_{ss}ωc​=ωL​cosθss​ is strongest dead center in the lock range and vanishes at the edges. When it fails to lock, the restoring force loses to the detuning, and the phase slides around in a "dwell-then-slip" sawtooth, spitting out one sideband per revolution — that's the pulling comb spectrum. Where this page sits: an advanced design page. The phase equation itself ([P3] Eq.(26)/(28)–(30)/(33)–(35)/(38)–(40)) and the beat frequency ([P4] Eq.(31)–(34)) have both been verified against the original PDFs; putting noise into the Adler equation and reading off the shaped PSD is textbook-standard but is not in the derivations of the five source PDFs on this site ([P4] p.2130 explicitly points its noise analysis to its own reference [29, Ch. 7], i.e. Hong's PhD thesis; the classic source is Kurokawa 1973, see the external-literature list at the end); this page derives it from scratch and cross-checks with simulation.

Which one is stable? Following [P3]'s stability criterion (Eq.(38)–(39), p.2115): substitute θ=θ0+θ^\theta=\theta_0+\hat\thetaθ=θ0​+θ^, expand to first order in Taylor series, giving dθ^/dt=Ω′(θ0)θ^d\hat\theta/dt=\Omega'(\theta_0)\hat\thetadθ^/dt=Ω′(θ0​)θ^; stable ⟺ Ω′(θ0)<0\Omega'(\theta_0)\lt0Ω′(θ0​)<0. Here Ω′(θ)=−ωLcos⁡θ\Omega'(\theta)=-\omega_L\cos\thetaΩ′(θ)=−ωL​cosθ, so the stable branch is cos⁡θss>0\cos\theta_{ss}\gt0cosθss​>0, i.e. the principal value θss=arcsin⁡(Δω/ωL)∈(−π/2,π/2)\theta_{ss}=\arcsin(\Delta\omega/\omega_L)\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)θss​=arcsin(Δω/ωL​)∈(−π/2,π/2); the other solution is unstable. Mechanical analogy: the tilted washboard. The classical Adler equation dθ/dt=Δω−ωLsin⁡θd\theta/dt=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\thetadθ/dt=Δω−ωL​sinθ is exactly the equation of motion of a ball rolling under overdamped dynamics (inertia negligible, velocity proportional to force) in the potential U(θ)=−Δω⋅θ−ωLcos⁡θU(\theta)=-\Delta\omega\cdot\theta-\omega_L\cos\thetaU(θ)=−Δω⋅θ−ωL​cosθ — overdamped particles obey dθ/dt=−dU/dθd\theta/dt=-dU/d\thetadθ/dt=−dU/dθ, and substituting confirms −dU/dθ=Δω−ωLsin⁡θ-dU/d\theta=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\theta−dU/dθ=Δω−ωL​sinθ ✓. U(θ)U(\theta)U(θ) is a "cosine corrugation" riding on a linear ramp: the ramp's slope is set by Δω\Delta\omegaΔω, the corrugation depth by ωL\omega_LωL​ — hence "tilted washboard." When r≡Δω/ωL<1r\equiv\Delta\omega/\omega_L\lt1r≡Δω/ωL​<1 the ramp is not steep enough to wash out the corrugation, so local dips (wells) remain and the ball falls into one and stops — this is exactly the geometric meaning of θss\theta_{ss}θss​ above. When r>1r\gt1r>1 the ramp overwhelms the corrugation, the wells vanish entirely, and the ball never stops rolling — corresponding to the pulling case in Part B below. The animation below turns this intuition into something you can drive interactively and watch cycle slips happen live: Adler tilted-washboard animation (mechanical analogy: a ball rolling in U(θ) = −Δω·θ − ω_L·cos θ) Δω / ω_L (r)0.60 noise strength0.00 state LOCKED (settling…) r < 1 well center θ* 36.9 deg cycle slips 0 count -2π-1π0π1πU(θ) = −Δω·θ − ω_L·cos θ PauseReset Reading the animation: the curve is the tilted washboard potential U(θ); the ball's horizontal position is the Adler phase θ, and it always rolls "downhill" (dθ/dt = −dU/dθ = Δω − ω_L sin θ, this page's boxed classical Adler equation). At r = Δω/ω_L < 1 the tilt is gentle enough that U(θ) still has local wells — the ball settles into one and stops: that is lock. At r > 1 the tilt has washed the wells out entirely — the ball rolls forever, one full 2π "slip" per beat period T_b = 2π/ω_b (ω_b = √(Δω²−ω_L²), derived in Part B below). Turning up "noise strength" adds a random-walk kick to dθ/dt each frame; near r ≈ 1 an unlucky kick can shove the ball out of a shallowing well before it would otherwise settle — each such escape is one cycle slip, counted live above. Model: pedagogical mechanical analogy (overdamped particle in a periodic tilted potential), not a literal circuit. ω_L fixed at 1 (normalized units); Δω = r·ω_L. Numerical integration: explicit Euler sub-stepped 4× per frame for stability; noise is a scaled sum-of-uniforms random-walk term (not exact Gaussian white noise, but statistically close for this illustration).

documents.t: The oscillator's own device noise current in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) runs through the same ISF machine ([P1] Eq.(11); [P3] Eq.(28)'s Γ~⋅i\tilde\Gamma\cdot iΓ~⋅i holds equally for a noise current). For white noise, after ISF-weighted averaging over one period it becomes equivalent to a white frequency-noise (white FM) drive n(t)n(t)n(t) added to the right-hand side of the Adler equation: dθdt=Δω−ωLsin⁡θ+n(t),\frac{d\theta}{dt}=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\theta+n(t),dtdθ​=Δω−ωL​sinθ+n(t), where n(t)n(t)n(t) [rad/s] has one-sided PSD denoted SnS_nSn​, units rad²/s (= (rad/s)²/Hz). This is exactly the drive that grows the 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt of a free-running oscillator: remove the injection (ωL=0\omega_L=0ωL​=0), so ϕ=∫n dt\phi=\int n\,dtϕ=∫ndt, and the transfer-function bookkeeping (one-sided in, one-sided out) gives Sϕ,free(ω)=Snω2,Sn=Γrms2qmax2 in2‾ΔfS_{\phi,free}(\omega)=\frac{S_n}{\omega^2},\qquad S_n=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\,\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}Sϕ,free​(ω)=ω2Sn​​,Sn​=qmax2​Γrms2​​Δfin2​​​ (the same result as the time-domain derivation in white_noise_to_phase_noise, Sϕ=Γrms2Si/(qmax2ω2)S_\phi=\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/(q_{max}^2\omega^2)Sϕ​=Γrms2​Si​/(qmax2​ω2) — the time-domain-/2/2/2-convention branch of it). Canonical numbers (true LC: Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC): Sn=0.5×10−24/10−24=0.5S_n=0.5\times10^{-24}/10^{-24}=0.5Sn​=0.5×10−24/10−24=0.5 rad²/s — this is exactly the value used by lab_26 (with the representative value Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5 it would be Sn=0.25S_n=0.25Sn​=0.25 rad²/s). Unit check: (−)2C2⋅A2Hz=A2sC2=1s\dfrac{(-)^2}{\text{C}^2}\cdot\dfrac{\text{A}^2}{\text{Hz}}=\dfrac{\text{A}^2\text{s}}{\text{C}^2}=\dfrac{1}{\text{s}}C2(−)2​⋅HzA2​=C2A2s​=s1​ (i.e. rad²/s) ✓. Linearization. When solidly locked, θ\thetaθ only dithers a little around θss\theta_{ss}θss​. Let θ=θss+δθ\theta=\theta_{ss}+\delta\thetaθ=θss​+δθ, sin⁡(θss+δθ)≈sin⁡θss+cos⁡θss⋅δθ\sin(\theta_{ss}+\delta\theta)\approx\sin\theta_{ss}+\cos\theta_{ss}\cdot\delta\thetasin(θss​+δθ)≈sinθss​+cosθss​⋅δθ, and Δω−ωLsin⁡θss=0\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\theta_{ss}=0Δω−ωL​sinθss​=0 cancels the constant term: d(δθ)dt=−ωc δθ+n(t),ωc≡ωLcos⁡θss=ωL2−Δω2 \boxed{\ \frac{d(\delta\theta)}{dt}=-\omega_c\,\delta\theta+n(t),\qquad \omega_c\equiv\omega_L\cos\theta_{ss}=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}\ } dtd(δθ)​=−ωc​δθ+n(t),ωc​≡ωL​cosθss​=ωL2​−Δω2​ ​ (the second equality uses cos⁡θss=1−(Δω/ωL)2\cos\theta_{ss}=\sqrt{1-(\Delta\omega/\omega_L)^2}cosθss​=1−(Δω/ωL​)2​, taking the positive root on the stable branch.) This ωc\omega_cωc​ is not a new object: it is exactly the pull-in frequency ωp:=−Ω′(θ0)\omega_p:=-\Omega'(\theta_0)ωp​:=−Ω′(θ0​) defined at [P3] Eq.(40), p.2115 (substitute Ω′=−ωLcos⁡θ\Omega'=-\omega_L\cos\thetaΩ′=−ωL​cosθ to get it), and it is also ωp=NωL2−Δω2\omega_p=N\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωp​=NωL2​−Δω2​ at [P4] Eq.(32), p.2130, with N=1N=1N=1. [P3] uses it to describe "how fast a perturbation decays" (θ^∝e−t/τp\hat\theta\propto e^{-t/\tau_p}θ^∝e−t/τp​, τp=1/ωp\tau_p=1/\omega_pτp​=1/ωp​); what we're saying now is: the same frequency is the corner of the noise shaping. And this correspondence is general: for any injection waveform, any topology, the noise-shaping corner =−Ω′(θss)=-\Omega'(\theta_{ss})=−Ω′(θss​) — the slope of the lock characteristic at the lock point.

documents.t: Fourier-transforming the linearized equation (δθ→Θ(ω)\delta\theta\to\Theta(\omega)δθ→Θ(ω), n→N(ω)n\to N(\omega)n→N(ω)): jω Θ=−ωc Θ+N⟹Θ(ω)=N(ω)ωc+jω⟹ Sθ(ω)=Snωc2+ω2 j\omega\,\Theta=-\omega_c\,\Theta+N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Theta(\omega)=\frac{N(\omega)}{\omega_c+j\omega} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\ S_\theta(\omega)=\frac{S_n}{\omega_c^2+\omega^2}\ }jωΘ=−ωc​Θ+N⟹Θ(ω)=ωc​+jωN(ω)​⟹ Sθ​(ω)=ωc2​+ω2Sn​​ ​ This is the Lorentzian PSD of an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. Dimension check: rad2/s1/s2=rad2⋅s=rad2/Hz\dfrac{\text{rad}^2/\text{s}}{1/\text{s}^2}=\text{rad}^2\cdot\text{s}=\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}1/s2rad2/s​=rad2⋅s=rad2/Hz ✓. Factor-of-2 discipline: Sθ=Sn/(ωc2+ω2)S_\theta=S_n/(\omega_c^2+\omega^2)Sθ​=Sn​/(ωc2​+ω2) is transfer-function bookkeeping "same side in, same side out" — SnS_nSn​ one-sided in gives SθS_\thetaSθ​ one-sided out (this page and its simulations are one-sided throughout); switch to two-sided and both sides just pick up a factor of 1/21/21/2, the formula shape is unchanged. And the suppression ratio Sθ/Sϕ,free=ω2/(ωc2+ω2)S_\theta/S_{\phi,free}=\omega^2/(\omega_c^2+\omega^2)Sθ​/Sϕ,free​=ω2/(ωc2​+ω2) cancels SnS_nSn​ entirely — it is independent of any one-sided/two-sided or /2/2/2//4/4/4 convention — the simulation measures the corner from this ratio, which is the cleanest way. Three limits, three sentences: ω≫ωc\omega\gg\omega_cω≫ωc​: Sθ→Sn/ω2=Sϕ,freeS_\theta\to S_n/\omega^2=S_{\phi,free}Sθ​→Sn​/ω2=Sϕ,free​ — far from the carrier, it is identical to free-running. The restoring force from the injection (bandwidth ωc\omega_cωc​) can't track fast jitter — it has no effect there. ω≪ωc\omega\ll\omega_cω≪ωc​: Sθ→Sn/ωc2S_\theta\to S_n/\omega_c^2Sθ​→Sn​/ωc2​ = a finite plateau. The free-running 1/f21/f^21/f2 divergence as ω→0\omega\to0ω→0 has been "cured" by locking: the phase no longer random-walks — it's pinned to θss\theta_{ss}θss​ with finite dither. (Compare with lorentzian_linewidth: the free-running case turns the divergence into a finite Lorentzian peak via "linewidth," but the variance still grows without bound over time; locking genuinely pins the variance to a constant — two different "cures.") Crossover ω=ωc\omega=\omega_cω=ωc​: the suppression ratio is exactly 1/21/21/2 (−3-3−3 dB) — the operational definition of the corner, and the simulation measures it this way. Total phase variance (one-sided integral): σθ2=∫0∞Snωc2+(2πf)2 df=Sn2π⋅π2ωc=Sn4ωc.\sigma_\theta^2=\int_0^\infty \frac{S_n}{\omega_c^2+(2\pi f)^2}\,df =\frac{S_n}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2\omega_c}=\frac{S_n}{4\omega_c}.σθ2​=∫0∞​ωc2​+(2πf)2Sn​​df=2πSn​​⋅2ωc​π​=4ωc​Sn​​. Numerically (lab_26 case A: Sn=0.5S_n=0.5Sn​=0.5 rad²/s, ωc=2π×5×106\omega_c=2\pi\times5\times10^6ωc​=2π×5×106 rad/s): σθ2=0.5/(4×3.14×107)=3.98×10−9\sigma_\theta^2=0.5/(4\times3.14\times10^7)=3.98\times10^{-9}σθ2​=0.5/(4×3.14×107)=3.98×10−9 rad² → σθ=63.1 μ\sigma_\theta=63.1\ \muσθ​=63.1 μrad; converting to time jitter (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz), σt=σθ/(2πf0)=2.0\sigma_t=\sigma_\theta/(2\pi f_0)=2.0σt​=σθ​/(2πf0​)=2.0 fs. Dimension check: rad²/s ÷ rad/s = rad² ✓; rad ÷ (rad/s) = s ✓. This is the power of locking an oscillator to a clean reference: unbounded accumulated jitter becomes a finite 2 fs dither.
documents.s: Step 3: the shaped PSD (a first-order Lorentzian)

documents.t: If the injection's own phase wanders: iinj=Iinjcos⁡(ωinjt+ψ(t))i_{inj}=I_{inj}\cos(\omega_{inj}t+\psi(t))iinj​=Iinj​cos(ωinj​t+ψ(t)) (ψ\psiψ slowly varying), redo the Step-0 average (product-to-sum, fast term averages out) to get Ω=−ωLsin⁡(θ−ψ)\Omega=-\omega_L\sin(\theta-\psi)Ω=−ωL​sin(θ−ψ), and linearize: d(δθ)dt=−ωc(δθ−ψ)+n⟹Θ(ω)=ωcωc+jω⏟low-passΨ(ω)+1ωc+jω⏟self FM→shapedN(ω)\frac{d(\delta\theta)}{dt}=-\omega_c(\delta\theta-\psi)+n \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Theta(\omega)=\underbrace{\frac{\omega_c}{\omega_c+j\omega}}_{\text{low-pass}}\Psi(\omega)+\underbrace{\frac{1}{\omega_c+j\omega}}_{\text{self FM}\to\text{shaped}}N(\omega)dtd(δθ)​=−ωc​(δθ−ψ)+n⟹Θ(ω)=low-passωc​+jωωc​​​​Ψ(ω)+self FM→shapedωc​+jω1​​​N(ω)Sθ,out=ωc2ωc2+ω2 Sψ+1ωc2+ω2 Sn.S_{\theta,out}=\frac{\omega_c^2}{\omega_c^2+\omega^2}\,S_\psi+\frac{1}{\omega_c^2+\omega^2}\,S_n .Sθ,out​=ωc2​+ω2ωc2​​Sψ​+ωc2​+ω21​Sn​. Reference phase noise is low-passed (corner is again ωc\omega_cωc​): below ωc\omega_cωc​ it's copied through fully (faithfully reproducing the reference), above ωc\omega_cωc​ it's rejected. Self-noise is high-passed: relative to free-running N/(jω)N/(j\omega)N/(jω), the ratio is jω/(ωc+jω)j\omega/(\omega_c+j\omega)jω/(ωc​+jω), ∣⋅∣2=ω2/(ωc2+ω2)\lvert\cdot\rvert^2=\omega^2/(\omega_c^2+\omega^2)∣⋅∣2=ω2/(ωc2​+ω2). This is exactly the transfer-function pair of a first-order (type-I) PLL — the same logic as the second-order ∣Hlp∣2/∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2/\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2/∣Hhp​∣2 in this site's lab_13, just with the loop degenerated to first order and bandwidth ωc\omega_cωc​. Block diagram: Honesty note: ωc\omega_cωc​ as the pull-in frequency is a native result of [P3] Eq.(40). Hanging n(t)n(t)n(t) and ψ(t)\psi(t)ψ(t) on it and reading off the high-pass/low-pass PSD is standard injection-locking noise theory (external literature, not among the five source PDFs: Kurokawa 1973; Razavi 2004 also has an accessible derivation; [P4] p.2130 points its noise analysis to its own reference [29, Ch. 7]).
documents.s: Step 4: what about the reference's noise? (the other half of the first-order PLL)

documents.t: ωc=ωL2−Δω2\omega_c=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωc​=ωL2​−Δω2​'s dependence on Δω\Delta\omegaΔω is an arc: highest at center, dropping vertically at the edges. Δω=0\Delta\omega=0Δω=0: ωc=ωL\omega_c=\omega_Lωc​=ωL​ (corner = the entire half lock range, maximum suppression bandwidth). This also gives [P3] Eq.(35) a second reading: ωL\omega_LωL​ is not just "the range over which it locks" — it is also "the ceiling on the noise-suppression bandwidth" (ωc≤ωL\omega_c\le\omega_Lωc​≤ωL​, equality at dead center). Δω=0.95 ωL\Delta\omega=0.95\,\omega_LΔω=0.95ωL​: cos⁡θss=1−0.952=0.312\cos\theta_{ss}=\sqrt{1-0.95^2}=0.312cosθss​=1−0.952​=0.312, ωc\omega_cωc​ is down to 31%, the low-frequency plateau is raised by 1/cos⁡2θss=10.3×1/\cos^2\theta_{ss}=10.3\times1/cos2θss​=10.3× (+10.1+10.1+10.1 dB) — still locked, but already dirty. Δω→±ωL\Delta\omega\to\pm\omega_LΔω→±ωL​: cos⁡θss→0\cos\theta_{ss}\to0cosθss​→0, ωc→0\omega_c\to0ωc​→0, suppression vanishes entirely; and the linearization itself breaks down (the potential well of the restoring force shallows out, noise starts kicking out cycle slips, transitioning toward Part B's pulling spectrum). In one sentence: the edge of the lock range is not a wall, it's a ramp — you start paying the phase-noise price well before you actually lose lock. When PVT drifts ω0\omega_0ω0​, Δω\Delta\omegaΔω quietly walks toward the edge, and the phase-noise plateau rises as 1/cos⁡2θss1/\cos^2\theta_{ss}1/cos2θss​ — this often bites earlier than "losing lock" itself. What you want to watch in design is the margin in Δω/ωL\Delta\omega/\omega_LΔω/ωL​, e.g. ∣Δω∣≤0.5 ωL\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert\le0.5\,\omega_L∣Δω∣≤0.5ωL​ keeps ωc≥0.87 ωL\omega_c\ge0.87\,\omega_Lωc​≥0.87ωL​ (plateau penalty only +1.2+1.2+1.2 dB).

documents.t: When ∣Δω∣>ωL\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert\gt\omega_L∣Δω∣>ωL​ (discuss Δω>ωL>0\Delta\omega\gt\omega_L\gt0Δω>ωL​>0), dθdt=Δω−ωLsin⁡θ ≥ Δω−ωL > 0\frac{d\theta}{dt}=\Delta\omega-\omega_L\sin\theta\ \ge\ \Delta\omega-\omega_L\ \gt\ 0dtdθ​=Δω−ωL​sinθ ≥ Δω−ωL​ > 0 is positive everywhere: θ\thetaθ rises monotonically, never stopping — locking fails, but the rise is highly non-uniform: Slowest near θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2 (sin⁡θ=1\sin\theta=1sinθ=1): dθ/dt=Δω−ωLd\theta/dt=\Delta\omega-\omega_Ldθ/dt=Δω−ωL​. The oscillator "almost locks" and dwells at the phase closest to lock (quasi-lock) — the description at [P3] Sec. V-G, p.2115–2116: spends a considerable amount of time "trying" to lock. Fastest near θ=−π/2\theta=-\pi/2θ=−π/2: dθ/dt=Δω+ωLd\theta/dt=\Delta\omega+\omega_Ldθ/dt=Δω+ωL​ — rapid slip, sweeping through a full revolution in one burst. So θ(t)\theta(t)θ(t) is a sawtooth staircase of "plateau + steep ramp" (see the simulation plot (a) below), net-sliding 2π2\pi2π per "beat."

documents.t: The period of one beat is the time for θ\thetaθ to traverse 2π2\pi2π. documents.t: Physical argument. The instantaneous frequency is ωosc(t)=ωinj+dθdt∈[ ωinj+Δω−ωL, ωinj+Δω+ωL ],\omega_{osc}(t)=\omega_{inj}+\frac{d\theta}{dt}\in[\,\omega_{inj}+\Delta\omega-\omega_L,\ \omega_{inj}+\Delta\omega+\omega_L\,],ωosc​(t)=ωinj​+dtdθ​∈[ωinj​+Δω−ωL​, ωinj​+Δω+ωL​], and the entire range sits on the same side of the injection (Δω>ωL\Delta\omega\gt\omega_LΔω>ωL​ guarantees a positive lower bound). And the time-weighting is extremely skewed: θ\thetaθ dwells longest in the dwell segment (ωosc≈ωinj+Δω−ωL\omega_{osc}\approx\omega_{inj}+\Delta\omega-\omega_Lωosc​≈ωinj​+Δω−ωL​, closest to the injection), while the slip segment flashes by — so spectral energy piles up on "the side of the injection frequency toward ω0\omega_0ω0​," hugging the injection and decaying outward; the other side of the injection is nearly empty. This contrasts sharply with symmetric FM (sinusoidal phase modulation → symmetric Bessel sidebands): the phase-modulating waveform of pulling is a sawtooth, not a sinusoid. Rigorous argument (advanced, one paragraph). Let z=ejθz=e^{j\theta}z=ejθ; the Adler equation becomes the Riccati equation z˙=jΔω z−ωL2(z2−1)\dot z=j\Delta\omega\,z-\tfrac{\omega_L}{2}(z^2-1)z˙=jΔωz−2ωL​​(z2−1). The Riccati solution is a Möbius (fractional-linear) transform of coefficients, letting us write the periodic solution as z=c+d w1+b wz=\dfrac{c+d\,w}{1+b\,w}z=1+bwc+dw​ (w=ejωbtw=e^{j\omega_b t}w=ejωb​t, ∣b∣<1\lvert b\rvert\lt1∣b∣<1); expanding the geometric series 11+bw=∑k(−b)kwk\dfrac{1}{1+bw}=\sum_k(-b)^k w^k1+bw1​=∑k​(−b)kwk leaves only powers k≥0k\ge0k≥0 — so in this idealized Adler model the comb is strictly one-sided, and the amplitudes decay geometrically, with ratio r=ωLΔω+ωbr=\frac{\omega_L}{\Delta\omega+\omega_b}r=Δω+ωb​ωL​​ (power drops by r2r^2r2 per line). This closed-form spectrum is a standard result (external literature, not among the five source PDFs: Armand 1969, see the end of this page); the rest of this page verifies it numerically with simulation. lab_27's 3-4-5 parameters: r=60/(100+80)=1/3r=60/(100+80)=1/3r=60/(100+80)=1/3, i.e. 20log⁡103=9.5420\log_{10}3=9.5420log10​3=9.54 dB per line.

documents.t: One of Part A's conclusions is that ωL\omega_LωL​ is not just "the range within which you can lock" — it is also the ceiling on the noise-suppression bandwidth (ωc≤ωL\omega_c\le\omega_Lωc​≤ωL​). So "for the same injection power, how far can ωL\omega_LωL​ be pushed" is a real-money design question. [P3] Sec. VI (pp. 2119–2120) gives an answer clean enough to memorize; this section re-derives it step by step, following the paper, and verifies it numerically on three ISFs. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the ISF is the dashboard showing "how persuadable the oscillator is right now." A fixed current budget should be spent entirely at the phases where ∣Γ~∣\lvert\tilde\Gamma\rvert∣Γ~∣ is large (where the node voltage transitions are steepest and the phase is easiest to push), and not a cent at the phases where Γ~≈0\tilde\Gamma\approx0Γ~≈0. A sinusoidal injection cannot do this — it is forced to spread its money uniformly across the whole period. The optimum is to "shape the injection waveform like the ISF itself" ([P3] Fig. 18, p.2118's concept cartoon).
documents.s: Injection waveform design: the ceiling on the lock range ([P3] Sec. VI, Cauchy–Schwarz)

documents.t: To compare waveforms of different shapes, you first need a common measuring stick for "equally big." A multi-harmonic waveform has no unique "amplitude," so [P3] uses the rms injection current ([P3] Eq.(43), p.2119, verbatim): Irms≡⟨iinj2⟩:=1Tinj∫Tinjiinj(t)2 dt .I_{rms}\equiv\sqrt{\langle i_{inj}^2\rangle}:=\sqrt{\frac{1}{T_{inj}}\int_{T_{inj}}i_{inj}(t)^2\,dt}\ .Irms​≡⟨iinj2​⟩​:=Tinj​1​∫Tinj​​iinj​(t)2dt​ . Units: A2=A\sqrt{\text{A}^2}=\text{A}A2​=A ✓. Why is rms the right proxy for "power"? [P3] p.2119 + Fig. 17: a practical injection circuit is usually a differential pair commutating a static tail current IbiasI_{bias}Ibias​; the instantaneous ∣iinj∣\lvert i_{inj}\rvert∣iinj​∣ is capped by the tail current, so Irms≤IbiasI_{rms}\le I_{bias}Irms​≤Ibias​, and the injection circuit's average power consumption is at least IrmsVDDI_{rms}V_{DD}Irms​VDD​ — fixing IrmsI_{rms}Irms​ ≈ fixing the floor of the injection circuit's power, and it is well-defined for any waveform.
documents.s: Step 0: define "how big" the injection is — why rms?

documents.t: Step 1: the lock range is the extremum of an inner product. The starting point is again the verified lock characteristic ([P3] Eq.(33), p.2114): Ω(θ)=1Tinj∫TinjΓ~(ωinjt+θ) iinj(t) dt.\Omega(\theta)=\frac{1}{T_{inj}}\int_{T_{inj}}\tilde\Gamma(\omega_{inj}t+\theta)\,i_{inj}(t)\,dt .Ω(θ)=Tinj​1​∫Tinj​​Γ~(ωinj​t+θ)iinj​(t)dt. At fixed θ\thetaθ this is precisely the time-averaged inner product of two periodic signals, ⟨u,v⟩=1T∫Tuv dt\langle u,v\rangle=\frac{1}{T}\int_T uv\,dt⟨u,v⟩=T1​∫T​uvdt, with uθ(t)=Γ~(ωinjt+θ)u_\theta(t)=\tilde\Gamma(\omega_{inj}t+\theta)uθ​(t)=Γ~(ωinj​t+θ) [rad/C] and v(t)=iinj(t)v(t)=i_{inj}(t)v(t)=iinj​(t) [A]. The lock condition (the generalization of Part A's Step 1; the steady state of [P3] Eq.(38)) is that Δω\Delta\omegaΔω falls within the range of Ω\OmegaΩ: the upper/lower lock edges are max⁡θΩ\max_\theta\Omegamaxθ​Ω and min⁡θΩ\min_\theta\Omegaminθ​Ω. So "make the lock range big" = "make the extrema of this inner product big" — the circuit problem has become a functional inequality. Step 2: the Cauchy–Schwarz bound. For every θ\thetaθ and every waveform (the integral form of Cauchy–Schwarz: ∣⟨u,v⟩∣≤∥u∥ ∥v∥\lvert\langle u,v\rangle\rvert\le\lVert u\rVert\,\lVert v\rVert∣⟨u,v⟩∣≤∥u∥∥v∥): ∣Ω(θ)∣ ≤ 1Tinj ⁣∫Tinj ⁣Γ~2(ωinjt+θ) dt⏟= Γ~rms (independent of θ)⋅1Tinj ⁣∫Tinj ⁣iinj2(t) dt⏟= Irms (Eq.(43))\lvert\Omega(\theta)\rvert\;\le\;\underbrace{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{T_{inj}}\!\int_{T_{inj}}\!\tilde\Gamma^2(\omega_{inj}t+\theta)\,dt}}_{=\ \tilde\Gamma_{rms}\ \text{(independent of }\theta\text{)}}\cdot\underbrace{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{T_{inj}}\!\int_{T_{inj}}\!i_{inj}^2(t)\,dt}}_{=\ I_{rms}\ \text{(Eq.(43))}}∣Ω(θ)∣≤= Γ~rms​ (independent of θ)Tinj​1​∫Tinj​​Γ~2(ωinj​t+θ)dt​​​⋅= Irms​ (Eq.(43))Tinj​1​∫Tinj​​iinj2​(t)dt​​​ The first factor is independent of θ\thetaθ: one injection period sweeps the entire 2π2\pi2π of Γ~\tilde\GammaΓ~ exactly once, and a mean square does not care at which phase the sweep starts. Units: rad/C×A=rad/s\text{rad/C}\times\text{A}=\text{rad/s}rad/C×A=rad/s ✓. Therefore, no matter what shape you give the waveform, the lock range can never exceed ([P3] Eq.(45), p.2120, verbatim) ωL∗=IrmsΓ~rms .\omega_L^*=I_{rms}\tilde\Gamma_{rms}\ .ωL∗​=Irms​Γ~rms​ . Step 3: the equality condition — the waveform = the shape of the ISF. Cauchy–Schwarz holds with equality ⟺ the two "vectors" are parallel: iinj(t)=λ Γ~(ωinjt+const)i_{inj}(t)=\lambda\,\tilde\Gamma(\omega_{inj}t+\text{const})iinj​(t)=λΓ~(ωinj​t+const). Normalizing the size of λ\lambdaλ to the given IrmsI_{rms}Irms​ via Eq.(43) gives the optimal injection waveform ([P3] Eq.(44), p.2119, verbatim; x=ωinjtx=\omega_{inj}tx=ωinj​t is the linear injection phase): iinj,0∗(x)=±IrmsΓ~rms Γ~(x) .i_{inj,0}^{*}(x)=\pm\frac{I_{rms}}{\tilde\Gamma_{rms}}\,\tilde\Gamma(x)\ .iinj,0∗​(x)=±Γ~rms​Irms​​Γ~(x) . Three key points: With the + sign, Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ) becomes the ISF's autocorrelation × Irms/Γ~rms\times\,I_{rms}/\tilde\Gamma_{rms}×Irms​/Γ~rms​, reaching +IrmsΓ~rms+I_{rms}\tilde\Gamma_{rms}+Irms​Γ~rms​ at the aligned point — optimizing the upper lock edge; the − sign likewise optimizes the lower edge ([P3] p.2120 states it explicitly: the positive solution for the upper edge, the negative for the lower). One waveform cannot push both edges to the ceiling simultaneously — see the numbers in Check 2 below. No manual alignment needed: θ\thetaθ is the oscillator's own degree of freedom; the locking mechanism adjusts it onto the stable branch satisfying Δω=Ω(θ)\Delta\omega=\Omega(\theta)Δω=Ω(θ). Waveform design only needs the shape right — the phase is found by the physics itself. Factor bookkeeping: Eq.(45) contains no 2 and no 4 — both sides are rms quantities. The 12\tfrac1221​ in the classical sinusoidal result ωL=12Iinj∣Γ~1∣\omega_L=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvertωL​=21​Iinj​∣Γ~1​∣ ([P3] Eq.(35)) is the projection integral ⟨cos⁡2⟩=12\langle\cos^2\rangle=\tfrac12⟨cos2⟩=21​, with IinjI_{inj}Iinj​ a peak value; rewritten in rms (Irms=Iinj/2I_{rms}=I_{inj}/\sqrt2Irms​=Iinj​/2​) it reads ωL,sine=Irms∣Γ~1∣/2\omega_{L,sine}=I_{rms}\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvert/\sqrt2ωL,sine​=Irms​∣Γ~1​∣/2​. All of these 2\sqrt22​'s and 222's are peak↔rms conversions and projection constants — nothing to do with the SSB /2/2/2, /4/4/4 bookkeeping conventions.

documents.t: The ideal LC's Γ~(x)=−sin⁡(x)/qmax\tilde\Gamma(x)=-\sin(x)/q_{max}Γ~(x)=−sin(x)/qmax​ is itself a single-tone sinusoid, so the waveform "shaped like the ISF" is a sine — the theorem predicts a sinusoidal injection already sits at the ceiling. Compute both sides (the true-LC Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​ branch, not the representative value 0.5): ωL,sine=Irms∣Γ~1∣2=Irms2 qmax,ωL∗=IrmsΓ~rms=Irms2 qmax⇒ratio=1.\omega_{L,sine}=\frac{I_{rms}\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvert}{\sqrt2}=\frac{I_{rms}}{\sqrt2\,q_{max}},\qquad \omega_L^*=I_{rms}\tilde\Gamma_{rms}=\frac{I_{rms}}{\sqrt2\,q_{max}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\text{ratio}=1 .ωL,sine​=2​Irms​∣Γ~1​∣​=2​qmax​Irms​​,ωL∗​=Irms​Γ~rms​=2​qmax​Irms​​⇒ratio=1. Numbers (reusing Part A's canonical case: qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, peak 62.83 μ62.83\ \mu62.83 μA i.e. Irms=44.43 μI_{rms}=44.43\ \muIrms​=44.43 μA): ωL∗=4.443×10−5×0.7071/10−12=3.14×107\omega_L^*=4.443\times10^{-5}\times0.7071/10^{-12}=3.14\times10^7ωL∗​=4.443×10−5×0.7071/10−12=3.14×107 rad/s → fL∗=5.000f_L^*=5.000fL∗​=5.000 MHz, identical to Part A's sinusoidal lock range. Dimension check: A × rad/C = (C/s)(rad/C) = rad/s ✓. (The simulation prints f_L sine = 5.0000 MHz, f_L matched = 5.0000 MHz, gain = 1.0000.) Teaching point: this is no coincidence — it is forced by "the ISF has only one harmonic." The only thing a sinusoidal injection can buy is Γ~1\tilde\Gamma_1Γ~1​, and a pure-sine ISF keeps all of its rms in Γ~1\tilde\Gamma_1Γ~1​. For waveform design to "make money," the ISF must hide energy where a sine cannot reach: DC (c0c_0c0​) or higher harmonics. The next two checks demonstrate one of each.
documents.s: Check 1: pure-sine ISF — a sinusoidal injection is "already" optimal (the ratio must be 1)

documents.t: The site toy Γ(θ)=cos⁡θ+0.3\Gamma(\theta)=\cos\theta+0.3Γ(θ)=cosθ+0.3 (α=0.3\alpha=0.3α=0.3, DC value c0/2=0.3c_0/2=0.3c0​/2=0.3; site convention: here α\alphaα is the DC offset of the toy ISF, unrelated to [P1]'s NMF α(ω0t)\alpha(\omega_0t)α(ω0​t)): Γrms=α2+12=0.7681\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{\alpha^2+\tfrac12}=0.7681Γrms​=α2+21​​=0.7681, c1=1c_1=1c1​=1. Closed-form gain: G=ωL∗ωL,sine=IrmsΓrms/qmaxIrms c1/(2 qmax)=2 Γrmsc1=1+2α2=1.0863.G=\frac{\omega_L^*}{\omega_{L,sine}}=\frac{I_{rms}\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}}{I_{rms}\,c_1/(\sqrt2\,q_{max})}=\frac{\sqrt2\,\Gamma_{rms}}{c_1}=\sqrt{1+2\alpha^2}=1.0863 .G=ωL,sine​ωL∗​​=Irms​c1​/(2​qmax​)Irms​Γrms​/qmax​​=c1​2​Γrms​​=1+2α2​=1.0863. (Simulation: gain = 1.0863, fLf_LfL​ from 5.0000 → 5.4314 MHz.) The matched waveform is just the shape of cos⁡+α\cos+\alphacos+α — the extra DC share of the current couples to the ISF's c0c_0c0​, something a zero-mean sine can never buy. But note the one-sidedness (the ±\pm± choice): in units of Irms/qmaxI_{rms}/q_{max}Irms​/qmax​, the simulation prints matched(+) upper/lower edges =+0.7681=+0.7681=+0.7681/−0.5338-0.5338−0.5338, versus the sine's ±0.7071\pm0.7071±0.7071 — the upper edge gains 8.6% while the lower edge loses 24%; for the lower edge, switch to the −-− sign. The DC injection shifts the whole lock characteristic upward — exactly the mechanism by which "the upper and lower lock edges can have the same sign," as the caption of [P3] Fig. 10 notes.

documents.t: A ring's ISF energy concentrates at the transitions. As a toy, use the [P2] App.B triangular-pulse construction (A=1A=1A=1, symmetric rise/fall): two opposite-sign triangular pulses, height h=1/f′h=1/f'h=1/f′, half-width w=1/f′w=1/f'w=1/f′ rad, with f′=ηN/πf'=\eta N/\pif′=ηN/π (from [P2] Eq.(54), p.803 with A=1A=1A=1). Sanity check: this construction's Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ lands exactly back on [P2] Eq.(55) (A=1A=1A=1): the simulation prints 0.05634 = the closed form 2π2/3η3/N1.5=\sqrt{2\pi^2/3\eta^3}/N^{1.5}=2π2/3η3​/N1.5= 0.05634 ✓. The narrow-pulse closed-form gain (three lines): a single pulse of area hwhwhw gives c1≈2hw/πc_1\approx 2hw/\pic1​≈2hw/π (the two opposite-sign pulses sit π\piπ apart, so their projections onto sin⁡\sinsin add with the same sign); Γrms2=12π⋅2⋅23h2w=2h2w3π\Gamma_{rms}^2=\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\cdot2\cdot\tfrac23h^2w=\tfrac{2h^2w}{3\pi}Γrms2​=2π1​⋅2⋅32​h2w=3π2h2w​; substituting h=w=1/f′h=w=1/f'h=w=1/f′, f′=ηN/πf'=\eta N/\pif′=ηN/π: G=2 Γrmsc1≈2⋅2h2w3π4h2w2π2=π3w=ηN3 .G=\frac{\sqrt2\,\Gamma_{rms}}{c_1}\approx\sqrt{\frac{2\cdot\frac{2h^2w}{3\pi}}{\frac{4h^2w^2}{\pi^2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3w}}=\sqrt{\frac{\eta N}{3}}\ .G=c1​2​Γrms​​≈π24h2w2​2⋅3π2h2w​​​=3wπ​​=3ηN​​ . N=17N=17N=17, η=0.75\eta=0.75η=0.75: G=4.25=2.0616G=\sqrt{4.25}=2.0616G=4.25​=2.0616 (full numerical simulation 2.0720; the 0.5% difference is the sinc2\mathrm{sinc}^2sinc2 correction for the pulses' finite width). With units attached: for the same Irms=44.43 μI_{rms}=44.43\ \muIrms​=44.43 μA and qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, sine 192.3 kHz → matched 398.4 kHz. This ×2 is not the toy congratulating itself: [P3] Fig. 19 (p.2119) runs transistor-level simulations of a 17-stage single-ended ring — injecting pulses shaped close to the ISF (Fig. 19(b), not a strict ISF replica), and p.2120 states verbatim: "the lock range is almost doubled compared to a sinusoidal injection of the same power." The toy's ηN/3≈2.06\sqrt{\eta N/3}\approx2.06ηN/3​≈2.06 agrees with the real circuit's "almost doubled" at the level of the factor 2, not the decimals (the real ISF's details differ). The gain is ∝N\propto\sqrt N∝N​: more stages → transitions occupy a smaller fraction of the phase → the sine wastes more — long rings are where waveform design pays off the most. An honest toy footnote: the site's cruder gamma_triangular toy is π\piπ-periodic (the rising and falling triangles repeat perfectly symmetrically), so it has even harmonics only — the simulation prints its c1=0.000000c_1=0.000000c1​=0.000000, c2=0.3625c_2=0.3625c2​=0.3625: a fundamental-frequency sine cannot lock it at all (effectively only superharmonic injection would work). This is a toy artifact (a real ring's rising and falling edges are never so symmetric that only even harmonics survive), but it demonstrates the same lesson in the most extreme way: a sine can only buy c1c_1c1​; if the ISF puts no energy in c1c_1c1​, the money is wasted.
documents.s: Check 3: ring-style narrow-pulse ISF — gain ≈ηN/3\approx\sqrt{\eta N/3}≈ηN/3​, ≈ ×2 at 17 stages

Model: on a 4096-point phase grid, write the periodic average of [P3] Eq.(33) as a circular correlation; for each of the three ISFs compute the lock characteristic under a sinusoidal and a matched injection (same IrmsI_{rms}Irms​); the extrema are the lock edges. Core code (full script: simulations/lab_39_optimal_injection.py): def lock_characteristic(gt, i_wave): # [P3] Eq.(33): circular correlation Gf, If = np.fft.rfft(gt), np.fft.rfft(i_wave) return np.fft.irfft(np.conj(If) * Gf, gt.size) / gt.size # Ω(θ) [rad/s] i_sine = np.sqrt(2)*I_RMS*np.cos(X) # sine of the same I_rms i_star = (I_RMS/gt_rms) * gt_p # [P3] Eq.(44), + sign wl_sine = lock_characteristic(gt_p, i_sine).max() # upper lock edge [rad/s] wl_star = lock_characteristic(gt_p, i_star).max() # should touch I_rms·Γ̃_rms Verified output numbers (PYTHONPATH=. python3 simulations/lab_39_optimal_injection.py): print(fL_sine_LC, fL_matched_LC) # -> 5.0000 MHz, 5.0000 MHz pure-sine ISF: sine already optimal (gain = 1.0000) print(gain_asym) # -> 1.0863 cos+0.3 matched gain = analytic sqrt(1+2α²)=1.0863 print(edges_asym) # -> +0.7681/-0.5338 matched(+) upper/lower edges (units of I_rms/q_max; sine ±0.7071) print(gamma_rms_ring) # -> 0.05634 = [P2] Eq.(55) closed form 0.05634 (construction sanity check) print(fL_sine_ring, fL_matched_ring) # -> 0.1923 MHz, 0.3984 MHz N=17 ring toy, same I_rms=44.43 μA print(gain_ring) # -> 2.0720 closed form sqrt(ηN/3)=2.0616 (0.5% difference = sinc² correction) print(matched_over_bound) # -> 1.0000 the matched injection exactly touches the Cauchy–Schwarz bound (all three cases) print(c1_site_triangular) # -> 0.000000 the site toy gamma_triangular is π-periodic: a fundamental sine cannot lock it (artifact) Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. V-H observation) "Size" measured by IrmsI_{rms}Irms​ (Eq.(43)) Optimum = Eq.(44), ceiling = Eq.(45) Change the constraint and the optimum changes: if the peak current is limited, ∣iinj∣≤Ipk\lvert i_{inj}\rvert\le I_{pk}∣iinj​∣≤Ipk​, the optimum becomes the square-like i=Ipk sign(Γ~)i=I_{pk}\,\mathrm{sign}(\tilde\Gamma)i=Ipk​sign(Γ~) with ceiling Ipk⟨∣Γ~∣⟩I_{pk}\langle\lvert\tilde\Gamma\rvert\rangleIpk​⟨∣Γ~∣⟩ (this site's extension, not in [P3]) The injector can generate the waveform Full GGG collected Narrow pulses need bandwidth up to ∼N\sim N∼N harmonics: at f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, a 17-stage pulse needs spectral content out to ~85 GHz — in practice the pulses are widened and GGG degrades smoothly along the ISF autocorrelation (no cliff) ISF known and stable Waveform can be designed offline The ISF must come from simulation ([P3] Sec. V-H's impulse-response method) or closed forms ([P2] App.B); when PVT drifts the ISF, GGG is discounted, but the locked phase θss\theta_{ss}θss​ re-aligns automatically The goal is the maximum lock range All of this section Sometimes you want to minimize it (multiple oscillators interfering, reducing coupling) — the same framework run in reverse ([P3] p.2120 closing explicitly flags this direction) Three design sentences: (i) for LC (near-sine ISF), don't bother — a sinusoidal injection is already at the ceiling (exactly gain 1.0000 for a pure sine; the residual gain for near-sine ISFs is second-order small); (ii) ring/relaxation (pulse-type ISFs) benefit the most from waveform design, with gain ≈ηN/3\approx\sqrt{\eta N/3}≈ηN/3​ growing as the square root of the stage count; (iii) this gain simultaneously scales Part A's ωc\omega_cωc​ — at the same power the noise-suppression-bandwidth ceiling also gains ×G, which is the number SerDes ILO deskew actually cares about.

documents.t: Push Δω\Delta\omegaΔω to the center of the lock range: the noise-suppression bandwidth ωc=ωL2−Δω2\omega_c=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωc​=ωL2​−Δω2​ is only maximal at Δω=0\Delta\omega=0Δω=0. The goal of a calibration/tuning loop is not just "get locked," it's "get locked in the middle." Two ways to increase ωL\omega_LωL​ ([P3] Eq.(35): ωL=12Iinj∣Γ~1∣\omega_L=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvertωL​=21​Iinj​∣Γ~1​∣): raise the injection current (at the cost of power and spurs), or use waveform design to align injection harmonics with ISF harmonics ([P3] Sec. VI's injection waveform design — effectively a free boost to ωL\omega_LωL​ and ωc\omega_cωc​; for the quantitative ceiling and the optimal waveform see the "Injection waveform design" section above: ωL∗=IrmsΓ~rms\omega_L^*=I_{rms}\tilde\Gamma_{rms}ωL∗​=Irms​Γ~rms​, with gain ≈ηN/3\approx\sqrt{\eta N/3}≈ηN/3​ for ring-type ISFs). Ceiling to watch: Iinj≪Imax=ω0qmaxI_{inj}\ll I_{max}=\omega_0 q_{max}Iinj​≪Imax​=ω0​qmax​ ([P3] Eq.(36)–(37)). Leave edge margin: the plateau penalty is 1/cos⁡2θss1/\cos^2\theta_{ss}1/cos2θss​. ∣Δω∣/ωL=0.5\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert/\omega_L=0.5∣Δω∣/ωL​=0.5 only costs +1.2+1.2+1.2 dB; 0.950.950.95 costs +10.1+10.1+10.1 dB. Budget for PVT drift should be counted against Δω/ωL\Delta\omega/\omega_LΔω/ωL​. Recognize the fingerprint of pulling: a comb next to the carrier that is one-sided, evenly spaced by ωb\omega_bωb​, with one edge pinned exactly at some fixed frequency → that fixed frequency is the aggressor's frequency. Countermeasures, in order: add isolation (layout, guard ring, supply/substrate filtering); move the frequency plan (pull Δω\Delta\omegaΔω larger, so the comb spacing ωb→Δω\omega_b\to\Delta\omegaωb​→Δω moves further out and the amplitude r→0r\to0r→0 shrinks); or, conversely, just lock onto it deliberately (make ωL\omega_LωL​ larger than ∣Δω∣\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert∣Δω∣, so the spur comb collapses into a clean locked carrier). The most dangerous case is neither near nor far: when Δω\Delta\omegaΔω is only slightly above ωL\omega_LωL​, ωb\omega_bωb​ is tiny, the spur sits right next to the carrier (in-band, can't be filtered out) and r→1r\to1r→1 (slow decay, a dense, tall comb). Connection to SerDes: injection-locked clock distribution (forwarded-clock / multi-lane ILO deskew) is using ωc\omega_cωc​ as the jitter tracking bandwidth — reference jitter below ωc\omega_cωc​ is copied through (a benefit for lanes with common jitter: shared source, correlated cancellation), while above ωc\omega_cωc​ cleanliness relies on the local oscillator itself (the same old homework of qmaxq_{max}qmax​, Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, design_tradeoffs). The trade-off structure is exactly isomorphic to a CDR: see serdes_clocking_connection, lab_13.

documents.t: Injection locking = a first-order PLL: linearizing [P3]'s generalized Adler gives d(δθ)/dt=−ωcδθ+nd(\delta\theta)/dt=-\omega_c\delta\theta+nd(δθ)/dt=−ωc​δθ+n, loop bandwidth ωc=ωLcos⁡θss=ωL2−Δω2\omega_c=\omega_L\cos\theta_{ss}=\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωc​=ωL​cosθss​=ωL2​−Δω2​ — exactly the pull-in frequency of [P3] Eq.(40) (general topology: ωc=−Ω′(θss)\omega_c=-\Omega'(\theta_{ss})ωc​=−Ω′(θss​)). Self-noise is high-passed, reference noise is low-passed, sharing the corner ωc≤ωL\omega_c\le\omega_Lωc​≤ωL​; under a white FM drive, Sθ=Sn/(ωc2+ω2)S_\theta=S_n/(\omega_c^2+\omega^2)Sθ​=Sn​/(ωc2​+ω2), low-frequency plateau Sn/ωc2S_n/\omega_c^2Sn​/ωc2​, finite total variance Sn/(4ωc)S_n/(4\omega_c)Sn​/(4ωc​) (simulation: corner and plateau both match theory to within 0.96-1.00×). Suppression vanishes at the lock edge: as Δω→ωL\Delta\omega\to\omega_LΔω→ωL​, cos⁡θss→0\cos\theta_{ss}\to0cosθss​→0, the plateau rises as 1/cos⁡2θss1/\cos^2\theta_{ss}1/cos2θss​ (+10.1+10.1+10.1 dB at 0.95 ωL0.95\,\omega_L0.95ωL​) — locked doesn't mean clean; margin must be budgeted. When it doesn't lock: θ\thetaθ slides in a sawtooth (dwell + slip), beat frequency ωb=Δω2−ωL2\omega_b=\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}ωb​=Δω2−ωL2​​ (derived step by step; [P4] Eq.(34)); the spectrum is a one-sided comb: lines at ωinj+kωb\omega_{inj}+k\omega_bωinj​+kωb​, one edge exactly at the injection frequency ([P4] Sec. V-B), amplitude decaying geometrically as r=ωL/(Δω+ωb)r=\omega_L/(\Delta\omega+\omega_b)r=ωL​/(Δω+ωb​) (external, Armand 1969; simulation matches −9.54-9.54−9.54 dB/line to the digit). Two faces of the same square root: inside lock, ωL2−Δω2\sqrt{\omega_L^2-\Delta\omega^2}ωL2​−Δω2​ = the noise-suppression corner; outside lock, Δω2−ωL2\sqrt{\Delta\omega^2-\omega_L^2}Δω2−ωL2​​ = the spur comb spacing. In design, you want one of them large (wide suppression) and the other either large or zero (spur far away, or locked out entirely). The ceiling of waveform design: at fixed IrmsI_{rms}Irms​ (= the proxy for injection power, [P3] Eq.(43)), the Cauchy–Schwarz ceiling of the lock range is ωL∗=IrmsΓ~rms\omega_L^*=I_{rms}\tilde\Gamma_{rms}ωL∗​=Irms​Γ~rms​ ([P3] Eq.(45)), with equality ⟺ iinj∝Γ~i_{inj}\propto\tilde\Gammaiinj​∝Γ~ (Eq.(44), the ±\pm± selecting the upper/lower edge). Pure-sine ISF: a sine is already optimal (gain = 1.0000); ring-type pulse ISF: G≈ηN/3G\approx\sqrt{\eta N/3}G≈ηN/3​, ×2.07 at N=17N=17N=17 — the same order as [P3] Fig. 19's "almost doubled."

documents.t: Prerequisites: tank_swing (L∝Γrms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​/qmax2​ and the swing lever), tank_Q_and_energy_restoration (what LC's "high-QQQ energy storage" actually buys, why ring lacks this advantage), rms_isf (Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, Parseval, ring's N−3/2N^{-3/2}N−3/2 scaling) | Next: serdes_clocking_connection, varactor_tuning_supply_pushing This page treats the ISF as a single unified ruler and measures the difference between LC and ring oscillators item by item. The point is not "which is better" (each has its use) but what the ISF framework lets us see, and what it doesn't. We first build an explicitly-labeled honest toy model, then quantify the differences using the [P1] / [P2] formulas. Physical intuition (conclusion first): LC is like a heavy pendulum — most of the energy is stored in the tank (LLL and CCC trading back and forth), with only a small device occasionally topping up the loss. The waveform is close to sinusoidal, the ISF is smooth (−sin⁡-\sin−sin), and phase sensitivity is spread across the whole period. ring is like a row of relay-passing gates — no energy-storage element, every stage is switching, every stage leaks noise, the waveform is close to a square wave, the ISF is concentrated at the transition, and phase sensitivity is sharp. LC buys low phase noise with "energy storage + high QQQ"; ring trades phase noise for "small area, tunability, multiphase output."
documents.s: LC vs ring oscillator through the ISF lens

documents.t: The following is a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level. It captures the qualitative difference but is not a measurement of any real circuit. LC: ideal sinusoidal state, V(θ)=cos⁡θV(\theta)=\cos\thetaV(θ)=cosθ, ISF ΓLC(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma_{LC}(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓLC​(θ)=−sinθ ([P1] Fig. 7(a)). Amplitude restoration is provided by the limit cycle ([P1] Sec. III-A). ring: NNN-stage inverter delay + independent timing noise per stage; ISF modeled as a triangular toy shape, peak ∼1/N\sim1/\sqrt{N}∼1/N​, energy concentrated at the transition (actual simulated ISF curve: [P2] Fig. 5, p.793; triangular approximation: [P2] Fig. 6, p.793). Accumulated jitter uses a random-walk model σΔt=σedgeΔN\sigma_{\Delta t}=\sigma_{edge}\sqrt{\Delta N}σΔt​=σedge​ΔN​ ([P2] Eq.(8)). Full scripts: simulations/lab_02_lc_toy_model.py, simulations/lab_03_ring_toy_model.py.

(d) N-independence conclusion (claim C7, verified): Key fact: [P2] Eq.(23)'s FOM contains no NNN at all — at fixed f0f_0f0​ and power PPP, a single-ended ring's phase noise is independent of the stage count NNN. documents.t: The N-independence above tells only half the story: it is the conclusion for a single-ended CMOS ring. [P2] Sec. V-B (p.796) redoes the same bookkeeping for a differential MOS ring (resistive load RLR_LRL​, tail-current biasing) and the ending flips — the phase-noise formula contains an explicit factor of NNN. All five formulas below have been verified verbatim against the original [P2] PDF, p.796 (rendered-page comparison). (a) The power bookkeeping turns from "dynamic" into "static" ([P2] Eq.(31), p.796): P=N Itail VDDP=N\,I_{tail}\,V_{DD}P=NItail​VDD​ The differential pair is biased by a tail current source: whether or not it is switching, each stage continuously draws ItailI_{tail}Itail​ from VDDV_{DD}VDD​ (class-A-style static bookkeeping); NNN stages means NNN shares. Unit check: (dimensionless)⋅[A]⋅[V]=[W](\text{dimensionless})\cdot[\text{A}]\cdot[\text{V}]=[\text{W}](dimensionless)⋅[A]⋅[V]=[W] ✓. Contrast with single-ended Eq.(21) P=2ηNVDDqmaxf0P=2\eta N V_{DD}q_{max}f_0P=2ηNVDD​qmax​f0​: there the power is the dynamic "charge/discharge qmaxq_{max}qmax​ every period" bookkeeping, automatically tied to f0f_0f0​; here the static power has no f0f_0f0​ in it — this bookkeeping difference is the seed of the flipped ending. (b) Frequency = tail current slewing the node charge ([P2] Eq.(32), p.796): f0=12NtD≈12ηNtr≈Itail2ηNqmaxf_0=\frac{1}{2Nt_D}\approx\frac{1}{2\eta N t_r}\approx\frac{I_{tail}}{2\eta N q_{max}}f0​=2NtD​1​≈2ηNtr​1​≈2ηNqmax​Itail​​ The physics of the last step: each stage transition is the tail current slewing the node charge qmaxq_{max}qmax​, so tr≈qmax/Itailt_r\approx q_{max}/I_{tail}tr​≈qmax​/Itail​, with the proportionality constant absorbed into η\etaη (the same stage-delay constant as Eq.(14)–(15), ≈1\approx1≈1). Unit check: [A]/([C])=[A/(A⋅s)]=1/s=[Hz][\text{A}]/([\text{C}])=[\text{A/(A·s)}]=1/\text{s}=[\text{Hz}][A]/([C])=[A/(A⋅s)]=1/s=[Hz] ✓. Factor-2 flag: the 2 in 1/(2NtD)1/(2Nt_D)1/(2NtD​) is the physical count "the signal must go around the ring twice to return in phase" (same as Eq.(15)) — it has nothing to do with the SSB/time-domain convention. (c) Raising NNN at fixed PPP, f0f_0f0​: two chains tighten at once Inverting Eq.(31): Itail=P/(NVDD)∝1/NI_{tail}=P/(N V_{DD})\propto 1/NItail​=P/(NVDD​)∝1/N — with power fixed, one more stage means cutting each stage's current. Substituting into Eq.(32): qmax=Itail/(2ηNf0)∝1/N2q_{max}=I_{tail}/(2\eta N f_0)\propto 1/N^2qmax​=Itail​/(2ηNf0​)∝1/N2 — the current shrinks (1/N1/N1/N) and the transition must complete within a shorter stage delay (another 1/N1/N1/N). [P2] p.797, verbatim: "increasing the number of stages at a fixed total power dissipation demands a proportional reduction of tail-current sources, which will reduce the swing, and hence qmaxq_{max}qmax​, by a factor of 1/N21/N^21/N2." Contrast with single-ended: Eq.(21) at fixed PPP, f0f_0f0​ gives only qmax∝1/Nq_{max}\propto1/Nqmax​∝1/N (first power). Why the differential ring gets squeezed once more: the power no longer self-scales with the f0f_0f0​ charge/discharge bookkeeping, so cutting the tail current is the only path — and cutting current directly cuts the swing. (d) The noise on each node ([P2] Eq.(33), p.796): in2‾Δf=(in2‾Δf)N+(in2‾Δf)Load=4kT Itail(1Vchar+1RLItail)\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=\left(\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}\right)_{N}+\left(\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}\right)_{Load}=4kT\,I_{tail}\left(\frac{1}{V_{char}}+\frac{1}{R_L I_{tail}}\right)Δfin2​​​=(Δfin2​​​)N​+(Δfin2​​​)Load​=4kTItail​(Vchar​1​+RL​Itail​1​) Two contributions: the differential transistor (subscript NNN, the NMOS differential device) plus the load resistor RLR_LRL​. VcharV_{char}Vchar​: (VGS−VT)/γ(V_{GS}-V_T)/\gamma(VGS​−VT​)/γ for a balanced stage in the long-channel limit, EcL/γE_cL/\gammaEc​L/γ in the short-channel regime ([P2] p.796, verbatim); for where the short-channel EcL/γE_cL/\gammaEc​L/γ comes from (Eq.(27)–(30)) and the Sec. VIII measured comparison see the paper_002 Eq.(27)–(30) section. Unit check: 4kTItail/Vchar=[J][A]/[V]4kT I_{tail}/V_{char}=[\text{J}][\text{A}]/[\text{V}]4kTItail​/Vchar​=[J][A]/[V]; with [J]=[V⋅A⋅s][\text{J}]=[\text{V·A·s}][J]=[V⋅A⋅s] this is [V⋅A⋅s⋅A/V]=[A2⋅s]=[A2/Hz][\text{V·A·s·A/V}]=[\text{A}^2\text{·s}]=[\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}][V⋅A⋅s⋅A/V]=[A2⋅s]=[A2/Hz] ✓. 2N2N2N nodes: each differential stage has two output nodes, so the whole ring has 2N2N2N single-ended nodes; [P2] p.796, verbatim: "The phase noise and jitter due to all 2N2N2N noise sources is 2N2N2N times the value given by (6) and (12)." — this 2 is a node count, not the SSB convention's 2. Where did the tail source go? Same page, verbatim: "Surprisingly, tail-current source noise in the vicinity of f0f_0f0​ does not affect the phase noise." — what does affect the phase noise is the tail's low-frequency noise (taking the symmetry/c0c_0c0​ 1/f³ path, see symmetry) and its noise near even harmonics (suppressible with a series inductor / parallel capacitor), so the white-noise bookkeeping counts only the differential device + load. (e) Convergence: the differential ring's phase-noise and jitter floor ([P2] Eq.(34)/(35), p.796): Lmin{Δf}=83η⋅N⋅kTP⋅(VDDVchar+VDDRLItail)⋅f02Δf2\mathcal{L}_{min}\{\Delta f\}=\frac{8}{3\eta}\cdot N\cdot\frac{kT}{P}\cdot\left(\frac{V_{DD}}{V_{char}}+\frac{V_{DD}}{R_L I_{tail}}\right)\cdot\frac{f_0^2}{\Delta f^2}Lmin​{Δf}=3η8​⋅N⋅PkT​⋅(Vchar​VDD​​+RL​Itail​VDD​​)⋅Δf2f02​​κmin=83η⋅N⋅kTP⋅(VDDVchar+VDDRLItail)\kappa_{min}=\sqrt{\frac{8}{3\eta}}\cdot\sqrt{N\cdot\frac{kT}{P}\cdot\left(\frac{V_{DD}}{V_{char}}+\frac{V_{DD}}{R_L I_{tail}}\right)}κmin​=3η8​​⋅N⋅PkT​⋅(Vchar​VDD​​+RL​Itail​VDD​​)​ (L\mathcal{L}L is the paper's L{Δf}L\{\Delta f\}L{Δf} in site notation; the paper states verbatim that both are "valid in both long- and short-channel regimes of operation with the right choice of VcharV_{char}Vchar​"; a bipolar differential ring folds its shot + load noise (Eq.(36), p.797) back into the same two equations with Vchar=4kT/qeV_{char}=4kT/q_eVchar​=4kT/qe​.) Compared with single-ended Eq.(23) there are only two differences: an explicit NNN, and an extra load-resistor share VDD/(RLItail)V_{DD}/(R_L I_{tail})VDD​/(RL​Itail​) in the bracket. Where does the NNN come from? Do the exponent bookkeeping of L∝(source count)⋅Γrms2⋅Si/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto(\text{source count})\cdot\Gamma_{rms}^2\cdot S_i/q_{max}^2L∝(source count)⋅Γrms2​⋅Si​/qmax2​ term by term (toy bookkeeping, fixed PPP, f0f_0f0​, fixed swing RLItailR_L I_{tail}RL​Itail​): Factor single-ended (the Eq.23 path) differential (the Eq.34 path) noise-source count ×N\times N×N (each stage's NMOS+PMOS already merged in Eq.18) ×2N∝N\times 2N\propto N×2N∝N (two output nodes per stage) Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ (Eq.16) ∝N−3\propto N^{-3}∝N−3 ∝N−3\propto N^{-3}∝N−3 per-source SiS_iSi​ ∝N0\propto N^{0}∝N0 (WWW unchanged at fixed P,f0P,f_0P,f0​) ∝Itail∝N−1\propto I_{tail}\propto N^{-1}∝Itail​∝N−1 (both terms of Eq.33) 1/qmax21/q_{max}^21/qmax2​ ∝N2\propto N^{2}∝N2 (qmax∝1/Nq_{max}\propto1/Nqmax​∝1/N) ∝N4\propto N^{4}∝N4 (qmax∝1/N2q_{max}\propto1/N^2qmax​∝1/N2) product N1−3+0+2=N0N^{1-3+0+2}=N^{0}N1−3+0+2=N0 N1−3−1+4=N+1N^{1-3-1+4}=N^{+1}N1−3−1+4=N+1 Single-ended cancels exactly (N0N^0N0 = no NNN in Eq.23); the differential ring's qmax∝1/N2q_{max}\propto1/N^2qmax​∝1/N2 contributes two extra positive powers, leaving a net N+1N^{+1}N+1 — exactly the NNN sitting in plain sight in Eq.(34). [P2]'s own conclusion sentence (pp.796–797, verbatim): "Note that, in contrast with the single-ended ring oscillator, a differential oscillator does exhibit a phase noise and jitter dependency on the number of stages, with the phase noise degrading as the number of stages increases for a given frequency and power dissipation. This result may be understood as a consequence of the necessary reduction in the charge swing that is required to accommodate a constant frequency of oscillation at a fixed power level as NNN increases." — At fixed frequency and power dissipation, a differential ring's phase noise gets worse as NNN increases; the culprit is the forcibly shrunken charge swing (qmax∝1/N2q_{max}\propto1/N^2qmax​∝1/N2). Convention flag (owed every time a 2 or 4 appears; corrected in v11): the prefactor 8/(3η)8/(3\eta)8/(3η) of Eq.(34) is of the same family as Eq.(23) — both are collected from [P2] Eq.(6), p.792 (Eq.(34) is 2N×2N\times2N×Eq.(6)), and the printed Eq.(6) has denominator 8π2foff2=2Δω28\pi^2f_{off}^2=2\Delta\omega^28π2foff2​=2Δω2, i.e. this site's L/2\mathcal{L}_{/2}L/2​ family — 3 dB above the /4/4/4 SSB family of [P1] Eq.(21) with its 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2 (e.g. example B's −148-148−148 ([P1] Eq.(21), /4/4/4) vs −145-145−145 (/2/2/2), see white_noise_to_phase_noise). So the absolute values −82.7-82.7−82.7/−78.0-78.0−78.0 dBc/Hz in example 3 below are /2/2/2-family numbers (in the [P1] Eq.(21) bookkeeping they read −85.7-85.7−85.7/−81.0-81.0−81.0 dBc/Hz); the ΔL\Delta\mathcal{L}ΔL in example 3 is a difference of two L\mathcal{L}L's, so the convention factor cancels — both conventions give the same answer. Example 3 (differential ring: N=4N=4N=4 vs N=12N=12N=12, same PPP, same f0f_0f0​ — what is ΔL\Delta\mathcal{L}ΔL?) Take f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, kT=4.0×10−21kT=4.0\times10^{-21}kT=4.0×10−21 J (300 K), P=1P=1P=1 mW, η≈1\eta\approx1η≈1, VDD/Vchar=3V_{DD}/V_{char}=3VDD​/Vchar​=3 (the same illustrative value as example 1 later on this page), and a fixed-swing design RLItail=VDD/2R_L I_{tail}=V_{DD}/2RL​Itail​=VDD​/2 ⇒VDD/(RLItail)=2\Rightarrow V_{DD}/(R_L I_{tail})=2⇒VDD​/(RL​Itail​)=2 (bracket =3+2=5=3+2=5=3+2=5; the design scales RL∝NR_L\propto NRL​∝N up to maintain the swing, so the bracket does not change with NNN). Use [P2] Eq.(34). Step-by-step substitution (with units): (f0Δf)2=(5000)2=2.5×107,kTP=4.0×10−21 J1×10−3 W=4.0×10−18 s,N=4: Lmin=10log⁡10 ⁣(83⋅4⋅(4.0×10−18)⋅5⋅(2.5×107))=10log⁡10(5.33×10−9)=−82.7 dBc/Hz,N=12: Lmin=10log⁡10 ⁣(83⋅12⋅(4.0×10−18)⋅5⋅(2.5×107))=10log⁡10(1.60×10−8)=−78.0 dBc/Hz,ΔL=10log⁡10124=10log⁡103=+4.77 dB.\begin{aligned} \left(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\right)^2&=(5000)^2=2.5\times10^{7},\qquad \frac{kT}{P}=\frac{4.0\times10^{-21}\ \text{J}}{1\times10^{-3}\ \text{W}}=4.0\times10^{-18}\ \text{s},\\[4pt] N=4:\ \mathcal{L}_{min}&=10\log_{10}\!\Big(\tfrac{8}{3}\cdot4\cdot(4.0\times10^{-18})\cdot5\cdot(2.5\times10^{7})\Big) =10\log_{10}(5.33\times10^{-9})=-82.7\ \text{dBc/Hz},\\[4pt] N=12:\ \mathcal{L}_{min}&=10\log_{10}\!\Big(\tfrac{8}{3}\cdot12\cdot(4.0\times10^{-18})\cdot5\cdot(2.5\times10^{7})\Big) =10\log_{10}(1.60\times10^{-8})=-78.0\ \text{dBc/Hz},\\[4pt] \Delta\mathcal{L}&=10\log_{10}\frac{12}{4}=10\log_{10}3=+4.77\ \text{dB}. \end{aligned}(Δff0​​)2N=4: Lmin​N=12: Lmin​ΔL​=(5000)2=2.5×107,PkT​=1×10−3 W4.0×10−21 J​=4.0×10−18 s,=10log10​(38​⋅4⋅(4.0×10−18)⋅5⋅(2.5×107))=10log10​(5.33×10−9)=−82.7 dBc/Hz,=10log10​(38​⋅12⋅(4.0×10−18)⋅5⋅(2.5×107))=10log10​(1.60×10−8)=−78.0 dBc/Hz,=10log10​412​=10log10​3=+4.77 dB.​ Result: stage count 4→12 (×3\times3×3) degrades the phase noise from −82.7-82.7−82.7 to −78.0-78.0−78.0 dBc/Hz, a difference of +4.77+4.77+4.77 dB. Same for the jitter constant: Eq.(35) gives κmin∝N\kappa_{min}\propto\sqrt{N}κmin​∝N​, so N×3N\times3N×3 → κ×3≈1.732\kappa\times\sqrt3\approx1.732κ×3​≈1.732.
