Python check: import numpy as np def L_ring_diff(N, kT, P, f0, df, eta=1.0, vdd_vchar=3.0, vdd_swing=2.0): # [P2] Eq.(34) return 10*np.log10(8/(3*eta) * N * (kT/P) * (vdd_vchar + vdd_swing) * (f0/df)**2) L4 = L_ring_diff(4, 4.0e-21, 1e-3, 5e9, 1e6) L12 = L_ring_diff(12, 4.0e-21, 1e-3, 5e9, 1e6) print(round(L4,1), round(L12,1), round(L12-L4,2)) # -> -82.7 -78.0 4.77 # Eq.(34) = 2N x Eq.(6); Eq.(6) denominator 8*pi^2*f^2 = 2*dw^2 -> these are /2-family values; [P1] Eq.(21) /4 family is 3.01 dB lower print(round(L4-10*np.log10(2),1), round(L12-10*np.log10(2),1)) # -> -85.7 -81.0 Applicability / failure conditions: Applies when: white-noise dominated (symmetry criteria already met, 1/f upconversion already suppressed — the stated premise at the start of [P2] Sec. V); fully switching differential pair with resistive load; Eq.(34)/(35) hold in both long- and short-channel regimes (with the right VcharV_{char}Vchar​); MOS or bipolar (the latter via Eq.(36) with Vchar=4kT/qeV_{char}=4kT/q_eVchar​=4kT/qe​). Caveats: Lmin\mathcal{L}_{min}Lmin​/κmin\kappa_{min}κmin​ are lower bounds (the same logic as Eq.(25)/(26) — extra noise sources, asymmetry, supply/substrate only make things worse); if the design fixes RLR_LRL​ instead of fixing the swing, then VDD/(RLItail)∝NV_{DD}/(R_L I_{tail})\propto NVDD​/(RL​Itail​)∝N and the degradation is steeper than 10log⁡10N10\log_{10}N10log10​N; the N−3/2N^{-3/2}N−3/2 of Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ carries over from Eq.(16) — [P2] Fig. 9 (p.795) measures the rms ISF of differential rings under three constraint scenarios (fixed power/fixed swing, fixed power/fixed RLR_LRL​, fixed tail current/fixed RLR_LRL​), all hugging the same scaling. One-line design rule: single-ended ring = phase noise immune to NNN (no NNN in Eq.23); differential ring = fewest stages wins (explicit NNN in Eq.34, +3.01+3.01+3.01 dB per doubling) — stop at the smallest NNN that phase margin, quadrature/multiphase, and frequency-division requirements allow.

documents.t: Ring is free-running with no absolute time reference; each stage transition adds a bit of independent timing noise, and the edge time performs a random walk, with accumulated jitter growing as the square root of the measurement interval ([P2] Eq.(8), p.792; κ\kappaκ = square root of Eq.(11), p.793 — the printed Eq.(12) is the time version κt=κ/ω0\kappa_t=\kappa/\omega_0κt​=κ/ω0​): σΔϕ=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta\phi}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔϕ​=κΔt​ This is phase jitter (dimensionless): per [P2] Eq.(11) σΔϕ2=Γrms2 in2‾/Δf2qmax2 Δt\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2\,\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{2q_{max}^2}\,\Delta tσΔϕ2​=2qmax2​Γrms2​in2​​/Δf​Δt, so κΔt\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}κΔt​ gives the phase jitter σΔϕ\sigma_{\Delta\phi}σΔϕ​. Time jitter then follows from [P2] Eq.(10)'s phase-to-time conversion σΔt=σΔϕ/ω0\sigma_{\Delta t}=\sigma_{\Delta\phi}/\omega_0σΔt​=σΔϕ​/ω0​. ω0\omega_0ω0​ lives in Eq.(10); this site's phase-version κ\kappaκ contains no ω0\omega_0ω0​, while the Eq.(12) printed on [P2] p.793 is the time version κt=κ/ω0\kappa_t=\kappa/\omega_0κt​=κ/ω0​ with Eq.(10) folded in (ω0\omega_0ω0​ in the denominator, units s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​). Unit check: κ\kappaκ has units 1/s1/\sqrt{\text{s}}1/s​ (in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf is [A2 ⁣⋅ ⁣s][\text{A}^2\!\cdot\!\text{s}][A2⋅s], qmaxq_{max}qmax​ is [A ⁣⋅ ⁣s][\text{A}\!\cdot\!\text{s}][A⋅s]), so κΔt=[1/s]⋅[s]=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}=[1/\sqrt{\text{s}}]\cdot[\sqrt{\text{s}}]=κΔt​=[1/s​]⋅[s​]= dimensionless ✓ (phase); dividing by ω0\omega_0ω0​ [1/s][1/\text{s}][1/s] gives σΔt=[s]\sigma_{\Delta t}=[\text{s}]σΔt​=[s] ✓ (time). κ2∝Γrms2/qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf\kappa^2\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2\cdot\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fκ2∝Γrms2​/qmax2​⋅in2​​/Δf ([P2] Eq.(11)–(12), p.793, re-verified in v11: phase version κ=(Γrms/qmax)(in2‾/Δf)/2\kappa=(\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max})\sqrt{(\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f)/2}κ=(Γrms​/qmax​)(in2​​/Δf)/2​ = square root of Eq.(11); the printed Eq.(12) is κt=κ/ω0\kappa_t=\kappa/\omega_0κt​=κ/ω0​) — the same core ratio shows up again. LC drifts much more slowly in phase (equivalently, small κ\kappaκ) thanks to high QQQ; but as long as it's free-running, both eventually drift — locking to an absolute time reference requires a PLL/CDR (see serdes_clocking_connection). documents.t: The steps above compared "whose ISF numbers are better, LC or ring." But the real design question is usually the other way around — given an application, which one do you pick? The answer depends not only on the VCO's own Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​, but also on whether a downstream loop filters out the VCO's close-in noise — CDR/PLL loop bandwidth is a high-pass filter on VCO phase noise (see serdes_clocking_connection Step 6). The table below collects the "who filters, who doesn't, and where the spec is dominated" evidence already derived elsewhere on this site into one selection table: Application Who filters the VCO (CDR/PLL BW, or none) Dominant spec region Choice ISF rationale SerDes TX PLL Narrow loop BW (filters the reference; VCO close-in appears directly at the output) close-in 1/f³ and in-band 1/f² LC-VCO No loop to help — low Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​/high qmaxq_{max}qmax​ is the only way to suppress close-in directly; see serdes_clocking_connection Step 7 SerDes RX CDR Wide loop BW, high-passes away VCO close-in (1/f³ and fast random walk) white noise left outside the loop / jitter tolerance ring-VCO viable The loop's high-pass stopband sits right on top of ring's weakness (close-in, fast random walk), and the multiphase outputs come free; see serdes_clocking_connection Steps 6–7 ADC/DAC sampling clock No CDR/PLL relief (free-running sampling, no loop to filter) close-in integrates straight into SNR (aperture jitter, no high-pass exemption) LC + clean reference No loop protection — low-offset noise counts in full toward σt\sigma_tσt​; see adc_aperture_jitter, reference_oscillators "Connection to SerDes" RF synthesizer (cellular/Wi-Fi) Narrow–moderate loop BW, spec dominated by spot offset 1 MHz spot L\mathcal{L}L and reference spurs (2–6 GHz class, order −120…−135-120\ldots-135−120…−135 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, external rule-of-thumb, not from this site's 5 PDFs, no citation fabricated) LC-VCO Spot spec pushes against the FOM ceiling — only the low-Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​/high-qmaxq_{max}qmax​ LC can get in; check feasibility against the fom_limit ceiling family Low-power BLE-class Power is the priority, but loop relief can't rescue ring's ceiling FOMreq\mathrm{FOM}_{req}FOMreq​ vs ring ceiling ([P2] Eq.(25) lower bound, ≈168.3\approx168.3≈168.3 dB, see fom_limit Step 2) Still LC Ring's FeffF_{eff}Feff​ ceiling is a hard limit — under N-independence, no power/NNN tweak buys it back; use the design_recipe Step 2 ceiling gate to check feasibility SoC internal digital clock Wide loop-BW PLL, tracks out VCO close-in in-band ps-level timing margin, not close-in dBc/Hz ring-VCO The wide loop filters away ring's weakness, trading in for small area, wide tuning, and easy digital-process integration Multiphase / wide tuning-range applications System-dependent; this row's choice is unrelated to filtering number of phases and tuning range, not phase noise ring-VCO Choosing NNN should be driven by tuning range/phase count/area, not phase noise (single-ended N-independence; this page's Step 2 "design implication") Instrumentation/radar reference chain No CDR; only the +20log⁡10N+20\log_{10}N+20log10​N of ×N multiplication (no cure) full-band close-in (Lorentzian linewidth) OCXO reference + LC multiplier chain The reference's close-in sets the whole chain's floor; multiplier stages still need the low-Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​/high-qmaxq_{max}qmax​ LC; see clock_chain_budget Rule 1, reference_oscillators Honesty banner (following the same rule as reference_oscillators Step 5): any row in the "dominant spec region" column that quotes a concrete dBc/Hz number is an industry-convention order-of-magnitude range (external literature, not from this site's 5 PDFs); different vendors/processes/vintages can differ by 10–20 dB, and real selection always goes by the datasheet's L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) curve and spur table — this site does not fabricate specific part numbers or paper figures. The other columns (who filters, ISF rationale) are direct applications of the ISF/CDR-high-pass/FOM derivations already verified earlier on this site, not new paper results. One-line summary: where a wide loop filters away close-in noise (RX CDR, SoC-internal PLL) — ring's weakness stays hidden; where no loop filters, or the spec is dominated by close-in/spot noise (TX PLL, ADC/DAC clocks, RF synthesizers, even power-first low-power designs that still must meet spec, instrumentation reference chains) — LC's low-Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​/high-qmaxq_{max}qmax​ advantage shows up directly in the spec.

documents.t: The following two examples use [P2]'s ring white-noise FOM to compute a concrete L\mathcal{L}L, and verify that "at fixed f0f_0f0​/power, phase noise is roughly independent of NNN." The formulas have been verified against the original [P2] PDF; below we take η≈1\eta\approx1η≈1 (stage-delay proportionality constant, entering the prefactor 8/(3η)8/(3\eta)8/(3η)), γ=2/3\gamma=2/3γ=2/3 (long channel, entering only through Vchar=ΔV/γV_{char}=\Delta V/\gammaVchar​=ΔV/γ), VDD/Vchar=3V_{DD}/V_{char}=3VDD​/Vchar​=3 (illustrative value); the numbers are an order-of-magnitude demonstration. Example 1 (use the ring FOM to compute 1/f² phase noise, comparing N=3/5/15) Take f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, offset Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, kT=4.0×10−21kT=4.0\times10^{-21}kT=4.0×10−21 J (300 K), P=1P=1P=1 mW, η≈1\eta\approx1η≈1, γ=2/3\gamma=2/3γ=2/3 (already absorbed into VDD/Vchar=3V_{DD}/V_{char}=3VDD​/Vchar​=3). One-line Python check: import numpy as np def L_ring_fom(kT, P, f0, df, eta=1.0, vdd_vchar=3.0): # [P2] Eq.(23), prefactor 8/(3*eta) return 10*np.log10(8/(3*eta) * (kT/P) * vdd_vchar * (f0/df)**2) vals = {N: L_ring_fom(4.0e-21, 1e-3, 5e9, 1e6) for N in (3, 5, 15)} print({N: round(v,1) for N,v in vals.items()}) # -> {3: -91.0, 5: -91.0, 15: -91.0} N-independence here is a direct consequence of "Eq.(23) simply contains no NNN" — and the toy exponents agree: Γrms2∝N−3\Gamma_{rms}^2\propto N^{-3}Γrms2​∝N−3 (Eq.16), qmax∝N−1q_{max}\propto N^{-1}qmax​∝N−1 (from Eq.(21) at fixed PPP, f0f_0f0​), and ×N\times N×N noise sources, so Γrms2/qmax2⋅N∝N−3+2+1=N0\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2\cdot N\propto N^{-3+2+1}=N^0Γrms2​/qmax2​⋅N∝N−3+2+1=N0, consistent with Eq.(23) (see lab_17 for the walkthrough). Example 2 (LC vs ring: how much better is LC under comparable-order conditions?) Use [P1] Eq.(21) to compute a representative LC number and place it side by side with ring's −91.0-91.0−91.0 dBc/Hz above. Take canonical Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Si=in2‾/Δf=10−24S_i=\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=10^{-24}Si​=in2​​/Δf=10−24 A²/Hz, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz. documents.s: Further reading

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: white_noise_to_phase_noise (L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​, the 1/f21/f^21/f2 mid-band, useful for back-solving SiS_iSi​), fourier_series_of_isf (the mechanism by which a spur is downconverted through the ISF's nnn-th harmonic cnc_ncn​), symmetry (back-solving c0/c1c_0/c_1c0​/c1​ symmetry from the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner) | Next: real_oscillator_topologies, lorentzian_linewidth The previous chapters carried phase noise from the ISF all the way to L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf) (SSB phase noise, units dBc/Hz) — all as "theoretical prediction." This page returns to the test bench and answers three questions that always come up in real measurement: How do you measure L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f)? Three mainstream methods — the spectrum analyzer (SA) direct method, the PLL/delay-line frequency discriminator (carrier-suppression method), and cross-correlation (correlating two independent channels to push the instrument floor down by a square root) — each with its own principle, pros/cons, and applicable range. How do you distinguish a spur (spurious tone, a deterministic sideband) from random phase noise? One is a discrete tone (units dBc, not /Hz), the other a continuous spectrum (/Hz). They look different on the spectrum, have different causes, and need different countermeasures. How do you read a real PN plot? Mark the 1/f31/f^31/f3, 1/f21/f^21/f2, and floor segments, the corners, and the spurs, then back out design information. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the fundamental difficulty in measuring phase noise is that the device under test's (DUT's) phase jitter is tiny (often −100-100−100 to −150-150−150 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset), while your own instrument jitters too. So every method does the same thing: find a way to remove the tall, clean carrier tone, leaving only the faint noise skirt beside it, while making the measurement system's own noise floor lower than the DUT's. The three methods are three engineering approaches to "remove the carrier + push down the floor." Honesty note: this page's measurement-instrument architectures and standards (PN spectrum analyzers, delay-line/PLL discriminators, cross-correlation analyzers — e.g. Keysight E5052B, R&S FSWP, Holzworth, etc.) are external engineering literature and instrument manuals, not among the five source PDFs. This page supplements with standard measurement theory and ties every result back to [P1]'s ISF framework. The underlying physics (carrier removal, PSD estimation, correlation averaging) is general DSP/communications knowledge; specific instrument models are used only as examples.
documents.s: Phase-noise measurement and spurs

documents.t: First, state clearly what we're measuring. Write the oscillator output as v(t)=V0 [1+a(t)]cos⁡ ⁣(ω0t+ϕ(t)),v(t)=V_0\,\big[1+a(t)\big]\cos\!\big(\omega_0 t+\phi(t)\big),v(t)=V0​[1+a(t)]cos(ω0​t+ϕ(t)), where a(t)a(t)a(t) is AM noise (amplitude noise) and ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) is PM noise (phase noise, this site's main subject). We want the single-sideband power spectrum of the phase part: L(Δf)≈12Sϕ(Δf)[dBc/Hz],\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\approx\tfrac12 S_\phi(\Delta f)\quad[\text{dBc/Hz}],L(Δf)≈21​Sϕ​(Δf)[dBc/Hz], (small-angle approximation, canonical Eq.16; see white_noise_to_phase_noise). The three methods differ in "how cleanly ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) is separated from v(t)v(t)v(t) without being contaminated by the instrument's own phase noise."
documents.s: Part 1: three methods for measuring L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f)

documents.t: Principle: connect the DUT directly to a spectrum analyzer and look at the power-spectrum skirt beside the carrier f0f_0f0​. At offset Δf\Delta fΔf, resolution bandwidth RBW\text{RBW}RBW, the measured sideband power PSSB(Δf)P_{SSB}(\Delta f)PSSB​(Δf) relative to carrier power PcarrierP_{carrier}Pcarrier​, normalized to 1 Hz: L(Δf)=10log⁡10 ⁣(PSSB(Δf)Pcarrier)−10log⁡10(ENBW/1 Hz) + 2.5 dB.\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P_{SSB}(\Delta f)}{P_{carrier}}\right)-10\log_{10}(\text{ENBW}/1\,\text{Hz})\ +\ 2.5\,\text{dB}.L(Δf)=10log10​(Pcarrier​PSSB​(Δf)​)−10log10​(ENBW/1Hz) + 2.5dB. The first term is "how many dB the sideband is below the carrier" (dBc). The second term normalizes the measurement bandwidth to per-Hz (using the equivalent noise bandwidth ENBW rather than the nominal RBW; e.g. for ENBW ≈1\approx1≈1 kHz you subtract 10log⁡101000=3010\log_{10}1000=3010log10​1000=30 dB). The +2.5+2.5+2.5 dB is a common correction: a log detector combined with video/sample averaging underestimates Gaussian noise by about 2.52.52.5 dB (Rayleigh-log bias), so about 2.52.52.5 dB must be added back to recover the true noise power (external literature: Keysight/Agilent AN-1303 spectrum analysis basics). This is a toy/illustrative approximation; real instruments auto-correct this in their built-in PN measurement mode. Unit check: 10log⁡10(dimensionless W/W)−10log⁡10(Hz)=dBc−dB(Hz)=dBc/Hz10\log_{10}(\text{dimensionless W/W})-10\log_{10}(\text{Hz})=\text{dBc}-\text{dB(Hz)}=\text{dBc/Hz}10log10​(dimensionless W/W)−10log10​(Hz)=dBc−dB(Hz)=dBc/Hz ✓. Advantages: Fastest setup — a single SA does it; you also see spurs (discrete tones) and the broadband noise landscape at the same time. Fatal drawback — the SA's own phase noise: What you measure is not the DUT's SϕDUTS_\phi^{DUT}SϕDUT​, but the sum of the DUT's and the SA's local oscillator (LO) phase noise: Sϕmeas(Δf)=SϕDUT(Δf)+SϕSA LO(Δf).S_\phi^{meas}(\Delta f)=S_\phi^{DUT}(\Delta f)+S_\phi^{SA\,LO}(\Delta f).Sϕmeas​(Δf)=SϕDUT​(Δf)+SϕSALO​(Δf). As long as the DUT is cleaner than the SA's LO, what you measure is the SA itself — you're measuring the instrument, not the DUT. Also, the SA measures the sum of AM+PM; near the carrier PM usually dominates, but it cannot separate AM from PM. Applicable range: when the DUT's phase noise is clearly worse than the SA's LO (e.g. measuring a noisy free-running ring VCO), or when you just need a quick look at spurs and the rough skirt shape. Not suitable for low-noise reference sources (OCXO, low-noise PLL), since you'll hit the SA floor.
documents.s: Method A: direct spectrum-analyzer method

documents.t: The problem with the direct method is that "the big carrier tone is still there, and the small noise beside it is swamped by the instrument's dynamic range and LO noise." The idea of carrier suppression: first cancel the carrier term cos⁡(ω0t)\cos(\omega_0 t)cos(ω0​t) with a phase detector, converting only ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) into a baseband voltage fed into a low-frequency FFT analyzer (whose floor is far below an RF SA's). There are two carrier-suppression methods: B-1: PLL (phase-locked loop) method — lock to a clean reference​ Feed the DUT and a cleaner reference source into a mixer (used as a phase detector), and use a PLL to lock the two at 90∘90^\circ90∘ (quadrature). At quadrature the mixer output is linear in the phase difference: vout(t)=Kϕ [ϕDUT(t)−ϕref(t)],v_{out}(t)=K_\phi\,\big[\phi_{DUT}(t)-\phi_{ref}(t)\big],vout​(t)=Kϕ​[ϕDUT​(t)−ϕref​(t)], KϕK_\phiKϕ​ is the phase-detector gain (V/rad). The PLL loop bandwidth is set very low, so that at the offsets of interest ϕref\phi_{ref}ϕref​ is tracked out by the loop, leaving only the DUT's phase fluctuation converted to voltage. FFT voutv_{out}vout​ and divide by Kϕ2K_\phi^2Kϕ2​ to get SϕDUTS_\phi^{DUT}SϕDUT​. Advantages: the floor can be made extremely low (limited by the reference source, mixer, baseband amplifier), making it one of the gold-standard methods for low-noise sources; it naturally measures only PM (a mixer at quadrature is insensitive to AM). Drawbacks: needs a reference source cleaner than the DUT (the biggest pain point); requires locking, so the DUT must be stable enough; offsets below the PLL loop bandwidth get eaten by the loop and need loop-transfer correction. B-2: delay-line frequency discriminator — using the DUT as its own reference​ When you cannot find a cleaner reference source (e.g. measuring a source that is itself the best low-noise part available), use the DUT delayed by τd\tau_dτd​ as its own reference. Split the signal into two paths, one through a delay line τd\tau_dτd​, the other through a phase shifter tuned to quadrature, then into a mixer. The delay converts frequency fluctuation into a phase difference, which the mixer resolves. Its transfer function (converting frequency noise SΔfS_{\Delta f}SΔf​ into output) is ∣H(Δf)∣2=(2πτd)2 sinc⁡2(Δf τd),sinc⁡(x)=sin⁡(πx)πx,\big|H(\Delta f)\big|^2=\big(2\pi\tau_d\big)^2\,\operatorname{sinc}^2(\Delta f\,\tau_d),\qquad \operatorname{sinc}(x)=\frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x},​H(Δf)​2=(2πτd​)2sinc2(Δfτd​),sinc(x)=πxsin(πx)​, here HHH maps frequency fluctuation δf\delta fδf to output. The discriminator senses frequency fluctuation, and frequency is the derivative of phase, so the bridging relation between the frequency spectrum and phase spectrum is Sδf(Δf)=Δf2 Sϕ(Δf)S_{\delta f}(\Delta f)=\Delta f^2\,S_\phi(\Delta f)Sδf​(Δf)=Δf2Sϕ​(Δf) (each extra derivative adds one Δf\Delta fΔf factor in the frequency domain). Substituting this back gives an extra Δf2\Delta f^2Δf2 in the denominator (i.e. (2πτd)2→(2π Δf τd)2(2\pi\tau_d)^2\to(2\pi\,\Delta f\,\tau_d)^2(2πτd​)2→(2πΔfτd​)2), so Sϕ(Δf)=Sv(Δf)Kϕ2 (2π Δf τd)2 sinc⁡2(Δf τd).S_\phi(\Delta f)=\frac{S_{v}(\Delta f)}{K_\phi^2\,(2\pi\,\Delta f\,\tau_d)^2\,\operatorname{sinc}^2(\Delta f\,\tau_d)}.Sϕ​(Δf)=Kϕ2​(2πΔfτd​)2sinc2(Δfτd​)Sv​(Δf)​. Physical meaning: the delay line converts frequency discrimination into phase, with sensitivity ∝τd\propto\tau_d∝τd​ — the longer the delay, the more sensitive. Drawback: sensitivity ∝τd\propto\tau_d∝τd​, but sinc⁡\operatorname{sinc}sinc has nulls at Δf=k/τd\Delta f=k/\tau_dΔf=k/τd​ — too long a delay narrows the usable offset range and blinds the measurement at the nulls; the delay line itself has loss (attenuates the signal, raises the floor). It's a "sensitivity vs. frequency coverage" trade-off. Advantage: needs no external reference source, self-sufficient; good for measuring a source that is itself extremely clean, with no better reference available. Unit check (delay-line): SvS_vSv​ is V2/Hz\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}V2/Hz; dividing by Kϕ2K_\phi^2Kϕ2​ (V2/rad2\text{V}^2/\text{rad}^2V2/rad2) gives rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz; the denominator (2πΔfτd)2(2\pi\Delta f\tau_d)^2(2πΔfτd​)2 is dimensionless, so overall rad2/Hz=Sϕ\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}=S_\phirad2/Hz=Sϕ​ ✓.
documents.s: Method B: PLL / delay-line frequency discriminator (carrier-suppression method)

documents.t: This is the signature technique of modern commercial PN analyzers (e.g. E5052B, FSWP, Holzworth), not among the five source PDFs, and belongs to external instrument literature. It addresses Method B's fundamental limitation: the measurement channel's own floor. Core idea: split the same DUT's signal into two paths, each connected to a fully independent carrier-suppression + measurement channel (each with its own reference source/mixer/amplifier, whose floors are mutually uncorrelated). The two path outputs are y1(t)=ϕDUT(t)+n1(t),y2(t)=ϕDUT(t)+n2(t),y_1(t)=\phi_{DUT}(t)+n_1(t),\qquad y_2(t)=\phi_{DUT}(t)+n_2(t),y1​(t)=ϕDUT​(t)+n1​(t),y2​(t)=ϕDUT​(t)+n2​(t), where ϕDUT\phi_{DUT}ϕDUT​ is the DUT phase shared by both paths (correlated), and n1,n2n_1,n_2n1​,n2​ are each channel's independent instrument floor (uncorrelated). Compute the cross-spectrum Sy1y2=⟨Y1Y2∗⟩S_{y_1 y_2}=\langle Y_1 Y_2^*\rangleSy1​y2​​=⟨Y1​Y2∗​⟩ of the two paths and average MMM times: Sy1y2(Δf)=Sϕϕ(Δf)⏟correlated, retained+1M(uncorrelated floor term)⏟drops with square root of averages.S_{y_1 y_2}(\Delta f)=\underbrace{S_{\phi\phi}(\Delta f)}_{\text{correlated, retained}}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\big(\text{uncorrelated floor term}\big)}_{\text{drops with square root of averages}}.Sy1​y2​​(Δf)=correlated, retainedSϕϕ​(Δf)​​+drops with square root of averagesM​1​(uncorrelated floor term)​​. Key physics: the DUT phase is correlated across the two paths, so it adds coherently in the cross-correlation and is retained in full; the two channels' instrument floors are uncorrelated, so in the cross-correlation they behave as random phase and, after averaging over MMM segments, converge as 1/M1/\sqrt{M}1/M​ (every 10× more averaging drops the floor by 555 dB, i.e. 10log⁡1010=510\log_{10}\sqrt{10}=510log10​10​=5 dB). How much you can gain: relative to the single-channel floor, you can additionally lower it by Δfloor=5log⁡10M [dB](5 dB per ×10 averaging).\Delta_{floor}=5\log_{10}M\ \text{[dB]}\quad(\text{5 dB per }\times10\text{ averaging}).Δfloor​=5log10​M [dB](5 dB per ×10 averaging). Dropping 202020 dB needs M=104M=10^4M=104 averages; beyond a certain point you're limited by residual correlation between channels (shared supply, reference distribution, thermal) and measurement time. Advantages: the floor can be pushed lower than any single reference source — you can measure world-class low-noise sources; the same architecture can separate AM and PM simultaneously. Drawbacks: needs two independent sets of hardware, expensive; near the carrier needs heavy averaging, so measurement time is long (MMM large); residual correlation sets a practical limit. Applicable range: measuring the lowest-noise sources (OCXO, low-noise synthesizers, integrated PLLs), the method of choice when you need to approach the physical floor limit. Three practical pitfalls of Method C​ The derivation above assumes the two channels' instrument floors n1,n2n_1,n_2n1​,n2​ are mutually uncorrelated. On a real cross-correlation analyzer there are three pitfalls that frequently trip up newcomers: (i) Cross-spectrum collapse: if n1,n2n_1,n_2n1​,n2​ are actually anti-correlated (Sn1n2<0S_{n_1n_2}<0Sn1​n2​​<0), the floor is not only not suppressed — it gets subtracted out of the cross-spectrum: Sy1y2=Sϕϕ+Sn1n2,Sn1n2<0 (when anti-correlated).S_{y_1y_2}=S_{\phi\phi}+S_{n_1n_2},\qquad S_{n_1n_2}<0\ \text{(when anti-correlated)}.Sy1​y2​​=Sϕϕ​+Sn1​n2​​,Sn1​n2​​<0 (when anti-correlated). Anti-correlation usually comes from a shared analog front end: AM noise converts to baseband differently through each channel's own mixer (different gain, different phase), or a power splitter's differential-mode thermal noise couples into the two paths with opposite sign — these are not each channel's independent instrument noise, but a systematic negative-correlation term. The result is a measured floor that looks "too good to be true" (much lower than any single channel, or even a notch or a negative real part in the estimate at some offsets) — this is a measurement artifact, not evidence that the DUT is really that clean. Diagnostic rule: if the floor suddenly looks abnormally low, or the cross-spectrum shows a negative real part or a notch, suspect collapse and re-measure with different hardware (a different power splitter, an isolated AM path) for comparison. This is a known phenomenon in the external measurement literature (external literature, not among the five source PDFs): C. W. Nelson, A. Hati, and D. A. Howe, "A collapse of the cross-spectral function in phase noise metrology," Rev. Sci. Instrum., vol. 85, no. 2, p. 024705, Feb. 2014 (DOI: 10.1063/1.4865715). (ii) The convergence check — the floor should saturate at the DUT's true floor, not keep dropping: 1/M1/\sqrt{M}1/M​ only holds for the uncorrelated residual; as MMM grows, the correct behavior is for the residual floor to approach (not keep falling below) the DUT's true floor, because the DUT-correlated term does not shrink with MMM. If you keep increasing MMM and the −5log⁡10M-5\log_{10}M−5log10​M slope never saturates (keeps dropping linearly forever, with no bend toward some floor), that means you are still measuring the instrument (or the uncorrelated residual has not yet dropped near the DUT floor) — you have not measured the DUT yet. The M=256,1024M=256,1024M=256,1024 points in the lab_35 simulation table below demonstrate exactly this saturation process: the straight-line fit is only valid for M≤64M\le64M≤64, and M=256/1024M=256/1024M=256/1024 visibly deviate from the pure −5log⁡10M-5\log_{10}M−5log10​M line (see the table and the "this is not an error, it is physics" discussion below) — the curve bending toward the true floor, and no longer dropping further, is the sign that the measurement is correct. (iii) Spur-included vs. spur-excluded integrated-jitter readings: when integrating jitter (σϕ,σt\sigma_\phi,\sigma_tσϕ​,σt​), instruments typically offer two numbers: integrating only the continuous PN (spur-excluded), or including discrete spurs in the total jitter (spur-included). A spur is a discrete tone; its power is computed as 10spurdBc/1010^{\text{spur}_{dBc}/10}10spurdBc​/10, counted once per sideband (a factor of 222), and added linearly into σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​ (not integrated like a continuous spectrum): σϕ2∣spur-included=σϕ2∣PN only⏟Sec. 3.3 integral+2∑k10spurk,dBc/10.\sigma_\phi^2\Big|_{\text{spur-included}}=\underbrace{\sigma_\phi^2\Big|_{\text{PN only}}}_{\text{Sec. 3.3 integral}}+2\sum_k10^{\text{spur}_{k,dBc}/10}.σϕ2​​spur-included​=Sec. 3.3 integralσϕ2​​PN only​​​+2k∑​10spurk,dBc​/10. A numerical feel: a single −60-60−60 dBc reference spur alone contributes σϕ=2×10−6=1.41\sigma_\phi=\sqrt{2\times10^{-6}}=1.41σϕ​=2×10−6​=1.41 mrad, i.e. σt≈45\sigma_t\approx45σt​≈45 fs at f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz — the same order of magnitude as the 27.627.627.6 fs buffer floor computed by Rule 4 in clock_chain_budget, showing that one unremarkable −60-60−60 dBc spur can hurt the total jitter budget about as much as an entire clock chain's white noise floor. When you get a jitter number from a datasheet or measurement report, always ask which convention it uses first — the two can differ by more than 2×2\times2× and mean very different things for spec margin (a spur can usually be removed by isolation/filtering; a continuous PN floor cannot). import numpy as np f0 = 5e9 spur_dbc = -60.0 sigma_phi_spur = np.sqrt(2 * 10**(spur_dbc/10)) # rad, spur-only contribution sigma_t_spur = sigma_phi_spur / (2*np.pi*f0) print(f"sigma_phi_spur = {sigma_phi_spur*1e3:.2f} mrad") # -> 1.41 print(f"sigma_t_spur = {sigma_t_spur*1e15:.1f} fs") # -> 45.0 Method C simulation: two-channel cross-correlation squeezes the instrument floor by a square root​ The 1/M1/\sqrt{M}1/M​ convergence above is only a verbal description; here is a reproducible numerical simulation that actually produces it, so you can see with your own eyes how "the single channel measures the instrument floor, while cross-correlation digs the true DUT floor back out" happens (full code: simulations/lab_35_xcorr_measurement.py; figure: static/figures/xcorr_floor.png). Methodology walkthrough: Synthesize a "true" DUT spectrum: use the site's canonical values (Example B: qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5; [P1] Eq.(21) gives L(1 MHz)=−148.0\mathcal{L}(1\text{ MHz})=-148.0L(1 MHz)=−148.0 dBc/Hz, i.e. Sϕ(1 MHz)=2×10−14.8=3.17×10−15S_\phi(1\text{ MHz})=2\times10^{-14.8}=3.17\times10^{-15}Sϕ​(1 MHz)=2×10−14.8=3.17×10−15 rad²/Hz) as the 1/f21/f^21/f2 mid-band, then add a white floor 202020 dB below it (SDUT,floor=3.17×10−17S_{DUT,floor}=3.17\times10^{-17}SDUT,floor​=3.17×10−17 rad²/Hz) — an honest "two-segment" toy DUT spectrum: 1/f21/f^21/f2 near the carrier, flattening far out. This is a known answer, so we can check whether the measurement method actually recovers it. Add instrument white noise to two independent channels: y1(t)=ϕDUT(t)+n1(t)y_1(t)=\phi_{DUT}(t)+n_1(t)y1​(t)=ϕDUT​(t)+n1​(t), y2(t)=ϕDUT(t)+n2(t)y_2(t)=\phi_{DUT}(t)+n_2(t)y2​(t)=ϕDUT​(t)+n2​(t), n1⊥n2⊥ϕDUTn_1\perp n_2\perp\phi_{DUT}n1​⊥n2​⊥ϕDUT​, each channel's floor set 151515 dB above the DUT floor (Sinstr=101.5×SDUT,floor≈1.00×10−15S_{instr}=10^{1.5}\times S_{DUT,floor}\approx1.00\times10^{-15}Sinstr​=101.5×SDUT,floor​≈1.00×10−15 rad²/Hz) — matching the comparison table's scenario where "single-channel floor === DUT floor +++ instrument floor." Compute both spectra from the same data: the single-channel auto-spectrum Syy=⟨∣Y1∣2⟩S_{yy}=\langle|Y_1|^2\rangleSyy​=⟨∣Y1​∣2⟩ (MMM-segment averaged) and the cross-spectrum Sy1y2=⟨Y1Y2∗⟩S_{y_1y_2}=\langle Y_1Y_2^*\rangleSy1​y2​​=⟨Y1​Y2∗​⟩ (also MMM-segment averaged), with M=1,4,16,64,256,1024M=1,4,16,64,256,1024M=1,4,16,64,256,1024 (powers of 4). In a high-offset band far from freff_{ref}fref​ (808080–959595 MHz, where the DUT's 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt has already decayed to below 1.5%1.5\%1.5% of the DUT floor and can be treated as "floor only"), measure how the cross-spectrum residual floor changes with MMM, and fit a straight line over M≤64M\le64M≤64 (where the residual floor is still clearly above the true DUT floor, i.e. "uncorrelated-noise-dominated"), comparing against the canonical slope Δfloor=5log⁡10M\Delta_{floor}=5\log_{10}MΔfloor​=5log10​M. At M=1024M=1024M=1024, compare the recovered spectrum against the true DUT spectrum: can cross-correlation dig out the DUT's true floor, which the single channel cannot resolve. Recovery performance (at M=1024M=1024M=1024, see panel (b) below): In the DUT floor region (near 909090 MHz): the true value is L=−167.95\mathcal{L}=-167.95L=−167.95 dBc/Hz; the single channel measures −152.74-152.74−152.74 dBc/Hz (masked by the instrument floor, off by 15.215.215.2 dB — what it measures is really the instrument); cross-correlation (M=1024M=1024M=1024) measures −166.15-166.15−166.15 dBc/Hz, only +1.79+1.79+1.79 dB off (# -> residual error at DUT floor after M=1024 averaging: +1.79 dB) — the DUT's true floor, completely hidden under the instrument floor, is dug back out almost fully by correlating two independent channels and averaging. Titles read: "(a) 互相關本底 vs M（擬合斜率=… dB/decade, M≤…）" = (a) the cross-correlation floor vs. M (fitted slope=… dB/decade, M≤…); "(b) 還原頻譜（M=1024）vs 真實 DUT" = (b) the recovered spectrum (M=1024) vs. the true DUT. Honesty note: what is verified here is only the statistical/DSP mechanism behind cross-correlation (the 1/M1/\sqrt{M}1/M​ convergence itself is a property of general complex-Gaussian statistics, not content from this site's five source PDFs, and not ISF physics), and in the model the two channels' instrument floors are set to be perfectly uncorrelated. On a real instrument, M→∞M\to\inftyM→∞ cannot push the floor down without limit — residual inter-channel correlation (shared reference clock distribution, shared supply/ground, thermal coupling) sets a physical floor not modeled in this simulation (external engineering literature, not among the five source PDFs; the simulation above only demonstrates the idealized 1/M1/\sqrt{M}1/M​ mechanism and one realistic finite-MMM outcome, not that the floor can be pushed arbitrarily low).

documents.t: A measured PN plot commonly shows two completely different things superimposed, which newcomers easily confuse. First, pin down the definitions: Item Random phase noise Spur (spurious tone) Nature Random (stochastic) process Deterministic sine tone Spectral appearance Continuous skirt Discrete single spike Units /Hz (dBc/Hz, power density) dBc (total power ratio, no /Hz) Vs. RBW Measured dBc/Hz does not change with RBW (already normalized) Spike height (dBc) does not change with RBW; but "appears" to widen/narrow with RBW Cause Device thermal/flicker noise, upconverted via ISF Reference leakage, supply ripple, external injection, and other periodic disturbances Countermeasure Improve ISF symmetry, increase qmaxq_{max}qmax​, lower device noise Find the interferer, isolate/filter/shield
documents.s: Part 2: spurs (deterministic sidebands) vs. random phase noise

documents.t: Random PN is a power density: phase is a continuous random process, so its power is spread across the frequency axis; only "power per Hz" is meaningful — hence dBc/Hz. Double the measurement bandwidth RBW and the measured noise power doubles too, but once normalized to per-Hz the number does not change. A spur is the total power of a discrete tone: a deterministic sine wave's entire power sits at a single frequency, with theoretically zero bandwidth. Its "density" is infinite (meaningless), so only the total power relative to the carrier, in dBc, is reported — no /Hz. Increasing RBW does not change its dBc value (all the power is in that one spike); it just looks "fatter." Measurement trap: on a PN analyzer, the continuous background is plotted in dBc/Hz, but if a spur is also plotted as "the density at the current RBW," it will drift up and down as you change RBW — this is an artifact. The correct approach is for the instrument to flag spurs separately in dBc (integrated total power). Discriminating rule: change the RBW setting and remeasure — the random PN's dBc/Hz number does not move, but the spur's "dBc/Hz reading" will change (because it is not a density). Whichever number moves is the spur.

documents.t: Spur frequency location Typical cause Physical mechanism (tied to ISF) Countermeasure freff_{ref}fref​ and its harmonics (reference spur) PLL reference leakage, charge-pump mismatch, PFD dead zone Periodic disturbance at the reference frequency, upconverted to near the carrier via the ISF's nnn-th harmonic Reduce CP leakage/mismatch, optimize PFD, strengthen loop-filter rejection Supply ripple frequency (e.g. 50/6050/6050/60 Hz, switching supply ∼\sim∼ hundreds of kHz) Periodic ripple on supply/ground coupling into tank/tail Periodic supply disturbance → upconverted via ISF's c0/cnc_0/c_nc0​/cn​ Regulator/LDO decoupling, layout isolation, lower PSRR sensitivity Nearby strong-signal frequency External RF injection, injection pulling Injected signal pulls the oscillator (see injection locking) Shielding, isolation, larger tank QQQ to resist pulling Digital clock and its harmonics Digital aggressor coupling via substrate/supply Periodic digital edges, upconverted via ISF Guard rings, separate supply domains, timing offset The key insight tying this back to the ISF: a deterministic injected single tone landing at nω0+Δωn\omega_0+\Delta\omeganω0​+Δω (near the nnn-th harmonic) gets downconverted by the ISF's nnn-th Fourier coefficient cnc_ncn​ to Δω\Delta\omegaΔω beside the carrier, producing a spur ([P1] Eq.(16/17), p.183, the single-tone version; see fourier_series_of_isf): ϕ(t)≈I0 cnsin⁡(Δωt)2qmax Δω.\phi(t)\approx\frac{I_0\,c_n\sin(\Delta\omega t)}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}.ϕ(t)≈2qmax​ΔωI0​cn​sin(Δωt)​. This uses the same ISF mechanism as random PN — the only difference is "whether the source is a deterministic single tone (→ spur) or white noise (→ continuous spectrum)." Design implication: if a spur lands near the nnn-th harmonic, lowering the ISF's cnc_ncn​ (by improving waveform symmetry) suppresses that spur too — the same knob set as for lowering random PN.
documents.s: 2.2 Typical causes of spurs and countermeasures

documents.t: Look at the shape: continuous skirt = random PN; isolated spike = spur. Change the RBW and re-weight: dBc/Hz unchanged is PN; a reading that changes with RBW is a spur. Check repeatability: a spur's frequency is fixed (locked to freff_{ref}fref​, ripple frequency, etc.); toggling nearby equipment (power supplies, nearby transmitters) makes the spur move/disappear; random PN is intrinsic to the DUT and cannot be switched off. Integrate power: integrating a spur gives a fixed dBc (independent of RBW); integrating PN gives jitter (see numerical_feeling).

It reflects ISF symmetry: the smaller c0c_0c0​ (ISF DC component) is — the more symmetric the waveform — the closer this corner sits to the carrier and the narrower the 1/f31/f^31/f3 region — this is the quantitative basis for "why pursue a symmetric waveform" (see symmetry). The noise-floor corner Δffloor\Delta f_{floor}Δffloor​: where 1/f21/f^21/f2 crosses the flat floor. It is usually the floor of the measurement system or output buffer, not necessarily intrinsic to the oscillator — when reading a plot, first confirm whether the floor is the DUT's or the instrument's (using cross-correlation from Part 1 to push down the instrument floor, so you can see the DUT's real floor).

documents.t: Height and width of the 1/f31/f^31/f3 region → device flicker magnitude (ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​) and ISF symmetry (c0c_0c0​). If close-in performance is poor → switch to a lower-flicker device, symmetrize the waveform/layout, use a tail filter to suppress c0c_0c0​. Height of the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region → Γrms2/qmax2⋅Si\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2 \cdot S_iΓrms2​/qmax2​⋅Si​. If too high → increase swing (qmaxq_{max}qmax​), lower device white noise, suppress Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (see tank_swing). A 202020 dB improvement per decade in the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region is a physical law — if the slope is off, suspect a measurement error. Floor height → confirm whether it is the DUT or the instrument. If it's the buffer, increase carrier power or switch to a lower-noise buffer. Spurs → identify each one: freff_{ref}fref​? ripple? injection? Apply the countermeasures in the 2.2 table respectively. This whole PN plot picture — the Leeson model and the ISF model produce the same three-segment broken line — this site's derivation_leeson and the leeson_vs_isf figure overlay both models; the three segments (1/f31/f^31/f3, 1/f21/f^21/f2, floor) and corners line up exactly. The only difference is that the ISF explains each segment's constant in terms of Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, c0c_0c0​, qmaxq_{max}qmax​, while Leeson uses the empirical QQQ, FFF. Relation to single-segment integration: the 1/f21/f^21/f2 mid-band, 1/f31/f^31/f3 close-in, and floor segments in 3.1 are all special cases of this general form at m=−2,−3,0m=-2,-3,0m=−2,−3,0; lab_08's Example C is just the closed-form solution for the m=−2m=-2m=−2 segment alone. Worked example: use a 6-point datasheet table for a typical free-running oscillator (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, reusing Example C's L(1 MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\text{ MHz})=-100L(1 MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz, the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner at 100100100 kHz from Sec. 3 Example 2, and adding a −150-150−150 dBc/Hz white floor summed with the 1/f21/f^21/f2 tail far out): fff 111 kHz 101010 kHz 100100100 kHz 111 MHz 101010 MHz 100100100 MHz L\mathcal{L}L [dBc/Hz] −20.0-20.0−20.0 −50.0-50.0−50.0 −80.0-80.0−80.0 −100.0-100.0−100.0 −120.0-120.0−120.0 −139.6-139.6−139.6 The first three segments (111–101010–100100100 kHz) have slope m=−3.00m=-3.00m=−3.00 (1/f31/f^31/f3); the next two segments (100100100 kHz–101010 MHz) have m=−2.00m=-2.00m=−2.00 (1/f21/f^21/f2, self-consistent with the corner in Example 2); the last segment has m=−1.96m=-1.96m=−1.96 — not a clean −2-2−2, because at 100100100 MHz L\mathcal{L}L is already the linear-power sum of the 1/f21/f^21/f2 tail (−140-140−140 dBc/Hz) and a −150-150−150 dBc/Hz floor (10−14+10−15=1.1×10−14→−139.610^{-14}+10^{-15}=1.1\times10^{-14}\to-139.610−14+10−15=1.1×10−14→−139.6 dBc/Hz) — the table uses a real mixed value, not an idealized single power law, which is exactly why you must compute mmm segment by segment rather than assuming m=−2m=-2m=−2 throughout. Integrating the SONET/OC-192-style 121212 kHz–202020 MHz band (the first segment spans four sub-segments: 121212 kHz–100100100 kHz, 100100100 kHz–111 MHz, 111–101010 MHz, 101010–202020 MHz): import numpy as np f0 = 5e9 # Hz, site canonical # datasheet-style table: (f [Hz], L [dBc/Hz]) table = [ (1e3, -20.0), (1e4, -50.0), (1e5, -80.0), (1e6, -100.0), (1e7, -120.0), (1e8, -139.6), ] def seg_integral(fa, La_dbc, fb, Lb_dbc): La_lin, Lb_lin = 10**(La_dbc/10), 10**(Lb_dbc/10) m = np.log10(Lb_lin/La_lin) / np.log10(fb/fa) if abs(m + 1) < 1e-9: return La_lin*fa*np.log(fb/fa), m return La_lin*fa/(m+1) * ((fb/fa)**(m+1) - 1), m def integrate_table(table, f1, f2): total, seg_detail = 0.0, [] for (fa, La), (fb, Lb) in zip(table, table[1:]): lo, hi = max(fa, f1), min(fb, f2) if hi <= lo: continue La_lin, Lb_lin = 10**(La/10), 10**(Lb/10) m = np.log10(Lb_lin/La_lin) / np.log10(fb/fa) L_lo = 10*np.log10(La_lin * (lo/fa)**m) L_hi = 10*np.log10(La_lin * (hi/fa)**m) I, _ = seg_integral(lo, L_lo, hi, L_hi) total += I seg_detail.append((lo, hi, m, I)) return total, seg_detail total, seg = integrate_table(table, 12e3, 20e6) sigma_phi = np.sqrt(2*total) sigma_t = sigma_phi / (2*np.pi*f0) print(f"integral = {total:.4e}") # -> 3.5217e-02 print(f"sigma_phi = {sigma_phi*1e3:.1f} mrad") # -> 265.4 print(f"sigma_t = {sigma_t*1e12:.2f} ps") # -> 8.45 print(f"frac from 12k-100k 1/f^3 segment = {seg[0][3]/total*100:.1f}%") # -> 97.2 Result: 121212 kHz–202020 MHz integrates to σϕ=265.4\sigma_\phi=265.4σϕ​=265.4 mrad, σt=8.45\sigma_t=8.45σt​=8.45 ps, of which 97.2%97.2\%97.2% of the variance comes from the closest-in 121212 kHz–100100100 kHz 1/f31/f^31/f3 segment (the steeper the slope and the closer to the carrier, the bigger the contribution — this is the quantitative version of the "close-in dominates" point in the 3.2 checklist). The same table integrated over 111–100100100 MHz (Example C's band): import numpy as np f0 = 5e9 table = [(1e3, -20.0), (1e4, -50.0), (1e5, -80.0), (1e6, -100.0), (1e7, -120.0), (1e8, -139.6)] def seg_integral(fa, La_dbc, fb, Lb_dbc): La_lin, Lb_lin = 10**(La_dbc/10), 10**(Lb_dbc/10) m = np.log10(Lb_lin/La_lin) / np.log10(fb/fa) if abs(m + 1) < 1e-9: return La_lin*fa*np.log(fb/fa) return La_lin*fa/(m+1) * ((fb/fa)**(m+1) - 1) def integrate_table(table, f1, f2): total = 0.0 for (fa, La), (fb, Lb) in zip(table, table[1:]): lo, hi = max(fa, f1), min(fb, f2) if hi <= lo: continue La_lin = 10**(La/10) m = np.log10(10**(Lb/10)/La_lin) / np.log10(fb/fa) L_lo = 10*np.log10(La_lin * (lo/fa)**m) L_hi = 10*np.log10(La_lin * (hi/fa)**m) total += seg_integral(lo, L_lo, hi, L_hi) return total total_c = integrate_table(table, 1e6, 100e6) sigma_t_c = np.sqrt(2*total_c) / (2*np.pi*f0) print(f"sigma_t (1-100 MHz) = {sigma_t_c*1e15:.1f} fs") # -> 448.5 # cross-check against np.trapezoid on a dense log-log-interpolated grid logf = np.log10([p[0] for p in table]); Ls = [p[1] for p in table] fgrid = np.logspace(np.log10(1e6), np.log10(100e6), 200_000) Lgrid = np.interp(np.log10(fgrid), logf, Ls) I_trap = np.trapezoid(10**(Lgrid/10), fgrid) sigma_t_trap = np.sqrt(2*I_trap) / (2*np.pi*f0) print(f"sigma_t (trapezoid) = {sigma_t_trap*1e15:.1f} fs") # -> 448.5 Result: 448.5448.5448.5 fs — reproducing Example C's 447.9447.9447.9 fs (a 0.60.60.6 fs difference, coming from the −150-150−150 dBc/Hz floor mixed into the table's 101010–100100100 MHz segment; Example C is pure 1/f21/f^21/f2 with no floor contribution). The closed form and np.trapezoid (dense log–log-interpolated grid) agree to floating-point precision — the two methods cross-validate each other. The same oscillator, changing only the integration band, gives a σt\sigma_tσt​ that differs by ≈18.8×\approx18.8\times≈18.8× (8.458.458.45 ps vs. 448.5448.5448.5 fs, 8447.8/448.5≈18.88447.8/448.5\approx18.88447.8/448.5≈18.8): this is exactly why "reporting jitter requires stating the integration bandwidth" (adc_aperture_jitter carries the same honesty warning) — for the same free-running VCO, a telecom-style narrow band (starting at 121212 kHz, folding in the full close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3) measures far more pessimistically than looking only at the wideband 1/f21/f^21/f2 segment; conversely, a free-running VCO will almost never pass a telecom integration-bandwidth spec unless a PLL/CDR tracks out the close-in noise (see pll_noise_budget). Common integration bands (application-dependent; external engineering convention, not content from the five source PDFs — check the specific numbers against the latest relevant spec): Application Common integration band Notes SONET/SDH OC-192 (telecom reference clock) 121212 kHz–202020 MHz Industry-standard lower bound; the exact clause is not verified here (Telcordia GR-253-CORE family; this site has not checked it clause by clause — see the same honesty note in pll_noise_budget) PCIe / OIF-CEI-family SerDes Not a fixed band — jitter is passed through a CDR jitter-transfer filter first, then integrated "Integration" becomes "filtering + integration" — see the dual-Dirac/CDR-filtered jitter discussion in dj_dual_dirac ADC/DAC sampling clock Lower bound ∼10\sim10∼10–100100100 Hz (set by the measurement system itself), upper bound fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 (Nyquist) See the aperture-jitter and sample-rate discussion in adc_aperture_jitter; the exact lower bound depends on the datasheet Interactive exercise: the PhaseNoiseCalculator component embedded in this site's interactive calculator page (interactive_calculator) provides a "datasheet segment table" mode where you can edit the 6 (f,L)(f,\mathcal{L})(f,L) points and the integration band [f1,f2][f_1,f_2][f1​,f2​] directly and watch σϕ,σt\sigma_\phi,\sigma_tσϕ​,σt​ update live — the default values are exactly the worked-example table above.

documents.t: The two problems below follow the strict format: problem (given plot readings) → step-by-step substitution (with units) → result → dimension check → one-line Python check. Using the same canonical values as Section 8 (qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz). Example 1 (back-solving the equivalent white noise SiS_iSi​ from a 1/f21/f^21/f2 reading): on a PN plot, the mid-band (1/f21/f^21/f2 region) reads L(1 MHz)=−148.0\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})=-148.0L(1MHz)=−148.0 dBc/Hz. Given qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5. Back-solve the equivalent white-noise current PSD Si=in2‾/ΔfS_i=\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fSi​=in2​​/Δf. Step-by-step substitution (inverting [P1] Eq.(21), p.185): Convert dBc/Hz to linear: 10L/10=10−14.8=1.585×10−1510^{\mathcal{L}/10}=10^{-14.8}=1.585\times10^{-15}10L/10=10−14.8=1.585×10−15 (dimensionless per-Hz). Offset angular frequency: Δω=2π×106=6.283×106\Delta\omega=2\pi\times10^{6}=6.283\times10^{6}Δω=2π×106=6.283×106 rad/s, Δω2=3.948×1013\Delta\omega^2=3.948\times10^{13}Δω2=3.948×1013 rad²/s². Eq.(21) is L=Γrms2qmax2⋅Si4Δω2\mathcal{L}=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\dfrac{S_i}{4\Delta\omega^2}L=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2Si​​; inverting, Si=Llin⋅4 Δω2 qmax2Γrms2.S_i=\mathcal{L}_{lin}\cdot\frac{4\,\Delta\omega^2\,q_{max}^2}{\Gamma_{rms}^2}.Si​=Llin​⋅Γrms2​4Δω2qmax2​​. Substitute: Si=1.585×10−15×4×3.948×1013×(10−12)20.25S_i=1.585\times10^{-15}\times\dfrac{4\times3.948\times10^{13}\times(10^{-12})^2}{0.25}Si​=1.585×10−15×0.254×3.948×1013×(10−12)2​ =1.585×10−15×1.579×1014×10−240.25=1.585×10−15×6.317×10−10≈1.0×10−24=1.585\times10^{-15}\times\dfrac{1.579\times10^{14}\times10^{-24}}{0.25}=1.585\times10^{-15}\times6.317\times10^{-10}\approx1.0\times10^{-24}=1.585×10−15×0.251.579×1014×10−24​=1.585×10−15×6.317×10−10≈1.0×10−24. Result: Si≈1.0×10−24 A2/HzS_i\approx1.0\times10^{-24}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si​≈1.0×10−24 A2/Hz — exactly recovering the canonical Example B input value (self-consistent). Dimension check: Llin\mathcal{L}_{lin}Llin​ (per-Hz === s) ×(rad/s)2⋅C21=s⋅C2s2=C2s=(A⋅s)2s=A2⋅s=A2/Hz\times\dfrac{(\text{rad/s})^2\cdot\text{C}^2}{1}=\text{s}\cdot\dfrac{\text{C}^2}{\text{s}^2}=\dfrac{\text{C}^2}{\text{s}}=\dfrac{(\text{A}\cdot\text{s})^2}{\text{s}}=\text{A}^2\cdot\text{s}=\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}×1(rad/s)2⋅C2​=s⋅s2C2​=sC2​=s(A⋅s)2​=A2⋅s=A2/Hz ✓. import numpy as np L_dbc, gamma_rms, qmax = -148.0, 0.5, 1e-12 dw = 2*np.pi*1e6 Si = 10**(L_dbc/10) * (4*dw**2*qmax**2) / gamma_rms**2 print(f"{Si:.3e} A^2/Hz") # -> 1.000e-24 A^2/Hz Example 2 (back-solving ISF symmetry c0/c1c_0/c_1c0​/c1​ from the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner): the plot reads a device flicker corner f1/f=1 MHzf_{1/f}=1\,\text{MHz}f1/f​=1MHz (ω1/f=2π×106\omega_{1/f}=2\pi\times10^6ω1/f​=2π×106), and the 1/f31/f^31/f3–1/f21/f^21/f2 crossover on the PN plot appears at Δf1/f3=100 kHz\Delta f_{1/f^3}=100\,\text{kHz}Δf1/f3​=100kHz. Back-solve the ISF's c0/c1c_0/c_1c0​/c1​ ratio and assess waveform symmetry. Step-by-step substitution (using [P1] Eq.(24), p.185's approximation Δω1/f3≈ω1/f(c0/c1)2\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}\approx\omega_{1/f}(c_0/c_1)^2Δω1/f3​≈ω1/f​(c0​/c1​)2): Invert: (c0c1)2=Δω1/f3ω1/f=2π×1052π×106=105106=0.1\left(\dfrac{c_0}{c_1}\right)^2=\dfrac{\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}}{\omega_{1/f}}=\dfrac{2\pi\times10^5}{2\pi\times10^6}=\dfrac{10^5}{10^6}=0.1(c1​c0​​)2=ω1/f​Δω1/f3​​=2π×1062π×105​=106105​=0.1. Take the square root: c0c1=0.1≈0.316\dfrac{c_0}{c_1}=\sqrt{0.1}\approx0.316c1​c0​​=0.1​≈0.316. Result: c0/c1≈0.32c_0/c_1\approx0.32c0​/c1​≈0.32 — the ISF's DC component is about one-third of its first harmonic, indicating "moderate symmetry." Design implication: c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0 means the waveform/layout still has asymmetry, with appreciable 1/f31/f^31/f3 upconversion still present. If further symmetrizing the waveform lowers c0c_0c0​ by another ×0.3\times0.3×0.3 (c0/c1→0.1c_0/c_1\to0.1c0​/c1​→0.1), the corner drops from 100100100 kHz to Δf1/f3=ω1/f(0.1)2=1 MHz×0.01=10 kHz\Delta f_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}(0.1)^2=1\,\text{MHz}\times0.01=10\,\text{kHz}Δf1/f3​=ω1/f​(0.1)2=1MHz×0.01=10kHz — the close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3 region shrinks 10×, substantially improving near-carrier noise (see symmetry, flicker_noise_upconversion). Dimension check: Δω1/f3/ω1/f\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}/\omega_{1/f}Δω1/f3​/ω1/f​ is rad/s ÷ rad/s === dimensionless; (c0/c1)2(c_0/c_1)^2(c0​/c1​)2 is also dimensionless ✓. import numpy as np w_1f = 2*np.pi*1e6 # device flicker corner dw_1f3 = 2*np.pi*1e5 # 1/f^3 corner read off the plot c0_over_c1 = np.sqrt(dw_1f3/w_1f) print(round(c0_over_c1, 3)) # -> 0.316

documents.t: The essence of measuring L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f): remove the carrier + push down the system floor. The direct SA method measures "DUT + instrument"; PLL/delay-line use carrier suppression to swap the instrument for a good reference or self-delay; cross-correlation correlates two independent channels to kill the uncorrelated floor by 1/M1/\sqrt{M}1/M​ (5 dB per ×10 averaging; simulation-verified fitted slope −4.73-4.73−4.73 dB/decade vs. theory −5.00-5.00−5.00, match 0.9460.9460.946, see lab_35). The three pitfalls of cross-correlation: (i) anti-correlated floors cause cross-spectrum collapse (a spuriously low floor, Nelson–Hati–Howe 2014); (ii) the convergence check — the floor should saturate at the DUT's true floor as MMM grows, not keep dropping without bound; (iii) spur-included vs. excluded integrated-jitter readings can differ by more than 2×2\times2× (a −60-60−60 dBc spur alone contributes ≈45\approx45≈45 fs at 5 GHz, the same order of magnitude as the 27.627.627.6 fs buffer floor in clock_chain_budget). A spur is a deterministic discrete tone (units dBc, density does not change with RBW); random PN is a continuous spectrum (dBc/Hz). Distinguish by: changing the RBW weighting, checking repeatability, toggling nearby equipment. Spur causes: reference leakage, supply ripple, external injection; downconverted to near the carrier via the ISF's nnn-th harmonic cnc_ncn​; countermeasures are isolation/filtering/shielding + suppressing cnc_ncn​. Reading a PN plot: 1/f31/f^31/f3 (flicker via c0c_0c0​) / 1/f21/f^21/f2 (white noise via the integrator) / floor (mostly instrument/buffer), plus two corners. Back-solve SiS_iSi​, c0/c1c_0/c_1c0​/c1​, device flicker to get design knobs. Integrating jitter from a datasheet table (Sec. 3.3): assume a single power law between adjacent table points, integrate in closed form, σϕ2=2Σ\sigma_\phi^2=2\Sigmaσϕ2​=2Σ; changing only the integration band on the same oscillator (121212 kHz–202020 MHz vs. 111–100100100 MHz) changes σt\sigma_tσt​ by ≈18.8×\approx18.8\times≈18.8× (8.458.458.45 ps vs. 448.5448.5448.5 fs) — reporting jitter requires stating the integration bandwidth. Numerical example: −148-148−148 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz back-solves to Si≈10−24S_i\approx10^{-24}Si​≈10−24 A²/Hz; a 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner of 100100100 kHz (flicker corner 1 MHz) back-solves to c0/c1≈0.32c_0/c_1\approx0.32c0​/c1​≈0.32.

documents.t: Prerequisites: white_noise_to_phase_noise (where the VCO term Svco∝Γrms2/qmax2⋅Si/f2S_{vco}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2\cdot S_i/f^2Svco​∝Γrms2​/qmax2​⋅Si​/f2 comes from), serdes_clocking_connection (the CDR/PLL's high-pass on the VCO, jitter integration bandwidth), lc_vs_ring (why ring's SvcoS_{vco}Svco​ is high and LC's is low) | Next: exercises, lab_13_pll_cdr_transfer This page answers a question a system-design engineer faces every day: for a phase-locked loop (PLL — a negative-feedback loop that locks an oscillator's phase to a reference clock), which sources contribute how much to the output phase noise, and which one dominates at which offset band? How wide should the loop bandwidth (the highest offset the feedback can still track) be chosen to minimize total jitter? We write out the transfer function of each of the five noise sources to the output, sum them as Sout=(SrefN2+Scp) ∣Hlp∣2+Svco ∣Hhp∣2S_{out}=(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})\,\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2+S_{vco}\,\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2Sout​=(Sref​N2+Scp​)∣Hlp​∣2+Svco​∣Hhp​∣2 (canonical Section 11.2, "PLL output noise budget"; for a fractional-N loop a third term — the ΔΣ quantization noise SΔΣ ∣Hlp∣2S_{\Delta\Sigma}\,\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2SΔΣ​∣Hlp​∣2 — must be added, see the section "The third term for fractional-N" on this page; it is zero for integer-N), then minimize ∫Sout df\int S_{out}\,df∫Sout​df (integrated phase variance, proportional to rms jitter squared) to find that famous U-shaped curve and its minimum. Physical intuition (conclusion first): a PLL is a low-pass tracker. Within the loop bandwidth fnf_nfn​, the feedback reacts fast enough that the output follows the reference — so the noise of the reference and the loop's front end (PFD, charge-pump, divider) is amplified and low-passed onto the output (and the reference is also multiplied by NNN, so its power is multiplied by N2N^2N2); meanwhile the VCO's own close-in drift is corrected away by the feedback (VCO high-pass). Beyond fnf_nfn​, the feedback can't keep up, and the output follows the free-running VCO — the VCO's 1/f21/f^21/f2 noise leaks straight through. So in-band tracks ref/CP, out-of-band tracks VCO, with the crossover at fnf_nfn​. Set fnf_nfn​ too narrow → too much VCO leaks through (U-shape's left arm rises); too wide → too much ref/CP gets carried through (right arm rises). There must be an optimal fnf_nfn​ in between. This page's PLL closed-loop transfer function (loop transfer / open-loop gain / type-II stability — the higher-order details) belongs to standard PLL literature (Gardner, Razavi, Best), not among the five source PDFs downloaded for this site; we only cite its type-II second-order closed-loop result (already recorded in canonical Section 10.2), and focus on "the ISF determines the VCO term SvcoS_{vco}Svco​" and "how the budget sums up and how the optimal BW is found." The microscopic origin of the VCO term (Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​) is precisely the output of this site's whole ISF theory built up so far.

documents.t: Phase noise is not a single number — it's a curve that varies with offset, and different sources dominate different segments of that curve. Doing a budget = plotting each source as one curve, and seeing where each one pokes up and what the total looks like. The value of doing this: Find the bottleneck: close-in too high? Usually the reference or the charge-pump (amplified by N2N^2N2). Far-out too high? It's the VCO. Treat the actual cause, don't swap parts blindly. Choose the loop BW: the crossover point and total jitter are both strongly tied to fnf_nfn​; the budget lets you quantify this trade-off. Connect to system metrics: integrate SoutS_{out}Sout​ to get rms jitter σt\sigma_tσt​, and feed it directly into the SerDes eye/BER (see serdes_clocking_connection).
documents.s: Why do a "noise budget"

documents.t: The skeleton of an integer-N PLL: reference clock → phase detector (PFD, phase-frequency detector) + charge-pump (turns the phase error into current pulses) → loop filter (integrates the current into a control voltage) → VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator) → divider (÷N, pulls the output back down to the reference frequency for comparison). The five noise injection points, shown below: Each source takes a different path to the output, so the shaping differs: Source Symbol Physical origin Transfer to output Shaping at output reference SrefS_{ref}Sref​ crystal/reference phase noise ×N\times N×N then low-pass N2∣Hlp∣2N^2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2N2∣Hlp​∣2 (in-band, amplified by N2N^2N2) PFD/charge-pump ScpS_{cp}Scp​ CP current noise, PFD dead-zone, mismatch low-pass ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 (in-band, flat floor) divider SdivS_{div}Sdiv​ jitter of the ÷N logic low-pass (same path as ref) ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 (in-band; often folded into ScpS_{cp}Scp​) loop filter SlfS_{lf}Slf​ filter resistor thermal noise modulating the VCO band-pass (peak exactly at fnf_nfn​) 4kTR Kvco2/(2πf)2⋅∣Hhp∣24kTR\,K_{vco}^2/(2\pi f)^2\cdot\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^24kTRKvco2​/(2πf)2⋅∣Hhp​∣2 (closed form in Step 2; not negligible for small IcpI_{cp}Icp​ / large RRR) VCO SvcoS_{vco}Svco​ tank/tail thermal noise via ISF (this site's main thread) high-pass ∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hhp​∣2 (dominates out-of-band) Why the reference is multiplied by N2N^2N2. The divider pulls the output frequency fout=Nfreff_{out}=N f_{ref}fout​=Nfref​ back down to freff_{ref}fref​ for comparison — equivalent to requiring output phase = N×N\timesN× reference phase (phase is also multiplied up). Phase amplified by NNN means power spectral density amplified by N2N^2N2. So a clean crystal (SrefS_{ref}Sref​ very low) combined with a large NNN (e.g. N=100N=100N=100) has its equivalent in-band noise floor at the output raised by 20log⁡10N=4020\log_{10}N=4020log10​N=40 dB — this is why an integer-N PLL's in-band noise is usually determined jointly by the reference ×N2\times N^2×N2 and the charge-pump, not the VCO. Design takeaway: the in-band floor ≈(SrefN2+Scp)\approx(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})≈(Sref​N2+Scp​); to suppress it, either lower NNN (use fractional-N or a higher-frequency reference), or lower the charge-pump's current noise. The VCO contributes nothing in-band (it's corrected away by the high-pass).

documents.t: The reference and charge-pump/divider take the same low-pass path (with the reference first multiplied by NNN), the VCO takes the high-pass path, and the three segments are uncorrelated — their powers add (canonical Section 11.2): Sout(f)=(Sref(f) N2+Scp(f)) ∣Hlp(f)∣2+Svco(f) ∣Hhp(f)∣2.S_{out}(f)=\big(S_{ref}(f)\,N^2+S_{cp}(f)\big)\,\lvert H_{lp}(f)\rvert^2+S_{vco}(f)\,\lvert H_{hp}(f)\rvert^2 .Sout​(f)=(Sref​(f)N2+Scp​(f))∣Hlp​(f)∣2+Svco​(f)∣Hhp​(f)∣2. Dimension check: Sref,Scp,Svco,SoutS_{ref},S_{cp},S_{vco},S_{out}Sref​,Scp​,Svco​,Sout​ are all rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz, NNN and ∣H∣2\lvert H\rvert^2∣H∣2 are dimensionless, so the three terms add in the same units — confirmed. Where did the divider go: SdivS_{div}Sdiv​ takes the same low-pass path as the charge-pump and is shaped identically by ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 at the output, so in practice SdivS_{div}Sdiv​ is often folded into ScpS_{cp}Scp​ as "the loop front end's equivalent in-band floor." This page's ScpS_{cp}Scp​ is the combined total of "PFD + charge-pump + divider." The loop-filter term (closed form): the thermal noise voltage of the filter resistor RRR (PSD 4kTR4kTR4kTR) adds directly onto VctrlV_{ctrl}Vctrl​, passes through the VCO's Kvco/sK_{vco}/sKvco​/s, and is then corrected by the loop as 1/(1+G)=Hhp1/(1+G)=H_{hp}1/(1+G)=Hhp​ (derivation in lab_13 §2): Slf(f)=Sϕ,R(f)=4kTR Kvco2(2πf)2 ∣Hhp(f)∣2[rad2/Hz],Sϕ,R(fn)=4kTR Kvco2(2ζωn)2S_{lf}(f)=S_{\phi,R}(f)=\frac{4kTR\,K_{vco}^{2}}{(2\pi f)^{2}}\,\lvert H_{hp}(f)\rvert^{2}\quad[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}], \qquad S_{\phi,R}(f_n)=\frac{4kTR\,K_{vco}^{2}}{(2\zeta\omega_n)^{2}}Slf​(f)=Sϕ,R​(f)=(2πf)24kTRKvco2​​∣Hhp​(f)∣2[rad2/Hz],Sϕ,R​(fn​)=(2ζωn​)24kTRKvco2​​ (KvcoK_{vco}Kvco​ in rad/s/V; rising ∝f2\propto f^2∝f2 at low frequency, falling ∝1/f2\propto1/f^2∝1/f2 at high frequency — band-pass, peak exactly at fnf_nfn​). It is not necessarily small: with lab_13's worked design (fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz, ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707, N=100N=100N=100, Kvco=50K_{vco}=50Kvco​=50 MHz/V, Icp=100 μI_{cp}=100\ \muIcp​=100 μA → R=178R=178R=178 kΩ, C=1.27C=1.27C=1.27 pF), Sϕ,R(1 MHz)=3.68×10−12 rad2/HzS_{\phi,R}(1\ \text{MHz})=3.68\times10^{-12}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}Sϕ,R​(1 MHz)=3.68×10−12 rad2/Hz (−117.4-117.4−117.4 dBc/Hz) — 2.5× above this page's in-band floor of 1.5×10−121.5\times10^{-12}1.5×10−12, but 27× below the ring VCO's 10−1010^{-10}10−10 at fnf_nfn​; integrated alone over 1 kHz–1 GHz it gives σt,R=91\sigma_{t,R}=91σt,R​=91 fs (compare the 259 fs optimum). At fixed fn,ζf_n,\zetafn​,ζ, R∝1/IcpR\propto1/I_{cp}R∝1/Icp​, so raising the CP current suppresses the resistor term and the CP term (2πN/Icp)2Si,cp(2\pi N/I_{cp})^2S_{i,cp}(2πN/Icp​)2Si,cp​ together (cost: power, capacitor area). The lab_20 figure (below) does not include this term (its IcpI_{cp}Icp​ is unspecified; marked illustrative); a real design must. import numpy as np from simulations.common.pll_utils import design_type2, H_highpass_mag2 R, C = design_type2(1e6, 0.707, 100, 50e6, 100e-6) # lab_13 worked design: Hz, -, -, Hz/V, A kv = 2*np.pi*50e6 # rad/s/V Sv = 4*1.380649e-23*300*R # V^2/Hz f = np.logspace(3, 9, 200001) S_R = Sv*kv**2/(2*np.pi*f)**2*H_highpass_mag2(f, 1e6, 0.707) i = np.argmin(abs(f - 1e6)) print(round(R/1e3, 1), f"{S_R[i]:.2e}", round(10*np.log10(0.5*S_R[i]), 1), round(np.sqrt(np.trapezoid(S_R, f))/(2*np.pi*5e9)*1e15, 0)) # -> 177.7 3.68e-12 -117.4 91.0 The fractional-N third term: if the divider modulus is dithered by a ΔΣ modulator (fractional-N), the quantization noise enters the budget as SΔΣ(f) ∣Hlp∣2S_{\Delta\Sigma}(f)\,\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2SΔΣ​(f)∣Hlp​∣2 — same low-pass path as the CP, but not multiplied by N2N^2N2, and shaped as a rising ramp of +20(m−1)+20(m-1)+20(m−1) dB/dec. Full derivation and worked example in the section "The third term for fractional-N: ΔΣ quantization noise" on this page. For integer-N (this page's lab_20 setup) this term is zero.

documents.t: SvcoS_{vco}Svco​ doesn't come out of thin air — it is exactly the output of this site's whole ISF theory. In the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region (white-noise upconversion), Svco(f)=Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf(2πf)2[rad2/Hz]S_{vco}(f)=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{(2\pi f)^2}\quad[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]Svco​(f)=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅(2πf)2in2​​/Δf​[rad2/Hz] (clean time-domain version, see white_noise_to_phase_noise; corresponds to [P1] Eq.(21), p.185, off by an SSB factor-of-2). So the answer to "why is the VCO term 1/f21/f^21/f2 in the PLL budget, why ∝Γrms2/qmax2\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2∝Γrms2​/qmax2​" is entirely in the ISF. A ring VCO has a large Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and small qmaxq_{max}qmax​, so SvcoS_{vco}Svco​ is high (see lc_vs_ring) — this is exactly the root reason a ring-PLL needs to open up fnf_nfn​ to suppress the VCO.

documents.t: Break SoutS_{out}Sout​ into three segments: Deep in-band (f≪fnf\ll f_nf≪fn​): ∣Hlp∣2≈1\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx1∣Hlp​∣2≈1, ∣Hhp∣2≈0\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\approx0∣Hhp​∣2≈0. Sout≈SrefN2+ScpS_{out}\approx S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}Sout​≈Sref​N2+Scp​ — a flat floor set by the reference×N2\times N^2×N2 and the charge-pump (if the reference contains 1/f1/f1/f, this segment tilts up slightly toward close-in). Out-of-band (f≫fnf\gg f_nf≫fn​): ∣Hlp∣2≈0\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx0∣Hlp​∣2≈0, ∣Hhp∣2≈1\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\approx1∣Hhp​∣2≈1. Sout≈Svco∝1/f2S_{out}\approx S_{vco}\propto1/f^2Sout​≈Svco​∝1/f2 — the VCO's −20-20−20 dB/decade skirt leaks straight through. Crossover (f≈fnf\approx f_nf≈fn​): the two segments meet. At ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707, at fnf_nfn​ ∣Hlp∣2≈1.5\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx1.5∣Hlp​∣2≈1.5 (+1.76+1.76+1.76 dB), ∣Hhp∣2≈0.5\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\approx0.5∣Hhp​∣2≈0.5 (−3-3−3 dB), and their sum ≈2\approx2≈2 (+3+3+3 dB) — this is the slight peaking, also the origin of the common "bump near the loop BW" seen in PLL output (the two curves are actually equal at f≈1.55 fnf\approx1.55\,f_nf≈1.55fn​, each about 0.850.850.85, −0.7-0.7−0.7 dB, not at fnf_nfn​). Too small a ζ\zetaζ (underdamped) makes the peaking sharp. The exact location and height of the peak actually have a closed-form solution — see the next section. Reading a PN plot at a glance: see a flat close-in floor → measure in-band, back out SrefN2+ScpS_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}Sref​N2+Scp​; see the floor start falling at −20-20−20 dB/dec from some offset → that knee is fnf_nfn​, beyond it is VCO. A sharp peak in the middle → insufficient damping or an overshooting loop-BW design.

documents.t: Step 3 measured ∣Hlp∣2≈1.5\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx1.5∣Hlp​∣2≈1.5 (+1.76+1.76+1.76 dB) at f=fnf=f_nf=fn​ — but that is not the maximum. This section solves analytically for the peak frequency and peak magnitude of the type-II second-order ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 (the canonical Section-10.2 form). The derivation itself is pure algebra (self-contained); the "ζ↔\zeta\leftrightarrowζ↔ phase margin mapping" and the "cascaded 0.1-dB rule" belong to standard control/telecom literature, each labeled as such (external literature, not among this site's five source PDFs).

The extremum condition of the quotient is N′D−ND′=0N'D-ND'=0N′D−ND′=0; expand term by term: N′D−ND′=4ζ2[u2+(4ζ2−2)u+1]−(1+4ζ2u)[2u+4ζ2−2]=[4ζ2u2+(16ζ4−8ζ2)u+4ζ2]−[8ζ2u2+(16ζ4−8ζ2)u+2u+4ζ2−2]=−4ζ2u2−2u+2 = −2(2ζ2u2+u−1).\begin{aligned} N'D-ND'&=4\zeta^2\big[u^2+(4\zeta^2-2)u+1\big]-(1+4\zeta^2u)\big[2u+4\zeta^2-2\big]\\ &=\big[4\zeta^2u^2+(16\zeta^4-8\zeta^2)u+4\zeta^2\big]-\big[8\zeta^2u^2+(16\zeta^4-8\zeta^2)u+2u+4\zeta^2-2\big]\\ &=-4\zeta^2u^2-2u+2\;=\;-2\big(2\zeta^2u^2+u-1\big). \end{aligned}N′D−ND′​=4ζ2[u2+(4ζ2−2)u+1]−(1+4ζ2u)[2u+4ζ2−2]=[4ζ2u2+(16ζ4−8ζ2)u+4ζ2]−[8ζ2u2+(16ζ4−8ζ2)u+2u+4ζ2−2]=−4ζ2u2−2u+2=−2(2ζ2u2+u−1).​ (The two 16ζ416\zeta^416ζ4 cross terms cancel exactly, leaving a quadratic with no ζ4\zeta^4ζ4.) Setting it to zero and taking the positive root: 2ζ2u2+u−1=0⟹u\*=1+8ζ2−14ζ2=21+8ζ2+1,fpk=fnu\*.2\zeta^2u^2+u-1=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u^\*=\frac{\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}-1}{4\zeta^2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}+1},\qquad f_{pk}=f_n\sqrt{u^\*}.2ζ2u2+u−1=0⟹u\*=4ζ21+8ζ2​−1​=1+8ζ2​+12​,fpk​=fn​u\*​. (The two forms are equal: multiply numerator and denominator by 1+8ζ2+1\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}+11+8ζ2​+1 and use 8ζ2=(1+8ζ2)2−18\zeta^2=(\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2})^2-18ζ2=(1+8ζ2​)2−1.)

documents.t: At u=0u=0u=0 (DC), N′D−ND′=4ζ2−(4ζ2−2)=+2N'D-ND'=4\zeta^2-(4\zeta^2-2)=+2N′D−ND′=4ζ2−(4ζ2−2)=+2 — positive for every ζ\zetaζ. The DC gain is 1 and the slope points up, so for any finite ζ\zetaζ, u\*>0u^\*>0u\*>0 always holds and the peak is necessarily above 0 dB. The physical reason: a type-II loop has two integrators (open-loop phase starts at −180∘-180^\circ−180∘) and can only be stabilized by the loop filter's zero (fz=fn/(2ζ)f_z=f_n/(2\zeta)fz​=fn​/(2ζ)) pulling the phase back early; that zero first lifts the closed-loop gain above 1 before the double pole pushes it down — peaking is the price of type-II stability, not a design mistake. Contrast: an ordinary second-order low-pass without a zero has no resonance peak for ζ≥1/2\zeta\ge1/\sqrt2ζ≥1/2​; a type-II with a zero always peaks, the peak merely getting lower and sliding toward lower frequency as ζ\zetaζ grows.

documents.t: Let s=1+8ζ2s=\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}s=1+8ζ2​ (dimensionless). documents.t: Cascade MMM loops with identical transfers (a chain of repeaters/CDRs on a long-haul link, each regenerating and re-transmitting the clock): the total jitter transfer is HlpMH_{lp}^MHlpM​ — the dBs add directly: the peak becomes M×PM\times PM×P dB. 2.09 dB per stage (ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707) ×\times× 20 stages === 41.8 dB: jitter near fpkf_{pk}fpk​ is amplified more than a hundredfold — the link is dead. 0.1 dB per stage ×\times× 20 stages === 2 dB: manageable. This is why the SONET/SDH era pinned the regenerator jitter-transfer peaking spec at the 0.1 dB level (external standards literature: Telcordia GR-253-CORE and the ITU-T G.783/G.958 family of telecom specs; this site has not verified the individual clause numbers — we cite the magnitude and the spirit). Inverting the closed form, 0.1 dB requires ζ≈4.32\zeta\approx4.32ζ≈4.32 (PM ≈89.2∘\approx89.2^\circ≈89.2∘, heavily overdamped) — completely different from the ζ≈0.7\zeta\approx0.7ζ≈0.7–111 that minimizes a single PLL's integrated jitter: single-loop optimal is not cascade optimal; a CDR's ζ\zetaζ is a system spec set by "which stage of the chain you are." Rigor note: adding dBs assumes every stage has the same fn,ζf_n,\zetafn​,ζ (peaks aligned — worst case); in practice the stages' fnf_nfn​ are slightly staggered and the compounding is milder than M×PM\times PM×P, but specs are written for the worst case.

documents.t: Closed form vs H_lowpass_mag2 from simulations/common/pll_utils.py (a 4-million-point fine sweep): import numpy as np from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_lowpass_mag2 def peak_closed(zeta): # closed form: f_pk/f_n and |H_lp|^2_max s = np.sqrt(1 + 8*zeta**2) return np.sqrt((s - 1)/(4*zeta**2)), (s + 1)**2/((s - 1)*(s + 3)) x = np.linspace(0.001, 5, 4_000_001) # x = f/f_n (take f_n = 1 Hz) for z in (0.5, 0.707, 1.0, 1.5): xpk, g = peak_closed(z) m2 = H_lowpass_mag2(x, 1.0, z) k = int(np.argmax(m2)) print(f"{z}: closed {xpk:.4f}/{10*np.log10(g):.4f} dB, " f"numeric {x[k]:.4f}/{10*np.log10(m2[k]):.4f} dB") # -> 0.707: closed 0.7862/2.0903 dB, numeric 0.7862/2.0903 dB (others: zeta=0.5→3.3339, 1.0→1.2494, 1.5→0.6514; closed = numeric to 4 decimals) zg = np.linspace(2, 8, 600001) # sweep zeta to invert for 0.1 dB peaking pk = 10*np.log10(peak_closed(zg)[1]) z01 = zg[int(np.argmin(np.abs(pk - 0.1)))] print(round(z01, 3)) # -> 4.319 (zeta required for 0.1 dB) Conditions of validity and failure (this section's closed form): Valid only for the ideal type-II second-order closed loop of canonical Section 10.2 (linearized charge-pump PLL, no extra poles). Real loops usually add 1–2 high-frequency poles in the loop filter (third/fourth-order loops); the peak location and height shift and must be computed numerically. The PM mapping assumes the crossover happens on the ideal G(s)G(s)G(s); extra poles eat PM, and PM≈100ζ\mathrm{PM}\approx100\zetaPM≈100ζ loses accuracy accordingly. This peak is a bump of the transfer function; the actual PN bump near fnf_nfn​ at the output must still be multiplied by each source's PSD (see Step 3).

documents.t: Besides random phase noise (a continuous skirt), PLL output also commonly has discrete spurs (single-frequency spikes). The most common is the reference spur: the charge-pump injects a current pulse every reference period, and this periodic disturbance appears at the output at integer multiples of freff_{ref}fref​ (i.e. offset =±fref,±2fref,…=\pm f_{ref},\pm2f_{ref},\dots=±fref​,±2fref​,…). Its source is CP current mismatch, leakage, and PFD dead-zone, which impose a small freff_{ref}fref​ ripple on the control voltage, converted by the VCO's KvK_vKv​ into phase-modulation sidebands. Spur vs. random PN: a spur is a deterministic, narrow line (a needle in the spectrum), random PN is a continuous skirt; in measurement, the spur's height doesn't change with resolution bandwidth RBW (its power is concentrated in one bin), whereas random PN's dBc/Hz is genuinely "per-Hz." Relation to loop BW: the reference spur at offset freff_{ref}fref​, if fref>fnf_{ref}>f_nfref​>fn​, is attenuated by ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2's low-pass (narrower loop BW → more spur suppression); this is consistent with "narrow BW favors random in-band noise," but it sacrifices VCO suppression — the same trade-off again. This page's budget only covers the random part (continuous SoutS_{out}Sout​); a quantitative spur analysis belongs to standard PLL literature (not among the five source PDFs) — here it's only a conceptual link.

documents.t: Write out the output's integrated phase variance (canonical Eq. 18): σϕ2(fn)=∫f1f2Sout(f;fn) df,σt(fn)=12πf0σϕ2(fn).\sigma_\phi^2(f_n)=\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_{out}(f;f_n)\,df,\qquad \sigma_t(f_n)=\frac{1}{2\pi f_0}\sqrt{\sigma_\phi^2(f_n)} .σϕ2​(fn​)=∫f1​f2​​Sout​(f;fn​)df,σt​(fn​)=2πf0​1​σϕ2​(fn​)​. σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​ is a function of fnf_nfn​, because SoutS_{out}Sout​ depends on fnf_nfn​ through ∣Hlp∣2,∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2,\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2,∣Hhp​∣2. Split it into in-band and out-of-band pieces to see the trend: σϕ2(fn)≈∫(SrefN2+Scp) ∣Hlp∣2 df⏟↑ as fn↑ (wider passband, more ref/CP carried through)+∫Svco ∣Hhp∣2 df⏟↓ as fn↑ (more VCO close-in suppressed).\sigma_\phi^2(f_n)\approx\underbrace{\int (S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})\,\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\,df}_{\uparrow\ \text{as }f_n\uparrow\ (\text{wider passband, more ref/CP carried through})}+\underbrace{\int S_{vco}\,\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\,df}_{\downarrow\ \text{as }f_n\uparrow\ (\text{more VCO close-in suppressed})} .σϕ2​(fn​)≈↑ as fn​↑ (wider passband, more ref/CP carried through)∫(Sref​N2+Scp​)∣Hlp​∣2df​​+↓ as fn​↑ (more VCO close-in suppressed)∫Svco​∣Hhp​∣2df​​. First term (ref/CP) increases monotonically with fnf_nfn​: the larger fnf_nfn​, the wider the low-pass passband, carrying more of the in-band floor (including the N2N^2N2-amplified reference) through to the output. Roughly ∝(SrefN2+Scp)⋅fn\propto(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})\cdot f_n∝(Sref​N2+Scp​)⋅fn​ (flat floor times passband width). Second term (VCO) decreases monotonically with fnf_nfn​: the larger fnf_nfn​, the more of the VCO's 1/f21/f^21/f2 close-in the high-pass corrects away. For Svco=k/f2S_{vco}=k/f^2Svco​=k/f2 passed through the high-pass, the residual integral ∝k/fn\propto k/f_n∝k/fn​ (wider BW → less leakage). One increasing, one decreasing → a U-shape. Setting the derivative with respect to fnf_nfn​ to zero gives a unique minimum: d σϕ2dfn=0⟹(marginal increase in ref/CP leakage)=(marginal decrease in VCO suppression).\frac{d\,\sigma_\phi^2}{d f_n}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{(marginal increase in ref/CP leakage)}=\text{(marginal decrease in VCO suppression)}.dfn​dσϕ2​​=0⟹(marginal increase in ref/CP leakage)=(marginal decrease in VCO suppression). Using the two rough estimates above (of the form a fn+b/fna\,f_n+b/f_nafn​+b/fn​, with a∝SrefN2+Scpa\propto S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}a∝Sref​N2+Scp​ and b∝Svcob\propto S_{vco}b∝Svco​'s coefficient) to find the minimum: ddfn ⁣(afn+bfn)=a−bfn2=0 ⟹ fn\*=ba ∝ Svco coefficientSrefN2+Scp.\frac{d}{df_n}\!\left(a f_n+\frac{b}{f_n}\right)=a-\frac{b}{f_n^2}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ f_n^\*=\sqrt{\frac{b}{a}}\ \propto\ \sqrt{\frac{S_{vco}\text{ coefficient}}{S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}}} .dfn​d​(afn​+fn​b​)=a−fn2​b​=0 ⟹ fn\*​=ab​​ ∝ Sref​N2+Scp​Svco​ coefficient​​. Physical meaning: the noisier the VCO (bbb large) → the larger the optimal BW (a wider loop is needed to suppress the VCO); the noisier the ref/CP, or the larger NNN (aaa large) → the smaller the optimal BW (you can't afford to carry too much of the in-band floor through). This relation fn\*∝b/af_n^\*\propto\sqrt{b/a}fn\*​∝b/a​ is the core intuition of PLL design, though the coefficients must be pinned down by numerical integration. Toy-model note: the afn+b/fnaf_n+b/f_nafn​+b/fn​ above is a heuristic estimate that approximates the shaping as an ideal brick-wall filter; the real integral needs the full ∣H∣2\lvert H\rvert^2∣H∣2 (including the peaking near fnf_nfn​), so below we use lab_20's numerical integration to give the exact minimum.

Core Python (full script: simulations/lab_20_pll_budget.py): import numpy as np from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_lowpass_mag2, H_highpass_mag2 def output_psd(f, fn, N, zeta=0.707): lp = H_lowpass_mag2(f, fn, zeta) hp = H_highpass_mag2(f, fn, zeta) S_ref = 1e-16 + 1e-18 * (1e6 / f) # clean crystal S_cp = 5e-13 * np.ones_like(f) # PFD/CP/divider flat floor S_vco = 2e-10 * (1e6 / f) ** 2 # ring VCO -100 dBc/Hz @1MHz, 1/f^2 return (S_ref * N**2 + S_cp) * lp + S_vco * hp # budget sum f = np.logspace(3, 9, 3000); f0 = 5e9; N = 100 fns = np.logspace(4.5, 7.5, 60) jit = [np.sqrt(np.trapezoid(output_psd(f, fn, N), f)) / (2*np.pi*f0) for fn in fns] k = int(np.argmin(jit)) print(fns[k]/1e6, "MHz", jit[k]*1e15, "fs") # -> ~6.90 MHz, ~259 fs
