Convert to σt=σϕ/(2πf0)\sigma_t=\sigma_\phi/(2\pi f_0)σt​=σϕ​/(2πf0​), with f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz. Result (lab_20 numerics): fnf_nfn​ σt\sigma_tσt​ What leaks through 0.30 MHz (too narrow) ≈867\approx867≈867 fs large VCO close-in leakage (U-shape's left arm) 6.90 MHz (optimal) ≈259\approx259≈259 fs balanced on both sides, the minimum 30 MHz (too wide) ≈396\approx396≈396 fs ref×N2\times N^2×N2/CP carried through (U-shape's right arm) Moving from the optimum toward narrow (6.9→0.36.9\to0.36.9→0.3 MHz), jitter rises to 3.3×3.3\times3.3×; moving toward wide (6.9→306.9\to306.9→30 MHz), it rises to 1.5×1.5\times1.5×. The U-shape's left arm is steeper than the right — because this is a ring VCO (SvcoS_{vco}Svco​ large, its 1/f21/f^21/f2 leakage very sensitive to BW), so "better to open it a bit wide than too narrow." This is exactly the design rule behind ring-PLLs' preference for large loop BW. Dimension check: ∫Sout df\int S_{out}\,df∫Sout​df: [rad2/Hz]×[Hz]=[rad2][\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]\times[\text{Hz}]=[\text{rad}^2][rad2/Hz]×[Hz]=[rad2] → σϕ [rad]\sigma_\phi\,[\text{rad}]σϕ​[rad]; σϕ/(2πf0)\sigma_\phi/(2\pi f_0)σϕ​/(2πf0​): rad/(rad/s)=s\text{rad}/(\text{rad/s})=\text{s}rad/(rad/s)=s — confirmed. import numpy as np from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_lowpass_mag2, H_highpass_mag2 f = np.logspace(3, 9, 3000); f0 = 5e9; N = 100 def Sout(fn): lp, hp = H_lowpass_mag2(f, fn), H_highpass_mag2(f, fn) S_ref = 1e-16 + 1e-18*(1e6/f); S_cp = 5e-13; S_vco = 2e-10*(1e6/f)**2 return (S_ref*N**2 + S_cp)*lp + S_vco*hp for fn in [0.3e6, 6.9e6, 30e6]: st = np.sqrt(np.trapezoid(Sout(fn), f))/(2*np.pi*f0) print(f"fn={fn/1e6:5.2f} MHz -> sigma_t={st*1e15:.0f} fs") # 867 / 259 / 396 fs

documents.t: The budget so far is integer-N: fout=Nfreff_{out}=Nf_{ref}fout​=Nfref​, so the frequency step can only be an integer multiple of freff_{ref}fref​. For fine steps (e.g. a 200-kHz channel spacing) without sacrificing freff_{ref}fref​, you need fractional-N (fractional division): dither the modulus between integers (÷NNN this reference period, ÷(N+1)(N{+}1)(N+1) the next, …) so the average modulus is N+αN+\alphaN+α (0≤α<10\le\alpha<10≤α<1). This pays a double dividend — freff_{ref}fref​ can be raised and NNN shrinks, so the in-band SrefN2S_{ref}N^2Sref​N2 floor drops directly — but the modulus dithering is itself a quantization error and becomes a new noise source. Generating the modulus sequence with a ΔΣ modulator (delta-sigma modulator — a feedback quantizer that shapes the quantization error toward high frequencies) pushes the error power out to high offsets where the loop's low-pass filters it away. This section writes it up as the budget's third term. The shaped result in this section belongs to standard ΔΣ frequency-synthesis theory (external literature, not among this site's five source PDFs); the classic source: T. A. D. Riley, M. A. Copeland, and T. A. Kwasniewski, "Delta-Sigma Modulation in Fractional-N Frequency Synthesis," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 28, no. 5, pp. 553–559, May 1993. The derivation below is self-contained, step by step.

documents.t: (i) The MASH-m output. An mmm-th-order MASH (MASH-1-1-1 means m=3m=3m=3: three cascaded first-order accumulators) produces the modulus-control sequence y[k]=α+(1−z−1)m e[k],y[k]=\alpha+(1-z^{-1})^m\,e[k],y[k]=α+(1−z−1)me[k], where e[k]e[k]e[k] is the last stage's quantization error, modeled as white: uniformly distributed over ±Δ/2\pm\Delta/2±Δ/2, variance σe2=Δ2/12\sigma_e^2=\Delta^2/12σe2​=Δ2/12, with Δ=1\Delta=1Δ=1 LSB (note: this Δ\DeltaΔ is the quantization step === 1 VCO cycle per reference period — not the Δ\DeltaΔ of the offset Δf\Delta fΔf). The (1−z−1)m(1-z^{-1})^m(1−z−1)m is the ΔΣ noise shaping: it pushes the error power toward high frequencies. (ii) The error accumulates into phase (one integration). In reference period kkk the divider swallows y[k]−αy[k]-\alphay[k]−α extra VCO cycles; each cycle is 2π2\pi2π rad of output phase, and phase is the accumulation of frequency error: ϕΔΣ[k]=2π∑j≤k(y[j]−α)=2π (1−z−1)m−1e[k][rad].\phi_{\Delta\Sigma}[k]=2\pi\sum_{j\le k}\big(y[j]-\alpha\big)=2\pi\,(1-z^{-1})^{m-1}e[k]\quad[\text{rad}] .ϕΔΣ​[k]=2πj≤k∑​(y[j]−α)=2π(1−z−1)m−1e[k][rad]. (Accumulation is 1/(1−z−1)1/(1-z^{-1})1/(1−z−1) in the zzz-domain, which eats exactly one order of shaping: mmm-th-order frequency shaping → (m−1)(m-1)(m−1)-th-order phase shaping.) (iii) PSD of the white sequence. A white sequence at sampling rate freff_{ref}fref​ spreads its power σe2\sigma_e^2σe2​ uniformly over ±fref/2\pm f_{ref}/2±fref​/2 (two-sided bookkeeping) → density σe2/fref=Δ2/(12fref)\sigma_e^2/f_{ref}=\Delta^2/(12f_{ref})σe2​/fref​=Δ2/(12fref​) per Hz; the discrete difference has magnitude response ∣1−e−j2πf/fref∣=2∣sin⁡(πf/fref)∣\lvert1-e^{-j2\pi f/f_{ref}}\rvert=2\lvert\sin(\pi f/f_{ref})\rvert∣1−e−j2πf/fref​∣=2∣sin(πf/fref​)∣. Putting it together (referred to the output phase, before the loop): LΔΣ(f)=(2πΔ)212 fref[2sin⁡(πffref)]2(m−1),SΔΣ(f)=2 LΔΣ(f)=(2πΔ)26 fref[2sin⁡(πffref)]2(m−1)\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\Sigma}(f)=\frac{(2\pi\Delta)^2}{12\,f_{ref}}\Big[2\sin\Big(\frac{\pi f}{f_{ref}}\Big)\Big]^{2(m-1)},\qquad S_{\Delta\Sigma}(f)=2\,\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\Sigma}(f)=\frac{(2\pi\Delta)^2}{6\,f_{ref}}\Big[2\sin\Big(\frac{\pi f}{f_{ref}}\Big)\Big]^{2(m-1)}LΔΣ​(f)=12fref​(2πΔ)2​[2sin(fref​πf​)]2(m−1),SΔΣ​(f)=2LΔΣ​(f)=6fref​(2πΔ)2​[2sin(fref​πf​)]2(m−1) (SΔΣS_{\Delta\Sigma}SΔΣ​ in rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz, single-sided). Factor-of-2 bookkeeping flag (flagged every time): the literature's customary 1/121/121/12 version is two-sided bookkeeping, which numerically happens to equal the SSB L\mathcal{L}L (because the 12\tfrac1221​ in L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​ cancels the ×2\times2×2 of single-siding); this site's strict single-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​ convention needs the ×2\times2×2 (giving 1/61/61/6). Both notations appear in the literature — always state which one you are reading. This is the same class of factor-of-2 issue as [P1] Eq.(21)'s /4 (SSB bookkeeping) vs the clean time-domain /2. (iv) No ×N2\times N^2×N2! This term enters the loop at the PFD like SrefS_{ref}Sref​ and is low-passed by the same ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2, but it is not multiplied by N2N^2N2: the error is counted in "VCO cycles" to begin with, so the 2π2\pi2π is already rad of output phase. If you insist on referring it to the divider output (only 2π/N2\pi/N2π/N rad per cycle), you must multiply by NNN (power ×N2\times N^2×N2) to get back to the output — the N2N^2N2 cancels exactly. The most common rookie budget mistake is multiplying this term by N2N^2N2 anyway. Dimension check: (2πΔ)2(2\pi\Delta)^2(2πΔ)2 [rad²] (Δ\DeltaΔ is a dimensionless cycle count) ×\times× 1/(12fref)1/(12f_{ref})1/(12fref​) [1/Hz] ×\times× shaping factor [dimensionless] =rad2/Hz=\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}=rad2/Hz — checks out.

documents.t: Sout(f)=(SrefN2+Scp)∣Hlp∣2+Svco∣Hhp∣2+SΔΣ(f) ∣Hlp∣2.S_{out}(f)=\big(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}\big)\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2+S_{vco}\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2+S_{\Delta\Sigma}(f)\,\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2 .Sout​(f)=(Sref​N2+Scp​)∣Hlp​∣2+Svco​∣Hhp​∣2+SΔΣ​(f)∣Hlp​∣2. It shares the CP noise's path (low-pass) but has a completely different shape: for f≪freff\ll f_{ref}f≪fref​, 2sin⁡(πf/fref)≈2πf/fref2\sin(\pi f/f_{ref})\approx2\pi f/f_{ref}2sin(πf/fref​)≈2πf/fref​, so SΔΣ∝f 2(m−1)S_{\Delta\Sigma}\propto f^{\,2(m-1)}SΔΣ​∝f2(m−1) — a rising ramp of 20(m−1)20(m-1)20(m−1) dB/dec (MASH-1-1-1: +40+40+40 dB/dec), capping out at fref/2f_{ref}/2fref​/2 (shaping factor at most 22(m−1)=162^{2(m-1)}=1622(m−1)=16, i.e. +12.0+12.0+12.0 dB). It is not a floor — it is a wall climbing up from low frequency; the loop must chop it with ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 before the wall climbs high enough to hurt. The two suppression knobs (why higher freff_{ref}fref​ and narrower BW work): Raise freff_{ref}fref​: at fixed f≪freff\ll f_{ref}f≪fref​, LΔΣ∝f2(m−1)/fref 2m−1\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\Sigma}\propto f^{2(m-1)}/f_{ref}^{\,2m-1}LΔΣ​∝f2(m−1)/fref2m−1​ — doubling freff_{ref}fref​ drops it by (2m−1)×3.01≈15.05(2m-1)\times3.01\approx15.05(2m−1)×3.01≈15.05 dB (m=3m=3m=3). Intuition: the total quantization power Δ2/12\Delta^2/12Δ2/12 is fixed but spread over a wider Nyquist bandwidth, and the freff_{ref}fref​ in the shaping denominator grows. Narrow the loop BW: the in-band spot value doesn't change (∣Hlp∣2≈1\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx1∣Hlp​∣2≈1), but the low-pass intercepts the ramp earlier — the third term's peak lands near ∼fn\sim f_n∼fn​ with magnitude ∝fn2(m−1)\propto f_n^{2(m-1)}∝fn2(m−1)​ (m=3m=3m=3: halving fnf_nfn​ drops the peak 12 dB); a brick-wall estimate of its integrated power scales as ∝fn2m−1\propto f_n^{2m-1}∝fn2m−1​ (fn5f_n^5fn5​ — extremely sensitive to BW). This pushes in the same direction as the U-shape's right arm ("narrow BW suppresses in-band"), but directly conflicts with a ring VCO's need for wide BW — fractional-N + a noisy VCO is the hardest budget combination, and one reason low-noise fractional-N synthesizers prefer LC VCOs. Honest toy-model warning (important): this page's type-II second-order ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 only falls −20-20−20 dB/dec beyond fnf_nfn​ — it cannot catch the +40+40+40 dB/dec rise of m=3m=3m=3. So in this toy model the third term keeps climbing at a net +20+20+20 dB/dec past fnf_nfn​ until the sin⁡\sinsin caps: with fn=100f_n=100fn​=100 kHz the peak is −103.6-103.6−103.6 dBc/Hz at ≈18.6\approx18.6≈18.6 MHz, about 22 dB above the VCO term at the same offset (−125.4-125.4−125.4 dBc/Hz). Real fractional-N loops therefore must add high-frequency loop-filter poles (third/ fourth-order loops) so the out-of-band rolloff beats 20(m−1)20(m-1)20(m−1) dB/dec (external standard practice — see the Gardner and Razavi textbooks; not among this site's five source PDFs). The design equation for that third pole (C3C_3C3​ in parallel with the RRR–CCC branch, ωp3=(C+C3)/(RCC3)\omega_{p3}=(C+C_3)/(RCC_3)ωp3​=(C+C3​)/(RCC3​); C3≈C/10C_3\approx C/10C3​≈C/10 gives fp3=11fzf_{p3}=11f_zfp3​=11fz​) and the phase margin it costs (65.5∘→53.1∘65.5^\circ\to53.1^\circ65.5∘→53.1∘) are in lab_13 §2 — note that a third-order loop only flattens the +40+40+40 dB/dec of m=3m=3m=3; a net decline needs a fourth-order loop. This is the classic origin of "the third term looks harmless on paper, then a high-frequency hump pops up in silicon."

Before the loop: 6.580×10−8×2.487×10−4=1.636×10−116.580\times10^{-8}\times2.487\times10^{-4}=1.636\times10^{-11}6.580×10−8×2.487×10−4=1.636×10−11 → LΔΣ(1 MHz)=−107.9\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\Sigma}(1\text{ MHz})=-107.9LΔΣ​(1 MHz)=−107.9 dBc/Hz. fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz: ∣Hlp(1 MHz)∣2=1.50\lvert H_{lp}(1\text{ MHz})\rvert^2=1.50∣Hlp​(1 MHz)∣2=1.50 (+1.76+1.76+1.76 dB) → −106.1-106.1−106.1 dBc/Hz — 15 dB above the −121.2-121.2−121.2 dBc/Hz floor; the in-band budget is wrecked: the BW is too wide, the ramp has already climbed to its top at 1 MHz and gets a boost from the peaking. fn=100f_n=100fn​=100 kHz: ∣Hlp∣2=0.0201\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2=0.0201∣Hlp​∣2=0.0201 (−17.0-17.0−17.0 dB) → −124.8-124.8−124.8 dBc/Hz — pushed 3.6 dB below the floor, safe on a spot basis (but the high-frequency hump still needs checking — see the toy-model warning above). Alternatively, leave the BW alone and raise freff_{ref}fref​ to 100 MHz: before the loop it becomes −122.9-122.9−122.9 dBc/Hz, a 15.04-dB improvement (theoretical asymptote 15.0515.0515.05 dB — checks out). Dimension check: rad2/Hz×\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}\timesrad2/Hz× dimensionless =rad2/Hz=\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}=rad2/Hz; after 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ it reads as dBc/Hz — checks out. import numpy as np from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_lowpass_mag2 fref, m, Delta, f = 50e6, 3, 1.0, 1e6 P = (2*np.pi*Delta)**2/(12*fref) shape = (2*np.sin(np.pi*f/fref))**(2*(m - 1)) raw = P*shape print(f"{P:.4e}", f"{shape:.4e}", round(10*np.log10(raw), 2)) # -> 6.5797e-08 2.4871e-04 -107.86 (prefactor rad^2/Hz, shaping factor, before-loop dBc/Hz) for fn in (1e6, 1e5): lp = H_lowpass_mag2(np.array([f]), fn, 0.707)[0] print(round(fn/1e3), round(10*np.log10(raw*lp), 2)) # -> 1000 -106.1, 100 -124.83 (L_dSigma(1 MHz) for fn=1 MHz vs 100 kHz, dBc/Hz) raw2 = (2*np.pi*Delta)**2/(12*100e6)*(2*np.sin(np.pi*f/100e6))**(2*(m - 1)) print(round(10*np.log10(raw/raw2), 2)) # -> 15.04 (improvement in dB for f_ref 50→100 MHz; asymptote (2m-1)x3.01=15.05) fs = np.logspace(3, np.log10(25e6), 200_000) LdS = P*(2*np.sin(np.pi*fs/fref))**(2*(m - 1))*H_lowpass_mag2(fs, 1e5, 0.707) k = int(np.argmax(LdS)) print(round(10*np.log10(LdS[k]), 2), round(fs[k]/1e6, 2)) # -> -103.6 18.55 (the third term's high-frequency hump under the toy 2nd-order loop: dBc/Hz, MHz)

documents.t: The PLL output's σt\sigma_tσt​ (this page's right-panel minimum, ≈259\approx259≈259 fs) is exactly the jitter budget fed to a high-speed serializer/deserializer (SerDes)'s sampling clock. In serdes_clocking_connection, this σt\sigma_tσt​ directly determines the eye diagram's horizontal closure and BER (bit error rate): the shorter the UI (unit interval, i.e. the higher the data rate), the larger the fraction of the eye width the same σt\sigma_tσt​ eats up. So choosing the right loop BW to minimize PLL jitter is the source of the entire SerDes link's budget. The CDR (clock-data recovery) itself is also a PLL, but two different quantities must be kept apart: the CDR's jitter transfer for input data jitter (how much of the input jitter the recovered clock "follows") is exactly this page's low-pass ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 (the same Sout=Sref∣Hlp∣2+Svco∣Hhp∣2S_{out}=S_{ref}\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2+ S_{vco}\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2Sout​=Sref​∣Hlp​∣2+Svco​∣Hhp​∣2 on this page; see lab_13_pll_cdr_transfer). But how much input jitter the CDR can tolerate without erroring (jitter tolerance, next section) is a different question, set by the complementary high-pass Hhp=1−HlpH_{hp}=1-H_{lp}Hhp​=1−Hlp​, not by ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2.

documents.t: Common mislabeling: writing the CDR's jitter tolerance as ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 too — that is actually the jitter transfer from the paragraph above. Tolerance asks a different question: the CDR's sampling clock ϕclk(f)≈Hlp(f) ϕdata(f)\phi_{clk}(f)\approx H_{lp}(f)\,\phi_{data}(f)ϕclk​(f)≈Hlp​(f)ϕdata​(f) tracks the input data's jitter ϕdata(f)\phi_{data}(f)ϕdata​(f), but the part it fails to track (the error) is what eats into the eye: ϕerr(f)=ϕdata(f)−ϕclk(f)=[1−Hlp(f)] ϕdata(f)=Hhp(f) ϕdata(f).\phi_{err}(f)=\phi_{data}(f)-\phi_{clk}(f)=\big[1-H_{lp}(f)\big]\,\phi_{data}(f)=H_{hp}(f)\,\phi_{data}(f).ϕerr​(f)=ϕdata​(f)−ϕclk​(f)=[1−Hlp​(f)]ϕdata​(f)=Hhp​(f)ϕdata​(f). JTOL criterion: let the eye's own margin (after subtracting DJ, sampling uncertainty, etc.) be UI−TJeye\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye}UI−TJeye​. The maximum single-tone sinusoidal input jitter (peak amplitude) the CDR can tolerate is JTOL(f)≈UI−TJeye∣Hhp(f)∣.\text{JTOL}(f)\approx\frac{\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye}}{\lvert H_{hp}(f)\rvert}.JTOL(f)≈∣Hhp​(f)∣UI−TJeye​​. Convention flag (peak vs peak-to-peak, a factor of 2): here the same formula is read as peak amplitude; cdr_bang_bang_jtol calls the same expression peak-to-peak, which is what matches an industry JTOL mask — the numbers are identical, only the reading differs by 2×, so be explicit about which one you mean. Here ∣Hhp(f)∣=∣Hhp(f)∣2\lvert H_{hp}(f)\rvert=\sqrt{\lvert H_{hp}(f)\rvert^2}∣Hhp​(f)∣=∣Hhp​(f)∣2​ is the linear (amplitude) transfer — a single-frequency sinusoidal disturbance goes through the amplitude transfer, not the power transfer ∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hhp​∣2 this page uses for summing PSDs; keep the units straight. At low frequency (f≪fnf\ll f_nf≪fn​) a type-II second-order loop has ∣Hhp∣∝(f/fn)2\lvert H_{hp}\rvert \propto(f/f_n)^2∣Hhp​∣∝(f/fn​)2 (the textbook −40-40−40 dB/dec slope), so the CDR tracks well and tolerance diverges as frequency drops; at high frequency (f≫fnf\gg f_nf≫fn​) ∣Hhp∣→1\lvert H_{hp}\rvert\to1∣Hhp​∣→1, the CDR cannot track at all, and tolerance caps out at UI−TJeye\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye}UI−TJeye​ itself (the static eye margin alone). Worked example (site values): UI =40=40=40 ps (the 25 Gb/s NRZ link in final_exam problem 10), free-running VCO σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs (Example C, this site's canonical value), CDR loop at this page's/lab_13's fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz, ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707. Find JTOL at 100 kHz, 1 MHz, and 10 MHz. documents.t: Oscillators have a FOM (fom_limit: it normalizes L\mathcal{L}L, (f0/Δf)2(f_0/\Delta f)^2(f0​/Δf)2 and PPP); a whole PLL has a commonly used quality metric too. A PLL's natural output quantity is not L\mathcal{L}L at some offset but the integrated rms jitter σt\sigma_tσt​ (Step 5; it already absorbs f0f_0f0​: σt=σϕ/2πf0\sigma_t=\sigma_\phi/2\pi f_0σt​=σϕ​/2πf0​), paired with the total power PPP: FOMjitter=20log⁡10 ⁣(σt1 s)+10log⁡10 ⁣(P1 mW)[dB]\mathrm{FOM}_{jitter}=20\log_{10}\!\Big(\frac{\sigma_t}{1\ \text{s}}\Big)+10\log_{10}\!\Big(\frac{P}{1\ \text{mW}}\Big)\qquad[\text{dB}]FOMjitter​=20log10​(1 sσt​​)+10log10​(1 mWP​)[dB] (External convention, not among this site's 5 PDFs; the definition was popularized by X. Gao, E. A. M. Klumperink, M. Bohsali, and B. Nauta, "A Low Noise Sub-Sampling PLL in Which Divider Noise Is Eliminated and PD/CP Noise Is Not Multiplied by N²," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 44, no. 12, pp. 3253–3263, Dec. 2009, already cited in sampling_pll.) Why σt2×P\sigma_t^2\times Pσt2​×P (20log⁡σt+10log⁡P20\log\sigma_t+10\log P20logσt​+10logP): in a thermal-noise-dominated PLL every term is ∝1/P\propto1/P∝1/P — the VCO term Svco∝Feff kT/PS_{vco}\propto F_{eff}\,kT/PSvco​∝Feff​kT/P (the universal form of Step 1 in fom_limit), the CP term (2πN/Icp)2Si,cp∝1/Icp(2\pi N/I_{cp})^2S_{i,cp}\propto1/I_{cp}(2πN/Icp​)2Si,cp​∝1/Icp​ (Si,cp∝IcpS_{i,cp}\propto I_{cp}Si,cp​∝Icp​), the loop-filter resistor term ∝R∝1/Icp\propto R\propto1/I_{cp}∝R∝1/Icp​ (Step 2 / lab_13). Hence σϕ2∝1/P\sigma_\phi^2\propto1/Pσϕ2​∝1/P and σt2⋅P≈\sigma_t^2\cdot P\approxσt2​⋅P≈ const — taking 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ gives the expression above. Doubling the power only buys σt/2\sigma_t/\sqrt2σt​/2​. Sign-convention flag: this expression is always negative, more negative is better (σt≪1\sigma_t\ll1σt​≪1 s); the opposite of fom_limit's oscillator FOM ("positive, bigger is better"). The two can neither be swapped nor added — one normalizes f0/Δff_0/\Delta ff0​/Δf, the other folds f0f_0f0​ into σt\sigma_tσt​. Dimension check: σt/1 s\sigma_t/1\ \text{s}σt​/1 s and P/1 mWP/1\ \text{mW}P/1 mW are both dimensionless → dB ✓. Worked example (this page's optimum): σt=259\sigma_t=259σt​=259 fs (the minimum of the Step 5 right panel, integrated 1 kHz–1 GHz), assumed whole-PLL power P=10P=10P=10 mW (lab_20 does not model power; this value is an illustrative assumption). Find FOMjitter\mathrm{FOM}_{jitter}FOMjitter​, and the improvement from halving σt\sigma_tσt​ or halving PPP. Step by step: 20log⁡10(259×10−15)=20×(log⁡102.59−13)=20×(0.4133−13)=20×(−12.587)=−251.720\log_{10}(259\times10^{-15})=20\times(\log_{10}2.59-13)=20\times(0.4133-13)=20\times(-12.587)=-251.720log10​(259×10−15)=20×(log10​2.59−13)=20×(0.4133−13)=20×(−12.587)=−251.7 dB. 10log⁡10(10 mW/1 mW)=+10.010\log_{10}(10\ \text{mW}/1\ \text{mW})=+10.010log10​(10 mW/1 mW)=+10.0 dB. FOMjitter=−251.7+10.0=−241.7\mathrm{FOM}_{jitter}=-251.7+10.0=\mathbf{-241.7}FOMjitter​=−251.7+10.0=−241.7 dB. Halving σt\sigma_tσt​: 20log⁡10(0.5)=−6.0220\log_{10}(0.5)=-6.0220log10​(0.5)=−6.02 dB (better); halving PPP: 10log⁡10(0.5)=−3.0110\log_{10}(0.5)=-3.0110log10​(0.5)=−3.01 dB. Halving the jitter is worth twice as much as halving the power — a direct consequence of the σt2P\sigma_t^2Pσt2​P bookkeeping. Distance to state of the art: the literature often quotes ≈−250\approx-250≈−250 dB as the order of magnitude of recent best PLLs (external convention; value to be verified, and it drifts with year and with the integration bandwidth definition). Reaching −250-250−250 dB at the same 10 mW needs σt=10(−250−10)/20=10−13\sigma_t=10^{(-250-10)/20}=10^{-13}σt​=10(−250−10)/20=10−13 s =100=100=100 fs; this page's −241.7-241.7−241.7 dB is 8.3 dB away — equivalent to a 2.6× larger σt\sigma_tσt​ at equal power, or 6.8× more power at equal jitter. The way forward is this page's knobs: lower SvcoS_{vco}Svco​ (LC instead of ring, the QQQ of fom_limit), lower the in-band floor (sub-sampling avoids the ×N2\times N^2×N2, sampling_pll), then re-optimize fnf_nfn​. import numpy as np sigma_t, P = 259e-15, 10e-3 # s (lab_20 optimum), W (assumed PLL power, illustrative) FOM_j = 20*np.log10(sigma_t/1.0) + 10*np.log10(P/1e-3) print(round(20*np.log10(sigma_t), 1), round(FOM_j, 1)) # -> -251.7 -241.7 print(round(20*np.log10(0.5), 2), round(10*np.log10(0.5), 2)) # -> -6.02 -3.01 print(round(10**((-250 - 10)/20)*1e15, 1), round(-241.7 - (-250), 1)) # -> 100.0 8.3 print(round(10**(8.3/20), 1), round(10**(8.3/10), 1)) # -> 2.6 6.8 Applicability and failure (FOMjitter\mathrm{FOM}_{jitter}FOMjitter​): before comparing two PLLs, align three things — (i) the integration bandwidth (this page: 1 kHz–1 GHz; the literature commonly uses 1 kHz–100 MHz or 10 kHz–40 MHz, and numbers with different bandwidths are not comparable); (ii) whether σt\sigma_tσt​ includes spurs (this page counts random PN only); (iii) whether PPP includes the reference and the output buffers. It also does not normalize foutf_{out}fout​ or the tuning range, so it is meaningful only within the same architecture class and frequency band; the thermal-noise-dominated ∝1/P\propto1/P∝1/P assumption fails when flicker or digital power (an ADPLL's logic, TDC) dominates.

In-band tracks ref/CP (amplified by N2N^2N2, low-passed), out-of-band tracks VCO (high-passed, 1/f21/f^21/f2 leakage), with the crossover at fnf_nfn​. The VCO term is exactly this site's ISF result Svco∝Γrms2/qmax2⋅Si/f2S_{vco}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2\cdot S_i/f^2Svco​∝Γrms2​/qmax2​⋅Si​/f2. The reference spur is a discrete spike (the freff_{ref}fref​ ripple from CP mismatch/leakage), suppressed by a narrow BW but at the cost of VCO suppression. Optimal loop BW: minimize ∫Soutdf\int S_{out}df∫Sout​df, fn\*∝Svco/(SrefN2+Scp)f_n^\*\propto\sqrt{S_{vco}/(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})}fn\*​∝Svco​/(Sref​N2+Scp​)​; too narrow leaks VCO, too wide leaks ref/CP. lab_20 numerics: fn\*≈6.90f_n^\*\approx6.90fn\*​≈6.90 MHz, σt≈259\sigma_t\approx259σt​≈259 fs. This ring-PLL's U-shape has a steeper left arm than right → favors a somewhat larger loop BW. The loop-filter resistor term has a closed form Sϕ,R=4kTR Kvco2/(2πf)2⋅∣Hhp∣2S_{\phi,R}=4kTR\,K_{vco}^2/(2\pi f)^2\cdot\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2Sϕ,R​=4kTRKvco2​/(2πf)2⋅∣Hhp​∣2 (band-pass, peak at fnf_nfn​); lab_13's worked design (R=178R=178R=178 kΩ) gives −117.4-117.4−117.4 dBc/Hz @1 MHz, σt,R=91\sigma_{t,R}=91σt,R​=91 fs — "omitted" does not always hold, and raising IcpI_{cp}Icp​ suppresses it together with the CP term. A type-II with a zero always peaks: fpk=fn2/(s+1)f_{pk}=f_n\sqrt{2/(s+1)}fpk​=fn​2/(s+1)​, ∣Hlp∣max2=(s+1)2/[(s−1)(s+3)]\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2_{max}=(s+1)^2/[(s-1)(s+3)]∣Hlp​∣max2​=(s+1)2/[(s−1)(s+3)], s=1+8ζ2s=\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}s=1+8ζ2​; ζ=0.707→2.09\zeta=0.707\to2.09ζ=0.707→2.09 dB @ 0.786fn0.786f_n0.786fn​ (the peak is exactly the golden ratio φ\varphiφ). In a cascade the peak dBs add → the 0.1-dB telecom spec (needs ζ≈4.3\zeta\approx4.3ζ≈4.3): single-loop optimal ≠\ne= cascade optimal. The fractional-N third term: LΔΣ=(2πΔ)212fref[2sin⁡(πf/fref)]2(m−1)∣Hlp∣2\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\Sigma}=\frac{(2\pi\Delta)^2}{12f_{ref}}[2\sin(\pi f/f_{ref})]^{2(m-1)}\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2LΔΣ​=12fref​(2πΔ)2​[2sin(πf/fref​)]2(m−1)∣Hlp​∣2 (SSB reading; this site's single-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​ needs ×2\times2×2), no ×N2\times N^2×N2, climbing at +40+40+40 dB/dec (m=3m=3m=3); doubling freff_{ref}fref​ gives −15-15−15 dB, a narrow BW chops the ramp; a 2nd-order loop cannot contain the m=3m=3m=3 high-frequency hump (add filter poles). CDR jitter transfer and jitter tolerance are two different things: transfer (how much input jitter shows up unchanged in the recovered clock) =∣Hlp∣2=\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2=∣Hlp​∣2; tolerance (how much input jitter the CDR can take without erroring) is set by the error transfer Hhp=1−HlpH_{hp}=1-H_{lp}Hhp​=1−Hlp​: JTOL(f)≈(UI−TJeye)/∣Hhp(f)∣\text{JTOL}(f)\approx(\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye})/\lvert H_{hp}(f)\rvertJTOL(f)≈(UI−TJeye​)/∣Hhp​(f)∣ — high tolerance at −40-40−40 dB/dec low frequency, capped at the static eye margin at high frequency. documents.t: Prerequisites: isf_definition, effective_isf, paper_003, paper_004 | Next: sampling_pll Quadrature (a pair of signals I and Q with a 90∘90^\circ90∘ phase offset) is a basic building block of modern transceivers: image-reject mixers, single-sideband modulation, 4-phase sampling in half-rate SerDes, phase detection in CDRs — all of them need a clean I/Q pair with small phase error. The problem: generating quadrature itself carries a phase-noise cost, and the cost structure differs completely between generation methods. This page answers: What this page answers: (1) What does the phase-noise cost of each of the three mainstream quadrature generation methods look like? (2) In a coupled QVCO (coupled quadrature VCO), why is coupling strength ↔ I/Q phase error ↔ phase noise a triangular trade-off? (3) For the coupled oscillator pair, is their noise common-mode or differential-mode correlated, and how does that determine the famous ∼3\sim 3∼3 dB? (4) How do you rigorously wire the "coupling injection" back to the ISF / generalized Adler of [P3]? Physical intuition (conclusion first): a coupled QVCO is just "two oscillators injection-locking each other" — A's output injects into B, B's output injects into A. Once you see it that way, the entire [P3] machinery applies immediately: the coupling current ici_{c}ic​ sees an effective ISF Γ~\tilde\GammaΓ~, "pulls" the other oscillator's phase through the harmonics cnc_ncn​ of Γ~\tilde\GammaΓ~, and the locking dynamics obey the generalized Adler equation ([P3] Eq.(30)). The stronger the coupling, the more tightly the two phases are bound (smaller phase error), but the coupling device also injects extra noise and pulls the frequency away from the tank resonance — that is where the triangular trade-off comes from.
documents.s: Quadrature generation and coupled-oscillator phase noise

documents.t: Put the three routes side by side first. Each route's "cost" is different; understanding the differences matters more than memorizing conclusions.
documents.s: 1. The three quadrature generation methods and their phase-noise costs

documents.t: Two identical LC VCOs, with a pair of coupling transistors injecting A's output into B and B's output (inverted) into A, forcing the two to lock at a fixed 90∘90^\circ90∘ phase offset. How it generates quadrature: under the constraint "total loop phase =0=0=0", the coupling arrangement forces the two oscillators to 90∘90^\circ90∘ (derivation in Section 4; this is the steady-state solution of the [P3] generalized Adler equation in the "mutual injection" case). Phase-noise cost: in theory it can be better than a single oscillator — differential/anti-phase coupling of two identical VCOs averages out the uncorrelated noise portion (a potential ∼3\sim 3∼3 dB benefit, Section 3); but the coupling device's own noise gets in, and strong coupling pulls the frequency off the tank peak, lowering the effective QQQ and raising phase noise instead. Whether the net is a gain or a loss depends on the coupling strength (the triangular trade-off of Section 2).
documents.s: (a) Coupled QVCO (coupled quadrature VCO)

documents.t: Run a 2f02f_02f0​ oscillator, then divide by 2. A master-slave flip-flop divider natively outputs two clocks 90∘90^\circ90∘ apart (because ÷2\div 2÷2 maps one input period onto an output half-period =90∘=90^\circ=90∘); or use an ILFD (injection-locked frequency divider) — inject 2f02f_02f0​ into an f0f_0f0​ oscillator and lock via the 2nd harmonic of the ISF down to f0f_0f0​ (this is exactly the ILFD of paper_004, subharmonic locking). The full lock-range derivation (ωL=Iinj∣Γ~N∣/2\omega_L=I_{inj}\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vert/2ωL​=Iinj​∣Γ~N​∣/2) and the "half-wave symmetry can't divide by 2" payoff have their own page: injection_locked_division. How it generates quadrature: the two complementary outputs of the ÷2\div 2÷2 (or the four nodes of a differential ÷2) are naturally 90∘90^\circ90∘ apart; quadrature accuracy is set by circuit symmetry, independent of tank detuning — its biggest advantage over the QVCO. Phase-noise cost: an ideal ÷N\div N÷N improves phase noise by 20log⁡10N20\log_{10}N20log10​N dB. Reason: division divides the phase by NNN, so the phase error is divided by NNN too, and the phase power (∝ϕ2\propto\phi^2∝ϕ2) by N2N^2N2: Lout(Δf)=L2f0(Δf)−20log⁡10N\mathcal{L}_{out}(\Delta f)=\mathcal{L}_{2f_0}(\Delta f)-20\log_{10}NLout​(Δf)=L2f0​​(Δf)−20log10​N For ÷2\div 2÷2 that is −20log⁡102=−6.02-20\log_{10}2=-6.02−20log10​2=−6.02 dB. But this only accounts for the "source" noise; you still have to build a clean 2f02f_02f0​ oscillator first (high-frequency VCOs usually have lower QQQ, smaller qmaxq_{max}qmax​, and are inherently noisier), and the divider (especially a CML latch) adds its own noise floor. The net benefit is the "−6-6−6 dB improvement" minus "the noisier 2f02f_02f0​ source + divider noise". This formula is a standard frequency-synthesis result (external literature, not among the five source PDFs), but its physical basis — the phase being divided by NNN — is consistent with this site's [P1] phase definition; the ILFD locking mechanism is the subharmonic injection locking of [P4]. Dimension / order-of-magnitude check: if a 2f0=102f_0=102f0​=10 GHz source has L(1MHz)=−110\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-110L(1MHz)=−110 dBc/Hz, an ideal ÷2\div 2÷2 gives 555 GHz, L=−116\mathcal{L}=-116L=−116 dBc/Hz. But if that 10 GHz VCO's Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ is more than 6 dB worse than a VCO built directly at 5 GHz, the ÷2\div 2÷2 gains nothing — a common practical trap.

documents.t: Purely passive: an RC low-pass on one path (phase −45∘-45^\circ−45∘), a CR high-pass on the other (phase +45∘+45^\circ+45∘); at ω=1/RC\omega=1/RCω=1/RC the two paths differ by 90∘90^\circ90∘. Cascading multiple stages (polyphase) widens the bandwidth. How it generates quadrature: passive phase shift, 90∘90^\circ90∘ set by RRR, CCC matching; no second oscillator needed. Phase-noise cost: a passive network generates no new phase noise (in theory), but it has two costs: (1) insertion loss — each RC-CR stage attenuates ∼3\sim 3∼3 dB, requiring a buffer stage whose thermal noise becomes additive noise (degrading SNR, raising the far-out noise floor); (2) quadrature accuracy is sensitive to the absolute values of RRR, CCC and to frequency — off 1/RC1/RC1/RC you get I/Q phase and amplitude error, requiring multiple stages and calibration. It does not change the close-in 1/f21/f^21/f2, 1/f31/f^31/f3 phase noise (that is set by the PLL/VCO), only raising the far-out floor slightly via buffer additive noise.

documents.t: This is the core triangular trade-off of QVCO design. Define the coupling strength first, then show how the three quantities pull against each other.
documents.s: 2. Coupled QVCO: coupling strength ↔ I/Q phase error ↔ phase noise

documents.t: Let each VCO's core (−GmG_mGm​) transconductance sustain its own oscillation, providing current IcoreI_{core}Icore​; the coupling transistors inject the other oscillator's signal into this one with injection-current amplitude IcI_{c}Ic​. Define the coupling factor m≡IcIcorem\equiv\frac{I_{c}}{I_{core}}m≡Icore​Ic​​ mmm is the dimensionless "how strong the coupling is relative to the core". As m→0m\to 0m→0 the two decouple and run independently; large mmm binds them tightly.
documents.s: Definition of the coupling strength mmm

documents.t: (i) coupling ↑ → I/Q phase error ↓: the coupling provides the restoring force that pulls the pair back to 90∘90^\circ90∘. Any mismatch that makes the two free-running frequencies differ (process variation in LLL, CCC, gmg_mgm​) tries to push the phase offset away from 90∘90^\circ90∘; the stronger the coupling, the larger the restoring force and the smaller the residual phase error. Intuition and order of magnitude (external literature, standard QVCO result): ΔϕIQ ≈ Qm Δω0ω0(order of magnitude; stronger coupling m shrinks the error; larger Q enlarges it)\Delta\phi_{IQ}\ \approx\ \frac{Q}{m}\,\frac{\Delta\omega_0}{\omega_0}\quad\text{(order of magnitude; stronger coupling }m\text{ shrinks the error; larger }Q\text{ enlarges it)}ΔϕIQ​ ≈ mQ​ω0​Δω0​​(order of magnitude; stronger coupling m shrinks the error; larger Q enlarges it) where Δω0/ω0\Delta\omega_0/\omega_0Δω0​/ω0​ is the relative detuning of the two tanks (caused by mismatch). An equivalent form is ΔϕIQ≈Δω0/ωL\Delta\phi_{IQ}\approx\Delta\omega_0/\omega_LΔϕIQ​≈Δω0​/ωL​, where ωL=m ω02Q\omega_L=\dfrac{m\,\omega_0}{2Q}ωL​=2Qmω0​​ is the Adler lock range of the mutual injection (the [P3] Eq.(35) form; external QVCO literature). Intuition: stronger coupling (large mmm) widens the lock range and strengthens the restoring force, so the residual I/Q error shrinks; but a sharper tank (large QQQ) makes the lock range narrower, so the same mismatch is harder to pull back to 90∘90^\circ90∘ and the I/Q phase error is larger. Numerical example (order of magnitude): take m=0.3m=0.3m=0.3, Q=10Q=10Q=10, tank mismatch Δω0/ω0=0.1%\Delta\omega_0/\omega_0=0.1\%Δω0​/ω0​=0.1%; then ΔϕIQ≈Qm Δω0ω0=100.3×0.001≈0.033 rad≈1.9∘.\Delta\phi_{IQ}\approx\frac{Q}{m}\,\frac{\Delta\omega_0}{\omega_0}=\frac{10}{0.3}\times0.001\approx0.033\ \text{rad}\approx1.9^\circ.ΔϕIQ​≈mQ​ω0​Δω0​​=0.310​×0.001≈0.033 rad≈1.9∘. That is, for a sharp high-QQQ (Q=10Q=10Q=10) tank, even with mismatch squeezed to 0.1%0.1\%0.1%, coupling of m∼0.3m\sim0.3m∼0.3 only brings the I/Q error down to about 1.9∘1.9^\circ1.9∘; to go smaller you must strengthen the coupling (larger mmm) or reduce the mismatch (smaller Δω0/ω0\Delta\omega_0/\omega_0Δω0​/ω0​). Unit check: (dimensionless)(dimensionless)×(dimensionless)=\dfrac{(\text{dimensionless})}{(\text{dimensionless})}\times(\text{dimensionless})=(dimensionless)(dimensionless)​×(dimensionless)= dimensionless === rad ✓. Conversely, to get within 0.5∘≈8.7×10−30.5^\circ\approx8.7\times10^{-3}0.5∘≈8.7×10−3 rad (same Δω0/ω0=0.1%\Delta\omega_0/\omega_0=0.1\%Δω0​/ω0​=0.1%), you need Q/m≲8.7Q/m\lesssim 8.7Q/m≲8.7, i.e. m≳Q/8.7≈1.15m\gtrsim Q/8.7\approx1.15m≳Q/8.7≈1.15 — for a Q=10Q=10Q=10 tank that means quite strong coupling, which is exactly the quantitative bound behind "high-QQQ QVCOs are hungrier for coupling strength". (ii) coupling ↑ → phase noise ↑ (two mechanisms): The coupling device injects its own noise: like the core devices, the coupling transistors have thermal/flicker noise; it hits the tank node directly, sees an effective ISF, and contributes extra phase noise (quantified via the ISF in Section 4). The stronger the coupling (larger coupling device, larger current), the larger this noise. The coupling pulls the oscillation frequency off the tank peak, lowering the effective QQQ: the coupling injection is a current out of phase with the tank voltage, so the oscillator must shift away from the tank resonance to keep the total loop phase =0=0=0 (this is the steady state of injection pulling). Off resonance → the tank's phase slope at the operating frequency (i.e. the effective QQQ) shrinks → by Leeson/ISF, phase noise ∝1/Q2\propto 1/Q^2∝1/Q2 rises. This is the main phase-noise penalty of a strongly coupled QVCO. (iii) net trade-off: so QVCO design is finding the sweet spot between "coupling strong enough to suppress I/Q phase error" and "coupling so strong it raises phase noise". Practical experience (external literature): there is an optimum mmm (typically of order m∼0.2 ⁣− ⁣0.5m\sim 0.2\!-\!0.5m∼0.2−0.5, topology-dependent); too small and the I/Q error and unlock risk grow, too large and the effective-QQQ degradation dominates the phase noise.
documents.s: How the three pull against each other (physics)

documents.t: parallel coupling series coupling How the coupling device connects in parallel with the core −GmG_mGm​ device at the tank node in series between the core device and the tail Current allocation coupling and core compete for the same tank-node current coupling current flows through the core, sharing the bias current Phase-noise intuition coupling device adds noise directly; larger frequency pulling coupling burns no extra current, smaller frequency pulling → generally better PN Cost noisier but simpler to design tighter headroom, harder to design Series coupling usually has better phase noise: it opens no extra noisy current branch into the tank, has smaller frequency pulling, and preserves more of the effective QQQ. This is one of the core conclusions of the QVCO literature (external literature, not among the five source PDFs; standard references such as the Andreani QVCO series, Romanò parallel vs series QVCO). This site does not redraw their schematics. Design knobs (coupled QVCO): Coupling strength mmm: trade I/Q error (wants large mmm) against phase noise (wants small mmm) → pick the optimum in between. Coupling hookup: series generally beats parallel (smaller frequency pulling, no extra current). Reduce coupling-device noise: use large-size, low-gmg_mgm​ / low-flicker coupling transistors to cut the Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ they inject. Reduce mismatch: good layout, common-centroid → smaller I/Q error at the same mmm, allowing weaker coupling.

documents.t: A QVCO is "two identical oscillators", so you must distinguish which noise is correlated between the two and which is not — that determines whether the famous ∼3\sim 3∼3 dB is a gain or a loss.
documents.s: 3. Noise correlation: common-mode vs differential-mode and the ~3 dB

documents.t: Think of the second oscillator (Q) as a "replica" of the first (I). For the phase-noise power of each of the I/Q paths: Differential-mode / uncorrelated noise (each VCO core device's own thermal noise, independent between the two): the phase noise of the two is uncorrelated. When you bind the two strongly into one oscillating system, the output phase is set jointly by both — two uncorrelated power contributions average, and the output phase noise is ∼3\sim 3∼3 dB (10log⁡10210\log_{10}210log10​2) lower than a single oscillator. This is the QVCO's theoretical "two oscillators buy 3 dB" benefit. LQVCO ≈ Lsingle−10log⁡102 = Lsingle−3.01 dB(uncorrelated core noise only)\mathcal{L}_{QVCO}\ \approx\ \mathcal{L}_{single}-10\log_{10}2\ =\ \mathcal{L}_{single}-3.01\ \text{dB}\quad\text{(uncorrelated core noise only)}LQVCO​ ≈ Lsingle​−10log10​2 = Lsingle​−3.01 dB(uncorrelated core noise only) Common-mode / correlated noise (noise hitting both oscillators simultaneously, or shared by the coupling path — e.g. shared tail, shared bias, coupling devices): the perturbations on the two are fully correlated, and averaging does not reduce it — correlated power gets no N\sqrt{N}N​ averaging. This noise cancels part of the 3 dB benefit.
documents.s: Bookkeeping of the two noise types

documents.t: The honest version of the ∼3\sim 3∼3 dB: "two oscillators → −3-3−3 dB" holds only for uncorrelated noise, and only if the coupling devices introduce no significant correlated noise and do not drag down the effective QQQ. In practice: Uncorrelated thermal noise of the core devices: enjoys −3-3−3 dB ✓. Noise injected by the coupling devices: it is added, and often correlated (shared coupling path) → cancels part of the benefit. Effective QQQ reduced by coupling-induced frequency pulling: phase noise ∝1/Q2\propto 1/Q^2∝1/Q2 rises → eats some more. So a real QVCO is not necessarily 3 dB better than a single oscillator — often only 1–2 dB, and under strong coupling even worse. The ∼3\sim 3∼3 dB is the upper bound of "averaging two uncorrelated sources", not a guaranteed value (external literature, not among the five source PDFs). Accounting mnemonic: correlated ↔ amplitudes add (total power ∝N2\propto N^2∝N2, no reduction relative to a single source) → no averaging benefit; uncorrelated ↔ powers add (total power ∝N\propto N∝N) → enjoys −10log⁡10N-10\log_{10}N−10log10​N. This is the same correlation-accounting logic as the Section 1 ÷N\div N÷N improvement of 20log⁡10N20\log_{10}N20log10​N (phase divided by NNN, a deterministic correlated scaling) — two faces of one bookkeeping rule.
documents.s: How to do the accounting (key caveat)

documents.t: This is the mathematical core of the page: the locking dynamics of a coupled QVCO are just the [P3] generalized Adler equation applied to "mutual injection". We invent no new theory; we use the equations of this site's paper_003 directly.
documents.s: 4. Wiring the coupling injection back to the ISF / generalized Adler ([P3])

documents.t: The coupling current ic(t)i_{c}(t)ic​(t) injected from A into B, like any injection current, drives B's phase through the unit-bearing ISF Γ~(x)=Γ(x)/qmax\tilde\Gamma(x)=\Gamma(x)/q_{max}Γ~(x)=Γ(x)/qmax​ (units rad/C, [P3] Eq.(26), p.2113). In other words, the coupling injection is nothing special — it sees B's effective Γ~\tilde\GammaΓ~ at the injection node, and "receives" the other oscillator's signal through the Fourier harmonics cnc_ncn​ of Γ~\tilde\GammaΓ~ ([P1] Eq.(12)): the better the harmonic alignment, the more effective the coupling (locking). The coupling device's own noise ic,n(t)i_{c,n}(t)ic,n​(t) travels the same Γ~\tilde\GammaΓ~, so its phase-noise contribution follows the [P1] recipe: L∝Γrms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​/qmax2​ ([P1] Eq.(21), p.185, with Γ\GammaΓ replaced by the effective ISF seen by the coupling injection). This is the quantitative outlet for Section 2's "the coupling device injects extra noise".
documents.s: Step 1: the effective ISF seen by the coupling current

documents.t: Now write B's injection into A as well. For oscillator A, the relative phase θA=ϕA−ϕref\theta_A=\phi_A-\phi_{ref}θA​=ϕA​−ϕref​ obeys the time-averaged generalized Adler equation of [P3] ([P3] Eq.(30), p.2113, with a plus sign in front of the averaged term): dθAdt=(ω0,A−ωref)+1T∫TΓ~(ωreft+θA) ic,B→A(t) dt\frac{d\theta_A}{dt}=(\omega_{0,A}-\omega_{ref})+\frac{1}{T}\int_{T}\tilde\Gamma\big(\omega_{ref}t+\theta_A\big)\,i_{c,B\to A}(t)\,dtdtdθA​​=(ω0,A​−ωref​)+T1​∫T​Γ~(ωref​t+θA​)ic,B→A​(t)dt where ic,B→Ai_{c,B\to A}ic,B→A​ is the coupling current B injects into A (proportional to B's output ∝cos⁡(ωreft+θB)\propto\cos(\omega_{ref}t+\theta_B)∝cos(ωref​t+θB​)). Write the symmetric equation for B. Key point: a coupled QVCO is nothing but two such Adler equations coupled to each other — θB\theta_BθB​ appears in A's equation and θA\theta_AθA​ in B's. Rearranged into the lock characteristic form of [P3] ([P3] Eq.(33), p.2114): dθAdt=(ω0,A−ωref)+Ω(θA−θB)\frac{d\theta_A}{dt}=(\omega_{0,A}-\omega_{ref})+\Omega(\theta_A-\theta_B)dtdθA​​=(ω0,A​−ωref​)+Ω(θA​−θB​) Ω(⋅)\Omega(\cdot)Ω(⋅) is the coupling-induced average frequency shift as a function of the relative phase difference (the stronger the coupling, the wider the range of Ω\OmegaΩ, the firmer the lock).
documents.s: Step 2: generalized Adler for mutual injection

documents.t: The QVCO's coupling arrangement (A injects into B in phase, B injects into A inverted, differing by a minus sign) means that in steady state (dθA/dt=dθB/dt=0d\theta_A/dt=d\theta_B/dt=0dθA​/dt=dθB​/dt=0, both at the same frequency), the two Adler equations are self-consistent only at the phase difference θA−θB=±90∘\theta_A-\theta_B=\pm 90^\circθA​−θB​=±90∘ — the plus or minus sign (I leading or lagging Q) is one of two symmetric stable solutions, decided at start-up. The 90∘90^\circ90∘ is not patched in; it is the steady-state constraint of the mutually injecting Adler equations. Any tank detuning (ω0,A≠ω0,B\omega_{0,A}\ne\omega_{0,B}ω0,A​=ω0,B​) nudges this 90∘90^\circ90∘ off a little, and how much is resisted by the slope of Ω\OmegaΩ (i.e. the coupling strength) — this is exactly the differential-equation version of Section 2's ΔϕIQ∝Q/m\Delta\phi_{IQ}\propto Q/mΔϕIQ​∝Q/m. Order-of-magnitude / dimension check: Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ) has the same units as (ω0−ωref)(\omega_0-\omega_{ref})(ω0​−ωref​), rad/s ✓. Strong coupling → wide range of Ω\OmegaΩ → the same detuning (ω0,A−ω0,B)(\omega_{0,A}-\omega_{0,B})(ω0,A​−ω0,B​) needs only a tiny phase shift to be compensated by Ω(θA−θB)\Omega(\theta_A-\theta_B)Ω(θA​−θB​) → small I/Q error. Weak coupling → narrow Ω\OmegaΩ → once the detuning grows there is no solution (unlock: the two no longer share a frequency, the phase slips periodically — exactly the injection pulling of [P3]).
documents.s: Step 3: steady-state solution → why 90∘90^\circ90∘

documents.t: Design phenomenon (Sections 2, 3) Corresponding [P3] / ISF quantity Coupling strength mmm width of the range of Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ) (= lock range; [P3] Eq.(33)) I/Q phase error vs mismatch detuning divided by the slope of Ω\OmegaΩ (strong coupling → steep slope → small error) Extra phase noise from the coupling device effective Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ seen by the coupling injection, via [P1] Eq.(21) Strong coupling pulls frequency, drops QQQ steady state θ\*≠0\theta^\*\ne 0θ\*=0 → operating frequency off the tank peak 90∘90^\circ90∘ appears naturally steady-state constraint of the anti-phase mutually injecting Adler equations One sentence: a coupled QVCO = two oscillators locking each other via the generalized Adler of [P3]; the coupling current travels the ISF of [P1], so "locking (quadrature)" and "extra phase noise" are two faces of the same Γ~\tilde\GammaΓ~ — fully consistent with [P3]'s point that "the same ISF accounts for both phase noise and injection locking".
documents.s: Step 4: stitching the three pieces into one picture

documents.t: The three steps above only "set up the [P3] equations". This subsection actually runs them: simulations/lab_42_coupled_qvco.py integrates the mutually injecting Adler pair numerically, to see (a) whether anti-phase mutual injection really locks itself to 90∘90^\circ90∘, and (b) whether the Section 2 worked number "ΔϕIQ≈(Q/m)(Δω0/ω0)≈1.9∘\Delta\phi_{IQ}\approx(Q/m)(\Delta\omega_0/\omega_0)\approx1.9^\circΔϕIQ​≈(Q/m)(Δω0​/ω0​)≈1.9∘" is right, and by how much it is off. Model (toy, phase-only): two ideal LC oscillators (Γ~(x)=−sin⁡x/qmax\tilde\Gamma(x)=-\sin x/q_{max}Γ~(x)=−sinx/qmax​, [P3] Eq.(26)), with phases θA,θB\theta_A,\theta_BθA​,θB​ relative to a common reference frequency ωref\omega_{ref}ωref​; the coupling currents carry a coupling-path phase shift ϕc\phi_cϕc​: ic,A→B(t)=+Iccos⁡(ωreft+θA+ϕc),ic,B→A(t)=−Iccos⁡(ωreft+θB+ϕc)i_{c,A\to B}(t)=+I_c\cos(\omega_{ref}t+\theta_A+\phi_c),\qquad i_{c,B\to A}(t)=-I_c\cos(\omega_{ref}t+\theta_B+\phi_c)ic,A→B​(t)=+Ic​cos(ωref​t+θA​+ϕc​),ic,B→A​(t)=−Ic​cos(ωref​t+θB​+ϕc​) (The minus sign is "B injects into A inverted", i.e. the QVCO hookup of Step 3.) Apply [P3] Eq.(34) to each oscillator (the lock characteristic for sinusoidal injection, Ω(θ)=12Iinj∣Γ~1∣cos⁡(θ+∠Γ~1)\Omega(\theta)=\tfrac12 I_{inj}\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvert\cos(\theta+\angle\tilde\Gamma_1)Ω(θ)=21​Iinj​∣Γ~1​∣cos(θ+∠Γ~1​), here with ∣Γ~1∣=1/qmax\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvert=1/q_{max}∣Γ~1​∣=1/qmax​, ∠Γ~1=+90∘\angle\tilde\Gamma_1=+90^\circ∠Γ~1​=+90∘), let ψ≡θA−θB\psi\equiv\theta_A-\theta_Bψ≡θA​−θB​ (the I/Q phase difference) and ωL=12Ic∣Γ~1∣=Ic/(2qmax)\omega_L=\tfrac12 I_c\lvert\tilde\Gamma_1\rvert=I_c/(2q_{max})ωL​=21​Ic​∣Γ~1​∣=Ic​/(2qmax​) ([P3] Eq.(35)), and subtract the two equations: dψdt=(ω0,A−ω0,B)−2 ωLsin⁡ϕc cos⁡ψ\frac{d\psi}{dt}=(\omega_{0,A}-\omega_{0,B})-2\,\omega_L\sin\phi_c\,\cos\psidtdψ​=(ω0,A​−ω0,B​)−2ωL​sinϕc​cosψ Steady state dψ/dt=0d\psi/dt=0dψ/dt=0 gives cos⁡ψ\*=Δω0/(2ωLsin⁡ϕc)\cos\psi^\*=\Delta\omega_0/(2\omega_L\sin\phi_c)cosψ\*=Δω0​/(2ωL​sinϕc​). Three immediate conclusions: At zero detuning cos⁡ψ\*=0⇒ψ\*=±90∘\cos\psi^\*=0\Rightarrow\psi^\*=\pm90^\circcosψ\*=0⇒ψ\*=±90∘ — this is Step 3's "90∘90^\circ90∘ is the steady-state constraint", and which one is stable is decided by the sign of sin⁡ϕc\sin\phi_csinϕc​ (for sin⁡ϕc>0\sin\phi_c>0sinϕc​>0, −90∘-90^\circ−90∘ is stable and +90∘+90^\circ+90∘ unstable). The leading 2 is the "mutual injection" factor: A pulls B and B pulls A, so the restoring force is twice that of one-way injection. Take ϕc=90∘\phi_c=90^\circϕc​=90∘ (coupling current aligned with the ISF fundamental, sin⁡ϕc=1\sin\phi_c=1sinϕc​=1); then ψ\*=−90∘+δ\psi^\*=-90^\circ+\deltaψ\*=−90∘+δ, sin⁡δ=Δω0/(2ωL)\sin\delta=\Delta\omega_0/(2\omega_L)sinδ=Δω0​/(2ωL​). Substituting Section 2's ωL=mω0/(2Q)\omega_L=m\omega_0/(2Q)ωL​=mω0​/(2Q): ΔϕIQ=δ=arcsin⁡ ⁣(QmΔω0ω0) ≈ QmΔω0ω0\Delta\phi_{IQ}=\delta=\arcsin\!\Big(\frac{Q}{m}\frac{\Delta\omega_0}{\omega_0}\Big)\ \approx\ \frac{Q}{m}\frac{\Delta\omega_0}{\omega_0}ΔϕIQ​=δ=arcsin(mQ​ω0​Δω0​​) ≈ mQ​ω0​Δω0​​ — the Section 2 order-of-magnitude formula is exactly the linearization of this arcsin⁡\arcsinarcsin, and it corresponds to Δω0/(2ωL)\Delta\omega_0/(2\omega_L)Δω0​/(2ωL​), not Δω0/ωL\Delta\omega_0/\omega_LΔω0​/ωL​ (the latter is the one-way-injection form and would be 2× larger — a factor-of-2 convention this page flags deliberately). Honest failure point: if ϕc=0\phi_c=0ϕc​=0 (the plainest parallel QVCO: coupling current in phase with the other oscillator's output), sin⁡ϕc=0\sin\phi_c=0sinϕc​=0 and the restoring term vanishes — the pure phase-only Adler pair cannot tell what ψ\psiψ should be (degenerate). A physical QVCO then relies on the amplitude channel (the two amplitudes must be equal ⇒cos⁡ψ=0\Rightarrow\cos\psi=0⇒cosψ=0, the AM dynamics of [P4]) or on a phase shift deliberately added to the coupling path (the phase-shift QVCO of [E-Romano-QVCO]; [E-Mirzaei-QVCO]). So Step 3's "the Adler steady-state constraint gives 90∘90^\circ90∘" strictly needs one more clause: provided the coupling phase is not orthogonal to the ISF fundamental (sin⁡ϕc≠0\sin\phi_c\ne0sinϕc​=0). The lock time constant is 1/(2ωL)=1.061/(2\omega_L)=1.061/(2ωL​)=1.06 ns (5.3 cycles). The black dashed line (ϕc=0\phi_c=0ϕc​=0) does not converge, confirming the degeneracy of point 3 above. For m=0.3m=0.3m=0.3 the unlock boundary is Δω0/ω0=3%\Delta\omega_0/\omega_0=3\%Δω0​/ω0​=3% (150 MHz at 5 GHz). documents.t: The three quadrature generation methods have different cost structures: the coupled QVCO pays with coupling-device noise + pulling-induced QQQ drop (net value depends on coupling strength); ÷2\div 2÷2 (ILFD) ideally improves by −20log⁡10N-20\log_{10}N−20log10​N but needs a clean 2f02f_02f0​ source first; RC-CR polyphase generates no new close-in PN, paying instead with insertion loss + buffer additive noise + narrow bandwidth. The coupled-QVCO triangular trade-off: coupling ↑ → I/Q phase error ↓ (stronger restoring force), but phase noise ↑ (coupling device injects noise + pulling drops the effective QQQ) → an optimum coupling strength mmm exists. Series coupling generally beats parallel (smaller frequency pulling, no extra current). The ∼3\sim 3∼3 dB is an upper bound, not a guarantee: only the uncorrelated core-device noise enjoys −10log⁡102-10\log_{10}2−10log10​2; coupling/shared noise is correlated, canceling part of the benefit; the pulling-induced QQQ drop eats some more → real QVCOs are often only 1–2 dB better, and under strong coupling even worse. Wiring back to [P3]: coupled QVCO = two mutually injecting generalized Adler equations ([P3] Eq.(30), p.2113); the coupling current travels the unit-bearing ISF Γ~=Γ/qmax\tilde\Gamma=\Gamma/q_{max}Γ~=Γ/qmax​ ([P3] Eq.(26)); the 90∘90^\circ90∘ is the steady-state constraint of anti-phase mutual injection; the lock range = the range of Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ) ([P3] Eq.(33)). Locking and extra phase noise are two faces of the same Γ~\tilde\GammaΓ~. Honesty note: the QVCO topology comparison, the ΔϕIQ\Delta\phi_{IQ}ΔϕIQ​ order-of-magnitude formula, the ∼3\sim 3∼3 dB, and the parallel/series conclusion are all external literature (not among the five source PDFs); the locking dynamics are strictly tied to [P3], and the ÷2\div 2÷2/ILFD subharmonic mechanism strictly to [P4].

documents.t: Prerequisites: effective_isf (cyclostationary effective ISF Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α, the common skeleton for all three topologies on this page), symmetry (c0c_0c0​ sets 1/f31/f^31/f3; why the tail's c0c_0c0​ is the real trouble), waveform_slope (deriving the ring stage's ISF from switching slope) | Next: lc_vs_ring, measurement_and_spurs The preceding pages all used the ideal-LC Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ as the lead character to lay out the mechanism white noise → 1/f21/f^21/f2, flicker → 1/f31/f^31/f3. But a real oscillator on silicon is not a clean LC plus a single white-noise source — it is several transistors, a tail (bias) current source, a tank, plus switching action. Different devices inject their noise at different nodes and different phase windows, so every noise source "sees" a different effective ISF. This page answers: What this page answers: in three of the most common topologies — the cross-coupled LC VCO, Colpitts, and the CMOS inverter ring stage — what does the ISF actually seen by each device-noise source look like? Where do its Fourier harmonics (c0,c1,c2,…c_0,c_1,c_2,\dotsc0​,c1​,c2​,…) land? And how do those harmonics set the close-in 1/f31/f^31/f3 and 1/f21/f^21/f2? We walk all of this by hand calculation plus order-of-magnitude estimation (not Spectre / not transistor-level netlist extraction), stringing device noise → ISF harmonics → close-in PN into one complete chain for each topology. Physical intuition (conclusion first): the ISF is "the shape of phase sensitivity to charge injected at some node." But the noise source does not inject uniformly over the whole cycle — the tail transistor only conducts during the switching instant, the Colpitts transistor only conducts during one narrow current pulse, and a ring's inverter only carries large current during transition. Multiplying "how much noise the device injects, and in which phase window" (i.e., the cyclostationary noise modulating function α(θ)\alpha(\theta)α(θ)) by "that node's ISF Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ)" gives the effective ISF Γeff(θ)=Γ(θ) α(θ)\Gamma_{eff}(\theta)=\Gamma(\theta)\,\alpha(\theta)Γeff​(θ)=Γ(θ)α(θ). The Fourier harmonics of this product — especially c0c_0c0​ (which sets flicker upconversion to 1/f31/f^31/f3) and c2c_2c2​ (which folds noise near 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ back onto the carrier) — are what actually drive real close-in phase noise. This page uses two signature close-in formulas from [P1] (verified verbatim): Flicker upconversion to 1/f31/f^31/f3 ([P1] Eq.(23), p.185): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(c02qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf8 Δω2⋅ω1/fΔω)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{8\,\Delta\omega^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​c02​​⋅8Δω2in2​​/Δf​⋅Δωω1/f​​) 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ([P1] Eq.(24), p.185): Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c022 Γrms2≈ω1/f(c0c1)2\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}\approx\omega_{1/f}\left(\frac{c_0}{c_1}\right)^2Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​≈ω1/f​(c1​c0​​)2 The white-noise 1/f21/f^21/f2 signature result ([P1] Eq.(21), p.185), used here to compute the floor: L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​) The cyclostationary effective ISF ([P1] Eq.(27), p.186 — replace Γ\GammaΓ with Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α, where α\alphaα is the noise modulating function, an amplitude-modulation function): Γeff(x)=Γ(x) α(x),α(x)∈[0,1]\Gamma_{eff}(x)=\Gamma(x)\,\alpha(x),\qquad \alpha(x)\in[0,1]Γeff​(x)=Γ(x)α(x),α(x)∈[0,1] Wherever a numeric cnc_ncn​ value is marked illustrative, it is a pedagogical constructed model (not extracted from a transistor netlist), whose purpose is to walk through the order of magnitude of a known mechanism; the ideal-LC Γ=−sin⁡\Gamma=-\sinΓ=−sin is exact. The specific mechanism behind the tail's effective ISF comes from the Hajimiri–Lee cyclostationary analysis ([P1] §IV.D) and from Andreani et al.'s tail-noise analysis (external literature, not among the five source PDFs — see end of page).

documents.t: The skeleton of a cross-coupled LC VCO: an LC tank across the two differential nodes V+,V−V^+,V^-V+,V−; below it, a cross-coupled NMOS pair (M1,M2M_1,M_2M1​,M2​, gates tied to each other's drains) supplies −Gm-G_m−Gm​ (negative conductance) to compensate tank loss; at the bottom, a tail current source MtailM_{tail}Mtail​ sets the bias current IssI_{ss}Iss​. Two fundamentally different noise-injection points: The differential tank nodes (M1,M2M_1,M_2M1​,M2​'s channel thermal noise lands directly on the tank) → sees the tank's ISF. The tail node (MtailM_{tail}Mtail​'s thermal + flicker noise) → sees the tail's effective ISF, because the tail current must first be "commutated" by the switching pair before it reaches the tank.
documents.s: Circuit and the two key noise sources

documents.t: The differential tank is a near-ideal LC resonator, with the two terminal voltages approximately V±=±Acos⁡ω0tV^\pm=\pm A\cos\omega_0 tV±=±Acosω0​t. Injecting charge into the differential node gives the ideal-LC phase-sensitivity result (see impulse_to_phase_shift): Γtank(θ)=−sin⁡θ.\Gamma_{tank}(\theta)=-\sin\theta .Γtank​(θ)=−sinθ. Its Fourier series has only one term, c1=1c_1=1c1​=1, with all other c0=c2=⋯=0c_0=c_2=\dots=0c0​=c2​=⋯=0. Γrms=1/2≈0.707\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2\approx0.707Γrms​=1/2​≈0.707. Physical meaning: −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta−sinθ is most sensitive at the zero crossings (θ=0,π\theta=0,\piθ=0,π) and zero at the peaks (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2) — the classic "a kick is most effective where the slope is steepest." Key benefit: c0=0c_0=0c0​=0. From [P1] Eq.(23), 1/f31/f^31/f3 strength is proportional to c02c_0^2c02​; c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 means differential tank noise barely upconverts flicker at all. This is why a differential LC VCO's close-in phase noise is cleaner than a ring's — provided the waveform is symmetric so c0c_0c0​ stays near 0.

documents.t: The story for tail noise is entirely different, because the tail node voltage swings at 2ω02\omega_02ω0​, and the switching pair applies full-wave-rectifier-like commutation to the tail current. Intuitively: On each half cycle, M1M_1M1​ or M2M_2M2​ alternately steers the entire IssI_{ss}Iss​ (including its noise) to one side of the tank; over one full RF period the tail current is "flipped" twice → the tail sees a 2ω02\omega_02ω0​-periodic modulation → this naturally produces c2c_2c2​ (second harmonic). The tail current's low-frequency/DC noise (especially flicker) gets averaged by switching into a common-mode swing, leaving a nonzero c0c_0c0​ (DC term) — this is the gateway for flicker upconversion. We write this shape down with an illustrative model (taken from lab_21_topology_isf.py, marked as a constructed model): Γtail(θ)=c02+c1,rescos⁡θ+c2cos⁡2θ,c0=0.30, c1,res=0.10, c2=0.55.\Gamma_{tail}(\theta)=\frac{c_0}{2}+c_{1,res}\cos\theta+c_2\cos 2\theta,\qquad c_0=0.30,\ c_{1,res}=0.10,\ c_2=0.55 .Γtail​(θ)=2c0​​+c1,res​cosθ+c2​cos2θ,c0​=0.30, c1,res​=0.10, c2​=0.55. c0=0.30c_0=0.30c0​=0.30: the DC term — the culprit behind flicker upconversion ([P1] Eq.(23) is proportional to c02c_0^2c02​). c2=0.55c_2=0.55c2​=0.55: the second harmonic — folds tail thermal noise near 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ back onto the carrier at offset Δω\Delta\omegaΔω. c1,res=0.10c_{1,res}=0.10c1,res​=0.10: a residual fundamental (should be 0 under ideal symmetry; asymmetry leaks a little through). This ISF's Γrms=(c0/2)2+12(c1,res2+c22)=0.0225+12(0.01+0.3025)≈0.42\Gamma_{rms}=\sqrt{(c_0/2)^2+\tfrac12(c_{1,res}^2+c_2^2)}=\sqrt{0.0225+\tfrac12(0.01+0.3025)}\approx0.42Γrms​=(c0​/2)2+21​(c1,res2​+c22​)​=0.0225+21​(0.01+0.3025)​≈0.42 (Parseval; see figure caption). Mechanism of the 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ fold-back (hand-calc intuition): tail thermal noise carries power in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf near 2ω0±Δω2\omega_0\pm\Delta\omega2ω0​±Δω. The ISF's c2cos⁡2θc_2\cos2\thetac2​cos2θ term acts as a "mixer that down-converts at 2ω02\omega_02ω0​" (see white_noise_to_phase_noise, step 3a): it moves noise at 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ to phase at offset Δω\Delta\omegaΔω. This is exactly why designers raise the tail current source's impedance at 2f02f_02f0​ (a tail filter): placing an LC trap or a large capacitor at 2f02f_02f0​ makes the tail node high-impedance (ideally open) at 2ω02\omega_02ω0​, so tail noise at 2ω02\omega_02ω0​ can no longer inject into the tank → the c2c_2c2​ fold-back is choked off.

documents.t: The Colpitts oscillator forms positive feedback with a single transistor plus a capacitive divider (C1,C2C_1,C_2C1​,C2​) and a tank inductor. Its signature feature: the collector (drain) current is not sinusoidal but a series of narrow, large current pulses followed by a long "quiet" interval. This is exactly what [P1] Fig. 13 shows — the collector voltage and collector current of the Colpitts oscillator of Fig. 5(a): the current is "a short period of large current followed by a quiet interval" ([P1] §IV.D, p.186).
documents.s: Circuit and current pulse

documents.t: Two independent periodic functions are multiplied here: The tank's own ISF Γ(θ)≈−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)\approx-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)≈−sinθ (the Colpitts tank is also near-sinusoidal), spread over the full cycle. The noise modulating function α(θ)\alpha(\theta)α(θ): the device only conducts — and only injects noise — during the current pulse, so α(θ)\alpha(\theta)α(θ) is a narrow pulse concentrated at some phase θp\theta_pθp​. The effective ISF is the product of the two ([P1] Eq.(27)): Γeff(θ)=Γ(θ) α(θ).\Gamma_{eff}(\theta)=\Gamma(\theta)\,\alpha(\theta).Γeff​(θ)=Γ(θ)α(θ). Because α(θ)\alpha(\theta)α(θ) is a narrow pulse, Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ is also "windowed" down to a narrow phase interval around θp\theta_pθp​ — this is the mathematical statement of "the Colpitts ISF concentrates in a narrow phase window (the current-pulse injection instant)," corresponding to [P1] Fig. 14 (which plots Γ\GammaΓ, Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​, and α\alphaα together).
documents.s: Key point: pulse timing vs. ISF shape

documents.t: [P1] §IV.D's key observation (quoted verbatim): "The surge of current occurs at the minimum of the voltage across the tank where the ISF is small." That is, the current pulse lands right at the tank voltage's minimum — and Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ is relatively small there (away from the zero crossings, in the low-sensitivity region). A well-designed Colpitts aligns noise injection with the phase window where ISF is small, so even though the device noise is large at that instant, multiplying by a small Γ\GammaΓ keeps Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ small; Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​ stays low → close-in phase noise is low. This is one of the core reasons Colpitts phase noise is excellent: not because its devices are quieter, but because it aligns the noise-injection instant with the least phase-sensitive window. Compare [P1] §IV.D: the ring oscillator's misfortune is that "the device current is largest at transition (where the ISF is also largest)" — the two peaks overlap, so Γeff≈Γ\Gamma_{eff}\approx\GammaΓeff​≈Γ and cyclostationary effects offer no help — this is one reason ring phase noise is worse.
documents.s: Why this is good news for Colpitts

documents.t: Example 2 (how a narrow window suppresses Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​, order-of-magnitude by hand): Colpitts, tank ISF Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ. The device current pulse width is about δ=10%\delta=10\%δ=10% of the period (conduction angle ≈36∘\approx36^\circ≈36∘), centered on where the ISF is small (take the representative value of Γ\GammaΓ within the pulse window as ∣Γ∣win≈0.3\lvert\Gamma\rvert_{win}\approx0.3∣Γ∣win​≈0.3). Compare Γeff,rms2\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2Γeff,rms2​ for "noise injected uniformly over the full cycle" versus "noise injected only in the narrow window." Case A (stationary, uniform over the full cycle): Γeff=Γ\Gamma_{eff}=\GammaΓeff​=Γ, Γeff,rms2=12π∫02πsin⁡2θ dθ=12=0.5.\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac12=0.5 .Γeff,rms2​=2π1​∫02π​sin2θdθ=21​=0.5. Case B (cyclostationary, narrow window): model α(θ)\alpha(\theta)α(θ) as a window of width 2πδ2\pi\delta2πδ and height 1/δ1/\delta1/δ (normalized so the average noise power inside the window is unchanged), located where ∣Γ∣win≈0.3\lvert\Gamma\rvert_{win}\approx0.3∣Γ∣win​≈0.3. Within the window Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α, with mean square: Γeff,rms2≈12π∫window(Γ(θ) α(θ))2dθ≈∣Γ∣win2⋅1δ≈0.32×10.1×δ=0.09×1=0.09.\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2\approx\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{window}\big(\Gamma(\theta)\,\alpha(\theta)\big)^2 d\theta\approx \lvert\Gamma\rvert_{win}^2\cdot\frac{1}{\delta}\approx 0.3^2\times\frac{1}{0.1}\times\delta=0.09\times1=0.09 .Γeff,rms2​≈2π1​∫window​(Γ(θ)α(θ))2dθ≈∣Γ∣win2​⋅δ1​≈0.32×0.11​×δ=0.09×1=0.09. (This is an order-of-magnitude approximation: window height 1/δ1/\delta1/δ, window width δ⋅2π\delta\cdot2\piδ⋅2π; after normalization, the average Γ2\Gamma^2Γ2 inside the window is taken as roughly the center value ∣Γ∣win2=0.09\lvert\Gamma\rvert_{win}^2=0.09∣Γ∣win2​=0.09. An exact value would require numerical integration — here we take only the order of magnitude.) Comparison: Γeff,rms2\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2Γeff,rms2​ drops from 0.50.50.5 to ≈0.09\approx0.09≈0.09, an improvement of about 7.47.47.4 dB (10log⁡10(0.5/0.09)=7.410\log_{10}(0.5/0.09)=7.410log10​(0.5/0.09)=7.4 dB). Chain closure (→ close-in PN): L∝Γeff,rms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γeff,rms2​/qmax2​ ([P1] Eq.(21) with Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ replaced by Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​), so aligning noise injection with a small-ISF window directly cuts close-in PN by about 7 dB — this is the order of magnitude of Colpitts' advantage. Dimension check: Γeff,rms2\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2Γeff,rms2​ is dimensionless (Γ\GammaΓ and α\alphaα are both dimensionless) ✓. Honesty note: δ=10%\delta=10\%δ=10% and ∣Γ∣win=0.3\lvert\Gamma\rvert_{win}=0.3∣Γ∣win​=0.3 are order-of-magnitude estimates (not precise values extracted from a netlist); the goal is to demonstrate how "a narrow window aligned with small ISF" suppresses Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​. See [P1] Fig. 14 for the exact curve. import numpy as np theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 20000, endpoint=False) gamma = -np.sin(theta) # Case A: stationary g2_A = np.mean(gamma**2) # ~0.5 # Case B: narrow window alpha aligned with small-ISF region (centered near theta_p ~ 1.5*pi, |Gamma|~0.3 region) alpha = np.zeros_like(theta) mask = (theta > 1.40*np.pi) & (theta < 1.50*np.pi) # ~10% window alpha[mask] = 1.0/0.05 # normalized height g2_B = np.mean((gamma*alpha)**2) * 0.05 # order of magnitude print(round(g2_A,3), round(g2_B,3)) # ~0.5 vs ~0.09 order of magnitude print(round(10*np.log10(g2_A/0.09),1), "dB") # ~7.4 dB improvement Design knobs (Colpitts): Align the current pulse with the tank-voltage trough (where ISF is small) — shrink the conduction angle, adjust bias so the pulse lands in the small-Γ\GammaΓ phase window. Narrower pulse (smaller conduction angle) — the narrower the window, the better it avoids the large-ISF zero crossings. Unlike cross-coupled: Colpitts is single-ended, single-device, and has no tail-switching c2c_2c2​ fold-back problem, but waveform asymmetry will make c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0 (still watch for flicker upconversion).

documents.t: A ring oscillator is a chain of NNN CMOS inverter stages in a loop. Each stage's output is "parked" at a rail (VDDV_{DD}VDD​ or GND) most of the time, flipping rapidly only during the brief switching transition. Question: what does this stage's ISF Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ) look like? Hand-calc reasoning (slope → sensitivity): phase sensitivity Γ\GammaΓ fundamentally measures "how far the phase is pushed by a kick at this phase." For a threshold-crossing digital stage, phase = when the edge crosses the threshold. A small charge Δq\Delta qΔq injected at the node produces a voltage jump ΔV=Δq/C\Delta V=\Delta q/CΔV=Δq/C, which shifts the edge-crossing instant by Δt=ΔV∣dV/dt∣=ΔqC ∣dV/dt∣,\Delta t=\frac{\Delta V}{\lvert dV/dt\rvert}=\frac{\Delta q}{C\,\lvert dV/dt\rvert},Δt=∣dV/dt∣ΔV​=C∣dV/dt∣Δq​, converting to phase via Δϕ=ω0Δt\Delta\phi=\omega_0\Delta tΔϕ=ω0​Δt. Comparing with the operational ISF definition Δϕ=Γ Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=ΓΔq/qmax​ gives Γ(θ) ∝ 1∣dV/dt∣∣θ(at the phase where the edge crosses the threshold).\Gamma(\theta)\ \propto\ \frac{1}{\lvert dV/dt\rvert}\bigg|_{\theta}\quad\text{(at the phase where the edge crosses the threshold)}.Γ(θ) ∝ ∣dV/dt∣1​​θ​(at the phase where the edge crosses the threshold). Intuition: a large dV/dtdV/dtdV/dt (steep transition) → the edge instant is shifted very little → local Γ\GammaΓ is small; but the edge only exists during the transition — on the rail (dV/dt≈0dV/dt\approx0dV/dt≈0), a charge kick just gets "reshaped" by the next stage's threshold and barely shifts the edge timing → Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0 on the rail. Conclusion: a ring stage's ISF is concentrated in the narrow phase window of the transition, near zero on the rails. Idealize it as a triangular toy shape — peak at the transition, width roughly equal to the fraction of the period the transition occupies. This agrees with the triangular toy in lc_vs_ring (gamma_triangular(theta, n_stages), see simulations/common/isf_utils.py): Γring(θ)≈triangular pulse, peak∼1N, width∼1N, concentrated at the transition.\Gamma_{ring}(\theta)\approx\text{triangular pulse, peak}\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt N},\ \text{width}\sim\frac{1}{N},\ \text{concentrated at the transition}.Γring​(θ)≈triangular pulse, peak∼N​1​, width∼N1​, concentrated at the transition. Comparison figure (ideal LC's −sin⁡-\sin−sin vs. ring's triangle): Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Title reads: "LC vs ring ISF (toy)：敏感度集中在 transition，N 越大 rms 越小" = LC vs. ring ISF (toy): sensitivity concentrates at the transition; the larger N, the smaller the rms.
documents.s: From transition slope to ISF shape

documents.t: Turning observation (b) around: a ring's device carries its largest current during transition (it must rapidly charge/discharge the node capacitance), so the noise modulating function α(θ)\alpha(\theta)α(θ)'s peak also lands at the transition. And the ISF Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ)'s peak also lands at the transition (just derived above). The two peaks overlap → Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α is barely reduced by windowing ([P1] §IV.D: the ring's Γ\GammaΓ and Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ are "almost identical") → cyclostationary effects cannot rescue the ring. This is one of two main reasons ring phase noise is worse ([P1] states this explicitly): (1) the noise peak overlaps the ISF peak, so cyclostationary effects cannot move noise into an insensitive window; (2) a ring dissipates all its stored energy every cycle (no high-QQQ tank to store energy). Compare with Colpitts: its pulse aligns with a small-ISF region — the two peaks are offset — which is why Colpitts is clean.
documents.s: Why the transition is both the most sensitive and the noisiest instant

documents.t: Example 3 (a ring stage's Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and 1/f21/f^21/f2 floor, order-of-magnitude by hand): a 5-stage CMOS ring, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, each inverter stage's equivalent white noise Si=4×10−23 A2/HzS_i=4\times10^{-23}\ \text{A}^2/\text{Hz}Si​=4×10−23 A2/Hz. Estimate Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ using the triangular toy, then compute L(Δf=1MHz)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f=1\text{MHz})L(Δf=1MHz) in the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region (single-stage contribution, order of magnitude). Chain link 1 (slope → ISF): triangular toy, N=5N=5N=5. From the [P2] Eq.(16) scaling (see convention §3), Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2; for the N=5N=5N=5 triangular toy, we take Γrms≈0.30\Gamma_{rms}\approx0.30Γrms​≈0.30 numerically (toy-level order of magnitude; gamma_rms(theta, gamma_triangular(theta, 5)) computes to about 0.260.260.26 — this example rounds to 0.300.300.30 for an integer-order estimate). Γrms2qmax2=0.302(10−12)2=0.0910−24=9×1022 C−2\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}=\dfrac{0.30^2}{(10^{-12})^2}=\dfrac{0.09}{10^{-24}}=9\times10^{22}\ \text{C}^{-2}qmax2​Γrms2​​=(10−12)20.302​=10−240.09​=9×1022 C−2. Si4Δω2=4×10−234×3.948×1013=10−233.948×1013=2.533×10−37\dfrac{S_i}{4\Delta\omega^2}=\dfrac{4\times10^{-23}}{4\times3.948\times10^{13}}=\dfrac{10^{-23}}{3.948\times10^{13}}=2.533\times10^{-37}4Δω2Si​​=4×3.948×10134×10−23​=3.948×101310−23​=2.533×10−37. Linear value inside parentheses =9×1022×2.533×10−37=2.28×10−14=9\times10^{22}\times2.533\times10^{-37}=2.28\times10^{-14}=9×1022×2.533×10−37=2.28×10−14. L=10log⁡10(2.28×10−14)=−136.4 dBc/Hz\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}(2.28\times10^{-14})=-136.4\ \text{dBc/Hz}L=10log10​(2.28×10−14)=−136.4 dBc/Hz (single-stage order of magnitude). Chain link 3 (summing over stages): N=5N=5N=5 uncorrelated stages each contribute one share, so total power ×5\times5×5 → +10log⁡105=+7+10\log_{10}5=+7+10log10​5=+7 dB: Ltotal(1 MHz)≈−136.4+7.0=−129.4 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}_{total}(1\,\text{MHz})\approx-136.4+7.0=-129.4\ \text{dBc/Hz}.Ltotal​(1MHz)≈−136.4+7.0=−129.4 dBc/Hz. Result: single stage ≈−136\approx-136≈−136 dBc/Hz; 5-stage total ≈−129\approx-129≈−129 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz (order of magnitude). Intuition: much worse than (a)'s LC VCO (Γrms=0.707\Gamma_{rms}=0.707Γrms​=0.707, single source ∼−148\sim-148∼−148 dBc/Hz) — but note the ring's Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ has already been suppressed by N−3/2N^{-3/2}N−3/2; the real penalty comes from summing over stages plus the lack of tank energy storage (only the +7+7+7 dB multi-stage-summing part is demonstrated here). Dimension check: same as [P1] Eq.(21) — the bracket reduces to s\text{s}s (per-Hz) ✓. import numpy as np import sys, os sys.path.insert(0, "simulations/common") from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_triangular, gamma_rms theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 4000, endpoint=False) g_rms = gamma_rms(theta, gamma_triangular(theta, 5)) # computes to ~0.26 (hand calc rounds to integer order 0.30) qmax, Si = 1e-12, 4e-23 dw = 2*np.pi*1e6 L1 = 10*np.log10((g_rms**2/qmax**2) * (Si/(4*dw**2))) # single stage L5 = L1 + 10*np.log10(5) # 5-stage sum print(round(L1,1), round(L5,1), "dBc/Hz") # computed ~ -137.7 / -130.7 (hand calc with 0.30 -> -136 / -129) Design knobs (CMOS ring stage): Steep transition (high slew rate) → smaller local Γ\GammaΓ, narrower transition window → lowers Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. More stages NNN → Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 decreases (but power, area, and per-stage noise summing all increase — needs trade-off). Symmetric rising/falling edges (NMOS/PMOS matched) → suppresses c0c_0c0​, curbs flicker upconversion (see symmetry). A ring has no tank energy storage, and cyclostationary effects offer no help → for the same qmaxq_{max}qmax​, close-in performance is inherently worse than LC.
