documents.t: (a)–(c) were about "in which phase window the device injects, and how large a Γ\GammaΓ it sees there." The designer actually holds two independent knobs: change the injection window (act on α(θ)\alpha(\theta)α(θ)) and change the waveform itself (act on the shape of Γ(θ)\Gamma(\theta)Γ(θ) and on qmaxq_{max}qmax​). Andreani's class-C / class-D and Staszewski's class-F are the three classic topologies that push each of these knobs to its limit (all external literature, not among the five source PDFs; volume / pages / DOI at the end of the page). This section stays at the topology level — no PDK, no transistor-level extraction; every number is produced by simulations/lab_43_classc_classf_isf.py.
documents.s: (d) Waveform engineering: class-C / class-D / class-F told with the ISF

documents.t: Circuit: the gate bias VbiasV_{bias}Vbias​ of the cross-coupled pair is pushed below threshold (Vbias<VthV_{bias}<V_{th}Vbias​<Vth​), and a large tail capacitor hangs on the common-source node (an AC ground, so the tail current can swing widely within a cycle). Each transistor therefore conducts only during the short interval when "its own gate (= the opposite drain) is highest, i.e. its own drain (tank voltage) is lowest"; the drain current is a train of narrow pulses — exactly as in the Colpitts of §(b): the pulse lands at a tank-voltage extremum, which is precisely a null of Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ (the same [P1] §IV.D sentence quoted in §(b)). First mechanism (injection window aligned with the ISF null): with the [P1] Eq.(27) convention (α=1\alpha=1α=1 while conducting, α=0\alpha=0α=0 while cut off), give each of the two transistors of the differential pair a window of half-width ϕ\phiϕ (conduction angle 2ϕ2\phi2ϕ), centred on θ=0\theta=0θ=0 and θ=π\theta=\piθ=π: Γeff,rms2=12π[∫−ϕϕsin⁡2θ dθ+∫π−ϕπ+ϕsin⁡2θ dθ]=1π∫−ϕϕsin⁡2θ dθ=ϕ−sin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕπ.\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2=\frac{1}{2\pi}\left[\int_{-\phi}^{\phi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta+\int_{\pi-\phi}^{\pi+\phi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta\right] =\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\phi}^{\phi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac{\phi-\sin\phi\cos\phi}{\pi}.Γeff,rms2​=2π1​[∫−ϕϕ​sin2θdθ+∫π−ϕπ+ϕ​sin2θdθ]=π1​∫−ϕϕ​sin2θdθ=πϕ−sinϕcosϕ​. Check 1: 2ϕ=180∘2\phi=180^\circ2ϕ=180∘ (class-B hard switching, each device conducts half a cycle) → Γeff,rms2=π/2π=12\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2=\tfrac{\pi/2}{\pi}=\tfrac12Γeff,rms2​=ππ/2​=21​, exactly the stationary value (§(b) case A) ✓. Check 2: 2ϕ=60∘2\phi=60^\circ2ϕ=60∘ (ϕ=π/6\phi=\pi/6ϕ=π/6) → 0.5236−0.5×0.8660π=0.0906π=0.0288\dfrac{0.5236-0.5\times0.8660}{\pi}=\dfrac{0.0906}{\pi}=0.0288π0.5236−0.5×0.8660​=π0.0906​=0.0288, i.e. 10log⁡10(0.5/0.0288)=12.410\log_{10}(0.5/0.0288)=12.410log10​(0.5/0.0288)=12.4 dB below 12\tfrac1221​ (lab_43 numeric value 0.0288 ✓). Compare the worst alignment (windows centred on the zero crossings θ=π/2,3π/2\theta=\pi/2,3\pi/2θ=π/2,3π/2): Γeff,rms2=(ϕ+sin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕ)/π\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2=(\phi+\sin\phi\cos\phi)/\piΓeff,rms2​=(ϕ+sinϕcosϕ)/π, which at 60∘60^\circ60∘ is 0.30450.30450.3045 — the same narrow window in the wrong phase buys only 2.2 dB. The narrow window itself is not the point; the narrow window aligned with the null is. Dimension check: ϕ\phiϕ is in rad and sin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕ\sin\phi\cos\phisinϕcosϕ is dimensionless, so the two are commensurate and can be subtracted; after dividing by π\piπ the result is dimensionless ✓. Honesty note (geometric window factor ≠ full FFF bookkeeping): the expression above assumes "the noise density while conducting does not change with the conduction angle." In reality, at the same IbiasI_{bias}Ibias​ a narrower pulse means a higher peak current and a higher gmg_mgm​, so the peak of α2∝gm(t)\alpha^2\propto g_m(t)α2∝gm​(t) from step 1 of effective_isf rises as well — the narrow window is no free lunch. Mazzanti–Andreani 2008 close that bookkeeping; their abstract frames the phase-noise relations of all specific LC topologies as special cases of one very general and very simple result, and under that bookkeeping the net advantage of class-C over class-B at the same current comes from amplitude — the second mechanism below. Second mechanism (fundamental tank current ×π/2\times\pi/2×π/2 at the same IbiasI_{bias}Ibias​). Single-ended, per-transistor bookkeeping (take care not to mix single-ended and differential): class-B: each drain current is a 0↔Ibias0\leftrightarrow I_{bias}0↔Ibias​ square wave (mean Ibias/2I_{bias}/2Ibias​/2). Square-wave Fourier series: Ibias[12+2πcos⁡θ−23πcos⁡3θ+…]I_{bias}\big[\tfrac12+\tfrac{2}{\pi}\cos\theta-\tfrac{2}{3\pi}\cos3\theta+\dots\big]Ibias​[21​+π2​cosθ−3π2​cos3θ+…] → fundamental amplitude I1B=2IbiasπI_1^{B}=\dfrac{2I_{bias}}{\pi}I1B​=π2Ibias​​. class-C limit: each drain current is an impulse train of area Q=Ibias2TQ=\tfrac{I_{bias}}{2}TQ=2Ibias​​T (mean still Ibias/2I_{bias}/2Ibias​/2). Impulse-train Fourier series: QT[1+2∑ncos⁡nθ]\tfrac{Q}{T}\big[1+2\sum_n\cos n\theta\big]TQ​[1+2∑n​cosnθ] → fundamental amplitude I1C=2QT=IbiasI_1^{C}=\dfrac{2Q}{T}=I_{bias}I1C​=T2Q​=Ibias​. (Differential bookkeeping gives 4Ibias/π4I_{bias}/\pi4Ibias​/π versus 2Ibias2I_{bias}2Ibias​; the ratio is the same π/2\pi/2π/2.) The tank keeps only the fundamental: A=RpI1A=R_p I_1A=Rp​I1​ → ACAB=Ibias2Ibias/π=π2=1.571\dfrac{A_C}{A_B}=\dfrac{I_{bias}}{2I_{bias}/\pi}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1.571AB​AC​​=2Ibias​/πIbias​​=2π​=1.571; qmax=C Aq_{max}=C\,Aqmax​=CA scales by the same factor. [P1] Eq.(21) has L∝Γrms2Si/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2 S_i/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​Si​/qmax2​; assuming Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and SiS_iSi​ unchanged: ΔL=−20log⁡10 ⁣(π2)=−3.92 dB.\Delta\mathcal{L}=-20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=-3.92\ \text{dB}.ΔL=−20log10​(2π​)=−3.92 dB. This is the "theoretical 3.9 dB phase noise improvement" of the Mazzanti–Andreani abstract (at the same current consumption). Applied to example B (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz, [P1] Eq.(21) SSB "/4" → −148.0-148.0−148.0 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz): class-C at the same bias →−148.0−3.92=−151.9\to-148.0-3.92=-151.9→−148.0−3.92=−151.9 dBc/Hz; with the time-domain "/2" convention (−145.0-145.0−145.0) it is −148.9-148.9−148.9 dBc/Hz — the factor of 2 between the two conventions has nothing to do with this section; the −3.92-3.92−3.92 dB difference is the same on both sides. Dimension check: I1 [A]×Rp [Ω]=[V]I_1\,[\text{A}]\times R_p\,[\Omega]=[\text{V}]I1​[A]×Rp​[Ω]=[V]; C [F]×A [V]=[C]C\,[\text{F}]\times A\,[\text{V}]=[\text{C}]C[F]×A[V]=[C] ✓; ΔL\Delta\mathcal{L}ΔL is the dB of a ratio, dimensionless ✓. Failure conditions: the amplitude is bounded by VDDV_{DD}VDD​ and by "the transistors must stay in saturation" (Vbias+AV_{bias}+AVbias​+A must not push the device into triode, or the class-C behaviour is lost); Vbias<VthV_{bias}<V_{th}Vbias​<Vth​ makes the small-signal gmg_mgm​ tiny, so start-up and bias stability are the engineering price of class-C (the original paper treats this specifically; not transcribed here).

documents.t: The class-D of Fanori–Andreani 2013 removes the tail current source; the cross-coupled pair is used as a switch, driven rail-to-rail: each drain node is clamped to ground by the switch for half a cycle and flung upward by the tank for the other half, with a single-ended swing well above VDDV_{DD}VDD​ (the original derives a peak of about 3VDD3V_{DD}3VDD​, not re-derived on this site, unverified). In ISF language: Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0 during the clamped half cycle: the node is pinned to ground through ronr_{on}ron​, dV/dt≈0dV/dt\approx0dV/dt≈0, and injected charge is simply eaten by the switch instead of entering the tank — the same argument as "Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0 on the rail" in §(c). Phase sensitivity is concentrated in the released half cycle and the switching instants. qmax=C Aq_{max}=C\,Aqmax​=CA is the largest attainable at a given VDDV_{DD}VDD​: the denominator of [P1] Eq.(21) is pushed to its limit, which is the main reason class-D phase noise stays good at 0.4–1 V supplies; in the language of fom_limit, the knob being turned is the ηP\eta_PηP​ term. Price: FFF is set by the switch's channel noise (4kTγgm4kT\gamma g_m4kTγgm​, at the switching instants) and by the loading of the tank through ronr_{on}ron​ — γ\gammaγ is the ceiling; the amplitude is proportional to VDDV_{DD}VDD​ → large supply pushing (see varactor_tuning_supply_pushing); the waveform is far from sinusoidal, so rise/fall asymmetry gives c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0 and 1/f31/f^31/f3 has to be suppressed by symmetric design (symmetry). This section gives no numbers for class-D: its amplitude, frequency and FFF expressions are the core contribution of the original paper and cannot be re-derived by this site's toy.

documents.t: Babaie–Staszewski 2013 use a transformer-based tank with an additional impedance peak at 3ω03\omega_03ω0​, so the third harmonic of the drain current is no longer filtered out by the tank and the tank voltage becomes V=Vp1sin⁡ω0t+Vp3sin⁡(3ω0t+Δϕ)V=V_{p1}\sin\omega_0t+V_{p3}\sin(3\omega_0t+\Delta\phi)V=Vp1​sinω0​t+Vp3​sin(3ω0​t+Δϕ), ζ≡Vp3/Vp1\zeta\equiv V_{p3}/V_{p1}ζ≡Vp3​/Vp1​ (original §II; that PDF is not among the site's five, equation / page numbers unverified). This site writes it as the dimensionless waveform f(θ)=sin⁡θ+ζsin⁡3θf(\theta)=\sin\theta+\zeta\sin3\thetaf(θ)=sinθ+ζsin3θ and derives the ISF from the waveform (method C of isf_from_waveform / the [P1] Eq.(38) shape, slope normalised to its own maximum — also the engine behind Tool 7 IsfSandbox): f′(θ)=cos⁡θ+3ζcos⁡3θ,Γ(θ)=f′(θ)fmax′,fmax′=f′(0)=1+3ζ.f'(\theta)=\cos\theta+3\zeta\cos3\theta,\qquad \Gamma(\theta)=\frac{f'(\theta)}{f'_{max}},\qquad f'_{max}=f'(0)=1+3\zeta .f′(θ)=cosθ+3ζcos3θ,Γ(θ)=fmax′​f′(θ)​,fmax′​=f′(0)=1+3ζ.Γrms2=f′ 2‾fmax′ 2=12(1+9ζ2)(1+3ζ)2⇒dΓrms2dζ=0 at 18ζ(1+3ζ)=6(1+9ζ2) ⇒ ζ=13,Γrms2∣ζ=1/3=12⋅24=14.\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{\overline{f'^{\,2}}}{f'^{\,2}_{max}}=\frac{\tfrac12(1+9\zeta^2)}{(1+3\zeta)^2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{d\Gamma_{rms}^2}{d\zeta}=0\ \text{at}\ 18\zeta(1+3\zeta)=6(1+9\zeta^2)\ \Rightarrow\ \zeta=\frac13,\quad \Gamma_{rms}^2\Big|_{\zeta=1/3}=\frac{\tfrac12\cdot2}{4}=\frac14 .Γrms2​=fmax′2​f′2​​=(1+3ζ)221​(1+9ζ2)​⇒dζdΓrms2​​=0 at 18ζ(1+3ζ)=6(1+9ζ2) ⇒ ζ=31​,Γrms2​​ζ=1/3​=421​⋅2​=41​. This agrees with the closed form in Babaie–Staszewski's §II (Γrms2=121+9ζ2(1+3ζ)2\Gamma_{rms}^2=\tfrac12\tfrac{1+9\zeta^2}{(1+3\zeta)^2}Γrms2​=21​(1+3ζ)21+9ζ2​, minimum 1/41/41/4 at ζ=1/3\zeta=1/3ζ=1/3; derived independently here with the [P1] waveform method — matches the original's Eq.(3), p.3121 term-for-term (external literature, checked against the original's abstract/equation numbers)); lab_43's numeric sweep (ζ∈[0,0.6]\zeta\in[0,0.6]ζ∈[0,0.6]) differs from this closed form by at most ∼10−16\sim10^{-16}∼10−16 (floating-point zero; the lab prints 1.7×10−161.7\times10^{-16}1.7×10−16, and the in-page block below, which integrates with trapezoid, gets the same ∼10−16\sim10^{-16}∼10−16 order), with the minimum at ζ=0.335\zeta=0.335ζ=0.335 (grid resolution 0.005). Conclusion produced by the lab: Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ drops from the sinusoidal 0.50.50.5 to 0.250.250.25, i.e. −3.01-3.01−3.01 dB. Why it works, in ISF terms (two things happen at once): Steeper zero crossings: the switching pair commutates at the zero crossings and injects its noise there; at the same VmaxV_{max}Vmax​ the pseudo-square wave's zero-crossing slope is f′(0)/max⁡∣f∣=2/0.943=2.12f'(0)/\max\lvert f\rvert=2/0.943=2.12f′(0)/max∣f∣=2/0.943=2.12 times the sinusoid's, and in the slope-dominated region the sensitivity is ≈1/slope\approx1/\text{slope}≈1/slope ([P1] Eq.(37), p.193 reduces to 1/f′1/f'1/f′ where f′′=0f''=0f′′=0) → ∣Γ∣\lvert\Gamma\rvert∣Γ∣ at the injection point drops from 111 to 0.4710.4710.471. Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0 on the flat top: the flat top where f′≈0f'\approx0f′≈0 is exactly when the gmg_mgm​ devices enter triode and, together with the loaded tank, inject a lot of noise — but Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0, so the noise gets in and the phase does not move (the argument of the original §II, corresponding to the ISF≈0 flat-top of Fig. 2(b); external literature, checked against the original's abstract/equation numbers). lab_43 then applies a ±30∘\pm30^\circ±30∘ zero-crossing injection window to get Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​: sinusoid 0.30450.30450.3045 → class-F 0.22120.22120.2212, a difference of 1.391.391.39 dB (toy order of magnitude). Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Titles read: "(a) class-C：電流脈衝落在 ISF 零點（tank 電壓極值）" = (a) class-C: the current pulse lands on the ISF's zero (the tank voltage extremum); "(b) class-C：Γeff,rms² 隨導通角（α=1 導通時，幾何窗因子）" = (b) class-C: Γeff,rms² vs. conduction angle (a geometric window factor when α=1 conducts); "(c) class-F：ω0+3ω0 諧振 → 準方波 → ISF 峰變窄、平頂處 ISF≈0（斜率歸一）" = (c) class-F: ω0+3ω0 resonance → a quasi-square wave → the ISF peak narrows, ISF≈0 on the flat top (slope-normalized); "(d) class-F：Γrms² 隨 ζ（ζ=1/3 時 1/2→1/4，−3.0 dB）" = (d) class-F: Γrms² vs. ζ (at ζ=1/3, 1/2→1/4, i.e. −3.0 dB). (Full script: simulations/lab_43_classc_classf_isf.py, run with PYTHONPATH=. python3 simulations/lab_43_classc_classf_isf.py, about 1 s. All topology-level toys: the class-C −sin⁡-\sin−sin is exact and the window follows the [P1] Eq.(27) α≤1\alpha\le1α≤1 convention; the class-F ISF is the slope-normalised "from the waveform" approximation, and panel (d) also plots the [P1] Eq.(37), p.193 second-order closed form as a cross-check — it has a pathological point at ζ=1/9\zeta=1/9ζ=1/9 where f′=f′′=0f'=f''=0f′=f′′=0 and shows spurious bumps at the flat-top inflection points of the fourth-order tank, exactly the failure case isf_from_waveform warns about, so it is kept as a reference and not as a conclusion.) The two normalisation conventions differ (be honest about it): slope normalisation (the Babaie–Staszewski closed form) and [P1]'s VmaxV_{max}Vmax​-normalised qmaxq_{max}qmax​ use different reference points — the former pins Γ(zero crossing)\Gamma(\text{zero crossing})Γ(zero crossing) at 1, the latter lets it fall to 0.4710.4710.471. Both agree on the conclusion "Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ drops by about 3 dB", but adding that 3 dB straight onto L\mathcal{L}L takes care: at the same Vp1V_{p1}Vp1​ the ζ=1/3\zeta=1/3ζ=1/3 waveform peaks at only 0.9430.9430.943, so the qmaxq_{max}qmax​ bookkeeping changes with it. Measured results of the original (external literature, checked against the original's abstract/equation numbers; Babaie–Staszewski, IEEE JSSC, vol. 48, no. 12, Dec. 2013, DOI 10.1109/JSSC.2013.2273823): 65 nm CMOS, 5.9–7.6 GHz, measured phase noise −142.2-142.2−142.2 dBc/Hz @ 3 MHz offset (measured from the 3.7 GHz carrier, after the on-chip ÷2 — not about −136-136−136), FoM 192.2 dB, 1.25 V / 12 mA. Engineering price: the 3ω03\omega_03ω0​ impedance peak has to be placed precisely via the transformer coupling coefficient, and the loop gain at 3ω03\omega_03ω0​ is not small either, so oscillation at the auxiliary peak must be prevented (discussed in the original §II). import numpy as np # --- class-C: geometric window factor (phi - sin phi cos phi)/pi, conduction angle 60 deg --- phi = np.deg2rad(60.0)/2 g2_null = (phi - np.sin(phi)*np.cos(phi))/np.pi g2_worst = (phi + np.sin(phi)*np.cos(phi))/np.pi print(round(g2_null, 4), round(10*np.log10(0.5/g2_null), 1), "dB") # -> 0.0288 12.4 dB (null-aligned) print(round(g2_worst, 4)) # -> 0.3045 (zero-crossing-aligned, worst case) # --- class-C: same I_bias, fundamental x pi/2 -> q_max x pi/2 -> Eq.(21) --- dL = -20*np.log10(np.pi/2) print(round(dL, 2), round(-148.0 + dL, 1), round(-145.0 + dL, 1)) # -> -3.92 -151.9 -148.9 (dB; SSB /4; time-domain /2) # --- class-F: ISF from the waveform (slope normalised), Gamma_rms^2 vs zeta --- th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 20001) def g2(z): f1 = np.cos(th) + 3*z*np.cos(3*th) g = f1/np.max(np.abs(f1)) return np.trapezoid(g**2, th)/(2*np.pi) zs = np.linspace(0, 0.6, 121) vals = np.array([g2(z) for z in zs]) print(round(g2(1/3), 4), round(10*np.log10(0.5/g2(1/3)), 2), "dB") # -> 0.25 3.01 dB (zeta=1/3) print(round(zs[np.argmin(vals)], 3)) # -> 0.335 (numeric minimum location, grid 0.005) eq3 = 0.5*(1+9*zs**2)/(1+3*zs)**2 print(round(np.max(np.abs(vals-eq3))*1e12, 3)) # -> 0.0 (vs the Babaie–Staszewski closed form; the difference is still 0 after ×1e12: floating-point zero) vmax = np.max(np.abs(np.sin(th) + np.sin(3*th)/3)) print(round(vmax, 3), round(vmax/2, 3)) # -> 0.943 0.471 (zero-crossing 1/slope at the same V_max) Design knobs (waveform-engineering summary table): Topology Which knob ISF mechanism Order of magnitude (this section) Price class-B (baseline) — Γ=−sin⁡\Gamma=-\sinΓ=−sin, each device conducts half a cycle Γeff,rms2=12\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2=\tfrac12Γeff,rms2​=21​ — class-C narrow α\alphaα window + fundamental ×π/2\times\pi/2×π/2 pulse lands on the ISF null; documents.t: The key point for real topologies: each device-noise source sees a different effective ISF Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α; close-in behavior is set by Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​'s harmonics c0c_0c0​ (1/f31/f^31/f3) and c2c_2c2​ (2ω02\omega_02ω0​ fold-back). Cross-coupled LC VCO: differential tank ISF =−sin⁡θ=-\sin\theta=−sinθ (pure c1c_1c1​, c0≈0c_0\approx0c0​≈0, clean); the tail's effective ISF is rich in c0c_0c0​ (flicker upconversion) and c2c_2c2​ (tail swings at 2ω02\omega_02ω0​, folded back by switching commutation) → the countermeasure is waveform symmetry + a tail filter tuned to 2f02f_02f0​ ([P1] §IV.D; Andreani tail-noise, external literature). Colpitts: the device current is a narrow pulse; α\alphaα windows Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ down to a narrow phase interval; the pulse aligns with the tank-voltage trough (small-ISF region) → low Γeff,rms\Gamma_{eff,rms}Γeff,rms​ → clean close-in ([P1] Fig. 13/14, Eq.(27)). CMOS ring stage: deriving Γ∝1/∣dV/dt∣\Gamma\propto1/\lvert dV/dt\rvertΓ∝1/∣dV/dt∣ from transition slope shows it concentrates at the transition (triangular toy); the ISF peak overlaps the noise peak → cyclostationary effects offer no help, and there's no energy storage → close-in is inherently worse. The three worked examples each walk the full chain (device noise → ISF harmonics → close-in PN): tail 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ≈255\approx255≈255 kHz, Colpitts narrow-window suppression of Γeff,rms2\Gamma_{eff,rms}^2Γeff,rms2​ by about 7 dB, 5-stage ring ≈−129\approx-129≈−129 dBc/Hz @1MHz (all hand-calculated order of magnitude). Waveform engineering (§(d)): class-C aligns the current pulses with the nulls of −sin⁡-\sin−sin (geometric window factor 0.02880.02880.0288 at a 60∘60^\circ60∘ conduction angle, versus only 0.30450.30450.3045 when aligned with the zero crossings) and raises the fundamental by ×π/2\times\pi/2×π/2 at the same IbiasI_{bias}Ibias​ → −3.92-3.92−3.92 dB (example B −148.0→−151.9-148.0\to-151.9−148.0→−151.9 dBc/Hz); class-D pushes qmaxq_{max}qmax​ to rail-to-rail with FFF bounded by γ\gammaγ; class-F builds a pseudo-square wave with a 3ω03\omega_03ω0​ resonance, and lab_43 derives from the waveform that Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ falls from 0.50.50.5 to 0.250.250.25 at ζ=1/3\zeta=1/3ζ=1/3 (−3.01-3.01−3.01 dB, consistent with the Babaie–Staszewski closed form). Sources: [P1] Eq.(21),(23),(24) p.185, Eq.(27) p.186, Fig. 5/13/14; figures cross_coupled_vco_isf.png (lab_21, illustrative), lc_vs_ring_isf_comparison.png (lab_03), classc_classf_isf.png (lab_43, topology-level toy).

documents.t: Prerequisites: clock_chain_budget (rule 3: in-band =N2Sref∣Hlp∣2= N^2 S_{ref}\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2=N2Sref​∣Hlp​∣2), tank_Q_and_energy_restoration (the three forms of QQQ, 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​, the Q↔Γrms/qmaxQ\leftrightarrow\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Q↔Γrms​/qmax​ bridge — every derivation on this page stands on it), derivation_leeson (the (ω02QΔω)2\big(\tfrac{\omega_0}{2Q\Delta\omega}\big)^2(2QΔωω0​​)2 shaping term) | Next: pll_noise_budget, fom_limit Every real clock chain — SoC, SerDes, sampling system, RF transceiver — sits on top of a reference oscillator: a crystal oscillator (XO) or a MEMS oscillator. System designers often spend more on it than on the entire PLL. The question is: why? What does it actually buy, and what doesn't it buy? This page answers using two bridges already built on this site: clock_chain_budget rule 3 explains why nothing downstream in the chain can clean up the reference's close-in noise; the tank_Q_and_energy_restoration Q↔Γrms/qmaxQ\leftrightarrow\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Q↔Γrms​/qmax​ bridge explains why a crystal's close-in noise is inherently orders of magnitude lower. Physical intuition (conclusion first): a crystal is not new physics — it is just an LC tank with an absurdly high QQQ. The quartz's mechanical resonance maps to an equivalent LLL, CCC, RRR, with QQQ typically 10410^4104 to 10610^6106 (industry-convention magnitude, external), versus an on-chip spiral-inductor tank at only Q≈5Q\approx5Q≈5–202020. The same Leeson/ISF formula, the same (f02QΔf)2\big(\tfrac{f_0}{2Q\Delta f}\big)^2(2QΔff0​​)2 shaping term, applied with QQQ going from 10 to 5×1045\times10^45×104: close-in phase noise drops ∝1/Q2\propto 1/Q^2∝1/Q2 — tens of dB, not from clever circuitry but from enormous energy stored in the resonator against a vanishingly small per-cycle loss. The clock chain's division of labor follows naturally: low offset is the reference's job, high offset is the VCO's job, and the PLL is just the tailor stitching the two segments together. Honesty note (read this first): none of the 5 downloaded PDFs on this site ([P1]–[P5]) cover crystal / MEMS content. Every place on this page that connects to ISF does so through the already-verified [P1] Eq.(21), p.185, and the site's own tank_Q_and_energy_restoration bridge; the Leeson shaping term belongs to [E1] Leeson 1966 (external literature, not among the five source PDFs, see references); the crystal equivalent circuit (BVD model) and the typical numbers for XO/TCXO/OCXO/MEMS belong to standard frequency-control industry knowledge (industry convention, external, not among the five source PDFs) — this page gives only order-of-magnitude ranges, does not fabricate specific paper citations, and selection should follow vendor datasheets.
documents.s: Reference oscillators (crystal / MEMS): the low-offset anchor of the clock chain

documents.t: clock_chain_budget rule 3 (PLL) states: Sout(f)=N2 Sref(f) ∣Hlp(f)∣2+Svco(f) ∣Hhp(f)∣2S_{out}(f)=N^2\,S_{ref}(f)\,\lvert H_{lp}(f)\rvert^2+S_{vco}(f)\,\lvert H_{hp}(f)\rvert^2Sout​(f)=N2Sref​(f)∣Hlp​(f)∣2+Svco​(f)∣Hhp​(f)∣2 In-band (f≪fnf\ll f_nf≪fn​, inside the loop bandwidth) ∣Hlp∣2→1\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\to1∣Hlp​∣2→1: the output's close-in phase noise is exactly the reference's phase noise plus 20log⁡10N20\log_{10}N20log10​N — not a single dB escapes this. Now look at what else in the chain can do (same page, rules 1, 2, 4): ×N, ÷N only scale (the entire curve shifts; clean in, clean out); a buffer can only add its own floor (power addition, only ever makes things worse). Conclusion: Nothing in the chain can improve the reference's close-in noise. The quality of the low offset (inside loop BW) is locked in the moment you "buy that reference." That page's worked chain is living proof: of the final 27.6 fs integrated jitter, 65.9% of the power comes from the reference's in-band floor after being lifted by ×N2\times N^2×N2, while the pretty −148-148−148 dBc/Hz VCO contributes only 0.42%. Conversely, far-out (outside loop BW) the reference is completely irrelevant — there, ∣Hhp∣2→1\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\to1∣Hhp​∣2→1, and it's the VCO's show. The reference is a low-offset anchor, not a full-spectrum savior (the worked block in Step 4 puts numbers to this). Example 1 (anchoring a reference into a ×50 PLL — canonical numbers): a 100 MHz low-noise XO has L=−150\mathcal{L}=-150L=−150 dBc/Hz at 1 kHz offset (low-noise-XO-grade, industry-convention magnitude, external). Locked into a ×50 PLL to 5 GHz, what is the in-band L(1 kHz)\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{kHz})L(1kHz)? How much better is it than a free-running on-chip LC? Substituting step by step (with units) — in-band, using rule 3's asymptotic form: Lout(1 kHz)=−150+20log⁡1050=−150+33.98=−116.02 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}_{out}(1\,\text{kHz})=-150+20\log_{10}50=-150+33.98=-116.02\ \text{dBc/Hz}.Lout​(1kHz)=−150+20log10​50=−150+33.98=−116.02 dBc/Hz. Control case: the site's canonical example B 5 GHz on-chip LC (L(1 MHz)=−148\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})=-148L(1MHz)=−148, 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt) extrapolated free-running to 1 kHz: −148+20log⁡10(106/103)=−148+60=−88-148+20\log_{10}(10^6/10^3)=-148+60=-88−148+20log10​(106/103)=−148+60=−88 dBc/Hz. Locking to the reference wins by 28.0 dB at 1 kHz — that's what "buying a reference" buys you. The two lines cross at 25.225.225.2 kHz (solving −148−20log⁡10(f/106)=−116.02-148-20\log_{10}(f/10^6)=-116.02−148−20log10​(f/106)=−116.02 for fff), which is exactly the first intuition behind pll_noise_budget's "the crossover point sets the optimal loop BW." Dimension check: dB addition = multiplying dimensionless ratios ✓; NNN in 20log⁡10N20\log_{10}N20log10​N is dimensionless ✓. One-line Python check: import numpy as np L_in = -150.0 + 20*np.log10(50) # rule 3 in-band: ref + 20logN print(round(L_in, 2)) # -> -116.02 L_lc = -148.0 - 20*np.log10(1e3/1e6) # canonical LC 1/f² skirt extrapolated to 1 kHz print(round(L_lc, 1)) # -> -88.0 print(round(L_lc - L_in, 1)) # -> 28.0 f_cross = 1e6 * 10**(-(L_in + 148.0)/20) print(round(f_cross/1e3, 1)) # -> 25.2

documents.t: A quartz crystal is a mechanical resonator: the piezoelectric effect (mechanical strain↔electric field interconversion) maps the quartz plate's mechanical vibration mode into an equivalent circuit at the electrical port — the standard BVD model (Butterworth–Van Dyke equivalent circuit, external textbook content, not among the five source PDFs): motional branch: series LmL_mLm​–CmC_mCm​–RmR_mRm​, representing the mechanical mass-stiffness-damping. Magnitude (industry convention): Lm∼L_m\simLm​∼ mH–H, Cm∼C_m\simCm​∼ fF, Rm∼R_m\simRm​∼ tens to hundreds of Ω\OmegaΩ. C0C_0C0​ (static capacitance): the ordinary capacitance of the electrodes and package, pF-scale, in parallel with the motional branch. Near the series resonance ωs=1/LmCm\omega_s=1/\sqrt{L_mC_m}ωs​=1/Lm​Cm​​, this is just an LC tank, with QQQ using the same definition as in tank_Q_and_energy_restoration (series form Q=ωsLm/RmQ=\omega_s L_m/R_mQ=ωs​Lm​/Rm​, or the energy definition Q=ω0Estored/PdissQ=\omega_0 E_{stored}/P_{diss}Q=ω0​Estored​/Pdiss​ — the same QQQ on both pages): Qcrystal∼104 to 106vsQon-chip LC∼5–20.Q_{crystal}\sim10^4\ \text{to}\ 10^6\qquad\text{vs}\qquad Q_{on\text{-}chip\ LC}\sim5\text{–}20.Qcrystal​∼104 to 106vsQon-chip LC​∼5–20. (The crystal QQQ range is industry-convention magnitude, external; the on-chip QQQ ceiling is covered in Step 5 of the tank_Q page.) Lm∼L_m\simLm​∼ mH against on-chip nH — a 6-order-of-magnitude difference in equivalent inductance paired with an even smaller equivalent loss — this is the circuit embodiment of "enormous stored energy against vanishingly small per-cycle loss." The oscillation waveform is close to sinusoidal, so the pedagogical-toy ISF is still Γ≈−sin⁡\Gamma\approx-\sinΓ≈−sin, Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​ (rms_isf) — the crystal's advantage does not come from ISF shape, it comes entirely from QQQ (equivalently: stored energy EEE and qmaxq_{max}qmax​). The next step turns this sentence into a formula.

documents.t: The bridge from Step 4(c) of tank_Q_and_energy_restoration: Leeson's 12Q\dfrac{1}{2Q}2Q1​ and ISF's Γrmsqmax\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}}{q_{max}}qmax​Γrms​​ are the same "noise→phase" conversion efficiency. Now walk this bridge step by step from [P1] Eq.(21) (sinusoidal LC toy, tank thermal noise only; active core handled separately): (1) Starting point — [P1] Eq.(21), p.185 (within the 5 PDFs, already verified): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​) (2) Substituting three quantities already derived on this site: Γrms2=12\Gamma_{rms}^2=\tfrac12Γrms2​=21​ (the rms of Γ=−sin⁡\Gamma=-\sinΓ=−sin, rms_isf), qmax=C Vpq_{max}=C\,V_pqmax​=CVp​ (canonical notation table), in2‾/Δf=4kT/Rp\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=4kT/R_pin2​​/Δf=4kT/Rp​ (tank loss thermal noise, tank_Q page Step 3): Llin=12C2Vp2⋅4kT/Rp4 Δω2=kT2 C2Vp2 Rp Δω2.\mathcal{L}_{lin}=\frac{\tfrac12}{C^2V_p^2}\cdot\frac{4kT/R_p}{4\,\Delta\omega^2} =\frac{kT}{2\,C^2V_p^2\,R_p\,\Delta\omega^2}.Llin​=C2Vp2​21​​⋅4Δω24kT/Rp​​=2C2Vp2​Rp​Δω2kT​. (3) Replacing RpR_pRp​ using QQQ (tank_Q page Step 1: Rp=Q/(ω0C)R_p=Q/(\omega_0 C)Rp​=Q/(ω0​C)): Llin=kT ω0C2 C2Vp2 Q Δω2=kT ω02 CVp2 Q Δω2.\mathcal{L}_{lin}=\frac{kT\,\omega_0 C}{2\,C^2V_p^2\,Q\,\Delta\omega^2} =\frac{kT\,\omega_0}{2\,C V_p^2\,Q\,\Delta\omega^2}.Llin​=2C2Vp2​QΔω2kTω0​C​=2CVp2​QΔω2kTω0​​. (4) Replacing CVp2CV_p^2CVp2​ using stored energy (tank_Q page Step 2: Estored=12CVp2E_{stored}=\tfrac12 CV_p^2Estored​=21​CVp2​, i.e. CVp2=2EstoredCV_p^2=2E_{stored}CVp2​=2Estored​): Llin(Δω)=kT ω04 Estored Q Δω2 \boxed{\ \mathcal{L}_{lin}(\Delta\omega)=\frac{kT\,\omega_0}{4\,E_{stored}\,Q\,\Delta\omega^2}\ } Llin​(Δω)=4Estored​QΔω2kTω0​​ ​ (5) Converting to power form using the energy definition (tank_Q page Step 2: Pdiss=ω0Estored/QP_{diss}=\omega_0E_{stored}/QPdiss​=ω0​Estored​/Q, i.e. Estored=Q Pdiss/ω0E_{stored}=Q\,P_{diss}/\omega_0Estored​=QPdiss​/ω0​): Llin(Δω)=kTPdiss(ω02Q Δω)2.\mathcal{L}_{lin}(\Delta\omega)=\frac{kT}{P_{diss}}\left(\frac{\omega_0}{2Q\,\Delta\omega}\right)^2.Llin​(Δω)=Pdiss​kT​(2QΔωω0​​)2. This is exactly Leeson's ([E1], external) 1/f21/f^21/f2 segment at F=1F=1F=1, thermal-only — the ISF version and the Leeson version meet exactly along this chain (the factor-of-2 SSB accounting convention still applies as usual, see white_noise_to_phase_noise; this page uses [P1] Eq.(21)'s /4 convention throughout). Dimension check (Step-4 form): [J][rad/s][J][rad/s]2=1[1/s]=[s]=1/Hz\dfrac{[\text{J}][\text{rad/s}]}{[\text{J}][\text{rad/s}]^2}=\dfrac{1}{[\text{1/s}]}=[\text{s}]=1/\text{Hz}[J][rad/s]2[J][rad/s]​=[1/s]1​=[s]=1/Hz ✓ (Llin\mathcal{L}_{lin}Llin​ is a per-Hz power ratio). Dimension check (Step-5 form): kT/Pdiss=[J]/[W]=[s]=1/HzkT/P_{diss}=[\text{J}]/[\text{W}]=[\text{s}]=1/\text{Hz}kT/Pdiss​=[J]/[W]=[s]=1/Hz, the bracketed square is dimensionless ✓. Three immediate corollaries (all backed by the numbers in Step 4 and Example 2): close-in L∝1/Q2\mathcal{L}\propto 1/Q^2L∝1/Q2 (fixed PdissP_{diss}Pdiss​): Q×10⇒−20Q\times10\Rightarrow-20Q×10⇒−20 dB. A crystal's QQQ is 10310^3103–105×10^5\times105× higher than on-chip LC — this term alone is −60-60−60 to −100-100−100 dB. The real lever is the Estored⋅QE_{stored}\cdot QEstored​⋅Q product (Step-4 form) — "how much energy is stored" × "how slowly it leaks." The same 4kT4kT4kT fluctuation, against a larger energy reservoir with slower leakage, converts to smaller phase. This is the energy reading of the Q↔Γrms/qmaxQ\leftrightarrow\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Q↔Γrms​/qmax​ bridge: a crystal's effective Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ (together with the noise it sees) is orders of magnitude lower than any on-chip LC — not because the ISF shape differs, but because the denominator qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (stored charge/energy) is enormous while the noise source (loss) is relatively tiny. The Lorentzian linewidth also ∝1/Q2\propto1/Q^2∝1/Q2: the close-in 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt corresponds to the phase diffusion constant DDD (single-sideband Sϕ=4D/Δω2S_\phi=4D/\Delta\omega^2Sϕ​=4D/Δω2, diffusion_dictionary), read off from Step 5 as Sϕ=2LlinS_\phi=2\mathcal{L}_{lin}Sϕ​=2Llin​: D=Δω2Sϕ4=kT ω028 Pdiss Q2,Δf3dB=Dπ=kT ω028π Pdiss Q2 ∝ 1Q2.D=\frac{\Delta\omega^2 S_\phi}{4}=\frac{kT\,\omega_0^2}{8\,P_{diss}\,Q^2},\qquad \Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=\frac{D}{\pi}=\frac{kT\,\omega_0^2}{8\pi\,P_{diss}\,Q^2}\ \propto\ \frac{1}{Q^2}.D=4Δω2Sϕ​​=8Pdiss​Q2kTω02​​,Δf3dB​=πD​=8πPdiss​Q2kTω02​​ ∝ Q21​. Plugging in numbers (how much energy does a crystal actually store) — crystal: f0=100f_0=100f0​=100 MHz, Q=5×104Q=5\times10^4Q=5×104, drive (dissipated) power Pdiss=100 μP_{diss}=100\ \muPdiss​=100 μW (typical crystal drive-level magnitude, industry convention, external); on-chip LC: the tank_Q page's canonical example (C=1.013C=1.013C=1.013 pF, Vp=1V_p=1Vp​=1 V, Q=10Q=10Q=10, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz): import numpy as np k, T = 1.380649e-23, 300.0 kT = k*T f0x, Qx, Px = 100e6, 5e4, 100e-6 # crystal: 100 MHz, Q=50k, drive 100 µW w0x = 2*np.pi*f0x Ex = Qx*Px/w0x # E = Q·P/ω0 (tank_Q Step 2 energy definition solved backward) print(round(Ex*1e9, 2)) # -> 7.96 C, Vp, Ql = 1.013e-12, 1.0, 10.0 # on-chip LC (tank_Q canonical example) El = 0.5*C*Vp**2 w0l = 2*np.pi*5e9 Pl = w0l*El/Ql # power the LC must dissipate print(round(El*1e12, 3)) # -> 0.507 print(round(Pl*1e3, 2)) # -> 1.59 print(round(10*np.log10((Ex*Qx)/(El*Ql)), 1)) # -> 79.0 print(round(10*np.log10((w0l/(El*Ql))/(w0x/(Ex*Qx))), 1)) # -> 95.9 print(round(10*np.log10(kT/Px), 1)) # -> -163.8 Reading: the crystal stores 7.96 nJ, about 1.6×104×1.6\times10^4\times1.6×104× the LC's 0.507 pJ — while dissipating 16× less power (0.1 mW vs 1.59 mW). The E⋅QE\cdot QE⋅Q product differs by 79.0 dB; factoring in one power of ω0\omega_0ω0​ as well, the same-offset thermal-only L\mathcal{L}L differs by 95.9 dB (amplitude ratio 3.9×109≈6×104\sqrt{3.9\times10^9}\approx6\times10^43.9×109​≈6×104 — this is what "effective Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ lower by nearly 5 orders of magnitude" means). The last line also gives the crystal's ideal floor at its own Leeson corner, kT/Pdiss=−163.8kT/P_{diss}=-163.8kT/Pdiss​=−163.8 dBc/Hz — the same order of magnitude as real low-noise XO floors of −150-150−150 to −160-160−160 (industry convention); the remaining gap belongs to the sustaining amplifier's noise factor and flicker (see the failure conditions). Example 2 (linewidth ∝1/Q2\propto1/Q^2∝1/Q2 — same two oscillators): plugging the two parameter sets above into Δf3dB=kTω02/(8πPdissQ2)\Delta f_{3\mathrm{dB}}=kT\omega_0^2/(8\pi P_{diss}Q^2)Δf3dB​=kTω02​/(8πPdiss​Q2), what is each oscillator's thermal-only Lorentzian linewidth? Substituting step by step (with units): crystal: 4.14×10−21×(6.28×108)28π×10−4×(5×104)2=2.6×10−10 Hz,LC: 1.02 Hz.\text{crystal}:\ \frac{4.14\times10^{-21}\times(6.28\times10^8)^2}{8\pi\times10^{-4}\times(5\times10^4)^2} =2.6\times10^{-10}\ \text{Hz},\qquad \text{LC}:\ 1.02\ \text{Hz}.crystal: 8π×10−4×(5×104)24.14×10−21×(6.28×108)2​=2.6×10−10 Hz,LC: 1.02 Hz. A ratio of 3.9×1093.9\times10^93.9×109 (95.9 dB) — exactly the same number as the same-offset L\mathcal{L}L ratio above (both ∝ω02/(PQ2)\propto\omega_0^2/(PQ^2)∝ω02​/(PQ2); a self-consistency check ✓). The crystal's thermal-only linewidth at the 10−1010^{-10}10−10 Hz level is unmeasurable within any achievable measurement time — this is the quantitative version of "the reference's carrier is essentially a delta function." Both numbers are thermal-only ideal values (no flicker, no sustaining amp) and are marked illustrative. Dimension check: [J][rad/s]2[W]=[J/s]⋅[J][W]⋅1[s]=[1/s]=[Hz]\dfrac{[\text{J}][\text{rad/s}]^2}{[\text{W}]}=[\text{J/s}]\cdot\dfrac{[\text{J}]}{[\text{W}]}\cdot\dfrac{1}{[\text{s}]}=[\text{1/s}]=[\text{Hz}][W][J][rad/s]2​=[J/s]⋅[W][J]​⋅[s]1​=[1/s]=[Hz] ✓. One-line Python check: import numpy as np kT = 1.380649e-23*300.0 lw = lambda f0, Q, Ps: kT*(2*np.pi*f0)**2/(8*np.pi*Ps*Q**2) print(f"{lw(100e6, 5e4, 100e-6):.2e}") # -> 2.60e-10 print(round(lw(5e9, 10.0, 1.591e-3), 2)) # -> 1.02 print(round(10*np.log10(lw(5e9, 10.0, 1.591e-3)/lw(100e6, 5e4, 100e-6)), 1)) # -> 95.9 (The LC's D=π×1.02≈3.2D=\pi\times1.02\approx3.2D=π×1.02≈3.2 rad²/s belongs to this page's illustrative parameter set, distinct input from diffusion_dictionary's toy parameter set D=0.125→39.8D=0.125\to39.8D=0.125→39.8 mHz; the formula is the same.)

documents.t: Now for this page's signature, fully checkable comparison: at the same offset Δf\Delta fΔf, how much does the Leeson shaping term 10log⁡10[1+(f02QΔf)2]10\log_{10}\big[1+\big(\tfrac{f_0}{2Q\Delta f}\big)^2\big]10log10​[1+(2QΔff0​​)2] differ? ([E1] form; comparing only the shaping term means assuming the same FFF and same PsP_sPs​ for both — a deliberately isolated variable, honestly noted below.) First compute the Leeson corner f0/2Qf_0/2Qf0​/2Q for both (where the shaping term rolls off from 1/f21/f^21/f2 to flat): crystal: 1082×5×104=1000 Hz,LC: 5×1092×10=2.5×108 Hz=250 MHz.\text{crystal}:\ \frac{10^8}{2\times5\times10^4}=1000\ \text{Hz},\qquad \text{LC}:\ \frac{5\times10^9}{2\times10}=2.5\times10^8\ \text{Hz}=250\ \text{MHz}.crystal: 2×5×104108​=1000 Hz,LC: 2×105×109​=2.5×108 Hz=250 MHz. The crystal's shaping term is gone (flattened) beyond 1 kHz; the LC's shaping term keeps falling as 1/f21/f^21/f2 all the way to 250 MHz — the LC is being penalized by (f02QΔf)2\big(\tfrac{f_0}{2Q\Delta f}\big)^2(2QΔff0​​)2 across the entire practical offset range. Computing offset by offset: offset Δf\Delta fΔf crystal term [dB] LC term [dB] difference (same offset, own carriers) normalized to same carrier (−33.98-33.98−33.98) 1 kHz 3.013.013.01 107.96107.96107.96 104.95104.95104.95 dB 70.9770.9770.97 dB 100 kHz 0.000.000.00 67.9667.9667.96 67.9667.9667.96 dB 33.9833.9833.98 dB 1 MHz 0.000.000.00 47.9647.9647.96 47.9647.9647.96 dB 13.9813.9813.98 dB 4th column: the raw difference at the same offset, same FFF, same PsP_sPs​. At 1 kHz, 104.95104.95104.95 dB (asymptotic ratio (2.5×108103)2=6.25×1010=108.0\big(\tfrac{2.5\times10^8}{10^3}\big)^2=6.25\times10^{10}=108.0(1032.5×108​)2=6.25×1010=108.0 dB; the crystal is 333 dB short of that at its own corner, from the 1+11+11+1 term). 5th column (the honest comparison): the 100 MHz and 5 GHz carriers differ, so a fair comparison must normalize the crystal ×50 up to 5 GHz, paying +20log⁡1050=33.98+20\log_{10}50=33.98+20log10​50=33.98 dB (clock_chain_budget rule 1). After normalizing, the 1 kHz advantage is still 71.0 dB; but note the advantage shrinks with offset (34 dB left at 100 kHz, 14 dB at 1 MHz), and beyond the boundary where both 1/f21/f^21/f2 curves meet the floor, the crystal's floor, lifted by ×50, can actually lose to the LC's far skirt — exactly what Step 1 called "the reference is a low-offset anchor, not a full-spectrum savior," and also why the PLL loop BW exists. Dimension check: f02QΔf=[Hz][Hz]\dfrac{f_0}{2Q\Delta f}=\dfrac{[\text{Hz}]}{[\text{Hz}]}2QΔff0​​=[Hz][Hz]​ dimensionless ✓; dB difference = ratio ✓. import numpy as np f0x, Qx = 100e6, 5e4 # crystal: 100 MHz, Q = 50,000 f0l, Ql = 5e9, 10.0 # on-chip LC: 5 GHz, Q = 10 term = lambda f0, Q, df: 10*np.log10(1 + (f0/(2*Q*df))**2) print(round(f0x/(2*Qx), 0)) # -> 1000.0 print(round(f0l/(2*Ql)/1e6, 0)) # -> 250.0 print(round(term(f0x, Qx, 1e3), 2)) # -> 3.01 print(round(term(f0l, Ql, 1e3), 2)) # -> 107.96 print(round(term(f0l, Ql, 1e3) - term(f0x, Qx, 1e3), 2)) # -> 104.95 print(round(term(f0l, Ql, 1e5) - term(f0x, Qx, 1e5), 2)) # -> 67.96 print(round(term(f0l, Ql, 1e6) - term(f0x, Qx, 1e6), 2)) # -> 47.96 print(round(20*np.log10(f0l/f0x), 2)) # -> 33.98 Honesty note: (1) Comparing only the shaping term assumes the same FFF and same PsP_sPs​; the real crystal drive power (∼0.1\sim0.1∼0.1 mW) is lower than typical LC tank dissipation (∼1.6\sim1.6∼1.6 mW), and folding power in as well would turn the 108 dB into Step 3's 95.9 dB (108.0−10log⁡10(1.59 mW/0.1 mW)=95.9108.0-10\log_{10}(1.59\,\text{mW}/0.1\,\text{mW})=95.9108.0−10log10​(1.59mW/0.1mW)=95.9, the two calculation methods are self-consistent ✓). (2) Thermal-only: a real crystal's measured close-in noise is often dominated by the sustaining amp's 1/f31/f^31/f3, and the floor is limited by the buffer — this table is "the lower bound set by resonator physics." (3) Q=5×104Q=5\times10^4Q=5×104 @ 100 MHz is a conservative value (100 MHz commonly uses overtone cuts, where QQQ can be even higher; industry-convention magnitude, external). The interactive component below is the general-purpose version of this worked block — drag QQQ, f0f_0f0​, offset, and watch the two Leeson curves and the normalized-×N gap: 參考源（crystal）vs on-chip LC：Leeson 整形項互動比較 crystal f₀100 MHz crystal Q = 10^x4.70 (Q≈50,119) LC f₀5.0 GHz LC Q10 noise factor F（兩者同）10 dB P_s（兩者同）1.0 mW 讀值 offset = 10^x3.0 (1.0 kHz) 把 crystal 折算到 LC 載波（×N，+34.0 dB，N=50.0） 1101001k10k100k1M10M100M-180-160-140-120-100-80-60-40-20f₀/2Q (xtal)offset Δf (Hz)L(Δf) [dBc/Hz]crystal（折算 ×N）on-chip LC crystal @ 1.0 kHz（折算後） -123.8 dBc/Hz LC @ 1.0 kHz -52.9 dBc/Hz crystal 優勢（LC − crystal） 71.0 dB 模型：Leeson（外部文獻 [E1]，thermal-only）L = 10·log₁₀[2F·kT/P_s·(1+(f₀/2QΔf)²)]， T = 300 K，兩顆振盪器共用同一組 F、P_s 以隔離 (f₀/2QΔf)² 項；未含 1/f³ flicker 與 sustaining amp 的實際雜訊，故為理想下限（illustrative）。crystal 折算 ×N 即 +20·log₁₀N（時脈鏈規則 1）。預設值對應本頁 worked block：Q=50,000@100 MHz vs Q=10@5 GHz，1 kHz 處折算後差 ≈ 71 dB。

documents.t: This entire table is an industry-convention order-of-magnitude range (external literature, not among the five source PDFs): it varies significantly by vendor, cut, frequency, and vintage; within the same grade, high vs low bins can differ by 20 dB. This table only builds intuition for "which magnitude lives at which tier" — selection must always follow the vendor's L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) curve and stability table in the datasheet; this site does not fabricate specific part numbers or paper citations. Grade Typical output frequency Frequency vs temperature (slow axis) L(1 kHz)\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{kHz})L(1kHz) magnitude far-out floor magnitude One-line positioning XO (plain crystal osc.) 10–100 MHz ±10…±100\pm10\ldots\pm100±10…±100 ppm −135…−155-135\ldots-155−135…−155 dBc/Hz −150…−165-150\ldots-165−150…−165 dBc/Hz Cheapest high QQQ; low-noise 100 MHz grade can reach −150-150−150 dBc/Hz @ 1 kHz TCXO (temperature-compensated XO) 10–50 MHz ±0.1…±2\pm0.1\ldots\pm2±0.1…±2 ppm similar to same-grade XO −150…−160-150\ldots-160−150…−160 dBc/Hz The compensation network fixes the slow axis (ppm), barely touching L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f); some designs are actually slightly worse close-in OCXO (oven-controlled XO) 5–100 MHz ±10−4…±10−2\pm10^{-4}\ldots\pm10^{-2}±10−4…±10−2 ppm −150…−165-150\ldots-165−150…−165 dBc/Hz −155…−170-155\ldots-170−155…−170 dBc/Hz King of close-in (specified even at 1–10 Hz offset); the price is watt-level heater power and size MEMS oscillator 1–700 MHz (PLL-synthesized) ±0.05…±20\pm0.05\ldots\pm20±0.05…±20 ppm depending on grade −120…−145-120\ldots-145−120…−145 dBc/Hz −140…−155-140\ldots-155−140…−155 dBc/Hz Silicon resonator + fractional-N PLL; wins on shock resistance/reliability/programmability, phase noise usually concedes to quartz Three points for reading the table: The XO→TCXO→OCXO ladder is mainly a "slow-axis" (ppm) ladder; the L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) difference is concentrated close-in (OCXO uses a higher-QQQ cut, a more careful sustaining amp, and the oven to suppress the 1 Hz–1 kHz region). The floor region (≥10\ge10≥10 kHz) is crowded into −150-150−150 to −170-170−170 dBc/Hz across all grades — the floor is set by the sustaining amp/output buffer (kT/PkT/PkT/P level, see Step 3's −163.8-163.8−163.8), not by QQQ; QQQ buys the 1/Q21/Q^21/Q2 inside the corner. Read MEMS's L\mathcal{L}L column carefully: its output frequency is PLL-synthesized, and the in-band shape is set by the PLL (N2N^2N2 floor + charge pump), not directly by the resonator's Leeson skirt — expanded in the next step.
documents.s: Step 5: typical-magnitude table — XO / TCXO / OCXO / MEMS

documents.t: MEMS (microelectromechanical systems) oscillators replace quartz with a silicon mechanical resonator (vacuum-packaged, Q∼104Q\sim10^4Q∼104–10510^5105 magnitude), then synthesize the MHz-level resonance frequency up to whatever output frequency the user wants via a fractional-N PLL. Two physical facts determine its phase-noise positioning (both industry-convention/materials-physics magnitude, external): (a) The f⋅Qf\cdot Qf⋅Q product ceiling. For a given material and loss mechanism (phonon scattering / Akhiezer damping, thermoelastic damping, anchor loss, etc.), the product of resonance frequency and QQQ has a magnitude ceiling — both quartz and silicon sit around f⋅Q∼1013f\cdot Q\sim10^{13}f⋅Q∼1013 Hz at room temperature (industry convention; the exact value depends on cut/mode/temperature, and this site does not give false precision). This ceiling ties QQQ and f0f_0f0​ into a see-saw: pushing f0f_0f0​ up forces Q∝1/f0Q\propto1/f_0Q∝1/f0​ down. (b) Optimal partitioning under the "multiplication tax." If f⋅Qf\cdot Qf⋅Q is fixed, the Leeson corner becomes f02Q=f022 (f⋅Q) ∝ f02,\frac{f_0}{2Q}=\frac{f_0^2}{2\,(f\cdot Q)}\ \propto\ f_0^2,2Qf0​​=2(f⋅Q)f02​​ ∝ f02​, and the resonator's own close-in shaping term (f02QΔf)2∝f04\big(\tfrac{f_0}{2Q\Delta f}\big)^2\propto f_0^4(2QΔff0​​)2∝f04​; normalizing it ×N to a fixed output carrier foutf_{out}fout​ costs 20log⁡10(fout/f0)20\log_{10}(f_{out}/f_0)20log10​(fout​/f0​), giving a net close-in Lout, close-in ∝ f04⋅(foutf0)2=f02 fout2\mathcal{L}_{out,\ close\text{-}in}\ \propto\ f_0^4\cdot\Big(\frac{f_{out}}{f_0}\Big)^2=f_0^2\,f_{out}^2Lout, close-in​ ∝ f04​⋅(f0​fout​​)2=f02​fout2​ — every 10× drop in resonator frequency nets a 20 dB gain in output close-in (same f⋅Qf\cdot Qf⋅Q, same FFF, same PPP). This is why reference sources all live at 10–100 MHz rather than being built directly as GHz resonators; it is also why MEMS (equally held hostage by f⋅Qf\cdot Qf⋅Q) chooses the MHz-resonator + PLL-synthesis architecture. Numerical check: import numpy as np fQ, fout = 1e13, 5e9 # f·Q product fixed (magnitude, industry convention), output 5 GHz rel = lambda f0: 20*np.log10(f0/(2*(fQ/f0))) + 20*np.log10(fout/f0) print(round(rel(10e6), 2)) # -> 67.96 print(round(rel(100e6), 2)) # -> 87.96 print(round(rel(100e6) - rel(10e6), 2)) # -> 20.0 (relrelrel = corner value + multiplication-tax relative dB; 10 MHz/Q=106Q=10^6Q=106 nets 20.0 dB better than 100 MHz/Q=105Q=10^5Q=105 ✓ the f02f_0^2f02​ law. Of course f0f_0f0​ cannot be lowered indefinitely: a larger N=fout/f0N=f_{out}/f_0N=fout​/f0​ raises the in-band floor ∝N2\propto N^2∝N2, and divider/PLL floor and flicker take over too — the practical optimum lands at a few tens of MHz, consistent with reference frequencies in the market.) MEMS's accounting consequence: the output's in-band is set by the fractional-N PLL's N2N^2N2 floor plus quantization noise, and the out-of-band is set by the built-in VCO — the resonator's extremely high QQQ mainly buys "frequency stability and a close-in anchor," not the whole curve. That's why in the Step 5 table, MEMS's L(1 kHz)\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{kHz})L(1kHz) is usually higher than a same-grade quartz XO (it's the PLL floor, not the resonator skirt), but this is adequate for many applications (Ethernet, USB, sensing), in exchange for shock/vibration resistance, lifetime, size, and arbitrary-frequency programmability (industry-convention positioning, external).
documents.s: Step 6: MEMS — the f⋅Qf\cdot Qf⋅Q product ceiling and the "multiplication tax"

documents.t: The datasheet's "stability ±25 ppm" and "−150-150−150 dBc/Hz @ 1 kHz" describe two nearly orthogonal things, and conflating them is one of the most common selection mistakes in system design: Fast axis: spectral purity (phase noise) Slow axis: frequency stability (frequency accuracy/stability) What it measures L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf), integrated jitter Δf/f0\Delta f/f_0Δf/f0​ drift vs temperature, time, voltage Units dBc/Hz, fs ppm, ppb Time scale offset ≥1\ge1≥1 Hz (sub-second fluctuation) seconds—years (temperature cycling, aging) Physical origin tank thermal noise (kTω0/4EQΔω2kT\omega_0/4EQ\Delta\omega^2kTω0​/4EQΔω2), amp's FFF and flicker cut's temperature coefficient, stress relaxation, electrode/package contamination migration (aging, industry-convention qualitative) What can fix it higher QQQ/larger PPP/cleaner amp; cannot be fixed downstream in the chain (Step 1) compensation (TCXO), oven (OCXO), calibration/discipline (GPS-disciplined) Damage to the system eye closure, BER, ADC SNR (fast jitter) frequency drifting out of the receive window, PLL/CDR pull-in failure, timestamp drift The oven and compensation network don't move L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f): OCXO's heater suppresses drift on an "hour—day" scale, with no effect at all on the 1 kHz offset skirt (the physics there is Step 3's kT/(E⋅Q)kT/(E\cdot Q)kT/(E⋅Q)); conversely, an ever-cleaner buffer cannot rescue aging. Each axis is fixed with its own means, at its own cost. Aging magnitude (industry convention): XO/TCXO first-year ∼±(0.5…5)\sim\pm(0.5\ldots5)∼±(0.5…5) ppm/year; OCXO can reach ppb/day–ppb/year. It is deterministic slow drift, not random phase noise. The bridge between the two axes is Allan deviation (allan_variance): the short-τ\tauτ region (white/flicker PM/FM) corresponds to the various slope segments of L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f), while the upturn at long τ\tauτ (random-walk FM, drift ∝τ+1\propto\tau^{+1}∝τ+1) is where temperature and aging enter — a single ADEV plot shows the handoff point between both axes at once. That's also why a reference's datasheet often gives an L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) table, an ADEV table, and an aging table together: three tables, three time scales, none dispensable.
documents.s: Step 7: aging/temperature vs phase noise — two distinct spec axes

documents.t: Knob Where it acts Cost/limit Reference grade (XO→TCXO→OCXO) Directly moves the low-offset anchor (Step 1: in-band =Lref+20log⁡10N=\mathcal{L}_{ref}+20\log_{10}N=Lref​+20log10​N, no cure downstream) Cost, power (OCXO oven is watt-level), size; TCXO/OCXO mainly buy the slow axis Reference frequency freff_{ref}fref​ (lower NNN) In-band floor ∝N2\propto N^2∝N2 (clock_chain_budget rule 3) The f⋅Qf\cdot Qf⋅Q see-saw: resonator close-in ∝f02fout2\propto f_0^2 f_{out}^2∝f02​fout2​ (Step 6), optimum at a few tens of MHz Drive level PdissP_{diss}Pdiss​ L∝1/P\mathcal{L}\propto1/PL∝1/P (Step 3, Step 5 form) Overdriving the crystal → nonlinearity, stress, accelerated aging (industry convention); datasheet has a max-drive spec Loop bandwidth fnf_nfn​ Sets "how far to trust the reference, where to hand off to the VCO" (crossover-point method, 25.2 kHz of Example 1) Full trade-off in pll_noise_budget (U-shaped curve) Output buffer/fanout Floor is clamped by it (rule 4, power addition) Even a great OCXO is ruined by one noisy buffer stage (clock_chain_budget rule 4) Quartz vs MEMS Phase noise vs shock/reliability/programmability trade-off (Step 6) MEMS in-band is the PLL floor; quartz is vulnerable to vibration (vibration sensitivity, industry convention)

documents.t: A TX PLL's in-band (inside loop BW) is exactly reference +20log⁡10N+20\log_{10}N+20log10​N — the reference's close-in determines the residual jitter of the TX clock at the edge of the CDR tracking bandwidth; anything fully inside the CDR bandwidth gets tracked out at the receiver (serdes_clocking_connection), so SerDes is relatively tolerant of the reference's L(10 Hz)\mathcal{L}(10\,\text{Hz})L(10Hz) but sensitive to the 10 kHz–few-MHz "handoff band" — right around Example 1's crossover point (25.2 kHz). Systems without CDR tracking (ADC/DAC sampling, radar) get no such exemption: aperture jitter integrates up from low offset, and the reference's close-in goes directly into SNR (adc_aperture_jitter). The slow axis bites too: the reference's ppm offset eats into the CDR's pull-in/tracking range and the SSC (spread-spectrum clocking) budget — this is Step 7's "two axes" made concrete in SerDes.

documents.t: Condition When it holds What happens when it fails Thermal-only, F=1F=1F=1 idealization (Steps 3, 4) 1/Q21/Q^21/Q2, E⋅QE\cdot QE⋅Q scaling holds cleanly Real close-in is often dominated by the sustaining amp's flicker (1/f31/f^31/f3), floor clamped by the buffer — the numbers here are the resonator-physics lower bound BVD equivalent near series resonance crystal ≈ an LC with extreme QQQ; the full tank_Q toolkit applies Far from resonance, at overtone/spurious modes, or where the C0C_0C0​ parallel path dominates, the single-LC model fails Drive level within datasheet range L∝1/P\mathcal{L}\propto1/PL∝1/P applies Overdrive: nonlinearity, activity dip, accelerated aging; underdrive: poor startup margin (industry convention) Small-angle approximation, Δf\Delta fΔf well beyond linewidth L=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12S_\phiL=21​Sϕ​, Leeson 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt Very close to the carrier it turns Lorentzian (crystal linewidth at the 10−1010^{-10}10−10 Hz level, practically never measurable there; lorentzian_linewidth) Measurement noise floor low enough Datasheet curve is trustworthy Measuring a low-noise reference requires cross-correlation, otherwise you measure the instrument (measurement_and_spurs) MEMS: look at system output in-band = PLL floor, resonator buys the close-in anchor and stability Reading MEMS output as a "bare-resonator Leeson skirt" is entirely wrong (Step 6)

documents.t: The reference is the low-offset anchor: in-band Lout=Lref+20log⁡10N\mathcal{L}_{out}=\mathcal{L}_{ref}+20\log_{10}NLout​=Lref​+20log10​N (clock_chain_budget rule 3), and nothing downstream can rescue its close-in; in the worked chain, 65.9% of the jitter power came from the ref ×N2\times N^2×N2 floor. Crystal = LC with extreme QQQ (BVD: Lm∼L_m\simLm​∼ mH, Cm∼C_m\simCm​∼ fF, Q∼104Q\sim10^4Q∼104–10610^6106, industry-convention magnitude); ISF shape unchanged (Γ≈−sin⁡\Gamma\approx-\sinΓ≈−sin, Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​), the entire advantage comes from QQQ (stored energy vs loss). Scaling derived from the site's bridges: [P1] Eq.(21) + 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​ + the QQQ definition ⇒ Llin=kT ω04EstoredQ Δω2=kTPdiss(ω02QΔω)2\mathcal{L}_{lin}=\dfrac{kT\,\omega_0}{4E_{stored}Q\,\Delta\omega^2}=\dfrac{kT}{P_{diss}}\big(\tfrac{\omega_0}{2Q\Delta\omega}\big)^2Llin​=4Estored​QΔω2kTω0​​=Pdiss​kT​(2QΔωω0​​)2; close-in L\mathcal{L}L and the Lorentzian linewidth both ∝1/Q2\propto1/Q^2∝1/Q2; the real lever is the E⋅QE\cdot QE⋅Q product (crystal example: 7.96 nJ vs 0.507 pJ, E⋅QE\cdot QE⋅Q differs by 79.0 dB, same-offset L\mathcal{L}L differs by 95.9 dB). Worked block: Q=5×104Q=5\times10^4Q=5×104@100 MHz vs Q=10Q=10Q=10@5 GHz — corner at 1 kHz vs 250 MHz; same-offset Leeson term differs by 104.95 dB (1 kHz), 67.96 dB (100 kHz); after normalizing to the same carrier (−33.98-33.98−33.98), still wins by 71.0/34.0 dB, but the advantage shrinks with offset — far-out has to be handed back to the VCO. Typical magnitudes (industry convention, external): XO floor −150-150−150 to −165-165−165, OCXO is king of close-in, the TCXO/OCXO ladder is mainly on the slow axis (ppm); floor is set by amp/buffer (kT/PkT/PkT/P level), not QQQ. MEMS: the f⋅Q∼1013f\cdot Q\sim10^{13}f⋅Q∼1013 Hz magnitude see-saw ⇒ output close-in ∝f02fout2\propto f_0^2f_{out}^2∝f02​fout2​ (a 10× drop in resonator frequency nets 20 dB) ⇒ the MHz-resonator + fractional-N PLL architecture; in-band is the PLL floor, buying stability, shock resistance, and programmability. Two spec axes: dBc/Hz (fast axis, set by QQQ/PPP/amp, cannot be fixed downstream) and ppm (slow axis, fixable by compensation/oven/discipline); the bridge is ADEV (allan_variance). Source discipline: [P1] Eq.(21) (within the 5 PDFs, already verified) + the site's tank_Q bridge; Leeson shaping = [E1] (external); crystal/MEMS equivalent circuit and typical numbers = industry-convention order-of-magnitude (external, not among the five source PDFs, no fabricated citations).

IEEE, vol. 54, no. 2, pp. 329–330, Feb. 1966 (volume/issue/DOI verified in references). Crystal BVD equivalent circuit, QQQ/drive level/aging/f⋅Qf\cdot Qf⋅Q product, typical numbers for XO/TCXO/OCXO/MEMS: standard frequency-control industry knowledge and textbook content — this page consistently labels these as industry convention, order-of-magnitude, and does not cite specific papers or part numbers to avoid fabrication; for engineering use, follow vendor datasheets and the IEEE International Frequency Control Symposium literature (field name, not a citation of a specific paper). The 5 PDFs on this site provide the key that connects all of this back to ISF: [P1] Eq.(21), p.185 (Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ and 1/f21/f^21/f2); [P2]–[P4] have no direct relation to this page.

documents.t: Prerequisites: pll_noise_budget (the five-source budget, where the in-band floor SrefN2+ScpS_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}Sref​N2+Scp​ comes from), clock_chain_budget (the +20log⁡10N+20\log_{10}N+20log10​N bookkeeping for ×N, ϕout=Nϕin\phi_{out}=N\phi_{in}ϕout​=Nϕin​), adc_aperture_jitter (aperture math: sampling error = slope × timing error) | Next: serdes_clocking_connection, exercises The conclusion of pll_noise_budget was: for the classic charge-pump PLL, the in-band floor is set jointly by reference×N2\times N^2×N2 and the PFD/charge-pump/divider — a cleaner VCO doesn't help at all. This page asks the next question: is the loop's front end (PFD, charge-pump, divider) a physical limit, or an architectural choice? The answer is the latter — the sub-sampling PLL (an architecture that samples the high-speed VCO sinusoid directly with a low-speed reference) removes the divider from the phase-detection path entirely, boosting the phase-detector gain (KPDK_{PD}KPD​) from "Icp/2πI_{cp}/2\piIcp​/2π divided further by NNN" to "gm⋅Ag_m\cdot Agm​⋅A." As a result, the divider noise term vanishes, and CP noise is no longer amplified by ×N2\times N^2×N2 — the in-band floor drops until only the reference term remains. This is one of the most important architectural breakthroughs in PLL design over the last fifteen years. External-literature note: the sub-sampling PLL architecture and the standard result "divider noise eliminated, PD/CP noise not multiplied by N2N^2N2" are not among the five PDFs downloaded for this site (external literature, not among the five source PDFs). Classic reference: X. Gao, E. A. M. Klumperink, M. Bohsali, and B. Nauta, "A Low Noise Sub-Sampling PLL in Which Divider Noise Is Eliminated and PD/CP Noise Is Not Multiplied by N²," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 44, no. 12, pp. 3253–3263, Dec. 2009. This page's derivation is self-contained, and every numeric value is labeled "illustrative"; the five source PDFs supply the other half of the physics — "sensitivity at the sampling point" ([P1]'s ISF). Intuition first (the punchline up front): in the classic PLL, phase comparison means "divide 5 GHz down to 100 MHz, then compare phase" — dividing shrinks the phase by a factor of NNN (the signal weakens by NNN), while PFD/CP noise enters unscaled, so the SNR takes an inherent N×N\timesN× hit; the divider then tacks on its own noise on top. Sub-sampling flips this: "don't touch the VCO — sample the 5 GHz sinusoid directly with the 100 MHz reference edge." At lock, the sampling instant lands on the sinusoid's zero crossing — where the slope is steepest (Aω0A\omega_0Aω0​, V/s) — so a tiny VCO phase shift produces a large change in the sampled voltage. The phase-detector gain is "volt-scale" (AAA, V/rad), several orders of magnitude larger than the charge-pump's "microamp-scale" gain. The same electronic noise (in A/√Hz or V/√Hz) divided by a much larger KPDK_{PD}KPD​ converts to phase noise that is orders of magnitude smaller. The price: the sampler hangs directly off the VCO (reference spur, kT/C folding), and every zero crossing of the sinusoid looks identical (can't lock in NNN without an auxiliary loop).

documents.t: First write "how front-end noise becomes output phase noise" as a chain whose units can be checked. The classic integer-N PLL's PFD (phase-frequency detector) compares ϕref\phi_{ref}ϕref​ against ϕout/N\phi_{out}/Nϕout​/N (the divider divides the output phase by NNN; see clock_chain_budget rule 2), and the charge-pump converts the phase difference into an average current: iˉcp=Kcp(ϕref−ϕoutN)+in,Kcp=Icp2π [Arad]\bar i_{cp}=K_{cp}\Big(\phi_{ref}-\frac{\phi_{out}}{N}\Big)+i_n, \qquad K_{cp}=\frac{I_{cp}}{2\pi}\ \ \Big[\frac{\text{A}}{\text{rad}}\Big]iˉcp​=Kcp​(ϕref​−Nϕout​​)+in​,Kcp​=2πIcp​​ [radA​] Where Kcp=Icp/2πK_{cp}=I_{cp}/2\piKcp​=Icp​/2π comes from: a phase difference Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ makes the CP conduct for a fraction Δϕ/2π\Delta\phi/2\piΔϕ/2π of each reference period, so the average current =Icp⋅Δϕ/2π=I_{cp}\cdot\Delta\phi/2\pi=Icp​⋅Δϕ/2π. Dimension check: A × dimensionless = A ✓; KcpK_{cp}Kcp​ is A/rad ✓. How the noise gets amplified. At lock, the loop drives the average current to zero, so the noise current ini_nin​ is "converted" into an equivalent phase error and absorbed by the output: 0=Kcp(ϕref−ϕoutN)+in⟹ϕout=Nϕref+NKcp in.0=K_{cp}\Big(\phi_{ref}-\frac{\phi_{out}}{N}\Big)+i_n \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \phi_{out}=N\phi_{ref}+\frac{N}{K_{cp}}\,i_n .0=Kcp​(ϕref​−Nϕout​​)+in​⟹ϕout​=Nϕref​+Kcp​N​in​. Converting to PSD (in-band, ∣Hlp∣2≈1\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx1∣Hlp​∣2≈1): Sϕ,out∣in-band=N2Sref+N2Sdiv+N2Kcp2 Si,cp[rad2/Hz]S_{\phi,out}\Big|_{\text{in-band}}=N^2 S_{ref}+N^2 S_{div}+\frac{N^2}{K_{cp}^2}\,S_{i,cp} \qquad[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]Sϕ,out​​in-band​=N2Sref​+N2Sdiv​+Kcp2​N2​Si,cp​[rad2/Hz] Dimension check: Si,cpS_{i,cp}Si,cp​ [A²/Hz] ÷ Kcp2K_{cp}^2Kcp2​ [A²/rad²] = rad²/Hz ✓; N2N^2N2 dimensionless ✓. Two amplification mechanisms stack: (1) CP noise is first divided by a small KcpK_{cp}Kcp​ (illustrative: Icp=1I_{cp}=1Icp​=1 mA → Kcp=159.2 μK_{cp}=159.2\ \muKcp​=159.2 μA/rad; the equivalent gain referred to output phase is further divided by NNN, leaving only 3.183 μ3.183\ \mu3.183 μA/rad); (2) once converted to output phase it's multiplied by N2N^2N2 (N=50N=50N=50 gives +33.98+33.98+33.98 dB). Divider noise SdivS_{div}Sdiv​ is injected at the PFD input, and likewise takes the ×N2\times N^2×N2 hit. This is exactly the microscopic origin of the Sout=(SrefN2+Scp)∣Hlp∣2+⋯S_{out}=(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2+\cdotsSout​=(Sref​N2+Scp​)∣Hlp​∣2+⋯ term in pll_noise_budget (that page lumps CP+divider together as ScpS_{cp}Scp​, already referred to the output). There are only three ways to suppress in-band noise: lower NNN, lower front-end noise, or — this page's topic — make KPDK_{PD}KPD​ larger.

documents.t: The sub-sampling phase detector (SSPD) is simply a track-and-hold: every rising edge of the reference samples the VCO's sinusoidal voltage onto a capacitor CsC_sCs​. "Sub-sampling" refers to the sampling rate fref≪f0f_{ref}\ll f_0fref​≪f0​ — sampling a 5 GHz sinusoid at 100 MHz is severe undersampling, but we only care about the phase error, and the phase error is exactly what gets aliased down near DC — which is what we want. (The idea of using a sampling phase detector for microwave synthesis is itself old — the step-recovery-diode sampler has long been a staple of microwave instrumentation (external literature, not separately cited); what turned it into an integrated CMOS PLL with a full noise analysis is the Gao et al. 2009 paper cited above.) Deriving KPDK_{PD}KPD​. At lock, ω0Tref=2πN\omega_0 T_{ref}=2\pi Nω0​Tref​=2πN (the VCO completes an integer number of cycles per reference period). Let the kkk-th reference edge land at tk=kTref+δtkt_k=kT_{ref}+\delta t_ktk​=kTref​+δtk​ (δtk\delta t_kδtk​ being the reference's own timing error, in s), with VCO output V(t)=Asin⁡(ω0t+ϕout)V(t)=A\sin(\omega_0 t+\phi_{out})V(t)=Asin(ω0​t+ϕout​). The sampled voltage: Vk=Asin⁡(ω0kTref+ω0 δtk+ϕout)=Asin⁡(2πNk⏟integer cycles, drops out+ ϕout+ω0 δtk)≈A(ϕout+ω0 δtk)V_k=A\sin\big(\omega_0 kT_{ref}+\omega_0\,\delta t_k+\phi_{out}\big) =A\sin\big(\underbrace{2\pi Nk}_{\text{integer cycles, drops out}}+\ \phi_{out}+\omega_0\,\delta t_k\big) \approx A\big(\phi_{out}+\omega_0\,\delta t_k\big)Vk​=Asin(ω0​kTref​+ω0​δtk​+ϕout​)=Asin(integer cycles, drops out2πNk​​+ ϕout​+ω0​δtk​)≈A(ϕout​+ω0​δtk​) The last step uses the small-angle approximation (the lock point sits near the zero of sin⁡\sinsin). This one equation immediately gives us three facts: Phase-detector gain: KPD=∂Vk/∂ϕout=AK_{PD}=\partial V_k/\partial\phi_{out}=AKPD​=∂Vk​/∂ϕout​=A [V/rad] — direct phase detection on the 5 GHz output phase, no division by NNN. It's just the zero-crossing slope converted: slope Aω0A\omega_0Aω0​ [V/s] divided by ω0\omega_0ω0​ [rad/s] gives AAA [V/rad]. Dimension check: (V/s)÷(rad/s)=V/rad ✓. Illustrative numbers: A=0.5A=0.5A=0.5 V, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz → slope Aω0=15.71A\omega_0=15.71Aω0​=15.71 mV/ps, KPD=0.5K_{PD}=0.5KPD​=0.5 V/rad. Back end: the sampled voltage passes through a gmg_mgm​ stage (transconductor, replacing the charge-pump) and becomes a current, with total gain (referred to output phase) KSS=gmAK_{SS}=g_m AKSS​=gm​A. Dimension check: [A/V]×[V/rad]=[A/rad][\text{A/V}]\times[\text{V/rad}]=[\text{A/rad}][A/V]×[V/rad]=[A/rad] ✓. Illustrative: gm=5g_m=5gm​=5 mS → KSS=2.5K_{SS}=2.5KSS​=2.5 mA/rad — 785× larger than the classic 3.183 μ3.183\ \mu3.183 μA/rad. (In practice the gmg_mgm​ stage is chopped by a pulser (duty cycle) to control loop gain and stability; this page illustrates with a continuous gmg_mgm​ — see the original paper for details.) Reference noise still gets ×N\times N×N: the δtk\delta t_kδtk​ term enters as ω0δtk=N⋅ωrefδtk=N⋅ϕref,k\omega_0\delta t_k=N\cdot\omega_{ref}\delta t_k=N\cdot\phi_{ref,k}ω0​δtk​=N⋅ωref​δtk​=N⋅ϕref,k​ — the reference's phase error is multiplied by NNN through the slope itself. Illustrative: a 1 ps reference edge error → 15.7115.7115.71 mV → 31.4231.4231.42 mrad =50×0.628=50\times0.628=50×0.628 mrad. This confirms clock_chain_budget rules 1/3: ϕout=Nϕref\phi_{out}=N\phi_{ref}ϕout​=Nϕref​ is an intrinsic property of "multiplying the frequency by NNN" itself, independent of whether a divider is present — what sub-sampling removes is the divider's "noise," not the reference's ×N2\times N^2×N2.

documents.t: Line up steps 1 and 2. Take the same noise current PSD SiS_{i}Si​ (A²/Hz) and refer it to output phase: Sϕ,outclassic=N2Kcp2 Si=(2πNIcp)2Si,Sϕ,outSS=Si(gmA)2,S_{\phi,out}^{\text{classic}}=\frac{N^2}{K_{cp}^2}\,S_i=\Big(\frac{2\pi N}{I_{cp}}\Big)^2 S_i, \qquad S_{\phi,out}^{\text{SS}}=\frac{S_i}{(g_m A)^2},Sϕ,outclassic​=Kcp2​N2​Si​=(Icp​2πN​)2Si​,Sϕ,outSS​=(gm​A)2Si​​, Dividing the two gives sub-sampling's suppression ratio for front-end current noise: Sϕ,outclassicSϕ,outSS=(2πN gmAIcp)2⟹20log⁡10N⏟removal of the divider multiplier+20log⁡10 ⁣2πgmAIcp⏟KPD gain bonus [dB]\frac{S_{\phi,out}^{\text{classic}}}{S_{\phi,out}^{\text{SS}}} =\Big(\frac{2\pi N\,g_m A}{I_{cp}}\Big)^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \underbrace{20\log_{10}N}_{\text{removal of the divider multiplier}} +\underbrace{20\log_{10}\!\frac{2\pi g_m A}{I_{cp}}}_{K_{PD}\text{ gain bonus}}\ \ [\text{dB}]Sϕ,outSS​Sϕ,outclassic​​=(Icp​2πNgm​A​)2⟹removal of the divider multiplier20log10​N​​+KPD​ gain bonus20log10​Icp​2πgm​A​​​ [dB] Dimension check: 2πNgmA/Icp2\pi N g_m A/I_{cp}2πNgm​A/Icp​ = dimensionless×(A/rad)/(A) — rad is dimensionless, so the whole ratio is dimensionless ✓, and the log is valid. Illustrative numbers (N=50N=50N=50, gmA=2.5g_m A=2.5gm​A=2.5 mA/rad, Icp=1I_{cp}=1Icp​=1 mA): 33.98+23.92=57.933.98+23.92=57.933.98+23.92=57.9 dB. The first term is exactly the "∼20log⁡10N\sim20\log_{10}N∼20log10​N removal of the divider multiplier": CP/PD noise in sub-sampling is no longer amplified by ×N2\times N^2×N2 (external standard result, Gao et al. 2009, cited above). The second term is the extra bonus from KPDK_{PD}KPD​ changing from Icp/2πI_{cp}/2\piIcp​/2π to gmAg_m Agm​A, and it varies by design. The divider noise term N2SdivN^2S_{div}N2Sdiv​ disappears entirely — there is no divider in the loop at all. (There's still a divider on-chip, but it only handles frequency acquisition inside the auxiliary FLL; once locked, it's silenced by the dead zone and is off the phase-noise path — see Step 5.) What remains of the in-band floor is ≈N2Sref\approx N^2S_{ref}≈N2Sref​ + the sampler's own noise — it becomes reference-limited. To go further, the only options are a cleaner reference or a higher freff_{ref}fref​ to lower NNN (there's no free lunch, per rule 1 of clock_chain_budget). ILCM comparison (same "kick the divider/CP out" goal, a completely different mechanism): the injection-locked clock multiplier (ILCM) also drives the in-band floor to reference-limited, but by a different route — the sub-sampling PLL is a continuous-time closed loop (the divider is reduced to an auxiliary FLL; sampling the zero crossing is the phase detector), while the ILCM is discrete-time, open-loop injection (there is no PFD/CP/divider at all — a pulse generator directly "pulls" the phase toward the reference). The in-band bookkeeping converges to the same destination by different paths: sub-sampling gives N2Sref∣Hlp∣2N^2S_{ref}\vert H_{lp}\vert^2N2Sref​∣Hlp​∣2 (the divider term disappears, CP is no longer ×N2\times N^2×N2); the ILCM gives N2Sref∣Href∣2N^2S_{ref}\vert H_{ref}\vert^2N2Sref​∣Href​∣2 with Href=β/(1−(1−β)z−1)H_{ref}=\beta/(1-(1-\beta)z^{-1})Href​=β/(1−(1−β)z−1), a first-order discrete-time low-pass (β\betaβ = the realignment factor) — the same ×N2\times N^2×N2, two completely different ways of kicking the divider out. The full derivation (lock range, β\betaβ, discrete-time noise shaping) is on subharmonic_injection.

documents.t: This step is where this site's main thread and sub-sampling elegantly intersect. The ISF of an ideal LC oscillator with output V=Acos⁡(ω0t)V=A\cos(\omega_0 t)V=Acos(ω0​t) is Γ(ω0τ)=−sin⁡(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=-\sin(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ)=−sin(ω0​τ) (lab_02, corresponding to [P1]'s LC example) — ∣Γ∣\lvert\Gamma\rvert∣Γ∣ is largest at the zero crossing (=1) and zero at the peak. The SSPD happens to fire exactly at the zero crossing, so this single location has two faces: (a) Maximum efficiency at reading phase, and naturally AM-rejecting. At the zero crossing, V=Asin⁡(ϕerr)≈AϕerrV=A\sin(\phi_{err})\approx A\phi_{err}V=Asin(ϕerr​)≈Aϕerr​: the voltage carries phase information "one-to-one" (the gain AAA V/rad is the maximum anywhere on the sinusoid); meanwhile an amplitude error δA\delta AδA enters as δAsin⁡(ϕerr)≈δA⋅ϕerr\delta A\sin(\phi_{err})\approx\delta A\cdot\phi_{err}δAsin(ϕerr​)≈δA⋅ϕerr​ — a second-order small quantity, so it doesn't enter at first order. Conversely, if sampling happened at the peak: ∂V/∂ϕ=0\partial V/\partial\phi=0∂V/∂ϕ=0 (no phase readout at all), while δA\delta AδA enters at full strength. This matches exactly the decomposition in phase_vs_amplitude_noise: the zero crossing is a "pure phase" window. The geometry of sampling is the same thread as the aperture math: step 1 of adc_aperture_jitter, "sampling error = slope × timing error," is noise on the ADC page (clock jitter dirtying the sample), but on this page it's flipped around and used as the signal (the reference edge's timing offset is converted into a measurable voltage via the slope Aω0A\omega_0Aω0​) — the same equation, one side is a liability, the other a phase detector. (b) Also maximum efficiency at hitting phase — kickback becomes a spur. Every time the sampling switch closes, it exchanges a small packet of charge Δq\Delta qΔq with the VCO node (charge sharing / switch feedthrough). Using [P1]'s operational ISF definition (canonical formula 5): Δϕ=Γ(ω0τ)qmax Δq\Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta qΔϕ=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​Δq Hitting at the zero crossing → ∣Γ∣=1\lvert\Gamma\rvert=1∣Γ∣=1 (maximum) → every kick lands with full force. Illustrative (following the scale of canonical example A, taking ∣Γ∣=1\lvert\Gamma\rvert=1∣Γ∣=1): Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC → Δϕ=1\Delta\phi=1Δϕ=1 mrad per reference period. This disturbance is deterministic, periodic at freff_{ref}fref​, so it isn't a continuous spectrum but a reference spur (canonical section 10.2's small-angle PM: a residual phase ripple of fundamental amplitude ϕp\phi_pϕp​ produces a sideband =20log⁡10(ϕp/2)=20\log_{10}(\phi_p/2)=20log10​(ϕp​/2) dBc; ϕp=1\phi_p=1ϕp​=1 mrad → −66.0-66.0−66.0 dBc, and if the loop suppresses it to 0.5 mrad → −72.0-72.0−72.0 dBc, illustrative). The same ∣Γ∣max\lvert\Gamma\rvert_{max}∣Γ∣max​ that gives you maximum phase-detector gain also gives you maximum kickback damage — this is sub-sampling's core trade-off, unpacked in the next step. (Distinguishing spurs from random PN is covered in measurement_and_spurs.)

documents.t: (1) Aliasing: wideband noise folds into ±fref/2\pm f_{ref}/2±fref​/2. The SSPD is a system that samples at freff_{ref}fref​ (the same math as the ADC in adc_aperture_jitter). The wideband voltage noise at the sampler input (thermal noise of the VCO buffer, PSD SvS_vSv​ V²/Hz, bandwidth Bn≫frefB_n\gg f_{ref}Bn​≫fref​) folds back into the single-sided band fref/2f_{ref}/2fref​/2 with power conserved: Sv,fold=Sv Bnfref/2=2SvBnfref⟹Sϕ,fold=Sv,foldA2 [rad2/Hz]S_{v,fold}=\frac{S_v\,B_n}{f_{ref}/2}=\frac{2S_v B_n}{f_{ref}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad S_{\phi,fold}=\frac{S_{v,fold}}{A^2}\ \ [\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]Sv,fold​=fref​/2Sv​Bn​​=fref​2Sv​Bn​​⟹Sϕ,fold​=A2Sv,fold​​ [rad2/Hz] Dimension check: [V2/Hz]×[Hz]÷[Hz]=[V2/Hz][\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}]\times[\text{Hz}]\div[\text{Hz}]=[\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}][V2/Hz]×[Hz]÷[Hz]=[V2/Hz] ✓; dividing by A2A^2A2 [V²/rad²] gives rad²/Hz ✓. (Dividing by A2A^2A2: the voltage-to-phase gain at the zero crossing is AAA V/rad.) For the sampling capacitor itself, the total noise power is the famous kT/CskT/C_skT/Cs​ (independent of bandwidth); once folded, Sv=2kT/(Csfref)S_v=2kT/(C_s f_{ref})Sv​=2kT/(Cs​fref​). Illustrative: Cs=100C_s=100Cs​=100 fF → kT/Cs=204 μ\sqrt{kT/C_s}=204\ \mukT/Cs​​=204 μV rms → L=−147.8\mathcal{L}=-147.8L=−147.8 dBc/Hz — much lower than the −126-126−126 reference floor (good news), but you have to account for folding before buying a wideband buffer: every doubling of BnB_nBn​ adds 3 dB to this term. (2) The reference-spur see-saw. The kickback from step 4(b) lands exactly where ∣Γ∣\lvert\Gamma\rvert∣Γ∣ is largest, so the spur is inherently worse than in a classic PLL. Every countermeasure is a trade: adding an isolation buffer (spur ↓, but the buffer's own noise folds in per (1), and it costs power); shrinking CsC_sCs​ (Δq\Delta qΔq ↓ → spur ↓, but kT/CskT/C_skT/Cs​ ↑ — noise and spur sit on opposite ends of the same see-saw); dummy-sampler cancellation. The same team's follow-up paper deals specifically with spur reduction: X. Gao, E. A. M. Klumperink, G. Socci, M. Bohsali, and B. Nauta, "Spur Reduction Techniques for Phase-Locked Loops Exploiting a Sub-Sampling Phase Detector," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 45, no. 9, pp. 1809–1821, Sep. 2010 (external literature, not among the five source PDFs; TODO: manual verification needed — volume/issue/page numbers should be manually verified before citing in a formal document). (3) Lock range: sin⁡\sinsin can't tell which cycle you're on. sin⁡\sinsin is 2π2\pi2π-periodic — every zero crossing of the VCO looks identical to the SSPD, so the SSPD has zero discrimination against "frequency error," and there's no hardware that defines NNN at all: any integer kkk satisfying f0=k freff_0=k\,f_{ref}f0​=kfref​ is a valid lock point (harmonic lock — locking to the wrong harmonic). So an SSPLL always pairs with an auxiliary FLL (frequency-locked loop: a conventional ÷N + PFD/CP) responsible for pulling the frequency close to the correct NfrefN f_{ref}Nfref​; it carries a dead zone — once locked, the phase error is tiny, the auxiliary loop goes completely silent, and the divider's noise never enters the main loop. In an SSPLL, the number NNN is defined by the auxiliary loop. (4) Effect on the optimal loop BW (tying back to the budget page). Using the afn+b/fnaf_n+b/f_nafn​+b/fn​ toy model from pll_noise_budget: if the in-band floor aaa drops by 7.1 dB (power ×1/5.12\times1/5.12×1/5.12, the illustrative numbers from the worked example below) → the optimum fn\*∝b/af_n^\*\propto\sqrt{b/a}fn\*​∝b/a​ widens by 5.12=2.26×\sqrt{5.12}=2.26\times5.12​=2.26×, and the minimum integrated jitter ∝(ab)1/4\propto(ab)^{1/4}∝(ab)1/4 improves by 5.121/4=1.5×5.12^{1/4}=1.5\times5.121/4=1.5× — a lower floor isn't just a lower floor, it also lets you open the loop bandwidth wider and suppress more of the VCO, so the total-jitter payoff is larger than the floor's dB number alone suggests.

documents.t: Format: problem → step-by-step substitution (with units) → result → dimension check → Python verification. All component values are representative / illustrative (not tied to any specific silicon process); bookkeeping conventions match clock_chain_budget (SSB, L=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12S_\phiL=21​Sϕ​; this page compares only ratios, so the /2-vs-/4 convention cancels out). Problem: fref=100f_{ref}=100fref​=100 MHz, N=50N=50N=50 (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz). Reference floor Lref=−160\mathcal{L}_{ref}=-160Lref​=−160 dBc/Hz, divider's own floor −160-160−160 dBc/Hz (at its output), CP and gmg_mgm​-stage equivalent noise current both in=4i_n=4in​=4 pA/√Hz, Icp=1I_{cp}=1Icp​=1 mA, gm=5g_m=5gm​=5 mS, A=0.5A=0.5A=0.5 V, Cs=100C_s=100Cs​=100 fF (300 K). documents.t: In a SerDes sampling-clock jitter budget, the in-band floor is often the dominant term (clock_chain_budget's worked chain: 65.9% comes from the in-band floor raised by ×N2\times N^2×N2). This page's illustrative numbers compress the in-band portion from 50.9 fs to 22.5 fs (2.26×2.26\times2.26×), and the optimal loop BW can then also widen by 2.26×2.26\times2.26× to suppress more of the VCO — a direct credit to serdes_clocking_connection's eye/BER accounting (RJ overhead =2Q−1σt=2Q^{-1}\sigma_t=2Q−1σt​). On the cost side: the reference spur is deterministic jitter (DJ, see dj_dual_dirac), which shows up on the eye diagram as a dual peak rather than a Gaussian tail — the "lower RJ, higher DJ risk" trade that sub-sampling buys is exactly what the system level needs to watch.

documents.t: Prerequisites: psd_phase_noise_jitter (SϕS_\phiSϕ​, L\mathcal{L}L, the four jitter "dialects," and phase↔time conversion), tank_swing (L∝Γrms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​/qmax2​ sets the VCO's own noise), lc_vs_ring (accumulated jitter σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ and the LC/ring trade-off) | Next: pll_noise_budget, exercises This is the capstone page of Chapter 06: it connects everything said so far about ISF / phase noise to what a SerDes (serializer/deserializer, high-speed serial transceiver) designer looks at every day — clock jitter, eye opening, BER (bit error rate). We derive, step by step, the two phase→time conversions, clarify how to choose the integration bandwidth, the difference between RJ and DJ, and why a CDR/PLL behaves like a high-pass filter that removes the VCO's close-in noise — which is why "the same VCO behaves completely differently under different loops." Physical intuition (conclusion first): an oscillator's phase noise is "the phase jittering." What a SerDes designer cares about is "how much the edge jitters on the time axis" and "the probability that the sampling instant lands near the center of the eye." Phase jitter → time jitter (Δt=Δϕ/2πf0\Delta t=\Delta\phi/2\pi f_0Δt=Δϕ/2πf0​) → the sampling point drifts off the eye center → the eye narrows → BER worsens. But not all phase noise, regardless of frequency, is harmful: the CDR/PLL tracks slow phase drift (low-frequency noise is absorbed by the loop), leaving only the fast noise the loop cannot follow to become jitter. So "integration bandwidth" and "loop bandwidth" are the two central knobs of SerDes clocking.
