documents.t: How does an oscillator's excess phase Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ turn into an edge timing error? One period T=1/f0T=1/f_0T=1/f0​ corresponds to 2π2\pi2π rad of phase, so phase and time are proportional (notation, Eq. 17): Δt=Δϕ2πf0 \boxed{\ \Delta t=\frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi f_0}\ } Δt=2πf0​Δϕ​ ​ Step-by-step derivation: the signal is V=Acos⁡(2πf0t+ϕ)V=A\cos(2\pi f_0 t+\phi)V=Acos(2πf0​t+ϕ). Treat a perturbation Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ of ϕ\phiϕ as a time shift Δt\Delta tΔt: requiring 2πf0(t+Δt)=2πf0t+Δϕ2\pi f_0(t+\Delta t)=2\pi f_0 t+\Delta\phi2πf0​(t+Δt)=2πf0​t+Δϕ and solving gives 2πf0 Δt=Δϕ2\pi f_0\,\Delta t=\Delta\phi2πf0​Δt=Δϕ, i.e. Δt=Δϕ2πf0.\Delta t=\frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi f_0}.Δt=2πf0​Δϕ​. Dimension check: [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] ✓ (2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ has units of rad/s, not Hz). Intuition (5 GHz): 1 mrad → 31.8 fs; 1 rad → 31.8 ps (≈ T/6.28T/6.28T/6.28, sensible).

documents.t: A single Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ is not useful — jitter is the sum of phase noise across all frequencies. First integrate the phase PSD to get phase variance (Eq. 18): σϕ2=∫f1f2Sϕ(f) df\sigma_\phi^2=\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_\phi(f)\,dfσϕ2​=∫f1​f2​​Sϕ​(f)df Then use Step 1 to convert rms phase to rms time (Eq. 19): σt=σϕ2πf0=12πf0∫f1f2Sϕ(f) df \boxed{\ \sigma_t=\frac{\sigma_\phi}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{1}{2\pi f_0}\sqrt{\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_\phi(f)\,df}\ } σt​=2πf0​σϕ​​=2πf0​1​∫f1​f2​​Sϕ​(f)df​ ​ Step-by-step explanation: Why integrate: Sϕ(f)S_\phi(f)Sϕ​(f) is "phase power per Hz" (rad²/Hz). Phase jitter at different offset frequencies is independent, so the powers add — integrating over fff gives the total phase variance σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​ (rad²). Dimension check: [rad2/Hz]⋅[Hz]=[rad2][\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]\cdot[\text{Hz}]=[\text{rad}^2][rad2/Hz]⋅[Hz]=[rad2] ✓ → take the square root to get rad. Convert to time: divide by 2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ (rad/s) → s. Connecting to measurement: a phase-noise analyzer reports L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) (dBc/Hz); use the small-angle approximation Sϕ=2⋅10L/10S_\phi=2\cdot10^{\mathcal{L}/10}Sϕ​=2⋅10L/10 (the factor-of-2 for single-sided → double-sided, Eq. 16) to convert L\mathcal{L}L to SϕS_\phiSϕ​ before integrating. Key intuition: the 1/f² integral is dominated by the lower limit f1f_1f1​ (the 1/f11/f_11/f1​ term is largest) — so "where you start integrating from" is critical. This is exactly the meaning of "integration bandwidth" and "CDR high-pass" discussed below. See numerical_feeling Example 3 for the full mental-math walkthrough.
documents.s: Step 3: numerical example (canonical example C)

documents.t: The SerDes receiver samples at the center of each bit. Let the bit period (UI, unit interval) be TbT_bTb​. Timing jitter σt\sigma_tσt​ at the sampling instant directly "eats into" the eye's horizontal opening from both sides. For the case of RJ (Gaussian) only, the BER at an offset ttt from the eye center is a bathtub curve (standard SerDes model, §10.2 of the spec): BER(t)=12[Q ⁣(UI/2−tσt)+Q ⁣(UI/2+tσt)],Q(x)=12 erfc ⁣(x2)\text{BER}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left[Q\!\left(\frac{\text{UI}/2-t}{\sigma_t}\right)+Q\!\left(\frac{\text{UI}/2+t}{\sigma_t}\right)\right],\qquad Q(x)=\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt2}\right)BER(t)=21​[Q(σt​UI/2−t​)+Q(σt​UI/2+t​)],Q(x)=21​erfc(2​x​) How to read it: the two QQQ terms are, respectively, the probability that "the left edge (at −UI/2-\text{UI}/2−UI/2) jitters past the sample point on the right" and that "the right edge (at +UI/2+\text{UI}/2+UI/2) jitters past the sample point on the left." At the exact eye center t=0t=0t=0 the two terms are equal and BER is lowest (the bottom of the bathtub). Solving for eye opening from BER: to meet a target BER (e.g. 10−1210^{-12}10−12), the one-sided margin at the bottom (t=0t=0t=0) must satisfy UI/2−Q−1(BER)⋅σt>0\text{UI}/2-Q^{-1}(\text{BER})\cdot\sigma_t > 0UI/2−Q−1(BER)⋅σt​>0. With Q−1(10−12)≈7.03Q^{-1}(10^{-12})\approx7.03Q−1(10−12)≈7.03: Eye horizontal opening (one-sided) ≈0.5 UI−(opposite-side ISI)−Q−1(BER)⋅σt\approx0.5\,\text{UI}-(\text{opposite-side ISI})-Q^{-1}(\text{BER})\cdot\sigma_t≈0.5UI−(opposite-side ISI)−Q−1(BER)⋅σt​, where Q−1(BER)Q^{-1}(\text{BER})Q−1(BER) is the inverse Gaussian Q-function value for the target BER (e.g. BER =10−12=10^{-12}=10−12 → Q−1≈7.03Q^{-1}\approx7.03Q−1≈7.03, total RJ ≈ 14σt14\sigma_t14σt​ peak-to-peak). Intuition: RJ is Gaussian and unbounded, so the stricter the BER target (the smaller the probability), the more margin must be reserved (larger QQQ). Each increment of σt\sigma_tσt​ eats ∼Qσt\sim Q\sigma_t∼Qσt​ off each side of the eye. Order of magnitude: in the example above, σt=448\sigma_t=448σt​=448 fs; at f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, if the data rate is 10 Gb/s (Tb=100T_b=100Tb​=100 ps), the RJ overhead for BER 10−1210^{-12}10−12 is ≈14×448 fs=6.3\approx14\times448\,\text{fs}=6.3≈14×448fs=6.3 ps =0.063=0.063=0.063 UI — clock RJ alone eats 6.3% of the eye. This is why high-speed links are so sensitive to VCO phase noise. ⚠️ The QQQ-value and 0.50.50.5-UI-opening eye/BER model is standard SerDes/communications knowledge (not in the five downloaded PDFs; supplemented from standard literature, e.g. the dual-Dirac jitter model, OIF-CEI, Razavi). [P1]/[P2] provide phase noise/jitter itself; they do not cover link budget.

documents.t: What a SerDes measures as "jitter" is actually several components stacked together, and they are treated completely differently (see the "four dialects" in notation): Type Source Statistics How it enters BER RJ (random jitter) oscillator phase noise, thermal Gaussian, unbounded, characterized by σ\sigmaσ peak-to-peak ≈2Qσt\approx2Q\sigma_t≈2Qσt​; margin grows with stricter BER DJ (deterministic jitter) ISI, duty-cycle distortion, crosstalk, PSIJ bounded, characterized by peak-to-peak added directly (bounded), does not scale with BER period jitter single-period length deviation Tk−TT_k-TTk​−T — clock internal spec cycle-to-cycle adjacent-period difference Tk+1−TkT_{k+1}-T_kTk+1​−Tk​ — sensitive to PLL stability accumulated / long-term free-running drift, σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ random walk open-loop only; suppressed once CDR/PLL is locked total jitter (TJ) @ BER: TJ=DJpp+2Q(BER)⋅RJrms\text{TJ}=\text{DJ}_{pp}+2Q(\text{BER})\cdot\text{RJ}_{rms}TJ=DJpp​+2Q(BER)⋅RJrms​ (dual-Dirac approximation; for the rigorous version and the gap between DJδδ≤DJppDJ_{\delta\delta}\le DJ_{pp}DJδδ​≤DJpp​, see dj_dual_dirac). ISF directly governs RJ and accumulated jitter (they originate from phase noise); DJ is mostly a link/pattern issue that ISF cannot see.

documents.t: This is the single most important idea on this page, and the answer to "why the free-running σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ does not grow without bound in practice." Put the VCO inside a PLL (locked to a clean reference) or a CDR (locked to data edges), and the loop tracks the VCO's slow phase drift: as long as the drift is slow enough (offset frequency below the loop bandwidth fBWf_{BW}fBW​), the loop corrects it. The result is that the VCO's own phase noise experiences a high-pass transfer function: ∣HVCO→out(f)∣2≈f2f2+fBW2⇒{below fBW: suppressed (loop keeps up)above fBW: passes unchanged\big|H_{VCO\to out}(f)\big|^2\approx\frac{f^2}{f^2+f_{BW}^2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\begin{cases}\text{below }f_{BW}:\text{ suppressed (loop keeps up)}\\ \text{above }f_{BW}:\text{ passes unchanged}\end{cases}​HVCO→out​(f)​2≈f2+fBW2​f2​⇒{below fBW​: suppressed (loop keeps up)above fBW​: passes unchanged​ Conversely, the reference clock (or the CDR's input data-edge) noise experiences a low-pass: low frequencies pass unchanged, high frequencies are filtered out. Design consequences: The integration lower limit f1f_1f1​ should be taken near the loop bandwidth (not DC) — because VCO noise below fBWf_{BW}fBW​ has already been absorbed by the loop. This directly answers "how to choose the integration bandwidth": closed-loop jitter is integrated from fBWf_{BW}fBW​ to f2f_2f2​ (Nyquist or half the data rate). Accumulated jitter is truncated: the free-running random walk (∝Δt\propto\sqrt{\Delta t}∝Δt​, energy concentrated at very low frequency) falls exactly in the high-pass stopband → it is suppressed into a bounded tracking error. So once locked, it no longer drifts without bound. Loop bandwidth is a trade-off: raising fBWf_{BW}fBW​ → filters out more VCO close-in noise (good), but lets more reference/input noise and the loop's own noise through (bad). The optimal fBWf_{BW}fBW​ sits near the crossover point of the VCO-noise and reference-noise curves. ⚠️ The PLL/CDR high-pass/low-pass transfer function is standard PLL theory (not in the five downloaded PDFs; supplemented from standard literature, e.g. Gardner, Razavi, Best). [P1]/[P2] cover open-loop oscillator phase noise theory; this section is the bridge to closed-loop clocking. TODO: manual verification needed — for an exact loop transfer function (including charge-pump and loop-filter order), consult standard PLL literature. What a real CDR looks like: this section draws the CDR as a linear-PLL black box. Practical SerDes receivers are almost always bang-bang digital loops (an Alexander PD that outputs only sign(Δt)\text{sign}(\Delta t)sign(Δt)) plus a phase interpolator — their loop gain is the reciprocal of the jitter, Kbb=2/π/σjK_{bb}=\sqrt{2/\pi}/\sigma_jKbb​=2/π​/σj​ (this site's σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs → 71.371.371.3/UI); the −40/−20-40/-20−40/−20 dB/dec segments of the jitter-tolerance mask JTOL(f)=(UI−TJeye)/∣1−H(f)∣\text{JTOL}(f)=(\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye})/\lvert1-H(f)\rvertJTOL(f)=(UI−TJeye​)/∣1−H(f)∣; and why tracking SSC spread-spectrum clocking (521 UI peak-to-peak phase) requires a type-II loop. See cdr_bang_bang_jtol.

documents.t: Scenario Intuition LC or ring? TX PLL (generates the transmit clock) Directly sets transmit jitter; usually narrow loop BW (absorbs ref noise), so VCO close-in noise matters High-speed lanes use LC-VCO (low phase noise); jitter requirements are strict RX CDR (recovers clock from data) Loop BW is set by data/jitter tolerance; high-passes away VCO close-in Commonly uses ring-VCO (wide tuning, multi-phase, small area — and close-in is filtered by the CDR, so it is less fatal) LC-VCO Low Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​, low phase noise, slow drift; large area, narrow tuning TX, reference, high performance ring-VCO Worse phase noise, faster jitter accumulation; but wide tuning, naturally multi-phase, small area; close-in is suppressed once inside a fast loop RX CDR, low-power/area-sensitive, multi-phase needs Core trade-off: the ring's weakness (close-in 1/f³, fast random walk) falls exactly in the loop's high-pass stopband — if the loop bandwidth is wide enough, the ring-VCO's close-in weakness is largely compensated. This is why many RX CDRs use ring instead of LC. Conversely, a TX PLL often uses a narrow loop to filter out reference spurs, so VCO close-in noise appears directly at the output → LC is preferred. For a more complete "which oscillator for which job" selection decision table (covering ADC/DAC sampling clocks, RF synthesizers, low power, SoC-internal clocks, multiphase/wide tuning range, instrumentation/radar reference chains, etc., each row labeled with "who filters the VCO" and the ISF rationale), see lc_vs_ring, "Selection decision table: which oscillator for which job."

documents.t: The following two examples work through this page's two core operations in detail: (1) using σt\sigma_tσt​ and the Q-function to compute the BER bathtub opening (UI=100 ps); (2) integration-bandwidth choice — how much jitter differs when the lower limit is taken at DC vs. the loop bandwidth. We reuse the canonical case: f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, L(1MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\text{MHz})=-100L(1MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz, 1/f² slope, example C gives σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs. Example 1 (compute the BER bathtub opening from σt\sigma_tσt​, UI=100 ps) Data rate 10 Gb/s → UI =100=100=100 ps. Clock RJ σt=448\sigma_t=448σt​=448 fs (example C, assuming no ISI/DJ). Find: (a) the BER at the exact eye center t=0t=0t=0; (b) the bathtub's horizontal opening (eye opening) needed to guarantee BER ≤10−12\le10^{-12}≤10−12. Step-by-step substitution (with units). First compute how many σ\sigmaσ's the center-to-edge distance is relative to σt\sigma_tσt​: UI/2σt=100 ps/20.448 ps=500.448=111.6,(a)BER(0)=12[Q(111.6)+Q(111.6)]=Q(111.6) ≈ 0 (≪10−300, far below floating-point precision).\begin{aligned} \frac{\text{UI}/2}{\sigma_t}&=\frac{100\ \text{ps}/2}{0.448\ \text{ps}}=\frac{50}{0.448}=111.6, \\[4pt] \text{(a)}\quad\text{BER}(0)&=\frac12\big[Q(111.6)+Q(111.6)\big]=Q(111.6)\;\approx\;0 \;(\ll10^{-300},\ \text{far below floating-point precision}). \end{aligned}σt​UI/2​(a)BER(0)​=0.448 ps100 ps/2​=0.44850​=111.6,=21​[Q(111.6)+Q(111.6)]=Q(111.6)≈0(≪10−300, far below floating-point precision).​ (b) The opening is set by "how far from center BER rises to 10−1210^{-12}10−12." Q−1(10−12)≈7.03Q^{-1}(10^{-12})\approx7.03Q−1(10−12)≈7.03, so the tolerable one-sided offset tedget_{edge}tedge​ satisfies (UI/2−tedge)/σt=7.03(\text{UI}/2-t_{edge})/\sigma_t=7.03(UI/2−tedge​)/σt​=7.03: tedge=UI2−7.03 σt=50 ps−7.03×0.448 ps=50−3.15=46.85 ps,eye horizontal opening=2 tedge=2×46.85 ps=93.7 ps=0.937 UI.\begin{aligned} t_{edge}&=\frac{\text{UI}}{2}-7.03\,\sigma_t=50\ \text{ps}-7.03\times0.448\ \text{ps}=50-3.15=46.85\ \text{ps}, \\[4pt] \text{eye horizontal opening}&=2\,t_{edge}=2\times46.85\ \text{ps}=93.7\ \text{ps}=0.937\ \text{UI}. \end{aligned}tedge​eye horizontal opening​=2UI​−7.03σt​=50 ps−7.03×0.448 ps=50−3.15=46.85 ps,=2tedge​=2×46.85 ps=93.7 ps=0.937 UI.​ Result: (a) center BER is astronomically small (σt\sigma_tσt​ is only 1/1121/1121/112 of half a UI); (b) the BER 10−1210^{-12}10−12 bathtub opening ≈93.7\approx93.7≈93.7 ps =0.937=0.937=0.937 UI — i.e., clock RJ eats 7.03σt≈3.157.03\sigma_t\approx3.157.03σt​≈3.15 ps from each side, ≈6.3\approx6.3≈6.3 ps =0.063=0.063=0.063 UI total. Consistent with Step 4's "448 fs RJ ≈ 0.063 UI." Dimension check: QQQ's argument [s][s]\dfrac{[\text{s}]}{[\text{s}]}[s][s]​ is dimensionless ✓; opening [s][\text{s}][s] divided by UI [s][\text{s}][s] gives a UI count (dimensionless) ✓. One-line Python check (using the real Q and ber_bathtub from simulations/common/serdes_utils.py): import numpy as np from simulations.common.serdes_utils import Q, ber_bathtub ui, sigma_t = 100e-12, 447.9e-15 print("BER(0) =", ber_bathtub(0.0, sigma_t, ui)) # -> ~0 (1e-300 floor) t_edge = ui/2 - 7.03*sigma_t print("opening =", 2*t_edge*1e12, "ps =", 2*t_edge/ui, "UI") # -> 93.7 ps = 0.937 UI Example 2 (integration-bandwidth choice: lower limit at DC vs. loop bandwidth) Same VCO (example C's 1/f² skirt, Sϕ(f)=2×10−10(106/f)2S_\phi(f)=2\times10^{-10}(10^6/f)^2Sϕ​(f)=2×10−10(106/f)2 rad²/Hz), upper limit f2=100f_2=100f2​=100 MHz. Compare rms jitter from "open-loop, integrated from f1=10f_1=10f1​=10 kHz" vs. "closed-loop, integrated from loop bandwidth f1=1f_1=1f1​=1 MHz." This is the numerical version of "why CDR/PLL high-pass reduces jitter." Step-by-step substitution (with units). The 1/f² phase-variance integral has closed form σϕ2=Sϕ(fref)fref2(1f1−1f2)\sigma_\phi^2=S_\phi(f_{ref})f_{ref}^2\big(\tfrac{1}{f_1}-\tfrac{1}{f_2}\big)σϕ2​=Sϕ​(fref​)fref2​(f1​1​−f2​1​); here Sϕ(fref)fref2=2×10−10×(106)2=2×102S_\phi(f_{ref})f_{ref}^2=2\times10^{-10}\times(10^6)^2=2\times10^{2}Sϕ​(fref​)fref2​=2×10−10×(106)2=2×102: (open-loop, f1=10 kHz):σϕ2=2×102(1104−1108)=200×(10−4−10−8)≈2.0×10−2 rad2⇒ σϕ=0.1413 rad,σt=0.14132π×5×109=4.50×10−12 s=4.50 ps,(closed-loop, f1=1 MHz):σϕ2=2×102(1106−1108)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2⇒ σϕ=14.07 mrad,σt=447.9 fs(i.e., example C).\begin{aligned} \text{(open-loop, }f_1=10\ \text{kHz)}:\quad \sigma_\phi^2&=2\times10^{2}\left(\frac{1}{10^4}-\frac{1}{10^8}\right)=200\times(10^{-4}-10^{-8})\approx2.0\times10^{-2}\ \text{rad}^2 \\[2pt] &\Rightarrow\ \sigma_\phi=0.1413\ \text{rad},\quad \sigma_t=\frac{0.1413}{2\pi\times5\times10^9}=4.50\times10^{-12}\ \text{s}=4.50\ \text{ps}, \\[6pt] \text{(closed-loop, }f_1=1\ \text{MHz)}:\quad \sigma_\phi^2&=2\times10^{2}\left(\frac{1}{10^6}-\frac{1}{10^8}\right)=200\times9.9\times10^{-7}=1.98\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}^2 \\[2pt] &\Rightarrow\ \sigma_\phi=14.07\ \text{mrad},\quad \sigma_t=447.9\ \text{fs}\quad(\text{i.e., example C}). \end{aligned}(open-loop, f1​=10 kHz):σϕ2​(closed-loop, f1​=1 MHz):σϕ2​​=2×102(1041​−1081​)=200×(10−4−10−8)≈2.0×10−2 rad2⇒ σϕ​=0.1413 rad,σt​=2π×5×1090.1413​=4.50×10−12 s=4.50 ps,=2×102(1061​−1081​)=200×9.9×10−7=1.98×10−4 rad2⇒ σϕ​=14.07 mrad,σt​=447.9 fs(i.e., example C).​ Result: raising the integration lower limit from 10 kHz (open-loop) to 1 MHz (loop BW) → rms jitter drops from 4.50 ps to 448 fs (roughly a 10×10\times10× reduction). Because the 1/f² jitter is dominated by the lower limit 1/f11/f_11/f1​, the loop's high-pass removes VCO close-in noise below fBWf_{BW}fBW​, equivalent to raising the integration lower limit to fBWf_{BW}fBW​ — this is the quantitative answer to "how to choose the integration bandwidth": closed-loop jitter is integrated from fBWf_{BW}fBW​ to f2f_2f2​. Dimension check: [rad2/Hz]⋅[Hz2]⋅[1/Hz]=[rad2][\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]\cdot[\text{Hz}^2]\cdot[\text{1/Hz}]=[\text{rad}^2][rad2/Hz]⋅[Hz2]⋅[1/Hz]=[rad2] ✓; [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] ✓. One-line Python check (using simulations/common/noise_utils.py): import numpy as np from simulations.common.noise_utils import leeson_one_over_f2, integrate_rms_jitter for f1 in (1e4, 1e6): f = np.logspace(np.log10(f1), 8, 6000) L = leeson_one_over_f2(f, L_ref_dbc=-100, f_ref=1e6) st, sp = integrate_rms_jitter(f, L, f0=5e9, fmin=f1, fmax=100e6) print(f"f1={f1:.0e}: sigma_t = {st*1e15:.1f} fs") # f1=1e+04: sigma_t = ~4500 fs ; f1=1e+06: sigma_t = 447.9 fs Example 1's BER/Q model is standard SerDes knowledge (not in the five PDFs; supplemented from standard literature, e.g. dual-Dirac, OIF-CEI); Example 2's loop high-pass truncation is standard PLL theory (not in the five PDFs). The phase noise/jitter itself comes from [P1]/[P2]. Example 3 (PAM4: 56/112 Gb/s — is RJ still enough once the UI shrinks to fs scale?) The first two examples used 10/25 Gb/s NRZ (1 bit/symbol). PAM4 (4-level pulse-amplitude modulation, 2 bit/symbol) turns the same bit rate into half the baud rate (symbol rate): bit rate=2×baud\text{bit rate}=2\times\text{baud}bit rate=2×baud. Here we run the same canonical VCO (example C, σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs) and the same clock_chain_budget PLL output (σt=27.6\sigma_t=27.6σt​=27.6 fs) through 56 Gb/s and 112 Gb/s PAM4, and see how much RJ margin is left once the UI shrinks. Step 1 (bit rate → baud rate → UI): 56 Gb/s PAM4:baud=56/2=28 GBd,UI=1/(28×109)=35.71 ps,112 Gb/s PAM4:baud=112/2=56 GBd,UI=1/(56×109)=17.86 ps.\begin{aligned} 56\ \text{Gb/s PAM4}:\quad &\text{baud}=56/2=28\ \text{GBd},\quad \text{UI}=1/(28\times10^9)=35.71\ \text{ps}, \\[4pt] 112\ \text{Gb/s PAM4}:\quad &\text{baud}=112/2=56\ \text{GBd},\quad \text{UI}=1/(56\times10^9)=17.86\ \text{ps}. \end{aligned}56 Gb/s PAM4:112 Gb/s PAM4:​baud=56/2=28 GBd,UI=1/(28×109)=35.71 ps,baud=112/2=56 GBd,UI=1/(56×109)=17.86 ps.​ Dimension check: [Gb/s]/[bit/symbol]=[GBd][\text{Gb/s}]/[\text{bit/symbol}]=[\text{GBd}][Gb/s]/[bit/symbol]=[GBd]; 1/[Hz]=[s]1/[\text{Hz}]=[\text{s}]1/[Hz]=[s] ✓. Intuition: PAM4's baud is half of an NRZ link at the same bit rate (56 Gb/s PAM4's 28 GBd equals the baud of a 28 Gb/s NRZ link), but each UI now has to resolve 4 levels instead of 2 — it is not simply "a bigger UI means an easier link." See the honesty box below. Step 2 (how much of the UI does the canonical VCO's RJ eat): using Step 4's eye-closure formula RJpp(BER=10−12)≈2 Q−1(10−12) σt\text{RJ}_{pp}(\text{BER}=10^{-12})\approx2\,Q^{-1}(10^{-12})\,\sigma_tRJpp​(BER=10−12)≈2Q−1(10−12)σt​, with Q−1(10−12)=7.034Q^{-1}(10^{-12})=7.034Q−1(10−12)=7.034 (the same precision used in final_exam problem 10): bare VCO (σt=447.9 fs):RJpp=2×7.034×447.9 fs=6.301 ps⇒ 6.301/35.71=0.176 UI @28 GBd,6.301/17.86=0.353 UI @56 GBd,PLL output (σt=27.6 fs, from clock_chain_budget):RJpp=2×7.034×27.6 fs=0.3883 ps⇒ 0.3883/35.71=0.011 UI @28 GBd,0.3883/17.86=0.022 UI @56 GBd.\begin{aligned} \text{bare VCO (}\sigma_t=447.9\ \text{fs)}:\quad \text{RJ}_{pp}&=2\times7.034\times447.9\ \text{fs}=6.301\ \text{ps} \\[2pt] &\Rightarrow\ 6.301/35.71=0.176\ \text{UI @28 GBd},\quad 6.301/17.86=0.353\ \text{UI @56 GBd}, \\[6pt] \text{PLL output (}\sigma_t=27.6\ \text{fs, from clock\_chain\_budget)}:\quad \text{RJ}_{pp}&=2\times7.034\times27.6\ \text{fs}=0.3883\ \text{ps} \\[2pt] &\Rightarrow\ 0.3883/35.71=0.011\ \text{UI @28 GBd},\quad 0.3883/17.86=0.022\ \text{UI @56 GBd}. \end{aligned}bare VCO (σt​=447.9 fs):RJpp​PLL output (σt​=27.6 fs, from clock_chain_budget):RJpp​​=2×7.034×447.9 fs=6.301 ps⇒ 6.301/35.71=0.176 UI @28 GBd,6.301/17.86=0.353 UI @56 GBd,=2×7.034×27.6 fs=0.3883 ps⇒ 0.3883/35.71=0.011 UI @28 GBd,0.3883/17.86=0.022 UI @56 GBd.​ Result: the bare VCO's RJ (no PLL filtering) already eats 17.6% of the UI at 28 GBd, and balloons to 35.3% of the UI at 56 GBd — unusable for a PAM4 link that has only a few percent of margin left over for DJ/ISI. The same oscillator, cleaned by the clock_chain_budget PLL to 27.6 fs, drops the RJ overhead to 1.1%/2.2% UI — close-in PLL/CDR filtering matters even more under PAM4's narrower UI (the same UI-percentage requirement bites harder because a PAM4 UI is only half that of NRZ at the same bit rate). Adding DJ: using Step 5's dual-Dirac TJ formula TJ=DJδδ+2Q−1(BER)σt\text{TJ}=\text{DJ}_{\delta\delta}+2Q^{-1}(\text{BER})\sigma_tTJ=DJδδ​+2Q−1(BER)σt​, with DJδδ=1\text{DJ}_{\delta\delta}=1DJδδ​=1 ps (the same value given in final_exam problem 10) stacked on the bare-VCO RJ: TJ=1 ps+6.301 ps=7.301 ps=7.301/35.71=0.204 UI @28 GBd.\text{TJ}=1\ \text{ps}+6.301\ \text{ps}=7.301\ \text{ps}=7.301/35.71=0.204\ \text{UI\ @28\ GBd}.TJ=1 ps+6.301 ps=7.301 ps=7.301/35.71=0.204 UI @28 GBd. One-line Python check: import numpy as np from scipy.stats import norm baud_28, baud_56 = 28e9, 56e9 ui_28, ui_56 = 1/baud_28, 1/baud_56 print(ui_28*1e12, ui_56*1e12) # -> 35.71 17.86 (ps) Qinv = -norm.ppf(1e-12) # -> 7.034 sigma_vco, sigma_pll, dj = 447.9e-15, 27.6e-15, 1e-12 rj_vco = 2*Qinv*sigma_vco rj_pll = 2*Qinv*sigma_pll print(rj_vco*1e12, rj_vco/ui_28, rj_vco/ui_56) # -> 6.301 0.176 0.353 print(rj_pll*1e12, rj_pll/ui_28, rj_pll/ui_56) # -> 0.388 0.011 0.022 tj = dj + rj_vco print(tj*1e12, tj/ui_28) # -> 7.301 0.204 # PAM4's three eyes split the same peak-to-peak swing into three segments, shrinking the effective level spacing to 1/3 of NRZ's: print(20*np.log10(3)) # -> 9.54 (standard PAM4 amplitude penalty, external literature) ⚠️ Honesty box (what this example deliberately leaves out): PAM4 slices one UI into three independent eyes (three decision levels). This example only computes "how much RJ/DJ eats the UI width," and does not touch (1) the ~9.5 dB amplitude penalty (three eyes split the same peak-to-peak swing into three segments, shrinking the effective level spacing to 1/31/31/3 of NRZ's; 20log⁡103=9.5420\log_{10}3=9.5420log10​3=9.54 dB, a standard PAM result, external literature, not from the site's five PDFs); (2) data-pattern-dependent transition jitter / DDJ (different levels have different settling behavior — PAM4-specific data-dependent jitter that the site's RJ/DJ dichotomy does not cover). Industry (external literature, not from the site's five PDFs) specifies these effects via OIF-CEI and IEEE 802.3ck CDR filtering (jitter tolerance) templates; this site does not transcribe their numbers. This page's ISF/phase-noise chain answers only "how much UI does clock RJ eat" — a full PAM4 eye budget must also stack the amplitude penalty and DDJ.

documents.t: Prerequisites: paper_003 ([P3] Sec. IV impulse train, Eq.(19)–(23), generalized Adler), paper_004 (the M:N time-synchronous average of [P4] Eq.(28)–(30)), injection_locked_division (the other half of the duality: division rides on the ISF's NNN-th harmonic), injection_locking_noise (a locked oscillator is a first-order PLL, corner =−Ω′(θss)=-\Omega'(\theta_{ss})=−Ω′(θss​)) | Next: lab_40_subharmonic_injection (independent simulation), sampling_pll, clock_chain_budget What this page answers: Fire freff_{ref}fref​ pulses into an oscillator running at f0=Nfreff_0=N f_{ref}f0​=Nfref​ — why does it lock? On whose harmonics? Why can a pure sinusoid at f0/Nf_0/Nf0​/N not lock? Why is the lock range ∝1/N\propto 1/N∝1/N? How do the two routes — the [P4] Fourier average and the [P3] impulse-train arithmetic — agree term by term? How much phase does each pulse "pull back" — what is the realignment factor β\betaβ, what sets it, how large may it be, how many pulses to settle? How is the phase noise of the locked output budgeted: reference ×N2\times N^2×N2, own noise shaped by a first-order discrete-time loop, closed-form output jitter, where the reference spur comes from? Design knobs: pulse width, ring vs LC, NNN, β\betaβ; how does an ILCM compare with a classic PLL and a sub-sampling PLL? Physical intuition (conclusion first): an injection-locked clock multiplier (ILCM) is not a "multiplier circuit" — it is an oscillator that already runs at f0≈Nfreff_0\approx N f_{ref}f0​≈Nfref​ and gets kicked by a reference pulse once every NNN of its own periods. One kick = one ISF phase step Δϕ=Γ~(θ) qinj\Delta\phi=\tilde\Gamma(\theta)\,q_{inj}Δϕ=Γ~(θ)qinj​; between pulses the oscillator free-runs, its phase drifts with the detuning and random-walks with noise. Locking = each kick exactly repays the phase owed over those NNN periods; noise suppression = each kick pulls the accumulated random phase back by a fraction β\betaβ. What makes the lock possible is the injection waveform's own NNN-th harmonic (the oscillator's ISF fundamental only hears things near f0f_0f0​) — the mirror image of the divider (ILFD): division rides on ISF harmonics, multiplication on injection harmonics. Scope of this page: advanced design page. The text, equations and footnotes of [P3] Sec. IV (p.2112) and [P4] Sec. IV (p.2129) were re-read from the enlarged PDF pages word by word (Section 0). [P4] writes out the closed form Eq.(30) only for the superharmonic case (M=1M=1M=1, a sinusoid at NωoscN\omega_{osc}Nωosc​); for the subharmonic (multiplier) side the paper gives only the general statement and footnote 10 — this page derives the multiplier closed form from Eq.(29) step by step, derives the 1/N1/N1/N law and the realignment factor from the discrete arithmetic of [P3] Sec. IV, and reconciles the two routes. Section 4, "putting noise into the discrete loop", is the textbook-level ILCM / realignment result (external literature, not in the site's 5 PDFs; two verified classics are listed at the end), derived here and checked term by term against this page's own Monte-Carlo. Every model is a phase-only, weak-injection pedagogical toy.

documents.t: paper_003 already teaches this section step by step: an ideal parallel LC fed by a train of current impulses of period Tinj≡2π/ωinjT_{inj}\equiv2\pi/\omega_{inj}Tinj​≡2π/ωinj​, each dumping a fixed charge qinjq_{inj}qinj​ (Fig. 3(a); the paper takes qinj≥0q_{inj}\ge0qinj​≥0 by convention, with the sign selecting Fig. 3(b) speed-up or Fig. 3(c) slow-down; the state-space impulse arrows in the figure are deliberately enlarged, not to scale). Four core equations: Δϕ=±qinjqmax (19),Δϕ2π=−ΔTT0=Δωωinj (20),Δω=ΔϕTinj=±1Tinjqinjqmax (21),Iinj=2qinjTinj (23)\Delta\phi=\pm\frac{q_{inj}}{q_{max}}\ \ (19),\qquad \frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi}=-\frac{\Delta T}{T_0}=\frac{\Delta\omega}{\omega_{inj}}\ \ (20),\qquad \Delta\omega=\frac{\Delta\phi}{T_{inj}}=\pm\frac{1}{T_{inj}}\frac{q_{inj}}{q_{max}}\ \ (21),\qquad I_{inj}=\frac{2q_{inj}}{T_{inj}}\ \ (23)Δϕ=±qmax​qinj​​ (19),2πΔϕ​=−T0​ΔT​=ωinj​Δω​ (20),Δω=Tinj​Δϕ​=±Tinj​1​qmax​qinj​​ (21),Iinj​=Tinj​2qinj​​ (23) The text states that for each qinjq_{inj}qinj​ there is an injection period TinjT_{inj}Tinj​ that makes the next impulse always land at the same place on the waveform, so the period is sustainedly lengthened or shortened while the amplitude never changes. That sentence carries two footnotes, both directly relevant here: footnote 7 (verified verbatim): the injection can also happen "every MMM periods (MMM a positive integer) … corresponding to subharmonic locking" — this is the starting point of this page: replace "one pulse per period" with "one pulse every NNN periods". The paper gives only this sentence; the arithmetic is completed in Section 2. footnote 8: injections that no longer preserve the amplitude (pulses not at the zero crossing) are left to the companion paper [P4] Sec. III-B — i.e. the APF / amplitude modulation of [P4] (paper_004). The phase-only model of this page ignores it; Section 3 points out where it bites.

documents.t: [P4] redefines the relative phase as (Eq.(28), M,NM,NM,N positive coprime integers) φ(t)≡MN ωinjt+θ(t)\varphi(t)\equiv\frac{M}{N}\,\omega_{inj}t+\theta(t)φ(t)≡NM​ωinj​t+θ(t) and obtains the generalized pulling equation (Eq.(29)) dθdt=ω0−MNωinj+1NTinj∫NTinjΓ~ ⁣(MNωinjt+θ)iinj(t) dt.\frac{d\theta}{dt}=\omega_0-\frac{M}{N}\omega_{inj}+\frac{1}{NT_{inj}}\int_{NT_{inj}}\tilde\Gamma\!\left(\frac{M}{N}\omega_{inj}t+\theta\right)i_{inj}(t)\,dt .dtdθ​=ω0​−NM​ωinj​+NTinj​1​∫NTinj​​Γ~(NM​ωinj​t+θ)iinj​(t)dt. The text then says that this M:NM{:}NM:N framework covers any rational ratio Mωinj=NωoscM\omega_{inj}=N\omega_{osc}Mωinj​=Nωosc​ under lock, and that a Fourier series shows at a glance that locking "requires the MMMth-multiple harmonics of the injection to interact with the NNNth-multiple harmonics of the oscillator's ISF"; it also notes that relative phases 2π/N2\pi/N2π/N apart are indistinguishable, so Ω(θ)\Omega(\theta)Ω(θ) has period 2π/N2\pi/N2π/N. Then — only for a superharmonic sinusoidal injection (at the NNNth superharmonic, amplitude IinjI_{inj}Iinj​) — the closed form is written out (Eq.(30)): Ω(θ)=12Iinj∣Γ~N∣cos⁡ ⁣(Nθ+∠Γ~N).\Omega(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}I_{inj}\vert\tilde\Gamma_N\vert\cos\!\big(N\theta+\angle\tilde\Gamma_N\big).Ω(θ)=21​Iinj​∣Γ~N​∣cos(Nθ+∠Γ~N​). What the paper does not write: a subharmonic (M≠1M\neq1M=1, multiplier) closed form for a sinusoid or a pulse. Footnote 10 honestly explains why: for M≠1M\neq1M=1 the higher-order harmonics the injection needs are often generated by mixing inside the oscillator, a nonlinear phenomenon "not explicitly captured by our framework", partly handled by the model of its reference [25] (which was used to design subharmonic injection-locked frequency multipliers). This page therefore assumes the injection waveform itself carries enough NNN-th harmonic (that is what a pulse generator is for), so that the first-order average of Eq.(29) applies directly, without relying on internal mixing outside the framework.

Where on the waveform is the lock point? (an APF reminder) The LC's Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ is zero at θ=0\theta=0θ=0 (the voltage peak) with maximum slope. So at zero detuning the pulse lands exactly on the peak — no phase shift, maximum β\betaβ, but that is where the [P4] amplitude ISF ∣Λ~∣\vert\tilde\Lambda\vert∣Λ~∣ (APF Δ=τ0Λ~\Delta=\tau_0\tilde\LambdaΔ=τ0​Λ~) is largest (ISF/APF quadrature, paper_004): each pulse kicks the amplitude, which then relaxes with τ0=2Q/ω0\tau_0=2Q/\omega_0τ0​=2Q/ω0​. What makes rings easy to realign in practice is a qmaxq_{max}qmax​ two orders of magnitude smaller (10 fF × 1 V = 10 fC vs pC-level for the LC): for the same 1 fC pulse, β\betaβ differs by 100×; β∼0.5\beta\sim0.5β∼0.5–111 is routine for a ring and nearly impossible for an LC (50 fC into a 10 fC node is qinj/qmax=5q_{inj}/q_{max}=5qinj​/qmax​=5, already outside the linear model). documents.t: Locked but detuned (Δω0≠0\Delta\omega_0\neq0Δω0​=0), the steady-state phase is a sawtooth: linear drift Δω0Tinj\Delta\omega_0T_{inj}Δω0​Tinj​ between pulses, a jump back at each pulse. Peak-to-peak Δθpp=∣Δω0∣Tinj\Delta\theta_{pp}=\vert\Delta\omega_0\vert T_{inj}Δθpp​=∣Δω0​∣Tinj​. The kkk-th harmonic of a sawtooth has amplitude Δθpp/(πk)\Delta\theta_{pp}/(\pi k)Δθpp​/(πk), and for small-angle PM each sideband's power is (amplitude/2)², so spurk≈20log⁡10 ⁣(Δθpp2πk) dBc,spur1=20log⁡10 ⁣(∣Δf0∣fref) \boxed{\ \text{spur}_k\approx20\log_{10}\!\Big(\frac{\Delta\theta_{pp}}{2\pi k}\Big)\ \text{dBc},\qquad \text{spur}_1=20\log_{10}\!\Big(\frac{\vert\Delta f_0\vert}{f_{ref}}\Big)\ } spurk​≈20log10​(2πkΔθpp​​) dBc,spur1​=20log10​(fref​∣Δf0​∣​) ​ The second equality uses Δθpp=2πΔf0Tinj\Delta\theta_{pp}=2\pi\Delta f_0T_{inj}Δθpp​=2πΔf0​Tinj​. In the linearized form often quoted: the fixed-point condition linearized gives β ∣θss−θ0∣=∣Δω0∣Tinj\beta\,\vert\theta_{ss}-\theta_0\vert=\vert\Delta\omega_0\vert T_{inj}β∣θss​−θ0​∣=∣Δω0​∣Tinj​ (θ0\theta_0θ0​ the zero-kick phase), so Δθpp=β∣Δθ∣\Delta\theta_{pp}=\beta\vert\Delta\theta\vertΔθpp​=β∣Δθ∣ — the step at each pulse = β\betaβ × the offset of the lock point from the zero-kick point. Example 4: Δf0=100\Delta f_0=100Δf0​=100 kHz, fref=250f_{ref}=250fref​=250 MHz ⟹ Δθpp=2π×105×4×10−9=2.51\Delta\theta_{pp}=2\pi\times10^{5}\times4\times10^{-9}=2.51Δθpp​=2π×105×4×10−9=2.51 mrad, spur1=20log⁡10(4×10−4)=−68.0\text{spur}_1=20\log_{10}(4\times10^{-4})=-68.0spur1​=20log10​(4×10−4)=−68.0 dBc (FFT of the sawtooth PM in the script: −67.95-67.95−67.95 dBc; at 2fref2f_{ref}2fref​ −73.97-73.97−73.97 vs theory −73.98-73.98−73.98 ✓). Δf0=10\Delta f_0=10Δf0​=10 kHz → −88-88−88 dBc; 1 MHz → −48-48−48 dBc. With β=0.05\beta=0.05β=0.05, a 100 kHz detuning corresponds to a lock point 50.350.350.3 mrad from the zero-kick point. Honest label: this is a first-order estimate — it assumes a linear phase ramp within the interval and ignores direct coupling (feedthrough) of the pulse itself, APF-induced AM, pulse-width effects and nonlinear kicks. What it says: the spur is set by the residual detuning and is independent of β\betaβ (for a fixed detuning the kick must equal the drift); β\betaβ enters through how far the FLL / calibration can push Δf0\Delta f_0Δf0​ down, and through spur ∝β\propto\beta∝β when a fixed phase offset (e.g. a path-delay mismatch) is present.

documents.t: Fixed area qinjq_{inj}qinj​: ∣IN∣=2qinjTinj∣sinc(f0τp)∣\vert I_N\vert=\dfrac{2q_{inj}}{T_{inj}}\big\vert\mathrm{sinc}(f_0\tau_p)\big\vert∣IN​∣=Tinj​2qinj​​​sinc(f0​τp​)​. τp\tau_pτp​ f0τpf_0\tau_pf0​τp​ sinc\mathrm{sinc}sinc ∣I20∣\vert I_{20}\vert∣I20​∣ (qinj=50q_{inj}=50qinj​=50 fC) 10 ps 0.05 0.996 24.90 μA 50 ps 0.25 0.900 22.51 μA 100 ps (T0/2T_0/2T0​/2) 0.5 0.637 15.92 μA 200 ps (T0T_0T0​) 1 0 0 The null at τp=T0\tau_p=T_0τp​=T0​ has a physical meaning: the pulse spans a whole oscillation period, the positive and negative half-cycles of the ISF cancel, and the locking force vanishes — not "a wider pulse is slightly less efficient", a cliff. Design rule: τp≪T0\tau_p\ll T_0τp​≪T0​ (compared with the output period; larger NNN means shorter T0T_0T0​ and harder pulses — one of the hard limits of pushing ILCMs to high frequency). The fixed height IpI_pIp​ view (a current-limited driver): qinj=Ipτpq_{inj}=I_p\tau_pqinj​=Ip​τp​, ∣IN∣=2IpπNsin⁡(πf0τp)\vert I_N\vert=\frac{2I_p}{\pi N}\sin(\pi f_0\tau_p)∣IN​∣=πN2Ip​​sin(πf0​τp​), maximal at τp=T0/2\tau_p=T_0/2τp​=T0​/2 with 2Ip/(πN)2I_p/(\pi N)2Ip​/(πN) (Ip=5I_p=5Ip​=5 mA, N=20N=20N=20: 159 μA) — the kick efficiency is then 0.64, but the total charge is 10× larger. Both views say: make the pulse a small fraction of T0T_0T0​, but there is no need to push it to the limit — 10 ps already captures 99.6%. The ring caveat (lab_40 (b)): the single sinc above holds only for "an ISF with just a fundamental". In general the kick is the box average of the ISF over the pulse window, and the mmm-th ISF harmonic is weighted by sinc(mf0τp)\mathrm{sinc}(mf_0\tau_p)sinc(mf0​τp​). A ring-type ISF concentrates its energy in triangular pulses about 1/f′1/f'1/f′ rad wide (Nst=17N_{st}=17Nst​=17 toy: 0.2460.2460.246 rad = 0.246/(2π)×2000.246/(2\pi)\times2000.246/(2π)×200 ps ≈7.8\approx7.8≈7.8 ps), so the pulse must also be narrower than that width: at the same 10 ps, the LC loses 0.4% while the ring toy's lock range drops to 0.68× (lab_40's unaveraged ODE agrees with the box-average prediction). A ring ILCM needs much narrower pulses than an LC — the flip side of the same node property as "rings win on qmaxq_{max}qmax​".

documents.t: Section 3's conclusion: β=(qinj/qmax) ∣Γ′(θss)∣\beta=(q_{inj}/q_{max})\,\vert\Gamma'(\theta_{ss})\vertβ=(qinj​/qmax​)∣Γ′(θss​)∣. The triangular ISF ties −sin⁡-\sin−sin on slope; the ring's advantage is all in qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (×100\times100×100). Practical meaning: a ring ILCM can run β∼0.5\beta\sim0.5β∼0.5–111 (nearly hard realignment every pulse, in-band almost purely reference), an LC only β∼10−2\beta\sim10^{-2}β∼10−2 (to stay in weak injection, and because a large qinjq_{inj}qinj​ kicks the amplitude). An LC ILCM relies on the oscillator being clean (small κ2\kappa^2κ2); a ring ILCM relies on frequent, forceful realignment. Section 5.4 quantifies this.

documents.t: Write Section 4's two terms together (time-averaged; the full form for small β\betaβ): σout2(N,β)=κ2NT0⋅1−β+β2/2β(2−β)⏟own: random walk between pulses ∝N+N2σψ2⋅β2−β⏟reference×N2\sigma_{out}^2(N,\beta)=\underbrace{\kappa^2NT_0\cdot\frac{1-\beta+\beta^2/2}{\beta(2-\beta)}}_{\text{own: random walk between pulses}\ \propto N} +\underbrace{N^2\sigma_\psi^2\cdot\frac{\beta}{2-\beta}}_{\text{reference}\times N^2}σout2​(N,β)=own: random walk between pulses ∝Nκ2NT0​⋅β(2−β)1−β+β2/2​​​+reference×N2N2σψ2​⋅2−ββ​​​ Own term ∝N\propto N∝N (σ∝N\sigma\propto\sqrt Nσ∝N​): the further apart the pulses, the further the random walk wanders. Reference term: ×N2\times N^2×N2 in the phase domain; but in seconds, Nσψ/(2πf0)=σψ/(2πfref)=σt,refN\sigma_\psi/(2\pi f_0)=\sigma_\psi/(2\pi f_{ref})=\sigma_{t,ref}Nσψ​/(2πf0​)=σψ​/(2πfref​)=σt,ref​ — the reference's time jitter is passed 1:1 to the output, independent of NNN (rule 1 restated: ×N\times N×N in phase = the same seconds). So for fixed f0f_0f0​ and fixed reference time jitter there is no interior optimum in NNN: smaller NNN is always better. With β\betaβ re-optimized for each NNN the script gives, for N=5,10,20,40,80N=5,10,20,40,80N=5,10,20,40,80, σt,min=5.99,7.12,8.46,10.07,11.97\sigma_{t,min}=5.99,7.12,8.46,10.07,11.97σt,min​=5.99,7.12,8.46,10.07,11.97 fs, log-log slope +0.250+0.250+0.250 — σt,min∝N1/4\sigma_{t,min}\propto N^{1/4}σt,min​∝N1/4 (small-β\betaβ closed form: σmin2≈σwNσψ\sigma_{min}^2\approx\sigma_w N\sigma_\psiσmin2​≈σw​Nσψ​, σw∝N\sigma_w\propto\sqrt Nσw​∝N​, NσψN\sigma_\psiNσψ​ fixed ⟹ ∝N1/2\propto N^{1/2}∝N1/2, then square-root). Doubling NNN costs only 19% more jitter — the noise penalty of NNN is mild. What really limits NNN is elsewhere: (i) the lock range ∝1/N\propto1/N∝1/N (398 ppm at N=20N=20N=20) is far below PVT drift ⟹ an FLL is mandatory; (ii) the pulse must be ≪T0\ll T_0≪T0​; (iii) a clean, high-freff_{ref}fref​ reference costs money (if the reference is itself multiplied up from a crystal, Sref∝fref2S_{ref}\propto f_{ref}^2Sref​∝fref2​ and N2SrefN^2S_{ref}N2Sref​ is independent of NNN — same conclusion). If an "optimum NNN" exists it is a system-level cost/power optimum, not an extremum of this noise equation.

Ring (L(1 MHz)=−100\mathcal{L}(1\text{ MHz})=-100L(1 MHz)=−100 dBc/Hz ⟹ κ2=Sϕω2/2=3948\kappa^2=S_\phi\omega^2/2=3948κ2=Sϕ​ω2/2=3948 rad²/s, σw=3.97\sigma_w=3.97σw​=3.97 mrad = 126 fs per TinjT_{inj}Tinj​): βopt=0.695\beta_{opt}=0.695βopt​=0.695, σout,min=123\sigma_{out,min}=123σout,min​=123 fs; 395 fs at β=0.05\beta=0.05β=0.05, 135 fs at β=1\beta=1β=1 — the ring wants a large β\betaβ, and its small qmaxq_{max}qmax​ can afford it. On the spur side (Section 4.4): at fixed detuning the spur is independent of β\betaβ; a larger β\betaβ does not worsen it, and a larger β\betaβ = larger lock range = an easier job for the FLL to squeeze Δf0\Delta f_0Δf0​. documents.t: Forwarded-clock architectures often take a low-rate forwarded clock (e.g. f0/4f_0/4f0​/4 or f0/8f_0/8f0​/8) and multiply it back to full rate at the receiver with an ILO / ILCM: this page's fcf_cfc​ is the jitter-tracking bandwidth — reference (forwarded-clock) jitter below fcf_cfc​ is copied onto the local clock (good for common jitter: transmitter and receiver correlate and cancel), above fcf_cfc​ the local oscillator is on its own (κ2\kappa^2κ2, i.e. the old Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ homework). The trade-off has the same structure as item 5 of injection_locking_noise and serdes_clocking_connection, only with N>1N\gt1N>1 and discrete updates.

documents.t: import numpy as np f0, qmax, kappa2 = 5e9, 1e-12, 0.125 # Hz, C, rad^2/s (canonical) N, qinj, tau_p = 20, 50e-15, 10e-12 # multiplication ratio, injected charge [C], pulse width [s] fref = f0/N; Tinj = 1/fref # 250 MHz, 4 ns I_N = 2*qinj/Tinj*abs(np.sinc(N*fref*tau_p)) # N-th injection harmonic amplitude [A] (sinc argument = f0*tau_p) wL = 0.5*I_N*(1/qmax) # route 1: (1/2)|I_N||Gt_1| [rad/s] beta = qinj/qmax*abs(np.sinc(f0*tau_p)) # realignment factor (lock-range centre, incl. pulse width) fc = beta*fref/(2*np.pi*(1-beta)) # corner [Hz] sw2 = kappa2*Tinj # phase variance accumulated per T_inj [rad^2] var_avg = sw2*(1-beta+beta**2/2)/(beta*(2-beta)) S_ref = 2*10**(-160/10); sig_psi2 = S_ref*fref/2 # assumed -160 dBc/Hz white reference var_ref = beta*N**2*sig_psi2/(2-beta) b_opt = np.sqrt(sw2/(N**2*sig_psi2)) print(I_N*1e6) # -> 24.90 μA print(wL, wL/2/np.pi/1e6) # -> 1.245e7 rad/s, 1.981 MHz print(qinj/(qmax*Tinj)/2/np.pi/1e6) # -> 1.989 MHz (impulse route, sinc=0.996 apart) print(beta, -1/np.log(1-beta)) # -> 0.0498, 19.58 injections (to 1/e) print(fc/1e6) # -> 2.085 MHz print(np.sqrt(var_avg)*1e6, np.sqrt(var_avg)/(2*np.pi*f0)*1e15) # -> 69.99 μrad, 2.228 fs print(10*np.log10(2*kappa2*Tinj**2/beta**2/2)) # -> -150.9 dBc/Hz own-noise plateau print(np.sqrt(var_ref)/(2*np.pi*f0)*1e15, 10*np.log10(N**2*S_ref/2)) # -> 16.08 fs, -134.0 dBc/Hz reference in-band print(b_opt, b_opt*qmax*1e15) # -> 0.00707, 7.07 fC print(20*np.log10(100e3/fref)) # -> -67.96 dBc (f_ref spur for a 100 kHz detuning) (β=0.0498\beta=0.0498β=0.0498 includes the sinc of the 10 ps pulse; the table in Section 4 uses the delta train's β=0.05\beta=0.05β=0.05, 0.4% apart.)

documents.t: Prerequisites: flicker_noise_upconversion (the full flicker → 1/f31/f^31/f3 derivation; this page is its design-facing counterpart), fourier_series_of_isf (the ISF's Fourier coefficients c0,cnc_0,c_nc0​,cn​ and Parseval), device_noise_mapping (the c0c_0c0​ of the effective ISF Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α is the real culprit) | Next: waveform_slope, serdes_clocking_connection This page answers a question that must be settled at the layout/topology stage: why does a waveform with symmetric rise/fall have noticeably lower close-in (near-carrier) 1/f³ phase noise? The answer is hidden entirely in one Fourier coefficient of the ISF — the DC term c0c_0c0​. Physical intuition (conclusion first): a device's flicker noise (1/f noise, slow-varying noise in the gate/channel) is a near-DC, low-frequency noise. Low-frequency noise should not normally contaminate a high-frequency carrier — but the ISF is a periodic function, and its DC component c0/2c_0/2c0​/2 acts like a "rectifier": it accumulates low-frequency device noise with a persistent sign into the phase, upconverting it to a close-in 1/f³ skirt near the carrier. If the rise/fall is perfectly symmetric, the ISF's positive and negative areas cancel over one period, c0→0c_0\to0c0​→0, and this upconversion channel is shut off.
documents.s: Waveform Symmetry and Flicker Upconversion

documents.t: Write the ISF as a Fourier series ([P1] Eq.(12), p.183): Γ(ω0τ)=c02+∑n=1∞cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=\frac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)Γ(ω0​τ)=2c0​​+n=1∑∞​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​) Substitute into the LTV phase response ([P1] Eq.(13), p.183), splitting the phase into contributions from each harmonic: ϕ(t)=1qmax ⁣[c02 ⁣∫−∞t ⁣in dτ+∑n=1∞cn ⁣∫−∞t ⁣incos⁡(nω0τ+θn) dτ]\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\!\left[\frac{c_0}{2}\!\int_{-\infty}^{t}\!i_n\,d\tau+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\!\int_{-\infty}^{t}\!i_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\,d\tau\right]ϕ(t)=qmax​1​[2c0​​∫−∞t​in​dτ+n=1∑∞​cn​∫−∞t​in​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)dτ] Key observation: device flicker-noise energy is concentrated near DC (Δω≪ω0\Delta\omega\ll\omega_0Δω≪ω0​). In the expression above, every cnc_ncn​ term (n≥1n\ge1n≥1) carries a cos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)cos(nω0​τ+θn​) factor, which multiplies the low-frequency noise by a high-frequency carrier — a mixing operation that moves the noise to near ±nω0\pm n\omega_0±nω0​, away from DC. Only the c0/2c_0/2c0​/2 term has no carrier: it performs a pure integration of the low-frequency noise. Low-frequency noise stays nearly the same sign over an extended interval, so the integral accumulates without cancelling, continuously driving the close-in phase → upconverted into 1/f³. In one line: cnc_ncn​ acts like a mixer (it moves the noise away), while c0c_0c0​ acts like an integrator (it retains and amplifies DC noise).
documents.s: Step 1: why only c0c_0c0​ upconverts flicker

documents.t: Feed the device flicker model ([P1] Eq.(22), p.185) in,1/f2‾=in2‾⋅ω1/fΔω\overline{i_{n,1/f}^2}=\overline{i_n^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}in,1/f2​​=in2​​⋅Δωω1/f​​ into the phase noise from the c0c_0c0​-only channel to get the 1/f³ region ([P1] Eq.(23), p.185): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(c02qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf8 Δω2⋅ω1/fΔω)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{8\,\Delta\omega^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​c02​​⋅8Δω2in2​​/Δf​⋅Δωω1/f​​) Slope dimension check: 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 (from the phase integration) times 1/Δω1/\Delta\omega1/Δω (from flicker's ω1/f/Δω\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omegaω1/f​/Δω factor) = 1/Δω31/\Delta\omega^31/Δω3 → −30-30−30 dB per decade, exactly 1/f³. ✓ Key point: the numerator is c02c_0^2c02​. A symmetric waveform drives c0→0c_0\to0c0​→0 → the entire 1/f³ region is suppressed. Intersecting the 1/f³ region with the 1/f² region ([P1] Eq.(21)) defines the 1/f³ corner ([P1] Eq.(24), p.185): Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c022 Γrms2≈ω1/f(c0c1)2\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}\approx\omega_{1/f}\left(\frac{c_0}{c_1}\right)^2Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​≈ω1/f​(c1​c0​​)2 Step-by-step algebra: how the corner falls out of "the two regions are equal." The corner is defined as the offset where the 1/f³ region and the 1/f² region are exactly equal in height. Setting the two (linear, not-yet-log) power spectral densities equal: c02qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf8 Δω2⋅ω1/fΔω⏟1/f3 region (inside the brackets of Eq.23)=Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2⏟1/f2 region (inside the brackets of Eq.21)c028⋅ω1/fΔω=Γrms24(both sides cancel qmax2, in2‾/Δf, Δω2)ω1/fΔω=Γrms24⋅8c02=2 Γrms2c02⇒Δω=Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c022 Γrms2.\begin{aligned} \underbrace{\frac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{8\,\Delta\omega^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}}_{\text{1/f}^3\text{ region (inside the brackets of Eq.23)}} &=\underbrace{\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}}_{\text{1/f}^2\text{ region (inside the brackets of Eq.21)}} \\[4pt] \frac{c_0^2}{8}\cdot\frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}&=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{4} \qquad(\text{both sides cancel }q_{max}^2,\ \overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f,\ \Delta\omega^2) \\[4pt] \frac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}&=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{4}\cdot\frac{8}{c_0^2}=\frac{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}{c_0^2} \\[4pt] \Rightarrow\quad \Delta\omega=\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}&=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2}. \end{aligned}1/f3 region (inside the brackets of Eq.23)qmax2​c02​​⋅8Δω2in2​​/Δf​⋅Δωω1/f​​​​8c02​​⋅Δωω1/f​​Δωω1/f​​⇒Δω=Δω1/f3​​=1/f2 region (inside the brackets of Eq.21)qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​​​=4Γrms2​​(both sides cancel qmax2​, in2​​/Δf, Δω2)=4Γrms2​​⋅c02​8​=c02​2Γrms2​​=ω1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​.​ What each step uses: the second line is just "dividing out the factors common to both sides" (pure algebra, no new physics); note that in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf, qmax2q_{max}^2qmax2​, and Δω2\Delta\omega^2Δω2 are the same value in both regions, so they cancel. Why Δω2\Delta\omega^2Δω2 also cancels: the 1/f³ region is 1/Δω31/\Delta\omega^31/Δω3, the 1/f² region is 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2; dividing leaves a single 1/Δω1/\Delta\omega1/Δω — exactly the ω1/f/Δω\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omegaω1/f​/Δω factor still on the left in line 2 above. Solving this linear equation gives the corner. Getting to ≈(c0/c1)2\approx(c_0/c_1)^2≈(c0​/c1​)2: using Parseval ([P1] Eq.(20)) 2Γrms2=∑cn22\Gamma_{rms}^2=\sum c_n^22Γrms2​=∑cn2​; if the ISF is dominated by its fundamental (c1≫c2,c3,…c_1\gg c_2,c_3,\dotsc1​≫c2​,c3​,…), then 2Γrms2≈c122\Gamma_{rms}^2\approx c_1^22Γrms2​≈c12​, giving Δω1/f3≈ω1/f(c0/c1)2\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}\approx\omega_{1/f}(c_0/c_1)^2Δω1/f3​≈ω1/f​(c0​/c1​)2. Dimension check: on the right, ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ is rad/s, and c02/(2Γrms2)c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)c02​/(2Γrms2​) is dimensionless/dimensionless = dimensionless, so Δω1/f3\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}Δω1/f3​ is rad/s ✓. The most important design implication (claim C5): the 1/f³ corner is not equal to the device's 1/f corner ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​! It is scaled by a factor c02/(2Γrms2)c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)c02​/(2Γrms2​). The smaller c0c_0c0​ is, the further the corner is pushed below ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ — i.e., for the same transistor with the same device 1/f corner, simply making the waveform symmetric can push the 1/f³ skirt's knee down several decades in frequency. Notation trap (see notation): c0c_0c0​ is the Fourier coefficient; the ISF's DC value is c0/2c_0/2c0​/2. Eq.(24) uses the coefficient c0c_0c0​ — don't drop a factor of 2 here.
documents.s: Step 2: 1/f³ phase noise and the corner formula

documents.t: c0c_0c0​ is (twice) the ISF's average over one period: c02=12π∫02πΓ(x) dx⇒c0=1π∫02πΓ(x) dx\frac{c_0}{2}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma(x)\,dx\quad\Rightarrow\quad c_0=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma(x)\,dx2c0​​=2π1​∫02π​Γ(x)dx⇒c0​=π1​∫02π​Γ(x)dx The ISF's shape is roughly proportional to the waveform slope (large slope near a zero crossing → large ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣; zero slope at the peak → Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0; see waveform_slope). If the rise and fall segments have symmetric shapes (rise slope = mirror image of fall slope), the ISF values over the rising and falling half-periods are equal in magnitude, opposite in sign, and cancel when integrated over one period → c0=0c_0=0c0​=0. An ideal LC's Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ is exactly this kind of odd symmetry: ∫02π(−sin⁡θ) dθ=0\int_0^{2\pi}(-\sin\theta)\,d\theta=0∫02π​(−sinθ)dθ=0, so an ideal LC naturally has c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 and very weak 1/f³ upconversion. Asymmetry (e.g. fast rise, slow fall, or even-order harmonics that make the waveform top/bottom asymmetric) shifts the ISF's average away from 0 → c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0. The figure below overlays a symmetric and an asymmetric ISF: the symmetric one has its DC average pinned at 0, while the asymmetric one is lifted by a "DC offset" of c0/2c_0/2c0​/2 — that offset is the culprit behind flicker upconversion. Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Title reads: "c0≠0 才會把 1/f noise upconvert 到 close-in phase noise" = only c0≠0 upconverts 1/f noise into close-in phase noise. Feeding actual device flicker into a simulation makes the close-in difference very clear: the asymmetric waveform shows a steep 1/f³ skirt, while the symmetric waveform shows almost none (only 1/f² and the floor remain). Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Title reads: "Flicker upconversion: ISF 對稱性 (c0) 決定 close-in 1/f³" = Flicker upconversion: the ISF's symmetry (c0) determines the close-in 1/f³ term. Both figures are pedagogical toy models (not transistor-level): the ISF uses an analytic shape (symmetric cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ, asymmetric cos⁡θ+0.4\cos\theta+0.4cosθ+0.4, etc.), and flicker is a synthesized 1/f sequence. They faithfully illustrate "c0c_0c0​ determines 1/f³" causally, but are not a measurement of any real transistor. Full scripts: simulations/lab_05_fourier_isf.py, simulations/lab_07_flicker_noise.py.
documents.s: Step 3: how symmetry drives c0→0c_0\to0c0​→0

documents.t: The first example uses an assumed c0c_0c0​ (illustrative); the second switches to the closed forms of [P2] Appendix B and computes c0c_0c0​ and the corner directly from the topology parameters (N,A)(N,A)(N,A) — full derivation in asymmetric_isf_closed_form. Symmetric waveform (c0≈0c_0\approx0c0​≈0): theoretically Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c02/(2Γrms2)→0\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)\to0Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅c02​/(2Γrms2​)→0, and the 1/f³ corner is pushed to extremely low frequency — in practice it is dominated by the small residual c0c_0c0​ set by mismatch (see the knobs table below). Asymmetric waveform (illustrative, c0c_0c0​ assumed): take c0=0.4c_0=0.4c0​=0.4, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5 (so c02/(2Γrms2)=0.16/(2×0.25)=0.32c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)=0.16/(2\times0.25)=0.32c02​/(2Γrms2​)=0.16/(2×0.25)=0.32). If the device f1/f=1f_{1/f}=1f1/f​=1 MHz, then f1/f3=f1/f⋅c022Γrms2=1 MHz×0.32=320 kHz.f_{1/f^3}=f_{1/f}\cdot\frac{c_0^2}{2\Gamma_{rms}^2}=1\ \text{MHz}\times0.32=320\ \text{kHz}.f1/f3​=f1/f​⋅2Γrms2​c02​​=1 MHz×0.32=320 kHz. Intuition: lowering c0c_0c0​ from 0.4 to 0.04 (10× smaller) drops the corner by 100× (c02c_0^2c02​) — from 320 kHz down to 3.2 kHz. In other words, each order-of-magnitude improvement in symmetry shrinks the reach of the 1/f³ skirt by two orders of magnitude — an extremely cost-effective design lever. Asymmetric waveform (computed, directly from ring topology parameters): a ring with N=5N=5N=5, η=1\eta=1η=1, whose rise is 1.5× steeper than its fall (asymmetry ratio A=frise′/ffall′=1.5A=f'_{rise}/f'_{fall}=1.5A=frise′​/ffall′​=1.5). The [P2] App. B closed forms (Eq.(55)/(56)/(57), p.803; derivation in asymmetric_isf_closed_form) directly give Γrms=0.2428,c0=2 Γdc=−0.1005,f1/f3=f1/f⋅32ηN⋅(1−A)21−A+A2=42.9 kHz.\Gamma_{rms}=0.2428,\qquad c_0=2\,\Gamma_{dc}=-0.1005,\qquad f_{1/f^3}=f_{1/f}\cdot\frac{3}{2\eta N}\cdot\frac{(1-A)^2}{1-A+A^2}=42.9\ \text{kHz}.Γrms​=0.2428,c0​=2Γdc​=−0.1005,f1/f3​=f1/f​⋅2ηN3​⋅1−A+A2(1−A)2​=42.9 kHz. Convention flag: 42.86 kHz is the [P2] Eq.(7)/(57) bookkeeping; substituting c0=2Γdcc_0=2\Gamma_{dc}c0​=2Γdc​ back into [P1] Eq.(24) above yields 2×=85.712\times=85.712×=85.71 kHz (a DC-channel weighting convention difference; see the flag on the new page. Scalings and ratios are unaffected). The numbers are verified by simulations/lab_33_asymmetry_corner.py (closed forms vs numeric integration, error ∼10−9\sim10^{-9}∼10−9). New design message ([P2]'s own sentence, p.803): at fixed AAA the corner is ∝1/N\propto1/N∝1/N — rings with fewer stages have a higher flicker corner (at A=1.5A=1.5A=1.5: N=3→71.43N=3\to71.43N=3→71.43 kHz, N=15→14.29N=15\to14.29N=15→14.29 kHz). White-region phase noise is approximately N-independent ([P2] Eq.(23)), but the 1/f³ knee is pushed down by the stage count. Corresponding experimental evidence: [P2] Fig. 17, p.802 measures ring-oscillator phase noise vs. "symmetry control voltage," which shows a minimum at the symmetry point — direct support for the design rule "symmetric → low 1/f³." (Verified: [P2] Fig. 17, p.802, "Phase noise versus symmetry voltage for oscillator number 7" — the y-axis is the 1/f³ corner frequency, showing a clear dip to a minimum at the symmetry point.)

documents.t: Knob How Why it lowers c0c_0c0​ Cost/notes Symmetric rise/fall NMOS/PMOS drive-strength or pull-up/pull-down symmetry (ring); differential topology ISF's upper and lower half-periods cancel → average → 0 needs sizing/bias tuning; process offset leaves residual c0c_0c0​ Differential / even-harmonic suppression fully differential, symmetric loads, suppress even harmonics even harmonics make the waveform top/bottom asymmetric → raise c0c_0c0​ 2× devices, area, power Symmetric load (ring) use a symmetric load ([P2]'s approach) instead of a single-ended inverter delay cell matches rise/fall shape [P2] Fig. 17's "symmetry voltage" tunes exactly this Reduce DC-bias-point drift control duty cycle near 50% duty deviating from 50% means a DC-asymmetric waveform → c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0 needs duty-cycle correction Directly lower device flicker use large-area, PMOS, buried-channel devices lowers ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ itself (does not change c0c_0c0​, but lowers the magnitude of 1/f³) large area → large parasitic capacitance → lowers f0f_0f0​ More on the duty-cycle row: a second path through tank QQQ — a high-QQQ LC tank filters out the higher harmonics of the drive waveform (e.g. the differential-pair current) on its own, pulling the output waveform's duty cycle toward 50% and thereby simultaneously lowering c0c_0c0​ / the even-order cnc_ncn​ ([P1] Sec. IV, end; see the "more linear loads" note in flicker_noise_upconversion). This path is independent of the other way high QQQ helps — lowering the white-noise 1/f21/f^21/f2 floor through Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (see the QQQ discussion in lc_vs_ring). The two mechanisms are different — one governs 1/f31/f^31/f3 (via c0c_0c0​), the other 1/f21/f^21/f2 (via Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​) — but both favor high QQQ. Conversely, a non-50% duty cycle generally makes the even-order cnc_ncn​ larger. Note the two categories: the first four knobs change c0c_0c0​ / the f1/f3f_{1/f^3}f1/f3​ corner location; the last one changes the device ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ / the overall height of 1/f³. Both can be used in design, but "making it symmetric" is usually free (no extra power) — take that shot first.

documents.t: The following two examples demonstrate the most cost-effective design lever — "improving symmetry lowers the 1/f³ corner" — reusing this site's canonical Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, device f1/f=1f_{1/f}=1f1/f​=1 MHz. Both use an illustrative assumed c0c_0c0​ (conversion practice); to compute the real c0c_0c0​ from topology parameters (N,A)(N,A)(N,A), see asymmetric_isf_closed_form. Example 1 (baseline: compute the 1/f³ corner for an asymmetric waveform; c0c_0c0​ is an illustrative assumed value) Given c0=0.4c_0=0.4c0​=0.4, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, device 1/f corner f1/f=1f_{1/f}=1f1/f​=1 MHz, find the 1/f³ corner f1/f3f_{1/f^3}f1/f3​. Step-by-step substitution (with units), using the just-derived f1/f3=f1/f⋅c02/(2Γrms2)f_{1/f^3}=f_{1/f}\cdot c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)f1/f3​=f1/f​⋅c02​/(2Γrms2​): c022Γrms2=(0.4)22×(0.5)2=0.160.50=0.32(dimensionless)f1/f3=f1/f×0.32=1 MHz×0.32=0.32 MHz=320 kHz.\begin{aligned} \frac{c_0^2}{2\Gamma_{rms}^2}&=\frac{(0.4)^2}{2\times(0.5)^2}=\frac{0.16}{0.50}=0.32\quad(\text{dimensionless}) \\[4pt] f_{1/f^3}&=f_{1/f}\times0.32=1\ \text{MHz}\times0.32=0.32\ \text{MHz}=320\ \text{kHz}. \end{aligned}2Γrms2​c02​​f1/f3​​=2×(0.5)2(0.4)2​=0.500.16​=0.32(dimensionless)=f1/f​×0.32=1 MHz×0.32=0.32 MHz=320 kHz.​ Result: f1/f3=320f_{1/f^3}=320f1/f3​=320 kHz — lower than the device's own 1 MHz corner, because c02/(2Γrms2)=0.32<1c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)=0.32 < 1c02​/(2Γrms2​)=0.32<1. Dimension check: [Hz]×[dimensionless]=[Hz][\text{Hz}]\times[\text{dimensionless}]=[\text{Hz}][Hz]×[dimensionless]=[Hz] ✓ (a ratio of frequencies works equally in Hz or rad/s, since f1/f3/f1/f=ω1/f3/ω1/ff_{1/f^3}/f_{1/f}=\omega_{1/f^3}/\omega_{1/f}f1/f3​/f1/f​=ω1/f3​/ω1/f​ and the 2π2\pi2π's cancel). One-line Python check (using the canonical conversion; simulations/common/ has no dedicated corner function, so compute it directly): c0, gamma_rms, f_1f = 0.4, 0.5, 1e6 f_1f3 = f_1f * c0**2 / (2 * gamma_rms**2) print(f_1f3 / 1e3, "kHz") # -> 320.0 kHz Example 2 (improving symmetry by one order of magnitude → corner drops two orders of magnitude) Make the waveform more symmetric so c0c_0c0​ drops from 0.40.40.4 to 0.040.040.04 (10× smaller), with Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and f1/ff_{1/f}f1/f​ unchanged. Find the new corner, and express in dB how much the heights of the two 1/f³ asymptotes (extrapolated skirts) differ. Step-by-step substitution (with units): f1/f3′=f1/f⋅(c0′)22Γrms2=1 MHz×(0.04)22×(0.5)2=1 MHz×0.00160.5=1 MHz×3.2×10−3=3.2 kHz.\begin{aligned} f_{1/f^3}'&=f_{1/f}\cdot\frac{(c_0')^2}{2\Gamma_{rms}^2}=1\ \text{MHz}\times\frac{(0.04)^2}{2\times(0.5)^2} =1\ \text{MHz}\times\frac{0.0016}{0.5}=1\ \text{MHz}\times3.2\times10^{-3}=3.2\ \text{kHz}. \end{aligned}f1/f3′​​=f1/f​⋅2Γrms2​(c0′​)2​=1 MHz×2×(0.5)2(0.04)2​=1 MHz×0.50.0016​=1 MHz×3.2×10−3=3.2 kHz.​ The corner drops from 320320320 kHz → 3.23.23.2 kHz (a 100× reduction === the square of the c0c_0c0​ ratio, 10210^2102). Note that after improvement the corner falls to 3.23.23.2 kHz, so Δf=10\Delta f=10Δf=10 kHz for the improved waveform now lies in the 1/f² region (no longer 1/f³); what follows compares the heights of the two 1/f³ asymptotes (extrapolated skirts). 1/f³ phase noise ([P1] Eq.(23)) ∝c02\propto c_0^2∝c02​, so the change in height is ΔL=10log⁡10 ⁣((c0′)2c02)=10log⁡10 ⁣(0.0420.42)=10log⁡10(0.01)=−20 dB.\Delta\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{(c_0')^2}{c_0^2}\right)=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{0.04^2}{0.4^2}\right)=10\log_{10}(0.01)=-20\ \text{dB}.ΔL=10log10​(c02​(c0′​)2​)=10log10​(0.420.042​)=10log10​(0.01)=−20 dB. Result: lowering c0c_0c0​ by 10× → the 1/f³ skirt overall drops 20 dB, and the corner drops 100× (to 3.2 kHz). "Each order-of-magnitude improvement in symmetry shrinks the reach of 1/f³ by two orders of magnitude" is exactly this c02c_0^2c02​ law. Dimension check: dB is a log of a power ratio (dimensionless) ✓; the corner is still in Hz ✓. One-line Python check: import numpy as np c0_old, c0_new = 0.4, 0.04 print("corner ratio:", (c0_new/c0_old)**2, # -> 0.01 (3.2 kHz / 320 kHz) "; dL =", 10*np.log10((c0_new/c0_old)**2), "dB") # -> -20.0 dB Both examples are pedagogical toys (not transistor-level): c0c_0c0​ uses assumed values representing "residual asymmetry." A real circuit's c0c_0c0​ must be extracted from the effective ISF (including cyclostationary α\alphaα); see device_noise_mapping.

documents.t: Only the ISF's DC coefficient c0c_0c0​ upconverts device 1/f noise into close-in 1/f³ ([P1] Eq.(23)). 1/f³ corner =ω1/f⋅c02/(2Γrms2)=\omega_{1/f}\cdot c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)=ω1/f​⋅c02​/(2Γrms2​), not equal to the device's 1/f corner ([P1] Eq.(24)). Symmetric rise/fall → the ISF cancels over one period → c0→0c_0\to0c0​→0 → the 1/f³ corner is pushed to very low frequency. Lowering c0c_0c0​ by 10× lowers the 1/f³ corner by 100× (c02c_0^2c02​): illustrative c0=0.4c_0=0.4c0​=0.4, f1/f=1f_{1/f}=1f1/f​=1 MHz → corner 320 kHz. A ring's c0c_0c0​ can be computed directly from topology: the [P2] App. B closed forms give c0=2Γdc=4πη2N21−A1+Ac_0=2\Gamma_{dc}=\frac{4\pi}{\eta^2N^2}\frac{1-A}{1+A}c0​=2Γdc​=η2N24π​1+A1−A​ and corner ∝(1−A)21−A+A2⋅1N\propto\frac{(1-A)^2}{1-A+A^2}\cdot\frac{1}{N}∝1−A+A2(1−A)2​⋅N1​ (N=5N=5N=5, A=1.5→42.9A=1.5\to42.9A=1.5→42.9 kHz; [P1] Eq.(24) convention ×2\times2×2) — see asymmetric_isf_closed_form. Design levers: differential, symmetric loads, 50% duty; must look at the c0c_0c0​ of the effective ISF (including α\alphaα). Experiment: [P2] Fig. 17, phase noise vs. symmetry voltage, shows a minimum.

documents.t: Prerequisites: white_noise_to_phase_noise ([P1] Eq.(21) signature result L∝Γrms2/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2L∝Γrms2​/qmax2​), impulse_to_phase_shift (why qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=CV_{max}qmax​=CVmax​ lands in the denominator), tank_Q_and_energy_restoration (why high QQQ is "nearly-free swing", where RpR_pRp​ comes from) | Next: varactor_tuning_supply_pushing, lc_vs_ring This page answers the question asked earliest — and most often underestimated — in oscillator design: why does making the tank's (LC resonator's) voltage swing larger lower phase noise? The answer is the cleanest scaling in ISF theory: phase noise is inversely proportional to qmax2q_{max}^2qmax2​, and qmax=CnodeVmaxq_{max}=C_{node}V_{max}qmax​=Cnode​Vmax​ is set directly by swing. Physical intuition (conclusion first): phase error =ΓqmaxΔq=\dfrac{\Gamma}{q_{max}}\Delta q=qmax​Γ​Δq — the denominator is qmaxq_{max}qmax​. The larger the swing, the more charge qmaxq_{max}qmax​ the signal carries, and the same lump of noise charge Δq\Delta qΔq becomes proportionally more "negligible" against it, so the phase it can push is smaller. Make the signal big, outweigh the noise — this is the first principle of every low-phase-noise design. The cost: swing is bounded by supply / headroom, and pushing swing up usually burns more power.
documents.s: Tank swing, qmaxq_{max}qmax​, and phase noise

documents.t: qmaxq_{max}qmax​ is "the maximum charge corresponding to the signal swing" at a node: qmax=Cnode Vmaxq_{max}=C_{node}\,V_{max}qmax​=Cnode​Vmax​ Unit check: [F]⋅[V]=[C][\text{F}]\cdot[\text{V}]=[\text{C}][F]⋅[V]=[C] ✓. It appears in the denominator of the impulse→phase relation ([P1] Eq.(10)–(11), p.182): Δϕ=ΓqmaxΔq\Delta\phi=\dfrac{\Gamma}{q_{max}}\Delta qΔϕ=qmax​Γ​Δq. Meaning: Δq/qmax\Delta q/q_{max}Δq/qmax​ is "the injected charge as a fraction of the signal charge." Larger qmaxq_{max}qmax​ → the same Δq\Delta qΔq produces a smaller relative disturbance → phase is more stable. Γ\GammaΓ (a dimensionless shape) itself does not change with swing; swing only moves qmaxq_{max}qmax​.

documents.t: The signature result for white-noise-induced 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise ([P1] Eq.(21), p.185): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4 Δω2)\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)L{Δω}=10log10​(qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​) The denominator has qmax2q_{max}^2qmax2​. So L∝1/qmax2\mathcal{L}\propto1/q_{max}^2L∝1/qmax2​. Scaling (claim C3): doubling qmaxq_{max}qmax​ → L\mathcal{L}L drops by 10log⁡10(22)=6.0210\log_{10}(2^2)=6.0210log10​(22)=6.02 dB. Every doubling of swing (with CCC fixed) improves phase noise by 6 dB. Step-by-step algebra: how "qmaxq_{max}qmax​ doubled → −6 dB" falls out of Eq.(21). Let qmax→qmax′=2qmaxq_{max}\to q_{max}'=2q_{max}qmax​→qmax′​=2qmax​, with everything else (Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf, Δω\Delta\omegaΔω) unchanged. Phase noise is "dB = 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​(power ratio inside the brackets)", so we only need the new/old ratio inside the brackets: PnewPold=Γrms2(2qmax)2⋅in2‾/Δf4Δω2Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4Δω2 = 1/(2qmax)21/qmax2 = qmax2(2qmax)2 = 14,ΔL=Lnew−Lold=10log⁡10 ⁣(PnewPold)=10log⁡10 ⁣(14)=−10log⁡104=−20log⁡102=−20×0.30103=−6.02 dB.\begin{aligned} \frac{P_{new}}{P_{old}} &=\frac{\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{(2q_{max})^2}\cdot\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\Delta\omega^2}} {\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4\Delta\omega^2}} \;=\;\frac{1/(2q_{max})^2}{1/q_{max}^2} \;=\;\frac{q_{max}^2}{(2q_{max})^2} \;=\;\frac{1}{4}, \\[6pt] \Delta\mathcal{L}&=\mathcal{L}_{new}-\mathcal{L}_{old} =10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P_{new}}{P_{old}}\right) =10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac14\right) =-10\log_{10}4 \\[4pt] &=-20\log_{10}2=-20\times0.30103=-6.02\ \text{dB}. \end{aligned}Pold​Pnew​​ΔL​=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​(2qmax​)2Γrms2​​⋅4Δω2in2​​/Δf​​=1/qmax2​1/(2qmax​)2​=(2qmax​)2qmax2​​=41​,=Lnew​−Lold​=10log10​(Pold​Pnew​​)=10log10​(41​)=−10log10​4=−20log10​2=−20×0.30103=−6.02 dB.​ What each step uses: line 1 cancels all common factors (Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​, in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf, 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2), leaving only the ratio of qmaxq_{max}qmax​; lines 2→3 use the log identity log⁡104=log⁡1022=2log⁡102\log_{10}4=\log_{10}2^2=2\log_{10}2log10​4=log10​22=2log10​2. Why "6 dB/octave" and not 3 dB: because L∝qmax−2\mathcal{L}\propto q_{max}^{-2}L∝qmax−2​ is an inverse-square law — a power ratio of 14\tfrac1441​ corresponds to −6-6−6 dB (not −3-3−3 dB; −3-3−3 dB is 12\tfrac1221​). Doubling voltage/charge → power ratio 4×4\times4× → 20log⁡10220\log_{10}220log10​2. Dimension check: the ratio Pnew/PoldP_{new}/P_{old}Pnew​/Pold​ is dimensionless (same units cancel) → 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ gives dB (dimensionless) ✓. Dimension check (the whole bracket must be dimensionless to give dBc/Hz): (dimensionless)2[C]2⋅[A2/Hz][rad/s]2=[A2/Hz][C2][s−2]\dfrac{(\text{dimensionless})^2}{[\text{C}]^2}\cdot\dfrac{[\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}]}{[\text{rad/s}]^2} =\dfrac{[\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}]}{[\text{C}^2][\text{s}^{-2}]}[C]2(dimensionless)2​⋅[rad/s]2[A2/Hz]​=[C2][s−2][A2/Hz]​. Using [A]=[C/s][\text{A}]=[\text{C/s}][A]=[C/s]: =[C2s−2/Hz][C2s−2]=1[Hz]=\dfrac{[\text{C}^2\text{s}^{-2}/\text{Hz}]}{[\text{C}^2\text{s}^{-2}]}=\dfrac{1}{[\text{Hz}]}=[C2s−2][C2s−2/Hz]​=[Hz]1​. in2‾/Δf\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fin2​​/Δf is itself already per-Hz, and it is exactly this per-Hz factor that makes the absolute L\mathcal{L}L per-Hz (dBc/Hz); and (as above) the ratio Pnew/PoldP_{new}/P_{old}Pnew​/Pold​ itself is dimensionless, so 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ gives dB ✓. The same 1/qmax21/q_{max}^21/qmax2​ also appears in the ring oscillator's accumulated-jitter proportionality constant ([P2] Eq.(11)–(12), p.793): κ2∝Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾Δf\kappa^2\propto\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}κ2∝qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δfin2​​​ So "larger swing lowers phase noise" and "larger swing lowers jitter" are the same statement — they share the core ratio Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​. ([P2] Eq.(12), p.793 as printed: κt=Γrmsqmax ω012 in2‾/Δf\kappa_t=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}}{q_{max}\,\omega_0}\sqrt{\tfrac12\,\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}κt​=qmax​ω0​Γrms​​21​in2​​/Δf​, the time version with ω0\omega_0ω0​ in the denominator; phase version κ=ω0κt\kappa=\omega_0\kappa_tκ=ω0​κt​, re-verified in v11.)
documents.s: Step 2: the phase-noise ∝1/qmax2\propto 1/q_{max}^2∝1/qmax2​ scaling

documents.t: qmax=C⋅Vmaxq_{max}=C\cdot V_{max}qmax​=C⋅Vmax​, so in principle either raising CCC or raising VmaxV_{max}Vmax​ raises qmaxq_{max}qmax​. But the two routes have completely different costs: Route Change in qmaxq_{max}qmax​ Effect on phase noise Side effect Increase VmaxV_{max}Vmax​ (swing) qmax∝Vmaxq_{max}\propto V_{max}qmax​∝Vmax​ L∝1/Vmax2\mathcal{L}\propto1/V_{max}^2L∝1/Vmax2​ (most effective) Limited by supply / breakdown / headroom; needs more bias current to sustain swing Increase CCC (tank capacitance) qmax∝Cq_{max}\propto Cqmax​∝C Looks like ∝1/C2\propto1/C^2∝1/C2, but there is a trap ↓ To hold f0f_0f0​, LLL must drop proportionally; sustaining the same swing needs a larger tank current (QQQ, gmg_mgm​ limited); f0=1/LCf_0=1/\sqrt{LC}f0​=1/LC​ is tied down Increasing swing is usually the first choice: direct, 6 dB/octave, and does not move f0f_0f0​. Increasing CCC has a trap: in an LC tank f0=1/(2πLC)f_0=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})f0​=1/(2πLC​), so raising CCC requires lowering LLL proportionally; sustaining the same swing voltage then needs more tank current (QQQ, gmg_mgm​ limited), and the real-world improvement is often eaten by "the extra power/noise spent driving the larger CCC." The genuinely clean lever is pushing swing to the headroom limit within the power budget.
documents.s: Step 3: two routes to raise qmaxq_{max}qmax​ — increase VmaxV_{max}Vmax​ vs. increase CCC

documents.t: Swing cannot grow without bound — it hits two walls, supply and device: Voltage headroom: the single-ended swing limit of a differential LC tank ranges from about the supply VDDV_{DD}VDD​ (current-limited regime) up to ∼4π IbiasRp\sim\dfrac{4}{\pi}\,I_{bias}R_p∼π4​Ibias​Rp​ (where RpR_pRp​ is the tank's equivalent parallel resistance). Once pushed into the voltage-limited regime, adding more current no longer adds swing — the phase-noise improvement saturates. Power: in the current-limited regime, swing ≈4πIbiasRp\approx\dfrac{4}{\pi}I_{bias}R_p≈π4​Ibias​Rp​ is proportional to bias current. Doubling swing → doubling current → doubling power. Putting the two together gives the FOM (figure of merit) trade-off: phase noise L∝1/qmax2∝1/Vmax2\mathcal{L}\propto1/q_{max}^2\propto1/V_{max}^2L∝1/qmax2​∝1/Vmax2​ (bigger swing is always better), but Vmax∝IbiasV_{max}\propto I_{bias}Vmax​∝Ibias​ (current-limited) → L∝1/Ibias2\mathcal{L}\propto1/I_{bias}^2L∝1/Ibias2​, while P∝IbiasP\propto I_{bias}P∝Ibias​, so does L∝1/P2\mathcal{L}\propto1/P^2L∝1/P2? — No. Because the noise current in2‾\overline{i_n^2}in2​​ also rises with bias current (more current → more device noise), typically in2‾∝Ibias\overline{i_n^2}\propto I_{bias}in2​​∝Ibias​, and the net effect reverts to L⋅P≈\mathcal{L}\cdot P\approxL⋅P≈ constant (roughly 1 dB of phase noise bought per extra 1 dB of power burned). This is why the industry uses FOM =L−20log⁡10(f0/Δf)+10log⁡10(P/1mW)=\mathcal{L}-20\log_{10}(f_0/\Delta f)+10\log_{10}(P/1\text{mW})=L−20log10​(f0​/Δf)+10log10​(P/1mW) to fairly compare oscillators at different power levels: it normalizes away this "phase noise × power ≈ constant" trade-off. ⚠️ The "current-limited / voltage-limited" boundary above and 4πIbiasRp\dfrac{4}{\pi}I_{bias}R_pπ4​Ibias​Rp​ are standard LC-oscillator design knowledge (not among the five downloaded source PDFs; supplemented from standard literature, e.g. the Hajimiri-Lee textbook, Razavi's RF Microelectronics). [P1] itself gives the 1/qmax21/q_{max}^21/qmax2​ scaling but does not expand the circuit-level detail of swing-vs-power. The exact swing-limit coefficients and phase-noise-factor floor can be found in E. Hegazi, H. Sjöland, A. A. Abidi, A Filtering Technique to Lower LC Oscillator Phase Noise, IEEE JSSC 36(12):1921–1930, 2001 (verified verbatim), and Razavi's RF Microelectronics (external literature, not among the five source PDFs).

documents.t: Using canonical example B as the baseline, we look at the effect of doubling swing. Baseline (example B): f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz: L=10log⁡10 ⁣(0.25(10−12)2⋅10−244(2π⋅106)2).\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{0.25}{(10^{-12})^2}\cdot\frac{10^{-24}}{4(2\pi\cdot10^6)^2}\right).L=10log10​((10−12)20.25​⋅4(2π⋅106)210−24​). First Δω=2π⋅106=6.283×106\Delta\omega=2\pi\cdot10^6=6.283\times10^6Δω=2π⋅106=6.283×106 rad/s, Δω2=3.948×1013\Delta\omega^2=3.948\times10^{13}Δω2=3.948×1013. Bracket =0.2510−24⋅10−244⋅3.948×1013=0.251.579×1014=1.583×10−15=\dfrac{0.25}{10^{-24}}\cdot\dfrac{10^{-24}}{4\cdot3.948\times10^{13}}=\dfrac{0.25}{1.579\times10^{14}}=1.583\times10^{-15}=10−240.25​⋅4⋅3.948×101310−24​=1.579×10140.25​=1.583×10−15, L=10log⁡10(1.583×10−15)=−148.0\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}(1.583\times10^{-15})=-148.0L=10log10​(1.583×10−15)=−148.0 dBc/Hz. Swing doubled (qmax=2q_{max}=2qmax​=2 pC, everything else unchanged): qmax2q_{max}^2qmax2​ becomes 4× → bracket becomes 1/4 → Lnew=−148.0−10log⁡10(4)=−148.0−6.02=−154.0 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}_{new}=-148.0-10\log_{10}(4)=-148.0-6.02=-154.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}.Lnew​=−148.0−10log10​(4)=−148.0−6.02=−154.0 dBc/Hz. Intuition: doubling swing → phase noise improves by 6.0 dB, exactly 20log⁡10220\log_{10}220log10​2. Trade-off reminder: but if this 6 dB comes from doubling bias current (current-limited, with in2‾∝I\overline{i_n^2}\propto Iin2​​∝I), SiS_iSi​ also rises by ~3 dB, so the net improvement is only about 3 dB — this is "phase noise × power ≈ constant" at work. The genuine free lunch is "raise VmaxV_{max}Vmax​ without adding current" (e.g., a higher-QQQ tank, higher RpR_pRp​).
