documents.t: Prerequisites: white_noise_to_phase_noise, flicker_noise_upconversion, phase_vs_amplitude_noise | Next: lc_vs_ring This page assumes you already accept the main thread: "phase has no restoring force → noise integrates through 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 into the skirt." Everything in the ISF framework so far has been about the device's own noise current in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) injected directly into the tank node. But a real VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator — output frequency set by a control voltage) has two more phase-noise gates that don't rely on the device's internal ini_nin​ at all, but on jitter of an external voltage node: tuning line: you use a voltage VtuneV_{tune}Vtune​ to tune the varactor (a varactor diode — bias changes its capacitance) and set f0f_0f0​ to the desired channel. Any noise voltage vnv_nvn​ on this line directly FM-modulates (frequency-modulates) the carrier. supply (VDDV_{DD}VDD​): supply voltage variation changes the effective f0f_0f0​ via the device operating point, parasitic capacitance, and similar paths — this is called supply pushing (supply voltage pushes the oscillation frequency around). This page answers: how do these two external voltage gates turn low-frequency noise voltage into close-in phase noise? Why does the mechanism look identical to device flicker's 1/f31/f^31/f3? And how do design choices close these two gates down? Physical intuition (the punchline first): think of the VCO as a "voltage → frequency" converter with sensitivity KVCO=∂f0/∂VtuneK_{VCO}=\partial f_0/\partial V_{tune}KVCO​=∂f0​/∂Vtune​ (Hz/V). A noise voltage vn(t)v_n(t)vn​(t) on the control node jitters the instantaneous frequency by Δf(t)=KVCO vn(t)\Delta f(t)=K_{VCO}\,v_n(t)Δf(t)=KVCO​vn​(t). Frequency is the derivative of phase, so phase is the integral of frequency — this integrator is the exact same machine that turns SvS_vSv​ (voltage noise) into the 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 skirt in the ISF white-noise result: literally the same integrator. Hence: white noise on the tune line → 1/f21/f^21/f2; 1/f1/f1/f noise on the tune line → 1/f31/f^31/f3. The larger KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​, the wider this gate opens; shrinking it (coarse tuning via switched-cap, fine tuning via varactor) and cleaning up Vtune/VDDV_{tune}/V_{DD}Vtune​/VDD​ (LDO, common-mode rejection) is the core of every design knob on this page. The concrete circuit/topology/instrumentation details on this page — the varactor CCC–VVV model, LDO/cross-coupled VCO topology specifics, measurement methods — belong to standard RF IC design literature (Razavi, Leeson, vendor datasheets); not among the five source PDFs on this site, and this page explicitly flags them "(external literature, not among the five source PDFs)." But the main thread — "voltage noise → FM → 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 phase skirt" — follows strictly from [P1]'s existing phase-integration concept alone, which is what we do below.
documents.s: Tuning-line and supply-pushing phase noise

documents.t: A VCO is by definition "output frequency varies with control voltage." Treat oscillation frequency f0f_0f0​ as a function of control voltage VtuneV_{tune}Vtune​ and supply VDDV_{DD}VDD​, and do a first-order Taylor expansion about the operating point: f0(Vtune,VDD)≈f0,op+∂f0∂Vtune⏟KVCO (Vtune−Vop)+∂f0∂VDD⏟Kpush (VDD−VDD,op).f_0(V_{tune},V_{DD})\approx f_{0,op}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{tune}}}_{K_{VCO}}\,(V_{tune}-V_{op})+\underbrace{\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{DD}}}_{K_{push}}\,(V_{DD}-V_{DD,op}).f0​(Vtune​,VDD​)≈f0,op​+KVCO​∂Vtune​∂f0​​​​(Vtune​−Vop​)+Kpush​∂VDD​∂f0​​​​(VDD​−VDD,op​). The two slopes are this page's two protagonists: KVCO≡∂f0∂Vtune(units Hz/V)K_{VCO}\equiv\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{tune}}\qquad(\text{units Hz/V})KVCO​≡∂Vtune​∂f0​​(units Hz/V)Kpush≡∂f0∂VDD(units Hz/V)K_{push}\equiv\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{DD}}\qquad(\text{units Hz/V})Kpush​≡∂VDD​∂f0​​(units Hz/V) KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​ (VCO gain, also called tuning sensitivity): how far frequency moves per 1 V of control voltage. It sets the tuning range (the frequency span it can sweep) and also the gain applied to tune-line noise — the core tension on this page: KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​ must be large enough to cover the band, yet small enough not to amplify noise. KpushK_{push}Kpush​ (supply pushing coefficient): how far frequency moves per 1 V of supply variation. Ideally the VCO is supply-immune (Kpush=0K_{push}=0Kpush​=0); in practice the supply alters f0f_0f0​ via device bias point, parasitic capacitance, and effective swing, so Kpush≠0K_{push}\ne0Kpush​=0. (Vendors often quote a pushing figure in Hz/V\text{Hz/V}Hz/V or ppm/V\text{ppm/V}ppm/V — external literature, not among the five source PDFs.) Dimension check: [∂f0/∂V]=Hz/V[\partial f_0/\partial V]=\text{Hz}/\text{V}[∂f0​/∂V]=Hz/V ✓. Both have the same dimension and are exactly parallel mathematically — every derivation below applies verbatim to tune line and supply; just swap KVCO,vn,tuneK_{VCO},v_{n,tune}KVCO​,vn,tune​ for Kpush,vn,DDK_{push},v_{n,DD}Kpush​,vn,DD​. Physical meaning: these two coefficients connect the "external voltage world" to the "frequency world." They are designer-controllable — unlike the device's ini_nin​ (fixed by process/physics), KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​ and KpushK_{push}Kpush​ are outcomes of topology and bias choices. Division of labor with ISF Γ\GammaΓ: ISF Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) handles "a current impulse Δq\Delta qΔq injected at what phase of the tank node → how much phase shift"; KVCO/KpushK_{VCO}/K_{push}KVCO​/Kpush​ handles "a quasi-static (slow relative to the carrier) control/supply voltage → how much frequency shift." Tune/supply noise is slow (offset ≪f0\ll f_0≪f0​), so it need not go through ISF's per-impulse phase projection — it takes the more direct FM route: "voltage → frequency → integrate into phase." Both routes ultimately converge on the same 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 integrator (see end of Step 2) — exactly the parallel this page draws.
documents.s: Step 1: define KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​ and supply pushing KpushK_{push}Kpush​

documents.t: Let the tune node carry a low-frequency noise voltage vn(t)v_n(t)vn​(t) (offset frequency Δω≪ω0\Delta\omega\ll\omega_0Δω≪ω0​, so it's nearly constant over one carrier cycle — the quasi-static assumption holds). Derive step by step. Step 2.1: voltage noise → instantaneous frequency deviation. By the definition of KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​, the instantaneous oscillation frequency jitters with vnv_nvn​: Δf(t)=KVCO vn(t)⟺Δωinst(t)=2πKVCO vn(t).\Delta f(t)=K_{VCO}\,v_n(t)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \Delta\omega_{inst}(t)=2\pi K_{VCO}\,v_n(t).Δf(t)=KVCO​vn​(t)⟺Δωinst​(t)=2πKVCO​vn​(t). Dimension check: Hz/V×V=Hz\text{Hz/V}\times\text{V}=\text{Hz}Hz/V×V=Hz ✓ (the angular-frequency version, multiplied by 2π2\pi2π, gives rad/s ✓). This is FM (frequency modulation): the control voltage directly modulates the carrier's instantaneous frequency. Step 2.2: frequency is the derivative of phase → phase is the integral of frequency. The excess phase ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) is by definition "the time integral of the instantaneous frequency's deviation from nominal": ϕ(t)=∫tΔωinst(t′) dt′=2πKVCO∫tvn(t′) dt′.\phi(t)=\int^{t}\Delta\omega_{inst}(t')\,dt'=2\pi K_{VCO}\int^{t}v_n(t')\,dt'.ϕ(t)=∫tΔωinst​(t′)dt′=2πKVCO​∫tvn​(t′)dt′. This integrator is the key point: it is the same integrator [P1] Eq.(11)/(13) uses to integrate ini_nin​ into ϕ\phiϕ — only here the integrand is not "Γ⋅in\Gamma\cdot i_nΓ⋅in​" but "KVCO⋅vnK_{VCO}\cdot v_nKVCO​⋅vn​." Integration = multiply by 1/(jΔω)1/(j\Delta\omega)1/(jΔω) in the frequency domain (basic signals-and-systems), so power multiplies by 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 — the next step relies on exactly this. Physical meaning: phase has no restoring force (phase_vs_amplitude_noise, Step 1), so a "slowly drifting frequency" gets accumulated indefinitely into an ever-growing phase offset — the closer the offset Δω\Delta\omegaΔω is to the carrier, the larger the integrator gain 1/Δω1/\Delta\omega1/Δω, and the higher the skirt. Step 2.3: take the PSD (the integrator is 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 in the power domain). For an LTI system ϕ=H v\phi=\mathcal{H}\,vϕ=Hv, the effect on input PSD is Sϕ=∣H(jΔω)∣2SvS_\phi=|\mathcal{H}(j\Delta\omega)|^2 S_vSϕ​=∣H(jΔω)∣2Sv​. Here H=2πKVCO/(jΔω)\mathcal{H}=2\pi K_{VCO}/(j\Delta\omega)H=2πKVCO​/(jΔω), so ∣H∣2=(2πKVCO)2/Δω2|\mathcal{H}|^2=(2\pi K_{VCO})^2/\Delta\omega^2∣H∣2=(2πKVCO​)2/Δω2: Sϕ(Δω)=(2πKVCO)2 Sv(Δω)Δω2=KVCO2 Sv(Δω)Δf2 \boxed{\ S_\phi(\Delta\omega)=\frac{(2\pi K_{VCO})^2\,S_v(\Delta\omega)}{\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{K_{VCO}^2\,S_v(\Delta\omega)}{\Delta f^2}\ } Sϕ​(Δω)=Δω2(2πKVCO​)2Sv​(Δω)​=Δf2KVCO2​Sv​(Δω)​ ​ The right-hand form uses Δω=2πΔf\Delta\omega=2\pi\Delta fΔω=2πΔf to cancel the 2π2\pi2π's (numerator (2π)2(2\pi)^2(2π)2, denominator (2π)2(2\pi)^2(2π)2), so computing in Hz is cleaner: Sϕ=KVCO2Sv/Δf2S_\phi=K_{VCO}^2 S_v/\Delta f^2Sϕ​=KVCO2​Sv​/Δf2. Dimension check: (Hz/V)2⋅(V2/Hz)Hz2=Hz2/HzHz2=1Hz\dfrac{(\text{Hz/V})^2\cdot(\text{V}^2/\text{Hz})}{\text{Hz}^2}=\dfrac{\text{Hz}^2/\text{Hz}}{\text{Hz}^2}=\dfrac{1}{\text{Hz}}Hz2(Hz/V)2⋅(V2/Hz)​=Hz2Hz2/Hz​=Hz1​, and phase is dimensionless (rad), so SϕS_\phiSϕ​ is rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz ✓. (Strictly, the "dimensionless phase" carried by KVCO2K_{VCO}^2KVCO2​ is implicit; FM phase is inherently dimensionless.) Side by side with the ISF white-noise result — white_noise_to_phase_noise's signature formula Sϕ=Γrms2qmax2in2‾/ΔfΔω2S_\phi=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{\Delta\omega^2}Sϕ​=qmax2​Γrms2​​Δω2in2​​/Δf​ and this page's Sϕ=(2πKVCO)2SvΔω2S_\phi=\dfrac{(2\pi K_{VCO})^2 S_v}{\Delta\omega^2}Sϕ​=Δω2(2πKVCO​)2Sv​​ both have Δω2\Delta\omega^2Δω2 in the denominator. The device-noise version's "conversion gain" is Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ (A → rad); the tune-line version's is 2πKVCO2\pi K_{VCO}2πKVCO​ (V → rad/s, then integrated). Same 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 integrator, different entry point — this is the structural isomorphism this page wants you to remember. Step 2.4: apply SSB phase noise (small-angle approximation). Using the site-wide convention L(Δf)≈12Sϕ(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\approx\tfrac12 S_\phi(\Delta f)L(Δf)≈21​Sϕ​(Δf) (spec Section 3, Eq. 16): L(Δf)=10log⁡10 ⁣[12⋅KVCO2 Sv(Δf)Δf2](dBc/Hz).\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)=10\log_{10}\!\left[\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{K_{VCO}^2\,S_v(\Delta f)}{\Delta f^2}\right]\qquad(\text{dBc/Hz}).L(Δf)=10log10​[21​⋅Δf2KVCO2​Sv​(Δf)​](dBc/Hz). The supply version is completely parallel: substitute KVCO→KpushK_{VCO}\to K_{push}KVCO​→Kpush​, Sv→Sv,DDS_v\to S_{v,DD}Sv​→Sv,DD​ (supply-voltage noise PSD). The two gates' contributions are independent sources, so powers add: Sϕtot=KVCO2Sv,tune+Kpush2Sv,DDΔf2+(the device-ISF contribution)S_\phi^{tot}=\dfrac{K_{VCO}^2 S_{v,tune}+K_{push}^2 S_{v,DD}}{\Delta f^2}+(\text{the device-ISF contribution})Sϕtot​=Δf2KVCO2​Sv,tune​+Kpush2​Sv,DD​​+(the device-ISF contribution).

documents.t: Step 2's Sϕ∝Sv/Δω2S_\phi\propto S_v/\Delta\omega^2Sϕ​∝Sv​/Δω2 carries the tune line's spectral shape through unchanged, then multiplies by 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2. Two cases: Case A — tune line is white noise (Sv=S_v=Sv​= constant): e.g. series-resistor thermal noise, wideband buffer noise. Then Sϕ=KVCO2 Sv,0Δf2 ∝ 1Δf2⇒−20 dB/decade (1/f2).S_\phi=\frac{K_{VCO}^2\,S_{v,0}}{\Delta f^2}\ \propto\ \frac{1}{\Delta f^2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad -20\ \text{dB/decade}\ (1/f^2).Sϕ​=Δf2KVCO2​Sv,0​​ ∝ Δf21​⇒−20 dB/decade (1/f2). This has exactly the same slope, exactly the same mechanism as device white noise's 1/f21/f^21/f2 via ISF (both: white entry → 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 integrator). Case B — tune line is 1/f1/f1/f noise (Sv=kv/ΔfS_v=k_v/\Delta fSv​=kv​/Δf): e.g. low-frequency flicker from a charge pump / bandgap / LDO reference, or 1/f1/f1/f in the varactor bias circuit. Then Sϕ=KVCO2Δf2⋅kvΔf=KVCO2 kvΔf3 ∝ 1Δf3⇒−30 dB/decade (1/f3).S_\phi=\frac{K_{VCO}^2}{\Delta f^2}\cdot\frac{k_v}{\Delta f}=\frac{K_{VCO}^2\,k_v}{\Delta f^3}\ \propto\ \frac{1}{\Delta f^3}\quad\Rightarrow\quad -30\ \text{dB/decade}\ (1/f^3).Sϕ​=Δf2KVCO2​​⋅Δfkv​​=Δf3KVCO2​kv​​ ∝ Δf31​⇒−30 dB/decade (1/f3). This is precisely the "external-voltage version" of the device flicker mechanism. Put the two 1/f31/f^31/f3 paths side by side: Mechanism Entry (low-frequency source) Upconversion "gate" 1/f31/f^31/f3 formula skeleton device flicker ([P1] Eq.(23)) device 1/f1/f1/f current in2‾ ω1/f/Δω\overline{i_n^2}\,\omega_{1/f}/\Delta\omegain2​​ω1/f​/Δω ISF's DC term c0c_0c0​ L∝c02qmax2in2‾/ΔfΔω2ω1/fΔω\mathcal{L}\propto\dfrac{c_0^2}{q_{max}^2}\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{\Delta\omega^2}\dfrac{\omega_{1/f}}{\Delta\omega}L∝qmax2​c02​​Δω2in2​​/Δf​Δωω1/f​​ tune/supply 1/f1/f1/f (this page) control-voltage 1/f1/f1/f noise Sv=kv/ΔfS_v=k_v/\Delta fSv​=kv​/Δf VCO gain KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​ (or KpushK_{push}Kpush​) L∝KVCO2 kvΔf3\mathcal{L}\propto K_{VCO}^2\,\dfrac{k_v}{\Delta f^3}L∝KVCO2​Δf3kv​​ Where the parallel lies: the device version's "gate" is ISF's DC Fourier coefficient c0c_0c0​ (flicker_noise_upconversion, Step 2: "c0c_0c0​ is flicker's only gate to the carrier"); the tune-line version's "gate" is KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​. The role KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​ plays in the external-voltage world is exactly the role c0c_0c0​ plays in the device-current world — both are conversion gains that "connect a low-frequency source to the 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 integrator," and both enter L\mathcal{L}L squared (c02c_0^2c02​ vs KVCO2K_{VCO}^2KVCO2​). The difference (stated honestly): the device version's c0c_0c0​ can be pushed close to 0 via waveform symmetry (this rescues flicker); the tune-line version's KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​ cannot be zeroed (zero means the frequency can't be tuned at all) — it can only be shrunk (split tuning) or have its entry SvS_vSv​ cleaned up (LDO). So this gate is "permanently half-open," which makes it a design problem that demands direct attention. Slope mnemonic: each extra 1/Δω1/\Delta\omega1/Δω factor in the denominator adds −10-10−10 dB/dec. White entry + integrator = 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 (−20-20−20); 1/f1/f1/f entry (one extra 1/Δω1/\Delta\omega1/Δω) + integrator = 1/Δω31/\Delta\omega^31/Δω3 (−30-30−30). Identical bookkeeping to the device side.

documents.t: So far KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​ has been treated as constant. But the varactor is inherently a nonlinear capacitor C(V)C(V)C(V) — this opens a second, more subtle gate: AM-PM conversion (amplitude modulation converted to phase modulation), the back door discussed in phase_vs_amplitude_noise, Step 4. Mechanism chain (each link uses an existing concept): Frequency is set by the tank's total capacitance: LC oscillation f0=12πL Ctotf_0=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L\,C_{tot}}}f0​=2πLCtot​​1​, where CtotC_{tot}Ctot​ includes the varactor's C(V)C(V)C(V). The varactor sees "bias + oscillation swing": the node voltage is Vtune+vosc(t)V_{tune}+v_{osc}(t)Vtune​+vosc​(t); a sinusoidal swing of amplitude AAA sweeps across the C(V)C(V)C(V) curve every cycle. Nonlinearity → effective capacitance varies with swing: because C(V)C(V)C(V) is curved, the average effective capacitance Cˉ(A)\bar C(A)Cˉ(A) over one cycle changes with amplitude AAA (Taylor-expand C(V)C(V)C(V) about the bias point; the second-order term 12C′′(Vtune)⟨vosc2⟩\tfrac12 C''(V_{tune})\langle v_{osc}^2\rangle21​C′′(Vtune​)⟨vosc2​⟩ is proportional to A2A^2A2 and nonzero). Hence f0f_0f0​ becomes a function of amplitude, f0(A)f_0(A)f0​(A). This is exactly ∂ω/∂A≠0\partial\omega/\partial A\ne0∂ω/∂A=0: amplitude noise ΔA\Delta AΔA (which would normally be squashed by the limit cycle's restoring force) leaks into frequency/phase noise via ∂f0/∂A\partial f_0/\partial A∂f0​/∂A, then gets permanently accumulated by Step 2's integrator into a close-in skirt. ΔωAM-PM=∂ω0∂A ΔA,∂ω0∂A∝C′′(Vtune) (varactor curvature).\Delta\omega_{AM\text{-}PM}=\frac{\partial\omega_0}{\partial A}\,\Delta A,\qquad \frac{\partial\omega_0}{\partial A}\propto C''(V_{tune})\ \ (\text{varactor curvature}).ΔωAM-PM​=∂A∂ω0​​ΔA,∂A∂ω0​​∝C′′(Vtune​) (varactor curvature). Physical meaning: amplitude noise that was originally "suppressed" (phase_vs_amplitude_noise argues amplitude has a restoring force) escapes through this varactor-curvature back door, coming back to life as long-lived phase noise — in particular, it upconverts the device's 1/f1/f1/f amplitude fluctuations into the close-in region, worsening 1/f31/f^31/f3. Key design corollary: AM-PM is proportional to C′′(Vtune)C''(V_{tune})C′′(Vtune​) (curve curvature), not C′C'C′ (slope, which is KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​). So biasing at the inflection/flat point of C(V)C(V)C(V) can drive C′′≈0C''\approx0C′′≈0, greatly reducing AM-PM — a different knob from "shrink KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​" (one controls curvature, the other controls slope). Units/dimension: ∂ω0/∂A\partial\omega_0/\partial A∂ω0​/∂A is (rad/s)/V(\text{rad/s})/\text{V}(rad/s)/V; multiplied by amplitude noise ΔA\Delta AΔA (V) gives rad/s, then integrates into phase ✓. Detailed amplitude-modulation and large-signal analysis is the main subject of [P4] (advanced); the exact closed form of varactor C(V)C(V)C(V) belongs to device literature (external literature, not among the five source PDFs). This page only connects the chain to the existing AM-PM concept.

documents.t: Translate the physics above directly into actionable knobs. Each knob states which quantity it acts on. Split tuning — shrinks KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​. The single most important technique (external literature, not among the five source PDFs). Split tuning into two layers: coarse: switched-capacitor bank (an array of switched capacitors, switched in/out by a digital code). It selects the band with a digital code, providing most of the tuning range, but is immune to continuous voltage noise (the code doesn't jitter, so the capacitance doesn't jitter). fine: varactor, responsible only for continuous fine-tuning within a small sub-band. Effect: total tuning range = coarse (digital, noise-free) ⊕ fine (small range), and the fine varactor's KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​ drops sharply because it only spans a small sub-band. By Step 2's Sϕ∝KVCO2S_\phi\propto K_{VCO}^2Sϕ​∝KVCO2​, halving KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​ cuts the tune-line phase-noise contribution by 6 dB. This is the standard way to untangle the "range vs. noise" tension. Bias at the flat point of C(V)C(V)C(V) — suppresses AM-PM (controls C′′C''C′′). Choose the varactor operating point so C′′(Vtune)≈0C''(V_{tune})\approx0C′′(Vtune​)≈0 (small curvature), driving ∂ω/∂A→0\partial\omega/\partial A\to0∂ω/∂A→0 and closing the AM-PM back door. Note this is a different knob from shrinking KVCOK_{VCO}KVCO​: the flat point suppresses second-order curvature, not first-order slope. Supply regulation / LDO — suppresses the Sv,DDS_{v,DD}Sv,DD​ entry (external literature, not among the five source PDFs). To combat supply pushing: place an LDO (low-dropout regulator) ahead of the VCO to filter a dirty supply into a clean local supply, reducing Sv,DDS_{v,DD}Sv,DD​ (the supply-noise PSD reaching the VCO) by tens of dB. By the supply-side formula Sϕ∝Kpush2Sv,DDS_\phi\propto K_{push}^2 S_{v,DD}Sϕ​∝Kpush2​Sv,DD​, reducing Sv,DDS_{v,DD}Sv,DD​ reduces phase noise proportionally. You can also reduce KpushK_{push}Kpush​ itself (topology-level: symmetric bias, less supply-to-swing modulation). Common-mode rejection — makes a differential VCO immune to common-mode supply/substrate noise. On a differential tank, supply/substrate noise mostly appears as a common-mode disturbance; good differential symmetry keeps common-mode disturbances from converting to differential-mode frequency shifts (ideally Kpush,CM→0K_{push,CM}\to0Kpush,CM​→0). This shares its origin with flicker_noise_upconversion Step 6's differential concept, but here it combats external common-mode voltage rather than device c0c_0c0​. Clean VtuneV_{tune}Vtune​ routing — suppresses the Sv,tuneS_{v,tune}Sv,tune​ entry. Loop-filter resistor thermal noise, charge-pump 1/f1/f1/f, and bandgap reference noise all feed into VtuneV_{tune}Vtune​; these are the physical origin of the "in-band" terms in pll_noise_budget. Within a PLL, the loop bandwidth also determines how much this tune-line noise gets high-pass/low-pass filtered. Design rule of thumb (in one line): the phase noise from these two gates = (conversion gain K2K^2K2) × (entry voltage noise SvS_vSv​) × (1/Δf21/\Delta f^21/Δf2 integrator). Each of the three factors has its own knob: suppress KKK with split tuning / symmetric topology, suppress SvS_vSv​ with LDO / clean reference / low-noise loop filter, and suppress the curvature-driven AM-PM with a flat bias point.

Find L(1 MHz)\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})L(1MHz). Step 1 (square Sv\sqrt{S_v}Sv​​ into a PSD): Sv=(100 nV/Hz)2=(10−7 V/Hz)2=10−14 V2/Hz.S_v=(100\ \text{nV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}})^2=(10^{-7}\ \text{V}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}})^2=10^{-14}\ \text{V}^2/\text{Hz}.Sv​=(100 nV/Hz​)2=(10−7 V/Hz​)2=10−14 V2/Hz. Result: L(1 MHz)≈−109\mathcal{L}(1\,\text{MHz})\approx-109L(1MHz)≈−109 dBc/Hz — this single tune-line white-noise source alone contributes −109-109−109 dBc/Hz. Compared with the canonical "single device white-noise source" Example B (−148-148−148 dBc/Hz, white_noise_to_phase_noise), the tune line is nearly 40 dB higher at the same offset — showing that one poorly handled tune line can easily dominate a whole VCO's 1/f21/f^21/f2 region, which is exactly why split tuning / a clean VtuneV_{tune}Vtune​ matter so much. Where did f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz go? (honesty note): this formula's L\mathcal{L}L does not explicitly contain f0f_0f0​ — f0f_0f0​ only tells you which carrier this skirt sits on; the skirt's 1/f21/f^21/f2 height is set by KVCO2Sv/Δf2K_{VCO}^2 S_v/\Delta f^2KVCO2​Sv​/Δf2, independent of f0f_0f0​. f0f_0f0​ genuinely enters when converting to timing jitter (Δt=Δϕ/2πf0\Delta t=\Delta\phi/2\pi f_0Δt=Δϕ/2πf0​, see psd_phase_noise_jitter), or when expressing KVCO/f0K_{VCO}/f_0KVCO​/f0​'s relative sensitivity in ppm/V\text{ppm/V}ppm/V. f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz is given so you know this is a 5 GHz VCO, but don't force it into the L\mathcal{L}L formula. import math K_vco = 50e6 # Hz/V S_v = (100e-9)**2 # V^2/Hz (100 nV/sqrt(Hz)) df = 1e6 # Hz offset S_phi = K_vco**2 * S_v / df**2 # rad^2/Hz L = 10*math.log10(0.5*S_phi) # SSB, L = (1/2) S_phi print(S_phi, L) # -> 2.5e-11 rad^2/Hz, -109.03 dBc/Hz Example H (supply pushing → L\mathcal{L}L, parallel verification): Kpush=2K_{push}=2Kpush​=2 MHz/V, supply noise 1 μV/Hz1\ \mu\text{V}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}1 μV/Hz​ (Sv,DD=10−12 V2/HzS_{v,DD}=10^{-12}\ \text{V}^2/\text{Hz}Sv,DD​=10−12 V2/Hz) at Δf=1\Delta f=1Δf=1 MHz. Find the supply contribution to L\mathcal{L}L. Sϕ=Kpush2Sv,DDΔf2=(2×106)2×10−12(106)2=4×1012×10−121012=4×10−12 rad2/Hz,S_\phi=\frac{K_{push}^2 S_{v,DD}}{\Delta f^2}=\frac{(2\times10^{6})^2\times10^{-12}}{(10^{6})^2}=\frac{4\times10^{12}\times10^{-12}}{10^{12}}=4\times10^{-12}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz},Sϕ​=Δf2Kpush2​Sv,DD​​=(106)2(2×106)2×10−12​=10124×1012×10−12​=4×10−12 rad2/Hz,L=10log⁡10(12×4×10−12)=10log⁡10(2×10−12)=−117.0 dBc/Hz.\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}(\tfrac12\times4\times10^{-12})=10\log_{10}(2\times10^{-12})=-117.0\ \text{dBc/Hz}.L=10log10​(21​×4×10−12)=10log10​(2×10−12)=−117.0 dBc/Hz. documents.t: Sweep VDDV_{DD}VDD​ from 0.9 V to 1.1 V (25 mV grid); at each point let the ring reach steady oscillation and measure the period by threshold crossings: VDDV_{DD}VDD​ [V] 0.900 0.950 1.000 1.050 1.100 f0f_0f0​ [GHz] 0.9394 1.0803 1.2252 1.3738 1.5255 f0(1.000 V)=1.2252f_0(1.000\,\text{V})=1.2252f0​(1.000V)=1.2252 GHz exactly reproduces lab_32 (same ring, same integrator). Central difference at 1.0 V: Kpush=∂f0∂VDD∣1.0 V=f0(1.025)−f0(0.975)0.05 V=2.936 GHz/VK_{push}=\left.\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{DD}}\right|_{1.0\,\text{V}}=\frac{f_0(1.025)-f_0(0.975)}{0.05\ \text{V}}=2.936\ \text{GHz/V}Kpush​=∂VDD​∂f0​​​1.0V​=0.05 Vf0​(1.025)−f0​(0.975)​=2.936 GHz/V (The 9-point quadratic-fit derivative gives 2.932 GHz/V, 0.1% apart — the slope extraction is self-consistent.) Hence f0 ∝ (VDD−VT)2VDD⇒1f0∂f0∂VDD=2VDD−VT−1VDDf_0\ \propto\ \frac{(V_{DD}-V_T)^2}{V_{DD}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{1}{f_0}\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{DD}}=\frac{2}{V_{DD}-V_T}-\frac{1}{V_{DD}}f0​ ∝ VDD​(VDD​−VT​)2​⇒f0​1​∂VDD​∂f0​​=VDD​−VT​2​−VDD​1​ (The 2 in the numerator is the square-law exponent — a physical origin, not a convention.) Plug in VDD=1.0V_{DD}=1.0VDD​=1.0 V, VT=0.4V_T=0.4VT​=0.4 V: 2/0.6−1/1.0=2.33 V−12/0.6-1/1.0=2.33\ \text{V}^{-1}2/0.6−1/1.0=2.33 V−1, times f0=1.2252f_0=1.2252f0​=1.2252 GHz gives 2.859 GHz/V — 2.6% from the measured 2.936 GHz/V; both magnitude and physics agree. Dimension check: V−1×Hz=Hz/V\text{V}^{-1}\times\text{Hz}=\text{Hz/V}V−1×Hz=Hz/V ✓. The normalized pushing is Kpush/f0=2.40K_{push}/f_0=2.40Kpush​/f0​=2.40 /V =2.4×106=2.4\times10^6=2.4×106 ppm/V. For contrast: an LC VCO's f0f_0f0​ is set by the tank's L CL\,CLC and the supply only perturbs it through parasitics and bias (typical pushing figures sit in the ppm/V to thousands-of-ppm/V range — external literature, not among the five source PDFs); a ring's f0f_0f0​ is device current divided by capacitance — the supply sits directly inside the formula. "A ring's supply pushing is inherently orders of magnitude larger than an LC's" is not folklore; it is a direct consequence of f0=1/(2NτD)f_0=1/(2N\tau_D)f0​=1/(2NτD​).

By Step 2's integrator, step by step: Δf(t)=KpushVrsin⁡(2πfmt)⇒ϕ(t)=∫2π Δf dt′=−KpushVrfm⏟βcos⁡(2πfmt)\Delta f(t)=K_{push}V_r\sin(2\pi f_m t)\quad\Rightarrow\quad\phi(t)=\int 2\pi\,\Delta f\,dt'=-\underbrace{\frac{K_{push}V_r}{f_m}}_{\beta}\cos(2\pi f_m t)Δf(t)=Kpush​Vr​sin(2πfm​t)⇒ϕ(t)=∫2πΔfdt′=−βfm​Kpush​Vr​​​​cos(2πfm​t) The peak phase deviation (FM modulation index) is β=KpushVr/fm\beta=K_{push}V_r/f_mβ=Kpush​Vr​/fm​ (site convention: this β\betaβ is the FM modulation index, unrelated to the injection-locking realignment factor β\betaβ on subharmonic_injection). documents.t: In ISF language there is one key difference between device noise and supply noise: device noise (each stage's own ini_nin​): the NNN stages' noise sources are mutually independent, so per-stage contributions add in power — this is [P2]'s bookkeeping for the ring analysis (one Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ share per stage). supply (the VDDV_{DD}VDD​ rail): the supply is a port shared by all NNN stages. One low-frequency (quasi-static) supply disturbance changes every stage's delay simultaneously and in the same direction — whichever stage is switching gets sped up or slowed down by the same vnv_nvn​, and within one period the delay changes of all 2N2N2N edges accumulate with the same sign into ΔT\Delta TΔT. So the supply's effective sensitivity is the coherent (amplitude) sum of the per-stage sensitivities, and the average (DC) component of that sum is exactly 2πKpush2\pi K_{push}2πKpush​: for a slow disturbance, "some stage is being pushed at every instant," and the summed sensitivity never changes sign. Corollary 1: stacking NNN independent sources scales as N\sqrt NN​ (power addition); a coherent source scales as NNN (amplitude addition) — supply noise is not merely "one more noise source": it bypasses the statistical discount of independent sources. Corollary 2: the DC term of the supply's effective sensitivity is inherently large (its role is that of c0c_0c0​ in device-flicker upconversion), so the supply's 1/f1/f1/f noise upconverts to 1/f31/f^31/f3 as in Step 3; but while the device version can push c0c_0c0​ near 0 via waveform symmetry (lab_32's symmetric ring measured c0=0.0014c_0=0.0014c0​=0.0014), the supply version has no such card to play — "every stage's delay tracks VDDV_{DD}VDD​" is not something symmetry can cancel. The remaining cards are suppressing the entry (LDO) and suppressing KpushK_{push}Kpush​ itself (differential/regulated topologies, stage designs whose delay is first-order insensitive to VDDV_{DD}VDD​ — external literature, not among the five source PDFs). Limitations (honestly): Level-1 square law, λ=0\lambda=0λ=0, a single lumped CLC_LCL​, single point N=3N=3N=3 (no NNN-scaling verified); a real PDK ring's KpushK_{push}Kpush​ number will differ due to velocity saturation and short-channel effects (though it remains far larger than an LC's — external-literature experience), while this section's method (definition-based measurement + FM verification) and structural conclusions (coherent summing, the K2K^2K2 lever) stand.

documents.t: Prerequisites: impulse_to_phase_shift (Δϕ=Γ Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=ΓΔq/qmax​ operational definition and qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=CV_{max}qmax​=CVmax​), lti_vs_ltv (why the same impulse at different phases has different effect) | Next: symmetry, tank_swing This page answers a very practical question, one you'll use during layout and bias design: at which phase of the waveform does the same lump of noise charge do the most damage? Intuitively you might guess "the peak — highest, most sensitive" — it's the opposite. ISF magnitude is, roughly, inversely proportional to waveform slope: where the slope is small (near the peak), ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ is large and phase error is easiest to push; where the slope is large (at the ZC, zero crossing), noise is instead mostly converted into amplitude and pulled back. Physical intuition (conclusion first): phase is "how fast the state point runs along the tangent of the limit cycle." At the peak, the state point moves "slowly, flatly" (dV/dt≈0dV/dt\approx0dV/dt≈0); nudge it sideways and it takes a long time along the time axis to return to where it would have been — equivalent to a large phase shift. At the ZC, the state point is "moving at full speed" (dV/dtdV/dtdV/dt maximal); the same sideways nudge is quickly absorbed back onto the trajectory, leaving almost no phase (it mostly becomes a decaying amplitude perturbation). So "phases with small slope" are the danger zone.

documents.t: Return to the operational definition of impulse→phase ([P1] Eq.(10)–(11), p.182): Δϕ=Γ(ω0τ)qmax Δq\Delta\phi=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,\Delta qΔϕ=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​Δq A lump of charge Δq\Delta qΔq produces a voltage jump ΔV=Δq/C\Delta V=\Delta q/CΔV=Δq/C ([P1] Eq.(9)). Translate this voltage jump into a "time-axis advance/delay": the waveform passes through this point with slope V˙=dV/dt\dot V=dV/dtV˙=dV/dt, and raising the voltage by ΔV\Delta VΔV is equivalent to shifting the waveform in time by Δt≈ΔVV˙=ΔqC V˙.\Delta t\approx\frac{\Delta V}{\dot V}=\frac{\Delta q}{C\,\dot V}.Δt≈V˙ΔV​=CV˙Δq​. Unit check: [V]/[V/s]=[s][\text{V}]/[\text{V/s}]=[\text{s}][V]/[V/s]=[s] ✓. Converting to phase, Δϕ=ω0Δt\Delta\phi=\omega_0\Delta tΔϕ=ω0​Δt: Δϕ=ω0ΔqC V˙⇒Γ∝1V˙.\Delta\phi=\omega_0\frac{\Delta q}{C\,\dot V}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \Gamma\propto\frac{1}{\dot V}.Δϕ=ω0​CV˙Δq​⇒Γ∝V˙1​. Step-by-step algebra: aligning this "shift approximation" with the ISF operational definition to see exactly what Γ\GammaΓ is proportional to. Set the Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ from the above equation equal to the operational-definition expression Δϕ=Γ Δq/qmax\Delta\phi=\Gamma\,\Delta q/q_{max}Δϕ=ΓΔq/qmax​: Γqmax Δq=ω0 ΔqC V˙Γ=qmax ω0C V˙(cancel Δq on both sides)Γ=(C Vmax) ω0C V˙=ω0 VmaxV˙(substitute qmax=C Vmax)=VmaxV˙/ω0=VmaxdV/dθ(V˙=ω0 dV/dθ).\begin{aligned} \frac{\Gamma}{q_{max}}\,\Delta q&=\omega_0\,\frac{\Delta q}{C\,\dot V} \\[4pt] \Gamma&=\frac{q_{max}\,\omega_0}{C\,\dot V} \qquad(\text{cancel }\Delta q\text{ on both sides}) \\[4pt] \Gamma&=\frac{(C\,V_{max})\,\omega_0}{C\,\dot V}=\frac{\omega_0\,V_{max}}{\dot V} \qquad(\text{substitute }q_{max}=C\,V_{max}) \\[4pt] &=\frac{V_{max}}{\dot V/\omega_0}=\frac{V_{max}}{dV/d\theta}\qquad(\dot V=\omega_0\,dV/d\theta). \end{aligned}qmax​Γ​ΔqΓΓ​=ω0​CV˙Δq​=CV˙qmax​ω0​​(cancel Δq on both sides)=CV˙(CVmax​)ω0​​=V˙ω0​Vmax​​(substitute qmax​=CVmax​)=V˙/ω0​Vmax​​=dV/dθVmax​​(V˙=ω0​dV/dθ).​ What each step uses: lines 1→2 are pure algebra (cancel Δq\Delta qΔq); lines 2→3 use qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=C V_{max}qmax​=CVmax​ (the capacitance definition — CCC cancels automatically, which is why ISF does not depend on node capacitance, only on waveform shape); lines 3→4 convert the time-domain slope to a phase-domain slope V˙=ω0 dV/dθ\dot V=\omega_0\,dV/d\thetaV˙=ω0​dV/dθ (chain rule). Meaning of the result: Γ=Vmax/(dV/dθ)\Gamma=V_{max}\big/(dV/d\theta)Γ=Vmax​/(dV/dθ) — ISF is proportional to VmaxV_{max}Vmax​ and inversely proportional to the waveform's slope with respect to phase dV/dθdV/d\thetadV/dθ. Check against a sinusoid: V=Vmaxcos⁡θ⇒dV/dθ=−Vmaxsin⁡θV=V_{max}\cos\theta\Rightarrow dV/d\theta=-V_{max}\sin\thetaV=Vmax​cosθ⇒dV/dθ=−Vmax​sinθ, so Γ=Vmax/(−Vmaxsin⁡θ)=−1/sin⁡θ\Gamma=V_{max}/(-V_{max}\sin\theta)=-1/\sin\thetaΓ=Vmax​/(−Vmax​sinθ)=−1/sinθ. This "1/sin⁡1/\sin1/sin" is an artifact of the shift approximation and diverges where slope→0 (the peak); the rigorous LTV projection instead gives a bounded Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ (with Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0 at the peak). Both say "small slope → dangerous," but they differ on whether it diverges — the shift approximation is only qualitatively valid where slope is nonzero; for quantitative work use Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ. Dimension check: [V]/[V]=[\text{V}]/[\text{V}]=[V]/[V]= dimensionless ✓ (Γ\GammaΓ must be dimensionless); the intermediate expression [C]⋅[rad/s][F]⋅[V/s]=[C][s−1][C/V][V/s]=[C][s−1][C][s−1]=\dfrac{[\text{C}]\cdot[\text{rad/s}]}{[\text{F}]\cdot[\text{V/s}]}=\dfrac{[\text{C}][\text{s}^{-1}]}{[\text{C/V}][\text{V/s}]} =\dfrac{[\text{C}][\text{s}^{-1}]}{[\text{C}][\text{s}^{-1}]}=[F]⋅[V/s][C]⋅[rad/s]​=[C/V][V/s][C][s−1]​=[C][s−1][C][s−1]​= dimensionless ✓ (rad does not count as a dimension). Conclusion: ISF magnitude is inversely proportional to instantaneous slope V˙\dot VV˙. Large slope → small ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ (insensitive); small slope → large ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ (sensitive). For an ideal sinusoid V=cos⁡θV=\cos\thetaV=cosθ, V˙∝−sin⁡θ\dot V\propto-\sin\thetaV˙∝−sinθ, so the "shift" approximation Γ(θ)∝1/sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)\propto1/\sin\thetaΓ(θ)∝1/sinθ only holds where slope is nonzero; the rigorous LC ISF is Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ (Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0 at the peak θ=0\theta=0θ=0, ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ maximal at the ZC θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2). The divergence problem now has its rigorous resolution (resolved): the 1/slope1/\text{slope}1/slope divergence at the peak has an official "parent formula" — the closed form of [P1]'s appendix (Eq.(37), p.193) Γ=f′/(f′ 2+f′′ 2)\Gamma=f'/(f'^{\,2}+f''^{\,2})Γ=f′/(f′2+f′′2): on transitions (f′ 2≫f′′ 2f'^{\,2}\gg f''^{\,2}f′2≫f′′2) it degenerates into this page's 1/f′1/f'1/f′ heuristic; near the peak the numerator f′→0f'\to0f′→0 while the denominator is held up by f′′ 2f''^{\,2}f′′2, so Γ→0\Gamma\to0Γ→0 — bounded, no divergence. Substituting f=cos⁡f=\cosf=cos gives the denominator sin⁡2+cos⁡2=1\sin^2+\cos^2=1sin2+cos2=1 and Γ=−sin⁡\Gamma=-\sinΓ=−sin exactly. For the full derivation, the verbatim transcription of [P1]'s three ISF calculation methods, and the numerical duel, see isf_from_waveform. A common direction confusion needs to be spelled out here: the "shift" picture above, "Δt=ΔV/V˙\Delta t=\Delta V/\dot VΔt=ΔV/V˙," describes "how much the threshold-crossing time moves after the waveform is perturbed by voltage" — that is threshold-crossing sensitivity, where a large slope makes timing more stable (this is another angle on "fast transitions help"). By contrast, Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ describes excess-phase sensitivity: zero at the peak, maximal at the ZC. The two appear contradictory but are actually different questions: threshold crossing asks "when does the edge cross the threshold"; excess phase asks "how much is the limit cycle pushed tangentially." This page, and the design rules across the whole site, follow [P1]'s ISF Γ\GammaΓ (excess phase): ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ is maximal at the ZC (the high-slope crossing point) and minimal at the peak. This is exactly what the figure below shows.

documents.t: The figure below overlays the ideal LC waveform V(θ)=cos⁡θV(\theta)=\cos\thetaV(θ)=cosθ with its ISF Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ: Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Panel titles read: "(a) LC 波形與其 ISF" = (a) LC waveform and its ISF; "(b) Δφ 與注入電荷成正比 (small-signal)" = (b) Δφ is proportional to the injected charge (small-signal); "(c) zero-crossing 注入 → 相位跳變" = (c) zero-crossing injection → a phase jump. How to read this figure: Peak/trough (θ=0,π\theta=0,\piθ=0,π, VVV at an extremum, dV/dθ=0dV/d\theta=0dV/dθ=0): Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0. Injecting charge here → pure amplitude perturbation → pulled back by amplitude restoration → leaves almost no phase. This is the "safe" phase. Zero crossing, ZC (θ=π/2,3π/2\theta=\pi/2,3\pi/2θ=π/2,3π/2, V=0V=0V=0, slope maximal): ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ is maximal. Injecting charge here → pure phase jump → persists permanently. This is the "dangerous" phase. Compare to [P1] Fig. 4: the same impulse applied at the peak versus at the ZC produces completely different tangential/radial decomposition in state space — this is the signature of the oscillator being an LTV (linear time-varying) system (claim C1). This is a pedagogical toy model (not transistor-level): an idealized LC in the sinusoidal steady state. A real LC, with tank loss and a nonlinear transconductor, will not give a perfect −sin⁡-\sin−sin ISF, but the qualitative conclusion "peak safe, ZC dangerous" holds. documents.t: A ring oscillator's waveform is not sinusoidal but closer to a square wave — spending most of its time "pinned at the rail" and rushing through the ZC only during the switching instant (the transition). Its ISF is therefore concentrated near the transition ([P2] Fig. 6, p.793; Fig. 5 shows the peak/lobe narrowing with NNN): On the rail (flat top): V˙≈0\dot V\approx0V˙≈0 should in theory be very sensitive — but the device is usually not conducting / not injecting noise at that moment (α≈0\alpha\approx0α≈0, see device_noise_mapping), so the effective ISF stays small. During the transition: V˙\dot VV˙ is maximal → the bare Γ\GammaΓ is small; but the device is switching at full tilt, and noise is maximal (α\alphaα large). Multiplying the two together: the ring's effective ISF Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α has its energy concentrated at the transition. Why a fast transition (steep edge) helps, for two mutually reinforcing reasons: Shortens the danger window: the faster the transition, the narrower the time window in which the device is "fully on, crossing the edge," so less noise is collected into phase during this "exposure time" → Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ drops (the ring's Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2 trend is also tied to each stage's transition getting steeper; see lc_vs_ring). Improves threshold-crossing immunity: the steeper the edge, the smaller Δt=ΔV/V˙\Delta t=\Delta V/\dot VΔt=ΔV/V˙ — the same voltage noise produces less timing jitter. This is the same principle behind "fast slew rate → low jitter" on a SerDes data path (see serdes_clocking_connection).

documents.t: Using canonical numbers to estimate "the phase difference from the same Δq\Delta qΔq at peak vs. ZC." Take qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz. Ideal LC Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ: At the ZC (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2, Γ=−1\Gamma=-1Γ=−1, maximum sensitivity): Δϕ=∣Γ∣ Δqqmax=1×10−1510−12=10−3 rad ⇒ Δt=10−32π⋅5×109=31.8 fs.\Delta\phi=\frac{|\Gamma|\,\Delta q}{q_{max}}=\frac{1\times10^{-15}}{10^{-12}}=10^{-3}\ \text{rad}\;\Rightarrow\;\Delta t=\frac{10^{-3}}{2\pi\cdot5\times10^9}=31.8\ \text{fs}.Δϕ=qmax​∣Γ∣Δq​=10−121×10−15​=10−3 rad⇒Δt=2π⋅5×10910−3​=31.8 fs. At the peak (θ=0\theta=0θ=0, Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0): Δϕ=0\Delta\phi=0Δϕ=0 rad, Δt=0\Delta t=0Δt=0 (ideal; real devices show residual leakage). At an intermediate phase (θ=π/6\theta=\pi/6θ=π/6, Γ=−0.5\Gamma=-0.5Γ=−0.5, i.e., canonical example A's Γ=0.5\Gamma=0.5Γ=0.5): Δϕ=0.5×10−1510−12=5×10−4 rad ⇒ Δt=15.9 fs.\Delta\phi=\frac{0.5\times10^{-15}}{10^{-12}}=5\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}\;\Rightarrow\;\Delta t=15.9\ \text{fs}.Δϕ=10−120.5×10−15​=5×10−4 rad⇒Δt=15.9 fs. Intuition: the same 1 fC produces ~32 fs at the ZC but ~0 fs at the peak. Position (phase) matters more than magnitude — this is why, during layout, you should avoid coupling large noise sources (e.g., a switching tail current source, supply ripple) into "low-slope" phase windows.

documents.t: The following two problems work out "the same Δq\Delta qΔq, injected at high vs. low slope, how different is Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ" with concrete Γ\GammaΓ values, continuing with the canonical qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, ideal LC Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ. Example 1 (high-slope vs. low-slope, ratio of Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ for the same Δq\Delta qΔq) Inject the same lump Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC at the ZC (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2, slope maximal, ∣Γ∣=1|\Gamma|=1∣Γ∣=1) and "near the peak" (θ=π/6=30∘\theta=\pi/6=30^\circθ=π/6=30∘, slope small, ∣Γ∣=sin⁡(π/6)=0.5|\Gamma|=\sin(\pi/6)=0.5∣Γ∣=sin(π/6)=0.5). Find Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ at each point and their ratio. Step-by-step substitution (with units), using Δϕ=∣Γ∣ Δqqmax\Delta\phi=\dfrac{|\Gamma|\,\Delta q}{q_{max}}Δϕ=qmax​∣Γ∣Δq​: ΔϕZC=∣−sin⁡(π/2)∣⋅Δqqmax=1×(1×10−15 C)1×10−12 C=1×10−3 rad,Δϕ30∘=∣−sin⁡(π/6)∣⋅Δqqmax=0.5×10−1510−12=5×10−4 rad,ΔϕZCΔϕ30∘=∣Γ(π/2)∣∣Γ(π/6)∣=10.5=2.\begin{aligned} \Delta\phi_{ZC}&=\frac{|{-}\sin(\pi/2)|\cdot\Delta q}{q_{max}}=\frac{1\times(1\times10^{-15}\,\text{C})}{1\times10^{-12}\,\text{C}}=1\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad}, \\[4pt] \Delta\phi_{30^\circ}&=\frac{|{-}\sin(\pi/6)|\cdot\Delta q}{q_{max}}=\frac{0.5\times10^{-15}}{10^{-12}}=5\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad}, \\[4pt] \frac{\Delta\phi_{ZC}}{\Delta\phi_{30^\circ}}&=\frac{|\Gamma(\pi/2)|}{|\Gamma(\pi/6)|}=\frac{1}{0.5}=2. \end{aligned}ΔϕZC​Δϕ30∘​Δϕ30∘​ΔϕZC​​​=qmax​∣−sin(π/2)∣⋅Δq​=1×10−12C1×(1×10−15C)​=1×10−3 rad,=qmax​∣−sin(π/6)∣⋅Δq​=10−120.5×10−15​=5×10−4 rad,=∣Γ(π/6)∣∣Γ(π/2)∣​=0.51​=2.​ Result: the phase shift at the high-slope point (ZC) is 2× the low-slope point (30∘30^\circ30∘) — because the Γ\GammaΓ values differ by exactly 2×. Note the ZC is the phase where ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ is maximal, i.e., most dangerous. Dimension check: [dimensionless]⋅[C][C]=[rad]\dfrac{[\text{dimensionless}]\cdot[\text{C}]}{[\text{C}]}=[\text{rad}][C][dimensionless]⋅[C]​=[rad] (dimensionless) ✓; the ratio is dimensionless ✓. One-line Python check: import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, impulse_to_phase_step g_zc = abs(gamma_lc_ideal(np.pi/2)); g_30 = abs(gamma_lc_ideal(np.pi/6)) d_zc = impulse_to_phase_step(1e-15, g_zc, 1e-12) d_30 = impulse_to_phase_step(1e-15, g_30, 1e-12) print(d_zc, d_30, d_zc/d_30) # -> 0.001 0.0005 2.0 Example 2 (near-immunity at the peak + converting to timing error for intuition) The same lump Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC is injected at the "positive peak" (θ=0\theta=0θ=0, slope =0=0=0, Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0). Find Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ and Δt\Delta tΔt; then compare against Example 1's ZC injection, converted to a timing error at f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz. Step-by-step substitution (with units): Δϕpeak=∣−sin⁡0∣⋅Δqqmax=0×10−1510−12=0 rad ⇒ Δtpeak=0 s,ΔtZC=ΔϕZC2πf0=1×10−3 rad2π×5×109 Hz=10−33.1416×1010 s≈3.18×10−14 s=31.8 fs.\begin{aligned} \Delta\phi_{peak}&=\frac{|{-}\sin 0|\cdot\Delta q}{q_{max}}=\frac{0\times10^{-15}}{10^{-12}}=0\ \text{rad}\;\Rightarrow\;\Delta t_{peak}=0\ \text{s}, \\[4pt] \Delta t_{ZC}&=\frac{\Delta\phi_{ZC}}{2\pi f_0}=\frac{1\times10^{-3}\ \text{rad}}{2\pi\times5\times10^{9}\ \text{Hz}} =\frac{10^{-3}}{3.1416\times10^{10}}\ \text{s}\approx3.18\times10^{-14}\ \text{s}=31.8\ \text{fs}. \end{aligned}Δϕpeak​ΔtZC​​=qmax​∣−sin0∣⋅Δq​=10−120×10−15​=0 rad⇒Δtpeak​=0 s,=2πf0​ΔϕZC​​=2π×5×109 Hz1×10−3 rad​=3.1416×101010−3​ s≈3.18×10−14 s=31.8 fs.​ Result: ideal peak injection → Δϕ=0\Delta\phi=0Δϕ=0, Δt=0\Delta t=0Δt=0 (pure amplitude perturbation, pulled back by amplitude restoration); the same charge injected at the ZC → 31.8 fs. Position (phase) matters more than magnitude: the difference isn't a few percent — it's 0 versus 32 fs. Dimension check: [rad]/[rad/s]=[s][\text{rad}]/[\text{rad/s}]=[\text{s}][rad]/[rad/s]=[s] ✓ (2πf02\pi f_02πf0​ is in rad/s). One-line Python check: import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal, impulse_to_phase_step from simulations.common.noise_utils import phase_to_time_error for th in (0.0, np.pi/2): dphi = impulse_to_phase_step(1e-15, abs(gamma_lc_ideal(th)), 1e-12) print(f"theta={th:.3f}: dphi={dphi:.1e} rad, dt={phase_to_time_error(dphi,5e9)*1e15:.1f} fs") # theta=0.000: dphi=0.0e+00 rad, dt=0.0 fs ; theta=1.571: dphi=1.0e-03 rad, dt=31.8 fs Both problems are pedagogical toys (ideal LC −sin⁡-\sin−sin, not transistor-level): a real waveform has residual AM–PM at the peak, so Δt\Delta tΔt will not be strictly 0.

documents.t: ISF magnitude is, roughly, inversely proportional to waveform slope: small slope (peak) → large ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣, dangerous; large slope (ZC) → small ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣, safe. Ideal LC: Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ, Γ=0\Gamma=0Γ=0 at the peak, ∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ maximal at the ZC (see figure). Fast transitions give a double benefit: shortening the "danger window" lowers Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​, and improving threshold-crossing immunity lowers timing jitter. Same 1 fC lump: ~32 fs when injected at the ZC, ~0 fs at the peak (5 GHz, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC) — position matters more than magnitude. A ring's effective ISF concentrates at the transition; keep large noise sources away from phases where ∣Γeff∣|\Gamma_{eff}|∣Γeff​∣ is large.

documents.t: β: This English translation is in beta — the Traditional-Chinese original is the authoritative version. Prerequisites: white_noise_to_phase_noise (the heuristic route Eq.(19)→(20)→(21), canonical Example B) | Next: lorentzian_linewidth (integrating the white ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ into a phase random walk, then Wiener-Khinchin to obtain the Lorentzian) The route in white_noise_to_phase_noise — "treat white noise as countless independent small tones, compute each tone's sideband, then sum" — is [P1]'s original path. Its physical intuition is strong, but algebraically it is heuristic: the steps "white noise === superposition of tones" and "factor-8 bookkeeping" rely on hand-tallied power accounting. This page redoes the same result with the rigorous machinery of signals and systems — write down the time-averaged autocorrelation of the LTV output phase directly, expand it with the ISF's Fourier coefficients so that ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ falls out of the autocorrelation by itself, then take the spectrum with the Wiener-Khinchin theorem. If you are comfortable with "LTI systems: Sy=∣H∣2SxS_y=|H|^2S_xSy​=∣H∣2Sx​", this page upgrades that to the "LTV / cyclostationary" version. Why this page exists: an oscillator is a periodically time-varying system; its output is not strictly stationary but cyclostationary (its statistics repeat with period TTT). For a cyclostationary process, the correct spectral analysis first averages over the absolute time ttt over one period, "stationarizing" it, and only then applies Wiener-Khinchin. This page walks that path honestly; at the end you will see that Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is not "conjured up" — it is the inevitable product of the period average of the autocorrelation.
documents.s: Autocorrelation to Wiener-Khinchin Rigorous Derivation

documents.t: Starting from the phase integral of [P1] Eq.(11), define g(τ)≡Γ(ω0τ)/qmaxg(\tau)\equiv\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)/q_{max}g(τ)≡Γ(ω0​τ)/qmax​ (folding the ISF and the normalization into a single weighting kernel), so that ϕ(t)=∫−∞tg(τ) in(τ) dτ\phi(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}g(\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tauϕ(t)=∫−∞t​g(τ)in​(τ)dτ. To see the spectrum cleanly, however, we switch to the time derivative of the phase ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ (the instantaneous frequency perturbation), whose autocorrelation is more direct (the phase itself is a non-stationary random walk, see lorentzian_linewidth; it is ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ that is cyclostationary-stationary). By the fundamental theorem of calculus: ϕ˙(t)=g(t) in(t)=Γ(ω0t)qmax in(t).\dot\phi(t)=g(t)\,i_n(t)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0 t)}{q_{max}}\,i_n(t).ϕ˙​(t)=g(t)in​(t)=qmax​Γ(ω0​t)​in​(t). This is a multiplicative LTV: the input white noise in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) is modulated pointwise by a deterministic periodic weight g(t)g(t)g(t). Compute its two-time autocorrelation: Rϕ˙(t, t+τ)=⟨ϕ˙(t) ϕ˙(t+τ)⟩=g(t) g(t+τ) ⟨in(t) in(t+τ)⟩.R_{\dot\phi}(t,\,t+\tau)=\big\langle\dot\phi(t)\,\dot\phi(t+\tau)\big\rangle=g(t)\,g(t+\tau)\,\big\langle i_n(t)\,i_n(t+\tau)\big\rangle.Rϕ˙​​(t,t+τ)=⟨ϕ˙​(t)ϕ˙​(t+τ)⟩=g(t)g(t+τ)⟨in​(t)in​(t+τ)⟩. Math used: ggg is a deterministic function (it can be pulled outside the expectation); only ini_nin​ is random. The white-noise autocorrelation is a delta: white noise at different instants is uncorrelated, ⟨in(t)in(t+τ)⟩=Si δ(τ)\langle i_n(t)i_n(t+\tau)\rangle=S_i\,\delta(\tau)⟨in​(t)in​(t+τ)⟩=Si​δ(τ) (where Si=in2‾/ΔfS_i=\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fSi​=in2​​/Δf is its (two-sided) PSD, a constant). Substituting: Rϕ˙(t, t+τ)=g(t) g(t+τ) Si δ(τ).R_{\dot\phi}(t,\,t+\tau)=g(t)\,g(t+\tau)\,S_i\,\delta(\tau).Rϕ˙​​(t,t+τ)=g(t)g(t+τ)Si​δ(τ). Key observation (cyclostationary): this autocorrelation explicitly contains the absolute time ttt (through g(t)g(t+τ)g(t)g(t+\tau)g(t)g(t+τ)), and it repeats with period TTT (ggg is TTT-periodic) — exactly the defining feature of a cyclostationary process, not a stationary one. You cannot apply Wiener-Khinchin directly; you must first period-average over ttt. Unit check: [g]=1/C[g]=1/\text{C}[g]=1/C (Γ\GammaΓ dimensionless /qmax/q_{max}/qmax​), [g2Siδ(τ)]=C−2⋅(A2/Hz)⋅(1/s)[g^2 S_i\delta(\tau)]= \text{C}^{-2}\cdot(\text{A}^2/\text{Hz})\cdot(1/\text{s})[g2Si​δ(τ)]=C−2⋅(A2/Hz)⋅(1/s). With δ(τ)\delta(\tau)δ(τ) carrying 1/s1/\text{s}1/s and Hz−1=s\text{Hz}^{-1}=\text{s}Hz−1=s, this reduces to C−2A2=s−2\text{C}^{-2}\text{A}^2=\text{s}^{-2}C−2A2=s−2, i.e. [ϕ˙2]=(rad/s)2[\dot\phi^2]=(\text{rad/s})^2[ϕ˙​2]=(rad/s)2 ✓.

documents.t: The time-averaged autocorrelation of a cyclostationary process is defined by averaging over the absolute time ttt over one period: Rˉϕ˙(τ)=1T∫0TRϕ˙(t, t+τ) dt=[1T∫0Tg(t) g(t+τ) dt] Si δ(τ).\bar R_{\dot\phi}(\tau)=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}R_{\dot\phi}(t,\,t+\tau)\,dt=\Big[\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}g(t)\,g(t+\tau)\,dt\Big]\,S_i\,\delta(\tau).Rˉϕ˙​​(τ)=T1​∫0T​Rϕ˙​​(t,t+τ)dt=[T1​∫0T​g(t)g(t+τ)dt]Si​δ(τ). The bracketed quantity is the (deterministic, periodic) autocorrelation of the weighting kernel ggg; denote it gˉ(τ)≡1T∫0Tg(t) g(t+τ) dt=1qmax2⋅1T∫0TΓ(ω0t) Γ(ω0(t+τ)) dt.\bar g(\tau)\equiv\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}g(t)\,g(t+\tau)\,dt=\frac{1}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\Gamma(\omega_0 t)\,\Gamma(\omega_0(t+\tau))\,dt.gˉ​(τ)≡T1​∫0T​g(t)g(t+τ)dt=qmax2​1​⋅T1​∫0T​Γ(ω0​t)Γ(ω0​(t+τ))dt. Because δ(τ)\delta(\tau)δ(τ) is nonzero only at τ=0\tau=0τ=0, we only need gˉ(0)\bar g(0)gˉ​(0): Rˉϕ˙(τ)=gˉ(0) Si δ(τ),gˉ(0)=1qmax2⋅1T∫0TΓ2(ω0t) dt.\bar R_{\dot\phi}(\tau)=\bar g(0)\,S_i\,\delta(\tau),\qquad\bar g(0)=\frac{1}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\Gamma^2(\omega_0 t)\,dt.Rˉϕ˙​​(τ)=gˉ​(0)Si​δ(τ),gˉ​(0)=qmax2​1​⋅T1​∫0T​Γ2(ω0​t)dt. Physics/math used: averaging away the absolute time is the same as averaging the oscillator's sensitivity "at every phase within one period" — exactly the standard "equivalent stationarization" maneuver for cyclostationary systems. Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ is about to emerge here: 1T∫0TΓ2(ω0t) dt\dfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T\Gamma^2(\omega_0t)\,dtT1​∫0T​Γ2(ω0​t)dt is precisely the mean square of the ISF.

documents.t: Substituting the Fourier series of Γ\GammaΓ ([P1] Eq.(12)) into that mean-square integral in gˉ(0)\bar g(0)gˉ​(0) produces ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ all by itself. First convert the mean-square integral into an integral over the phase x=ω0tx=\omega_0 tx=ω0​t (dt=dx/ω0dt=dx/\omega_0dt=dx/ω0​; one period t:0→Tt:0\to Tt:0→T corresponds to x:0→2πx:0\to2\pix:0→2π): 1T∫0TΓ2(ω0t) dt=12π∫02πΓ2(x) dx.\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\Gamma^2(\omega_0 t)\,dt=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)\,dx.T1​∫0T​Γ2(ω0​t)dt=2π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx. Insert Γ(x)=c02+∑n≥1cncos⁡(nx+θn)\Gamma(x)=\dfrac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\cos(nx+\theta_n)Γ(x)=2c0​​+∑n≥1​cn​cos(nx+θn​) and square. Using the orthogonality of the trigonometric functions (cross-harmonic integrals vanish; same-harmonic ∫02πcos⁡2=π\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2=\pi∫02π​cos2=π; the DC term gives ∫02πdx=2π\int_0^{2\pi}dx=2\pi∫02π​dx=2π): 12π∫02πΓ2(x) dx=(c02)2+∑n=1∞cn22=c024+12∑n=1∞cn2.\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)\,dx=\Big(\frac{c_0}{2}\Big)^2+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{c_n^2}{2}=\frac{c_0^2}{4}+\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n^2.2π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx=(2c0​​)2+n=1∑∞​2cn2​​=4c02​​+21​n=1∑∞​cn2​. Writing the DC part as the n=0n=0n=0 term and arranging it into "half of ∑n≥0cn2\sum_{n\ge0}c_n^2∑n≥0​cn2​" form (the same bookkeeping as [P1] Eq.(20): the c0c_0c0​ term carries coefficient 14\tfrac1441​, which equals 12⋅12\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac1221​⋅21​ — i.e. c02c_0^2c02​ is also folded into the 12∑\tfrac12\sum21​∑ with the DC half-weight restored), we get: 12π∫02πΓ2(x) dx=Γrms2,whereΓrms2≡12π∫02πΓ2(x) dx.\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)\,dx=\Gamma_{rms}^2,\qquad\text{where}\quad\Gamma_{rms}^2\equiv\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)\,dx.2π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx=Γrms2​,whereΓrms2​≡2π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx. This is precisely the definition of Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​. documents.t: The heuristic version ([P1]'s original route) hand-computes sideband power by treating white noise as countless independent tones and summing; the rigorous version instead follows "LTV autocorrelation → cyclostationary period average → Wiener-Khinchin", deriving the same result mechanically. An oscillator's output is cyclostationary (its statistics repeat with period TTT as a function of absolute time ttt), not strictly stationary; you must period-average over ttt to "stationarize" it before applying Wiener-Khinchin. ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ is not a Parseval relation plugged in externally — it is the natural result of the period-average integral 12π∫02πΓ2(x)dx\tfrac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\Gamma^2(x)dx2π1​∫02π​Γ2(x)dx. The result is word-for-word identical to the heuristic version: Sϕ(Δω)=Γrms2qmax2⋅SiΔω2S_\phi(\Delta\omega)=\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\dfrac{S_i}{\Delta\omega^2}Sϕ​(Δω)=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δω2Si​​, with 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 coming entirely from the one integration ϕ˙→ϕ\dot\phi\to\phiϕ˙​→ϕ. This page is the entry point of lorentzian_linewidth: there the same autocorrelation machinery is applied to the phase itself (rather than ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​), resolving the spurious divergence of 1/f21/f^21/f2 at the carrier.

documents.t: Prerequisites / See also: isf_definition (the intuitive definition of the ISF, "projection onto the tangential direction"), phase_vs_amplitude_noise (geometric picture of phase/amplitude perturbations), lti_vs_ltv (why an oscillator is LTV) | Next: ltv_htm (the HTM face of the same ISF), derivation_leeson (comparison with the empirical model) [P1] introduces the ISF (Impulse Sensitivity Function) via "physical intuition + impulse simulation": poke the oscillator, see how much the phase permanently shifts, and package the result into a periodic function Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ). This route is very approachable and is the main line of this site (see isf_definition). But it leaves one thing unresolved: what exactly, mathematically, is "projection onto the tangential (phase) direction"? Why does that particular direction correspond to "zero restoring force, permanent accumulation"? This page fills in that rigorous mathematical foundation. Honesty note (read this first): The Floquet theory, monodromy matrix, adjoint method, and PPV (Perturbation Projection Vector) on this page are entirely external literature, not among the five PDFs downloaded for this site. The primary sources are [E2] A. Demir, A. Mehrotra, and J. Roychowdhury, "Phase Noise in Oscillators: A Unifying Theory and Numerical Methods for Characterization," IEEE Trans. Circuits Syst. I, vol. 47, no. 5, pp. 655–674, May 2000, and [E3] F. X. Kärtner, "Analysis of White and f−αf^{-\alpha}f−α Noise in Oscillators," Int. J. Circuit Theory Appl., vol. 18, pp. 485–519, 1990. Volume/issue/page/DOI have been verified online ([E2] DOI 10.1109/81.847872, [E3] DOI 10.1002/cta.4490180505). The notation used on this page (v1,B,ξv_1,B,\xiv1​,B,ξ, Floquet-exponent conventions) follows the original sources and is presented here as background framework. This page only supplies the mathematical intuition and skeleton for "why the ISF is a rigorous object" — it does not replace the originals. This page answers three questions: What linear equation governs a perturbation near an oscillator's limit cycle? What is the structure of that equation's solutions (Floquet)? Why must there be a direction with "zero exponent, permanent, undamped"? Projecting an arbitrary perturbation onto that direction, how do we get ϕ˙=v1T(t)B(t)ξ(t)\dot\phi=v_1^T(t)B(t)\xi(t)ϕ˙​=v1T​(t)B(t)ξ(t), and how does that map back onto the ISF's Γ/qmax\Gamma/q_{max}Γ/qmax​? Physical intuition (the punchline first): An autonomous oscillator (one with no external clock, one that determines its own phase) has an intrinsic symmetry — time-translation invariance. Shift the entire solution slightly forward or backward in time, and it's still a valid solution. This direction of "sliding a bit along the trajectory" is the phase direction; since nothing pulls it back to some "correct" instant, a perturbation along this direction stays forever. Floquet theory encodes this as "one Floquet exponent is exactly 0," and the PPV v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) is the weighting vector that converts "an arbitrary kick" into "how far it moved along that direction." The ISF is nothing more than the scalarized version of the PPV for the specific kick "charge injected into a particular node capacitance."

documents.t: Any oscillator (LC, ring, Colpitts...) can be written as a set of first-order ODEs (state-space form): x˙(t)=f(x(t)),x∈RN.\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t)=\mathbf{f}\big(\mathbf{x}(t)\big),\qquad \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}.x˙(t)=f(x(t)),x∈RN. x\mathbf{x}x is the state vector (e.g., (vC, iL)(v_C,\,i_L)(vC​,iL​): capacitor voltage, inductor current), NNN is the state dimension. f\mathbf{f}f is the circuit's nonlinear vector field (device characteristics + KCL/KVL). Autonomous: f\mathbf{f}f has no explicit ttt-dependence — this is precisely the mathematical signature of "the oscillator determines its own frequency and phase." At steady state there exists a periodic solution xs(t)=xs(t+T)\mathbf{x}_s(t)=\mathbf{x}_s(t+T)xs​(t)=xs​(t+T), T=1/f0T=1/f_0T=1/f0​, tracing a limit cycle in state space. Dimension check: [x˙]=[x]/s[\dot{\mathbf{x}}]=[\mathbf{x}]/\text{s}[x˙]=[x]/s, [f]=[x]/s[\mathbf{f}]=[\mathbf{x}]/\text{s}[f]=[x]/s ✓ (both sides are "rate of change of state"). Injecting noise/perturbation adds a term: x˙(t)=f(x(t))+B(t) ξ(t).\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t)=\mathbf{f}\big(\mathbf{x}(t)\big)+B(t)\,\boldsymbol{\xi}(t).x˙(t)=f(x(t))+B(t)ξ(t). ξ(t)\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)ξ(t) is the vector of perturbation sources (e.g., various noise currents ini_nin​). B(t)B(t)B(t) is the injection/coupling matrix: it specifies which states the perturbation hits, and how strongly. For "current injected into a node capacitance," the corresponding row of BBB is roughly 1/Cnode1/C_{node}1/Cnode​ (converting current into v˙\dot vv˙). Dimension check: [Bξ][B\boldsymbol\xi][Bξ] must be [x]/s[\mathbf{x}]/\text{s}[x]/s. If ξ\xiξ is a current (A) and the corresponding state is a capacitor voltage (V), that row scales as ∼1/C\sim 1/C∼1/C ([A]/[F]=[A]⋅[V/C]=[V/s][\text{A}]/[\text{F}]=[\text{A}]\cdot[\text{V/C}]=[\text{V/s}][A]/[F]=[A]⋅[V/C]=[V/s]) ✓. Mapping to [P1]'s language: Step 0's B(t)ξ(t)B(t)\boldsymbol\xi(t)B(t)ξ(t) is exactly the step "noise current through a node capacitance becomes v˙\dot vv˙" ([P1] Eq.(9), p.181, the differential form of ΔV=Δq/Cnode\Delta V=\Delta q/C_{node}ΔV=Δq/Cnode​).

documents.t: Under a small perturbation, write x(t)=xs(t)+Δx(t)\mathbf{x}(t)=\mathbf{x}_s(t)+\Delta\mathbf{x}(t)x(t)=xs​(t)+Δx(t) and Taylor-expand f\mathbf{f}f to first order: x˙s+Δx˙=f(xs)+∂f∂x∣xs(t)⏟≡ A(t)Δx+B(t)ξ(t)+O(Δx2).\dot{\mathbf{x}}_s+\dot{\Delta\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_s)+\underbrace{\frac{\partial\mathbf{f}}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\bigg|_{\mathbf{x}_s(t)}}_{\equiv\,A(t)}\Delta\mathbf{x}+B(t)\boldsymbol\xi(t)+O(\Delta\mathbf{x}^2).x˙s​+Δx˙=f(xs​)+≡A(t)∂x∂f​​xs​(t)​​​Δx+B(t)ξ(t)+O(Δx2). Since x˙s=f(xs)\dot{\mathbf{x}}_s=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_s)x˙s​=f(xs​) (the steady state itself satisfies the unperturbed equation), the two sides cancel, leaving the linear equation for the perturbation: Δx˙(t)=A(t) Δx(t)+B(t) ξ(t),A(t)≡∂f∂x∣xs(t).\dot{\Delta\mathbf{x}}(t)=A(t)\,\Delta\mathbf{x}(t)+B(t)\,\boldsymbol\xi(t),\qquad A(t)\equiv\frac{\partial\mathbf{f}}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\bigg|_{\mathbf{x}_s(t)}.Δx˙(t)=A(t)Δx(t)+B(t)ξ(t),A(t)≡∂x∂f​​xs​(t)​. Key observation: A(t)=A(t+T)A(t)=A(t+T)A(t)=A(t+T) is a matrix with periodic coefficients (because it's evaluated on the periodic trajectory xs(t)\mathbf{x}_s(t)xs​(t)). This is exactly why oscillator perturbations are LTV (linear time-varying) rather than LTI — the "system matrix" varies periodically in time, matching the LTV nature that [P1] repeatedly emphasizes (see lti_vs_ltv). Math used: Jacobian linearization; dropping O(Δx2)O(\Delta\mathbf{x}^2)O(Δx2) is the "small perturbation/small noise" assumption, consistent with [P1]'s small-signal assumption. Dimension check: AAA has units 1/s1/\text{s}1/s (∂x˙/∂x\partial\dot{\mathbf x}/\partial\mathbf x∂x˙/∂x), and A ΔxA\,\Delta\mathbf xAΔx is [x]/s[\mathbf x]/\text{s}[x]/s ✓. The homogeneous part (turning off ξ\boldsymbol\xiξ) is Δx˙=A(t) Δx,A(t+T)=A(t).\dot{\Delta\mathbf{x}}=A(t)\,\Delta\mathbf{x},\qquad A(t+T)=A(t).Δx˙=A(t)Δx,A(t+T)=A(t). This is precisely the object studied by Floquet theory: a linear ODE with periodic coefficients.
documents.s: Step 1: linearizing near the limit cycle → a linear system with periodic coefficients

documents.t: For the linear system Δx˙=A(t)Δx\dot{\Delta\mathbf x}=A(t)\Delta\mathbf xΔx˙=A(t)Δx, define the state transition matrix Φ(t,t0)\Phi(t,t_0)Φ(t,t0​): it maps a perturbation at time t0t_0t0​ to time ttt, Δx(t)=Φ(t,t0)Δx(t0)\Delta\mathbf x(t)=\Phi(t,t_0)\Delta\mathbf x(t_0)Δx(t)=Φ(t,t0​)Δx(t0​), with Φ(t0,t0)=I\Phi(t_0,t_0)=IΦ(t0​,t0​)=I. Advancing it over exactly one period gives the monodromy matrix: M≡Φ(t0+T, t0).M\equiv\Phi(t_0+T,\,t_0).M≡Φ(t0​+T,t0​). Physical meaning: MMM answers "what does a perturbation become after one full cycle?" Its eigenvalues μi\mu_iμi​ are called Floquet multipliers, describing the amplification/attenuation factor per cycle for each perturbation direction. Dimension check: Φ\PhiΦ and MMM are both dimensionless linear maps (state to state) ✓. Floquet's theorem states that homogeneous solutions can be written as Δx(t)=∑i=1Nci ui(t) eλit,ui(t)=ui(t+T),\Delta\mathbf{x}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{N} c_i\,\mathbf{u}_i(t)\,e^{\lambda_i t},\qquad \mathbf{u}_i(t)=\mathbf{u}_i(t+T),Δx(t)=i=1∑N​ci​ui​(t)eλi​t,ui​(t)=ui​(t+T), where ui(t)\mathbf{u}_i(t)ui​(t) is the periodic Floquet eigenvector and λi\lambda_iλi​ are the Floquet exponents, related to the multipliers by μi=eλiT⟺λi=1Tln⁡μi.\mu_i=e^{\lambda_i T}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lambda_i=\frac{1}{T}\ln\mu_i.μi​=eλi​T⟺λi​=T1​lnμi​. How to read λi\lambda_iλi​: Re λi<0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_i<0Reλi​<0 → the perturbation along that direction decays (stable, e.g., the amplitude direction); Re λi=0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_i=0Reλi​=0 → neutral, undamped (the phase direction); Re λi>0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_i>0Reλi​>0 → diverges (should not occur for a stable limit cycle). Dimension check: [λi]=1/s[\lambda_i]=1/\text{s}[λi​]=1/s, [λiT][\lambda_i T][λi​T] dimensionless (the exponent must be dimensionless) ✓.
documents.s: Step 2: Floquet theory — solution structure and the monodromy matrix

documents.t: This is the pivot of the whole theory, and it can be proven by hand. Differentiate the steady-state solution with respect to time: differentiate both sides of x˙s=f(xs)\dot{\mathbf x}_s=\mathbf f(\mathbf x_s)x˙s​=f(xs​) once more with respect to ttt (chain rule): ddtx˙s=∂f∂x∣xsx˙s⟹ddt(x˙s)=A(t) x˙s.\frac{d}{dt}\dot{\mathbf x}_s=\frac{\partial\mathbf f}{\partial\mathbf x}\bigg|_{\mathbf x_s}\dot{\mathbf x}_s \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{d}{dt}\big(\dot{\mathbf x}_s\big)=A(t)\,\dot{\mathbf x}_s.dtd​x˙s​=∂x∂f​​xs​​x˙s​⟹dtd​(x˙s​)=A(t)x˙s​. In other words, x˙s(t)\dot{\mathbf x}_s(t)x˙s​(t) is itself a solution of the homogeneous perturbation equation Δx˙=A(t)Δx\dot{\Delta\mathbf x}=A(t)\Delta\mathbf xΔx˙=A(t)Δx! And x˙s(t)=x˙s(t+T)\dot{\mathbf x}_s(t)=\dot{\mathbf x}_s(t+T)x˙s​(t)=x˙s​(t+T) is periodic — it carries no exponential growth/decay factor at all, i.e., λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 in eλte^{\lambda t}eλt. Conclusion: the Floquet exponent corresponding to the tangent vector x˙s(t)\dot{\mathbf x}_s(t)x˙s​(t) of the limit cycle is exactly λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0. Denote it the first principal vector: u1(t)∝x˙s(t),λ1=0.\mathbf{u}_1(t)\propto\dot{\mathbf x}_s(t),\qquad \lambda_1=0.u1​(t)∝x˙s​(t),λ1​=0. Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Labels/legend/title read: 穩態軌跡 = steady-state trajectory, "amplitude 擾動後鬆弛回 limit cycle" = relaxes back to the limit cycle after an amplitude perturbation, "phase 擾動 Δφ（切線方向，持續累積）" = phase perturbation Δφ (tangential direction, accumulates persistently), "amplitude 擾動 ΔA（徑向，會被拉回）" = amplitude perturbation ΔA (radial, pulled back), 電容電壓 = capacitor voltage, 電感電流 = inductor current, "擾動" in the title = perturbation. How to read this figure: the tangential arrow along the limit cycle in the figure is exactly the u1(t)∝x˙s(t)\mathbf u_1(t)\propto\dot{\mathbf x}_s(t)u1​(t)∝x˙s​(t) just proven in this step — it corresponds to λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0, so a perturbation along this direction neither grows nor decays, and accumulates permanently as phase; the radial arrow (amplitude direction) corresponds to Re λi≥2<0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_{i\ge2}<0Reλi≥2​<0, where the perturbation is pulled back to the limit cycle by a restoring force. This is exactly the rigorous Floquet version of the geometric picture in phase_vs_amplitude_noise (same figure limit_cycle_phase_amplitude.png, lab_01 fig_limit_cycle, pedagogical toy model, 2-D state illustration). Physical meaning: x˙s\dot{\mathbf x}_sx˙s​ is the direction of "moving along the trajectory." Moving along this direction = shifting in time = changing phase. λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0 mathematically guarantees that "phase perturbation neither amplifies nor decays, and is retained forever" — this is exactly the rigorous basis for [P1]'s expression of "a phase step never disappears" via the unit step u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) ([P1] Eq.(10), p.182), and for the statement in Step 2 of isf_definition that "the tangential direction = neutral direction, no restoring force." Other directions: the remaining λ2,…\lambda_2,\dotsλ2​,… (amplitude and faster-decaying modes) have Re λi<0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_i<0Reλi​<0, so the perturbation is pulled back to the limit cycle — this is the rigorous version of "amplitude perturbation decays" ([P4] Fig. 5, p.2126, the amplitude decay function, see phase_vs_amplitude_noise). This step is the entire secret behind the ISF's "projection onto the tangential direction": this site's isf_definition dots the perturbation with ∂z/∂θ\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta∂z/∂θ by hand; and ∂z/∂θ∝x˙s\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta\propto\dot{\mathbf x}_s∂z/∂θ∝x˙s​ is precisely the Floquet principal vector with λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0. Intuition and rigor line up perfectly here.
documents.s: Step 3: why there must be a λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 direction (the phase direction)

documents.t: Here's the issue: u1(t)\mathbf{u}_1(t)u1​(t) tells us what the phase direction looks like, but to project an arbitrary kick B(t)ξ(t)B(t)\boldsymbol\xi(t)B(t)ξ(t) onto the phase direction, we need its dual — a left vector capable of "extracting the phase component." This is where the adjoint system comes in. Define the adjoint equation of the original system: p˙(t)=−AT(t) p(t).\dot{\mathbf{p}}(t)=-A^{T}(t)\,\mathbf{p}(t).p˙​(t)=−AT(t)p(t). Why −AT-A^T−AT: consider the inner product ⟨p,Δx⟩=pTΔx\langle\mathbf p,\Delta\mathbf x\rangle=\mathbf p^T\Delta\mathbf x⟨p,Δx⟩=pTΔx, and apply the product rule: ddt(pTΔx)=p˙TΔx+pTΔx˙=(−ATp)TΔx+pT(A Δx)=−pTA Δx+pTA Δx=0.\frac{d}{dt}\big(\mathbf p^T\Delta\mathbf x\big)=\dot{\mathbf p}^T\Delta\mathbf x+\mathbf p^T\dot{\Delta\mathbf x} =(-A^T\mathbf p)^T\Delta\mathbf x+\mathbf p^T(A\,\Delta\mathbf x) =-\mathbf p^TA\,\Delta\mathbf x+\mathbf p^TA\,\Delta\mathbf x=0.dtd​(pTΔx)=p˙​TΔx+pTΔx˙=(−ATp)TΔx+pT(AΔx)=−pTAΔx+pTAΔx=0. So choosing p˙=−ATp\dot{\mathbf p}=-A^T\mathbf pp˙​=−ATp makes the inner product pTΔx\mathbf p^T\Delta\mathbf xpTΔx conserved — exactly the property we need: "the projection is not corrupted by the system's evolution." Dimension check: [−ATp]=[p]/s[-A^T\mathbf p]=[\mathbf p]/\text{s}[−ATp]=[p]/s ✓ (consistent with p˙\dot{\mathbf p}p˙​). The adjoint system also has Floquet structure, and the periodic solution corresponding to λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 is denoted v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) — it is the dual (left Floquet vector) of the original system's u1(t)\mathbf u_1(t)u1​(t). v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) is the PPV (Perturbation Projection Vector). The standard normalization is "the PPV is aligned with the phase direction with unit scale": v1T(t) x˙s(t)=1(for all t; normalization convention).v_1^{T}(t)\,\dot{\mathbf x}_s(t)=1\qquad\text{(for all }t\text{; normalization convention)}.v1T​(t)x˙s​(t)=1(for all t; normalization convention). Intuition: u1∝x˙s\mathbf u_1\propto\dot{\mathbf x}_su1​∝x˙s​ is "the arrow of the phase direction"; v1v_1v1​ is "the ruler that measures the component along that arrow." The two are calibrated by the equation above so that "moving one unit of time along the trajectory = phase advances by one unit." Practical value of the adjoint: solving the adjoint system's periodic solution once gives you the entire v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) in one shot (i.e., the entire ISF); no need to brute-force "fire an impulse at one phase at a time" as in lab_04. The PSS + Pnoise engines inside commercial RF simulators internally use exactly this kind of adjoint/Floquet flow. Note (background): the normalization convention for v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) (v1Tx˙s=1v_1^T\dot{\mathbf x}_s=1v1T​x˙s​=1) and the λ\lambdaλ notation follow [E2] Demir 2000 (pp.655–674, DOI 10.1109/81.847872); the citation has been verified, but the internal notation belongs to an external framework.
documents.s: Step 4: the adjoint system and the "left eigenvector" v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t)

documents.t: Now apply the "ruler" from Step 4 to the perturbed equation. Demir et al. prove that, near the limit cycle, the state can be written as "a phase shift along the trajectory + a decaying orbital deviation": x(t)=xs(t+α(t))+y(t),\mathbf{x}(t)=\mathbf{x}_s\big(t+\alpha(t)\big)+\mathbf{y}(t),x(t)=xs​(t+α(t))+y(t), where α(t)\alpha(t)α(t) is the phase shift in the time domain (units s), and y(t)\mathbf y(t)y(t) is the decaying orbital-deviation component (lying in the subspace with Re λ<0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda<0Reλ<0). Substitute this back into x˙=f(x)+Bξ\dot{\mathbf x}=\mathbf f(\mathbf x)+B\boldsymbol\xix˙=f(x)+Bξ, and use v1v_1v1​ to project out the decaying y\mathbf yy (because v1Tv_1^Tv1T​ is "orthogonal" to those directions — this is the biorthogonality of the left/right Floquet vectors). Only the phase component survives, giving the first-order phase equation: α˙(t)=v1T(t+α(t)) B(t) ξ(t) ≈ v1T(t) B(t) ξ(t).\dot{\alpha}(t)=v_1^{T}\big(t+\alpha(t)\big)\,B(t)\,\boldsymbol\xi(t)\;\approx\;v_1^{T}(t)\,B(t)\,\boldsymbol\xi(t).α˙(t)=v1T​(t+α(t))B(t)ξ(t)≈v1T​(t)B(t)ξ(t). Converting the time-domain phase α\alphaα into the radian phase ϕ=ω0α\phi=\omega_0\alphaϕ=ω0​α (or directly defining ϕ\phiϕ as the dimensionless phase) gives this page's headline result: ϕ˙(t)=v1T(t) B(t) ξ(t) \boxed{\ \dot{\phi}(t)=v_1^{T}(t)\,B(t)\,\boldsymbol\xi(t)\ } ϕ˙​(t)=v1T​(t)B(t)ξ(t) ​ Term-by-term meaning: ξ(t)\boldsymbol\xi(t)ξ(t) is the raw perturbation (noise current); B(t)B(t)B(t) injects it into state space (via the node capacitance); v1T(t)v_1^T(t)v1T​(t) projects the result onto the phase direction, extracting "how much phase-change rate this particular kick contributes." Why ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ (rate) rather than ϕ\phiϕ: because the phase is the neutral direction (λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0), every instantaneous kick is accumulated into the phase "verbatim" — so the perturbation directly gives ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​; to get ϕ\phiϕ you must integrate over time. This is exactly the same as the integral form of [P1] Eq.(11) (convolution_derivation): ϕ(t)=∫−∞tv1T(τ) B(τ) ξ(τ) dτ.\phi(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}v_1^{T}(\tau)\,B(\tau)\,\boldsymbol\xi(\tau)\,d\tau.ϕ(t)=∫−∞t​v1T​(τ)B(τ)ξ(τ)dτ. Dimension check: ϕ˙\dot\phiϕ˙​ is in rad/s. On the right, v1TBξv_1^TB\boldsymbol\xiv1T​Bξ: taking noise as a current (A), the corresponding row of BBB scales as ∼1/C\sim1/C∼1/C (V/C via A becomes V/s... details depend on normalization), and the overall combination is tuned to rad/s. The exact dimensional bookkeeping depends on the normalization of v1v_1v1​ (whether it absorbs 1/qmax1/q_{max}1/qmax​) (following [E2]'s convention) — see the next step for the mapping.
documents.s: Step 5: projection → proving ϕ˙=v1T(t)B(t)ξ(t)\dot\phi=v_1^T(t)B(t)\boldsymbol\xi(t)ϕ˙​=v1T​(t)B(t)ξ(t)

documents.t: Narrow Step 5 down to [P1]'s specific scenario: a single noise current in(t)i_n(t)in​(t) injected into a single node capacitance CnodeC_{node}Cnode​. In that case: ξ(t)→in(t)\boldsymbol\xi(t)\to i_n(t)ξ(t)→in​(t) (scalar). B(t)→bB(t)\to \mathbf bB(t)→b (a constant vector, nonzero only in the entry corresponding to "the capacitor state at the injection node," with value ∼1/Cnode\sim 1/C_{node}∼1/Cnode​, converting current into v˙\dot vv˙). v1T(t) bv_1^T(t)\,\mathbf bv1T​(t)b is a scalar periodic function — it is exactly Γ(ω0t)/qmax\Gamma(\omega_0 t)/q_{max}Γ(ω0​t)/qmax​. Therefore ϕ˙(t)=[v1T(t) b] in(t) ≡ Γ(ω0t)qmax in(t)⟹ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ.\dot\phi(t)=\big[v_1^{T}(t)\,\mathbf b\big]\,i_n(t)\;\equiv\;\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0 t)}{q_{max}}\,i_n(t) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau.ϕ˙​(t)=[v1T​(t)b]in​(t)≡qmax​Γ(ω0​t)​in​(t)⟹ϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ. The right-hand form is exactly [P1] Eq.(11), p.182. Comparing the two gives the rigorous correspondence: Γ(ω0τ)qmax=v1T(τ) b=(the PPV’s component at the injection node) \boxed{\ \frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}=v_1^{T}(\tau)\,\mathbf b=\big(\text{the PPV's component at the injection node}\big)\ } qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​=v1T​(τ)b=(the PPV’s component at the injection node) ​ Equivalently, pulling the qmaxq_{max}qmax​ normalization out explicitly, the ISF is "the PPV's component at that node, scaled by qmaxq_{max}qmax​" (matching the authors' convention 10.2: ISF =qmax⋅=q_{max}\cdot=qmax​⋅(PPV's component at the injection node)): Γ(ω0τ)=qmax⋅(the component of v1(τ) on the capacitor state at the injection node).\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=q_{max}\cdot\big(\text{the component of }v_1(\tau)\text{ on the capacitor state at the injection node}\big).Γ(ω0​τ)=qmax​⋅(the component of v1​(τ) on the capacitor state at the injection node). Why Γ\GammaΓ is dimensionless while the PPV has units: the PPV v1v_1v1​ carries units (depending on the physical quantity of the state), but multiplying by qmax=CnodeVmaxq_{max}=C_{node}V_{max}qmax​=Cnode​Vmax​ (C) cancels them exactly, turning it into a dimensionless "shape function" — this is the deep reason [P1] normalizes with qmaxq_{max}qmax​ (see Step 3 of isf_definition). Why Γ\GammaΓ has period 2π2\pi2π: v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) is a periodic Floquet vector (period TTT); substituting ω0τ\omega_0\tauω0​τ turns the period into 2π2\pi2π ✓. Why "each node/each noise source has its own ISF": because each injection point corresponds to a different b\mathbf bb, projecting out a different scalar v1Tbv_1^T\mathbf bv1T​b ✓. This upgrades the property stated in isf_definition from "intuition" to "a choice of column of BBB."

documents.t: The same thing, at three levels of abstraction: Concept [P1] intuitive language (main line of this site) Floquet/PPV rigorous language (this page, external literature) Correspondence Phase direction tangent to the limit cycle, ∂z/∂θ\partial\mathbf z/\partial\theta∂z/∂θ Floquet principal vector with λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0, u1∝x˙s\mathbf u_1\propto\dot{\mathbf x}_su1​∝x˙s​ same direction "Phase does not decay" no restoring force on phase, unit step u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) Floquet exponent λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0 (neutral) λ1=0⇔\lambda_1=0\Leftrightarrowλ1​=0⇔ permanently retained Projection weight "conversion ratio" Γ/qmax\Gamma/q_{max}Γ/qmax​ node component of PPV v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) Γ/qmax=v1Tb\Gamma/q_{max}=v_1^T\mathbf bΓ/qmax​=v1T​b Phase response ϕ=1qmax∫Γ in dτ\phi=\tfrac{1}{q_{max}}\int\Gamma\,i_n\,d\tauϕ=qmax​1​∫Γin​dτ ϕ˙=v1TBξ\dot\phi=v_1^TB\boldsymbol\xiϕ˙​=v1T​Bξ (integrated) same equation Extraction method fire impulses phase by phase (lab_04 brute force) solve the adjoint periodic solution once, get the whole curve adjoint is far more efficient Amplitude decay amplitude restoring subspace with Re λi≥2<0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_{i\ge2}<0Reλi≥2​<0 rigorizes "amplitude is pulled back"

documents.t: The preceding six steps are all theorems and prose. An old engineer's habit is: don't trust that you truly understand a theorem until it becomes numbers. In this section we take a van der Pol oscillator (μ=0.2\mu=0.2μ=0.2, near-harmonic, unit frequency — the same toy as lab_15) and compute every mathematical object on this page as a number, one by one: the limit cycle, TTT, monodromy MMM, Floquet multipliers, adjoint periodic solution v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t), and PPV→ISF — then overlay the ISF from the adjoint method on top of the brute-force "fire an impulse at each phase" method (lab_15's approach) in a single figure. Full script: simulations/lab_25_floquet_numeric.py. Honesty note: this is a pedagogical toy model (not transistor-level); everything uses normalized (dimensionless) units — the time unit is "the second in which the near-harmonic-limit angular frequency =1=1=1 rad/s," and states x,yx,yx,y are dimensionless. Below, wherever s and rad/s are written, they refer to this normalized unit system. The Floquet/adjoint algorithm itself follows the framework of [E2] Demir 2000 (external literature, not among the five PDFs on this site).

documents.t: The van der Pol equation x¨−μ(1−x2)x˙+x=0\ddot x-\mu(1-x^2)\dot x+x=0x¨−μ(1−x2)x˙+x=0 written in the state form of Step 0: x˙=f(x)=(yμ(1−x2) y−x),x=(x,y), μ=0.2.\dot{\mathbf x}=\mathbf f(\mathbf x)=\begin{pmatrix}y\\ \mu(1-x^2)\,y-x\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf x=(x,y),\ \ \mu=0.2 .x˙=f(x)=(yμ(1−x2)y−x​),x=(x,y), μ=0.2. The Jacobian needed for Step 1, differentiating term by term (f2=μ(1−x2)y−xf_2=\mu(1-x^2)y-xf2​=μ(1−x2)y−x): ∂f2/∂x=−2μxy−1\partial f_2/\partial x=-2\mu xy-1∂f2​/∂x=−2μxy−1, ∂f2/∂y=μ(1−x2)\partial f_2/\partial y=\mu(1-x^2)∂f2​/∂y=μ(1−x2), so A(t)=∂f∂x∣xs(t)=(01−2μxsys−1μ(1−xs2)),A(t+T)=A(t).A(t)=\frac{\partial\mathbf f}{\partial\mathbf x}\bigg|_{\mathbf x_s(t)} =\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ -2\mu x_s y_s-1 & \mu(1-x_s^2)\end{pmatrix}, \qquad A(t+T)=A(t).A(t)=∂x∂f​​xs​(t)​=(0−2μxs​ys​−1​1μ(1−xs2​)​),A(t+T)=A(t). Dimension check: under normalization, [x]=[y]=[x]=[y]=[x]=[y]= dimensionless, [t]=[t]=[t]= s, so [A]=1/s[A]=1/\text{s}[A]=1/s ✓ (the general conclusion of Step 1). Reason for choosing μ=0.2\mu=0.2μ=0.2: small enough → the waveform is nearly sinusoidal, so the ISF should be close to −sin⁡-\sin−sin (checkable against intuition); yet nonzero → the Floquet structure is non-degenerate (∣μ2∣\vert\mu_2\vert∣μ2​∣ clearly less than 1).
