documents.t: Method: starting from (2,0)(2,0)(2,0), integrate with RK4 (step size 10−310^{-3}10−3 s) for 300 s — the transient decays as e−μte^{-\mu t}e−μt, and μt=60\mu t=60μt=60 already reaches machine precision; then take the Poincaré section "x=0x=0x=0, y>0y>0y>0 (rising zero-crossing of xxx)," and use a Newton step Δt=−x/x˙=−x/y\Delta t=-x/\dot x=-x/yΔt=−x/x˙=−x/y to correct the crossing point to ∣x∣<10−13\vert x\vert<10^{-13}∣x∣<10−13; average over 5 consecutive returns to the section to get TTT. import numpy as np from simulations.lab_25_floquet_numeric import find_limit_cycle, monodromy s0, T = find_limit_cycle() # step 1: settle + Poincare section + Newton print(round(T, 4)) # -> 6.2989 print(round(2 * np.pi / T, 4)) # -> 0.9975 M, states, hf = monodromy(s0, T) # step 2: dPhi/dt = A(t)Phi integrated over one cycle mults = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvals(M).real)[::-1] print(round(float(mults[0]), 6), round(float(mults[1]), 4)) # -> 1.0 0.2828 print(round(float(np.log(mults[1]) / T), 4)) # -> -0.2005 print(round(float(np.linalg.det(M)), 6)) # -> 0.282827 tr = 0.2 * (1 - states[:, 0] ** 2) # tr A = mu(1 - x^2) print(round(float(np.exp(np.trapezoid(tr, dx=hf))), 6)) # -> 0.282827 Result and cross-check: T=6.2989T=6.2989T=6.2989 s, ω0=2π/T=0.9975\omega_0=2\pi/T=0.9975ω0​=2π/T=0.9975 rad/s. The Lindstedt–Poincaré perturbation expansion gives the standard van der Pol result T=2π (1+μ2/16+O(μ4))T=2\pi\,(1+\mu^2/16+O(\mu^4))T=2π(1+μ2/16+O(μ4)) (external literature, not among the five PDFs on this site: A. H. Nayfeh, Perturbation Methods, Wiley, New York, 1973): substituting μ=0.2\mu=0.2μ=0.2 gives 2π×1.0025=6.29892\pi\times1.0025=6.29892π×1.0025=6.2989 s — matching the numerical result to four decimal places; equivalently ω0≈1−μ2/16=0.9975\omega_0\approx1-\mu^2/16=0.9975ω0​≈1−μ2/16=0.9975 ✓. Amplitude A=max⁡∣xs∣=2.0004A=\max\vert x_s\vert=2.0004A=max∣xs​∣=2.0004 (the well-known result A→2A\to2A→2 in the harmonic limit). Dimension check: [T]=[T]=[T]= s, [ω0]=[\omega_0]=[ω0​]= rad/s ✓; rad is a dimensionless bookkeeping unit.

documents.t: Method: turn Step 2's definition directly into a numerical problem — integrate "state + fundamental matrix" simultaneously along the cycle just found: dΦdt=A(t) Φ,Φ(0)=I2,M=Φ(T),\frac{d\Phi}{dt}=A(t)\,\Phi,\qquad \Phi(0)=I_2,\qquad M=\Phi(T),dtdΦ​=A(t)Φ,Φ(0)=I2​,M=Φ(T), RK4, 12000 steps per period (A(t)A(t)A(t) is evaluated directly from the current xs\mathbf x_sxs​ at each RK4 stage's Jacobian; no analytic form of A(t)A(t)A(t) is needed). Result (printed by the same code block above): μ1=1.000000,μ2=0.2828,\mu_1=1.000000,\qquad \mu_2=0.2828,μ1​=1.000000,μ2​=0.2828,λ1=ln⁡μ1T=1.5×10−13 1/s≈0,λ2=ln⁡μ2T=−0.2005 1/s.\lambda_1=\frac{\ln\mu_1}{T}=1.5\times10^{-13}\ \text{1/s}\approx0,\qquad \lambda_2=\frac{\ln\mu_2}{T}=-0.2005\ \text{1/s}.λ1​=Tlnμ1​​=1.5×10−13 1/s≈0,λ2​=Tlnμ2​​=−0.2005 1/s. Three things worth reading twice: μ1=1\mu_1=1μ1​=1 is not something we put in — it's something that came out. The program was never told at any point that "there is a phase direction"; the deviation of μ1\mu_1μ1​ from 1 (∼10−13\sim10^{-13}∼10−13) is simultaneously numerical evidence for Step 3's theorem (tangent direction ⇒λ1=0\Rightarrow\lambda_1=0⇒λ1​=0) and a self-diagnostic that "the cycle was found accurately enough, TTT was measured accurately enough" — if settling is insufficient or TTT is wrong, μ1\mu_1μ1​ immediately deviates from 1. λ2≈−μ\lambda_2\approx-\muλ2​≈−μ has an analytic counterpart. So the first-order prediction is λ2=−μ=−0.2\lambda_2=-\mu=-0.2λ2​=−μ=−0.2, versus the numerical −0.2005-0.2005−0.2005 (0.25% difference, an O(μ3)O(\mu^3)O(μ3) correction) ✓. The amplitude-perturbation time constant τamp=1/∣λ2∣=4.99\tau_{amp}=1/\vert\lambda_2\vert=4.99τamp​=1/∣λ2​∣=4.99 s ≈1/μ\approx1/\mu≈1/μ — this is exactly the Floquet-rigorous version, on this toy, of the amplitude decay function d=e−t/τ0d=e^{-t/\tau_0}d=e−t/τ0​ in [P4] Fig. 5, p.2126 (LC oscillator τ0=2Q/ω0\tau_0=2Q/\omega_0τ0​=2Q/ω0​). Abel–Liouville cross-check. The determinant identity det⁡M=exp⁡ ⁣(∫0Ttr⁡A dt)\det M=\exp\!\big(\int_0^T\operatorname{tr}A\,dt\big)detM=exp(∫0T​trAdt), with tr⁡A=μ(1−xs2)\operatorname{tr}A=\mu(1-x_s^2)trA=μ(1−xs2​): left side μ1μ2=0.282827\mu_1\mu_2=0.282827μ1​μ2​=0.282827, right side — numerically integrating along the cycle and exponentiating — =0.282827=0.282827=0.282827 — matching to six decimal places. documents.t: Why integrate "backward": first turn Step 4's conservation law into a map. For any initial perturbation Δx(0)\Delta\mathbf x(0)Δx(0), p(T)TΔx(T)=p(0)TΔx(0)\mathbf p(T)^T\Delta\mathbf x(T)=\mathbf p(0)^T\Delta\mathbf x(0)p(T)TΔx(T)=p(0)TΔx(0) and Δx(T)=MΔx(0)\Delta\mathbf x(T)=M\Delta\mathbf x(0)Δx(T)=MΔx(0), so MTp(T)=p(0)M^T\mathbf p(T)=\mathbf p(0)MTp(T)=p(0) — the adjoint's "one-cycle map" is M−TM^{-T}M−T, whose eigenvalues are 1/μi1/\mu_i1/μi​: namely 111 and 1/0.2828=3.541/0.2828=3.541/0.2828=3.54. Integrating forward, that 3.54 mode amplifies numerical impurities by 3.54× per cycle, quickly swamping v1v_1v1​; integrating backward, it decays by a factor of 0.2828 per cycle, so the integration automatically "self-cleans" and converges to the periodic solution v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t) — this is exactly [E2] Demir 2000's backward-adjoint numerical procedure (external literature). We start from the eigenvalue-111 left eigenvector of MTM^TMT and integrate backward along the cycle: p˙=−AT(t) p(integrated from t=T back to t=0).\dot{\mathbf p}=-A^T(t)\,\mathbf p\quad(\text{integrated from }t=T\text{ back to }t=0).p˙​=−AT(t)p(integrated from t=T back to t=0). import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_rms from simulations.lab_25_floquet_numeric import ppv_pipeline res = ppv_pipeline() # steps 1-3 done in one call print("{:.1e}".format(res["const_err"])) # -> 2.2e-14 print("{:.1e}".format(res["per_err"])) # -> 9.5e-13 theta = res["theta"] g = res["omega0"] * res["v1"][:, 1] # step 4: Gamma/qmax = w0 * v1_y print(round(float(np.max(np.abs(g))), 4)) # -> 0.5011 print(round(res["qmax_toy"], 4)) # -> 2.0442 print(round(float(gamma_rms(theta, res["qmax_toy"] * g)), 4)) # -> 0.7258 gn = g / np.max(np.abs(g)) print(round(float(np.sqrt(np.mean((gn + np.sin(theta)) ** 2))), 4)) # -> 0.0555 Two machine-precision-level checks: Periodicity: ∥p(0)−p(T)∥/∥p(T)∥=9.5×10−13\Vert\mathbf p(0)-\mathbf p(T)\Vert/\Vert\mathbf p(T)\Vert=9.5\times10^{-13}∥p(0)−p(T)∥/∥p(T)∥=9.5×10−13 — integrating backward over one cycle does indeed return to itself (the left Floquet vector, λ=0\lambda=0λ=0). Constant normalization (the inner-product conservation theorem of Step 4): p(t)Tx˙s(t)\mathbf p(t)^T\dot{\mathbf x}_s(t)p(t)Tx˙s​(t)'s maximum relative deviation over the full cycle =2.2×10−14=2.2\times10^{-14}=2.2×10−14. This inner product should not move by even a constant, theoretically; numerically only round-off error remains. Dividing by this constant completes the normalization v1T(t) x˙s(t)=1v_1^T(t)\,\dot{\mathbf x}_s(t)=1v1T​(t)x˙s​(t)=1 (for all ttt). Dimension check: the normalization condition v1Tx˙s=1v_1^T\dot{\mathbf x}_s=1v1T​x˙s​=1 (dimensionless) gives [v1]=s/[x][v_1]=\text{s}/[\mathbf x][v1​]=s/[x]; hence the time-domain phase Δα=v1TΔx\Delta\alpha=v_1^T\Delta\mathbf xΔα=v1T​Δx obtained from a kick Δx\Delta\mathbf xΔx has units of s ✓ (the units of α(t)\alpha(t)α(t) from Step 5).

For this toy we fire the impulse along the yyy-axis (exactly the same kick as lab_15's impulse_dy, b=e^y\mathbf b=\hat{\mathbf e}_yb=e^y​), so Γ(θ)qmax=ω0 v1,y(θ),θ=ω0t (measured from the rising zero-crossing of x).\frac{\Gamma(\theta)}{q_{max}}=\omega_0\,v_{1,y}(\theta),\qquad \theta=\omega_0 t\ (\text{measured from the rising zero-crossing of }x).qmax​Γ(θ)​=ω0​v1,y​(θ),θ=ω0​t (measured from the rising zero-crossing of x). Predicted peak 1/(ω0A)=1/(0.9975×2.0004)=0.50111/(\omega_0A)=1/(0.9975\times2.0004)=0.50111/(ω0​A)=1/(0.9975×2.0004)=0.5011 — the numerical peak is exactly 0.50110.50110.5011 ✓. import numpy as np from simulations.lab_15_nonlinear_isf import extract_vdp_isf from simulations.lab_25_floquet_numeric import ppv_isf, extract_isf_impulse_axis theta, g_ppv, res = ppv_isf() # adjoint solved once th15, isf15, T15 = extract_vdp_isf(0.2) # lab_15 brute force: 36 phases, impulses rms = np.sqrt(np.mean((np.interp(th15, theta, g_ppv) - isf15) ** 2)) print(round(float(rms), 4)) # -> 0.0016 g_ppv_x = res["omega0"] * res["v1"][:, 0] # x-component of the same v1 thx, isfx = extract_isf_impulse_axis(res["s0"], res["T"], axis=0) rms_x = np.sqrt(np.mean((np.interp(thx, theta, g_ppv_x) - isfx) ** 2)) print(round(float(rms_x), 4)) # -> 0.0023 Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Axis labels/titles read: "x（無因次）" / "y=ẋ（無因次）" = x (dimensionless) / y=ẋ (dimensionless); "θ/2π（自 x 上升零交越起算）" = θ/2π (measured from x's rising zero crossing); "Γ/qmax（rad／單位 Δq，正規化）" = Γ/qmax (rad per unit Δq, normalized); "(b) 一次 adjoint 解 → 每個注入軸的 ISF\n歸一化恆定誤差 …，x 軸 rms 差 …" = (b) a single adjoint solve → the ISF for each injection axis; normalized constant error …, x-axis rms difference …; "注入相位 θ/2π（自 x 上升零交越起算）" = injection phase θ/2π (measured from x's rising zero crossing); "(c) PPV = ISF：兩種方法疊在一起\nrms 差 …（vs 脈衝）, …（vs −sin, 歸一）" = (c) PPV = ISF: the two methods overlaid; rms difference … (vs. impulse), … (vs. −sin, normalized). How to read this figure (script: simulations/lab_25_floquet_numeric.py, figure floquet_ppv_numeric.png): (a): the gray line is the transient (absorbed into the limit cycle as eλ2te^{\lambda_2 t}eλ2​t — a visualization of Re λ2<0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_2<0Reλ2​<0); the blue circle is xs(t)\mathbf x_s(t)xs​(t); the red arrow is the tangent x˙s\dot{\mathbf x}_sx˙s​, i.e., the Floquet principal vector u1\mathbf u_1u1​ with λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0. (b): a single adjoint solve gives the whole v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t), and its two components are simultaneously the ISFs for the two injection axes — the blue line (kicking yyy) hugs −sin⁡θ/(ω0A)-\sin\theta/(\omega_0A)−sinθ/(ω0​A); the orange line (kicking xxx) shows a visible deviation from the harmonic limit +cos⁡θ/A+\cos\theta/A+cosθ/A (dotted line). This deviation is genuine physics (waveform distortion at μ=0.2\mu=0.2μ=0.2), not numerical error — the evidence: the orange squares are from a separately performed, independent impulse sweep (kicking the xxx-axis, 18 phases), differing from the orange line by an rms of only 0.00230.00230.0023. Step 4's claim, "solve the adjoint once and get the ISF for every injection point," becomes a computed fact here: the xxx-axis ISF was obtained without re-solving the adjoint — just reading off a different component of the same v1v_1v1​. (c): the headline overlay. Blue line = ω0v1,y\omega_0v_{1,y}ω0​v1,y​ (adjoint method); red circles = lab_15's impulse-firing method (36 phases, Δq=0.02\Delta q=0.02Δq=0.02); black dashed line = −sin⁡θ/(ω0A)-\sin\theta/(\omega_0A)−sinθ/(ω0​A). Tying the toy back to the site's canonical numbers: taking the toy's qmaxq_{max}qmax​ as the maximum swing of the kicked node, qmax toy=max⁡∣ys∣=2.0442q_{max}^{\,toy}=\max\vert y_s\vert=2.0442qmaxtoy​=max∣ys​∣=2.0442, the de-normalized dimensionless ISF Γ=qmax toy⋅(Γ/qmax)\Gamma=q_{max}^{\,toy}\cdot(\Gamma/q_{max})Γ=qmaxtoy​⋅(Γ/qmax​) has rms Γrms=0.7258\Gamma_{rms}=0.7258Γrms​=0.7258 — only +2.6%+2.6\%+2.6% away from the true LC canonical value 1/2=0.70711/\sqrt2=0.70711/2​=0.7071 (see rms_isf): a near-harmonic oscillator's ISF is "almost exactly" the ideal LC's −sin⁡-\sin−sin, with the deviation being exactly the distortion introduced by μ\muμ — connecting to the lesson of lab_15 (at large μ\muμ, the ISF departs far from −sin⁡-\sin−sin).

[P1]'s impulse-firing intuition and [E2]'s rigorous adjoint method give the same curve on the same oscillator, differing by 0.3%. Applicability and limits of this section's numerical method (honesty clause): fixed-step RK4 + Poincaré/Newton is more than adequate for this near-harmonic toy; if μ≫1\mu\gg1μ≫1 (relaxation oscillator, very steep waveform), an adaptive step size and more careful section selection are needed; if the system dimension is high and ∣μ2∣→1\vert\mu_2\vert\to1∣μ2​∣→1 (very slow decay, e.g., ultra-high QQQ), the eigenvector separation of MMM degrades and backward-integration convergence slows — these are exactly the engineering details handled by commercial shooting-PSS/Pnoise engines. Also, this toy uses additive, single-point injection; for cyclostationary modulation, see effective_isf.

documents.t: An oscillator perturbation near the limit cycle → a linear system with periodic coefficients Δx˙=A(t)Δx+Bξ\dot{\Delta\mathbf x}=A(t)\Delta\mathbf x+B\boldsymbol\xiΔx˙=A(t)Δx+Bξ, A(t+T)=A(t)A(t+T)=A(t)A(t+T)=A(t) — this is the root of LTV behavior. Floquet's theorem gives Δx=∑ciui(t)eλit\Delta\mathbf x=\sum c_i\mathbf u_i(t)e^{\lambda_i t}Δx=∑ci​ui​(t)eλi​t; the eigenvalues of the monodromy matrix M=Φ(t0+T,t0)M=\Phi(t_0+T,t_0)M=Φ(t0​+T,t0​) determine the per-cycle amplification factor, μi=eλiT\mu_i=e^{\lambda_iT}μi​=eλi​T. The tangent vector x˙s\dot{\mathbf x}_sx˙s​ is automatically a homogeneous solution → λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0 (phase is neutral, permanently undamped); amplitude and other directions have Re λ<0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda<0Reλ<0 (decaying). The adjoint system p˙=−ATp\dot{\mathbf p}=-A^T\mathbf pp˙​=−ATp conserves pTΔx\mathbf p^T\Delta\mathbf xpTΔx; its λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 solution is the PPV v1(t)v_1(t)v1​(t). Projecting gives ϕ˙=v1T(t)B(t)ξ(t)\boxed{\dot\phi=v_1^T(t)B(t)\boldsymbol\xi(t)}ϕ˙​=v1T​(t)B(t)ξ(t)​; narrowing to single-node current injection → Γ/qmax=v1Tb\Gamma/q_{max}=v_1^T\mathbf bΓ/qmax​=v1T​b, i.e., the ISF is the PPV's component at the injection node (scaled by qmaxq_{max}qmax​). The entire Floquet/adjoint/PPV apparatus belongs to the external literature of Demir 2000 and Kärtner 1990, not within the five PDFs; the citations (volume/page/DOI) have been verified — see references. Numerical verification (lab_25, van der Pol μ=0.2\mu=0.2μ=0.2): T=6.2989T=6.2989T=6.2989, μ1=1.000000\mu_1=1.000000μ1​=1.000000 (λ1≈0\lambda_1\approx0λ1​≈0), μ2=0.2828\mu_2=0.2828μ2​=0.2828 (λ2=−0.2005≈−μ\lambda_2=-0.2005\approx-\muλ2​=−0.2005≈−μ); v1Tx˙sv_1^T\dot{\mathbf x}_sv1T​x˙s​ constant to 2.2×10−142.2\times10^{-14}2.2×10−14; the adjoint-computed ISF differs from the impulse-firing method by rms 0.00160.00160.0016 — "PPV = ISF" is a computed fact, not just prose.

documents.t: Prerequisites / See also: tank_Q_and_energy_restoration (the energy definition of QQQ, why the tank shapes 1/f21/f^21/f2), psd_phase_noise_jitter (4kTR4kTR4kTR thermal noise and PSD basics), white_noise_to_phase_noise (the ISF-version 1/f21/f^21/f2 derivation) | Next: symmetry (using c0c_0c0​ symmetry to suppress the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner), references (external literature [E1]) Before Hajimiri–Lee's ISF theory ([P1], 1998) appeared, engineers estimated oscillator phase noise using the Leeson model (1966). It is a semi-empirical formula: the physical skeleton (tank filtering + feedback) is correct, but it packs in a noise factor FFF that is "unknown where it comes from — has to be fit from measurement." This page derives Leeson from scratch, then maps it term by term onto the closed-form ISF result — you'll see that ISF theory "explains why Leeson looks the way it does, and replaces that mysterious FFF with a computable physical quantity." Honesty note (read first): the Leeson model comes from [E1] D. B. Leeson, "A Simple Model of Feedback Oscillator Noise Spectrum," Proc. IEEE, vol. 54, no. 2, pp. 329–330, Feb. 1966, not among the five source PDFs downloaded for this site. This page relies only on standard-literature knowledge for background and comparison; the volume/issue/pages/DOI have been verified online (DOI 10.1109/PROC.1966.4682); FFF (noise figure) is inherently an empirically fitted parameter of the Leeson model (implementation-dependent), not a fixed constant. By contrast, the ISF formulas in the right half of this page ([P1] Eqs.(21),(23),(24)) are authoritative, verified expressions from within the five source PDFs. This page answers: Physically, where does each term of the Leeson expression (floor, 1/f21/f^21/f2, 1/f31/f^31/f3) come from? Why are the slopes 1/f21/f^21/f2 and 1/f31/f^31/f3, and where is the corner? Which ISF quantities do Leeson's QQQ, FFF, ω1/f3\omega_{1/f^3}ω1/f3​ correspond to? Which ones does ISF explain more clearly? How does [P1] itself prove that "existing LTI models are simplified cases of ISF" (Sec.III-F Eq.(28)–(29))? Where does the famous 2× difference come from? Physical intuition (conclusion first): Leeson treats the oscillator as "a feedback system continuously fed by thermal noise and narrowband-filtered by a high-QQQ tank." Three things stack up: (1) the amplifier/tank injects a white noise floor (2FkT/Ps2FkT/P_s2FkT/Ps​); (2) because it is an autonomous oscillator, phase perturbations near the carrier have no restoring force, so the closed loop multiplies the noise by a (ω0/2QΔω)2(\omega_0/2Q\Delta\omega)^2(ω0​/2QΔω)2 "phase-integration" transfer function, producing the 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt; (3) the device's 1/f1/f1/f flicker noise gets upconverted by one more order, producing the 1/f31/f^31/f3 closest to the carrier. ISF theory tells the same three-part story, only it replaces 1/2Q1/2Q1/2Q with Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​, and replaces FFF with a physical quantity computable from Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​.

documents.t: Leeson model (spec 10.2, external literature, not one of the five PDFs): L(Δω)=10log⁡10 ⁣[2FkTPs(1+(ω02Q Δω)2)(1+ω1/f3∣Δω∣)]\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega)=10\log_{10}\!\left[\frac{2FkT}{P_s}\left(1+\Big(\frac{\omega_0}{2Q\,\Delta\omega}\Big)^2\right)\left(1+\frac{\omega_{1/f^3}}{\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert}\right)\right]L(Δω)=10log10​[Ps​2FkT​(1+(2QΔωω0​​)2)(1+∣Δω∣ω1/f3​​)] Symbols: FFF = amplifier noise figure (empirical quantity, dimensionless); kkk = Boltzmann constant (J/K); TTT = temperature (K); PsP_sPs​ = oscillation signal power (W); QQQ = tank quality factor (dimensionless); ω0\omega_0ω0​ = carrier angular frequency (rad/s); Δω\Delta\omegaΔω = offset angular frequency (rad/s); ω1/f3\omega_{1/f^3}ω1/f3​ = flicker corner (rad/s). Below, the three factors inside the brackets are derived one at a time.
documents.s: The full formula (state it first, then derive step by step)

documents.t: Treat the oscillator as a "feedback loop of amplifier + resonant tank." The thermal-noise source in the loop is the tank's loss resistance RRR (parallel-equivalent), whose single-sided thermal-noise voltage PSD (Johnson–Nyquist) is: vn2‾Δf=4kTR.\frac{\overline{v_n^2}}{\Delta f}=4kTR.Δfvn2​​​=4kTR. Physics used: resistor thermal noise 4kTR4kTR4kTR (standard result; see psd_phase_noise_jitter). Dimension check: [kT]=J=V⋅C[kT]=\text{J}=\text{V·C}[kT]=J=V⋅C, [kTR]=V⋅C⋅Ω=V2⋅s=V2/Hz[kTR]=\text{V·C·}\Omega=\text{V}^2\text{·s}=\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}[kTR]=V⋅C⋅Ω=V2⋅s=V2/Hz ✓. The amplifier itself also adds noise; the whole thing is lumped into a single noise figure FFF (which packages "actual total noise" over "input thermal noise alone" into one ratio). Normalizing the noise power against the carrier power PsP_sPs​ gives the phase-noise floor near the carrier: Lfloor=2FkTPs.\mathcal{L}_{\text{floor}}=\frac{2FkT}{P_s}.Lfloor​=Ps​2FkT​. FFF is Leeson's "empirical escape hatch": it absorbs all the noise that isn't explicitly modeled (amplifier, conversion loss, cyclostationary effects, ...) into a single measurement-fit number. This is exactly what ISF later replaces (see Step 5's comparison). Where the 2 comes from: this is a bookkeeping convention of the Leeson model (not the only way to write it — it varies by reference). Physically there are actually two factors, pulling in opposite directions: (1) AM/PM equipartition — thermal noise perturbs amplitude and phase simultaneously, and phase gets only half the power (×12\times\tfrac12×21​); (2) single-sideband (SSB) accounting converts double-sided power to single-sided (×2\times2×2). The two cancel, so the "cleanest" way to write the floor is actually FkT/PsFkT/P_sFkT/Ps​; writing it as 2FkT/Ps2FkT/P_s2FkT/Ps​ leaves the SSB convention explicit in the leading constant without folding the AM/PM 12\tfrac1221​ into FFF. This is the same kind of SSB/double-sided bookkeeping difference as [P1] Eq.(21)'s 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2 vs. the time-domain 2Δω22\Delta\omega^22Δω2 (see the factor-of-2 discussion in white_noise_to_phase_noise). (FFF is an empirically fitted parameter, and the leading constant varies slightly by reference — this is precisely what ISF later replaces with Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​.) Dimension check: [2FkT/Ps]=J/W=J/(J/s)=s=1/Hz[2FkT/P_s]=\text{J}/\text{W}=\text{J}/(\text{J/s})=\text{s}=1/\text{Hz}[2FkT/Ps​]=J/W=J/(J/s)=s=1/Hz ✓ (L\mathcal{L}L is relative power per hertz, dBc/Hz).
documents.s: Step 1: tank thermal noise — the noise floor 2FkT/Ps2FkT/P_s2FkT/Ps​

documents.t: The tank is a narrowband filter. Near the carrier, at offset Δω\Delta\omegaΔω, the phase/amplitude response slope of the parallel RLC is set by QQQ. The standard result: the (half-power) transfer of the tank at offset Δω\Delta\omegaΔω can be written as ∣H(Δω)∣2 ∝ (ω02Q Δω)2(Δω≪ω0/2Q).\left|H(\Delta\omega)\right|^2\;\propto\;\left(\frac{\omega_0}{2Q\,\Delta\omega}\right)^2\qquad(\Delta\omega\ll\omega_0/2Q).∣H(Δω)∣2∝(2QΔωω0​​)2(Δω≪ω0​/2Q). The physics of QQQ: Q=ω0/Δω3dBQ=\omega_0/\Delta\omega_{3dB}Q=ω0​/Δω3dB​ = "how sharp the resonance peak is" = stored/dissipated energy ratio per cycle ×2π\times2\pi×2π. The higher the QQQ, the narrower the tank bandwidth, the steeper the phase slope, and the stronger the suppression of offset noise. Why 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 (i.e., −20-20−20 dB/dec): an autonomous oscillator's phase is a neutral direction (no restoring force, echoing λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0 in derivation_floquet_ppv). The closed loop is equivalent to one integration of the phase perturbation, which in the frequency domain is ×1/Δω\times 1/\Delta\omega×1/Δω; squaring for power gives 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2. This is the fundamental reason phase noise must be 1/f21/f^21/f2 in the mid-band, slope −20-20−20 dB/dec — it shares the same origin as ISF's 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 ([P1] Eq.(21)). Dimension check: ω0/(2QΔω)\omega_0/(2Q\Delta\omega)ω0​/(2QΔω) is dimensionless (rad/s ÷ rad/s) ✓, so the whole transfer is dimensionless. Multiplying Steps 1 and 2 (floor × tank shaping) gives the first two terms in the brackets: L1/f2+floor=2FkTPs(1+(ω02Q Δω)2).\mathcal{L}_{1/f^2+\text{floor}}=\frac{2FkT}{P_s}\left(1+\Big(\frac{\omega_0}{2Q\,\Delta\omega}\Big)^2\right).L1/f2+floor​=Ps​2FkT​(1+(2QΔωω0​​)2). The 111 in "1+1+1+" is the white noise floor (dominant at far offset, flat); (ω0/2QΔω)2(\omega_0/2Q\Delta\omega)^2(ω0​/2QΔω)2 is the 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt (dominant near the carrier). Where the two are equal is the corner where 1/f2→1/f^2\to1/f2→ floor, Δω≈ω0/2Q\Delta\omega\approx\omega_0/2QΔω≈ω0​/2Q.
documents.s: Step 2: narrowband filtering by the high-QQQ tank → the 1/f21/f^21/f2 skirt

documents.t: The device's low-frequency 1/f1/f1/f (flicker) noise gets "upconverted" near the carrier by the oscillator's nonlinearity, and after the phase integration of Step 2, becomes a 1/f31/f^31/f3 steeper than 1/f21/f^21/f2. Leeson attaches it with a multiplicative factor: (1+ω1/f3∣Δω∣).\left(1+\frac{\omega_{1/f^3}}{\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert}\right).(1+∣Δω∣ω1/f3​​). When Δω≫ω1/f3\Delta\omega\gg\omega_{1/f^3}Δω≫ω1/f3​: this factor ≈1\approx1≈1, flicker is invisible, leaving just 1/f21/f^21/f2 and the floor. When Δω≪ω1/f3\Delta\omega\ll\omega_{1/f^3}Δω≪ω1/f3​: this factor ≈ω1/f3/∣Δω∣∝1/Δω\approx\omega_{1/f^3}/\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert\propto1/\Delta\omega≈ω1/f3​/∣Δω∣∝1/Δω, which further multiplies the 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 from Step 2 → total 1/Δω31/\Delta\omega^31/Δω3, i.e., 1/f31/f^31/f3, −30-30−30 dB/dec. ω1/f3\omega_{1/f^3}ω1/f3​ is the "flicker corner of the phase noise", not the device's own 1/f1/f1/f corner. Leeson never explains what determines it — this is exactly the key physics ISF fills in (Step 5, [P1] Eq.(24)). Dimension check: ω1/f3/∣Δω∣\omega_{1/f^3}/\lvert\Delta\omega\rvertω1/f3​/∣Δω∣ dimensionless ✓. Multiplying all three terms gives the full Leeson formula from the top. Three slope segments: floor (flat) → 1/f21/f^21/f2 (−20-20−20 dB/dec) → 1/f31/f^31/f3 (−30-30−30 dB/dec), from far to near.
documents.s: Step 3: device flicker → the 1/f31/f^31/f3 region closest to the carrier

documents.t: Plotting the Leeson formula and the ISF result ([P1] Eqs.(21),(23),(24)) on the same log–log axes, the three segments (1/f31/f^31/f3, 1/f21/f^21/f2, floor) overlap — the two models describe the same curve, just with different physical meanings assigned to the parameters: Translator's note: this figure is generated by a script with Chinese text baked into the image. Title reads: "Leeson vs ISF：同樣的 1/f³ / 1/f² / floor 三段" = Leeson vs. ISF: the same three segments — 1/f³ / 1/f² / floor. Formula correspondence: left half is the Leeson expression from the top (external literature); right half is [P1] Eq.(21) (1/f21/f^21/f2), Eq.(23) (1/f31/f^31/f3), Eq.(24) (1/f31/f^31/f3 corner). script / function: simulations/lab_16_leeson_vs_isf.py (main), corresponding to leeson_vs_isf_overlay.png in the spec 10.1 table (lab_16). This is a pedagogical toy model, not transistor-level; the Leeson curve is drawn illustratively for the 1/f21/f^21/f2 segment using functions like leeson_one_over_f2 from simulations/common/noise_utils.py, and the constants used to stitch the three segments are for teaching illustration only. How to read it: the two curves are exactly parallel in the mid-band 1/f21/f^21/f2 region (both slope −20-20−20 dB/dec, since both come from "phase integration 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2"); near the carrier both turn into 1/f31/f^31/f3; far out both flatten to the floor. The only difference is where the corner falls and the absolute level — which is set by the parameter correspondence, see below. Note: in the overlay, the Leeson segment's F,Q,ω1/f3F,Q,\omega_{1/f^3}F,Q,ω1/f3​ and the ISF segment's Γrms,qmax,c0,ω1/f\Gamma_{rms},q_{max},c_0,\omega_{1/f}Γrms​,qmax​,c0​,ω1/f​ are illustrative teaching values (lab_16 parameters), used to show the three-segment slope overlap, not measurements of a specific circuit.

documents.t: This is the core of this page. Putting the corresponding terms of both models side by side: Segment Leeson (empirical, [E1] 1966, not one of the five PDFs) ISF ([P1] 1998, within the five PDFs) Correspondence and where "ISF is clearer" 1/f21/f^21/f2 shaping (ω02Q Δω)2\Big(\dfrac{\omega_0}{2Q\,\Delta\omega}\Big)^2(2QΔωω0​​)2 Γrms2qmax2⋅1Δω2\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\Delta\omega^2}qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δω21​ ([P1] Eq.(21)) Both give 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2. Leeson's 12Q\dfrac{1}{2Q}2Q1​ ↔ ISF's Γrmsqmax×\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}}{q_{max}}\timesqmax​Γrms​​× (including carrier/noise-power normalization). QQQ↔Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​: high QQQ = low Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ = low phase noise. Noise source/level 2FkTPs\dfrac{2FkT}{P_s}Ps​2FkT​, FFF empirically fit in2‾/Δf4\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4}4in2​​/Δf​ paired with Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ (including cyclostationary) Empirical FFF vs ISF physical: Leeson's FFF is "you only know it once you measure it"; ISF splits it into a computable device noise PSD × Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​, which can even fold in cyclostationary gating (see effective_isf). 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner ω1/f3\omega_{1/f^3}ω1/f3​ (Leeson never says what sets it) Δω1/f3=ω1/fc022Γrms2≈ω1/f(c0c1)2\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\dfrac{c_0^2}{2\Gamma_{rms}^2}\approx\omega_{1/f}\Big(\dfrac{c_0}{c_1}\Big)^2Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​2Γrms2​c02​​≈ω1/f​(c1​c0​​)2 ([P1] Eq.(24)) ISF's signature insight: the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner is not equal to the device's own 1/f1/f1/f corner ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​, but is scaled by (c0/Γrms)2(c_0/\Gamma_{rms})^2(c0​/Γrms​)2. Waveform symmetry → c0→0c_0\to0c0​→0 → corner pushed far below ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​. Leeson gives no visibility into this design lever at all. Key comparisons expanded: (a) Q↔Γrms/qmaxQ\leftrightarrow\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Q↔Γrms​/qmax​. Both are "the efficiency with which noise is converted into a phase skirt." Leeson says "higher QQQ is better"; ISF says "smaller Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ is better." But ISF is more general: it also holds for ring oscillators with no high-QQQ tank (a ring has no QQQ to speak of, but does have Γrms,qmax\Gamma_{rms},q_{max}Γrms​,qmax​; see lab_03). This is the first way ISF goes beyond Leeson. (b) Empirical FFF vs ISF physical. Leeson's FFF is a black box: you must first build the oscillator, measure the phase noise, and back out FFF, before you can "predict" with the model — which is really post-hoc fitting, not prediction. ISF writes the same level as in2‾/Δf4qmax2Γrms2\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4q_{max}^2}\Gamma_{rms}^24qmax2​in2​​/Δf​Γrms2​ ([P1] Eq.(21)), where every quantity can be computed ahead of time from the device model and waveform, and cyclostationary behavior (device leaking noise only at certain phases) can be folded in via Γeff=Γ⋅α\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\cdot\alphaΓeff​=Γ⋅α — this is exactly why the Colpitts's "effective FFF" is much lower than a naive Leeson estimate (see effective_isf). (c) 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner. Leeson simply takes ω1/f3\omega_{1/f^3}ω1/f3​ as an input parameter, effectively admitting "I don't know where it comes from." Early engineering practice even mistook it for the device's own 1/f1/f1/f corner. ISF's [P1] Eq.(24) settles it: Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c02/(2Γrms2)\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅c02​/(2Γrms2​) — it is set by the ISF's DC coefficient c0c_0c0​ (waveform symmetry). Making rise/fall symmetric → c0→0c_0\to0c0​→0 → the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner drops sharply → near-carrier phase noise falls substantially. This is a design rule Leeson simply cannot give, and it is the theoretical basis for [P2]'s use of symmetry to suppress ring phase noise (see symmetry, flicker_noise_upconversion).
documents.s: Step 5: term-by-term comparison (Leeson ↔ ISF)

documents.t: The first five steps are an external comparison, "Leeson versus ISF." [P1] itself also performs an internal reduction in Sec.III-F (p.187): take the general ISF expression Eq.(19), impose every simplifying assumption of the LTI model, and see what it collapses to. This is the most persuasive evidence on this page — the two models do not merely "overlap as curves"; one is a special case of the other's formula. (1) What the LTI assumptions mean in ISF language. [P1] p.187 lists the four assumptions of the LTI models (its references [3] and [8]): linear time-invariance, all noise sources stationary, only noise in the vicinity of ω0\omega_0ω0​ matters, and a noise-free waveform that is a perfect sinusoid. Translated through the ISF Fourier series ([P1] Eq.(12)): discard every term except c1c_1c1​, and set c1=1c_1=1c1​=1 ([P1] p.187, verified on the rendered page). That is exactly the ISF of the ideal LC oscillator (lab_02, capstone): Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ=cos⁡ ⁣(θ+π2) ⇒ c0=0,c1=1,cn≥2=0,Γrms2=12π∫02πsin⁡2θ dθ=12.\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\theta=\cos\!\big(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\big)\;\Rightarrow\;c_0=0,\quad c_1=1,\quad c_{n\ge2}=0,\quad \Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=\tfrac12 .Γ(θ)=−sinθ=cos(θ+2π​)⇒c0​=0,c1​=1,cn≥2​=0,Γrms2​=2π1​∫02π​sin2θdθ=21​. Parseval ([P1] Eq.(20)) is self-consistent: ∑cn2=c12=1=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=c_1^2=1=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=c12​=1=2Γrms2​ ✓, hence Γrms=1/2≈0.707\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2\approx0.707Γrms​=1/2​≈0.707 (this site's "true LC" value; the representative 0.50.50.5 is a deliberately conservative teaching value, see white_noise_to_phase_noise). c0=0c_0=0c0​=0 also explains something: an ideal sinusoidal LC has no 1/f31/f^31/f3 upconversion — the LTI model cannot see what sets ω1/f3\omega_{1/f^3}ω1/f3​ precisely because it threw c0c_0c0​ away along with everything else. (2) Inject the thermal noise of the tank's parallel resistor ([P1] Eq.(28), p.187). Consider the RLC oscillator of [P1] Fig. 2 and count only one noise source, the tank parallel resistor RpR_pRp​: in2‾Δf=4kTRp,qmax=C⋅Vmax.\frac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}=\frac{4kT}{R_p},\qquad q_{max}=C\cdot V_{max}.Δfin2​​​=Rp​4kT​,qmax​=C⋅Vmax​. 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​: the Norton (current) version of Step 1's 4kTR4kTR4kTR (single-sided PSD, A²/Hz). qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=CV_{max}qmax​=CVmax​: the maximum charge swing on the tank capacitor — this is the paper's origin of the site-wide definition qmax=C⋅Vmaxq_{max}=C\cdot V_{max}qmax​=C⋅Vmax​, and it is the "translation dictionary" between LTI variables (CCC, VmaxV_{max}Vmax​) and the ISF variable (qmaxq_{max}qmax​). (3) Substitute into Eq.(19) to get Eq.(29). [P1] Eq.(19) (white-noise summation, p.185): L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(in2‾/Δf ∑n=0∞cn28 qmax2 Δω2).\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f\;\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2}{8\,q_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}\right).L{Δω}=10log10​(8qmax2​Δω2in2​​/Δf∑n=0∞​cn2​​). Substituting ∑cn2=c12=1\sum c_n^2=c_1^2=1∑cn2​=c12​=1, in2‾/Δf=4kT/Rp\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f=4kT/R_pin2​​/Δf=4kT/Rp​, qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=CV_{max}qmax​=CVmax​: L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣(4kT/Rp8 C2Vmax2 Δω2)=10log⁡10 ⁣(kT2 Rp C2Vmax2 Δω2)=10log⁡10 ⁣[12⋅kTVmax2⋅1Rp (Cω0)2⋅(ω0Δω)2].\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\} &=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4kT/R_p}{8\,C^2V_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}\right) =10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{kT}{2\,R_p\,C^2V_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)\\ &=10\log_{10}\!\left[\frac12\cdot\frac{kT}{V_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{1}{R_p\,(C\omega_0)^2}\cdot\Big(\frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}\Big)^2\right]. \end{aligned}L{Δω}​=10log10​(8C2Vmax2​Δω24kT/Rp​​)=10log10​(2Rp​C2Vmax2​Δω2kT​)=10log10​[21​⋅Vmax2​kT​⋅Rp​(Cω0​)21​⋅(Δωω0​​)2].​ The last line is [P1] Eq.(29), p.187 (verified verbatim against the rendered page) — it merely rewrites C2Δω2C^2\Delta\omega^2C2Δω2 as (Cω0)2(Δω/ω0)2(C\omega_0)^2(\Delta\omega/\omega_0)^2(Cω0​)2(Δω/ω0​)2 so that the "tank admittance Cω0C\omega_0Cω0​" and the "relative offset ω0/Δω\omega_0/\Delta\omegaω0​/Δω" can be read separately. Dimension check: [kT/Vmax2]=J/V2=C/V=F[kT/V_{max}^2]=\text{J/V}^2=\text{C/V}=\text{F}[kT/Vmax2​]=J/V2=C/V=F; [1/(Rp(Cω0)2)]=1/(Ω⋅S2)=Ω[1/(R_p(C\omega_0)^2)]=1/(\Omega\cdot\text{S}^2)=\Omega[1/(Rp​(Cω0​)2)]=1/(Ω⋅S2)=Ω; F⋅Ω=s=1/Hz\text{F}\cdot\Omega=\text{s}=1/\text{Hz}F⋅Ω=s=1/Hz ✓; (ω0/Δω)2(\omega_0/\Delta\omega)^2(ω0​/Δω)2 is dimensionless ✓. Physics: 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2 (phase integration), ∝1/Rp\propto1/R_p∝1/Rp​ (larger RpR_pRp​ = higher QQQ = smaller noise current), ∝1/(CVmax)2=1/qmax2\propto1/(CV_{max})^2=1/q_{max}^2∝1/(CVmax​)2=1/qmax2​ (larger charge swing is better) — every cell of the Step 5 table has a counterpart in this one expression. Cω0=1.013×10−12×3.1416×1010=3.182×10−2C\omega_0=1.013\times10^{-12}\times3.1416\times10^{10}=3.182\times10^{-2}Cω0​=1.013×10−12×3.1416×1010=3.182×10−2 S; Rp(Cω0)2=314×1.0128×10−3=0.3180R_p(C\omega_0)^2=314\times1.0128\times10^{-3}=0.3180Rp​(Cω0​)2=314×1.0128×10−3=0.3180 S, reciprocal =3.145 Ω=3.145\ \Omega=3.145 Ω. (ω0/Δω)2=(5×109/106)2=2.5×107(\omega_0/\Delta\omega)^2=(5\times10^9/10^6)^2=2.5\times10^7(ω0​/Δω)2=(5×109/106)2=2.5×107. Multiply: 2.071×10−21×3.145×2.5×107=1.628×10−132.071\times10^{-21}\times3.145\times2.5\times10^7=1.628\times10^{-13}2.071×10−21×3.145×2.5×107=1.628×10−13 (units F·Ω = s ✓) → L=10log⁡10(1.628×10−13)=−127.9\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}(1.628\times10^{-13})=-127.9L=10log10​(1.628×10−13)=−127.9 dBc/Hz. Recomputing with Eq.(21) must give the same value (Γrms2=12\Gamma_{rms}^2=\tfrac12Γrms2​=21​, qmax=CVmax=1.013q_{max}=CV_{max}=1.013qmax​=CVmax​=1.013 pC, Si=4kT/Rp=5.276×10−23S_i=4kT/R_p=5.276\times10^{-23}Si​=4kT/Rp​=5.276×10−23 A²/Hz): 0.5(1.013×10−12)2⋅5.276×10−234 (2π×106)2=1.628×10−13\dfrac{0.5}{(1.013\times10^{-12})^2}\cdot\dfrac{5.276\times10^{-23}}{4\,(2\pi\times10^6)^2}=1.628\times10^{-13}(1.013×10−12)20.5​⋅4(2π×106)25.276×10−23​=1.628×10−13 ✓. Against canonical Example B's −148.0-148.0−148.0 dBc/Hz (Si=10−24S_i=10^{-24}Si​=10−24 A²/Hz, Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5, qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC): here SiS_iSi​ is 52.8× larger (+17.2+17.2+17.2 dB), Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​ is 2× larger (+3.0+3.0+3.0 dB), qmax2q_{max}^2qmax2​ is 1.01321.013^21.0132× larger (−0.1-0.1−0.1 dB): −148.0+17.2+3.0−0.1=−127.9-148.0+17.2+3.0-0.1=-127.9−148.0+17.2+3.0−0.1=−127.9 ✓. (5) The Craninckx–Steyaert 2×, and the true face of this site's factor-of-2. [P1] p.187 then notes that its reference [8] (J. Craninckx and M. Steyaert, "Low-noise voltage controlled oscillators using enhanced LC-tanks," IEEE Trans. Circuits Syst. II, vol. 42, no. 12, pp. 794–804, Dec. 1995; external literature, not among this site's five PDFs; [P1]'s reference list prints pp. 794–904, evidently a misprint for 804) assumes equal contributions from amplitude and phase to Ltotal\mathcal{L}_{total}Ltotal​, so the result of [8] is exactly twice Eq.(29). In other words, the chain Eq.(19)→(29) counts only the phase half; the LTI model's Ltotal\mathcal{L}_{total}Ltotal​ (the measurement definition of [P1] Eq.(2), p.180, AM included) also counts amplitude noise. This site adds one more cross-check of its own (not in the paper; rerun it with the Python below): take the Leeson-form Eq.(6) of [P1] p.181 with F=1F=1F=1 and convert with Q=ω0RpCQ=\omega_0R_pCQ=ω0​Rp​C, Ps=Vmax2/(2Rp)P_s=V_{max}^2/(2R_p)Ps​=Vmax2​/(2Rp​): 2kTPs(ω02Q Δω)2=4kTRpVmax2⋅ω024 ω02Rp2C2 Δω2=kTRp C2Vmax2 Δω2=2×[Eq.(29)].\frac{2kT}{P_s}\Big(\frac{\omega_0}{2Q\,\Delta\omega}\Big)^2=\frac{4kTR_p}{V_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\omega_0^2}{4\,\omega_0^2R_p^2C^2\,\Delta\omega^2}=\frac{kT}{R_p\,C^2V_{max}^2\,\Delta\omega^2}=2\times\big[\text{Eq.(29)}\big].Ps​2kT​(2QΔωω0​​)2=Vmax2​4kTRp​​⋅4ω02​Rp2​C2Δω2ω02​​=Rp​C2Vmax2​Δω2kT​=2×[Eq.(29)]. So within [P1]'s own bookkeeping, Eq.(6) at F=1F=1F=1 is also 3 dB above Eq.(29) (−124.9-124.9−124.9 vs −127.9-127.9−127.9 dBc/Hz) — even though [P1] notes just below Eq.(6) that its 12\tfrac1221​ comes from neglecting amplitude noise. This 2 is the same 2 as the "clean time-domain /2/2/2 vs Eq.(21)'s /4/4/4" of the factor-of-2 note in white_noise_to_phase_noise (canonical Example B's −145-145−145 vs −148-148−148 dBc/Hz), and it is the well-known minor controversy in the literature. This site lists it honestly and does not adjudicate which constant is "right": the scaling (∝1/(RpC2Vmax2Δω2)\propto1/(R_pC^2V_{max}^2\Delta\omega^2)∝1/(Rp​C2Vmax2​Δω2)) and the −20-20−20 dB/dec slope are physics; the 2 is AM/PM and SSB bookkeeping convention. (6) Closing the loop with the Step 5 FFF/QQQ mapping. From the identity above, Eq.(29) =12⋅2kTPs(ω02QΔω)2=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{2kT}{P_s}\big(\tfrac{\omega_0}{2Q\Delta\omega}\big)^2=21​⋅Ps​2kT​(2QΔωω0​​)2, i.e. L{Δω}=10log⁡10 ⁣[kTPs(ω02Q Δω)2]\mathcal{L}\{\Delta\omega\}=10\log_{10}\!\left[\frac{kT}{P_s}\Big(\frac{\omega_0}{2Q\,\Delta\omega}\Big)^2\right]L{Δω}=10log10​[Ps​kT​(2QΔωω0​​)2] (ideal sinusoidal LC, tank RpR_pRp​ thermal noise only). This is the 1/f21/f^21/f2 term of the Leeson expression, and its leading constant lands exactly on the "cleanest form" FkT/PsFkT/P_sFkT/Ps​ of Step 1 with F=1F=1F=1; forcing it into the 2FkT/Ps2FkT/P_s2FkT/Ps​ form at the top of this page is equivalent to F=12F=\tfrac12F=21​. [P1] p.187 states that (29) together with (24) yields (6) — the whole difference is how much bookkeeping constant FFF absorbs. Explicit identity for Q↔Γrms/qmaxQ\leftrightarrow\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Q↔Γrms​/qmax​: ISF side Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf4=12⋅4kT/Rp4C2Vmax2=kT2RpC2Vmax2\dfrac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\dfrac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{4}=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{4kT/R_p}{4C^2V_{max}^2}=\dfrac{kT}{2R_pC^2V_{max}^2}qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅4in2​​/Δf​=21​⋅4C2Vmax2​4kT/Rp​​=2Rp​C2Vmax2​kT​; Leeson side kTPs⋅ω024Q2=2kTRpVmax2⋅14Rp2C2=kT2RpC2Vmax2\dfrac{kT}{P_s}\cdot\dfrac{\omega_0^2}{4Q^2}=\dfrac{2kTR_p}{V_{max}^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{4R_p^2C^2}=\dfrac{kT}{2R_pC^2V_{max}^2}Ps​kT​⋅4Q2ω02​​=Vmax2​2kTRp​​⋅4Rp2​C21​=2Rp​C2Vmax2​kT​ — the two sides are identical term by term ✓. This turns Step 5(a)'s "1/2Q↔Γrms/qmax1/2Q\leftrightarrow\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}1/2Q↔Γrms​/qmax​ (with normalization)" into a checkable equation. The ISF version of FFF is no longer a black box: for any real ISF, the role of FFF is taken over by ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​ (relative to the ideal LC's c12=1c_1^2=1c12​=1) and by Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​ (cyclostationarity); ω1/f3\omega_{1/f^3}ω1/f3​ is taken over by Eq.(24)'s c02/(2Γrms2)c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)c02​/(2Γrms2​). [P1] p.187 states explicitly that the generalized approach can compute the fitting parameters FFF and Δω1/f3\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}Δω1/f3​ of Eq.(3) from the ISF coefficients cnc_ncn​ and the device ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ — that sentence is the paper's original source for all three rows of the Step 5 table. Python verification (# -> lines are actual run output): import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_rms, compute_fourier_coefficients # (1) Ideal-LC ISF Γ(θ) = -sin θ: only c1, and c1 = 1 (the LTI setting of [P1] p.187) theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 4097) # endpoint included, for the trapezoidal rule gam = -np.sin(theta) c0, _, _, c, _ = compute_fourier_coefficients(theta, gam, 3) # c[n] = c_n Grms = gamma_rms(theta, gam) print(round(float(c0), 4), round(float(c[1]), 4), round(float(c[2]), 4), round(float(Grms), 4)) # -> 0.0 1.0 0.0 0.7071 (c0, c1, c2, Γrms; Parseval: c1² = 1 = 2Γrms²) # (2) [P1] Eq.(28): the 5 GHz tank of the tank_Q page (L=1 nH, C=1.013 pF, Rp=314 Ω, T=300 K), Vmax = 1 V k, T = 1.380649e-23, 300.0 f0, C, Rp, Vmax = 5e9, 1.013e-12, 314.0, 1.0 w0 = 2*np.pi*f0 Q = w0*Rp*C Si = 4*k*T/Rp # A²/Hz qmax = C*Vmax # C dw = 2*np.pi*1e6 # Δω @ 1 MHz print(round(Q, 3), f"{Si:.3e}", f"{qmax:.3e}") # -> 9.993 5.276e-23 1.013e-12 (Q, i_n²/Δf [A²/Hz], q_max [C]) # (3) [P1] Eq.(29) vs Eq.(19) (c1 only) vs Eq.(21) (Γrms² = 1/2) — all three must agree L29 = 0.5*k*T/Vmax**2 / (Rp*(C*w0)**2) * (w0/dw)**2 L19 = Si*c[1]**2 / (8*qmax**2*dw**2) L21 = Grms**2/qmax**2 * Si/(4*dw**2) print(round(10*np.log10(L29), 2), round(10*np.log10(L19), 2), round(10*np.log10(L21), 2)) # -> -127.88 -127.88 -127.88 (dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz) # (4) Leeson-form cross-check: [P1] Eq.(6) with F = 1, and the closing form (kT/Ps)(ω0/2QΔω)² Ps = Vmax**2/(2*Rp) L6 = 2*k*T/Ps * (w0/(2*Q*dw))**2 L29_leeson = k*T/Ps * (w0/(2*Q*dw))**2 print(round(10*np.log10(L6), 2), round(L6/L29, 4), round(L29_leeson/L29, 4)) # -> -124.87 2.0 1.0 (Eq.(6)|F=1 is 3 dB above Eq.(29) = exactly 2×; Eq.(29) ≡ (kT/Ps)(ω0/2QΔω)²) Applicability: Eq.(29) is an equality only when all four LTI assumptions hold (ideal sinusoid, c1c_1c1​ only, stationary noise, only the neighborhood of ω0\omega_0ω0​ counted). A ring oscillator (cn≥2≠0c_{n\ge2}\neq0cn≥2​=0, Γrms∝N−3/2\Gamma_{rms}\propto N^{-3/2}Γrms​∝N−3/2), an asymmetric waveform (c0≠0c_0\neq0c0​=0 → 1/f31/f^31/f3), or cyclostationary device noise (Γeff=Γα\Gamma_{eff}=\Gamma\alphaΓeff​=Γα) all break it — then go back to Eq.(19)/(21) with the real cnc_ncn​ and Γeff\Gamma_{eff}Γeff​, and FFF is computed automatically instead of being fitted.

documents.t: Example (1/f31/f^31/f3 corner comparison): take a device 1/f1/f1/f corner f1/f=1f_{1/f}=1f1/f​=1 MHz (ω1/f=2π×106\omega_{1/f}=2\pi\times10^6ω1/f​=2π×106 rad/s). Compare the phase-noise 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner of a "symmetric" vs. an "asymmetric" waveform. ISF's [P1] Eq.(24): Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅c02/(2Γrms2)\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot c_0^2/(2\Gamma_{rms}^2)Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅c02​/(2Γrms2​), take Γrms=0.5\Gamma_{rms}=0.5Γrms​=0.5. Asymmetric waveform (large c0c_0c0​, set c0=0.4c_0=0.4c0​=0.4): Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅(0.4)22(0.5)2=ω1/f⋅0.160.5=0.32 ω1/f.\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{(0.4)^2}{2(0.5)^2}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{0.16}{0.5}=0.32\,\omega_{1/f}.Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2(0.5)2(0.4)2​=ω1/f​⋅0.50.16​=0.32ω1/f​. That is, f1/f3≈0.32×1 MHz=320f_{1/f^3}\approx0.32\times1\ \text{MHz}=320f1/f3​≈0.32×1 MHz=320 kHz — the 1/f31/f^31/f3 skirt extends far from the carrier. Symmetric waveform (small c0c_0c0​, set c0=0.04c_0=0.04c0​=0.04, 10× smaller): Δω1/f3=ω1/f⋅(0.04)22(0.5)2=ω1/f⋅0.00160.5=3.2×10−3 ω1/f.\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{(0.04)^2}{2(0.5)^2}=\omega_{1/f}\cdot\frac{0.0016}{0.5}=3.2\times10^{-3}\,\omega_{1/f}.Δω1/f3​=ω1/f​⋅2(0.5)2(0.04)2​=ω1/f​⋅0.50.0016​=3.2×10−3ω1/f​. That is, f1/f3≈3.2f_{1/f^3}\approx3.2f1/f3​≈3.2 kHz — the corner drops 100× (because c0c_0c0​ is squared: a 10× reduction in c0c_0c0​ → 100× reduction in the corner). Dimension check: c02/Γrms2c_0^2/\Gamma_{rms}^2c02​/Γrms2​ is dimensionless, ω1/f×\omega_{1/f}\timesω1/f​×dimensionless === rad/s ✓. Intuition: Leeson treats ω1/f3\omega_{1/f^3}ω1/f3​ as "fixed by nature"; ISF tells you it is a knob the designer can turn by two orders of magnitude via symmetry. This is ISF's practical value. One-line Python verification (corner ratio): import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_rms # Ratio of the 1/f^3 corner for a symmetric vs asymmetric waveform = (c0_asym/c0_sym)^2 c0_asym, c0_sym, Gamma_rms = 0.4, 0.04, 0.5 w1f = 2*np.pi*1e6 corner_asym = w1f * c0_asym**2 / (2*Gamma_rms**2) corner_sym = w1f * c0_sym**2 / (2*Gamma_rms**2) print(corner_asym/(2*np.pi)/1e3, "kHz ;", corner_sym/(2*np.pi)/1e3, "kHz") # -> ~320.0 kHz ; ~3.2 kHz (a symmetric waveform pushes the 1/f^3 corner down 100x) (For gamma_rms and related library functions, see simulations/common/isf_utils.py; this example computes the corner directly by hand from [P1] Eq.(24).)

documents.t: The Leeson model itself: [E1] D. B. Leeson, Proc. IEEE 54(2):329–330, Feb. 1966 — not among the five downloaded source PDFs; volume/DOI verified (10.1109/PROC.1966.4682, see [E1] in references); this formula is the standard Leeson form (FFF is an empirical noise factor, leading constant varies slightly by reference). ISF comparison equations (within the five PDFs, verified): 1/f21/f^21/f2 [P1] Eq.(21), p.185; 1/f31/f^31/f3 [P1] Eq.(23), p.185; 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner [P1] Eq.(24), p.185; device flicker [P1] Eq.(22), p.185. Cyclostationary (explaining "effective FFF"): [P1] Eqs.(25)–(27), p.186 (see effective_isf). [P1]'s internal reduction (Step 6): Sec.III-F Eq.(28)–(29), p.187 (c1=1c_1=1c1​=1, 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​, qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=CV_{max}qmax​=CVmax​); Leeson-form Eq.(3), p.180 and Eq.(6), p.181; measurement definition Ltotal\mathcal{L}_{total}Ltotal​ Eq.(2), p.180; its reference [8] Craninckx–Steyaert, IEEE TCAS-II 42(12):794–804, Dec. 1995 (external literature, not among this site's five PDFs). Overlay plot: /figures/leeson_vs_isf_overlay.png, simulations/lab_16_leeson_vs_isf.py (spec 10.1, lab_16).

documents.t: Leeson (1966, external, not one of the five PDFs) = a semi-empirical three-term expression: L=10log⁡10 ⁣[2FkTPs(1+(ω02QΔω)2)(1+ω1/f3∣Δω∣)]\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}\!\big[\tfrac{2FkT}{P_s}(1+(\tfrac{\omega_0}{2Q\Delta\omega})^2)(1+\tfrac{\omega_{1/f^3}}{\lvert\Delta\omega\rvert})\big]L=10log10​[Ps​2FkT​(1+(2QΔωω0​​)2)(1+∣Δω∣ω1/f3​​)]. Three segments: white-noise floor (2FkT/Ps2FkT/P_s2FkT/Ps​) → tank-shaped 1/f21/f^21/f2 (−20-20−20 dB/dec, from phase integration 1/Δω21/\Delta\omega^21/Δω2) → flicker-upconverted 1/f31/f^31/f3 (−30-30−30 dB/dec). Term-by-term correspondence: Q↔Γrms/qmaxQ\leftrightarrow\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Q↔Γrms​/qmax​ (high QQQ = low Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​); empirical black-box FFF ↔ ISF's computable in2‾⋅Γeff\overline{i_n^2}\cdot\Gamma_{eff}in2​​⋅Γeff​ (including cyclostationary); mysterious parameter ω1/f3\omega_{1/f^3}ω1/f3​ ↔ [P1] Eq.(24), set by c0c_0c0​ (symmetry). ISF's three big advances: (1) also holds for no-QQQ rings; (2) computable ahead of time, not fit-dependent; (3) turns the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner into a design knob that symmetry can move by two orders of magnitude. The two models overlap on all three segments in a log–log plot (leeson_vs_isf_overlay.png) — the same curve, different physical languages. [P1]'s own reduction (Sec.III-F): LTI assumptions ⇔ keep only c1=1c_1=1c1​=1 (Γ=−sin⁡θ\Gamma=-\sin\thetaΓ=−sinθ, Γrms=1/2\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2Γrms​=1/2​); substituting 4kT/Rp4kT/R_p4kT/Rp​ and qmax=CVmaxq_{max}=CV_{max}qmax​=CVmax​ into Eq.(19) gives Eq.(29) =kTPs(ω02QΔω)2=\tfrac{kT}{P_s}(\tfrac{\omega_0}{2Q\Delta\omega})^2=Ps​kT​(2QΔωω0​​)2 — Leeson's 1/f21/f^21/f2 term is a special case of ISF (5 GHz, Q=10Q=10Q=10, Vmax=1V_{max}=1Vmax​=1 V example: −127.9-127.9−127.9 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz); [8] Craninckx–Steyaert (external) is 2× larger because it counts AM and PM equally — the same 2 as this site's factor-of-2.

documents.t: See also: notation (rigorous symbols and units), math_identities (math toolbox), references (source codes [P1]–[P5], external [E1]–[E4]) The biggest friction when reading English papers alongside Chinese teaching pages is "one concept, two languages." This page pairs the site's terminology Chinese–English, each with one line of Chinese intuition (not a rigorous definition, just "get the feel first") plus the page it comes from. Click through for depth. How to use this page: when you hit an unfamiliar term on some page, come back here, scan a one-liner, then decide whether to click through to the source page for detail. For rigorous symbols and units, cross-reference notation. Terms marked (external) mean they are not among the five downloaded PDFs, supplemented from standard literature.

documents.t: English Chinese One-line intuition Source page ISF (Impulse Sensitivity Function) 脈衝敏感度函數 The oscillator's "phase-sensitivity weighting" to noise — tells you "kick it at this phase of the waveform, and this much phase results." Dimensionless, 2π2\pi2π-periodic. isf_definition excess phase 多餘相位 ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) The deviation beyond the ideal phase ω0t\omega_0 tω0​t; both phase noise and jitter live here. impulse_to_phase_shift phase noise 相位雜訊 Random jitter of the oscillator signal's phase, appearing in the frequency domain as skirts on either side of the carrier. white_noise_to_phase_noise timing jitter 時間抖動 The time-domain statement of the same thing: the random error of when an edge actually occurs relative to ideal. psd_phase_noise_jitter phase perturbation 相位擾動 The component of noise that pushes the state point "tangent to the limit cycle"; no restoring force, it persists forever. phase_vs_amplitude_noise amplitude perturbation 振幅擾動 The component of noise that pushes the state point "radially"; a restoring mechanism pulls it back, does not persist. phase_vs_amplitude_noise limit cycle 極限環 The closed trajectory the oscillator circles in steady state in state-space; phase = how far along the cycle, amplitude = how far off the cycle. oscillator_phase

documents.t: phase noise vs timing jitter: the same thing, the former in the frequency domain (dBc/Hz), the latter in the time domain (fs); interconvert via σt=σϕ/(2πf0)\sigma_t=\sigma_\phi/(2\pi f_0)σt​=σϕ​/(2πf0​). phase perturbation vs amplitude perturbation: phase stays, amplitude gets pulled back — which is why phase noise is the star of the show. LTI vs LTV: the difference is whether the impulse response depends on the absolute time τ\tauτ; the oscillator is LTV. c0c_0c0​ vs the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner: c0c_0c0​ determines whether flicker upconverts at all; the 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner =ω1/f(c0/c1)2=\omega_{1/f}(c_0/c_1)^2=ω1/f​(c0​/c1​)2, is not equal to the device's ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​. device 1/f1/f1/f corner ω1/f\omega_{1/f}ω1/f​ vs phase-noise 1/f31/f^31/f3 corner Δω1/f3\Delta\omega_{1/f^3}Δω1/f3​: two different things, do not confuse them (see flicker_noise_upconversion).

documents.t: Prerequisites: lti_vs_ltv (intuition for LTV vs. LTI), convolution_derivation ([P1] Eq.(11)'s LTV convolution), fourier_series_of_isf (ISF Fourier coefficients cnc_ncn​) | Next: derivation_floquet_ppv (the PPV/Floquet face of the same ISF) This site's main thread ([P1]) introduces the ISF via "physical intuition + impulse simulation," and convolution_derivation uses superposition to generalize a single impulse to arbitrary noise. That path works very well, but leaves a gap: we keep saying the oscillator's response to noise is LTV (linear time-varying), "it acts like a time-varying mixer that shifts noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ to the carrier" — but in the language of signals and systems, exactly which rigorous object do these statements correspond to? Can "frequency gets shifted, gain is ckc_kck​" be written as a clean transfer function? This page fills in that system-theory foundation. Starting from the convolution/LTI framework the reader already knows, we work up to Zadeh's time-varying transfer function H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t) and the harmonic transfer matrix (HTM), and then prove one statement: The ISF (together with 1/qmax1/q_{max}1/qmax​) is exactly the "conversion vector from each input-harmonic band to the phase output" — its kkk-th component is precisely the kkk-th Fourier coefficient ckc_kck​ of the ISF. In other words, the ISF's Fourier series {ck}\{c_k\}{ck​} is not merely a set of numbers — it is exactly the "phase-output row" of this LTV system's HTM. Honesty note (read first): this page's Zadeh time-varying transfer function H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t), bi-frequency function, and harmonic transfer matrix (HTM) belong to the broader theory of linear time-varying systems and are not among the 5 PDFs hosted on this site. The original concept comes from [E5] L. A. Zadeh, "Frequency Analysis of Variable Networks," Proc. IRE, vol. 38, no. 3, pp. 291–299, Mar. 1950 (DOI 10.1109/JRPROC.1950.231083); the HTM formulation is standard in periodic-time-varying/RF circuit literature (e.g., cyclostationary, LPTV system analysis). These are external mathematical frameworks; the formal [E5] citation (Zadeh 1950, Proc. IRE 38(3):291–299, DOI 10.1109/JRPROC.1950.231083) is recorded in references. This page only uses them to "re-derive the ISF"; every correspondence to the ISF converges back to [P1] Eq.(13) (within the 5 PDFs, verified verbatim). This page answers four questions: How does LTI convolution generalize to LTV? (First connect to the reader's signals-and-systems background.) How does Zadeh write "the LTV response to each input frequency fff" as a time-varying transfer function H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t)? When this LTV system is periodic (as an oscillator is), what structure does H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t) collapse into — why does the input frequency fff only get shifted to the discrete set f+kf0f+kf_0f+kf0​, with gain ckc_kck​? This is the HTM. Narrowing to the "phase output," how do we prove the ISF is exactly that conversion vector?
documents.s: Rigorous LTV framework: Zadeh's time-varying transfer function and the harmonic transfer matrix

documents.t: The LTI (linear time-invariant) systems taught in signals-and-systems courses are completely determined by a single impulse response h(τ)h(\tau)h(τ). For an input x(t)x(t)x(t), the output is a convolution: y(t)=∫−∞∞h(t−τ) x(τ) dτ.y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h(t-\tau)\,x(\tau)\,d\tau .y(t)=∫−∞∞​h(t−τ)x(τ)dτ. Key feature: the kernel hhh depends only on the time difference t−τt-\taut−τ, not on absolute time. "Kicking it now" and "kicking it one beat later" give the same effect, just shifted in time. The frequency domain is diagonal: LTI's signature property is that complex exponentials are eigenfunctions. Substituting x(t)=ej2πftx(t)=e^{j2\pi f t}x(t)=ej2πft, y(t)=∫h(t−τ) ej2πfτ dτ=ej2πft∫h(σ) e−j2πfσ dσ⏟= H(f),y(t)=\int h(t-\tau)\,e^{j2\pi f\tau}\,d\tau =e^{j2\pi f t}\underbrace{\int h(\sigma)\,e^{-j2\pi f\sigma}\,d\sigma}_{=\,H(f)},y(t)=∫h(t−τ)ej2πfτdτ=ej2πft=H(f)∫h(σ)e−j2πfσdσ​​, (change of variables σ=t−τ\sigma=t-\tauσ=t−τ). The output is the same frequency fff multiplied by a complex gain H(f)H(f)H(f). This is the essence of LTI: input frequency fff in, only frequency fff out — no new frequencies are generated. So a single transfer function H(f)H(f)H(f) suffices to describe everything — in the frequency domain, LTI is diagonal (different frequencies do not couple). Dimension check: [h]=[y]/([x]⋅s)[h]=[y]/([x]\cdot\text{s})[h]=[y]/([x]⋅s) (convolution carries a dτd\taudτ); H(f)=∫h e−j2πfσdσH(f)=\int h\,e^{-j2\pi f\sigma}d\sigmaH(f)=∫he−j2πfσdσ differs from hhh by one s\text{s}s, so [H]=[y]/[x][H]=[y]/[x][H]=[y]/[x] (a pure gain) ✓. Why is an oscillator not LTI? Because "kicking at the peak" and "kicking at the zero crossing" give wildly different effects — the kernel depends on the absolute injection instant (through Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ)), not only on t−τt-\taut−τ. This is exactly what lti_vs_ltv and impulse_to_phase_shift Step 4 ("hϕ(t,τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)hϕ​(t,τ) depends on τ\tauτ") describe. Below we systematize this.

documents.t: Relax LTI's "depends only on time difference" assumption: an LTV system's impulse response depends on two instants — "when the impulse is applied (τ\tauτ)" and "when it is observed (ttt)." The output is written (per convention 11.2): y(t)=∫−∞∞h(t,τ) x(τ) dτ \boxed{\ y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h(t,\tau)\,x(\tau)\,d\tau\ } y(t)=∫−∞∞​h(t,τ)x(τ)dτ ​ h(t,τ)h(t,\tau)h(t,τ) reads as "the response measured at time ttt to a unit impulse fired at time τ\tauτ." LTI is a special case: if the system is time-invariant, h(t,τ)=h(t−τ)h(t,\tau)=h(t-\tau)h(t,τ)=h(t−τ), and the expression above collapses back to convolution. LTV loosens "t−τt-\taut−τ" into the "independent pair (t,τ)(t,\tau)(t,τ)" — the extra degree of freedom is exactly the mathematical container for the physical fact that "when you kick it matters." Correspondence to the ISF: [P1] Eq.(10), p.182's excess-phase impulse response hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)=\dfrac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau)hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ) is exactly such an h(t,τ)h(t,\tau)h(t,τ) — its dependence on τ\tauτ is entirely encoded in Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ), and its dependence on t−τt-\taut−τ is just a unit step (the phase step is retained permanently). Substituting into the box above gives [P1] Eq.(11)'s ϕ(t)=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ\phi(t)=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tauϕ(t)=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ (see convolution_derivation). So ISF theory was already an LTV convolution all along — just with a particularly simple kernel. Dimension check: same as LTI, [h(t,τ)]=[y]/([x]⋅s)[h(t,\tau)]=[y]/([x]\cdot\text{s})[h(t,τ)]=[y]/([x]⋅s) ✓.
documents.s: Step 1: LTV — the kernel becomes a two-variable function h(t,τ)h(t,\tau)h(t,τ)

documents.t: LTI needs only one H(f)H(f)H(f). For LTV, the response to "each input frequency" varies with the observation instant ttt, so Zadeh (1950) defines a time-varying transfer function H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t): feed a pure sinusoid x(τ)=ej2πfτx(\tau)=e^{j2\pi f\tau}x(τ)=ej2πfτ into the system, and write the output as "ej2πfte^{j2\pi f t}ej2πft times a gain that varies with ttt": y(t)∣x=ej2πfτ=H(f,t) ej2πft.y(t)\big|_{x=e^{j2\pi f\tau}}=H(f,t)\,e^{j2\pi f t}.y(t)​x=ej2πfτ​=H(f,t)ej2πft. Substitute Step 1's LTV convolution into this, and change variables σ=t−τ\sigma=t-\tauσ=t−τ (i.e., τ=t−σ\tau=t-\sigmaτ=t−σ): y(t)=∫h(t,τ) ej2πfτ dτ=∫h(t, t−σ) ej2πf(t−σ) dσ=ej2πft∫h(t, t−σ) e−j2πfσ dσ⏟≡ H(f,t).y(t)=\int h(t,\tau)\,e^{j2\pi f\tau}\,d\tau =\int h(t,\,t-\sigma)\,e^{j2\pi f(t-\sigma)}\,d\sigma =e^{j2\pi f t}\underbrace{\int h(t,\,t-\sigma)\,e^{-j2\pi f\sigma}\,d\sigma}_{\equiv\,H(f,t)} .y(t)=∫h(t,τ)ej2πfτdτ=∫h(t,t−σ)ej2πf(t−σ)dσ=ej2πft≡H(f,t)∫h(t,t−σ)e−j2πfσdσ​​. This yields Zadeh's time-varying transfer function (convention 11.2): H(f,t)=∫−∞∞h(t, t−σ) e−j2πfσ dσ \boxed{\ H(f,t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h(t,\,t-\sigma)\,e^{-j2\pi f\sigma}\,d\sigma\ } H(f,t)=∫−∞∞​h(t,t−σ)e−j2πfσdσ ​ How to read it: H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t) is the "instantaneous complex gain at this instant ttt, for input frequency fff." Its dependence on fff resembles LTI's H(f)H(f)H(f); the extra dependence on ttt is the entire content of being time-varying. Degeneracy check: when time-invariant, h(t,t−σ)=h(σ)h(t,t-\sigma)=h(\sigma)h(t,t−σ)=h(σ) is independent of ttt, so H(f,t)→H(f)H(f,t)\to H(f)H(f,t)→H(f), recovering LTI ✓. Dimension check: same as H(f)H(f)H(f), [H(f,t)]=[y]/[x][H(f,t)]=[y]/[x][H(f,t)]=[y]/[x] (a pure gain) ✓. Why this still isn't "elegant" enough: H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t) is an arbitrary function of ttt, carrying the same amount of information as the entire h(t,τ)h(t,\tau)h(t,τ) — no compression. The real magic comes in the next step — when the system is periodic, H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t)'s dependence on ttt reduces to only discrete Fourier components, and the whole LTV system collapses into a matrix (the HTM).
documents.s: Step 2: Zadeh's time-varying transfer function H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t) — "the instantaneous response to each frequency"

documents.t: In periodic steady state, an oscillator's LTV kernel is TTT-periodic: h(t+T,τ+T)=h(t,τ)h(t+T,\tau+T)=h(t,\tau)h(t+T,τ+T)=h(t,τ) (invariant when τ\tauτ and ttt are both shifted by one period). This class of systems is called LPTV (linear periodically time-varying). Periodicity makes H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t)'s dependence on ttt become TTT-periodic, so it can be expanded in a Fourier series in ttt: H(f,t)=∑k=−∞∞Hk(f) ej2πkf0t,f0=1T,H(f,t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}H_k(f)\,e^{j2\pi k f_0 t},\qquad f_0=\frac1T,H(f,t)=k=−∞∑∞​Hk​(f)ej2πkf0​t,f0​=T1​, where Hk(f)=1T∫0TH(f,t) e−j2πkf0t dtH_k(f)=\dfrac1T\displaystyle\int_0^T H(f,t)\,e^{-j2\pi k f_0 t}\,dtHk​(f)=T1​∫0T​H(f,t)e−j2πkf0​tdt is the kkk-th harmonic transfer function. Physical meaning (key): feeding a pure sinusoid x=ej2πfτx=e^{j2\pi f\tau}x=ej2πfτ into the system, the output is y(t)=H(f,t) ej2πft=∑kHk(f) ej2π(f+kf0)t.y(t)=H(f,t)\,e^{j2\pi f t}=\sum_{k}H_k(f)\,e^{j2\pi (f+kf_0) t}.y(t)=H(f,t)ej2πft=k∑​Hk​(f)ej2π(f+kf0​)t. A single input frequency fff scatters into an entire row of discrete frequencies f+kf0f+kf_0f+kf0​ (k=0,±1,±2,…k=0,\pm1,\pm2,\dotsk=0,±1,±2,…), with the complex gain of the kkk-th line being Hk(f)H_k(f)Hk​(f). This is the rigorous statement of "the oscillator is a time-varying mixer" / "frequency gets shifted": in the frequency domain, LPTV is no longer diagonal — it couples an input band to every band "spaced by an integer multiple of f0f_0f0​." The harmonic transfer matrix (HTM): index both input and output by "harmonic bands spaced by f0f_0f0​"; the entire LPTV system is then described by a matrix H\mathbf{H}H whose elements [H]m,k=Hm−k ⁣(f)[\mathbf{H}]_{m,k}=H_{m-k}\!\left(f\right)[H]m,k​=Hm−k​(f) map "input band kkk" to "output band mmm." It has Toeplitz structure (elements depend only on the band difference m−km-km−k), because the shift amount only depends on "how many multiples of f0f_0f0​ apart." This is the harmonic transfer matrix — LPTV's "transfer function" is not a single number but this matrix that couples the harmonic bands to one another. Degeneracy check: if the system is time-invariant, only H0(f)=H(f)H_0(f)=H(f)H0​(f)=H(f) is nonzero, and the matrix becomes diagonal (the k=0k=0k=0 line), recovering LTI's "no new frequencies generated" ✓. Dimension check: every Hk(f)H_k(f)Hk​(f) is a pure gain (same dimension as H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t)) ✓. This diagram is identical to the one in fourier_series_of_isf: that page's mermaid diagram draws "noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ folded back to the carrier via cnc_ncn​" as a row of arrows; here HkH_kHk​ is the rigorous name for those arrows. documents.t: Now we narrow the abstract HTM to [P1]'s phase channel. The phase output's LTV kernel (with respect to noise current) comes from [P1] Eq.(11), written in Step 1's h(t,τ)h(t,\tau)h(t,τ) form (phase is the cumulative integral of noise, so the kernel carries a unit step): hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ)[P1] Eq.(10), p.182.h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau)\qquad[\text{P1] Eq.(10), p.182}.hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ)[P1] Eq.(10), p.182. Substitute the ISF's Fourier series ([P1] Eq.(12), p.183) into Γ\GammaΓ: Γ(ω0τ)=c02+∑n=1∞cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn)=∑k=−∞∞c~k ejkω0τ,\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=\frac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n) =\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\tilde c_k\,e^{jk\omega_0\tau},Γ(ω0​τ)=2c0​​+n=1∑∞​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)=k=−∞∑∞​c~k​ejkω0​τ, where the right-hand side rewrites the real-valued cosine series as a complex exponential series (c~0=c0/2\tilde c_0=c_0/2c~0​=c0​/2, c~±k=12cke±jθk\tilde c_{\pm k}=\tfrac12 c_k e^{\pm j\theta_k}c~±k​=21​ck​e±jθk​, k≥1k\ge1k≥1; this is the standard real↔complex Fourier conversion, see math_identities). Core algebra: the phase channel is "ISF-weight, then integrate." First look at the "ISF weighting" — an instantaneous multiplication (we leave the integrator to the next step, since it multiplies every band uniformly by 1/(j2πf)1/(j2\pi f)1/(j2πf) and does not couple bands). Weight a pure sinusoidal noise in(τ)=ej2πfτi_n(\tau)=e^{j2\pi f\tau}in​(τ)=ej2πfτ by the ISF: Γ(ω0τ) ej2πfτ=∑kc~k ejkω0τ ej2πfτ=∑kc~k ej2π(f+kf0)τ.\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,e^{j2\pi f\tau} =\sum_{k}\tilde c_k\,e^{jk\omega_0\tau}\,e^{j2\pi f\tau} =\sum_{k}\tilde c_k\,e^{j2\pi (f+kf_0)\tau}.Γ(ω0​τ)ej2πfτ=k∑​c~k​ejkω0​τej2πfτ=k∑​c~k​ej2π(f+kf0​)τ. (using kω0τ=2π(kf0)τk\omega_0\tau=2\pi(kf_0)\taukω0​τ=2π(kf0​)τ). Comparing against Step 3's y=∑kHk(f)ej2π(f+kf0)ty=\sum_k H_k(f)e^{j2\pi(f+kf_0)t}y=∑k​Hk​(f)ej2π(f+kf0​)t, term-by-term matching reads off the harmonic transfer function of the ISF-weighting stage: Hk(Γ)=c~k ⟺H0(Γ)=c02,H±k(Γ)=12ck e±jθk (k≥1).\boxed{\ H_k^{(\Gamma)}=\tilde c_k\ }\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad H_0^{(\Gamma)}=\frac{c_0}{2},\quad H_{\pm k}^{(\Gamma)}=\tfrac12 c_k\,e^{\pm j\theta_k}\ (k\ge1). Hk(Γ)​=c~k​ ​⟺H0(Γ)​=2c0​​,H±k(Γ)​=21​ck​e±jθk​ (k≥1). This is half of this page's signature result: the harmonic gain of the ISF-weighting stage's HTM is exactly the ISF's Fourier coefficient. "Input frequency fff is shifted to f+kf0f+kf_0f+kf0​ with gain ckc_kck​" is now a theorem that holds verbatim, not an analogy. H0=c0/2H_0=c_0/2H0​=c0​/2 (the DC band, shifting fff right back to itself) — this is exactly the band by which c0c_0c0​ upconverts baseband flicker; H±1∝c1H_{\pm1}\propto c_1H±1​∝c1​ folds down the band near ω0\omega_0ω0​ — this exactly matches fourier_series_of_isf Steps 4 and 5. Dimension check: ckc_kck​ is dimensionless, 1/qmax1/q_{max}1/qmax​ carries C−1\text{C}^{-1}C−1; the ISF channel turns current (A) into a phase rate of change, with the dimension being reconciled to rad by 1/qmax1/q_{max}1/qmax​ together with the following integrator (see next step) ✓.

documents.t: The block below can be run directly (it depends on this site's simulations/common/isf_utils). It tests the claim Hk=c~kH_k=\tilde c_kHk​=c~k​ verbatim: separately inject equal-amplitude single-tone noise near 1ω01\omega_01ω0​, 2ω02\omega_02ω0​, 3ω03\omega_03ω0​ (each offset by Δf\Delta fΔf), integrate into phase ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t), take the FFT of ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t), and measure the amplitude of the "sideband down-converted to baseband Δf\Delta fΔf." If Hn∝cnH_n\propto c_nHn​∝cn​, these sideband ratios must equal the ratios of the ISF's Fourier coefficients c1:c2:c3c_1:c_2:c_3c1​:c2​:c3​. import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import ( compute_fourier_coefficients, integrate_phase_from_noise) f0, qmax = 5e9, 1e-12 # 5 GHz carrier, q_max = 1 pC w0 = 2 * np.pi * f0 fs = 8 * f0 # resolves up to ~3 w0 without aliasing df = 5e6 # injected single-tone offset near each harmonic [Hz] N = 1 << 21 # large N -> cleanly resolve the baseband df sideband t = np.arange(N) / fs # same pedagogical ISF as this page's figure / lab_05 (nonzero c0, several nontrivial harmonics): def gamma(theta): return (-np.sin(theta) + 0.35*np.sin(2*theta) + 0.18*np.cos(3*theta) + 0.25) g_traj = gamma(w0 * t) # Gamma(w0 t), sampled along the trajectory th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 4000, True) _, _, _, c, _ = compute_fourier_coefficients(th, gamma(th), 4) print(np.round(c[:4], 3)) # -> [0.5 1. 0.35 0.18] (c0, c1, c2, c3) I0 = 1e-6 def phi_sideband(n): # inject I0 cos((n w0 + df) t), measure phi's sideband at df i_n = I0 * np.cos((n*w0 + 2*np.pi*df) * t) phi = integrate_phase_from_noise(t, i_n, g_traj, qmax) P = np.abs(np.fft.rfft((phi - phi.mean()) * np.hanning(N))) / N f = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, 1/fs) k = int(np.argmin(np.abs(f - df))) return P[k-5:k+6].max() a1, a2, a3 = (phi_sideband(n) for n in (1, 2, 3)) print(f"a1/a2 = {a1/a2:.3f} c1/c2 = {c[1]/c[2]:.3f}") # -> a1/a2 = 2.857 c1/c2 = 2.857 print(f"a1/a3 = {a1/a3:.3f} c1/c3 = {c[1]/c[3]:.3f}") # -> a1/a3 = 5.556 c1/c3 = 5.556 The two sets of ratios match digit-for-digit: ϕ\phiϕ's response strength to "injection near nω0n\omega_0nω0​" is proportional to cnc_ncn​, which is the numerical witness to Hn(Γ)=c~nH_n^{(\Gamma)}=\tilde c_nHn(Γ)​=c~n​ — the HTM's folding gain is the ISF's Fourier coefficient, not an analogy. (This also corresponds to the arrow heights on the left side of the band-folding figure above, ∣c~±1∣=c1/2|\tilde c_{\pm1}|=c_1/2∣c~±1​∣=c1​/2, ∣c~±2∣=c2/2|\tilde c_{\pm2}|=c_2/2∣c~±2​∣=c2​/2.)

documents.t: The full phase channel is "ISF weighting →\to→ multiply by 1/qmax1/q_{max}1/qmax​ →\to→ integrate" (see the block diagram in white_noise_to_phase_noise). In the frequency domain, the integrator multiplies the "post-shift" frequency f+kf0f+kf_0f+kf0​ by 1j2π(f+kf0)\dfrac{1}{j2\pi(f+kf_0)}j2π(f+kf0​)1​. But what we care about is phase noise near the carrier: noise falling at f=−kf0+Δff=-kf_0+\Delta ff=−kf0​+Δf (i.e., "the kkk-th harmonic band offset by Δf\Delta fΔf") gets shifted by HkH_{k}Hk​ to baseband Δf\Delta fΔf (following Step 3's HTM convention y=∑mHm x(f−mf0)y=\sum_m H_m\,x(f-mf_0)y=∑m​Hm​x(f−mf0​), shifting input −kf0+Δf-kf_0+\Delta f−kf0​+Δf to Δf\Delta fΔf requires m=km=km=k), and the integrator there multiplies by 1j2πΔf\dfrac{1}{j2\pi\Delta f}j2πΔf1​. So the gain of the entire chain "noise in the kkk-th band → phase at Δf\Delta fΔf near the carrier" is 1qmax⋅c~k⏟ISF shift⋅1j2πΔf⏟integrator → ∣⋅∣ ∣ck∣2 qmax⋅12πΔf(k≥1).\frac{1}{q_{max}}\cdot \underbrace{\tilde c_{k}}_{\text{ISF shift}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{1}{j2\pi\Delta f}}_{\text{integrator}} \;\xrightarrow{\ |\cdot|\ }\; \frac{|c_k|}{2\,q_{max}}\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi\Delta f}\quad(k\ge1).qmax​1​⋅ISF shiftc~k​​​⋅integratorj2πΔf1​​​ ∣⋅∣ ​2qmax​∣ck​∣​⋅2πΔf1​(k≥1). This is exactly [P1] Eq.(16/17), p.183's single-tone sideband result ϕp=I0 ck2qmax Δω\phi_p=\dfrac{I_0\,c_k}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}ϕp​=2qmax​ΔωI0​ck​​ (Δω=2πΔf\Delta\omega=2\pi\Delta fΔω=2πΔf) — we've re-derived it from the HTM, with every piece (ISF shift =ck=c_k=ck​, integrator =1/(j2πΔf)=1/(j2\pi\Delta f)=1/(j2πΔf), normalization =1/qmax=1/q_{max}=1/qmax​) cleanly separated out. Collect this entire row of gains "each input harmonic band → phase output" into a vector (this is the row of the HTM corresponding to the "phase output"): gϕ=1qmax[…, c~−2, c~−1, c02, c~1, c~2, …] \boxed{\ \mathbf{g}_\phi=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\big[\dots,\ \tilde c_{-2},\ \tilde c_{-1},\ \tfrac{c_0}{2},\ \tilde c_{1},\ \tilde c_{2},\ \dots\big]\ } gϕ​=qmax​1​[…, c~−2​, c~−1​, 2c0​​, c~1​, c~2​, …] ​ The kkk-th component =c~k/qmax=\tilde c_k/q_{max}=c~k​/qmax​: maps "the noise band a distance kf0kf_0kf0​ from the carrier" to phase. The sum of squared magnitudes ∑k∣c~k∣2=(c0/2)2+12∑n≥1cn2=Γrms2\sum_k|\tilde c_k|^2=(c_0/2)^2+\tfrac12\sum_{n\ge1}c_n^2=\Gamma_{rms}^2∑k​∣c~k​∣2=(c0​/2)2+21​∑n≥1​cn2​=Γrms2​ (the DC term contributes as (c0/2)2(c_0/2)^2(c0​/2)2, consistent with lab_05's Parseval correction and [P1] Eq.(20)) — this is the HTM version of white_noise_to_phase_noise's use of Parseval to convert ∑cn2\sum c_n^2∑cn2​ into Γrms2\Gamma_{rms}^2Γrms2​: the total phase-noise weight = the energy of this conversion vector. Dimension check: each component c~k/qmax\tilde c_k/q_{max}c~k​/qmax​ carries C−1\text{C}^{-1}C−1; multiplying by the noise band's charge (A·s/...) and the integrator afterward yields rad ✓.
documents.s: Step 5: adding back the integrator and 1/qmax1/q_{max}1/qmax​ — the complete HTM row of the phase channel

documents.t: Combining Steps 4 and 5, this page's signature theorem holds: Theorem (ISF = HTM row of the phase output): treat the periodic-time-varying oscillator's phase channel as an LPTV system, indexing input/output by harmonic bands spaced by f0f_0f0​. Then the kkk-th component of the conversion vector gϕ\mathbf{g}_\phigϕ​ mapping "each input harmonic band → phase output" is exactly the (complex) ISF Fourier coefficient divided by qmaxq_{max}qmax​: [gϕ]k=c~k/qmax[\mathbf{g}_\phi]_k=\tilde c_k/q_{max}[gϕ​]k​=c~k​/qmax​. Equivalently, the ISF's Fourier series {ck}\{c_k\}{ck​} is exactly the content of that row of the phase output in the HTM. This upgrades three statements that had been treated as "intuition/analogy" into theorems of LTV system theory: What this site has said (intuition) Rigorous HTM statement Correspondence The oscillator is a "time-varying mixer" LPTV system, H(f,t)=∑kHk(f)ejkω0tH(f,t)=\sum_k H_k(f)e^{jk\omega_0 t}H(f,t)=∑k​Hk​(f)ejkω0​t, off-diagonal Input fff → output f+kf0f+kf_0f+kf0​ "Noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ is shifted to the carrier" H±k(Γ)=12cke±jθkH_{\pm k}^{(\Gamma)}=\tfrac12 c_k e^{\pm j\theta_k}H±k(Γ)​=21​ck​e±jθk​ Shift gain =ck=c_k=ck​ "The ISF's Fourier coefficient ckc_kck​ is the mixer gain" [gϕ]k=c~k/qmax[\mathbf{g}_\phi]_k=\tilde c_k/q_{max}[gϕ​]k​=c~k​/qmax​ ISF === HTM row of the phase output "Total weight ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​" Conversion-vector energy ∑k∣c~k∣2=Γrms2\sum_k\vert \tilde c_k\vert ^2=\Gamma_{rms}^2∑k​∣c~k​∣2=Γrms2​ Parseval = vector norm Relation to [P1] Eq.(13) (within the 5 PDFs): [P1] Eq.(13), p.183 writes phase as "the c0c_0c0​-term integral plus the sum of integrals weighted by each harmonic cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn)c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​)." That is exactly the time-domain version of "applying the conversion vector gϕ\mathbf{g}_\phigϕ​ to the noise, then integrating" — the HTM is its frequency-domain counterpart. The two are the same thing in two languages (time-domain series vs. frequency-domain band matrix). Relation to PPV/Floquet: derivation_floquet_ppv proves the ISF === the PPV's component at the injection node (Γ/qmax=v1Tb\Gamma/q_{max}=v_1^T\mathbf bΓ/qmax​=v1T​b). The HTM is the frequency-domain/system-theory face of "the same ISF"; the PPV is its state-space/differential-geometry face. All three ([P1]'s intuition, PPV, HTM) describe the same object Γ\GammaΓ, just at different levels of abstraction.

documents.t: LTI is described by a single h(t−τ)h(t-\tau)h(t−τ)/H(f)H(f)H(f), diagonal in frequency domain, generating no new frequencies; LTV's kernel becomes h(t,τ)h(t,\tau)h(t,τ), with output y=∫h(t,τ)x dτy=\int h(t,\tau)x\,d\tauy=∫h(t,τ)xdτ; the oscillator's hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmaxu(t−τ)h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}u(t-\tau)hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ) is exactly one example. Zadeh's time-varying transfer function H(f,t)=∫h(t,t−σ)e−j2πfσdσH(f,t)=\int h(t,t-\sigma)e^{-j2\pi f\sigma}d\sigmaH(f,t)=∫h(t,t−σ)e−j2πfσdσ describes "the instantaneous gain at frequency fff right now"; it degenerates to H(f)H(f)H(f) when time-invariant. Periodic LTV (LPTV): H(f,t)=∑kHk(f)ejkω0tH(f,t)=\sum_k H_k(f)e^{jk\omega_0 t}H(f,t)=∑k​Hk​(f)ejkω0​t; an input frequency fff gets shifted to an entire row f+kf0f+kf_0f+kf0​, with gain HkH_kHk​. This set of harmonic gains forms the Toeplitz harmonic transfer matrix (HTM). Substituting the ISF kernel → Hk(Γ)=c~kH_k^{(\Gamma)}=\tilde c_kHk(Γ)​=c~k​ (the ISF's Fourier coefficient); adding back 1/qmax1/q_{max}1/qmax​ and the integrator re-derives [P1] Eq.(16/17)'s single-tone sideband. Signature theorem: the phase-output conversion vector [gϕ]k=c~k/qmax[\mathbf g_\phi]_k=\tilde c_k/q_{max}[gϕ​]k​=c~k​/qmax​ — the ISF is exactly the conversion vector from each harmonic band to the phase output (the HTM's phase-output row); its energy ∑k∣c~k∣2=Γrms2\sum_k|\tilde c_k|^2=\Gamma_{rms}^2∑k​∣c~k​∣2=Γrms2​ is Parseval. The entire Zadeh/HTM apparatus belongs to external LTV system theory, not among the 5 PDFs ([E5] Zadeh 1950); together with [P1] Eq.(13) and PPV, it is the same ISF in three languages.

documents.t: See also: notation (authoritative symbols and units), glossary (Chinese–English term intuitions), convolution_derivation (LTV convolution uses the tools on this page), white_noise_to_phase_noise (application site for Parseval/integrator response) ISF theory looks very "circuits," but its skeleton is really a handful of standard math tools combined repeatedly. This page collects them, gives each a short proof or citation, and marks which page on the site uses it. Come back here when a derivation stalls — it beats memorizing formulas by rote. How to use this page: each section first gives "one line on what it says," then "why it holds" (proof or citation), and finally "where on the site it's used." Every quantity carries units — doing a dimension check is always the fastest way to catch mistakes.

documents.t: One line: any 2π2\pi2π-periodic real function can be split into DC plus a set of harmonics; its "total energy" equals the sum of each harmonic's energy. This is the mathematical basis for splitting the ISF Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) into c0,c1,c2,…c_0,c_1,c_2,\dotsc0​,c1​,c2​,…. The ISF is a dimensionless, 2π2\pi2π-periodic function, written as a cosine series ([P1] Eq.(12), p.183): Γ(ω0τ)=c02+∑n=1∞cncos⁡(nω0τ+θn)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)=\frac{c_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)Γ(ω0​τ)=2c0​​+n=1∑∞​cn​cos(nω0​τ+θn​) Write the argument as x=ω0τx=\omega_0\taux=ω0​τ. Parseval's relation ([P1] Eq.(20), p.185): ∑n=0∞cn2=1π∫02π∣Γ(x)∣2 dx=2 Γrms2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n^2=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma(x)|^2\,dx=2\,\Gamma_{rms}^2n=0∑∞​cn2​=π1​∫02π​∣Γ(x)∣2dx=2Γrms2​ Why it holds (short proof): square the series and integrate from 000 to 2π2\pi2π. Cosines of different harmonics are mutually orthogonal, ∫02πcos⁡(mx+θm)cos⁡(nx+θn) dx=π δmn(m,n≥1),\int_0^{2\pi}\cos(mx+\theta_m)\cos(nx+\theta_n)\,dx=\pi\,\delta_{mn}\quad(m,n\ge1),∫02π​cos(mx+θm​)cos(nx+θn​)dx=πδmn​(m,n≥1), so the cross terms all vanish, leaving only the square terms: each cncos⁡(⋅)c_n\cos(\cdot)cn​cos(⋅) term contributes cn2⋅πc_n^2\cdot\picn2​⋅π, and the DC term (c02)2\left(\frac{c_0}{2}\right)^2(2c0​​)2 contributes (c02)2⋅2π=c022π\left(\frac{c_0}{2}\right)^2\cdot 2\pi=\frac{c_0^2}{2}\pi(2c0​​)2⋅2π=2c02​​π. Dividing both sides by π\piπ gives ∑n=1∞cn2+c022\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n^2+\frac{c_0^2}{2}∑n=1∞​cn2​+2c02​​. Hajimiri–Lee write the DC term as c022\frac{c_0^2}{2}2c02​​ (note the n=0n=0n=0 term is counted as only half in the sum), and rearranging gives exactly the form above. rms definition consistency check: Γrms2=12π∫02π∣Γ(x)∣2 dx\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\Gamma(x)|^2\,dxΓrms2​=2π1​∫02π​∣Γ(x)∣2dx (rms is just "root mean square": square first, average, then take the root). Substituting into the right-hand side of Parseval: 1π∫=2⋅12π∫=2Γrms2\frac{1}{\pi}\int=2\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi}\int=2\Gamma_{rms}^2π1​∫=2⋅2π1​∫=2Γrms2​ ✓. Numerical feel: for the ideal LC, Γ(θ)=−sin⁡θ\Gamma(\theta)=-\sin\thetaΓ(θ)=−sinθ, only c1=1c_1=1c1​=1 (all others 0). Γrms2=12π∫02πsin⁡2θ dθ=12\Gamma_{rms}^2=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac12Γrms2​=2π1​∫02π​sin2θdθ=21​, so Γrms=1/2≈0.707\Gamma_{rms}=1/\sqrt2\approx0.707Γrms​=1/2​≈0.707; the right-hand side of Parseval, 2×12=1=c122\times\frac12=1=c_1^22×21​=1=c12​ ✓. Used on this site: fourier_series_of_isf (splitting the ISF into harmonics, explaining how noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ downconverts), rms_isf, lab_05 (numerically verifying ∑cn2=2Γrms2\sum c_n^2=2\Gamma_{rms}^2∑cn2​=2Γrms2​).
