documents.t: One line: an LTI (linear time-invariant) system's impulse response depends only on "how long ago" t−τt-\taut−τ; an LTV (linear time-variant) system also depends on "at what instant it's kicked" τ\tauτ. The oscillator's response to noise is LTV — this is the core of ISF theory. LTI superposition is standard convolution: y(t)=∫−∞∞h(t−τ) x(τ) dτ.y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h(t-\tau)\,x(\tau)\,d\tau .y(t)=∫−∞∞​h(t−τ)x(τ)dτ. Core feature: hhh depends only on the difference t−τt-\taut−τ (time-invariant). Delay the input, and the output is delayed unchanged. The oscillator's excess-phase impulse response, however, is ([P1] Eq.(10), p.182): hϕ(t,τ)=Γ(ω0τ)qmax u(t−τ).h_\phi(t,\tau)=\frac{\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)}{q_{max}}\,u(t-\tau).hϕ​(t,τ)=qmax​Γ(ω0​τ)​u(t−τ). It simultaneously depends on τ\tauτ (via Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) — at what phase of the waveform it's kicked) and on t−τt-\taut−τ (via the step u(t−τ)u(t-\tau)u(t−τ) — it persists permanently after being kicked). Superposing all past noise ([P1] Eq.(11), p.182): ϕ(t)=∫−∞∞hϕ(t,τ) in(τ) dτ=1qmax∫−∞tΓ(ω0τ) in(τ) dτ.\phi(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h_\phi(t,\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau=\frac{1}{q_{max}}\int_{-\infty}^{t}\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)\,i_n(\tau)\,d\tau .ϕ(t)=∫−∞∞​hϕ​(t,τ)in​(τ)dτ=qmax​1​∫−∞t​Γ(ω0​τ)in​(τ)dτ. Why it's LTV, not LTI: because Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) is a periodic function of the absolute instant of injection. The same impulse, kicked at the peak (Γ≈0\Gamma\approx0Γ≈0), barely changes phase; kicked at the zero crossing (∣Γ∣|\Gamma|∣Γ∣ maximal), changes it the most. This is exactly [P1] Sec. III's claim C1: "the oscillator's response to noise is linear time-variant, not LTI." Unit check: hϕh_\phihϕ​ has units of 1/C1/\text{C}1/C (Γ\GammaΓ dimensionless, qmaxq_{max}qmax​ in C, uuu dimensionless), ∫hϕ in dτ\int h_\phi\, i_n\, d\tau∫hϕ​in​dτ has units =(1/C)⋅A⋅s=(1/C)⋅C==(1/\text{C})\cdot\text{A}\cdot\text{s}=(1/\text{C})\cdot\text{C}==(1/C)⋅A⋅s=(1/C)⋅C= dimensionless === rad ✓. Used on this site: impulse_to_phase_shift, convolution_derivation, lab_04 (lti_vs_ltv_impulse_response.png: LTI's step height is fixed, LTV's step height varies with injection phase).

documents.t: One line: phase is the "integral" of noise current (the upper limit of Eq.(11) is ttt); an integrator in the frequency domain is 1/(jω)1/(j\omega)1/(jω), and in power terms 1/ω21/\omega^21/ω2. This is the source of the −20-20−20 dB/dec slope. For an ideal integrator y(t)=∫−∞tx(τ) dτy(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}x(\tau)\,d\tauy(t)=∫−∞t​x(τ)dτ, with a single tone x(t)=ejωtx(t)=e^{j\omega t}x(t)=ejωt: ∫tejωτ dτ=1jωejωt ⇒ H(jω)=1jω.\int^{t}e^{j\omega\tau}\,d\tau=\frac{1}{j\omega}e^{j\omega t}\;\Rightarrow\;H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{j\omega}.∫tejωτdτ=jω1​ejωt⇒H(jω)=jω1​. Magnitude: ∣H(jω)∣=1/ω|H(j\omega)|=1/\omega∣H(jω)∣=1/ω. Power (PSD multiplier): ∣H∣2=1/ω2|H|^2=1/\omega^2∣H∣2=1/ω2. dB slope: 10log⁡10(1/ω2)=−20log⁡10ω10\log_{10}(1/\omega^2)=-20\log_{10}\omega10log10​(1/ω2)=−20log10​ω, −20-20−20 dB per decade — exactly the 1/f21/f^21/f2-region slope of phase noise. Connecting to the ISF: taking Γ\GammaΓ's rms as an effective gain, the noise-current PSD SiS_iSi​, after "multiplying by Γrms/qmax\Gamma_{rms}/q_{max}Γrms​/qmax​ then integrating," gives the phase PSD: Sϕ(Δω)=Γrms2qmax2⋅SiΔω2.S_\phi(\Delta\omega)=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{S_i}{\Delta\omega^2}.Sϕ​(Δω)=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅Δω2Si​​. Unit check (using C=A⋅s\text{C}=\text{A}\cdot\text{s}C=A⋅s): 1C2⋅A2/Hz(rad/s)2=A2/HzC2⋅s−2=A2/HzA2=1Hz=rad2/Hz ✓\frac{1}{\text{C}^2}\cdot\frac{\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}}{(\text{rad/s})^2}=\frac{\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}}{\text{C}^2\cdot\text{s}^{-2}}=\frac{\text{A}^2/\text{Hz}}{\text{A}^2}=\frac{1}{\text{Hz}}=\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}\ \checkmarkC21​⋅(rad/s)2A2/Hz​=C2⋅s−2A2/Hz​=A2A2/Hz​=Hz1​=rad2/Hz ✓ Factor-of-2 note: using the equation above (a clean time-domain derivation) gives L=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}=\frac12 S_\phiL=21​Sϕ​, corresponding to a denominator of 2Δω22\Delta\omega^22Δω2; whereas [P1] Eq.(21), p.185 writes 4Δω24\Delta\omega^24Δω2. The factor-of-2 difference is an SSB bookkeeping convention, a well-known minor point of contention in the literature, and does not affect the Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ scaling or the −20-20−20 dB/dec slope. See white_noise_to_phase_noise for details. Used on this site: white_noise_to_phase_noise, lab_06.

documents.t: One line: a stationary stochastic process's "power spectral density" (PSD) is the Fourier transform of its "autocorrelation function." This connects time-domain noise (autocorrelation) with frequency-domain noise (PSD), and is the foundation of every phase-noise calculation. For a stationary stochastic process x(t)x(t)x(t), the autocorrelation is Rx(τ)=⟨x(t) x(t+τ)⟩R_x(\tau)=\langle x(t)\,x(t+\tau)\rangleRx​(τ)=⟨x(t)x(t+τ)⟩. Wiener–Khinchin theorem: Sx(ω)=∫−∞∞Rx(τ) e−jωτ dτ.S_x(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}R_x(\tau)\,e^{-j\omega\tau}\,d\tau .Sx​(ω)=∫−∞∞​Rx​(τ)e−jωτdτ. White-noise special case: Rx(τ)=N02δ(τ)R_x(\tau)=\frac{N_0}{2}\delta(\tau)Rx​(τ)=2N0​​δ(τ) (completely uncorrelated at different instants) ⇒Sx(ω)=N02\Rightarrow S_x(\omega)=\frac{N_0}{2}⇒Sx​(ω)=2N0​​ (frequency-independent — that's what "white" means). This site uses the single-sided PSD Si=in2‾/ΔfS_i=\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta fSi​=in2​​/Δf (A²/Hz). Variance (total power): σx2=Rx(0)=12π∫−∞∞Sx(ω) dω=∫0∞Sx(1-side)(f) df.\sigma_x^2=R_x(0)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_x(\omega)\,d\omega=\int_0^{\infty}S_x^{(1\text{-side})}(f)\,df .σx2​=Rx​(0)=2π1​∫−∞∞​Sx​(ω)dω=∫0∞​Sx(1-side)​(f)df. This is where the phase-variance formula σϕ2=∫f1f2Sϕ(f) df\sigma_\phi^2=\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_\phi(f)\,dfσϕ2​=∫f1​f2​​Sϕ​(f)df comes from: phase variance is the integral of the phase PSD over frequency ([P1]'s usage convention; a standard stochastic-process result). Unit check: SϕS_\phiSϕ​ is in rad²/Hz, ∫Sϕ df\int S_\phi\, df∫Sϕ​df has units =rad2/Hz⋅Hz=rad2=\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}\cdot\text{Hz}=\text{rad}^2=rad2/Hz⋅Hz=rad2 ✓. External source: Wiener–Khinchin is a standard stochastic-process theorem (not among the five downloaded PDFs, standard textbook material, e.g. Papoulis; [P1] uses its conclusion directly). Used on this site: psd_phase_noise_jitter, stochastic_processes_recap, lab_06 (estimating PSD via Welch's method), lab_08 (integrating PSD to get jitter).

documents.t: One line: dB is a "log scale of a power ratio"; dBc/Hz is the phase-noise unit "power relative to the carrier, per Hz of bandwidth." Remembering "×10\times10×10 power =+10=+10=+10 dB, ×2\times2×2 power ≈+3\approx+3≈+3 dB" is enough to get by. Definition (power ratio): XdB=10log⁡10 ⁣(PPref).X_{\text{dB}}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P}{P_{ref}}\right).XdB​=10log10​(Pref​P​). Voltage/amplitude ratio: because power ∝\propto∝ amplitude2^22, XdB=20log⁡10(V/Vref)X_{\text{dB}}=20\log_{10}(V/V_{ref})XdB​=20log10​(V/Vref​) (an extra factor of 2). Inverse conversion: P/Pref=10XdB/10P/P_{ref}=10^{X_{\text{dB}}/10}P/Pref​=10XdB​/10. SSB phase noise L(Δf)\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)L(Δf)'s unit is dBc/Hz: "c" = relative to carrier, "/Hz" = per unit bandwidth. Its relation to the phase PSD (small-angle approximation, see Section 6): L(Δf)≈12Sϕ(Δf)⟹LdBc/Hz=10log⁡10 ⁣(12Sϕ), Sϕ=2⋅10LdBc/Hz/10 rad2/Hz.\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\approx\frac12 S_\phi(\Delta f)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal{L}_{\text{dBc/Hz}}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\tfrac12 S_\phi\right),\;\; S_\phi=2\cdot10^{\mathcal{L}_{\text{dBc/Hz}}/10}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}.L(Δf)≈21​Sϕ​(Δf)⟹LdBc/Hz​=10log10​(21​Sϕ​),Sϕ​=2⋅10LdBc/Hz​/10 rad2/Hz. Numerical feel (canonical example C): L=−100\mathcal{L}=-100L=−100 dBc/Hz ⇒10−100/10=10−10\Rightarrow 10^{-100/10}=10^{-10}⇒10−100/10=10−10, Sϕ=2×10−10S_\phi=2\times10^{-10}Sϕ​=2×10−10 rad²/Hz. 10× better in power (−110-110−110 dBc/Hz) = 10≈3.16×\sqrt{10}\approx3.16\times10​≈3.16× better in amplitude (rms). documents.t: One line: when phase jitter is small, the single-sideband power of a phase modulation is about half the phase PSD. This is the bridge that converts "phase PSD" into the "dBc/Hz" on a datasheet. Consider a phase-modulated carrier: v(t)=Acos⁡ ⁣(ω0t+ϕ(t))v(t)=A\cos\!\big(\omega_0 t+\phi(t)\big)v(t)=Acos(ω0​t+ϕ(t)). When ∣ϕ(t)∣≪1|\phi(t)|\ll1∣ϕ(t)∣≪1 rad (small-angle), expand trigonometrically and approximate cos⁡ϕ≈1\cos\phi\approx1cosϕ≈1, sin⁡ϕ≈ϕ\sin\phi\approx\phisinϕ≈ϕ: v(t)=A[cos⁡ω0tcos⁡ϕ−sin⁡ω0tsin⁡ϕ]≈Acos⁡ω0t−A ϕ(t)sin⁡ω0t.v(t)=A\big[\cos\omega_0 t\cos\phi-\sin\omega_0 t\sin\phi\big]\approx A\cos\omega_0 t-A\,\phi(t)\sin\omega_0 t .v(t)=A[cosω0​tcosϕ−sinω0​tsinϕ]≈Acosω0​t−Aϕ(t)sinω0​t. The first term is the pure carrier; the second term −A ϕ(t)sin⁡ω0t-A\,\phi(t)\sin\omega_0 t−Aϕ(t)sinω0​t is the "phase sideband" — it moves the baseband ϕ(t)\phi(t)ϕ(t) to either side of the carrier. For a phase component at a single offset frequency Δf\Delta fΔf, the sideband power is proportional to the power of ϕ\phiϕ; converting to the single-sideband (SSB) density relative to the carrier gives L(Δf)≈12Sϕ(Δf).\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\approx\frac12 S_\phi(\Delta f).L(Δf)≈21​Sϕ​(Δf). That 12\frac1221​ comes from the bookkeeping of "total phase power split evenly between the upper and lower sidebands." Applicability condition (important): holds only for σϕ≪1\sigma_\phi\ll1σϕ​≪1 rad. If the integration bandwidth is wide enough that σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ approaches or exceeds 1 rad, this approximation fails (the carrier gets "smeared out"), and a more complete treatment is needed. Canonical example C's σϕ=14.07\sigma_\phi=14.07σϕ​=14.07 mrad ≪1\ll1≪1, so it is safe. Used on this site: psd_phase_noise_jitter, numerical_feeling, Eq.(16) of the spec (L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\frac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​).

documents.t: One line: when multiplying "some harmonic of the ISF" by "an injected single tone" and integrating over time, you use product-to-sum identities to split the product into a slow term (survives) and a fast term (vanishes after integration). For an injected single tone i(t)=I0cos⁡(Δω t)i(t)=I_0\cos(\Delta\omega\,t)i(t)=I0​cos(Δωt) near DC, the phase response ([P1] Eq.(13), p.183's c0c_0c0​ term) requires computing ∫tI0cos⁡(Δω τ) dτ=I0sin⁡(Δω t)Δω\int^{t}I_0\cos(\Delta\omega\,\tau)\,d\tau=\dfrac{I_0\sin(\Delta\omega\,t)}{\Delta\omega}∫tI0​cos(Δωτ)dτ=ΔωI0​sin(Δωt)​, directly giving [P1] Eq.(15), p.183: ϕ(t)≈I0 c0sin⁡(Δω t)2qmax Δω.\phi(t)\approx\frac{I_0\,c_0\sin(\Delta\omega\,t)}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}.ϕ(t)≈2qmax​ΔωI0​c0​sin(Δωt)​. When the tone is near nω0n\omega_0nω0​, use product-to-sum: cos⁡(nω0τ+θn)cos⁡((nω0+Δω)τ)=12cos⁡((2nω0+Δω)τ+θn)+12cos⁡(Δω τ−θn).\cos(n\omega_0\tau+\theta_n)\cos\big((n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau\big) =\frac12\cos\big((2n\omega_0+\Delta\omega)\tau+\theta_n\big)+\frac12\cos\big(\Delta\omega\,\tau-\theta_n\big).cos(nω0​τ+θn​)cos((nω0​+Δω)τ)=21​cos((2nω0​+Δω)τ+θn​)+21​cos(Δωτ−θn​). The first term has frequency ≈2nω0\approx2n\omega_0≈2nω0​ (fast); after integration its amplitude ∝1/(2nω0)\propto1/(2n\omega_0)∝1/(2nω0​), tiny, negligible. The second term has frequency Δω\Delta\omegaΔω (slow, near DC); after integration its amplitude ∝1/Δω\propto1/\Delta\omega∝1/Δω, survives. Keeping only the slow term and integrating gives [P1] Eq.(16)/(17), p.183: ϕ(t)≈I0 cnsin⁡(Δω t)2qmax Δω.\phi(t)\approx\frac{I_0\,c_n\sin(\Delta\omega\,t)}{2q_{max}\,\Delta\omega}.ϕ(t)≈2qmax​ΔωI0​cn​sin(Δωt)​. That 12\frac1221​ is exactly what falls out of the product-to-sum step. Physical meaning: the ISF's nnn-th harmonic acts like a mixer, "downconverting" noise near nω0n\omega_0nω0​ into low-frequency phase modulation near the carrier — this is the frequency-translation picture of phase noise. Common identity quick reference: Identity Use cos⁡Acos⁡B=12[cos⁡(A−B)+cos⁡(A+B)]\cos A\cos B=\tfrac12[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)]cosAcosB=21​[cos(A−B)+cos(A+B)] separating slow/fast terms (Eq.16/17) sin⁡2θ=12(1−cos⁡2θ)\sin^2\theta=\tfrac12(1-\cos2\theta)sin2θ=21​(1−cos2θ) computing Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ (rms of −sin⁡-\sin−sin is 1/21/\sqrt21/2​) ∫tcos⁡(ωτ)dτ=sin⁡(ωt)/ω\int^{t}\cos(\omega\tau)d\tau=\sin(\omega t)/\omega∫tcos(ωτ)dτ=sin(ωt)/ω integrator 1/ω1/\omega1/ω (Eq.15) Used on this site: fourier_series_of_isf, convolution_derivation, the orthogonality used in Section 1's Parseval.

documents.t: One line: an open-loop oscillator has no absolute time reference, so each period's phase error accumulates independently like a "drunkard's walk"; the variance of the error grows linearly, so the standard deviation grows as Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​. Suppose each period injects an independent, zero-mean phase error δk\delta_kδk​ with variance σ12\sigma_1^2σ12​ (the result of white noise integrated over one period). After MMM periods the total phase error is ΦM=∑k=1Mδk\Phi_M=\sum_{k=1}^{M}\delta_kΦM​=∑k=1M​δk​. Because each δk\delta_kδk​ is independent, the variances add (cross-correlation terms have zero expectation): Var(ΦM)=∑k=1MVar(δk)=M σ12.\mathrm{Var}(\Phi_M)=\sum_{k=1}^{M}\mathrm{Var}(\delta_k)=M\,\sigma_1^2 .Var(ΦM​)=k=1∑M​Var(δk​)=Mσ12​. The measurement interval is Δt=M⋅T\Delta t=M\cdot TΔt=M⋅T, so M=Δt/TM=\Delta t/TM=Δt/T, Var(ΦM)=σ12T Δt∝Δt\mathrm{Var}(\Phi_M)=\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{T}\,\Delta t\propto\Delta tVar(ΦM​)=Tσ12​​Δt∝Δt. Converting to time jitter (σt=σϕ/(2πf0)\sigma_t=\sigma_\phi/(2\pi f_0)σt​=σϕ​/(2πf0​), i.e. the phase-to-time conversion of [P2] Eq.(10), p.793) and taking the square root: σΔt=κ Δt([P2] Eq.(8), p.792).\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\,\sqrt{\Delta t}\qquad([P2]\ \text{Eq.}(8),\ \text{p.792}).σΔt​=κΔt​([P2] Eq.(8), p.792). κ\kappaκ is a proportionality constant specific to each device, with units s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​; it is determined by the same Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​ ratio ([P2] Eq.(12), p.793 as printed: κ=Γrmsqmax ω012in2‾Δf\kappa=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}}{q_{max}\,\omega_0}\sqrt{\tfrac12\tfrac{\overline{i_n^2}}{\Delta f}}κ=qmax​ω0​Γrms​​21​Δfin2​​​​, with ω0\omega_0ω0​ in the denominator, hence units s\sqrt{\text{s}}s​; re-verified in v11. The phase version κϕ=ω0κ\kappa_\phi=\omega_0\kappaκϕ​=ω0​κ is in diffusion_dictionary). Key intuition: variance (power) grows linearly, standard deviation (rms) grows as a square root. This is the hallmark of a random walk; it appears whenever phase errors accumulate independently with no restoring force (contrast: with a PLL locked, there is a restoring force and jitter is suppressed, no longer growing without bound). Corresponds to claim C6. Numerical feel: at a spacing of 1000 periods (at 5 GHz, Δt=200\Delta t=200Δt=200 ns), σΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}σΔt​ is 1000/10=100=10×\sqrt{1000/10}=\sqrt{100}=10\times1000/10​=100​=10× that at a spacing of 10 periods (Δt=2\Delta t=2Δt=2 ns) — a 100× longer interval gives only 10× more jitter. Used on this site: lab_03 (ring_oscillator_timing_noise_accumulation.png: σΔt=σΔN\sigma_{\Delta t}=\sigma\sqrt{\Delta N}σΔt​=σΔN​ random walk), psd_phase_noise_jitter, serdes_clocking_connection.

documents.t: One line: Section 6's small-angle PM result (L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\frac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​) is only the first-order approximation of "large-angle phase modulation" valid for β≪1\beta\ll1β≪1; the full solution is an infinite ladder of Bessel sidebands, with the carrier and each sideband having amplitude J0(β)J_0(\beta)J0​(β) and Jn(β)J_n(\beta)Jn​(β) respectively. This section builds the full ladder and quantifies exactly when the small-angle approximation starts to break down.
documents.s: 9. Large-angle PM: the Bessel sideband ladder and where the small-angle approximation fails

documents.t: For any real β\betaβ (the modulation index) and angle Ωt\Omega tΩt, the Jacobi–Anger expansion (a standard special-function identity, e.g. Abramowitz & Stegun 9.1.42; external literature, not in this site's 5 PDFs): ejβsin⁡Ωt=∑n=−∞∞Jn(β) ejnΩte^{j\beta\sin\Omega t}=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(\beta)\,e^{jn\Omega t}ejβsinΩt=n=−∞∑∞​Jn​(β)ejnΩt where Jn(β)J_n(\beta)Jn​(β) is the Bessel function of the first kind, order nnn. Why it holds (one-line provenance): ejβsin⁡Ωte^{j\beta\sin\Omega t}ejβsinΩt is 2π2\pi2π-periodic in Ωt\Omega tΩt; expanding it in a Fourier series, the integral defining its coefficients 12π∫−ππej(βsin⁡x−nx)dx\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{j(\beta\sin x-nx)}dx2π1​∫−ππ​ej(βsinx−nx)dx is exactly one of the standard integral representations of Jn(β)J_n(\beta)Jn​(β) — that integral representation itself is not re-derived here, only its result is cited. Properties (used below): J−n(β)=(−1)nJn(β)J_{-n}(\beta)=(-1)^n J_n(\beta)J−n​(β)=(−1)nJn​(β) (symmetric for even nnn, antisymmetric for odd nnn), and the Bessel Parseval-like identity: ∑n=−∞∞Jn(β)2=1(∀β)\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(\beta)^2=1\qquad(\forall\beta)n=−∞∑∞​Jn​(β)2=1(∀β) This can later be used to check "the sideband ladder's total power is conserved" — a complete analogy to the Parseval relation for the ISF's Fourier coefficients in Section 1.
documents.s: 9.1 The Jacobi–Anger expansion (external literature, not in this site's 5 PDFs)

documents.t: Consider a carrier phase-modulated by a single audio tone Ω\OmegaΩ (writing Section 6's ϕ(t)=ϕpsin⁡Ωt\phi(t)=\phi_p\sin\Omega tϕ(t)=ϕp​sinΩt as ϕ(t)=βsin⁡Ωt\phi(t)=\beta\sin\Omega tϕ(t)=βsinΩt, where β\betaβ is the modulation index, i.e. the peak phase deviation, units rad): V(t)=cos⁡ ⁣(ω0t+βsin⁡Ωt)V(t)=\cos\!\big(\omega_0 t+\beta\sin\Omega t\big)V(t)=cos(ω0​t+βsinΩt) Writing this as Re{ejω0t ejβsin⁡Ωt}\mathrm{Re}\{e^{j\omega_0 t}\,e^{j\beta\sin\Omega t}\}Re{ejω0​tejβsinΩt} and substituting the Jacobi–Anger expansion: V(t)=Re{ejω0t∑n=−∞∞Jn(β)ejnΩt}=∑n=−∞∞Jn(β)cos⁡((ω0+nΩ)t)V(t)=\mathrm{Re}\left\{e^{j\omega_0 t}\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(\beta)e^{jn\Omega t}\right\} =\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}J_n(\beta)\cos\big((\omega_0+n\Omega)t\big)V(t)=Re{ejω0​tn=−∞∑∞​Jn​(β)ejnΩt}=n=−∞∑∞​Jn​(β)cos((ω0​+nΩ)t) This is the full Bessel sideband ladder: Carrier (n=0n=0n=0): amplitude J0(β)J_0(\beta)J0​(β), located at ω0\omega_0ω0​. nnn-th sideband (n=±1,±2,…n=\pm1,\pm2,\dotsn=±1,±2,…): amplitude Jn(β)J_n(\beta)Jn​(β), located at ω0+nΩ\omega_0+n\Omegaω0​+nΩ. Because J−n=(−1)nJnJ_{-n}=(-1)^nJ_nJ−n​=(−1)nJn​, the upper and lower sidebands have equal magnitude (∣J−n∣=∣Jn∣|J_{-n}|=|J_n|∣J−n​∣=∣Jn​∣), differing only in sign (phase). Unit check: β=ϕp\beta=\phi_pβ=ϕp​ is the peak phase, arising from the integral ∫ϕ(t)\int\phi(t)∫ϕ(t), with units rad; Ωt\Omega tΩt and ω0t\omega_0 tω0​t are both dimensionless phase angles (rad), and Jn(β)J_n(\beta)Jn​(β) itself is dimensionless (an amplitude ratio), so substituting into cos⁡(⋅)\cos(\cdot)cos(⋅) raises no unit issue; V(t)V(t)V(t) has the same units as the original cos⁡(ω0t+ϕ(t))\cos(\omega_0t+\phi(t))cos(ω0​t+ϕ(t)) (normalized amplitude) ✓.
documents.s: 9.2 The sideband ladder for single-tone PM

documents.t: Small-argument expansion of the Bessel functions (standard external-literature result): J0(β)≈1−β24,J1(β)≈β2(β≪1)J_0(\beta)\approx1-\frac{\beta^2}{4},\qquad J_1(\beta)\approx\frac{\beta}{2}\qquad(\beta\ll1)J0​(β)≈1−4β2​,J1​(β)≈2β​(β≪1) Substituting back into the sideband ladder: the carrier amplitude J0(β)≈1−β2/4≈1J_0(\beta)\approx1-\beta^2/4\approx1J0​(β)≈1−β2/4≈1 (barely attenuated at first order), and the first-sideband amplitude J1(β)≈β/2J_1(\beta)\approx\beta/2J1​(β)≈β/2. The single-sideband relative power: L(Δf)≈J1(β)2≈(β2)2\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\approx J_1(\beta)^2\approx\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\right)^2L(Δf)≈J1​(β)2≈(2β​)2 This is exactly Section 6's small-angle PM result L≈(ϕp2)2=12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\left(\frac{\phi_p}{2}\right)^2=\frac12 S_\phiL≈(2ϕp​​)2=21​Sϕ​ (β=ϕp\beta=\phi_pβ=ϕp​ is the peak phase, Sϕ=ϕp2/2S_\phi=\phi_p^2/2Sϕ​=ϕp2​/2 is its power) — the Bessel sideband ladder automatically converges to the small-angle PM formula as β≪1\beta\ll1β≪1; the two are the first-order and full versions of the same thing. The higher-order sidebands J2(β)≈β2/4, J3(β)≈β3/48,…J_2(\beta)\approx\beta^2/4,\,J_3(\beta)\approx\beta^3/48,\dotsJ2​(β)≈β2/4,J3​(β)≈β3/48,… vanish rapidly as β≪1\beta\ll1β≪1 (Jn(β)∼(β/2)n/n!J_n(\beta)\sim(\beta/2)^n/n!Jn​(β)∼(β/2)n/n!), which is why it is reasonable for the small-angle approximation to keep only the first-order sideband.
documents.s: 9.3 The small-β\betaβ limit: recovering Section 6's small-angle approximation

documents.t: The small-angle approximation replaces J1(β)J_1(\beta)J1​(β) with the first-order term β/2\beta/2β/2; as β\betaβ grows, this approximation drifts from the true value. Define the error (comparing the amplitude ratio of the two, in dB): errdB(β)=20log⁡10 ⁣(J1(β)β/2)\text{err}_{\text{dB}}(\beta)=20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{J_1(\beta)}{\beta/2}\right)errdB​(β)=20log10​(β/2J1​(β)​) (errdB→0\text{err}_{\text{dB}}\to0errdB​→0 as β→0\beta\to0β→0; as β\betaβ grows, J1J_1J1​'s growth slows, the ratio drops below 1, and errdB<0\text{err}_{\text{dB}}<0errdB​<0, i.e. the small-angle approximation overestimates the sideband.) Solving numerically for errdB(β)=−1\text{err}_{\text{dB}}(\beta)=-1errdB​(β)=−1 dB (root-finding scipy.optimize.brentq on scipy.special.jv, see the Python block below): β1dB≈0.950 rad(≈54.5∘)\beta_{1\text{dB}}\approx0.950\ \text{rad}\quad(\approx54.5^\circ)β1dB​≈0.950 rad(≈54.5∘) In plain terms: as long as the peak phase deviation β≲0.95\beta\lesssim0.95β≲0.95 rad, the small-angle approximation L≈(β/2)2\mathcal{L}\approx(\beta/2)^2L≈(β/2)2 is accurate to within 1 dB; beyond this range (e.g. wideband FM, large-index PM, or an integration bandwidth wide enough that σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​ approaches 1 rad), the full Bessel sideband ladder must be used — the small-angle formula no longer applies. This echoes Section 6's qualitative statement that it "holds only for σϕ≪1\sigma_\phi\ll1σϕ​≪1 rad," now with a quantitative boundary.
documents.s: 9.4 Failure boundary: where does the small-angle approximation err by 1 dB?

documents.t: Carrier suppression: as β\betaβ grows to the first root of J0(β)=0J_0(\beta)=0J0​(β)=0, the carrier vanishes completely and all power is transferred to the sidebands — a classic phenomenon in FM/PM systems: J0(β)=0’s first root: β=2.405(numerical solution, see the Python block below: J0(2.405)≈−9×10−5≈0)J_0(\beta)=0\text{'s first root: }\beta=2.405\quad(\text{numerical solution, see the Python block below: }J_0(2.405)\approx-9\times10^{-5}\approx0)J0​(β)=0’s first root: β=2.405(numerical solution, see the Python block below: J0​(2.405)≈−9×10−5≈0) Carson's bandwidth rule (external literature, an engineering rule of thumb, not in this site's 5 PDFs): in practice the sideband ladder has infinitely many terms, but Jn(β)J_n(\beta)Jn​(β) decays rapidly to negligible size once n>β+1n>\beta+1n>β+1, so an effective bandwidth is defined (fm=Ω/2πf_m=\Omega/2\pifm​=Ω/2π): BWCarson≈2(β+1)fmBW_{\text{Carson}}\approx2(\beta+1)f_mBWCarson​≈2(β+1)fm​ At β=2.405\beta=2.405β=2.405, BW≈6.81 fmBW\approx6.81\,f_mBW≈6.81fm​; at small-angle β=0.1\beta=0.1β=0.1, BW≈2.2 fmBW\approx2.2\,f_mBW≈2.2fm​ (barely more than a single sideband pair, consistent with the picture that "small-angle PM has only the ±1\pm1±1 sidebands").

documents.t: import numpy as np from scipy.special import jv, jn_zeros from scipy.optimize import brentq for beta in [0.1, 1.0, 2.405]: print(f"beta={beta}") for n in range(5): print(f" J_{n}({beta}) = {jv(n, beta):.6f}") # -> beta=0.1: J0=0.997502, J1=0.049938, J2=0.001249, J3=0.000021, J4≈0 # -> beta=1.0: J0=0.765198, J1=0.440051, J2=0.114903, J3=0.019563, J4=0.002477 # -> beta=2.405: J0=-0.000091(≈0), J1=0.519110, J2=0.431783, J3=0.199032, J4=0.064763 # carrier null (classic 2.405) z0 = jn_zeros(0, 1)[0] print(f"first zero of J0: {z0:.6f}") # -> first zero of J0: 2.404826 # small-angle approximation vs exact for beta in [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0]: J0, J1 = jv(0, beta), jv(1, beta) print(f"beta={beta}: J0={J0:.6f} vs 1-b^2/4={1-beta**2/4:.6f} | " f"J1={J1:.6f} vs b/2={beta/2:.6f}") # -> beta=0.1: J0=0.997502 vs 0.997500 | J1=0.049938 vs 0.050000 # -> beta=1.0: J0=0.765198 vs 0.750000 | J1=0.440051 vs 0.500000 # 1 dB failure boundary: 20log10(J1(beta)/(beta/2)) = -1 dB f = lambda b: 20*np.log10(jv(1, b)/(b/2)) - (-1.0) beta_1dB = brentq(f, 0.5, 1.5) print(f"beta_1dB = {beta_1dB:.4f}") # -> beta_1dB = 0.9505 # Parseval check: sum J_n^2 = 1 for beta in [0.1, 1.0, 2.405]: s = sum(jv(n, beta)**2 for n in range(-50, 51)) print(f"beta={beta}: sum J_n^2 = {s:.8f}") # -> all beta give 1.00000000 Used on this site: Section 6's small-angle PM (this section is its full version), white_noise_to_phase_noise (the small-angle premise behind the single-tone sideband Eq.(16)–(18)), psd_phase_noise_jitter (the applicability boundary σϕ≪1\sigma_\phi\ll1σϕ​≪1 rad, now with a quantitative number ≈0.95\approx0.95≈0.95 rad).

documents.t: The paper then switches to the second route — stating up front that timing jitter is the standard deviation of the timing uncertainty: σΔϕ2=1ω02E{[ϕ(t+ΔT)−ϕ(t)]2}=E[ϕ2(t)]ω02+[ϕ2(t+ΔT)]ω02−E[ϕ(t)ϕ(t+ΔT)]ω02(Eq.(45), as printed)\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=\frac{1}{\omega_0^2}E\big\{[\phi(t+\Delta T)-\phi(t)]^2\big\} =\frac{E[\phi^2(t)]}{\omega_0^2}+\frac{[\phi^2(t+\Delta T)]}{\omega_0^2} -\frac{E[\phi(t)\phi(t+\Delta T)]}{\omega_0^2} \qquad(\text{Eq.(45), as printed})σΔϕ2​=ω02​1​E{[ϕ(t+ΔT)−ϕ(t)]2}=ω02​E[ϕ2(t)]​+ω02​[ϕ2(t+ΔT)]​−ω02​E[ϕ(t)ϕ(t+ΔT)]​(Eq.(45), as printed)Rϕ(τ)=E[ϕ(t)ϕ(t+ΔT)](Eq.(46), as printed)R_\phi(\tau)=E[\phi(t)\phi(t+\Delta T)] \qquad(\text{Eq.(46), as printed})Rϕ​(τ)=E[ϕ(t)ϕ(t+ΔT)](Eq.(46), as printed)σΔϕ2=2ω02[Rϕ(0)−Rϕ(ΔT)].(Eq.(47))\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=\frac{2}{\omega_0^2}\big[R_\phi(0)-R_\phi(\Delta T)\big]. \qquad(\text{Eq.(47)})σΔϕ2​=ω02​2​[Rϕ​(0)−Rϕ​(ΔT)].(Eq.(47))Rϕ(τ)=∫−∞∞Sϕ(f) ej2πfτ df(Eq.(48), the Khinchin theorem)R_\phi(\tau)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_\phi(f)\,e^{j2\pi f\tau}\,df \qquad(\text{Eq.(48), the Khinchin theorem})Rϕ​(τ)=∫−∞∞​Sϕ​(f)ej2πfτdf(Eq.(48), the Khinchin theorem)σΔϕ2=8ω02∫0∞Sϕ(f)sin⁡2(πfτ) df.(Eq.(49))\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2=\frac{8}{\omega_0^2}\int_0^{\infty}S_\phi(f)\sin^2(\pi f\tau)\,df. \qquad(\text{Eq.(49)})σΔϕ2​=ω02​8​∫0∞​Sϕ​(f)sin2(πfτ)df.(Eq.(49)) plus the two practical corollaries restricted to white noise (the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region) — Eq.(50) is obtained by combining the main text's (6)+(12), and Eq.(51) then follows "based on (8)" (i.e., σ=κT\sigma=\kappa\sqrt Tσ=κT​); neither comes from integrating (49): κ=Δff0⋅10−L{Δf}/20(Eq.(50))\kappa=\frac{\Delta f}{f_0}\cdot10^{-\mathcal{L}\{\Delta f\}/20} \qquad(\text{Eq.(50)})κ=f0​Δf​⋅10−L{Δf}/20(Eq.(50))σCTC=ff01.5⋅10−L{Δf}/20.(Eq.(51), as printed)\sigma_{CTC}=\frac{f}{f_0^{1.5}}\cdot10^{-\mathcal{L}\{\Delta f\}/20}. \qquad(\text{Eq.(51), as printed})σCTC​=f01.5​f​⋅10−L{Δf}/20.(Eq.(51), as printed) As-printed disclosure (verified under magnification; symbol overloading and printing slips listed honestly): σΔϕ2\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2σΔϕ2​ does double duty: in Eq.(40)–(44) the LHS is phase jitter (rad²); from Eq.(45) on, the LHS is still printed σΔϕ2\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2σΔϕ2​ yet carries an extra 1/ω021/\omega_0^21/ω02​, and the text explicitly calls it timing jitter — it is really σΔT2=σΔϕ2/ω02\sigma_{\Delta T}^2=\sigma_{\Delta\phi}^2/\omega_0^2σΔT2​=σΔϕ2​/ω02​ (s², i.e., the Eq.(10) conversion). That page names σΔϕ\sigma_{\Delta\phi}σΔϕ​ and σΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}σΔt​ separately precisely to defuse this mine. The expansion line of Eq.(45) drops two symbols: the middle term is missing its EEE, and the cross term is missing its factor 2 (the cross term of [a−b]2[a-b]^2[a−b]2 is 2ab2ab2ab; under stationarity the first two terms combine into 2Rϕ(0)2R_\phi(0)2Rϕ​(0), so landing on Eq.(47) requires the cross term to be 2Rϕ(ΔT)2R_\phi(\Delta T)2Rϕ​(ΔT)). Eq.(47) itself is printed correctly — the slip does not propagate. τ\tauτ and ΔT\Delta TΔT are mixed: Eq.(46) writes Rϕ(τ)R_\phi(\tau)Rϕ​(τ) on the LHS but uses ΔT\Delta TΔT on the RHS; the kernel of Eq.(49) is written sin⁡2(πfτ)\sin^2(\pi f\tau)sin2(πfτ), where this τ\tauτ is the delay ΔT\Delta TΔT. The numerator of Eq.(51) is printed as fff: multiplying Eq.(50)'s (time-version) κ\kappaκ by T=f0−0.5\sqrt T=f_0^{-0.5}T​=f0−0.5​ gives σCTC=κT\sigma_{CTC}=\kappa\sqrt TσCTC​=κT​, so the numerator should be the offset frequency Δf\Delta fΔf — the printing swallowed the Δ\DeltaΔ (the transcription in "Corresponding papers / equations" is annotated accordingly). The integration limits ∫−∞∞\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}∫−∞∞​ of Eq.(48) declare that SϕS_\phiSϕ​ here is a two-sided spectrum — the only place in the whole paper where the convention leaks out; the 8 of Eq.(49) therefore has one bookkeeping 2 built in (see the table below).

documents.s: A.3 Step-by-step mapping: the paper's two routes ↔ that page's derivation

documents.t: Skipped by [P2], filled in by that page: The stationarity rigor gap: Eq.(45)–(47) needs Rϕ(0)R_\phi(0)Rϕ​(0) finite; a free-running oscillator's ϕ\phiϕ is a random walk, so Rϕ(0)R_\phi(0)Rϕ​(0) diverges (exactly the confession at the start of that page's Route A). The difference Rϕ(0)−Rϕ(ΔT)R_\phi(0)-R_\phi(\Delta T)Rϕ​(0)−Rϕ​(ΔT) is finite and the conclusion survives, but making it rigorous requires that page's Route B (which only demands that ν=ϕ˙\nu=\dot\phiν=ϕ˙​ be stationary) — the paper does not address this step. No convention declared: not one sentence in the paper says whether SϕS_\phiSϕ​ is one- or two-sided; only the integration limits of Eq.(48) give it away. That page's three-column table in Step 0 lays that out in the open (v5 used exactly those limits to infer "two-sided" and reconcile the literature's "coefficient-8 version" with the one-sided 4sin⁡24\sin^24sin2 kernel). The two routes are never interlocked in the paper: Eq.(44) stops in the time domain, Eq.(49) stops in the frequency domain; the paper never substitutes the white-noise spectrum into (49) to check that it lands back on (44). That page's 4.1 integral ∫0∞sin⁡2(ax)/x2 dx=πa/2\int_0^\infty\sin^2(ax)/x^2\,dx=\pi a/2∫0∞​sin2(ax)/x2dx=πa/2 plus the substitution in 4.3 is that missing closed loop (the code below computes both routes — same number). Neither the time-domain flicker 1/f31/f^31/f3 closed form (Step 5's log formula) nor the c2c 16sin⁡416\sin^416sin4 kernel (kernel (c); Eq.(51) is only the one-period version) appears in the paper. Glossed over by that page, written out in full by [P2]: The general double integral of Eq.(42): Section 4.2 jumps straight to "white-noise δ correlation ⇒ single integral"; the paper writes out the general form Γ(ω0τ1)Γ(ω0τ2) E[i(τ1)i(τ2)]\Gamma(\omega_0\tau_1)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau_2)\,E[i(\tau_1)i(\tau_2)]Γ(ω0​τ1​)Γ(ω0​τ2​)E[i(τ1​)i(τ2​)] — the starting point that accepts any colored-noise autocorrelation, with white noise merely a special case. The validity condition printed inside the equation: Eq.(44)'s "for ΔT≫T\Delta T\gg TΔT≫T or ΔT=mT\Delta T=mTΔT=mT" prints right next to the equals sign the condition for ∫Γ2→Γrms2ΔT\int\Gamma^2\to\Gamma_{rms}^2\Delta T∫Γ2→Γrms2​ΔT to be exact; this page's 4.2 only mentions it in a parenthesis. For short or non-integer ΔT\Delta TΔT there is an O(T/ΔT)O(T/\Delta T)O(T/ΔT)-level Γ2\Gamma^2Γ2 ripple residual.

documents.t: import numpy as np from simulations.common.isf_utils import gamma_lc_ideal F0, T = 5e9, 2e-10 W0 = 2 * np.pi * F0 QMAX, SI, GRMS = 1e-12, 1e-24, 0.5 # canonical parameters N = 100 DT = N * T # ΔT = mT (the validity condition of Eq.(44)) # Route 1: [P2] Appendix A time-domain autocorrelation route — substituting R_ii=(S_i/2)δ into Eq.(42) collapses it to Eq.(43) tau = np.linspace(0.0, DT, 200 * N + 1) gam = np.sqrt(2.0) * GRMS * gamma_lc_ideal(W0 * tau) # LC-shaped ISF with Γrms=0.5 var_43 = 0.5 * SI / QMAX**2 * np.trapezoid(gam**2, tau) # Eq.(43), numerical integral var_44 = 0.5 * SI / QMAX**2 * GRMS**2 * DT # Eq.(44) = main text Eq.(11) print(f"{var_43:.4e}") # -> 2.5000e-09 rad^2 (Eq.(43), σ²_Δφ @ N=100) print(f"{var_43/var_44:.4f}") # -> 1.0000 (at ΔT=mT, ∫Γ² is exactly Γrms²ΔT) # Route 2: that page's kernel route — one-sided S_φ=2κ²/(2πf)² times the 4sin²(πfΔT) kernel kappa2 = GRMS**2 / QMAX**2 * SI / 2 # κ²=Γrms²S_i/(2q_max²) print(f"{kappa2:.4f}") # -> 0.1250 rad^2/s (the same prefactor as Eq.(44)) x = np.linspace(1e-8, 1e4, 4_000_001) # x = fΔT core = np.trapezoid(np.sin(np.pi * x)**2 / x**2, x) + 0.5 / x[-1] # tail: sin²→1/2 var_kernel = 2 * kappa2 * DT / np.pi**2 * core # = κ²ΔT (the 4.3 analytic value) print(f"{var_kernel/var_43:.4f}") # -> 1.0000 (frequency kernel = Appendix A route, same number) # Reconciling [P2] Eq.(49): 8/ω₀² × two-sided S_φ^DS=κ²/(2πf)², LHS is the time-version variance var_49 = 8 / W0**2 * (kappa2 * DT / 4 / np.pi**2) * core print(f"{var_49/(kappa2*DT/W0**2):.4f}") # -> 1.0000 (8 = 2(two-sided→one-sided)×4(kernel)) print(f"{np.sqrt(var_49)*1e15:.2f} fs") # -> 1.59 fs (σ_ΔT @ N=100 = √100×0.159 fs) The first two prints walk [P2] Eq.(43)→(44) (the time-domain autocorrelation route); the remaining four walk that page's kernel (b) and the two-sided bookkeeping of Eq.(49) — one oscillator, two routes, one number, κ2ΔT=2.5×10−9 rad2\kappa^2\Delta T=2.5\times10^{-9}\ \text{rad}^2κ2ΔT=2.5×10−9 rad2. Appendix A and Steps 3/4 of that page are two proofs of the same theorem; the only difference is that the paper hides its convention inside the integration limits, while that page prints it in Step 0.

documents.t: [P2] Appendix A proves the same thing along two independent routes: A.1 the white-noise time-domain autocorrelation route (Eq.(40)-(44), converging on the main text's Eq.(11)), and A.2 the autocorrelation + Khinchin route (Eq.(45)-(49)), plus two white-noise-special-case corollaries Eq.(50)/(51). A.3's step-by-step table pins every equation in the paper back onto that page's matching derivation and convention (which 2 belongs to which step); A.4 honestly accounts for what each side skips and spells out in full (the paper never states its SϕS_\phiSϕ​ convention and never interlocks the two routes; that page never writes out the general double integral of Eq.(42)). A.5's Python computes the time-domain autocorrelation route (Eq.(43)) and that page's frequency-domain kernel route separately, for the same oscillator, landing on the same number κ2ΔT=2.5×10−9 rad2\kappa^2\Delta T=2.5\times10^{-9}\ \text{rad}^2κ2ΔT=2.5×10−9 rad2 (every # -> prints 1.0000). The paper itself has a few printing slips (the expansion of Eq.(45) drops EEE and a factor of 2; the numerator of Eq.(51) is printed as fff and should read Δf\Delta fΔf) — this page transcribes them exactly as printed and annotates them alongside, without correcting the paper.

documents.t: See also: notation (symbol conventions for function arguments), the simulation lab pages (e.g. lab_01) reference the common/ functions here | to regenerate all figures: python scripts/run_all_sims.py Every figure on this site is produced with a Python pedagogical toy model (not transistor-level). This page covers: how to set up the environment, what the directory layout looks like, how to regenerate all figures with one command, and what each module and function in common/ does. All function names correspond to actual existing code, and can be imported directly to verify. Design philosophy: the simulations aren't meant to "look like a real circuit" — they exist to turn formulas into numbers and plots you can touch. Each lab reduces one ISF formula to the smallest runnable program, with a fixed random seed so results are fully reproducible.
documents.s: Python Environment

documents.t: Requires Python 3.12; only three packages are needed: # Recommended: use a virtual environment # python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # Then install: # pip install numpy scipy matplotlib Package Recommended version Purpose numpy 1.26+ vectorized numerics, FFT, random number generation scipy 1.11+ scipy.signal.welch (PSD estimation), integration, interpolation matplotlib 3.8+ render figures to static/figures/ Why only three packages: dependencies are kept deliberately minimal, so anyone can install everything with one line on a clean Python 3.12 install and reproduce every figure with one command. No deep-learning framework or circuit simulator (SPICE, etc.) is used — again, this is a toy model.
documents.s: 1. Setting up the environment

documents.t: Figures carry Chinese labels (axis names, legends); matplotlib's default font doesn't cover Chinese and renders "tofu boxes" instead. The site does not hardcode a single font name — instead, simulations/common/plot_utils.py scans the fonts actually installed on the machine with matplotlib.font_manager and picks the first one that exists from a preference list (the import is at plot_utils.py:24; the scan/pick logic is at plot_utils.py:26–29): import matplotlib.font_manager as _fm _available = {f.name for f in _fm.fontManager.ttflist} _cjk_prefs = ["Heiti TC", "Arial Unicode MS", "STHeiti", "Hiragino Sans GB", "Songti SC", "PingFang TC"] _cjk_font = next((f for f in _cjk_prefs if f in _available), None) plt.rcParams["font.family"] = ([_cjk_font] if _cjk_font else []) + ["DejaVu Sans", "sans-serif"] plt.rcParams["axes.unicode_minus"] = False _available: _fm.fontManager.ttflist is every installed font object matplotlib scanned at startup; collecting their .names gives "the font names this machine actually has." _cjk_prefs: an ordered preference list of 6 common macOS Chinese fonts (Heiti TC, Arial Unicode MS, STHeiti, Hiragino Sans GB, Songti SC, PingFang TC). _cjk_font = next(...) picks the first font that is both in the preference list and actually present on this machine; if none of the six are present it returns None. Graceful degradation (not a hardcoded Heiti TC): when no CJK font is found, ([_cjk_font] if _cjk_font else []) becomes an empty list, so font.family falls back to just ["DejaVu Sans", "sans-serif"] — matplotlib's built-in font that has no CJK glyphs. Figures still render normally in that case (no exception is raised); only the Chinese labels turn into boxes. axes.unicode_minus=False is still critical: matplotlib defaults to the Unicode minus sign U+2212, which many fonts lack the glyph for, turning the minus sign in "−100-100−100 dBc/Hz" into a box; setting it to False switches to the ASCII hyphen and fixes this. Non-macOS platforms: _cjk_prefs currently lists only 6 macOS fonts. To get correct Chinese labels on Linux/Windows, add a CJK font your system actually has (e.g. Noto Sans CJK TC on Linux, Microsoft JhengHei on Windows) to the front of _cjk_prefs — the detection logic will automatically pick it up; no other code needs to change.

documents.t: Every lab that uses randomness (white noise, flicker, jitter accumulation) uses NumPy's modern random generator with a fixed seed, so that anyone re-running it gets a bit-identical figure: import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=12345) # fixed seed -> fully reproducible i_n = white_noise(n=2**16, psd=1e-24, fs=fs, rng=rng) # pass in the same rng Why default_rng(seed) instead of the legacy np.random.seed: the modern Generator object-based API passes random state explicitly (rng as an argument into functions), avoiding global state being silently mutated elsewhere — this is best practice for reproducibility. Sanity check: with a fixed seed, the numerically integrated jitter in lab_08 settles stably near the analytical values σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs, σϕ=14.07\sigma_\phi=14.07σϕ​=14.07 mrad (canonical example C), fully consistent with theory. To see different realizations: change the seed (e.g. default_rng(1), default_rng(2)) to see the Monte-Carlo spread; but the figures pinned on the site always use the fixed seed.

documents.t: Chaining together everything above, the snippet below needs no lab script at all — using only common/ it reproduces canonical example A (qmax=1q_{max}=1qmax​=1 pC, Δq=1\Delta q=1Δq=1 fC, Γ=0.5\Gamma=0.5Γ=0.5, f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz): from simulations.common.isf_utils import impulse_to_phase_step from simulations.common.noise_utils import phase_to_time_error dphi = impulse_to_phase_step(delta_q=1e-15, gamma_value=0.5, qmax=1e-12) dt = phase_to_time_error(dphi, f0=5e9) print(dphi, "rad", dt * 1e15, "fs") # -> 0.0005 rad 15.92 fs This gives Δϕ=5×10−4\Delta\phi=5\times10^{-4}Δϕ=5×10−4 rad, Δt=15.9\Delta t=15.9Δt=15.9 fs, consistent with impulse_to_phase_shift (example A).

documents.t: The seven mainline labs each have a corresponding Jupyter notebook (interactive notebook, runnable cell-by-cell with parameters you can change and re-run) available for direct download, to play with the formulas offline as numbers and figures: Notebook (click to download .ipynb) Contents Corresponding page lab_01_sinusoidal_oscillator limit cycle, phase (tangential) vs amplitude (radial) perturbation, impulse injection timing lab_01 lab_05_fourier_isf ISF Fourier coefficients cnc_ncn​, Parseval verification, c0c_0c0​ and symmetry lab_05 lab_06_white_noise_phase_noise end-to-end white noise →\to→ 1/f21/f^21/f2 phase noise simulation vs theoretical line lab_06 lab_08_jitter_integration integrating L(f)\mathcal{L}(f)L(f) into rms jitter (canonical example C) lab_08 lab_18_lorentzian phase random walk →\to→ carrier Lorentzian lineshape and 3-dB linewidth lorentzian_linewidth lab_22_capstone_lc_end_to_end full ideal-LC chain: Γ→Γrms→Sϕ→\Gamma\to\Gamma_{rms}\to S_\phi\toΓ→Γrms​→Sϕ​→ linewidth →σt→\to\sigma_t\to→σt​→ BER capstone lab_24_jitter_kernels TIE / period / cycle-to-cycle: three jitter weighting kernels + Monte-Carlo verification jitter_kernels How to run it: the notebook imports modules from simulations/common, so you first need to git clone https://github.com/gmcycle7/isf-teaching-site.git, and then run the downloaded .ipynb from anywhere within the repo directory tree (each notebook's setup cell automatically searches parent directories for simulations/common and adds it to sys.path). Dependencies are the same as in section 1, pip install numpy scipy matplotlib, plus pip install jupyter, then open with jupyter lab. Honesty note: these notebooks are generated snapshots that scripts/make_notebooks.py automatically produces from the corresponding simulations/lab_*.py — they are not hand-written; the authoritative version is always the lab script in the repo. After a lab is updated, running python scripts/make_notebooks.py regenerates all notebooks. There are exactly two deliberate differences from the original script: savefig is replaced with inline display within the notebook (not written to static/figures/), and the path setup is handled by the setup cell automatically locating the repo root (the original script uses __file__ for this).

documents.t: Python 3.12 + numpy/scipy/matplotlib; the CJK font is auto-detected from plot_utils.py's _cjk_prefs list (falls back to DejaVu Sans if none is found), with unicode_minus disabled. The seven common/ modules (isf_utils, noise_utils, oscillator_models, pll_utils, serdes_utils, signal_utils, plot_utils) hold the authoritative implementation; each lab only sets parameters. python scripts/run_all_sims.py regenerates all 60 figures into static/figures/ in one command (from 52 lab_*.py/fig_*.py scripts). Everything is a toy model; a fixed default_rng(seed) guarantees bit-identical reproducibility. The seven mainline labs have downloadable Jupyter notebooks (section 8), automatically produced as generated snapshots by scripts/make_notebooks.py.

documents.t: A. Hajimiri and T. H. Lee, "A General Theory of Phase Noise in Electrical Oscillators," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 33, no. 2, pp. 179–194, Feb. 1998. (file general.pdf, paper_001) One-line contribution: establishes the view that an oscillator's response to noise is LTV (linear time-variant) rather than LTI, introduces the ISF Γ(ω0τ)\Gamma(\omega_0\tau)Γ(ω0​τ) and qmaxq_{max}qmax​ normalization, and derives closed forms and design rules for 1/f21/f^21/f2 and 1/f31/f^31/f3. Used on this site in: impulse_to_phase_shift, isf_definition, convolution_derivation, fourier_series_of_isf, white_noise_to_phase_noise, flicker_noise_upconversion. Key equations: Eqs.(1),(9),(10),(11),(12),(13),(15)–(24), pp.180–185 (see equation_index).

documents.t: A. Hajimiri and R. Heald, "Design Issues in Cross-Coupled Inverter Sense Amplifier," Proc. IEEE ISCAS, 1998. (file Hajimiri_ISCS_98.pdf, paper_005) Honesty note: this is a paper on cross-coupled-inverter sense amplifiers, on the topic of regeneration speed and mismatch offset — unrelated to oscillator phase noise / the ISF. It appears in the download folder only because it shares an author (Hajimiri). The only conceptual link: the cross-coupled-pair's regeneration / positive feedback mechanism, which is also the underlying mechanism for startup in latch-type and LC oscillators — this site uses it only as a peripheral note and does not draw any ISF formula from it (corresponds to claim C12). Key equations: TODO: equations not transcribed because this PDF is unrelated to ISF/phase noise.

documents.t: D. B. Leeson, "A Simple Model of Feedback Oscillator Noise Spectrum," Proc. IEEE, vol. 54, no. 2, pp. 329–330, Feb. 1966. DOI: 10.1109/PROC.1966.4682. Role: the most widely used empirical phase-noise model before ISF theory; [P1]'s introduction treats it as "the special case that ISF theory subsumes and surpasses." For the comparison and derivation see derivation_leeson: L(Δω)=10log⁡10 ⁣[2FkTPs(1+(ω02Q Δω)2)(1+ω1/f3∣Δω∣)].\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega)=10\log_{10}\!\left[\frac{2FkT}{P_s}\left(1+\left(\frac{\omega_0}{2Q\,\Delta\omega}\right)^2\right)\left(1+\frac{\omega_{1/f^3}}{|\Delta\omega|}\right)\right].L(Δω)=10log10​[Ps​2FkT​(1+(2QΔωω0​​)2)(1+∣Δω∣ω1/f3​​)]. Status: volume/issue/pages/DOI verified; FFF (noise figure) is an empirically fitted parameter (varies slightly by implementation), used here for comparison only.
documents.s: [E1] Leeson 1966 — empirical phase-noise model (for comparison)

documents.t: A. Demir, A. Mehrotra, and J. Roychowdhury, "Phase Noise in Oscillators: A Unifying Theory and Numerical Methods for Characterization," IEEE Trans. Circuits Syst. I: Fundam. Theory Appl., vol. 47, no. 5, pp. 655–674, May 2000. DOI: 10.1109/81.847872. Role: using the PPV (Perturbation Projection Vector) and a nonlinear phase equation, gives the ISF a rigorous mathematical foundation (the PPV is the first principal Floquet vector, obtainable numerically via the adjoint). Background equation: ϕ˙(t)=v1T(t) B(t) ξ(t)\dot{\phi}(t)=v_1^T(t)\,B(t)\,\xi(t)ϕ˙​(t)=v1T​(t)B(t)ξ(t). Status: volume/issue/pages/DOI verified; the PPV framework is detailed in derivation_floquet_ppv.
documents.s: [E2] Demir–Mehrotra–Roychowdhury 2000 — PPV (rigorizing the ISF)

documents.t: F. X. Kärtner, "Analysis of White and f−αf^{-\alpha}f−α Noise in Oscillators," Int. J. Circuit Theory Appl., vol. 18, no. 5, pp. 485–519, 1990. DOI: 10.1002/cta.4490180505. Role: one of the perturbation analyses of oscillator noise predating [P1], often listed alongside Demir as a "mathematical precursor of the ISF/PPV." Status: volume/issue/pages/DOI verified; mentioned on this site as background only.
documents.s: [E3] Kärtner 1990 — perturbation analysis of oscillator noise (background)

documents.t: R. Adler, "A Study of Locking Phenomena in Oscillators," Proc. IRE, vol. 34, no. 6, pp. 351–357, Jun. 1946. DOI: 10.1109/JRPROC.1946.229930. (Reprinted in Proc. IEEE, vol. 61, no. 10, pp. 1380–1385, Oct. 1973.) Role: the original source of the classical Adler equation; [P3] generalizes it to arbitrary oscillators / arbitrary injection waveforms. Status: volume/issue/pages verified; the classical and generalized Adler equations appear in paper_003.
documents.s: [E4] Adler 1946 — the original injection-locking paper (the target of [P3]'s generalization)

documents.t: L. A. Zadeh, "Frequency Analysis of Variable Networks," Proc. IRE, vol. 38, no. 3, pp. 291–299, Mar. 1950. DOI: 10.1109/JRPROC.1950.231083. Role: defines the time-variant transfer function H(f,t)H(f,t)H(f,t) (system function), the source of the harmonic transfer matrix and of the strict LTV view that "the ISF is the vector that maps phase output onto each harmonic." Status: volume/issue/pages/DOI verified; the framework appears in ltv_htm (not among the 5 PDFs).
documents.s: [E5] Zadeh 1950 — frequency-domain analysis of linear time-variant systems (the source of the HTM)

documents.t: Site-internal citation format: inline usage like [P1] Eq.(21), p.185; every definition/formula/conclusion/figure drawn from a paper is tagged with its source (see Section 1 of the author's spec). Codes: the core 5 papers use [P1]–[P5] (corresponding to paper_001–paper_005); external supplements use [E1]–[E5], and always carry the note "not among the 5 downloaded PDFs." LaTeX sources: the formula LaTeX in [P1] has been confirmed against the PDF rendering pages (manual_verification_needed=false); some constants/forms in [P2]–[P4] are flagged ⚠️, see the TODO below. Units and notation: consistently follows notation site-wide.
